Like Danelectro's other effects pedals in this series, the body has a very solid feel -- it's metal.  The controls allow for a wide range of depth of temelo and speed of the tremelo.  At first, I wasn't sure to what extent the middle switch on the pedal -- hard/soft -- would be something that I would use.  However, the hard setting completely cuts the signal in between the pulses for a very interesting sequencer-like effect that, while non-traditional, might have a place in some styles.  This, like Danelectro's other pedals in the series, also has a true, direct, pass through when the pedal is turned off.  Highly recommended!

There is something quite fishy going on in regard to this 2nd Tier Keyboard stand and its reviews. Before purchasing it, I noticed that it had standalone reviews for it at maybe 300-400 total; it wasn’t combined with other items, and you could clearly see that the ratings were not spectacular. After purchasing it, it seems like somehow all the reviews have been merged with other keyboard stands to make it look like it has a better rating. Sorry, but that seems sketchy to me, and after having purchased it, I understand why. It seems like the seller is trying to mask the horrible quality of this item.

Why do I say it’s horrible? Well, for one, there were visible scratches and rust (so bad that it was even on the bag) on various parts of the 2nd tier stand. Furthermore, the screws on the middle crossbar were bent as well, making it super hard to screw in while attempting to assemble this thing. It doesn’t stop there though. The description says that the diameter of the fitting/clamp was 1 1/8”, but even though the bars on my keyboard stand were only 1” (measured with a very precise measuring caliper), they didn’t fit; on my first one of these, I had to tap the clamp parts with a hammer to get them to slide on to the bars of the main stand. This was not ideal because doing so left scratches on the main keyboard stand. Did I mention that the crossbar didn’t fit into one side of the side bars properly? Well, yeah, that also happened.

These were all problems I had with my first 2nd tier stand from this company. I returned it, obviously, and got a replacement. Was the replacement any better? Yes, and no. There was still rust, but less. There were still scratches on one of the components. The screws on the cross bar were straight – but the hole on the right side bracket was so small that it barely fit the cross brace (the other side was fine, so why was only the right side incorrect?)

Please take a look at some of my pictures so that you can see a reference to what I’m talking about.

Will this item work for you? Maybe. If you manage to get a version that isn’t damaged. If you plan on using it in a studio and the keyboard you’re placing on it is on the lighter side and will remain stationary, it should be ok. I would NOT use this if you plan to take it on the road. I would NOT put one of my heavier keyboards on it. No way. It is far from sturdy. It’s not worth the risk to damage your heavier gear.

This is really a case of “you get what you pay for”. This 2nd tier stand really is terrible. I know a lot of products sold on Amazon are cheaply produced and have bad quality workmanship, but this item is just horrible: rust, scratches, bent parts, other parts that don’t fit. Yikes! It shouldn’t have to be this way. You shouldn’t be subjected to buying a product that is of inherently low quality out of the box. I don’t understand why sellers like this are allowed to sell things on Amazon (or anywhere, really). And the fact that this seller is trying to mask bad reviews by merging the item with 5 or 6 other items seems super shady. Amazon, please take note of this. Text:
I've owned this throne for some time and recently purchased a lighter one to further lighten my hardware bag. In less than a month I have come back to this one for a few reasons.

First, it is a lot more comfortable than the lighter one. Although my gigs are in retirement homes and relatively short, I needed something comfortable or risked back pains. This throne had served me well in that respect and is now serving me again after the pains associated with the lighter throne were starting to become more intense.

To be sure, this is not the best or most comfortable throne for four plus hour gigs and heavy gigging schedules, or even prolonged home and studio use. For those I recommend spending the money for one of the top tier thrones.

I do want to make one correction: the product specs claim that this throne has six adjustable positions - it only has five - so that may be a typo. Still, the range and increments are more than sufficient for most folks. Also, while this uses the older style of tube that is adjustable by inserting a bolt in one of the holes, it is also absolutely non-slip. I own a Tama throne that uses a friction clamp as well as a memory clamp, and it slips. This one may be more low tech, but slip it will not.

Finally, at around seven pounds with the 12x2.5 padded seat it is lighter than most thrones, easy to pack, and very stable.

Text:
The ergonomics are really well done for a desktop interface: The shallow angle makes the top controls comfortably accessible while the front phone jacks sit parallel to my desk surface, providing clearance for all cable jacks while the unit itself sits flush.

How you feel about XLR and MIDI jacks on the back panel depends on your workflow. For me it’s a big plus: I don’t like a mess of heavy cables between my arm and the unit and I prefer the flexible lengths of standard DINN MIDI cables (they’re also more reliable IMO than USB at the controller end).

I use Alesis M1Active monitors on a desktop PC for general work, music notation/playback, and ‘sketchpad recording’ (single mic/MIDI keyboard). I still prefer volume knobs versus software sliders and the M-Track’s large master volume knob is perfect – easy to grab and turn in small increments, right where I want it.

To give a benchmark, I’m running Win10 64-bit on an 8 year-old HP Pavilion p6330f with 6GB RAM – far from state of the art but adequate for my needs.

Easy download and install of the latest driver package for 64-bit Windows 10 – the package includes the M-Audio ASIO driver that installed flawlessly. I have an Axiom-61 for MIDI input use a pair of ¼” phono to RCA adaptors to run output from the M-Track to my monitors. A nice side-effect of getting the cables out from under the desk is it’s easy to connect an A/B switch to share the monitors with my Linux box.

Initially I plugged the M-Audio into a powered USB multi-bay shared with a Wi-Fi adaptor and an external drive – bad idea. The performance was ok for sustained pads and slower voiced synth and organ textures. But I experienced drop outs while playing piano-like with a lot of moving inner voices – frustrating but not exactly a surprise with all that shared USB traffic through the bay.

I installed an Inateck PCI-E to USB 3.0 5-Port PCI Express Card that I now use exclusively for the M-Track – drop outs are gone, regardless of keyboard texture and patch.

A couple of relatively minor construction points:

The corner feet didn’t sit flush on my desk – a surface that other equipment (and my steel straightedge) tells me is pretty flat. Fortunately shimming a corner of the M-Track with electrical tape did the trick.

A second concern is the large output level knob scrapes lightly against the rim of the case opening beneath – it’s a little noisy (in the context of close-listening) and ‘kills the design vibe’ a bit.

There’s a thin protective plastic layer that takes quite a bit of pulling at a corner to tear loose – I hoped it might be what the knob was rubbing against, but no luck, it’s the casing itself. By pulling the knob out slightly I managed to eliminate most of the scraping sound but it feels as though the knob stem itself has some loose wobble it in.

Software-wise, the M-Track 2x2 ASIO driver works great on Win 10 64-bit: With a default 256k buffer keyboard playback latency is around 12ms – barely detectable and more than usable for my needs. It’s comparable to what I got from my EMU 1010 card with its flaky beta Win7 driver (my main reason for abandoning PCI cards and going with an external interface.

I tried Reason, Ableton, Sonar X3, notation programs that include sound packages and VST output including Sibelius, Finale and Notion - as well as standalone software instruments including Kontakt, and the Dimension XP soft synth.

I’m very pleased with the response of the driver. I will say the driver crashed twice on Windows 10 – both times while clicking from a playing YouTube video to one queued in the sidebar – and both times the enhanced Win 10 blue screen fingered the M-Audio driver file as the culprit. That’s two times over the past several months of daily use – as a long-time Windows user, unless that rate noticeably increases, I don’t consider it a big deal – and hopefully it will be addressed in a future update.

Audio recording with a Shure SM-57 and mid-priced Rode condenser mics is clean with adequate gain from the phantom power. I tend to record mostly acoustic instruments with a lot of space that’ll expose noisy gear.

Bottom Line: The single most useful and reliable piece of gear I’ve added in years. I’m only sorry I waited so long to dump my old cards.

Text:
On the unit I received yesterday, the headphone monitoring is too faint to suit the purpose.

Since this microphone arrived I have invested about 10 hours with it. The volume of the headphone monitoring is simply not loud enough. On the unit received, all functions listed in the manual do operate, multiple different computers recognize the mic instantly, and multiple different headphones all get signals...so it is not the computer, headphone, or operator.

Chances are you want to purchase this unit so you can hear yourself loud and clear while podcasting, narrating, or singing. Unfortunately, with the volume control at 100% and recording settings correct, the monitor sound is too soft to be fit for use. (Playback through the mic/headset connection after recording is plenty loud, however.)

This problem occurs on a certain percentage of the units, and the responses on forums, bulletin boards, and FAQs all say "Contact Technical Support."

Calling the Audio-Technica help line during normal business hours resulted in a recorded "We are all busy serving other customers so please leave your name, phone number, model number, and a detailed message and someone will get right back to you."

About an hour later, a polite fellow called back. After a lengthy detailed discussion, he was stumped, and pointed out he is a customer support person, NOT a technician. He forwarded me to the voicemail of their technician. Can you guess what the technician's voicemail said? Yes... she is busy right now, but she checks her voicemail often, and if I will leave my name, telephone number, etc., she will call me back...

A couple of hours later, a very kind and helpful technician called back. She and I went over a complete, thorough, lengthy and detailed diagnosis. Finally she determined that the unit was defective from the factory. She instructed me to send the unit back to Amazon and get a refund.

RECOMMENDATION: Test this thing immediately upon receipt, and save the packaging materials.

Ask yourself: "Is my time worth anything?" Audio-Technica has nice front-line people, and I don't blame them for anything. The front-line people are very courteous and friendly, doing exactly what their management is asking them to do. They cannot prevent defective units from the factory. But their management system has minimized their staffing while shifting the time, effort, trouble, and frustration onto you.

THANK YOU to Amazon for their return policy!
Summary: Headphone monitoring not loud enough -- Audio Technica said return to Amazon

Each unit has a bright back-lit display that shows the levels but doesn't seem to drain the battery. The meters aren't super responsive but are responsive enough. The sound quality isn't bad at all. The receiver and transmitters can also be charged using a USB type C cable if needed and a 3 way charging cable is included if you prefer to travel light without the charging case. They also provide furry windscreens for the transmitters built-in microphone if you needed to record in a hurry. No furry windscreens are included for the lav mics but the pre-installed windscreens are nice and thick so you shouldn't have any issues unless you are outside on a very windy day but a good high pass filter should help.

Overall I'm impressed by these. They look presentable and sound nice. The battery lasts a very long time and the meters make setting the levels super easy. The charging case is super convenient and closes with force and doesn't creak or wobble. I feel confident that the case will hold up well and protect the units as long as it isn't dropped hard. The hinges are also plastic so being put in a bag shouldn't be an issue but a hard drop on concrete might be. I can't complain though. This is probably the best value out there right now and has become my favorite small setup for outdoor videos. It is so much easier not having to sync audio. Text:
After seeing many reviews for these pickups, all positive, I decided to get a pair.

I was looking to upgrade my Glarry GJazz bass. While it was okay stock, I wanted to wake up the tone, among other things.

The pickups came sooner than promised, well-packaged, and in perfect condition. Mounting springs and screws are included.

These things are MASSIVE. The pole pieces, magnets, and apparently the base plate are all huge and heavy. They are sealed with flexible epoxy, to prevent microphonic feedback and hold it all together.

I made a routing template out of 1/4" acrylic by tracing around the base. The stock depth was used when I enlarged the pickup holes to accept these. You can also use MDF to make a template, purchase one, or if you are REALLY steady, use a tracing and rout freehand.

They are wired with 4 color-coded conductors, plus a bare braid for ground. The conductor wires are red for hot, black for neutral with a white and green soldered together joining the coils. This is cool, because these two wires can be separated and wired to a switch, or push-pull pot, to tap the coils. I didn't do that, but insulated the connections and taped them to the harness, so I have the option to do this mod later.

I wired them in with 4 new 500k ohm pots from TAOT, and some new .022 microfarad poly capacitors. A switch was used as a pickup selector, and it was wired using a Les Paul patterned circuit.

Well, once it was done and plugged in, I was blown away! These pickups have some OUTPUT, and the sound is incredible!! Even my little 70-watt GK Backline 110 sounded big and powerful.

The tonal response is WIDE. They are bright and punchy, with a crystal clear top end end and a huge thundering bottom end. There is no noise whatsoever, and they respond really well to both tonal and volume input.

These pickups have given fresh life and lots of power to my Glarry, it's like a whole new instrument.

If you don't mind a bit of routing and wiring, then these bargain pickups are a good upgrade option for you.

Text:
For my main rig, I have a monstrous TC Triple Delay (3 independent delay pedals in one box). Love it but it’s overkill for most things.

For just goofing around and getting simpler tones when I’m composing / tracking, my go-to has been a cheap “MoozikPro” delay (discontinued but probably floating around rebranded) that has slightly dark repeats but does solid, works-for-any-situation short delays (think EVH).

Was pretty excited when I requested the Pigtone PP-22, as it has a mix knob (something the Triple Delay has but MoozikPro lacks) that allows you to fine tune how much your dry signal is effected. Simple feature but lacking on many classic delay pedals.

I was able to quickly dial in a short delay with minimal repeats that made me smile as I rocked out. See pic for settings.

You can also bump up the repeats for a more cascaded effect, and increase the delay time for greater ambient effect.

The knobs can be a little sensitive, and there’s no digital readout to know your tempo / no tap tempo etc. Recreating settings and tempo matching might be a challenge and there are other (more expensive) units out there better suited for that purpose.

For what it is - an affordable analog delay - this does everything I hoped it would and I’m now retiring the trusty old MoozikPro.

I've been an advocate of Mackie studio monitors from their original HR series for pros to their original MR series for home studio. Personally, I've feel Mackie has been pressured to create a lower MR speaker line to keep up with KRK's growing base of Rockit series users. And with that I'm glad they brought out their MR series which impressed me from the start with it's crisp sonic quality and clean audio output. This is compared with KRK's Rockit speakers which is more prone to electrical interference. In professional environments, there shouldn't be a problem in isolating electrical against audio wiring. But in home use, this can be a problem with power cables crossing against audio cables. And in this case, Mackie MR is very forgiving.

I loved the sound of my previous MR5 and it's good to see how far Mackie has gone with their third revision since they launched this series. The best design I've seen is the MR5 mk2. While this latest MR mk3 is a bit gimmicky in design that my visual sight is distracted from my listening experience.

Design:

- Gone is the simple led blue light to indicate the presence of power. They have instead succumbed to KRK's style once again in illuminating their own remade logo in the form of the "running man". Of course they didn't stop there, they had to light it up in bright green.

- I can live with the curvaceous fascia, but what is with the painted silver accents on the tweeter and woofer. Too overdone and too amateurish in design I had to do a double-take if this was by Mackie.

Sound:

- For those unfamiliar with studio monitors, the flatter the response the better because you want a speaker that outputs the true tonality of your audio source. This is versus other speakers that have been built to "enhance" the music by the use of passive or active equalization. In this case Mackie MR mk3 for it's price point, earns 4 out of 5 stars in my personal opinion. Like I earlier said, sound output is clear especially on the high range.

- I'm very impressed with the clean output and little static that you can hardly discern. To the normal ears, what static? Which is good. And besides this won't matter once the audio starts.

- Mackie has stuck to it's guns in having a rear port. Unlike the previous two MR series, they built their porting up top as a round tube. Again, personally, I'm not a fan of rear porting because I can't control the refraction as much as if it were front ported.

Overall:

Choosing this specific MR5 mk3 means you will eventually want to have their MR10S mk3 subwoofer. Having both will be a perfect pairing. It won't take you down to 20Hz, but unless your in a pro studio environment or an audiophile it really won't matter. A word of caution is that their subwoofer is also rear ported. You need to have a solid padding or your walls will vibrate like crazy more than a front ported speaker.

If you don't have space for a subwoofer, then I would chose to go with its bigger brothers - MR6 or MR8. (Another caving in to competition for adding a 6" speaker line which is great.)

Unfortunately if space really is an issue and the reason why you're choosing the MR5 versus a bigger speaker and no chance for a subwoofer, then I would suggest choosing instead switching to the KRK RP6 series. Unlike the MR6, the porting is up front and therefore more controlled especially for amateur audio creators. It's a bit taller only because of the front porting which gives you a solid, tight bass output and no annoyingly bright green light up front to distract you from your audio mixing especially in a close and dark environment. The only downside is if you don't have a clean wiring and cable layout, then electrical interference will bog your workflow.

If I had to chose only one studio monitor in this price range, a year ago I would go with Mackie's MR5 mk2. The latest MR5 mk3 or the mk3 series in general is too overdone in design that it detracts from how good of a lower end studio monitor that it can be.

My advice to Mackie is to go back to the drawing board and retrace your roots why you have made a name in the industry. Forget the kitschy styling and accents. Design is important of course so give us a sexy speaker with clean curves and lines. But most of all give us great sound as close as possible to your HR speaker line.

I've also tried the felt ukulele picks and didn't really like those all that much after awhile. The texture was too weird for me. I've tried plastic guitar picks too, and those are OK, but a little too harsh on ukulele strings.
I think these are great for the best tone on a ukulele. I think the Hards are too hard though for most ukulele's. The Hard's may work for baritones or electric's/solid bodies. The Hard's are about twice as thick as the Medium and Soft. The Medium and Soft are essentially the same thickness; the only difference is the tension in them. I find that the Medium is the best though because of that extra little resistance. The Soft sometimes can drag on the strings/snag on the strings a little bit.
Thus I think Medium are the best for the ukulele (5-star), Soft next best (4-star), and Hard least-best (3.5 but rounding up since I like the product overall).

There are some inexpensive wireless solutions out there. I guess some of them may be ok, but frankly, as someone who has worked as a live sound professional, wireless devices terrify me. I've seen horrible devices ruin shows, but I've also experienced well made devices that were completely trouble/worry/problem free, set it and forget it. I looked around and thought long and hard before I a purchased this device for a couple reasons:

I'm going to have a pedal board with me anyway. And a tuner pedal. Any little wireless device the plugs into my existing tuner pedal runs a high risk of being stepped on and broken. On the other hand if the receiver IS the tuner pedal, it's more durable than the little plug in things and easier than carrying around a separate receiver that I have to put on top of my amp or somewhere else. It also makes power easy.

This is a digital device, and its a well known name in wireless reliability. The technology allows the signal to find a clean frequency space, and hop around if needed to stay clean. That means the sound quality should always be good.

The rechargeable battery in the transmitter pack means I don't have to worry about having a fresh set of batteries for a show. Battery life on the pack is claimed at more than enough to do a sound check and a show, even if the pack accidentally gets left on for the couple hours in between the two.

Now you have the reasons, you have to wonder if my expectations have been met, and it works as I hoped - the answer is yes, yes, yes. The tuner feature is every bit as good as the dedicated tuner pedal I was using. My sound has not changed or been altered in any way by the device that you can distinguish by listening. Even though I have a large/powerful multi-band wireless router in my practice room, there is no interference from that.

In short, sometimes if you want a solid product, you simply have to pay for it, and there are no shortcuts. Yes, I might try a $40 wireless system if I just wanted to not have a cord from my amp to my guitar in my bedroom or something, but for playing out - I simply don't trust it. I can go to a show with the band and know that this won't let me down, and I won't let the guys in the band down, and we won't let the audience down. And the peace of mine is worth it.

Text:
I have a small apartment in a small but densely populated apartment complex - space and noise is an issue. As a beginning guitarist, I contemplated a small amp but decided on the Mini Tone Master (because in my apartment, the smaller the better). Also, I had no need for ample volume or a variety of controls being at the level that I am... I just wanted something no-frills that was small, compact with enough quality sound to help me as I practice. The Mini Tone Master delivers well.

I was pretty surprised at the range of sounds the little guy can produce (from distortion grungy to a softer bluesy tone). It does not come with a power adapter but we already have on in the apartments and works well with that or with a battery. Battery life is also pretty good. I've had the same battery in there for several months already, playing several times a week and sometimes leaving it on accidentally for a day or two and no signs of battery drain so far.

It is a little frustrating sometimes, as another reviewer mentioned, to remove the distortion but with enough fiddling, I found a setting that was acceptable to my ears.

While I didn't need volume, this little guy can be loud! No weakness there.

I also plugged an acoustic-electric classical guitar into the mini tone master and it also worked surprisingly well.

The good is that it doesn't leak.  The bad is that in my normal house in the northeast, it has to be filled every 3 days or so.  If the guitar is in storage or swapped out among several others, you don't always remember to fill it.  I suppose most are this way, but maybe not and, with this much trouble, I rather dedicate a closet and electric humidifier to my guitars.
Summary: Works but not my cup of tea.

I came back multiple days, just to be sure.  I mean, who'da thunk it?  Despite what the description may elude, it is not a solid-wood instrument.  It's a laminate with high gloss.  But it was easy to play and, like I mentioned earlier, it sounded great!  The uke it's replacing is also a Kala uke, but side by side, the BG is *so* much better.  I think it's a keeper and may even have a MiSi pickup installed.  Do your due diligence and see the different ukes in person, but please consider the Kala KA-BG if you're looking for a baritone.  Like I said, I wouldn't have even bothered checking out the BG had I known it was Kala right off the bat.  You just can't beat the sound for the price.

The Clairevoire dust cover is also quite thick so it provides probably more protection than this cover, is easier to get on and off since it does not use an elastic band, and the top is quite pretty so it makes my piano look nicer than this dust cover, which makes the piano look quite utilitarian. If you do not have any such reason to desire superior protection, though, and are mostly just looking for something to keep basic dust off of your digital piano, then for $12 I don't think it can hurt to try this one first. The worst case scenario is that the elastic band randomly breaks when you are taking it off or putting it on your piano, and then you can upgrade to the Clairevoire dust cover or another more expensive dust cover, but it is possible that the one I got was a lemon and maybe your dust cover will last much longer and you'll get your $12 of worth out of it.

Life-changing harmonica

No offense if you just skip the following elucidation and acquire one in your favorite key.

I’ve been carrying a harmonica with me for over 70 years, yes, literally. I purchases my first harmonica at the local “find-and-dime” at about age 10 or 12, and I got, or traded for, not sure which, for another soon after.

One is the “American Ace,” made in Ireland; the other is a Hohner “Blues Harp,” made in Germany. Both in Key of G. They hung around for decades as I struggled to try to figure out how to play them. I didn’t accomplish very much. Decades later, with the internet replete with instructions for everything, I finally learned a bit about the ordinary Richter harmonica. I had occasionally stumbled onto an old tremolo harmonica, but was put off by what I later learned was deliberate dissonance. Musically, I was never into dissonance.

That led to well over 20 Richters, a few minor harps, and two Suzuki Chromatixs.

Recently I stumbled across a promo for the Seydel Orchestra. I immediately ordered one. I might never play a Richter again.

The Seydel Orchestra is the harmonica I needed 70 years ago, and, if I had one then, I have no idea how my life would have been different, but certainly it would have been very different. It is all but frightening to think about it. I sang at school, I sang at church, and I sang at family gatherings. But my harmonica stayed in my pocket, contributed nothing to any of these activities. I played only in my solitude while walking rural trails and sitting on river banks and tree limbs.

In contrast, a Seydel Orchestra, especially one for each of the more popular keys, would have enabled me to play in all those otherwise unavailable settings.

I glad to have the Seydel Orchestra, but wonder why it took so long to produce a harmonica almost anyone who sang could master, easily playing most of their favorite folk songs, gospel songs, and popular songs.

Glad I lived long enough to own a C and G, and hope eventually to acquire others, especially an E, but they don't make one in E.

So, why only four stars? Because it only comes in A, C, D, F, G. Strange selection seems to me.
Why those keys?

I want one in E.

Perhaps their Key options will soon expand.
Summary: Best harmonica ever, especially for beginners

I'm a performing singer-songwriter, and I don't dance around a lot on stage, so I have always been content to stay plugged in. Also, I guess I also never trusted the idea of a wireless system that did not cost hundreds of dollars. I've always thought that it would be nice to be cord-free, at least in rehearsals, so I finally decided that I would take a shot.

I have no idea who Brian Faye might be, but I have to say that I really like this wireless system a lot. They come in a very classy storage box with a built-in charger. You just plug the box into a USB port, drop the transmitter and receiver in the cradles, and they're ready to go when you need them.

When you hit the power button they power right up, and pair automatically. Changing the channel is super easy and intuitive, in case you're using more than one set of these in the same area, or if you're getting UHF interference from something else.

I'm not a sound technician, so when I tested these I used my ears. To evaluate the sound, I used the Bose S-1 Pro that I use to play small rooms and my favorite acoustic guitar with a K&K passive pickup.

First I went straight from the transmitter in the guitar straight to the receiver in the amp. I got a lot of signal, but the tone was thin and tinny compared to connecting directly with a cable. Using the Treble and Bass EQ on the amp I could not get it sounding anywhere near as good as it did with the cable.

Then I moved the receiver to the Fishman EQ/Preamp I normally use on stage, and I could easily bring the sound in the range of what I'm used to by boosting the mid-range and the bass, and pulling back the attack a bit. I know that with a little bit of experimentation and fine-tuning I can get this sounding great.

I could not get the sound to drop out at all, no matter what I did. I even went into a separate room separated by a concrete block wall, and could not kill it. I also tried it with a bass guitar and it sounded great after I got it EQ'd.

So even though I have not put it through a strenuous gig yet, I can enthusiastically recommend this wireless system. At the price, it would be fantastic if I only used it in rehearsals to de-clutter the studio. However, I really can't see any reason that any professional would not be happy with this on a casual stage after they got it dialed in.

The "Product Dimensions" as shown must be for the product in a package. The actual pad itself measures 16.25" long by 17.0" tip-to-tip on the wide end, and 13.5" tip-to-tip on the narrow end. The important thing to know is that for it to work as designed, one of the flaps needs to be resting against the inside of the drum head at a fairly steep up-angle, so that it can "bounce" away from the head when it's struck, and then settle back to rest against the head again to dampen the ringing. This means that with the EQ Pad you will only be able to muffle either the batter head or the resonant head, but not both. It seems that the pad is really designed to work behind the batter head, so, the resonant head could still need something else for ring control.

As another reviewer mentioned, you will not get that deep, pillow sound with this pad. But then, that's not what it's intended to do.

As far as the Velcro not sticking, mine stuck fine. I thoroughly dry-dusted the inside of the shell first, paying special attention to the area where the Velcro would mount. You could even do a light wipe-down with rubbing alcohol on a rag to prepare the surface first. I would just be sure to let it air dry completely before sticking down the Velcro pads.

For my purposes, although the EQ Pad worked as Evans designed it to, in the end I wound up using a small pillow instead to get the "warm thud" sound I wanted. But the EQ pad is definitely worth trying out. Maybe in the future I'll find another drum that it's perfect for.

Absorbtion, diffusion and isolation are three different animals. Some reviewers are a bit confused about what this item is and is not. This is not in any way, shape or form a sound absorption (dampening/deadening) panel. Generally both actions are needed in order to create that perfect, perky sweet spot that sits between out of balance echoey-ness and flat, dull lifelessness. Neither is this something you would use to isolate any space, large or small, from external noise.

Rather than reflecting pressure waves at the usual, specific, predictable, opposite angle like a wall does this panel disperses that energy in multiple, more random, directions. So while no pressure waves get significantly absorbed or muffled by diffusers the benefits are that frequency build up (standing waves) and cancellations are reduced. You are not getting less sound so much as a more evenly (and randomly) dispersed/controlled/natural sound across the spectrum.

NOTE that something thin like this reflects high to mid frequencies AND will leave low and low-mid frequencies pretty much unaffected. That's why it will do little or nothing to stop noise coming in from outside a room or home. For a reflective surface to truly block sound it needs to be thick, dense and pretty much air tight. Like how much more outdoor noise you hear when you crack open a door or window even just little bit. So even a massive number of these panels coating your walls will be pointless for blocking outside noise. They are only for manipulating the sound energy WITHIN a room. Again, using these will not protect you from noisy neighbors or visa-versa.

Quadratic diffusers probably are the more "proper" panels for dispersing pressure waves but these cheaper plastic reflectors will still likely put you ahead of untreated, flat, parallel opposing, walls. Aesthetically you get what you pay for. Wood diffusers definitely look classier and are better than plastic in pretty much every way; density, paint/stainable, durability...

By themselves diffusers do not reduce volume across the board though they may cut down reverberation/echo times and combat frequency build up caused by standing waves. In that sense they can make a room sound and feel less acoustically out of control.

While every situation is unique the principles are the same whether it be a small studio, living room or event space. I like thick absorbers for controlling low end build up with diffusers mixed in to maintain liveliness, spaciousness and evenness throughout the mid and upper ranges. Pay an expert thousands to calculate everything to perfection or experiment a bit and find that balance point that sounds right to you.

Text:
***UPDATE: Glad that several like my review, so if you want this amp you better find it, because Fender discontinued it (apparently) for the newer version. It's no longer on their product list. This little amp may be costing them money elsewhere!*** I may buy this amps big brother. Sorry for the interuption, please read on:

I'll spare you my guitar playing resume (30+ years), and get right to it. So, I purchased the Super Champ XD outside of Amazon, but am so impressed with it, I don't mind supporting the other excellent Super Champ XD reviews herein. After a few weeks of viewing piles of reviews on various effect/amplication items and actually field-testing many amps and interests.. I happened back on my trusty old Fender series of amps. I sat down and played the Mustang 2 first and then the SCXD. The Mustang 2 was neat, but more for a beginning home-player wanting a full solid state amp with a-bizillion gizmos. The SCXD is more of a player's amp (for the musician who wants tube-driven warmth with "modeling" or "voicing" built-ins, manueverability, and ease of use. The expression "modeling", or "voicing", simply means that this amp has built-in pre-set distortion settings and effects (16 distortions and several effects combinations - chorus, delay, tremelo, Fender spring reverb, and Vibratone - which is a phase-like effect). And, they are adjustable (gain, and intensity). As such, you have two different knobs; one which controls your distortions, and the other which controls your effects (there is an intensity knob for the effects too). The 16 distortions range from very light to crunch, so it's not completely accurate to say that some are all that "distorted", but you get the idea. To add each distortion setting, and effect setting may be tuned to your liking with gain, treble, bass and intensity knobs. So, this amp is pretty customizable for what it is. No, it's not a fully customized pedal/effects board. However, you will admire the versatility of this set-up, and all the many tones it produces. Plus 15 watts of tube power is a lot! (Guessing here - similar to a 60 watt solid state amp in power output). The pre-set distortions are all usable for varying tastes of music. For hard rock and lead, I use setting 8 (plexi-Marshall) and 3 (Fender, driven tweed) each used with full gain, and higher treble and bass settings. Go ahead, and add some delay/reverb, or plain delay for soloing.. This setting is great either way. Or, for a blusey vibe, I'll use setting 2,6, and 7, with/without some temelo.. there are so many ideas and tones you can get out of this amp. The hard-rock distortion is very good and toothy (setting 8). It's my opinion that setting 8 is an excellent general setting (w/without delay, or verb). Just adjust your tone and pick-ups with this setting, and you'd be happy, but you've got plenty of others to choose from too. I also really like to work the tubes on this thing.. Many times, I crank up the volume to a 5-7 level, and the gain all the way up!! This little thing sings, cries, and rocks.. nice and loud! All tube amps need volume to do their magic - so, it's no different on this amp.. Testing it in a store on level 2, or 3 is great, but go ahead, turn it up to level 5-7 to get this thing into groove.. If the store will let you do it go ahead and try it (use setting 8 on the voicing knob, and pick out a Les Paul to work this horse). Or, you got to, take it home for a little while.

The fit and finish are usual Fender-look, and quality. Everything feels good as you adjust and play with the amp. I also like that this amp is small/midsized and will stow away without taking up too much space, but, at the same time, deliver fairly rich base response and fat tone (notable with Fender tube amps). This amp is about the size of an average microwave oven (more boxy though). The SCXD offers versatility and big sound in a compact package; it is absolutely perfect for home-space playing without all cords/gear/mess that larger amps/stacks/pedals/cords give you. Could you gig with it? Hell yeah, but depends on your set-up and other things. The speaker inside the SCXD gives good bass and lush/fat tone; but also will render the crunchy/crispy metal tone too.. This speaker sounds pretty fantastic people..; many have suggested, you've got to break-in a speaker, my stock speaker is getting more edgy after about 100 hours and sounds really good - I doubt I'll ever replace it.
I also dig the old-school power-on indicator light. It glows and looks old-school-cool.

Overall - I would replace this amp at a higher cost if it were stolen from me.. . It's like adding 20 pretty good pedals to your small tube amp without all the cords, adapters, mess etc.. Therefore, it's a great home-use amp (plug and play). Purists argue that modeling/voicing amps (also known as hybrids) are not full-tube sound which is partly true, but you'll never hear a difference. So, I disagree in context as to how tube sound works to begin with. As for the SCXD, the sound on both channels is still moving through vaccume tubes, it's just that, the overdrive is processed from transistors, instead of extra tubes which are in "full-tube amps, therefore making the OD gain in the SCXD solid-state. This is no different than pros using solid-state pedals to run throuh their "full tube" amps (clean or dirty channel).. It's all snobbery to me.. Don't be fooled, the SCXD sounds tube-wonderful for the price (and the SCXD clean channel; for you purists, is full tube anyway). Alright.. we move on.. Fender sought out to try and please everybody who is an avid home-playing musician and they'll win-over most with the SCXD (not everyone, but most). They included settings, tones, and effects which would cover just about everything in general. Plus, you get the much of the character, feel/sound of a a fully tube-driven Fender. When I finally tripped into this amp, there were folks who stopped by to ask me which one I was playing out of. The store was set up with Marshall, Egnater, Tiny Terror, Vox etc.. and, I played them all, and for the money, the SCXD is what I bought - it just sounded the best and I got tubes too! Is it stage worthy? Absolutely, but please be realistic; you'd have to mic it for large events or club playing. (so, it depends on the stage and intended use - YES, for uses in churches and less sized areas). There are other amps which have a lot more included effects, but most are solid state, and don't offer the warmth, resonance, and bass response of tube sound. OK, this amp doesn't have everything, but it has the many commonly used distortions and effects. The Fender Mustang series, Peavey Vipyr and the VOX + series offer piles more effects, but they don't sound like the SCXD. The Peavey Tube Vypyr is the only exception here, but I've not heard it live and it's $449.. So, not really price-comparable.. Still, the XD kicks effen a**. For me, less effects and a better distorition-sound was what I wanted for my money, and I got it with the SCXD. If you compare the Fender Vibro Champ to this one, beware that it's only 5 watts, and an 8 inch speaker. The SCXD has a 10 incher, another channel, and 15 watts.. It's plenty loud enough to small-gig (clean or dirty), at an average 300 person church without a mic (in my opinion).

Negatives? none really; are there a few things I'd consider? Well... before I mention any kinda-cons, I paid $243 for this amp (on sale), and it's very hard to argue against it for that little money. ***Now you can find this amp for $199.00...I must admit, that the preset distortions try really hard, but I can't find my exact sweet spot within them (However, it's fairly close on setting 8 - I wish there were a bit more saturation within this setting). There are many settings which are very good sounding for most styles/tastes (country, rock-a-billy, blues, jazz, rock, hard-rock, metal, crunch). As for the SCXD, I would say that in it's size, weight, features, and SOUND-class, there is nothing that will really compare. No, this is NOT a Fender Super Sonic, or a Hot Rod Deville 212 - both have larger cabinets, with larger speakers and full tube-driven gain (no solid state voicing). So, with the SCXD, you won't get stage-big, and full tube sound (comparitively) but, what you will get, is big-enough-for-your-house tube sound, with piles of add-ons at a great price. This is a fantastic amp for intermediate/avid home players, studio guys, or grab and go musicians.. No clutter, no mess - lightweight etc. Some people upgrade the tubes and speakers.. Perhaps, I'll look into that, or not. So, if you have reasonable expectations, this amp will really surprise you. If you're really picky; have space; muscle; and have the coin, spend a lot more and check out the Super Sonic, Hot Rod Deville 212, Blackstar HT, Engl Screamer (which is incredible), or the Mesa Boogie 5 X 50, and a few others I could mention. These offerings have it all, big tube amp sound with excellent clean, and gain personalities. Especially the Engl Screamer, Fender Super Sonic or Blackstar HT20, or 40.. Saving my money.. Until then, this will work really really well for most anyone and is at least half the cost of the Blackstar HT 20 (which is a full tube amp, with no voicing, or effects).. You won't be displeased with this purchase - there is an army of folks on the Fender blogs who would likly support my review. Read-up for yourself. Please find an excellent You Tube demo of this amp; this guitarist is terrific and goes through the voicings (but doesn't use the effects much).[...] Now you can find this amp on Ebay for $100-150. The clean channel alone works great for pedal usage and is very loud!. Also works great with external cabinets (check ohms before doing this!).
Summary: Best small-midsized tube amp on the market - BUY THIS.

Text: Always revamping my board, I needed this thin-jack style for the latest incarnation. I was looking for a pack of the usual brand-names, but came across these, read the reviews & took a chance. Very glad I did. They're really well made, robust, flexible, no noise, just a pro cable all around. Well worth the very decent price.

The strength of these cables is that they are fairly cheap for low capacitance cable, and of course they can be cut to any length. The drawbacks are that assembly is not foolproof and worse, some pedals don't like the plugs.

To save you some trouble, yes, watch YouTube. But if you really want to make life easy, use a high quality wire stripper, not that boxcutter thing they throw in. Not over-cutting or under-cutting is half the battle. Next, study the inside of the plug. You'll see that the center of the cable, the stiff part, needs to be dead straight, so it will go down the tiny center hole in the plug. If your center wire isn't perfectly straight it ain't gonna happen. Lastly, even if your center wire is straight, it won't always make a "snap" sound, but this doesn't appear to make any difference as long as you've done everything else correctly.

So now you have low capacitance custom cables with tiny plugs that fit in very tight spaces. But there can still be issues. A few pedals, like my Truetone Rt 66 will not accept the plugs. They only go part way in. On pedals where the jacks are too close together, like the Keeley Aria, you have the reverse problem; it's hard to get a grip on the small plugs to pull them out. Obviously only an issue if you frequently move your pedals around. Lastly, watch for the caps on the plugs to start unscrewing.

Despite these drawbacks, I've had no sound problems and no tone loss, and when I need a 13 inch cable, I can just make one on the spot. Having color options is nice, too, to help keep track of things.
Summary: Not that difficult to assemble but not perfect, either

Just got the Behringer Xenyx X1204USB mixer and I really was impressed. The knobs, faders, and switches all felt solid (compressor pots feel flimsy though), but there is one button that now sticks in the engaged position which is on channel 7/8. It's the Pre fader button, and that shocked me since every other one is flawless (knock on wood), and even the first time I tested the one that is now bad worked like a charm. I didn't even press that hard (these are like ball point pen buttons in which they latch when pressed down) on it before it would not disengage.

For $200 I do expect a product that doesn't break after a simple test (engage/disengage). Is it worth returning for a new one? To be honest I am debating this, but here's the issue. If could get a replacement that is worse and half of the buttons could stick in the engaged position, or perhaps I could end up with other issues such as bad faders, POTS or whatever. One switch isn't the end of the world, but it does stink.

One thing to note before buying the X1204USB (or any in the Xenyx family) is that while this is USB, it WILL NOT (repeat) WILL NOT multi track record for you. Unlike a Studio Live mixer from Presonus which can muti track record into the DAW, all you can do in a XENYX is record in 2 track stereo into your DAW. Definitely not what you'd want in your home studio. Even podcasting you have to send it all to 2 tracks (even with 4 mic outs and instrument (line in). Makes it tough to isolate the audio for a good mix down.

Over all this is a decent entry level mixer, but don't expect everything under the sun. Even with what this has, it is still very basic. I've been recording for years, and have been a musician for many years, my experience say this is okay, but there are better mixers out there if you spend a bit more.
Summary: Channel 7/8 Pre button sticks in the engagued position when pressed, and won't release.

People describe the sound of parlor guitars as "boxy" or "full" but the truth is they sound pretty bad when compared to a full size acoustic. However, it's that lo-fi sound that makes this guitar fun to play. Basically "boxy" means too much bass, messy mids, flat sounding highs and a body that resonates in a bit of an ugly way. It almost sounds like a toy guitar. Oddly, this is the sound you want for fingerpicking in a delta blues style. This is not a good pick strumming guitar but it's really good for fingerpicking. It's super fun to play and the small size and tiny price tag makes it a great travel guitar.

I look forward to hearing/seeing how this guitar mellows with age.

These extra-heavy's are considerably smaller than a classic Fender heavy. Rough measurement tip to top for the heavy is 1 3/16" while the extra-heavy is just less than an inch, perhaps 31/32". This applies to the width as well, and the shoulders are more rounded, so these picks feel considerably different in the hand. Most important for tone is the tip of the extra-heavy is considerably sharper than the heavy which, in my experience, produces more high end.

Fender sells their large tri-corner picks in extra-heavy with the same dimensions as a heavy, so I'm not sure why they don't here with the classic shape. If you like the classic heavy shape but want a little more weight, D'Addario sells a Planet Waves pick but the material feels (and I believe sounds) a bit different - I'm talking primarily about acoustic tone for guitar and mandolin.

Bottom Line: The tip is too sharp for the tone I prefer on mandolin but these feel and sound fine for acoustic and electric guitar.
Summary: Image is Misleading, But They're Still Useful Picks

Text:
Azor is following in the footsteps of their parent company Caline by releasing a new line of colorful budget pedals.  Caline's  recent "G" series of pedals was hit or miss, with some being very good and some being not so good.  Judging from this chorus pedal, Azor is not off to a great start.

Positives:

1.  Build quality is good, everything functions as it should.

2.  I did not notice that this pedal added much - if any - noise to my chain at lower volumes.

Negatives:

1.  The Azor mini-chorus pedal (AP309) gave a noticeable treble boost when engaged, which is generally typical of chorus pedals.  This new pedal, however, seems to boost the low end slightly and lower the treble, which makes for a muddier-sounding chorus effect.  

2.  There is a small amount of gain introduced when the pedal is on.   It is therefore difficult to get a clean sound - again, it is sort of muddy.

3.  No matter how I tweak the knobs, I was never able to get the kind of lush, shimmery chorus effect that was so popular in the 80's.  The pedal sounds like it's 2/3 of the way there but never quite gets to the place where you are playing through it and are just fascinated and delighted by the tones you are getting.  

OVERALL SUMMARY:   This is a serviceable chorus pedal if nothing else is available, but you can do better.  I do not use chorus often so for quick and dirty tones this will do in a pinch, but it is not that great. Considering that the Azor Mini-Chorus AP309 is half the price of this one, I would recommend that one over this.
Summary: Not As Good As The AZOR Mini-Chorus AP309

Text:
I very recently bought this guitar for my young daughter based on the previous reviews. She's joined the jazz band at her school and since she is smaller than the average 12 year old, she needed a smaller sized guitar. It was packaged very well and it took a while just to get the guitar out of the packaging. The only thing I have found so far that sort of disappointed me was that there were some dark stain blemishes on the white pick guard. Trying to get the stains off with a damp paper towel didn't work so I took a special soft, damp sponge made to remove stains and gently rubbed it over the spots. They came off but the finish on the plastic pick guard is dulled where I had rubbed the stains off. That sort of irked me. However, it didn't seem to bother my daughter nearly as much as it did me.

Despite the blemish episode, it fits her perfectly. I tried to tune it using a clamp-on Snark tuner. That didn't work at all for some reason so we went to Guitar Center and bought an electric guitar tuner which you plug the cord into from the guitar. That really worked well to tune the guitar. The tuning pegs (gears) were stiff and a bit hard to turn. When I change the strings I will adjust them to make them easier to turn. The strings the guitar comes with are very cheap so I'll need to change those out soon for a much better set, but they'll have to do for now.

I plugged the guitar to my old Crate amp and it sounded pretty good. The knobs on the front of the guitar turn well an did what they are supposed to do. It's easy to control the tone and volume from the guitar without having to dicker much with the amp. My daughter had a great time getting used to it. She's a great classical guitarist (I teach classical guitar) so playing an electric guitar was a new experience for her. My old Strat is just too big and heavy for her and this black one looks good (despite the dullness that only I can see) on her and she was awesome playing jazz guitar in her school concert the other night. Since this guitar is so inexpensive and is just right for a smaller person, I really can't find anything major wrong to say about it. I'm glad I bought it, just wish it didn't come with the stains. It feels solid, well-constructed, and not very heavy. I like playing it too!

I've ordered a really good gig bag, new cord, a Pignose amp just for her and of course, a bunch of new electric guitar strings. She'll find the small stuff in her stocking this Christmas! I can't wait for us to do some mother and daughter electric guitar duets!!

Instead, I drilled the f-hole slightly larger. The rest of the installation went off without any problems. I drilled a hole for the jack and fished it through with little difficulty. We'll see how long the adhesive holds the transducer in place. I'm thinking a few bumps might knock it loose. I plugged it in and it worked. The sound was about what I had expected and about what I had paid for. A lot of the depth of the tone is lost and come's through in the high-mid range. It isn't terrible, though. I think with a little EQ I might improve on the sound a little bit. I might work on placement of the transducer as well. There is a little body noise that gets picked up if you bump the instrument as well, but it isn't too bad.

The bottom line is that this pickup does what you expect. If you want spectacular sound, or have a spectacular instrument, don't be so cheap on the pickup. If you have a $200 mando like mine, this pickup will probably suit your needs.

Text: Donner's doing great stuff lately, and this trio of effects in a solid, nicely laid-out unit is a keeper. The reverbs can get you the nice usual subtle underlay but they can also dial in pretty extreme if needed- anything from a large room to deep dark caves. The delays are interesting- the digital delay is a hair tighter than the slightly warmer analog, and both can be dialed to durational taste. The reverse mode is nicely psychedelic- this effect has never been readily available in a lower-budget pedal till the last few years, but it's popping up more often now in delay pedals, and it's a credit to Donner to have included such a unique effect in this (one of the reasons i got it). The Phaser/Chorus/Flanger... well, they're not subtle, and could be considered as an alternative to the usual pristine, more backgroundish versions out there. They're all thick & syrupy, and they seem to add a little bit of bottom & volume. Not a bad thing, just different from the light wisps of, say, a Roland JC40.  The unit's got a reasonably low but not invisible noise floor, looks very cool (think Tony Stark's brushed silver metal suit #2), super easy to carry around. It went on an overdub session today and sounded great. Recommended.

I started on a soprano uke, and while it was small and portable and easy to start learning on... I started having trouble when I needed to use any note below the third or forth fret with my adult sized hands. The little bit of extra size on the tenor makes it so much more usable and now I can go down nine or ten frets before I have to be careful and precise. So for that reason I definitely recommend starting with a tenor for anyone with size 8 fingers or above. Another nice comfort thing with this uke is it includes two pegs for a strap (included), which is a lot more ergonomic than tie or clip on straps.

The sound is nice clear and bright, although I prefer the warmer sound and softer feel of nylgut or nyltech strings than these. These strings are also taking their time being broken in, but they're getting close and when they are in tune the intonation between the strings is true and the same note played on a different string sounds the same. If you already have guitar callouses or if you like bright Hawaiian sounding ukes then you may be perfectly fine with these, although I plan on changing them out with gut like strings and maybe with a low G string as well.

The build quality is nice, they chose a nice compromise of style and function for this price point. It doesn't in any way look, feel or sound like a toy and looks great in the hand or the stand. Although, I doubt it would be confused for a high-end professional instrument for a performing musician. It is a however a great choice for someone who want to start learning without dropping a lot of money. There's no gotchas that will make learning harder other than maybe getting different strings which are reasonably cheap. The best part is even if the new hobby doesn't take off it makes for very functional and decorative piece for the home.

Text:
The Ernie Ball Expression Series Ambient Delay SCREAMS quality. The build quality is absolutely stellar. Check out the size of the expression pedal pivot in the pictures. I can't say I'm a fan of the copper color finish, but that's trivial. The expression pedal itself is dead smooth. The knobs are dead smooth with just the right amount of friction to keep them from moving. No noise. No artifacts.

The effects themselves are excellent. Good reverb with a good range of effective room/stage sizes. Good delay. But the real benefit is controlling the mix with the expression pedal. Dial it back to sink back into the mix. Hit it for full effect. I will say I'm more of a fan for this for the delay than reverb, but if you really are sinking back into the mix, going dry with the reverb is less of an issue than with the delay.

No bypass. Basically you're on the pedal's buffer with the pedal back. Not a problem for me, but I don't have a board with a zillion pedals, either. The pedal can use tap tempo, but doesn't have a tap switch - the expression pedal presumably prevents that, so if you want it, you'll have to use a separate switch ... pretty much essential for live use.

Packaging could be better (see pic). No damage to the pedal itself, though. I've also included a pic of the "documentation" - a simple, small fold-out. Nothing more needed, really.

Excellent pedal and excellent concept.
Summary: Ernie Hit the Ball Out of the Park

Lots of great features and excellent sounds. This is a decent keyboard, but there are some things to keep in mind: 1. Even if you are a beginner, you might soon get frustrated with the limited amount of keys on this instrument. I'd say get a keyboard with at least 76 keys. And if you are serious about playing classical, and/or taking piano lessons, either buy a piano or a keyboard with weighted keys (which are quite different from touch-sensitive keys) and one that has the full 88 keys. Unfortunately, keyboards with these features, with the exception of one or two models made by Williams, are more expensive. Sorry, I don't know if those Williams keyboards are very good, I've just played on some in a store.

Secondly, lighted keys are a bad idea. If you are focusing on and playing the keys as they light up, you might as well be playing a video game like Rock Band or Guitar Hero.

Why? If you are watching and playing the lighted keys, you are not learning what notes the keys are, and you are not learning how to read music. The notes do show up on the display at the center of the keyboard, but it is kinda tough to watch the display and also the keys as they light up. Trying to learn with the lit keys feature, in my opinion, will actually slow your growth as a musician, not speed up your improvement.

If you don't need a keyboard with 88 weighted keys, and want a good synth, I'd say go for the Yamaha PSREW300AD 76-Key Portable Keyboard & Power Supply (if one is sold with portable power supply). These features are not on the keyboard, but the app works. Strangely, I just found that sound controller listed under "iphone apps," not "ipad apps," but I was still able to download it to my ipad.

The PSREW model I just mentioned does not have lighted keys, has 76 keys, and has more and better features. It doesn't cost much more than this model. Watch the demo on youtube. Pretty cool.

Thirdly, the display on this keyboard is not backlit, and is therefore not easy to see unless you are somewhere with good lighting. The keyboard I just mentioned does have a backlit display that is easier to see.

Lastly, this model, as of 1/15/18, when I am writing this review, is not sold with a power supply in the box. You'll have to buy one extra.

Some other things I just thought of.. the "survival kit" that is often sold as part of a bundle is not worth buying. The headphones are terrible, the expression pedal is really really tiny, and there's a bunch of offers for online programs which you may or may not be interested in. Better to buy a full size sustain pedal and a power supply separately. Skip the survival kit.

And keyboard stands.. X-brace stands, whether single or double braced, are wobbly. Z stands are not wobbly, but might not be adjustable high enough to make playing standing up comfortable, depending on your height.

National NP2B Brass Fingerpicks
INTRODUCTION: Metal fingerpicks protect your fingers and produce a loud, clear ringing tone when plucking a metal string. They are typically used for playing acoustic guitar, dobro, banjo, or steel guitar.
I have purchased and used all the picks in this review. I compared them on Gretsch Lap Steel Guitar, Martin Acoustic Guitar, and Gibson RBT Banjo strung with Dunlop and Fender extra-light strings.
COMPOSITION: Brass fingerpicks alloy usually contains 66% copper and 34% zinc. It contains no nickel or steel. Brass can kill bacteria on contact.
COMPARISON: I compared National NP2B Brass fingerpicks with National NP2 and Dunlop 156/33P Nickel Silver fingerpicks, National NP2SS Stainless Steel fingerpicks, Dunlop 81/37R Brass fingerpicks, ProPik Split Wrap Brass fingerpicks, my bare fingers without fingerpicks, and a variety of plastic fingerpicks.
DESCRIPTION: The National NP2B Brass fingerpicks are 0.025 inches thick with a single band and flat wings that hold the slightly rounded paddle around your fingertip. They were softer and easier to fit than the Nickel Silver or Stainless Steep fingerpicks.
SOUND: The National NP2 Brass fingerpicks were loud, bright, and they emphasized the treble end of the fundamental tone of each string without adding any unnatural overtones. They were almost as bright as the National and Dunlop Nickel Silver fingerpicks without producing high harsh, treble overtones.
CONCLUSIONS: All metal picks sounded louder than naked fingertips and plastic picks. The National NP2B fingerpicks sounded loud and bright without changing the fundamental sound of the strings.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Metal fingerpicks can make a string sing and increase enjoyment of the music you make. I liked the National NP2B Brass fingerpicks and my bare fingertips best. I will be using these brass fingerpicks from now on whenever I want brighter sound.

Compared to the GT the Tauren sounded a lot smoother (and I don't mean less gain, more like less harsh). It blended well with the natural gain of the amp. On the clean channel I got some killer blues tones, and on the lead channel I was in metal territory all day long. I never had the gain turned past 9 O clock on the pedal, it broke up and sounded really good right at 9. It's very responsive to guitar volume and pick attack. With the volume rolled back, it cleans up nicely. But dime the volume on the guitar and it screams. I really like the ambient light on the edges of the pedal. I like to block the LEDs on my pedals because they're too bright and make it difficult to see my settings. After taping off the LED on the Tauren, the ambient light was clearly visible, but wasn't glaring off the top. A small subtle detail that is just awesome. As for construction I'd say this is built really well. All metal, nice feeling switch and the pots feel buffered. I'm really impressed with this pedal, probably gonna snag another one just to have a spare. Text:
This power supply provides flexible power for a wide variety of guitar effects pedals. There are 6-9V 100 mA connections, 2-9V 500 mA connections, 1-12V 100 mA connection and 1-18V 100 mA Connection. What all that means is, you have power available for most any types of guitar pedals you may be using. The majority of modern pedals are 9V and that means that you have lots of availability with this supply. For most the 100 mA connection is more than adequate, but if you need more you have 2 500 mA ports as well. Analog pedals generally use less power than their digital counterparts. You should always check the requirements of the specific pedals you may be trying to utilize with this power supply. The pedal will only draw what it needs, so you can use these outputs so long as they meet the pedals max requirement. The 12V and 18V outputs are for the rare pedal that might need that higher voltage. You should not use those outputs for 9V pedals. There are an additional 4 AC outlets on the top of the unit should you need to plug in something that uses that sort of power. The combined max output for the 4 plugs is 600 W.

The box itself is lightweight and seems well constructed. It is made of some sort of plastic. While it is not very rugged and might not hold up to continued abuse when moving from place to place, it is fine for my home setup here. The unit comes with 10 connectors (wires) for the most common pedal power connections. They are wired for a center negative pole which is the most common configuration. There is a polarity reversal adapter if you should need it for an odd bird that requires a +POS center pole.

The unit seems to be well isolated and does not seem to introduce a lot of extra noise into the system. There is separate short circuit protection on all 10 outputs. If one channel shorts the rest should continue to operate. There are leds at each output that indicate that the output is operating. If there is a short circuit, the corresponding led should go out making it easier to find the offending unit.

In my experience with it so far, it seems to be operating well. I only have use for the 9V outputs at this time, but they seems to be functioning properly. I have not noticed any noise being introduced.

The manual provided is written in decent English and is not difficult to understand.

If I were a professional travelling musician, I don't know that I would use a power supply like this, as I don't know that it would hold up to the constant abuse. For home use where you are going to set it up and forget it, I think it is great. I think the price at under $40 is a good value and am pleased to have it in my gear.
Summary: Nice Guitar Pedal Board Power Supply

One young man selected the music industry careers as his topic for the semester. I asked if he played an instrument and his response of "no, but I want to" started a group quest to find what might work for him. Fairly soon I was working with half a dozen students wanting to try the Ukulele. One of the young men said he know someone who could play and would ask him to come to teach some of the basics. He agreed and the quest for instruments began.
After several days of research, begging family and friends to help, we finally received a couple of classroom instruments. One teacher, six students, and 2 ukuleles make learning next to impossible. One of the girls told me she found the ukulele she was going to get for class. Her eagerness to share the find caused me to slow down and take a look. She had actually found a ukulele that was not too expensive and looked a lot better than the "toy" ones she first wanted. I agreed to order it for her and she could pay me back in installments.

Please watch her video final where she discusses the Ukulele and explains why she choose this one.

Fast-forward to now, Ukulele fever is spreading and I believe we have found one of the BEST Beginner Ukuleles Amazon has to offer. Text: If it's good enough for the Opry, it's good enough for me.

This is a very versatile mic stand that can be used in many ways.

The main support post telescopes from about 28" to about 54". But it does become less sturdy when expanded to full length. The best part is that the boom is attached to a part that can slide up and down the upper portion of the main post, unlike many other stands where the boom can only be positioned at the very top of the pole. You can also remove the boom entirely and just use the main pole to hold your mic as it has threads at the top of it.

It came with two mike clips. One is pretty standard and the other is an adjustable pinch type and will fit many sizes. At first I found them hard to screw onto the threads and thought they might be the wrong size. Be careful not to force it as you might strip the threads. After getting them to screw on a couple of times, they now screw on easily. They have an adapter which lets them attach to the smaller diameter connectors on this stand. You can remove the adapter and use them other stands which have a larger diameter connector.

The tripod legs seem very stable but the stand itself is fairly lightweight. That works very well for me, but might not for others.

This is so flexible that you can use it in many ways. I think it's a great bargain. Much more versatile and can be made smaller than my other stand.

I should add that for some reason this took three days to deliver using Amazon Prime while other items in my order arrived in two days.

Update: Nov. 29. 2017:
This stand also works well as a smartphone holder if you want to make a video. You can use the pinch style mic clip to hold your smartphone steady. This is a real added bonus.
Summary: Versatile and well-designed mic stand at a great price. Also works as a smartphone stand for making videos.

Text:
The Mooer Blues Crab, simply put, is a faithful clone of the fabled 90's-era Marshall Bluesbreaker pedal. That pedal was long ago discontinued, but has experienced a surge of interest in the past 15 years or so with pedals either cloning or "inspired by" the original Bluesbreaker. That list includes the King/Prince of Tone, JHS Morning Glory, Snouse Blackbox, and Wampler Panthon, among many others. I actually owned a v1 Snouse Blackbox, but sold it, and have been pleasantly surprised how close this Mooer Blues Crab reproduces that sound.

A few things note about the Blue Crab and this style of overdrive. First, this is very much a light-to-medium gain overdrive pedal that is valued for its transparency. Similar to how one would use a Klon, it's meant more to enhance the flavor of the rest of your signal chain, as opposed to completely taking it over. But I find that it excels with both clean and dirty amps. Into a fully-clean Fender Twin, it adds just a bit of "tube-like" grit while retaining that clean "sparkle" on the upper end.

Second, this is a clone - not a mod - of the original 1990's circuit...for better and worse. The original Bluesbreaker did not have a ton of output, and I find that the Blues Crab is at unity gain around 2:00 or 3:00 on the volume knob with most setting. But because it is meant as an "always on" overdrive, this is not really a problem, and you can stack it with additional drives afterwards if you are looking for more gain or output.

Finally, I want to say a word about Mooer. Yes, these are Chinese-made clones, often based on or copying popular circuits from years ago. But Mooer, in particular, was also hugely influential in the "micro pedal" trend of the last 10-15 years. I'm not even sure it's fully accurate to call a pedal a clone when they were among the first manufacturers to take pedals like Bluesbreakers, Tubescreamers, and OCD's, cramp them in to enclosures 1/3 or 1/2 the size of the original, and sell them at more affordable prices. Some of the Chinese budget pedals are made poorly, but the Mooers are solid, and the Blues Crab is one of their best efforts.
Summary: An excellent (and affordable) micro version of the Marshall Bluesbreaker

After some research I bought this Midi Interface Cable because it was the cable of choice for my needs. I am using it to interface my Korg Volca FM2 with my Macbook Pro and Arturia Keystep 32 Keyboard. This allows me to connect the Volca FM2 to my MacBook Pro in order to us the DEXED and SYNTHMATA Applications (and some others) to edit the Volca FM2 sounds and also to Upload Sysex Files into the Volca FM2. At the same time I can use my Keystep 32 to play the Volca FM2.

Part of this review is to help others as the included instructions were useless.

It's important to first download the Drivers for the MacBook Pro (or what ever computer you are using, such as Windows), install them and then Restart youy computer. Once you do this the Roland UM-ONE-MK2 should be recognized by your computer. Also there is a little switch on the side that needs to be in the COMP position. It's TAB (Tablet) to the left and COMP (Computer) to the right as you face the unit. Make sure you set this before you connect it to your Computer (or Tablet). The switch is recessed and a bit tricky to see and move, I needed a thin paperclip to set it and was not sure at first if the switch even moved so I tried it a few times just to be sure and it did. Roland could have designed this a little better.

One of the important points about the Roland UM-ONE-MK2 is it handles Sysex File Transfer perfectly. Many of the off brand Midi Interface cables do not, they either drop parts of the file, corrupt it or won't transmit them at all.
