(Edited 1/6/15 after conversations with Focusrite rep)
I purchased this after reading multiple recommendations for Focusrite equipment, and because I liked the aesthetic appeal of this unit. Today, after testing it for two weeks on my Windows 8 production PC with an Electro-Voice RE320 microphone, I am returning it. Here are my specific reasons:

- I experienced major issues during the installation process. After installing the drivers from the Focusrite website and restarting, the unit prevented my PC from booting past POST (the first screen you see after powering on a PC). This happened multiple times and eventually required me to unplug the unit and adjust my BIOS settings.
- The unit would generate a series of loud clicks and pops every time I booted into Windows. The pops would register on both of the gain knob LEDs as well as the power light. It almost seemed as if the unit was having some sort of electrical short, but the pops would always stop after a minute or so.
- My microphone required a ton of gain to even register on the LEDs. Unfortunately this also meant that the monitors required a ton of gain. The Scarlett Solo has no on-unit mixing control which meant that I was constantly fiddling with the monitor volume knob as well as my computer's own volume output controls. A mix knob seems like a huge omission in hindsight.
- Ableton Live Lite is junk. I'm sorry. Downvote this review if you want to. It won't change reality. It is totally befuddling that an audio interface this aesthetically pleasing would be bundled with a program that looks as if it was developed for Windows 3.1. The Ableton code that was shipped with my unit did not work, so I contacted Ableton and they unlocked the program for me. Unfortunately this did not mean that any additional functions became available. Linear editing was virtually impossible. The unit did work with my primary DAW application, Adobe Audition, though low gain continued to be an issue.
- The Scarlett Plug-in Suite that was included with the Scarlett Solo was plagued by technical issues. Every single plug-in introduced a skip in my edited audio about 2.5 seconds into any recording after the effect was applied. I confirmed that this was a software issue by recording audio with my old preamp, a Shure x2u, and editing the audio with the Scarlett plug-ins. Note that the skips occurred *after* activating the plug-in suite with Focusrite's included code. So, basically, none of the software is usable, at least for voiceovers or people who care about audio fidelity.

Now I want to say a word about customer service at Focusrite. I have gone back since my original review and docked the Scarlett Solo another star because of the approach of their customer service. I have received multiple messages from Focusrite since posting this review, none of which actually take ownership over their product and the issues it has. What Focusrite did not know is that I am an audio producer with more than ten years of experience, including about five years in engineering. I have worked in small home-based setups and brand-new broadcast studios. What I know from experience is that this product simply does not rise to the level of other products at the same price point. I've worked with preamps and processors from the biggest names in the business, all of whom stand behind their products with customer service that stays with you until it works. I've had a company's lead product designer call me personally to assist with tweaking a processor. I've even had another company go so far as to offer to fly their own engineer to my studio, at their own cost, to diagnose and fix a technical issue in person. While I wouldn't expect that from Focusrite, I also don't expect for them to put the issues with the Scarlett Solo back on me and my setup. The greatest piece of advice someone has ever given me is, "When you make a mistake, own it." That means that if a more-than-qualified customer with a newer PC that has already been used as an audio workstation can't get this thing to work, then at least introduce the thought that there might be something wrong on the manufacturer's end. Offer to walk the customer through the setup and tweaking process over the phone or a live chat. Offer to replace the unit. Don't just be concerned with negative reviews on Amazon. Own it.

I am disappointed in the Scarlett Solo and would like to think that it is not a reflection on the rest of their product line. For my needs, I will continue to search for a better audio interface.

I bought the stand to better organize my personal studio space and I'm satisfied enough to consider purchasing a second (too many instruments for my own good).

Still, it could use some tweaks: I'd recommend putting lock washers under all the nuts - very inexpensive and keeps the bolts tight - especially on carpet where there's even more tendency for the pieces to shift about under stress. It also protects against over-tightening the bolts that can bend the relatively lightweight metal arms and support bars.

I can imagine people feeling queasy about storing expensive instruments on a stand that feels like it wouldn't take much to tilt over forwards, but you should be able to convince yourself that the downward force of the instrument bodies (especially electrics) counteracts the weight of the necks leaning into the top support - making a forward fall unlikely.

Still, for sanity's sake, I'd position the stand close to a wall. At first, this causes a dilemma because your headstocks will extend beyond the front plane of the stand. But it's easy to rig up one or two 6-8 inch support pieces from wood or pipe insulation-covered metal to brace the stand against the wall while providing comfortable clearance for the headstocks. Removing any worry of a fall is worth the effort.

The design can hold a variety of instrument body shapes; the trick is to find the optimum balance point but it's not hard: I fit an acoustic bass guitar, a 335-shaped Ibanez Artist, Strat, SG-shaped bass, J-Bass, a Martin OM-1, a long neck bouzouki, six-string banjo and a Nick Lucas-shaped Recording King acoustic on it. That said, I don't max out the seven slots - I'll use at most 5, simply because different shapes make catching a strap and banging an instrument too easy when they're that close. If I were storing all electric guitars or basses with similar shapes, I might be comfortable with six or even seven.

I wouldn't use this stand on stage - and by 'on stage' I mean any setting with people moving about who might come into contact with it, including a house party, basement jam session, etc. It's simply not sturdy enough, physics or no. But for my needs it works well and saves me a lot of floor space where it's tight to begin with.

Been using the humiditrak for a few weeks now. I attached the sensor INSIDE the actual guitar to the side using a Command Picture Hanging strip which is similar to velcro. In this way, I know the exact conditions of the guitar in and out of the case. Also bear in mind that the humidity levels are different in various parts of any given guitar case and may not reflect the actual humidity inside the guitar itself, which is where it matters most.

What I like:
-Keeps record even when out of range and updates when you get reconnected. So far this is the only solution that allows you to keep record hour by hour. Other in case hygrometers will only tell you the current conditions when you open and see it. This has allowed me to make several observations such as how effectively my in case humidifier works, how quickly the humidity inside the guitar drops when I take it out for practice, if my guitar changes temperature when I walk outside to my car on a cold winter day, what the conditions were while the guitar was checked in a plane, etc. These things you simply can't do with other hygrometers.
-Having the hygrometer inside has allowed me to make observations of what humidity and temperature my guitar sounds at its best and worst.
-I'm able to track the humidity/temperature while out of the house by connecting another device. I have a Nexus 7 Android tablet as well as my Android phone (Oneplus 3T) connected to the humiditrak. Interestingly I didn't have to pair the sensor with the second device, yet they both have the ability to connect directly to the sensor via Bluetooth. When I am out of the house, the Nexus 7 tracks the humidity and uploads the data to the cloud via wifi. As long as my phone has wifi, I also see the updates on my phone wherever I am.

What needs improvement:
-The sensor seems to only gather data in EXACT 30 minute intervals. In between those 30 minutes, I cannot force an update or reading it seems. I understand that the 30 minute interval is probably to save battery, but I wish I could force an update through the app if desired... a lot of conditions can change within a 30 minute period.
-I wish the app could allow you to calibrate the humidity reading then restore to default if desired. I compared the humiditrak with 2 other digital hygrometers and the humiditrak read 5-7% higher than the other two. I suspect the humiditrak is pretty accurate since I put two humidipaks inside my guitar when I went on vacation for a week and the reading stayed at a solid 50-51% the entire time. Still, I think there should be a calibration feature and should be easy to implement in the app.
-Since I started using the humiditrak with a second device, one device or the other or both randomly loses Bluetooth connection inexplicably and will not reconnect. Sometimes it connects instantly, sometimes it doesn't even after several hours even though I am only a few feet away. This lack of reliability is concerning.
-I'd like the ability to export data from the app to a tablet or computer for future reference.

If my complaints are addressed, I'd easily give this device a 5 out of 5. I believe the whole concept of the humiditrak is by far the best idea in instrument care.
---
Update March 30, 2017 - I've discovered that if my device isn't connecting to the sensor, I just need to turn the Bluetooth OFF then ON on my device and they suddenly discover each other.

This product has hundreds of reviews, so I doubt this review will ever be read. Alas, when searching for just the right recorder, I didn't see a review such as this so I'm writing it because I wish I had a review like this when I got it.

Let me begin by saying my experience with audio is very low. I'm a video guy, and I only care about audio because a video without audio is incomplete. I have been doing production for many years, but I've only ever been a backup sound man, and I'm pretty happy with that arrangement to be honest. When tasked with recording video of a live performance though, the need for recording the audio arises. When running a BFC from the sound board to the video camera for everyone to trip over isn't the best solution, enter the Zoom H4N.

What a terrible device if that's all you need it for. It's expensive, it's noisy, it hates any input that's not mic level, and you'll never take advantage of the sweet combo XLR & 1/4" inputs or the phantom power it can provide (the biggest selling points to me, I'll get there...)

If you're in my position though, a VIDEO guy, and not an AUDIO guy, it MIGHT be the perfect swiss army knife do-it-all audio solution for you, like it was for me. Without further adieu, I am just going to lay it all out and try not to bore you to death with my rambling.

Situation: Recording from a pre-mixed source, such as a sound board during a live performance.

In this scenario, beware the terrible shortcoming of the H4N. It's been said many times before, I'll say it again, this recorder hates line-level inputs. It seems that even on the lowest record level setting, it just can't handle the power. I am quite sure that's because there is a pre-amp that's always engaged. Fortunately for you, I've done a ton of experiments and will give you a tip right now that will make all of your confusion vanish when it comes to the strange clippiness of the H4N. If you read nothing else in this review, read this...

****************************************
PRO-TIP
Pretend any "mic level" below 1 DOES NOT EXIST. I don't know what kind of crank the makers of the H4N were on when they decided to include these useless levels, but just don't use them, here is why.

If you have something and it clips with the mic level set to 1 (in stereo mode, but this applied to other modes in my limited testing in those modes), it will still internally clip at a mic level below 1 *clips occur at the exact same input levels that it clips at mic level of 1*. In other words, a mic level of 1 is technically the lowest the recorder can go, but they included levels 0.1-0.9 to give the illusion of higher recording resolution than is truly possible.

END PRO-TIP
****************************************

If you want a way around this from a sound board, boy do I have an easy solution for you!
1) Set the mic level to 1 on the H4N (might as well go as low as you can, the pre-amps in the h4n are horribly noisy)
2) Use a headphone-to-headphone jack to connect the phones/monitoring port to the mic input on the H4N
3) Set levels using the phones volume adjustment on the soundboard.
4) If you still desire to monitor, you can! Just hook up your headphones to the monitoring port on the H4N.

Issues: 1) Your sound guy wont be able to "solo" anyone, meaning listen to them outside of the mix to fine tune their sound. 2) The monitoring jack on the H4N blows, it adds a strange and extremely tinny EQ curve to the sound - almost zero bass at all, I'm guessing it peaks around 5K. Great if all you need to listen for is bad handling/environment noise in the recording. Terrible if you're a sound technician trying to get a proper sounding mix off of that thing. Also terrible if you try to do the old trick many people suggest by connecting the H4N directly to your camera's microphone jack from the monitoring port of the H4N. Really bad idea, if you want usable audio that is.

In the end, the solution ends up being somewhat beneficial. I recommend getting the ROLLS DB24 Stereo Direct Interface or similar (suggested in a prior review, thanks!). Then (so long as you are actually recording mono like I know 99% of you who do live performances are), you can set your mic level on the H4N to 1, and independently attenuate each channel AND have the option of a ground lift on each channel.

"How does that benefit me?" you may ask. I'm glad you asked, first by lifting the ground you can stop a ground loop hum that will often show up especially if you have the unit plugged into AC power. Further, you can attenuate each channel independently and set for example one level to average of -6db, then the other average at -12db. This means if the band gets too excited (that never happens), and blows out your recording causing it to clip, you've got your left channel to fall back on. If they are really bad about it, you could increase the separation from 6db to 12db etc. The options are endless, and in situations where you only get one shot at recording it, the ability to do this is priceless! For the 1% of you that need stereo, the same thing applies, you can get 2 DB24's and record in 4 channels.

Situation: Recording in the field with one or more microphones plugged directly into the unit.

The shortcomings outlined earlier all apply still, but I'd like to re-iterate a couple of points.
1) The pre-amp in this thing really is very noisy (try recording as close to mic level 1 as you can)
2) The headphone monitor port is terribly inaccurate sound wise. It's very tinny, with almost no bass and seems to peak around 5K. Not important for voice, but it is important when it comes to instruments, environment, etc.

The good news is, there's a good dose of the good stuff too though:
1) Can record 4 channels at once
2) The built-in mics are actually half decent, but to my ear they suffer from the same strange EQ issue as the headphone monitoring does.
3) XLR & 1/4" combo jacks, along with phantom power & plug in power options, really make this guy the jack of all trades. You can basically use any mic you've got laying around.
4) I have complained about the quality of the headphone monitoring, but it's really not a dealbreaker at all. At least you CAN monitor your sound with this. Can't say the same with most on-camera mics.
5) Stamina mode is pretty decent, you just have to fully understand how it operates.
6) Many onboard goodies like a tuner.

Overall, the unit is an exceptional do it all field recorder that fits my video production needs perfectly so long as I learn how to work with its shortcomings. I wouldn't recommend it to someone needing a recorder just for recording live performances. Nor would I recommend it to the person who just needs a microphone for interviews, or "run and gun" type shoots. There are far better options for those type things (aka rode videomic). With someone who has diverse needs such as mine though, this one fits the bill and makes everything "doable". I can do the contorting to fit the needs of the equipment, so long as it's cheap and the end result is quality. If this unit sold for twice as much though, I would be dissatisfied.

Sorry for the long review, I hope at least one person found it helpful!

Text:
[[VIDEOID:79ba78f0e6835502b6f3b5cf481a33e2]] This is a review of the Donner Tutti Love chorus pedal. The pedal was supplied by the manufacturer in exchange for a fair review.

My first impression of the pedal was good. The pedal is made of metal, and has a really solid feel. It's smaller than my other pedals, due to the fact that it doesn't have a battery. In order to use the pedal you will need a power supply that is properly set up for 9 volt devices. Donner sells one for a reasonable price, if you don't already have one. I originally tried to use the power supply from a different device and found that it was really noisy. As soon as I got the proper supply it worked perfectly.

When evaluating a chorus, it's important to remember that it's not like other effects, such as a wah-wah pedal. Chorus is much more subtle than most effects, and is typically more about filling in the sonic space with a wider sound than it is about making itself known in the mix. You might use it, for example, with an acoustic guitar to create a more full sound, or with a rhythm guitar to widen and soften the sound on mellow songs. Like any other musical gizmo, though, it's up to you to figure out how to use it for best effect.

The controls are simple. There are three knobs and a stomp switch. The Level knob mixes the signal with the effect and the dry signal so that you can change the relative amount of the effect. Turning it to the left removes the wet signal (the effect), while turning it to the right increases the relative amount of the wet signal. The Depth switch basically controls the volume of the wet signal. Turning it to the right increases the depth and turning it to the left decreases it. Although everyone has their own musical vision, I tend to turn up the level and the depth to make the effect a little more intense. Finally, the Rate switch changes the rate at which the chorus oscillates (for lack of a better description). When it's turned to the left it slows down the timing of the effect, while turning it right speeds it up. When the Rate is turned all the way up you get a sort of tremolo-like sound, with a spacey "blurred" edge to the notes. The accompanying video will probably make the above descriptions a bit more clear.

Overall, I think that the Tutti Love chorus pedal is a good value. It's well-built, inexpensive, and it does what I'd expect a chorus to do. I did ding it one star, due to the lack of a battery option, but that is as much a matter of personal taste as anything else. If you already have a power supply for your pedals, or if you are aware that you will need one, it's really not going to be much of a problem.
Summary: Donner Tutti Love chorus provides good performance at a reasonable price

I'm a bit of a controller junkie, with 10 MIDI keyboards, a bunch of drum control surfaces, a handful of other controllers, synths, and keyboards in my collection, but I feel like I know what works for effective MIDI control because of it.

This Graphite 49 has a lot going for it. The build quality, in terms of case design and weight, is GREAT. It's quite heavy relative to other controllers at this size/feature point, but I like that. The weight gives it a substance that makes it feel solid and sturdy when I'm playing it.

The key action is really good, too, with a semi-weighted feel and aftertouch that's distinct and almost 'clicky', but without feeling artificial. I've read comments from other reviewers that the mechanism Samson used to facilitate these features can be faulty, but I've not experienced any problems. As always, compare reviews.

The total package is nice here, as well, as it comes with an introductory software suite that, while mainly designed as an entree to more robust (re: expensive) options, nevertheless offers a nice swath of sounds. It won't replace a dedicated library of samples and plugins, but it's certainly enough for the budget musician or beginner to make some good music.

Now, to the problems. They're really pretty simple, and they all parse down to design choices. The knobs and sliders simply aren't conducive to good control over software parameters. The knobs are 'clicky', and this is a major impediment to functional granular control. Audio control knobs should ALWAYS turn smoothly. The sliders are difficult for my fingertips to grab unseen and slide with precision. These are small design accents, but in music production, God and the devil both reside in the details.

Additionally, I don't prefer the feel of the four drum/control pads. I applaud Samson for adding them (more value added), but the feel and playability misses for me. They're too hard and they don't receive with the precision that I'm used to (though they DO have aftertouch, which is very cool). I have a bunch of Akai MPC controllers, so I'm used to a certain feel, and these are different. This is totally a function of what I'm used to, though, and others' experience may be quite different.

At the time of this review, the Graphite 49 goes for about $30 more than the M-Audio Oxygen 49, which has better controls; however, the Graphite has more piano-like playability and it comes with that nice software bonus.

I'm giving this four stars because, even though the controller-oriented features are lacking, the playability is still very nice, and that's really the most important part of a keyboard controller. Also, as noted, there's a lot of value in this package for someone who's just starting out or who needs a controller but is also on a budget and likes the added value of getting some sounds.
Summary: Nice design and build, but spoiled by some unfortunate design choices; fair value for beginners or budget musicians

I'm reviewing the Angel chorus pedal. now these days, chorus does not come up too often in my guitar playing, but when it does, it needs to be something cool and not something cheesy. I didn't have high expectations for this pedal considering it's fairly low price point.

However, I'm super impressed with the range of tones that this pedal can put out. At the sort of standard setting, both knobs pointed at 12 position, you get that GNR Paradise City intro sound, or The Pretenders "Chain Gang". The 80s chorus sound springs to life. If you crank the knob is all the way to the right, however, you can create some pretty crazy mutated sounds. and crank them both almost all the way to the left and toggle between the clean sound and the chorus sound, what you get doesn't sound 80s, it doesn't sound like a chorus pedal. It sounds like just an nice unobtrusive thickening of your tone. To me, this is the bonus sauce. I'm impressed!!

There is no internal 9 volt battery option. You are given a short cord with a 9v attachment on it, so you can plug a 9v battery into it externally. This is kind of weird. I imagine you could also plug a standard 9v power supply from your pedalboard into it, but I did not have one on hand to test.

the only drawback for me is I would prefer the 9v battery inside the unit option, but this is a pretty minor complaint. So I would give this 4.8 stars, and if you're looking for an affordable chorus pedal, this is it!

Text:
Sometimes I like to practice my guitar when everyone else is busy doing other things. We live in a small house, so I have to have a private way to practice.

HOW THIS COMES

PERFORMANCE

EFFECTS

WIFI
I have not used this in tandem with online practice yet as I have just been doing work on my own. I can not comment on that because I did not get it for that purpose.

CHARGE
I did not use this for months, as I had misplaced it. When I found it, I plugged it in and it still had a full charge.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is perfect for private practice of my guitar. I like it, but it can be a bit bulky in the spot I need to plug it into.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. I like this and figured out ways around the bulk, but if it had a more friendly hinge or something to move it out of the way on some guitars, I would like it better. I still like it and use it however. It is a great thing to have for me in a small house.

Just leave it off. No matter what hype they throw at it, this circuit sounds like crap. If you really need OD or grit, purchase a pedal. The money spent on that could have given us an XLR. Other than that, it’s a great little amp. One has to consider however, that you could purchase a used G-K 1x10 or other small pro quality amp for the same price, and that is something to think about. Update: I have been trying the SGT circuit a lot today. It’s not as bad as I made it out to be. I still think that the money could be better spent on a d.I. The cabinet is ported, and fully lined with dampening material too. Update #2: I removed speaker to discover that it’s the same poo-poo driver from the BA-108. Text:
My Ortofon 2M Blue came with a Fluance RT-85 turntable I bought here on Amazon.
I have been using it on and off for over a year. Here are my impressions:
*Compared with other options from other manufacturers like Audio Technica, the sound output is louder and more compressed sounding.
*Compared with the Ortofon 2M Red, which more than 2x cheaper, the sound profile is almost exactly the same.
*Compared with the Audio Technica VM520EB, especially through speakers, the sound quality is about the same, despite the fact that the VM520EB is half the price. I prefer the VM520EB because it has more detail.

If you are considering the Ortofon 2M Blue, and are a casual listener who will be listening with speakers, I can say with confidence that there's virtually no difference between it and the 2M Red in sound. Don't waste your money.

If you are an audiophile who listens with high-end headphones, you will notice better tracking with the 2M Blue vs the 2M Red but generally will not notice a big difference in sound quality. The 2M Red is no slouch with the tracking though.

In my honest opinion, you will get virtually the same results with the Ortofon 2M Red or the Audio Technica VM520EB for less than half the cost. If money is no object, just ignore what I'm saying because the 2M Blue is a great setup, even if it has virtually the same sound profile and literally the same physical appearance as the 2M Red.
Summary: Sound profile is almost exactly the same as the Ortofon 2M Red at more than 2x the cost.

Text:
Because everyone wants to know, both my old Squier Bullet Stratocaster and my new IYV LP copy fit, the LP just barely, but fine.
First impressions were not helped by rolling it into a ball, which after arrival in Minnesota Winter, unrolled with some crackling and stiffness. Warming to room temperature, it was still not very supple and has some ugly creasing and wrinkling. But nothing cracked or broke. The fabric is medium weight, not thin like the free bags sent with some guitars and not as thick as "ballistic" nylon. It should do, you wouldn't subject your guitar to anything that would destroy the bag. It's probably a good match for my cheap Squier Bullet strat, I'd probably go upscale for a spendier guitar. I'd say this is fine as long as _you_ are using it, probably not for baggage handlers. A bare guitar is very vulnerable and nerve wracking to handle. This bag will help a lot with that.

What I got this for, and what it should be ideal for, is shuffling around and storage. Without any protection, guitars tend to pick up nicks and scratches and dings. Look at most old guitars, they show history and grunge from just everyday shuffling and standing in a corner. And if I occasionally put it in the car and take it someplace, it should be fine.
The various pockets are handy for the things you might want keep with the instrument. I have not seen a stand that would fit, but a cable, strap, extra strings, tuner, sure. I wouldn't pack pedals or things with sharp edges.
I can keep my strat in an unheated bedroom when I'm on a Les Paul copy jag and maybe save the finish from checking. And vice versa. I'm gonna give it a while and maybe buy another for when both guitars have to go into hiding. For the LP type guitar, I'd save a couple of those shipping air pillows to support the neck and avoid breaking the peg head off.
I like that the handles span the zipper, so if it fails the guitar won't go skidding. The bottom end has a bumper, but it's so narrow it might make it tippy. Just in case I get the urge to take it along on my ebike, I already supplanted the dodgy square rings on the shoulder straps with sturdy cable ties.
To sum things up, shopping for gig bags was discouraging, the cheapest bags weren't as cheap as they should be, offering only a dust cover. And the nicer bags cost as much as the guitar. This seems to be a reasonable compromise. As a final thought, I have an old Harmony Sovereign ca. 1970. If it had ever had any kind of bag, it would look a lot better now.
Summary: Good for what I need it for.

For my purposes - they're a spare pair of headphones that I leave in my office, and for that, I'm very pleased.

One of my Strat partscasters has a swamp ash body and a one-piece maple neck, and it's been frustrating to find the right sound in that guitar.

The original pickups I chose was a set of Seymour Duncan SSL-1s, which are widely thought of as providing a 'standard Strat sound'--kind of scoopy, bright highs, warmish but firm lows. But that's not what I heard after I put them in--I heard an aggressive, loud, mid-focused sound, eager for gain, and they didn't clean up easily. That wasn't at all what I expected.

First, I took out the 0.1 uf cap and replaced it with a 0.047 uf cap, then a 0.022 uf cap, trying to find that characteristic chimey Strat sound in these well-regarded pickups. The 0.022 uf cap was an improvement, but it still wasn't what I was trying to hear. Then I considered swapping the pots for a known-good set of CTS 250k audio taper pots. But it didn't seem like the pots were the problem. So I held off.

I figured trying another set of pickups might give me some perspective on things. One of my favorite sets of Strat pickups is a set of Fender Pure Vintage '65s, which I had in a MIM Standard Strat. Those pickups are magical in that guitar, maybe due to its alder body, I suppose. So I pulled the PV65s from that guitar and put them into the partscaster. The result was inconclusive. They sounded better than the SSL-1s, but they did not sound as good as they did in the alder-bodied MIM Strat.

Hmm. More head scratching.

It was time for me to realize a particular truth--my ash-bodied, maple-necked partscaster Strat is, historically speaking, a 50s style Strat, and I needed to outfit it like one. It made sense to give it pickups like those in the original 50s ash-bodied Fender Strats. So I zeroed in on one set of pickups--the Fender Original 57/62s.

They're black-bottom pickups with output in the 5.9-6.1k range--the hottest of my set tested at 6.05k. They don't have a reverse-wound middle, so there's no hum-cancelling in the 2 and 4 positions. Like my set of PV65s, the mount plates of the 57/62s did not come pre-threaded, so before mounting them on the pickguard I carefully threaded each side, to make sure they would go on easier. Just keep that extra step in mind when you buy a set.

I've now had these pickups in the guitar for a few weeks. They can do gain sounds pretty well, but now I'm realizing the guitar really shines with cleans. There's some truth in the saying that you should let the guitar be what it wants to be--and I think this guitar is my 'clean' Strat. It also has some of the best in-between sounds I've ever heard in the 2 and 4 positions. It could probably be a great Nile Rodgers-like R&B Strat, if I could do that style any justice.

These are the right pickups for this guitar. If you're like me and you have an ash-bodied, maple-necked Strat that just doesn't seem to sound right, try a set of Fender Original 57/62s. The guitar will let you know the truth.
Summary: Perfect cleans for a 50s style Strat

Text:
I have only recorded one major event at my church with this recorder so far, but I am completely delighted with the results. In the setup I used, I added two external mics on XLR cables (also using the built-in phantom power from this recorder). The first thing I noticed in my post-production review was how sensitive this device is (in comparison to my less-expensive mic-recorder). There is also noticeably LESS background noise (noise floor) from this device. Recordings sounded crisp and clean.
The H6 comes with two different mic capsules for recording. My first recording was using the X-Y capsule (adjusts for either 90 degree or 120 degree pattern). I plan on trying out the front-side capsule on a recording event coming up in the near future.
TIPS: I definitely recommend using the backup audio track feature built in to this device. It is easy to ruin an entire recording by having unexpected loud bursts from your talent (singer, orchestra, choir, etc.) causing over-modulation. There are some safeguards (such as dynamics and hard limiters) but those often end up sounding like post-production 'repairs" to bad sound. A better choice is to use the backup track feature to ensure you have a duplicate of your mic capsule tracks made at a significantly lower gain setting.
Also as others have commented, the design of the control panel makes it really easy to accidentally move the volume level controls for the XLR inputs while you're handling this H6 unit (but I already knew that when I bought it - so I simply remind myself to double-check everything just before the recording starts). There are several "cottage industry" entrepreneurs who are selling after-market knob guards for this device - so you might want to look at those if you are concerned about that.
Bottom line for me: I bought this device only needing two of the four external mic inputs, but I eventually will "grow into" using all four of them in addition to the mic capsule(s) once I purchase the additional mics. The front-side mic capsule (included with this unit) and a protective carry case were items I planned to buy even if I had gotten the H5 instead, so the price difference between the two units, for me, is much less than it seems. The recording quality of the H6 is superb. The controls and display are extremely intuitive, and make it easy for me to set up and use this recorder. I am completely happy with this device so far. I may update this review later on, as I get more recording venues 'under my belt' with this unit.
Summary: So far this recorder is amazing!

I just received my new Paisley overdrive - the one replacing the last one I had (and reviewed here) because of road damage. And to my surprise and disappointment, Wampler has changed a few things. #1, the 'stomp switch' is no longer the sturdy standard one that you actually feel under your toe when it "clicks". Now Wampler has chosen to use the cheaper momentary contact type switch instead, which means the actual switching is being done electronically, not mechanically; just one more potential thing to go wrong. #2, they moved the damn input and output jacks! - which means I have re-configure my pedal board set-up to accommodate new wiring. #3, the direction of the mini-switch movement which controls the EQ curve and brightness is now side-to-side instead of up-and-down, making these even more prone to breakage than before. During a show, one's boot-toe is very likely to hit one of these switches because of their placement.

All that said, this is a good sounding pedal. Unlike many distortion/overdrive pedals, it doesn't suck the bottom end out of your signal when in use as so many others do. The tone shaping switch combined with the tone control and brightness switch offer many possibilities to the user.

I spent several months trying to find a review to help me figure out if I wanted inexpensive (sub $200 a pair) or low price ($200 to $500) a pair pencil condensers. Most reviews are simply product listings with no actual opinions, of the few sites that do provide opinions I've not found any that bridge the gap despite the large number of options exactly at $200. So after trying a borrowed pair of Behringer C-4 mics I bought a pair of Behringer C-2 and a pair of Lewitt LCT 040-Match. Here's my attempt to resolve the review problem.

I'm a hobbies audio junkie and have been mixing and recording my rock cover band for a few years with a combination of Shure PGA58, SM58, Beta58, and a Lewitt MPT 350CM and recently started dabbling in recording a church choir. I generally record through a Behringer XR18 to multi channel for later editing. For ear calibration I hear a clear difference between the Behringer XM8500 and other $20 dynamics and the $50, $100, and $150 mics above. For backing vocals and instruments in a mix the PGA58 generally holds its own against the others, but for solo work it clearly isn't a clean or pleasing as the others. The SM58 and Beta58 are clearly different but as a matter of character not quality. The MPT 350 is dramatically different as a solo mic in that it is clearly a condenser and sounds like it, though a condenser tuned to sound like a stage dynamic. With that baseline here are my thoughts:

Using simple low volume desktop testing where the differences between the PGA58 and Beta58 and MPT 350 aren't all that large the C2 sound similar, though the high end extends a little further and sounds a little brittle. The LCT 040 sound exactly like the MPT 350 for my speaking range, but clearly extend dramatically further up and down the frequency range with typical condenser clarity.

Moving on to the rock context, as drum overheads the C2 were dramatically better than any of the dynamic options. The LCT 040 as drum overheads are clearly better than the C2 when soloed but not obviously so in the mix and any differences were easily fixed with EQ.

The big difference came in the church choir context. Here I'm recording (and live streaming) in a quiet environment where the acoustics are pretty classic "church". Specifically when in the room you can hear a person speaking pretty easily but loose clarity due to the reverberate in the room. Before we started streaming and recording we only put a mic on spoken word and left choir, piano, and any other instruments fully acoustic. Now that we stream we could get away with just a stereo pair on the choir and catch the piano and optional solo from the reverb, but it sounds a bit muddy so we close mic the piano and solo instrument for clarity. I first tried using the C2 as a XY Pair and the LCT 040 as a wide pair. They were level matched at about 48 db of gain on the C2 and 33 db of gain on the LCT 040. In this range there was a lot of noise coming off the C2, specifically something that sounded like feed back that was fixed by putting a -18 db cut with a Q of 10 at each of 1k 2k 3k and 4k with a high cut at about 16k. I still ended up favoring the LCT040 in the mix. The next week I used the C2 in place of the close mics on the piano and the solo cello with the LCT 040 in the XY pair. In this configuration I ran all 4 mic with a gain of 39 db and -5db on the mix for the piano and cello and -6.3 db for the XY with no evidence of the "feedback" self noise from the C2.

In summary:
Would I buy the C2 again? depends on the situation.
* For studio recording, no the quality just isn't there.
* For live use in close mic applications where you don't need high gain, absolutely, you won't hear the difference in quality.
* For non studio recording in cases where you have a full mix, again yes.
* For high gain live use (XY mic on a choir) no, the self noise is way too high with high gain.

In conclusion:
When placing the C2 and LCT 040 on the much better understood range of dynamics mics:
The C2 feels a lot like a $50 mic such as the PGA58, ie dramatically better than the $20 dynamics.
The LCT 040 feel more akin to the $150 to $200 dynamics.
Both are a valuable part of your mic locker. If you have unlimited budget you won't miss the C2 but if you have a real world budget the C2 are great for filling in the rest of the locker around the stars.

Text: I have had, for years, a cheap Chinese knockoff of a Fender P-Bass, in a vintage style, which I bought specifically because it had a Jazz neck. I've considered, off and on, buying a "real" bass, but that's another 500-1000 dollars and so I figured it may make more sense to see what I could do with the original to make it a better bass without that much of an investment. The first thing to do in any instrument upgrade is to replace the pickups, and I am glad that I went with these. They are, first of all, EXTREMELY loud. I had to pull them back from the strings a few millimeters further than the original pickups were positioned, and even then the output level is more close to "active" than passive. But the versatility that they have really can't be overstated. The tone with the tone knob turned all the way up is biting, aggressive, sharp, and articulate. The tone with the tone knob rolled all the way back is rich, warm, and creamy. Rolling the volume back a bit and the tone knob only a touch forward from rolled all the way back gives it a warm, jazzy tone, and I can crank it up all the way for an abrasive, overdriven sound more keyed for punk or metal. My $100 bass sounds like it cost 10 times more, and only cost me $65. Great, great pickups.

Design comments:
- Fits my Martin D and Taylor dreadnought series guitars perfectly. Snug but not so tight that it is hard to get the guitar into it like a Taylor gig bag is.
- The straps are mounted closer to the head than my other gig bags so that I don't bump the head when going through doorways.
- The pockets are huge! One could be tempted to pack too much stuff in there (change of clothes for the weekend?)
- Extra stitching at stress points (strap attachments and handle). Real stitching not just an additional row.
- The handle and zippers are much stronger than they need to be for an acoustic guitar. The heavy duty design should last for decades.

The bag comes with a LIFETIME guarantee on materials and workmanship. Where on this planet can you find a lifetime guarantee anymore?

Overall I am very pleased with this bag and highly recommend it.

Text:
Takes a while to understand how the pre-amp section and the distortion stomp-box sections work together. Once you figure that out -- and learn to use a headphone jack to turn on the cab simulator -- then this thing is the full bag of tricks. But it does take a LOT of time to learn what works well with your amp. At first all I could get was variations of harsh-fizzy. Then with experimentation with both pre-amp and distortion together I began to find sounds that worked for my styles and preferences. I only have two gripes. First, there should be a software way to turn the cab simulators on. The pre-amp section is an amp simulator, not a cab simulator. But the tone and dynamics improve markedly when you use an old 1/8 male headphone plug on the headphone input which turns the cab simulator on for all outputs. Why this can't be done via a global setting is beyond me. Second, in Memory mode (using pre-defined patches) I wish the CTRL (control) feature would trigger manual on-off for the effects foot switches. The CTRL is sort of that, but it basically acts like a second sub-patch turning effects within a patch on and off, but still not allowing manual foot control.
EDIT: Ok, so I got tired of fiddling with it and not finding easy ways to edit patches on the fly, so I traded it on a Fender Mustang GT40. Although a small amp, the Mustang GT40 is 10,000 times easier to edit and manage effects than with the ME-80. I really wanted to like the ME-80, but the longer I had it the more frustrated I got. The patches are named only with numbers -- so you have to remember what sound is where. The knobs are not dynamic when editing. Say you have several patches and you decide that your venue's acoustics demand a little more reverb, chorus, or whatever. If you try to edit, you have no idea what the actual effect parameters were, and the knobs will become active in their current physical setting, not the settings for that patch when it was saved. The only real option is to use it in pure manual mode, which can be done but defeats the purpose of having an integrated floor unit vice separate pedals.
Summary: Takes a while to find the right sound. Cab sim makes all the difference in the world.

I've only had the Scarlett 18-20 for a day but I feel compelled to review it. I've been using a Tascam US-1641 for years. It's a similar interface with 8 mic pre's, which I need for recording drums, but I wanted to upgrade to something more stable and with better preamps. The Tascam is a budget interface that definitely gets the job done, but bland preamps, dodgy construction, and buggy drivers make it a love/hate relationship. It wasn't until I bought a new computer and upgraded to Sonar X3 that the device finally became stable, but a bug required that I reinstall the drivers every few days, and I could only get latency down to 15ms round trip. I was really just looking for an all-around upgrade: better pre's, stable drivers, lower latency.

I was considering Tascam's newest iteration, the US-16x08, which would hopefully give me stable drivers with ongoing support. But besides that, the device appears to be merely a re-skin of the US-1800, which is a re-skin of my US-1641; definitely not worth the price tag. So I've been looking at the Behringer U-PHORIA UMC1820, which has an almost too-good-to-be-true price. The only question is if the thing will ACTUALLY EVER BE RELEASED. It was announced a year ago and there's still no word on when we can finally get our hands on one.

So I finally considered the Focusrite 18i20. It was a little out of my price range, but all the reviews said it was pure quality. Focusrite has a reputation for stable drivers and good support, but I was most excited about the award winning preamps. I took the plunge and bought an open-box item at a good discount. Much to my expectations, the build quality is excellent. The knobs are sturdy and turn smoothly, unlike the plasticky feel of the Tascam. The inputs and outputs are all tight and sturdy as well. After installing the drivers, the unit was literally plug & play. My computer recognized it instantly and routed sound to my monitors. Sonar X3 also recognized it immediately and configured inputs and outputs automatically. I'm able to get latency down to 11ms with only the occasional stutter on larger projects. For the Tascam, 15ms was a struggle.

The required Scarlett Mix Control software is also quite useful and simple enough for basic operations. Also, I was delighted to see that the software is lightweight and opens and closes instantly without any delay. I noticed that the interface itself does not have a knob to control the direct monitor vs computer mix. This is handled within the Mix Control software. You can adjust the level of each input INDEPENDENTLY (which is impossible on most consumer interfaces) as well as the level of your DAW. Dialing in a decent mix is a simple task. Beyond that, you have full control over input/output routing options. I haven't experimented with anything more advanced, but I know there are many possibilities.

Finally, the highly praised preamps lived up to their reputation. I didn't know what to expect, but when I tried punching in some vocals on a recording I had made only a day prior (with the Tascam), the difference was immediately apparent. Compared to Tascam, the Focusrite 18i20 has a much warmer and fuller sound. It was like playing through a tube amp vs a solid state amp. Audio recorded with the Tascam was more harsh and sterile. The Focusrite warmed things up without sacrificing presence and clarity.

My only complaints are that the rack attachment plates are not removable and the chrome monitor/headphone volume knobs are a little too shiny, making it hard to see where they're set. I am completely happy with this interface and can say that it fully lives up to it's reputation. If you're looking for pro quality, but on a budget, the 18i20 is definitely the way to go. If you're just starting out but need the inputs and outputs, I'd recommend the latest product from Tascam. While I struggled with the US-1641, it's a solid product, and I'm sure the latest iteration has better support and compatibility. If anything significant occurs I'll be sure to update my review.

UPDATE 4/22/15: I've had the unit for a few days now and was able to experiment with the Mix Control software. I'm pleased to say that I REALLY like it. I've read reviews saying that the software is confusing and difficult to set up, but I couldn't disagree more. The software is only as complex as your routing is. A quick visit to the Focusrite webpage will give you all the information you need. From there it's just a matter of figuring out exactly what you want to do. For my purposes, I wanted Zero-Latency monitoring of vocals while applying compression. I merely had to plug a mic into an input (IN 3) and then route the signal to an output (you can choose any of the Line, SPDIF, or ADAT outs). The output (Line Out 3 in this instance) then went into the input on my compressor. I then ran a cable from the compressor's output to a free input on the interface (IN 4). I just had to make sure to MONITOR the input that my compressor was feeding, and RECORD the mic input that I started with (IN 3). In Mix Control, this simply means muting 'IN 3' and bringing up the fader on 'IN 4'. In the end I'm able to monitor with compression (or reverb/delay etc.) but record a dry signal. It was all done with a few simple mouse clicks. So for anyone wondering about Mix Control capabilities, it's easy to use and you can route any input to any output while maintaining full control over each channel in the headphone mix.

Text: I am a confessed and unrepentant hoarder of dirtboxes and I like this pedal a lot.  This is my 5th Joyo pedal- I already own the Ultimate Drive, Vintage Overdrive, Crunch Distortion, and Octive Fuzz pedals.  I consider Joyo and the Dano Cool Cat line to be some of the best values in stomp-boxes these days.  You've already heard the particulars about this pedal, so I won't go into the features.  The build quality does appear to be a hair shoddier than all my other Joyo pedals (which are earlier versions).  The switch seems a little less heavy-duty, and the case seems to be thinner metal.  That said, the case is still metal and isn't going to fail in any way.  The switch- well, we will have to wait and see.  For $35 or so, I'm not going to complain.  Soundwise, this product offers excellent gain for this price level.  It's not particularly suited for Pantera, but you can do modern mid-gain up to Metallica without any problems.  This is not an overdrive, so it doesn't do the 'just on the verge of breakup' thing like a tubescreamer does.  That's not what it was designed to do.  I run it into a cleanish tube amp and it sounds very good.  I've also boosted it with the following with a good result:  SD Pickup Booster, Cool Cat Transparent Overdrive, Tubescreamer (TS9,Joyo Vintage OD, Behringer TO800), Tech 21 Comptortion.  If you play rock/ hard rock through a single channel amp (like a Blues Jr, Valve Jr or Pro Jr) and you want to make it a two channel amp, this will get you there. Most people compare this pedal to the Suhr Riot.  I do not own that pedal, so I can not fairly make a comparison.  I have seen several videos comparing the two and as far as that is concerned, I hear enough similarity that I am not compelled to shell out $200 for the Riot. Another comparison that gets made is that the US Dream is close to a ProCo RAT.  I own an original 80s RAT and I don't think they are all that similar.  The US Dream has a tighter low end and more treble.  Not better or worse- just different enough that they don't completely cover the same sonic territory.  Admitedly, I don't own a newer RAT-  maybe that one is closer to the US Dream.  For what they are charging, this is another home run for Joyo-
Summary: Five stars for this amout of joy for so few dollars

Text:
I believe I got a unit that is operating as intended. It's just poorly designed. I am really surprised at the number of positive reviews. I bought this because of a lot of recent negative reviews indicating that Snark had a run of fragile plastic. What a mistake... This is no Snark. Not even close.

PROS:
- Bright clear display
- Supports setting to +/- 10Hz from A440

CONS:
- It has all sorts of modes that only work with particular instruments. And it's really easy to accidentally switch it to the wrong mode. I've found no way to just lock it into chromatic tuning mode. The only way to fix this is by cycling through everything... Twice if you miss the stop.
- Buttons are on opposite sides of it, so it is difficult to turn on or off without inadvertently changing to A442 or a half step flat (and it's easy to miss the change and get your instrument out of tune next time because of it.
- When it is in any of the non-chromatic modes, it completely ignores notes that are not in the tuning. If you are way flat of your guitar's A-string, it doesn't tell you you have tuned to a low F or G. It might think you are tuning a different (low E) string and tell you to tune more flat.
- It has two-axis rotation, but one quickly finds that you need 3... You can't put it on the back of your headstock unless you are willing to read it upside down (or at least sideways).
- It is incredibly slow. It takes between 1/2 and 1 full second to update. So if trying to tune quickly, you can overshoot the correct tuning before the tuner updates. I've taken to using very small turns of the tuning peg and then playing a different string to see "E" change to "A" for example. Then playing the original string so that I know it has updated when the display reads "E" again.

I think I threw the box away, because "how could a tuner be worth returning"... D'oh!
Summary: Poor User Interface. Slow. Difficult to position.

When I got my first guitar, it spent a lot more time in its case than out -- keeping it off the floor saved space and kept away from sticky fingered rug-rats. But I soon realized that when its in its case, I wasn't thinking about playing it.. being in a hard case in the closet - it just wasn't accessible for a quick break from whatever I was into. When I finished renovating my home office, I picked up a String Swing to put the guitar where I could reach it and yet, away from the low to the floor crew.

The result is that I played it more often, I enjoyed seeing it as a good looking art piece when not in use, and it wasn't underfoot. I now have 4 of these in my office and my kids that play, have one for their guitar in their room. Very functional -- yet they look good too. I chose the metal based bracket because its lower profile. It holds the guitar far enough away from the walls that you don't have any wall-mark damage from the guitar -- or even dust marks. Keeping guitars off the floor in kids rooms prevents them from being toppled over, dented, or otherwise damaged worse than they do in their normal little path of destruction...

Someone else mentioned to plan your layout well in a previous review. Good advice. While the bracket comes with drywall mounts, anything that gets this much use should be anchored to a stud. If you mark your studs, 16"OC... a good layout is to have the first bracket up high - mines at 6'3". The next stud over the bracket is lower at 4'6". The next stud over the bracket is at 6'3".. and so on. This makes it possible to hit every stud in a normal wall and stagger the height of the guitar bodies to prevent them from bumping together. Looks nice this way too.

The swings come with little collars that I leave on. Just a little security for keeping them in place. I have both 3+3 and inline 6 head-stocks and it doesn't matter to the swing, it holds everything. These are solid and you could hang 100 lb's on them if they are anchored in wood. In any case, these are great -- they work -- no hype.
Summary: Safest place to put your guitar, and still be at arms reach

Certainly I love my collection of Boss, electro-harmonix and all the other name brand pedals I've amassed over the years. But about a year ago, I noticed all these micro pedals on Amazon and figured, why not experiment? And I've found some surprisingly low priced gems and only two duds. This is one of the good ones.

It shines driving my combo tube amp, especially while playing a guitar with single coil pickups. It pushes the volume of your guitar enough for the amp to break up into a pleasant overdrive, even with the drive knob set to minimum. For a clean boost, you can back off on your guitar volume, which is a great way to shape your tone in general. You, too, can get a Tom Petty worthy sound. From my experience, boost pedals like this don't add a whole lot to most humbucker pickups except as an overall volume boost, which can be what you're looking for in a live setting. But even on my Roland JC-20, which is a solid state amp, it added some unexpected spank out of the single coil and humbucker pickups on my Jaguar.

Tech-y type stuff now. With all knobs of the pedal set to zero, it appears to boost about 3-5 dbs depending on how hard you hit the strings. At max on the drive setting, it was closer to ten dbs, according to my sound level meter. The bass and treble controls are very responsive, and nice to have if you need to do some extra tone shaping. I didn't notice that adding either of them added volume. The nose floor rose a tiny bit when the pedal is maxed out, but really, if you're using distortion, you're going to get a little noise with any set-up. It's not excessive in any way. Oh, one thing to note: it requires a 300ma adapter, which isn't too unusual. I had a couple laying around. It's worth pointing out that most Boss pedals, for example, are powered by 100ma. Just be sure you get the right adapter for the best sound, or that you plug it into the higher current but ONLY 9 Volt outlet of your power brick, if you're using one. 9 volt 500ma won't hurt any 9volt pedals, but 12 or 18volts...yikes. Don't do it, unless your manual states that is an option. It's usually not.

Manuals are your friends! If you just can't stand to read one, at least look at the tech specs in the back.

Most of the time, a pedal will list the ma along with the tip/sleeve requirement on a diagram. This pedal did NOT indicate on the back that it needs 300ma. I was about to plug it into a standard 100ma Boss adapter, so my habit of checking the manual, even on something as basic as a boost pedal, paid off. Pedals that require 300ma sound nasty and power starved on 100ma. I know. I've made that mistake before.

The point is, if an effect sounds good, it is good, whether you paid $20 or $200. In over 30 years of playing, believe me, I've demo-ed, bought and sold a ton of pedals. So, even though I admit I sorta chuckled when I saw pedals made by Amazon, I realized I was being a brand snob. I have tried MANY booster pedals (and I won't name them all here). This sounds just as good, and better than some four times the price for my set up. In fact, I wonder which Chinese company makes these? I mean, the name Amazon Basics somehow sounds cheaper and more generic than Joyo or Mooer. But rest assured, you don't have to cave into pressure and be a brand snob if you don't want to.

After getting a replacement for the first guitar I ordered, I was presented with new issues. The second guitar came with blemishes, little nicks and scratches all over the pick guard and some of the body. It’s not noticeable until you get close to it, but still. The first guitar was immaculate. The new one had slightly better tuning pegs, less jumpy. The jack was not showing any issues, but after just a few uses, it’s starting to crackle. Also, I feel like the first one was setup right out of the box (neck was straight, action was good). The replacement needs a setup and a string replacement (which is pretty standard). The neck is also really fat, fatter than a strat.

Based on my experience the money you save isn’t worth the hassle. Buy a used guitar or spend just $30-50 more and get an Ibanez RG series or something (thin and very playable necks!). If you REALLY need a strat copy, this will do as a cheap option, but I’d bet a squire is just as good if not better.

YouTube guitar reviewers are too generous.

**** ORIGINAL REVIEW ****
I want to love this guitar, but it’s got serious pros and cons.

Pros:

- Looks great. I like the look just as much if not more than a real strat. I like the dark fretboard and the pick guard. *wish they made it with the oversized headstock like some strats had, that’s just my taste though.

-It’s got some weight to it, doesn’t feel cheap.

-It’s got a humbucker instead of 3 single coil pickups.

-The gig bag (case) it comes with is actually better than the one I bought with my first guitar.

-I couldn’t believe how low the action is straight out of the box. Plays great in the hands for such a cheap guitar.

Cons:
-the single coil pickups are cheap and useless. They don’t sound too bad, it’s that they have no output... I can hear my strings acoustically over the output of the signal. The humbucker is really the saving grace of this guitar.

-tuning pegs are also junk. Won’t stay in tune (though my next problem is why I can’t definitively speak on this yet), they’re very jumpy on the G and B strings (this could potentially be fixed with a setup, changing the strings, and tightening the bolts on the pegs themselves).

-however my jack is crackly and cutting out, right out of the box. This is disappointing, I’m going to exchange it, but I can’t even sit and play into my computer without it cutting out (yes, I tried other patch cables). I did a lot of research, and these were not complaints of the Donner guitars, in fact it’s the reason I didn’t go with a Glarry or unbranded. Yet I’m experiencing hum, crackle and cut outs, the tuning pegs were also praised yet they’re as chincy as expected.

I’m going to return this for another one and hope it performs better. Like I said, I WANT to love this guitar, I could deal with the lousy single coils (I prefer the bridge channel and a humbucker anyway). I could even deal with the jumpy tuning pegs, though it’s annoying.

If the next one is better, I will update and add stars.
Summary: 2 stars for now, will update if fixed.

Text:
First, a few claims about XLR cables that are not subject to debate.

A search reveals that the consensus of audiophiles urgers that wire gauge (most range from 16 to 24 AWG) has little, if any, influence in sound quality output.

The build quality of the cable affects durability and flexibility. A thick outer jacket offers protection from damage, while the material used allows flexibility and radical bends without breaking even after long-term use.

Shielded cables, especially braided shielded, in conjunction with a foil layer greatly reduces EMF interference.

Self-locking connectors are just as stable as their screw-on cousins (not seen very often today) and are quickly connected/disconnected.

The copper- (resists corrosion) nickel- (high Vickers hardness) plated pins suggest enduring positive contacts, especially in cases where components suffer routine, frequent connecting/disconnecting.

Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large
Guitar slides are metal tubes that slide across the strings, producing notes without depressing strings against the metal frets. Slides produce a clear ringing tone that is distinctive, and allow you to play notes between frets and glide smoothly from one pitch to another (glissando). Most guitar slides are flat, but if your guitar neck, frets, and/or bridge are radiused (curved), you will find that curved slides will help you hit all strings without buzzing or clanking down on the frets. If you want to slide and play multiple strings or chords, you probably need one of these slides. The weight of the brass helps provide sure slide action and a positive ringing tone.
I compared three curved slides, the Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large, the Dunlop 227 Concave Brass Slide, Heavy Wall Thickness Medium, and the Dunlop 285 Preachin Pipe Large. I used Fender Telecasters American and MIM, a Martin 00-15M acoustic, and a 1970 Lotus F215 acoustic, strung with Dunlop extra-light strings, for comparisons,
DESCRIPTION: The Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large is made of heavy polished brass that is flared only on one end. The 232 fits all of my ring and little fingers, and fits down to the knuckle on my first and middle fingers. It also comes in a medium size. The 232 is 64 mm long and 3.2 oz.
COMPARISON: The Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large is much like the 227 flared on one end only. It was shorter than the Dunlop 227 Concave Brass Slide Medium and longer than the Dunlop 285 Preachin Pipe Large. It felt more comfortable on my fingers than the Dunlop 227 Concave Brass Slide Medium, but not as comfortable as the Dunlop 285 Preachin Pipe Large.
SOUND: The heavy brass of the Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large gave a good ringing tone, better than many of the thinner, lighter straight slides I have used. It provided a chiming note with good sustain. Because the Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large was longer and flared on only one end, it sometimes produced string buzzing and sometimes missed contacting strings in a chord. The longer you practice with this slide, the more accurate it will be.
OVERALL: The Dunlop 232 Harris Slide Large has a good tone. Its flare may fit your fingers better than the Dunlop 227 Concave Brass Slide Medium. Nevertheless, you will have to learn to move the slide around to hit all the strings accurately. If you do a lot of single string or solo work, this slide may work best for you. You will like the tone it brings to your music.
HELPFUL HINTS: If you are undecided, take a look at the nut, the frets, and the bridge on your guitar to see if they are radiused (curved). Look at your fingers and decide if you play light or heavy on the strings. Then try one of these slides and rely on your ear. It will tell you what sound you want.
Enjoy playing.

The new one was 11mm ish which was great, they can be lower to get good string action but not higher and you’d have to shim the neck. Everything worked great expect string spacing. The G and D string were too far towards the center of the neck. This was on a jazz bass, one of the most narrow string spacing on a bass you can find and this bridge spacing was TOO narrow?!? I’m glad I wasn’t putting it on a P bass or other wider spaced bass. So my fix was to take some nut files and slot a new saddle groove and it seemed to work fine. But kind of annoying since this is a FENDER bridge and was too narrow for their most narrow bass. Also, the listing says brass saddles... ok they might be, but when I was cutting the new saddle grooves, I saw no yellowish brass under the chrome plating. There was even a sticker on the bottom that said “brass”, however I see no physical evidence to support that claim. Who knows. It does look and sound a bit better than the stock bridge but honestly it’s so minor. Luckily I did not have to shim the neck, if I did I would not reccomended this bridge. Also the lack of adjustable string spacing (although I didn’t think I would need it seeing as it’s a FENDER bridge going on a FENDER bass). I didn’t want to use the Kickass hipshot because I’m not a fan of having the saddle as a separate piece inside the bridge, I feel like you would loose vibrational energy. Someone needs to make a better alternative for 5 hole Fender replacements, they could make a lot of money.

Because I wanted two stands and was limited by the seller or by amazon (don't know who or why) from buying more than one of this type of stand, I also bought and On Stage SM7122BB folding music stand with a case for roughly fifteen dollars(https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0006NDF76/ref=cm_cr_ryp_prd_ttl_sol_16).  The OnStage case is clearly a better quality case as it is heavy canvas-like material with a Velcro closure instead of the rather thin nylon zippered case that came with the ChromaCast.  The On Stage stand also came pre-assembled.  Whether one stand is better than the other remains to be seen---I won't know until I use them both. Neither stand appears to be a heavy duty stand for using with big book, but instead both stands seem to be just right for taking along to music events. Both stands, once folded down and put into their cases, are about 18 x 3.5 inches.  Neither takes up very much space and would easily fit into a carry bag or a suitcase.

As thrilled as I have been with the Chinese-made Joyo overdrive and distortion pedals I've tried out in the recent past, I felt like the JF-10 Dyna Compressor was somewhat of a risk. I had been using the very excellent MXR Custom Comp already, but was frustrated with its lack of external controls and versatility. Also, it's one thing thing for Joyo to "clone" the circuitry of a distortion pedal, but could they do it accurately with an "always on" effect like compression?

Well, Joyo has absolutely done it, and they've done it well enough that I'm selling my MXR. Compressors are hard to explain, and even harder to demonstrate on a YouTube video, so let me offer my explanation of what this pedal does, and why you should give it a try for only around $40.

The primary effect of compression is to "level" or normalize the output across frequencies. Particularly with a clean signal, aggressive playing can lead to annoying volume swells. Also, certain notes sustain, while others seem to die out too early. Compression "smooths" over these problems and levels everything to a polished, presentable sound.

The secondary effect of compression is that the pedal can sustain single notes and chords by increasing their level after they would normally die out. In this area, the Joyo JF-10 is superior to many other compressors because it gives you "Attack" and "Sustain" knobs. "Attack" refers to how soon the compression effect kicks after the note is struck. Turning the knob up produces a "chicken picking" effect where the note is very clear and pronounced. Adjusting the "Sustain" knob, obviously, increases the length of time that the note or chord continues to play at volume. Like most compressors, there is also a "Level" control to change the volume of the compressed sound.

Of the compressors you can actually find under $100 (such as the MXR Dyna Comp and BOSS CS-3 Compression Sustainer), I like this one the best. The MXR models have a good clarity of tone, but with only two knobs, the lack of customization is a problem. You may want high sustain or attack for playing U2-type guitar parts, but might find excess sustain too "messy" for punchy AC/DC riffs. The Joyo allows you to make this change easily.

The BOSS CS-3 is a good pedal that has controls for attack, sustain, and also tone, but the pedal produces a lot of noise, and the resulting tone sounds too digitized. Also, a "tone" knob on a compression pedal strikes me as an admission that the pedal is CHANGING your tone, which good compression really shouldn't do. The Joyo Dyna Compressor sounds like MY guitar and amp, it just puts some polish on the final product, and allows me to add sustain and "punch" if I see fit. Great pedal, and amazing value!
Summary: Boutique quality and customization at a great price!

Text:
First of all, received this chair lightning fast - like < 2 days w/free shipping. It must have been in a warehouse real close to here.

As always, I read all the reviews on this thing. You wouldn't think that necessary with something rated almost 5 starts and only a 30-buck investment, but I like to see what the people have to say who rate it 3 stars or less. I have to agree with the 5-star people and the comments that have already been written by them, though I cannot speak to longevity. I weigh a little over 200 pounds, but when I sit on this bench it supports me well and doesn't have the type of give that lets me know my rear will be hurting within a few minutes. Very firm, but enough give to probably be comfortable for an extended period of time. I haven't given it a couple hour practice session yet, but you can kinda tell how something is gonna perform based on your first few minutes. I'll update if it proves to not hold up for an extended session.

Assembly is quite easy, adjustment really shouldn't be an issue unless you are adjusting it on a regular basis and fully tightening it every time. And by "issue", I mean something that takes much time: it is not difficult to adjust at all. You have the "option" of not tightening the legs once they are in position, and this would make adjustment actually faster. To be clearer on what I mean, the legs form a "T" at the top just as they do at the bottom, and at the ends of the T's are spring-loaded pins that lock into place in your choice of holes in a two rails on the seat bottom. There are four screws that allow you to hand-tighten these pins into place once they spring into position, but you don't really HAVE to tighten them for the pins to still stay in place. I am not ADVISING that you don't tighten them (I did), but if you had to frequently adjust the height of the chair, I imagine that not tightening them would be tempting, and would speed up the adjustment process. I don't see how they would pop out even without being tightened unless you were like subjecting the chair to some kind of unusual stress or like rocking it back and forth and causing the legs to kinda twist. This bench is VERY sturdy (probably more sturdy than the old wooden bench I used to sit on as a kid with our upright piano), but anything that is adjustable is OBVIOUSLY not going to be as sturdy as something that is permanent.

As for the width of the chair, it has sufficient space for pretty much any adult. There is little space left over when I sit on it, but probably 2 smaller kids could use it. Anyone who thinks two bigger people could fit on this must be sitting back-to-back length-wise. I am not extraordinarily wide and it is spacious, but this is a one-adult bench.

After getting hooked on "drumming" playing Rock Band for a while, I decided to take it one step further. A real drum set wasn't an option because of the noise, so electronic was the only way to go. And I didn't want to spend a lot of money. The Alesis DM6 looked like a good option.

I still think it is a fair deal, but with some notable limitations. After the suggested firmware update, the cymbals are fairly responsive, and the unit operates reliably. But the module is fairly noisy, with a hum in the background that changes in intensity depending on what the display shows (!?). I also noticed that all sound samples have the same length (duration), and those that create short sounds, like the ride, create some noise until the end of the sample.

The selection of voices is very limited, and there are almost no configuration options (e.g. for sensitivity, cross-talk, noise rejection). But for a beginner, that may be a blessing. The triggers are connected via a proprietary cable with a multi-pin connector on the module (brain). You cannot add any triggers (e.g. extra tom) to the setup. What you get in the package is what you will use.

The hi-hat pedal is velocity sensitive, allowing you to vary the volume of the hi-hat sound and also allowing for a "splash" (rapid closing and opening), features that you'll only find in much more expensive sets.

The brain has a USB port to connect to a PC, for recording and for updating the firmware. It also has 1/8" output connectors, which is a bit annoying. And it does NOT have a MIDI connector. So if you were thinking about using this as a MIDI trigger without a PC, forget it. (And forget about using this with the Rock Band 3 MIDI controller.)

(Added after some use): I got tired of the low quality output and the limitations of this unit after a very short time. I replaced the DM6 brain with a used DM5 and am much happier now. This will be OK until I get better at drumming.

The good: Easy hook-up, simple operation, out-of-the-box solution, great hi-hat control
The bad: Noisy, limited voices, limited configuration options, not expandable, no MIDI out
Summary: Recommended for beginners who are not sure they want to get into drumming. All others, avoid.
