Text:
First, I have to say I am very, very impressed with the build on the Ampero Hotone MP-100. This pedal not only looks good and sounds good, but it really is built like a tank with a nice aluminum chassis, beautiful layout around a very nice “touch screen” control and very versatile back panel with just about all the inputs/outputs you could need for live performance, rehearsal, recording or any other application. This review is based on the “Limited Edition” version, which comes in what Hotone (pronounced Hot Tone) calls “Pink”. I think it is more of a “salmon” color and it looks very good with the gold backplate too! As far as what the “Limited Edition” includes that’s not on the standard unit, as far as I can tell the only difference is the color and a “Tetris” type game they included. Not sure what the “thinking” was, but I honestly don’t think most will be playing Tetris on their guitar modeling unit, but it’s there just in case.
In the MP-100 you get a versatile modeling/amp/speaker simulator along with tons of effects that you can edit to your hearts content. Just about every parameter can be edited and modified. You can have up to 9 different effects running simultaneously, including 3 different FX, amp and cabinet IR, noise reduction, delay, reverb and EQ and they are all adjustable, and you can even place them in different spots in your signal chain. You can adjust and select/change from using the touch screen, along with 3 adjustment knobs located under the the touch screen and you can also download the editor on your computer (Mac/Windows) and plug in using the included USB cable and edit/change/save just about anything you can think of from there as well. This is also the way you can update the software or firmware for the unit, and use it for USB audio to your DAW.
On the back panel you have stereo outputs in both balanced and unbalanced, a switchable 1/4” input (guitar, line, keyboard, etc) a ground lift switch, a on/off switch, a 1/8 stereo input and 1/8 headphone output, a USB connection, a midi in connection, a external foot switch input and a 18v input for the included 18v power supply. The unit powers up quickly, and the touch screen is bright and responsive.
In a lot of units like this, the programmed patches (sounds) are many times, less than stellar. I can honestly say that in the case of the Ampero Hotone, this is NOT the case and many of the included patches are very nice and usable right out of the box. Of course, you can tweak them in just about every way to get them how you like them, but many are very useable already.
I won’t go into every different amp, cabinet, effect, reverb, delay, EQ, that is available, but you have over 240 to play with, each editable based on the controls for that particular unit. You have four “assignable” foot switches on the unit, and you can add another foot switch on the back panel for even more control. You also get a small, but very usable volume pedal that can also be assigned to different functions, including wah-wah. The switches light up with “halo” style LED lights, with (again) assignable colors. You can even change the colors of the touch screen!
I don’t use midi control, but if you do midi automation to set your patches you will also appreciate having midi input also available on this unit.
This is a very well thought out unit, with control for just about any aspect of it, including a global EQ, sending cab IR’s on left or right outputs, turning off cab and amp sims, controlling volume, adjusting and changing cab microphones, and the list goes on and on!
I suggest that if you are in the market for this type of unit, to give the Ampero Hotone a go. Download the full manual from Hotone and look at what this unit includes and is capable of. You can bring a nearly endless amount of guitar rigs to your show, rehearsal or recording session in your backpack! A seriously impressive unit!

Plenty of bookshelf-sized speakers are advertised as studio monitors, but these actually deliver the goods. The MR4’s sound is exactly what you want from quality monitor speakers: detailed, controlled, and flat. Of course, that’s "flat" in the good sense, with the various audio frequencies presented equally and accurately.

The MR4 is very well tuned, allowing good audio recordings to shine while revealing the shortcomings of weaker ones. The treble is smooth and articulate without being exaggerated or fatiguing. Bass is tight (not boomy) and nicely covers the musical frequencies, but as expected for small speakers, there isn’t much deep-bass thump or rumble. Imaging is excellent when the speakers are at ear-height, so you’ll want to use stands (or at least place wedges underneath to tilt the speakers toward your head).

The speakers offer both "monitor" and "music" sound modes, with the latter adding a modest bass boost and slight vocal-frequency emphasis. The difference between modes is quite subtle, but the "music" setting does add a little punch when you’re listening for fun (instead of production).

Physically, the speakers are nicely built, with sturdy MDF cabinets measuring about 9"H x 5.5"W x 7"D. The right speaker houses all the controls and electronics, while the left one has a passive design. There are some monitors on the market that allow the left/right speaker roles to be reversed, but this pair does not include that feature. I don’t mind the omission, but it did mean that the included 5.5ft-long cables were too short to reach my tower PC (which sits on the floor to the left of my desk).

Overall, the MR4 is an excellent pair of studio monitors for near-field listening. While they don’t have bells and whistles like Bluetooth connectivity, these speakers deliver on sound quality, which is what matters most.
Summary: Impressively accurate and detailed sound. Great for music production.

I’m almost embarrassed to use the word “sexy” to describe the design of the Scarlett 2i2, but it is a sexy looking box. In my opinion, it is a beautiful piece of design. The ergonomics are excellent. I have more than a touch of arthritis in my very old hands which can make knob-twiddling difficult. But even in the limited front panel space, Focusrite designers provided plenty of room for fingers to grasp and turn knobs or flip switches.

Physical setup is simple: plug your cables into one or both inputs and connect the 2i2 to your computer via the included USB cable. The inputs can be switched between Line and Instrument. Each input also has an independent Gain control. Switchable 48v Phantom Power is available. The monitor is also switchable and has its own volume and gain controls and a ¼ inch female socket. There are two line outputs on the back.

Setting up the computer is more complex. I’m running Windows 10 and believe I had to install drivers. The instructions are, in my opinion, unclear. I’ll experiment further when I am not as tired and maybe things will make more sense.

Focusrite provides a rich software bundle with the 2i2. It is, in fact, almost overwhelming in some ways. The Avid Pro Tools DAW has numerous secondary downloads of effects – and I will have to install another driver, I think, when I install Pro Tools. Several other packages are provided as well, altogether aggregating almost 6GB so far – and I haven’t downloaded all of it yet! As I install and experiment with the tools, I will amend as appropriate.

I conducted some basic voice tests using Audacity and the audio was beautiful. No noise. No hiss. No distortion. Just nice clean audio. Tomorrow, I’ll install Pro Tools, which I’ve never used before, and do a reading. I do only spoken word kinds of things, so I won’t be reporting on interfacing with instruments.

Overall, this a beautifully designed box with preamps that deliver nicely shaped audio. It could not be easier to use, though I am still struggling to understand all the driver options.

What I am is an occasional lecturer in venues like public libraries and law offices that lack sound systems of their own. In addition, I belong to several organizations that meet in libraries, field houses, church meeting rooms and other venues without sound systems. I also have a couple of significant disabilities that restrict my mobility and, sad to say, my hearing.

Thus, The Freeplay Personal PA System is a miracle on wheels?

On wheels? Yes. Really. It’s light, weighing in at about eleven pounds. It’s fairly small, measuring 9.5 x 17.8 x 9.1 inches.

Since I have difficulties walking and use a rollator (a fancy walker), I just lash the Freestyle to the seat with a pair bungie cords, drop my mic and cable into the messenger bag hanging from the rollator and maybe a stand and I’m off and sort of walking. Everything I need to provide very crisp, clear and (if necessary) very loud audio is right there. I can bring good sound with me to law office conference rooms, libraries, field houses and even the occasional room at a bar where some groups choose to meet. Using the Freestyle sure as heck beats shouting to be heard.

The Freestyle is simple to use. First, for ultimate ease of use, read the manual. Second, download the iOS or Android app for your smartphone or tablet. Next, hook up your devices. There are two XLR / ¼ inch balanced inputs and a 1/8 inch unbalanced input. (If you think you need more inputs, just use a mixer.) Each input can be controlled from the back panel, but in my opinion , you’re better served by using the Freestyle app. It takes a few minutes to learn how to use the controls directly on the back panel – some have dual-functions and can be a tiny bit confusing. With the asp, however, everything is very straight forward.

The Aux input is perfect for inputting your tracks or other audio from your smartphone, tablet or other device.

Basic equalization is available for each channel and there are several Fx. (Yes, I did have a lot of fun playing with the Reverb.)

Can you hear me now? Mackie says the unit is rated at 300 watts peak Class D power. I don’t know what that means. What I do know is that I walked about 50 feet away from the Freestyle and heard the music I was playing loudly and clearly. Frequency response is quite nice. It isn’t boomy or distorted when turned all the way up. The audio level is more than adequate for goodly sized rooms, but never overpowering. It’s unlikely you’ll see many audience members sticking their fingers in their ears – unless, of course, they don’t like what you’re saying.

You can power the Freestyle from the included AC adapter, eight D cells or a rechargeable lithium-ion battery which was included with my review sample, but is otherwise a purchasable option. There is also an optional combination angled stand and tripod adapter. Coming soon is a fitted carrying case that carries a fairly hefty price tag, but is probably going to be worth it. I’m using a duffel bag right now, but would prefer a fitted case, which I believe will also have some padding.

Build quality is of the “battleship” variety. It’s solid.

No doubt about it: I love this unit. After years of putting up with poor or no audio in the venues I speak at, I can bring my own quality sound in a light, easy to manage package. That is fantastic!

Jerry
Summary: One of those "best thing since sliced bread" inventions

Well what do you know? For the hobbyist and other non-professional musicians who just want a serviceable instrument microphone, you don't need to go with the SM-57 from that big name-brand manufacturer. Yep, if you're a hobbyist or someone who's just not super-picky about audio stuff, you can get this knockoff SM-57 for less than half the price. It's still quite sturdy-feeling, comes with a good-fitting clip, and it definitely picks up sound.

I got this to use with my all-chrome resonator guitar, for which I built a magnetic microphone mount. I took that mount to a big-box music equipment store (you know which one), and they claimed that only a supercardioid super-expensive microphone would work with my guitar. Of course, they tried out various other microphones, but sure enough only the 200-dollar microphone worked with my guitar. So they said, of course. I took a chance and rolled the dice with this GLS ES-57, and I'm glad I did. It picks up plenty of sound on a typical house PA-system at open mic nights, and that's all I really wanted. The one downside -- and this is almost surely an artifact of the instrument and other equipment -- is that it picks up a lot of feedback from the monitor speakers. Who cares, though? The guitar is loud enough for me to hear it on stage, and the audience can definitely hear the signal coming out of the other speakers.

So unless you're a professional audio person -- and heck, maybe even if you ARE a professional audio person -- this is a good value for a microphone. I'm sure that a professional ear and discerning audiophile would pick up all kinds of differences between this microphone and the big-name equivalent -- but my ears and most audience members can't tell the difference. These might be good backup microphones for a professional sound engineer on a tight budget, or if a bar has a house PA system and doesn't want to invest money in microphones that drunk bands will beat up and damage anyway, or for a hobbyist who wants a decent microphone but just doesn't want to spend the money on the supposed "gold standard" name brand.

I have been using delay pedals for over 20 years (wow), I had the digitech one with the two pedals, the old school one, that was great and beloved, and have had other non looping ones through the years. I few other ones that were way too noisy in playback. this is the best one yet, since they seem to improve as the years go by. that said, there are better for more, but for most this will be enough.

the only thing I found frustrating is there is no counter/meter on it, so if you are trying to loop a song then add parts over it, you have no idea where one part ends, and so on. I stopped trying to record that long with it, and usually do about 3 different parts then loop it. the sound quality is good, and is as good as the source that goes in. as my guitar setup has gotten better, the quality of the loops sounds way better. one thing I would recomment is to turn the volume on the pedal up pretty high when you record, so you can adjust as you go along. I would start with the output loop volume at like 2-3 o'clock and then you can adjust it to the volume of the second loop. this is all pretty self explanatory, but may save you a little time. not much of a learning curve, though you will forget how to do some stuff and need to go back to reference things. that said, this is as good as most will need save for recording onto a computer. very fun to just work out ideas and try stuff over them right away as opposed to recording and laying down track after track. with this you can create mini super songs and it helps you with your timing, layering and learning how to overdub and let other parts breathe so every sound isn't fighting for position.

UPDATE: I have recently run a drum machine, bass and guitar through this and it sounds awesome! I made an incredible melody that I am going to add vocals over asap. This thing handles all those instruments so well it blew me away. I am going to figure out how to set everything up and will be able to create songs instantly! Before I was just layering guitar and not trying to really push this thing. I give it 10 stars for figuring this out. The mire instruments the better. This could totally be used live, I told someone it couldn't and I was wrong. Other than no counter for measures (boo), this thing is brilliant. Every musician needs one.

Feb 2017 Update: The "Tuner On" button had been getting fussy for a while, like I had to really press it with whatever fingernail I could manage (I play cello, so they are very short) and yesterday the button just stopped functioning. I cannot turn the tuner on, period. I haven't even been using it since I now use apps for most all of its functions, but if my iPod is charging I will use the Korg to tune before practicing.m Well, no more I guess. I paid a lot for mine, twice what it is selling for today, so I am not happy at the waste of $. The batteries are alkaline, only a couple months old, and I barely use the Korg. I will not be replacing it. My former teacher had the basic Korg tuner and used it many times per day for years, so some of them do last and take a beating. The last thing I will say now is that I went to a 1 day local cello camp and one person had a tuner which lit up the note in bright one inch high green light. Not sure what brand, but that was nice. This Korg was a little hard to see the # and b notations unless you use the bright light, and if you have any vision problems, the note names will be hard to see.

Mid-2015 Update:
Ok, I'm sure that I tried "everything" to improve the volume when using the Recorder function before I wrote my review below, but the other day I recorded something using the contact mic clipped to the bridge of my cello, and The volume on playback was good! Now, the quality of the recording is not great, but it is useful for hearing what you sound like if you are working on a piece (assuming you are not a pro of course.) i also see that the price is even lower now, and there is a "new and improved" contact mic with a more robust connection between the wire and the device. My older version has started to separate there, so I would recommend the new version.

I paid up for the TMR50, which on the day that I bought it was $50 more than the TM50 (today it is only $40 more; insult on top of injury). I wanted the "sound back" feature and I really wanted the recording feature. I also paid $5 more for the black than the white (that day) because the white gets smudged with use.

I play the cello. "Your mileage may vary."

* The tuner itself is very fussy / sensitive, more so than my basic Korg tuner. I don't consider that a huge negative, but the fluctuation from flat to sharp to flat while bowing an open string may drive some people crazy. And sometimes it just stays green so it is not impossible to get in sync with it. It's just fussy. I have a very resonant cello with lots of overtones, which may have something to do with that. I am not an expert.

* The metronome is great. Does what you would expect, and I like the tap feature.

* The "sound back" function is sort of annoying, but I still use it. I turn it on and sometimes when I clip the contact mic (required additional purchase) onto my bridge, it causes a lot of buzz when I play; if I then move it onto my tuning peg, before I even play a note or make any extraneous sound, it starts playing a tone and does not stop until I unclip it from the peg or turn it off. Once I get it to stop sounding, I start over, playing somewhat slowly to play in tune with the function. Then when I stop, at least half the time it continues to sound until I unclip it or turn it off. Sometimes it will stop on its own after a few seconds, but usually not. That is annoying. It also flips back and forth from, say, F# to B, or G to C on the higher strings, which I also find annoying. That said, I don't know where else I could find this function, so I put up with it. But it is annoying.

* The recording function is awful. It is nothing like the video demo of the product. The volume, which I have turned all the way up, is very, very soft. I am using new batteries, and holding the mic on the front very close to what I am trying to record. If I play back through an external speaker, the volume improves a bit but the sound quality is horrible. I think this feature will prove to be useless to me, although I will experiment a bit more because I could really use it both to record myself playing (I have to wedge it on top of my tailpiece to have adequate volume) and to record segments off of youtube to play with (that is really not working well). Again, your experience may vary.

Lastly, I had asked a question to other reviewers about the volume. One responded with the helpful suggestion of using an external speaker. (Thank you!). Another asked if I had something covering the mic. I don't, and I always have it close to the source (I am a reasonably bright person). It was also suggested that I use 6v batteries, if I remember correctly. However, this device takes 2 AA batteries, which are 1.5 v each for a total of 3v. I googled to see if there are stronger AA batteries and there are not. They are all 1.5v. I am not using rechargeable batteries, but good quality brand new.

If anyone else has a suggestion that has worked to improve the volume and / or quality of the recordings, please comment! Thank you.
Summary: Pluses and minuses; utility depends on your purposes

I purchased this budget priced preamp on the glowing recommendations and reviews here and on other sites. However, as a preamp, it functions worse than even the cheapest preamps found on any basic interface or mixer board. Further, the device generates a low level static/crackling/popping sound that is very low but enough to dirty your recordings ruining any type of clean vocal/guitar takes you'd get with it. I tried many different types of cables, power outlets, and power conditioners, and found the low level static/buzzing to be present in any condition.

As a preamp for a distorted guitar signal, it may work alright, but the noise the Art TubeMP generates makes it completely unusable for any type of clean recording situation.

There are times when the phrase "you get what you pay for" really rings true, and this is it. If you are in a position where you even need a preamp, do yourself a favor and invest a little more into a piece of equipment that is vital to getting a good sound out of your mics and instruments.

I have since returned the device and gotten a refund.
Summary: Functions on only the most basic of levels

Text:
I did quite a bit of research before deciding on this instrument. None of it was done "hands on" though. I chose this Ukulele because of the design, and the descriptions of it's tonality as well as endorsements from professional players. All of the pros chose this brand and model due to the warm tone. It's a fun little instrument with a distinctly Hawaiian tone without being "tinny". I play classical guitar. I also have a travel classical guitar, however, even that is too large to play comfortably when actively traveling (By "active" I don't mean playing at the hotel when I get there, I mean playing in the car as I'm going there).

I first started looking at the Baritone Ukes because I felt they would be easier to play being set up with the four highest strings of a guitar. Then I saw the Guitaleles. There were a different tuning than a guitar, so that was out for me. There were the Ukes that had 6 strings but with two singles and two doubled up... there were the Ukes that had 4 string pairs (8 strings altogether)... I considered all of them.

All of these proved too expensive for a first Uke. As many many others have stated to go with a cheaper one to start with. So then I looked at a Tenor. The tenor can be tuned either gCEA (standard) or like a baritone (DGBE). I was pretty set on a tenor... then I listened to a comparison of a Uke tuned to gCEA and GCEA (high "g" vs low "G") and although I liked both, I really did like the high "g" more than I thought I would. So then I started looking at the sopranos. Ok, maybe the soprano was too small. I REALLY wanted something small, but not toy-like. I wanted more notes than that could offer. So then I got to seriously considering a Concert Uke. Small, but large enough, and in the right price range. I could start with the high "g" tuning and switch it out with a low "G" at any time. I could also get close to mandolin tuning (one of my other "toys") with available CGDA strings (also read about tuning a Concert Uke to mandolin and the problems with GDAE tunings with the high "E" having too much tension for this size of Uke - however, the standard mandolin strings GDAE are available for soprano sized Ukes).

Anyway, so I ended up with this one and so far am very satisfied with it. Am planning on getting that lower G string as well as the CGDA set after I mess around with this standard stuff for awhile... then again, I just may get another one to set up differently.... Cus this really does have a nice sound!

This comes with a gig bag. The bag is pretty thin and doesn't have any cushioning, but if you are on a budget, it will keep your Ukulele from immediate damage - water, something lightly hitting it, air moisture changes, etc. It just won't protect it much if you throw it in the back of a car with other luggage. By the time I do any traveling with it hopefully I will have a hard case by then cus this bag won't protect it enough for hard traveling (luggage, pets, and such).

Oh yeah, and tuning it was easy. Within a week the strings were staying in tune and didn't need much fine tuning after that.
Summary: Nice instrument. Warm tone. Recommended by others

I have upgraded my rating, which was concerned with system crashes caused by Mixcraft. The program is much more stable and crashes are rare. It is my main composing program, and in many ways, despite the "intuitive" interface, it is a drag. Aside from minor amenities (an auditing function, via raking the cursor across material, like in Cakewalk, would be nice, if not necessary), my main complaint is that the program does not interface with the computer HD directly, via Windows Explorer, as found for example in Sony Acid, and so "loading" the library with loops, even those supplied by Mixcraft, is tedious. Switching around a library category can trigger a "loading". The import and edit library functions are poor, albut useless. There is no library--typically accessible via an interface with WIndows Explorer-- for MIDI loops, just audio (WAV) loops or sounds. One loads a MIDI file thru the menu, and auditing in advance of loading is not possible, unless whatever virtual instrument will be playing file already has a pre-load feature--for example Cake Studio Drums has this feature.

There are too manygood qualities to list here, but imo this issue is very important. THis is loop based composition, after all, and immediate and fluid access to one's own library of loops, both MIDI and audio, is crucial.

This last criticism is maybe asking too much from the developers ar MC. Arranging a composition in the usual linear timeline can result in chaos, dozens of tracks, and difficult to insert changes which affect the whole piece. I'd love to see an arranging grid or tabs, like in a browser, which can load or unload all the tracks, both MIDI and audio, for any and every of the user's predefined part--intro, chorus, verse, lead, chorus, ending. As I understand Personus has this, and maybe Bitwig too.
Summary: A sorely missed feature causes my low grading

If you are looking for a handheld recorder to replace a large professional recording unit with lots of high end features, this is not the right choice. The lack of XLR inputs should be the first clue this is not what this recorder is designed for.

If, however, you need a handy recorder for field notes, audio memos, on the spot interviews and casual recording, this is one great recorder. We purchased several of these where I work for people to take into the field to record customer satisfaction comments and they are ideal for that purpose. The people using them had no prior training and we had them up to speed in something on the order of fifteen minutes . . . including a Q&A session.

Admittedly, they are not the most rugged recorder, but they will stand up to normal travel related wear and tear. The built-in microphones are more than adequate for one-on-one interviews and will also do a credible job recording meetings if placed in the middle of a conference table. If you do this, I strongly suggest using some type of table top tripod, as opposed to hand holding the recorder or putting it directly on the table top, as the recorder's body does conduct contact noise. The fixed position of the microphones is another limiting factor, so that contributed to the less than perfect score. There is a mini-jack for line input, but the less said about that for use with a microphone, the better. It is another big negative.

All in all, well worth the current street price for business people or students looking for a good quality, no frills, voice recorder. For anything more, you should consider a different recorder.

******* SUMMARY ********
I have a lot of experience with various Fender amps, and other amps (Orange, Mesa, Marshall, Vox, Roland, Crate, Line 6, others.) This is now Rev 6 of my review, and I've had the amp for more than a year, used it for band practices, and several gigs.

All in all, I love the amp, and just wish fender had included a dust cover, rubber feet, tilt back legs, a better footswitch -- and eliminated the "pop" when going into standby. You can probably negotiate 15-20% off the sticker price if you try locally or mail order. You can also save on the tax buying online, which is a significant savings on an item in this price range. I love amazon but that savings from negotiating makes some of the suggested upgrades easier to swallow like the cover, rubber feet, tilt-back legs, etc. Overall, I don't think you will be disappointed buying this amp, unless you are looking for a Rectifier or Marshall sound. It's not that, but with the right pedals in front, might be able to get close. (For instance a wampler triple wreck can get you there.) It is after all, a combo amp. And it's a pretty great combo amp in a lot of ways. It was also available as a head only, although they stopped making those now. Another similar option is the '68 Custom Deluxe Reverb which is claimed to take pedals better. But I don't find the '65 has any trouble with any of the 30 or so pedals I've tried with it. I recommend getting an "Always On" Plug(tm) from ebay/reverb. Best $10 you'll spend.

******* PROS ********
- It's a good size for gigging...doesn't break your back, plenty loud for the stage, sounds good.
- As usual nothing beats fender cleans, and fenders cut great in the mix.
- Nice reverb, as usual from Fender. In fact...TONS of reverb...I don't run that beyond 2 except in very specialized situations!
- You can add an extension speaker for a little more coverage and air movement. Or you can plug in your favorite 8 Ohm extension speaker and disconnect (or not) the internal speaker if you just want a different sound. It's too bad Fender doesn't make a "matched" extension cabinet. And it seems the major cabinet builders charge an arm and a leg for a matched extension cabinet. Search on SactoCabs and soon you will find affordable high quality extension cabs to match the Deluxe Reverb.
- Learn to play "Gimme Shelter" and use that tremolo/speed/intensity - sounds amazingly great.
- Did I mention it gets loud? That can be a "pro" if gigging...and a bit of a pain at home for practice if you want overdrive, unless you use a pedal or an attenuator. I highly recommend a high quality attenuator like the "ultimate attenuator" you can find on e-bay, or just adding a tubescreamer or other overdrive.
- It's a two channel amp. (But you need to provide your own A/B switch to really take advantage of that, and be aware no channel is a "drive" channel.) If you happen to play harmonica as well as guitar, you can plug a shure green bullet microphone into channel 1 and play your guitar through 2.

******* CONS ********
There are a few nits that really bug me at the $1100 sticker price. I deducted one star for value and for these items.

1) No dust cover included, not even the cheapo vinyl Fender cover. C'mon Fender, they only cost you about 2 bucks to make in China. Just about every other cheaper fender I've had comes with one, so why not the $1100 DRRI? They aren't very expensive even retail ($18 on amazon), but really ought to be included. That said, there are better ones available (I picked up the D2F, but they are out of business now. Tuki makes similar covers, or Studio Slips makes canvas padded clamshells and slips that are nice - i bought those for my Mesa gear - very nice.)

2) The ever present, crappy metal feet that fender puts on their amps. They are cheap and they scratch the hell out of anything you sit the amp on. Take a flat screwdriver and simply pry them out, replace them with 1 1/4" round rubber feet...about $5 retail on the Carvin site or from a variety of speaker building websites or from Mojotone. I normally use an amp stand for combos, but still...who wants to scratch stuff up with metal feet. (Yeah, Yeah...it's a reissue, matching the original, blah blah....the feet are cheesy and destructive. Ditch 'em.)

3) The footswitch for the reverb and vibrato...is the odd duck two button oval footswitch Fender has used for years. I get it that this is a re-issue, but the switch is just el-cheapo. The buttons are too close together, and the plastic base is like a margarine lid. Fender, with their volume purchase power, could easily put a nice 2 button switch in a metal stomp box for this amp for probably $10 cost or less. Not a big deal but...Fender could do better. These switches are odd on a pedal board, require their own run of cable, etc. etc. I replaced mine with an "always on" plug...see below. (Also sometimes called a "shorting plug"). Works great.

4) No "Fender Tilt back legs" included. This is obvious, so I'm not saying I thought they were included...I'm saying at the price point, they should have been included. Tilt back legs work great to get the sound pointed up at you, without having to carry an amp stand to your gig. Good news, if you negotiated a discount, then you can afford to add them as an "upgrade". Available on Amazon, shipped prime for $30 to $40 on any given day. There are no instructions, but search "Fender 14" Tilt back leg kit" and see my review for where I placed them on my DRRI to achieve about 30 degrees of tiltback. My placement works great when gigging in small bars or larger stages. Others have replicated my measurements and said it worked well for them too.

5) When going on standby, this amp POPS kind of loud. None of my other amps do that when I flip the standby switch. It's annoying...

******* DETAILS, UPGRADEs, TONE CHASING, ETC. *******

It is similar to many other Fenders I have had, and most notably similar to a Super Reverb I used to own - at least in terms of the controls. Those are the same with the exception of the DRRI lacking a midrange control on the reverb channel. It sounds Fendery, albeit a bit harsh until the Jensen breaks in. That should mellow out nicely once the Jensen C12K breaks in. I've had other Jensen C12's and they are like an ice pick in the eardrum at first until broken in, then they mellow out, sound great, and cut great in the band mix. Meanwhile, that's what that treble control is for. Or plug into #2 instead of #1 that helps a little too. The first brand new Jensen I had, I HATED, until it got some use...then it became one of my favorite speakers after it mellowed out. I also have hooked this up to a single Jensen 1x10 P10R (of the super reverb variety) and it sounded even more super reverby. I think with a pair of them, you could almost call it a mini-super-reverb. My point -- the 12" C12K has a little different voice than a super with P10R's. Enough said.

It's a great clean amp, and you can still get it for under a grand if you negotiate...at $1099 list, I think it is slightly overpriced for what it is, but nice amps cost money. I bought mine new for $882 plus tax (so $950 out the door) new in a sealed box. (20% off) So before you get excited about prime shipping...talk to your local dealer. I love amazon and I buy tons of stuff prime shipped (in fact almost every day it seems...) but for amps....kinda like to go get 'em in person. Plus you can't really negotiate on Amazon. You can save tax online from some sellers ad that can be significant. The savings help pay for some of the deficiencies Fender decided not to include. But still, even at $1099, it's a lot of amplifier and certainly not the most expensive one I've bought. So it's a decent value but better on sale or with a negotiated discount. Anyway on the topic of clean - it's sparkling clean up to about 6 which is pretty darn loud, then starts to break up a little.

Past 6 or 7 she starts to growl, and it is pretty loud when you get there. I've seen FSR versions that use a different alnico Jensen speaker (a P12Q) and I recently picked one up used. I installed it and tried it, and it broke up earlier and was quieter and lighter to carry. But it totally lacked bass and was too farty in the low end for my taste. I didn't keep that speaker.

As of late, I put a Celestion Creamback -65 in the amp and it removed the slight shrillness I was getting with the Jensen. I still like that stock Jensen quite a bit but for the particular material I'm performing right now, the Celestion works better.

I just heard an '68 Deluxe Reverb in a club, cranked up pretty loud, and using a Warehouse Guitar Speakers 12" knockoff of the Jensen C12N, and it sounded great. He also did the bright cap mod on that amp, and had upgraded tubes. I haven't done any of that to my amp, but his did sound good. I'm not sure it sounded that much better than stock though.

I connected an ULTIMATE Attenuator and cranked her up to 10, and it was good dirty blues tone between 7 and 10. With a T-Rex clean boost pedal in front, the amp on 10, and the attenuator turned way down - nice tubey overdrive, pretty thick, and relatively low volume. Still responsive and so much treble it was no problem to bring back what the attenuator trimmed away. In fact, I don't think I would ever be able to experience this amps overdrive beauty properly without an attenuator...it's so dang loud on 10 otherwise. Not as bad as a super, but pretty darn loud. The attenuator is the bomb with this amp. But now I get my overdrive from pedals in front, set the amp about 5 for gigs, and use a T-Rex booster on solos. I ultimately installed a Dr Z Brake lite attenuator inside the amp...not quite as adjustable as the ultimate attenuator, but works great for gigging.

Because I am also potentially interested in the "head" model of this amp that is available now as a FSR, I also ran this over to a Mojotone (Markshall-like) 2x12 (looks like a 4x12) that contained two eminence legend GB128's. (these are eminence's take on a greenback celestion). This, with the attenuator, and the amp on 10...is "bluesbreaker" sounding. Pretty awesome. Wow...what a difference in the low end for chunking on your low E-string. This did highlight that the low end of the DRRI isn't "great", although I haven't really ever heard a combo that was...It's still ok and a heck of a lot better than a blues jr, or in my opinion, any of the hot rod fenders. So if you are after a small combo for gigging...this is a pretty good choice, especially if you want great Fender cleans.

If you want to have a two channel switchable amp, use an A/B switch between the guitar and amp, sticking an overdrive on the "plain" channel, and setting the reverb channel for clean -- effectively converting this to a two channel amp with a clean and a dirty. I like the Radial Bones Twin City ABY Amp Switcher. Whatever you get, make sure it has a 180 degree phase switch as the inputs between the two channels are out of phase with each other. It doesn't matter for A or B, but if you hit BOTH and they are out of phase, it sounds like crap and doesn't give you the boost you would expect. With the phase switch set correctly, this becomes an A/B Boost switch, in effect.

I already added a set of Fender Tilt back legs...and when this isn't sitting atop my mojotone marshall knockoff cab, its ready to go club in "tilt back" mode. A nice addition...and eliminates the need for an amp stand to get your combo up where you can hear it. They were $35 when I bought them, then Amazon dropped them to $29 right after that (of course). Pretty easy to install...just remember measure twice, cut once. You have to drill a couple holes to mount...be careful and pay attention to where you are drilling and it's very easy. I posted a review on the 14" Fender tilt back legs and included the locations I placed the holes to achieve approx 30-35 degrees of tiltback. See my separate review for that.

Because I don't like the footswitch, and don't really want to switch the reverb and vibrato off anyway, I constructed an "always on" plug. (Or "shorting plug") When this plug is inserted in place of the footswitch, reverb and vibrato/speed/intensity are all turned on. Normally, you would need to have the footswitch for the vibrato/speed/intensity to work. The reverb is "normally on" without the switch, and then is turned off by stomping the switch. To make an "always on" plug for your DRRI, buy a TRS (that's TIP-RING-SLEEVE) metal 1/4" plug that looks like the one on the fender pedal. Unscrew the screws, and solder a small piece of wire from the center terminal to the inside of the metal plug, grounding that terminal (like closing the switch.) That's it...screw the cap back in, plug it into the pedal jack, and wala...all the features of the vibrato channel are turned on. UPDATE -- even though I have told you exactly how to make one of these, if you don't solder, or would just rather spend your time PLAYING your guitar than messing with parts, I've now made some of these plugs and placed them on reverb.com and ebay.com. Search "Always On Plug Fender Reverb" to buy one from me.

All in all, I love the amp, with the upgrades I've made. It has become my favorite amp for going out to small gigs and local jams, because it sounds good, gets plenty loud, and is "amp & speaker under one handle" for transport. Not too heavy, not too big.

I've also got a Princeton Reverb and I like it a whole lot too. It is even easier on the back for taking to practice or gigs, and the only downside of that is it doesn't have the second channel. The upside is that it is slightly lower power at 15 watts so gets into the "break up" zone a little easier. And do not be fooled, the Princeton Reverb is plenty loud for a band situation and playing bar gigs.

Plug in, turn up....enjoy.
Summary: Very nice amp, a couple minor nits, my suggested upgrades

This is a multi-mode distortion pedal and there are 6 “flavors” to choose from.

Out of the 6, I REALLY like modes 1 and 6 (named Classic and Djent respectively).

However, I strongly dislike modes 2-5. They’re shrill and actually hurt my ears, emphasizing all the wrong frequencies in a deeply unpleasant way. Maybe if you’re into death metal and want what sounds like brick wall limited, absolutely crushed, wasps-in-a-jar tone but I’m more into dynamics.

But modes 1 and 6 rock. Classic is, as the name suggests, more of a Marshall stack / classic rock tone. It can get VERY dirty and will definitely scratch some EVH itches.

Djent gets a little more aggressive and tight, really good for harder, percussive lines.

The 3-band EQ help shape your tone really well.

I run pedals in a loop switcher, so the buffer doesn’t bother me or affect my tone when the pedal is turned off.

Tested with the green (clean) channel of an EVH 5150III, guitars used were a Les Paul with Duncan JBs and an Ibanez with Fluence KSE pickups. In both humbucker and single coil modes, able to get a good amount of note clarity and can tame the pedal’s gain somewhat from the volume knob.

Not sure this is the best choice for low to medium gain tones (I’d get an OD pedal for that) but for outright dirty tones, this is a lot of fun.

Yes, there are 4 modes I’ll never use but, for $45, you still get 2 really good distortion pedals in one.

Really happy with the pedal and happy to recommend it.

This little gem is a game changer for guitar practice for me and at only 40 bucks it may the best toy I ever purchased for my guitar playing. Here is why I love it so far.

1. I can practice with headphones now and all I have to do is plug in my guitar, headphones, and the iRig2 into my iPhone or iPad.
2. Portable and small.
3. No batteries needed!
4. The free app has several useful practice features allowing me to do away with having several apps open at one time to practice. The free amplitube app has a tuner, can import and play backing tracks, can slow down tracks, can add effects without pedals, can access the iPad's mic, can record my practice sessions, has a metronome and more. One app to rule them all!
5. I can also plug into an amp if I don't want to use headphones.
6. I don't wake my wife and kid up when I practice and don't annoy them when they are watching TV.
7. The sounds quality is excellent for my intended use. No feedback yet and the external gain control is nice too.
8. The free app is easy to use. I figured out everything I will use in five minutes.
9. Plug and play even for a newbie.
10. I get to try more amps and effects than I could ever afford to buy or even want to buy without ever leaving the house. Of course, some of those will cost extra as in app purchases so keep that in mind.
11. I practice more now because it is less of a pain to get going.
12. I practice any where I want without having to bring an amp. Just my guitar and a few small items in my gig bag.

A few observations. For the record, I am using an iPhone and iPad without issue so I can't speak to how it works with Android or others. Seems pretty sturdy. The mic velcro could be useful in the future for live use. Packaging is nice. It is smaller than I thought it would be. The extra cost for in app purchases may annoy some but after reading some complaints, I was pleasantly surprised by what is included. I can't believe it only cost $40 and that it works as advertised. Big surprise. I expected more bugs but I guess this is pretty basic technology. Unless you are playing live for money or you need professional quality recordings, I would skip the HD version and save $60 by getting this one.

Extra pedals, drums, and amps cost more. They range individually for as low as $2.99 and as high as $99 for an "everything they sell" bundle. You can download the Amplitube app for free and have a look at all the extras before you even buy the irig2 if you like and then delete the app if you choose later.

I should have purchased something like this a long time ago. Happy playing everyone!
Summary: Game changer for guitar practice for me!

It's not severe enough to request a replacement, & doesn't rise to the level of dampening my thumbs-up on the product. But, it's A Thing. ;)

This is a special purpose wire set that is designed for orchestral use. I typically use [[ASIN:B0002D0KT6 PureSound Custom Series Snare Wire, 16 Strand, 14 Inch]] on most of my snare drums. My review of those wires explains why. However, this model is sometimes the only one that will work for general purpose use.

The occasions when these wires are perfect for general purpose use is when you are changing out damaged or lifeless snares on a vintage snare drum or a modern one with narrow and deep snare beds. Anything wider than this snare set will not give optimum results. And while I have not seen the 10-strand model on the market, if you come across one of those sets you will immediately notice that they are physically wider than this model!

Of course this set is perfect for orchestral work because it is significantly more responsive than the general purpose set I cited above, and the decay is super fast. Each note is articulated, and if installed properly this set will give you sensitivity to the edge of your drum (unless you are using Yamaha style wood hoops, which will attenuate some sensitivity.)

One other snare drum this set works beautifully with is the older Ludwig pioneers with two piece shells and other drum brands and models of their era that were originally equipped with gut snares. This modern set retains some of the original characteristics of those snares, and when used with calf (or Fiberskyn) heads also make great orchestral snare drums.
Summary: Very responsive, fast decay and also great for some vintage drums

An E-bow is an electromagnetic feedback device to use with a guitar. You can use this to add infinite sustain, note swells, string like bowing, saxophone like blowing, and synth-like arpeggiation depending upon the hand technique & positioning you use.

I had the second generation black w/ red logo E-bow for 20 years before I decided to sell it on Ebay and get this model. My other unit performed like a champ with much use both in guitar and bass work.

I decided to upgrade to the "Plus" version due to the high harmonic mode that my version did not have. It is interesting because that mode basically doubles the rate of electromagnetic vibration so that the feedback sounds an octave higher than normal mode.

Other than that mode, the only other differences between the two units is the weight/thickness of the plastic and the two mode switch. My original Ebow felt like it was made of a heavier grade ABS plastic. I guess to cut costs and weight, they went with a lighter grade plastic. So far, after 6 months of use, the E-bow plus shows no signs of cracking or damage, so I guess the plastic is not as big of a concern as I thought it might be. The switch feels a little less substantial, but it has held up under use, so again I guess it is not as big an issue as I might have thought.

If you take the time to woodshed on it, you can really do some creative things with this tool.
Summary: Amazing Unit for What it Does!

Text:
A very tight fit for the XR18 but nothing half a brain can't figure out how to do.
Wiggle it an inch at a time per side with the the mixer face up/visible as it sits in the bag. No need to remove the rubber end pieces. Material has a little give and likely relaxes a bit over time; I've only actually used the bag a couple of times so can't verify that. Bought it along with the mixer but should have waited until I'd had the XR18 a while and figured out just what it was I really needed. I knew I'd needed something and impulsively bought this "recommended" accessory. Now it's money wasted unless I can come up with another good use for the bag.

You can not (NEVER TRY) to use the mixer while it's in this bag; For storage and transportation ONLY! The power input and switch are on the side of the XR18 BUT most importantly, even if you could work around that, this mixer gets warm and needs ventilation. The mixer's vents are also on it's side plus it has no internal fan. This isn't a knock on the bag but just the reality. To reemphasize- storage and/or transportation, period.

Decent for it's intended/limited purpose but a little too pricey for what it is, imo.

The better option for my application was to install the XR18s' rack ears and mount it in a shallow 4u rack case/bag. Now the mixer is always ready to use and has plenty of air space all around. For good measure I added a 1u rack fan to bring fresh air in across the top of the mixer.

Ended up getting this: rack; https://www.amazon.com/Odyssey-BR408-Space-Shoulder-Strap/dp/B0002DV18A

Here's the fan I choose: https://www.amazon.com/PROCOOL-TV440-Cooling-Industrial-Cabinets/dp/B07N1V29Z5?dchild=1

Reviewed those items as well if you want to check them out.

Any very shallow 3u or 4u case that you can just leave the mixer screwed into all the time would likely be a better option than this Gator bag UNLESS, for some reason, a rack case takes up too much space for you. For compact storage/transportation this bag is well made and probably your best and only option. In general I'm definitely a fan of Gator products, just wished I'd passed on this one.
Summary: Good Bag but wish I'd held off

If you want to go a bit lower, opt for the 10 or 14. I was really hoping that the 12 hole would be the same which would actually give it an orchestra tuning (what Seydel calls it).

Those extra low notes really come in handy and I find myself playing the 10 most often.
The 14 is really nice, but it's a bit too large to conveniently carry.
Obviously, the 10 is also easier to cup without adjusting your grip.

The 8 hole might be fun, but rather limited. I'm thinking I'd rather recieve one as a gift than have to pay for it.

If you do buy one, make sure it has the fancier raised relief lettering stamped into the top. Those were made in Germany. The newer ones without raised relief lettering are made in Asia somewhere by a toy company.
I would never pay as much for one of those. As far as I'm concerned, not the real deal!

You can also tell if one is really made in Germany by looking at the label on the case. The German ones will have the original German label under the new Chinese label. I carefully remove the top label with a hair dryer set to low and use a sharp knife to lift the edge. You can carefully remove the sticky leftovers with a damp washcloth, wiping from the center outward. If done gingerly, you can retain the original German label on the case without damaging it. I've done it successfully three times.

The German label will say "OKTAVE" rather than octive or octave. Even most German harps will have the original label covered due to the buyout. To me, it's just nicer being able to look at the old label. It's really sad that Hohner had to sell out.

I bought my GSR100EX from Sweetwater, and I originally got it to mod it. I wasn't expecting much, so I was very surprised when it arrived. First off, mine looks nice, the neck is barely a hair wider than more expensive Ibanez Soundgear basses, and it's so little that i don't even notice - it's not chunky by any means. Another surprise is that it was pretty well set up and sounded pretty good. I started wondering whether I wanted to mod it, actually, and I haven't because I'm pretty happy with it.

This is the cheapest brand-name long scale bass you can buy. The Squier Bronco bass costs even less, but it's a 30" scale, and when I ordered my GSR100EX i was looking for a 34" scale. Mine weighs in at 6 pounds 2 ounces, which is extremely light for a non-hollow body electric bass; it's got no neck dive, so I'm a happy camper. The single Music Man-style pickup sounds pretty good, the neck is fast and slim and a good shape - Ibanez players will find it familiar.

One negative is that the fretwork isn't great, although not in ways that affect me. The edges of a few frets, instead of being filed, are bent and pushed into the side of the neck. To be honest, it doesn't bother me because there are no sharp edges, and if there were, I'd file 'em down using fret files. The wood isn't perfectly matched, but mine looks nice, and for under $200 I couldn't care less.

When the bass arrived, I slapped a set of La Bella Nickel Plated Rounds (not the RX series - these but for 4 strings https://www.amazon.com/Bella-767-6N-Bass-Strings-Roundwound/dp/B012BO2L36/ref=sr_1_26 ) on the bass and for my preferences, they sounded better, but the strings it came with weren't bad. Set up was okay. Not much neck relief, but that's easy to dial in, and besides, I like my strings fairly low. A new bass player could rock the bass I got happily without making any changes.

If you're looking for a lightweight, long scale bass with a slightly smaller body - good to carry around, play 4 hour shows or to play if you have back or shoulder issues - this is a very good bass. I have more expensive basses and I have shorter scale basses, but this one is as light as an Ibanez Mikro bass but with the longer scale. In fact, I'm ordering another one to route and drop some Fender Mustang pickups in - I might get the black one. The GSR100EX bass is a great value, a great player and if you're not looking for perfection, it may be as good as it gets.
Summary: Lightweight and plays well and cheapest 34" scale bass from a major brand

Every time I put on my headphones and turned on my Bugera G20 to practice, I'd hear a ton of very loud static and what I thought was amp hum. It was totally annoying. It only became bearable when I'd start playing, as the guitar was loud enough to drown the noise out. But when I'd stop playing, between songs and exercises, the noise would just come back and be constant... and LOUD.

I had thought the multi-outlet pedal power supplies I'd picked up for both of my amp setups were isolated, and noise filtering, as that's what I had been searching for back when I bought them, but I couldn't afford a $200+ model, so I got a couple of them in the $40 or so range.

A few days ago, thinking not all of that noise can be coming from the amp, I thought I'd take a chance and try a different power supply and ordered an OTraki when I saw someone else saying how it had made their pedals quiet in their review.

It just arrived a little while ago, and I immediately brought it upstairs, plugged it in, swapped all my pedals over to it, and turned the amp on and waited for the tubes to warm up. I was shocked when there was only the very slightest, and quite normal amp hiss. The annoying noise was GONE. TOTALLY GONE. The amp was totally quiet. The amp was so quiet, in fact, that I impulsively reached for my guitar sitting on it's stand and plucked the low E string, just to make sure the amp was actually working properly. When the low E sounded through the amp, loud and clear, I was like "holy crap... my amp is quiet...! It's finally quiet...! it's finally, finally unbelievably quiet...! Wow...!"

This thing weighs nothing. You wouldn't think there's even anything inside of it, it's so light. So, it won't add any weight to your pedalboard, even slightly... and it's length is short enough, I can easily mount two of them side by side on my mini pedal board (maybe even three).

My one and only disappointment, which is more of a wish list item, really, is that it only provides one 500ma outlet, with all the other ones being 100mA. Up until a couple of years ago, this would have been more than adequate, but some companies, like Strymon, are designing more power hungry pedals these days. Mooer, in particular, came out with an entire series of amp-simulating preamp pedals, that are just to die for if you're a tone hound like me, and those pedals require 300mA or they don't fully work as designed (or so the folks at Mooer Support have told me more than once). So, if they made this with 4 or 5 300mA outlets, then it would be just perfect for folks with a bunch of more power-hungry pedals like me. .

But as far as a standard 100mA multi-outlet pedal power supply, the OTraki can't be beat, especially if you're just looking for quiet, isolated power for your effects pedals.

I'm so totally impressed with it, I just ordered another one to replace the other power supply I have powering the pedals in my larger amp setup downstairs. There's just no contest... the Otraki is light years ahead of the others in its price range.

It's unbelievable just how quiet this thing actually is... and it's unbelievable how inexpensive it is for this kind of quiet, isolated power.

I may actually write to them and ask if they could made a model with multiple 300mA outlets for those of us with more power-hungry pedal collections, like the Mooer amp-simulator series of preamp pedals... that would just be awesome, if they could...
Summary: Wow, My Amp Is Quiet Now...  Really, Really Quiet...

The problem that the Dare Guitar Strap seeks to address is the comfort of playing a heavy guitar or bass for lengthy sessions with a standard strap that might cut into your shoulder. Rather than a wider strap (which has worked wonderfully for my bass playing), D’Addario has gone the route of two straps that potentially distribute the weight on two shoulders. Unfortunately, due to the design of a guitar and the way it is played, this strap actually adds to the discomfort that it seeks to alleviate.

Unlike a saxophone strap which attaches to the horn at a single point, a guitar strap attaches on the horn or near the neck and at a second point at the bottom of the instrument. If you are right-handed the standard strap lays over your left shoulder. On the Dare strap a second strap lays over your right shoulder, snapping to the ‘standard’ side of the strap. If the guitar hung from this united point you might gain some benefit but the other end of the strap is still attached to the base of the guitar. No matter how I adjusted the ‘second’ strap to shift some of the weight of the instrument to my right shoulder, as soon as I started playing and the guitar moved around, the weight distribution shifted and the second strap would cut into my neck making the whole experience measurably more uncomfortable.

Kudos for trying to improve the players experience but this needs to go back to the drawing board.

I have not used a true “fuzz” box in my pedal board since the 80’s, but saw this and thought I would give it a try.  I have a number of overdrive pedals that I really like, but every once in awhile you want that “heavy fuzz” sound.  This Pigtone PP-29 is a full size stomp box, and like many, it’s a 9V powered effects pedal that needs power from your pedal board, or separate 9V power supply.  It does ship with a 9V battery pigtail if you want to use a battery.  It’s a metal casing (somewhat light) with the power input on the side of the box next to the output jack.  I wish the power plug was on the back, as the other pedals I have as they set better on the board that way.  The controls are pretty simple, with 3 chicken head type knobs for level, sustain and tone.  It also has another toggle style switch for “normal” and “special” along with your standard stomp switch to turn effects on/off and a light so you can see what position it is in.  All standard stuff, with the exception of the toggle.  In the “normal” mode, you get a bit of a octave style fuzz that sounds pretty good.  In the “Special” mode, it just seems to add a bit more low frequency to the fuzz mix.  It’s a interesting pedal that I experimented with on a number of guitars, including humbucker, single coil, and P90 equipped guitars.  I think it sounded best with my P90 equipped guitars.  I also found it sounded much better with a EQ pedal pre fuzz in the chain.  I was able to get better articulation with the EQ.  I think overall, especially for the $$ it’s a decent pedal, however with limited usefulness in my rig.  Of course, your mileage may vary, but I find it a bit too mushy.  With a EQ however, you should be able to coax out some pretty gnarly sounds.

This review is for Finale PrintMusic 2014 for Windows.

Computer: Win 8.1, core I7, 6GB RAM.

Musical skill level: Complete novice older adult using Gibson's Learn and Master Guitar course.

I purchased the Finale software to help me with learning the guitar and reading music. I have had the software for 2 days.

The software installed from DVD quickly and easily. I installed as a normal user. It properly asked for administrative password on installation. Even though the software ships with a software "key", it still requires you to create an account on their web site to register the software, or it quits working in 30 days.

When setting up the account at their site, the following is at the bottom of the page if you don't have Javascript enabled:
"Javascript appears to be disabled in your browser. This page requires Javascript to be enabled to better protect your security."

As a computer/network security architect, this is not only incorrect, it is exactly opposite of what is correct. Enabling Javascript REDUCES your security. All web sites should be programmed to work whether Javascript is enabled or not.

Within 2 hours, I had the software installed, and had entered two practice songs. Both display the music, guitar tab, lyrics, and guitar chords with the fret and fingering. Printing was flawless. I found the software easy use to perform these common tasks.

I downloaded several midi files from the Internet, and opened them with Print Music. These files were almost instantly converted into sheet music, and could be played back on my computer, or printed. Couldn't be simpler.

I want to play along with Finale to learn to read the music, and learn the songs. I can adjust the tempo to start slowly, and speed up as I improve. The tempo adjusts well, but the music begins as soon as you press the playback button. I haven't found any way to enter a delay so I can get my hands back on the guitar.

I know I am just scratching the surface of what this software is capable of. My use is probably not their normal target audience, but I would like some features added for beginning learners like myself.

CONS: (and the reasons this software didn't get a five from me)
1. The confusing and misleading statement on the website about Javascript.
2. The requirement to have Javascript enabled to use the website.
3. The requirement to create an account on their website to register the software.
4. The apparent lack of playback controls for learners.

The weighted key feel, and the sound quality were right up there with some grand pianos that I've played. You can check it out in the video that I've posted. I hooked up some good headphones to the keyboard, and placed a small microphone in my ear, so you can hear exactly how it sounds when you play it. You can even play other instruments using this keyboard, or make your own music recordings, with MIDI sound software (e.g., Ableton, Reaper, Cubase, or a freeware equivalent) by connecting a USB cable between the keyboard and a computer that has the software installed.

Text:
This looper distinguishes itself by really only doing one thing but doing it really really well at a very affordable price. To record you simply press the button and the led will turn red, continue playing. When done simply tap again and the LED goes to green and plays back. At any time in the looping process if you want to overdub simply tap the button and record and tap to finish. No need to line it up with the loop, it places your overdub exactly where you played it in the loop. If you don't like the take a simple press and hold will erase the overdub. Want to stop and clear (two presses and press and hold) and your back to a clean slate. I don't know the limit of overdubs but I haven't reached it. The amount of time for the looping I believe is 5 min so you can record an entire song and overdub to your hearts content. The tone preservation is excellent and haven't noticed any issues there. You can get a nice variety if you put this at the end of your effects change so that you can record a rhythm that is dirty and crunchy and overdub and record, then turn off your distortion and overdub a very nice clean lead over it. If I have something I like, I then output it to Sonar to play with some more.

Pros- Small, very easy to use (1 level knob and a stomp button), designed by guitarists and it shows, true bypass and plenty of room for recording.

Cons- You may consider lack of battery a con, I don't, everything goes on the effects rack and is powered through AC. No drum track or click track but then again, the aim for this device was to keep is simple, I believe.

UPDATE: I was having an issue with the looper one night being able to record but not hear myself. I contacted support and their response was quick but they basically said it sounds like it is broken, replace at the store which I did. It worked great then one night again, I couldn't hear myself recording. I played for about an hour with different configurations, it seems not all 9V AC adapters are equal. Out of the 4 I have it only liked 2. When I used that adapter it seemed to work just fine. So beware if you are having an issue you might want to look at the 9V AC Adapter.
Summary: Best looper I have used in 30 years

I play heel down and have the dynamic control to use a regular beater in an acoustic trio setting, so I don't love this because of any shortcomings in technique. Where this beater shines is the full, resonant musical note you can get from an unmuffled bass drum - a sound I cannot produce with hard felt beaters no matter how softly I feather my beater.

For folks who play heavier music most of the time and are not used to a felt-but-not-heard approach to bass drum playing, this beater will save a lot of frustration, especially in very small venues where normal playing and a typical, modern beater would be overwhelming.

To get the best results you need an unmuffled bass drum - or a very lightly muffled one. On my bass drums I use [[ASIN:B0002GFPN4 Remo Ambassador Coated Bass Drum Head - 20 Inch]] (or the size that fits my 18" bass drums, depending on configuration), as both batter and resonant heads. If I use muffling at all it's [[ASIN:B0002F783A Gibraltar SC-BF Bass Drum Felt Strips 2/Pack]], and typically on the batter side, but in some rooms on both sides. You can hear and feel every note using such a configuration with this beater. Not a thump, but a real, resonating note.

This beater is too one dimensional to use in every situation (unless you only play in acoustic trios), but is a valuable tool in your arsenal. For jazz and authentic blues players it is essential.
Summary: Another part of your beater arsenal

Text:
I recently purchased this guitar at a local guitar center, in the special edition Olympic White color (picture attached) and within a few hours of play time, this is quickly becoming my favorite guitar.

I've been playing guitar seriously for roughly 20 years now, but grew up with a guitar in my hands from birth. I've owned Gibson SG's, Epiphone Les Pauls, Fender Mustangs, a Squier VM Mustang at one point, an Ibanez RG series guitar, and a vintage 1960s Silvertone. Of all the guitars I've played Mustangs have always felt like "the one" that one special guitar that just plays perfectly for me. This model is no exception.

Stock, out of the box you get a fixed bridge, as opposed to the standard floating vibrato bridge that is both really unique and cool, and also a disaster for keeping in tune. The machine heads are decent, but I'd recommend swapping them for locking tuners (perhaps fender locking tuners) eventually. The stock pickups aren't half bad, but I personally intend to upgrade them. I'm getting a couple more of these for different configurations (one to be setup like a Cobain mustang with a humbucker at the bridge, and a single coil Myth at the neck, another with a duncan '59 neck, and JB at the bridge, with coil tapping, and yet another perhaps to have dual single coils, or active humbuckers, I haven't decided.) Regardless, even bone stock, this guitar is pretty close to perfect for the price. Great for a beginner no doubt, but will be enjoyed by anyone at any skill level. For a modder or someone who wants to have a guitar customized to their specs like myself, $150 is cheaper than buying a body blank and neck from most places ($175 through warmoth just for the mustang body alone) and you get a complete guitar that you can play the second it reaches your door. That is amazing.

The setup is pretty close to perfect, at least the one I got (which I was assured Guitar Center usually doesn't mess with unless it's completely out of whack) intonation seems to be almost dead on, and the action is incredible. I haven't had to adjust anything yet, though when I switch to hybrid slinkys, I anticipate minor adjustments to be needed.

The strings it comes with feel very nice to the hand, very easy to bend, I believe them to be .09-.42 gauge strings, definitely great, but because I play down tuned by a half step, with a low Drop C# where the low E would be, so for me a slightly thicker low end (going to .46) helps keep things in tune nicely.

Overall, buy this guitar, you're going to love it, and if you don't you can always give it to me ;) I'd love to have a few spares hanging around.
Summary: Amazing guitar, especially for the price.

So, I had one of my Focal Solo6 midrange amps die, and ordered a quick, cheap standby when I ordered these from Sweetwater. However, I had no idea that they would sound so darned good! I'm hearing a few things that the Focals didn't provide, but there are clear benefits to the Focals as well.

At first, I just unpacked and connected these. After being astounded by what I was hearing, I began playing some CDs (yes, CDs) through them. There was a tremendous amount of detail, the timbre of instruments in acoustic jazz and classical work was excellent. However, I listen to rock an metal, so I popped on some prog metal. Dream Theater's "Awake" was literally awakened by this pair. The bass reproduction was amazing for a 5" mid, though you need to place these at least 1ft out from the wall behind them in order to avoid any muddiness, or low frequencies running together. The tweeter was never harsh, and even metal wasn't fatiguing to listen to over long periods. These are amazing.

After listening for a while, I checked around my wiring just to verify the sensitivity switch was correct, and IT WASN'T! So, I switched to +4dB (connected to "pro" level outputs), and the sonic character changed from being pleasantly forward, to far more recessed, but still very good. Personally, I believe I liked them better in the wrong position, so I wrote to JBL about what I heard, and what they did from the factory, and look forward to their response.

The bottom line is, I will probably keep these, and A/B them with my Focals when I get the repaired one back! I beleive they can serve both the "Pro" community and consumers rather well.
Summary: Better than they deserve to be!

I have played guitar for about 30 years, mostly in the novice-intermediate range. I am no Eddie Van Halen. That said, I am a gadget guy, and I was excited to try something that falls into the gadget genre that would also be a "luxury" for me, since I don't really perform publicly. This is an extremely cool product. Out of the box, it took a little bit of configuring (which mostly came down to "reading the directions") since you need to plug the receiver into your amp and make sure it "pairs" with the transmitter (which you plug into your guitar and attach somewhere on your body - a pocket or belt is ideal). After 5 minutes of messing around with the settings, my teenage daughter (a budding guitarist who fell in love with this product, by the way) and I were soon fighting over who would get to use it. There was no fuzziness or static at fairly close range (up to 10 feet) and very little from being in the next room and 20 plus feet away. The guitar sounded very clean. Some very positive things: cord length for the transmitter is perfect - not too long and not too short - to attach on your body and keep it out of the way; the receiver can work with up to 8 transmitters (a bit mind boggling), and I plan to test that functionality out soon. Obviously, anything that uses the same cord - a keyboard or a mic, for example - would operate well with this product. The "stomp" mechanism is great, and this product is well built, not flimsy or cheap looking. I can see it being used on stage at some clubs here in Nashville, or conversely, for the home user who does not want to be anchored to an amp (like me) and can stand up and walk around with your instrument. Very happy with this product and plan to use it a lot!

Text:
I wanted an audio interface that I could use to record the stereo output of my Akai MPC Live II and then use to record and overdub vocals. I have many years of experience working in radio and audio production so I know...I had high hopes for such an inexpensive piece of equipment! At the end of the day it will serve me perfectly!

This unit is USB powered so it must be plugged in to receive power and to interface with your PC. Once plugged into my PC, I noticed that it set itself up for use. Within a minute or so, it was ready. I opened Adobe Audition. I was able to select my interface from the options and immediately was able to arm a track and record. First I used it in stereo mode by making sure the phantom power was turned off and the instrument/line input was selected. Then I used the two input knobs to set the levels of the L and R channel. It worked well and the quality was surprisingly good.

Next I attempted to record my voice. I used a condenser mic that requires phantom power, which gave me a chance to try that feature and it works great!

The build quality is good. The sound quality is good, but if the lowest latency possible with this unit is 30ms, it is not usable. I have wasted a day trying this unit with other recording programs trying to eliminate this issue to no avail. I posted my original review that was very negative toward this unit after that day of struggle. The company reached out after contacting its engineers. They suggested bringing the rate down to 44.1k, which would bring down the latency. I had already tried to this, but after great customer service, I decided to try again. With fresh eyes and a different mind set, I was able to find the settings and actually adjust it. I went into Cubase 12 and Audition 2023 and had success; however, I realized the issue was partially software related. Long story short, I can bring the quality back up to 48k and get the latency needed.

In conclusion, the issues I had were mainly due to my being out of audio for so long and needing to make changes differently. This interface is surprising easy to use. It doesn't even require a driver download. The sound quality is good enough for my current needs and the latency is not an issue anymore! Great unit for the money!
Summary: Works well and great customer support!  Awesome budget interface!

Text:
I've used a wide variety of harp mics including vintage Green Bullets and JT-30s. This mic isn't bad. It's not as easy to overdrive as my Shure Commando or my Astatic 300 shell with a relatively new JT-30 ceramic element, but with the right amp it's a good sounding mic. It's also relatively high output. A plus is that the volume control that comes with the mic has a useful range. You don't have to crank it all the way up and leave it there in order to get the best tone. I have an amp with both preamp and power amp gain controls. I can get as dirty a sound as I please with that one. With some amps the sound will be cleaner.

There are always 3 variables in tone: the player, the mic, and the amp. A truth not universally acknowledged but true nonetheless is that the player is the most important variable. If you want a dirty sound you must be able to produce a somewhat dirty sound without amplification. The mic and the amp can influence your sound but good tone originates from inside the player. A second truth is that gear is personal. The best gear for you may not be the best gear for anyone else.
