[[VIDEOID:e675cd5ff4e2af34d793dab3d874d4b5]] So here is my setup: I have a whole mess of budget pedals, and I'm using those cheapo daisy-chain 9v cables to plug them all in. When 2 or 3 of the pedals are engaged, I get a really bad high-pitch whine (which hopefully you can hear in my video). It's the worst. But with this noise gate, it almost completely wipes it out. There is a little trail of noise after you play a note and go quiet, but overall, this really wipes out the high pitched squeals.

In my video, I have the Fuzz, tube screamer and distortion all going (pretty much a worst-case scenario in terms of amplifying noise). After I engage it, the squeal is 90% gone, I would say. If I only use 2 distortion pedals, it's entirely gone.

In the picture, you can see my current settings. I'm keeping it closer to -20 than -30, and I think it's in that range where this is most useful. Beyond -20, and it just kills all sound. Let than -30, and it lets the noise through. I experimented with the hard vs soft switch, and found hard just sounds better.

I hope you found this review helpful! This seems like a great budget noise gate for those of us with noisy setups.

Text:
This is a comparative review of Samuel Kolstein's Bass rosin vs Pop's Bass Rosin. Both are very good but this is why I prefer Kolstein's.

While Pop's is great and one of the standard rosin brands for Double Bassists, I have always preferred Kolstein's brand (and not because I owned a bass and bow from the luthier Sam Kolstein for years- comparatively, it just surpasses Pop's performance). Pop's is just too soft and with Kolstein it is just the right consistency to give you a good grip without being too sticky, runny etc especially in warm weather. It also does not get too hard or have a tendency to crack in colder weather as Pop's does. You can tell by the sound when someone has too much rosin on their bow and with Kolstein, even if you use a little more than you need it won't "glob" up on your bow hair and create that kind of "gravely" sound behind the note when there's too much. It gives you an excellent grip but still allows the bow hair to have a natural feel and sound on the string (also a little secret is that I always carry a toothbrush and brush off any excess rosin and separate the hairs). Pop's is so soft that with more inexperienced players, they can easily use far too much rosin and suffer from too much rosin build up on the bow hair which affects sound negatively.

You can see from the posted images that there is a much smaller quantity of the Kolstein brand than the Pop's. Why? Contrary to belief you really don't need much rosin at all if you have quality bow hair- (if you go with "AAA" level Moroccan horse hair in either salt and pepper or black, you really need very little rosin- if you use this same quality but in white, you just need a bit more on it than you'd use for the salt-pepper and black because the hair is naturally not as course. Ask your bow repairer/ luthier for this type of hair and you will hear a major difference in the bow sound before you even use any rosin. NEVER use synthetic bow hair. Synthetic hair combined with rosin equals bad tone.

Also the actual Kolstein rosin itself comes encapsulated inside a rubber sleeve (see images) that maintains the structure of the rosin itself within the outer gold cardboard casing and won't allow the rosin to stick to the sides in any weather. All I do is roll down the rubber just enough to draw the bow across it a couple times, let the rubber go and it keeps everything nicely in its place. This is an upgrade from back in the day when it was encased in a cardboard casing you had to peel off.

As you can see from the Pop's rosin (given to me to use from an instrument rental shop with a piece of the paper cup torn off ---huge mistake!). The rosin melts out of the cup often and once it gets out of its paper cup holder it sticks to the plastic cup. When it is not melting, it's generally cracking.

I suggest getting Kolstein's All-Weather grade (this is the ultra which works too) and you will be covered for well over a year by using sparingly on good bow hair. HAPPY PLAYING!!
Summary: Fantastic Double Bass rosin - recommendation from a classically trained bassist

I've been searching for a set of string for my Martin D28 for some time now. I have probably tried various gauges and types from at last 10 different manufactures. I just could get the nice warm mellow sound I was looking for. A few were close or at least when they were new, but tended to get a tinny sound after a short time.

I had thought of trying Elixir string in the past but never did as I had read reviews about them breaking. But a friend recommended them so I decided to give them a try. I tried a set of the Nanoweb first and they were okay but when I tried the Polyweb I struck gold. It was the combination of the string design and also the gauge size. The light/medium works out very well. Easy enough on the fingers but still produces a nice full sound and I normally play finger style.

Very pleased with these strings and think my search is over. I have had this set on for a couple of months now and I play daily, and they are holding up well.

Highly recommended for the Martin D28 for sure, but if you are searching for a set of strings, I would give them a try on any guitar too. Guitar strings are not a one size fits all, so you might not get the same results, but they are worth a shot in my opinion.

UPDATE Nov 26. 2019

Just a quick update on the Elixir Polyweb strings. I have used them for a while now and can comment on their longevity. I would say they are on the high side, meaning they last longer than most. When they do start to wear they get a little thin sounding and do not resonate as well.

Overall though they have become my string of choice for all my acoustics. I have an older Wasburn Dreadnought and the Custom Lights sound great. I did find that it takes some use before they sound their best. When you first install them you might not fall in love with the sound. Just give them some time before making a decision. Stretch them a little and play for a few sessions and you might notice a difference.

This review will cover both the utility of the GJazz for beginners, and its value as a platform for upgrades/modification.

My Glarry arrived earlier than expected, well protected and completely undamaged.

Unboxing it revealed a mixed bag. Most issues I have revolve around the neck, and the finishing.

Neck is solidly made of hard maple and a nice rosewood slab fretboard. The edges on the headstock are done a bit crudely, and the Glarry logo appears to be silkscreened on. It isn't coated, and might easily rub off. It is sharp and clear.

The frets are installed cleanly. The fret ends are not sharp, but could use more finishing. Frets themselves could use a final buff. The tuners are a trifle rough; easy fix with a dab of light grease. They do have a bit of backlash. They tune well enough, and do hold tune.

The GJazz is sold as a substitute or analog for the Fender Jazz Bass, but the neck is completely different in profile. Width at the nut is more like a Precision, and it is thicker too. Players with smaller hands will need to get used to it. It is not heavy enough to neck dive, and it does-JUST- balance.

The neck plate, bridge, and control plate are all heavy steel stampings, well-chromed. The pickguard is a good quality laminated vinyl part, black/white/black in color with good beveled edges. It fits well.

The body is by far the best feature. The grain is beautiful, and the clear yellow finish is deep, flawless, and accents the wood grain.

So how does it work?

Setup was pretty good. Intonation is in, but the string action is high. It plays well, but when the action is lowered, it plays GREAT. There are no buzzy frets or dead spots. The tones available are varied, and it sounds good on either or both pickups. There is some 60-cycle hum present, but this cancels with the volume full on both pickups (like a Jazz Bass).

It has a nice, snappy high end, especially on the bridge pickup. It lacks some punch on the bottom end, but still sounds good.

Controls all work as they should.

This bass is VERY light, and easy to handle.

Overall, this bass would make an excellent first choice for a beginner. It's not perfect, but it plays and sounds really good. It is beautiful to look at, too! Recommended.

For you modders and hot-rodders, it's still a good choice. I didn't especially like the neck and tuners, but the knobs, control plate, neck plate, pickguard, and body were all quite good and I used them. I added two knobs from IKN. The bridge is good quality too, but I went with a Musiclily cast zinc bridge and Wilkinson brass saddles for more mass.

The body is GORGEOUS and ready to use. Neck pocket routing was slightly rough, but exactly right for a standard Fender-style heel block.

Controls work fine, but the pots are light-duty and small. Pickups are NOT standard Jazz Bass sized, they are a bit smaller. Not a problem for my build, as I upgraded to BQLZR musicman type humbuckers. Pots were replaced with TAOT 500k, and capacitors replaced with 22microfarad polys. A switch was added, and a Les Paul patterned circuit was used for fully independent control of the pickups. On the control plate, all 4 holes were drilled to accept 4 fullsized pots. A Musiclily endplate with jack was added to move the input jack to the edge of the body.

The tuners were replaced with Fender Highway Ones, and the neck with a Kmise paddle headstock in Jazz Bass profile. Headstock was shaped like a Jazz, decaled, and lacquered. I fabricated a brass nut from a piece of music-grade 1/8" brass plate.

The strap buttons were replaced with Planet Waves oval strap keepers.

This was an easy and fun build. The hardest part was making a routing template to mount the pickups, and freehand routing a switch pocket and channel!

All assembled, my GJazz was transformed into a funk monster. Action is low and soft, it has tons of output, and the tones are KILLER. It is so punchy and bright! It's also completely hum-free at all settings.

You may question the amount of work investment in this project, but look at it this way: Where else can you get a gorgeous brand new Jazz Bass body, finished, for a paltry $103? All the other useful pieces are a bonus!! Cost of this project all-in is about $250, and it is EXACTLY what I was looking for.

To sum up, I recommend the Glarry GJazz enthusiastically. It works right in both roles that it's suitable for, and it would also be a fantastic backup or spare bass.

I've used a lot of different metronomes: Taktells, seiko style, qwiktime, numorous card style metronomes, my teacher's dr beat which I loved (and was a major reason I chose to practice in his studio) and my mother's seth thomas electric metronome when I would come home. Of all of these, my favorite besides the dr beat was the seiko style ones. They were durable with one movable knob only, no display- nothing fancy to break down (the seiko one i used for teaching, I must have dropped a hundred times) - and they were loud! I'd leave one in a practice room or somewhere and it was no big loss. Those card style digital ones in particular were like 10 bucks anywhere 15 years ago! I've always been nervous to get an integrated metronome such as the one above because I figured the more features, the more possibilities for something to stop working. This has been sort of proven to me in my experiences with some of these integrated tuner/metronome combos. The only tuner I've ever owned, on the other hand, was my beloved korg CA-30. I had it for 15 years. Practiced intonation using the tone generator for an hour each day for something like 5-6 of those years. It never failed. In fact, I lost it last year during a move. I bought a few decent looking tone generators to try and replace it (I only use the tuner when setting up instruments, not when practicing), and finally picked this one up. It doesn't have any fancy roll wheels to change tempo (like that dr beat). In fact, on the surface, the design looks pretty clunky: It's a little large. Separate sides for both functions with dedicated buttons, no color display or anything, but i've gotten used to it and i really appreciate its design now. The metronome tap feature I use all the time and is quite accurate. I also like that when i turn it off and on, it returns to the tempo at which I had previously left it. That's a nice touch. There are beat subdivisions and you can set it to a few different meters. I don't really use any of those features much, but some will appreciate them in so portable a unit. It's pretty loud, though I wish it were a little louder and my main gripe on this side is that i can't track the tempo as subtly as i would like.. Sometimes, I'll click it up a hair and the tempo divisions seem to go between 3 and 4 bpm at around 50 bpm to 8 (!) at around 200 bpm. This is a minor inconvenience though. Taktells, for example have this lack of precision borne into the design. The tone generator is great, just like the one in the CA-30. In fact I don't remember that unit having a 3 octave range, which this does. Good strong square wave tone, great for practicing intonation drills. I can't comment on the tuner as I haven't used it yet but i'm sure it's just as fine as the one in my ca-30. It has an adjustable backlight so you can use it in poorly lit conditions, but the controls are so intuitive, you really shouldn't even need it other for just tuning. I haven't needed to change the provided batteries yet, in several weeks of use from an hour or two a day or more so i'd say it doesn't kill batteries quickly. Now, it's strange that this was the last of the metro/tuners that i bought given how well my previous Korg products seem to hold up but I'll just add that of the two other metro/tuners I've bought over the last year, this is the only one that still works. Granted, I've only used it heavily for a few weeks, but the first one i bought (using this forum- you might find my review online, i don't want to mention it here) died several months in. The second one, which i dropped some money on for a few more features failed as well and i was able to return it for store credit. There's, in short, a rash of cheaply made items about that have feature well above their ability to maintain those features. caveat emptor. If it looks too good to be true for the price, it probably is. Get the reliable one instead.

Edit: Two years in and everything still works as it should. I think i did get around to changing the batteries but only once so far.. This is about the performance I expected. Good ol' KORG!

Let me start off by saying that I picked up the TD-11 hoping to use it in the studio and for practice. I have not been disappointed. I did not buy this kit through Amazon but I know how much traffic passes through these pages and thought a proper review posted here would get the most hits. For me, the usability and quality of performance can be broken down into three distinct categories; the brain, the pads and triggers and the stands and rack where everything is mounted.

The TD-11 Brain is a very easy to use piece of technology. I wont waste your time with the specifications. What I like most are the large, well-lit LED, an extremely ergonomic and easy to grasp button interface and the intelligently designed software that doesn't get in the way of playing. For instance, you can change kits while playing and sample tails of instruments that are still sounding while you change will continue to play. Also nice, the first five quick recordings created are automatically stored as general MIDI files to an inserted USB flash drive. The audio and MIDI computer interlink has been extremely reliable in controlling DAW-based drum plugins and samples...MIDI notes can even be reassigned individually for any pad without effecting the brain's onboard drum assignment for that pad! Ultimately, I knew what I was getting with this brain but was still very pleased once I plugged it in and used it.

The pads that ship with the TD-11KV are definitely not Roland's best pads. I've had a lot of experience with rubber pads but had never played a mesh head before. I have to say that the PDX-8, which serves as the snare pad for this kit, is an amazing pad to play on. The sensitivity of the head and rim triggers is quite amazing. Of course, the creation and refinement of mesh pads has been one of the crowning achievements of the Vdrum line. The PDX-8, really delivers in my opinion. So much so that I will definitely be upgrading all of the rubber tom pads to mesh pads as I prefer playing on them. I find the PD-8A rubber tom pads to be a bit stiff however they do reliably trigger and do not seam susceptible to false triggering in the slightest. In fact, the entire kit plays very smoothly with a well-balanced dynamic range right out of the box. As a side note, the TD-11 brain does support dual trigger pads for all of the toms. The rubber pads this kit ships with are only capable of triggering one sound at a time. Some people might prefer the rubber pads so I definitely recommend anyone interested in the TD-11KV check one out at a local music store to see which pad type you prefer, as there is an all-mesh version of this kit available as well.

In my opinion, the weakest component in the TD-11KV is the MDS-4V rack and the associated mounting brackets. The rack itself is reasonably sturdy but not very "solid" feeling on the floor. I haven't experienced any wobbling or swaying while playing so I can say that it's definitely usable. The rack could be bigger, or at least taller. I found that I needed to come up with a custom configuration to raise the height of the snare and toms to a level that feels more comfortable. This is another component I'll probably upgrade at some point in the future. The clamps also seem very susceptible to wear. I've not had any issues with them yet but I am somewhat concerned as they are made of plastic, which may lead to easy breakage or stripping. Fortunately, the clamps provided are pretty standard 1.5" L bracket type connecters so I expect I can replace them as needed with sturdier versions.

The TD-11 does not come with a case but I'm not sure I would gig with it anyway as the rack and pads really are too small to comfortably manage in a stage environment where lighting is always changing. That said, this is am extremely capable studio kit that captures much of the nuance and finesse of one's technique. The bass trigger will accommodate a double bass pedal and there's even an extra crash trigger jack allowing one to add a 3-trigger ride for a total of 3 cymbals.

Overall, I'd rank this a very solid 8 out of 10 as a solid project studio kit this setup works well. For quiet practicing or even the odd gig I could see this kit filling in nicely. If you were really interested in playing live, I would probably consider the TD-15KVs.

NOVEMBER 2013 UPDATE:

I'm not one to file revisions to a review. However, the unwavering quality of the TD11K after more than a year of pretty heavy use has motivated me to expand upon my original musings about this product. To be honest, I've added to and upgraded my edrum kit quite a bit since this purchase. Even so, much of the TD11K remains at the heart of my setup.

One of the things I had some concerns with initially were the drum and cymbal rack clamps. I'm happy to say that these have proven to be quite sturdy and robust. I've yet to have a problem with any of them slipping or breaking -no matter how tightly they are fastened or how hard I hit the drum. In fact, one of the original TD-11K mounts is holding a PD-120, which is one of Roland's 12 inch mesh pads that currently serves as a snare drum in my setup. This is certainly one of several triggers that receives the most pounding and that clamp has remained solid and unmoving.

The CY-8s that shipped with the TD-11K have also been extremely reliable. After purchasing the kit, I read through some less than favorable reviews that suggested these pads do not always hold up well. For me at least, this has not turned out to be the case. These cymbal pads trigger very reliably and continue to perform superbly.

I no longer use the PD8a toms that ship with this particular configuration but can indeed confirm that the TD11 brain will accommodate dual piezo or piezo/trigger pads which allow you to trigger a different sound from the head and the rim. For those so inclined, a special Y-cable can also be purchased which provides you with the ability to connect two single-trigger pads to one dual trigger cable.

I decided to upgrade the stand to something substantially larger. This was a decision driven by a desire to expand the kit as much as the need to move the individual pads into more comfortable positions. Truth be told. the stand really is the worst part of this setup. To be fair, It was reasonably stable during the time I used it. However, the pad positioning was very cramped. This lead to bad posture and an occasional cramp.

Ultimately, whether you are an aspiring drummer or a veteran time-keeper, the TD11K is a fantastic instrument that will provide years of service.
Summary: Great eKit that's Worth the Cost

I just got this little cart, and it really is a very nice product. I took it on a gig last night and had a good 5 minute walk through a large parking lot with rocks, some gravel, mini-craters, and even speed bumps. On the cart I had about 50-60 lbs of bass gear. All of my gear, including the electric bass itself, loaded nicely on to the cart. 12" speaker cabinet, amp, music stand, guitar stand, and bass with case. 2 bungee cords adjusted for the size of the load, and I was on my way! The cart sets up easily and quickly to the size of the load, which is important. Last night it was cold out!

The only problem I can foresee other than spontaneous collapse, which seems unlikely given the cart's seemingly sturdy construction, is that the 2 adjustment screws that tighten on the bottom of the frame to lock it into the size you want could potentially loosen due to vibration while rolling the cart. Since the screws face down, they could be lost and gone forever before I notice since the weight of the load would prevent the cart from falling apart if the screws fell out. So I may try to find a way to attach the screws to the frame with a velcro strap in the event they become unscrewed. But I do think that it is unlikely that I would lose both, or even one. And if I did, the worst case scenario is that I would have to always set it up to the largest position, which is locked in place by a spring mechanism.

I love the fact that it rolls so easily, and does not have inflatable tires. Anyone who owns a wheelbarrow or hand truck with inflatable tires knows what I am talking about. They go flat!

I'll update this review over time to let people know how the cart holds up to regular use.

One of the big things you can't tell when you look at something online is whether the build quality of an item is as good as the picture makes it look. This pedal's build quality, however, really exceeded what I was expecting. It seems super-sturdy. The housing is metal, and it's hefty for nano. It takes up hardly any room on the pedal board. Operation is simple enough. There's a little three-position mode switch and a level knob. It comes with a small memory card in an adapter for the regular SD slot on the side of it so you can bring external sound files into the pedal. There are a couple of foot pedal codes to remember, and they mean different things depending on what state the LED is indicating, so it takes a little practice, but I'm a one-man band after a day. Sound is great. You can loop, layer more loops on top of the first loop, delete the last layer, or delete the whole loop with only the following foot button commands: tap, hold, and double-tap.  You get to store layers of loops with the total of all layer lengths equal to or less than ten minutes. You can loop things backwards, too, but I probably won't use that feature much. I have always wanted to get a looper, but my pedal board was a little crowded already. I wish I could shrink my other pedals to this size. Two thumbs up, especially when space on your pedal board is scarce.
Summary: Built like a tank. Saves space on the pedalboard.

I love this drawer. I needed a locking drawer able to handle a lot of weight and this one certainly does the trick.

I found it very nice that when I posted a question (see “Questions” area) prior to purchasing one of these asking how much weight it could handle, that the manufacturer, Penn-Elcom Online, responded quickly. Often, you won’t get an answer from a product’s manufacturer or distributor quickly, or EVER, but Penn obviously was monitoring the Amazon.com page and questions posted by potential buyers, and they offer customer service greater than most as evidenced by their rapid reply. Customer service means a lot to me, so this impressed me a lot and was partly why I purchased this unit. By the way (since it isn’t, or at least wasn’t when I purchased mine, given on the product page):

WEIGHT CAPACITY (according to Penn-Elcom): 40 lbs.

Customer Service is all-too-neglected these days & Penn-Elcom passes the test, but ultimately, it’s the product itself that matters, and this one is well worth its cost if you need such an item.

The drawer flows smoothly with its ball bearing mechanisms, even after I’ve placed a lot of weight inside of it! That’s a huge consideration for me. The drawer is easy to use, placed in the lowest spaces (just off of the floor) in the rack it’s in.

The fact that it locks was significant to me as well, and the locking mechanism seems as secure as I’d expect or want.

The drawer is also very attractive, having a nice, plain, black appearance that fits well within the mostly black color scheme of its environment, and lacking obnoxious product labeling on it. I don’t like the brand or model or any other text plastered on my gear, and this drawer fulfills this criterion nicely.

Recently, I had to turn the rack this drawer is in on its back, thus turning the drawer perpendicular to the ground rather than in its usual horizontal position. The drawer was full of items of various sizes, yet nothing fell out of the well-secured back, as I’d want. Other drawers come with holes for cables, which I didn’t want. This drawer COULD have holes cut out of the back if you need that, but if you don’t, I love that it comes sealed up tightly, not only lacking cable holes, abut also lacking gabs around the edges, so that contents will remain securely inside (and inaccessible to people who might seek to remove something via the rear).

The drawer clicks into position when shut all the way. You must press down after inserting fingers into the space on the front where you can release the catch. It’s great that it clicks firmly into position, which means that if the rack/case it’s in is moved, tilting it without it being locked will still not allow the drawer to open without you wanting it to. The only thing I’d have preferred is for the release to occur upon listing upward on the latch. You have to press downward instead to release it, which isn’t as easy given that mine is installed so low in the rack. But that’s a small matter, and overall, the latch feature is very nice.

19” rack gear fitting with adjacent devices can sometimes be a problem. Some devices make adjacent devices difficult or impossible to fit in a manner that makes use of every space, sometimes, for example, due to extending “feet” (such as little rubber extending bits you’d want if the device was resting on a desktop). But I have no problem fitting a device immediately above this thing and although mine is the lowest position, it seemed like I’d have no problem putting something immediately below it. Thus, it doesn’t seem like it would waste any spaces in your rack.

I highly recommend this unit, and I’d guess that the 2U (i.e., take up 2 spaces) and 1U comparable models would also be very nice from Penn. I noticed that the review rating for the larger 4U unit isn’t as good as for the models that are smaller. I didn’t need a 4U unit so I didn’t read the text of the reviews and don’t know why that’s the case, but maybe there’s an upper limit in the size of these things before problems appear.

If you need something 3U or smaller, I’d highly recommend these models from Penn. If you need something 4U or larger, I’d recommend considering buying multiple smaller models perhaps if there are problems with the four-space models that concern you. I’m thinking of buying one or two more of these myself, and if I did so, I’d stick with 3U or smaller models even if that meant buying, for example, two 2U units instead of one 4U unit.

My background in audio is as a home recording enthusiast; I play electric guitar and bass, recording into a DAW (old Mac running Logic Pro X). I prefer close mic-ing my cabs with a 57 / ribbon combo instead of DI usually.. haven’t tried experimenting much with room mics yet.

Signal chain for me is mic > Focusrite LS56 > Mac (Logic). Simple. The LS56 Liquid Channel is emulating the Manley Slam.

My usual mic for vocals is an SM7B with a Soyuz Launcher, although I’ve got some other dynamics (Heil PR30B, SM58 derivatives) and an MXL ribbon on hand for comparison. My only actual condensers are a pair of Behringer B-2 Pros.. which cost around $100 less per mic than the Stellar.

Don’t want to focus too much on bundled accessories but I was a little underwhelmed. They seem to be of a lower standard than the mic itself. Possibly it’s just that the mic feels pro-level and the accessories are more budget feeling.

Because the mic is heavy. Like.. reassuringly “this is a nice piece of kit” heavy and well made. More than makes up for the cheap accessories. The money saved there definitely went into making the mic what it is: a handmade (right here in California!) LDC that punches way above its price point. It’s got a fixed polar pattern (cardioid), no switches or toggles to worry about. Plug it in and hit record.

On vocals, the smoother top end of the X2 Vintage is a better fit to my voice than my other condensers (there’s a reason my main mic is a darker sounding dynamic). The Behringer B-2 Pro has a lot more presence / detailed top end but I hate how that makes me sound and never use it for voice. But the X2 Vintage never gets harsh. Really like that a lot. Super important to seek out a mic that compliments YOUR tone; if you have a darker tone, the X2 (non Vintage) might be a better fit based on it having more going on in the high end / less roll off.

The Vintage’s slight roll off / smooth top end is what makes it a great alternative to the SM7B for multiple applications for me, as the X2 Vintage still has an overall more detailed sound (and is easier to drive thanks to its sensitivity and 48v powered JFET output). I HAVE to use a mic booster with the SM7B for spoken word stuff, otherwise it’s too quiet (and cranking the interface too noisy). With the X2 Vintage, I can dial the interface gain back and there’s no unwanted noise generated by the preamp.

Something that doesn’t impact the SM7B as much is room treatment (or lack of). I’m spoiled by the SM7B’s excellent rejection and hadn’t realized how badly I need to treat my room acoustics and deal with the many reflections present in my workspace.

With the Stellar X2 Vintage, you’re gonna hear EVERYTHING. So I immediately noticed an increase in room noise in recordings. If you’ve got a recording booth, a well-treated room, a closet you can sing into, etc. then you’re all set. But if you’ve got a square, untreated room that echos, it’s gonna be part of whatever you record. That’s just the nature of condensers and afflicts the mighty Neumann U87 just as much as the Stellar X2 Vintage. Yes, cardioid has some side and rear rejection but reflections coming over your shoulder will be picked up for example.

Haven’t had a chance to record acoustic yet (something the SM7B is NOT great at, at least for my guitar) but will update review ASAP, along with notes on how it fares as a room mic for recording my old Marshall.

But so far I’m loving the Stellar X2 Vintage and feel like it’s worth investing in some room treatment to really make it shine.

I bought this bridge in hopes of solving the intonation problem I was having with the stock tune-o-matic bridge on my Epiphone Les Paul Special II LTD. I have Ernie Ball Classic pure nickel .009-.042 strings on it, and the intonation was always sharp on the first three strings, even with the tune-o-matic saddles all the way at the end of their travel. I also had a problem with the G string sounding flat and squawky, and I believe that was related to the saddle because I could loosen the string, wiggle the saddle a little, then re-tighten the saddle and the string would sound normal again for a day or two before going dead again.

So, first things first. This solved my intonation problem. I know I probably didn't really need a roller bridge to get more travel on the saddles, but I figured that I could also help lengthen string life by taking away the sharp edge of the tune-o-matic style bridge at the same time. It works for that purpose, but it took some extra work.

The first problem I had was that some of the rollers wouldn't actually roll! I used a bit of tri-flow and a pair of needlenose pliers to get them going, and they now work for the most part but I really had to crank on them with the pliers to get them moving and a couple of them still don't spin as freely as I would expect. I discovered that the rollers are not black chrome, but actually just painted brass. This begs the question, why did they bother painting them? If you want a roller saddle bridge for use with some kind of tremolo, I would strongly encourage you to look elsewhere because these rollers don't work well. They are working for my non-tremolo guitar just fine, but I won't be actually using the rollers much.

The next problem I had was the post size. Now, I know that Gibson bridge posts are smaller than those by Epiphone, but based on some of the other reviews I was under the impression that the included posts should screw right in to the threads in my guitar body. That is not the case. The threaded portion of the included posts is a larger diameter than those on my Epi. As a result, I was left with two options. I could either try to pop out the original thread inserts from the guitar body or I could pull out the Dremel and chase out the post holes on this bridge to make it work with my original posts. I chose the latter because I couldn't justify hacking into my guitar and risking permanent damage for the sake of this experiment. So, I chased out the holes to fit my posts and it is working but if you look closely it is fairly obvious that I am not a machinist.

With all of that said, I am giving this bridge three stars because of the problem with the rollers and not because of the modifications I had to make for it to work on my Epi. The rollers are their primary function, and that function does not work well.
Summary: Required work right out of the box

For the money these are 5-star headphones. The quality mids and highs and respectable bass in this compact package is what I expected from Beyer. I own a larger more expensive pair of the DT-770s and these are no match for the 770s as far as bass, but again all things considered the 240s rock pretty hard. If money is no object, they are probably a strong 4.5-star item.

I got these because I want quality audio around the house and office without blasting speakers and without lugging my large studio cans (770s) on my head half the day. The 240 model delivers plenty of volume with amazing crisp mids and highs totally lost in other headphones. The bass is good, not great, but still good and not overwhelming. Better than other 4 sets of headphones I own from various manufacturers under this price point. I've found there are some good EQ apps which really bring out the headphone bass on my Android phone, this has been great listening to YouTube music but even before this the 240s did a fine job. If you're looking for headphones to pound techno and hip hop these aren't for you. For all other music including dance, top 40, and metal these handle the music well in a small package.

Now the pressing issue I see raised in many other reviews ...that these headphones are too tight. They absolutely are tight, not the tightest ever but definitely tight, I was having trouble wearing them for more than a half hour and I'm an average sized guy.
The solution is that they are adjustable, but you have to do it at the right place. At the top of the headphone band feel around and you can tell where the plastic meets a thinner metal spine (this is the same spine that is exposed when you stretch the earcups fully extended). when you find the spine at the top by feel, it's in two places at the top but it's under wraps so you can't see it. When you feel this area, use TWO HANDS and carefully bend this to expand the unit. It worked for me. I'm not sure this is recommended, as I supposed you could break it if you aren't careful. but for me I had to, and the first time I bent it a little far and then bent it back so it was much more comfortable than stock. Make sure you are bending the metal part not the plastic and you'll have much less chance of cracking something.
I dont recall seeing this in the tiny paper insert provided, but I can tell you this will work and make these cans less tight. Warning - if you loosen them up too much, you will notice less bass and more outside noise, this is because they aren't pressing into your head a much and the speakers are a fraction of an inch further from your ears. Since volume follows the inverse square law, any loss of distance does show a loss in sound but you can make it up by turning up the volume a bit. If you do it right this will be negligible, plus comfort is arguably the most important thing

Good luck, and enjoy your new compact sonically superb headset. You really can't go wrong with Beyerdynamic.

First: manage your expectations. This is an insane price for a decent instrument. I believe many people think of ukuleles as toys, but getting a decent, playable stringed instrument for under $100 is pretty darn incredible. I've been playing guitar for about 40 years, and it's really easy to find dirt cheap, terrible guitars. This is my second uke - my other is a more expensive tenor.

I like the tenor size and find that it gives more of the "standard ukulele" sound. Baritones get into classical guitar territory - which isn't a bad thing, it just depends on what you're looking for.

PROS:
- Good tuners - tunes and stays in tune surprisingly well. Tuners at this price point are often a weak link. These seem fine, though the plastic buttons look and feel cheap. Other than that they work just fine.

- Built in tuner works great! A very pleasant surprise.

- Good playability . The action could be lowered a little, but I haven't messed with it yet.

- The sound is good. Not super loud and, as I said, you get into classical guitar territory with the range. From many demos I've watched it seems that baritones can sometimes seem a bit muddy when strumming (of course some of that is up to the player and how it's played) - the voice of this uke is not bright, but not overly dark. It's good enough - and string choice can make a difference. I recently changed the strings to Martins, which I like better than the stock...Aquilas?...not sure.

- Fret work seems good enough, and they're good sized frets. My tenor uke has TINY frets - which I don't like, as it makes playing a bit more difficult. Larger frets allow you to have a lighter touch, IMO.

- Intonation seems good enough (meaning it plays in tune up the neck)

- The truss rod actually works! This was one of the selling points for me. A truss rod allows you to straighten the neck, or give it a touch of bow to allow for string vibration. Very helpful, and a useful feature whose importance shouldn't be overlooked.

- Pickup is decent! Really, the fact that this thing has a pickup at this price is crazy. So if you want/need to amplify your uke, this is great. And it sounds good enough.

CONS:
- Workmanship is sloppy in places. The finish isn't perfect, and where the neck is glued to the body, and the fretboard is glued there is some slopiness. I take these things as they come, and for this price I don't really care. I'm bringing this up because some people will pick this apart. Just be aware that you're not buying an expensive instrument.

- Playability is decent, but could be better. Again, for the price, it's fine. I don't know that I'll ever get this to play as well as I'd like, but it's good enough, and I'd say it's good enough to gig with, if that's your thing.

- As one would expect from a low cost, mass-produced instrument, it's a bit overbuilt, has a thick poly finish and isn't super resonant. Which means that the tone (while not bad at all) and volume feel a bit muted. There is always a trade off: building lighter instruments with thinner tops (the soundboard) that resonate more easily is more difficult to do so those end up being more expensive. Those instruments are often more fragile, as well - but you can and do get a more resonant instrument.

You get a lot of instrument for the money here. The zebra wood is attractive, the playability is pretty darn good, the tone is good enough, and the thing tunes properly, and stays in tune (those two are things I can't do without. An instrument that won't tune or stay tuned is a deal-breaker for me. I've seen far too many students with super cheap beginner guitars that sound terrible, primarily because they're difficult to tune and won't stay in tune. I believe this simple issue can be a big factor in keeping a newcomer's interest in playing an instrument. )

I think a baritone uke can be a friendly transition for guitar players - OR as an introduction for someone who eventually wants to play guitar. I've taught youth guitar lessons for years, and a common issue is finger strength & length, even with smaller guitars. Many younger kids find guitar difficult because of the physical difficulties with playing - the strength needed to press strings down to fret notes, and also with small fingers forming chords can be a challenge. A baritone uke is much easier to play, and you can transfer your knowledge over to guitar, if you so choose.

Overall, I think this ukulele is a great starter instrument at a very reasonable price.

Text: Great Product

I love this pedal. I was going to write an article-length review, but it's the best "clone" of that mythologically-themed man-beast pedal from the 90s. Three-band EQ, higher-gain setting waiting with the switch of a toggle. Brian Wampler went there. We were all thinking it. We all knew it needed to happen, so he went and did it. Thank you, Mr Wampler. Just when I was getting tone fatigue out of my pedalboard, I got the Tumnus Deluxe and I suddenly fell in love with my guitar and amp again. I remembered that I actually like the sound of my guitar, pickups, amp, etc. I plug in, stomp on the Tumnus and hear this . . . well, the image that always comes to mind is that clarity of a pre-dawn morning where everything is covered in dew and the air has such a sweet purity that every breath you take is deep and mindful. It's such a fresh sound, without preservatives, weed killers or insecticides. I never realized just how much my other pedals were affecting the color of my sound, or that I could get so much variation just from using the tone and volume knobs on my guitar. I can throw on reverb and delay and it still sounds great drenched and trailing. If I could change anything about it, I'd love an extra footswitch for normal/high gain, or at least for a boost. The only real complaint I have is that it now I have to upgrade my other pedals because they all seem lacking.

I put it in my pedal board chain at the end before effects input to try out. I run a stereo Digi Tech effects out to 2 custom 64' Fender Deluxe amps. That brought on a real nice sustain much like turning up those Deluxe amps for a natural tube overdrive. I use several "high end" pedals on gigs. I turned the Drive down to about 2/3 the way, the Voice to about 1/2 way and used it in combo with my original TS808 Tubescreamer and it took that sound to another dimension. Same effect when I added it in with my Boss DS1. Even a combo with my Dunlop EJF1 for some burnin' saturation and sweet feedback. The Voice control is fun to play with.
Needless to say I have been using this pedal as a line driver in the chain on leads or by itself as a crunch on rhythm. Even makes a nice "Bassman" blues lead sound. Been using it now for about 3 weeks and I only hope it holds up to constant use.

I previously purchased a Behringer Q502USB to use along side my AT2020... For the longest time I thought the Q502USB had 45v of phantom power, but it didn't. I had always just turned the mix volume and gain up really high. After testing and seeing it only provided 14~v I switched to another simple $30 audio interface that provided 45v. I wanted more features and I had used the scarlett 2i2 and wasn't impressed at all.. dunno why ppl rave about that interface. I thought it was noisy and very limited in features. I finally decided I would not cheap out on an audio mixer/interface and found this.

Huge pro.. it has an actual on/off button unlike all the other mixers I've used. The buttons and knobs are all extremely solid. It feels amazingly well built and I just feel very confident with it.

The only problem I had was figuring out that the Fader adjustment didn't work with DRY CH 1-2G.. it only works with the other two modes. I really wish I had just started out by purchasing this mixer. Would have saved a lot of time, money, and frustration. It also comes with some software which is a huge plus.. none of the behringer products I used came with anything.

I'm currently only using it with an AT2020 xlr mic and a logitech 231 headset.. I will be getting some JBL monitors soon to use with it. I would highly recommend this mixer.. though, I've only had it for a few days... things could go wrong in the future, so I will update if anything bad happens whilst using it.

It would have been nice if it had come with a USB outlet plug for mobile use.

I'm a singer-songwriter (TATYAYA on YouTube) and I like the way I sound with this AT2035 -- much better than Rode NT1-A which is an over-hyped mic to newbies. The Rode NT1-A has a frequency boost at 100-200 that will cause what sounds like a low hum from your guitar, and it also boosts the high frequencies too much so your voice sounds brittle on the Rode NT1-A. The AT2035 has a nice meaty sound without overemphasizing any range of frequencies-- don't believe me? Then google the two Frequency Response Charts fo the two mics.

BUT, for home recording, consider bypassing condenser microphones and getting quality dynamic mics like the:

--Shure SM7b (for voice)
-- Electrovoice ND 468 (for guitar

Dynamics 1) cost less, 2) have much better rejection of room/outside noise, 3) are more durable, 4) less sensitive to humidity, 5) less sibilance (the S sounds) and 6) less plosives (the P and B sounds)

If you want a condenser mic for home recording, I think the AT2035 is a great value. But, it will pick up all the cars passing by, the air conditioner, the cat's meow, the couple arguing two doors down, etc. After recording many songs on the Rode NT1-A, I switched to the AT2035 for some songs, and the Shure SM7B / EV 468 combo others.

If you want to hear what I'm talking about regarding the Rode NT1-A, listen to some of my earlier songs on YouTube: TATYAYA

It will be worth your time if you are buying a mic for home recording. Good luck and have fun. Remember, it really is not about the gear, but the heart and emotion you put in to your song. You will NOT be disappointed with the AT2035, and I predict you will like it not just for the price, but as probably the best value condenser mic you can buy.
Summary: Tatyaya says: Best value condenser mic for singer-songwriter home recording studio

I have the AC4TV10. How can words describe the greatness of this amp? For one thing, it sounds so much better than anything I've heard in this price range that my choice was easy. Comparing this to the [[ASIN:B002GHBZ4U Bugera V5 5-Watt Class-A Valve Amplifier Combo with Reverb And Power Attenuator]] A/B in the store, the difference was unreal. The Bugera sounds okay, I guess, but pretty dark and muddy. I went in intending to buy the Bugera, but was underwhelmed with the sound, so I started playing all the small amps. After I played the Vox I quit auditioning and took it home.

The Vox is a revelation. Always musical, harmonic, chimey, and rich... Strat > Cable > AC4TV sounds better than you could believe 4 watts, no pedal, no reverb could sound. Clean, it's powerful enough for practice, even with weak single coils, and sounds so sweet. Volume up halfway, (noon) and it starts breaking up a little and sounding sweeter. By 3 o'clock the tubes are working hard, and there's a range of great tube distortion sounds on tap.

Oh, and that's 4 _tube_ watts. At full volume, (4-watt setting) it's maybe louder than you'll want it in the bedroom. But thoughtfully, it has an attenuator so you can get dirty tones at lower volumes.

Any bad points at all? Hmm... Well, it doesn't have much clean overhead. Want real loud clean tones out of single coils, like for a gig? Buy something else, or mic this. The tone control is a bit subtle, and only seems to work if the volume is up at noon or better. The attenuated sounds aren't wonderful; it definitely sounds best on the 4-watt setting. Okay, I can't really find much to criticize here.

I can't get over how much amp you get for the money. I'm running a Line6 M13 into my AC4, and so far, all I've gotten out is sweetness. From chimey chorus-o-heaven to crunch, growl, scream, this thing does it all and does it well. I'll probably end up modding this amp a bit, swapping tubes, maybe a different speaker, but I must say I could not be happier with it as it is right now, box stock.

If you're on the fence, don't hesitate- just buy this thing. If you don't like it, there are plenty of folks who'll be happy to take it off your hands. There seems to be a real cult springing up around this amp online, and I believe I just joined. See you at the clubhouse!

[Edit to add- I've had the amp for a while now, just put in the bitmo mod switch and new tubes. It just gets better, although you do have to invest in new tubes from time to time... After I've tried a few more, I'll post. In the meantime, I'm enjoying it.]
Summary: Greatness in a small creamy box!

Then I watched a couple reviews which honestly didn't sell me on them, but I figured what the h*ll and gave them a try.

So, I've used these a lot since I got them and have wandered all over the house, into the garage out in the yard and haven't lost signal yet. So if you're playing a small stage you'll probably be 100% ok with these, in a bar situation it's a no brainer, I have places in my house where my wifi and my phone get crap signal but this had no issues.

Thankfully most of the guitars I am actively playing are V's with the jack placement in the upper horn so it's pretty well out of my way at all times.

Honestly there is only one thing I would change about the physical pieces of this unit, as far as it's doing it's job it does it very well and I'd recommend it.

Things I would actually change, instead of this being one piece, put a removable jack cable on it (or have a model with this feature) and put a metal click on the back of this to slide on belt or guitar strap. that is my only real complaint about this, and honestly it's not a strong complaint..

There has been a bit of a boom, so to speak, in multi jointed, extendable, swing arm microphone support arms for podcasts and so forth. There are dozens of them on offer on Amazon. Most of these are obviously just the same light weight arms and mounts used for desk lamps, usually with the flex function supported by springs and weak clamps. These are OK, for what they are, as long as you're using a fairly light microphone. But they are inherently cheap and flimsy. That has created an opening for the more "professional", solid and substantial type of boom arm.

The Squarock Mic Boom Arm is a good example of the more substantial, desk mounted microphone swing arms that have come on the market. Although it has the same weak point that all these types of arms have, i.e. the small footprint of the clamp used to attach it to the edge of a table or desk, the arm itself is solid, and the joints and clamps that control the flex of the arm seem pretty stiff. It's rated for up to four pounds. I don't have a microphone that weighs that much. But I did try it with a Rode Pod Mic which is a pretty hefty item, and definitely heavier than the typical cheap condenser microphone, and had no problems.

The only complaint I have is, as mentioned that the desk clamp has a tiny footprint. To me upping the surface are of the table clamp would be a good selling point. The Squarock Mic Boom Arm is another Chinese made product with promo and instruction text in near gibberish English that barely makes any sense. But after a bit of deciphering, head scratching and re-translation the meaning was usable. The guy in the Squarock promo video seems to speak English properly. Maybe he ought to write the advert and instruction copy for use in the USA as well. Just saying. The Squarock Mic Boom Arm is a good choice in general and especially for heavier microphones and competitive with more expensive arms from Rode etc.
Summary: Solid microphone boom arm and competitive with more expensive options

The MC6000MK2 is the right intersection of price and performance; it's also tank-like and has a very pro feel. In many ways the device is more pro than controllers two or 3 times its cost; while it doesn't have features like performance pads etc, those can be added easily (and more flexibly) through Akai finger-drum pads or a Novation Launchpad, but you can't take something like Pioneer's controllers and turn them into super-solid all-metal construction.

I'd say the only disadvantage, and only JUST a disadvantage, is that it's about 18.75" wide and so its four channels can be a little cramped. But overall, its rock-solid construction, uncluttered "everything a dj needs and nothing they don't" layout, and an amazingly good internal ASIO soundcard (also, it now comes with the full version of Serato DJ) means that the unit is ready whether you are in a club, a studio, or you're taking it around as a mobile DJ.

You cannot go wrong with it. Between this and the Prime series gear, Pioneer has a LOT to be worried about. I used to run all pioneer gear since ~2000, but I am slowly transitioning to Denon.

Lastly, in the image you'll see a stand. It is this one: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B01BH7VV8Y/ref=cm_cr_ryp_prd_ttl_sol_0
And as you can see it's like it was made for the unit. It's a perfect compact solution for getting the device at the right height for efficient practice or as a backup if you need to play out and all they have is a regular-height table to play on.
Summary: The only real "pro" controller below $1200 dollars... and it's half that!

* input and output jacks are on the right and left, which I think is the most optimal location.
* tunes guitars or bass in strobe mode, or needle mode, or "poly" mode i.e. all 6 strings at once
* good build quality
* available in mini format, for those who like that. I don't care for it but some do.
* available in a clip on format also, I haven't tried that.

CONs
=====
* Honestly the only negative I can think of on this tuner is that the display can be a little hard to see in sunlight. My recollection is the Boss is a little more visible in bright sunlight. So if you play a lot of afternoon outdoor gigs, that may be a consideration.

SUMMARY
========
A really great tuner for guitar and bass. Does what it is supposed to and does it accurately. Supports a whole variety of altenate tunings -- see the manual for details.

This is an awesome little reverb, for a really good price. If someone asked for a recommendation for their first, low cost reverb pedal, this is easily the one I would recommend. It’s definitely the best in its price range (and I’ve reviewed many). In the past I’ve designed a few reverb pedals, and I like how Azor designed this one, because it’s almost identical to how I would have done it. This is a DSP based pedal, and uses 78.5 mA.

The pedal is white, with very nice looking matte-finish artwork. The matte finish feels strong (I couldn’t scratch it with my fingernail), but I did notice a few paint blemishes and a circular scratch in the artwork where someone scratched it during assembly putting on the nut on the 3PDT stomp switch. It’s barely noticeable since it didn’t scratch all the way through, and the scratch is black underneath. I couldn’t even get a good picture of it, that’s how hard it was to see. It comes with both a Velcro and grippy back, so you can install either one you prefer.

The mix knob ranges from zero to full, and at zero, there is really nothing mixed in. The signal passes through at unity gain, with no additional coloring of the tone (verified by oscilloscope). Just as it should be.

The Decay knob ranges from very short delay (metallic bathroom type sounds) to fairly long (about 8 seconds) but not infinite. You can get some really cavernous sounds.

The tone knob only seems to affect the tone of the reverb tails, not the fundamental guitar tone. Again, this is exactly how it should be, IMHO. It seems to me to be just a standard treble-cut type of filter, and it can really help tame the “metallic” characteristic of sounds by rolling down the tone. It has a fairly good range, with a noticeable effect on the reverb tails.

All of the sounds that come out of this sound good, from short hallways to huge stadium reverb. The tone knob really helps, and is worth dialing in to different settings for different decay times. Overall, I really think it sounds great, and this has replaced my previous reverb on my economy pedalboard. I really think you’ll be pleased. There is nothing janky about it. I've tested with multiple guitars, and two different amps, and it sounds great on all of them.

Final Rating: 5 stars. A few minor blemishes in the finish, but the sound is first class in this price range, and overall this is an excellent value.
Summary: I really, really like this reverb!

This is a sturdy, well designed monophonic volume pedal. It is the size of a standard [[ASIN:B0002F4V5S Dunlop pedal]] (which I had on my board), but unlike the Dunlop, it has its inputs and outputs on the back panel - can we get more manufacturers to please start putting jacks on the back panels? It makes for much neater cabling on crowded boards. Additionally, this has a tuner output, which is awesome - you can have [[ASIN:B06ZXZCVBL one tuning pedal]] always on, or, if you're like me - put a tuner pedal in the front of the pedalboard (for fast muting when that [[ASIN:B004D8KX7K tuner pedal]] is on) and another one on the output of this pedal, for quick tuning on the fly. It works great, if you have the funds and real estate.

The throw on this is a bit longer than on the Dunlop, which is awesome. That makes it good to sub in with lap and console steel guitar, as the throw feels in the ballpark of a steel guitar volume pedal. It also means you have more throw for your foot, which can make things a bit easier to control.
For an anniversary model, I would love to see a few selectable volume curves, or even an on / off effect selectable for stutter effects. This is just a single volume curve - nothing to set, just plug it in and go. For that it works beautifully, but a few more functions would be welcome. Likewise, the polarity is not reversible.

The construction is very solid - the grip on the pedal itself is more rough than on the Dunlop, and it feels a bit more substantial under the foot. This is a strong, steel bodied pedal that feels like it could take a fair amount of punishment. I wouldn't feel any reservations about taking out for a rowdy bar show - It definitely gets a nod for the construction quality. You might need to remove the unit's 'feet' if you mount this to a pedalboard, but that would be true of any other such pedal.

Finally, you can always use the output of this pedal for the expression input of another piece of gear. I sometimes use it with a [[ASIN:B012XIZ592 Line 6 Helix Floor Controller]] and it works perfectly. Of course it's also a passive effect, so no need for batteries or an external power supply.

All in all, a sharp looking, well built pedal with a tuner output that only suffers from a lack of volume curves and selectable polarity. Even without those few missing features, this has replaced my Dunlop as the main volume pedal in my arsenal (for both six string and console steel guitars). Recommended!
Summary: A strong, nice feeling volume / expression pedal

for those looking to block sound, I'll tell you how below.

a couple things first:

1.) these do not block sound. they do not offer to do so. if you go to the Audimute website, you can find a lot of info on how to block sound. You're looking at a fairly major investment. Their isole blanket will block a window or doorway somewhat. Tips on how to block sound further down.

2.) these DO actually absorb sound and give a room audio treatment. They are superior to the adhesive foam panels, giving you more square footage of coverage AND better absorption per square foot for generally less money.

OK. People looking to "block sound" see below. remember you're thinking in terms of sheer mass between you and the sound source and sealing air gaps. There is no magical substance that will block sound but be relatively light and non intrusive.

First, do you rent or do you own? (further down if you own)

If you rent, consider getting some closed headphones. If you like quality sound, consider Audiotechnica M50's although any closed headphones will do. Or some comfortable shooting/construction earmuffs. Some of them have built in headphones for listening to things as well. Also consider a white noismaking machine. You could replace a hollow core door to a bedroom with a solid core and add weather stripping to block sound from a living room if your landlord allows it. If your neighbor likes bass heavy stuff, it will be incredibly difficult and expensive to block the bass part of the sound. You'd be better off getting them to stop making the noise or moving.

To not modify the structure you are living in but block sound for a ROOM, you would need to sort of build a room within a room. You could lay down a floor made of rubber exercise flooring (the kind on which you put heavy exercise equipment) then build a box on it (possibly with Ikea Billy shelves? The books would help further dampen sound) - with glassed in windows if you like - with a roof. You'd want to coat that box in Mass Loaded Vinyl and then add some Roxul or Corning 703 paneling on sides and top. Use Green Glue to seal all cracks. Give it an exterior with plywood, wood paneling, whatever. Put more mass loaded vinyl on the inside of that sheathing if you like. You'll want a HEAVY solid core door with high quality weather stripping to get in. You'll want to remember ventilation - a long baffled tube for air to come in and another go out and a fan to move it.

There, now you can block sound as a renter - simply build your own structure isolated from the existing structure --- resting on the rubber flooring with its own ceiling with walls and ceiling not touching the existing walls and ceiling and with the proper soundproofing, it WILL block sound.

If you OWN your home, then add drywall like soundbreak XP over all the walls and ceiling of the room. Put in a dampened rubber floor and put more flooring or carpeting over that if you want. Replace the existing door with a heavy solid core door with weather stripping all the way around. Add sound - baffled ventilation with a fan - making sure to provide both a way IN and a way OUT for air that are not too close together. If you need to block sounds coming through the window, try a heavy, thick rubber-gasketed piece of plexiglass cut to fit and inserted in the window frame if you can. (again, it is often simply a matter of MASS to absorb and stop sound. that and establishing an air seal)

Even adding another layer of drywall of any kind using Green Glue can probably give a homeowner a decrease in sound from noisy neighbors. Or you can put a layer of Mass Loaded Vinyl in between the old and new drywall layers.

Hopefully it can be understood now how much was being asked of an audio blanket when people said it didn't block sound.
Summary: Good for room audio treatment bad for things it was not made for

Well pleased with the String Swing guitar wall mount. It is well made, sturdy and looks great. Most important of all...I feel that my guitar is safe! It was shipped in a sealed plastic bag inside the larger Amazon carton. It surprised me that String Swing did not box their quality and relatively expensive product. I find that many companies are cutting cost in this way now days. Or maybe it is because it was purchased through Amazon. No matter, it arrived on time and in perfect condition.

The String Swing mount is fairly easy to install, but placement can be tricky. The guitar I have mounted in my music room (see pic) is not a very expensive instrument. It has much more sentimental value. It belonged to my brother who lost his battle with cancer about a year ago. I may have displayed it higher on the wall than your needs, but this guitar is not going to be taken up and down to play. I do have a few expensive axes in my collection but when I am not picking at them, they are in their cases. WHERE THEY BELONG! IMHO.

The first step for installing is to find a stud in your chosen wall. Then take the provided plastic wall anchors and throw them away! If you are not going to use a STUD to mount your cherished instrument, then I have nothing more to say to you. Unless you are hanging some p.o.s. you don't care about... in which case you can just drill a hole in it, use a nail, and save yourself 40 plus dollars!

Next, temporarily put the two parts of the mount together on a bed or other safe surface. Make sure the nuts and bolts are just loose enough to experiment with the angle you want. YES, you can mount your guitar at almost any angle you want but remember.... the steeper the angle, the lower the body of the guitar will be to the floor. Now, carefully place the guitar in the mount on the bed. You can now move things around to see different angles and where each support arm will end up against your guitar. In my case I needed the bottom of the guitar to be 60 inches up from the floor and I liked the playing angle I have it at. (About 15 degrees.) Use the edge of the bed as a guide to find the angle you prefer. Then sneak a tape measure under the guitar and measure STRAIGHT DOWN from the bottom mounting hole towards the edge of the bed. Get an eyeball estimate on how much lower the bottom of the guitar is from that bottom mounting hole. In my case it was 10 inches. So, if I wanted the bottom of the guitar to be 60 inches from the floor.... I needed the bottom mounting hole to be 70 inches from the floor. Mark the wall for that bottom mounting hole and the rest is cake.

I did get someone to help hold the mount, making it easier to drive the screws. I knew there was a reason I married her!
Summary: Excellent product... read review for some install tips

I have a nice Custom Shop Hummingbird that I elected not to have any electronics put in to it. I should have realized that meant no neck strap pin. (There is one at the base of the body.) I do a lot of recording of acoustic instruments, and for some song types that require a specific more aggressive strumming technique, I prefer to stand. The choice is to drill into the base of the neck and install a strap pin (like the Planet Waves Solid Brass Pin) or to try this strap tie. So...I did both. I have a Martin 12-string that I installed the strap pin and my Hummingbird has the Martin Strap Tie.
The Martin Strap Tie works as advertised. And so long as I am careful to insure that the strap connects properly to the Tie, I have confidence that my guitar will stay secure.
The strap pin works better. Here's why:
- the guitar has a better balance with your strap attached to the strap pins due to gravity pulling downward on the body of the guitar with your guitar strap in an inverse U shape.
- conversely, when the guitar is on the Martin Strap Tie, the guitar wants to pivot using the strap tie and the pin at the base of the body. Your guitar strap is now more horizontal than with strap pins and the guitar will shift.
- the guitar rides too high with the Strap Tie. You look like Hank Williams I. (No offense to HW I. He's one of my musical heroes.) Lengthening the strap just gives more slack to make the guitar shift more.
The Martin Tie just doesn't really work for me. I'll probably continue to use it on the Hummingbird as needed - but for performance, I'll pick a guitar with neck and body strap pins.
Summary: The alternative to drilling a hole to mount a strap pin

Ive been ordering and returning boutique dirt pedals for months now. Finding that perfect distortion pedal: its difficult if your a tone snob such as I. There are people that can get off on generic Boss or Electro Harmonix distortion/OD pedals, and then there are people who have a higher attention to musical detail and aren't satisfied with substandard.

This is the pedal for people seeking the ultimate boutique quality distortion pedal. I went through most of Wamplers dirt pedals, which have a near mythic level of gravitas in the industry, and didn't find any that were truly superb. The BE-OD is an incredible pedal, and dare I say an "amp in a box."

It has a roaring yet smooth tone, is capable of obscenely high clipping levels for even the heaviest metal, and is extremely versatile due to a functional presence and tight knob. For classic rock/metal like Zeppelin, Hendrix, Steppenwolf or Iron Maiden it is KING. I cant recommend this pedal enough. After playing dozens of dirt pedals, and half a dozen boutique dirt pedals, this is the ONLY one I found to be truly incredible. The tone is sexy and sweet, and can be shaped to fit almost any genre. Theres even an "internal gain trim pot" which means there is a dial on the inside of the pedal that can be turned for more or less gain. This unique and almost unheard of feature is brilliant and should be a standard for dirt pedals. Lucky it does have it, because ho boy does it have a LOT of gain. Even with gain knob ALL the way down to nothing, its still a strong overdrive soft clipping sound. With the gain maxed, and the tight knob turned you can get the sweetest palm muted E chugging, great for Metallica and Slayer style thrash metal.

10/10 - literally perfect score, I cant think of a criticism for this beauty. Its very cheap for a boutique distortion pedal too, the other heavyweights like Wamplers Deluxe pedals, Revv, Bogner and Diezel pedals cost $70-200 more. $200 for this pedal feels like a steal.
Summary: After going through half a dozen boutique distortion pedals... I found the ONE!

But, I got it wet yesterday and it was in the guitar all night and today. The sponge was a little drier, I noticed.

The hard plastic ring, according to the manufacturer's instructions, is made of a plastic that won't react with the guitar's finish. So, I left it on. Basically, get the sponge wet and then squeeze out all excess water. Use a towel and thoroughly dry the exterior of the humidifier. I remove the hard plastic ring for that. It's easy because the rest of the humidifier is a soft plastic material. So, once dry, put the humidifier over the sound hole, under the strings. Slip the "wings" under the sound hole. The hard plastic ring is between the body of the guitar and the humidifier.

I purchased this AC adapter to use with my Tascam DP-008EX portastudio home recorder specifically because the title, photo and description of the adapter led me to believe this was an OEM Tascam adapter - which is what I expected. What I received did not look anything like the adapter in their ad, plus it was not a Tascam product. It is made by a company called "UpBright". See the photos I've attached which show the adapter I received. However, this adapter does power my Tascam recorder and so far seems to work just fine. The jack does not insert all the way into the device, but it still seems secure. I'm not pleased that it was not at all what their ad depicts tough.

PROS: It works and powers my Tascam DP-008EX recorder
CONS: It is not what I was led to believe I was buying. It is not a Tascam OEM adapter. It is significantly overpriced for a no name generic adapter (there are identical generic ones for much less money available). The jack does not insert completely into the device (about 3/16" gap between the device and the black plastic grip on the adapter jack where the metal part of the jack in put is exposed).

The seller should revise their ad to show an actual photo of what they are selling and provide the correct name of the manufacturer of the adapter (UpBright) so buyer will know exactly what they are buying and not confuse it with an OEM adapter.
Summary: It works but it is NOT what is pictured, and not OEM.

I have been on the hunt for a desktop audio solution for casual listening and occasional mixing for many years now. I've tried the Vanatoo T0s, which just didn't have enough lowend headroom at a "fun" listening volume, the JBL 305p MkIIs which have a very fun sound to them but are a bit harsh on treble and have a bit of a "plastic-y" timbre that's impossible to quite put your finger on. I've tried the Adam T5vs which were amazing but again struggled with bass. Treble through the AMT was incredible, however. Adding a subwoofer is not preferable for me because I've found that you have to spend an *unbelievable* amount of money to find something that's not a boomy mess.

Enter the Kalis. My first impressions out of the box were "Wow, these speakers are huge. Like, almost comically huge even on my giant 98" desk" quickly followed by "Wow, these are uh... kind of ugly." I chose the white thinking that the cabinet and speaker being contrasting colors would help the sex appeal a little bit but it ends up drawing more attention to their size. Seriously though, pictures don't do it justice. These are massive speakers and completely dwarf the JBL 305s.

Then, I plugged them in and went through my test tracks and let me tell you- “there's no replacement for displacement” as the car guys say. The added "kick" that I felt I was missing could only be remedied by physically larger speakers, and with the LF trim upped 2db they definitely provide that fun sound that I was itching for. Let me clarify- I'm by no means a basshead, but there's something primally appealing about feeling a bassline or kick drum in your chest- and I don't want to have to crank to ear-bleeding volumes to experience it. This is the best bass experience that you can get without a completely ridiculous 8" monitor or a subwoofer. Quantity is there, and it's incredibly tight and controlled thanks to the front-ported design. For my fellow desktop users who have no choice but to position their speakers right up against the wall, this design is a godsend and prevents the bloated, boomy nastiness that happens with rear ports against a wall. It lets you comfortably turn them up without destroying the sound.

For as much as I've ranted about the bass, you might be thinking of these as having a KRK Rokit-esque sound signature- let me be clear! This is NOT the case. The reason I obsess about bass is because so many cheap monitors completely fall apart in that category even when they do well elsewhere. This is a decent but not overwhelming quantity of nice, controlled low end. But it's not even what impressed me most about these guys...

Kali claims that they sacrificed on cabinet design to squeeze a nicer woofer into the LP6 than the JBL 305 or 306 lines, but in practice they're not worlds apart from one another. The Kalis have noticeably better midrange which is appreciated, but they're not incredibly different from one another. The tweeter appears as though it might literally be the same part, but whatever Kali has done with their tuning has reigned in the piercing nature of JBL's implementation to a degree where it ends up having a lot of the "smoothness" of an AMT design. JBL's ridiculous looking waveguide might have something to do with it, but who knows.

Overall, the Kalis are legitimately very very well engineered monitors for their price point and the guys have outdone themselves for their first product. They're good to a degree where they really start getting into the territory of being unforgiving on poorly mixed and mastered music, which is exactly what you want from a production tool but hurts my heart a little bit as my use for them so often includes casual listening. The tradeoff of how these come to life on well produced albums is entirely worth it, though.
Summary: Maybe one of the best audio deals ever?

The tuners and bridge are serviceable cheapies. I replaced the tuners on mine with some Fender tuners I had and the bridge with a Hipshot Kickass bridge. I would have had to move the bridge anyway since it was installed too far forward to intonate this bass. I had to fill holes and re-drill for the new bridge. The wiring harness is a joke. Dime sized no name pots and a resistor that is so tiny you need a magnifying glass to see it. Fine for a beginner but not a pro. The pickups had a hollow weak sound. I changed the harness and pickups. The cavity was big enough to use American size pots. If you’re going to change pickups keep the original pickup covers and put them on the new pickups as the original covers themselves are oversized and it will leave a very noticeable gap if you use the covers that come with standard P-Bass pickups.
Would I buy another? Not in this lifetime.
