So I'm using the Behringer XM8500 dynamic microphone. Hooked up via XLR to a U-Phoria 204HD. Sometimes to other things. But mainly needed it to be positionable for meetings, recordings, etc.

The XM8500 is pretty hefty. So I was concerned that this arm might have wiggle or would be loose. It was not. The springs on the arms give it a great deal of resistance to change, but not so stiff that it is problematic to move about.

As you can see in the photo, I mounted it to the left side of my desk, have the XLR cable velcroed in place with the provided velcro strips, and have the pop screen screwed onto the mic holder and the flexible arm kinda going around and above the mic, ultimately lowering the screen over the front of the mic facing where I would be speaking into the mic.

I've got sound dampening cloth all around my work space.

After bolting into place on the table and test moving it around, the arm and microphone moves where it needs to move and stays put once I move it. The screen, being mounted to the mic mount, is always in the right spot without needing to be repositioned. The springs do not make any sound when the arms are moving. So +1 for that.

So far, I like it. Definitely worth the low price I paid for it.

Text:
Mystified as to why Amazon lets sellers get away with this. If an instrument is advertised as “Solid Mahogany,” and if the description says, “the ukulele is made of solid mahogany,” then all the major body components — top, back and sides—should be solid (I.e., not laminated) wood.

Careful examination of the uke I received shows that the grain of the sides, on the inside, is running at 90 degrees to that of the outside. The back grain on the inside also does not perfectly match the outside. So, clearly, only the top is solid wood, and the seller should, ethically, describe this as “solid-topped,” and not “solid.”

This is still a pretty good uke for the price point, but it is not the steal it appears to be, and it irks me that the potentially more gullible entry-level customers at whom this uke is marketed are being misled in this fashion.

The Montage is amazing and it has so much going on that it would take years to explore all the sounds you can get out of it. But it is not a "workstation". This is because its sequencer is not designed to handle editing tasks. For this you need to connect to the DAW on your computer. Once you have done this, you can edit all you like. Also, Montage OS 2.5 allows you to control your DAW remotely, including transport controls, track volume and other things, as well as integrate your DAW output through the Montage itself, this makes it possible for the Montage to form the heart of an extremely powerful system.

There is very little not to like. The keyboard on the 8 is excellent and very sensitive, the sounds are fantastic and the ability to dive in and program is great. Along with everything else, it can also import Motif patches and performances. Plus, Yamaha's online converter allows you to take your old patches - going back to the DX7 - convert them to Montage format, and then download them. This means that the Montage has access to thousands of extra sounds.

When you combine, power, features, sound quality, ease of programming and UI, I am not aware of any other supersynth to compare with it. Compared with the Kronos, for example, you may not be able to set up eight zones, but with the Montage and its ability to set up multiple layers of different zones and switch zones while switching performances, this is not much of an issue. As regards everything else, it handily beats the Kronos and at a similar price.
Summary: A truly amazing instrument truly deserving to be called a supersynth,  but not a workstation.

OK, lets get this right, it is a $99 guitar from Fender / Squire.  One person spoke of wishing it's strings were a few inches longer.  If you want that, and a normal strat 25.5 inch scale, buy a Strat.  This is for smaller hands, or a smaller person, or a youngster, or someone like I who had broken his left hand.  MIne came set up very well, but I lowered the action, adjusted intonation, which, though some reviewers disagree, was a total breeze.  I changed the strings to 10's which naturally on a short scale guitar, helped the tone.  If you can handle 11's, they would probably be even better.  If you are just starting, stick with the 9's on there.  String spacing is a little close for me, but not unhandelable.  Just remember is is scaled down in all measurements, not just scale length.  I have found it such a good guitar that I invested in new pickups that have this thing singing.  Everyone has their own taste.  There are reasons to get this guitar and there are reasons to upgrade it if you want.  All in all, for $99 you would be hard pressed to find anything better.  Every Strat I have owned has needed fret leveling.  This may need some, but for $99, who cares.  It is when you buy a $1500 guitar and then find the frets need some work that you get angry.  This also is so much easier to play then an acoustic guitar for kids just starting out.  Not saying one is better, but if I had this as a kid, I would have played much more.  It is just a fun instrument and can sound incredibly good.

I've uploaded customer-supplied images above to show just how much gear one of these is capable of holding and how small the stage or studio footprint is. When you factor in the price it's plain to see that this rack is not only a bargain, but a flexible platform for mounting components.

One other characteristic that the images reveals is this is not a table-top only rack. They work very well on the floor.

The rack itself is easy to assemble and is built like a tank. I have a bass amp head and a power amp, plus a power conditioner in one of my racks that, combined, weighs around 50 pounds. The rack is not stressed or strained by this weight, and could probably hold another 50 pounds safely and reliably. Another plus is it comes with a bag of high quality mounting screws for components, eliminating that expense (I was expecting to have to order [[ASIN:B0001FTVD6 Raxxess Rack Screws With Washers Hardware (Pack of 25)]], which turned out to be completely unnecessary.)

My only complaint is the rubber feet caps easily fall off, but a little glue rectified that rather trivial problem.

If you need portability, reliability and value for smaller gear suites that are frequently moved (such as setting up on stages) this is an ideal solution for rack mounted equipment. I am so pleased with mine that I intend to purchase another one, bringing the total to three.

This is a pretty decent little low-profile patch cable. I actually measured it's length at 26 inches, rather than 2 ft, if that matters at all. If you use just these low profile cables, you can get two pedals to be within 3/4 of an inch of each other. With standard patch cables, you are lucky to get them about 1 1/8 inch apart. This very low profile adds up to maybe let you squeeze just one more pedal on your board. So, basically, that's what you're getting for the price. . . the ability to squeeze one more pedal in.

I am always concerned with tone-suck in longer signal chains, so I measure the capacitance. This 2ft patch cable introduces about 92pf of parasitic capacitance. That's a little high for just a 2 foot cable, and I was a little surprised, but it's also not horrible. It's in the typical range for average quality patch cables (e.g. not-pro grade). I must admit, for the D'Addario name brand and price, I was expecting a bit better (like 60 or 70pf). I've noticed these higher capacitance ratings on several low profile cables, and I assume it just has something to do with the physical shape of the cable (i.e. flat, rather than round).

Otherwise, I really like these cables, and I use them on my own pedal board. They are not bulky at all, and the low profile is nice. However, I am subtracting just one star for the price being a little high without an audio quality justification to go with it. I think you're mostly buying the name here. But part of buying the name is also buying D'Addario's lifetime guarantee of the cable (the guarantee is stamped right on the cord!).

Final Rating: 4 stars. Great low-profile cable, with a lifetime guarantee, but the price is a little higher.
Summary: Nice low profile cable for pedalboard - 92pf capacitance

This Korg tuner is a real learning tool because it responds to notes fast enough to indicate whether you're playing in tune while you're playing a piece (admittedly, a slow piece).

I play violin and playing in tune has become a real driver for me. Here's how I've used the Korg to help. First, I rip a CD of the piece I'm playing to a wav file using Windows Media Player. Then I import that wav file into Audacity, which is wonderful FREE downloadable sound-editing software. Ok, so now I see the wave diagram of the piece before me on the screen.

Finally, I use headphones to listen to the piece while Audacity plays it, and the Korg sits on my music stand while I play along. There it is... thanks to the Korg, I discovered that I was playing consistently about 15-20 cents sharp almost all the time. I've had to re-educate my ear.

Sometimes I record what I play on a second track in Audacity, while listening to the CD (the first track) through the headphones. Audacity makes that easy. Later I can go back, mute the CD track, and play my recorded track through the speakers -- the Korg picks that up and once again tells me how in tune I was (or not).

Really a useful device! I had it with me today in a quartet rehearsal, and at one point one of the other players stopped everyone and said to me, "You're flat!" I had the Korg on, and I hadn't moved my finger so I played the note -- I was dead on. They were all sharp. Now that is cool...

The only thing the Korg is missing, for me, is a metronome. Oh well.
Summary: A real help learning to play in tune

The included software is nice especially if you're just starting out.

Not exactly a negative but more something to bear in mind. The Motu M2 is basically the exact same interface but with fewer inputs and outputs. If you don't think you need the extra inputs and outputs that the M4 has, the M2 is a much better deal for you.

Edit after a couple years of ownership: the Motu M4 is still my absolute favorite interface, however there is one quirk that I have found. I'm not sure whether it's MOTU's fault or Windows, but at least partial blame goes to MOTU considering no other interface I've used has had this bug. Occasionally it would output and record sound as if it had been pitch shifted (think Alvin and the Chipmunks). I believe it is some sort of clock sync error with Windows. After getting into contact with their technical support (who deserve props for not just regurgitating the same useless copy-pasted answers and actually problem solving effectively), I was presented with a simple solution: disable fast startup on your PC. Once I did that, the problem was immediately solved and has not occurred again for well over a year.

Personally, I still think it's an excellent interface and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it despite that bizarre quirk. Latency is still incredibly impressive and the preamps are still very clean. I've also come to love the monitoring screen, it's become very difficult to go back to an interface without it.
Summary: If you need the extra I/O the Motu M4 is perfect. If you don't, get the M2

Text:
I'm not a drummer, but thought I'd like to pretend to be. That said, the default voices sound pretty darn good to my ears. I've not had any problems with volume but on rare occasion the hat sounds are clipped.

Being able to play through headphones is a real plus since I rent and relentless banging probably wouldn't fly with the neighbors.

As others have mentioned, setup wasn't straightforward, as the diagrams are a little vague as to the orientation of some of the joint and mount pieces. All told it took me about two hours to assemble, but I'm also a perfectionist.

The included drumsticks are serviceable, but feel like they just came off the lathe and have a fine layer of sawdust on them. They discolor the pads and cymbals, but it wipes off with a damp cloth. I recommend investing in a better set sooner than later. Also, a throne isn't necessary, but I picked one up before this was delivered, so I can't comment on comfort and usability with a chair, but I can't imagine it'll have much disadvantage.

The two pedals have a very strong Velcro on them. I have hardwood floors, so before assembling I bought a 4'x6' low pile area rug. I've had no issues with them sliding. Additionally, I recommend some zip-ties or Velcro strips for the cables, as they are a bit messy otherwise.

I also chose to keep the packaging (every piece comes in its own box all packed in the main box) so if/when I move I can pack it back up. Unfortunately, I didn't photograph the arrangement of boxes in the main box as I unpacked, so getting everything back in was like a losing game of physical Tetris. However, some other reviewers did take photos and those helped, so many thanks to them.

I didn't get this for free for a review (if I'd known it was a possibility I might have explored that avenue!) and I'll admit sometimes I've almost had a tinge of buyer's remorse. Not on the kit itself, but that I plunked down $500 for it. Then I look at prices of some of the higher end kits available, and for what I got, have to admit it's a pretty good deal. In the end I don't regret it. In fact, a friend (who's a much better drummer than I) was telling me he bought the Alesis model one step down a couple years ago for about $650, so this set really does seem to be a good deal.

One final note: once my skill gets to a passable level, I'm looking forward to using it in my home recordings. The thought of plugging this in directly rather than having to mic an acoustic set is very appealing.

As owner of an original Juno, I found this item to be an abomination, since it is not analog but digitally modeled. Although once I started to use it, I found myself more and more attracted to it, to the point where I decided to get one for various projects that require that typical Juno sound, but that does not require me to spend 8K to get one, and repair it every other day.

The build is plastic but the top is metal; all is doll-house sized; but I can operate controls with ease. Chords on the buttons are not feasible, but single bass lines or lead in monophonic mode are something doable. Faders are also small, and I don't get why didn't they make the device using knobs that takes less space, and selector switches, but I guess they wanted to keep the look of the Juno. Personally I could care less how something look like, and are more focused on what it does.

So, how does it sound? Like a Juno. Not 100% but 96% similar, to the point where some patches are identical almost, to the point where the humming and noise are perceivable like on the original; but being a modern device, takes the space of a book, use batteries and it is much more reliable.

What I don't like is that some features are deep down the menu diving experience, and the display is a segment display that can barely display base numbers and few characters; I would honestly spend more on a small multiline LCD like the ones used on Korg minilogue for example; which would help with readability and usage.
You can expect a simple display like this on a Volca, which cost 3 times less than this device, but not on something in this price range.

Another thing that I do not like is the patch management. Roland as usual did nothing to make available for users a librarian or editor of some sort; so you are forced to rename patches in a way that bring you back to the 80s; with fixed naming for patches; and upload them to the device via USB. On this, it feels like being in the 80s and not on a modern device.

Another issue that some people complained about is the 4 voices polyphony instead of 6. It is different from the Juno, true; but for the price; feels OK. I don't know too many 6 voices synths in this price range, beside the Deepmind maybe.

Also beware; the keyboard module is not included. The picture is deceiving, you are buying the module and the module only, so do not expect the keyboard with it.

Overall great device, great sound, a bit on the small side for controls but I use it mostly via MIDI, so it is not a deal breaker. Patch management and editors are a mirage, but if you know your way around Sysex and midi, you can make your own editor. Worth with a 20% discount maybe, but even at full price it is a great Juno replacement.

Text:
This stuff is just fine. I think people get upset thinking it's poison from some big company. Looking at the poison facts sheet (which they publish, apparently, to sell this stuff in Germany- It's on the Thomann website) the ingredient they list as toxic is "white mineral oil". I have that stuff in my medicine cabinet. Sometimes I take a pull on it just for kicks. That's all it lists as a hazard..
To be clear, there is no actual "lemon" in this oil save for the artificial smell. Any "natural" oils would turn rancid after a period of time. And it's not the same stuff marketed for furniture or wood restoration. See, the association with "lemon oil" was a desirable one in the market at at some point. Techs would tell you to get a "bottle of lemon oil" (old english say) so these companies started making products more for guitar using that association. Now, it's kind of a dirty word: people want "natural" ingredients or, at the very least to pamper their guitars so these products are now victims of the very association that they originally wanted. The bottom line is: who knows all-in-all what's in this stuff. In any of the similar products really. It's quite thin and is actually a good fretboard cleaner as well on its own. I doubt it is more or less "natural" than any other product. Goodness, white petroleum and the distillates thereof are ubiquitous.
I admit, for my pricier instruments, some of which may need more nourishment, I've always used a fingerboard oil by "Roche Thomas". It's a bit thicker and is more of a straight oil. I've had the same bottle for at least 30 years.. It's great stuff. I finish my bass fingerboard with it only on the rare occasion I use Naptha to clean the rosin off. It rehydrates well. I also use it on my classical guitars. But now I set up guitars and end up cleaning and in some cases restoring guitars - call it a professional adjunct. For most of my players, and for my students' instruments which may have ne'er seen a rag before they see me, this Dunlop stuff is the exact right thing. I will say, I wish they would publish the ingredients. One star off that I had to go to Germany to get ANY info on this.

About a month ago I picked up three new picks at my guitar store--the 2.0 mm Jim Dunlop Delrin pick (the dark purple one in the photo), a Jim Dunlop 208 jazz pick, and 1.52 mm Clayton USA teardrop pick. Mere weeks before that, my lovely wife got me a gift of a pack of the well-known and very expensive V-Picks (you won't find those on Amazon). Also, strewn about my house are tons of 0.60 mm Jim Dunlop nylon picks (my standard for over a decade), and Jim Dunlop .71 mm Gator Grip picks. Among all those choices, I keep a very close eye on where my 2.0 mm Delrin pick is, because it's really the only one I want to use anymore.

Its features that might be of interest to you would be:

1) it does not flex or bend. At all. Apparently they're designed to be that way.
2) it has a very smooth texture--no grip built into the surface. Much to my surprise, though, I've never dropped it, and I use it literally every day.
3) it lasts. As I said, I use it every day. I've used it for at least an hour, usually 3 or more, per day, for the last month. I've got some wear on the normal spots on either side of the pick, but my gray nylon Dunlop would be a stub by now, and the V-pick that I use the most is just as worn as the Delrin one is, but I've used it only a fraction of the time in comparison.
4) the 2.0 mm feels comfortable. I know full well that's a preference thing, but I'm still fascinated that I enjoy the feel of a thick pick so much.
5) the tone is strong and bright with these, and the pick itself is quiet. I primarily play a Gretsch G-5122 with 12-guage DR strings. My lighter picks provide big sound, but they have almost have a "pop" to them when I strum or play individual notes. My V-picks grate across the winding on my lower strings, and produce a much mellower tone. My Delrin doesn't grate and creates a big sound.
6) it's reasonably fast. I mentioned earlier I also have a Jim Dunlop 208. If you want a fast pick, go with that bad boy--it's designed for nothing else. I have had a few overdrive mini pedals, so I am familiar with how they sound. When I plugged this one in, I was bracing for some great overdrive sound. What I got instead was quite different.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes with a box and of course, foam glued on the back of it so that if you want to use velcro, you have to scrape off the foam. I wish these companies would include both velcro and foam pads so we can choose what we want.

NOISE
This was just a little noisy when I first turned it on, but not too bad. When I turned my guitar on, it seemed to get less.

BYPASS
This seems like a true bypass, but there is a small hum occasionally which I am not sure about. When I swap this mini pedal out and try another, the hum is gone (same single pedal unit same power source, cords, etc).

PERFORMANCE
Well, to put it bluntly, no matter what I tried to do, this sounded like I was playing at the next door neighbors house in their closet. I kid you not.

I thought perhaps something was wrong with my settings. I fiddled with my guitar, and then the other settings, but every time no matter WHAT I did, the stupid thing sounded like I was playing in the closet at the next door neighbors with the DOOR SHUT.

I put another pedal in swapping that one out and almost blew myself across the room. That pedal was clear and very loud and pronounced.

I put the Vintage Overdrive pedal back and same muffled almost not there sound again.

I tried every combination of dials and nothing seemed to change the muffled sound much at all. I was beginning to wonder if vintage meant like listening on a very old record player on batteries .. in the closet .. with the door shut. HAHAHA Sorry, there seems to be a recurring theme here..

THE BOTTOM LINE
This pedal must have been a dud. I know others have gotten this pedal and it is a great over drive pedal. In my case, it is awful. If I got this pedal as the first overdrive mini pedal ever, I probably would never have gotten another one again. It is THAT BAD.

MY RATING
ONE STAR. This should sound way better than this. I think I got a dud. I feel like Charlie Brown trick or treating.. I got a rock. Except if I got a rock, it would sound way better than this, right? *chuckles*

UPDATES
If somewhere along the line I find out that there is a silly explanation for this and the pedal works, I will update my review. I never had to work this hard to make a pedal work, but there is always a first time. Unless that happens, I will leave it as it is.

I have Komplete 10 Ultimate and Maschine Studio. I got this keyboard for a steal. My ONLY reason for purchasing was to experience its integration with my NI software. I have 3 separate opinions for this keyboard:

Using with NI software in 3rd party DAW: I get basic transport functionality to the DAW and good integration with NI software, especially recent instruments like Rounds, Polyplex, etc. Older Reaktor ensembles won't be as fluid...but that is not an issue for me. Arp, Scale, transpose and advanced knob functions will be limited to Komplete Kontrol plugin (which can now host AU/VSTi inside). Several developers have adopted the NKS format, which makes Kontrol software plugin more versatile with popular and well-maintained plugins

Using with Maschine 2.x: This has been the best case scenario for me. Inside of Maschine, I can use Arp, Scale, Transpose with BOTH native and 3rd party plugins...knobs are also automapped and pages are generated as necessary. If you own Maschine, the Komplete keyboard will be a pleasant addition.

Using as midi keyboard without software: It will work fine as a standard keyboard with pitch bend, modulation, and assignable CC knobs. No arp, scale, transpose function.

Note that the anchor screw on these is larger than most guitar strap buttons, so your guitar will need to be drilled out a little to make them fit. If you have any reservations about doing this yourself, I would highly recommend getting the straplocks installed professionally.

One potential issue with these that I have encountered is that the straplocks are not all the same size. I have Schallers on two guitars and straps and I cannot use the straps interchangeably because one set of straplocks is larger than the other and the strap adapter will not fit with out getting stuck. Keep this in mind if you like to use the same strap on multiple guitars.
Summary: Great Straplocks, but Beware - Not All of Them Are Interchangeable!

The Mackie Reach, while small in stature, packs a decent wallop. It boasts 720 watts through a class D amplifier into two 6.5” and three 1” drivers, along with a 4” driver on either side. With four XLR/tip ring sleeve (Neutrik style) inputs, it’s 3mm stereo input and Bluetooth, there is no shortage of connectivity.

The onboard controls take a bit of practice – and reading glasses – to obtain proficiency in their use, but with a bit of intuition and the online manual, they become increasingly user friendly. With a bit of practice, one can control all aspects of the Reach from these physical dials and buttons. Volume can be adjusted as input per channel and summed into one channel to adjust the overall volume. The effects are similarly accessed, and provide a decent array of reverbs, choruses, delays and combinations thereof. Individually, the effects parameters can be adjusted for the amount of the effect desired per channel.

The Reach can also be controlled from an IOS device or any compatible Bluetooth capable cellphone or device. The application, called “Mackie Connect”, works well and is rather intuitive, but does have some issues. When first installed, it will open in a “Demo” mode, which gives the user an idea of its capabilities and how to use the app. One simply has to pair the Reach with a Bluetooth device, and the opening screen of the app switches from “Demo” to “Mix” mode. Once there, you can control the Reach from anywhere within range of the Bluetooth device. This is where it gets a bit tricky and mildly frustrating. The app defaults back to Demo mode if somehow the signal from the Bluetooth device is interrupted. The problem is that it is not clearly discernable that the app has defaulted to demo, and I caught myself making futile attempts to control the Reach, not aware that it had gone to demo mode. At this point, I needed to reboot the application and pair it with the Reach again. This happened several times during my tests of the Reach. Additionally, several times the Bluetooth settings in my IOS device indicated that the Reach was indeed connected; yet the app remained in the demo mode. It took a bit of patience and finagling to get the two to pair. During a performance or presentation this could be devastating.

Also, if you want to stream Pandora or similar music services, the Connect app is overridden by the IOS devices controls for sound. If streaming, the app defaults to demo, and there is only access to the functions via the onboard controls.

As far as what it can and cannot do. It can serve as a very capable PA for presentations or behind the screen for a projector movie night. There is plenty of volume for a coffeehouse acoustic gig. It handles dynamic microphones nicely, but has no phantom power for condenser microphones. I tested it with two microphones and two very active test vocalists for an evening of high volume gibberish testing for volume, tone, effects and feedback. It is loud. Very loud. Amazingly loud for a package this small. The feedback destroyer functions as a notch filter, so the sound remained quite clear even with the mic very close to the speakers. We tinkered with the reverbs and delays, which, while not from the latest Waves plug in catalog, served their purpose satisfactorily.

The next evening, I set up the Reach as a PA for a musical combo including guitar, drum set, saxophone, Theremin, bass and keyboards, featuring a caterwauling male and female singer. They were staged “in the round”. The Reach was used exclusively for vocals, and it delivered clear and audible results. The side speakers widened the sound enough for the whole combo to hear. The reverb gave a gentle softening of the vocals, allowing them to blend nicely into the mix.

At another event, I linked a signal from a house board to the Reach and used it as a supplement to the main PA, which was rather small. The Reach provided enough extra power that together with the small house system was audible over a rather loud rock band, and worked well as a monitor system.

As far as sound quality is concerned, the Reach’s two 6.5” “woofers”, while producing a decent low end, cannot compete with a larger loudspeaker for those bass heavy moments, but that is not the goal of this PA. There is a bit of hiss when cranked up, but it is likely to be used in a fashion that rarely requires full volume, so it’s not that much of an issue.

All in all, I find that the connectivity and versatility of this speaker are what makes it desirable. Great for small crowd PA use, music at a barbeque, coffeehouse gig, and similar applications. It’s light and loud enough for a small musical combo, but would likely be overwhelmed if used for a traditional rock band. The app, while frustrating at times, is versatile and intuitive, and when it works, it does what it is designed to do adequately. One thousand bucks (!) puts the Reach out of reach for what is essentially a specialty speaker. There are louder PA systems available for similar costs, but the portability and versatility of the Reach can’t be beat.

Sound________________________A- to B
Quality of build______________A
User friendliness____________B (The Connect app__ B-)
Versatility____________________A
Portability____________________A
Price point___________________B
Overall impression__________I like it and will have many uses for the Reach.

Got this cabinet as a Warehouse deal for $98 vs $109 brand new. No cosmetic flaws, cabinet’s clean, no obvious problems. Paired with an Orange Micro Terror 20w head- obvious nice Orange crunch or clean sound depending how you set it. For distortion, have settings of high gain/low volume on the head, guitar volume at 1/4-1/2 up versus high guitar volume/12 o’clock head gain. Clean is with the head gain at 12 o’clock, and whatever volume you want.
For me the first setting for distortion works best without having to blast the Orange cabinet past its capacity for the same effect. On stage, you can mic the cabinet or go through the PA for decent results. Nita Strauss has shown us what she can do with just a Roland board through Alice Cooper’s PA.
Got this cabinet and the Roland Mini (7 watt amp) as alternatives to lugging around 25-50 lb Fender tube amps for intimate-small gigs.
Overall, the Roland Mini with its loaded features and very light weight case offers more versatility. One could argue the Orange’s Micro Terror tube/solid state technology head offers more warmth/sound variation and wattage though there’s no delay or EQ feature as the Roland. Both amps only have one input jack.
My hot rodded Squier Tele bridge pup sounds its country best on the Orange. My Gretsch Duo Jet sounds warm, though its filtron pups are beefier, less twangy than the Tele. The Roland is dependable, well built. Jazz/clean sounds are good on both amps though subjectively, the Orange is warmer on the same aforementioned guitars.
Overall, you’re paying for the Orange name with this cabinet- it’s overpriced for what it is, though matches nicely with the Terror head. Gotta decide if you want a girl with nice tubes or one with a plastic/solid state figure.
Summary: Wanna Orange or Roland Mini girlfriend?

I play an American Standard Strat, manufactured in the year 2000. The guitar is equipped with the two point (two screw) bridge, with the block bridge pieces. According to 3 days of my own research (and zero help from Fender, by the way...), I determined that this was the correct bridge, because Fender also makes an almost identical trem arm for Vintage Strats, which come with the six point (six - screw) older style bridge, with the rolled steel bridge pieces.

There is also a Mexican Strat trem arm which also looks very similar, but is too big in diameter to fit the American Standard bridge. Upon receipt of this arm, it fit beautifully. It came with a bright white knob, and a off-white, kind of eggshell color knob, to fit with vintage style pickguards and volume and tone knobs. It is threaded, and so it screws on and off. It is meant to be installed with a trem arm spring, to keep it in place, as sometimes it can be screwed in, and have enough play to make noise, and the trem spring is designed to hold it in place. Not strictly necessary though.

TO ENSURE THIS TREMELO ARM WILL FIT, CONFIRM THAT:

* The touch screen is a not terrible responsive, I find it difficult to set it at the tempo I want..

* I find the quiet blinking option almost unusable (YMMV). The blue horseshoe blinks, but it's not terribly bright relative to the rest of the screen,

*The blue horseshoe may start up to light up the same time as the beat, but it takes the merest fraction of a second to reach full intensity. That causes the impression, in the 120 bpm range, that the blink and the beat are the slightest bit out of agreement as though the beat ever so slightly leads the blink.

* There is a flip out stand on the back so that the metronome doesn't have to lie flat on the table. In what I consider a major design flaw, the portion that flips out from the back runs up and down the length of the battery cover. It's designed in such a way that the battery cover comes off when the stand is flipped out too far.

The SM-1 is compact, but so is the Korg MA-1 (http://www.amazon.com/Korg-MA1BL-Visual-Counting-Metronome/dp/B0055BMQG0/)..

The Korg KDM-2 (http://www.amazon.com/Korg-KDM-2-Advanced-Digital-Metronome/dp/B001EWN72Q) remains my own personal favorite. However, I admit it has been years since my last exhaustive look-see at metronomes.

Text: Just what I Needed

I love these things. I have one for each of my guitars. (NOTE: Make sure you get the correct size. Measure. My two smaller Martins needed the "classical" version; my larger martins and Gibson needed the regular size.)

What I love is that it holds the humidity inside the guitar. This is especially useful if your home is almost humid enough but not quite. You can leave your guitars out with this in the soundhole (however, if it gets below 30%, I either humidify the room or put them in their cases and humidify the cases).

I have these in the soundholes most of the time. If they're in the case, I still have them in the soundholes, but then I also stick in a Herco clay humidifier or something else in the case. The case itself sucks up humidity, as does the neck. But, primarily, what needs humidity is the naked wood inside the guitar, and that's what these do.

These can actually also help protect your guitar from too much humidity, too, though I'm not sure how effective they are for that purpose.

Some people have complained about the rubber discoloring their guitar. I have not had that issue or experience at all. Others have complained about leaks. I also have not experienced that. Don't overfill the sponge, and it'll be fine. (You can even overfill it somewhat and it's still fine.) As for the rubber ring, some folks take it off. I have left mine on, as they are intended. It works great.
Summary: Great alternative humidifier--cheaper and holds the humidity INSIDE the guitar

I've used more than a handful of USB/Firewire interfaces over the past decade. In the past, it's always been a crapshoot, regardless of brand or reputation. Instability, incompatability, and frustration abound with audio interfaces. That being said, this has been the best interface I've ever owned.

The size is fantastic, the preamps sound great, it has phantom power, it looks cool, and most importantly, it's been rock solid ever since I installed it two and a half months ago.

I frequently leave my PC on 24 hours a day with this plugged in, and as of yet I haven't had a single crash, dropout, 'pop' etc. It's performed flawlessly since day one.

Regarding sound quality, my recordings have never sounded better. I've used this to record electric guitar straight into the unit, acoustic guitar via condenser mics, dynamic mics, hammered dulcimer, cello, synth via direct input, and it handles it all flawlessly. I'm seriously impressed with the quality.

Finally, it's small enough to take with me when I want to record at a friends house on my laptop.

I've used it with Reaper, Sonar X1, Guitar Rig 5, Cubase LE, all without a hitch, on two PC's - Both Win 7 64-bit. The drivers gave me no hassle installing, and as I said above, ROCK SOLID.

Your mileage may vary, as I stated earlier audio interfaces can be quite the crap shoot. Same setup, same hardware, etc, and one person can have wildly differing results. That being said, I would definitely recommend this unit, as it is my favorite of all time, and I've used everything from crappy firewire mixers to high-end MOTU interfaces.

Great for the price, and if 2-in/2-out works for you, it should perform better than interfaces costing twice as much. It performs better than my old MOTU 828 mkII that I got for five hundred.

The Venue is a complete toolbox for amplified acoustic tone. The entire design shows that a great deal of thought went into it.
I had already been using LR Baggs Element pickups exclusively on four acoustic guitars, so I felt very confident that they had gotten
it right. I have not been disappointed. If you have been plugging directly into a console, no matter how good, I think your instrument
will sound better through this.

Here's my recommendation:

One feature that attracted me was the ability to battery power the box. I don't like to deal with any more plugs than necessary when gigging. <g>
However, when a battery died just before a gig, I found that this box works MUCH better if you use a power supply. Using it over the last six months, I had noticed occasional distortion and a compressed sound when strumming, even with a fresh battery and carefully adjusted gain. Those
problems have disappeared with the use of a wall wart. The sound is smoother and more transparent with a power supply.

Asking a 9V battery to deliver the current apparently needed for this box is a bit much. There is a great deal of headroom and fidelity built in, but it is only available with a power supply. I highly recommend that you use one.

I am very happy with the Venue.
Summary: Use a power supply to get the full benefit of this excellent device.

I think it's clear that one has to get their expectations to be realistic. If you're expecting this $140 unit to be exactly as good as one of the industry leaders that costs five to ten times as much, you'll probably be let down. If you need a very specific monitoring setup that this device does not support, it makes little sense to try and save money here, and you should just purchase another device that does do what you need.

That being said, for stereo recording from two microphones, this device does the job very well, with a relatively clean signal and fairly simple software. I use it in a fully mobile recording setup with a MacBook Air M1 running Big Sur and Logic Pro in a concert hall with orchestral musicians to produce symphonic backing tracks for a variety of applications, and it's exactly what I was looking for. Small, simple, and bus-powered. I have a variety of nice microphones available to me these days, but am happy with the results that I get from even inexpensive mic pairings like the Audio-Technica AT2020 cardioid condenser and the MXL R144 ribbon, and for my music students who are getting into recording for the first time, they are able to put together a functional setup for their machines for under $400 including the interface, mics, cables, and stands.

The Big Stubby has a pretty good feel, the depressed area for the fingers does help to maintain grip, and beveled edge helps reduce drag on the strings. This tuner is more than I expected. It is extremely accurate and Very, very sensitive. When they mention "Tight" tuning, they are not just spewing sound bites. I found that my other tuner had been allowing me to tune a few cents sharp, which was annoyingly off register, whereas this nifty little Snark tuner helped me correct that. It allows you to gently creep up from below pitch to stop dead on when the green light begins to flicker. It is so sensitive that you can hardly ever get the green light to Stay on without the slight purple flicker of the Sharp indicator. I tune up from flat and when the Green light blinks, I stop and retest. If there are any flickers of the Sharp indicators, then I know I'm venturing sharp. Of course guitar necks are flexible to an extent, so if you pull or push the neck, you are going to change the pitch. And this little gem detects the Slightest variation in pressure on the neck. That's why I'm careful not to allow any sharp frequencies, because when playing the natural tendency is to pull on the neck, which sharpens the notes. THIS PRODUCT IS EXCELLENT. NEVER HAVE I SEEN BETTER.

Be aware that the screw collars are 14 mm diameter and the original holes in the head are 13.8 mm diameter. You can either open up the holes a little with a 14 mm drill, sandpaper, or do as I did and push them in with a G-clamp. They'll be a tight fit.

Also be aware the original tuner mounting screw holes will be visible. You can leave them or fill them with toothpicks or wood filler. Your choice.

The newer models are marketed to have better more realistic / bigger tone, but sadly it's the case of marketing tactic (I can't get into a marketing dissertation here, but marketers frequently take a liability/flaw and write copy that turns it all around. It's how we're taught. Sorry.) One last word of advice: Unless you can touch and test drive a pre-owned APX STAY AWAY!! These guitars lend themselves to the kind of abuse that uses up and instrument. Combined with the MDY-12 mount this ride swings and rocks around a bit like a real cymbal, which certainly adds some life to an otherwise static kit, and makes it more fun to play since it reciprocates your movements.

Due to Roland's modularity, this wasn't a "for feel only" luxury upgrade; rather, it's an outright expansion. The CY-8 and arm it replaced, instead of sitting sad and forgotten in the closet, simply shifted over and plugged into the Crash 2 slot to become a second dual-zone crash cymbal, which is fantastic with stock and user kits alike and allows for more variation in the cymbal patterns. So if you have an identical setup to mine and asked yourself "is an extra zone really worth this much?", the answer is you're actually gaining three, which certainly justifies the cost to someone like me who practices solo 95% of the time and needs as many variations as possible to generate interesting patterns.

I did not share my fellow reviewers' opinion on the bell's sensitivity, I find that it sits comfortably among the other triggers and can be played with proportional force at stock settings. This is my subjective opinion however, so nobody is wrong to feel otherwise. That said, with the TD11 brain, even if I were unhappy with the sensitivity of the bell (or any zone on my kit), I have the option to adjust their sensitivities individually, which is something I've already done with the stock HH and kick pad and took less than a minute of painless adjustments to accomplish.

The bell DOES take a bit of precision and practice to trigger reliably, as it can be sort of hard to zero in on exactly where you have to hit it at first, but it only took a day or three to improve my accuracy to the point where I could easily trigger it when and how I wanted.

The quality of the construction doesn't need much detail. It's Roland. This baseline TD11k kit is my first piece of Roland gear, but that's all it took for the name to become synonymous with peace of mind when looking for robust build quality.

Aesthetically, it looks like it's always been part of the kit (save for the all-chrome arm it's sitting on). The underside of this cymbal has an attractive glossy white surface that contrasts nicely with the mostly-black kit and matches the mesh heads. The strike face on the bell is already starting to get its texture beaten flat just a bit but it's an entirely cosmetic effect and it shouldn't effect you unless resale value is a major concern for you.

In summary, if you're looking to expand on your TD11 kit, this is a great place to start.
Summary: A lively addition to my TD11K

I have played, listened to, and used audio amps for over 4 decades, and while I haven't owned every name brand amp on the planet, I do know my way around them well enough to spot a good deal when I see one. This is a nice little practice amp for electrified acoustic guitar, with an input for a mic (XLR - no phantom power) and a CD player or other audio source. It also has a headphone output (1/4 inch). It has three tone controls and separate volume for the guitar and mic inputs.

I got this originally for my mother, who used to sing in an Andrews Sisters-type group back in the day. She still loves to sing, and wanted a small amp and mic to practice and do the occasional small jam. She hasn't had the opportunity to do that yet, but I have tested the amp and put it through its paces. I think it will work fine for the kind of thing she has in mind. The lack of reverb or processing for the mic is a bit of a drawback, but considering what I paid for it, I can't complain.

Now, this is not a gigging amp, at least not in my opinion (your mileage may vary). It is small, solid state, with an 8 inch speaker, and 15 watts of power (I haven't measured the exact output, so I'm taking Behringer's word on that). I like Behringer, and they can turn out some pretty good gear, within its limits.

I like the sound of the amp with my Carvin acoustic guitar with a Fishman preamp. It is an inexpensive practice amp, so I don't expect the same kind of quality I would from a more serious combo amp. The 8 inch speaker is obviously not going to give the kind of sound quality as a good 12 inch, no matter what. The question is, does this amp provide the sonic quality and flexibility needed to allow serious practice work, composition, or just moderate entertainment value? For me, that answer is a clear "yes."

However, this is an inexpensive practice amp, and if you approach it with that attitude, I think you will find it a nice little amp. Don't plan on using it for your next tour with Manhattan Transfer, Seal, or Celine Dion.

Text: Overall great value

When a product's rating on Amazon is substantially different from my own rating, it is usually an indication of one or more of the following:
- Other ratings are superficial and nobody has taken the time to write an in-depth review
- I am using the product in a very different way and see things that other's don't
- There are fake or bought reviews

I can't tell which of the above applies here. Maybe there is a fourth reason. Either way, the American Dj Vertigo does not impress me. I purchased it to make a family event a bit more interesting. I tested the light at home in my living room, and I deployed it at a venue large enough to hold 200 people. I wouldn't purchase this light again for either scenario. At home, the individual light spots, when projected on the walls and ceiling, have the same hourglass shape as the openings on the fixture. This looks a bit cheesy.

At the event hall, I would have needed 5 of these lights to make an impression. I do like the way it responds to the music, but as others have noted, it needs to be close to the speakers and the volume has to be relatively high, definitely beyond the point where people can have conversations. Because of this, I do not recommend this light for an outdoor party. It is limited to the use on a small dance floor.

And lastly, the fact that it cannot be remote-controlled (other than synchronized with another ADJ light that supports this) or programmed makes this light a dead-end for the aspiring DJ who wants to start out small, but add on to his or her equipment over time. This will have to be replaced as you start getting into DMX lighting.

So, in conclusion, for $80 you get an effect light that is better than a $20 laser pointer with different patterns, but cannot compete in the realm of DJ effect lights for the ambitious amateur or professional.
Summary: American Dj Vertigo - not sure where it's sweet spot is

Text:
This does a lot of processing that would take a ton of expensive equipment if you did it all on the rack. But it's not so clear what exactly it's doing. For example, it claims "adaptive EQ," but getting an idea of what it really does to the response curve is not easy. I've done some RTA on it. I use the "less bright mode" (which isn't mentioned in the manual but is noted online), and there doesn't seem to be much change in the EQ. That's good.

I use this primarily for the Tone button, and the pre-amp. I could just use a TC Helicon T1, but I felt getting reverb and pitch correction for a little more and not having more pedals was worth it.

Having all this on a pedal means I don't need a preamp on my mixer. I can I use a line input on a mixer, or even just a powered speaker. With line input levels, there's not a demand for a good preamp which would require spending more on a better mixer with quality preamps and more channels of them.

I debated about getting this or the newer Perform V. The Perform V has a few more bells and whistles like doubles, and could do harmony with a downloaded preset, but for my purposes the main difference would be the floor pedal form factor versus the mic stand clip-on. I decided I prefered the simplicity of the Mic Mechanic and that the floor pedal would be durable and easier to tuck out of the way when I would not need to be pressing any buttons (just using it as a preamp and leaving the tone button on all the time, no effects to adjust or turn on and off).

Roland has a similar box that seemed slightly more complex to me. And then there's much more complex multi-effects like the Voice Live series and equivalents from Roland and others. I chose the MM for simplicity.

Overall, I think this is a great tool to add to a simple microphone setup when you want to have good sound, but focus on singing, or your instrument, and not on a lot of effects manipulation, looping, and other tricks.
Summary: This does a lot of processing that would take a ton of expensive equipment if you did it all on the rack

Text:
Since so many other reviewers said it would be necessary to change the stock tube, I went ahead and ordered a TungSol 12AX7 at the same time. It's a good thing I did, because the pedal arrived with... no stock tube at all! This, of course, meant no sound, so I was getting nervous until I opened it up and realized what was up. With the TungSol in it, it actually produces a fairly nice Marshall-ish crunch tone, and the noise gate works really well. It responds quite dynamically to being boosted with other pedals, but it doesn't clean up much when you turn the guitar down. I don't generally use overdrives that way anyway, so I don't care. I'm using this guy between my existing pedalboard and the amp (Blues Jr), and I like it there. I still have a jones for a Butler Tube Driver, but this is a very, very usable pedal for the money.
UPDATE 10/17/16... I've been experimenting with tubes as many of you have. One important point: the power supply Behringer included is 9V, 300mA. In my pedal at least, a 12AU7 tube will only function if the power supply is at least 500 mA. Drove me crazy for a while, until I decided to try that. It sounds very cool with the low gain tube in it- I think I may even get a second pedal to put a higher gain tube in, and cascade them. What the heck, at this price?
Summary: Great deal for the money- be sure to order a tube!

I recently purchased the Triple Play (not through Amazon), but thought I would leave some feedback for others considering this product. After 1 week since purchase, here are my thoughts so far:

* As others have mentioned, you'll spend a decent amount of time getting the software and hardware setup. While not the worst, I think Fishman needs to do a better job of combining all of the info/instructions/faq in one place. I had a lot of questions that I had to find the answers to elsewhere as well. Their info and help guides seem to be all over the place, and some of their instructions are not very clear. I spent a lot of time in the virtual guitar forums trying to understand how some of this works.

* The hardware installs fairly easily, however the one thing I didn't like was I had to elevate my stratocaster's neck to achieve reasonable string action. Why? Because the midi pickup that comes with the Triple Play controller wouldn't allow me to lower my saddles. Fishman should have made their pickup not so tall...this would prevent this issue.

* Once you get the software setup and hardware installed, the anxiety diminishes and the fun is near. From my understanding so far, the Triple Play software is your home base. From there you can call upon various effects from the included free software. I was unable to install the SampleTank software because only the 32bit version is available. Since Logic Pro X only runs in 64 bit mode, SampleTank 32bit is useless. SampleTank does have a 64bit version now, but unfortunately Fishman doesn't offer this with the included software. Hopefully they will in the future. This seemed odd to me and causes a bit of confusion.

* Aside from the countless hours I've had to spend trying to understand how all of this works, I've had a blast experimenting with the various midi sounds offered. The latency seems pretty good (some better than others)...many of the sounds are cool, some not so much. And where are the bagpipes? I haven't seen them yet lol.

* I have my audio setup through my Yamaha THR10x guitar amp, which is also acting as my output speaker and audio interface. I love the setup because I can have the guitar volume controlled separately from the midi sounds. Yes, that's right...you can play guitar signal and midi alongside each other. I find that pretty cool.

* I've yet to record with the Triple Play. That's next for me now that I have everything setup. I do wish Fishman offered some various hardware setup diagrams. I'm finding it confusing how to setup my amps, guitar pedals, foot controllers, etc.

Anyway...if you're on the fence (as I was) with this product, and you're a guitarist who doesn't know how to play keyboard...this product is for you. If you're looking for a live setup, I'd probably go with a Roland GR-55 or something, but for home recording and tinkering around, this setup works for me. If you consider all of the software that comes with the device, I think the price is not as bad as everyone else is saying.

Things that Fishman could do to better their product:

1) Make their pickup less tall so that people don't have to raise their neck. This is a stupid design. And I have a common American strat.

2) Offer a more in depth FAQ and have all instructions better written and in one easy to find place. I have a bunch of bookmarks just to find anything.

3) More quality hardware...things feel very "made in china"....because they are.

4) Offer multiple diagrams to users, exploring various audio setups (guitar amps, pedals, audio interfaces, monitors, foot controllers, etc). Or have a support line for helping new buyers getting setup.

5) Have a dedicated forum on the Fishman website for users. I had to visit the Virtual Guitar forums to find 1/2 the info I needed.

6) Let users know which software works and which does not...how to back up all sounds and samples to prevent future loss of effects and/or loops.

7) Include all software on a disc or usb device with every purchase rather than having customers download software. For $400 this should be a given.

8) Stop including useless 32bit version of SampleTank with your bundle when a 64bit version is available. Everything is moving to 64bit so why not prepare your users for the future? This seems very stupid to me.

9) The software needs reworking....while not the worst, things could be less confusing. I don't believe there are any hover over help tips for anything...that would be a start.

10) There are certain midi sounds where I could play everywhere on the fretboard, except just a couple of frets on the E string? I know there are certain midi samples that only allow certain strings to be played (visible through the interface's fretboard diagram on the screen), but no mention as to why frets 1-3 on the low E are not playable for certain midi samples?
Summary: If you don't mind the frustrating setup, the reward is lots of fun with your guitar.

The Epiphone Les Paul 100 is a lot of guitar for the money. First of all it has two wonderful humbucker pickups (at the bridge & neck), separate volume & tone controls for each pickup and of course the classic Les Paul 3-way toggle to select bridge pickup, both Bridge & neck, or neck pickup. It has a bolt-on neck (rather than a glued neck) which IMO is not a bad thing, it is a bit thinner than your typical Les Paul which makes it light (a good thing). Still for the $250-$300 usually paid for a Les Paul 100, you get proper tuners (which are very good) a nice finish (mine is Hertitage Cherry Sunburst) and the wonderful Les Paul sound in a well-constructed, nicely-crafted guitar. The 12" radius neck feels wonderful, and I found no sharp fret-ends on the rosewood fretboard. All controls work just as they should (volume, tone, pickup selectors) and the tones this guitar is capable of are wonderful.
This is a guitar that although it is value-priced, it isn't and doesn't look, feel or sound 'cheap'. It's a guitar you can happily play for many years and want to keep.
What you don't get on this guitar that you might get on a higher priced guitar is as previously mentioned - a glued-on neck (this one is bolted on) fancy large inlayed fret markers (this has the usual dot markers common on many guitars) and binding on the body. The later two are more cosmetic than anything and doesn't change the fact that this guitar looks & sounds wonderful.
I own many more expensive guitars, but I find that the Les Paul 100 is a very enjoyable guitar to play. My 8 year-old daughter refers to it as my "pretty" guitar, and indeed it is very nice-looking. The proof is in the playing, and this is a guitar that you won't want to put down. The lighter weight also makes playing very enjoyable and I've yet to experience a sore back playing (the weight is one of the reasons I choose this over other Les Paul models).
Don't let the reasonable price fool you - this is a very good guitar that you won't be sorry you purchased -not a month from now, not a year from now & most likely you'll still be enjoying it years & years from now. It's that good & it's a great value. Highly recommended!

Text:
A little smaller than I expected it to be but for the price it does a fair job.

Horns tend to be a little thin and tinny in general and this allows them to "cut through" and project the sound so it can be heard over ambient noise levels such as a car, shop noises, etc.

Comes with a good length of cable that should be suitable for use for when mounting in the grill or underside of an automobile. It uses an 1/8" mono mini connector for plugging into standard speaker outputs such as the PA system built into many CB radios.

Is this a fantastic speaker? No, but for the inexpensive price tag it is easily justifiable and can be used for many situations where needing to hear over noisy conditions or use for a terrific outdoor speaker that will hold up to rain, sleet & snow. Great for camping or hooking up to that CB radio in the car, not only for use with the PA address system, but many times, you want a horn/speaker to cut through the noise.

Made of weather resistant plastic, this should hold up under most conditions and it handles up to 15 watts of power, and at 15 watts, this horn can get quite loud and shrill! Be careful not to place your ear(s) in direct or close proximity when playing loud sounds through this horn/speaker.

Nice circular bracket allows for mounting on and at various angles and is adjustable.

I gave it 3-stars for rating because although it is a great little bargain, I didn't want people to think it was going to sound like a police car speaker or an expensive bullhorn. The horns they use in police cars are very expensive, high quality, handle much more power and sound professional. This is a cheap little horn that does a good job for under ten bucks!

This one will be used mainly for a patio outdoor speaker, but I plan using it for camping, CB radio speaker and PA address, and for my scanner which has a tiny low level output speaker. When connected to it, it makes it about 5 times louder than the internal speaker and I can hear it clearly from another adjacent room.

This will also make a nice outdoor speaker for a Halloween decorated spooky house!
One more thing - The box/packaging that it comes in is a rather nice looking box suitable for a nice wrapped present or gift.

Don't get your hopes up too high and this horn/speaker will do a fine job...at what it is good at doing.
Summary: Good Horn/Speaker for Under Ten Bucks!

Text: I have played the same Alvarez acoustic guitar on stage an average of at least one time per week for the past 25 years, and I have never been as pleased with its sound as I was the moment I plugged it into the LR Baggs Session DI. Over those 25 years, I have used the LR Baggs Para Acoustic DI, and I have generally been quite pleased with it. It is obviously very durable, and it has a host of useful features. However, even when plugged into effects processors, there was a persistent abrasiveness to my tone that the Para Acoustic couldn't eliminate. The Session DI, however, eliminated the abrasiveness immediately and beautifully, and it is producing the smooth and even sound I have always wanted. At least for my guitar, the compression EQ and saturation options are brilliant. If you have a guitar that already has top-notch electronics, the Session DI may not be as helpful for you. If, however (like me) your guitar is equipped with a simple passive pickup, I cannot recommend this device highly enough.

Text:
Disappointed. I purchased this assuming it would be a step up from my Behringer X1204USB mixer. but one minor and one major issue may cause me to return this. Using this primarily for production of vocal shows. The minor issue: no matter whether I use decent dynamic mics or some good condenser mics, I have to crank the gain up to almost 100% on the channels in order to get any response at all on the output LEDs. But the major issue is that when I connect my MXL 990 condenser mics up to the board and turn on the phantom power, I get a loud whine that does not go away. It is present in the headphones and also in the recording. I have switched mics, switched out cables, tried everything but the whine makes using my condenser mics impossible. Same mics plugged into my Behringer board, quiet as can be, no whine at all. (and this is a LOUD whine.)

Very disappointing, this is my first Mackie product, and I was really expecting a step up in quality.

EDIT: Follow up - when I had an issue with my Behringer, I sent them a note and tech support called me up, asked for a time convenient to me where I could be in front of the board, called me at that time, walked me through the problem, resolved the issue, then also asked about any other questions I had while I was still on the line with them and in front of the board. I have a 2006 Mexican Standard, and the plastic accents were getting a little scuffed so I figured it was time for a makeover. The finish was tobacco sunburst with white, and I didn't like how dirty the white got, and how readily the scuffs showed in the white, so I decided I was going to get off-white, and was surprised by how many options there were. I was back and forth between Aged White and Parchment, and I will admit that the final decision was literally a coin toss. Man am I ever glad that it came up heads, because I love this finish. it is the perfect degree of yellowed white, and really does look like legitimately aged bakelite. I decided to replace the pickguard with a red tortoise, and the off-white/cream color of these accessories really complements that better than the white does, and I'd suspect probably better than the Parchment as well. I'd strongly recommend looking up on google a comparison between all the finishes, I was able to find someone who had purchased all of them and laid them out side by side.

The major critiques I have though, and which lost this set a star, were primarily due to the small details. The backplate didn't fit perfectly right. I don't know if this is sized for the American standard or what, but the hole placement was about 1/16" off. I had to bondo and redrill. Similarly, the holes in the backplate where the strings were supposed to go through were 1/8" off, and it's a pain to get the strings into and out of the holes without taking the whole thing off. It's minor but it's worth mentioning.

The spindle-shaped accent that goes on the end of the vibrato arm was similarly just-slightly-the-wrong-size-for-my-Mexican-guitar, I'd guess somewhere in the realm of 1/64" too small of a diameter. I couldn't even hammer the thing on all the way. I couldn't heat it up and get it to mold around the arm. It's currently on about halfway and looks good enough, but that's the absolute best I could do. I don't know if there's a secret science to these or what but in the past when I've changed them out I've just slid the old one off and the new one on but for whatever reason this was just slightly too small and impossible to get on all the way.

Besides those complaints, it's more or less exactly what I wanted and overall love it.

I ordered this drum set because I had always wanted to get into drums, but was not keen on the noise level it would entail for neighbors, so had stuck to electronic pianos. When this set became available, I jumped at the chance to try it. Here is what I found:

1. Do NOT expect this set to have the same performance level as an $8700 set from Yamaha! That being said, the sounds that this set is capable of producing is VERY good and you have a lot of room for making custom changes.

2. This set assembles fairly quickly. It took me about an hour from start of opening box to sitting down to try it out. The instructions consist of a pictograph. Use the picture on Amazon on your computer, it is a better picture to show you where everything goes. Keep in mind that all of the mounts for drums and cymbals go to the outside of the u-shaped frame you sit inside of. The wiring diagram does NOT really exist. Instead, what you are looking at is the name for each part of the set and its location. Take the cable assembly and look at the tag on the end of each cable. Match name on the tag with item in the picture and you have your wiring diagram!

3. Once you have everything where it belongs and have all of the cables connected, use the velcro straps provided to bundle the cables along the rack. It makes for a very neat installation!!

4. The control module is powered by a very small transformer. The reach on the cable to that plug in transformer is about 5 feet! It is really VERY short so plan accordingly. You will either need an amplifier and speakers to plug into the unit or a set of headphones. I used a set of studio grade Sony headphones and the sound is incredible!!! You have a separate volume control for headphones and for output. So, you can adjust accordingly. If you want to use it in a house, the headphones keep it very quiet. You will still hear the sticks hitting the devices, but they are made of rubber and what you basically hear is dull clacks.

5. Now is where we start to get into issues. There are supposed to be 120 songs pre-recorded that have separate volume controls for the drum set and for the song. This lets you listen and play along or to turn off the drum section and just play with the song. There is also a record feature and a start feature for the record. The problem is that only the first 50 work correctly. The next twenty have only the drum section, and the rest do nothing but play a single note every time you press start.

6. So, I went to contact the company and get help. Guess what? NO contact phone number!!! They point you to user groups to solve your issue. Nice, except this product is so new there is NO user group for it! Ok, you can then go to a commonly asked questions section. Nice, except there is NO section for this product! Ok, last resort, you can send e-mail and they are supposed to respond. Fine, it has been 5 days and I still have not heard from them!!!!!

7. One of the other things they try to do is to point you to a seller of their equipment for technical support since they are music stores selling musical equipment and they service that equipment. Great, except I got this from Amazon!!!

So, while the sounds of the drums are very good and I am quite happy with the functional design, the support from the company at this point is non-existent and the equipment is NOT doing what they say it will do. Now, I have not tried to modify all of the drum sets, so I have no idea if that functions correctly or not, but if it has short comings like the pre-recorded songs do , then you are up a creek without a paddle since support seems to be non-existent.

Based on the fact that this appears to be a very new product and the fact that support is non-existent at this point in time for the product, I would NOT recommend buying this unless you are willing to fully check it out yourself in the 30 days you have to return it with Amazon and you do not mind if some of the features are missing.

I will update this review if something changes.

Text:
Some say "daw-dare-e-o", "de-ah-dare-e-o", "dad-ar-ee-oh", or "dee-ah-dare-e-o"
Others shorten it to "D-adds" or even "Daddy-O's". Took me a while to figure that last one out.
I was trying to find out info about "Daddy-O strings" and why people thought they were so great. Duh.

While people may disagree on how to say the name, few debate the idea that these are great strings.
* Less expensive that most string sets out there, especially if you buy multi-packs
* Color-coded to make string changes easy
* Easy to find from most any vendor or music store
* Made in the USA
* You can collect "players points" for SWAG
* They are sealed in a special "environmentally friendly" package to keep them fresh and corrosion-free
* They have one of the widest range of string-size combinations available

If you are just starting out and do not know what to put on your new guitar then the phrase "set it up with EXL-120s" or "put on some Da-Dairy-O" nines" is a good choice, at least for a strat or tele-like guitar.

I personally like them better than Ernie Ball Super Slinkys aka "EB Pinks", but I cannot quite put my finger on "why".
You can pay more for coated strings, cryogenic frozen strings, boutique strings, and all that but if you do not know what any of those are then you probably haven't been playing long enough to find value in them.
Almost every guitarist has a set of strings they "swear by" because they work wonders that no other string can - they make them play smoother or faster, their last set of strings lasted for 6 years, or whatever.

I just appreciate a great value, and D'Addario strings are just that.

BTW, for the record the official pronunciation is "Da-Dairy-O":
>> "We receive letters each week regarding the correct pronunciation of the D'Addario name. Some years back, we even ran an ad that illustrated an easy way to pronounce the D'Addario name. The name is pronounced phonetically as follows: Da-Dairy-O. A simple way to pronounce the most difficult name in musical accessories!"
Summary: "Da-Dairy-O" produces great USA-made strings at a great value

Biggest miss is if I adjust the volume level in monitor mode while using, I start to get a little more noise on monitoring. No idea why. Support knows that you need to pick either the computer audio controls or the mics in a session. But I now find that the front audio control is pretty much also unusable like the mute button. Still like the gain, though it is a miss too for not having any markings to see where it’s set (you have to look at the software, which makes sense for ultimately checking but it would be nice if you know you like it at, say, a specific mark for a specific application if you could possibly know there that is. I ended up making markings on it with a Sharpee. Does not help the aethetics but that’s on the back. Still LOVE the acoustic qualities. But adjusting anything while live is just not good. On the focused stereo setting the rejection of sounds from other directions seems exceptional. I present online often and sometimes stream video as part of that, and Mac Mini fan starts up and runs. It’s not super loud (the fan) but a less focused condenser mic would pic that sound right up. This does not when pointed toward me (not toward the mini) and on the focused stereo setting. That’s a very strong feature.

In pamphlet that comes with it, it says to first go download the latest firmware. There is NOT firmware update available and support has confirmed this. And, there needs to be. I want to love this mic but I am now looking for something else. So, a couple months in now, I’m moving this rating back down. if they put out a firmware update that fixed these things, it would get 5 stars from me even with the useless mute button.

This could easily be the best microphone available for streaming, gaming, podcasting, under $200 but these misses had me looking at a Blue Yeti tonight. I doubt that could sound as good as this but I imagine all the features might work better.

UPDATED 3-27-2020:

This is a great design with fabulous features all of which are easily accessible. The sound is fantastic. I mean, it's exceptional and the choices in pattern of pick up are better than anything I've seen. The weight and heft are very nice in this day and age of plastic body mics. This is substantial. And it is quite retro. It's cool. One of the things that fairly makes it great is the presence of an actual, working, smooth gain control, right on the mic. It works really well.

I have a few concerns though. I thought one of them was more serious that it maybe is. The other is just a fail in the design but relatively more minor as an issue.

1. The volume control on the front has a type of interface issue with the volume control on the device you plug this into. I now know the key to this, and it seems to hold up: Only use one mode of managing the volume back to you through the headphone jack on the mic. Don't start with using the knob on the mic and then sometimes use the system volume, too. Or, don't start with system volume control and then reach for the knob. Pick a lane. Pick one or the other during a sessions, because it does weird things switching between one or the other. Their tech support confirmed this to me. This checks out on my Mac and it works best for me to just do this in this order:
- Plug in the mic
- First thing, go to settings/sound, and select the AKG mic for input (It will already have selected itself, I believe) and then go to output and select AKG for output. It will NOT have automatically moved to that by you just plugging in the mic. Now, if you are using external monitoring like through headphones or ear buds, only use the knob on the front of the mic to dial in your volume.
- Second, dial in your input level as desired. Many programs like Zoom will auto control this but you may first have wanted to set it where you want it in the sound settings on your device (mac or PC). So, go there, and play with that gain button on the back until it's where you want it in that range.

I will try later some more with this on iPad Pro and see it I get that working well enough. iPad pros have some funky issues in such things. I do KNOW that it works but the control issues are greater.

2. The mute button is just a fail. It's functionally worthless. You have to press just right for it to work, and it makes a bit of a "thunk" and, at least on mine, sometimes it works and sometimes it does not. So, it's just not useful for quick muting and unmuting. It will make noise every time you press it and it will also not reliably work and you'll have to press again. Maybe mine is defective but I think it's a poorly designed button/switch. It will work however to press when you want to make sure that the mic is off. Otherwise, you will want to mute by software and not hardware if using this for something like recording or being on a webinar.

The sound is what matters most, and this is terrific for that. And, the volume control is better than I thought. It truly does not work as well as the volume control on my Shure MV5 but it's quite good if you do what they suggested to me and set it up how I suggested above. It is easier to access and actuate than the one on the Shure.

Minor note: The pamphlet that comes with it says to first do a firmware update. It gives you a website to go to. There is no firmware update. I checked with tech support. There is no firmware update to find.

I have moved my rating up to a 4. It may yet get to a 5, but it won't be because of the mute button. It will be the sound, the robustness of the design (the heft is very nice), and the ability to select those four settings for sound pick up patter. Very nice.
Summary: I want to love this mic but it has issues.  Probably needs a firmware update that does not exist.
