I am primarily a guitarist, and the guitars I own are all American, handmade and custom built. I wanted to try my hand at tracking bass on some original material, and not being a bass player, didn't need something handmade for that purpose. So I decided to try the Sterling Music Man SUB 4.

This instrument has active electronics, powered by a rear compartment 9 volt battery (included). The bass comes packed nicely, but will only arrive with a registration card - no tags, spec sheets or schematics, no gig bag or strap or cable. I expect the lack of case and cable at this price point, but it is a little strange to not have any tags on the guitar - it's the first time I've sen that (but again, I am a custom shop person).

The bass has very low action, buzzing midway across the fretboard. The fretboard is maple, and the fretwork is good - intonation is good as well (where were quality budget instruments when I was learning?) and the frets have a nice feel to them. The instrument looks good, tunes well, and most importantly holds tune - very important for any instrument, and it happens here.

The pickup sounds aggressive without being too hot - I ran it through a [[ASIN:B00FEX380M Wampler Ego Compressor]] and a [[ASIN:B009G44J7Q Hot Wired V2]] for a little boost and got a nice even tone with just a smidge of dirt and grease. Very nice.

Is this the equivalent of a USA handmade instrument? No. Not even close, honestly. Is it playable, does it stay in tune, and is the intonation good? Yes, absolutely.

So you may need to get it set up to remove the fret buzz, and get a gig bag or case for it - the construction quality seems fine (what can a CNC machine not do nowadays?) and the electronics are good for recording or practicing at home. I have not (and will not) gig with this, so can't speak to its durability and performance in that regard, but for learning songs and laying down bass tracks in Pro Tools for demo work, this is fine.

All in all worth the money. Great if you want to play bass but you're not a bassist, need a general tracking instrument, or want to see if the bass is for you without going broke doing it. Hey, despite my owning high-falootin' guitars, this will also stay with me, and it will be played and recorded.

Recommended!

I am not yet a drummer, but I feel like this purchase was a good step in that direction. I have prior experience with an inexpensive acoustic student set, and the Alesis Nitro is a much more satisfying way to get my feet wet with drums. Some of the sounds are quite good, the kit is compact, and I have found playing with headphones to be very liberating, because it removes my self-consciousness.

In the plus column, the metronome and the various play-along modes are proving to be very useful learning tools. I feel like I have made more progress on drums in three days than I did on trumpet in three weeks, or maybe even three months. It is very useful having immediate feedback, in the form of an indicator that flashes SLOW, FAST, or GOOD! while you play along. Many of the play-alongs are set up with graduated difficulty levels, such that the first level only has you play two or three drums, and the highest level may have you running the whole kit. I've barely gotten started, but that feels productive.

In the minus column, the number of usable on-board sounds is pretty limited, and most of the stock kits pretty much sound the same. The brain box says DM7X on the bottom, and the Nitro is obviously a DM7X "lite," which I find mildly disappointing. I feel like the thing has features locked away inside its brain that I can never use. The stand is highly flimsy, and now that I am just starting to develop a tiny modicum of skill, I find it kind of scary to look down and see what the pedals are going through as I play. Are those going to hold up? They'll be the first thing to go, I imagine; especially the hi-hat controller. Finally, there is persistent "solid state hiss" background noise in the audio signal that is probably bad enough that you won't want to record these drums for anything serious.

I plan to play this kit to death as fast as I can, and the buy the Roland I probably should have bought in the first place. When am I going to learn to stop buying things twice? On the other hand, this attractive price point is what finally got me to come off the fence and take the plunge in the first place. If I hadn't popped for the Nitro kit, I would be planning to buy the Roland eventually without any drums to play in the meantime, and I would be much less likely to ever get there at all.

I do have to say that this thing has grown on me more and more every day, and I am really enjoying myself.
Summary: More fun than an entry level acoustic kit

This review is from a Classical Guitar teacher's point of view:

I like this guitar dock a lot but I don't love it.

Pros:
- It clears up space in my studio by eliminating a guitar stand which holds my teaching classical guitar. My students previously had to move around it to get to their chair or I would have to physically move it and my guitar out of the way so they could easily enter my studio. The guitar dock completely ends that necessity.
- It was easy to install on my bookshelf next to my teaching chair.
- It seems to clamp down tightly onto the shelf, so I'm not too worried about it being accidentally knocked off my shelf and my guitar falling down to the floor.
- The back of the guitar will not get scratched because it has a rubberized pad to protect it.
- It's convenient to take with you as long as you have something to attach it too, otherwise a guitar stand always works.

Cons:

- Be aware that the bottom of your guitar might be direct contact with the floor and if the floor is rough, or uncarpeted, your guitar will probably get scratched on the bottom. My floor is carpeted but I still might put down a very soft cloth for my guitar to rest on.
- The two rubber tongs will not automatically flip out to cover the front of the guitar neck. You will need to physically pull them over your strings to add a little extra security so your guitar will not fall out forward facing.
- Also be aware that anything you attach your guitar dock to could have objects or items on it lower down that could scratch the back of your guitar. I have attached mine to a 3-shelf book cabinet and had to move some large books to another spot so they would not touch my guitar.
- The trick to getting the guitar dock out of the packaging is to not cut the enormous tie-down. Just rip the cardboard in half sideways and the guitar dock will come out.

Overall, I think this is a good product and I'm glad I got to try it out for review. I will continue using it and update this review if needed.

I used #4x1/2'' Stainless flat head phillips sheet metal screws made by Everbilt that I bought at Home Depot. The top of the screw is flat and it fits perfectly flush with the top of the pick guard. They come in a bag with 8 screws in it. You will need to use a small headed philips screwdriver. The cost was under $2 for the bag of screws.
This is the way I installed my pick guard: I placed the guard in place and made a small dent in the wood of the guitar, using a finishing nail, in the center of the hole of the pick guard. Next I removed the pick guard and used a very small drill bit to drill down into the guitar's wood a little less than 1/2" on the spot where I put the dent in the wood. If the pilot hole is still too small, use a slightly larger drill bit. If you made the hole too large, use the same screws and put a small amount of wood glue on the screw and gently screw it in. You are done!
Summary: My SGJ Pickguard fits good and looks great!

I didn’t expect this low-cost wireless microphone system to work as well as it does.

I tested the system indoors at distances up to 35 feet and non-line-of-sight, approximating my normal use situation.

The Fotowelt AIR transmitter has a built-in microphone and a 3.5mm female socket for an external microphone.

My tests were conducted using the default settings of the unit. I changed nothing. My test device was an iPhone SE. Definitely not a top-of-line device, but one I use for casual shooting and adequate for that task.

The internal microphone clipped to my shirt pocket surprised me. No hiss. No static. No popping. No effect from my walking and talking. Voice fidelity was excellent. I deliberately walked into rooms along the way to take me out of line-of-sight and put some solid walls between transmitter and receiver. I was very surprised that there was interruption of the transmission. One small pop as I went from line-of-sight into the room.

I clipped the supplied lavalier microphone to the front of my shirt – big mistake. It picked up rustling noises as I walked and talked. Next time I will be more careful and clip it to my collar and test more extensively. Though omni-directional, the lav rejected sound from the sides, including my soft-spoken wife’s voice. My subjective impression is that the internal mic produced better audio. I’ll be trying it later with higher quality lavalier microphonesa.

The OLED screen, small as it is, is highly readable. In the upper-left corner is a signal strength meter on the receiver. Battery level is in the upper-right corner of both receiver and transmitter. Channel information is along the bottom the screen. The middle displays a VU meter. There are controls to choose which of the 36 channels you want to operate on and volume. Operation is very, very simple.

The unit comes packaged in a nice semi-rigid case. TRS – TRS and TRS – TRRS cables are included, along with the lavalier microphone. A single Type-C charging cable is provided. I suggest the user add a second Type-C cable and one of those little block chargers with two Type-A slots. The units came partially charged and bringing them to full charge status didn’t take long. My tests so far barely dented the battery charge. I don’t have a firm idea yet of how long a charge will last or if the units can be operated while being charged. A cold-shoe adapter is also provided.

Overall, I am very impressed with this unit. It delivers solid audio, even through walls, indoors at 35 feet and less. That’s my work radius.

My hope is that the unit will prove durable and continue to deliver this kind of performance.

Jerry

I read a lot of reviews and discussions on forums before purchasing the Spark amp. A lot of people were saying some misleading things so let me start off this review by telling you what this amp isn't. This isn't a gigging amp. I don't think you are going to want to run it to a PA or anything like that. It isn't a replacement for a nice, loud, tube amp. It doesn't sound like one and it doesn't feel like one when playing it. A lot of people were saying it sounded better than their main amp. Either they are lying or they have a terrible amp.

That said, it is an excellent practice amp. The ability to search virtually any song, have it play through the amp with a close approximation of the chords used (more on that later), and have a selection of preset tones for that song is amazing. I can search for an ACDC song, play it, have an angus-like tone right at my fingertips then do the same for a Jack White song without ever fiddling with my pedals and pedal board and amps.

It sounds good for a practice amp. It doesn't play loud very well, but it will play loud enough to annoy your housemates. It also sounds good with headphones. I've played through many practice amps with headphones where it would sound very harsh and poppy, this doesn't do that at all. I'm just as happy playing through the headphones as I am the speakers.

The biggest negative at the moment is chord recognition. The software does an okay job at recognizing chords of songs and generating an on the fly chord chart for whatever you happen to search. It isn't perfect though and you're probably still going to want tabs or instructional videos. The jam feature though is pretty terrible. I have a digitech trio+ that does a much better job than this, but it's a $200 pedal that does nothing else. The good news is, this is all software based so Positive Grid may be able to improve it over time.

Overall, this amp does what I had hoped. It allows me to play a lot of different styles easily and learn a lot of different songs. This inspires me to practice. Which in turn inspires me to go plug into my AC15 or Marshall 50 watt amp and play these new songs loud.
Summary: Excellent practice amp that actually makes me want to learn new songs!

The newest batch of these that showed up came with sponges that were oversized, especially once moistened. You have to shove it in the holder and push the top down forcibly to close it. Ones ordered last year had smaller sponges that fit in the holder perfectly, even when dampened. I guess the sponges can be trimmed, but the holders are curved inside and have a triangular shape that slopes and gets more narrow at the bottom than the top. The oversized rectangular sponges would need a lot of trimming to make them fit perfectly, and you would end up with a fidget sponge after cutting enough of it away. I cannot say if this is a one time aberration or a new design. I’ve gotten a few of these new Caline 2022/23 model pedals, and I’m quite impressed with them. Physically, these pedals look beautiful. I love the cohesive artistic/animal theme, and how well the entire product line matches in artistic style. The Artwork is very glossy and appears to be covered by a thin acrylic sheet. They are not “cheap” but also nowhere near “boutique” pricing. I would say they are squarely in the “very good value for the money” range.

The physical dimensions of the pedal are: 9.9cm (tall) x 4.9cm (wide) x 2.5cm (thick, body only without pots/switch). They are somewhat smaller than a “compact size” 1590B, but a bit taller and wider than a “mini size” 1590A. I’d say the size is a good mix of not being too small, but also not taking up too much space on the pedal board. They feel rock solid, and are pretty heavy. They come with stickers for both a velcro back, or a grippy back, already perfectly sized to fit.

For this review, the pedal was powered by a Caline CP-04 pedal board power supply, and tested alone (no other pedals in the loop) with a Carvin DC127, plugged directly into the FX return of a Carvin SX-200 amp. No coloring from anything but the pedal itself. Any oscilloscope pictures are generated from the open B string. The yellow trace is the input signal, and the green trace is the output signal. The pedals are absolutely silent with zero input: there was no hum or anything.

The LEDs on all of these pedals are blue, which I love! Interestingly, it seems that on these whole series of pedals, the power jack also lights up --though not always the same color as the FX LED. In the Nasty Bear case, the colors do match (blue for both).

Subjective analysis: This Nasty Bear Fuzz pedal sounds great. It’s your fairly standard “vintage” fuzz sound. I’d call it a medium-thickness fuzz, not a super-thick fuzz, if that makes sense. It sounds like a standard transistor fuzz. I’m guessing the tone is a tilt style (e.g. big muff), because it sounds a lot like it. The tone is very dynamic, and gives very different sounds as you sweep across the full range. This is a pretty versatile little fuzz box.

Objective analysis: Indeed, it is a transistor fuzz – 3 transistors in fact. When unscrewing the back panel, you can see the footprint of 3 transistors on the circuit board. No op amps or anything, unless they are surface mount on the other side. I didn’t do a full disassembly and circuit trace, since that’s a bit overkill for these reviews. The total current draw was a very steady 5.6 mA, even though the product page says 50mA. So, for your power management purposes, this is important to know. This very low current draw is pretty typical of transistor-only fuzz circuits. (A standard 9V battery could power this for about 100 hours.)

The gain control is labeled as “sustain” and it really does draw out the sustain, to over 20 seconds (see oscilloscope pic). The max voltage output, at max volume, is about 1.4V at either side of the tone sweep, and about 900 mV with tone in the middle. Again, typical of a Big Muff style tone control. The tone-centered fuzz waveform is shown in the oscilloscope picture. You can see the characteristic fuzz waveform with some high frequency coming through. I’m not sure how helpful the waveforms are to anyone else, so I didn’t take pictures of all of them. But the waveforms are pretty similar to a Big Muff Pi, as you sweep through the tone range. However, this doesn't sound, to me at least, exactly like a Big Muff Pi -- it's similar, but it's its own animal.

The only super minor thing that is a bit janky is the fit of the enclosure around the power jack. It’s not a super tight fit, and there just a tiny gap (see picture). This is the case on all my Caline pedals from this lineup, so it looks like a consistent thing. Really not a big deal, but worth pointing out.

Final Rating: 5 stars! This is a great Pi-style fuzz pedal, with a super solid build, perfect size, and very attractive artwork.
Summary: Excellent Pi-style Fuzz: Attractive artwork, solid build.  Good size. Only draws 5.6 mA

What makes this drum set for beginners?

The bass drum vibrates (again different from the more professional bass drum at school).

Anyway, that's what makes this more for beginners, it uses cheaper material than the professional one. But if you are a beginner, it's a good buy for the price. (Or you can buy an electric drum set like the Ion which you can also use for Rock Band. That one's got everything as well and you can lower the volume so neighbors don't hear you.)

Update: I'm really glad we purchased this drum set. I have been playing every day (2-3 hours per day) and it's awesome. The sound of the cymbals still bother me a little, I know I like to replace them with the nicer ones [[ASIN:B0007MU1L4 Zildjian 14-Inch ZBT Rock Hi-Hats Cymbal Pair]] like the ones we play at school.

The bass drum stopped vibrating and it's terrific. We're using [[ASIN:B000FREODC Vic Firth Cymbal Pack w/ 10, 12, 14(2), 22, Hi-hat and Cymbals]] to keep the sound down and that's working well for us. Everything works, it's helping me practice, awesome for the price!

Update to my Update: It's Feb. 27, 2011, about 7 mo's since I got this drum set and I love it even more now. I have replaced the hi hats and ride/crash cymbals with a Zildjian 22" and a Sabian 14". And when my drum teacher came by the other day and played it, he gave it 2 thumbs up.

I mean, that's my drum teacher. He just said, "put a pillow inside the bass drum otherwise it's all good." He added that the hardware (screws, nuts, bolts) aren't as high quality as the more professional ones but if I'm not hauling it to gigs anyway, if it's just going to stay in one place then it's perfectly fine.

So, there you go, it's drum-teacher-approved, replacing the drum heads is unnecessary, good luck to all you drummers out there--drumming on this set is FUN!!!

p.s. My drum teacher did suggest I get a second Ride Cymbal (like an 18" since different size cymbals produce different sounds)

First ... let me say I'm a total beginner. I purchased this for my used Yamaha FG JR1, small 3/4 guitar. As expected, due to its small size, its sound seemed small as well. So I decided to invest in a few upgrades. First I put on a high end set of Elixir NANOWEB, 11/52 strings and added bone bridge pins which, real or imagined, seemed a bit better with more sustain. The B & E strings just didn't seem to ring out nicely as they should ... or could.

Since I have no intention of buying another guitar, I contacted GraphTech for the proper TUSQ part numbers for my JR1. They replied quickly and I ordered as recommended. Then I replaced both the nut and saddle with TUSQ.

The nut suggested fit almost perfect with only a very minor adjustment. The saddle required a bit more work. It was very slightly too thick and too long. I made those adjustments first. Next came the height adjustment. Hand sanding off 1/16 inch would take forever so I marked carefully and used a belt sander to knock of the bulk of the material. When I got close I hand sanded the final amount. Plus I had to lower it a very small amount as the action was too high. Yes, the fitting of the saddle was a rather tedious. You need to go about it patiently.

The end result was satisfying. The little Yamaha now plays probably as good as it ever can. The small strings seem brighter and cleaner sounding. For such a small body guitar I think it now puts out a nice, big sound. Pretty and plenty satisfying for my at home learning. Yes, the change was fairly small but occurred where I wanted it to.

This inexpensive mod was worth the time and effort. It was the first time I ever changed a nut or saddle and it wasn't that hard. Watch a couple videos on YT. Take your time. You can do it too. If you get even a 10 or 15% improvement in tone it will be worth it. Especially if you have a low end guitar like me.

(Don't cheap out on strings either. Get the best ones you can for your guitar and playing needs. Added all up, your cheapie or high end instrument will surely sound better)
Summary: Nice Upgrade from Original YAMAHA Plastic Nut

This cabinet is more like a "kit" than a finished unit. The outside is finished well with fairly good attention to detail on the tolex covering and good fit and finish of the plywood components, but open it up to install speakers and you get an entirely different story. The two 12" holes for the speaker were completely unfinished, Sharp shards of splintered plywood stuck out everywhere around them and had to be sanded to prevent them from puncturing a speaker. It's as if they were cut with a dull jigsaw, and when measured the fact was they were not even perfectly round (companies like Avatar laser cut their speakers holes for a perfectly consistent finish).

The unit was "set-up" for front loading of the speakers but with the gaskets on the speakers would actually rub against the grill cloth if installed in front. So I removed the front loading hardware that was installed on the soundboard (it was actually too small for a standard Celestion speaker anyway so it was essentially worthless), only to find out that the holes already drilled did not line up with the speakers. SO... after drilling some new properly spaced holes in the soundboard, going to Home Depot to buy the correct sized mounting bolts, and removing the many screws that held the back on, I was able to properly rear mount my pair of 12's.

Oh, and the wiring is already pre-setup for parallel and I needed series wiring. Would have been better to just provide the wires and let the consumer decide IMHO.

Here's the good news: Once I finished doing the job that should have been done at the factory in the first place, the cabinet sounded great. I have my Marshall TSL602 combo on top of it and the combination has added a great deal of bottom and depth to the overall sound.
Summary: Good sounding cabinet in the end - BUT it's truly a do it yourself project...

I do a lot of video interviews and live stream setups where I need real-time control over audio. I used to bring a large 6-track XLR board around which was kind of overkill for something as simple as controlling a dual-mic setup. This mixer is a perfect alternative! It is super portable and a super low-footprint, and it uses the 1/4" jack setup that my wireless mic system already outputs, which makes cables without adapters easier!
The doubled-up stereo plugs took a little getting used to compared to the "every plug is an isolated track" setup of the XLR board, but I'm impressed at the solid performance and sound quality for the price and size of this thing. I'd recommend it for low profile setups like mine.

I generally dislike digital effects, but this pedal provides very clean and versatile sounds. The stereo features are very useful for recording. But you might want to keep the instruction manual handy until you learn the many tricks to setting up the varied modes. There's a lot more to the pedal than just delay and depth. The external tap-tempo feature works very well, but I was very disappointed to hear a very audible clicking sound when tap tempo was engaged. The clicking (or popping) sound was evident regardless of whether the pedal was engaged, and remained until the delay was manually reset. The problem turned out to be an inadequate 9V power supply (from one of those multi-output bricks). This delay uses a lot of power compared to most pedals, so when I moved the 9V supply to a 500ma outlet (rather than 100ma as on the other 9V outlets) the click/pop went away. I haven't tried it on battery power, but I suspect it will deplete a battery very quickly.
Summary: Clean and versatile delay, but use a high power 9V supply to avoid clicks/pops during tap tempo

For yourself or as a gift, especially for a kid, get a harmonica that one can comfortably play, and more likely enjoy, such as most any Hohner, Suzuki, Seydel, Lee Oskar, or other professional level harmonica that costs over $30, such as the Hohner Special 20, at only $32.90, used by professionals worldwide.

I'll admit it: I'm OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE about my instruments being in tune.

I've been using the Snark SN-2 tuner for 4 years now, with my masterworks acoustic guitar and LE Koa classical guitar. I owned a Korg and a Planetwave tuner, both of which I found hard to read, especially in the sun (and very expensive compared to the Snark). After using the Snark for 2 weeks, I ordered a second one for my classical guitar. It's accurate (I mean DEAD-ON), and extremely sensitive. It's intuitive, so it's very easy to use. The unit uses little energy, so the battery is long lasting. It's so light weight, you'll forget that it's on the head stock. The clamp is protected by heavy rubber feet, that contact the guitar, so it doesn't harm the wood. The readout is mounted on a 2 ball heads (where the readout is attached to the neck; also where the curved neck attaches to the clamp). You can manipulate the thing into almost any position for easy reading. The bottom jaw of the clamp is mounted on a hinge, so that it can accommodate strange angles. The display is a vibrant colored; you'll have no problem reading it in the Sun and there will be no doubt when you're in tune. I'm about to order a 3rd SN-2 for another classical guitar that I have en-route (I like to have one in each case). Beware, this particular Snark has a microphone (which is the difference between the SN-1 and this unit) so that it can be used Chromatically; I didn't realize it until it tried to "tune" my television! So, the unit can be used either by vibration sensor, or microphone. It can be programed to different vibration frequencies, so it's useful for different instruments. It's a very well thought out, and executed product.

1. Total weight: 1.4 ounces (34 grams)
2. Read out head 1 1/2" diameter
3. 1 1/2" tall from top of clamp to top of readout (when in the position as pictured)
4. Uses CR2032 battery
5. Built-in Metronome (which is also adjustable)
The clamp will open to almost 1 1/2", so it would fit on a thick headstock The rubber lower jaw rotates, so it will accommodate strange angles.

The M87 also has a foot switch that allows you to have the pedal on, or in true bypass mode with a blue light as an indicator to let you know which mode is currently functioning. The M87 can be powered with one 9 volt battery or with an adapter/power supply. The housing is small and durable. Everything is detailed to read in an easy way and this device is a powerhouse that everyone should have in their lineup. The instructions that came with the M87 are very thorough, which makes it easier for those that may not yet fully understand the aspects and effect that a compressor can have on your sound.

My last gig was a jazz trio last night in about a 50 person capacity bar. Still did the job very well.

Here's my gear: Shure Beta 58. Taylor 12 fret acoustic. Eastman AR 371ce archtop.

PROS:
-Small & Lightweight.
-Superb CLARITY!
-My Taylor 12 fret acoustic guitar absolutely SHINES through this thing
-Vocals with the Beta 58 are top notch. No EQ needed! Just sing into it and it flatters your voice.
-Fast setup and breakdown.
-Impressing all your friends at the gig with how simple it is and how great it sounds

CONS:
-My biggest criticism is that there is no EQ for the instrument input. It is already voiced for acoustic guitar, which sounds incredible. But Archtop guitars with humbuckers have way too much bass and midrange. The bottom end is just too woofy with archtop use. I still give the L1 Compact 5 stars because I do not think it was intended to be used as an archtop amplifier. Also my issue can be solved by simply using a cheap EQ pedal like the Boss GE-7 when using an archtop.

-Only 2 inputs, one XLR for vocals, and one 1/4 inch input for guitar. I was hoping the guitar input would accept a TRS balanced signal, but it doesn't. It only accepts regular instrument signal. But again, the L1 Compact is designed for solo act use: one instrument, one mic. Still giving it 5 stars.

Summary:

I'm VERY happy with my purchase. IMHO, it far exceeds the performance standard of any competing equipment in its class. If you aren't ready to dive deep into a wide-ranging app and website with a steep learning curve, you won't like this amp at all. I showed what I've learned so far to a friend (a pro musician with a bit of tech-phobia) and he backed away like i was demonstrating my pet rattlesnake. I'm a software/firmware guy and this software is about as user-friendly as Pro Tools or most DAWs. It can do some cool things, but it will take a while to find them. It's too bad Positive Grid didn't see fit to create apps for Win11 and OS X for people who would rather be messing with this kind of software on an actual computer rather than a phone.

The order of pedals/effects is oddly fixed and, likely, not at all what the app indicates. I suspect the plug-ins are ordered depending on what the Positive Grid programmers anticipate users will like. For example, the noise gate is listed as first in the signal chain and it clearly isn't, since it quiets the buzz and noise from the distortion pedals, which come next. One gross absence is a multi-tap delay, necessary for all sorts of modern jazz guitar sounds and, again, you can't change the signal path order which really limits the sounds possible. Most of the compressors are just variations in graphics and provide no difference in sound quality or sustain.

My current irritation is that every time I open the app (on a Samsung tablet) the app starts playing a selection from my MP3 player through the amp. The Positive Grid (PG) folks claim it is because of a Bluetooth "autoplay" setting in the MP3 player, but I have several Bluetooth speaker/phone devices and the Spark Mini is the only one that demonstrates this problem. The company's "customer service" department is, typical of the low-end MI industry, notorious for deflecting product problems on to the users.

After a week, I came off of the fence about keeping the amp and returned it. It does some cool things, but not $250 worth. There is no way the amp/speaker combination produces the advertised 90dBSPL of acoustic output at anything less than 50-100% distortion. A clean sound of any sort is more in the 65-75dBSPL @ 1m territory and even then you're likely to experience a lot of low end clipping or speaker overload at that volume. A clean sound from the amp can't keep up, acoustically, with a strongly strummed acoustic guitar. That and software glitches proved, to me, that this product is not ready for prime time. Returns go directly to Positive Grid, which means the company issues an Amazon credit rather than charging back to the card that you asked Amazon to use. I would avoid doing business with this company through Amazon. You might as well take your chances with Positive Grid directly.
Summary: Hyper-flexible, low power output, incredibly complicated and somewhat glitchy

For anyone that owns a Yamaha Revstar, you know that the plastic nut on those is pretty sucky. The tuners are pretty sucky too if we're being honest. They look great, but need to be replaced for good tuning stability. For those interested go check out some Gotoh SG301-MG-T, button style 04. All the Revstar's have the same nut and have the same neck radius. One Revstar model in particular, the RSP20CR, is the only model that has a TUSQ nut as basic equipment from Yamaha. Since the neck is identical on my RS502T to the RSP20CR, i reached out to yamaha and asked what was the part number they use on the RSP20CR. They provided me with Part #WU137900. This correlates to graphtech part number BT-6114-00. BT-6114-00 is equivalent to PT-6114-00, except the BT means bulk packaging. This is why I bought the PT-6114-00 for my revstar RS502T.

Now, those that are looking for a drop in replacement need to understand that you cannot just drop this in. I had to sand the bottom of the TUSQ nut quite a bit to get to a close height where the strings would lie correctly. After i was satisfied with the height, there was further adjustment that was required to get the string height from the first fret appropriate so the strings were not sharp when fretted. I did need to nut slot file the upper 4 string slots a fair amount to get the position I wanted. I didn't own a set of files, so I bought the Stew-Mac nut slotting files, and they worked perfectly.

Overall I am much happier with the TUSQ nut than the Urea plastic nut Yamaha ships these Revstars with. But beware that you probably will need to be savvy enough to do some nut fitment, or take it to a luthier if you are not.
Summary: Great replacement nut for Yamaha Revstar 502T

Text:
Not all of these "brick" or "wall wort" power supplies are built the same. Although the standard center negative adapters are common-place, not all of them have sufficient filtering. The adapter's purpose is to transform the wall voltage (120VAC in the USA) down to 9V DC. It does this by rectifying and then filtering the resulting voltage. In non-musical applications, a certain amount of AC "ripple" voltage can be acceptable, but NOT in the case of audio products, like the effects pedals used for electronic music reproduction. In these applications, almost no amount of ripple is acceptable. At any rate, this converter produces negligible ripple. I am using it, through a "daisy chain" to power two pedals and the result is excellent - no external noise is introduced.

In most pedals, to keep the cost down, the use of high quality filter capacitors is minimal to non-existent. Pedal manufacturers rely on end users either using a 9v battery to power the effect (pure DC = absolutely NO ripple) or a power supply that has excellent filtering. That is why choosing the correct power supply for your pedals is so important. This one definitely does the job!
Summary: Very Well Made - Does Not Introduce Noise Into The Signal Chain

[[VIDEOID:94cdcc03a98548ba51e9fed590cedc92]] What is not to like about a less expensive alternative phase min-pedal? I normally run my output through a multi-pedal for effects, but it's not always possible to lug the pedal bag around with my guitar and a mini-pedal is just the thing for some quick jam sessions.

For the equipment: Guitar is an Epi LP strung with elixir nanoweb ultra lights, amp is an acoustic 15 watt. I played a simple DCG progression (yes, I know my timing is off...but my drummer was busy and I can't keep a beat!)

In the video clip, you can hear the guitar clean, then with the phase pedal (at full throttle), and then for some fun the last bit is the pedal with some distortion through the amp. Here are my thoughts:

1: At the lowest setting, you do get a touch of the phase. Just enough to let you know it's there.
2: As you crank the phase up, you do get more and more of the effect.
3: The effect sounds good. I don't have great hearing, but it sounds just as good as the multi-pedal that I use for gigs.
4: It seems to be pretty solid. The bypass switch has a loud tactile click with a bright red LED so you know it's on.
5: Bypass works as it should.
6: It does not come with a power supply, but does use a standard pedal AC converter power supply.
7: This pedal shines with some gain/distortion. Fine-tune it and you can get some neat hard rock sounds out of it.
8: I love the color.

If you're looking for a small footprint phaser pedal, go for it. If your ears are super sensitive and you can differentiate between the soft tones of a far-away bird tweet, then go ahead and buy it anyway for comparison. It's not going to break the bank!

Full Disclosure: I received this product for testing. Fuller disclosure: I would buy this pedal again without testing it, and will be looking at the other pedals offered.

First, the '68 Custom Princeton is neither like the '65 Princeton Reissue, nor is it a reissue of an actual '68 Princeton except in appearance. Rather, it's a '68 Princeton with modern modifications. A few of these mods include: the tone circuit is more like a Bassman, the amp breaks up early (after 4 on the Volume), the speaker is designed to help the early breakup, and the amp is very sensitive to picking dynamics. Anyone who is expecting a pristine clean tone above 3 or 4 on the Volume should look somewhere else entirely.

Having said that, this amp is designed for pristine cleans below 4, and then heavy breakup at 5 and above. The tone at low volumes is arguably like a Princeton, but bassier and slightly less "chimey". It still sparkles like a typical Princeton, but that ends after 4. Beyond 4 the amp begins to break up and gets very beefy in the lows and low-mids, some may even call it 'muddy". My first instinct was to roll off the bass to almost zero, which then made me want to roll the treble back to about 3. However, I soon realized that's the wrong approach. This amp needs the bass set to 5 or above and the treble at 7 or 8. With that EQ, plus Reverb set to 3 or less and Volume above 5, this amp starts to shake walls in small rooms. In fact, it made a piece of live rock near the top of my reef aquarium fall to the bottom of the tank from 5 feet away!

Reverb is nice and lush, though at 3 and above expect a long tail, especially at higher amp volumes. Tremolo is very useful and adds a very warm effect. If I am correct, reverb and tremolo are tube-based.

-The amp comes complete with a Fender embroidered dust cover and footswitch for Reverb and Tremolo.
-It sports Fender-branded Groove Tubes: two 6V6, three 12AX7, one AT7 and one 5AR4 (rectifier).
-Speaker is Celestion TEN-30. Though I am not a huge believer in speaker break-in, mine seems to have loosened up after the first 2 hours of use, and does seem to sound better: warmer, less brittle and more defined.

Pedals: I'm using a Fulltone OCD (v1.7) for rhythm drives, and a Wampler Pinnacle for additional volume and gain for solos. This works phenomenal. This amp takes pedals very well, and was specifically designed to do so. I have yet to try time-based effects, and wonder how they would translate.

If you run your guitar straight into the amp under Volume 4, you'll get nice clean Fender tones, especially with a single coil guitar. Les Pauls will be very bold and great for Jazz tones. At Volume 5 and above the amp will start to break up and vibrate and sound like the whole thing's going to explode. With a distortion pedal in the front set to moderate gain, you're going to get one heck of a LOUD, thick, punchy, bassy, HUGE sound! But you can still get great low-volume bedroom levels with a pedal too.

I hope my descriptions help you. I highly recommend this amp for anyone who wants the best of two worlds: low-volume Fender cleans, and loud tube amp breakup that will scare nearby fish but not the neighbors. If you want louder pristine cleans, look to the Deluxe models: '65 black face and the new '68 silver face. This amp shimmers down low, and gets nasty up high.

Overall I'd give this a 9 out of 10. Highly recommended.

***UPDATE: I have been using a few time-based effects with this amp and they work unbelievably well. Typically you wouldn't put time-based FX into the front end of an amp that's going to distort, but I'm not turning it up much past 4 so in this case it's producing great results. I'm currently using:

- TCE Flashback delay
- TCE Corona chorus
- TCE DITTO looper

Cheers!

When designing a product, one always has to ask the main question, first: "Who are you designing for?" or "What environment would the customer use this product in?"

I've written some very glowing reviews of Singing Machine Karaoke players in the past. I've probably made this company a fair bit of money as I had the spotlight review on a previous model for three years. I must've answered close to 50 customer emails regarding my review for would-be purchasers. Each time I edified this company to the utmost. Here -- this particular device is about as wrong as it can be.

First of all, the menus built into the software are klunky and difficult to find, use and adjust. When I plugged my unit in, the echo was cranked all the way up. I kept digging around trying to find how to normalize it but the menus looked to be designed by someone using COBOL or Fortran. Wow. I couldn't believe it. It was like dealing with machine code. I thought it was a joke. If you think an entry level user is going to be okay with this, guess again. The on-screen software is ugly and unfriendly.

Second, the device opening is about as awkward as everyone has stated in the other reviews and sometimes even moreso. The moment you stand up and sing with a wired mic, you're always looking at the thing hoping your're not going to launch the device across the room if you whip the mic cord too hard.

Third, the microphone is probably the worst I've seen since something bought at radio shack in the 80s. It's really bad. I mean bad. The voice projection is hollow and tinny, like you're singing through a tin can even at a basic singing level. If this is for kids, with softer voices -- guess again -- most kids belt into the mic in their natural loud kid voice. Nothing but distortion. This mic is nothing like previous wired mics from this company and they should probably just recall this thing and forget it.

So, who would use this and where? Kids? I don't think so. This thing is difficult to use, sounds bad, looks dumb and just all-around unfriendly. So, we have to conclude that it's for adults ... who live in quiet, small, spaces like those micro-apartments reported on the news of 250 square feet in San Francisco ... or the other side of the same coin ... adults in correctional facilities. Karaoke for Prisoners. Fantastic idea.

Need a karaoke machine for the kids? Try this one by the same company, it's fantastic. I own one and have given several as Christmas presents.

[[ASIN:B001AW3UHC Singing Machine SML-385 CDG Karaoke System With Sound and Disco Light Show]]

Don't be fooled by this hunk of garbage, Singing Machine makes the best entry level Karaoke Machines, without doubt. This thing must be just an experiment by them that got out of control. I expect greater things from them, but it definitely won't look anything like this nasty device.

The Saramonic Blink-Go system is very good for use with my mobile devices.

The system comes with a soft carrying case that is nothing to write home about. I wish it comes with a case that has organization -- to separate the transmitters and the receiver, for example. Saramonic includes two USB-A to USB-C charging cables in my double transmitter bundle which is nice. I can charge the transmitters with all my regular USB-C to USB-C PD charging setup as well, a big plus.

The mics come with a small foam wind shield -- the ones that can easily be lost. They just fit over the rectangular ends of the transmitter, so any generic version should work.

The sound quality: The sound quality is good. It is better than a built in mic on any mobile devices. The main attraction of the Saramonic system is that I can be much further away from the receiver / iPhone / iPad, and the sound quality is still constant. The system records in simulated stereo, meaning both mics are mixed to equal left and right channel.

The range is good. When I am 30 feet away the sound is just as good. The noise cancelling mode is so-so. It reduces the gain and also limit the high and low end, muffling the sound. I can definitely hear the difference. Unless the surrounding is extremely noisy, you are better off with just the standard mode.

Overall -- a very nice system -- especially the two mics version for a very flexible audio setup for both indoors and outdoors.

I am updating this review because I have discovered something amazing. I always felt this mic was a little sharp in the highs.  But recently, I added a foam pop-filter "within" another larger foam pop filter.  The resulting sound is absolutely amazing when running the flat (no low cut) switch -- especially if you eat the mic.  It completely cured the high-end issue, yet allows me to get right on top of the mic for near zero P-pop issues.  To make it sound even more natural, EQ it a bit around the ESS-range.  I dropped it about -4.5db around the 6000hz range, creating a long dip when ends between 5,000 and 12,000 hz to make for a more natural sound without that excessive top end many mics have, these days.  Move an inch off, and it's perfect. This mic is now out-performing large-diaphram condensers costing 10x as much, and it's also dead-on perfect for Zoom, and virtually no need to de-ess.  It's like a Shure SM7b with no need for a cloudlifter, if you add two sponge filters (smaller within a larger one).  I'm so giddy about it, I'm going to make a video, soon.
Summary: Add two layers of foam pop-filter on the head, and it's absolutely stunning.

Text:
This is a very fun and relaxing tongue drum. It is tuned to F major, which also places it in mixolydian C (the Bb being a flat seven, just like playing a diatonic harmonica in fifth position).. It sounds good with the mallets when it on a hard surface - not so good on a lap - and it is tuned very well. According to my orchestral tuner, these pitches are all spot on. So if you want to play with another instrument, or record with it, you can do that easily. That's a very big plus.

This also comes with finger mallets, but those are a bit tougher to get a solid tone from. It can be done, but it takes a bit of practice. Playing with the stick mallets is much easier. Of course, playing with your fingers makes triads possible, so if you want to harmonize, that's a better way to go. The times are spaced in thirds next to each other, so going from a one to a four to a five is easy. Actually, any diatonic triad is easy. Likewise, if you play it in C, you have only a flat seven, which can be useful in the correct context - so you get two keys out of this drum.

It comes with a songbook, but it's really fun to just improvise on and relax. This is an excellent tool for someone who wants to explore music without being overwhelmed. It sounds nice as well, metallic but deep, with a strong second harmonic that fades in a lovely way after stringing a tongue.

Highly recommended.

I've been playing guitar more than 35 years and have used a lot of electronic tuners. The first was slightly larger than a paperback book and cost what a cheap guitar sells for today. But it was a godsend tuning up backstage while another band was playing. Over the years tuners have gotten smaller, cheaper, and easier to use. The Planet Waves PW-CT-12 is my new favorite.

It is very small - a little bit larger than a grape. Despite some of the other reviews I have used it with good results on a Strat, Tele, Les Paul, and ES-335 electrics and on acoustics from Martin, Gibson, National Resophonic, and Voyage Air. I clamp it on the headstock between the nut and the low-E tuner. I didn't expect it but it is out of the way enough to leave on while playing. Previous to this my favorite tuner was a chromatic ukulele tuner built to clamp on the top of the headstock. Small and accurate but to use it behind the headstock I have to read it upside down. The PW-CT-12 is nicely out of the way even when I play an F chord with my thumb on the low E string. It's so light I don't notice it's there.

The display is bright and easy to see in most light. A bit hard to read in direct sunlight but I do my best to avoid playing without shade anyway. The display is small - a dime can cover most of it - but the characters are large enough to read in normal playing position. The '#' sharp symbol is small but once you are familiar with the display you recognize it. (No flat symbol. Bb is displayed as A#.) The tuner has auto shutoff to make the battery last longer. The display uses bars to the side of the note letter and color to indicate tuning. It's red until you get close then green with a bar on each side when you are in tune (for example, |E|). I found it to be stable enough to be easy to use for quick tune ups between songs.

These are inexpensive and intended to be discrete so the clamp is small and thin. Rough handling will probably break it. I notice that the clamp is easily removed so I'm guessing Planet Waves may sell replacements. The clamp was not intuitive the first time but the instructions do cover it. It is a ratchet rather than a clamp. You press a small tab and gently pull the clamp out then push it down on the guitar neck. For this reason this is not a tuner to pass around. It's meant to be left on an instrument. (It's small enough that you can leave it on in the case.) If you need a tuner that is moved frequently there are better (and larger) choices. It can be moved but it is a good tuner to set and forget. I'm going to buy a couple more to leave on my most frequently used guitars.

Other reviewers commented on accuracy. If you want strobe accuracy there are better choices. For that kind of accuracy you also need a larger display. This tuner will get you close quickly and you can use your ears to fine tune if necessary. I haven't had a problem except with guitars that have built-in intonation problems (like old Nationals) and they need tweaking even after a Peterson Strobe.

Soapbox: especially if you are a new player, do yourself a favor and learn to tune your guitar by ear! Try tuning the strings to a reference pitch or each other then use the tuner to check. Learning to tune by ear will help you in more ways than I have time to list. Being able to hear the intervals in a chord and know which string is off is an invaluable skill. People that can only tune with a tuner will take much longer to develop that, if ever.

I have now purchased two MOTU M2's from different sellers about 4-6 weeks apart and both exhibited similar behaviour. The first one gave me 10-20s of recording then died and came up on the USB port with an error with unable to handshake (on any PC I threw it on). Now the second gave me about 8-10 minutes and I turned it off then I turned it back on to do some recording about two days later and it didn't turn on. Fear came over me that it had blown up my port while it was off but after I swapped it over with my keyboard the keyboard worked but not it. YAY, at least my USB port was fine. I then remove the USB-C plug from the back of the unit and put it back in, and flip the on switch, and power again. YAY. I talked into the microphone and the meters moved (as did the first one even after death) but when I loaded up the DAW, and OBS, nothing. I looked and sure enough the pc didn't even see it. I then looked at a few other programs, including their driver, and nothing saw the interface. I unplugged the cable, rebooted, plugged the cable back in, turn the unit on but nothing changed.

I have other USB devices (including a camera) and I have never had an issue with them so something is really flaky with the M2 in these covid times and I firmly believe this is the problem as they are rushing, or at least were, to try and keep up with demand and in that rush issues came.
Summary: Two M2's dead in under 10 mins.

If I am to be honest, I have largely been a skeptic when it comes to IR Amp/Cab simulators. I've always thought that the best sounds come ONLY from running a guitar through an amp and letting the sound waves fly through the air. The few times I've tried digital amp/cab sims were through various DAWs and old gen pedals. Sometimes they were passible, but they never really hit that itch for me.

Things change however when children become a part of your life and thus aren't able to blast the amp all the time. So I was looking for a solution for 3 main reasons: 1) I want to still be able to write and record musical ideas into my DAW. 2) I need an effective mainstay unit that can be used for live performance since it will serve as also become my main practice unit. 3) won't wake the kids.

Simply put, I was impressed with the capabilities of this unit. I'll list some of my favorite highlights:
1) Responsive and sensitive to how I play the guitar. It captures the nuances and expresses them well
2) Detailed controls to set up the digital amps (and many choices) and Cabinets (can even set mic distance/placement)
3) Many useful presets
4) Can work well using it as an "amp" and just running your pedal board through it.
5). A variety of useful effects that can be turned on/off and adjusted in detail (the effects chain order is fixed however).
6) Moore has an online community producing more IR presets...and you can add your own, too. The community is still small, but you can find some neat sounds there.
7) Though editing can be done on the unit, using the App makes it way easier...and you can store to your computer too.

I am currently using it for a project and it is delivering and even spawning some ideas I never considered.
All in all this is a great "all in one" unit. Great for beginners who love exploring possibilities and also great for more seasoned musicians that require space savers, mobility, or maintaining peace with sensitive children without losing quality.

Things to be aware of when working with these:
1. This is a digital unit so firmware updates are possibilities and so you should connect it to the computer from time to time.
2. In similar theme to the above, there will ALWAYS be a chance that as technology progresses, the unit will eventually lose support from MOORE. It happened to one of my favorite digital amps, the Mustang IV by Fender and even to one of my boss pedals (ME-25). What this means is that there may be a time where you won't be able to connect it to a computer if the App becomes "obsolete" or that the company may choose to not support certain operating systems. Just know that you can still use these units...you'll just either have to use the App and store locally without using the online features OR you can still do your edits on the pedal itself. I still effectively use and edit my Mustang IV even now. This unit is even easier.
3. The effects editing process on the unit is actually really simple, but you will just need to get used to how it's down since knobs are multi-use.

Text: I've used these strings before on my classical guitar, and loved them. I ordered this new set since I do change strings every few months. The sound of the black trebles is very clear and warm., and I like the way the strings look on my guitar.  The strings have ball ends which actually makes no difference to me, since  I have had no problems with tying on traditional nylon strings either. They settle in very quickly--after a couple of days--but it depends on how often you play your guitar. There is no stated tension for these strings, so when I bought my first set and opened the package I was a little appalled because they looked so thick.  I have some arthritis in my fingers which flares up from time to time, and smallish hands (and classical guitars have wider necks as well), so I was surprised that they were not hard to press down on at all. It would of course depend on the action on your own particular guitar.  The manufacturer website describes the strings as having medium tension, and this seems about right. Despite the label as "folk singer",  I don't thiink these would work that well on a steel stringed acoustic guitar.  Those want a really bright tone to their guitars might not like these strings either. While the tone is very clear and pure, it is also very mellow and warm, which is what I personally prefer.
Summary: One of my favorite classical guitar strings

You are required to not only register and fill out an annoying form, but you have to first make an actual account on their website, too. And of course, while you're doing that, they're pitching you on upgrades and additional purchases that you have to skip in order to finally reach your download. Plus if you're the type of person who uses the same password on multiple websites (hopefully people aren't doing that anymore), this is one more location for your data to be potentially stolen and used on other sites that you have the same password on.

Fortunately, you only have to go through this ordeal once, so after that, it's smooth sailing and the unit is great. But I had to deduct a star for the initial setup.

Text:
I am quite pleased with my purchase of the newly-released Vox AC10C1, a 10-watt combo amplifier featuring a 10" Celestion speaker. I apologize in advance for the length of this review, but I did quite a bit of research on the AC10C1 and its place in the Vox lineup. I hope my comments prove useful for prospective buyers, and I will amend my review if my thoughts on the amp change or evolve over time.

BACKGROUND - The AC10C1 is in some respects a resurrection of a discontinued vintage product and, in other respects, a completely "new" product. Vox manufactured an "AC10" from 1959 to 1967, but the similarities between the two basically end with the model name and wattage. The original AC10 was a square "TV front" combo amplifier that was offered both in a single 10", or as a 2x10" "Twin" configuration. The original AC10 featured multiple inputs, vibrato, an open-back cabinet, and an assortment of 5 tubes under the hood.

FEATURES OF THE AC10C1 - In 2015, Vox released the AC10C1, but the amp is far from a "reissue" of this original design. Rather, Vox seems to created a completely new design targeting something that the famed AC15 and AC30 do not offer - a sub-$500 tube/valve combo amplifier capable reasonably suited for portability, and home/studio use at reasonable volumes. The feature set of the AC10C1 is somewhat limited, but mostly in line with similarly priced "entry-level" tube amplifiers. There is a single input jack, and extension cabinet jack for 10 watts in a 16-ohm cabinet, a separate gain and master volume control, and knobs for bass, treble, and reverb. There is also a main power switch but no standby switch (my understanding is that this is commonly missing on many modern lower powered tube amps).

PROS - I had the opportunity to try out the AC10C1 a few times before I bought it, and I was instantly enamored with the tone. It somehow marries the "chime" and "dirty cleans" of a signature Vox tone with a fuller low end presence - almost like a Fender Deluxe Reverb. One thing important to point out is that this amp becomes loud fairly quickly. I am using it exclusively as a hobbyist for bedroom/basement levels, but if controlling volume for your neighbors is a priority, there are other amps I would consider first. But the nice about the AC10C1 is that it is at least capable of bedroom level cleans (or overdriven tones, due to the master volume control), while also having horsepower for keeping up with other instruments and possibly some smaller gigs. I've been in love the tone of an AC30 for years, but it wasn't until the AC10C1 was released that Vox made an all-tube amplifier that I could realistically consider owning.

The aesthetics of this amp nail vintage Vox, and I believe that is a step in the right direction for this company, which has spent the last 15 years or so releasing some decent products (Night Train, Valvetronix, etc.) that are either divisive or downright ugly in appearance, depending on whom you ask. The rectangular shape not only makes the amp look like a smaller AC30, but I believe it benefits the sound. Some 10" combo amps develop a "boxy" sound that can be quite directional. The wider, closed-back cabinet deflects bass frequencies forward across a wider field, and I would argue that this amp can compete with some 12" combos in terms of fullness in a home practice setting.

Vox advertises that the AC10C1 features the famous "Top Boost" circuitry made popular on the AC30 and popularized by players like Brian May and The Edge. People who understand amp circuitry better than I do have remarked that the tube configuration of the AC10C1 is quite different from the authentic Top Boost circuit. Whatever you call it, however, the amp is extremely warm-sounding and versatile. Low wattage, single-channel tube amps seem to fail more often than not at offering a combination of clean headroom and rich, saturated overdrive tones. The AC10C1 nails both, and can do so at a variety of volumes. At 27 pounds (versus 47 pounds for the AC15), it is also surprisingly lightweight and portable.

CONS - Despite my overwhelming positive impressions of the AC10C1, this is far a perfect product both in design and in execution. Let's get the elephant in the room out of the way first - the amp is manufactured in China, much a like an increasing portion of affordable gear nowadays. If your expectation for a tube amplifier is that it is hand wired in the US or UK, then those products are available for you, but usually at a considerably higher cost. Chinese construction is a reality of globalization in 2015, especially in the more affordable end of the guitar gear spectrum. My personal view on it is that guitar playing is a hobby for me, and my gear does not need to "perform" or be thrown into vans at 2am. If it is built well enough to sit in my basement, I hope that I can take care of it and get many years of enjoyment, while saving money that I don't have to spend on $1,000+ amplifiers. But the fact remains that this is the first run of a new product, so nobody can say for certain if there are any pressing design flaws.

I have not removed the back of the cabinet, but have seen pictures of the amp's internals from other people who have. The components, including the two pre-amp and two power amp tubes are arranged and fastened in a manner that seems more focused on keeping the size compact, as opposed to convenience or long-term durability. Also, I have heard that speaker replacement on this amp can be quite difficult because there is simply not much room to install a speaker of a different size/shape. So, if you are into modding, this is almost certainly not the right amp for you, but I like amp stock, and as long as it continues function for many years, I will be happy enough.

Feature-wise, the amp does not have an effects loop, which is a bit disappointing for me, as I like to use effects pedals, and the loop can really expand the way effects are used. The on-board reverb is digital, and I actually like the initial attack and quality of its tone. But if this amp is ever revised, I hope they re-tune it a bit because it seems to favor long decay times even on very low settings. I found that using the reverb on "1" or even less than "1" was all that I needed, but that setting would usually correspond to a "3" or a "4" on a Fender amp, for example. At the end of the day, it's not a great reverb, but it's better that it's there versus not having one at all. I do plan on using it, and an amp with on-board reverb is more tempting to plug directly into, which means it is more likely to get played.

ALTERNATIVES TO THE AC10C1 - As written above, I bought the AC10C1 exclusively to use as a home combo amp. I wanted it to get just slightly louder than I would ever need, while retaining fullness and clarity at bedroom levels. I believe the AC10C1 does that exceptionally well. It nails the character of "Vox clean", which adds in tube saturation and sustain to a tone that otherwise remains brilliant and expressive, walking a delicate line between "clean" and "overdriven".

But if you are looking for a solid tube amplifier without being married to the idea of owning a Vox, there are other options out there. The VHT Special 6 is one such option, and retails for nearly $200 less. Vox offers the Night Train 15 for nearly the same price, and it has an effects loop and more tonal versatility (though I preferred the sounds of the AC10C1). Fender offers a Pro Junior (10") and Blues Junior (12") which are quality tube amplifiers with a longer track record than the new AC10C1. For gigging, the AC15 is a larger, louder relative of the AC10C1, and may be worth the additional money. I do not recommend the AC4-112, which is slightly cheaper, but lacks the low end presence of the AC10C1.

For a very affordable bedroom solution, however, I would also recommend checking out the Vox Pathfinder 15, which is a now-discontinued solid state 8" combo. It can be found used for about $75 to $125, and is an absolute freak of nature in its ability to offer Vox cleans (and even some overdriven tones) in a portable, inexpensive package with no tubes involved.

Time will tell if the Vox AC10C1 is a reliable amp. But I think there is little question they have made a great sounding, 10" combo that covers the full range of classic Vox tones. It offers the authentic warmth of an all-tube amplifier and manageable volumes and a decent price point. I wish I was playing mine right now.

UPDATE (10/08/15) - Posting a quick update only a couple of weeks after buying the amp to report that my factory-shipped model functioned absolutely perfectly and sounds great. I did some research on the tubes (which are Chinese-made and of debated quality), and after verifying from Korg/Vox that these can be replaced without re-biasing, I ordered some Tungsol 12AX7's for the preamp and (matched) JJ EL84's for the power amp. I will be leaving the stock Celestion speaker as is. The tube change may or may not make an appreciable difference, but I'm going to try it out, as I have heard several AC10C1 users reporting a noticeable improvement.
Summary: Classic Vox tones with warmth and fullness in a home/studio-sized package

I have a number of these devices used in around-the-clock radio production.

To use these devices with WindoZe, you MUST load the Behringer (or other equivalent) USB drivers. This is because the stock drivers provided by Microsoft do not support line level audio, which is the only kind this device does. Failure to load the drivers will result in a level mismatch, and consequent bad quality audio. This is not a problem with the device, it is a problem with the WinDowZe stock drivers.

I have a Behringer mixer with built-in USB, however, I use the UCA202 (family) device because it has no detectable electronic noise, while the built-in USB interface does. Counter-intuitive, but that's my experience.

The devices do seem susceptible to failure. I've had two fail, in environments that _should_ be free of ground loops, etc. -- connecting only to electrically isolated devices (incl. laptop). However, given the price and utility of the devices, I still give them 5 stars.

I would recommend buying the UCA222 instead of the UCA202 because it's a newer design. The UFO202 is designed for use with turntables that do not have their own pre-amps.
Summary: Very high quality audio, but some have died

Text:
My experience with the ATW-1102 system is limited so, consider this review a first impression.

Judging from the lack of reviews, there's not many of these out there just yet. But, this technology seems to be the direction of wireless sound systems. The only down-side I've seen so far is excessive battery consumption. Sound reproduction is excellent. So, four stars for incredible sound reproduction. Minus one star for battery consumption. Read on.

I bought two of these from a local source to replace a couple UHF wireless mics which operated in a frequency range that was re-dedicated to public service entities by FCC in about 2010, i.e. 698 to 806 MHz wireless microphones are now illegal to use in US & Canada. (Mexico might also have adopted the same protocol). The ATW-1102's are UHF mics (300MHz to 3 GHz) and operate at 2.4 GHz. (That's over-simplifying everything).

Wireless mics require batteries. And, most wireless mics do not have a battery meter to tell you when your power source is about to die.. So, you'll find yourself replacing good batteries 'just to be safe' and to make sure the thing doesn't die mid-sentence or mid-song. The 1102's are no different in this regard. There is no battery meter on these; they have a blinking green light that indicates low battery....and you have to be looking directly at the microphone to see the green light flashing on and off. There's no indicator on the receiver.

I've found that mics which require 9v batteries operate longer and are more reliable. (arguable). Those which require AA's and AAA's usually require more frequent battery replacement. The ATW-1102 owners manual suggests that two AA batteries should be good for 7 hours "depending on usage pattern". My experience is that you 'might' get 3 hours with the 1102 mic continuously on and actually used for 45 minutes of that time speaking normally into the mic at 50-62 db.

They're simple to set up, easy to adjust and are engineered in such a way as to virtually eliminate feedback by manipulating on board gain adjustment. I could stand maybe four feet in front of a speaker with a hot mic and not be afraid of feedback.

Were it not for the battery consumption issue, which I don't think is all THAT inconsistent with other wireless mics which require AA or AAA batteries, these things would be perfect. Battery consumption is what it is: there's better and much worse out there. But, for the current price of these units, battery consumption might be a deal breaker. Had I known beforehand that they'd suck this much juice, I might've considered other manufacturers. But AudioTechnica quality is hard to beat. The reason I bought these is because I also had some ATW-700's. Excellent quality stuff!

At this writing there is a rebate of $25 if you buy two of the System 10 ATW-1102's. It seems also that they can be purchased cheaper locally than on Amazon. That certainly will change as the price will certainly have to come down.

And, that's my first impression. Hope it's helpful.

I LOVE TC Electronic products, but this one misses the mark. I think they've over engineered the thing.

I like to use some compression to fatten up my clean tone for some funkier rhythm playing. I play both a strat and a tele through a Marshall tube combo amp. I run my signal through a compressor, a Blues Driver with the gain real low that stays on all the time, and then an overdrive pedal as needed. All this goes into the Marshall's clean channel with the gain set at about 50%.

There were a few things about the HyperGravity that led me to return it:
1) It's not plug-and-play friendly. Yes, it has the ability to dial in some custom tones, but that takes work. I want something I can drop on a pedal board and tweak right out of the box, and this pedal doesn't do that.
2) It makes my overall tone dark, swampy, muddy. Strats in particular have this great shimmering tone, but the HyperGravity kills that.
3) It adds noticeable gain. In one sense, this pedal by itself adds some of that subtle gain that I get from running my Blues Driver all the time. There's a quality similar to a transparent overdrive. But, unfortunately, this just isn't practical. It makes it more difficult to dial in a true clean sound, and then there's what it does down the signal path..
4) It makes my other pedals sound like garbage. Though when used by itself it makes the tone muddy, it also somehow manages to make overdrive pedals farther down the signal path tinny, with a less pleasing breakup.

I've previously been using the Joyo compresser, which costs $37: https://www.amazon.com/JOYO-JF-10-Dynamic-Compressor-Guitar/dp/B007T8CUNG/

With the Joyo, I had a real nice twangy sound with my bridge pickups and a great bluesy, funk thing going with neck pickups. Just swapping out the Joyo for the HyperGravity, I ended up with very aggressive tones, with a lot more breakup and distortion from the drives. It's as if the HyperGravity was trying to do [[ASIN:B007T8CUNG JOYO JF-10 Dynamic Compressor Guitar Effect Pedal]]more to my signal than it was supposed to, and just not playing well with others.

I could see this pedal playing an important role for a musician that maybe plays through solid state gear, or primarily uses clean tones. Otherwise, it's honestly just not fun to play with. It's too much work to get good tone.
Summary: Muddy tone and too much work to dial it in.

As a guitarist who has been happily and successfully tying classical guitar strings for 50 years, I didn't see a need for this product, but I was curious. Call me a sceptic. I put these on a good, handmade classical guitar, that has a naturally warm, round sound (cedar top.) The instructions were easy but for someone who is used to tying strings, it seemed like an awfully fiddly process. I didn't like doing it and almost didn't bother. The set of beads I received were not a consistent color, so I opted to put the darker ones on the 2 E strings and keep the lighter ones in the center. See photo 1. You ned to be sure whatever strings you use has a generous length G string -- in my experience, not all string makers' strings are the same length, and with the extra inch+ the bead requires, it might make a difference.

I took a photo in-process to demonstrate the slightly harder angle at which tying with the beads angles the string downward from the saddle of the bridge. If I didn't see that increased angle, I would not have continued. See photo 2.

Because I am a skeptical user, I feel compelled to say that I can hear a volume increase on my guitar. I didn't really want to believe it and though I was just being suggestible, but a couple of my students noticed the slight change in projection. So, I am giving this product a reluctant 5 stars. Reluctant for 2 reasons - neither major.
1 - the non-matching color
2 - it took me 3 times longer to tie my strings than without them. I will probably cut that time down as I (if I) continue to use the beads.

Extremely interesting product. If you're a new nylon string player/owner, I definitely recommend them. If you've been happily tying your strings for decades, give them a try but plan to spend much more time with this process than it usually takes you, for the pay-off of enhanced projection. If you have a student or entry level guitar, they may make a nice, inexpensive upgrade in sound for you.

Text:
I’ve had the Boss Katana for a while now. I have several different amps, tube and modeling. The Katana is a great amp at a great price. The tone is really exceptional compared to the other amps I own in this price range...the fender mustang GT100, the katana air, or the Orange 20 watt. Functionally, it has 5 voices that cover pretty much any tone. The effects and reverb options are extensive. It also has variable output power, which is very useful at home. You can hook it up to your phone for backing tracks or to access tone central with hundreds of different presets. I don’t use these features, which brings me to the downside of this amp...it does not have Bluetooth connectivity, requiring a wire connection, which is inconvenient. Additionally the effects selection is displayed by various colored lights which you cannot remember.

If this amp had Bluetooth and a small LCD screen it would blow away the competition. Compared to the Fender Mustang GT100, the katana sounds a LOT better, but the mustang has a very intuitive interface and WiFi and Bluetooth connectivity that works great. The Mustang is a modeling amp that has dozens of different amps modeled, but in truth this functionality is pretty worthless. All the different amp models fall into more or less the same categories as the Katana. I thought the modeling functionality would be really worthwhile, but it really isn’t as useful as it sounds. The Orange 20 watt has its own voice, but the amp is very primitive in terms of functionality. The Katana Air is a portable amp that sounds nowhere are good as the katana 50, but does have Bluetooth functionality. Final comparison...to a hand wired ‘57 tweed deluxe tube amp. While a tube amp always makes you feel good, I really have to put the Boss Katana 50 clean tone right up there with it.

Overall a great amp at a great price. Hopefully, Boss will include Bluetooth and an LCD interface in future models.
Summary: Wonderful tone and functionality for a bargain price...comparison to a few other amps below

I specified this assembly on two drum kits I had custom made and agree with another reviewer that bass drum shell mounted cymbal arms do not affect the sustain in the least. That said, I did have problems with this particular assemble leaning if the tightening screw backed off in the slightest, which was more often than I cared for. When I acquired a [[ASIN:B0046W328A Gretsch 4pc Catalina Club Jazz Shell Pack]] I naturally planned to install a mounted cymbal arm, and when searching for this one I discovered the [[ASIN:B001U0ORMG DW Drum Workshop SM770 Bass Drum Mounted Cymbal Arm w/L-Arm & Bracket]], which I purchased, installed and became a true believer in that model. See my review for why and also for one issue I had with installing it.

Back to this one: the mounting bracket that ships with this is as solid as a rock and is engineered to hold just about anything inserted into it. It is also hinged, and will hold 12 and 10.5 MM arms. The arm that ships with this assembly is the weak link in my opinion (it's 10.5 vs the DW's 12.5 MM diameter.)

The main point of comparison between this assembly and the DW is price. The DW is nearly twice as expensive, but - and this is my personal opinion only - I think the additional cost is worth it for the peace of mind it gives me knowing that a cymbal is not going to lean or fall over while I am playing. Granted, I have never had one fall over, but I have had them lean, and I am a light hitter who plays mainly jazz. For the record, my right side ride sizes range from 21" (K Custom Special Dry Ride) to various 22 and 24 inch rides, most of which are relatively thin and light.
