Text:
This compact wireless microphone system works well - a package which comes in a case with plenty of adapters. The receiver terminates in a 3.5 mm plug, and there is both an 1/4 inch adapter for professional gear, and a 3.5 mm cell phone adapter that allows you plug in the microphone and a pair of headphones. The lavaliere microphone comes with a metal clip and a foam windscreen (a spare is included as well). It is permanently attached to the transmitter. Also included is a belt clip for the transmitter.

The receiver and transmitter can be charged simultaneously through a USB cable that has two microUSB connectors, and a standard USB plug. This is a great feature, as it means there is no unique charger to lose, and it can be charged off a convenient source such as a laptop. Turn on the transmitter and receiver when they are close together, and they pair automatically. I

have used this wireless microphone system to record presentations with my iPhone Xr. Since my iPhone doesn’t have a headphone jack, I used a lightning to 3.5 mm adapter, and then plugged the included cell phone adapter plug into it. The manufacturer states this microphone has a distance of 50 feet - in my case I was at a maximum of 25 feet away, and it worked fine.

Sound quality is good enough. It is designed for recording a speaking voice, not music. The transmitter has a rocker switch on the side for setting the microphone output level. It took a little experimentation, but I managed to get a good level for recording.

This microphone’s big strengths are that it is compact and can be charged via USB. The case for the microphone is well designed and fits in a laptop bag easily. This makes it ideal for my use, recording presentations so that I can put them online later. In all this is a decent wireless microphone system at a good price.
Summary: Affordable and Compact - Charges off USB

I'm a podcasting addict--I've tried just about every popular mic on the market. Out of the other options, this one ranks very low for me.

The Blue microphones have always sounded "robotic" to me. In fact, sometimes I listen to a podcast and can tell right off that they're using a Snowball. However, they are reliable and I certainly couldn't say the same for the MXL 770.

For the same price, you could pick up an Audio Technica ATR2100, which I'd consider to be superior in every single way. It's XLR AND USB, the sound signature is far more clear and natural, and it's even a little less expensive.

For about $100 you can also get a Shure SM58. That mic truly is legendary, and it's great for podcasting. The audio is a little better than the ATR2100 and it's more directional (cuts out room sound better). The trouble with choosing the SM58 is that you don't get USB (Same as Rode Procaster mentioned below). So in this case you'll need a Zoom h5 or Zoom h6 to be your audio mixer and recorder in one. This provides a MUCH higher quality recording and is easier to do.

Compared to higher-end mics, the ATR2100 leaves a little to be desired. At the top of the market I'd put the Rode Procaster above even the venerable Heil PR40--and I've tested all of these mics side-by-side multiple times.

In short, it's not a BAD mic, but there are better options out there for the money.

As an English Man, this Distortion seemed right up my alley!

Definitely some type of MIAB (Marshall In A Box), which is a pretty common distortion type.

Controls have the usual Level, Drive and Tone but they’ve included a “PRES” (Presence) knob, which is described as adjusting the “thrust of the effector” … which doesn’t really match my understanding of a presence control! The Presence and Tone both raise / lower treble but the EQ curves are different and seem to impact bass and mids differently. So there’s definitely value in having both and it does allow for a lot of fine tuning. Overall, you can get pretty muffled by reducing either knob to zero, and ice-pick high-end by maxing either out. The sweet spots I found were usually a little left or right of noon.

There’s plenty of gain on tap, definitely enough for classic and hard rock, which is probably the target audience for a classic Marshall.

Doesn’t seem to introduce much hiss when engaged (unless you’re going crazy with the Drive AND Tone/Pres controls). True bypass, so no issues when it’s turned off.

Text:
"Mouth organ," "pocket harp", call 'em what you will, a good harmonica is a wonderful thing. And the Eastar 24 Holes Harmonica Admiral Performance Competition Harmonica takes that "wonderful" and extends it for another entire octave.

This is a melody player, not a "blues harp." It's principles sonarities come from being "blown" in the named key, not so much 'inhaled' and "bent" in the named key's 4th.

That makes the key of C a good choice. (Blues harps are usually better in the named keys of A and D so that their pentatonic inhaled and bent notes work in the oft preferred guitar keys of E and A.)

And it's also why the extended range is so, SO nice. Especially since the upper notes on this excellent harmonica are sonically rich, not thin and piercing as they often are on a lesser instrument.

The quality of a harmonica is best revealed by its sound -- the place where this one most particularly shines. But along with its rich sound there are other indicators that this, despite its very reasonable price here on Amazon, is no "cheapy."

One is the quality of it chrome covers and its comb. -The later of which has white indicators to help you find your place when starting a song. A nice touch I've missed even on some pretty pricey 'harps.'

Its case, too, is solid. "Deluxe" if you will. The Admiral Performance Competition Harmonica is thus one you'll be happy to take with you and, even more, proud to pull out and play.

Well, at least I will! More amazing because my own playing is most commonly blues.

But this 'harp' will be going places with me. After all, we should always be ready to break out in song!

Highly recommended.
Summary: An Extended Range Harmonica with Rich Full Tone

I decided to try these out on an old T. Haruo Model 80 acoustic guitar that I had bought back in the 1970s.

I leveled the frets first and then crowned them with a fret crowning file that I'd also just bought. When I was done crowning the frets, I used the coarser fret eraser on them. Without taking the trouble to look it up, I think the grits on the erasers are 180, 400 and 1000.

The 180 grit does a very nice and quick job on the frets. I didn't notice too much more improvement with the 400 grit. Of course, there was some improvement, but the improvement from crowning the frets with a file and then to polishing them with the 180 grit eraser was the biggest and quickest improvement. In fact, you could probably get by with the 180 grit eraser alone.

I didn't care too much about the guitar. I hadn't played it in decades. I didn't care if I ruined it. However, I found out that I was able to do a perfect job on the frets without even touching the fingerboard. Don't do this, though!

I had a box full of various Martin acoustic strings, so I went ahead and strung up the guitar. Surprisingly, the guitar sounds beautiful. The workmanship, if you look close, is no where near the quality of a Martin guitar, but the sound is probably as good as an upper end Martin, surprisingly. I know because I also have a Martin HD-28 acoustic guitar. The T. Haruo guitars, like many other guitars, were styled after the Martin guitars, especially the Martin Dreadnought guitars. The Dreadnoughts are the largest or "jumbo" Martin guitars.

Anyway, if you are going to use the fret erasers, you probably care about your guitar or you wouldn't be taking the trouble to polish the frets. In that case, I'd suggest using masking tape between all the frets that you are working on. You can buy different widths of masking tape. You'll need a narrow width for the higher frets, so it's best to buy one roll of wide width and one roll of narrow width tape. I doubt very much that the fret erasers are going to hurt your frets, but the 180 grit will brighten the dirtiest and nastiest frets very quickly, for starters. If you want to spend enough time, you can bring the frets up to a pretty good shine using the other erasers.
Summary: They do what they're supposed to do.

THREE of my students have these. Every one of them plays in tune, stays in tune and sounds great.
Two of them came from the box with perfect intonation and low action. The other one required only minimal tweaking to get perfect. ( about five minutes)

The pickups are passive single-coils, so there WILL be some noise if you use only one pickup at a time.
Use BOTH pickups simultaneously and the noise cancels.

The MOST IMPORTANT thing is, these are REAL instruments, not cheap walmart toys. That's CRUCIAL if you want your budding bassist to practice.

Playing a crummy toy that never sounds right, won't play in tune and looks cheap is a perfect storm of misery that prevents anyone ( especially kids) from ever practicing. That's especially true if the instrument is difficult to play because of high action. Most basses and guitars have some mechanism for adjusting the action, but that is useless unless the neck and other components are stable and solid. On a crummy instrument ( bass or guitar) you can't lower the action beyond a certain threshold where the strings buzz, fret-out or even play the wrong notes!

Ibanez makes even their least expensive to higher standards than most other makers, so you actually CAN adjust these when needed.

For the price, these are an incredible bargain. I could easily use one on a professional gig and no one would notice the difference unless it was a fellow bassist who SAW me with the bass. You can make this sound just like a pro bass. It's just smaller and easier for little hands.

Highly recommended.
Even pro players love these little things for fun, travel, tour-bus practice, back-stage warm up;
THAT is how good these inexpensive little beauties are!

Text:
This is a great package for beginners. I never played a ukelele before but I learned to play guitar many years ago. I have no idea on how to tune a ukelele so I downloaded an app called "Easy Ukelele" available in Amazon and Google Playstore for free. That is the only ukelele tuner I can recommend for beginners as it actually listens to your Ukelele and tells you when your device is in tune. I purchase this as gift to my son's 5th birthday that is coming up in 2 weeks so I have not yet preview the DVD and CD that came with it. I did however, checked and played with the ukelele while my son is at school, sleeping or playing outside to make sure that it is properly working when he open the box on his birthday and before the return period runs out.

My Review:

1. The Package: The box comes with the Ukelele, Beginners Manual, DVD, CD, carry pack, and 2 extra set of Ukelele strings. Tuner is not included so I advise that you either buy a tuner or download the "Easy Ukelele" app I mentioned above.

2. The Ukelele: The Ukelele looks and feels decent. It has a sticker that says made in china. It comes pre-strung but it is out of tune. I tuned it using the app I downloaded but it would not hold a tune. It is very bad that the sting gets out of tune before you even finish tuning all the other strings. Basically, the ukelele sounded like an out of tuned toy when you first take it out of the box and even after a few adjustments. Since the string is nylon, I gave it a chance to settle. I would tune it really sharp and leave it alone for at least 10 minutes or more then pick it up and strum on it and push the string from side to side. I actually position the tuner pegs horizontally so I can see if it is moving when the string gets more tension. The tuner pegs stays in place so I know that the problem is with the string. It could be that the string included is a cheap one. After doing this a few time on day 1, I was able to play my first song I grabbed from the book (Clementine). But after 1 song, you have to tune it again. I just repeat what I did for the next 2 days, tuning it sharp and leaving it alone and play songs. Yesterday morning I tuned it sharp before leaving to work and when I came back in the afternoon, I checked the strings and they are still tuned to the same key I left them in the morning. I played with it for at least 10 minutes just trying to learn the music from the book and I was able to play at least 4 songs without any problem. This morning, I checked the note again and they stay close to the G-C-E-A range. I could see this improving more as the ukelele gets used more. Even if I have to tune it every day I would not have any problem with it.

So, for the reviews complaining about the device being out of tuned, just give the string a try to settle. This are cheap string that they included here and it will take time to settle in. Or you can buy a better quality string that costs around $9.00 for a set. Another place you can check is the tuner, make sure that it does not get pulled back when the strings tension. If it would not hold its place then just grab a philips screw driver and tighten it a little. That is an easy fix.

2. The String: As I mentioned above, it is a cheap string that needs a lot of adjusting until it settles. Even if you buy a good quality strings, I am sure that it will also need a few adjustment in the beginning. It comes with 2 extra set in case you accidentally snap the one that is already installed. The problem is that the extra set does not have a label so you have to eyeball it. From some research I found online they said that the Thinnest string will be the A string. The second thinnest is the E string, The thickest is the C string and the second thickest is the G string. The extra string package says "Gangia Brand" on it so I assumed that that is the brand of the string.

3. The Book: I just scanned the book and I could tell that it is written well for beginners. The songs included progress from only needing 2 chords in the beginning and they add more chords on the succeeding lessons. Each song have a chart on which chord you will use.

4. The Case: The case will protect your ukelele from dust, water and from getting dirty while you are transporting it but will definitely protect the device from being damage in case of a drop.

5. The DVD's and CD's: I have not tried the DVD and CD's yet but the DVD's I believe will have the lesson and the CD will have the songs on the books so you can listen to it and have an idea on how to play the songs on the book. I will come back and edit this item once I get the chance to watch the DVD and listen to the CD.

Overall. This is a great price for the package.
Summary: Great Package. It finally stayed in Tune after multiple adjustments

I've been a HUGE fan of the guitar version of the Blackstar Fly3 for a couple of years now - it arguably gets played the most frequently out of any my amps at home due to sheer convenience and quality at (very) low volumes. So imagine my surprise when I was at a local guitar store and came across a product I somehow didn't even know existed: the BASS version of the Blackstar Fly3. I'm not much of a bass player, but I do have a bass at home I use with headphones and for entry-level recording, so I had to give it a try.

So far, my thoughts on it are mixed - though if you were simply in the market for a $70 mini-amp of this size to use with a bass, it really doesn't have many competitors to speak of. The form factor of the Fly3 bass is nearly identical to the guitar version. It substitutes a metallic grill cover for the black one, and instead of the digital delay, it has a compression effect, which is probably there as much to keep you from blowing out the amp as it is for how it sounds. The tone control works a little differently also - instead of the ISF feature that goes from "British" to "American" voicing, the tone becomes more "scooped" in the mids and, therefore, darker sounding as you rotate clockwise. There are separate controls for level and gain, and an overdrive button that actually sounds pretty convincing for a little transistor amp.

PROS - Much like the Fly3 Guitar, the bass version puts out a good amount of volume, and while it is massive or room-rattling in any way, shape, or form, it does sound like you're playing a bass. This is no small acheivement on a 3" speaker powered by 6 AA batteries. I haven't run the batteries down yet, but I believe it's something like 20 hours of play on a single set, and it seemed even longer than that on the Fly3 Guitar. The Fly3 bass was also receptive to a broader range of tones than I accepted. It could do bright and funky, or growling and saturated.

I think my favorite experience with the Fly3 Bass was using it as a headphone amp. The speaker sim on the headphone jack sounded GREAT, and it's tough to imagine a headphone output on a larger amp sounding appreciably better. Even if the 3" speaker sounds just too small for you, it might be worth having the Fly3 around just to use with headphones.

CONS - I need to work some more with the amp (and I'm about to try out a new bass), but the amplified sound through the little 3" speaker is a bit of a disappointment. Unless my unit is defective, which doesn't seem to be the case, the speaker sounds like it is overdriving or giving off a fizz-like distortion even at volumes that seem like it shouldn't be pushing the unit very hard. I was more convinced of what I was hearing after trying it with headphones and hearing how great the amp sounds with the speaker removed from the equation. I didn't expect any appreciable low end from the unit - that would be pretty unrealistic. But I'm a little disappointed with the unit as a combo amp thus far, if only because the Fly3 Guitar impressed me so much with how convincing it sounded.

VERDICT - So the amp hasn't blown me away yet for low volume practicing, but it certainly does well enough to practice the instrument, and I think it excels as a headphone amp. Which is just a more satisfying experience for bass practice anyway unless you're getting the size and wattage you really need to push out the low frequencies. It isn't a perfect product, but it's affordable and has enough features to warrant a look.
Summary: Bass practice aid - held back by over-matched speaker, but excelling at headphone practice

Text:
If you want a budget guitar that sounds and feels like a telecaster, this is a good option, and a few years ago, I may have said it was the best option. When I bought mine just 2-3 years ago, I paid under $200, if I remember correctly. At the prices I'm seeing for these now, I'm not sure I'd buy another one, unless the quality has gone up significantly.

I love cheap guitars, but don't usually play off the shelf stuff like this due to a nickel allergy. However, this was was fine for me short term. The tone was surprisingly good and it definitely played like a telecaster. I had no issues with the workmanship and it played it buzz free with no noticeable sharp frets. The truss rod worked and the electronics are fine. I still have the guitar, and while I don't play it much, there's nothing wrong with it several years after purchase. This is definitely a real guitar and not a toy, everything is adjustable and upgradable.

The only issue is that I've seen a lot of fantastic budget guitars from smaller, more generic brands popping up over recent years. The market is fairly saturated with low cost imports so buyers have more options than in years past. Still, I'd recommend this to someone looking for a cheap tele style guitar, it just wouldn't be my only recommendation anymore.
Summary: One of the best budget/beginner guitars available.

I wrote a more detailed review after I bought the Snark. I already had a couple Boss PSA120S's and a One Spot. I never compared them all closely until now. After doing so, the one spot is the best choice for quality and value.

Why?
- The Snark has a wimpy thin 6' cord. Boss and 1-spot have a 10' cord. The 1-spot has the heaviest most durable cord.
- The Boss is nearly twice the price of the 1-spot and has an annoying inline pod about 1 foot from the pedal end of the cord.
-Output Specs - all 9V but One spot can deliver 1.7A, Boss 0.5A, and Snark 0.4A....so the One Spot can power more equipment.
- Snark and Visual Sound both have provided me helpful customer support at times in the past. Boss is not very good in my experience. If you have an issue, you're pretty much hosed with Boss. Visual Sound (now TrueTone actually) seems to have GREAT customer support, at least on their pedals. I've had good support from Snark too, just not Boss.

One thing the Boss has that the others don't is a power LED. That actually is kind of useful sometimes, but it's a high cost differential to pay for that so unless you really want that power indicator....get the 1-Spot.
Summary: Best Choice - compared here to Boss and Snark

The clean channel didn't sound any crisper or better in any way, and the trade off was severely limiting high gain options.

When they say this is a low-gain pre-amp tube, they really mean it. I was shocked by how little gain I was able to squeeze out of it. Maxing the gain knob to 10 on my Blackstar (which is a "metal" amp) didn't even give enough distortion to have a 60's British palm mute crunch, and wasn't even remotely enough for any more than that. Such limitations for no noticeable benefits makes this a deal breaker for me. I think I either had unrealistic expectations, or this tube simply isn't for my tastes, hence the 3 star review. I can recognize the craftsmanship and decent build quality on the tube though.
Summary: Decent quality but not the tube I was looking for

I would like to preface my review of these headphones with the following: Everybody hears differently, and everyone "listens" differently. We don't all enjoy the same types of music, and similarly, every set of headphones is not necessarily suited for every genre of music. We all own different source components, and most of us have a limit as to what we are willing to spend on our gear. I believe every headphone review should include a brief summary of the reviewer's musical tastes, sources, and gear and should always including references to other sets of cans they own, have auditioned, liked, or disliked. With so many variables affecting peoples like or dislike of any pair of phones it is my goal to help those with similar musical tastes and similar gear to determine whether or not these headphones will be a good investment for them personally.

To that end; I listen to music in practically every genre. I tend to go through different phases, but I enjoy Mozart as much as Metallica, 80's one hit wonders and New Orleans Jazz, Lady Antebellum or Lady Gaga, Eminem to Zedd. Music has so much to offer in all genres that one could spend a lifetime discovering new things they like. I use my computer to play all the usual manner of digital files, and an Onkyo C-7030 CD player to handle disk duty. Both feed into my Nuforce Icon DAC/Headphone Amp. The digital files via USB and the CDs via analog RCA (the Onkyo has excellent onboard D/A conversion). I use no equalizer to modify the sound. My headphones include Sony MDR-V6s and MDR-7506s, V-Moda Crossfade LPs and M-100s, Audio Technica ATH-M50s, Sennheiser HD 598s and HD 600s (my personal favorite) as well as my 4th pair of Koss Porta-Pros (easy to exchange when you live in Milwaukee) . I've tried Grado SR 80s and SR 225s (just too darn uncomfortable), and my son even owns a pair of Beats Solo phones (Yuk). The other day I threw away some Denon's (no clue what model, but circa 1990) and a set of MDR V600s that were both totally worn out. I also own lots of buds as well (my Klipsh X10s being my favorite).

So what do I think of these DT 990 Pro 250s? In short, and for my personal tastes , I think they're just okay. Let me put it another way. When I got my Sennheiser HD 600s I plugged them in, fired up Chris Isaac's "Wicked Game" and in less than 30 seconds had a chill running up my spine. I spent many, many hours with those 600s over the next couple days tearing through my music collection like a kid in a candy store who'd just gotten his first taste of sugar. With the 990's I spent a lot of hours listening and a lot of hours feeding white, pink, brown, etc. noise in hopes that the middle range would open up and the dynamics would improve, but any change was negligible. Do I think the 990's are bad headphones with terrible sound? Not at all. I spent many years listening to music with my EQ looking like a couple of deep V's, making for accentuated treble and bass and a subdued midrange. But as I stated earlier, I now use no equalization in my system and have really come to appreciate a more flat and balanced presentation. I've also come to prefer the sound of open phones to closed cans. For $140 these are an excellent way to get into a pair of high quality open phones, especially if you're looking for those boosted lows and highs. They clamped a little tight and the pads were a bit stiff when I first put them on, but they have become very comfortable over the past week and a half. They are made very well and being able to replace any broken or worn part is a big benefit. I like the coiled cable and the plug with the screw-on ¼" adapter (though I wish it was detachable), and I think the phones are nicely styled. I wish the midrange had a bit more presence and that the phones had better dynamics (difficult with the subdued middle). The soundstage is very good, though it doesn't feel quite as wide as my HD 598s or 600's (at least to my ears). All in all the DT 990's are very good cans; they just aren't for me. Still I debated for quite a while as to whether or not I would keep them. But, in the end I decided I would send them back.

UPDATE: I didn't want to give up on Beyerdynamics, so the day after I returned these 990s I ordered a set of DT-880 Premiums. I'm hoping that the sound will be more what I like, and based on most of the professional reviews I have read I think they may be. I admit I was being cheap when I chose the 990 Pros over the 880s. Not that the 990s are cheap in any way other than price, or that they aren't an excellent value (probably one of the best in the world of headphones). I will add to this update when I've had a chance to audition the 880s, and I will be sure to review those as well.

FINAL UPDATE: So I got the DT 880s (250 ohm Premium) today, and I knew right away that I liked them. Much more in line with my personal preferences. Still a tiny bit of sizzle on the top, but the mids are much more "up-front". The bass is very detailed, but also less pronounced than the 990s. The 880 Premiums clamp A LOT lighter than the 990 Pros as well (super comfortable, though I could probably sneeze them off). In the end, I was glad I auditioned both sets, and even though the 880s are almost double what I got the 990's for I will be keeping them. I can see the appeal of the 990s, but still, for me they were just okay (and I'm talking sound wise only). Beyerdynamics makes some really nice cans, but a person needs to do their research to figure out which model will suit them best.
Summary: They Just Didn't Do It For Me.

I purchased this case for use with an Inyen Vina (IYV) Les Paul clone. I was originally planning to carry the IYV to gigs in a gig bag, since the guitar itself sells for under $200, however, the thing ended up being so much nicer than I'd expected that I decided to invest in a hard case for it. As it turns out, this was the one to get.

The build quality of the case seems about what you'd expect at this price point. It's definitely solid enough to withstand the "rigors" of the band trailer, backseat or trunk. The guitar fits perfectly with virtually no wiggle room, and the interior construction and padding offer plenty of protection. Like other reviewers have noted, this case isn't meant for the meat-cleaver/sledge-hammer handling of a baggage claim agent at the airport, but for the average weekend warrior traveling a couple hours to a gig, it's plenty.

I especially like the fact the handle is slightly padded! Though the case itself isn't heavy, my Paul knock-off is, so the padded handle is a nice little bonus. Also, the body-hugging shape of the case gives it a form factor that takes up a little less room than, say, my Fender Tele case. So if space is an issue for you, there's another plus.

I'm not wild about the Epiphone label on the case; it's fairly large and prominent. But I figure the next time we play a festival somewhere, I'll buy a bumper sticker and cover it up. Meanwhile, there's no shame in playing an Epi, so what the hell. If the brand was good enough for the Beatles, I guess I can live with the logo for a while.

Finally, the interior "fur" is VERY nice. Frankly, I'm a little jealous of my guitar. I'd like a bed made outta this stuff! It's very soft, but seems quite durable. The latches all close as they're supposed to; hopefully, that will continue to be the case in the years to come.

It's not the most interesting case out there, nor the cheapest, nor the best. But it is reasonably priced and will handle pretty much any abuse, other than that proffered by the aforementioned baggage claim people at the airport.

My main “everything” pedal board uses 2 power supplies: a Decibel Eleven Hot Stone Deluxe and a Pigtronix Power Supply (got several Pigtronix and other pedals running 18v). They’re great but they’re also big, heavy and expensive.

My 2nd board consists mainly of mini pedals and is / was powered by a Snark “one spot” style adapter with a daisy chain cable. That worked fine until I tried using a pedal with a higher current draw, which causes that one pedal to simply shut down.

So! The Vangoa VSM-08 advertises having a 9V output with up to 500mA, which sounded perfect.

Pulling it out the box, this thing is TINY. Like super compact and I have to question how “isolated” these outputs are when everything is smushed together. It’s powered by an external 18v wall wart PSU (included), so it’s more like a breakout box than a power supply itself.

There is an included cable for each output, no spares or reverse polarity cables (but at this price point that’s fine).

My current setup has an EX “chicken head” distortion, an EQD Pyramids (9V, 460mA), an EX Gemini mini chorus, a Moozikpro mini Delay (generic brand analog delay / echo), and a TC HoF2 running into the front of a Marshall Artiste 2x12.

The VSM-08 handles those 5 pedals without issue. No significant noise is evident (and playing with single coils in close proximity to a vintage amp is always gonna generate a little hum regardless).

Not much else to say. It’s the perfect size for a mini pedal board and having 6 outputs running 9V at 100mA means it’s able to power a bunch of pedals simultaneously, with an extra couple outputs for some higher draw pedals. If you’re building your first pedal board (or a 2nd or third!) then this is worth checking out.

I have tried every small amp on the market over the years to try and get a good tone and feel at low "quieter than TV" volumes.
None of them could really sound like a big stack but at low talking level volumes.
This Yamaha comes the closest by far.
I should mention it was never my goal to record with this amp since I have a studio setup that allows me to use larger and real tube amps .
I just wanted an amp with small speakers that was voiced to sound and feel like a big amp -- miniaturized to very low levels ----- imagine your favorite rock tone coming from a CD playing at low volume thru a small stereo -- THAT is what I was always looking for.
Yamaha has achieved this here.

Perhaps the tones are a bit cloudy and muffled and not as clearly defined as the real thing, but for portable practice and other applications this is a winner
Why 4 stars ?

A few gripes .....
1) The military green looks great but they use a dull gold lettering that is almost impossible to read and will only be harder as the years pass by and these gold pigments fade even more as they are prone to do.

2) You need the Editor software to control all options which I don't really mind - however there are only a few extra options (like mix and match speaker cab, gate, etc...) that are only available in the software -- so it seems 4-5 extra controls on the panel would have solved this.

3) Only a few of the speaker cabs are usable --- the others have too much of a harsh high end HISS and SIZZLE to them.

4) The sound differs slightly between headphone jack and monitoring with same headphones via the USB interface

5) Limited amps models --- You basically have an Engle Powerball sound, the heavily saturated EVH Brown Sound , Clean Sound and a Solid State Metal Sound.
This covers most of the hard rock territory -- but you have to dial out some of the oversaturation emulation in the BROWN models if you want a standard Marshall JCM800 type of rock tone that does not have the Variac induced mushiness of the Brown sound

So it would have been nice to see at least 2 more models
A straight up 80s-90s era Marshall JCM800 kind of thing and maybe a Mesa or similar.

The little amp does take pedals well, so this would have made it more versatile

I will find use for this out by the pool and other places I want a small portable low volume "stack" -- BUT, I will not use it as much as I originally thought.

WHY ?

I discovered the Torpedo CAB that is a high end Cabinet Simulator using IR Cabinet Impulses that I can use with my REAL tube amps.
Thus when I am at home, I can now use my real amps instead of a simulation at super low volumes via the Torpedo Cab.
Of course this apprach is not portable - but it serves the purpose for much of my home practice

For portability and totally quiet practice thru headphones, I find I prefer the Zoom G3
The Zoom sounds better thru headphones than the Yamaha
It has built in drum patterns/metronome which is great for practice.
All the settings can be controlled from the front panel without a need for connection to a PC
The quality of the tone and touch response are comparable to the Yamaha on the "Marshall -like" models.
It is even smaller to fit in suitcase or briefcase when traveling, sitting in hotel rooms late at night, etc..
Of course the Zoom G3 does not have built in speakers like the Yamaha, but again this it not important for this application where you are doing headphone practice.
Summary: Best of the small practice amps by far .... but I think a Zoom G3 fits my needs better

Text:
I've had this amp for an afternoon and had to give it a go right away.

The amp modeling is selected by the dial on the front. Generally, the setting all the way to the left is the cleanest amp, and each one past that gets a little dirtier. They all have suggestive names, but don't straight-up say an exact amp that's being modeled.

On the top, you have standard gain control and low, mid, and high equalizer, then volume. Then you have multi controls for the effects. There is a button to tap-set the modulation rate and delay rate for those controls.

On the reverb pot, the "hall" effect is pretty useless - it's just too much reverb, but the other settings (room and hall) are fine.

The dials all work as expected in live mode, but if you want you can go into patch mode where you can save the particular settings you like and it ignores where each dial is set.

Bluetooth works fine for inputting a backing track. I haven't tried the 1/8 inch input on the back, but I expect that's fine too.

The amp is light. It's not fragile, but I also don't think it's built to be gig-tough. That's okay since this is clearly just a practice amp anyway, though you could use it for a small public performance. The lack of a proper handle makes this a little inconvenient, even though it does have a recessed "handle" built into the back, you'll still need two hands to move it.

There's a lot to like about this amp. It looks nice enough and has more than enough sound for my den. It sounds good with both of my guitars and my electric ukulele.

It's hard to say how well it will work in the long run, but I have Fender Princeton Reverb 68 Custom and a Vox AC15C1 so this won't by my primary amp setup. This is for my home office and lower volumes while I'm watching videos/movies, taking a break, whatever. I was a little afraid that the 8" speaker wouldn't be all that great, even if it is a Celestion because I have another 8" speaker in a similarly powered solid state amp of about the same wattage. This amp destroys that in every way. I don't think I'll be in any hurry to build a 10" speaker cabinet and head enclosure for it just yet, but I do plan on at least giving it a test-run with the Princeton speaker as an extension cab just to see how it goes.

This to me sounds like your basic Fender Champ tube amp. I"m fairly certain that's what it's based on. It is a Fender-y amp you can crank without destroying your hearing, which is nice, because even my 12W Princeton is waaay loud and while the Vox does have a master volume and sounds pretty good at low volumes, cannot be cranked at the pre and power amp stages without reminding everyone a few houses away that 15w still means loud. I don't think you need to crank either of those amps to get a really good sound, but I digress. This is an amp you can crank, it's still fairly loud, and it's going to blow away any clean/slightly overdriven practice amp you can pick up for $100. No problem.

The construction seems solid. It is actually spec'd as plywood, which depending on your opinion on speaker cabinets might actually be better than my Princeton which I"m fairly sure is MDF. The tolex is applied well. The back seems to be well designed to let just the right amount of air in and out. It's dead quiet and doesn't seem to pick up any interference when the guitar isn't plugged i.

Cons: This is a simple amp. You only get one tone knob. Not the end of the world, but it would have been nice to see that at least split into a two band EQ. Also, it takes a little longer to warm up than my other tube amps and unlike the others, you don't get any sound from the amp until it's properly warm. Also, no reverb, no trem. Again, not the end of the world, or even to be expected at this price. This is a nice mini-pedal platform amp, so just bring your own.

**UPDATE:** OK, this is only day 2 and the power amp tube is showing no signs of life. I can't tell if it's the tube of the amp. This thing has not be moved more than 5 feet since it's first power on, hasn't taken any spills, and the writing was on the wall with that long warm-up I mentioned earlier. I'm setting this to a 1 star review until I find out, because that's going to be _really_ frustrating to a new player to get this amp and have it croak on the first day. It could be the tube, but I do not have any spare 6V6 tubes lying around, tubes last a lot longer than 20 hours, especially only being powered on for 3 of those hours, and until I get confirmation that this is a fluke, it doesn't matter how good it sounds, if QC is this bad. There should be no expected maintenance on a new amplifier for several months to several years. Very disappointing.
Summary: If you like tube amps and you like Fender amps, you can't really go wrong ...unless the QC is really this bad.

Update- I wanted to post an update since I have now had this guitar for a while, some posts I have seen where they were saying the tuner doesn't work, saying it's useless, there is a trick to it, tune it down to the letter below and tune it slowly up to the note you want, where it shows green on both sides of the letter, every letter has two displays, one is right on the note in perfect pitch, the other allows you to tune it to a perfect sharp for the note you want, both look very similar, the difference being there is a small red dot next to the letter....If you tune it green on both sides of the letter and the dot is there....It will be sharp....If tuning down, the first display will be for the note tuned sharp...Many reviews say it always tunes wrong and that it needs re-tuned with a separate tuner to make sure it is in tune....Look closely, if it says it's tuned sharp, there will be a red dot....You need to tune it further down, the next display will be the note, tune it so there is green on both sides on that one and that will have you in tune....That's why I prefer tune it down to the letter lower than you want and slowly tune it up since tuning up the first display is for in tune, but if you just tune straight down, the first display is for you to tune it in tune as a Sharp tuning ....I'm surprised the setup isn't more obvious, I mean to just know it's tuned sharp the only indication is a small dot if tuning to a sharp note vs in tune....The other thing is I don't know if all the stock strings are the way mine were but while it sounded good and played good, the lowest string tended to be more muted and in some cases you might say it was buzzing...I switched to a pair of strings I like, they are actually a set of D'Addario strings, I had a set on one of my other guitars so I bought a set for this one, it solved the quieter sometimes almost buzzing on the lowest string, it wasn't a big problem and turns out it wasn't the guitar that was causing it, especially I noticed the low string was less responsive when tuned down slightly, or when using a Capo, I'm not sure if it was the fact the strings were just gone stale or what, I will keep the stock strings as a back up pair for those unfortunate emergency strings situation...But I thought I would add that, in case anyone else ends up where they feel some strings, like in my case the low E string just wasn't sounding out as loud as the others, and/or if you feel it is hard to get a clean note ....A fresh set of strings can make everything come to life....I would also advise, go with a good brand name, like how I went with a set I have used on another guitar.... A good set of strings, a name brand set is best, it will only cost a couple dollars more, and it's well worth it....The guitar was great with the stock strings, but having a set of strings I have used on another guitar was a great move, They have great booming low notes and clear and clean mids and highs....A new set really has made the guitar sound even better than it already did....Even if you use the stock strings (which are good) Make sure you take the time to stretch the strings, tune it, run your finger under each string work it up the fretboard...It will likely be flat...Tune it again and repeat, a few times, do it on each string one at a time.... then before you know it the guitar will stay in tune....(although even the most expensive guitars and strings do need to be re-tuned after playing, sometimes while playing....Especially if you do lots of bends....And if there have been wide changes in humidity and/or temperature, especially if it's been sitting and unplayed for a while....And when the strings are new, they will go out of tune....I play it all the time, both unplugged and plugged into the Fender Acoustic amp I bought with the guitar. Just some things I wanted to share based on my experience, This is a very well made and great sounding, very easy to play guitar....Well worth the Price! Some things which hopefully will be helpful for someone who is thinking of buying the guitar, or someone who has the guitar and isn't very happy with it for sound issues and tuner issues, and if the guitar seems to not be staying in tune.....Before sending it back, I've pointed out some things I have learned about the guitar as I've been playing it quite regularly....

So I have several guitars but I didn't have an electric-acoustic guitar, I did a ton of research on brands, and styles of electric acoustic guitars before narrowing things down, I have 2 Fenders already, both are different types from this one...Also since I didn't want to buy a bundle and just needed a guitar alone without all the extra stuff that are in various bundles this guitar deserved a look and consideration, from my experience with bundles....They seem to go really cheap on the guitar quality. I am guessing they do that because they figure "Hey, they are beginners....They don't need a really expensive guitar to start with....This way they get a guitar and accessories for an affordable price...." But actually that works against the whole idea of being a beginner wanting to learn guitar because the sound quality and build of the guitar, as well as quality of strings, and the "playability" things like how easy or difficult it is to depress strings and make a good sounding chord are big problems with cheap "beginner" guitars. and there are many people who end up giving up on the idea of learning guitar because the cheap guitars are built poorly and as cheaply as possible and thus everything sounds terrible, and often the beginner has so much trouble fingering chords they think it's them and not the guitar, but a well built guitar, or even a moderate guitar are much easier to play which builds confidence. Glad I chose this one,. It sounds great both played acoustic or paired with a good amp. It's easy to play and is so far well worth the price which is in a decent price range....Its not one that is built cheaply but it's not a real top of the line expensive guitar either. So you get a well made and great sounding guitar that is in a good price range. For me, I also paired it up with a Fender acoustic electric guitar amp which is also in the middle of the road range for a good amp, and a decent amp is important too but since it is easy to play and sounds really good both unplugged and with an amp, I don't think somebody could go wrong with this guitar. It's not cheap but won't totally break the bank. The guitar keeps sounding better and better over time too which is a sign of a good guitar....As they say a good guitar seems to get better with age.
Summary: Awesome guitar! Well worth the money :)

I was really, really, excited to try out this new microphone and show it off in stream; however, I never really got the emotes on the Razer Seiren Emote Streaming Microphone to work correctly. First, the program needed to use the microphone's emotes is called the "Streamer Companion App"; however, there's no instructions to download this program included in the manual. You are only instructed to download the Razer Driver app ("Razer Synapse").

I think all guitarists whether a beginner or an advanced player should have one of these if you're looking to dial in your perfect tone. This is of course a cheap pedal so i recommend treating it with care, but it's a steal for $30. The construction seems to be of good quality hard plastic, one of those confusing is this metal or plastic kind of materials. Either way it feels pretty sturdy. The button has quite a loud click compared to say, MXR, but again you're ppaying less than half of that of the MXR compatible. Also, the size is a little thicker than that of say an MXR pedal, but only slightly. The sliders are very nice, and light up with a sinister red glow which just looks really cool. I wouldn't mind just setting it flat and having some extra lighting on my pedal board. The sliders also have a little notch in the middle so you'll never lose your starting point.

99% of amps nowadays of course come with a 3 band eq (bass/mid/treble) or at least a tone knob. Either way, this little pedal is great to have, since you can fine tune any of the aforementioned tones to perfection. Think of it this way: every 2 of the sliders on here represents either bass, nids, or treble. So that means you can fine tune EXACTLY what you want, like a shrilly high end, or a not as harsh high end; or a rumbly or subtle bass.

To start using this pedal, i would recommend sliding everything at 0, then turn up just one slider at a time, just to hear exactly what that slider does. This is gonna help you because you can hear exactly what each slider sounds like, and will be able to dial in what you want to hear.

So get this thing please. All guitar players should have one!
Summary: Great tool all guitarists should have!

This powered, dual 15”, 2-way is comprised of 2- 15” JBL 275 woofers and 1- 2408H-237.5mm driver. Out of the box, it feels every bit of 80 pounds. The handles and case feel sturdy, and it has 8- M10 suspension points.
Setup is performed over wifi via an app on an iPad (NOT iPhone) or Android device. I used an Android tablet. The wifi is nice when you have a full stage worth of speakers set up and need to tune all them from different parts of the room. There are two options when setting up. First, you can connect directly to a speaker’s wifi with the tablet and just set it up individually. Or, you can connect all your speakers to a central wifi, and then connect to them over the central wifi with the tablet. I found the latter to be clunky, and did not get it on my first try. Connecting to one individually was very easy and straightforward.
Once connected, setup was nice with 8 available bands on the software driven EQ. You can change center frequency and curve shape. I do wish the crossover was adjustable, but it is fixed at 2.4kHz. Navigating the app is not super intuitive, but after setting one up it became much easier.
The sound quality is excellent, with extremely low distortion even at the highest of volumes. The highs are clear and the bass is very clean. The max SPL is rated at 138 dB peak, and you can feel and hear every bit of that. I am using mine as part of a DJ setup, the input to the JBLs are coming from an auxiliary output from an old powered mixer being fed directly from my DJM-800 DJ mixer.
The PRX825 would be a great addition to your setup, maybe fingers crossed for an app update.

I'm coming to multi-track recording late in the game - doing it for the first time in my mid-30's and having actually learned to do it first on my iPad and iPhone (using a variety of interfaces for guitar and audio sources into a DAW). So it's a little hard to articulate why I was drawn to the TASCAM DP-008EX, when it arguably offers far less editing capability and flexibility than a DAW. But, for me, I found the affordability, variety of input options, and simplicity for capturing ideas quickly to be very appealing with the DP-008EX. It even motivated me to purchase a dynamic microphone (SM-57 copy) and mic stand to finally attempt to mic and record some of my amps at home!

I will keep this review short, since I'm somewhat of a novice user and haven't put in the hours yet to fully explore this device. But I found relatively simple to get working "out of the box". There are a few design choices that feel archaic, such as the way inputs are assigned and pretty much anything having to do with the LCD interface. But keep in mind that those choices are part of what keeps this an affordable product for people who might not have used a multi-track recorder before, and for whom basic functionality (off a set of batteries, nonetheless) is more important than bells and whistles.

I found that the purchase of the DP-008EX led to a few other inexpensive purchases, including a 1/8" to 1/4" mono cable and the XLR cable for the aforementioned dynamic mic purchase. (I've actually heard the on-board condenser mics aren't half bad, but positioning those in front of a guitar amp while trying to start a recording seemed like a non-starter to me). One early concern I've read about and experienced with the use of an external mic is that the recording levels seemed low. However, there are a number of settings that impact this, including a switch on the back of the device, and a series of recording levels you can designate in the LCD menus. So, come to think of it, I might not have explored all of those options, in addition to being a total novice when it comes to mic placement and recording levels. I did record some other audio sources (iOS instruments and Korg Volca synths and drum machine) and had little problem getting the levels where I wanted them.

So, why buy a DP-008EX when you can purchase a $10 DAW and an interface and record directly on a mobile device? For me, it's much the same reason why I still enjoy playing real life guitar amps and effects pedals versus modeling software offering far more variety in sounds...it's just a much more satisfying experience working with physical gear. In my case, I already had the guitars, effects pedals, and even preamp "direct" pedals, so the DP-008EX was an affordable way to capture recordings without getting bogged down in a bunch of software.

The lack of an included power supply is a bit disappointing at this price point, but I might try using Eneloop rechargeable batteries for awhile in lieu of being tied to a wall plug. Really liked the level control, pan, and reverb send knobs laid out physically on the display. Getting content off of the device sounds a little harder than it should be in 2016, but I'd rather have difficulty on that end than hassle on the front end when I'm trying to record ideas.
Summary: Solid budget 8-track recording device with a variety of input options for guitars, mics, synths, and other audio sources

[[VIDEOID:6b12efa26195ac65a80c9179561ccb9b]] So far the sound quality is acceptable. However something that absolutely blows my mind is how she the enclosure is for this unit. In my hands, it seems to make creaking noises. When you rotate it or move it from side to side you will hear a noise that sounds like a piece is rattling around on the inside. This is actually the volume control rocker. If they had used a silicone rocker it would’ve dampened the sound. Also, the battery compartment door opens very easily. If this unit or to fall just a foot or two, I would imagine that the battery compartment door would fly off and the batteries shoot out all over the place. I would have gladly spent an extra five dollars on this unit if it had a more robust Enclosure.

Why would a volume rocker shifting around be a problem? Because these microphones are so sensitive the shifting of the volume rocker within its slop causes a rattle sound in the audio recording.

A quick fix for the volume rocker is putting a piece of tape over it. This prevents it from shifting when you rotated or move it around and eliminates the sound.

Aside from these quirks it seems to record very well.
Summary: Cheaply made enclosure, good sound BUT…

Text: This thing is super light. Clamps like a vice grip...my one gripe is the pin puller is very sharp. Potential to go through my gig bag.

Our 3YO is outgrowing some of his musical toys, including his old sit-down keyboard / piano.

This seemed like a great option for introducing him to more keys, more sounds and also having some drums / beats to play along to.

Key size is pretty small. My adult hands can hit the notes pretty accurately for the most part but it’s very cramped. Definitely aimed at younger / smaller hands.

The keys have pretty short and squashy travel. It’s easy to make notes sound but I noticed some occasional issue playing chords where a middle note wouldn’t sound. It’s not an issue with polyphony; the keyboard can simultaneously play as many notes as you can hit, as far as I can tell. The issue is just that I struggled to press with equal pressure due to my hands being larger than this keyboard is designed for I think (middle finger needed to press slightly harder). Probably more a technique issue than keyboard issue; I’m not a pianist.

The built-in speakers are pretty LOUD. You’ll hear this from the other side of the house. Hopefully you’re little one gets good fast!

Sound quality is pretty decent. I’m thinking back to my first “real” keyboard, some old cheaper Yamaha with a sampler, and feel like a lot of the synths and pads available on the Kmise 32 Key are actually better sounding. Maybe the speakers are better. Either way, sounds pretty good! The basic piano sound is not bad either. The strings are ok and the guitar sounds are, as always on synths, terrible. The bass tones are fine but I couldn’t figure out how to play LOWER notes.. no option to transpose that I can see.

Which leads me to my first and probably only complaint: if you want to record from this, the headphone out is your only option. It’s not terrible, at least there’s that option, but it’s not ideal. I was hoping to use this as a basic midi controller / add some keys to tracks in my DAW but only the 88-key model supports that.

In terms of IO, there are 2 power inputs (9V and 5V) and the headphone output.

Battery compartment takes 6xAA batteries. For testing, I used a cheap 5V cellphone charger, worked perfectly. The 9V power port needs a positive tip polarity, and all my 9V adapters are for guitar pedals that use center-negative polarity. If you’re unsure, batteries are the 5V microUSB port are safer options.

Build quality seems robust but there’s something loose / rattling inside. Not causing any issues, probably just a little piece of plastic molding.

Overall.. this a lot of fun! For learning basic keys and chords, it’s great for kids and toddlers to make some noise on.

I bought this several months ago just to try it out. I clipped it and my Snark onto the headstock of my acoustic guitar. As far as accuracy, I think the Micro and the Snark SN-5 are about the same. The first big difference is the time it takes to register the frequency of the string.

The Snark is almost instantaneous. So, I usually keep plucking or strumming the string until it's in tune. The Micro takes longer to register. You have to get used to playing the string once and waiting for the tuner. The only place this is a problem is the higher strings, where you start to get overtones and harmonics very quickly. If you mute the other strings while tuning, this problem goes away.

The other difference is the size and the ability to mount the Micro just about anywhere on the head stock. I always attached the Snark with the head on the back. It worked great except when tuning the D string with my hand in the way. I've started using the Micro exclusively attaching it to the headstock just below the 6th string tuning head. I can swivel the display so it's very close and pointed right at me. I also like the fact that the tuner itself is very unobtrusive when attached to the guitar.

Many reviews say you can leave the tuner attached all the time, because it's so small. I worry about the nitrocellulose finish on my guitar, so I generally take it off when I'm not playing.
Summary: I've grown to love this little tuner.

When I was nearing 18, the legal age for drinking in New York State at the time, I noticed that my violin teacher recommended alcohol spirits (the drinkable variety) for cleaning the rosin from my violin strings. It does work, by the way. When I was in Philadelhia attending Ceili dances where Eugene O'Donnell performed, I was told that the only spirit "approved" for this use was Jameson's Irish Whiskey. Many Irish fiddlers used it and would take a dram before playing at a dance (akin to the Riverdance, but authentic Irish folk dancing). I actually enjoyed this, and never had a hangover from Jameson's. The case was closed in my mind.

Then drinking ages were raised to 21 universally in the U.S., and I could not recommend Jameson's to any college student I knew, or teenager at music festivals. The answer is a commercial string cleaner, which I can recommend now to any young fiddler. I've tried this product for that reason, and it works, is not expensive, so I recommend it.

I love these strings. I play mostly jazz, on an Les Paul style guitar, and I was finding the regular boomers (11-52) well, a little bright and boomy. These strings sound so creamy and warm, and the wound strings feel nicer to move around on also. While I may play mostly jazz, I also wanted to be able to rock out if I felt like it, and these strings can really growl! Firstly I will say that the style of rock/blues/metal I like, is warm and fuzzy (zztop, Sabbath, etc.), and these strings really deliver. The vintage tones I'm getting out of my instrument are killer, and I really like the stiffer feel but smoother glide of the rollerwound wrapping. I don't think my guitar will see anything but nickel rockers any time soon.

As far as GHS brand goes, I highly recommend them. I've used many styles of their strings on a variety of instruments and I've always been extremely pleased. The durability is solid, never had a string failure, and they hold their tune until they are pretty well shot. I've only broken high E strings, and always at the nut or bridge (the places with the most tension and friction), and I have to say, I am rough on my strings. Yes I play jazz, but I also love blues and fingerstyle and am not squeamish about bending to next week or even yanking a string away from the fretboard for effect. These strings also endured being tuned back and forth between C# standard, open E, D, and G, standard and even drop C when I feel silly.

The electric part I could do without - it's not a bad thing, but I have a ukulele with a hold in the place where this electrics are mounted on this instrument. But for the rest - I love that this comes with everything a beginner really needs including the wall-mounted hook which is the first time I've seen that item included and it is much appreciated.  I mean, having a stringed instrument laying on the coffee table or a desk top or wherever? Text:
I bought one of these used at Guitar Center for about $120 USD (plus shipping) . It is good for the price but I would not pay list for it. I also have a Roland A-300 pro. Here are some comparisons.

Keybed - Well aside from more keys from my A300 pro, I also like the type of key. Technically not a "waterfall" but more like a piano (slight edge at the front of a key. Keys squeak slightly but not noticeable unless you are using it with no sound (which is kinda pointless)

Velocity is a bit to sensitive no matter what velocity curve I choose. (even after updating to latest firmware.

Knobs and buttons, many more than the Roland A-XXX series. The primary reason (beyond the keys) that I bought this unit.
I would give up a few knobs and buttons however for 9 sliders (for organ drawbars).

Software for setting up keyboard works but it would be nice if it was more self documenting (had ability to put comments for each control before saving the file. Also the Roland A-300 pro displays the comment you placed for each control as you use it. All the VI61 displays is either the controller value, velocity value or after touch. For instance if I assign a controller on the Roland and call it "Patch One", the Roland will display "Patch One". The VI61 does not.

Roland has these features that the VI 61 does not have.

You can assign a know to program change without having to select bank. On the roland I can select my bank with one control and then the program with another, so I only have to press bank if I call a new patch from a different bank. On the VI61, every program change requires bank change.

VI61 cannot send free form, SysEx, NPRN or PRN values. A-300 can.

VI61 has 24 available patch bays. A-300 has 19.

Roland has midi in that you can use for midi through. VI61, no midi in.

Well these are the highlights. All in all good value for the price I paid but I would have not paid full list for this one. If you can find one under 150 USD then you will probably be happy.
Summary: Bought used which made for good value.

An hour before an live event was to begin, a presenter needed audio out from their laptop to my mixer about 15’ away. I used a 30’ 3.5 to RCA cable into the mixer, played a video on the laptop, and a lot of ground loop humming buzzed the main speakers. It was a near disaster because the laptop audio played a key role in showing attendees videos with sound for the venue. Both of my speakers and mixer were connected to furman power conditioners and it was hard to tell what was making the buzz. It was definitely coming from the laptop audio output so against the instructions of the ebtech hum x, I inserted the electrical outlet adapter in front of a normal surge protector that had a laptop and projector plugged into it. Says you’re not supposed to do that. The ebtech hum x immediately cut the noise and the event was a great success. Next time I’ll just connect it to the laptop or trouble causing device’s plug. I have used it with guitar ac adapters for pedals as well and if it is ground loop you’re trying to suppress, it works as advertised! I’ve never done audio at a venue where the electrical was sketchy like that and I’m glad I packed the hum x. 5 stars but $78+USD is way too much I think… $45 USD maybe…
Summary: Ebtech Hum X saved my live gig!!

I decided for the price, I would give the o-port a try, and I'm so glad I did. I chose the small size in ivory to complement my pink sunburst guitar. The sound hole measurement was the smallest option.
Installation was easy. I loosened the strings (without a capo as the video suggests) and just spread them to the sides for installation vs. pulling the bridge pins. It took some serious folding/squeezing and manipulation to get it in to the sound hole. The ring is much larger than the hole, so that extra material has to go somewhere to get it in. The piece is malleable plastic as described, but it has a rigidity to it as well. I got it in just fine, but then had to use a thin tool (smooth end of nail clipper lever) to coax the part of the o-port that lacks a rim out of the guitar to fit along the inner edge of the top of the sound hole. At first it kind of folded to the inside, and since there isn't a lip on that part, it stayed in until coaxed out. I wasn't sure at first, but then I remembered it's job is to smooth out the interior of the guitar, and if there is a ripple of any kind it can't do that as well, so I worked it out. It fits very snugly, I am glad I don't have any plans to remove it because I believe it would be a challenge. It fits very snugly into the sound hole, and would be hard to find a edge to lift.
The final step was to tighten and tune the strings. Total installation time was around 5 minutes.
Once installed, I immediately noticed a change in the sound. So did my children, and they aren't musicians. The guitar sounds richer and fuller as described. The thin tinny quality I sometimes had seems to be replaced by tones and harmonics that are much more pleasing to hear. The guitar is also louder. I don't have to play as hard to get a louder sound.
Overall, I feel like my guitar just got an upgrade. I don't plan to gig with this guitar, but I love how it sounds now. For all of you who have a smaller sized instrument, consider an o-port if you want a passive, inexpensive way to improve and amplify your sound.
FWIW I'm currently using Martin Silk n' Steel strings.

Two weeks later, and a friend who had heard the Daisy Rock before the o-port heard it for the first time with the o-port. They didn't know what changed, but noticed the guitar sounded much nicer.

Text:
I bought one of these nearly 8 years ago. Now I really wanted to learn how to play. This was not one of those "maybe" kind of purchases for me. I give lessons now. I know a thing or two.

If you're getting this because you're not sure if you, or the person you're gifting this to, really has the interest then by all means get one. However, plan on replacing it fast. It's cheap for a reason and it feels cheap. With guitars, you get what you for up to a certain price point. This is an OK starter guitar for someone who may not have the drive or patience.

If you're looking at this as a first guitar and you plan on playing, learning, practicing then pass on this. Epiphone makes great guitars and for double the price you get a much better feeling and sounding instrument. I've played on more than of these and a common issue is staying in tune and not sounding right in anyrhing but standard tuning. For examoleexample, if you want to learn metal this guitar will not satisfy you.

The epiphone les paul standard, typically around $300 is where you should go. They fret easier and sound richer. You may also want to check out a fender telecaster modern player around the same price. It's a different feel due to the maple fretboard and really is fantastic for chords - where all beginners should start anyway.

I've gone through a number of guitars since I bought one of these. The lesson learned is when you get to the $300 - $500 you'll get quality not only in build but in comfort and tone.

I love epiphone, but depending on your level of interest in the guitar this particular model may be something to pass on. Go put your hands on one of these at guitar center and then compare to a slightly more expensive lp standard. There's a difference and it does matter. Try various models and pick the one that fits your hands, your body, and whispers "buy me". Craigslist is full of blind buys for a reason.
Summary: If you're serious about learning pass on this

The Pignose Hog 30 is a battery powered amplifier for electric guitar, electric bass, keyboards, microphone, and just about anything else that, according to the owner's manual "works at 20 watts, with 35 watts of peak power."  In reality, the 20 watts is probably the more accurate number, as I have a fairly inexpensive Washburn 30 watt bass amp that provides more sound at about "4" than the Pignose does turned all the way up (and with the funk bass switch activated, to boot).  This amplifier seems, though, to hold a charge nicely and would therefore seem to be the ideal amplifier to take along to any al fresco situation.  My 4 star review is bassed (spelling intentional) on the fact that it has a "5" tone for clean-tone electric guitar, but is more of a "3" for electric bass.  Mine seems to have an inherent buzz on F (10th fret, G string, electric bass).  The speaker looks fine, the screws are all tight, but there's a buzz.  I have tried three different basses and the buzz is most annoying on a short-scale bass, but it is noticeable on all three.  Cutting the treble and mid-range and boosting the bass on the amplifier helps quite a bit, but still this amplifier clearly emphasizes the upper harmonics.  At some point, it might be interesting to see what a larger speaker would do, although several non-Amazon reviews that I've read suggest that the relatively small (for a bass amp) speaker might not entirely be the culprit.  I would recommend the Pignose Hog 30 without question for guitarists (the buzz is not really noticeable on guitar, so it does seem to be connected somehow to the harmonic series (overtones) of the bass.  It is a crisp guitar amp and with effects pedals will do just about anything you'd need for practicing or for a small outdoor gig.  With a classical acoustic/electric, it is also quite nice, especially for the price.  On bass, it's just more fussy.  I did connect through an emulator pedal that changes the overtones and the tone was better; however, ideally an amplifier should not require the use of an effects pedal.  It is not a bad bass amp, provided that the music you are playing avoids the resonating frequency and the notes adjacent to it.  Since I play both bass and guitar, I am happy with the amp, and will use it for both.  If I only played bass, however, I might be looking for another battery powered amp.

Despite having played guitar for quite a few years, my experience with electric guitar pedals has only been a few years so far. However, I am more the creative type so having unusual tools is something I always like to have in my line up. This pedal is quite a unique pedal.

BACKING
The foam backing of this mini pedal came off easily. It comes with velcro so you can prepare it for a pedal board if you like.

CONTROL DIALS
The top two controls on this are pretty small. That means you have to work with them to find what you like BEFORE you plan to use them in a public or performance setting. They are pretty difficult to find the sweet spots, but it is possible. The main dial for decay is easy to see and access, however.

ON/OFF BUTTON
This is a mini pedal. That means if you have big feet or shoes, it can be tricky to quickly turn on and off. A button cap helps some.

LIGHT
The light on the pedal is bright blue so you can see when it is on clearly or if it is in bypass mode (off)

BUILD
The build of this seems to be pretty nice. It seems solid. The two top dials are pretty small and hard to see in dull light, but otherwise it seems like this is a decent build.

SOUNDS
Where do I begin? This pedal is AWESOME. But then again, I am talking from an ultra creative mind who does not necessarily want to sound like everyone else all of the time.

The ROOM setting when you mess around with the others sounds pretty typical reverb on a more controlled side. When you move it to the SPRING setting, it gets a bit more ballad in sound bordering on sci fi at times.

When you put it in SHIMMER mode, OMG it is GREAT! What you can get varies from special effects and new agey sounds to actual sounds that resemble angel choirs singing and church music. It is really unique and lends itself to some pretty creative music compositions.

I know you are probably thinking I am nuts, but it really does sound like angels singing and church music on shimmer setting. I tried to record it for you, but it isn't working out yet. I hope to update with a sound video so you can see what I mean.

ALONE OR WITH OTHER PEDALS?
I like this with the GIHUBO Overdrive pedal (a more tame overdrive pedal) before it because it adds a nice boost without disintegrating the signal so much that it sounds like a mess. The possibilities with this pedal in combination with others are very interesting.

USEFULNESS?
If you are a plain and simple down the middle rocker with classic rock, or other high energy distortion rock, you might not be interested in this pedal. If you like to have unusual creative options in your set up that would allow for some out of the box thinking, this pedal is really fun.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This pedal is really unique and interesting. I love the sounds of the this pedal on certain settings as it is unusual. It gives me more options in creating unusual music. If you are not interested in unusual effects, this might be boring for you.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This pedal is not only attractive (aqua color) but it has some interesting possibilities. If I didn't have many pedals, I probably would not make this top priorities. Since I have the basics covered, this was a great addition to my board. I am very excited to explore it with other instruments from mandolin and uke to perhaps even bass.

I have been playing guitar for over 30 years. I have a variety of instruments including an older Roland Guitar Synth.
I read a few magazine reviews, notably Sound on Sound, and I was intrigued.

Let me first say something about guitar Synth's and Midi Guitar controllers. They will never ever replace a guitar. There are nuances, picking types, hammering, pull off's and On's that a controller cannot emulate to an extent of an acoustic instrument (Or electric). With that being said, it's nice to play with other sounds using the guitar mindset. This controller does it, and does it in a very inexpensive way. It looks insanely cheap, but the electronics for the sound triggering are unique. There are no strings on the fretboard, but an emulation of strings in a touch sensitive / pressure point interface. As a guitarist, I wanted to bend at the fret level. This is not possibile, but the midi tremolo device assists on this end.

Ok. I've owned this unit for about two weeks. I am using the controller not for it's onboard sounds (Which suck tremendously), but for triggering virtual synths through Steinberg Cubase 4.3 64 bit. I am using not the MIDI port, but USB. It works incredibly well at triggering the sounds. Tracking is pretty good but a guitar controller is not forgiving....You must pick a bit harder to trigger the midi Communication. I have downloaded the supplemental console software and I plan to play with the string sensitivity and velocity settings and see if I can adjust to my playing style (Which is far lighter than it's pre-programmed configuation).

I would never ever play this virtual instrument live. It would not hold up. It's strength is the midi controller. It does this the best in my opinion and at or under 200.00 which nothing compares at this price point.

OK, this unit failed right out of the box:  It worked for about ten minutes and then the blue light started flashing.  No sound could get through it.  I changed out the battery with a brand new one and---nothing.  Zzounds sent me a new one in a few days.  The return process was painless.  The new unit works well, so far, although you have to remember to disconnect both in and out cords after each session or the battery will drain.  That is a terrible engineering flaw.  Even with the pedal off, you still get a dead battery if you leave your cords plugged in.  Have a four-hour gig?  Better remember to bring a new pack of nine-volt batteries, or get a 9V/100mA adapter with sleeve-hot configuration.  As far as changing out the battery is concerned:  This is the worst effects pedal I've ever owned.  Using a ballpoint pen, you need to push in the spring-loaded rod, on both sides, through two holes drilled in the plastic pedal.  It is truly hit or miss.  Once you get the pedal top off, be very careful.  The pedal spring is loose.  It can pop right out and be gone, leaving you to grope around, onstage, to find it, and you probably won't. All in all, I would not order another pedal made by Behringer.  This unit is made in China, and I suppose its other effects pedals are, as well.  While some Chinese stuff is OK, I suspect the factory churning out these units is strictly bottom-of-the-barrel.  The only reason I gave this unit two stars is that it sounds pretty darned good, once it's operating.  Its design flaws are too numerous to give it any other stars, though.  UPDATE: 5/6/12: The replacement unit went through a brand new Duracell battery in one hour!  We were rehearsing, thankfully, so I put in another new battery and things were OK.  I have a converter on the way, and I'll update, in here, once I try it out.  In all honesty, I have a feeling both units may go back.  In the end, you do get what you pay for, most of the time.  UPDATE: 7/18/12:  I have now had my second unit on its converter for over two months.  It works great and sounds great.  I can now recommend this unit, but only with the converter, as it eats batteries.  UPDATE: 1/23/16:  Unit is still OK.
