I have a vintage Kay resonator/tone ring banjo that sounds and plays decently when I'm performing Bluegrass or playing with an amplified string band, but I wanted an open back banjo for a more authentic sound on Civil War-era music (think "Cold Mountain").

Also, my old Kay is too loud - even picked without fingerpicks - to jam with folks who are playing unamplified acoustics - it's like playing bagpipes in a flute ensemble. So I was thinking about getting an open-backed banjo as a way to "level the playing field" at (real) acoustic jams. If I didn't spend too much on it, I'd consider using it as a travel or "beach banjo" as well.

I picked up a "standard" Goodtime up to try it and was blown away by the quality of the neck. The maple neck reminds me of playing a US-made Fender maple-necked Strat, and action is very similar.

For (relatively) quiet practicing, I can mute the sound by playing it close to my too-ample belly. To make it loud enough to keep up with most unamplified acoustic guitars, I play it out away from my body. Again, if I wanted to blast people, I'd bring the Kay.

There's also a lot to be said for having a banjo that's about 15 pounds lighter than I'm used to.

I'll be honest, I would like a darker finish. But that is the ONLY thing I would change.

Back to the sound itself - it sounds great on proto-Bluegrass stuff (think Cold Mountain) and on Celtic and most Folk (think Pete Seeger). If you NEED a big loud banjo to keep up with a modern Bluegrass group, this won't necessarily do the job. But to me it provides a more appropriate sound for most of the music I like. I may (gasp) add a piezo pickup for the times when I need to be louder but want to keep the old-timey sound of an open back.

Finally, the Goodtime just made its first trip to the beach. Actually I also brought along a $100 banjo that was supposed to be the one I exposed to sand and salt water. But the Goodtime is just so much more fun to play, the other one stayed in the case. I WAS careful to keep the Deering out of the sand and salt water, in case you wondered.

The only real problem this has caused me is that I'm now dissatisfied with the action on my Kay, which I thought was QUITE acceptible before. What about that Goodtime 2? . . . .

If you order one of these mail-order, you'll need to get someone who knows what they're doing to "set it up" for you, like you would with any other banjo that lists for less than a thousand dollars and some that list for more. If you're just starting on banjo and you have the money for a flashy mid-range banjo, consider getting one of these instead. You'll learn the things you really need to know more quickly on a banjo that plays like a pro model.

Just received this bass the day before yesterday. I did a lot of looking around for a lightweight short-scale bass and this is probably the best one out there short of having one custom built. My main reason for going short-scale is to replace my old G&L bass which weighed 11 lbs, and was aggravating my back problems. Holding it up side-by-side with my American Stratocaster it weighs less than the guitar. The Strat probably weighs in around 7 - 8 lbs. I'm also only 5'7" with short, stubby fingers, and have always found full 34" scale basses difficult to navigate quickly around the fretboard. It's like they're made for giants.

For beginners it's a decent bass to start out with. It's great for those with small fingers, guitarists who just play bass occasionally (like me), kids starting out, or anyone else who just wants a short-scale to goof around with. It still booms the low frequencies like my old bass, so don't worry about the short scale nerfing your tone. And there's something about the scale and weight that makes it a lot of fun to play. For my purposes I'm using the body and neck as a platform to make a pro quality bass. I'll be replacing the hardware, electronics, nut, and pickups with high quality components since I may be using it onstage with my band and it's replacing a high-end G&L. I'll probably be spending another $250 or so past the initial investment to get it to where I want it to be. Already ordered some Fender American Standard pickups. Very exciting!

One of the major drawbacks is that it's really hard to find a case for. Fender offers a hardshell case but it costs as much as the instrument. They just started making a gig bag called the Fender Urban Short Scale Bass Gig Bag. I ordered one of those.

This bass is better built than the Ibanez Mikro Bass or the Steinberger Spirit XT-2, and has better tone than a stock Epiphone EB-0. It's also a bolt-on neck which I see as a big plus since it can be swapped out easily. That's about all that's out there for short-scales. So unless you're willing to pay a lot for a custom one, the Squier Vintage Modified Jaguar is probably your best bet.

Text:
I've been playing a Fender Deville 410 since 2004 and there aren't enough good things to say about this line of amp. These amps are rock solid and can take some abuse. They're highly mod-able if that's your thing, and of course sound awesome. I've only come to owning a Mark III because my old warhorse 04 Deville finally gave out on me after years of serious gigging and abuse, and frankly, it was probably fixable, but I just didn't want to deal with it.

The Deville is not your typical fender amp - it has a great clean sound as can be imagined, but has more in common with the tweed era of Fender amps which means it has a much dirtier sound than what would be considered 'classic' fender tone. The deville has 2 channels, and the overdriven channel has two distortion modes, so with the included footswitch you can go from "clean" to "dirty" to "on fire". This is a fender open-back cabinet, so while the distortion can be pretty intense, it's probably not the best amp if your thing is full-blown metal: the amp can handle it but the open back cabinet means it gets a little muddy in the lows.

This amp is LOUD. and HEAVY. Did I mention it was LOUD? It's a relatively compact amp, but with four 10" speakers and a 60 watt amp, this thing moves an enormous amount of air and can easily compete with any half-stack. The downside is this thing is ridiculously heavy - the shipping weight is 70lbs, and there's practically nothing in the box EXCEPT the amp, so this amp is close to that in weight. This is even more surprising when you see it - it's not dramatically bigger than a typical 1x12

The Mark III improves upon the original model of the Deville by replacing the master volume & treble pots with audio-taper pots. This means the fine tuning is much more responsive. For those used to the original models, whereas you got to 90% volume by 3-4 on the knob (and there being a HUGE jump between 2-3), the volume curve is much smoother - you'll reach a comparable volume level at around 6 on the knob with a much smother control of the change up to that point. This doesn't mean the output of the amp is any different overall - 10 is still 10 - but the knob responds more smoothly. Likewise, treble response is more noticeable overall for the same reason - the knob is audio-taper. This was one of the major flaws of the original design and frankly you find this in a lot of low-to-mid market amps because amps with linear volume pots get louder lower on the dial, which translates to generally being louder at the store. Fortunately for us Fender realized that this amp doesn't need to sell itself with cheap tricks, and have given us what real musicians have been asking for for years.

Other minor improvements include a black faced switchboard, which makes it much easier to read in a dim bar at night, the preamp tubes are now in a cage, and some minor cosmetic changes.

Overall this amp sounds exactly like it's older brethren. It's just as sturdy as ever, and if my previous amp is any indication, will last for years through serious abuse, up to an including ingesting an entire glass of beer and surviving (don't try this however - I probably just got lucky).

5 Stars - a real home run, unless you're trying to play heavily palm-muted metal. In that case, you really should be looking at a Marshall, or if you're looking for that "classic" fender clean tone, in which case you should be looking at a Super Reverb.
Summary: The best gigging amp on the market just got better

It also sounds great on my acoustic guitar with silk and steel strings. A word of caution: buy these new (probably good advice for all ribbon mics). I bought one on ebay that said it was in good condition, but was busted. They can break and people probably aren’t as familiar with ribbons as other mics, so they don’t know what to look for. You can do a “light breathing” test on each side of the mic and there should be no rattling; if there is rattling, it’s broken. I didn’t think I’d like the color of the Heritage Edition, but it looks much better in person than in the Amazon pictures. The case and shockmount make it a good bundle, so spring for the HE or you’ll have to deal with buying a separate shockmount and case that may or may not fit each other, etc. Also FYI, you can register your mic on the MXL website for 2 years of warranty protection.

Update: Ordered a second one and it arrived with a rattling ribbon..lol. Returns are easy but check your ribbons!

Update II: Just uploaded a video showing what to listen for in a healthy v. damaged ribbon mic. Breathe lightly on each side like you're fogging up a mirror and if you hear crunching/knocking/rattling, the ribbon is damaged, stretched, or out of alignment. Even the manual for these mics says to test the ribbon right away because they're fragile and can damage in shipping! Let me know if this video is helpful or not! These are great sounding mics if you get one that's not damaged.

Update III: The replacement for the broken mic was also broken and looked like it had been a previous return, so I'm taking off a star for inconsisent build quality. Still, if you have the time to retension these, they can sound good; but if time is of the essence for your project, I would look elsewhere for something that's going to be reliable out of the box.

P.S: When I mention "light breathing" like you're fogging up a mirror, it's just that: a super light and gentle breath, not a hard and forceful blow. It doesn't take much to test for a bad ribbon and a hard stream of air could cause damage. So be careful! These ribbons are crazy fragile. Light and gentle: hah...hah...hah; not: FFFFF!-FFFFF!-FFFFF!.

The reason I like this particular design is it allows you to feather the bass drum or lay into it depending on what the music requires. I can achieve a wide dynamic range with it. The beater itself is densely packed, so you can get near the same effect as you can from a wooden beater head. But because it is felt, you can get softer notes if you feather it.

With a non- or minimally-muffled bass drum you can easily coax old school sounds with this beater - something you will be hard pressed to do with some of the modern beaters with light heads and multiple faces. Of course, you will still need the technique to do so, but this beater allows it more than most other ones on the market.

I held off buying this keyboard for a long time because I read comments that said it did not work with Android. But that is not correct (at least in 2019) ... the keyboard works just fine with Android over Bluetooth. I tested with Android 8 and up, using the app FluidSynth (which allows you to use downloadable sf2 soundfont files).

The only tip: you must connect to LE Bluetooth from inside the Fluidsynth app, not from Android's system.

The only limitation you might run into on Android is the typical limitation with apps: not all the apps will yet support LE Bluetooth. App manufacturers do favor iOS because it's more tightly controlled. But there are apparently a couple general purpose LE Bluetooth apps that may work for older midi apps.

Otherwise, USB OTG or USB C will of course work too.

Aside from that, yes these are mini keys. The depth of the key is a bit more challenging to get used to than the width. Still, it's quite fun to play, and super portable.

I got the 49 key version, which has plenty of room for composing music (half a piano). You probably want the 61 key version if you want to use it for performance (where even 5 octaves is a bit small).

What I was expecting this product to be isn't what it is. I expected it to allow me to use my Audio Technica AT2020 condenser mic, which requires 48 Volt phantom power and microphone preamp, so that I could use it with any device with a mic input, connecting it to either the iRig Pre headphone jack or its TRRS output plug (plus a TRRS-to-TRS mic adapter I already have).

But here's some things you need to know about the iRig Pre:

1) The headphone jack produces no output whatsoever unless you have the TRRS cable connected to a PC or phone configured to send speaker/headphone output to the iRig Pre's TRRS connector. The headphone jack is merely a pass-thru of the audio produced by the PC/phone from the TRRS connector.

2) The built-in amplifier of the iRig Pre has a much lower output than a standard microphone preamp. A microphone preamp should be able to convert a mic level signal to a line level signal (about 1.2 Volts). At its highest gain setting, the average output I measured from the iRig Pre directly was 0.035 Volt, maximum was 0.150 Volt. This is too low to be usable for any of the devices I wanted to connect it to directly e.g. powered speakers, mixers, etc. I got some signal but it was extremely low, for example barely audible when I had my powered 40W speakers turned all the way up.

3) Because of this low level output from the iRig Pre, it actually requires the use of an PC/phone to further boost the signal. On my PC I had to set the microphone level to 80 AND set the PC mic boost to +20dB. This is apparently what it's designed to do, to leverage the amplification performed by the PC or phone since it's unable to do itself.

4) The overall quality of the sound was not very good after I got it set up the way it apparently supposed to be configured with the iRig Pre. The iRig Pre does some kind of gain regulation which limits the dynamic range and muddles frequency response. Clarity and sound quality was not as good, making my $100 mic sound not much better than using my built-in PC or phone mic.

All this said, this might work for you, depending on what kind of mic you have and if you always intend to use it with a PC or iPhone. But if you want versatility and great sound, I would suggest you get a decent 4-6 channel mixer with mic preamps designed and built with higher quality than what is in this single-purposed iRig Pre.
Summary: Doesn't perform as expected, low quality

Design(5 stars): I give the design a 5 star (that's the design).
Finish(3 stars): Meh - it's a smooth piece of wood. it has a stain and seal - but that's it. There is nothing special about it.
Cost (2.5 stars): it's literally two pieces of wood with a super cheap wood seal and finish. The cost between walnut and oak is insane - 99 vs 199 (and again - the finish isn't anything to write home about).
Quality(5 stars): they are well made. they are not just slapped together. You can rest assured they Weill be solid after you assemble them. (not to be confused with the finish quality - which isn't bad - just very basic).

This is one of, if not the, best selling large diaphram condenser microphones of all time. This is one of the most useful mics you will ever buy and no matter how many mics you end up with, this one will always have a place in your mic locker. Simply the best for the money.

SUMMARY
These are my favorite cables. They don't break the bank, but aren't cheapo. The clip-on tie proves to be more useful than you would expect, especially if you gig. Buy it - and enjoy for a long time.

PROs
- Never have to tighten the molded plug covers.
- Cable is a good quality, fairly heavy gauge material
- Includes a clip on "bungee cord" cable tie -- VERY HANDY -- I wish I could buy a bag of those and clip them on other cables
- Seem to last as well or better than other instrument cables I have

CONs
- Lack of a dual right angle plug option
- Lack of a 25' length

NEUTRAL
- Gold coated plugs. Makes no difference at all...conducts electricity, just like the silver ones.
- Bungee cord cable ties do stretch out over time and become useless. But they work for quite a while and you can buy replacements from D'addario though, which is actually awesome.

DETAILS
I've been playing for about 30 years and these are my favorite cables. I've owned all sorts of cables. some had metal casings around the plugs in flatter configurations, or round metal casings. Some were metal with plastic coating, some are molded plastic. I have had cloth covered cables, rubber covered cables, plastic covered cables and cables of various gauges. I've had gold plugs, silver plugs, smooth plugs and ribbed plugs. I've had $5 cables and $55 cables...bargain basement and mogami.

These are the cables that I find myself grabbing for - they seem stay to in place well when plugged in, don't have problems with the cable wanting to coil, twist or tangle, and they have a very handle cable tie (Like a little clip on bungee cord), that turns out to be very useful and a lot quicker than hunting for a velcro cable tie. Seem to hold up as well or better than the others I've had.

I've also tried the planet waves CLASSIC series and had problems with those always wanting to tangle up, so I do NOT recommend the CLASSIC series -- the cable is thinner and cheaper and it is always tangled. This CUSTOM series is much better.

First, let me say this transmitter/receiver combo is great. This is my first wireless transmitter, and I don’t know how I lived without this! Having a wireless connection from the guitar (to whatever) is just very convenient, freeing, and awesome. No tangling or tripping over cords. This alone makes it 5 stars, despite anything I say below.

It fit most of my guitars, but I must admit, I did have one guitar that this didn’t fit into. I suspected this one might be a problem before I even orderd this. It has a VERY recessed, angled front jack with no guard plate. This transmitter would NOT fit in that guitar (see picture, the red guitar) because the jack is just too deep. It only goes about 3/4 of the way in. It fit all my other guitars just fine, including a standard strat-style jack, and the hinge allows you quite a bit of freedom in how you position it. For guitars with body-edge jacks (Les Paul style), this is designed to fit along them snugly like a puzzle piece. This is a nice little design feature, which makes it feels pretty solid. Often I sit on my couch to play, and the jack/cable rubs and bends on the cushion (so I always have to use cables with right-angle connectors). I was worried that it might put too much stress on the transmitter, but it feels quite stable, and not likely to break in this scenario.

I used this for a guitar-to-pedal board connection, and just loved it. I didn’t experience any electrical noise/interference/hum or anything. They came paired right out of the box. It sounded great, better than my 10ft cable, so I thought about eliminating more cords and buying another one of these transmitter/receivers for a pedalboard to amp connection. But, before doing this, I figured I ought to take some technical/objective measurements.

I used a function generator to observe the behavior with various waveforms (sine, triangle, square waves). For all of the oscilloscope pictures the YELLOW trace is the input to the transmitter, and the GREEN trace is the output from the receiver. This receiver mimics the guitar signal voltage at about a 1-to-1 ratio at lower voltages, but clips the signal at 2.4 volts peak-to-peak (see oscilloscope pictures). Natural signals coming out of a guitar (or even a bass) are rarely above this threshold. So, connecting the transmitter to your guitar and the receiver to the first pedal in your board (or directly into your amp) works great. Everything goes as expected. If you are going to use it this way, you will be very happy!

But, you need to know a few things if/when you decide you want to wirelessly transmit from your last pedal to the amp. For that approach, here are a few items to note:

1) If you are trying to boost your signal with a boost pedal, or high gain distortion, or anything else that’s high gain, (say, to slam the front of a tube amp with 5 or 6 or 7 volts), and wirelessly transmit that to your amp, this thing won’t go over 2.4V. So, you can’t use this to wirelessly connect the output of your boost pedal to the input of a tube amp and get the expected behavior, since the receiver cannot deliver more than a 2.4V signal. You cannot send ANY kind of signal above 2.4 volts without clipping. Again, only a problem sending from pedal outputs to the amp, since you are never going to get 2.4V from the guitar, only from a gained/boosted pedal.

2) The slew rate of this device is only about 0.05 V/us. That’s actually pretty poor but doesn’t actually matter much here for relatively slow guitar signals. It’s just fine for sending sinusoidal waves in a guitar or bass’s natural frequency range to the pedal. However, if you are sending from your last pedal to your amp, then for some pedals it may slightly color the tone of any effects that exit the pedal and get sent to the amp that are higher than "natural" guitar frequencies. Many distortion effects with very rapid voltage swings (e.g. “hard-clipping” distortion that produces sharp square waves, or DSP effects with sharp spikes) have frequency content that goes into the several kHz. In the pictures, you can see how the green transmitted signal keeps up with the true output pretty well, but not perfectly.

3) Even though I measured the slew rate with a function generator, I couldn’t actually hear any audible difference. The transmitter sounded EXACTLY the same to my ear as a patch cable, and I tried this will all of my distortion pedals (Red Llama, OCD, Big Muff Pi, Tube Screamer, Multi-Distortion). I was actually surprised I couldn't hear a difference, so I rigged up my oscilloscope to the output of my highest frequency distortion pedal (this was no easy task, splitting the signal so I could get one unaltered output, and the other to go through the transmitter/receiver). The effect was EXTREMELY MINIMAL when viewed on the oscilloscope, which is why it was not audible to me (or probably to anyone). There is just the slightest lag in the slope on some of the sharper transitions. But, I COULD NOT HEAR THIS difference. You can barely even see it on the oscilloscope (for real pedal signals).

4) I’m not saying this will be a problem for you, because it probably won't be. I’m just saying, be thoughtful if you use this for pedal-to-amp transmissions, and be aware of both the 2.4V clipping and the possibility of high frequency tone roll-off. This would be similar to the tone loss from just using a guitar cable (all of which suck just a little tone from their excess capacitance). Really nothing to get worried about.

Other reviewers have commented on the 10+ hours of battery life, so I didn’t test that here. I’ll just trust the other reviewers. I've been using it all day for these tests, and it still has juice.

Again, I LOVE this thing. I am done with plugging a cord into my guitar! I do have one guitar it doesn’t fit in, but I know that’s a weird situation with an extra deep jack, so I’m not subtracting a star. It fits fine in standard jacks and works great. The 2.4 volt clipping prevents it from being able to transmit from a boost pedal to really send a Tube amp hard over the edge (again, if transmitting from the pedal board only), but that’s not really a big deal here, and not worth subtracting a star for.

Final Rating: 5 Stars! If you’ve never had one of these, you will love it!
Summary: Great wireless system!  Just know it clips at 2.4V.  Signal analysis included.

When I heard about the line of 13 inexpensive pedals offered by TC Electronics, the Skysurfer Reverb was the one that instantly stood out to me, if only because there aren't a lot of $50 reverb pedals - even "bad" ones. But I tried out at a Guitar Center a few months back and was not at all impressed. More recently, I gave it a second chance, and found that it's a bit of an oddball unit that requires non-conventional settings to acheive a "traditional" reverb sound. Therefore, while it isn't a standout unit, it's still a highly useful offering at this price point, and I plan to use it with a lot my amps that don't have built-in reverb.

Part of the confusion over this unit has to do with the "Reverb" and "Mix" controls. Most reverb pedals have either a single "reverb" control (which controls either decay or intensity) or some combination of both parameters. But the Mix control actually switches between dry and wet signal. I've heard that the reverb is actually the most intense at around the 12:00 setting. With the Mix knob all the way up, you are getting essentially ONLY the reverberated audio, which can lead to some strange pre-delay and swell effects.

The "Reverb" knob is supposed to control decay, but I think it's actually more like "intensity". If you set all the knobs to 12:00 and start playing, you'll have a washed out, swampy mess, which is part of the problem this pedal. But, actually, I was able to make it behave like a fairly standard reverb unit with both the Reverb and Mix knobs at about 9:00, or possibly a bit lower. From there, the Tone control darkens or brightens the reverberated sound.

There's also a 3-way switch to select from Spring, Plate, and Hall. I have a DigiTech Hardwire RV-7 with Lexicon reverb algorithms, and I clearly prefer each version of those sounds on the RV-7. But there's actually a good variety of types in the Skysurfer for such an inexpensive unit. The "Spring" lacks that famous "pling!" or "boing" effect when you really attack notes, but does have the liveliness of a vintage spring unit. The "Plate" setting actually surprised me - it was probably my favorite of the three, and I'm not usually a Plate reverb fan. It's bright and expressive, but as with all three settings, needs to be set carefully to keep it from getting out of hand. Finally, there's the Hall setting, which is usually the easiest for cheap reverb pedals to handle. On the Skysurfer, it's just okay, but gets the job done.

I had considered a lower rating for the Skysurfer, but after using it a bit, I got used to its quirks, and it's a very well-built unit with a solid tank-like enclosure. It's hard to be too hard on it when I can't even name a competing $50 standalone reverb unit. A digital multi-effects like the Zoom G1on comes to mind, but not a dedicated reverb unit like this, and certainly not one backed by a Western manufacturer. Don't expect it to be the only reverb pedal you'll ever want, but it's a nice offering from TC Electronic at a great price point.
Summary: Affordable reverb with unconventional controls; easily can get swampy or excessive

Starting with the charging case, this system screams quality.  The “lollipop” send/receive units are light, small and unobtrusive especially for a Strat style guitar.  If using with a front/side output jack, they may not be as unobtrusive as they do not fold down, but I knew that going in.  If your guitar is equipped with a trem arm, and your output jack is on the front of the guitar, just be aware.  The units paired easily, simply by turning them on and holding the button for a few seconds.  I tested them using a number of different guitars, and in each case I could not tell the difference between wired or wireless…no noise and no latency could be detected.  I also left the studio and stood outside, separated by two walls and a concrete wall with no issues.  The case acts as the charging unit and includes a USB charging cable.  I just used my powered USB cube from my computer to charge, though the case showed a full charge from receipt.  The lollipops simply lay in their slots to charge from the case.  These have 4 different channels as well.  I played for well over a hour testing these, and still showed full battery!  The only change I could think of on these, were if they could be made to fold from the jack somehow, then any type of guitar could be used without worry of them getting in the way.  As they are, they are a very elegant way to go wireless in your Strat style guitar, or other guitars depending on where your output jack is located.
Summary: Unique Design | No Noise | Clean Signal

First, the quality of the effects are better with this unit than others in the below $300 price range. I've owned and used a great many budget effects units. Most of the cheap-o's are fine for live use but in the studio they really muddy up a mix, sound quite grainy, have a noise "floor" that could better be referred to as a desk halfway between the floor and the ceiling. You won't have those problems with this unit.

But, a few negatives. One, the VST plug-in to integrate this unit into your DAW is 32-bit only. It will not work in a 64-Bit DAW. I have PreSonus StudioOne 2 Professional (full) version, and it would not recognize the DLLs for this reason. Nowhere on the box, nor in the owner's manual, nor in the product description in any of the online sales listings I've seen do they mention this substantial limitation. When I contacted Lexicon, they did reply promptly and claimed that this "product page" serves as notice of the limitation: http://www.lexiconpro.com/en-US/softwares/mx-edit-mx400-v231-windows. I find that disingenuous, as this page is a page for the 32-bit version of the VST plug-in download and is buried accordingly. And, a brief, buried statement that the 32-bit driver only works on 32-bit systems does NOT convey that there exists no 64-bit driver and the entire selling point of using this device as a plug-in is limited to 32-bit systems. They should include that on the box, in the manual, and in the sales literature that promotes the plug-in feature.

Also, I bought the unit in January 2015 and the included CD-ROM would not install on my system, which is Windows 7. I got an error message from the installer that indicated my operating system is not compatible. It would not successfully install in compatibility mode either. Hard to believe they are shipping CDs in 2015 that only support Windows XP-era operating systems. No problem here, really, as you can download the latest from Lexicon's website. But, it just makes you go "hmmmm" and fosters some unflattering perceptions.

Second, the USB connection only controls the unit. It does not pass audio. Therefore, if you are going to integrate this with your DAW using the VST plug-in, you are going to have to pass audio from your computer, to the Lexicon unit, and back- either via analog or S/PDIF at a max of 48KHz. This will eat up inputs and outputs in your interface. As such, if you're currently using all of your I/O channels, you'll need to buy a bigger interface. So, this unit's plug-in feature is really not much different than using any external hardware processor with a DAW- only the fact that you can control the effects parameters from your computer instead of having to mess with the front panel of the device. And again, that is assuming that you have a behind-the-times 32-bit DAW.

Third, I'm not all that impressed with the reverbs. While they are better than other processors in their price range, you can hear the tail of the reverbs drop off in a very stair-stepped pattern. The decay is not smooth. They also sound a bit dark to me. To be fair, if this weren't a Lexicon I'd think it was quite good for the $ (and it is), but it's not what you used to get from the company's previous mid-tier products.

Another thing- none of the effects really blew me away. I much prefer the old LXP-15 II. That unit had a number of patches that would instantly add a WOW factor to a vocal or instrument track. With this model, I can get good results that sound professional and lack that "cheap reverb/amateur studio" sound, but I don't get the wow-factor.

Also, as is typical with higher-quality effects units, you don't have as much flexibility to combine multiple effects and fine-control the routing. For example, I have another manufacturer's budget reverb where I can feed into a de-esser effect, route that to an EQ effect that feeds a slapback delay, and in parallel route the output of the de-esser effect to a plate reverb, then sum the paralleled effects together into an exciter that feeds the output. You don't have as many effects or routing options with this one. BUT, that is typical on a unit in this category- your dollars are going toward increased sound quality.

Lastly, part of my decision to purchase was that I could use it as two MX200 units in dual stereo mode. Two discrete Lexicon effects boxes in one physical package. The drawback here, is that the two separate units are summed together internally and sent to one pair of outputs. So, you'll have to mix the levels between the two processors inside the Lexicon unit. That means you can't feed each effect unit's output into its own stereo pair on your console and apply channel strip EQ to each effect independently, which I always like to do.

On the plus side, the chorus effects are quite clean for a budget unit.

Overall, this device is serving a purpose- I needed decent verbs and choruses that won't muddy up a mix or sound cheap for my project studio. I would recommended if you need to fill that need.
I expected to love it, but due to some of the shortcomings I view it as a necessary tool in my arsenal like one of the wrenches in my garage as opposed to an object of affection.
Summary: Better sound than other under $300 effects, but a few disappointments.

Text:
I wouldn't dock them a star, because for what these are, they are very nicely made, with very good leverage for opening the jaws--and I really like getting two choices of color, for different guitars/settings!... but if your needs are anything like mine, you may want an elastic capo, due to less hardware obstruction to hand position **behind the neck**.

I'm a blues player who uses a baritone electric guitar so that on songs in keys below "E", I can still do all the cool open-string runs, droning, etc. that you can in 'E'.

(A capo on the fifth fret of a baritone guitar sets you at the same tuning as open strings on a regular, vanilla, non-baritone six-string guitar...successively lower frets are thus like "capo-ing DOWN" from what your regular axe can play...giving songs in "C" & "D" a bass-base-basis [lol] you can't get solo on regular tuned guitar...&, for vocalists, you get a few more chances for your 'cowboy chords' to match YOUR range. ;) )

Doing some of the necessary chording & wrist positioning for that conflicts with so much hardware behind the neck, & an ELASTIC capo just has drastically lower profile back there. (It also boasts that you more easily "slide" from key to key without first releasing it, but that's not something I've tried enough to vouch for it as a technique--i.e., not snagging/scratching/detuning etc.)

But if you're a "cowboy chords" player, or otherwise not concerned with bending your wrist in various ways that invade the "airspace" of this capo [which, probably, is most players, but this caveat is for the oddballs whose scenario is like mine], it's a very good choice.
Summary: Can't dock them a star, but if you're like me, you may want an elastic capo

Text:
As many of you will know, finding a controller that works really tightly with Logic Pro X makes for slim pickings. I tried an Novation Impulse and the Automapping was a nightmare. This on the other hand is REMARKABLE. The integration borders on spectacular and requires ABSOLUTELY NO mapping on your part unless you want to get deeper. Out of the box, with only their latest driver installed and working transparently, there is a huge amount of intuitive mapping.

Please know that all my comments are based on use with Logic but I am sure there are many out there that would love to know how well this works with it!

PROS:

1) A relatively high resolution screen provides detailed information on the parameter mappings so you always know what your controls are mapped to.

2) Very high integration in several modes:
a) MIXER MODE - maps faders and left encoders to banks of 8 tracks with the buttons below toggling between solo, mute, select and arm. It also provides control access to Sends and Inserts such as compressors, etc.
b) INSTRUMENT MODE - The instrument name appears on your display and the P4 provides instant control on BOTH sets of encoders (16 in all!) and the faders for various instrument specific controls. It maps very intuitively and because the display provides feedback you always know what you're doing. One nice touch...the faders become draw bars on many organ patches.
c) TRANSPORT MODE - Love this. Lots of access to turning punch on and off, setting starting and end points, using the master encoder as a jog wheel and the drum pads can be set to create, delete and navigate markers easily. You can even turn count in on and off. Of course, there are permanent transport buttons (some backlit!) too for recording, playing, navigating, starting, stopping and turning cycle on and off.
d) INTERNAL MODE - this allows you to use the controller in pure midi form.
I am just scratching the surface. Even without a single bit of customization this baby is ready to go with endless well mapped plugins and instruments. But if you want, you can definitely customize and rearrange to taste. But for me, that is more than I need. Note, you can switch between modes easily on the fly.

3) The keybed is quite reasonable. I have a Yamaha MOXF8 which has a much more true weighted feel but this is a nice "synthish" alternative. It also has monophonic aftertouch which my MOXF doesn't.

4) Motorized fader - this is really quite nice. The leftmost fader, which sits alone in the white plastic is motorized (if you plug in the second USB power supply, and it is great. It is always set to the CURRENT track automatically, and adjusts to the correct level when you switch. The other manual faders don't "jump" when you touch them and only engage once they are set to the current setting on the track, but this isn't nearly as awesome as the motorized fader. I love it. Also, the dedicated SOLO, MUTE and automation read/write mode buttons are great for quickly working with the CURRENT TRACK.

5) Easy track/patch navigation using dedicated buttons.

6) Build Quality. It's not only beautiful, but also solidly built. Nothing cheap feeling about it.

7) SUPPORT. The support team at Nektar are INCREDIBLE and highly responsive. Ask a question and they are not only going to help you, but they are going to help you with a really positive attitude. They stand behind their product passionately and so they should. It's awesome and so are they.

CONS:

Note, these are all MINOR cons. I again reiterate that I have never seen better DAW integration with Logic. PERIOD.

1) Since OSX 10.11 there is no more QUERTY mapping to the the 11 function keys. A real shame because I would like to have programmed in things like REDO, SAVE, etc. Not critical given the very high degree of integration in general, but definitely a small disappointment.
2) Not critical but just a design thing I'm not crazy about. There is nothing protecting either end white key on the keybed. It just "feels" exposed even though both ends are set back from the edge of the unit. Also, this stays on my desk and doesn't get gigged or anything like that but if I was travelling with it, it seems like the most likely part that would get accidentally damaged. It's not a big deal at all so I don't want to overstate the issue.
3) The drum pads - honestly, these are more a function of the age of the system than anything else. But to be fair, there are far nicer ones out now, including on their own more recent products and on other cheaper controllers so if drumming is your thing, you should still get this but supplement it with a dedicated drum pad, a decent one of which can be had for about a hundred bucks and even less if used.

So, final impressions?

YES. YES. YES. FOR LOGIC, IT'S A NO BRAINER. People who say it's tough to set up with Logic either wrote their review before Logic support (i.e., years ago), or are having other issues. This thing requires no more than a driver install and you are away in a manner that no other controller that I have encountered can rival.

I LOVE THIS THING. It lets me work without reaching for my mouse as much and that keeps me more in the zone. Also, it's just cool. I love that the screen is always giving meaningful feedback. If you take the time to read the documentation, you will become much more productive. Just take the time to practice using this and eventually you'll find you can work more and more smoothly.

HIGHLY recommended for Logic Pro X.
Summary: OUTSTANDING Controller Integration for Logic Pro X

Text:

It has a "serial" mode that jumps from string to string. It works fine but you have to silence the string you just tuned before going to the next. Takes a little getting used to. No big deal.
A little awkward to hold, and the chuck bumps the other tuners on some guitars.
--
What I don't like:
It should always tune below then note and then back UP. If you've played guitar for more than 2 weeks you should know this. This device, with all it's clever technology, can't seem to manage that. As a result, if you give you strings a quick tug after tuning, as I always do, you're outta tune again. The tug is to make sure the string does not bind at the nut, and then release while I'm playing. This is a no-brainer.

So my recommended workaround is to detune your strings before using the Roadie, and then I will still give them a tug and retune once more.

Second complaint.

Anybody who uses a capo knows even the best capo can throw a guitar out of tune. Maybe it's intonation. Maybe it's the capo tension on the strings. Some guitars seem more prone than others.

The roadie has "standard" tuning, plus a laundry list of suggested alternate tunings, plus the ability to create your own alternate tunings. You can also name them, which is great for finding them fast.

What it does NOT have is a simple capo mode, where you can effectively say, "tune this in standard mode for the 6th fret." Standard plus 6. That should be it.

INSTEAD, you have to create an alternate tuning for Bb Eb Ab Db F and Bb. And another one for the first fret, 2nd fret, 3rd fret, and any other fret you want to put a capo on.

I am hoping they will update the app with a capo mode some time in the future. As it stands now, I'm still testing. Mandolin and 12 string (both tuned down half a step) are next.

--

If you want to share this device with someone else, you will need to add the guitar to the device and sync it up. Easy enough, but if you're in a hurry and need to tune a guitar not sync'd up, then it may be easier to use a standard tuner.
Summary: Nice but pricey, and some glaring omissions in current app. Hope they will update.

Great little practice amp, but be sure that you understand what you are getting into.

Pros:
Very small and light. I use it a lot because it isn't a hassle at all to bring it out and set it up. Honestly, it's probably more of a hassle to set up my mini pedal board.

Great tube sound that is nice and warm. The reverb on it is also very nice.

I love the drive button that this amp features which allows you to very quickly (without a pedal board if you don't have one) get distorted tones

The build quality is great and the amp is very nice to look at. The strap on the top is very nice and comfortable to hold, the knobs are very sharp looking as well

Cons:
I personally have no problems with this amp, however, I understand fully what niche this amp fills. I could see someone complaining that the amp is not loud enough, or that it is too bright. But to be fair, it is a 1-watt amp, with a tiny speaker. You just can't move much air with that, and you aren't going to get the rich sound out of such a small driver. If I am practicing and my wife jumps on the upright piano, she can easily drown me out.

Conclusion:
If you are looking for a practice amp that is very light and portable, this is the one for you. It is a bit quiet and you will perhaps miss the full range of tones from a bigger amp, but you will be able to drive the tubes without rattling the windows. If this is what you need, and you are tired of lugging around big amps and are pressed for space in your home, this is a great amp for you. If you are looking to get better sound out of your amp and you want to hear every detail of your guitar, you might need something a bit bigger (and probably a lot more expensive). Please think about what your needs are before you buy it.

I got mine gently used, not from Amazon, but I have to say I'm very impressed! This is my first rack compressor, and I bought it for my home studio set up. Let me say, first off, that I'm not a recording pro! However, I've been playing music for a long time, and have a generally good working knowledge of gear and whatnot. The MaxCom was perfect for my needs, and even at the 'new' price quite affordable.

Pros:
-Easy to figure out. If you're unfamiliar with what a compressor does, google it- there's plenty of info out there. Then spend some time messing around with different settings. I'd say it took me a couple hours to get familiar with how each control affects the signal, and once I got a handle of it, I was able to get a range of cool tones.
-Sonic Maximizer rules. I love that this has the SM built in to each channel. I use this for recording mainly acoustic guitars, and the SM is awesome for "unblanketing" acoustic guitar tone... I was skeptical at first, but a few minutes of tweaking the lo and hi contour made a believer out of me with a quickness.
-Dual channel with a "channel on/off" button that allows you to hear a bypassed signal for comparison. This is really nice after a long session when your ears are tired. The Sonic Maximizer also has this feature. I like having 2 channels, since I mostly record acoustic guitar and vocals- this way I can have one channel set up for each without having to re-configure my settings as I move between takes.
-Light and good looking: full rack size but pretty light (without feeling cheap) and the graphics are attractive (let's not pretend looks don't matter.) The knobs are plastic, but sturdy and the pots are smooth and tight. I have the red colored model and it looks great.

CONS:
- I'm sure there are better compressor units out there, and this might not be top of the line studio grade- I'd think that if you have the money a nice vintage tube compressor would be the best, but for me, this is a good-sounding, multi-functional unit at a good price.
-This is super picky, but I dislike the way the lo contour and process knobs are stacked on the SM. I have big fingers and it's really hard to turn one without moving the other. I understand that BBE did this to save space, but it is annoying.

Overall, a great unit that does it's job well and won't break the bank.
Summary: Squeezing out Bang for your Buck!

I generally have good experiences with Planet Waves. I ordered five LARGE celluloid finger picks to try with nylon-stringed instruments for some extra volume. I ordered large, butnI could barely squeeze them onto my little finger, so they would be right for, maybe, a ten year old girl. These can of course be played with steel string guitars or other instruments where you need finger picks, but celluloid sounds different than steel or brass. Use what sounds right for your instrument, to your ears. Unlike steel picks, it is possible to use files or fingernail files to thin the ends to get a more fingernail-like sound. The picks can also be roughed a little so they are less slippery at the end. That changes the tone. Or polish them for more speed.

I agree with what Strube writes, but note that reforming the picks requires, ideally, rapidly boiling water. Hold the pick with needle nose pliers or, better, a surgical needle holder or clamp. Wear one rubber glove on your left hand and TWO on your right. After holding the pick for five seconds in the boiling water, push the pick onto your finger and press it into shape. If you want to bend over the tip a bit more, now is the time. If you are doing a batch of five (one at a time!) you may burn your finger, but not badly, and thanks to the gloves, it will feel better in a few minutes. If it starts burning your skin, pull off the pick for a couple seconds. If it is still too small or if it is now too big, put it back in the water and try again.
Summary: Too small, but can be reformed. Expect a celluloid sound

It would take me well over an hour to get my drums to how I wanted them after replacing heads. And then of course, things change as you play them more, so then I would take a lot of additional time to re-tune them to ear. I finally broke down and bought a DrumDial and it quite possibly was the best purchase I've ever made for my drum set. I got frustrated with tuning and then when it sounded perfect, I barely wanted to touch it because I was nervous to how I would get it back to that perfect sound again. I really just should have gotten one of these a loooong time ago.

I got this in the mail the other day and immediately took it down stairs to my drum set, read through the instructions/recommendations and started using it. I started by loosening all the screws completely and then hand tightened them as I would normally. Then, I put the drum dial on the drum and begin tuning each screw to 78 (per the recommendation - the number you like may be different) until they were all 78. I followed the further recommendations and did this for each drum. I then tried a basic one or two hits on each drum. Most sounded pretty good, but the few that sounded slightly off, I went back with the drum dial, loosened all the screws on the drum that sounded too tight/high pitched and tightened all the ones on the drum that sounded too dull/dead. Then I got both sticks and started to play. I was honestly BLOWN AWAY. I don't think my kit EVER sounded this good. It took a middle of the line Yamaha drum set and made the shells sound like 10k shells. I'm not lying to you when I tell you I don't think I've ever heard ALL my drums sounding quite THAT perfect all together at the same time.

If you ever have been frustrated or let down with how your drums sound or have taken more than 5 minutes to tune each of your drums, you need to get this. It's amazing and it will bring out the TRUE potential in your drum set.

In a word, "WOW"! I am amazed at the quality of my Epi ES-339 Pro. I thought long and hard before ordering it, mainly because of where these are made. I have owned several USA Gibsons over the years (two ES-335s, four Les Pauls), so I'm familiar with Gibson and truly love the Gibson sound. However, I really can't justify spending the money Gibson wants for the models I prefer (and money is not really an issue for me). So I researched the ES-339 extensively and was impressed by the overwhelming positive reviews this guitar (as well as other Epi models being made today) received. I watched a ton of YouTube product reviews as well. In the end I decided to take a chance and order one. I'm glad I did.

The only things I had to do was lower the action for my likes, adjust the pickup height a smidge for better balance between the neck and bridge pickups, put on my preferred strings, replace the strap buttons with Strap Loks and replace the control knobs with Speed Knobs. Sounds like a lot, but all of these tweaks reflect personal preferences. It was fine out of the box.

Fit and finish are flawless. Very solid guitar and extremely stable. It stays in tune. As far as the action, I simply lowered the bridge. I expected I would have to tweak the truss rod and mess with intonation adjustments (things I always had to do with EVERY USA Gibson I've bought new). The neck couldn't have been more perfect. No adjustment needed. The fretwork was spot on.

I love these Classic Pro pickups. I generally do not like the stock pickups on USA Gibsons and ALWAYS replaced them with DiMarzios. I really wasn't expecting much from these Epi PUPS, but wow. They sound great and are perfect on this guitar (I played this through a Fender Twin). Very articulate, clear, warm and crisp at the same time. I like what I'm hearing. A lot. And the coil spit is subtle but usable, and will work great for a couple of countryish songs I do, where I don't need all the meat of the full humbuckers. I do mainly blues so I think I found the perfect blues guitar.

If you're on the fence about buying because of the "China" thing, do yourself a favor and give it a try (heck, you can always return it). The Epiphone ES-339 will surprise you.

Also, the upright bars are not padded, so you have to be careful not to bang your guitar into them. Especially if you are using more than two or three guitar slots. It probably wouldn't be much more costly to pad the upright bars to make the stand safer. However, after leveling the frame and a couple of days of use, it is very handy to be able to have more than one guitar out at a time and be able to grab the guitar that is needed. It also looks nice to have a rack of guitars in your practice or performance space. After the initial set-up, the stand works pretty well.

Text: This is without a doubt the best mouthpiece I have come across.  I have tried Vandoren V16 A5, Selmer Soloist D tip, Meyer 5M and an Otto Link 5* this year. I got this guitar as a project platform and to practice my luthier skills. For this purpose, it's an ok guitar. It is not playable out of the box though. It had sharp fret ends, uneven frets, fret sprout on three frets, a nut that needed filing (factory filed it crooked), saddles needed replacement (saddle buzz), and it desperately needed a setup. So, I got to work.

Work that I did to get it playable: hammered in frets that were sprouting, leveled and dressed the frets and fret ends, filed the nut, replaced the saddles, put on a decent set of strings.

In addition, I oiled the fretboard, replaced the pickguard with a nice dark blue pearl 3ply version (had to pull out my router to trim it a bit to fit), and gave it a good polish.

After completing the above, I finished setting it up, and now it plays pretty well. That took me about 3 hours to do all the work. At some point, I will replace the pickups. The bridge pickup is bad microphonic. The neck pickup is good though.

While it didn't affect the playability, I should note that the blue body had some poor paint work on the back, with spots where you could see where it ran and they tried to sand it down before clear coating it. The finish flaw was minor overall though, so it wasn't worth sending back.

If you are looking for a project guitar, or a guitar to learn/practice guitar repair and maintenance, then this guitar isn't a terrible one to start with. If you are a beginner, or are looking for a budget t-style guitar to play and want it playable out of the box, I'd look elsewhere.

The terrible fretwork and faulty hardware is what gives it two stars. Also, pictures showed string through and it wasn't string through.
Summary: An ok project platform. Not for beginners.

This is an interesting cable: There is a mute switch on each of the 1/4” TR connectors. Sometimes, depending on the static charge over the cable, there can be quite a loud POP when engaging the mute button. Nevertheless, it does work and, when used correctly, will completely eliminate the “I’m plugging in the guitar” noise we, as musicians, all despise. Counterintuitively, the mute is ON when the button is in the UP position. I will say this: the push-on-push-off action of the mute buttons feel well engineered.

My only concern is that the cable picked up a lot of EMF noise (Hum, white noise, pops) when it was unmuted and not connected to an instrument. This indicates that either it is lacking in shielding coverage and/or the unmuted condition of the switching mechanism themselves are acting as antennas.

However, it should be noted that this is not be a “normal” use of this cable, so I don’t see this as a big deal as when plugged into an instrument and amp the EMF noise is attenuated so as not to be noticeable - at least to my ears. Besides, the whole concept is that you turn the mute on (UP position) before removing it!

While I can't speak to the longevity of this cable I can say that the mute function works well and if feels pretty solid overall - not a skinny cable. I tested this cable with both an electric guitar and bass. Both sounded crisp and clear and no apparent high end roll off. Bass response was just fine.

This mic came recommended highly as the number one vocal mic to buy if you're on a budget, and maybe even one of the top five even if money isn't a consideration. It's no secret that a lot of great vocal performances have come from the SM7, including "Thriller." But just because it was recommended to me by a couple of engineers who I trust, or just because it was used on some classic recordings doesn't mean everyone should own this mic- everyone should own it because it's incredibly versatile and makes it really easy to get great sounding performances, as long as you account for a couple things:

-First, you do need a good preamp, with plenty of gain (60 DB seems to be conventional wisdom, but you may get away with less if you work it very close, which sounds good as it has a nice proximity effect that resists muddiness unlike a lot of other mics.)
I like this mic a lot with the Warm Audio WA12 preamp, which has plenty of gain to drive it and sounds fantastic. It also works well with the Cloud Lifter, although I find that the CL can push a preamp into too much gain even at low settings, thereby loosing the color that a higher gain setting gives a particular preamp.
-Second, you do have to play around a bit with the mid and presence boosts that are adjustable on the back of the mic body- these will be useful in different ways depending on the tone of your voice.
-Third, This mic does sound a lot better up close than further back, as is pretty standard for a dynamic mic, so take advantage of the nice, thick pop-filter and get all up in it. You can, however, get a bit more crisp tone by removing the pop filter (very gently wiggle the plastic ring at the base of the foam free from the metal body). You will have to use a conventional pop screen to avoid plosives, but if you have a very dark or low voice it helps tighten things up.

Overall, this is a great addition to anyone's studio, whether it be a home studio like mine or a professional space. The quality of vocal recordings that I've gotten with this mic paired with a good preamp are far better than what I was getting with my MXL condenser (even with a decent preamp), and I'd say it's perfect for someone (like me) who isn't exactly a novice but isn't an expert either. It also sounds pretty good close-micing an acoustic guitar, especially when paired with a small-diaphragm condenser.

This mic isn't exactly cheap, but it's not that expensive either, and it proves that for a bit more money than something generic and "just ok" you can have an industry-standard piece of gear that anyone who knows a bit about recording will instantly recognize as a classic.

Solidly built. High quality preamps. For simplest applications.

PROs
- Very affordable for a stombox tuner
- Reasonably accurate (Boss is a little better)
- Nice Big display of notes, and uses # sign (not a tiny dot or other weird LED notation.)
- Battery or standard 9V (center negative) power supply (i.e same as Boss and "many" pedals)
- Good size, jacks are all in the right places to be convenient on a pedal board

CONs
- The pitch adjustment/calibration buttons are on the back vertical surface -- I'm a little concerned if they get bumped in transit that I might get pulled out of calibration and not know it.
- The battery compartment is accessed from the bottom, using a Very Large phillips screwdriver, or a quarter. You wont have that size screwdriver at a gig, so use a coin.
-Lacks a "passthru" jack. Signal is automatically always muted if you are tuning. There is no option like on a Boss to pass the signal thu or do silent tuning. Just silent. Not a big deal, unless you want to compare to other pedals.
- While the tuning is "accurate enough", if you put this next to a Boss TU-2 you can be slightly out of tune on the boss and see it, and this will show you on the center bar as if perfectly tuned. So it isn't as precise as the Boss.

SUMMARY
Overall, this is a good tuner for the money, and frankly a lot better than the Snark (and other) clip on tuners in terms of accuracy. If you want mutable stompbox tuner that doesn't break the bank, this is it. Nice big display, easy operation. Not sure how it performs outdoors in bright sunlight but I've found most pedals are next to impossible to see in those conditions.
Summary: Good deal at $35, Tunes pretty well, Good Visibility.

But I am reminded of Katana's greatest shortcoming every time I look at the GA-FC. The amp has so much more under the hood than can be accessed by this very basic little pedal. I bought the pedal because it gives me quick access to the four preset channels (called LiveSets by Boss, and disregard the panel settings) and the panel, which does represent panel settings. Tap a button and you can then turn effects on and off within each of the 5 preset options. So it does a lot, for what it is.

You can create presets from the panel, but to really tweak them requires a computer and USB cable. Nothing for IOS or Android as far as I know, and I don't see it coming unless someone comes up with a hack.

Conclusion - they do a LOT with a bare bones GA-FC pedal, and it is essential for Katana owners who take the amp out and plan to use the amp's channels. But you would do fine with the panel setting and your own effects pedals.

Not for all instruments. This works very well for strings, but poorly for brass. These are super popular for guitar and other strings, so I think most people who play strings have seen one before. I have an older one that I use regularly to tune my classical guitar and my two sons' two electrics. I bought this one for four reasons: it's claimed to be for all instruments, it's advertised with a transpose feature, it has the hertz readout, and it's claimed to be faster. It also has an upgraded display but I could see the display on the old one fine.

I tried to understand the transpose feature from the description and online manual but I could not figure out if it would transpose for Bb or not. When I actually got one, I realized it won't. The transpose feature works with a capo. It tunes up by one, two, three, or four semi-tones. It does not work with instruments that are tuned down, like a Bb trumpet, Flugelhorn, or Cornet that are tuned down two semitones from concert pitch. It might work with an Eb instrument, but it will not work on Trombones, French Horns, Baritone, Euphonium, or Tuba in G, F, etc.

The Hertz readout simply does not work with brass at all. I verified it worked with my guitar, but I tried sustaining notes is various places of the trumpet's register and the Hz display only showed 000.0.

I also tried with voice, the best instrument of all. Again, the Hertz function failed to work at all. If I sustained a note, it would display the letter, but the Hertz display would only show 000.0.

Fast pitch readout would be valuable for developing intonation with brass, but this tuner would require the user to transpose themselves unless they play a C instrument.
Summary: For strings only; not for all instruments

Text:
I did buy this not because I use Maschine app, but to have a more well-rounded controller that can help me to use the keyboard and mouse to the minimum. I am no DJ nor live performer; but I play classic instruments since when I was 7, so I am not exactly the target for this device.

I like the build; it is solid as most of the German NI products are. I paired this device with a NI Komplete Kontrol keyboard, and they do work well together; except that NI is still figuring out how to handle their ecosystem.
While the KK keyboards works very well with their KK software, and overall integrate seamlessly, can't say the same of the Jam. Fundamentally the JAM works great if you use Maschine app, because that's what it was meant to do; but as far as other Native instruments software; you get mixed results. Some of the features are not implemented, like browsing or transport features; while other works.

So if you want to use the JAM with other DAW or software, even from NI itself, be ready to work a bit around the limitations.

As far as applications, it works fine with Maschine, and with Ableton Live; although there is a whole sequence of file copying and setup to do; so it is not working out of the box. Nothing too hard, but takes you some time to figure out where to place files and how to set up config parameters in the options, and you just need to do it once.

If you use mostly Ableton Live; it is still a good buy, considering that the Push cost much more than the JAM, and it does exactly the same things. If you use Cubase, you are out of luck because NI hate Cubase; most of the features do not work, and you need to fiddle with midi signals to get it to work. I just gave up, and hope that NI will release an updated firmware to work out of the box with Cubase.

Logic and Garageband are fully supported; it works fine on those applications, if you are a OSX user. Before you ask...no, it does not work with the ipad.

As far as controls and features, the JAM is awesome. Its main thing is the old school visual step sequencer; so you push buttons and sounds get placed in a specific position, so you can visually program music, and not only the bass or drum part, but also the melody. It is a weird concept if you are used to classic instruments and you did study music theory, but for everyone else, it is easy, and you may end up making something that sound nice, even without even knowing what are you doing.

Buttons and strips are very solid and while not clicky, give you a good resistance when pressed. The pads are not velocity sensitive, and there is no LCD, so you need to look at the screen.
The strips are quite fun to use; since the JAM can be set in note mode to use either the button pads, or the strips. It is similar to what you do in garageband on the iphone or ipad, strumming with your fingers, or playing with single notes. The downside is that the strips are small, so at least for me, it was hard to get used to which note I was playing, ending up with something that remind me when I play with the pitch wheel on my keyboard. It is just a matter of getting used to it, I assume.

The strips control also parameters, in the same way that knobs on a KK keyboard or on a Maschine MK3 do; so you can set them either to be volume controllers, like on a mixed, or change parameters for an instrument you are playing, at the press of a button. You can also automate these functionalities for live performance; which is something I don't really use... I set them once I find what I like and I don't touch the parameters anymore.

The other features on the JAM are mostly aimed at Maschine, so you get the usual quantize, transport controls and such; which help a lot to not use the keyboard and mouse. Moving around tracks, groups and sounds, using the knob and the 4 directional buttons is easy and intuitive. I just wish NI would allow this workflow also in other applications, but sadly, only Maschine and Ableton (once you set it up), works out of the box.

As far as exotic things; there is a slew of features for live performances, which rely on changing parameters on the fly using the touch strips, or lock memory positions, which allow you to set up a specific subset of parameters you may want to change, and record it in the device at a specific position, so while performing, you can swap between parameters sets at the touch of one button. Never used it, don't really care for it, so can't say how good it is.

I would give it 5 stars if NI would actually support Cubase, and if they would actually allow the JAM to be integrated better with their own software; because as is now; if you have a JAM, a MK3 and a KK keyboard, you have devices that are overlapping a lot, but each is its own niche product, instead of being universal with NI software, as far as functionalities and features.

To give you an example, I can play on the KK keyboard and on the JAM at the same time; a melody, because the pads and the keys do the same exact thing, on the same exact midi channel. Same for the knobs on the KK and strips on the JAM. If you want to specialize the JAM to play only some octaves or have different properties for the strips, it is not as easy as you would assume, or in some cases, impossible to achieve.

To summarize; the device is solid, built like a tank and worth the money. The software included is amazing and worth the money they ask for it (you get the Maschine software, which is 99 USD, plus the base Komplete software that cost 149, so in the end your controller cost barely 100 dollars). The functionalities of the device are clearly aimed at live performances, and for musicians that like to make beats in a visual way, but it works, with some limitations, also as generic MIDI controller, so anything that can assign CC inputs works with it.

If you want an extension to your keyboard, maybe you can look at other devices, if you are committed to the NI ecosystem, the JAM is a solid device, and if you are mostly a Maschine user, it does most of what the MK3 does, but at a lesser price; and you can use it for live performances, so it all depends from the usage you have in mind, what kind of musician you are, and what kind of music you create.
Summary: Great Midi device with some confusing areas

Text: God carry bag for my Yamaha

I play a Gibson A-style mandolin and prefer to wear the instrument about medium chest high. That works best for the length of my arms and playing comfort.

I'm buckling the first notched hole in the short strap piece, with the other end looped around the head stock right above the nut. This gives me the maximum strap length. It's usable, but I'd prefer 3-4 inches more with the option to take it in if I'm wearing heavy clothing.

I can punch one more hole in front of the first, spaced like the others, or place one as close to the edge as the little buckle can handle. That'll give me about 1 1/2-2 inches more without weakening the strap structurally.

If the longer strap segment were a few inches longer, the little buckle wouldn't be sitting on the back of my neck behind my ear. With the back of the strap touching me I don't really feel the buckle but, should the strap flip from motion, shirt collar, etc. it would be irritating.

For those who don't like the strap touching their hand at the first fret, this strap is one of the better fits I'm come across. You can slide the loop up and away just enough that there's barely any contact at all.

Finally, the strap is real leather and smells like it. It's secure fit on an A and like the style. Extra length would have earned it five stars but it's still a good deal.
Summary: Barely Long Enough As-Is, But Can Be Modified

I bought this because I had 2 MOTU interfaces (ultralight MK3 and 4pre) that where overkill for PC gaming. Just the amount of interconnect wires, wall wart power supplies and all the mess came with it gave me anxiety. This K3+ device just connects a single micro USB (outdated plug), but its very efficient and can use my Keyboard plug to power it on.

I also had other interfaces from Native Instruments and Headrush that worked amazingly well for PC gaming. But like I said, i wanted something small without a mess of wires, so I bought this Sound Blaster K3 on sale and it works pretty darn good. Its got a high resolution audio output for headphones, phantom power for XLR mics, an instrument input for guitars, and it even worked as a pre- amp for my turntable to my powered speakers.
It worked well, it was kind of chunky but small enough and had some good monitoring features. The built in sound effects kind of sucked though. It had some dumb one-shots like babies crying and bird sounds. The sound effects like reverb and delay were pretty bad too.

I also never tried it out as a portable interface, apparently it can plug into a mobile device, like a phone, and use an xlr cardiod mic to record on the go.

I regret returning it because during the 1st week of buying it, I ordered a more permanent solution which was a Sound Blaster AE-9 HiFi sound card and control module. Yes, the AE-9 is better for me because I run HiFi powered speakers on my PC, but tbh, the K3 is a much better choice for gaming. The AE-9, which is SoundBlaster's flagship product, doesnt have an instrument input. So if your a musician, a guitarist, that likes practicing with modeling amp software or plugins, then the K3+ does it right out of the box, but the AE-9 doenst.
I kind of miss that simplicity. Now I have to connect another interface if I want to hook up my guitar to use modelling software.

Also, a huge bummer for me was that this K3+ interface isnt supported by SoundBlaster's Command PC software. Soundblaster Command is the software that controls settings, resolution, and sound profiles for Soundblaster sound cards. Its one of the reasons I decided to return the K3+.
Summary: Good mixer and interface for the price. Simple set up and very streamlined for XLR mic inputs.

I am not a "drummer" per se, but I have a number of electronic percussion instruments that I enjoy playing.

I was looking for something that was portable that I could use to practice my timing and develop muscle memory, and this Yamaha unit fits the bill quite nicely.

It can run off batteries if you need to go that route - I got it with the included AC adapter and token drumsticks (you'll definitely want to spend a few bucks and get some better sticks).
The onboard sound system sounds good, yet surprisingly it isn't that loud (or my hearing is worse than I thought), though it's adequate if you don't want to use headphones. If you want to use this in a live setting (i.e. with other musicians), you'll need to output the sound to a separate amplification system. For practice, it's plenty loud with headphones.

The next major concern are the included "foot pedals" - they are really more like "foot switches", and are apt to drive you crazy. The high-hat switch actually works, and I can get a decent 'open/closed' rhythm going with it, but the kick switch is impossible. Luckily, you can hook up real pedal controllers - I have a Roland KT-10 Kick Trigger pedal that I love, and it works perfectly with this kit. So, if you buy this, you'll either need to accept the poor performance of the foot switches, or shell out the money for something better.

For this model, Yamaha made the entire device a uniform color - I think it would have been better if the pads had been a contrasty color, like light grey or something, but maybe it's just me.

Now for the good - I very much like the bouncy feel of the pads, and the way they are positioned at varied heights. You can indeed use this casually on a tabletop, or if you want a more authentic/versatile setup, you can place the DD75AD on a snare drum stand. It's an awesome yet compact layout that's enjoyable to play.

The sounds are heavily weighted towards authentic acoustic kits and to my ears, they are wonderful, including the cymbals. Most of the built-in kits are actually subtle variations of each other - one kit may have the exact same sounds as the previous kit, with the exception of a different single cymbal sound swapped out. Again, I am not a drummer - I assume that a dedicated drummer or student would be able to appreciate these subtle differences between the kits. There are a lot of one shot samples on this instrument (over 500), and you can make your own custom kits by assigning any sound to any pad you wish. Just don't expect a lot of lot of exotic/ethnic/electronic percussion sounds, though it does have some. Also worth noting - other than timpani, the DD75AD has no tuned or melodic kits, like a marimba.

For practice, there are many flexible features on this instrument - there's a metronome with a wide tempo range, variable time signature, adjustable volume and "click" sound options. There are also a lot of preset patterns that you can practice along with, and it allows you to silence different layers if you want to concentrate on improving your skills in a specific area. The backing instruments on some of the patterns are cheesy, yet they get the job done.

Some of the more in depth functions are buried in a sometimes cryptic sub menu system - Yamaha includes an excellent printed manual that explains every aspect and function pretty clearly.

If you love acoustic drums and don't have the room for the real deal, you'd probably enjoy the DD75AD (with a proper set of pedals). Ditto if you are just starting out or trying to hone your chops. If you are looking for a device with a lot of very different sounding kits, or one that includes melodic kits, you'll need to look elsewhere. :)

Text:
I got this product to use in college while my 16-input Tascam US-1600 stays at home. It does the job nicely, at least for what I need. I mainly use it for the audio drivers, because my laptop can't handle much DAW work on its own. It's also nice to have audio hardware driving my studio monitors instead of a laptop's line out. Since my primary use of this product is mixing and listening to music, I can't speak too much for, nor am I bothered by the less-than-perfect recording experience. I have only used a condenser mic with it so far, and there is a clearly audible high-pitched whine present in the audio at all times (probably due to phantom power). It's covered up by playing usually, but I'd imagine it could be audible in certain recordings under certain situations (quiet source, high gain). While this doesn't bother me since I won't be doing too much serious recording in my dorm, I'm sure this would be quite an inconvenience for some. Some people might complain about the outputs and the headphone jack being tied to the same volume knob, but this doesn't bother me at all. The overall build quality is decent; I can't complain about it.

Pros:
-Made by Tascam; good hardware in general
-Small and portable; powered by USB
-Great for on-the-go recording/mixing

Cons
-Subpar preamps; constant noise heard through mics
-USB power can be finnicky sometimes; one time it wouldn't stay on until I rebooted my laptop
-Some switches are on the back of the unit

It's hard to fully utilize the space. Putting top-plug types in the upper left helps, but most of mine are side-plugs. Generally I find it hard to use the top-left and bottom-right of the board the way I would like to even if I have enough space there.
