Text:
One of the hassles of carrying multiple instruments is how much room their stands take up. This little number is a big help in that department. It's very light and folds up in a nice compact way -- much less bulky than the ProLine A-frame guitar stands that I also use. Its one down side is a consequence of its diminutive size/weight: it would be easy to tip it over if bumped into from behind. Although the single leg that is at the back of the stand helps it resist falling in that direction, the 2 legs on the front effectively form a pivot point on which the stand -- with the guitar on it -- can easily pitch over. Still, I like the convenience the stand provides, so I'm always careful to place it where it is unlikely to get bumped in that direction.

Fender claims (on the box) that it will "fit in most gig bags or cases." This is ludicrous. Gig bags, yes, if they have -- as most do -- an outside compartment. But hard-shell cases? No way. The best you can do is to strap the stand to the outside of the case.

Bottom line: not perfect, but a reasonable compromise if you're looking to save space and weight.

The only reason I still buy SM58s is because it's the same and model people expect to see, but functionally there's no quality difference, except for a little handling noise when hand held, only really noticeable when pee are speaking and there's no music.

A lot of cheap mics seem to sound good for the money, but when you kick them up they feed back a bunch... Not the case with these. They sound good completely flat, similar in tone and gain to the 58. They're not THE SAME, though. They will feed back at different frequencies than 58s do, so of you're having to get loud and notch out feedback frequencies in monitors you may want to stick with all the same make and model on stage.

Text: After opening the package, the device comes in its own plastic carrying case. That's a nice touch. All the parts are rock solid. I read about other low priced units that were cheap plastic. The Transmitter is in a steel case. I like that it has its own volume control. I also like that the transmitter has a headphone out, peak meter and limiter. It would be nice if it had a control knob for the limiter, but just watching you output source volume keeps it reasonable (update: limiter on off is in the receiver--hold right button down for a few seconds). There is enough volume on the earphone end to cause hearing loss, so you really can't ask for more there. As with all common sense, the included ear buds can be donated to your local thrift store. Someone else mentioned Easy KZ ZST Colorful Hybrid Banlance Armature with Dynamic In-ear Earphone 1BA+1DD Hifi Headset (colorful ZST NOMIC). I got those ($19.00), and they are about 6 db louder than the included set and have much better sound separation. The Easy KZ wires fall out with the slightest movement (crazy glued them) and they fall out of your ears (ordered expandable earphone tips from  (Comply™ Foam Tips) --I will see if they work. I play guitar and sing on stage, so its important that I can move around. All the knobs and inputs on the transmitter are rock solid, including the antenna. I don't recall being this impressed by a new product before. I hooked it all up, figured out how to change the settings (basically just hold the right button down for a few seconds and the middle and left buttons help you change things). The receiver is rock solid too. It seems to be made of some kind of aerospace metal of some kind--feels like a military grade device. The whole package seems like it is made to last. The sound quality is acceptable for my purpose. Very little or no hiss is noticed with no sound present--cleaner at the low db setting. No need for the high db setting if you set other output volumes correctly--enough to injure your ears. I enjoyed getting the mix right and then turning the volume on the receiver down to a safe level. The sound is clean, loud and full--especially with quality ear buds (critical). I haven't found anything negative yet, but if I do, I will update this review.

Well I was gigging with this throne on my Roland E-kit and the screw post broke in half! Unacceptable! I weigh 170lbs and was on an E-kit. Not playing hard at all. Lucky I had my Roc-N-Soc nitro with me as a back up just in case. NO MORE off brand equipment for me. I will stick to well know brand names.

First your throne is the most important piece of equipment that a drummer owns. Please don't cheap out on buying one
I don't care if you're a beginner and know nothing about drums. Always have a good sturdy comfortable throne! I don't care how great of a player you are, how great your kit is. If you have butt and back pain, you're not going to be playing at your best. I been playing drums since I was 11 years old. I am now 53. Played thru all of school and college. Been in a lot of bands and also am a session drummer. Only reason I considered this was on a recommendation from a friend. I have owned to many thrones to be honest. DW, Gilbralter, Pearl, Roc-N-Soc. The Roc-N-Soc Nitro is by far the best throne. At a cost over $200, it's worth every penny. I bought this for my Roland TD-50 kit. E-kits are a while different beast then aocustic. I was very surprised by the build quality and how comfortable it is. Not sure about the other guys review in how he wants to add lock washers and not having instructions to put it together. Basically takes 2 minutes. Open the base, screw in the post, attach saddle. Get it behind your kit. Dail it in and tweak it. Once you're happy, tighten all the key screws. Do not use a wrench or add washers. They're not gonna help and the throne doesn't need help. Once you tighten it, the throne doesn't lossen up. Over tighting can damage the screw post and key screws. I was pretty impressed by it so I decided to take it with me to some gigs. Put it thru some paces. I have gigged with the throne 4 times. 3 on my aocustic kit and once on my Roland E-Kit. Happy to say it worked very well. No pain in my butt or back after playing 2 hours straight before a break. Then another 2 hours. The real test was standing up. That's when you really feel it with a subpar throne. I felt great. No pain and the throne stayed put, felt very stable throughout the night. Only thing I missed on the aocustic kit was the Lil bounce I get from my Roc-N-Soc. I didn't buy to replace any of my thrones. I bought it for my E-Kit. I hit hard and go thru pedals, cymbals and always breaking sticks. E-kits you're not hitting no where as hard. It's more about finesse. When I used it at a wedding gig with my Roland's, it again preformed excellent. I have enough time on it to where I have it broken in. I'm still amazed by the comfort and build quality at this price point. It passed the hard hitting aocustic test and is a great fit for my Roland's. Would actually work excellent for either. But I love my Roc-N-Soc. I own 2 nitros. Again I wasn't happy with the bounce from the nitro on my E-Kit. I almost bought a DW until a friend recommended this. Glad he did. I saved some money without compromising comfort and quality. One pointer if you're new to drums. Don't tighten the saddle keys to where the saddle won't turn. I have mine setup to where the saddle moves with me. Makes for better passes in the toms and getting up from behind the kit. Spin a lil to the left and I walk out. Then it's there for me when I go to play. Just sit and spin back inwards to the kit.

PROS: Very comfortable and stable while playing. No pain in the butt or back. The cut of the saddle is deep enough to where my upper thighs aren't free resting on it and interfering with my pedals. But not so deep where it's not supporting them. Well designed. Plush top is a plus. Very well built. Rubber on the legs are over sized and keeps the throne put. Easy to adjust on the fly. Great value.

CONS: Haven't really found any. One thing I like is a four leg throne. But at this price point it's not an issue. Just a personal preference.

The arm requires both hands to push up and pull down if you want to position it properly, but be careful to not tug or push too hard as the joints, when tightened, give off noises that sound like you're about to break something. Be that as it may, when you do have the arm just the way you like it, the whole thing will stay and not slouch or slowly lose its shape.

The big pro here is the price tag. For what it can do, this is easily one of the least expensive boom arms available on the marketplace. If you are looking for that professional feel, but don't want to shell out the dough for a Blue Compass, then this will do nicely.

I have a very expensive collector edition Sabian cymbal that had fingerprints from the music store on it and I was concerned with the finish. My Sabian rep told me that this would do the trick, so I gave it a shot on the rest of my cymbals first. I have an assortment of vintage Zildjian, Sabian and newer Paiste and Wuhans. This stuff worked wonders on them all. DO NOT leave it on for more than 30 seconds, as the directions state, because it is an acid base. If you follow the directions and wipe it off you will not be disappointed. Several of the cymbals need two or even three applications, but it worked wonders on them.

I finally trusted it with my collector edition cymbal and it removed every fingerprint flawlessly by just applying and wiping slightly until the prints were gone. This simply works on the brilliant finish cymbals without any scrubbing. I also wiped the cymbals down afterwards with a damp cloth to make sure the cleaner was removed entirely.

I also bought Nomad cleaner to test out and had exactly the opposite results with that. It turned everything BLACK, way worse than Brasso, and was impossible to completely clean off of the cymbals, especially the milled vintage ones. I'll stick with the Sabian cleaner from now on.
Summary: This works great as long as you follow the directions

After having used a Peterson VS-1 original strobe tuner for forever, I realized that it was getting harder and harder to read the small LCD display. That unit had been a workhorse and quite reliable. Recently I dropped it and it started having trouble detecting the B and E strings. I had purchased the Peterson Strobosoft app for my iPod Touch and was quite happy with that but it didn't offer any of the "sweetened tunings" for guitar. If any of you are too cheap to buy the StrobPlus, stop here and go get the Strobsoft app for your iPhone/iPad. I digress, anyway, did a little research and found people were giving this StroboPlus a pretty good reviews.

$120.00 seems high for a tuner but those familiar with Peterson products know it will probably worth it. I was not disappointed. First the screen is very, very, easy to read even in bright light. The old VS-1 was almost unusable sometimes from glare off its screen. Instead of the traditional Peterson vertical scrolling block-pattern strobe, the StroboPlus has a half-circle back-lit orange screen with only two sets of strobe blocks. The rotate either clockwise or counter-clockwise on the edge of a semi-circular display face and is much easier to interpret versus the older format. If you wear glasses, you'll appreciate this.

This tuner reads info really quickly and accurately. If you work on guitars especially if you do set-ups, this is your only choice. It charges its Lithium-Ion battery via a USB cable that plugs into your computer. No more hand fulls of AA batteries.

You register on-line and on their website, you can load all sorts of specialized tunings, sweetened tunings, and even your own custom tunings. When loaded into the StroboPlus, with the press of a button and the turn of a wheel, you now have access to your saved tunings. There's a tone generator as well which is a nice touch. There's also pay to download additions programs like their BodyBeat metronome feature.

This is probably the best and most accurate tuner I have ever owned and that includes various Boss, Intellitouch, Sabine, Korg, and various miscellaneous units. It finds the note faster and with more accuracy than anything I've ever used. The only thing that is even in the same ballpark is the the Peterson Strobosoft app.

The original Peterson VS-1 was the size of a brick, the StroboPlus with its almost square shape reminds me of a clock radio or a really big sandwich. It has "ruberized" antishock material wrapped around most of its perimiter. There's a very sturdy stand on the back that folds out and makes the unit quite stable on any flat surface. It's sturdy and well built, logically designed, easy to use and is so much better than what's currently out in the market. I've know there's a following for the tuners that have the rotating led lights but when you work on guitars and do a lot of setups, those flashing led's will probably fatigue your eyes or give you a grand mal seizure, take your pick.

The StoboPlus website page is easy to navigate and for those in the audience that have issues with with the ability to read instructions, there's even a very well done user video. The StroboPlus is NOT a stomp box and really has no place on a pedal board. They have a metal case version for that. If you do any kind of guitar or stringed instrument work, you need this. I've seen a lot of tuners come and go over the years and this is by far the best. It even comes in a very nice box with magnetic closure, closed cell foam interior, and a slot to store the USB cable.
Summary: This is the one to get...

I was in the market for a beginner banjo, and really didn't know where to start. In the interests of full disclosure, I am a veteran guitar player. I used to play banjo many, many years ago, but I played it like a guitarist. This time around, I wanted to learn to play it as a banjoist, as it should be played, so for all intents and purposes I am a beginner. I don't know anyone who plays banjo, so I couldn't get any recommendations from friends or family. After considerable Internet research - a lot of which involved checking out Amazon reviews - I settled on this Jameson instrument.

Many of the "name" brands in the music stores seem to start in the $250 range and go right up to the $700s and $800s, and I even saw some over $1,000. Even the $250 range was beyond my budget. In Amazon (rather than the music stores) there were instruments within my budget in the $150 - $200 range, but none of the names was familiar to me. Then again, I admit, I don't know enough about the banjo world to really know the names.

Anyway, to make a long story short, I am really glad I decided on this instrument. It is a beautiful piece of workmanship, really attractive and nicely put together, and it sounds great. During my research, I had seen several reviews of other brands where people had said not to expect your banjo to arrive ready to play. You would have to install the bridge, the strings and so on. Not so with this Jameson - it arrived nicely packed and ready to play. It only needed minor tuning, which is of course understandable (for which I recommend the [[ASIN:B004XNK7AI Snark SN-5 Tuner for Guitar, Bass and Violin]], which works fine for banjo even though they don't mention that). It even included a tuning and chord chart.

Note that this instrument has a (removable) resonator back, which is a bonus in this price range, since a resonator back usually hikes up the price. Another nice bonus is that Jameson provides free basic lessons on their website ([...], which links to [...]).

I noticed that in the questions above, one answer said it was made in USA. However, mine was made in China. This is not an issue for me and shouldn't be for you (unless you are of the "buy-only-American" persuasion); it's a beautiful instrument regardless of where it was made.

All in all, I highly recommend this banjo, especially (but not only) for beginners. It is an excellent value for a really fine instrument. Five stars without any reservations!

Text:
This review is gonna be pretty short, as I just wanna throw in my 2 cents and support the positive reviews this keyboard has already received. Until recently, I didn't do much electronic music production. I'm a multi-instrumentalist, and if ever I want to add a synth/piano to a track, I would just play my Korg R3 or digital piano and track it live. But I'm not much of a pianist, and I wanted to start making more involved arrangements, so I started getting into MIDI. While the R3 makes an okay MIDI controller, the small number of keys and lack of customization made me want something more.

So when I saw the new Alesis VI series I had to give it a try. It seemed like the perfect solution for those of us who want more than those little grey M-Audio keyboards but can't justify spending the dough on an Akai MPK, and the Alesis does not disappoint. The build quality is better than I expected, greatly surpassing the plasticky build of my Korg R3. The keyboard is light, but feels sturdy and substantial. The matte black finish looks great in the light, and the semi-weighted keys have a great feel to them. Some of the black keys were a little stiff at first, but they quickly loosened up.

The Alesis VI functions as advertised. I was able to set it up in Cakewalk Sonar and Fruity Loops with ease. It truly is plug & play. The downloadable software editor works well too. It allows you to change the parameter mappings on the keyboard with ease. Just keep in mind that the keyboard is almost useless without the editor, as you can't change anything through the keyboard itself; you can only cycle through presets made in the editor.

My last gripe is that the pitch and mod wheel are in a weird location. Not a deal breaker for me, but might be for those who are more performance oriented. In short, the Alesis VI61 is a quality MIDI controller that won't break your bank. Everything functions as you would expect. No surprises, neither good nor bad. A great mid-range contender.

Text:
For an inexpensive plastic ukulele, this instrument has surprisingly good sound quality and volume for a thinline concert-sized ukulele. I like the thinline travel shape for easy portability. Resonance is good. Dynamic range is better than expected and it doesn't sound real plasticky. It is harsher and less warm than a decent solid wood instrument (even after changing the strings), through good solid wood ukuleles will cost more than twice as much as this ukulele.

While they advertise this instrument as "carbon fiber", the carbon fiber content is very small (around 30%) and the majority of the build is polycarbonate plastic. This ukulele has more in common with mostly plastic instruments (like Outdoor or Waterman) than with mostly carbon (and much more expensive) ukuleles like Klos or Blackbird.

The instrument is mostly easy to play. Action is pretty low, especially at the nut, like most beginners like. Barre chords are easy to hold at any fret, even in that cutout area above the 13th fret. The neck is stiff and straight and intonation is accurate up the fretboard. I would prefer a wider nut to make chords like "E" easier to hold, though this is not the worst ukulele for that.

I like that they included a carrying case, since this instrument has a non-standard shape. Unfortunately, the case isn't very good. The zipper is low quality and slides very roughly. The case has very little padding, though the semi-stiff outer shell is more protective than thin soft gig bags. The case does not have a shoulder strap, which I would really like for travel use. I hesitate to sew my own strap onto the case since the thin outer shell may tear from the stitching.

The strings that came with the instrument were surprisingly harsh sounding even after several days of breaking in. I replaced them with Aquila Red strings (which you can see in the photo) and I think those sound much richer.

This is my second Enya ukulele. My first was the HPL (high pressure laminate) model. That one got good reviews from various internet reviewers, but I was disappointed. It had a warm vibrant sound quality, but surprisingly low volume and it lacked brightness. Also, it was very heavy, making it uncomfortable to hold and play. I like this plastic Enya Nova much better. It is lighter weight and easier to play. The sound quality is not as warm as the HPL Enya (even after changing the strings), but the volume is much louder.

This isn't the best sounding ukulele that I own, but I'm still giving it 5 stars because it has very good sound quality and playability for this price and the it is much better than other plastic ukuleles in the under-$100 price range. The plastic construction should be crush-resistant and temperature-resistant and humidity-resistant, which are all very important features of a travel ukulele.
Summary: great sound and playability for a plastic ukulele, after I changed the strings

This is a surprisingly great little compressor. It doesn't have much character to speak of, just a good solid clean compressor.

It accepts either a single mono signal, or a single stereo signal, and does great on both.

All of the controls are exactly what you'd expect if you've used other hardware or software compressors. The Super Nice mode cascades 3 compression circuits so you can get a substantial amount of gain reduction without it sounding too conspicuous.

My main gripes are few, but here's what I'd like to see if they ever do a "revision 2":
- A dual mono option. That'd require a 2nd set of knobs to control each side, but it'd make this a slam-dunk winner over the ART PRO VLA II. The ART's dual mono and stereo link make it pull ahead in the bang-for-buck category for me.
- less (or more pleasant) distortion at higher gain reduction. It gets pretty nasty sounding when you really slam it, and not in a good way. It'd be nice if it maintained its clean sound as I really dig into the GR.

I can't really say that this adds much over what you could get with a good software compressor, but its small form factor and mono-or-stereo operation make it a good choice for a portable live rig, and of course it is right at home in a home recording studio like mine.

At this price, it's a really attractive option.

HOW THIS COMES

QUALITY
These tools are plenty good enough to do basic work on your instruments. There might be a few things here or there which could be better, but honestly, I would rather have this than nothing. My guitar guy said it is pretty decent and he has worked on instruments for a long time.

INSTRUCTIONS
Honestly, I know that the company says that they will show you how to use everything in the kit, but if you plan to give this as a gift or if your internet is out (like ours often is) then having instructions IN THE KIT TO LOOK AT ON PAPER is essential. I think they should print out the information and put it in the kits.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a good quality kit to work on your own instruments. It is great for home or on the road. The company needs to put in the directions for each tool so it is easily referred to even if not accessible online.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. One star off for not including paper instructions or a booklet in the case. They have some great photos on the listing they should just put it on a paper or booklet to include. Products come and go quickly on Amazon, so equipping people with instructions is vital.

However, you would think that because of this coating that this would deaden the sound, but it absolutely does not... "Bronze are our brightest acoustic guitar strings", and I like that the sound is bright but not overly-bright. It's a clear, ringing tone that I am enjoying so far. I'm a little perplexed by the unnecessary complexity of the bag... "our premium re-sealable VCI bag, so every set is kept factory fresh until you're ready..." Well, okay. It seems as though if you're changing a whole set of strings, this packaging is excessive and unnecessary. And with all the strings in one pouch, rather than in individual paper sleeves, it's not the idea set to use as your quick go-to when you need to change one string on the fly.

It also might be a touch weird for beginners, as again instead of one string inside a sleeve labeled "D string" (etc.), you get all of them in one bag with slightly different-colored ball ends, with color codes listed on the packaging. Nothing crazy, but worth mentioning.

d'Addario is well-established mainstay in the guitar string world, and these strings, representing this "tremendous leap forward", are another worthy edition to their arsenal, and even though they are a bit on the pricey side, they are worth trying. Guitarists can have some weird quirks, like they can only use a certain brand/color/gauge pick or else everything is ruined... so maybe these will be your go-to strings. 4.4 stars.

I'm using this microphone with my Google Pixel 2 Android smartphone's USB-C port. This phone does not have a regular stereo jack, just the USB-C port. The Shure microphone comes with a USB-C cable that plugs right into my phone. I tried using the microphone with my old audio recording app and the sound quality was poor. Then I tried Shure's recording app and the sound quality is tremendous. Audio quality is very clear and dynamic; much better than the phone's built-in microphone or any other external microphone that I have tried (none in this price range, though). Unlike cheap microphones, this is a microphone that I would gladly use to record live music performances (I am a music student).

No documentation is included with the microphone, but there is a picture of their apps on the side of the box, so I looked them up and downloaded them. The apps say that some phones will not work with the microphone and the only phones that they approve of are recent Samsung and Apple phones. I can confirm that the Google Pixel 2 also works fine. The app does have links to download more detailed documentation if you need that.

Shure has separate Android apps for audio recording and video recording. The video app is still in beta release, but it does work OK. The apps have lots of settings to control the microphone's recording geometry, compression, volume, video resolution, as well as tools to edit your past recordings or save them in different formats. This is a great set of tools to have on my phone. Everything works great on my phone.

My only complaint is that the port on the microphone is micro-USB so I need an unusual micro-USB to USB-C cable to connect it to my phone. A 16" cable is included, but if I lose that or if I need a longer one, then additional cables are not that expensive, but if they used a more standard USB-C to USB-C cable, then I bet all their customers would already own a bunch of cables that they could use.

Personally I like this mic for vocals more than the [[ASIN:B000CZ0R42 Shure SM58-LC Cardioid Vocal Microphone without Cable]] and I also believe that it is as good - if not better - than the [[ASIN:B000CZ0R3S Shure SM57 Microphone]] for micing instruments and amps.

One reason is the Blue mic is hotter, requiring no boost (I run Shures through a [[ASIN:B0002D0KG4 PreSonus Tubepre Single-Channel Vacuum Tube Mic Pre]] to compensate while the Blue is so much hotter that the tube pre provides too much gain at the lowest gain setting.)

There is a negative side, especially for vocalists who are used to the SM58 running through quasi-professional PA systems: the Blue will pick up every flaw that is sometimes masked by the SM58. In other words, while the Shure is somewhat forgiving of vocal 'deficiencies' because of its frequency profile and power range, the Blue will expose every flaw it 'hears'. On the other hand, this is a major plus when using the blue to mic instruments in lieu of an SM57 (or 58). My only real complaint is weight - the Blue is very heavy and I often fret over whether or not it is being securely held by holders such as the [[ASIN:B0002ZO60I On Stage MY325 Dynamic Shock Mount Microphone Clip]], which is the strongest I have found. Thus far I have had no problems, but it still is a nagging concern because of the weight of the Blue.

Back when I purchased my Blue it was priced substantially below its Shure competitor models, but today the Blue, the 58 and the 57 are all in the same price range. On such a level playing field I still prefer the Blue and will continue to opt for them over the venerable (and aging) SM58 and SM57.

Text: Excellent product

Steinberg has outdone itself in producing this amazing interface and I'll try to explain why I think so. The ordering of the below points was arbitrarily chosen without sequencing by importance.

Pros:

1. Build quality: Right away you see the quality of the device, as the device comes in a rugged full metal body which looks like it can stand the test of time. The Neutrik combo jacks are an industry standard. The knobs and buttons feel very very solid. The smooth finish and grey/black color combinations are a touch indeed. It is however more heavy than it would seem, which gives me confidence in quality anyway. Simply a 10/10 for build.

2. Mic Pres: One of the most important qualities of an interface. and in this regard the UR44 shines again. The pres are very quiet both at low and high gain settings. I can compare with the Presonus 44VSL which had pres which were far more noisy.

3. Good I/O options: 4 mic, 2 line input and Midi I/O. Plenty for my needs. 2 headphone outputs with 2 mixes is again a killer feature. Invaluable while recording music with other people.

4 . DSP features: DSP is fast becoming a standard feature in interfaces even at this price range. UR44 kicks the butt of most interfaces in this regard. This interface works in conjunction with the dspMixFX software interface. It offers EQ, compression, high pass filter, phase and guitar amp both while monitoring and recording (You can use these effects as an insert). This software control is even better integrated into Cubase. Reverb you can use only for monitoring, or for recording using the loopback feature.

5. Standalone use: This is what simply takes the cake imo. Artists can use the interface standalone on stage. All the levels, effects, compression and other settings can be stored onto the device. So you can even hear reverb without computer processing. To change settings or recall profiles however, you will need to control the dspMixFX software using a computer or iPad. I always add some reverb to my vocal or instrument mic while performing live. Yamaha's reverb FX is surprisingly good.

6. Performance: It is simply rock solid while in use. The drivers are well written leading to very low latency performance. The software control never failed on me. The AD/DA conversion is top notch. I use it with the Studio One DAW, and it hasn't caused me problems one single time. Forums are in high praise of this kind of stability.

Cons:

1. The biggest con is that the pres seem a little under powered. It hasn't been an issue with the mics that I own, but with some mics that require lot off gain, you have to crank it all the way up. With some dynamics or tube mics, I could even see it not being sufficient. Again, it depends on the requirements of your mics. So do some research first. But gain is very clean overall.

2. I/O options are plenty enough. But I like RCA line inputs usually. Of course, that problem is easily solved using cables. But I would have still preferred RCA to connect line level devices like mp3 players, etc.

3. Headphone outputs are not the loudest: My older interfaces, be it the Presonus 22VSL or the Yamaha Audiogram 3, gave me a louder headphone output. So again look into the specs for your requirements.

4. Reverb: I wish reverb could have been recorded as well on each individual channel. It sounds so good. But I am asking for too much at this point. :)

Overall, have no doubt about buying this interface. It is a steal at this price!
Summary: Perfect interface for the modern musician, Solid top to bottom!

Wanted to like it, it is such a classic. I still have it on my pedal board, but it is coming off, even though I was just playing through it yesterday. Here are the problems:

1. Too Limited - It has only one sound in it, and you can only make it go faster or slower.

2. The high and low points of the phasing/frequencies affected are fixed, and they are fixed in terrible spots/frequencies. The Phase 90 always goes too low in frequency and then when it's down there it makes the low end super loud, it essentially blows up the low end, making the low end of the guitar stick out in the mix only for that time it approaches, hits and then ascends out of the low end of its cycle. When the phase is low, it makes the guitar step over everything else, bass, vocals, drums, keys, other guitar. I dread the phaser reaching the bottom of its cycle, I cringe in anticipation each time. You can't set your guitar volume low so you sit well in the mix in the low part of the Phase 90's cycle because you won't be heard for the rest... most of the Phase 90's cycle. Basically you'll be playing, and no one will hear you until the Phase 90 goes into the bottom of its cycle, then the guitar will be super bassey and whack and still conflict with all other elements of the band/mix, and then when the phaser cycles up, you'll disappear again.

3. There is only one depth of the phasing effect. - There is no subtlety with this effect. If you just want to add a little movement in your guitar sound, the Phase 90 can't do the job, it is too heavy handed, it will take over your guitar sound. It doesn't matter if you put it in front of or behind your gain stages (dirt pedals or in the fx loop of a driven amp), the effect will be too prominent, too loud, the sound of the guitar, overdrive, distortion or whatever other effect you have on the guitar will be lost to the domineering swooshing of the Phase 90. And again, that is with the Phase 90 before or after anything else. It IS less offensive before everything else, so first in line of distortion, overdrive or other effects, but it is still too overpowering before. If you put it after, forget about it, you're only hearing Phase 90 swooshing, it doesn't matter what you play or how your guitar/amp sounds.

4. It is not true bypass. - There is a lot of propaganda against true bypass pedals nowadays, but trust me, you want your pedals to be true bypass, and if you have a large pedal board, you can have a buffer, either in a pedal, or a separate dedicated buffer, at the start of your fx chain to boost your guitar signal through the fx chain, and at the end of the fx chain to drive the signal to your amp. The thing is, you want to be intentional about this, you want to use either a pedal with a HIGH QUALITY buffer, or a dedicated buffer that is HIGH QUALITY. Just having one crappy buffer, like in the Phase 90, in the chain, even if the pedal is switched off, it can still lower the resolution of your sound, making it blurry. If you've taken pains to select high quality fx, pickups, amp, speakers, whatever, it can all be diminished by a low quality buffer, and especially by a series of unnecessary low quality buffers. Each one will suck your tone. I may be sounding like a tone snob, I'm not, I guarantee I'm more budget than you are, out of necessity. But if you ever hear what buffers are doing to your sound, like playing through your fx chain with no pedals on, but with several pedals with crappy buffers, then plug your guitar straight into your amp, you'll be amazed at how much better your guitar sounds. How you can hear more detail. Your multiple crappy buffer sound is like a forzen microwave burrito and your straight into the amp sound will be like taking your ingredients FRESH out of the ground and putting them into your real, FRESH burrito. You won't be able to go back to microwave burritos, or multiple crappy buffers, you'll know what you are missing, and how good it CAN be. So, be skeptical of this recent trend to diminish true bypass pedals, there is some sense to what these guitar "pundits" say, again, if you have long cable runs, and/or a long fx chain, you may need two HIGH QUALITY buffers, but that DOES NOT mean you need all of your pedals to have buffers. NO. NO. NO.

5. The Phase 90 compresses your guitar signal, just flattens it, and not in a good way, not like a good compressor, overdrive, or tube amp will compress your signal, helping to even it out, but retain the dynamics in your playing and the character of your sound. This is the worst aspect of the Phase 90... among other really bad attributes, but still, this is just the worst. As soon as you turn on the Phase 90, it will FLATTEN your guitar signal. It doesn't matter if you play with dynamics, like light picking/strumming in parts of a phrase, and then heavy picking/strumming in other parts of the phrase, or one phrase/section being light, and another phrase/section being heavy, it doesn't matter, anything you play will be as flat as hammered... brown clay. This is the worst for me, not that I'm some maestro on the guitar (or bass, or keys/synth/sampler, the other instruments I've tried to make the Phase 90 work with), but everybody has some dynamics in their playing, that is part of your unique sound, how you relate to the guitar, and it is all just steamrolled by the Phase 90. But it is worse than that. Even your guitar, fx, and amp tone all have subtleties to them, little aspects of how each of these sound, it's what makes the guitar sound "three-dimensional" (air quotes - I know this is a buzz word, but it is the best description of this aspect of your instrument's overall sound), and in combination, it is a large part of what makes you sound like you, your guitar sound like your guitar, your fx sound like your fx, and your amp sound like your amp, and the Phase 90 just BAMB! flattens all of that. All nuance of your sound, and all the nuance of the parts that make up your sound, they're all lost, totally flattened and erased. Just having the Phase 90 on in your fx chain makes everything super low resolution, like drawing with crayons vs a photo or high quality printing, or even an oil painting. Having the Phase 90 is like petroleum jelly smeared on the lens of your camera, or your glasses, everything becomes blurry, with no detail at all... you'd essentially be blind.

Honestly, I could go on... this is a classic pedal, I recognize that, but for any of the wide range of guitar styles/genres, tempos, even instruments beyond guitar, I've not been able to make this pedal work on anything. It is probably my largest disappointment in all of my pedal purchases. (AND I have two of them, don't even ask!) But I'm going to sell these, and buy a phaser at half the cost of the Phase 90 that has controls for the range of the phase cycle, the depth of the phase effect, is true bypass AND is high resolution, meaning all dynamics will be kept, as well as all character of my sound. You don't need a digital pedal to do this, I'll stay in the analog domain, and get these features.

MXR is just milking the "classic" status of this pedal. I know companies need to make money, I'm all for it, but the performance to price ratio here is WAY off. And for what it is worth, it is in a solid enclosure, if you need to hang some pictures, you could use this pedal as a hammer to drive some nails... unfortunately, this would be a better use of this pedal than letting any instrument's sound pass through it.

Years and years ago I had a 12 string guitar. I was a poor college student, so went from 12 string to 11 string to 10 sting... I could eventually afford only 6 new strings, so became a 6 string. When I could finally afford a new 6 string (a real 6 string), I gave my 12/ 6 sting to a young man who wanted to learn guitar. Ever sense then I had in my memory what a 12 string sounded like and wanted to try it again. I am not an expert, but after playing for almost 40 years, I know a bit.

This guitar is an inexpensive "made in China" guitar, which did make me a bit nervous, even though many guitars are made in China now. When it arrived it was left in the 33 degree rain, upside down, leaning against my door (thanks UPS man), so when I opened the door it fell down through the door banging on the floor. But when I unpacked it, the cold, wet and fall did not appear to have damaged it (I would not suggest you try this however). It comes strung, and with 12 strings you tune, tune, and tune again, as the neck does flex a bit as more and more tension is applied to the strings. Plus they are adjusting to being stretched, so just plan to spend some time tuning a few times to get a decent sound out of it, then tuning again and again to get it right. It does come with a little clip on tuner (with a battery, thank you for including that strange size battery), which makes tuning easier.

It comes with an extra set of strings, some picks, a pick guard sticker, some sandpaper (I am not sure what that is for, very fine so maybe if there is a scratch?), some picks a strap and capo. Capo said "for 6 string guitars" but works fine for 12 also. Also comes with a padded case. This is also an electric acoustic, it has a small control panel, volume and a few other adjustments. This is a powered pick-up, so takes a 12 volt battery (included, always nice when an unexpected battery is included). Honestly I really like the sounds of an acoustic 12 string, so don't see myself ever plugging it in. 12 strings tend, in my opinion, to be a bit louder and "fuller" than a 6 string, so unless you are playing for a larger group, you probably will not need this.
This is geared more toward beginners, price is very good. But it does sound good also. It is not a high end guitar that sings, but sound is very good, especially for the price. Neck is adjusted right, but also includes a wrench if your does need a bit of adjustment. Action is great, no buzzing, but not too hard to hold strings down. And guitar looks good on top of it. Really it is a quality instrument.

Only negative I found, which I debated taking a star for, but decided not to, is that the case has a bunch of loose threads. For every product, I feel like quality control should have a pair of scissors to clip those off. If they missed those, did they miss anything else? After a few days of playing, I can find nothing else wrong with it.

Very good guitar, which I am very happy with. My current main guitar is about 35 years old, so hopefully this one will last just as long or longer.

Beringer has made great budget priced pro audio equipment for years. It's no wonder that they got into the podcasting/prosumer mic business just like the big name brands did.

Bheringer's Bigfoot is an obvious copycat of Blue Microphone's Yeti mic. I'm sure somewhere out there another company also makes a “Sasquatch” microphone to complete the names of the elusive creature. The Bigfoot has all of the features of the Yeti including four different polar pickup patterns, a microphone gain control, a mute switch, a headphone amplifier with a volume control and a desk stand. I don't own a Yeti, so sonically I'm not sure how they compare, but visually I actually like the Bigfoot better. The more oblong mesh screen with the flat top just fits the design better than Yeti's half spherical top. Just keep in mind that the pickup surface is on the sides and not the top.

The build of the Bigfoot is great. The mic is has a heavy metal casing and a sturdy metal stand. I just hope the inside is as durable as the outside. Probably the weakest points in the Bigfoot are the plastic knobs and switches, but they should last quite awhile. The mic also has a thread at the bottom so it can be mounted to a boom arm which is highly recommended to isolate desk noise and other vibrations. Also on the bottom is the mini-USB jack, which at this point is outdated, but I believe is what is found on the Yeti, so being true to the clone it was duplicated on the Bigfoot. The included cable has a standard USB-A on the other end so it is compatible with most computers. This mic is truly plug and play. No software is required to use the mic, it uses a standard ASIO driver that is usually part of the operating system drivers. Behriger does have a downloadable driver on their website if necessary.

Since the Bigfoot is a condenser microphone it requires a power source. This is supplied by USB power. Normally with a standard microphone a preamp or computer interface would be required for power. Since this mic is designed to be used with a computer that is not necessary.

Condenser mics are highly sensitive and will pickup any noise in the area. That includes fan noises, air conditioners, etc. That is why you usually see vocalists recording in well soundproofed isolated booths to keep out extraneous noises in the studio. The Bigfoot has this quality and despite being on the tightest cardioid pickup pattern will still pickup the fan noise from my desktop computer, so the best way to use this mic is to get as close as possible to it and keep the mic gain down to its lowest usable level.

I've used most of the popular broadcasting microphones over the years including the Shure SM7-B, EV RE20 and the Sennheiser MD 421 and while the Bigfoot doesn't have the sound characteristics of those mics since they are all dynamic, it has a good proximity effect like them. Basically the closer you get to the microphone the more emphasis is placed on the lower end giving it a warmer, more present sound. But, with four different pickup pattern the Bigfoot is quite a versatile microphone. Each one has it's own purpose but you should always use the one that sounds best for your particular application. On the back of the mic is where the pickup pattern switch is that will turn on a combination of the three capsules within the mesh area of the microphone. Above that knob is the gain that controls the volume and sensitivity. On the front of the mic is a mute switch that turns off the pickup but keeps the it powered up. Below that is the headphone volume level. There is jack on the bottom to plug headphones into which allows real time monitoring without any latency. That makes it perfect for podcasting.

For the price Bheringer's Bigfoot is a great buy with great sound quality. It works in just about every application that a mic can be used in and its multiple pickup patterns provide great versatility. Even though it's a copycat it stands out well on its own.
Summary: Even though it's a copycat, it standsout well on its own

Got this to upgrade the synthetic nut on my strat. Took a little work but in the end it looks great and improved the look and tone of my guitar. I recommend anyone with intermediate guitar maintenance experience do this if you have a synthetic nut. This particular nut was nicely machined and sanded easily. I've shared some helpful tips below for installing it yourself because it can be a process if this is your first time and it's easier to learn the easy way from someone who has learned it the hard way.

The nut is intentionally taller, wider, and longer so sanding is a must. If you bought the curved nut, use the the radius of your guitar to keep the shape consistent. Lay some 120 grit sandpaper on the top of the first fret of the fretboard (grit side up, obviously) and place the bottom of the nut on it and sand it back and forth until it's most of the way down to where it needs to be height wise. This will ensure it fits your guitar's radius exactly. center te nut and figure out how much to take off the sides.

The curved nuts come with lightly cut string slots but these are really there as a guide and will need to be cut deeper for your strings. To deepen the slots for the string gauges you will be using, you can either purchase a string nut file but these can get expensive so in a pinch, you can actually just use the old wound strings to deepen them. The ribs on the wound strings will act like a file. Use this to deepen the slots and hold the string in place. For the three low strings which are not wound, just use the D string. It is thin enough that it won't leave too much play for the G, B, And E strings.

After everything is sanded and ready for installation, do a quick smoothing and polishing with either extremely fine sandpaper (800+ grit) or my personal favorite, a fingernail buffer. These are super cheap (like, $1 at the grocery store) and work great for smoothing and shining up the nut (and frets, but that's a different process) before installing.

Finally, using a toothpick, put a SMALL DROP of Elmer's glue or wood glue, NOT SUPER GLUE and NOT a ton that covers the whole bottom of the nut slot. Just enough to hold the nut in place when the strings are off the guitar. Firmly press the nut into the slot and make sure it's properly centered. You can either wait for the glue to set or you can go ahead and restring it. The strings, once tightened, will hold the nut firmly in place

This is an amazing starter unit. If you just want an all-in-one package for streaming games, then this is what you want. Don't even hesitate, buy it. It has a really nice "Denoise" function and the soundpad and controls are perfect for this use case, additionally it has all the plug-in options you will need.

However, if you want this for something more, then there are a few things to keep in mind here. I have run this unit with several microphones and done audio tests with them using various settings, and I have integrated the unit into my desk now with my other audio/video gear and have used it in recorded training meetings and interviews.

- The provided 40db microphone (PM320) is adequate but most pod casters will want to replace it with a different microphone as the sound quality does not stack up. There is switch on the back to support other microphone sensitivity (50db and 60db) ... I ended up using a different microphone.
- There are two USB-C ports, one for dedicated power (recharging) and one for connecting to your computer. If you just use the one for your computer, you will need to recharge this every few days. This is bizarre, as USB-C can be used for power and data simultaneously.
- There is only one XLR jack, but they added an instrument jack there. This really needs two XLR jacks so you can pick between an instrument and a second XLR microphone. Most podcasters will be using two XLR microphones so this seems like a miss.
- There is no full recording feature which doesn't make any sense—this is supposed to be a mobile unit that has a battery so you can take it with you. If it had a micro SD slot, this would be fantastic.
- You hear your own voice when you are monitoring content. Unless there is something I missed, there is no way to not hear your own voice.
- The buttons are those soft ones you mash on and it takes a second for the system to show you have selected a button. The reverb button never turns off, it is always some color.
- The unit is plastic. I looked at the previous version and they made it of aluminum. This is a pretty big change to make to a product line, especially one advertised as "on the go" and then they don't ship it with a protective case. I would need to buy some kind of case if I wanted to take this on the road.

Even with the above issues that I noted, for the newer podcasters who are using phones/bluetooth and streaming from their consoles, this unit is a perfect fit. If you have a more classic podcast setup, this may not work into your system unless you are willing to make the leap and swap to wireless lavalier microphones and bluetooth.
Summary: Great starter unit with a few issues.

Text: Straps come in all sorts of designs which I boil down to materials, ergonomics, and adjustments. The Rico uses a chamois/velvet-like material against the neck or shirt depending on one's dress. This material is both soft, to avoid chaffing, and slip resistant. The inner layer consists of about a one-half inch of foam padding which cushions and spreads the weight of the instrument over a large area, i.e., it does not dig into the neck. The outer layer is a vented nylon mesh that allows the neck strap to breath. From the neck strap extends a singular, small nylon cord on each side. I particularly like this design because often, instrument straps continue unchanged from the neck to the hook with the same thickness/width of material - which I find too bulky. Where the Rico especially shines is its length-adjusting system. Most straps (instrument, camera, backpack, binocular, etc.) adjust their length by threading the strap through a series of buckles/clasps; there simply is no quick adjusting. The Rico, however, employs a pulley-like system that shortens or lengthens the strap by sliding the adjusting disc (for lack of a better word) up or down; it's that simple. So, you want to fine tune the length, a slight pull up or down on the disc while you are "wearing" the instrument and you're set. I especially like this feature because, although there is a defined, set position of the MPc (mouthpiece) relative to the mouth, assuming a given posture, I sometimes have the need to slightly raise or lower the instrument, e.g., when I am sitting v. standing. All things considered: a terrific strap.

I'm not sure how much I can say about a mute. It's easy to put on and take off, and it does its job. It mutes the violin to a reasonable level. I used an SPL meter at a distance where a sustained open G string gave a reading of about +2db. With the mute, it dropped to -6db. I then tried a Yamaha silent electric violin (unplugged) and from the same distance, it barely registered. I recalibrated the meter so the muted acoustic violin read about 1db, and the Yamaha read about -6db at that distance and setting.

So it won't make your instrument completely silent, and from a purely subjective perspective, it seemed to bring things closer to the silent violin, perhaps seeming about 10 to 20% louder had I not measured it.

With accessories, tonal quality is typically important. But with a mute, you expect it to deteriorate. Surprisingly, there was still a lot of tone left, especially compared to the unplugged electric, yet there were no buzzes or other horrible artifacts introduced.

You can't expect this to give great sound or complete silence, but it won't disturb the neighbors or their dogs, and it won't make the instrument sound dead. This is about 15 times cheaper than the cheapest silent violin, and the latter will probably sound worse. It's not the ultimate solution for quietness but it lets you stick to your instrument of choice.

Absolutely astonishing reverb pedal! I have many amps, all of them tube amps that range from 5 watts up to 150 watts. Some have built in spring tanks, some have a digital reverb simulation, and some have none. I bought this pedal for the ones that don't have reverb built in, but after hearing this pedal, I probably will just use it instead of the built in reverbs, as this thing is able to dial in MANY sounds / reverbs in one sitting as opposed to the single kind you get with certain amps. I was impressed! Some people in the review sections have mentioned that it's sub par, and sounds like crap, etc. But I am willing to bet they may not know how their particular amp / amps work. With many years of experience, you come to find out that not all amps are equal, and some you need to put certain pedals, such as a reverb, in the FX loop, and others, in front of the amp. I have one in particular that this pedal doesn't sound quite right in the FX loop, where other pedals do, but putting this reverb in front of it was the cure to the issue at hand (which was minor anyway, I could have lived with it after tweaking). That particular amp in pretty picky about pedals anyway. Some other amps I have, this thing sounds killer IN the FX loop and NOT in front. So, if you have this pedal, and you find yourself not liking the tone, change it around, it probably has to do with your particular amp and how it likes to take pedals. This pedal is well worth the price I paid, which was full listed price, and I would absolutely buy it again!
Summary: Great Reverb pedal, know your AMP!

Light- a bit dry but not severely. I got this light rosin cake since the price was good and I was going to order dark rosin anyway. As a previous reviewer has noted, it's a bit dry for air conditioned environments, but now that it is the fall some of my playing is outdoors in the still-humid late August air. It goes on fairly well, isn't too soft nor too dry. The cracking that other reviewers have noted isn't very severe on this cake. It has a single tangential crack at one corner of the bottom, which doesn't run all the way through to the other end.

One can rejuvenate rosin, but it is a real bother: heating to melting point in a double boiler, adding a few drops of turpentine then re-casting into its holder. Too much trouble at the current price, but a strong consideration if the piece happens to be one of those sixty dollar brands. Or I guess they could even buy a press for up to a hundred dollars or a heated press for more. But this cake was cheap so if it shatters or gets too dry I'll just pitch it or grind it up to use as a powder on newly haired bows.

Text: I've been using sax stands for a LOT of years (40+) and have used Hercules stands for the past 5-6 years, as they make a very durable and easy to transport stand.  I play soprano/alto/tenor/bari saxes on many gigs.  One of the things that always made me nervous on gigs was that the Hercules (and almost all other) sax stands did not really "secure" the horn.  What I mean is they were pretty stable, but the "grip" on the bell was not consistently "snug" without being so tight you couldn't pick up or place a sax out/in the stand quickly and safely.  This all changes with the new design!!!  Just to see how well it does hold the horn in place when in the stand, I put my alto sax in the stand the picked up the stand/sax and held it by the upright bar...and turned it over to see if the sax stayed in place (of course my test had a hand ready to catch the horn if/when it fell out of the stand.)  To my delight, the horn stay in place without ANY movement!!!  I guess I could actually walk around carrying it by the stand's upright bar...but I'm not that brave!  This is a great improvement of an already really fine sax stand!  I expect they will update all versions they make to incorporate this new bell "grip" mechanism...at least I hope they do.  My recommendation is that you buy this new model...if you love your horn.  It's definitely an excellent investment and will keep your "baby" in place much better!

This is the second Music Area gig bag I have reviewed, the first one was their lowest end model. I was impressed with that model, and even more impressed with this one. Every aspect of this case is well thought out. The fabric outside is a black/silver denim type of look. The bottom has heavy rubber bumpers, and it seems pretty stable leaned up against the wall.

There are 2 compartments in the front. The biggest one will hold larger music books, it actually held my largest on with room to spare. It has a mesh compartment inside, a slot for a tablet, and a loop to carry a cord. This is also a smaller compartment in front of that one as well; both are padded. Moving up there is a small area that I assume is for lifting the guitar. Moving to the top of the case there is a strange pocket with entry on both sides, it has a picture of an airplane and a "carry tag"; not sure exactly how to use that. Behind it though is an area for a phone, id, pen and some other small stuff, it's padded as well.

Moving to the back, there is a metal loop that is heavily reinforced. The backpack harness tucks into the case, or pulls out easily if you need to wear the guitar as a backpack. Tucking it all in makes the case extremely sleek, no flopping buckles or straps. The backpack harness is well ventilated, and there are large bumpers on the back to make wearing it comfortable. The carrying handle is padded, rigid and very comfortable. The last external detail is a flap that folds over the zippers so they don't inadvertently open.

Moving to the inside, it is again brilliantly thought out. The padding is thick and my strat doesn't move at all when buttoned up. The bottom has a split for the strap button. There is a patch of tough fabric that goes over the bridge/tremolo system so that they don't shred the padding. The neck has a large pillow, with a flap that goes over the strings to keep in tight.

This company seems to have come out of nowhere and is making brilliantly designed cases that provide excellent protection. When I brought this case to my last lesson my instructor was admiring this case quite a bit. He is a well known touring musician, so pretty familiar with gig bags...

These wall hangers operate smoothly once they’re installed. Place a guitar in the hanger and release… the pads on the ends of the hanger arms are pushed down by the weight of the guitar and two tabs come up to ensure your guitar can’t be pulled out or knocked out by accident. I like that bit.. but there’s a lot about these hangers that I don’t like.

First of all, they’re BIG. They look like robot arms on your wall and they hold the guitar a full inch further from the wall than the old style hangers I’ve used for many years.

Second - they feel flimsy. Yes, I know the pads on the ends of the arms are supposed to move up and down when you place or remove your guitar from the hanger but the whole arm sags noticeably under the weight of the guitar. I put my Fender Strat in the hanger and the arm itself sagged more than a 1/4 inch. It just feels flimsy. You can see in the photo of the Classical guitar how even the relatively light weight bends the arms down.

Mounting them is pretty straightforward if you know what you’re doing but the rudimentary diagrams on the box don’t help much if you’ve never done something like this before. For example: each hanger comes with two mounting screws and two each of two different types of wall anchors. One style I am familiar with.. it’s meant for hanging the hanger from drywall if there’s no wooden wall stud framing behind the drywall where you want to hang the guitar. But the other style is for some other type of wall material. I’m not sure which, and no explanation is provided for either. They also do not explain the way that’s preferred by many to mount the hanger on a timber framed wall by locating the studs, pre-drilling the holes properly, lubricating the screws with candle wax, and screwing them directly through the hanger and into the framing.

I know the hangers are rated for up to 8kg but to be honest, I will only hang my lightest guitars from them….and that’s with them mounted directly to the wall framing.
Summary: I like the locking arms but…

I know that many people who review guitar pedals are experts who use these all of the time. I am starting my pedal board up so I am approaching this as a beginner with mini pedals. That is how my review will be written.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
When building a pedal board, a power pack is usually the best way to go, but for me who is just starting, I decided to go with the daisy chain power. My pedals are all mini and take 9v so this seemed like a good place to start.

PLUG
The plug is a smaller sized transformer plug. It will fit on an open receptacle, but it will be a tight fit on a power strip or a crowded outlet.

DAISY CHAIN PLUGS
The plugs on this are all decent length, they fit well with my mini pedals, and the have plenty of room for my pedals to be spread out a bit on the board to allow room for the patch cables.

SOUND
The sound is pretty good for me, but since I do not have a power block to compare it to, it does seem like there might be a little room for cleaner sound than what I am getting. It is not BAD, I am just saying, it seems like perhaps it might be a bit cleaner with a power pack.

However, the sound is good for me who at this point is not doing any gigs, so I only need it for practice and messing around at home.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This cord works, it allows me to use my pedals and it is affordable until I can get myself a power box. I have no bad issues with this.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. There is nothing wrong with this, I do recommend it. I am just not sure it is five stars at this point. If I get a power block and test this again to check and it is not at all different, I will update my review and rating.

A BIG plus for this device is it doesn't require special software to interface with it. Plug it in as USB and it looks like a memory stick. This means it will work with other operating systems like Linux, and won't become obsolete in the future if they decide to no longer bother to keep their software compatible with future generation computers..

I also should point out that some people complain about how complex its usage is. Some of these commenters don't seem to realize that you can change the behavior of some of the functions. For example, I reconfigured mine so it goes from initial record into playback mode (instead of overdub mode) with one click. And another click will then go into overdub. I find this much better for how I like to use it.

Also, I don't use the tempo or rhythm functions at all, if I want drums I'll record a drum loop. But it would be useful as a metronome I would think, at least. So I really can't say much about these features.

It use to be the only option for locking tuners was either Sperzel or Schaller, which are great locking tuners. The downside to those was that one had to drill new holes into their guitar to install them, and then you'd have the hole left from the original tuners. I'm so glad that Grover has a locking tuner that's a direct fit with no heavy modification. I have a set of these on 2 Les Pauls, and they work just as well as the Sperzel tuners I've had on other guitars in the past. Very smooth operation, and the locks work the same as the other guys. Plus, they look just like the tuners their replacing with just a little extra knob that's barely noticeable. The lock knob is lower profile than the aforementioned lockers. Overall weight is about the same as a standard set of Grover 102's (the non-lockers that come stock on most Epiphone guitars).

Being a bass player who plays rhythm guitar on the side, I hated changing strings on guitars (guitar strings are so tiny). Locking tuners make everything so much easier. No winding, no messing around with anything. Plus they help stay in tune better than the standard tuners. I know guitarists who use these for the quick string change factor. When they break a string on stage, they just throw a new one on in less than a minute.

If its too tight you have to retune, if its too loose it deadens the strings and If you use mediums, its different than lights or extra lights. Slightly curved radius types work best for obvious reasons and some capos are better made for certain brand guitars. I've learned of late that there's problems with all of them.
On a breedlove 12 string pursuit factory setup and other 12 string guitars I have, the Shubb is dependable, adjustable, and if you get the tension ju-u-st right you don't have to retune depending on size strings your playing. It can't be too tight and it surely can't be too loose and the perfect placement is not necessarily right behind the fret. The problem there is if you do get it ju-u-st right you have to go through the same fussbudget process as before and it takes more time than if you just retune the guitar and i use the addario in hole tuner making it a quick process. I have not tried the d'addario pro with flex fit for about $30 but I'll bet it will work perfectly without retuning. I had a J Cash brass that was my favorite and worked great but you cant find 'em anymore. Anyway, the Shubbs are a great capo and worth the money. Text:
I'll echo what others have said: this is a superbly built instrument for the price, and I don't know how Epiphone can make them to sell so inexpensively. It looks, feels and plays like an instrument that cost at least twice as much.

A few notes: what looks in the product photos like a black finish around the edges and on the back and sides of the "Vintage" model is actually a super-rich deep, deep mahogany/maroon color, and it's unbelievably beautiful.

As others have said, the factory-supplied strings are crap; if you judge the instrument by them, you'll be disappointed. Include a set of Aqila Nylgut strings when you order this ukulele, and restring it as soon as you get it.

I was a little surprised that the sound was quieter than my $60 Kala soprano uke--normally, one expects a concert ukulele to have a louder, fuller sound. But the Les Paul has a relatively small soundbox compared to an all-acoustic ukulele, and that probably accounts for the quieter tone. I think it's a *better* tone, and I'm more interested in delicacy than in loudness, so I'm happy with it. If I wanted stadium-filling volume, I could always plug this into a stack of Marshall amps.

Oh, I almost forgot one important note to all owners: IT IS POSSIBLE TO REMOVE THE STUPID, UGLY PICK GUARD! Since ukulele players rarely use picks, and when we do, we use soft rubber or felt ones, there's no need to protect the finish from scratching, and that white pick guard really detracts from the instrument's looks.

I applied gentle heat from a hair dryer on its low power setting for about ten minutes, and very slowly and gently pried up the edges of the pick guard with my fingernails--no sharp tools! It came off pretty cleanly, leaving only a few small spots of adhesive residue. I was able to get rid of those with small amounts of rubbing alcohol on cotton, without any damage to the luscious ultra-glossy lacquer finish. And the ukulele looks SO much better now! If you feel as I do, feel free to do likewise. Just remember the key words: SLOW and GENTLE. Don't force anything, and you should be fine.
Summary: An exceptional value... and you can get rid of the pick guard!

PROS:

+ Becoming a bit of a "studio standard" for "accurate enough" affordable reference phones.
+ Flat (almost) frequency spectrum represented, little hype. Also, by way of functional design to a point, very little "air" in the soundstage, a good thing (or bad thing for you stylish kids with open back headphones that are not so good for studio reference/isolation). Honest enough to "mix in cans" with some minor user compensation, low-mids sound a touch boxy and up front to my ears, but it's not overly fatiguing.
+ Very good isolation almost rival hearing protection sets or big clunky traditional studio cans.
+ Comfortable enough on average head size/shape (short term-ish).
+ Adjusts pretty far out for us with fatter heads.
+ Foldable/collapse and store.
+ Good all hard plastic all week. construction/physical design, have survived heavy use and multiple drops onto hard floors and rocks (when field recording) with no issues....not even much obvious cosmetic damage.
+ Ear cushion cover does not flake off and wear nearly as easily as other sets in it's price point.

CONS:

- Long term comfort suffers from cheap cushion material. As seemingly intended to wear out, be replaced at more expense/hassle than they should be, and all too often.
- Cushions NEED TO BE THICKER, MORE COMFORTABLE, and MORE RESILIENT. Please from big ear fat head people. Our ears "bottom out" on the painful inner plastic grill in the first 8 months of heavy use. This can be more painful and annoying than a shirt with a harsh label back right over your right nipple.
- (Crown appears to be improved (partially on newer with thicker crown cushions. Thank you I think, have not used them yet). Stock original head crown cushion are about the cheapest you'd ever want to not cushion your cranium. Tends to slip along the axis of the top of headphones. Come un-ziplocked over time, pointlessly difficult to "stretch the un-stretchable" when replacing. This appears to remain the same. To add injury to insult...they tend to flatten out pretty quickly, so you feed the hard plastic headaches, then order replacements, repeat every 5-6 months or so.

NEUTRALS:

= Cord, while old school curly is fun and functional to wrap around a headphone hook under desk and provide strain relief. This one get's janky almost immediately, perhaps the nature of this unruly beast to get the curly cord at a price point?

BOTTOM LINES: They're good workhorses. With required maintenance and modification in ways that are pure laziness and manufacturing cost cutting measures. They sacrifice long term usability and general comfort for pennies on the dollar, could be easily improved. I'm not near ready to drop 2300 dollars on a pair of HD820's that appear to have addressed the issues, so maybe apply a couple of these changes to the bargain set?
Summary: Almost perfect...flawed by comfort and maintenance issues caused by manufacturer cost cutting.

Text:
I'm a noodler, fiddling with mostly blues. This was my first all-tube amp.

Tested out a lot of amps at Guitar Center, and pound for pound, this was the clear winner for bluesy tone-price ratio -- so I took one home. It has a small footprint albeit on the heavy side for its size. Despite its compact form, it's loud. Never played in a band setting so can't comment on how it cuts through.

The Good
- It has lush cleans, nice reverb, handsome vintage looks
- The Junior NOS has that distinctly Fender tone. Lenny type, glassy super cleans from my Strat
- The overdrive sounds much nicer when the master is cranked, but I can't play at those levels from home. In terms of power and headroom, it's more than adequate power for home practice -- in fact, even at its lowest volumes my wife still pounds on my door.
- The tone gets better when the master is above 5 (10:00). (I have never cranked it beyond 7 (1:00), and can't comment on performance at those levels.
- Supposed to be a great platform for modding -- do a Google search for BillM mods.
- Pedal friendly, and it becomes much more versatile with colored pedals for different amp sounds. It does fuzz, overdrive, distortion, modulation and delay very well. I've reviewed a few of my pedals, so you can have a look at my profile if you're in the market for Blues Jr. effects.

Tips
- A compressor pedal was the best investment I made for this amp. Evens out the dynamics so their not as biting at higher volumes and it helps dial in some of the amp's best tonal characteristics.
- Because I practice at very low apartment levels, I tend to prefer OD from pedals over the amp's volume knob. I generally run the amp loud and clean and drive the tubes from my boosts and OD pedals.

The "Meh"
- I find it can get a bit noisy with the volume knob (dirt knob) at high levels. Probably typical for gain to amplify the noise floor.
- The polished stainless control plate gets very hot when the tubes are lit up. Again, probably typical for a tube amp.
- Mids make things slightly muddy, so I roll them way back to scoop -- doesn't sound scooped as such. I read the BillM mods tighten this up nicely, but I've found my settings sweet spot for the kind of stuff I play, and I'm happy with the results using my pedals.
- Would like to have an effects loop. I run my pedals off the front.
- IMO the bass could be tighter and punchier. There are mods for this, but my compressor has been useful here as well.
- I could really use a line in/out for headphones/backing tracks. IMO this is an essential feature for a home/apt. amp.
- Increasing the volume or engaging the Fat Switch increases the noise floor. I rarely use the fat switch anyway. Moreover, I can almost always dial out most/all of the hiss with settings on the amp and pedals. FYI, this is not single coil hum. Generally, the hiss is non existent, except with more cranked settings and/or the Fat Switch.
- The amp is quite loud, and could really use attenuation for apartment practice. The Bugera V5 is going to be a much better and more versatile practice amp, although its cleans and headroom are at a relatively significant deficit next tot he Blues Jr. I really wanted a V5, but after A/B-ing it with the Blues Jr. there was just no comparison.
- Frankly, I think the best type of apartment practice amp (alone, not with band setting) is going to be a combo solid state modeler like Line 6 amps. Much more versatile and suited for practice. But for beautiful organic tones of a tube amp, the Blues Jr. NOS is killer.

Summary
- Great blues/country/rock amp for the money.
- IMO it's not versatile like some more expensive do-it-all tube amps like my dream machine--the Mesa Boogie Express, but it's a ton of fun and can achieve some beautiful tones. Pedals make it really shine.
- For solo apartment practice I'd recommend looking at a more versatile combo amp that has line in/out, attenuation, etc.
- I give it 4.5 stars, but Amazon doesn't allow fractions.

All in all, I recommend the amp. The compromise in features is balanced out by the great tones.
Summary: Great all-tube blues amp for the money

I love my Snark SN5 tuner. It works smoothly without any issues, and allows me to tune my guitar swiftly and accurately. All you need to do is clamp the tuner to the headstock, and it is ready to go. The SN5 is smaller than I expected, but the multicolored meter is easily readable, and the meter can adjusted so that it can be seen clearly from any position.

Using the color coded meter, you can tell whether a string is flat or sharp, and adjust the string tension accordingly. With a little practice, tuning becomes a quick and easy process. The unit is powered by a CR 2032 battery, which generally has a long life.

Although the clamp has rubber pads, apparently the finishes of certain guitars could still be prone to damage. The instructions states that the Snark is not recommended for guitars with the following finishes, polyurethane, French polish, and nitrocellulose lacquer. Those with Gibson, Gretch, or Taylor guitars may want pay particular attention to this warning. I have had no problems using this tuner on Kramer, Ibanez, Charvel, Epiphone, and ESP guitars. The tuner also works for bass guitars and violins. I do not have either of those instruments, but I imagine the tuner would work much the same.

As there are a number of guitar tuners that attach to the headstock, it took me a little while to decide on the SN5. Even after eliminating tuners by D'Addario and Planet Waves, selecting the SN5 wasn't that simple, as Snark makes a number of similar tuners. I am completely satisfied with the SN5, and believe that it fully deserves a 5 star rating. It is also the least expensive, of the tuners I was considering buying. If the finish of your guitar isn't an issue, you may find the Snark to be very helpful.
Summary: compact and inexpensive, the Snark SN5 is terrific, if you have the right kind of finish...
