Today I completed the 52nd lesson, so I'm 1/7th of the way through the set and can comment on how this book has helped me progress in guitar. First, I've been playing guitar for about 45 years - primarily self-taught - although I had a prior formal music background in clarinet. In all that time I never really advanced past what could be intermediate level, and I recently bought new electric and acoustic-electric guitars and decided to seriously pursue improving my proficiency through various resources on the internet, software like guitar pro and powertabs, playing with others, and through books, with a mental commitment to Guitar Aerobics.

My first impression echoed what several have already noted, that there is little descriptive detail in the exercises. However, there are usually one or 2 key tips relevent to the lesson and the sample CDs are very helpful. I copied the CDs onto my laptop music player, so when I start a new lesson at the slowest tempo, it automatically advances to the next faster, and so on, and I try to play the 2 bars for the whole minute and a half at each tempo (sometimes pausing or rewinding if needed), which usually means more reps than the 10 per tempo suggested. I rarely get all the reps perfect, but I can tell that my proficiency at speed has improved thus far, so I am encouraged and see improvement.

The excercises are broken down into 7 techniques per week: alternate picking, string skipping, bending, arpeggios, sweep picking, legato, and rhythm. I was never very good at picking, knew nothing of sweep picking, and was pretty basic at bending and legato. I have learned several new things from the book and improved my technique in these areas. I'm definitely much more comfortable with a pick in my hand than before.

I've found some of the lessons to be quite easy and some almost impossible (even at slow speeds). For example stretching from the 3rd fret to the 7th for a pull off is difficult because my hands are not that large. I try it anyway - after all it is "aerobics" and who knows? But sometimes, I'll just make things easier by moving up the neck where the frets are smaller. Another thing I do is review the past lessons of the current week so it stays fresh. What I don't do is agonize and compulsively seek perfection before moving on. I'm happy noticing my gradual improvement and know I'm becoming a better player. One last thing - I still practice songs and other techniques about every day. Two measures of an exercise isn't enough, even if repeated 200 times.

Good luck with your playing...
Summary: You get out what you put in

Text:
Because of my profession, I suppose I might be something of a speaker snob. My regular monitor system is carefully calibrated and my room is treated. I'm in other high-quality rooms on a regular basis and I know how good speakers are supposed to sound. So what to do a a pair of inexpensive little desktop monitors?

The out-of-the box impression is fairly positive. The speakers are light and the enclosures are a rigid high-impact plastic. While not the MDF frame you might find in more expensive monitors, it's really the rigidity that's important. These are satisfactory in that regard. The overall appearance is attractive--not Mercedes attractive, but not overly cheap either. Provided cables are on the short side: just enough for mounting by a computer but a little too short for anything else. The first thing I didn't like was the fact that the cable carrying the amplified signal to the left speaker uses a 1/4" jack. Quarter-inch cables rarely carry that much current and this opens the door to a misstep. I think a banana plug would have been a better choice.

Connection to the outside world is simple, using either RCA or 1/4" TS jacks. The power switch is on the back. I'd have preferred it on the front when you consider the jumbled mess that's often on the backside of a computer desktop. There's also a bass-boost switch on the back which I found not to be necessary. On the front is a headphone jack (nice touch) and a volume knob.

I put the speakers on stands in my treated room to give them the best possible audition. I used several types of material: jazz, samba, classical. My first impression was positive. Bass was sufficient for small speakers and highs were sharp. After a couple of minutes, some deficiencies in lower midrange became evident as well as a certain unevenness in overall midrange. But bear in mind that these aren't Genelecs. These are low-cost speakers that deliver more than adequate power and quite acceptable sound. And after a one-cent modification, they got even better---

If you've spent any time in a recording studio over the last 20 years, you'll know the ubiquitous NS-10 monitor. It's a low-cost monitor that has served as a general stand-in for the inexpensive speaker that's likely to be in most homes. Not a great monitor, but it's predictable. You'll notice that many of those NS-10s will have a little bit of, ahem, bathroom tissue across the tweeter. That's just enough to damp the more unpleasant parts of the high-end response. And it works very well on these little Alesis speakers. I found a single ply did the job well (two-ply was just too muffled). Most of the harshness was gone and these speakers became something you might even be able to trust (at least well enough to check out a mix for smaller speakers).

If you're really serious about listening, you're likely to go for more expensive monitors. But if you're just starting out or simply looking for a pair to use for a mix (when you're supposed to be on vacation), you can do a lot worse that these little guys.

The Source Audio C4 Synth was being developed around the same time BOSS announced its $200 SY-1 compact synth pedal. Apart from the timing of their release and the fact that both pedals involve “synthesis”, they actually differ quite a bit. In fact, I own (and like) the SY-1, but a lot of that pedal’s limitations are what drove me to check out the C4 Synth. The developers of the C4 Synth are great, and have been very responsive online.

OVERVIEW:
I would not exactly describe the C4 Synth as “plug and play”. Whereas the BOSS SY-1 has approximately 120 sounds accessible on the face of the pedal itself, the C4 really only offers six presets. However, the C4 has an online (and phone) editor and preset manager that allows for a much wider variety of patches. Critically, there are already hundreds of community patches, so even if you know nothing about synthesis or how to set one of these presets up, you’ll still have a wealth of sounds to choose from.

I think it fair to point out that navigation of those presets could be much better implemented, and Source Audio has basically admitted as much. But the C4 Synth grew accidentally out of the development of another pedal (the Spectrum Filter, I believe), and Source Audio felt that it was more important to offer one at a (relatively) affordable price point in a compact package. There are only two assignable control knobs for each preset, but this also prevents the user from becoming overwhelmed. Most presets use these to tweak controls like an EQ/filter roll-off, or to adjust modulation speed/depth.

MONOPHONIC PITCH TRACKING:
Note tracking on the C4, for the most part, is MONOPHONIC, which is a critical difference from the SY-1. However, Source Audio preferred this method because they feel like it results in much purer (and cleaner-sounding) waveforms. Bassists love this pedal for that reason, but single note bass and lead sounds are also excellent on guitar. Since bass sounds are one area where the SY-1 mostly fails to deliver, the two pedals sort of compliment one another in that regard. With the C4, I get everything from vintage analog basses, to 808-style sub bass, to searing leads and galloping note sequences. You can blend in dry guitar signal if you like, but if you go full-on with the mix, it’s amazing how non-guitar-like your guitar becomes.

I should note that you do need to “calibrate” the output of our instrument to each patch (this can be adjusted with the top left knob on the pedal without using the editor). Otherwise, the note tracking might work poorly, or not at all. I suspect that when you come across reviews where the person is saying that the C4 is terrible and didn’t even make sounds, this is one of the mistakes they are making. In addition to setting the input correctly, there is a bit a “C4 playing style” that you need to use in order for it to track each note and sound, well, like a synthesizer. It’s actually relatively easy to learn, but it is true that if you just pick up a guitar and expect to play chords and non-articulate phrases with legato….that’s not something the C4 is going to respond well to.

The C4 has some additional tricks up its sleeve, and I’ve only just begun to explore them. The editor actually has quite a few effects built in, so while its primary trick is to do monophonic synthesis, you can also just use it as an effects pedal, including drives, bitcrusher, tremolo, etc. The pedal can be played normally for this purpose, since it is applying effects, as opposed to using note tracking to produce the sound.

MIDI IMPLEMENTATION & TIPS FOR SWITCHING PRESETS:
I probably spent a week online (before the pedal even arrived) planning out how I would integrate the C4 into my pedalboard, and what I could do to expand access to the 128 preset slots that can be stored on the device. First off, it is a point of frustration that there is no “up/down” button for presets, nor is there a simple LED screen or other indication as to what preset you are currently playing. You get a 3-way switch with a modifier button for a total of 6 presets.

However, if you have a USB MIDI controller (and possibly a Source Audio Neuro Hub, sold separately), there are ways to cycle through presets, or simply recall specific presets, using MIDI commands. The Morningstar MC3/6 is a popular option for this, but requires purchase of the Neuro Hub in order to make it work. It might be worth checking out some of the MIDI controllers from Disaster Area, however. Some of their controller have the unique ability of acting as a USB Host, and with a simple $5 adapter cable, I was able to hook my MIDI Baby 3 directly to the C4 and access 24 different presets with just a few footswitch presses.

But if you don’t want to get that complicated, keep in mind that you can simply pick 6 of your favorite synth presets and assign them to the slots accessible directly on the pedal. The iPhone app is a little dodgy at times due to some login issues, but can pretty quickly switch and re-order presets using the included 3.5mm to 1/4” cable. Honestly, some of these presets are so convincing and unique that any one of them could have been sold as a standalone pedal. Therein lies the power, versatility, and (arguably) the value of the C4 Synth.

CONCLUSION:
It’s frustrating to see a few of the 1* and 2* reviews on this pedal and wonder what might have happened had: (a) done a little more forum/YouTube research on how to load and change presets on the pedal; or (b) purchased the pedal with more realistic expectations for what it can do. Yes, the C4 has a learning curve. No, you can’t just pick up your guitar, play sloppy chords, and expect the C4 to spit that out as a “synth” sound. But the C4 Synth is INSANELY powerful at a size and price point that guitar player routinely shell out just to get ONE type of overdrive or modulation effect. The C4 can make my guitar sound like a bass. Or like a vintage Moog. Most importantly, it sounds like nothing else I can create with any other pedal I’ve ever tried (including anything in the Helix HX Stomp). And no, it’s not just for bass players, and I actually use my guitar to conjure some of my favorite bass synth tones out of it. It’s an amazing tool that has really expanded my view of what guitars are capable of, all in a box the size of a typical compact effects pedal.

UPDATE (04/14/22): Wanted to update my review because I took a brief hiatus from the C4 (and guitar in general), but am returning to the pedal now and am excited about it all over again. I highly recommend viewing the YouTube tutorial by Zachary Rizer - it's about 52 minutes long and is essentially the real "instruction manual" as to what the C4 is capable of. My initial use of the C4 was limited to search for community presets, but that was also limiting and disappointing because the C4 can be used in so many different ways. One example of why that matters: the note tracking for each preset is calibrated different instrument and note ranges, and I found immediately better results when I specified that I wanted it to read the E to E range of a 6-string electric guitar (instead of a bass or whatever).

Once the concept of programming your own presets "clicks" for you, the C4 becomes not just one synth pedal, but a potential replacement for several - sort of like a "signal chain in a box." If you want the C4 simply to take the audio signal of your guitar and transpose it down (or up) 1 or 2 octaves - maybe with some fuzz and filtering applied - it can do that very effectively. If you want to take that same monophonic note and transform it into a swirling, synthesized soundscape with up to 4 different waveforms, you can do that too. And there's a whole world of polyphonic, harmonizing, and sequencing applications that I won't even attempt on the C4, but a more advanced user would certainly appreciate. This isn't a pedal for everyone, but there's insane value and functionality here that can be infinitely explored, customized, and enjoyed.
Summary: A library of synth sounds - played with your guitar - in a compact package

When I started up my band a couple of years ago, I bought 3 Shure SM58s--the industry standard since they're durable, don't make much noise on handling, and cut through the mix with most voices. But no mic is the best for every singer--some people just sound better with particular mics! A couple of months back I started working with a great female singer whose own mic was, ahem, rather cheap. We had her using one of the SM58s in practice--but when we sound-checked our first gig, we found that her voice sounded really thin and chirpy through the PA. I had bought this mic a year ago just to have an extra in my collection, and had brought it to the gig just in case. Popped this mic on the stand, and voila--her voice was strong and warm, with ten times the body it had on the 58, yet with a smooth, detailed high end!!!

The moral of this story is that no mic is perfect for everybody. I sound great on an SM58, muddy on this one. But if you happen to have somebody who already has a crisp high end and doesn't need the SM58 accentuation in that range, this is a very reasonably priced, well-made alternative with a warmer, fuller sound, that MIGHT work nicely. Text:
Disclaimer: I backed this on Kickstarter and the company is incentivising reviews.

That disclaimed, though somewhat biased, I legitimately love this thing, and have since five minutes after I got it out of the box.

Back in, lemme think... 2009? In my band at the time, we had a chaotic end to a song in which, while the keyboard went wild with pitch shifting and octaves, on bass I used a screwdriver sliding near the bridge, to hit the strings, and to make noise on the pickups, along with a slide and lots of slapping. I would've loved to have this then, as it's a lot better than a screwdriver for some of the things I was doing.

Not that it's just for noise, by any means. You can achieve some really pretty and unique sounds with it, and it's just as important to have as an Ebow. It is essentially the complimentary opposite to an Ebow's lack of attack and infinite sustain, too. This gives percussive attack and can give at least the impression of faster decay, such as with a mandolin, due to that, giving you a sound that is very similar to a hammered dulcimer, without having to have, and learn, another instrument for over $100. It is a wonderful tool to have in your toolbox if you don't just want to play "traditional" guitar. It isn't insanely versatile, and you will want it only for specific things, but there is still a lot you can do with it.

That said, you do still have to learn, just not nearly as much as the switch to a dulcimer. There's a lot you can do with this, but it takes some practice and experimentation to find. The company has some basic tutorials and demos on youtube that make it very easy to pick it up and start getting cool sounds with just a few minutes' practice, but the amount of things you can do with it does stretch beyond that, and I'm genuinely excited experimenting and writing with it. And I find a song with one part using an Ebow and one using this sounds great and incredibly unusual.

And to follow the Ebow comparison, it certainly gets bonus points for being under $20, instead of $100, and not needing batteries.

The build quality and plastic are quite good, with quality matte plastic, not slick ABS, and the design is clever, with an area to grip between the fingers that is quite comfortable. It's possible the "bulb" on the other side of the gripping area could be bigger to prevent it sliding better, but that might also interfere with the action, preventing it from bouncing. The only minor gripe I have is that there is a fairly prominent molding seam going right along the sides you'll be using, the sides that hit the strings. I can't imagine it affects the usage of the triller in any way, but it could've been buffed down, especially the injection site at the end, which is just ugly.

Also, really stretching to find negatives, the box is just a little odd. It's needlessly large and just that plastic with a big, hollow, cardboard insert. I get the idea of letting you see the actual triller, but it really doesn't need to be that big.

I've played this thing on six and twelve string guitars, acoustics and electrics, a bass, a mandolin, a ukelele, and a bass ukelele. It doesn't work too well on a ukelele as it already has such quick decay, and the plastic strings on a bass ukelele don't work with it well at all, but on everything else, I love the sounds I can get.
Summary: An important part of your toolbox.

The vid (for sound only) is from a live concert, playing these reeds on the M30 mouthpiece and R13 Buffet clarinet.

As you can see from the pictures, these are well polished reeds with consistent characteristics like density, fibrosity, thickness and finish. Each reed comes individually sealed and with a plastic holder.

All reeds are made of cane, known as Arundo Donax. It is not wood or bamboo, but more closely related to tall grasses. It grows around river banks and lakes with moving water. It absorbs the water for growth and nutrients. It MUST be properly collected when the stalk is drained of water in the winter (dry season) and it must be drained and dried to avoid including biological and chemical impurities. The climate also affects its density, which limits where good reed stock can grow. Cane will absorb whatever is in the water where it grows.

Good reeds should have a smooth vamp (shaped upper part) and have a golden- yellow or light yellow color without much variation. The bark can be of varied tone (glossy-looking bottom part). That's OK. You should not be able to see longitudinal lines or fibrous streaks on the vamp (part that goes inside the mouth). Green looking reeds have not been properly dried and drained. Throw them away. Grey looking reeds or ones with dark spots or streaks may have mold. Throw them away also. (This is highly unlikely in Vandoren or Daddario reeds).

Good reeds are expensive. However, with proper care, you CAN make them last months.. or longer. Just teach your kids proper care skills. It's a wonderful way to teach being responsible.

Always take the reed off after playing. Always put them back into the holder (or get a special case). NEVER touch the tip of the reed (I see kids do it all the time.. and they break the reeds). Practice securing the reed to the mouthpiece with the ligature without tripping the tip. Carefully wash the reeds with water once a week, wiping with clean fingers, bottom to top. And lastly, don't play one reed all the time. Have a few ready to go and rotate them. If you do this, or teach your kids, a box of quality reeds will last you a very long time... and you won't have to buy cheap non-reeds made in china..
Summary: Love these. Listen to vid for sound!

Ask any professional DJ and they will tell you that Pioneer is one of the few top brands of DJ equipment out there. Pioneer can be found out at the most famous clubs and is used by the most well known DJs.

The Pioneer DDJ-200 is designed as an entry level controller for those DJ’s who are just starting out and are on a budget. At the same time, a professional DJ could use this unit with ease and sound great since the layout of the controls are the same as a pro unit. I’m sure Pioneer figured that it would be in their best interest that the user should have to make as minimal as an investment as possible to get started. In fact, almost everyone has the equipment to start: a phone, tablet, or computer, a pair of headphones, a speaker they can plug their output into, and a music library.

The technology Pioneer has developed is pretty smart on one hand but limits the unit on the other hand. They have decided not to include any sort of audio interface, either input or output which means program or cueing. Instead that will be handled by the audio source either phone, tablet or computer. By doing this, it limits the program output to be in mono, splitting the stereo output of the device into two mono signals, one for the headphone the other for the output. The headphone output is controlled on the unit so that the cue/program/solo mix can heard in one channel and the program output is controlled by the level controllers for each channel as well as the master output via software. The split is achieved using an included cable with two 3.5mm jacks (If using an iPhone or iPad a lightning to headphone jack dongle is required but not included).

On the smart side, Pioneer uses Bluetooth technology for all controls on the unit to communicate to the software on the phone or tablet making it completely wireless. The DDJ-200 requires a USB power source, which kind of baffles me why they did not build in a rechargeable battery on this unit which would make it truly portable since it is small and light enough. Maybe it would make the controller bigger and heavier or just too expensive. I’m sure Pioneer thought about adding a battery and there is some logic behind why they did not include one. You can still use the DDJ-200 with an external power bank and I’m guessing Pioneer figured that most people will have one of those laying around as well.

Without going into a lot of detail, the controller layout is pretty much the standard with the eq, headphone control, and sound processing, levels and crossfader in the middle, pitch control for each channel to the right, 8 pads for looping, effects, etc. and cue and play/pause buttons. Above that is the beat sync button and platter. The pads, cue, play pause, beat sync, headphone and transition fx buttons are all backlit by either a red yellow or green LED. The unit is just big enough to use comfortably, but is small by comparison to the pro decks. All of the controls feel nice and solid, even though it is entirely plastic it is very well built. Pioneer has even included a touch sensitive surface on the inside of the platter, so maybe that is metallic.

Overall, I’m quite impressed with what the DDJ-200 offers for the price, but it does have some limitations. Here are some Pros and Cons below.

Cons
No built in Rechargeable Battery, must provide a power source
No built-in audio interfaces – no audio inputs or outputs at all
No microphone input
Bluetooth is for control only, not for audio
If using headphones output will always be in mono, even if using a computer with multiple sound cards
When using iPhone or iPod requires Lightning to 3.5 mm dongle (not included)
Only 2 Channels
Colors on pads and controls cannot be changed
No meters on unit
Not really designed for gigs, more for casual use

Pros
Can use with streaming services such as Spotify, Soundcloud, Beatport Link, etc providing an endless music library (Internet connection required of course)
Professional layout and controls
Touch sensitive platters
Good build quality
Includes Rekordbox software as a free download
Can interface with popular DJ software such as dJay, WeDJ, and virtual DJ
Can be used with iPhone/iPad or computer
Many controls backlit by LEDS
Summary: Excellent Beginner Controller With Some Limitations

They use color-coded "flags" (for lack of a better term) that make it somewhat difficult to determine which string is which gauge. There's a chart on the package telling you which color denotes which gauge, but that's not as easy as just reading an envelope. Overall, depending on the price, or if you prefer the all-in-one packaging, these are good strings and a valid alternative to Elixir strings.

Text:
I purchased this to save batteries on my [[ASIN:B0035JI8J8 Boss ME25 Guitar Multi-Effects Pedal]], which has a healthy appetite for them. I did consider a few after-market supplies, but opted for this one because I felt it was a safer choice.

This will work with any 9 volt DC device that consumes up to (but does not exceed) .5 Amps. To make sure this is right for a non-Boss device check your connector receptacle. The male barrel connector on this adapter is 2.5mm x 5.5mm (inner x outer diameters). The piece right behind the barrel connector houses two coils that function as RF filters, and they do work on my BE-25, because it is noise-free.

Another feature that makes this safe and handy for non-Boss devices is it has a protection circuit that will go into overload mode if the device to which you connect this requires more than 9 volts DC or attempts to draw more than .5 Amps.

The wall wart is less than an inch thick and is about 2.25 inches long, so should not interfere with adjacent plugs in a power strip. The wire itself is fairly thick - much beefier than many power supplies I own, and there are four separate strain reliefs in the total wire run, so with care this power supply should last a long time.
Summary: Well made and will work with some non-Boss devices too (see measurements I provide in the review)

Look for the designation 12-"AWG". That means the American Wire Gauge, the standard for sizing cable diameter since 1857! Did Pyle try a "fast one" by labeling the casing "12-GA." Maybe that's the Chinese size.
I am sending this cable back because the website description does not match the reality of the product. I bought GLS speaker cables on Amazon. It's family run California company. They're the real deal - 12AWG strong cables.

I spend 125+ nights a year in hotels, and wanted a ukulele I could take with me without upsetting my much practiced road warrior packing system. I played the concert-sized travel Kala uke at my local music store (they didn't have the soprano in stock), and loved the action and the tone. Easy to play, sweet sound. I put the uke into its nice gig bag, took it out to the car, and tried to fit it into my 25" suitcase. It would just barely go diagonally corner to corner, tight to the point that I was concerned that a sharp blow to the end of the suitcase might damage the uke. So I went back in and ordered the soprano. Waited a few weeks, went back to the store, they said it was back-ordered for at least another month, so canceled that order, and bought one online.

The soprano showed up, and I was almost immediately disappointed. One of the zippers on the cool looking gig bag would not operate. Took the uke out, tuned it, and started playing. Within minutes it was wildly flat, particular the E string. And the instrument's tone was just too harsh, not at all mellow like the concert version I had played earlier. I continued to noodle around on it for the next two weeks. Everytime I picked it up, the same problem -- way way out of tune.

Now I own two other ukes (both Gretcsh solid-bodies) and I understand that the strings have to "settle"; that initially you have to keep tuning until they are properly stretched. But the Kala was ridiculous. I couldn't get through a two-minute song without it going flat. In contrast my Gretsch tenor will stay in tune for days, even weeks at a time.

Nonetheless I took the uke along on a trip. It fit easily in my suitcase, and seemed quite safe and secure in its well-padded bag placed among the packing cubes I use to organize my stuff. It was great being able to pull it out at night and practice in the hotel, but OMG, I was tuning it 15 times an hour (and I have crappy sense of pitch so it takes awhile for me to realize when it goes flat). And even in tune the tone somehow was just not right, too brassy, too harsh.

Yet there were a lot of good things about the Kala, as other reviewers have noted. It was well made and well finished. I liked the balance and the look. It had nice tuners, nice binding and inlays. The Kala had good sustain and remarkable projection for an instrument this size. I just really wanted to love it, but couldn't. Sent it back to the online retailer and returned to dragging around my Gretcsch in its hard case when I travel.

Given my positive experience with the concert Kala travel uke, and the largely glowing reviews of the instrument on this site and elsewhere, it's possible I just got a dud, or bad strings, or something. And perhaps the issues could have been addressed had I bought it locally (as I prefer to do) so the guys at the music shop could work on the set up. I'll go by there again and see if they have one in stock I can play, and talk to them about the issues I experienced. I don't rule out buying another one, but only locally this time.
Summary: Wanted to love it, but just couldn't

It does what it claims. It's not a combination neck reset and top flattening, but it does reduce the bow in the top considerably. I have a 1963 Guild F-30 that I bought new. I didn't take very good care of it when I was younger and the top has a pronounced bow. It's a very nice sounding guitar. It's horrible looking and people are often surprised by the sound. I figured that the worst that would happen would be that the device wouldn't do anything. One little installation surprise was that I had to cut it down a bit. It was bigger than the cross section of the body under the bridge plate. A couple minutes with a razor saw solved that. The rest of the installation was a snap. To drill the hole in the bridge I made a pilot hole with an electric drill and then used a quick change bit in a ratchet screw driver to enlarge the screw hole. No problems. If I did a couple of these I think I could get the installation time down to under 30 minutes.

I've adjusted it a couple of times and reduced the bow. Bonus, there is a bit more sustain. Because the neck angle is changed there is a bit of buzz that wasn't there before. I haven't gotten around to that yet.

All in all this is a good way to improve a guitar you care about but don't want to spend a huge amount on. This is much cheaper than getting the top flattened professionally. It improves the action and, in my case, changed the tone a bit for the better. Expect to need some set up after installation. You are changing the geometry of the guitar. One con. The piece of plastic described as MOP was dark grey in mine. I used a bit of silicone putty to anchor it in the hole.
Summary: Surprisingly useful.  Unlike most miracle gizmos this thing actually does what it says

I just received these tubes in the mail yesterday, and I installed them right away in the preamp section of my Jet City 20w combo amp (JCA2112). The tubes in the amp previously were marked "made in china" and were 12ax7R, which I think must be the same as the ax7s, do to their pretty high gain tendency. I picked the JJ's at the recommendation of the Jet City's product support guy, and based on some positive feedback from fellow musicians.

I've only had the tubes in for about 36 hours now, but last night I put them through about 3 hours of gig time and they sounded great. The item description that Amazon provides is really pretty right on- these tubes increase clean headroom nicely. The original stock chinese tubes broke up almost instantly, and while that was fun for heavier rock, I've always been displeased with the lack of clean tones my amp could provide. The JJs changed all that in a hugely noticeable way. I'm reserving my final judgement for a few weeks from now when they've had another 10 hours of playing time, but here's what I've noticed so far:
-Great headroom and very musical, lush breakup- not harsh, jagged distortion, but creamy, bluesy drive.
-tight lows, very pronounced mids, and a nice, chimey high-end that isn't brittle at all.
-The note separation that the increased headroom gives is really great, and even with the preamp gain cranked, lead runs and hammer-on pull-of stuff has a nice, clear quality to it that allows notes to cut through the breakup in a really cool, vintage sounding way.

I guess I should also add that while this 3-pack isn't eligible for Prime, I received the package in 3 days and it was very well-protected. I would recommend the JJs, especially if you have an amp that comes stock with chinese tubes. These really do make a difference in tone.

Text: My new electric guitar isn't particularly comfortable to play while sitting, so I needed a strap.  I've played with straps in the past and always found them to be uncomfortable, so I hoped to find a padded strap that didn't break the bank.  This strap fits the bill just fine.  Depending on the angle that your pegs are set, however, you may find that the holes in the strap will with time enlarge to the point that the guitar is always in danger of falling.  If your pegs are set at an angle, like on a Strat, this strap will last forever.  If you're on a guitar with a horizontal peg, like a LP, you'll probably want to invest in some strap locks as well.  This will move the pressure from the strap holes to the metal locks and both extend the lifetime of the strap and its security. Don't love it, it's 2 x 3" speakers... but 5 star for meeting all expectations.

1st) get the extension cabinet. Some people say the extension cabinet does not make much difference but it does. This Amp had everything I wanted and nothing I didn't want. One of the things I wanted and can be hard to find in a mini amp is a level control on delay/reverb. If find that very valuable in dialing in just want you want for delay.

2nd) I wanted at "headphone" amp since most of my playing is through headphones. The single cabinet is small enough to sit on a table and the physical knobs are much easier to deal with than the small buttons on a headphone amp (like the mustang micro mini).

Observations: It goes loud enough for what I want a very quiet bedroom practice amp. With only the amp, it can kind be pretty quiet with low gain. With the extension speaker it better fills the room. The OD is better than I thought it would be. Use the OD channel and dial back the gain, turn up the volume, and get a nice fat sound. The ISF "EQ" makes a difference but it's not a big difference. But between ISF, which pickup I use and the tone control on my amp I have no problem dialing in a sound I like.

The construction feels cheap, it's made of plastic and not particularly heavy plastic but how strong do you need for sitting on a table? The knobs feel fine for a cabinet this small. I run it with batteries, even though it comes with a power supply, to have fewer "wires" attached and to give it some more weight to stay put on the table. With the batteries and some better rubber feet, I think I will feel very stable. You are not going to drag it off the table if you stand up.

I like the cabinets in a stack but the rubber feett are not very good so I plan to either get better pads or some velcro to hold them in a stack. (to my ear the stack sounded better than side by side).

At the end of the day, it's exactly what I wanted. It gets to the volume I want (with the 2nd cabinet) for playing in my bedroom and with the one cabinet it makes a nice little tabletop "headphone amp". I did not want a bunch of modeling but wanted enough controls to dial in the amp sound I want and with Gain Volume and OD, and some delay with level control I can do that. It's not a miracle but for two 3" speakers I'm impressed with the sound that comes out. At the $100 it cost me (the green model) I feel like I got a lot for my money.
Summary: Don't love but like it a lot

Has three different polar patterns - omnidirectional (all around), cardioid (in front) and bidirectional (front and back). Knob is easy to switch between the settings. For 90% of my uses, I'll be sticking with cardioid, but having the options to use this in an interview or when recording a music session is really nice.

Has built in controls for the line in (IT HAS A LINE IN! WOO!), the mic gain, and the monitoring volume (IT HAS A LINE OUT!) Didn't get any lag from mouth to ears, so completely comparable to more expensive mics and much better than expected. No issues with monitoring.

Also has a mute button that is very quiet and easy to press. Probably the coolest built-in feature, though, is the LED. Not only do you know when your mic is powered on (green), but also when it is on mute (orange), AND when you're audio is peaking (red). THAT IS AWESOME.

The sound quality is better than anything within fifty bucks of this price, for sure. My voice is deep and rich without doing anything in post. There's no line noise, no background hum, no clicks or pops. It just picks up what I need and sounds fantastic. The Line In on the back works well and my guitar sounded just fine. Was able to do stereo recording so I had the guitar on one track and my voice on another. Work on each independently in post to get the best possible sound.

This is the same price I paid for the podcast mic I bought a couple years ago and the G-Track Pro just blows it away in every possible way. I love the size, I love the heft, I love the features, and I love the audio. Definitely a sound investment. Pun intended.

Text:
I have many so-called travel size acoustic guitars and have changed out all of the over sized strings that were installed on them (typically 12-54's) with these 10-47's (or 11-52's for beefy 7/8 and 3/4 scale guitars) in all cases, has brought the smaller guitars from duds to nice playing instruments.
Three radical samples come to mind: On an old 1931 Gibson L1, the 12-54's pulled the bridge out.
On an SX Traveler, you could not hear the Low E until I got rid of the 12-54's.
On my Lil Martin, the lower bout started to delam under the pressure of the bridge pull.
Short scale acoustic guitars are someplace between a full size acoustic and a Ukulele and in most cases are not set up for heavier gauge strings (even though the manufacturers insist on delivering them this way) due to their short scales, small frets, and light construction.
If you can't hear the low E, or you are having problems fretting your strings, try these, what can it hurt?
Summary: Best strings for parlor size or travel acoustics

I have a small home studio and I wanted to have the ability to swap out amp tones without having to lug out a big head or a combo. i needed to be able to plug into my I/O and on to my DAW.

I like heavy bass tones and wanted something that would be clean but deep with an option to overdrive like tubes might. Digital often sounds lacking to me and before the days of digital we tried to get that tube sound with solid state. Rectifiers took the place of tubes and had much of the warmth of tubes and could be made more portable, lighter, and cheaper, even with shipping from Japan! That’s what we have here, solid state, and while it’s not tubes, it’s also not digital.

The Thunder bass amp has good tone, simple operation, converts to line impedance (via the headphone output), is capable of driving a decent speaker cabinet and sounds pretty damned descent while doing so.

Text:
I received the Behringer U-Phoria UMC204HD as a gift, and my early impressions of it are quite good. The first thing you notice is the build quality. Behringer got a bit of a poor reputation in guitar circles for putting out cheap plastic-enclosed clones of BOSS pedals. But this interface has a solid metal construction with no immediately-apparent durability concerns.

I opted for the UMC204HD as an affordable all-in-one budget home recording interface with my iPad Pro. For its price point, this unit packs in a lot of functionality. I actually did have a variety of dongles and standalone interfaces to do digital audio conversion, 5-pin DIN MIDI, etc. But it was impractical switching all of these in and out when you only have the single USB jack to work with using the Apple Camera Connection Kit. Now I can record with guitars, line-level audio equipment (synths, drum machines, etc.), and even dynamic and condenser microphones all with one box, and it can also receive and transmit MIDI data using the ports in the back. A good interface that solves all of these problems at once really does a lot to merge music hardware with the software instruments and DAW capabilities on the iPad.

On the negative side, I've heard (but have not experienced yet) some problems with low output if you plug a instrument-level guitar directly into the interface. That might be a concern, though I plan on using it with preamp and cab simulator pedals that shape the sound before it even gets to the interface, so I anticipate being able to compensate for that issue. Also, unless I am mistaken, there is no input for USB MIDI on the UMC204HD. This is almost a nonsensical complaint on a PC, but with an iPad, it does require an external hub to use a MIDI keyboard, assuming that works.

That reminds me: the device is USB powered, so it did require an external USB2.0 hub to supply power to it, as the iPad Pro's power is not enough to run the device. Frankly, I'm not sure I would want draw that much power from the iPad battery anyway, and I had a small hub already on hand. The device seems to work as I intended it to, and time will tell if there are audio quality issues or other concerns I haven't thought of. So far, I'm quite happy with it.
Summary: Versatile, budget-friendly, class-compliant USB audio interface for use with desktop computers or iPad

One weird thing that at first annoyed me that the treble-clef is shown "lower" on the high stickers than the bass-clef is shown on the stickers for the bass notes. When you first start applying the stickers, working out from the center, this seems like a stupid and annoying "got it backwards" design error. Only when you get out to the higher octaves does it start to make sense: they put the treble clef "low" on the sticker, to have room for the higher ledger lines above the staff. Same with putting the bass clef "higher" on the other end of the keyboard, it's to accommodate the additional ledger lines that go below the bass staff.

I think this also explains why a lot of other sets of keyboard stickers do not include the higher and lower octaves. If you try to show the grand staff on each sticker, you will run out of room for additional ledger-lines. So the choice is basically, do you want the stickers to show the grand staff from low to high across the keyboard, and not show the highest and lowest octaves notated, or do you prefer this odd configuration, which shows notation for all 88 keys, but sort of inverts the placement of the treble staff vs the bass staff?

If you have a smaller 49-key keyboard, you might prefer a set with fewer notated keys, but that "looks" more like the grand staff from top to bottom. But if you have a bigger keyboard, you might prefer this set, even though there is kind of an abrupt visual change at middle C.

[[VIDEOID:5107d118d478090262f4e91c71f1d74e]] This 5-in-1 light has 5 modes...surprise surprise!

1-Strobe: Works well. Can adjust the strobe speed from the remote control. Personally I don't use strobe too much for concerts but if you need to plan a Halloween party, this would work well.

2-UV: This black light isn't too bright but it can make bright/white objects glow from about 10-15 feet away.

3-Laser: It has a red and green laser that make circles and patterns. I wish the laser was brighter. Any ambient light will make it difficult to see the laser. To really appreciate the laser effects, you need a nearly dark room. If you have a dark room, the effects are nice.

4-Wash Light: You can change the color of the wash light (solid light) with the remote. I posted a few pictures of the wash light in action along with 2 OPPSK wash lights so you can gauge relative brightness. The 5-in-1 isn't quite as bright as the dedicated wash lights, but is more than adequate for a larger living room area.

5- LED "Rotating Magic Ball"- The rotation LED lights are where this light really "shines". These are very bright and go over a larger area. When placed on a small coffee table, the rotating LED lights fill the entire living room. I have brand name lights which cost 3 times more than this light and I think this light is brighter and has a wider angle. This is perfect for a dance floor or ceiling effects. You can change the color of the rotating LED light. White rotating lights with a blue wash light make for a cool slow dance scene.

Auto/sound mode works well. If you are a DJ you could set this behind you and it would add decent lighting effects to your event.

There are only two downsides I have found with this light:
-With the remote you can't seem to turn on more than one effect at a time, however in auto-mode, more than one effect comes on at a time.
-The magic rotating ball isn't "smooth" when it rotates. It seems to grind some which isn't a problem, but we will see if this impacts the life of the light...but you aren't exactly breaking the bank when you buy this light. The rotation light also doesn't continue in one direction. It goes in one direction for about 180-360 degrees then reverses direction.

Overall I'm impressed with this light. It also comes with a bracket so you can mount it or use the bracket to angle the light.

THIS is the BEST way to split your guitar signal between an amplifier and Rocksmith to eliminate feedback.  Just use a cheap Y fitting to split your guitar signal into 2 imputs into this filter.  Then 2 outputs of this filter will be isolated from each other and you won't get any hum!  I tried using a normal A-B splitter box to send my Bass guitar signal to both Rocksmith and a Separate Amp but I would get lots of feedback.  This is because my PC's power was plugged into a 110V home circuit shared by my amplifier and ground loops caused the feedback.  I opened this up and was pleasantly surprised to find small audio transformers inside that isolate the grounds in the signals.  I tried it and it has been working great for weeks.  If this doesn't eliminate your hum its because there is something wrong with your equipment

Text:
I’ve had this for 2 years. I’m an Army Chaplain and got it for a chapel band. It was originally meant to drive a Roland drum set, but then was found useful as a PA. It is way more capable than originally anticipated.

I’m a Peavey, Marshall, Fender or Carvin fan, so this had to establish its own reputation with me. Well it has proven reliable and flexible. I’ve used it to pump background music for parties with about 75 people in a 50X50 room, used it at a Strong Bonds even in an even larger room with even more people. I’ve used it for ceremonies with a Shure 58 mic and it was very clear and projected well with plenty of power left. I’ve used it for an electric piano and it was clear and captured the frequency needed. I’ve used the Bluetooth, 1/8” plug, the XLR and RCA inputs with no hassle whatsoever. I’ve used the Bluetooth for music while playing electronic drums through it at the same time. It was extremely clear and dynamic. Finally, I’ve used it in a chapel and outdoors to hook up to a TV and it sounded great in every situation –with more volume available than needed.

It even has an SD slot/USB port and music player function, if you use this media. The thing has a remote control too. I’m amazed at everything this simple PA can do and after two years of use I haven’t had a single issue with it. It’s been carried around and thrown in the trunk more than a couple of dozen times too.

When I find a terrific value, I’m obliged to leave a review reflecting my satisfaction as a civic duty. Others ought to know the product’s performance and the manufacturer ought to be praised for their excellent work. Hopefully that’s what I’ve done here.

And where are the 707 or 606 sounds? They are still some of my favorites.
Who are they trying to sell this to? It's the hardware people, who want the above features.
This could have been great. But it missed the mark.
They did give it good build quality, and an attractive design. But what good is it without the features you need?
There are plenty of software emulations of these boxes for 1/4 the price. So why shell out so much for so little?
I was really hoping this would replace my cranky old boxes, but it doesn't.
I'll just have to keep praying the originals don't break down on me... which they haven't in almost 30 years!

Text:
Let me start off by saying I am NOT a Strat / Tele guy. I am more of a Single Cut type of guy with humbuckers. I have always thought that twangy sound from single coils was nice in some instances, but I wanted to strike heavy thick ringing, DRIVEN chords more than anything. Nothing personal against Strats / Tele's etc, but just personally wasn't what my search was about..... Until now.
in 1992 my parents, when I was 15, bought me my first REAL guitar (I had a guitar I was playing prior, a "Harmony" guitar... I put a large bolt about the size of the original bridge in place of where the bridge used to be (first time using it, I lost interest quickly as "Mary Had a Little lamb wasn't what I wanted to play, so it sat in a corner, and the bridge got lost lol) in order to play... I was serious! lol).
That guitar was an Alvarez Dana series electric guitar. Up until a few years ago, I had no idea that was basically a "super strat", but as you delve into guitars, and origins, repair, the whole nine, you learn those things.. lol
Anyway, I still have that Alvarez, but it saw better days. It's pickups were Neck Single Coil, Middle Single coil, and "tri force" bridge humbucker. Apparently that was a pretty impressive pickup, some people still talk about the Tri Force.
Anyway, This guitar was my "practice" guitar for repair, as the bridge was broken, the pickups sounded awful, were rusted, frets needed leveled and crowned, etc. So I took on the project after using it for practice, and wanted to make my folks proud, and bring this back to life like it was (to me) basically 28 years ago.

I bought these Wilkinson Single coils, and MAN.... I don't know what I was expecting, but for the price I wasn't expecting a lot... but I sure got a TON. These things are loud, clear, musical, have that twang, and most of all, match up perfectly with the humbucker I put in there as well!

These pickups sounded so good, they have inspired me to build my own KIT "Strat" style guitar and use these in it!
Don't hesitate to get you some of these pickups, I am glad I did, and I love every minute of them!

All reeds are made of cane, known as Arundo Donax. It is not wood or bamboo, but more closely related to tall grasses. It grows around river banks and lakes with moving water. It absorbs the water for growth and nutrients. It MUST be properly collected when the stalk is drained of water in the winter (dry season) and it must be drained and dried to avoid including biological and chemical impurities. The climate also affects its density, which limits where good reed stock can grow. Cane will absorb whatever is in the water where it grows.

Good reeds should have a smooth vamp (shaped upper part) and have a golden- yellow or light yellow color without much variation. The bark can be of varied tone (glossy-looking bottom part). That's OK. It should not have fibrous longitudinal protrusions on the vamp (part that goes inside the mouth). Green looking reeds have not been properly dried and drained. Throw them away. Grey looking reeds or ones with dark spots or streaks may have mold. Throw them away also. (This is highly unlikely in Vandoren or Daddario reeds).

Good reeds are expensive. However, with proper care, you CAN make them last months.. or longer. Just teach your kids proper care skills. It's a wonderful way to teach being responsible.

Always take the reed off after playing. Always put them back into the holder (or get a special case). NEVER touch the tip of the reed (I see kids do it all the time.. and they break the reeds). Practice securing the reed to the mouthpiece with the ligature without tripping the tip. Carefully wash the reeds with water once a week, wiping with clean fingers, bottom to top. And lastly, don't play one reed all the time. Have a few ready to go and rotate them. If you do this, or teach your kids, a box of quality reeds will last you a very long time... and you won't have to buy cheap non-reeds made in china..

Text:
The NR300 is a decent little pedal. Does what it says it does. It took a little bit of experimentation to get it right, though. It's a little slow to shut the gate, but for the price I wasn't expecting a Decimator II.

For me, I placed the pedal up front, after the wah and Boss Acoustic Simulator (which, if you haven't tried, is brilliant). More importantly, before all of the noisy overdrive and distortion pedals. I also keep the threshold low and the delay at minimum. That way, when I mute the strings, the gate shuts off the sound before it gets distorted so there's no residual noise that has to be shut down making for really quick and clean mutes. Well, as quick as the unit allows. Remember, I said it was a little slow. Not silly slow, though. We're talking milliseconds, not whole seconds. Although, the latter was what I experienced when I put the unit after the distortion. When the gain levels are boosted, the signal is louder and necessitates the need to up the threshold. The problem with that, is if I need to let the distortion ring on, the threshold would kick in and shut it off early. That makes you turn up the delay and really kills the ability to get real quick and clean mutes. Placing the gate before the distortion and turning everything down solves all those problems.
Summary: Takes a little work to get right, but it's good for the money!

The only thing that kept me from giving this product 5 stars is that the holes in the pickguard didn't line up with the ones from the original on my Mexican Strat. I think that two of the eleven were spot-on. Some were off by a lot, but some were off by just a tiny bit. This made it really hard to drill new holes, as the drill bit skipped into the original hole despite my best efforts. I suppose I should have taken the time to first plug the original holes, but I tried to keep them available in case I wanted to go back to the "factory" pickguard and electronics.

Other than that, I couldn't be happier with the sound of the new electronics. The pickups are very clear and have about the same output level as the originals (maybe even a little bit more). Perhaps there are purists who wouldn't be thrilled with them since they don't sound EXACTLY like single-coils. But they are pleasing to my ears. I just hope the pots and switch don't get noisy with age as inexpensive components sometimes do. Time will tell...

I will add that what I DON'T hear makes me even happier than what I do hear. They are vastly more silent. Depending on the amount of gain used in amplification/effects, there is little-to-none of the annoying 60-cycle hum from these puppies! In fact, getting rid of the hum was the reason I purchased this. So mission accomplished on that front.

Bottom line is I'm glad I upgraded my guitar with this product (yes, I consider it an upgrade). And although I would have preferred a white pickguard, the green is light enough in color to not be too objectionable in my opinion, even though my wife said it looks a little "psychedelic".

Text:
While I have heard that these devices can be great for recording concerts and have heard some great recordings to back that claim up my review will be focusing on my main use which is podcasting. After using the Zoom H4N for a few weeks I've found it to be a very versatile tool that should be in any podcaster's arsenal of gear.

I mainly use the H4N to record my podcasts using a Allen & Heath ZED14 mixing board. I usually do a two person podcast where I am in one location and the other person is brought in via Skype. Using the Aux sends of the board and the 4 track mode of the H4N I can record myself in one channel, the other person in another channel and all of the sound effects and music supplied by my iPad into its own stereo channel. This makes editing a breeze as everything is on its own track.

The sound quality of the H4N is excellent and it is very easy to hook up external microphones to the unit. You can hook up either two XLR microphones or two 1/4" jack sources (or a combination) to the bottom of the unit and there is one 1/8" input on the back of the unit that will accept a stereo microphone or any line level stereo source. It's the combination of these that lets me record the podcast onto the 4 separate tracks.

The H4N will also let you record using two attached microphones and the internal microphones at the same time as well, which could be useful if you're looking to capture some background noise if you are recording something on location or say to mix the crowd reaction to a soundboard feed.

Overall this is a great device for podcasters both in the studio and out in the field, letting you produce high quality recordings in both environments. Five stars without a doubt.

Text:
I have owned 3 of these for 2 months. Using Hosa STP-202 insert cables off insert points on our Yamaha soundboard. I use one for Lead vocals, one for Chorus group and one for a group channel which I can group any other vocal or instrument to.

On +/- 12db these things are perfectly responsive to the ear for adjusting a voice or an instrument during a live performance. I am utterly delighted with the performance and effect these things have, they've enhanced our vocals tremendously. Input gain is very sensitive, anything much over unity causes feedback potential, of course.

We have a crystal clear system, I was worried about introducing hum or noise with these... no such problems at all. Would highly recommend these for live applications. They push too much bandwidth around at 9 channels to be used for anything precise... don't expect to dial in your venue with one of these... but to shape any instrument or vocal they are great! Kudos to Behringer for the design and the price. Reviews on their other products leaves one skeptical to purchase their products, but I love these things.
Have purchased 1 more and am planning on yet another for a total of 5.

For the price of two of these one could buy a two channel 15 band eq and double your precision for this same application, but then you start to intimidate people. Our other sound guy is even a little intimidated by these... a little working w/ them he'll love em, I'm sure.

Realistically these are easier to use than the semiparametric 3 band on a mixer's channels and yet work beautifully with them, taking a voice where three bands can't.
Summary: 1 or 2 channels off mixer insert points, excellent

If you end up with a faulty unit I can understand being displeased with the product. But the fact of the matter is, these pedals can only be sold this cheaply when they keep manufacturing costs way down.  That means mass production in China with a tiny chance that you will get a faulty product out of the box.  I own more than half a dozen of these inexpensive Behringer pedals and I have yet to have a single problem, but they do not have the bullet proof construction of some of my more expensive pedals.  If you read the reviews, no one is faulting the tone you are getting for the money. So buy it new and in the off chance you get a lemon, Amazon will make good on your purchase. I am fond of saying that it doesn't matter which type of tuner you use because they've pretty much become a commodity. They all tune well with the same accuracy, so it comes down to looks and price.

I bought the Pro I/O single channel elsewhere, but I review mostly on Amazon, so here's my review... I wish I had bought it here to make my return easy and I'd get a *verified purchase badge for my review too.

**fTHIS IS ONLY TRUE WITH THE DUO VERSION :
"DIRECT MONITOR WITH YOUR HEADPHONES: Connect your earbuds directly to the headphone jack to monitor your sound in real-time, with no latency or echo. Ensure you always sound your best."

There is no direct monitoring on the single-channel, non-duo. This is dumb, because you're out in the field and can't listen back to your microphone with headphones to see if the audio is OK. You have to record, and then play back to check the audio, which isn't in real-time, so you can't constantly monitor to make sure everything is 2irking and you get the best sound plus you can't monitor in real-time to get the best mic placement.
***The absence of this feature makes it nearly useless, and the duo is too expensive and bulky (twice the size) to be practical to strap into a mic pole and be nimble. Imagine doing a whole bunch of work, getting what you thought was the perfect take, just to find out your audio dropped out or something! Ridiculous.

Someone said you need a power supply for direct monitoring. I cannot verify this is true, because it didn't come with a power supplyx and the manual didn't mention direct monitoring at all for the single channel version. Either way, that doesn't help you when you're not near a wall outlet!

For the price, I expected at least direct monitoring right out of the box, on the go.

IT'S NOISY AS HELL!
Unless you have a good quality condenser with a lot of output, you're going to get noise from the built-in preamp. Dynamic microphone? Forget it! You have to boost the mic preamp to 8 or more to get an OK signal, but that will come with hiss. The way around this is to drop another $90 on a Triton Audio FetHead, to get more clean signal from the mic. The trouble is that you will further drain the unit's batteries, defeating one of the purposes of using a dynamic microphone, which is to not use batteries.
Summary: Noisy preamp, single channel version DKRS NOT have direct monitoring

This is a good uke for the price, especially considering it comes with a tuner, a gig bag and a miniature song book to get you started. It's the second one I ordered from Amazon and is far better than the Kala that came first: it is louder with better tone, but most important the intonation is very good.

If you are new to fretted instruments and don't know what good intonation is, what you need to know is that when you play notes down on the neck, the notes will be correct and not sharp or flat. If the intonation is off, no matter how good you get on an instrument, your playing will sound off.

The sound is good for a small instrument made of laminated wood. The tuners are lose and need to be tightened a bit. I've been tuning it for a half hour now and the strings have finally stopped stretching so much that I can finally play chords. Even $3000 ukes with new strings would have the same problem.

As for the complaint about the tuner not being like the one in the picture, it's not a problem because it is a better tuner. The tuner in the picture is half the size of the uke - this one is about the size and weight of two quarters laid side by side. it is much easier to leave on the instrument when playing because it doesn't un-balance it.

I know that if I get better on the uke, I'll want a better instrument, but right now as a beginner, I am very happy with this purchase.

I have purchased several Snark tuners, including the black SN-5 for tuning an electric bass guitar and a dobro. The SN-5 is a decent tuner, it's not as fast to register as the Intelli IMT-500, but it's very accurate. Another plus is the easy to read display. My main problem with the entire Snark product line is the reliability of the swivel joint that couples the arm to the clip and the display. Almost all of my Snark tuners, SN-1 (blue), SN-2 (red), and the SN-5 (black) have broken within the first few months of ownership. Out of 4 purchases, I've got one SN-5 that is still alive. They all break at the same location, the 3 prong clip that grabs the ball on the armature. One of those tabs will eventually break. I've had them break during the first week or last a couple of months. I'm still searching for a great clip on tuner that will work well with both acoustic guitars and electric bass. While the Intel IMT-500 has a great clip, it doesn't register well on the low E string of my Martin guitars or at all with my Fender Jazz bass. It also does a lot of hunting when trying to tune banjo. The Snark SN-5 registers well on bass and dobro, but it's too fragile to be reliable for gigging. Attached is a photo of my last SN-1 that broke. The SN-1,2, & 5 share a common mechanical design with differing color and electronics.
Summary: Works well but not a robust or reliable mechanical design.

Text:
This little amp packs a lot of power in a mighty small package. True, compared to my Champion 40 it just doesn't have the power to compete, but it's a tough call when deciding on a practice amp between this and the Champion 20. The 20 has many more features (and twice the power) however this little dynamo sounds great, really surprises you in overdrive and is extremely portable, making it a wonderful practice amp.
No you won't get the same volume you get from a Champion 20, but you get as much volume as you will need in a practice amp with very little distortion unless you turn the volume to the max on your guitar & amp. The 'overdrive' basically is an on/off switch for the gain, which you can increase or decrease using a rotary knob. I really love the bright, clear, clean sound that this amplifier provides with the overdrive button in the 'off' position, but it's also a lot of fun to turn on the overdrive, turn up the gain and play a little Hendrix.
In power, sound quality and overall quality of this little amplifier is actually quite amazing.
In fact it is hard to believe this little guy only packs a six inch speaker - as the Frontman 10 packs some big sound.
Great for the bedroom, office, basement or to carry to lessons, and at this price you will be very pleased. The Frontman 10 is a Fender product, and this little guy is built with the same great quality as the big Fender amps. I've yet to own a Fender product that I haven't really enjoyed, and this amp is no exception. In fact although I also own two larger & more expensive amplifiers, the Frontman 10 is the amplifier I enjoy using the most, due to it's crystal clear, clean, bright sound - it's actually quite extraordinary in an amp of this size.
Summary: Wow! More than I expected in a tiny amp.

First impressions are are good. Will need to play with it some more to really understand all the setting variations but everything seems to work. I'd say the best part is getting a dmx light that has motion for so cheap. With or without sound-activation it really livens up a room or dance floor. For a huge area you'd want additional units (or a really large one) but for a normal dance floor area or a medium-ish party room you'll be fine. The UV lights on the side are a nice touch but if you really want I major black light effect I suggest you buy multiple, larger black lights. I have an OPPSK UV light bar and while it's pretty good, I would want a few more if I were trying to really bathe large area in black light. In any case this light gives you a measure of the effect without having to buy something more. Don't expect a $200 light for this price. It is what it is but it does a three things for cheap and does them good enough for my purposes (not a career dj using it every weekend or something). Not extremely bright but I have other lights for that while this one adds what I was missing which is some lively action to go along with the music. A nice addition that I'm happy with.

The little remote seems to do the job but in general I prefer to use the buttons on the back of the light to find (visually see the setting) a scene I like and then mainly use the remote to turn it on and of... at least until I get a dmx controller. Works well when you have some some other, static, lights so you aren't left with total darkness when you want a break from all the motion. I don;t have a dmx controller yet so can't speak to how well it works with this light or my other2 OPPSk lights that are on the light stand in my photos.

I'm sure if you a pro dj or something you will want something bigger, badder and brand named but for anybody who throws an occasional party or dj's for dances once in while then this is a great option imo. For someone like me who doesn't want to spend a lot on something that gets used maybe a few times a year this light is great. I could barely rent something for what this costs.

Note that my old smart phone does not do too well with light and color and somewhat darkened rooms! All the colors, from all the lights pictured, are more distinct and vibrant in real life. Not like a high end 150 watt fixtures, but much, much better than the photos would make you think. Hope this helps, thanks for reading.

The obvious competitors for this kind of product are from Behringer and Mackie. They both make compact mixers but what they offer is very different. I found that Alto's mixers sit right in the middle and offer the best of both worlds. This mixer seems to be designed with knowledgeable sound engineers as the intended users. I opted against Behringer's line because they all seem to be riddled with XLR inputs and pretty on-board fx, yet cost merely pennies. Not to be skeptical, but we all know Behringer isn't a "quality" brand, and I wanted to make sure I got something with good pre's that would last me a lifetime. On the other end of the spectrum is Mackie. Their prices suggest top quality preamps, but what they offer in terms of connectivity is lacking (usually a single post-fader aux and a handful of mic inputs). It's also hard to justify spending that kind of coin for a glorified headphone amp.

This Alto mixer on the other hand, has a price that sits right between the "cheap" and the "fancy". It doesn't boast on-board multi-effects but is one of the only compact mixers to offer 2 aux sends (one for monitors and the other for FX), 3-band EQ for each channel, and separate Control Room and Main Mix outputs. This is truly a miniature version of a real live-sound desk. It has the capabilities to simply mix audio going into a computer, or route sound to a PA & monitors and control sound for a small band. The preamps are quiet and deliver enough gain as I would expect at this price. The only bad thing I can say is that some of the knobs are tight while others are really loose. Not a dealbreaker, but I honestly can't find anything wrong with this mixer.

To put it simple, the Alto ZMX862 is a compact mixer that you can buy with confidence. It doesn't boast a price as low as Behringer's equivalent and doesn't promise Mackie's 1st class preamps and performance, but it can handle everything from splitting an iPod signal to mixing a full band.
Summary: Perfect for many applications. Good value

Text:
This is an excellent minimalist pedal board. You can only fit about 5 standard size pedals (size 1590B), or about 7 mini pedals (size 1590A), so it’s intended to just let you travel easily with the bare necessities. You could get creative, and fit a few more if you really Tetris them in there or get creative with the geometry, but It’s not really intended for that. You can’t really fit two rows either, just one nice row down the center. It’s nice metal (steel, aluminum?) construction, and feels very sturdy. It has little plastic feet that are just soft enough you don’t need to worry about it scratching a hardwood floor. Also, I love that it doesn't look cluttered when it's full. See pictures.

It comes with 2 patch cables, each 15 inches long. I measured the stray capacitance of the cables to be 61pf (blue cable) and 76pf (black cable). These are fairly standard “averagely good” capacitance values for the length, and typical of “averagely good” quality cables (not super high end pro-grade, but good). They shouldn’t suck too much tone. The choice to include two 15 inch cables was interesting, instead of a few 6 inch patch cables. . . but really, including ANY patch cables is a bonus. Pedal boards typically don’t come with these at all.

Mine also came with 40 inches of Velcro (more than the 28 inches advertised), which is more than enough to cover both top and bottom strips of the pedal board, which is only 14 inches long by 5 ½ inches wide. The strips of Velcro are just a bit too wide (maybe a millimeter or two) for the pedal board, but it’s not a problem at all. You’ll even have about a foot of Velcro left over for some other pedals, or whatever.

You can NOT fit a brick-shaped pedal board power supply underneath, even a small/thin one, but there’s really no reason to. Since you can only fit 5 or so pedals, a simple daisy-chain power cord works fine. Yes, I understand the limitations of those, but this is intended to be a super compact rig, and so a few sacrifices are in order. However, when you need a super compact, but sturdy rig, this fits the bill.

Since it’s only 14 inches long, it easily fits in an old laptop case, which leaves plenty of room for some other gear too. I think there is a version of this that comes with a carrying bag, but I didn’t get that version, and my old laptop case works fine. I think the version with the case can fit over the top of a gig bag, which might be nice. . . but really, I don’t have any issue throwing it in a laptop case with my cables and sheet music, and other stuff.

The whole pedal board is pretty low profile, and while you can’t fit a PS underneath, you CAN easily route your patch cables underneath. It also came with some zip ties, I presume to help tidy up your patch cables, but I don’t use these. They are slightly too permanent of a solution, and I move stuff around a lot, so I prefer velcro ties.

My board also came with a nice hand-written note, and two random acoustic guitar strings. Not two SETS, just two individual strings. . . for an acoustic. I think it’s on the rarer side for an acoustic player to be using many pedals. . . but I suppose it happens. Still, including a random 010 gauge and 016 gauge 75/25 bronze acoustic strings makes zero sense to me. Maybe in a pinch they could work for a broken E or B? But they are for acoustic? Maybe for these lighter gauges they are all steel and may still work for electric, and they’re just trying to give you a spare, if you break an E or B? Still odd.

On the whole, for a minimal rig, this really is a great pedal board. I highly recommend it. The board itself is good, plus it comes with plenty of Velcro and a few patch cables. The handwritten note was a nice touch, but I just didn’t understand why the 2 random acoustic strings were in there. All told, this was an easy 5 stars! I'm very happy with it!
Summary: Excellent mini pedal board for a very minimal/portable rig - fits in a laptop case!

I consider this to be absolutely amazing and well beyond what I was hoping for.

Now I paid good money for that DAC and its well worth its cost and then some IMO; it still is the single best audio purchase i have ever made. This cart obviously has varying defects in reproduction compared to it and truth be told, it's not worth going over. What is most important to note is that there is zero problems with any sort of sibilance. It has pretty much bomb proof tracking @ 1.8g and beyond. For my ears 1.9g had the best sound on my Sony PS-X2 and its stock tone arm and an Audio Technica AT-HS10 headshell.

What impressed me most is how clearly synthesized sounds sound synth and how naturally correct brass horns and anything stringed. The instrument separation, soundstage, everything is rendered in just a lovely and natural way.

I purchased this amp in 2005 to use in church as my monitor and DI for an acoustic electric guitar. I was totally happy with the natural acoustic sound, and the amp had more than enough power to fill the church on the few occasions where the main PA failed.

My criticisms may be minor to some, and admit that I am very picky:

1) I really wish that the line level XLR outputs had a switchable pad to allow for connection to a microphone level input. As it stands I need to use a XLR attenuator or direct box to tame the signal by -20 db. It works fine but it is another piece of gear I have to remember to bring along.

2) I would have also liked a sturdier kickstand clip -- the stock nylon clip is reminiscent of an old zip tie, and it broke one winter's day -- not at all consistent with the rest of the package.

3) I like the shoulder bag but the strap gets cinched at it's attachment point on the bag. Also, the strap cannot be shortened maximally, and there is no top handle on the bag, which means it has to stay on your shoulder or you need to use two hands to carry the bag.

Ultimately I decided it was easier to carry the unit by the handle and only use the bag to protect it in my vehicle. Nevertheless, the true test of this unit is that I have continued to use it for the past 4 years, even after experimenting with all sorts of direct box combinations including a Roland AD-8, Roland CM-30 monitor, Behringer GI-100, UltraSound PDI, Demeter Tube Direct, and BBE DI-1000 direct boxes. I still use this amp with a Guild Peregrine, a Whirlwind -20 db XLR pad, a Korg CA-30 tuner, and a FS-5L switch to control muting.

At that point a metric socket can unclamp the power cord. When I soldered on the new cord, one of the terminals came loose from the PCB board but fortunately it was able to be reattached. While I was there I sprayed the pots and dusted it out. I can now see the value of having a detachable power cord. I turned the kickstand around as it had gotten bent out of shape over time. Amp still functions perfectly. Also, I'm now using the 1/4" output into a JDI direct box because the small XLR pads kept breaking and making lots of noise. My wish list for this amp would be a true effects loop, better built in direct out with pad, and courtesy AC outlet. Maybe also a built in tuner.
