I've worked with Teac/Tascam equipment for like, 40 years. In fact, I still have two of their reel-to-reels, a 2 and a 4 track, that I've had since the 1970s, and a 4-track Portastudio cassette deck from a couple of decades later, and they all still work. The tech is out of date, so I don't use them except to digitize my old tapes, but they still work. Well designed with attention to details, and solidly built. They set the quality standard for decades.

However, I don't get the sense that the new hand-held digital recorders are up to those standards anymore. Read the reviews of the recent Tascam recorders. Some don't do WAV format without a time-consuming conversion. Most don't come with an A/C adapter. Some are noisy or sensitive to RF interference. Lack of durability is a common complaint. Some of these things may seem minor quibbles for a cheap recorder, but they reveal a lack of attention to detail.

Zoom on the other hand seems to get it. My purchase of the H4n is my third zoom device, and for each one my response was the same-- they exceeded my expectations. The only area for this device that didn't was the price-- at this writing, it's going for a full 2X the price of the roughly feature-equivalent Tascam DR-40. And close to 3X the price of a DR-006. And I like to be as frugal as the next guy. But I want something that works well, and is reliable, otherwise, what's the point? In this case, I think what you get for the money here is well worth it. Here's some of the features of the H4n that sold me on it:

Solid construction
Able to record all 4 channels at once
Guitar-oriented effects chain, amp modeling, etc.
WAV format (also does Mp3, but I usually want WAV).
AC adapter included

Necessary features that all the competing recorders have:

Ability to take a 2 track recording and record one or two extra tracks along with it
SD card storage (all include a 2G but can handle up to 32G)
Built-in stereo microphones
AA battery operation as well as (often optional) AC adapter
Stereo Line-in capability
Headphone/Line Out

So yeah, I could have saved some money, but I think in this case you get what you pay for. Some of the incidental extras that exceeded my expectations with the Zoom were:

Foam wind screen
Durable (rigid but not brittle, PVC?) plastic protective case
Free Cubase LE download
Mic stand adapter (will fit into a standard dynamic mic sleeve)
MicroSD to SD card adapter (memory card supplied was a microSD)

I thought the SD card adapter was a particularly nice touch, again -- attention to detail.

So if price is what's most important, by all means, buy one of the others. And while it smarts to pay nearly $300 when I could have gotten nearly the same functionality (supposedly, anyway) for half as much, I don't think I'll regret the confidence I have in its ability to perform and hold up in any normal music recording situation-- and my music is important to me...
Summary: Dependable & full featured.  Zoom gets it right

There's a little button on the unit that flips the digital display, so it still reads right-side-up if you install it on the under side of your instrument, like I did. I was complimented by a fellow mandolin player recently on my ability to tune by ear. He didn't see a tuner, so he thought I wasn't using one. I laughed and flipped over my mandolin to show him my "stealth" tuner.

These tuners work well. I've tested them by using them at the same time as two other types of tuners and they showed the same results. If the note is right on, the letter will display in green with one bar on either side. The letter changes color if the note is out of tune and the number of bars to the left or right of the letter increase, depending on how flat or sharp the note is.

The second thing is that the "Sapphire Mix Control" was not very intuitive. It reminded me a lot of PC software, where everything is overcomplicated and overdone. This pickup has a good physical design and is manufactured well. The sound is very thin and the output is extremely weak and so it should be used with a preamp or sound modeler to be totally useful. I bought two of these and put one on a Gibson J200 and one on an imported Fender 12 string and the output from both pickups was so low that a tc Helicon modeler with tuner wouldn't activate steadily enough to even tune the guitars. I even tried mounting the unit so close to the strings that they touched it when fretting high notes, and it still didn't have the output to activate the tuner long enough to tune a single string. I had been using a $15 HDE pickup on these guitars and thought that I would upgrade to something that had so many good reviews. What a total disappointment. The HDE pickup has much better frequency reproduction (lows and highs) and has enough electrical output to activate my tuners even when the strings are lightly plucked.

The Markley pickup produces a very tinny, metallic sound even when adequately amplified. Frankly, it bears no resemblance to the sound of an acoustic guitar. It's more like a very poor quality hollow-body electric. After 45 years of playing just about every kind of guitar and amplification system I would have to recommend that you search out something better than this for amplifying an acoustic guitar. I love the convenience of Amazon, but the majority of the reviews for this product were incomplete and in my opinion incorrect. I should have gone down to the music store and researched pickups before purchasing--unfortunately I believed the reviews. Shop around and if your local music store has some demo units you should try to find a product that performs better than this one. It's a shame really. The design and construction are so well done. It's like a Ferrari without an engine--looks great in the driveway but can't get you down to the grocery store.

I have several trombones, have played semi-professionally in the past, and this caught my eye. I took the plunge and bought it. I've encountered plastic trombones before - someone I play with in a marching band uses one. It has some obvious advantages.

It makes sense to use this instead of a far more expensive instrument on the street. It's a lot lighter than a brass trombone, also important when marching any distance. It's supposedly more resistant to casual bumps, etc. It can be used without having to lubricate the slide. It should be easier to use in cold weather jobs. So for marching purposes, this makes a lot of sense.

The sound is decent considering the construction and materials, surprisingly so. I wouldn't use it for symphony work, but it's not bad. It's comfortable to hold, and easy to assemble. The bell section goes onto the slide with a simple friction lock; the joint there and the slide are both molded with projections that make it difficult to assemble it in any but the correct way.

The carrying bag is simply that - a bag with no cushioning to protect the trombone. It does make it easy to carry though and is very compact. The plastic mouthpiece that comes with it is comfortable and plays well, and the Conn 2 metal mouthpiece I normally use works just fine with the horn also.

I'm taking an extended trip; this trombone is compact enough and light enough that I plan to take it with me. I have a suitcase long enough to fit it in comfortably with room to spare. I have a concert coming up, so this will let me practice while I'm away.

I may revisit this review after more time with the horn, but so far I'm very pleased with it.
Summary: Portable, light weight, and decent sound

The idea of the Zero-Glide is great, but getting the nut to fit is no fun.  May not have helped that my guitar's neck is 1 11/16 inch, for which there is no Zero-Glide nut.  Stewart Mac suggested I buy the nut with the closest string spacing without going wider.  That is what I did, but then spent about 10 minutes each day for 2 weeks to file it down, and it still wants a little more.  Really hard material, but brittle as well.  I tried using a vice to hold the nut and speed the filing, but that only cracked the top of the nut and a small part of it chipped off; fortunately it is still usable, so I continued filing by hand.  I've reached the point where it fits okay for now so I stopped until I change strings next time, when I will file a bit more to even the bottom up.  It does sound good, though, so when all the work to make it fit is forgotten, I will be quite happy with it.

The Rosen Solid Top Dreadnought Acoustic Guitar is a starter guitar, so we need to think about it that way. This isn't a name brand and is about half the price of a named brands starter. There is no installed tuner and the one it comes with isn't good at all, but your cell phone can download good ones for free anyway. The strings it comes with are okay, but give it a very "tinny and twangy" sound that isn't very enjoyable. I immediately replaced the strings with a much nicer set.

When tuned with a good set of strings the Rosen Solid Top Dreadnought Acoustic Guitar is a decent sounding guitar with smoother action than I expected and is perfect for any beginner. It comes with a case, strap and starter picks also.

All-in-all, as someone with 8 guitars, I would definitely buy this guitar for any beginner in my life. It is perfect for the beginners in your life.
Summary: Great starter guitar with decent sound and good action, once better strings installed.

I understand that this is a cheap guitar and you get what you pay for. I had two of these and both of them had some issues.

1. This thing smells awful fresh out of the box. I'm pretty sure I was exposed to numerous carcinogens. It would probably air out eventually, but I sent this puppy back already.

2. Numerous high frets caused buzzing and some notes to be the same on different frets. I'm sure that with a good set up these issues could be fixed, but again I sent this puppy back.

3. The fret edges are very sharp. To the point that my fingers were scratched from playing for less than a half hour. Filing down the fret edges is time consuming if you do it yourself and expensive if you send it out.

I wasn't expecting a perfect guitar for this low of a price, but I was expecting something that was playable. All in all it looked like a toy and didn't feel much better. Evaluating controller keyboards comes down to few main concerns: Playing feel and ease of access/functionality of the onboard controls. Overall construction and durability usually rounds it out.

I have access to a number of acoustic and electronic keyboards and hope to give a sense of where the Samson Graphite Controller slots in: The semi-weighted action of the white keys is slightly softer than those on the M-Audio Axiom61. The Samson keys spring back more crisply, which I prefer for repeated notes and overall control of articulation. In contrast, the white leys of the Axiom feel noticeably `mushier' and tend to slow me down.

The difference in the black keys is, curiously, even more pronounced: the Samson keys are considerably softer than the Axiom and all the other keyboards I compared - including an Alesis Q25 that doesn't even pretend to be semi-weighted. It's quite unexpected - but nice to play - particularly if your setup has the keyboard at desktop level where your finger/hand leverage may not be optimal, compared to sitting at an acoustic piano.

The keyboard itself is surprisingly rugged and I'd have no qualms transporting it in a live setting - whether that be a gig or someone's house for a party. The Samson works fine on USB power and did not require a specialized driver on Windows 7 64-bit. It uses a `D-shaped' USB plug at one end and the cable is included. There's a 9v DC power input if you want to omit the computer and go old school to control a synth or sound module directly - but there's no power adaptor included - my guess is the majority of users will be USB-based.

The layout in the pictures is clear but, for comparison, the sliders, buttons, knobs and rhythm pads are positioned very similarly to those on the Axiom. In line with the overall durable construction, these controls feel a bit more substantial and all worked as expected. I found the LED screen more highly contrasted and easier to read than the Axiom's.

For notation input I tried the Samson with Finale 2014, Sibelius 7 and a recent version of Notion: it was detected fine and performed with acceptable latency. I played it `real-time' through Kontakt 4 using `Alicia's Keys' and an M-Audio sustain pedal and it sounded terrific. I also `step-sequenced' it using Reason 5, Ableton 9 and Sonar X1: I was able to map controls easily and found it responsive and comfortable.

Finally, I recommend giving some thought to the range of keyboard that suits what you do - it can be frustrating to run out of keys at creative moments. I find 49 keys very usable for entering notation and experimenting with sounds. In such `non-real time' contexts I can make do with the octave shift buttons. But for actual playing, composing , working out harmony, arranging, orchestrating, etc., 61 is the practical minimum and, let's face it, 88 is best.

Some acoustic purist friends laugh when I talk about subtleties of synth and controller keyboards. To some people they're toys that don't deserve serious consideration. But I spend time in both classical and contemporary worlds and like to think I can appreciate the expressive potential in both kinds of instruments. As I like to say, it's ultimately the music not the tool. I'd recommend the Samson Graphite as a solid, responsive tool that'll meet a lot of needs - the rest is up to you.

I have to disagree with the other reviewer who said this pedal doesn't play well with other pedals. It does, indeed, play very well with all other twenty pedals on my board. I absolutely love this compressor. I have played around with the toneprint and the vintage settings, but where this pedal really shines is the Spectra setting. You basically get your signal split into three different eq sections and compressed separately; so what this means is that everything sounds even without being overbearing like some other compressors out there. There is also a blend control to keep your dry signal in the mix.
I personally don't like a squashed tone for most the music I play. I primarily play praise & worship but also occasionally play in a gospel funk group. For the latter, I opt to use the vintage mode as it does squash your sound more, and hence appropriate for funk (and country) styles. With my church, I use the Spectra setting. It's one of my few "always on" pedals and I couldn't be happier with it.
All in all this is a great compressor and sounds amazing for church or funk styles. I can't speak to how this pedal sounds for extreme gain, but for moderate gain and overdrive it does great. As with any compressor that I have EVER tried, there is some associated hiss. That is to be expected as when the sound is being evened out, some extraneous noise gets into the mix. That's why I use as noise gate and I would recommend that to everyone as well regardless of your compressor choice. If this were to be stolen, I would definitely get another (and hunt down whoever stole it - lol).

I have to admit that I'm still quite new to all things MIDI, and it was a constant frustration to me that so many of the inexpensive MIDI controllers are USB-only. So, if you have an older MIDI keyboard (with the 5-pin DIN round connection) or a piece of hardware that only accepts old-school MIDI connections (including the popular Korg Volca series), your options become limited.

The midiplus Tbox 2x2 is a sturdy metal box approximately 3.75" x 2.5" x 1.5" in size. It rests on rubber feet and is built like a tank. It has two MIDI In/Out connections (as seen in the picture) for a total of 32 MIDI channels. But to be honest, I only wanted it for the most basic MIDI functions, such as hooking up a keyboard to a computer DAW, or sending MIDI sequencer data to a Korg Volca. The Tbox could not be more beginner-friendly. There's no drivers to install or anything to do other than plug it into the USB jack. My Windows 10 computer instantly recognized it and any MIDI-supporting program listed it as an input or output.

Even better, the Tbox 2x2 is a class-compliant (and USB-powered) MIDI device. This allows it to be plugged into a PC, Mac, and even iOS. Plug a 5-pin MIDI keyboard into the Tbox, and then run the USB output of the Tbox into a Camera Connection Kit into the Lightning jack of your iDevice - it worked instantly and with no discernible latency. There are cheap Chinese cables you can try for less than $10, and name brands sold at Guitar Center and elsewhere for $30 to $40. I've seen spotty reviews of those, and think that this is a much better option. It just works.
Summary: Sturdy 5-pin DIN MIDI interface for connecting traditional MIDI devices to PC, Mac, or iPhone/iPad

Text:
I've had the mic for two weeks now and I'm using it w/a Canon HV30 and a NRG 59111 bracket. In quiet shooting situations, the mic will pick up a lot of motor noise if mounted directly to the camera; this is normal. The bracket suspends the mic about 5" above the camera and motor noise pickup is eliminated. The supplied windscreen does a pretty good job. I would prefer if there was a "power on" LED to serve as a reminder to shut the mic off but that would just draw power too. I understand the rationale behind not having one, but want one anyway. The mic cord is NOT detachable as shown in the picture. Maybe newer versions are, but the one I received does not detach. The shockmount is not that great. The upper/lower parts of the mount are connected by hard rubber squares. So, it's not really "shock mounted" but more of a "dampened mounted." Some handling noise/tapping the camera will be picked up by the mic. This is due to the "not really a shockmount" shockmount.

That said, I'm very happy with it. Note: This is not a shotgun mic, so don't expect to pickup conversation-level sound from 30 feet away. This mic is a true stereo mic and outputs two distinct L/R channel. This mic beats the pants off the stock in-camera mics in every way. There is much more clarity as compared to the stock mic. The best way to describe it is that with the stock mics, all the sounds are "mixed together and indistinct." Whereas with the SMX-10 each sound "stands out from all the others." Frequency response is also better with the SMX-10; I find there is a lot more high-end frequency information in recordings made with it vs. stock.

The mic is very light, not too long (doesn't hang over the front of the camera) and the cord is of the coiled variety so it doesn't hang all over the place. It's designed very well. Body is all-aluminum and very solid feeling. Switches are recessed into the body of the mic, so it would be very difficult to accidently slide them one way or the other. There really isn't anything else in it's price range that is better. Another option/very popular video mic is the Rode Stereo Videomic, but it is literally 2x the price and twice the size. I took a chance with the SMX-10 and am very happy with my purchase.
Summary: Great external mic for the Canon HV30

Text:
I've tried two of these now with the same result. I bought it at full price and was riddled with drop outs so I returned it. I saw it again on a lightning deal during prime day and decided to try again as it was too good of a price to pass up. Maybe the first one was just a bad unit? (Spoiler alert, it wasn't.)

At first, everything seemed like it was going to be awesome. I charged the battery to full, then took it for a spin. Everything paired quickly and seemed great. My studio is in the corner of a very large finished basement so I walked around. Everything was great. Walked up to the main level and walked around... no drop outs. Impressive. Walked up to the second story... still no drop outs. I was shocked. I was in the furthest corner of the second story and still jamming away.

Then I walked back down to the basement. I got 2ft from it... drop out. Not even for a note or two, it dropped for about 10 seconds. "Hmm... that was weird." So I played more while right next to it. When I'm close to it, I'm lucky to go two minutes without a significant drop out where it has to rescan and reconnect. I have tried every group and troubleshooting technique in the manual with no results.

I do have 3 wireless access points in the house, though they're not super close to my pedal board. Next gig is in a few weeks but I don't trust this thing at all. If the wifi really is the problem then if you live in a super connected house like mine this is probably a non-starter.

Before I bought this I tried the Line6 G50 and I had no issues with that one at all. My only beef with it was it didn't fit on my pedal board, but I might just have to move some stuff around and make it fit because it at least worked, despite being a bit dated.

Additionally, once the rubber cover is pulled back on the body pack to charge the battery you can't get that flap to go back on, which was quite frustrating as well. (UPDATE: This was not a problem with the second unit, only the first.)

In summary, this could be environmental. But if it can’t hang in my house I have no idea how it would hold up in a venue. During practice it would drop out for sometimes twenty seconds, once perfectly timed starting with the first note of a lead and lasted the entire thing, so I certainly won't experiment with it live and just must be returned.

My other gripe with it (other than the fact that it doesn't work), I would opt for one without a tuner if it could be smaller. Because of the inconsistency, even if I had kept it, I would have to keep a tuner on my board anyway. I have a very hard time believing anyone would have 100% consistency in a venue with this unit and you'd have to switch to cable at some point. If you rely on this tuner, where does that then leave you? Nowhere good. So this unit either needs a direct in bypass or drop the tuner.
Summary: It's super reliable... at dropping signal

The cymbals:
18" ride - very nice bounce from the sticks, great for practicing at low volume. Great for working on your "Jazz Ride" pattern(s). Great for crashing, very low volume when crashed, Id say more than 80% reduction in volume when crashed on. Also a ton of stick definition. Great for paying attention to all those little subdivisions when playing your ride. Lets you really hone in on your ride cymbal when keeping Jazz time.
16" crash - feels like a real crash when struck, sounds like a real crash as well. Pretty amazing how real it sounds and how low the volume is. Awesome for low volume practice. As they advertise Id agree the volume is reduced by at least by 80%
14" Hi Hats - produce the "chick" sound nicely when played with the foot, not *quite* the same as regular hh's but very close, MUCH closer to anything else made for a reduced volume that Ive ever tried - leaps and bounds better than using regular hi hats with cymbal mutes on them FYI - Only minor complaint would be that when played with the foot they sort of sound a bit like a tambourine, you do still get a chick sound but with a tambourine-esque tone mixed in. When played with the sticks they sound great, both open and closed sounds are at an equally reduced volume (perfect balance between the two). The hi hats are very quiet and very close to real hi hats.
By comparison using cymbal mutes in conjunction with real hi hats:
When played open (open hi hat sound) there is a loud predominant CLANK instead of a smooth swish and/or when quickly opened and closed "hi hat bark"... very non-musical.
In contrast L80 hi hats are almost exactly like real hi hats, but at a very reduced volume. Zildjian did a great job with these. Very nice.

And as if it should ultimately matter, they do look cool as well - see the pictures - look better on my practice set than expected - although tbh I was under the impression they would look good, just a pleasant surprise they do look so nice.

Highly recommended if you want "authentic" sounding (and feeling) reduced volume cymbals.

Massive QC problem but I feel the problem is deeper at the design level. Generally, you think reverse engineers would stay out of design space but not here. The chamfer on the locking pin is gone, the throw of the lock is shorter. The V seems more U shaped which just makes it harder to put on.

Combine these design elements with poor QC and you end up with a recipe for paying fender to your guitar at risk.

Text:
We have a lot of ukulele players in my community and in fact, there's a group that practice weekly together. Ukuleles have become popular with many major artists though its roots began in Hawaii. The most notable song played that you may have heard is "Under the Rainbow", which has become popular amongst many players and on YouTube.

I have been playing the Banjo and electric guitar for some time, and I wanted to try this ukulele out. The kit comes with a owner's manual and guide that includes a few chords and two songs (Imagine and Somewhere Over the Rainbow).

There is a nice padded black nylon gig bag with a small exterior zippered compartment to place spare strings and a nylon carrying handle.

The ukulele is made of mahogany with a nice rosewood fretboard and bridge. The Rosette and frets inlays have inlaid abalone. The tuners appear to be simulated mother of pearl. The standard wood in a ukulele is koa.

The size, weight and balance are perfect for a beginner or intermediate player. This particular model is a Soprano or Standard ukulele. This particular model has a warm tone. The body is in a figure 8 pattern. This has four nylon strings which I tuned in C (G-C-E-A).

Tuning this instrument was pretty easy using a digital tuner, which is not included. However, digital tuners aren't terribly expensive ($15-$30, on average). You can use a piano, which I could have done also. I acquired the Hal Leonard App from the Apple AppStore which you can use to tune the ukulele by ear, and learn a lot about how to get up and running with playing. Being a four stringed instrument, it's not complicated to learn.

Considering entry level ukuleles run around $40-$70, and custom professional ukuleles run in upwards of a few thousand dollars, this is a great instrument for learning or getting started.

Two thumbs up!
Summary: Nice moderately priced entry level ukulele

I am a professional guitar tech of 40 years, which means pretty much nothing... other than the fact that I am constantly fixing and replacing guitar output jacks. I have seen every output jack there is, from Russian to Asian and everything in between.

The USA-made Switchcraft #11 and this longer bushing version, the L11, have been used on every American made Strat and Les Paul since both their inceptions. Besides the much higher quality metal and phenolic material used on this jack compared to jacks made overseas, the clever design of the spring is actually "two springs in one". This double-sprung tip not only gives the #11 a positive feel when you plug in your cord, it also makes for a better electrical & ground connection. It forces the plug shaft to touch the jack's inner sleeve harder which makes for a better ground connection, even after years of use when the plug and jack have become a bit oxidized.

A word of warning... Due to the Switchcraft's slightly larger heft than most Korean jacks, sometimes the fit may be a little tight when installing it into an Asian guitar. You may need to make room for the larger diameter or longer spring length and / or throw.

I can't say enough great things about the Switchcraft #11. It is the ONLY jack to use on a guitar!

ps. this does not hold true for Switchcraft's (or any other manufacturer's) barrel jacks. They ALL stink! : )

I was not paid in any way for this review and I am not affiliated with Switchcraft in any way.

This review is for the Pyle PMKSH04 Suspension Boom Scissor Microphone Stand.

When I ordered this I really didn’t have high expectations; let me tell you how pleasantly surprised I was.

We are using two of these in our studio along with the LEAGY L-58 Home Recording Sound Studio Dynamic Pro Audio Condenser Microphones.

I was skeptical on whether or not it would be strong enough to hold up the microphones when extended from a distance. I found that the scissor stand was able to reach further than I expected and still be positioned out of the way so it wasn’t blocking our faces. It held up really well with only about a half inch drop when fully extended after setting the position. This can easily be compensated for by just positioning it a half inch higher than needed before using it.

For the cost the construction was very good. These have been connected and removed several times and there is no ware on it as I can see. They hold tight to the table where attached and move freely for adjusting. The only complaint I have is that the screw on the base of the clamp when left loose tends to loosen up even more. For our needs it is beneficial to be able to swivel the boom from side to side. To solve this I just removed the hand twist screw and put a nut on the end; then screwed it back in; by using the nut to secure the screw in place it solved the problem.

The XLR cable is permanently threaded through the boom and is a nice feature. The cable isn’t a great length, but for plugging into a mixer you have more than enough cable.

Final conclusion
Well worth the money. It is more than you can expect from anything priced under a hundred dollars.
Summary: You don't have to look at anything else!

Text: My son and grandson both play guitar (both acoustic and electric guitar) and I thought they might like trying to play/learn a similar stringed instrument.  They both loved this banjo and have been having fun learning tunes to play on it.  Music is wonderful, but playing music is a gift that each person should try with whatever instrument they like and feel comfortable with.  Stringed instruments are my own favorites - I play a lap steel guitar - it is played very different than this banjo (and acoustic/electric guitars) so was not really in a place where I could play it.  Lap steel guitars do not have raised fret boards and you do not play chords with finger placement - they are placed with a slide placed against the strings.  I also play the hammered dulcimer - a stringed instrument - which is played with wooden hammers, so my own instruments are not easily interchangeable with this banjo unlike my son and grandson.  The full-size banjo I received had all the accessories including a nice carry bag and with a little bit of tuning, it was ready to play.  My son in particular is really having a blast learning to play Dueling Banjos on the banjo with his son (my grandson) playing the dueling part on his acoustic guitar.  If you have a guitar player in the family or someone wanting to learn to play the banjo, this is a nice and very reasonably-priced one.
Summary: Great qualify for a decent price

I bought this for podcasting, so I could use the mix-minus technique over Skype. I found a video on YouTube that described how (with this exact mixer). It took awhile to get used to the setup, but then I finally got it. I routed the audio to an external recording device with no problem.

However, this device has no on/off switch. So I had to plug in the power supply through the rear port, which was not easy to do. At first I always made sure to unplug it after I used it. Then I began to use the mixer as a way to use a decent mic over conference calls during COVID, sometimes (unitentionally) leaving the power supply plugged in for a few days afterwards. That was a mistake, and it didn't take long for something to go wrong. The power on the Behringer mixer is now dead, and although my computer still recognizes the USB input when it's plugged in, there's no power for the device and therefore it's now useless.

There might be better ways to do podcasting now, 18 months later. I'm going to look into some of the online services that allow you to record in the cloud... and also look into audio interfaces and apps that might allow me to record an interview onto separate tracks without needing to use a mixer anymore.

I wish the Behringer had an on/off switch. I could have avoided this issue, because apparently the power supply burns out really easily.

I had never used a strobe tuner before and, when I saw them, they appeared to be confusing. I was wrong. I was using this tuner literally within seconds of clamping it to my guitar head. Some of the Q&A questions indicate there's some confusion about how these tuners work and that's perfectly understandable. Just think of it as a very accurate chromatic tuner. Nothing could be simpler. It tells you what note your playing and you just adjust each string until the squares stop spinning. It's that simple. It's as easy to use as a regular chromatic tuner. That said, I don't think this is a true strobe tuner because I think of those as using a blinking strobe light which this obviously doesn't have. But as far as I can tell, this simulates a regular strobe digitally with great accuracy.

The only reason I am giving this one star is that I'm a bit disappointed with Peterson's customer support. After receiving the tuner, I contacted them to ask if there was some kind of documentation that gave better descriptions of the many sweetened tunings that come installed on the tuner from the factory and also the tunings for download on their site. They did get back to me within a day but they didn't answer my question. Instead, they sent me a bunch of links to information that had absolutely nothing to do with my question. I wrote back to let them know that they didn't answer my question but they never responded to that message. Then after I registered on their site and signed in, I couldn't download more sweeteners. I contacted them and they, again, got back to me within a day and said I had never registered. But not only did I have the confirmation that I had registered but when I tried to download a sweetened tuning and a message popped up saying I had to register, I went to the registration page and it said I was already registered (???). It must have been a glitch in their system because I could download sweetened tunings the next day.

I guess it's because I'm getting old but their website didn't seem user-friendly at first. But after a little time, I had it pretty much figured out and was able to delete all the sweetened tunings that have no application for guitar and download a couple that do that didn't come pre-installed on the tuner. However, since I often play in Drop-D and Double Drop-D, I downloaded those sweetened tunings and they were terrible. The low E string was way off with those tunings so I deleted them and simply used their standard sweetened tunings and dropped the E(s) down. I now have on my tuner the following tunings: EQU (standard tuning), ACU (the James Taylor tuning) GTR (for my electric guitar), 12s (for my 12-string guitar) and a couple others. Deleting all the tunings that have no use for guitars just eliminated having to possibly scroll through them but the tuner has a great feature that, by default, puts the tunings that you use most tunings at the top of the list and adjusts the list according to how often you use each tuning.

At first, I was a little worried as I played around with deleting and adding tunings that I might mess up something but I quickly found that you can revert back to the factory set of tunings instantly. But that really isn't necessary once you figure out how things work on Peterson's site and if I can do that quickly, just about anyone can.

All-in-all and so far, I really like this tuner. I just wish Peterson's customer service was a bit better but, again, they did respond quickly to my questions. They just didn't answer them.
Summary: Excellent tuner but Peterson has a bit to be desired for their customer service.

It has a MASSIVE variety of expertly done pedal sims as well as great amp sims. Some of the pedals included (Lexicon Reverb, Digitech Whammy) are worth the price of admission alone. Also, if you are looking for the "church sounds" (swells, delays, etc.), you can save a lot of cash and dial it in flawlessly. It may not be TC Electronic and Strymon, but no one in the crowd will know the difference.

I will tell you now that other than changing your strings to a lighter or heavier gauge, there is not a cheaper way to change the tone of your guitar. You don’t realize just how much the plastic nut, saddle, and bridge pins muddy up the sound until you upgrade to bone. With a little know-how, sanding, and patience, you can improve your guitar’s sound, tone, and resonation.

This purchase was actually a replacement for a nut in the Blisstime nut, saddle, and bridge pins set that I ended up sanding down to far and couldn’t use. So For about a week I was just playing with a bone saddle and bridge pins and the stock plastic nut on my Alvarez until the new nut came in. During that time, I wasn’t loving the sound. I didn’t seem to hear that dramatic difference in the tone and resonation that I was expecting to hear and was kinda bummed. But once I got the replacement nut, sanded it right this time, and installed it, it was amazing to hear the difference. I didn’t think the nut had that much to do with the sound but it evidently does. It seemed to complete the tonal transformation. It has noticeably improved the sound of my guitar in terms of tone, brightness, clarity, sustain, and resonation. I can literally feel the vibrations of the guitar against my body a lot more now. I highly recommend upgrading.

Advice for sanding: Sand initially with 120 grit paper. This will bring you down to where you need to be quickly. Once you’re where you need to be, you can polish with 320 or 400 real quick to make it buttery smooth before installing. Take your time, make sure the pieces are flush on the paper and distribute the pressure evenly. I didn’t do this the first time and I ended up with an uneven sanding job. My attempt to even it out again brought it down too far and had to be throw away. Sand for 10-15 seconds and then check. No one ever won a trophy for sanding the fastest

Text:
People love the Yeti, at least to judge by most of its reviews on Amazon. Let me tell you why I don't.

I bought it because the Yeti offers a functionality -- USB, and a choice of four polar patterns -- that you won't find on any comparable product, and the price is on the low end. Plus, it looks cool.

But you get what you pay for: the build quality is junk. Seriously, the screws that hold it in the stand are the cheapest plastic you can imagine -- I worried they'd break as I struggled to loosen them to set up the mike. The volume control knob on the front is flimsiest knob I've ever encountered on any electronic product, including the cheapo radios you'd find in a dusty clearance bin at a dollar store. It wobbles and makes a scraping sound as you rotate it.

I sent my Yeti back because the mute button above the volume button did not work -- well, it worked occasionally, but you never knew if two, three, or four presses would be required. I also found that the Yeti made an unacceptable amount of noise when connected to my MacBook air, but to be fair, there are a number of factors that could have been responsible.

I should mention that I have nothing against Blue as a company. In fact, my favorite vocal mike at the moment is Blue's Bluebird, a $300 (street price) mike that sounds better on my voice than mikes that cost a lot more.

But my overall impression is that the Yeti is a toy. It is, to a professional microphone, what the toy plastic typewriter in my 1960s Sears Roebuck Christmas catalog was to my Dad's real typewriter, or a kid's first microscope is to a real one.

So why do some people love this mike? The Yeti might well meet the needs of many bloggers and a number of other users. I have no doubt that it can make decent recordings -- if you were using something a lot cheaper before, this will be a big step up. It's convenient to connect a mike via USB, especially to a laptop. The Yeti's built in headphone jack (also found on some competing USB mikes) is also a convenience, though Blue could have put it in a more accessible location.

It might also have been nice if Blue offered a carrying case for the Yeti, even as an option -- there is no convenient way to lug this thing around, and a decent carrying case from a third-party will cost more than the Yeti. But given the build quality, you should probably leave it on your desktop, anyway.

The alternatives? I haven't looked at every USB mike out there, but it's probably fair to say that anything a lot a better will cost you more.

Since the Yeti isn't really all that portable anyway, one alternative worth considering is a basic USB audio interface from somebody like Focusrite or Presonus, which will cost you $100 to $130 or so. You could pair that with any mike you like, or you could find a package deal for the interface, a mike and accessories for $200 or so. More than the Yeti, but a lot more quality and options.

Or you can buy a Yeti. If you are gentle with it, never take it on location, and are very lucky, it might serve your needs for a long time. But if you're expecting professional equipment or anything close to it, the Yeti should either make you laugh, or cry.
Summary: Great features, poor build quality -- you get what you pay for

The EX-Analogy Analog Delay Pedal is another mini style foot pedal that will not take up a lot of precious real estate on your pedal board, and here is the first couple of small “cons” which caused me to deduct 1 star from this review.
These type of small 9v pedals are really designed to add to a pedal board. As such, many (if any) ship with a power supply, as they figure you are adding it to your board and using your existing power supply to power the pedal.
However, some competitors pedals do ship with a Velcro mounting pad, and or a pigtail to your supply.
Unfortunately, this pedal ships with neither. I know it seems to be a small issue, but they ship it in a nice carry bag that almost no one will use. Drop the bag and at least add a pre-cut Velcro backing to mount.
So, how does the pedal sound? It sounds good...nice analog repeats that can be dialed from a near “reverb” style repeat up to some pretty nice long delays. It’s true bypass which is nice, but the volume function needs to be just about maxed to allow full bypass (equal bypass volume) levels between effect and non effect.
The Footswitch seems sturdy, as does the casing itself. Time and repeat knobs work fine. Not a huge fan of the “tiger stripes” finish, but hey....you know which pedal is the delay when looking down on your board.
This is my first pedal from EX, and like most of the other companies making inexpensive mini effects pedals these days you wonder how they can produce these at this price point.
Can’t comment on the reliability, having just received it a couple of days ago, but will update this if any issues come up, but wouldn’t expect any.
Overall, a nice sounding, fairly versatile delay pedal that with the inclusion of a Velcro pad and a pigtail would have earned it 5 stars.

I don't know whether they have "warmed up" with use as some people claim, but I've had them on there for a couple of months and they are now awesome! I use a thumb pick and the lows and base runs are great and the picked E and B strings are fine even with nails. In addition the guitar chimes like a bell! Seriously, I haven't touched my 60's Martin in weeks. I just can't get enough of the way the that Yammie battleship rings when picked or strummed. I'm using it for my gig tomorrow and I sure don't feel like I'm giving up anything. I'm buying more of these to try on all my acoustics.

On a separate note, there were some comments on lack of stretch when new (I agree, but it's a good thing) and about string breaking. I have found these strings to be surprisingly forgiving. Since I was setting up the guitar (truss rod, saddle, nut, intonation), I had this first set of Earthwoods on and off that guitar dozens of times with nary of problem. I've been struggling with microphone/audio hassles in my recent Youtube channel videos. I used to merely record music straight into the PC and edit, then sing into a SM57/58 over the backup tracks I created, etc...
Live recording with lav mics and the like is a new experience for me. With a history of mixing audio and using separate tracks, I understand the benefits of blending acoustic alterations from one part of the room into another (as well as for backup/redundancy). Unfortunately, I had a heck of a time over the last couple years finding a device that could record separate inputs onto individual tracks.
Finally, FINALLY I saw the Zoom H6 for sale in September 2018. I hadn't tried looking for new devices since around January 2018. When the Zoom H6 popped up on Amazon's list, I couldn't believe I missed this device in the past. Turns out I didn't, that it's a newer release.
Well, I must say that this does everything I wanted, and then some. It not only allows for mono AND stereo recording from separate inputs, AND splits it into individual recordings, but it ALSO has really good attachable microphones to go with it. I'm shocked at how much better my stuff has been sounding lately.
The fight with my crappy Movo wireless mics and their whiny pitched hum, and/or the hassle of trying to ensure input balance gets equalized after bouts of silence as the camcorder attempts to predict input levels is gone. The time spent trying to noise cancel pitch whine while also not crushing dynamics is gone. So, too, is the up/down, up down yo-yo of sectioning out the first 4 seconds of speaking as the input attempts to reduce volume on-the-go... so much time is saved with the H6's dead silent noise floor and crystal clear recording.
Also great is the portability, snappy menu response (not lightning quick, but certainly acceptable), and portability. The issue is NOW deciding which tracks sounds BEST, and/or whether I should attempt to merge two microphone tracks in order to catch the bass of vocal timbre while also EQ'ing 3-8k range with ambient reverb, etc... it all sounds so GOOD that the time spent being frustrated with making BAD audio sound "passable" has been replaced with how to make all these good sounding options sound the best it can. This is something I can live with.

I bought this interface for the 4 outputs. I had an Alesis io2 before this and it only had the 2 outputs. I needed the second pair for cueing DJ sets. First thing I noticed when I plugged the US200 in was how much louder it was. At this point I was only using the phones on the front panel because I neglected to get RCA cables. The second thing I noticed was the single volume control for the outs. I figured it was no biggie and proceeded to plug my monitors into outs 3 and 4, once I got my cables, and my headphones into the phones jack on the front. The next thing I noticed was the blood coming from my ears as soon as the first notes came from my monitors...

Ok, it wasn't quite so dramatic, but BEWARE! The master volume nob on the front panel does not control the volume to outs 3 and 4, only 1,2, and the phones, which are stereo of 1 and 2. Outs 3 and 4 pump out max volume all the time, regardless of the volume nob on the interface or the volume control on the computer if you redirect the main computer sounds to outs 3 n 4. What I'll have to do is get a volume control to reduce signal from the interface to my monitors.

Text: Hosa  makes great products

Just a quick review to say the G3 Effects Unit and Amp Simulator is Excellent.

I have played real tube amps all my life.

In the past I had tried products like the POD, Line 6, V-amp , J-Station, Amplitube I, Korg, Digitech RP-series, and other amplifier simulators.

I did not like the sound of any of them.

None really emulated a guitar amp when used DIRECT with Speaker Emulation.

They all sounded fizzy, fuzzy and buzzy.

I liked the Zoom G2 -Dave Mustaine series as an Effects Pedal feeding a real amp, but even it was a little weak sounding and "fuzzy', "buzzy" when used in the DIRECT mode with speaker emulation thru headphones or direct to mixer.

But the G3 is the first amplifier simulator that sounds good thru headphones or direct to mixer.

I love it.

My only criticism, I wish it could handle four effects with noise reduction, then it would be perfect
(Overdrive + Noise Reduction + Amp + Delay + Reverb)

But it is still great and a leap forward in the technology and sound.

I am guessing in the past all the research was done on the amp simulation part of the equation, but only recently have they started focusing on the equally important part of speaker/mic emulation.

I say that because until the G3, every single unit I ever tried to use for practice listening thru headphones still had that nagging and irritating fuzzy, buzzy , fizzy edge to the sound as though the speaker emulation was just not quite right yet.

The G3 is the first one I have tried that I can say ........ Hey, they are finally on the right track with these devices.

Line 6 Pod, Behringer V-amp, Korg Pandora, Digitech RP ....... Yuk, Yuk, Yuk for direct use to mixer or practicing thru headphones.

Zoom G3 ...... YEAH !!!!

I am going to start paying more attention to Zoom
I had never really taken them all that seriously in the past !
Summary: Finally .... digital amp emulation is getting real, real close

Dunlop 81/37R Brass Fingerpicks
INTRODUCTION: Metal fingerpicks protect your fingers and produce a loud, clear ringing tone when plucking a metal string. They are typically used for playing acoustic guitar, dobro, banjo, or steel guitar.
I have purchased and used all the picks in this review. I compared them on Gretsch Lap Steel Guitar, Martin Acoustic Guitar, and Gibson RBT Banjo strung with Dunlop and Fender extra-light strings.
COMPOSITION: Brass fingerpicks alloy usually contains 66% copper and 34% zinc. It contains no nickel or steel. Brass can kill bacteria on contact.
COMPARISON: I compared Dunlop 81/37R Brass fingerpicks with National NP2B Brass fingerpicks, ProPik Split Wrap Brass fingerpicks, National NP2 Nickel Silver fingerpicks, Dunlop 156/33P Nickel Silver fingerpicks, National NP2SS Stainless Steel fingerpicks, and a variety of plastic fingerpicks.
DESCRIPTION: The Dunlop 81/37R Brass fingerpicks have a single band with wrap-around wings that are slightly curved to keep them from digging into your fingertip. The picks come in 0.013, 0.015, 0.018, 0.020., 0.0225, 0.025 inch thicknesses. Thinner picks such as 0.018 are easier to bend around your finger, while 0.020 and 0.025 have a more substantial feel. I used 0.025 inch thick picks in this review.
SOUND: The National Dunlop 81/37R Brass fingerpicks were loud, bright, and they emphasized the treble end of the fundamental tone of each string without adding any unnatural overtones. They were almost as bright as the National and Dunlop Nickel Silver fingerpicks without producing high harsh, treble overtones.
CONCLUSIONS: All metal picks sounded louder than plastic picks, or my naked fingertips. The Dunlop 81/37R Brass fingerpicks sounded loud and bright without changing the fundamental sound of the strings.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Metal fingerpicks can make a string sing and add to your enjoyment of the music you make. I liked the Dunlop Brass Fingerpicks almost as well as the National Brass fingerpicks, and I carry them with my guitar.

You need to pay attention when attaching the ratchet, so it is firmly enough clamped to the headstock. (3) because the display is in a low-profile form factor, it can require a little head tilting to read. Nothing uncomfortable or that makes you look odd. Text:
I wasn't really sure what to expect when I ordered this pedal. I'd tried some of the other, more popular brand acoustic simulator pedals and thought they all sounded pretty much like garbage. After watching some review/demo vids of this one, I figured I'd give it a shot before giving up on my life long dream of trying to make my Les Paul sound like my Martin...

I have to say, this little pedal does a pretty damn good job. No, it's not "perfect". But honestly, you're not going to get much of a better acoustic tone unless you use an actual acoustic guitar.

This pedal has a lot of options jammed into its little housing - tonal controls are "body" and "top" (which are essentially low end and high end EQs, respectively) and then you've got the style switch. I've been getting a lot of cool, completely distinct sounds while switching between Standard, Piezo and Jumbo. These settings vary from the low, boomy-ness of a dreadnaught body to the twangy sparkle of an electrified shallow body.
Finally, you've got your basic volume level knob. It's fairly sensitive, so a little bit increases/decreases volume exponentially.

When all is said and done, this pedal does not make your electric sound like an "in person" acoustic... but it does sound like a great "plugged in" acoustic. Best way to describe it is like an unplugged hollow body electric guitar.
All in all, I'd definitely recommend it.

Text:
UPDATE1 : I misplaced the plastic cover for the connector on the main unit. I was promptly sent a new one from Zoom at no charge. This kind of service is commendable. While it doesn't overcome the technical limitations, it shows that they stand behind their product and for those that it suits perfectly, that is comforting.

UPDATE 2 : After a couple of years, the vulcanized rubber which covers almost the entire exterior became tacky and sticky to the touch. That was the final straw for me and caused me to dock a further star from 3 to 2. I gave up on it completely and sold the unit.

------ END UPDATES ----

For field recording, or location recording, I think this is a lot of power in a rather small package. With that said, my primary purpose in purchasing this was because of the convenience of an XY microphone head in a small package which I mount use over a grand piano for home recordings. Frankly for the cost of two microphones alone, this was a viable and cost effective solution and it does fulfill this role reasonably well.

While I am about to go over the fairly serious limitations this unit has to those who might have hoped it was a stand in for a multitrack recorder, it should be noted, that the unit DOES serve as microphone interface to your computer so the mics can be used in conjunction with any DAW you may use more regularly. For me this is what, despite it's shortcomings below, will continue to be of value to me which is why I gave it a neutral if not stellar rating.

It is also worth pointing out that if you are trying to record live (vs. multi-take multitrack) performances, this IS a good buy because you can have up to 4 mics plus the onboard all at once. These tracks can then be either mixed onboard (good luck with that - the interface is cumbersome), or the tracks can easily be imported into a DAW for further treatment and remixing.

So, with that said, it's undeniable that this unit could and I would argue should have offered so much more than it does and that's why I am reluctant to give it more than 3 stars. There are several shortcomings that will inevitably quickly cause problems for musicians who want to use this as a low key multitrack recorder for overdubbing. And the reason I dock them for this is because this is clearly a firmware related matter.
The general ergonomics of this unit are poor and with the possible exception of the hardwire connection between tracks and inputs, most matters could have been resolved with better firmware.

1) Overdubbing using the built in mics is NOT possible. That's right. The connectable mics are not assignable to any tracks other than L and R (and not to 1 through 4 in any mono or stereo configuration). Indeed, none of the inputs are assignable at all. So, every time you want to record on a different track, you will need to reconnect your mic. More importantly, this means if ALL you have is the connected mics, then you are completely unable to overdub because a) the inputs are not assignable (probably a hardwire limitation) and b) the tracks you have recorded can't easily be bounced or transferred to another track. How easy would that be to implement? VERY, I assure you. This is just poor limited firmware functionality.

2) In overdub mode, all Global Phantom Power assignments are ignored and by defaul turned off. You are instead forced to set them again, for each individual track. This is on a per project basis. Why? Who knows. No good reason I can think of. If I appreciate being able to toggle it again in in overdub mode but I want it to default to it's global setting. Not just an arbitrary "Off." Especially given that MOST mics used with something like this do require phantom power.

3) Overdub mode would likely be used almost ALL musicians so why bury it in a project file. A physical button would have made sense. Or at least easy top level menu access. Speaking of which, a "custom" menu which is user configuable would be very helpful. Having to search in deeply nested menus for commonly used functions is again, something that a little ergonomic user design would have remediated to some degree.

4) The metronome doesn't work AT ALL unless in overdub mode. Why? You created one. Let me turn it on whenever the hell I want.

5) Another shortcoming for a musician. I need to point my XY mic down at the grand piano's stings and operate it from the keys. This means the unit is upside down making menus and meters harder to read. The ability to orient the screen either way would have been a HUGE benefit. I was actually surprised that I couldn't determine that by way of a setting.

All in all, I can't argue with this is a robust field recorder, but if it wasn't for the XY microphone, I would not have any reason to purchase this as a musician. I'd be much better off in getting something that is more suited to the task like a true multitrack recorder. After all, You are going to need external mics anyway to multitrack on this thing even if you want to use this in overdubbing mode.

Physical build, etc. is very good. It seems like a it will handle a little bit of punishment and certainly does have solid feeling controls. It just seems that this remarkable small and high quality recorder falls very short due to lazily implemented firmware that is poor in both layout and also functionality.
Summary: Not recommended for Musicians (unless it's for the XY or live performance recording)

Text:
It's small. It's cheap. It's brown. ...But not in a turd-like manner. It's not like there's a lump of poo on my pedal board; this is much more than that. It's an inexpensive, small, passive potentiometer you control with your foot. You can use it to attenuate (but not boost) your overall volume, or you can use it to control parameters on some pedals. E.g. I've used it to control the EQD Avalanche Run.

This gets five stars not because it's "the best" of the four expression pedals I have, but because it's the best value in a passive volume/expression pedal. I don't expect this to stand up to years of abuse, but I don't plan to abuse it, so it might very well last my lifetime, unless modern science catches up to the challenges of entropy, gravity, and their increasingly annoying effects on my creaky-ass body, making me live an absurdly long time. ...But I digress.

This pedal is almost identical to another one I have. It's orange, made by Valeton, which I found out is made by the same company as Sonicake, hence the similarities. The other two pedals I have are more expensive: The DOD mini expression pedal, which feels better to the feet and seems more durable, despite its internal plastic gears, and the full-sized Moog expression pedal. The latter two have more expression pedal options, but both lack native volume control. ...So the Sonicake and Valeton have a leg up in that regard.

So, that's why this is a five star pedal. BROWN!
Summary: Let me tell you why this is five stars.

I went through a private sale of a friend to obtain my Zoom H4n, so it's not going to confirm that I ever purchased it via Amazon. The deal was that my friend works at a production company and his boss bought a ton of them, then realized he bought too many. So, he started to sell them at a cut-rate to get rid of the extras. My experience is a little unique but I felt it should be documented anyway.

Anyway, I bought it brand new in the box, unopened, untampered with, everything still in the factory wrapped plastic and tape. Immediately, I opened everything and the contents were all in the box (no missing parts). I put batteries in and started doing tests. First, I stood in one room and tested the mics. Everything worked fine, very clear microphones. Sounded like I was standing RIGHT there when I went to listen back to my recording. I was very happy and impressed. Then I went into another room and plugged in an external lavalier mic into the "ext mic" input jack located on the back. Although it was plugged in and both the transmitter and receiver were on, and I could hear myself through the headphones...as soon as I hit record, the Zoom would start recording with the external built-in mics instead of my plugged in lav mic.

Confused, I recorded anyway, unplugged my lav mic and then plugged in another lavalier mic. I could hear myself, everything sounded okay, I pressed record and it recorded through the lav successfully, no problems. I plug in the lavalier I just had problems with one more time, recorded, and I could hear myself fine...it recorded successfully. So, it went from not receiving signal to receiving signal.

SO here's where it gets really interesting. After a couple of days and using it maybe three times on the job, I think to myself, "Well, it's been a couple of days since I got this thing, let me take it home from work (where we do productions involving automobiles) and do a review on it." I put it into the plastic Zoom carrying case it comes with, drive home (40 minute highway drive), pull it out, pull my camera out, flip it over and the power switch on the side is loose. So loose that you can rock the Zoom back and forth and watch the switch slide back and forth by gravity.

Luckily, my friend spoke with his boss who is going to come in this morning and give me another Zoom from his stack of Zooms and handle returning this one for me since we have a deadline we have to fulfill for our next segment.

Anyway, happy but disappointed. Assembly error maybe? Who knows?
Summary: Sounds great but had some problems. Power switch became VERY loose.

Worth every penny and then some. I never played a reed instrument before buying this, and I was dubious whether I'd get an instrument, or a clarinet shaped object. When I pulled it out of the case, I didn't even know how to put it together. I'd never touched a reed before let alone assembled a ligature. I couldn't even get a note to come out at first. That's how new I was to this.

It's been 2 months now with near daily practice. I have no teacher. I can play several songs, circular breath, play across the break in intermediate songs like The Pink Panther theme, and I can hold a note for 55 seconds without circular breathing. I am not some kind of wood wind prodigy. I credit having a GREAT instrument with my progress.

Out of the case I was shocked at how heavy this clarinet is. It's heavier than my flute, which is all metal. The key material is also solid and did not require any adjustment in several weeks of playing now. The tenons are tight, but soon get to a comfortable resistance with frequent cork greasings at cleaning time.

I ditched the stock mouth piece after a month and a half and got a Vandoren 5JB 88 with a Vandoren 1.5 reed. Just do it. You won't look back. I now have an instrument that is going to last me a long time before I need to upgrade, and to me that is what makes a good starter instrument. One that you don't need to immediately toss because it's holding you back or breaks.

I also replaced the ligature with a single screw leather one which makes reed cleaning easier. The pads are still in good shape, no leaky keys, and it plays from bottom of the cleff up to the 3rd octave without any off or slow notes.

I have a few minor nit picks though. As it came out of the box, it was 1/2 a semitone flat with either barrel in use. Changing the mouth piece solved that problem. You can compensate with your embouchure but as a new player I found it hard to do that AND concentrate on my scales at the same time. Mine did not come with a replacement reed either so be sure to buy a box of reeds. The stock mouth piece played best for me with a 3.0 reed strength. 2.0 was too easy to over blow and squeak in the lower register.

I also recommend you get a stand that stores in the bell. I rarely disassemble my instrument now, and instead keep it next to my favorite chair, ready to grab and practice at any time.

I've bought a few inexpensive instruments before on Amazon like a trumpet and a flute, which were around the same price as this clarinet, but far inferior in terms of quality, weight, and build. I feel like I got a really good deal on this clarinet at $180. With the new mouth piece I'm about $270 in, and feel like I have a $800 instrument.
Summary: This is a real instrument, very well built, not at all like many of the cheaper band instruments I've purchased on Amazon.

Text:
Ok, it's basically an aluminum RGB flashlight with a pretty durable plastic tube that you screw 2 srews with an allen key into, a small speaker and a basic motion sensor setup. But it's still pretty cool and the more you use and learn what makes it give off what sounds it behaves like an ok lightsaber. Even though it doesn't have the full look of a genuine lightsaber.

Biggest thing I found is that it doesn't have a very sensitive accelerometer sensor or whatever senses the impacts. You cannot limp wrist or hold this loosely and expect it to make the striking sounds. It will mostly make the vibrating whooshing sound for light strikes and taps when your hand and wrist absorb the shock. If you hold it (like in the first image) with your hand below the power button firmly and strike you get the strike sound isn't of 1-5% of the time it becomes more of a 80-90%+. So if you're just getting whooshing sounds try firming up your grip.

I also ran into my saber was really quiet when I got it and the issue was that at some point from manufacturing to arriving at my door the mesh screen ring that protects the speaker got pushed right up against the speaker which prevented it from moving and giving off the full sound. I took a needle and put the tip under mesh and pried it up gently and it popped back to its proper spot (I assume) and the volume went up drastically. It's not enough to drown out other noise in a room, but you can definitely hear it from several feet away. So if you're experiencing a very quiet one, check the speaker in the base of the handle.

Features wise it doesn't have any volume control, you get what get. There is the 1 sound for turning on and the other for off, 4 variations of whooshing and a few more for strike/clashing. The lightsaber idle sound is more of the Kylo Ren aggressive hum than a light hum. The light saber color is 7 colors and it defaults on Red and you have to switch to the color you want. I haven't been able to set any other color as default which is where I took the star away, because no matter what you start out as a Sith despite any preference you may have.

Overall it's pretty fun once you learn to time you grip for striking and get the sounds matching up. It seems pretty durable as the tube for the blade seems to take some pretty decent blows and force on padded poles or other plastic sabers and there is no risk and shattering it. Just be careful of environmental collateral and enjoy.
Summary: Not bad, but definitely not a super high end lightsaber.

Text:
I'm probably not experienced enough of a drummer to warrant getting a double pedal yet, but they just look like so much fun, I have been wanting to try it out for some time now. As such, I'm no expert in what makes a good or bad set, so I'll just give my impressions here--take them for what they are worth.
1) The beaters are harder than I'm used to. The single-pedal beater that I was using was a softer felt that gave a more gentle "thud" than these beaters do. It isn't bad, but it does change the sound quality a bit. It does appear that one could easily take the beaters out and replace them with something else.
2) I wish the shaft was a bit longer. When I get the pedal where it is comfortable and doesn't interfere too much with my hi-hat pedal, the shaft is at its very most extended position. If I tried to go any longer, it would fall out. This works, but with no room to spare and that could be a problem, so -1 star.
3) There is velcro on the bottom of the left pedal which sticks furiously to my carpet, so it's perfect for me but I have a very low-pile carpet. Not sure how it would do with a shaggier carpet and I'm certain it would be a big problem for a hard floor.
4) There were 0 instructions of any kind, so I just had to figure out how to get it together. That wouldn't have been any kind of problem, except somehow the left pedal and chain had gotten twisted and rotated so that it almost looked right, but was backward and it took me a while to figure out how to get it oriented correctly again. I'm assuming that was a fluke, but... (shrug)
5) Both pedals feel balanced and I can adjust the tensions independently to get the feel dialed in just the way I like

Very happy with this set. As noted, I think the shaft should be a bit longer, but other than that, I don't know what I would do to improve on it.

Text: I was excited to use these triggers for an A to E conversion with mesh drum heads (to use for practice and low volume gigs), but ended up being disappointed. The build quality and seamless integration with the drum module are excellent.  What was terribly disappointing was the poor fit, which prohibited proper seating on the drum head.  I purchased two RT-30H triggers, one RT-30HR trigger, and one RT-30K trigger.  Despite being advertised to fit most common rims/hoops, they did not fit my hoops for the desired application; and I have standard triple flange hoops.  Here's the issue: With mesh drum heads, you have to tighten the lug screws more than you would on an acoustic head to maintain sufficient tension on the head.  In doing so the hoop ends up dropping into a low position.  These triggers have a deep "pocket" that allows for hoops that sit well above the drum head, but they do not allow for hoops that sit shallow with respect to the drum head.  Because of this, I could not get the triggers to seat correctly.  I had a separate seating problem with the RT-30K, because my bass drum hoops have a subtle outward flange toward the edge of the hoop.  I may still use these with my other acoustic set to add triggering layers to acoustic sound during live performances, but I originally purchased these for a full A to E conversion.  I would not recommend them for that!
Summary: Does not fit all rim/hoop styles

I am one of those guys (like so many of us) that just can't leave my music equipment alone and have to experiment a little (sometimes a lot). In the case of the Champ 40, I wanted to see what a Celestion G12-65 Creamback would do in the place of the stock Fender speaker.
The results,
Creamback: More hiss, was not as clean, had more drive.
Stock speaker: Better on clean, less hiss, had less drive.
My conclusion, is that you probably will never get a better sound from another speaker than the one the Champ 40 comes with.
This is not that surprising, as most of the low end amps are designed to match speaker and amp to come up with an acceptable product. I use this amp for practice, and upgraded from a Frontman 25R that has a 10" speaker. I was looking for a fuller sound with some limited amp modeling, in a small package/footprint, and that is what I got with the Champ 40, along with front controls like the Frontman, as I stack or shelf my amps 2 or 3 high, and (for this application), top control amps are a hassle. The overall sound is much better than the 25R. My only wish for the Champ 40, is that the gain would work on both channels, and I have seen the same request from other reviewers. The overall sound is a bit tinny, which is a Fender thing (I have many Fender amps), but not so much that it bugs me. The drive channel Voice (Amp models) and FX (Effects) are just enough to keep it simple.
When you pull it all together; Price, Value, Functions, 12" Speaker, Ease of operation, Small size, I just don't see anything available at this time that can out do this combo.
While the Mustang II V.2 may (I have never used it) be a better amp (I don't know), it has top controls which knocks it out of contention going in.
I just bought a second Champ 40 for a teenager I am musically supporting.
Summary: Don't bother changing speaker. Best bang for the buck

I am probably not the ideal reviewer for the Arturia MicroBrute, since I am primarily into guitars and relatively new to synthesizers. As such, I don't have a long-standing knowledge of the history of analog synthesis to fully appreciate how amazing it is that Arturia can offer this device in such a compact (and relatively affordable) package. At the same time, the price point and feature set of the MicroBrute are meant to attract newcomers who would never have paid $1,000 or more to try out some of the vintage equivalents of this technology. So in that sense, I come to my review with a perspective similar to a lot of prospective MicroBrute owners.

Overall, I am liking the MicroBrute a fair amount, though it has some complexities and limitations that will likely hold it back from being even more useful. Let's make perfectly clear - this is a MONOPHONIC synthesizer, which means it is capable of playing only one note at a time. Therefore, it is not capable of doing chords and a lot of familiar synth melodies (and a lot of people recommend against having a monophonic synth as your "first" or "only" synth for this reason). But monophonic synths are useful for baselines or syncopated sequences, and the tones of the MicroBrute are rich and full.

As new as I am to synthesis, I actually did appreciate the paper manual that comes with the MicroBrute - it offers not only a crash course on synthesis and what the different parameters do, but some "Init" patches you could set up as a starting place to make your own sounds. Arturia also includes 15 nice cards that slip over the dashboard and indicate settings for 10 of their sample patches plus blank cards for 5 of your own (using dry erase marker). The MicroBrute does not use presets and cannot save your settings to switch quickly between sounds - it simply does whatever the knobs have it set to do.

The device cannot be run by batteries (Arturia says this was to protect sound quality), but it does have a headphone jack so you can listen directly out from the synthesizer. I was disappointed, however, to learn that the USB jack is not for audio out, but only for firmware updates and some MIDI functionality. Arturia is a software company, so I anticipated they would have included a class-compliant USB audio interface, but that is not the case. Audio can be captured using 1/4" line out jack(s) or even the 1/8" headphone out jack.

I should also point out that as I review this analog synthesizer in early 2016, there is a huge library of great sounding synthesizer apps on iOS, which you can play with a relatively inexpensive MIDI controller. I more or less wanted to try a hardware unit because it was affordable and because of the novelty aspect. But I do hope to learn more about synthesis from working with the MicroBrute, and it's a quality device capable of powerful and rich sounds that punch well above its weight class.

UPDATE (02/09/2016) - Writing back briefly to affirm my 4-star rating. Actually, my enjoyment of the unit was increasing as I began to understand how to program it better - there are some rich, wonderful sounds to be had from this little beast. And I was able to hook up the Line Out and record into my iPad via an Apogee JAM interface (1/4" instrument cable). The fun really begins if you have some guitar effects pedals lying around that you can throw in between the line out and your interface to modify the sound. (Just keep your Master Volume around 9:00 or 10:00 so as not to pump too much signal into a pedal expecting instrument level signal).

But my particular unit (which admitted, was purchased lightly used) turned out to have a defect in it, and I've read enough anecdotes about other people having hardware issues that it's worth pointing out in the review (and deducting a star from my score). The defect in my unit is some sort of oscillator "bleed through" that you can hear at all times, even if you aren't playing a note. It's a minor nuisance when playing live, but becomes really noticeable using headphones or recording. So, I'm returning the unit, but I'd certainly like another one if I can find it at the right price. I think it's just part of the "deal with the devil" Arturia made to produce an analog synth at this size and price...there's bound to be some glitches with some units.
Summary: Affordable, powerful monophonic synthesizer, but perhaps not the ideal "first synth".

40 years playing guitar, complete newbie to the violin. First, the instrument looks beautiful and comes with everything you need safe and sound in it's own case. It's completely set up and ready to tune and play. The white has a subtle sparkle to it that I really like. It does smell like paint upon opening but that will dissipate, albeit slowly, very slowly. It is very loud unplugged and sounds like itself when plugged into an amp. I had no trouble getting it to produce distinguishable notes using the bow, rosin and strings that it comes with. Yes, the back of the neck is unpainted but that is how it's supposed to be. I replaced 2 of the 4 strings with D'Addario preludes when I accidentally broke them by using the wrong peg for the wrong string and I actually prefer the sound of the stock strings, they seem more articulate. I've had no trouble tuning it and it keeps it's tune for a few days at a time, although I always tune any of my stringed instruments before playing them.

Before changing anything, whether bow, strings, rosin or shoulder rest, take a look at Fiddlerman's "109 dollar violin test" on youtube where he takes it out of the box, tunes it very quickly, and plays with everything it comes with. It's the same violin as this one in black without the electronics. It sounds fantastic when he plays it and he is quite impressed and he is also quite impressive. The only thing I've had to add to this outfit is a mute because it's so loud it was hurting my left ear. I would also recommend a snark clipon tuner if you don't already have one. I play with the tuner clipped behind the scroll which makes it easier to know where to put your finger when you are starting out.
