It's hard to really describe what this pedal does-  It doesn't distort, flange, echo, or produce a chorus.  I'd heard it described as making your amp sound like someone had thrown a blanket off of it.  And because words don't do an accurate job in describing it, I would have probably never pulled the trigger on one (even though they are pretty cheap as pedals go).  As luck would have it, I acquired one on trade, and I have to admit that I agree with the whole blanket euphemism.  This stompbox helps correct the boxy sound of my Blues Jr. when placed at the end of my pedaltrain- right before I run into the amp. I don't feel it needs to be run on a dedicated effects loop to improve an amp's tone, though I do believe it works even better in a loop.  I placed it in the effects loop of both a Palomino V8 (USA/Ampeg made) and a Crate VC508 (a 5 watt USA made EL84 tube amp with Celestian speaker) and it was transformative to both amps' tone (in a great way). It does very well with single coils.  It's a pedal that I would leave on all the time once my tone is dialed in.  I don't think it works as well when I run my LP into a Jet City combo - particularly when trying to coax out subtle textures / harmonics. That amp also lacks an effects loop and I imagine it would have a different effect if placed after the preamp phase.  I guess it's rig dependent, but it's a keeper for what it does to the sound of my Fender.

WARNING- This is an in depth review of this ukulele set. If you prefer a brief summary, see section marked THE BOTTOM LINE
----------------------------------------------------------------
I have a few Ukuleles. They are nice and I do enjoy them, but for some reason, this one really hits home with me. Let's take a look.

WHAT IS THIS SET LIKE?
This ukulele is a wonderful set. Not only is the ukulele a nice size and easy to play, but the sound is great. Let's see what all comes in this set.

UKULELE
This comes with the strings all strung so you don't have to do it yourself. You will have to tune it. The keys are easy to turn and the strings sound pretty nice too. The body is a nice quality and the construction seems to be good as well. It does have knobs on the end for the straps- more on that in a minute.

REPLACEMENT STRINGS
There is a full set of nylon replacement strings in this which is a great feature.

PICKS
Three picks come with this. They are on the thinner side- not rigid.

STRAP
There is a lightweight cotton webbing adjustable strap for this. I have never had one with a strap before, so it took me a while to find the 2nd knob. When you put the ukulele up to play it., there is a knob on the end near your right hand. The other knob is facing the FLOOR at the top of the sound chamber. It is tricky to find at first if you are not sure where to look. The strap slips over each knob and is quite comfortable. If it is large enough for you, it won't interfere with your playing.

CAPO
I have never seen a capo for ukulele either- perhaps I am not professional enough. HAHA Anyway this fits the ukulele just fine. You can also use this on a guitar if you have one of those. It works well and I had no issues with it.

CASE
There is a cloth case that it comes in as well as a box. The case has a front pocket on it for protection of the basic accessories that come with it. Everything fits in there well.

CHROMATIC TUNER
This is epic. It has a setting for each instrument that you are trying to tune. When you turn it to ukulele it shows you what the note of the string you are using is. When you are at the right setting, it shows you which string this is for. The light turns green when the sound is lined up. It works so well. My last tuner experience was not good. This one is great.

BOOKLET
That is where at least this has a decent booklet, but it has barely any information in it. It does tell you how to tune the ukulele. It tells you the basic parts of the instrument, and how to tune it. I would have liked to see more instruction on basic songs or something, however.

There is a scan code for a facebook support group.

HOW DOES THIS SOUND?
This sounds beautiful. The tones are very rich yet very ukulele without sounding like a toy. It has a really nice depth to the tone and I love playing it.

WHAT DO WE HAVE TO BE SURE TO DO?
GET YOURSELF A HUMIDIFIER! I say that because a long time ago I learned that the biggest mistake people make is not putting a humidifier in with their wood stringed instruments. After I put a humidifier in the case and let it set for a few days, it is amazing how much richer the sound and the beautiful smell of the wood that this has.

You can get guitar humidifiers on Amazon here, and they are not too expensive. Be sure to use DISTILLED water.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a great kit for beginners and even enthusiasts like me who might have had a basic ukulele, but wanted something a little nicer sounding. Be sure to line up some lessons online or in person and get a humidifier for this. You will be glad you did.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is my favorite ukulele yet and I love that it has a strap for those times I want to tool around the house and play at the same time. Okay, so I am weird. ;)
Summary: Something About Summer And Ukuleles - I Love This One- MAKE SURE YOU DO ONE THING!

I am lead singer for a classic rock band, and also perform occasionally as a solo with acoustic guitar. I mostly got this to add some spice to my solo shows, but I am also finding it very cool to use with the band. Plusses: when set right for the song you are performing it works great! Negatives: it is sometimes a little slow to adjust to a chord change, so it sounds like on of your backup singers is searching for the right note. I've only put a couple of hours into using it so far, but I have already found that you have to alter your guitar playing slightly when using the H1. Where you might normally play a chord slightly behind the beat for a more emotional effect, that causes the H1 to delay getting the info it needs to match you. This is of course, when you are using the guitar a guide. Much better when set to the correct key for the song. I also noticed that when finger picking on the acoustic, I have to kind of sweep my finger across all the strings when switching chords. That might sound like a bigger deal than it is...it only took me a few minutes to get used to it. Of course, you can't do a cappela when set to the guitar as a guide, but I have been using it on the Eagles "Seven Bridges Road" very effectively by strumming the chords quietly behind the vocal. It sounds awesome!

On some songs the "two voice above" setting sounds better; on others maybe a single voice, or one above and below might work. It will depend on your own voice (mine is baritone), the material and what effect you want. The controls are very easy to use, but I did find the manual helpful to answer a few simple questions. One reviewer complained that the controls are not recessed, therefore too easy to hit with your foot, and I have found that to be true also. Minor issue, but annoying.

I will probably order a second one to have as a backup, and also to have set to a different type if harmony for faster changes when playing solo; also to use with both my electric and my acoustic when playing with the band. Overall, as I said I think it is an excellent value for the money!

FOLLOW UP: After having the H1 for a couple weeks, I still think it is awesome, but I did experience the issue of accidentally hitting the knobs with my foot and changing the settings. Since the knobs are not recessed it's easy to do. Plus I think the switch is too small, meaning I have to look down to see where the button is while playing a song. It's very disctracting to have to do that...get to the end of a verse, look down, stomp on the switch for the chorus, look down again at the end of the chorus, etc. But I love the sounds I'm getting so I went to an electronics store and bought an $8 metal project box, and a $2 hinge. I cut up the box with a Sawzall, and cut down the lid to make a wide cover for the button. Now I can rest my foot against the edge of the pedal and push the switch without looking. Plus I can't hit the knobs. Cost me about $11, and about an hours work. Works great. I wish I could post a photo of it for anyone else who is interested in making one!

Of all the things I use in my day-to-day business life, this is probably my most used device. It's essentially a portable "recording studio" and I've used it for audio books, coaching calls, recording at events, off-camera microphone capture, and so forth.

It makes a great podcasting microphone if you set it up on a stand and maybe a shock mount with a pop filter as I did for many years. It also makes a great capture device for your boom microphone or whatever external mic you might want to use, including a lapel.

NO you don't get XLR inputs and basically you're limited to 3.5mm inputs and outputs. That's okay for a lot of stuff though. It has a lot of great features (I like the onboard compressor and limiter).

It can be plugged into your computer and used as a microphone or pre-amp, it can go in your travel bag for on-the-road recording, and I hear it's excellent for musicians. I've never used it for music so I can't say.

The microphone quality is very high for the price point. For many years I preferred the internal mics to a lot of my other mics.

Battery life is good, I used rechargeables. The unit CAN power a mic if it needs some external power (some lav mics do). It can also run on USB power alone.

If you do a lot with the spoken word (especially for information products), this is a great tool to have in your arsenal.

Text:
Let's face it - banjo gig bags are problematic compared to guitar gig bags because banjos have long narrow necks and no gig bag is going to protect the neck from any really bad handling. But after I picked up a Deering Goodtime open-back banjo, I wanted something to give it basic protection from from scratches and from things poking holes in the head or snagging on the strings, bridge, or tuning pegs. Plus something to carry an extra set of strings, etc., along with the banjo.

I suppose that I COULD have bought a hard shell case, but that would have defeated the purpose of buying the Goodtime - I wanted a "travel banjo" with a killer neck that I could take along on trips without having to worry about where it would fit.

I toyed with the idea of getting the Deering bag, but I thought it would be a little silly to pay extra for a "brand-name" bag - what would I gain from that, except maybe that people would see that and assume I had a $2000 banjo instead of a $350 one. Right up there with the guy who used to buy Izod socks so he could sew the little alligator on his off-brand shirts. The only downside to NOT having Deering's name on the case it that the "pot end" is so small, it could get overlooked, causing people to wonder if I was carrying a rifle or something. Not a good look for airports or certain other public places. I recently saw one guy in the Atlanta airport with a Martin Backpacker case, on which he had scrawled in white paint "This is a guitar."

Of course if I was going to paint things on my banjo case it would say something like "This machine kills fascists," but that wouldn't go over well, either, I suppose.

I appreciated the folks on other sites whose reviews included the kind of banjo they owned. Several folks specifically recommended this gig bag for the open-back Goodtime, so I gave it a try.

Again, no gig bag will prevent a banjo neck from snapping if you drop a combo amp on it the wrong way. But assuming you're not a moron and will put your banjo places they don't drop combo amps, this bag will probably protect it about as well as any bag on the market.

I also notice that nearly all of the "bad" reviews of this bag resulted from people who didn't read the ad carefully and ordered this for a resonator banjo. Do NOT order this case if your banjo has a big wooden snack-bowl-shaped thing on the back.

The overall takeaway is that this bag accomplished my goals - it helped me add reasonable protection to a small, light-weight instrument without adding bulk or significant weight or expense. Since I don't plan to check it on airplanes or let other people throw it in their car trunks, I'm sure it will serve its intended purpose for years to come. The only reason I didn't give it five stars the first time I reviewed it is that it's not the best you can buy.

Update: A few months after I purchased this bag, I had some experiences with low-end bags that increased my respect for this one. There's a LOT to be said for a bag that fits your instrument, versus a bag that lets your instrument slop around like it was in a pillowcase. I'm sure you can do better than the Superior bag if you go "upstream" in pricing, but I assure you that you can do a lot worse for about the same amount of money. Just thought I'd let you know.

Update for 2014: To have a $100 open-back banjo I could leave in the car with no worries, I recently bought an old Samick with a wooden pot and took the back off. For a few months I dragged it around in a spare resonator banjo case - the thing slopped around like it was in a pillowcase, but it was SOME protection. I thought about ordering a new Superior case for it, but then I figured I'd have to tie different colored ribbons or something on them so I wouldn't grab the wrong banjo by mistake. I'm not really a "ribbony" kind of guy though.

Finally, I "bit the bullet" and bought the more expensive Deering-labeled gig bag for my GoodTime and put my Samick into the Superior case. Ooops, the Samick is almost an inch-and-a-half longer than the GoodTime, so it was a tighter fit, lengthwise. I tried the Samick in the Deering bag and it was a tight squeeze there, too. This gave me an opportunity to compare the two gig bags, though.

The padding seems very similar in quality. The Superior case has two zippered compartments on front of the bag, while the Deering bag only has one. The Deering case's zippered compartment is bigger, but it's also flatter, so no sandwiches. Neither bag's compartments will hold, say, a lesson book. The backstraps on the Deering case are wrapped with vinyl which might make it easier on your shoulders, but these resonator-less tone-ring-less banjos weigh so little that that isn't a major concern. The backstraps on the Deering case can be removed, however, if that's of interest to you. Both bags have double zippers on the main compartment.

Here is one possible advantage of the Deering bag - the Deering's "handle" is actually two straps you have to bind together with a velcro thingie before you can pick the bag up properly, while the Superior's handle is one nice solid handle that you don't have to bind together. Why is that a plus in the Deering's column? Because if you accidentally pick the Deering bag up by the handle without zipping it shut, you won't throw your banjo across the room like you would with the Superior bag. That might not affect you, but it might affect anyone careless or absent-minded, like, say, a student.

Summary: All things being equal - the bags are very similar in quality. As far as I can tell, the only real reason to spend the extra money for the Deering bag with the shiny gold embroidered letters is so you can have a cool-looking bag with shiny gold embroidered letters on it. On the other hand, the name Deering may get you more respect from hipsters, or help you avoid starting a panic at an airport. Tip: No matter which case you're using, if the cops or TSA tell you to put it down, don't argue with them.

Best of luck, all,

Paul Race - Creek don't Rise

P.S. I have since used one of these for a Samick 5-string resonator banjo (sb-4) that I took the back off (I prefer backless for most of my music). The samick's headstock has a silly extension with a big S on it that almost makes the banjo too long to fit. But it does fit. In addition, I've used one of these on a Davison/Jameson 6-string banjo that I took the back off. Again, it's a little tight, but once the banjo's zipped in I prefer that to having a case in which the banjo slops around.

Text:
I got a kalimba which was out of tune when I got it. The key was F major, and I wanted to tune it accordingly.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This has all of the features as listed in the product description. It has a jack in it where you plug it into the clip which you put on the instrument and you can tune your instrument. There is also a charging port to recharge the tuner.

HOW LONG TO CHARGE?
This came partially full, and it only took under an hour to charge fully. It shows the battery usage. After several uses, I have 4 strips of battery left.

HOW DOES IT PERFORM?
I love how easy this is to read and tune with. The clip was big enough to fit on the outside of the kalimba which is pretty thick. The tuner shows a red light over or below the goal tune you are looking for. When it is green, you are there.

Incrementally, you can turn this to whatever key you want on the list. This works perfectly. I could not believe how easy it was to tune. It has a lot of indicators so that you can tune just below or above the goal tone which a lot of people like to do.

METRONOME
This is a handy feature when I want to play a variety of instruments with a cadence. It works well and I like it.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This tuner is fabulous. I like this a lot as it seems accurate, has a great readout that is easy to see with colors so it is quick to read. The accuracy seems good and it works quickly and easily. Having it rechargeable is fantastic too.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is one of my favorite tuners. I like that it also has a metronome when I want one. For now, however, I use it mostly for tuning. The specific tuning set ups give a lot of choices which I can use for my instruments (which I have quite a few of).

I've been a fan of high quality headphones for some time and have had little issue with paying a bit more for them. In the past, this usually meant buying Sennheiser.

These headphones blow away any Sennheiser headphones or headsets I've had.

Sound: The sound reproduction is quite good. The high dynamic range is probably the best I'd heard, and tuned quite well. Despite having high impedance, my computers seem capable of driving them well, and I can get adequate performance from my phone without my portable amp. Still, I recommend using a headphone amp for the best sound if you purchase the 250 Ohm model.

These are closed back headphones, so outside sound will be more difficult to hear, and the sound reproduction will be...I guess the best way to put it is "less broad."

Comfort: This is really important to me when it comes to headphones I intend to wear for long periods of time. Given I bought these to use at work, I wanted to make sure they would be comfortable. With the velour pads, rather than the vinyl covered foam found in many headphones in this range, the comfort is quite good.

Construction: While there are plastic bits, the stressed parts (ie: the headband) are metal. This makes for very sturdy construction.

I like that when off of my head the ear cups clamp together. The pads and the closed back will silence the headphones if there is still audio playing through them. I find this useful in preventing disturbing my coworkers if I have to step away from the desk and I forget to hit pause on my music.

If you don't mind pay a little extra, I highly recommend these headphones. They are cheaper and sound better than the Sennheiser headphones I've used in this performance range, and far outperform Beats headphones that can cost twice as much. If you don't want to be fiddling with a headphone amp, portable or not, then there are options for lower impedance (ie: 80 Ohm).

I received this item as a Christmas gift (by request) with plans to install it on an Epiphone acoustic. I took my time with the installation, used a Forstner bit to drill the hole, bought the right type of gel glue, read the instructions carefully, did practice runs, and all went very smoothly. Then, the moment of truth to plug it in to my acoustic preamp. Wow, with a little EQ (boost the treble and mids, cut the bass) this pickup makes the guitar sound pretty close to what it sounds like unplugged. I was surprised. My prior experience with electric acoustics involved sound hole magnetic pickups (ugh, terrible!) and built-in piezo under saddle pickups. The piezo under saddle pickups can be good, but they give the guitar a whole different sound - very trebly, lots of attack and string noise - hard to avoid making finger squeaks on the strings. The K&K are still piezo, yet behave differently because they are picking up way more of the overall soundboard, not just the saddle/strings. You get more of the natural resonance of the guitar and they are very sensitive to taps on the body if percussive sounds are part of your style. While I was at first disappointed that these didn't sound like I expected piezo pickups to sound, I realized after playing plugged/unplugged that these sound much more like what the guitar is supposed to sound like. The only reason I deducted a point from my score is that these do require some EQ to sound right. Although every guitar and install will be slightly different, if you don't have an acoustic preamp with EQ, you may not like what you hear.
Summary: Sounds very close to real acoustic!

Text:
I'm a novice to guitar repair, so if you are like me don't be afraid, it's not that hard (just need a soldering iron of course!). Just got this today and put it in a cheap mini strat. The wiring is not always the same color code apparently (i.e the photo has a yellow wire, mine didn't). I used another reviewer's instructions (Robert Johnson) and they were quite good except my wire colors were in a different order. Just know that whatever wire is connected to the shield wire is ground (my shield wire had black shrink wrap, and the other wire was green). I capped off the the other two that were wired together (in my case red and white) and the remaining wire was the hot wire and went to my switch. If you read the other reviewers instructions this will make sense. The wires are already soldered together as they should be. Now a couple of issues, and forgive me if I don't have the correct nomenclature for some of the parts:

The part of the pickup that has the holes to be screwed to the pick guard is plastic. The holes are small, and so are the screws that come with it-really small-and they almost go through the pick guard. I found two small washers and was installing them when the screw hole in the pickup stripped. I was being careful, but it stripped anyway. I used a small screw to bore out the hole to accommodate the bigger screws that came with the guitar. This seemed to work, but I'm a little concerned that the plastic part of the pickup may break or strip out. I was very careful doing this, so hopefully it will hold-only time will tell.

t. The only other issue is that the wires are a very thin gauge-thinner than the wire in the cheap guitar. Nothing broke, but it was a concern when working with the pickup.

For the price, it's pretty hard to complain. I just wanted to point out this stuff so you know what you're getting. It sounds pretty good, way better than the single coil that was already in it. This is my first pickup installation and it works and has definitely improved the guitar. Hope this helps and let me know if you have any questions, I'd be glad to help you if I can.

I have used four other lav mics, wired and wireless, and this Rode is by far the best I've used.

I make tutorial videos, and good sound is not just important, it's critical. Sometimes, I need to roam quite a distance from the camera, so I tried a wireless lav mic. Not being ready to shell out $600 for the really good ones, I bought a $45 wireless lav mic, and it works ... okaaaay, but I wasn't happy with the sound.

Now my setup is the Zoom H1n digital recorder, which is small enough to carry with me, and this Rode SmartLav lavalier microphone, wired to the recorder. So far, this is by far the best voice recording setup I have found.

In testing this unit, I fastened it to the front of my shirt, about 4" below my chin, and spoke a number of test sentences, including rotating my head from the far left to the far right while speaking. If you've ever worked with lav mics before, you know this can produce a very distracting difference in sound and volume. With the Rode, the difference in speaking volume was nearly indistinguishable.

Additionally, the sound quality of the voice was spot on. Very little background noise, almost zero distracting mouth noise (such as smacks, clicks, pops).

I've only been using this for a few days, so cannot yet attest to its durability, but as of now I'm very happy with this item.

DigiTech is a company that gets a lot of flak from guitar effects "elitists" for two primary reasons: (1) They are a mass-produced, "cheap" effects pedal manufacturer (similar to the criticisms of Boss; (2) They absorbed much of the catalog of the now-defunct DOD pedal company, which made a lot of inexpensive, yet often poor, pedals in terms of reliability and tone. I am increasingly of the opinion that these criticisms are no longer fair. While the "digital" X-Series offered by DigiTech (Hot Rod, Tone Driver, Distortion Factory, etc) is somewhat of a mixed bag, DigiTech does offer a number of excellent analog pedals, such as the Hot Head, Bad Monkey, and Screamin' Blues, which are basically modified versions of the Boss DS-1, Ibanez TS-9, and Boss BD-2, respectively.

So why consider a Screamin' Blues instead of the Boss BD-2 Blues Driver? First, it's cheaper. Most of the DigiTech pedals can be had for $50 or less new, or often in the $20-$40 range used, which is about as good of a price as you could expect. Second, it actually offers two features that the BD-2 does not have: a split mixer/amp output jack, and a two-band tone control that allows you to dial up (or down) the bass.

The latter of these "improvements" is critical to the success of the pedal. Both the Blues Driver and Screamin' Blues start from a Tubescreamer platform, but offer additional gain and an overall brighter sound. The Screamin' Blues can actually become fairly raucous if you turn up the gain, much more so than a Tubescreamer. In my opinion, this pedal has more output than a Tubescreamer, and therefore, would work better as a booster for amps or other pedals. High notes really sing on this pedal, and there's even enough gain to do blues and rock rhythm parts without adding other effects.

If there was subjective "criticism" I would have, it might be that the higher-gain tones aren't as transparent as a TS-9 or an SD-1, but I believe that is intended as part of the pedal. It's also hinted at in the name "Overdrive/Distortion" - this pedal is meant to give your tone some additional grit. It's definitely staying in my collection, and might just become a permanent fixture on my board!
Summary: Great value and quality from DigiTech's answer to the Boss BD-2 Blues Driver!

Text:
I bought this cable to connect my bass to my amp in a very tight setting on a small stage. Regular straight cables would just drop to the floor and I hate walking on them. This coil cord was just what I needed for this cramped stage. The cable does not touch the floor and gives me all the length I need to get 5-6 feet away comfortably from my amp (which is still impossible on this one stage).

I unscrewed the barrel on each of the plugs to check the soldering. I was pleased to see that there was a length of heavy heat shrink tubing completely covering the entire joint almost to the bottom of the jack threads. The connections appear to be well made. If I ever needed to repair this myself, I could cut the heat shrink off with a razor, resolder and reapply my own heat shrink tubing. The coil cord itself is nicely thick. I looks like it will last a good while.

One note, and this is not a complaint. The photo shows the straight ends of the cord sticking straight out as if the ends are molded that way. They are not rigid or molded that way at all. The ends are free to move or hang straight however you need them. This may be something to consider if you think a 90 degree plug on one end might fit your application better. I normally use a 90 on the instrument side and loop the end through my strap like a strain relief. I was fooled by the photo.

At $12, I would buy another one of these if needed. Very satisfied.

My first shipment came complete with a defective receiver. I contacted the manufacturer and they quickly sent a replacement which worked well beyond my expectations. Make no mistake about it, this isn't a Sennheiser or Shure wireless system, but it sounds good for voice (my particular use) and has a range of about 150+ feet, maybe more under the right conditions. For the price, it is an amazing value. They give you both a hand held mic and a lavaliere mic with an additional head-worn mic, which is handy for hands free operation with little chance of feedback. The only thing missing is a mic clip to allow the hand held mic to be used on a standard mic stand. That's an easy fix for around $5, although I wish they had included one. If you have non critical wireless mic needs, this might be for you.

Addendum: Since the seller did not seem to want me to send back the defective unit, I decided to open it up to see what was wrong. Only one wire was connected to the audio output - a manufacturing defect. The 1/4" phone jack was also intermittent. Rewiring it correctly and replacing the jack made it work. While doing this, I discovered that the "Balanced Output" is not balanced at all. It is just a male XLR connector wired in parallel with the unbalanced phone jack. In most instances, that probably won't be a problem, but it could be in some cases. Further, the output is neither mic level nor line level, but somewhere in between - although it is controlled by the volume control on the receiver. That may not be an issue for most people, but it is another thing that could potentially be a problem, depending on what you are using it for.

We are using one of these to feed a speech only PA system for tour guide use in a museum. It is fine for that, and quite a bargain at that. Call it "casual use." For more critical applications, you would be better served by sticking with a wireless system for Sennheiser, Shure, Audio-Technica or others. Some times you do get what you paid for.
Summary: Hard to argue with, or maybe not....

I have used several different brands of "strap locks," and they are all a pain in the butt compared to these little marvels. I hate trying to screw straplocks onto thick leather strap ends (and all the quality straps have thick ends). And they're ridiculously expensive. And to top it all off, you are stuck using one particular strap on one guitar (unless you're a rock star and have multiple guitars all outfiltted with the same kind of straplocks). These little buggers are brilliantly engineered to fit in a straps end easily and then hold on well (unless you're really acrobatic with your guitar). They let you use the strap you want with the guitar you want. And best of all, they're affordable enough you can use them on multiple guitars.
TIP: Yes, they DO swivel around a bit - which is why you need to put a few drops of Gorilla Glue in the hole before you screw them in, making sure the eye-shaped button part is pointed the right direction to hold onto the strap once you're done. Let the glue cure over night with the screw in it and you'll have a rock-solid strap lock.

Being that this is my first ukulele, I'm not sure how to review the Fender. I will have to compare it to other ukes that players in my ukulele club have.

I spent the extra money to get the Nohea All Koa uke. Afterwards I found out that the "All Koa" is a bit misleading. I've been told, and pro reviews say that it isn't all Koa wood body construction, rather it is a veneer of Koa wood over a composite. So you are probably going to get virtually the same sound from the cheaper mahogany tenor.
In my opinion it doesn't matter a lot about the wood, the polyurethane coating finish (at least that's what it feels like) is so heavy that I doubt there is much resonance from the wood affecting the sound.
The Fender does not produce a loud or particularly rich sound compared to other ukuleles in its price range. The body isn't very deep (front to back dimension) as a result, the sound is thinner than other tenors. I bought this sight unseen because I had $200 in gift cards. I should have gone to a music store to try out a few different brands before making a decision.
I love the head design. Just like the signature Fender guitars. I like having the tuner keys all on the side and that all turn the same direction to tighten the strings. And it looks great.
The neck is narrower than what's on many tenor ukes. I have somewhat short fingers for my height, so this makes reaching some of the chords easier, if somewhat crowded on a few. The smooth finish makes moving up and down the neck a breeze. However, the fret bars are VERY ROUGH on the ends and can scratch your fingers if you are a little over the side when you hammer a string. (As I said: I'm new at this and I am not very accurate yet with placing my fingers. I'm hesitant about filing the burrs off myself, because of the possibility of scratching the finish. But I suppose I'll have to do it. That's a BIG "con" in my book.
The strings seem to be about the right height above the fretboard & fretbars. They seem to uniform in height. But the action on the first fret is difficult for all of the strings. So I may see if I can find someone willing to adjust the action. Since I didn't buy it locally, I may not be able to find anyone willing to do it.
Asthetically, the workmanship is good, but not great. The join between the neck and the body looks like a filler was used. The thick gloss finish hides any mistakes pretty well. I'm not a fan of the plastic mother of pearl inlay decoration, but many other people have complimented me on its looks. So, a matter of personal taste.
The Koa wood is handsome looking.
All in all, I think this sounds more like a travel uke. A nice sound, but not a particularly rich sound for a tenor. So I can't give it more than 4 stars. In fact, I was considering only 3. Maybe 3.5?
UPDATE: I took my Fender Uke to a music shop and asked them to adjust the action. The owner/repair tech played it and said: "You're right the action is terrible!" When I picked the instrument up three days later, he said he lowered both the bridge and the nut. What a difference! Played much better. A few days ago I removed the Aquila nylon strings, which are close to the strings that came with the Fender, and replaced them with thinner Martin fluorocarbon ones. Wow! Big change in tone! The Aquilas made the uke play dull and muddy. The Martins are louder and have a much brighter sound. (I'll also try the D'Addario bright strings.) The first fret is now far easier to barre chords due to the thinner strings. (Though harder on my fingers.) The sound is also much better. I give the uke a solid 4 now.
My advice is to try different strings to find the sound you like best.
Summary: Nice, but Not as Good as I hoped

If you have a Fender electric guitar (meaning a guitar that is fitted with a 3- or 5-way PU selector switch that looks like this switch), this should hold enormous appeal to you. I build a Telecaster or Stratocaster for fun every now and then, and I have come to keeping one of these on hand either for my building or to help my friends upgrade their Fender guitars.

If you do not know why a "4-pole 5-way" is so useful look to Seymour Duncan's and Stewart McDonald's sites; there are many more, too. These sites will explain the versatility that is within your reach with this switch.

If you can read simple schematics go to DBG Studio for Guitar Players and Builders' site; you will find the mother lode of guitar wiring schematics. It will take a while to figure out how the schematics work at DBG, but the enormous versatility this switch offers in irresistible and should propel you to `get it.' Just use the index for "4-pole 5-way" and check it out. In and out of phase, add a capacitor for different tones, parallel or series, coil taps, are all no problem with this.

And if you want, you can swap out your 500k volume or tone pot with a 500k push/pull pot to get 10 PU options - or you can just drill a hole in your pickguard and put in a mini-toggle switch to get the same advantages. But I like to just use a push/pull pot because the guitar has that `stock' look but has 10 PU options. Wow!

Assuming that you can solder (or learn to, it is not hard) you can have enormous fun with this switch.
Summary: A 'no-brainer' for Fender players. Buy it now!

I wanted something I could record to without worrying about DAW latency issues, software compatibility, etc., and this unit seemed like my best option. I'm not looking to make the White Album, just some backing tracks for solo gigs and maybe a few demos and vanity "sell at the gig for ten bucks" CDs. At that, the DP-24 SD excels.

It's a very solid piece of hardware and more than capable of producing professional-sounding recordings without a HUGE learning curve. Not to say there's NO learning curve; there is. It took me a couple weeks to become fairly proficient with the thing, and that only after several hours alone with YouTube tutorials, of which there are many. If you're willing to put in the time, though, it quickly becomes second nature and you can crank out decent recordings in a fairly quick and painless fashion.

It's also easy to transfer WAV files to and from the unit and into (or out of) your DAW. I've finally decided on a workflow in which I record all my tracks to the DP24, then load them into my laptop for final mix-down and mastering. It's all fairly seamless once you get the hang of it.

I also plan to use the unit as a live mixer at solo gigs, since it has all the effects (verb, exciter, compressor, etc.) that I need for live shows, and will allow me to easily play the backing tracks along with my live performance.

I paired my DP24 with a good set of earphones, some mid-priced studio monitors, a mid-priced mic, studio pre-amp, pop filter, acoustic panels, etc., to make a fairly decent little home studio that fits in one corner of my dining room. All told, I probably dropped less that a grand for the entire set up and the results I've been getting are at least as good as what I've gotten in "real" studios in the past.

For the money, this unit is an amazing piece of hardware!
Summary: Great Starting Point for Home Studio

This pedal board is pretty solid for what it promises to deliver. It is pretty rugged, but it isn't up to the standards of ATA flight cases. Clearly Boss expected this to be used by mature professionals, or folks who take good care of their toys. I bought this more for the organization rather than protection, but I am 100% certain that this pedal board will stand up to the light to medium abuse I plan to put it through. If you are really hard on your gear, or going on tour, you should definitely look into ATA grade cases.

Many people have written about the hinges on this particular pedal board, but there had to be a compromise made in the design, because the pedal board was meant to separate at the hinges, so that you can lay it flat. I could see that after a few hundred times of taking it apart, it may not be the most secure, but it's just an example of a trade off of durability vs convenience.

One of my favorite aspects of this pedal board is that all power cords are hidden under a rail, secured with thumb screws, so there is very little clutter from cables. Once you lock down the layout of your pedals, you can secure the cables and never have to deal with tangles, and the usual difficulties working with multiple power cables.

This pedal board was meant for use with BOSS pedals, but it can also accommodate wah-wah pedals, double-pedals, and most compact stomp-boxes, as they supply a padding blank, that you can cut to the custom shape of whatever pedal it is you need!

PROS:
+ Durable enough for someone who takes care of their stuff, not indestructable
+ Hinges detach for ease of use
+ Includes 1000mAh power supply (no more 9v batteries!)
+ Includes all the patch cables you need
+ Everything is secured with thumbscrews, no tools needed to modify

CONS:
- A bit expensive for what it is
- Takes a while to set up initially
- Padding material is a little tough to cut
Summary: More for convenience than for protection, but does both well!

When you think about it a guitar cable has a pretty simple job. All it has to do is accept the tiny signal produced by the guitar pickups and deliver it faithfully, over the span of several feet, to the amplifier. What’s the big deal? Well, it also has to deliver that signal without introducing any external noise, it has to stay connected at both ends while being stepped on, slapped against the stage, and dragged back and forth, stretched, coiled up and bent and do so for hours at a time. The Rig Ninja cable does all this and more at a value price.

Not only does this cable look good with its vintage woven sheath, it resists kinking and tangling while you are playing or later when you’re packing up your rig. The builder uses high quality plugs with both a stress relief and heat shrink applied over the solder points. It doesn’t excellent job of carrying my guitar signal to the amplifier with no loss in the build quality leads me to think that it’s going to last a long time. This is an excellent value and beats some name brand cables costing twice as much and more.

HERE'S THE SKINNY; I string a LOT of guitars, and have since 1977. I use a high-speed 600RPM dedicated cordless screwdriver (the Ryobi Tec 4V). I really wanted to like this PW Drill Bit Peg Winder adaptor, but I find it too cumbersome to work with at high speed. Although most people would find its multi-instrument design to be an asset, I find it makes this adaptor too big and clumsy for my guitar work. This is why I ONLY USE IT ON BASSES.

On guitar tuners, it utterly engulfs the tuner knobs in its behemoth maw and disconnects me from one of the important things I monitor while stringing at industrial speeds. (I monitor the string wrap, string tension, turning post and knob while aligning the string in the nut and on the saddle). If I can't see the knob, I feel like I'm disconnected from what's happening.

Another thing is that this winder adaptor is made from a resin that is IMHO is too hard to have spinning at the speed I'd be using it at right next to expensive guitar wood and metal with delicate finishes. However, because bass tuners are much larger, this adaptor usually doesn't come too close to the headstock of a bass.

IMHO, Planet Waves usually makes pretty decent and innovative products, although I've heard from a lot of techs that they dislike PW stuff. I'm not sure why. I know Daddario's CS is obnoxious to communicate with and doesn't listen to their customers (anymore), but they do arguably make one of the best strings and other neat products for the musician.

Although I don't personally like the Planet waves Drill Bit Peg Winder, it does have a metal shank and it should last two lifetimes. Maybe it'll work for you?

Hope this review helps someone.

Text: When I bought my first electric guitar, a Telecaster, the sales person suggested the Fender 25R Frontman amplifier to me. However I decided to go with a Champion 40 instead, thinking I wanted something with a few more 'bells & whistles' as the Champion has many voices &  effects built into it. After I was playing a while the number of amps and guitars in my collection started going up as I added a Frontman 10 bedroom amp, a Champion 20, as well as a few Stratocasters and a Les Paul guitar. It seemed every time I went into my local guitar store to try out a few different guitars, I found myself seeking out that neat red amplifier with the nice reverb on it. I would pass by the expensive large amps with all kinds of features, and would plug into the 25R. I love the clear clean sound that the 25R amp provides in spades. At times a 25R wasn't available and I would plug into a much more expensive amp, but when one became available I would switch amps. I especially love the wonderful reverb. Also the overdrive & volume of this amp are very impressive. I also appreciated the straightforward controls the 25R has. Input jack, Rotary knobs for Volume, Gain, (a button to turn the drive/gain on or off)  Rotary knobs for Drive Volume, Treble , Middle,  Bass, & Reverb level - auxilary jacks, Foot Switch Jack, Earphone Jack, & Power (On/Off) switch - There you have it - all you need for great sound out of a 25 Watt amplifier. Again the sound of this amp is extremely impressive and I found it perfect to compare various guitars abilities for clean sound, overdrive, and of course the outstanding reverb that this amp has in spades. Finally I saw that fewer & fewer 25R amps were available and decided to get one before they were all gone. I called the manager of my local guitar store and he found me a brand new one still sealed in its box and had it shipped to the store for me. I have bigger amps, I have amps with a lot more features, but I find that my Frontman amps (both the diminutive 10, and it's impressive big brother the 25R) are the shining stars of my sound equipment. I truly find that the 25R is all I need in a home amplifier - excellent sound and excellent reverb. I highly recommend this amplifier - Get one before they are gone.

There are a TON of pluses for this interface:

- Low price
- Audio quality is unmatched at this price point or even 2-3x higher (192kHz, 24-bit compared to most others 48kHz, 16-bit)
- Ultra-low latency and direct monitoring
- Solid 45-48V Phantom Powering via USB bus and the MIDAS preamps sound really, really good (really!)

And so on. This has worked incredibly for desktop recording, streaming, and voice chat. You have to know what you're doing -- ASIO drivers means this is more of a pro-level recording product, not a desktop WDM interface -- which meant using with voice chat programs like Skype and Discord cause some difficulty, which can be resolved through using a software routing program like Voicemeeter Banana or similar (routes ASIO audio streams to virtual WDM I/O). If you're just using this for recording, there's no issue whatsoever, but for voice chat applications, be advised that this works but requires some time to setup. The direct monitor switch lowers all other audio output, which I wasn't a fan of. Luckily if your computer can process with ultra low latency you get near real-time monitoring. The only other disappointment I have is that this doesn't come bundled with any software. So for only a few bucks more, unless you can get this on sale, you can get a Scarlett Solo/2i2 or M-Track 2x2 and have at least minimal recording software. This isn't a huge issue for those that have recorded before (like myself) but, for people who are looking at this as their entry to recording, be advised that you'll need to get some software to record. There are free products out there, but are very feature-limited.

In all, I'm glad I made this purchase. This has some of the best preamps I've heard even among $400-500 products I've used. You can't go wrong. The feature set and some of the design choices, plus the lack of software keeps this from being a 5-star product. You can still buy with confidence as long as you know what you're getting.
Summary: Great entry-level and low-cost way to get impressive preamps and desktop recording.

I'm a big fan of Ultimate Support equipment because it's always engineered and manufactured to a high level... when I open the box my expectations are met or exceeded.

Well this is not really Ultimate Support gear, and if they're going for a budget line with the JamStands label then I think they'll tarnish their name. It only takes 15 seconds to see that this boom arm will not take abuse and will likely fail eventually with normal use. It will suffice for someone who sets it up, leaves it alone, and uses it personally. But don't plan on breaking it down and packing it, or changing the adjustments too often. This is a frail bit of gear that will need to be babied. It has all the hallmarks of cheap Chinese manufacture... including the tell-tale noxious paint smell (I truly pity the workers that build this stuff and live in those factories). But I guess that's what $19 delivered gets you.

Edit: I knocked it down to two stars bc after setting it up, it really doesn't perform its function without modification... the central pivot (where the arm meets the stand) slips and doesn't hold the angle no matter how hard you tighten it. And I have it set up without the extension out and with the boom about half back... basically about 12" in total length. I do have a condenser diaphragm mic on it, but it should certainly be able to hold that short of a reach.

The reason it slips is that the housing... the sleeves on the outside of the joint... are smooth inside and they squeeze two rubber disks. The rubber is too hard and the housing is a bit large, so the rubber just slips and doesn't hold. I modified it by cutting disks of that 3M tread stuff you can buy at Home Depot... its an aggressive grit and has strong glue on the back. I put two disks facing the rubber washer on each side (4 disks total) so that they press on the rubber, since that will wear slower and can be replaced. It's now fairly stiff even before it's tight, and locks up nicely when tightened down. Took about 30 minutes, but I already had the 3M stuff and some Wiss snips to cut it.

I'd normally return it but I need it for the weekend. And I'd normally give it one star but I was able to modify it quickly and effectively. If you don't enjoy that sort of thing, you're better off looking elsewhere and paying more. When you buy inexpensive gear you really buy more of a kit than a finished product, and some extra ingenuity seems to be needed more often than not these days
Summary: A bit frail and doesn't function without modification (see edit)... not Ultimate Support quality.

[[VIDEOID:338f711d56b11498cdf36107fa922a60]] PreSonus Eris E5 is an excellent, small, beautiful monitor. It is a bit warm with excellent bass response, and very nice build quality. With three inputs (XLR, 1/4" and RCA) and both a high and mid boost dial, it provides a lot of options. The front-side port is great for the (common) desktop or against the wall placement so many people use.

The biggest con I have with this is that I got distortion at volume levels that I felt I shouldn't be getting it at considering the 102 DB SPL and 80 watts of power. With that said, it's a solid speaker that you can feel good about owning.

I've attached a video of me comparing it against the JBL SLR305, which is in a similar price category and gets similarly great reviews.

The differences are highlighted in the video, including:

Eris Pros relative to JBL LSR305:
Much smaller for the same speaker size and power output (and weight)
Front bass port, making them better for near-the-wall placement many people will prefer
Produced a richer, bassier sound than the JBLs, despite their higher HZ rating and smaller size... impressive
Aesthetically more pleasing... modern, expensive looking, clean deisgn, esp the kevlar cone and lit logo
Requires quite a bit less input volume to attain the same output volume (contrary to the SPL rating... so I find JBL's numbers suspicious)
RCA Input for additional input options w/o modification - helpful for people outputting from their computer or other component without 1/4" or XLR outputs
More fine-tuning adjustments for mid and high as well as room on the back of the speaker.

Eris Cons compared to JBL:
Breaks up more at the same volume (this was on bassy dubstep with lows and highs... they started to get muddy and a bit broken up)
Has a less efficient A/B class amplifier, gets warmer
Not as good at capturing highs, not as flat (good for home use though, but I question the accuracy in mixing)
A bit more expensive
Narrower "sweet spot" making less ideal for "whole room" uses
Summary: Presonus Eris 5 vs. JBL LSR305 Monitors

The Yamaha YPT260 is an inexpensive digital 61 key keyboard which packs in features. Notable are the breadth of built in voices, full-sized keys, decent amount of rhythm accompaniment and teaching features. The controls are for the most part intuitive and easy to learn. Voices, patterns and songs are entered with a row of numbered keys, and some of the more often voices and rhythms are printed on the keyboard itself. There is a rotary volume knob, and a recessed power button, so that the keyboard can't be accidentally turned off.

In the middle of the keyboard is a LCD display which gives information such as voice, rhythm or song being used. On the left of the display is the note being played, and on the bottom is the key being pressed. This information is necessary when using the built-in teaching mode of the keyboard. There are three different settings for teaching; Listen and Learn, Timing and Waiting. Timing is where you play along with one of the several built in songs, focusing on the rhythm of the notes. Waiting is a mode where the accompaniment will pause until you press the right note on the keyboard. The problem with this mode is the display showing the keyboard, and which key to play, is small. It would have been good for this display to be much larger, so that you can easily see what note to play.

The Yamaha YPT260 and YPT360 are siblings that have many the same features. Both are full-sized keyboards with a large array of built in sounds. But the key differences (beyond the YPT360 costing more) is the the YPT 360 is touch sensitive, and has USB. The first feature allows for more nuanced playing, the second feature is nice in that it allows you to connect the keyboard to a computer, and use it with music software. The YPT 260 has a headphone jack, and also a jack to connect in an audio player. With that, you can play along with songs you like - it is mixed together.

The voices are a mixed bag - the piano has a full sound with a touch of reverb, but other sounds, like the saxophone does not come close. There are a bevy of other sounds as well, some useful, some whimsical (sound effects). Since there are so many to choose from, keep the manual handy. Rhythms are the stock rock, "soul", disco and so on - but there are plenty to choose from. They work well enough as background for playing.

In all, this is a nice, inexpensive keyboard with a large number of voices, probably many more than most people will use. The user interface is OK, but a larger display would be much appreciated. The sounds such as the piano are full, and the keyboard will play loudly with no distortion. It includes both a power supply and music holder. It is affordable, lightweight, and has all the features you would expect on an inexpensive keyboard.

I bought the Mini Tone Master as a practice amp for my Dean EVO electric guitar, and love it -- but there are a few things you should know before a possible purchase:

1. When they say "mini," they mean it. It's a tiny little thing about the size of a hardcover book (or smaller), and about as thick (2" thick or so).

2. It also runs off a 9V battery, though if you have a DC9V adapter, there's a plug for it. it also has a 1/4 jack for standard headphones or earbuds as well.

3. It's LOUD. Even when at low volume its tones will fill a room. This is a major plus for such a tiny, inexpensive amp.

Controls on the amp are great; it has a gain/distortion knob that is almost as good as having an overdrive or gain effects pedal hooked up to a full-size amp. It's strong enough to where if you're playing small gigs such as coffeehouses or hole-in-the wall small bars, you won't need to lug along your 10W (or larger) amp with you, though that may depend on the tone your guitar puts out to begin with. Still, this is an awesome deal; I paid about $30 here on Amazon for it, so if you need a practice amp but don't want to spend a ton of cash, snatch up one of these little bad boys. You won't be sorry.
Summary: Inexpensive, compact, and LOUD = great little amp.

Text:
I did some research before purchasing the Zoom H4n Pro. I wanted to be able to record myself or others outside of a studio setup. After comparing the various options and tradeoffs between cost and features, I settled on this model. I watched some reviews and was aware of how to use the basic features without reading a manual. The UI is similar to a modern digital camera with a menu and scrolling capability. The buttons are laid out in a reasonable manner and are self-explanatory.

My first session with it was outside. I had purchased a 32GB SDHC card (no storage comes with the device). I bought a little tripod with the proper threading to mount this for about $15. That first session was on a windy day and I had not yet received the Dead Cat noise filter accessory I had also ordered from Amazon. That session was unusable because of the gusting winds. Next I tried it inside within my studio so I could compare it to recording via condenser or dynamic mics going into my audio interface This time the recording was very nice. Clear, rich, low noise. Using the built-in XY mics in default 90% phase captured the acoustic guitar really well. It rivaled several old standards such as an SM58 (or SM57). Setting back a few feet from the guitar with the little tripod allowing the height and angle to be well-positioned gave me nice natural stereo.

The Zoom H4n Pro has a great set of features for a device under $200USD. If you are looking to have a portable, hi-fidelity recorder with up to 4 tracks, this device is a grand slam home run. Because I had researched the product, I knew it came without an SD or SDHC card and ordered one. I also got a nice desk/tabletop tripod, AC adaptor and Dead Cat wind filters (I bought two accidentally). The H4n Pro comes with a manual, some licenses to software (I haven't touched these yet), and a fitted clear plastic hard case. You might also want to get a mini-USB cable. It seems most devices are micro-USB these days which is flatter so I ordered a 5 ft mini-USB for docking it to my MacBook Pro. I also have a SD/SDHC reader on one of my USB C->to->other hubs. Rather than buy Zoom's accessory pack, I researched the individual components I wanted or ordered the from Amazon.

This device makes very nice sounding recordings. I record straight to WAV. If doing that, all you need to do is put appropriate SD-type card in, power it on, press record once to see the input levels and adjust if needed, and press record again. The ring turns solid red indicating recording. The default settings using the built-in XY mics exceeded my expectations and I am very happy I bought this unit. Why only a 4 star review? It's fairly tough to get the 5th star out of me. The failure to package everything needed (SD card of some sort, dead cat, AC power adapter, stand, usb cable) was a bit of a con, but it also allowed me to hand pick components. On overall value for the price, I'd say this is a five star review.
Summary: Nice audio quality and rich feature set for less than $200 USD

Text:
Decent jingle quality and volume. Appears well-made. One possible improvement would be to supply it with adjustable replaceable strap with quick release buckle or velcro rather than the elastic one, which is a little tight even on my narrow size 9 foot. It's definitely a two-handed procedure to apply it, but once on it stays in place well. Also, that would address the possible issue of strap breakage and replacement after repeated heavy use.

One other observation about the sound, and this is not a fault; it's just due to the very nature of it's design: it's difficult to attain a sharp attack like you get when striking a tambourine with your hand, a stick, or a foot tap (when resting your foot on top of one on the floor). The LP188 (and probably any foot tambourine) jingle is initiated with foot motion before impact with the floor, so it can sound a bit blurred and delayed. Tapping your foot harder will mask this effect somewhat, but might lead to fatigue if you're not used to doing that. Another trick I've found helpful for this is to strap the tambourine up higher onto the midfoot rather than the forefoot. There is a little less motion there so the jingles will be less sensitive until impact. Also they will respond almost as well to heel tap as well as forefoot tap, giving you the option of heel up and heel down playing, thereby lessening fatigue.
Overall, a very handy inexpensive instrument, especially for cajon players.
Summary: it's difficult to attain a sharp attack like you get when striking a tambourine with your hand

Text: I ordered a bunch of different electric and acoustic strings last week. I like to use different gauges, materials, or brands. I came back around 8pm and decided to capture some ideas in my head. So I tuned up and recorded the entire 40 minute session with the guitar uninterrupted stream of consciousness. I never needed to pause and tune up. It was bright and exhibited all the delicious tones that a Dreadnought in the hands of hippie should make! Everything felt right while I was playing so I just powered on from idea to idea. It's a warm humid day so I I put the guitar down after that session and played back the recording. These strings sound amazing. 40 minute session of various intensity playing with string, picking and palm muting. Lots of light hammer on/offs. The strings were bright as sunshine and they broke in amazingly fast. They both felt and sounded good. Wow. I am just going to order a few more sets so always have these around. Next month I try a different Ernie Ball set with .11-.52 which is more my norm.

We have a small band that needs lights on occasion.  In the olden days when there was just white lights, the controller just had to control the brightness.  Now, the new LED lights use at least 7 channels just for one light to control the colors, brightness, flashing, etc.  This unit has 12 scanners preprogrammed with 16 channels each (1-6, 17-32, 33-48, etc).  There are only 8 physical slidders and a button to switch between 1-8 and 9-16 channel control. The 12 scanners can be turned on and off with a button assigned to each scanner.  So, now a single LED takes 7 channels (other lights may differ on the number of channels used) so each scanner would be able to control 2 lights by switching between A & B for the slidder control.  You could control all 24 lights (12 scanners times 2 lights each) if you select all the scanners on, but all the lights would act the same to whatever the slidders are set at.  But, there is the capability to program scenes so that each light can be set to what you want it to be and each light can be programmed differently.  This is what takes the extra time learning to program each scene.  Over all, I think for a small number of fixtures (8 or so) this would be ok for like a school play or small band.  If you just have white lights, this woukd work great.

I can't believe this thing is getting 5 stars across the board. Obviously it is from people who do not know instruments at all and think they scored one heck of a deal. This banjo is nothing more than a cheap chinese made fake that is churned out by the millions, the jamison name is just stamped on it because they bought "X" amount. This same banjo has about 12 different names stamped to it, it's all the same. The only thing this product does so well is look like a nice banjo.

Onto the banjo itself, it has no tone ring. For those who don't know banjos, the tone ring is the brass ring that sits below the head and against the rim and gives the banjo a nice "ring" (essentially giving the banjo it's sound that makes a banjo a banjo). This is just a cheap remo head laid against a poorly made rim, giving it a plunking sound as soon as you actually try to play a real note instead of a strum. The neck is so narrow the strings want to go over the edge, making it almost unplayable. As soon as you hold this banjo, then pick up a "real" one from a music store, you will want to throw this thing in your kids toy box where it belongs.

If you don't believe me just google cheap banjos and read from real musicians about this poorly made junk. Spend money and get a good quality instrument that has a good resale value. If you decide the banjo isn't for you the better ones hold their value well. This pile of junk will make you discouraged and will make you give up because you think your terrible and will ever learn, when in reality it's this clone that is mostly at fault. (And remember the heavier the banjo is, the better it is).
Summary: The only thing this product does so well is look like a nice banjo

Ugh. This has to be one of the worst sounding and underperforming amps I have ever heard.

Where to begin? Firstly, there is some sort of noise gate on the output, so any volume below a certain point will have an intermittent cutting in and out. That makes it useless for scale playing or quiet practicing.

The stock sounds it ships with are unuable to the point of being some sort of bad joke. Do the folks at Line 6 really think that anyone with the ability to play more than five notes wants their tone to be completely masked by inferior DSP and thin EQ? Why on earth would I want to bathe a custom shop Fender in a wash of cheap effects?

As for the distortion, it is thin and weedy and nowhere near usable to anyone who actually overdrives amps or uses a real distortion. I would go so far as to say that if you are a beginner, DO NOT get your ear into the bad habit of thinking this is what a distorted guitar should sound like. It will only hurt you later on if you decide to get serious. If you already are serious, you know this thing sounds as lousy as a cheap AM radio.

Stretch a little. Pick up a [[ASIN:B00EM5UOE6 Fender Champion 20]] and a [[ASIN:B002QKRUJG MXR Fullbore Metal Distortion]] pedal - you'll thank me later.

This kind of cheap, beginner oriented junk is useless to anyone - again there is no good to be had in developing bad habits early on, and buying any gear that you inevitably outgrow (and is completely unsuitable for either live play or recording).

Do yourself a favor and pass on this, even at the price.

Text:
Below I’m going to review the product but also shed some light on the creator of this product. The overall score is a reflection of the product itself and not the creator because these are product reviews, not seller reviews, but it’s worth talking about both.

About the product itself:

This tool is fantastic for everyone from weekend warrior string instrument players to luthiers. Primarily this is a string height measurement tool, everything is kinda plays second fiddle, however, I imagine these secondary gauges will be really useful when the time is right. It’s nice that the creator maximized its usefulness.

As far as accuracy is concerned it’s dead-on from what I can tell, I tested with a very high precision caliper.

In the past for set up I used this same caliper but I found it annoying because getting precise measurements is an exercise in patience. For maximum accuracy I would use my very expensive caliper to measure the string width, then I would measure from the top of a fret to the top of the string using the depth gauge and then subtract the string width, I would do this three times and then average the results. I didn’t like measuring from the top of the fret to the bottom of the string because it’s hard (for me anyway) to do this precisely. We’re talking thousandths of an inch and it was difficult for me to tell if I was too low or too high using this method. I have also used feeler gauges in the past, but these are very one-dimensional and there was never a feeler gauge that was quite right, so I would stack them together, but I never felt confident.

I do like that all markings are laser etched and not printed. I work on bicycles as well and I have some tools with printed markings which have faded over time, I’m confident that this tool will last me a very long period without rubbing or fading.

There are only a couple notable (though minor) nitpicks. First, it really is expensive for what it is. You can find very similar tools for less than $10. I’m a big supporter in local economies and I trust that the FretGuru is near 100% accurate, so I went with this tool over saving cash and buying something made in China. In the end I knew what I was buying and paying for, so I can’t knock it down.

Second, the tool is very busy with markings. “FretGuru 2” is etched in a large font and and there are five arrows with descriptions etched as well. These arrows/descriptions are only useful once, after which they don’t have any use and only clutter things up. I would prefer a small instruction pamphlet describing each tool because knowing what the gauges are for is easy after learn it the first time. I really like cleanliness and minimalism, but in the grand scheme this is pretty much a non-issue.

Finally, I really wish I could choose an option that had markings measured in metric. There is a handy conversion chart on the back, but I would prefer metric markings over flipping it back and forth for conversions, that being said this is another small nitpick.

About the creator:

It really rubbed me the wrong way when I learned that Bernie basically bribed people for positive reviews. Apparently he offered the leather case if the customer gave a positive review. The product should speak for itself. Thankfully this seems to be an issue from the past because a leather case was included with mine and my tool didn’t come with a piece of paper trying to bribe me into leaving positive feedback. I learned about this issue after ordering and I was prepared to return this item if I received it along with a piece of paper trying to persuade me into leaving a positive review because that goes against my morals. Thankfully this is no longer an issue.

Also, Bernie comes across as a bit too impassioned in his responses to low rated reviews. He tends to respond verbosely with heaps of sarcasm when paying customers have complaints. I like his passion for this product, but you have to take these complaints in stride, not yell at your customers telling them that they are wrong. This will only put potential future customers off, had I read these reviews and responses before purchasing this product then I probably would have looked elsewhere.

Finally, this product is a bit oversold by Bernie. I get that he is impassioned but he acts like this tool is the second coming. Yes it’s accurate, yes it’s useful, but he treats this as the be-all and end-all of gauges for guitar/bass setup. Yes this tool will help you achieve good results, but so will many other tools. We have been setting up guitars/basses successfully long before this existed, so it’s not as revolutionary as Bernie might lead you to believe. That being said, he is trying to run a business and make money (aren’t we all?) so overselling your product(s) is to be expected, Bernie just goes a bit too far.

Conclusion:

There are many great features here and it’s a fantastic tool. It’s not perfect in every way possible (what is?) but it will help amateurs and pros alike achieve optimal results. The creator can come across as overbearing, but he is passionate about his product which I suppose is a good thing overall. I do highly recommend this product, especially if you are like myself and want to support local economies, but like everything else in this world it’s not completely without flaws. Thank you Bernie for creating this! I wish you continued success!
Summary: A great tool with few caveats

I really wish I could give this camera a better rating. I am classical musician, and the audio quality from a smartphone or consumer grade vlogging camera simply doesn't cut the mustard for what I do. On recommendation of a colleague I bought this Zoom Q8.
The audio is as close to professional grade as one can get for a small under $500 cam, and par to other Zoom audio recorders (I have an H4).
The camera is small, compact and light weight. Who works with an E-keyboard or an external microphone set & mixer has a direct audio plug-in option for recording, with no humming, white noise, distortion, or unwanted "sound enhancement". Each channel has an individual gain adjust. So fat I haven't tested the built-on X/Y mics but the audio quality of recordings done by others who own the same camera is really superb. You get a real HIFI quality here; so far the BEST.

But there are too many shortcomings outside that.
Let's start with the video quality. It's Sub par, comparable to a first gen surveillance camera at best. The fish eye effect is extremely annoying. The cheapest vlogging camera, even my phone, do MANY times better. With the "Stage / low lighting" setting, and tweaking the (digital) zoom, I get something close to acceptable, and since video quality is NOT my priority, let's keep it like that.

The battery comes next. It drains in no time. Getting a spare battery and a charger (not included) is an absolute MUST, unless one wants to keep the camera "running on juice" with the charging cable. Speaking of that, the charging port is of the OLD micro USB style. This might be done on purpose so nobody plugs the juice into the 'video out' new style micro USB port, but be aware if you need to replace or get a longer power cable.

The biggest problem however is the video format. It ONLY does .mov videos, and has no on-board converter to other, more standard / popular formats like mp4. So be prepared to invest in a video format converter, since .mov is not widely accepted... Instagram i.e. doesn't take it.

In conclusion, if we could put a man on the moon and fly a helicopter on Mars, why the industry isn't capable to build a consumer grade camera that gets BOTH video and audio quality right without breaking the bank is out of my comprehension. Honestly.

I have not heard a better sounding handheld, dynamic microphone. I have heard several that may sound just as good, some of which are much less expensive, but I can't say I've heard a better sounding one.

The biggest drawback I see with this microphone is it seems to have a stronger tendency to feedback than any other I've tried. I evaluated both feedback from the side and back and made a subjective evaluation of this and the polar pattern, and my perception tells me the e945 has a fairly broad pattern for a supercardioid, about the same as what many cardioid mics like the SM58 have. Although the e945 has significantly more gain than a SM58, it still tended to be more likely to produce feedback from the side even when the additional gain was compensated for in comparison.

It could be a great microphone where feedback is not a concern, or very likely, such as for recording or when the mic and monitors are in fixed locations and all precaution has been taken to avoid feedback.

Comparing it to other dynamic vocal mics, I appreciate the e945 as quite possibly the best of them. I felt it was better than the Telefunken M80, the Beyerdynamic TG-V70D, and several Audix models, as well as the SM58. However, I am a lot more doubtful the e945 has anything worth the much greater price. Comparing careful recordings using studio-quality headphones, I could just barely perceive a difference in sound qualities compared to good microphones costing 1/3rd the price. I wasn't really able to identify anything that would convince me it is certainly worth three times as much money as an alternative. Many of the differences I did perceive could have been due to small changes in the gain, distance and proximity effect that I couldn't perfectly compensate for.

I have a lot of long-term experience with Sennheiser microphones, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend them in general. You won't go wrong with this high-end microphone unless you have high stage volumes and feedback is a major concern, in which case you would be better off with a much tighter pattern.

Everything else I can think of is mostly subjective, and based on my testing, mostly in your head. I think people believe one mic sounds better than another simply because they heard it with more gain, or with the amount of their preference of proximity effect. I compared several mics without EQ or other processing, but when you add the EQ and compression that is typical in live sound environments, and consider that the PA and the room probably have anything but a flat response, the sound of a mic is going to be totally different. Ideally, you might compare them in the venue where they're to be used, but if that's constantly changing, then what really makes one mic better than another? Some are more dependable than others, but one certainly doesn't need to spend over two hundred dollars to get a reliable mic.
Summary: Great sounding, more prone to feedback than others
