I received the R144 as a gift, although it was on my wish list so I did want it. I have been slowly acquiring gear for my modest home "studio" plus gradually learning to be a "recording engineer". I'm not a complete newbie at this but also not an expert. However, I have been able to record songs with good quality so I've apparently learned some things along the way.

Prior to receiving the R144 I owned/used these microphones, choosing one or the other based on need or simply experimentation: Shure SM57, Shure SM58, MXL 603, AT3035. I had never used a ribbon mic but became aware of them through various Internet forums and musical web stores. The R144 receives generally good reviews and the price is low enough, so it went onto my "things to get" list.

I was concerned that the R144 would require a pre-amp with good gain, which I read is typical for ribbon mics. I hoped my ART TubePAC would suffice. In fact, the TubePAC provided plenty of gain for the R144 so I thought I'd try plugging the mic directly into my Soundcraft Notepad mixer (which I use prior to my M-Audio Delta 44 interface). The R144 worked fine with the mixer, providing sufficient mic volume, so now I don't bother using the TubePAC.

My first recording with the R144 was basic acoustic guitar, then vocal. Upon playback I thought "this isn't good, sounds dense and muddy". Then I adjusted EQ but increasing treble just a bit and the recordings came to life. The sound was now warm and clear. Very nice.

I have not noticed any noise from the R144, although it is sensitive and seems to pick up every little sound happening within 1/4 mile radius. That is somewhat of an exaggeration but it really is sensitive, although the same is true for my condenser mics. Luckily I live in the country where it is fairly quiet, although it's best to record when no other family members are home (and take the phone off the hook!). While my condenser mics are sensitive to 'plosives so I use a pop filter, the R144 seems somewhat more sensitive, especially to words beginning with P. I use the pop filter on the R144, which is mandatory for not only sound quality but to help protect the ribbon, but I also must place myself 6-12" inches further from the pop filter than I do when using the condenser mics. Otherwise the 'plosives can sometimes get through. Maybe my pop filter is low grade!

Although I've owned the R144 only six weeks I've used it several times, primarily for vocals but sometimes also for acoustic guitar. It is not better than my AT3035, which was my primary mic, but it does provide a different sound that is perfect for certain songs. While I feel the AT3035 is less warm than the R144, it is clearer and brighter so it also has its place. I did record upright bass with the R144 but I'm not as pleased with that, although in fairness I haven't spent much time to verify that acoustic bass is suitable to the R144. But mid to higher range instruments/voices work very nicely with the R144 after minor EQ tweaking. All told, I am satisfied having the R144 in my microphone selection as it provides for increased variety for me.

Update:
I have since stopped playin the violin with a shoulder rest or sponge. I use a Kreddle adjustable height chin rest and now play better than I used to and without any pain. The violin sits on my collarbone and I hold it up with my left hand while lightly resting my chin on the chin rest. I flip the Strad Pad upside down and attach it to the violin with a rubber band. This provides the perfect amount of cushion between the bottom of the violin and my collarbone, as well as adding a bit of friction to keep the violin from slipping. It also protects my neck from the metal bracket that holds the chin rest on.

————————-
I've been working on changing how my violin is set up. The neck and shoulder pain was getting to me. Different shoulder rests. No shoulder rest. Foam shoulder support. New chin rests. Chin rest pads. This is one option I tried. It didn't work for me but that doesn't mean it won't work for others. I use it occasionally with double stick tape for a temporary attachment. It is well made and provided a nice cushion. However, I needed to learn to not clamp down with my chin, which was the core problem, so for now I'm not using it. But I kept it just in case.

I've posted this review almost identically on all the products that I went through.

Where I've ended up is with a sponge as a shoulder rest. I bought just a car wash sponge and carved it out a bit to fit the contour of my collar bone and shoulder. I wish I could play without a shoulder rest at all but I have a tall neck and my shoulder is narrow and slopes quickly away. For my chin to even touch the chin rest without a shoulder pad I have to really crank my neck down. Not good. I had been taught years ago as a kid to use a shoulder rest and clamp down on it with my chin. Now I'm reversing that and holding the violin up with my left hand while I play. The chin lightly touches on the chin rest but my head and neck are in line with my spine and I don't have to bend my neck down. So my head can move freely while I play. The thick sponge shoulder pad keeps me from the reflex of pulling my left shoulder up while I play. I'm much more comfortable playing now even though I have to learn everything over again. It's amazing how much freer my movement is with the head not clamping down. The violin and my head can move more easily with the context of the music.

The sponge does change the tonal quality of the violin. But I just play for myself--I'm not in an orchestra or playing for the public, so it doesn't really matter.

This product may work for others, so I wanted to explain my story and let you know that I didn't choose to use it for reasons other than quality of manufacture or design.

You can look at all the comparison videos and see that each reviewer has their favorite, Kawai ES8, Roland FP-90 and the Yamaha P-515.  They are all excellent digital pianos.  Because of the Pandemic I was forced to by the last remaining digital piano at an online piano store, the P-515.  Everything is now out of stock.  To make a long story short my church has had a Clavinova since 1995 and its still going strong.  I don't think you can beat the build quality of a Yamaha.  In addition there are some little things that make the Yamaha stand out.  A heavy key action,like an acoustic.  Two headphone jacks on the front of the keyboard bed.  The USB slot is located on the front of the keyboard unlike the Roland's back location.  The Bookshelf is easily removed as the feet fit in two holes on the top of the keyboard.  This makes it is easy to remove and lay it flat on the keyboard for the Yamaha keyboard plastic cover.  It's also wider than the Kawai metal Bookshelf.  Roland has built in bluetooth connectivity for both backing tracks and computer connectivity for accessing the pianos extensive settings along with USB connectivity.  Yamaha takes a different approach.  Yamaha provides the USB connectivity along with MIDI in/out connections and also has Bluetooth connectivity for music only.  Using the MIDI connections you can purchase Yamaha's MDTB-01 Bluetooth MIDI connector to get the same wireless connection as the Roland.  Yamaha's approach, IMHO, is a better solution since it is external to the piano and not built in.  Bottom line, I really wanted the FP-90, but I am really glad I got the P-515.  I think this is a smarter choice from a longevity point of view.  Lot of features, dig deep into the menus for Duo mode, turning off or keeping the internal speakers on when using the line out or head phones.  Roland has a better registration process if you want to store and change sounds on the fly.  This was not a deal breaker for me on the P-515.  Plenty of volume for my home music room.  Yamaha stood out as the choice for my needs.  If your on the fence about the P-515, you won't be sorry with this purchase.

This is the first USB MIDI controller I've used, but I've used soundboards and mixers in the past so it wasn't completely foreign to me. And while none of the faders, buttons or keys felt luxurious, mechanized or very finely weighted and crafted... they didn't feel nearly as cheap as they should for this price. The controller is attractive and does not seem like it will break easily. Getting it installed and going did take some unnecessary time. You need to register your keyboard, download some very large apps/packages, register for and download Abelton Light (for free), and go through the installation steps. It can take an hour or more to set up depending on your connection speeds. Once I got the drivers and Abelton installed I thought I'd just be able to start playing around... not quite. I could control some things, but the keyboard and other options wouldn't work. There is an important step after installing, which is in the manual but I missed it at first, that has you set the correct MIDI ins and outs for Abelton. But once you do that, there's no mapping necessary. Which is a huge time saver and more than makes up for the lengthy downloads. It took a little bit of poking around to get used to Abelton, but after a couple of nights I was able to make some fun little jams. It's going to take some time before I can make anything good, but this is just the controller to get me there.

On a side note, I also used it to control my photos in Lightroom using a program call MIDI2LR. It was fun to be able to use real sliders to control the virtual ones, and each button could issue a command like ratings, navigating photos, and changing modes. This controller (the 49key) is a little bit too big to use like this all the time, but I may just pick up a smaller or keyboardless unit for that purpose in the future.

Overall, it's a really nice entry level controller that's easy to get going and will grow with you.
Summary: Great value for the money, excellent entry level controller

Text:
This capo is easy to position and release. It's design is an artistic work of grace. I am an acoustic player and use the capo primarily on my resonator guitars.

When I first started playing regular guitar, I used capos a lot, but as I became more proficient on the neck I put them aside and I believe I went for at least a decade or more without using one. Then I got into non-standard tunings and resonator slide guitar - a whole new world. Out came the old capos and I didn't feel comfortable with any of them. (I had about a dozen.) I had elastic wrap arounds, thumb screw tightened ones, cam locked ones, spring loaded lever ones and even a couple which I made myself based on an old 19th century design. Then I discovered the G7th Capo.

The G7th is heavier than my other capos, but not in a significant way. It is infinitely adjustable and does not pressure the strings out of tune. I have a vintage 1920s Washburn with a beefy V-profile neck and it does not fit that guitar all that well, but none of my other modern capos do either. The exception being the elastic band one and my home made one.

My National Resophonic baritone has a neck 2" wide at the nut and a brace of bowling balls would weigh less than this brass monster so the weight of the capo is negligible. The neck is thick and robust, but I have no difficulty with the G7th. My strings are heavy gauge (15 - 64). The capo is a bit tight up around the 7th fret, but not so I can't use it. (For some positions it clamps the strings more evenly if I use it with mechanism on the 1st string side of the neck.) After reading some of the other reviews, I gave it a try on my Ovation and an antique Austrian parlor guitar I have. It fit both of them just fine.

Realizing one man's wine can be another man's vinegar, I like this capo a lot and I would certainly recommend it.

Do they last longer? Probably. Even when I'm in situations where I'm gigging regularly I rarely change strings more than every few months, just because I don't see the need. I think the main benefit to coated strings is if you have guitars that you can't play regularly the strings won't corrode. But these sound great and feel fine, and the're the least expensive coated strings I've found. I've always found D'Addario quality to be great.

I am capable of properly setting up a new guitar including leveling and polishing frets (if necessary) and making truss rod adjustments. This guitar was far enough out of whack that I was uncertain there was sufficient range of adjustment to get it where it needed to be. Rather than make big changes and perhaps not being able to return it, I decided just to send it back. Fit, finish and materials all seemed fine. It looked great, had good sound and decent fret ends. However, even at this price point a guitar needs to be set up sufficiently on final inspection to have been properly tested and passed QC. What this guitar needed was probably 90 minutes of work by a competent amateur like myself to dial it in (and I expect to do that with any inexpensive guitar even from name brand manufacturers), but this one was far enough out that it was questionable that it could be adjusted to where it needed to be. I'm not trying to trash Donner or their products (especially at the prices they charge), but a beginner or someone who needs to have the work done for them may be disappointed. In the end, however, it was easy to return the guitar under Amazon's return policy. Maybe your copy of this guitar will be better than what I received.

Text:
These were a good set of monitor speakers for my needs, until one of the speakers blew after not much use. I contacted Presonus expecting they'd have me ship the speaker in for a repair for maybe around $50, or better yet - stand by their product and offer a replacement speaker.

But all I got was the runaround by a condescending rep after spending far too much time having to jump through hoops just to submit a repair request (apparently it's out of the question for companies to offer a simple phone number to call these days). Anyway, after inquiring about a repair/return I had obviously requested an approximate repair cost. The rep said he couldn't provide me one (not even a ball park or a max amount).

Ok... so I'm supposed to just send in the speaker with my credit card info on file, and just hope I'm not charged $250 for a repair for a $200 set of speakers? Not to mention the $30 to ship the speaker to and back. Is it really that difficult to just offer a standard fee for electronic repairs of a particular item? Eventually the costs for repairs would even out. And besides, the customer should be getting the benefit of the doubt when it's your company who sold me a faulty product to begin with.

Based on this ridiculous policy I'm still without a set of monitor speakers years later. What can I say, I'm on a very tight budget due to ongoing health issues and am unable to work much at all; having to live mostly on whatever my wife brings in. I still don't know if it would be less costly to have the speaker repaired or just buy a whole new set. Either way, with my lack of funds to spend on non essential items (music is a hobby for me), I don't have another $200+ to be spending on a second set of speakers. I've searched for just a used single speaker on occasion, but with no luck.

I do not recommend buying from Presonus. If you do, just hope you don't have to deal with a broken item and having to play price roulette with a repair.

We have a mandolin case from the same series, so I knew the overall quality of this Gator case before purchasing. It's well made, surprisingly lightweight, and should be quite protective of any guitar that fits properly. Do note the criticisms of the backpack straps, and replace the straps with something that doesn't come apart.

So, this brings us to the question of size. To quote the old saying, Size Matters. We bought the Classical size case for a Martin 000-18 and a Martin OM-1. THE CASE IS SIGNIFICANTLY SMALLER THAN THE INDICATED DIMENSIONS both here and on the Gator website. In fact I went to the Gator site and used the "case finder" app, entering the exact dimensions of both guitars. The suggested cases included this one. I measured carefully and looked at interior dimensions on several other sites. One of the other sites has smaller dimensions than listed here -- but still large enough to hold my two guitars. The guitars *do not fit*. Our Yamaha Classical fits perfectly, of course, but the guitars that *should* fit based on the printed inside measurements do not.

I can force my 000-18 into the case, but that's not very protective - every shock gets transmitted directly to the guitar. The OM-1 is the same body size but has a longer neck, and doesn't fit at all -- too long overall.

I wish Gator made a 000 or OM size case in this series.

Edit: measuring the inside of the case, the Body Length is 19.5 inches (not including the cutout for the end pin), the lower bout is 15.5, middle is 10, and upper bout is 11.25. Overall length is 39.5. Height is about 4 inches since there's a little extra in the lid and a cutout for the saddle. What appears to be tripping me up is the body length and the shape of the upper bout with the 000-18. The OM-1 is physically too long to fit in the case even though the body area might loosen up - the printed dimension for overall length is 41 inches, but the actual length inside is 39.5 (again, not including the end pin.) Hope this helps. If you have a classical guitar in the general size of the old Yamaha, it's a great case.
Summary: Classical case is smaller than published dimensions!!

I got these strings to convert my Enya tenor ukulele to a low G.  There is quite a bit of stretch but after a couple of days the strings settled in.  They're so easy on my fingers and I love the warm tone.

EDIT: After I have set this guitar up (which involved mostly lowering the nut height, lowering the action overall and polishing the fret surfaces and ends) this guitar won me over. It just became mine. I put Eric Clapton strings on it which are slightly warmer and less bright and this guitar sings! I’m adding not one but two stars making it a perfect five!

Original review:
I've read a lot about how this guitar is a great value and a surprisingly good instrument at this price so maybe my expectations were too high, but I'm somewhat disappointed.

First of all, the guitar arrived poorly set up. The action was extremely high due to, both, a very high nut and very high saddle. While updating the saddle I realize the original one was too thin: it fell out of the slot right away when I removed the strings. This caused it to lean forward in the slot, which affects the sound. It also affects intonation as it shortens the scale just a few micrometers (intonation was pretty good out of the box though but not perfect). After the saddle upgrade the intonation is perfect. I don't understand how it is possible that Yamaha does not care to install a saddle of a correct thickness, it does not cost more to simply install a matching saddle. The nut had a poorly cut slots, there was a lot of strings binding. The fret ends are quite sharp and not properly finished. The middle of the frets are very poorly polished: if you try to bend a note you will feel grinding. Very sloppy! I have no idea what Yamaha is bragging about when they say that the fretboard has "rolled edges" - no such thing.

When changing the strings I inserted a small webcam into the sound hole to inspect the interior of the guitar. The bridge plate has lots of splinting and rough edges around the string holes, it's as if a 4-year-old drilled those wholes with a dull drill bit from a toy set (sad thing is that maybe it was ?). Lots of glue squeeze everywhere, bracing not being of correct length - don't look inside if you want to love this guitar!

After the upgrades and a basic common sense setup the guitar is very easy to play. Not the most inspiring guitar to play as it does not have what one would call a character, but very playable. The sound is quite decent actually but lacking in bass response for sure. Also, in my sample, the low E string sounds thudy, as if made of rubber. I tried several strings and now have a good quality bone nut and saddle - unfortunately it has more to do with the resonance of the guitar and/or the neck's ability to transfer vibrations. It just sounds thudy with no sustain on anything other that open string. It is not a very nuanced guitar, does not respond to dynamics in playing well.

However, somehow, I still like it. It is a very honest guitar. Very sincere. Does not pretend to be anything else that it is - an entry level guitar. It is not flashy, pretentious, fake. I still think that at $200 it is a great buy. Great as an everyday instrument that will not make me too precious about it, instead I will just play it without too much reverence towards it.
Summary: You get what you pay for. Very poorly setup out of the box.

I was excited waiting for the arrival of a new Yamaha Pacifica I purchased online. But when it arrived, I found that it's fretboard was a lot lighter that it had appeared to be in the pictures that had been shown.

since I liked everything else about the guitar, I started looking for ways to remedy this. After coming across a number of articles and videos that recommended staining the fretboard, I figured I'd give that a try, as I was familiar with staining furniture, and like how they penetrate the wood and bring out the grain, rather than coating it the way leather dye's seem to do, which was the other option I found.

The staining itself went well, with the fretboard coming out perfect, reaching just the right shade I desired after multiple rounds of staining over a number of days, but after I'd finished staining it, and the stain had fully dried after a couple of days, I found it had changed the feel of the fretboard, and the fretboard just felt very "dry" afterward when I played it.

I happen to have quite a selection of fretboard conditioners on hand (D'Addario, Fret Doctor, Goby Labs, Dunlop, etc.), and so, naturally, I thought applying one of these would quickly and easily solve the problem, but to my surprise, none of them made the fretboard feel any less "dry" after a couple of days had gone by after applying them, when they'd fully soaked in and had a chance to dry.

Over about a 2 week period, I tried one conditioner after another, with the fretboard initially feeling better, but after letting each of them dry a day or two, I'd find the fretboard felt just as "dry" as it did before I applied them. So, I'd try another, hoping it would do the trick, until I went through them all. NONE of them did anything at all for this fretboard and it always felt "dry" again a couple of days after applying them.

I began wondering if perhaps there might have been some "particulates" from the stain that might have created some kind of microscopic roughness that was causing the problem, so I tried using some 1200 grit sandpaper with a sanding block on the fretboard, as that had done wonders on a couple of other fretboards on other guitars of mine in the past, but it didn't make any difference at all with this one. It still felt just as "dry" as before even after sanding it as smooth as it was possible to be. (and no, the sanding didn't affect the staining at all, if you were wondering).

I ended up watching a bunch of videos on fretboard conditioning, and one thing led to another, and I became interested in boiled linseed oil and began looking for more information on it...

While investigating the possibility of using linseed oil to solve the problem, I came across an article that mentioned the Ernie Ball Wonder Wipes Fretboard Conditioner. While I didn't really want to "seal" the woods pores, wanting the wood to always be able to absorb the conditioners I used, I'd already tried everything else... so I picked up a 6 pack.

To my surprise, the Ernie Ball Fretboard Conditioner did what no other fretboard conditioner could do - it brought my fretboard back to life...! I found my fretboard was smooth as glass after I had let it dry overnight, and it didn't feel "dry" under my fingers anymore at all... in fact, it felt great...!

I liked the results so much, I ended up trying it on another guitar in my collection, and again I found I just loved the results. The fretboard was smoother, my fingers slid over the fretboard easier, even my bends were easier. It improved my playing enjoyment so much, I decided to try it on a third guitar, and the results were just as satisfying.

Then, as is my nature, I began wondering if there might be another linseed oil based conditioner that might work as good or possibly even better.

So, I did some searching and found reviews claiming that the Mohawk Fretboard Conditioner was "the best" of the linseed oil based conditioners, so I bought a container of that and tried it on another guitar of mine. After it had dried for a day, I was disappointed to find that the fretboard didn't feel as good as the ones I'd used the Ernie Ball conditioner on, so, I applied the Ernie Ball conditioner to that fretboard, and voila...! Just like magic, the fretboard was perfect even after it had been allowed to soak in and dry for 2 or 3 days.

I ended up using the Ernie Ball Fretboard Conditioner on all 8 of my guitars (using a couple of string separators to fully expose their fretboards and avoid having to change strings on all of them}. At one point, I used one of the wipes to do 2 or 3 of my guitars at the same time, and found the wipes are wet enough to do more than one neck at a time... and I loved the results on every one of them after they were treated. Every one of them felt better than the results of any of the other fretboard conditioners that I've used since I started using them (rather than the lemon oil I used to use), over the past 20 years or so.

I ended up buying a couple of extra boxes of the Wonder Wipes Fretboard Conditioner, just to be sure I had them on hand, and have ended up using them on some other guitars I've worked on as well, with the owners loving the results as much as I do...

All I can say is I wish I'd found these sooner...!

There are absolutely the best fretboard conditioner I've ever used...

Most highly recommended...! (and yes, take your strings off when you use them, and let it soak in for 10-20 minutes for deep penetration before wiping off and buffing, then let it dry overnight so it can harden for best results).

The best fretboard conditioner I've ever found, bar none...!

Highly recommended...!
Summary: I've Used a LOT of Fretboard Conditioners, But THESE ARE THE BEST...!

What you've already probably read or heard is pretty much accurate... this is a fairly decent instrument that doesn't cost a lot, but it needs some setup to work properly. I've been having fun playing the horn and I consider it worth the money. I only gave it four stars because it has a specific problem for which there is a workaround. As you may have already read elsewhere, this horn is overall pitched very low relative to concert pitch. So you have to push the mouthpiece in as far as it will go (until it almost hits the octave key arm) to get it to play in tune with other instruments. For this you will have to sand the cork on the neck until it is quite thin. If you push the mouthpiece all the way in, that should get it up to pitch. That doesn't mean all the notes on horn play consistently in tune... they don't. But it plays reasonably in tune for an instrument at this price level. I found that I couldn't get any of the palm keys to play using the mouthpiece supplied. So I bought a Rico Metalite with the M7 opening. With the Rico I can get most of the palm key notes to play more consistently, depending on the stiffness of the reed. (It's my understanding that getting the high notes to speak can be a problem on soprano sax in general, and is not specific to this instrument. But it's something to be aware of if you're more used to tenor and alto, as I was.) Even with the cork sanded very thin, the Rico wouldn't slide far enough on the neck to get the horn up to concert pitch. So I had to sand out the inside of the Rico as well. (The Metalite is a plastic mouthpiece. If you choose a metal mouthpiece, obviously sanding it could be a problem.) The cheap ligature provided is also very small and didn't even really fit the terrible mouthpiece that came with my horn, so I bought a Rovner dark, which fits the Rico Metalite fine. So to summarize: sand the neck cork, push the mouthpiece way in, probably buy a new mouthpiece and ligature, (you will want to for sound quality anyway), possibly sand the inside of the new mouthpiece barrel, depending on the fit, until you can slide it far enough in to get to concert pitch. These are the minimum steps required to get the horn to playable condition. I would also recommend buying a set of Key Leaves, because your G#, Eb and C# keys are going to stick. I've been using the Key Leaves and it really helps if you use them consistently. I would not recommend this horn for a beginner because it's so hard to play it in tune. But if you're a sax player who would like a soprano to fool around with, and you don't want to spend a lot of money, it might be for you. Personally I'm happy I bought the horn. The action feels okay and it doesn't seem to leak. There are a few little fit & finish glitches but no major defects, apart from the horn playing way below concert pitch, which has a workaround. It comes with a bunch of reeds, which I've been using although they're not very good. It also comes with a strap that's not very good, but I've been using that as well. I had to tie a knot in the strap to get it to raise the horn up high enough to be comfortable. The case is perfectly fine though. Its made of a stiff foam (lined with velvet) with a fabric covering, and opens with a zipper. It's light and compact and provides some protection, though I wouldn't call it a hard case. The horn was delivered very quickly and didn't get damaged. To do all this sanding you can use a 150 grid oxide sandpaper or something similar, and keep it wet as you're working. Go slow and don't overdo it, because you could ruin the mouthpiece or the horn. To sand the cork, cover the neck and octave key with blue painters tape so they don't get scratched. Wrap the sandpaper around and use a rolling motion to evenly remove layers of cork. When sanding the mouthpiece, roll the sandpaper into a tube and slide it in and out while also rotating the mouthpiece so you get even removal all around with no low spots. Check the fit every once in a while so you don't sand too much. That's about it.

UPDATE: Having had the horn a few months I'm going to add something else here I would not have expected. Black gunk comes off the horn and gets on my hands and fingers. Yeah. I have to scrub it off with soap and water. Then I have to wipe down the horn. Little spots of sticky black gunk, not every time I play the instrument but sometimes if I hold it a certain way. Seems to be coming from the posts, from the joints, the bearings where the keys move. I guess maybe it's graphite they used to lubricate the bearings? Or maybe when they painted the horn black, some of the paint got down in the holes where the key rods fit, and their constant motion from playing grinds the paint into a fine powder, and it mixes with the lubricant to make... black gunk? Maybe a little of both. Anyway, it's not cool. Also, the black paint is flaking off a little in a few places. That's really no big deal to me at all, but the sticky gunk is kind of a bummer. I'm not going to take away a star though, because I like the horn and I'm enjoying it quite a bit. Just be aware. Black gunk.

FURTHER UPDATE: A few months down the road and I'm still glad I bought the horn, I play it every day. I just want to add that I bought a black horn, and the paint is really weak. You can easily scratch it off with your fingernail. You will start to accidentally fingernail the paint off just from handling the horn. The sax I bought is covered with bare areas now, especially inside the bell where I pick the horn up. I don't really care, except the flakes of paint stick to things, like your hands and your phone. They kind of make a mess which then has to be cleaned up. It's too bad these guys didn't offer a version of the horn with just bare brass and no finish on it. I would have picked that one. That would have been a nice looking horn, and they could have saved a couple bucks by not spraying it with this crummy defective paint.
Summary: A Lot Of Horn For The Money

The Mustang GT 100 is the amp I wish I'd had thirty years ago. I’ve played acoustic since I was a teenager, and always wanted to take the plunge into electric – but I never did, because I’d have to roll the dice on an amp (wrong amp for the sound you want? Gosh, that's too bad), spend a bundle on pedals and controllers, and invest countless hours setting the gear up and learning to use it. Along comes the Mustang GT, and BOOM, problem solved! Everything you need for home play, jam groups, and maybe gigging, is right there in one box.

Read plenty of other reviews and check out the videos – especially if you’re an advanced player and have specific needs. I play at home and in jam/improv groups, and I’m very happy with the provided voices and models, especially the classic Fender reverb amps. I play blues and jazz, so I don’t need the dozens of distortion/fuzz/OD voices that Fender loads in. OK, the Fender Tone app (Android): D-minus, almost a total failure. UPDATE: Design Flaw Could Drop Your Guitar

Normally the guitar button and the screw that holds it are separate pieces. Those buttons can rotate without affecting the screw. With the “S” version the screw that goes into the guitar is an integral part of the button. If you rotate the button, the screw will rotate. This is a particular problem if, as in this case, the strap part fits tightly over the guitar button and can “grip” and rotate it with normal playing motions.

I’ve had these on 2 guitars now. In both cases the buttons have tended to get unscrewed from the guitar over time. The screws are long, and the chances are that you’ll notice the button coming out, but why buy into this unnecessary failure mode??? I highly recommend replacing all S style buttons with the old style. The S strap part works great with the old style buttons.

STRAT PLAYERS BEWARE! Just a quick review to say these strings may or may not work well for you. I am an older professional guitar tech, so what I'm telling you comes from genuine hands-on experience.

These cobalt-coated strings are certainly made well, as are most Ball products, however, they may exacerbate a VERY common issue many Strat players already have with their guitars; LOSS OF THE LOW E STRING'S HARMONIC DEFINITION.

Most Pro players with Strats know this issue very well. It has to do with the fact that there are 3 pickup magnets pulling on the low E string (they are simply too close to the string and need to be adjusted away from the string), and thus, causing the low E string to lose its tonal clarity as you play it up past the 12th fret. This issue usually only affects the low E string due to it's heavier magnetic mass.

To test if your Strat is mis-adjusted, simply play each note on the low E past the 12th fret with a clean setting on your amp (we're just testing the low E only. No other strings are involved). If each note loses more and more clarity and definition as you get to the last fret, your pickups are too close to the string and needs to be backed off (lowered equally).

If your guitar has this problem when using normal nickle-coated string, these M-Steel cobalts will make the issue worse as they are more magnetic. BTW, all 3 Strat pups should be lowered down to pickguard level (on the low E side only) and all 3 pups should be brought up equally until the low E fretted notes past the 12th fret begin to lose tonal definition. Then, back off the height screw one half to a full turn.

If the guitar is set-up properly, the rest of the strings will not be affected by the magnets in the pups, unless you tune low and your string height is mis adjusted.

I'm not sure why this is getting so many good reviews. I have a feeling that it's because the product page is merged with other models. The FCT-2 is by far the worst clip on tuner I've ever used (and I've used many manufacturers and models). I'm really surprised that a company like Fender would think this gadget is acceptable quality, because I'm definitely a Fender fan when it comes to guitar, bass, and amplifiers.

Anyhow, there are so many things wrong which basically makes this tuner unusable:

- The display is way too dim. I mean, you can barely tell if it's on or off (and there's no way to adjust it that I've found).
- When you pluck a string, you can barely see the meter change, and you absolutely can't see the note (i.e. G, A, C, etc). You can see where the letter should go more than the displayed letter itself. Duh
- The clip is way too tight. I can understand that they'd want it tight enough so that it detects the vibration better, but I have other tuners that aren't nearly as tight and they do a great job (I'm thankful to still have a few Intellitouch PT10's lying around). It's so bad that it's close to the point where I need to position my hand correctly just to put the device onto the headstock.

So there you go. They failed on almost everything a clip on tuner needs to be.
Summary: This is the worst tuner I've tried yet (FCT-2)

It has 2 wire mic ports, but 1 is the big size that comes with standard mic's and the other is a small port which you'd have to have a standard to mini plug adapter (not included). Text:
I recently picked up an Ibanez SRX 400 bass in a trade deal. It has become my knocking around bass here at home. Since it didn't come with any case and I can't see paying the $120.00 or so dollars for the Ibanez HSC I decided to go with a gig bag. Target price was under $30 and so I thought the ChromaCast CC-BPB-BAG at under $20.00 would do OK.

Upon arrival I was surprised at how decent this bag is for the price. A few hanging threads and some seams on the inside that could have had the excess material trimmed off, but overall the construction is very good for a bag under $20 dollars. Zippers work smoothly but feel a bit stiff. They do work fine though and no snags of any type. Was nice to see a pad on the bottom for some added protection where the strap button rests. Wish it had a loop sewn in at the top for hanging though.

The Ibanez is a tight fit in the bag and there's very little room to spare inside the bag. The bag does zip closed but I wish it had a bit more wiggle room. IMO the padding could be thicker. It's there but don't expect a large amount of shock resistance or drop protection if it takes a small tumble or falls over in the bag. This is a basic bag that's designed for general purpose storage and transportation.

Bag has multiple zippered storage pockets. So I started to see what I could fit in the bag (see pics). I wanted to be able to toss my tc electronic BH-250 micro head ( 9 1/2 x 8 1/2 x 3) into a compartment on the bag. It did fit in the outside compartment but it was a tight fit with little room to spare. There is easily more than enough storage on the bag as I was also able to get other stuff I need in there too.

So here's the total of the stuff in my bag. The Ibanez bass, strap, lead cord, tc head, cords for speaker, extra cord, and power, spare set of strings and my tuner. Still have space available to stash a few smaller items or a tablet and phone. Fit with the Ibanez bass is tight. Don't expect to fit much in with the bass. For a gig with the bag loaded like this my load in would be the bag in one hand and my tc RS112 in the other. All under 50 pounds. Possibly add a small over the shoulder messenger bag too if needed.

This is really a decent bag for the price. If all you need good basic storage and transportation for your bass at a decent price, this bag will work fine. If you need a bag that will hold up to daily use, IMO you will need to spend some extra money and get a higher quality bag. With items like this you really do get what you pay for.

As someone who has played String Bass for about 50 years,
I've tried and used a lot of various Rosin's over the years.
There are even some Rosins no longer made.

By every stretch, Kolstein rosin the absolutely the best rosin I've ever tried.

1: Unlike other rosins, over time the rosin doesn't "glaze", it remains consistent.

2: It has excellent aggressive gripping power on the strings. I love that.

3: It has excellent tone. You'd be surprised at the differences between rosins.

4: It does not take a long time to rosin up your bow. Other rosins you have to really warm them up
with many strokes. Kolstein rosin applies easily to the bow.

5: It doesn't create a lot of dust, good for allergic type issues and keeping the bass clean.

One thing to note, all Rosins are NOT compatible. Use up or clean off the rosin on bow before
changing over to Kolstein or any other rosin.

Kolstein Music has been probably the most reputable and expert bass dealer in the United States.
It's an incredible treat to visit their store and see their incredible array of vintage and new basses.
They have engineered a number of products over the years, various strings, cases, bridges, all with excellent quality
and integrity.

Text:
This relatively small PA head has some great features for the price, and is perfect for inside venues of up to 100 people (assuming that you are playing at sound pressure levels of less than 100dB.) It's also perfect as a dedicated keyboard amp head or for other instruments, but the best use is for solo, duo and trio acts.

I love the features - it has a feedback location system that consists of five LEDs positioned over the sliders on the graphic equalizer. It will not find the offending channel. but a light will display over one of the five bands, alerting you to the specific band that needs to be lowered until the feedback has been eliminated. The bands are 80, 250, 1K, 3K and 10K. The sliders have a range of -12 to +12 dB per band. There is also a speaker protection circuit that will automatically engage to prevent distortion at certain thresholds. On the front of the PA is an LED display that show the amp levels.

Another thing I love is the small form factor. This head is a small 9" x 9" x 14" form factor that weights fourteen pounds. That makes it ideal for small stages or even floor area that has been cordoned off for performers. I use mine with a pair of 10" Kustom speakers, daisy chained to a pair of 10" monitors.

The front jacks will accept XLR or 1/4" plugs, which saves a lot of real estate by not having both types of input for each channel like older heads have. And although this is claimed to be a five channel head, the fifth channel is actually a pair of RCA jacks for MP3 devices. It also has a parallel 1/8" jack to give you flexibility in connecting players. That is a nice touch.

If you find that you truly need more than four mic inputs you may want to consider sharing channels using a Y-cable like the [[ASIN:B0061OPQK8 GLS Audio 6 Inch Patch Y Cable Cords, XLR Male To Dual XLR Female Cables, 6 Inch Y-Cable Cord Splitter XLR-M to Dual XLR-F]].

There is also a record out (two RCA jacks) and a 1/4" line out to a power amp for even more flexibility.

A few things I do not like, but can live with. First, the reverb is not too good. To be honest it's better left turned off. Also, the outputs are 1/4" jacks - I would have preferred connectors that can accept Speakon and 1/4", but I understand the need to also cut costs to keep this affordable.

This has some surprising features for such an inexpensive head, and are missing some as noted above. It is perfect for small spaces or for micing amps or drums and feeding into a master PA, or as a dedicated keyboard amp. But it excels as a small footprint PA for small ensembles, or for practice.
Summary: Ideal for smaller venues and a few specific uses

I bought the SR-18 to replace my old Zoom RT-123 that finally started failing after over a decade of serving me well. I have a full computer recording setup with high quality drum plugins but I still love the vibe and hands-on immediacy of a good old-fashioned groove box, and the SR-18 does not disappoint. It sounds better than I expected, with a good selection of surprisingly decent acoustic kits, but it's those deliciously dated kits and samples I actually like the most. My philosophy is, if you're going to use a standalone drum machine these days, embrace its mechanical nature and look to software if realism is what you're after.

My favorite features:
Fully customizable drum kits. You can either edit a factory kit or start fresh by choosing from an awesome selection of basic samples and then tweaking volume, pitch, panning, envelope and other parameters to taste. Super flexible.
Multiple parts/fills. For each sequence you get an A part, B part and a corresponding fill for each.
Record a song live. In song mode you can hit record and the unit will capture your pattern changes and fills in real time, making it fun and easy to arrange entire songs. I much prefer this style of arranging to the tedious and time consuming step editing song mode of other machines, though that mode is still an option here if you prefer that workflow.

Deeply customizable. I like how much control you get over every aspect of the machine, including very extensive midi settings which is great for me since I'm using this in conjunction with other synths and sequencers
Onboard effects. They aren't anything fancy but the eq and compression effects are very useful. There are only a few useful reverb settings but those few sound good and are nice to have on hand.

Drawbacks:
There are a few drawbacks keeping me from giving the SR-18 five stars but they're minor and by no means deal breakers.
No USB. This machine was released in the late 2000s as an update to it's predecessor, the SR-16. It really seems like oversight that they didn't include a USB port for midi communication and firmware updates. It's not a big problem but should have been a no-brainer
Doesn't automatically save. If you're editing a pattern, song or kit and you turn off the machine without saving, your work is lost. It should save your work automatically and perhaps provide an undo function if you need to reverse any mistakes
Settings don't always save. Some of my record settings and system settings seem to get lost when I tirn off the unit. This could be user error but the manual isn't clear if you need to manually save settings or not. Again, this should be automatic
No dedicated "exit" button. It's easy to get buried in a menu and not quite know what mode the machine is in. It would help to have a dedicated cancel or exit button that gets you completely out of whatever context you're in
Pad response. I find that I really have to pound on the pads to get higher velocities from them, and it shouldn't be that difficult. They should have included a setting for pad sensitivity so this could be tailored to the user's playing style. Perhaps the pads will get "broken in" over time as I continue to play on them
Low output level. The line outputs are pretty quiet compared to the output of all my other line-level instrumens. An option to boost the output level would be nice. I have to boost it on my mixer instead

Overall I'm in love with this little box and for the price and what it is you really get a ton of samples, kits, beats and options. It is also just plain fun! I can spend hours tapping out beats, tweaking kits and arranging songs. It is really helping as a songwriting tool because you can organize all your parts, even with bass lines, and then jam over it on guitar or keys to get ideas and try things out. Overall I highly recommend the SR-18

If you are thinking of buying this but the "Groovy" review claiming "false advertising" concerns you. please read:

Set the unit so it mimics/matches the mixer's VU output level display. Should read in the high yellow at loud but system safe volumes. It will now warn you with red lights when you start to overdrive your mixer output level. It is therefore doing the exact same thing the mixer's VU lights do. So this "protects" the speakers from you over driving them in-as-much-as 1. your amp and speakers are properly matched, 2. you have your gain structure set properly and 3. that you are making volume corrections only at the mixer (not at the amp or on a powered speaker itself). Basically it gives you a visual or your mixer's output level. BUT how you set the rest of your gain structure will also determine the signal level entering your amp. And then your amp level has the final say as to how hard your speakers are being driven. So while this does not DIRECTLY protect your system they are giving you some credit I think. I don't think they are expecting the you to take the leap and believe that this in anyway functions as a limiter that will automatically protect the system or speakers.

These are studio monitors. My review will talk about what they do, what they don't do, who should buy them, and the value. I'll mention a few small issues.
So what are studio monitors? Basically, if you record or mix down your own music, you need a special pair of speakers to check your mix. You can't do that on headphones--your mix--the way the different tracks of music sound together--won't resolve spatially (there's no real space with headphones). So this special product was designed to address this issue, as well as provide a live playback in the studio, and so on.
Studio monitors do not have an exact definition, and there are different kinds. If you go into a music studio, the monitors are usually set up wrong, anyway. And so it goes. These tend towards what I would call "near field" which means, well, you sit near them. Not really near, but near. High frequencies lose energy over distance, so if you sit too far away they will sound dull.

How are they different from a pair of stereo speakers in a hifi system? Well, they are designed in most cases to be flat and neutral, and not impart an attractive EQ, color or bias to the sound. So as far as speakers go, they sound, well, flat and colorless. And that's good for checking your mixes, but not so good for easy listening. Ideally, they should be revealing and mostly unforgiving. You want the truth, just like the ad says. Also, since these are not shielded (more on this later) they are a dud for computer speakers. And, they are for a solo listener. You have to be in the focus point, they focus like a good camera lens--that makes them special, but also a specialty item.

So, so far, they from my description they sound like the box they came in. But in fact, they are great. Because when set up properly, you--the listener--and the speakers form the three points of a triangle. And after a few experiments (depending on your room acoustic), when they are set up right, the stereo image snaps into focus, and you can use them exactly they way they should be used--to check a mix. Any little problem in the mix is revealed, and you can quickly find the best mix (assuming you know how to mix). Note that in this triangle, the speakers angle towards the listener, at around 30 degrees. If you move a foot to the right or left, the image snaps out of focus.

So basically, if you are looking for studio monitors for mixing on a budget, look no further. These do the job and do it well. They do it better.
There are a few minor issues, again, remembering that these are a bargain. First is that the bass port fires towards the back wall. This is always problematic, depending on the room you are in. Having said that, in the focus position in the triangle the bass is reasonably well controlled. Also, the bass really does hit around say 42-48 Hz--it won't hit the lowest note of a large church organ, but double bass or electric bass, pretty good.

Next, there is a resonant frequency in the case. That is, if you tap on the case, it has a note. This is surprising for a JBL design, and I guess this in one area where they cut corners. You could open up the case and apply some damping material, but then you risk the warranty and you might make it worse. If I find an easy mod or see one I'll try to post it. Resonant nodes are a common problem in audio, and this is a present, but minor quibble.

Much has been written about the tweeter of this speaker and the diffracting pattern supposedly borrowed from more expensive designs. First of all, almost all speakers make this claim of "porting" expensive design components to lower models. In this case, the high frequencies, according to the hype, are less directional--more evenly dispersed. Well, this is pretty much rubbish, it is a cheap plastic design, and the high frequencies are very directional.

But the fact is, that's what you want in a studio monitor--you want to sit in the focus point and hear a very accurate representation of the mix. It's a decent sounding tweeter, but if you want good sounding speakers, get JBL "regular" speakers, not these, or the perennial favorite Bowers & Wilkins. These are studio monitors.

Next on the minor annoyances list is the overall shielding and hum rejection. There are two inputs, one for phono jacks and one for XLR cables. Now, you can hook up an RCA or banana plug combo--using adapters--from a stereo and drive these speakers (these are powered speakers, so they work with or without an amp or preamp).

But the fact is, they just don't work well. Drive them from a sound card, they just don't do the job, they pick up hum and the sound is a bit off. But drive them from, say, an RME interface, or anything with decent balanced XLRs (say a mid range Focusrite, or, my fave, Grace audio), flip the switch from "consumer" to "professional" input level (they are "consumer" by default, at least on my set) and be prepared to be surprised, they do pretty well. The noise goes away. They are also susceptible to hum from dimmers, or electromagnetic hum.

The tweeter is just a little bit less bright than flat--that is, there is almost a hint of ribbon in the sound. Not a bad thing, but don't set your mix too bright to compensate. Lastly, there is a very slight color to the sound, a hint of dark chocolate, sometimes edging ever so slightly towards murk. No biggie, but a slight coloration. As another reviewer perspicaciously noted, the coloration is similar to the Audio Technica ATHM50 headphones, so they make a complimentary pair. Compared to my Sennheiser HD600s, they are slightly darker.

JBL claims the speakers are "pre" broken in, mine settled in and sounded noticeably different after about twenty hours, so don't mix anything serious until they have moved some air, IMHO.

Again, these are some problems, but if set up right with the right cables, you are in business.
And so, recommended. And better than anything in the price range.

Who are they for: the budget home recording studio
Not for: not for home stereo, computer speakers, multiple listeners

Other notes: You will need XLR cables, and longer power cords than the ones supplied. There's no protective grill. The speakers have a very wide range for such a small box. Since there is no shielding, they are not too heavy--save the boxes for transport owing to the exposed cones. Do not forget to follow the setup pattern indicated in the obtuse instructions--if they aren't angled in (a very common setup mistake), the highs will be seriously skewed. There's a minimalist EQ switch on the back, I recommend you don't use this. Have fun, and happy mixing.
Summary: Very good for the price: flat, neutral & professional

I got this pretty fast. I took it out of the box and wanted nothing more than to give it 5 stars just for value alone. I'm still shaking my head in disbelief that I got this guitar for the price. First, the 'tuner' issues that I've been reading about. Replace the strings! I stretched and stretched these things and they would not stay in tune. A set of D'Addario 10's cured that straight away (or whatever you prefer just change them). The tuners aren't the best but they are not to blame, it's the cheap strings. Now, technically if you only play open chords this was playable out of the box. The neck angle was so off the A string rattled no matter how high I set the bridge. The guitar would not intonate due to the ridiculous angle. Yes I could have sent it back but I suspect I would have gotten another just like it. I had to spend about 6 hours shimming the neck AND the nut (Never had to do this to the nut on an electric, not even on a used guitar. The nut slot was cut too deep), as well as working on leveling nearly every fret to make it playable. It required 3 business cards to shim the neck which is the most I've ever had to use. After I got that straight I removed a bit of paint from the neck and set it with wood glue in the pocket and on all the screws. In my opinion this helps a great deal with these and all bolt ons for that matter.
If I bought this used none of this would have been a big deal. But as I'm looking at this horrid neck angle and doing all this work I'm steadily staring at the 'QC passed' sticker. Must have been built on a Friday afternoon or something.--- NOW--after I did this it is sweet!!. I play through a Peavey Valveking 100 and it rocks as good as my Strat w/ Duncans and Dimarzios. The quality of the electronics is not sub par at all. After adjusting the pickups screws to match the string height and getting all the horrible wax off them, I'd argue that this is as good as any Epi I've ever played as far as pups and all, so don't hesitate there because I don't really care for Epis and I'm in love with it. (I bought this to sell mainly, but now????) The build quality; hmm, if you can do guitar work go for it. Otherwise I'd highly recommend a more expensive model. The $299 models are great right out of the box usually.

SUMMARY
Great pedal, buy it, you'll probably keep it! At its price point - 5 stars. I am keeping it and it is probably going to become a permanant addition to my pedalboard. Only time will tell but I like adding some vibrato for clean sounds. It reminds me a lot of how I used to set up my Super Reverb amp. Compared to all pedals, I'd actually give it 4 stars - downgrading 1 star for the plastic case and the limited functionality of the Rise control. But I liked it so much I decided to score it "at its price point".

PROS
- dirt cheap at $25 for a new pedal
- sounds great - does not add or subtract any frequencies or add any noise (I wish I could say the same for some $200 pedals I've tried.)
- Latched/Unlatched mode -- the best feature on the pedal. I love that I can put this in unlatched mode and use it to vibrato in short bursts.
- Small form factor - normal "single pedal" size
- Standard power supply - 9V Center negative - runs from pedal board power or a battery
- The larger foot pedal surface (compared to just a silver bullet switch) is nice for the unlatched mode use

CONS
- Cheap plastic case - I doubt its durability and would have preferred to pay more for a more durable case.
- Latched/unlatched switch is small (hard to reach, have to bend over, can't do with a toe)
- Rise control has only the most subtle impact on sound. Probably not needed on this pedal. Two larger controls for the other controls would be a better design for usability.
- Like most pedals - the knobs are super small and not easily controlled with a toe, and the settings are hard to see. My favorite pedals have large knobs, well marked settings you can see from a distance, enough space between the knobs to set one without bumping another, and in the best cases, enough space, size, and durability for the knobs to be tweakable by a foot or toe bump.

Suggested Redesign, "Super Vibrato" or "Vibrato II"
1) Change to a metal case
2) Lose the Rise control altogether
3) put the latched/unlatched modes on a 2nd stomp switch so you can stomp to go between modes
4) Increase the size of and space between the other two controls -- put large "foot controllable" knobs with high visibility knobs.

Then again, at 25 bucks, I might just buy a 2nd one and put one in latched and one in unlatched mode.

I've used a lot of different tuners for my weekly gig at church, including pedals and handheld. Over the years I have settled on using the cheapest Korg guitar tuner connected to the tuner output of my Roland AC-60. It worked pretty well, in that the tuning was decent and if the tuner broke I could replace it inexpensively. However, my tuning quality changed dramatically when the church changed their sound system and I began experiencing AC hum in my signal. I was able to squash some of it using the anti-feedback circuit but the little bit of hum that was left over made it impossible to get an accurate reading from the tuner.

Enter this headstock tuner. It fits on my Guild Peregrine guitars perfectly, discretely, and stays put even if I put it in the case. The tuning isn't like my Petersen Stroborack, but it is good enough and easily replaced if it breaks. Finally, it isn't dependent on guitar output signal. So I can now tune without plugging in. The negatives are that the calibration function is too easily accessed -- the other day I started tuning a half-step down to 430 Hz until I noticed that it is labeled in the bottom corner of the tuner display. Also, depending on where the tuner is attached in relation to the tuning pegs, one's hand can block the display. I'm learning to use more of an "OK" grip on the tuning pegs with my thumb and forefinger, which seems to help me see the display.

UPDATE 6/2014: The battery life of this tuner is not so great, I estimate I had it on 10-15 minutes every week for 3-4 months before it died. It doesn't have a true battery life indicator except for the device shutting off unceremoniously. So, I actually went back to the cheap Korg tuner that uses AAA batteries. It turned out my guitar's piezo pickup had broken and was the source of the hum. I keep the clip on tuner as a back-up and for use when I'm practicing unplugged.
Summary: Discrete and works great if you have to deal with ground loop hum

People love comparisons so here you go.... Based solely on the sound of the mic pres, the Blackjack Onyx is king of the under-$150 2 channel audio interfaces. This includes the also Focusrite 2i2, Presonus Audiobox, Behringer umc202hd, Propellerhead Balance, Tascam US-42, Alesis I02, Avid Mbox 2, and others. These interfaces are all excellent for different reasons and despite some of them boasting more features or higher bit-depth/resolution specs, the Blackjack simply produces a better sound when recording vocals and electric guitars. This kind of thing is of course subjective and for that matter a lot of folks probably wouldn't recognize a difference sound-wise in any of these devices. I have put them all through a lot of testing however as I have had a home studio for many years now and 2 channel interfaces are all I require for recording my own music.

So whats the catch? If the preamp's sound so good why is the Blackjack at under $100 not dominating the stiff usb interface competition? Well, a quick search online will reveal Windows users far and wide with major driver/install problems. The Windows 7 and earlier driver problems have largely been taken care of with the latest version 3 driver but Windows 8 and 10 users are still left to dry at least at this point. Fortunately I have found an easy way to get around this issue in Windows 10 but you have to follow these steps exactly and in this order.
1. Unbox the device but do NOT plug it in yet and set it aside while you go get the latest driver.
2. Download the newest version of Onyx Blackjack driver. It is 3.0 as of right now and you'll notice it says it supports up to windows 7.
3. Unzip the installer and then navigate to the extracted installer. Right click on it and run it in compatibility mode for Windows 7 from the menu.
4. After it is completed plug the device in and wait until you see the yellow LED on the device light up.
5. You will also notice a little green Mackie "running man" icon in the bottom right with your other icons.
6. Do not try to use the device or open your recording software just yet. Do a fresh restart of Windows and log back in.

I have done this exact series of steps on 4 different Windows machines, 3 being Windows 10 and 1 of them Windows 8 with the exact same results each time. It also worked immediately using Linux I might add.(My dad and I run a computer business for a living in case your wondering why or how I would do this) I have had the device now for a little less than a year and its been very reliable and consistent. For this reason I give it a full 5 stars since sound for me is the most important feature in a 2-channel interface. Outside of that it's also built like a tank, looks cool on a desk, and (much like the brilliantly designed Balance by Propellerhead) has a nice clean front with all your controls while hiding your cable mess neatly in the back. If you Windows 10 users can get the drivers installed correctly, you'll have yourself quite the little gem in the Onyx Blackjack.
Summary: If you can get the drivers installed correctly, the Onyx Blackjack is one great sounding dual channel interface...

That's the whole point right? The high E and B strings of both the Elixirs and D'addario's "plonk" out. They have no sustain and "fleshy-ness" to them. These Martin SP strings do though. I have to confess to a particular image that comes to mind when I think of capos. It's the image of an earnest folkie, with mastery of C, G and D, but still struggling with the A. A good player should be comfortable in any key. But there's still an occasional place for a capo, and that's when you need open strings in a chord.

I tested this capo on several guitars, and with one exception it worked well. Steel-string dreadnought, archtop jazz box, and Les Paul worked nicely. Not so much on a flat fretboard classical. The capo has a slight curve that works well on any curved neck. But on a flat neck there's a little string buzz on the D and G strings. While the capo's grip is good, it still needs to be fitted right behind the fret. This means that it can get a little bit in the way for passage work. That's probably a rare problem for the intended user.

All in all it's a nice little capo. Goes on and off with no fuss and fits the majority of necks.

⦁ Sound absorption and sound insulation:

As you can see from the picture, sound insulation products
can be divided into sound absorption and sound insulation. This
sound - absorbing material suppresses reverberation, improves
sound clarity, and prevents sound leakage to the outside. On the
other hand, unlike sound insulation, sound absorption is a method
of suppressing the reverberation of sound in the room where the
sound is emitted.

⦁ Sound absorption principle:
The sound enters the porous sound-absorbing material, and
the sound is diffused in a large amount, so that the air vibration
is directly transmitted to the air in the inner bubble part. At that
time, viscous friction of air occurs on the surface of the bubble,
part of the sound energy is converted into heat energy, and the
reflected sound is reduced, which is sound absorption.

Generally, in order to reduce the reflected sound to zero, it is
necessary to select a sound-absorbing material whose thickness
is more than 1/4 of the wavelength. In this way, the resistance to
air movement attenuates the vibration, and the sound-absorbing
material serves the purpose of reducing sound.

⦁ What is the sound absorption coefficient?
When sound waves enter the sound-absorbing material, they
will be reflected, transmitted and absorbed. The sound absorption
coefficient, which represents the performance of a sound-absorbing
material, is the ratio of the energy of the unreflected sound to the
energy of the incident sound.

Bought this for the power and flexibility you get for the price. Arrived quickly, but there was a problem from the moment I first plugged it in. There was an annoying "frying bacon" sound when I turned it on, even with gain and volume set at zero. I checked the output at the effects send and it had no noise, so I knew it was coming from the power section. Tried re-seating the power tubes to no avail. Contacted Amazon through their online chat function to report the problem and told them I could probably fix it with a matched set of JJ EL84 tubes for $26. They talked to Monoprice real time while we were chatting and they said go ahead and order those and they would give me a credit. Got the new tubes (sold by Sam Ash through Amazon) and plugged them in and the noise has gone away. So great service from Amazon/Monoprice to fix my problem.

After the tube swap, I am really happy with the amp so far. Sounds great with with my Fender, Gibson, home-made and even cheaper guitars (Danelectro, Epi and Teisco) which have a range of humbuckers, single coils and lipstick tube pickups. I can get a wide range of clean and dirty tones by adjusting the relative levels of gain vs volume on the amp. The switch to cut from 15W down to 1W really helps for quieter practice sessions without destroying the overdrive and overall tone. Haven't gigged with it yet, but the 15W volume seems beefy enough for small venues. The weight of this Monoprice (less than 30 pounds) will be greatly appreciated over my 62 pound Roland JC-120.

Note that a Fender Blues Junior cover available on Amazon fits this well (brown version looks really nice). The one thing I'm not crazy about is the light cream vinyl covering on the amp. Although it might grow on me (looks like the early 1960s Fender Brown Faced amps), I'm thinking about buying some tweed fabric from Amazon and re-covering it.

Will update if I have any issues long term, but for now I'm really happy with it!

The Yamaha MD-BT01 is a well-engineered product that works mostly as advertised, with the exception that you have to jump through a few hoops to get it working at all on iOS device. I should start out by saying that this a $50 Bluetooth adapter that functionally performs the same task as a $10 5-pin DIN MIDI cable...it just does it wirelessly. Therefore, I consider it more of a convenience item than a true necessity. One exception to that argument might be that you can have several of them running at once (five, I believe). So you could imagine having an interface with only 1 MIDI connections, and now you could have MIDI running (wirelessly) to several different hardware units, which is pretty cool.

The two important "issues" for you to be aware of before buying the MD-BT01 are: (1) It requires MIDI power and both the IN and OUT jacks; and (2) iOS Bluetooth doesn't recognize it natively, so Yamaha has engineered a software workaround. The device runs off the power of the hardware you plug it into IF your device offers MIDI power. There are more units than you'd think that do not have MIDI power. This would include all of the Korg Volca series, which only has a MIDI in jack. By contrast, the Korg Minilogue and Roland Boutique series do provide MIDI power to run the device.

Once powered up, you can't just go to your Bluetooth menu in "Settings" and find the MD-BT01. You have download Yamaha's utility app to find the device and connect to it. You can also rename the unit or do firmware updates from that utility. As several reviewers have pointed out, I think you also have to identify it as a MIDI destination in an app that supports it. There are several of these, but I found that if I skipped this step, I couldn't just load up a sequencer app (like Inifinite Looper or Xequence) and make the connection. But once it works, it generally works.

I should point out that my primary concern prior to buying the device - latency - really isn't much of an issue at all. The latency seems pretty minimal, and if you're just using the MIDI connection for sequencing or to mess with control parameters on a synth, it's basically a non-factor anyway.

The device is a little bulky, and maybe a little expensive for what it does. I suspect that this is the type of device that will seem archaic in 5-10 years, but then again, MIDI is still with us, and has been since around 1983. The primary reason I like and wanted the MD-BT01 is to connect my iPhone or iPad to a hardware synth with needing to use a MIDI interface. If you're willing to deal with a few steps along the way, it works pretty well for that objective.
Summary: Works well and with low latency, but not exactly "plug and play"

For my situation this thing is awesome! I have my main studio where all the big toys are but as a test I wanted to build a lightweight secondary studio in my living room (in reality I just wanted the cheapest M1 Mac Mini to play with, but this was a good enough excuse).

I’m loving this laid back setup, instead of hunching over my computer with a 61 key Arturia KeyLab 2, I’m laying back on my couch with my big screen making music! I love it! The only problem was choosing a wireless MIDI keyboard.

I like to keep my living room clean so not having wires running across that I have to worry about was a must, but that left me very limited in regards to options. There are only a handful of bluetooth MIDI keyboards on the market, which had me worrying (mostly about latency). Ultimately I ended up picking this one and it’s a thing of beauty!

The build quality really is topnotch, it feels like a genuine Apple product (though of course it’s not made by Apple). It’s made with aluminum and it has a nice bit of heft to it without actually feeling too heavy. The keys are super responsive and the overall build quality is an easy 10/10. It’s nice and compact, which is perfect, it’s small enough to fit in my backpack but still usable enough for my living room studio. I have a full length 88 key digital piano, so going down to 25 keys felt super limiting at first, but I’m not trying to use this thing as a piano, it’s more so I can throw down chords for software instruments and lead lines. If I must throw down some piano then I’ll go to my regular studio and go to town, but for day to day music making it’s perfect.

I grew used to the keys way faster than I thought I would, they are “chicklet” style keys, similar to an Apple typing keyboard. I thought they would be annoying to play on but since they are full sized and they were smart enough to raise the black keys, I felt right at home quickly. I had no issues adapting from my full length hybrid with grand piano keys to this, sure it feels different, but it’s far from feeling bad. One small downside is that they can be quite noisy if I’m really getting into the groove, but that just means I have to turn my monitors up louder!

Although I definitely do prefer pitch and mod wheels over the pitch/mod buttons on the Xkey Air, I still find the buttons to be quite usable. They’re not perfect by any stretch but they are a reasonable compromise considering that this keyboard is so low profile that you can easily slip it in a backpack without anything catching.

It’s not all roses though, there are a few (nit-picky) faults. First, I really wish it was USB-C, this isn’t a dealbreaker by any stretch, but it would be nice. The biggest offender is the software for configuring the keyboard. It’s nice that software exists where I can adjust velocity curves and shut off time, among other things, but it’s quite buggy and the product registration link sends me to a 404. One thing I do like is that in the software you can configure the sustain button into a switch (press it once to turn sustain on, press it again to turn it off), this is much more usable than having to hold the button for sustain.

Overall this is a fantastic keyboard that’s built like a tank. There are some compromises that come with it, but they are reasonable compromises. Finally, the latency is surprisingly minimal. I was worried about this going in, but it’s actually quite responsive and feels like it’s sub 10ms. If I concentrate hard enough I can detect it, but it’s more than usable and when I’m laying down tracks I don’t notice any lag.

To conclude, this is a great purchase! It’s a bit expensive but the build quality and feel make up for it. At times I do wish I would have gone with the 37-key version, but then it would be less portable and more annoying to deal with in a laid back setting, so I just had to get used to the small form factor and for laying down basic chords and lead lines it’s amazing.

I’d give it 4.5/5 but rounded up to 5. It’s great! Also, it works flawlessly on the new M1 Macs and Big Sur, I have had no issues setting it up.
Summary: Darn near perfect! Works well with M1 Mac Mini (running Big Sur)

For me I was looking for a functional boom arm with a bit of style, I'm not a podcaster or content creator and my gear does not appear on camera. I had been scrapping along with my ultra-budget grade microphone mount (see second photo) for most of the pandemic. I wanted a more substantial microphone mount, but I didn't want to pay three bills for it. My old cheap mount was too short, it could barely get the microphone above my monitors. And it had no cable management.

The Squarock product checked ALL the boxes for me. It's quite a bit taller and with a longer horizontal reach than my old cheap mount. I've included a side-by-side photo so you can see the difference in size versus a standard budget mount.

It has an integral cable management channel and clips, plus four branded velcro cable ties for below-decks management.

The Razer Siren Emote is meant for use with streaming for professional streamers. You will need to set the microphone recording quality in Windows to DVD quality to get the best recording (it defaults to CD quality for some reason). After that, though, the microphone works flawlessly. It comes well packaged, and with the micro-USB to USB connector, as well as the base that you can use with the optional shock mount that allows you to tilt the microphone in any direction. The microphone also has a headphone port at the bottom that you can connect headphones to if you want to a pass through connection for 3.5mm connected headphones.

The big feature on this microphone is that it has an 8 x 8 LED panel for customizing lighting effects. You will need to download the Razer Synapse software to get going with that. It is not too challenging to use, but if you want to configure custom animations and icons for various events while you are streaming (like tips and cheers) then you will need the streaming companion app, which is a separate download. I find the streaming companion app to be a little more challenging to get working correctly. It is a little bit of a pain to have to download separate software to enable this feature. Also, I find that often the Synapse software does not turn the LEDs on after a reboot. Unplugging the microphone and plugging it back in will usually resolve this issue.

You don't need to bend your head towards this mic as it has a good range. If you really want the fancy streaming features then you can't go wrong with this. Once you get used to operating it and messing with the display it is much easier, but I find this is a pricey option for a mic that does not include a boom arm.
