Text:
Update 01-17-2023: I heard back from AKAI support, and apparently they have a process by which the hardware (and I assume software) licenses will be automatically revoked when a new owner registers and uses the keys, so that’s good. It would be even better if the documentation was updated to reflect that, rather than having me waste my time filling out a support request. However, this is the internet and it’s possible there is up-to-date info about this on some link I didn’t happen to click.

Original review:
So I’ll take the hit on buying something that is probably not the best match to what I might need. I generally run a DAWless studio, but thought maybe the DAW transport controls could come in handy at least sometimes, say if I want to knock out a tune in GarageBand. That, plus some simple on-board sequencing sounded pretty interesting, too. Jury was out on mini-keys, since I’m not a huge fan.

Anyway, I get the unit and am immediately annoyed that it cannot be self-powered. OK, my bad — I missed that, and as a DAW-oriented device, it actually makes sense. But here I am hooking it up to my iPad for power, and just leaving the iPad off. Inconvenient. But here’s the real kicker — dropped and stuck notes over MIDI. Just a regular old MIDI DIN connection. Nope, not going to put up with that. Aside from that, the key feel is not great, and honestly the device feels very cheap and lightly constructed, overall. If you’re going to carry it around in a backpack, that makes total sense, but it’s not really my use case.

So I thought maybe a firmware update would address the issue since the firmware was something like 0.54 (who rolls out a 0-point-something release of software/firmware?). I figured it would be as simple as grabbing the update and connecting the device via USB for a quick load. Oh, hell no. I had to first create an account on the AKAI/InMusic site, register the MPK, download a “software manager” app to my MBP … then I could actually download the firmware installer. What a pain in the ass.

Along the way, I somehow convinced myself I needed to go through the licensing manager required for the included production software (really a pretty good bargain if you’re into that sort of thing), so I did all that garbage, too, to get those things installed (note that the instructions for getting the software licensed are HORRIBLE — Sweetwater.com has a better version of the instructions, FYI).

Remember that I went through all this garbage hoping that the key sticking/note dropping would be fixed with the update. Call me an optomist. Well, the firmware update didn’t fix anything I would notice. So, I decided I’d return the thing. Amazon makes that easy.

But now the responsible thing to do would be to de-register the product and properly de-license the software, right? You’d think I could just go to the site and de-register, right? No, I have to start a ticket with AKAI support. And skimming a bit further it on the site, it sounds like I’ll need to have a conversation with them about de-licensing the software, too. What a pain.

Most companies do not require you to create an account and register your product just to get a firmware update. For example, in contrast, as much hate as Behringer gets, their SYNTHTRIBE app is freaking gold. You attach your iPad (yeah, iPad or computer, whichever) to the device, and it figures out what the device is, figures out whether there’s an update, and applies it in a jiffy. Totally owns the AKAI experience in every way imaginable.

Anyway, I decided to get an Arturia KeyStep Pro, which probably matches my needs a lot better. Should have just started there, but it’s a lot more expensive (and probably worth it if my BeatStep Pro is any indication). I guess let myself be convinced by some YT reviews of the MPK and its cheaper cost.
Summary: Not for me, unfortunately, and AKAI new user experience is crap

I've been recording exclusively in home studio's(actually all in my apartments spare bedrooms) for the past 10 years plus, so I know a thing or two about setting up to record in less than ideal situations. The audio interface, to me, is a central part of that kind of set up where recording is getting more and more mobile. If having numerous single or dual channel interfaces has taught me anything, its that most of these out there will fit the bill for 90 percent of us recording in our own home. There is not a wildly huge margin of sound quality were talking about here at least when dealing with these "under $300" units, despite what the internet might have you believe. With that said, this little guy was a very pleasant surprise indeed. First off, the Midas preamps caught me off guard in that they were much cleaner and better sounding than other Behringer Mic Pres I've heard. For under $70, I got an interface that rivals the now-famous Scarlett 2i2 in terms of sound. Actually, the fact that this one has a pad button for use with high output guitar signals makes it preferable to my Scarlett in many situations. The build quality is very nice and feels durable, and it's all black and silver casing looks pretty sharp on my desk. It was very easy to set up and was a breeze to get going on my Windows 10 Pro 64 bit PC. Its one of the lowest latency devices I've used which is pretty important if you record lots of Vocals and Guitars. I have to say well done to Behringer on this one. At the current price, it simply can not be beat in terms of quality or feature set. Highly recommended.
Summary: The new "top of its class" in this price range

My bassist plays with fingers and picks now and then.

Also I was VERY disappointed when I got the product and opened it to only find ONE pack/set of strings. I grabbed the box and had a look to see where on earth I got the notion that I was getting 4 packs/sets of strings. Well have a look at the product image for yourself, it says 4 set, they should really take that off or find another way to phase what they are trying to say. Their intent obviously was to say it's one pack of strings for your bass that contains strings for a 4 string bass guitar. Marketing is a funny thing huh.

Anyways to wrap up I liked the sound of the strings initially (although there was a coating over it, it didn't 'damp' the sound as I had suspected). For the price and the protective coating shedding issue I won't purchase another pack. Too expensive and doesn't live up to the hype.

This switcher/looper includes a very nice tuner, and two buffers- one input and one output buffer. These three functions are worth the cost of this device before you even get to the switching capability.

The L6 includes a "tuner out" port, but since it has a tuner built-in, it really should be labeled "Aux Pre-Out". I use it when recording. I record my guitar on two channels, one on the tuner out and one output from my effects. That way, I have the unmodified guitar on a channel and I can post-process using different tools if I want to.

The buffers are very clean, and do a good job of line leveling signal regardless of what effects are in the loop, or if I'm using my guitar active pickups or passive.

Note that this isn't a switch matrix, so you won't be changing pedal order. But there are plenty of -pre-programmed banks. With six loops, that's a lot of options.

The build is quite sturdy, the display is bright and the screen cover doesn't seem like it will break under most circumstances. I have the switch toppers, and these dress the looper up a bit and make switching comfortable in bare feet.

Look, I haven't gigged with this yet. I'm kinda moving away from my TC Helicon Voicelive III and toward more flexible, discreet pedals. This looper seems like a great way to get some of the flexibility of the Voicelive, but without putting all my eggs in one basket. It will likely graduate to become my stage kit- after I pick up an octaver and a chorus pedal.

I hope this review helps!

First, I like this product and plan to get many years of good use from it.  It's made of sheet metal but is not too heavy and is fairly stiff from underneath supports. Slots and holes were plenty big for all my wires. I'm never sure about terminology since one person's big is another person's small. It's sold as a medium size board, and certainly many would agree. I consider it small. I have 5 pedals on it and am planning for #6.  (This is my bass board.  My guitar board has 14 pedals.)  It will be a tight fit, and I haven't yet tested my layout for toe switch-pushing space.  Four of the pedals are Boss-size pedals.  The remaining two are about 1.33 times that size.  3 are faced out from the board edge to make room for cable plugs which I have to unplug to get the board in the case. I believe the board would easily accommodate 5 pedals.  Give the power supply good thought. It comes with a bracket that was too tall for my Caline power supply.  But I fixed that with two stick-on rubber chair foot pads stuck on the bracket.  They compressed nicely for a tight fit. Sadly, making the PS nice and tight caused the top rail to very slightly bend inward. But no big deal; everything still worked nicely.  I also had to reverse the direction of the power supply to have enough room for all the power cables coming out the front of the unit.  I trace around my pedals onto card stock and make cutouts to test for pedal placement.  That's how I managed to get six pedals on the board. There are no carry handles on the board, but it's small and light enough to easily pick it up.  I think it looks nice as well.  I was surprised to find the carry bag more than adequate. It appears to be about the size of my computer case made for a 14" computer.  The top where the pedals will meet the inside case top has some padding.  In fact, all sides are lightly padded.  There's a zip pocket on the front that covers 2/3 of the bag top.  Another piece of foam in the pouch would give adequate protection for bumps. (Unless it's a flight case, no bag is going to protect from a serious drop. And even a flight case...).  I consider this board a good value for the price. In an apartment (or large household) it would be a good choice to keep the volume down, as it wouldn't ever get too loud. But I wanted something with a little more beef to it. First of all, these whistles are essentially clones of the ABS Susato whistles made by Kelischek Workshop though far cheaper. Woodi USA appears to be one of the countless brands on Amazon and elsewhere that sells what musicians call "stencil" instruments that come from the same, usually Chinese, factory that different fly-by-night companies stamp their name on. Sometimes these instruments are passable and sometimes they're not but in general there's always poor quality control. You could get a great set of whistles or you could get terrible ones. You can find the exact same whistles as these ones branded Thomann, Woodnote, Smart and probably more.

In the world of cheap tin whistles, questionable quality isn't the end of the world as even trusted brands like Generation can be a roll of the dice. The biggest issue with this market however is they can be produced so cheaply that they price out more reputable brands and it's especially shady when they lift someone else's designs like they did in this case with Susato. Stencil instruments and companies like Woodi USA have sort of become a blight on the musical instrument market since they flood it with inferior, copied instruments and beginners end up thinking they found a bargain when they're more than likely purchasing a lemon that will stunt their learning progress. I'm not innocent of buying some of these instruments to mess around with knowing full well what I was risking, but in the particular case of these whistles I purchased them before I knew they were clones based on some positive online and video reviews.

Getting that out of the way, the whistles themselves are pretty decent. They have large bores so they're loud and require a ton of air in the upper octave which may not be suitable for beginners or children. On the other hand they're cheap and durable so giving these to kids isn't the worst idea. The fipples are removeable and tunable which gives them a leg up on their competition at this price point.

The case they come with is worth the price alone though it does have a strong and unpleasant pleather smell and needs to be aired out for a few days. It has room for three whistles, more if you double them up.

The sound is cleaner than the traditional roughness expected of tin whistles and whether you like that or not will be subjective. I personally think they sound a bit too much like a recorder, especially the C whistle. The high octave also isn't as pleasant as the low octave, especially without proper breath support. They are loud as I said earlier and since they're made of plastic they're great for playing outside in the elements since they won't be affected by the weather or humidity as harshly as a whistle made of metal or wood.

I would say it's worth buying these if you want a cheap whistle to take with you places that will survive rough treatment and you're not afraid to break. If you want a quality plastic whistle save up for the Susato that this design was stolen from. Dixon is also an excellent choice for a quality tunable plastic whistle. I'd ultimately suggest other cheap whistle brands like Clarke, Generation and Feadog for beginners and to stay away from the Chinese knockoffs even if they can sometimes be decent like these whistles.

The TB-4 Trembucker is the same pickup as the SH-4 JB, only the former is spaced for Fender-style guitars (or many guitars with tremolo systems), which have slightly wider spacing at the bridge than a fixed bridge, such as a Les Paul. The difference subtle, and either pickup would probably sound just fine even if the strings didn't line up perfectly with the pole pieces. But check your spacing at the bridge pickup - if it is more than 50mm E to E (many Fenders are around 52 or 53mm), the Trembucker version will be the better fit.

As for how it sounds, I have absolutely no complaints. I'm mostly a home player and a hobbyist, but I do have a number of different guitars and have really gotten involved with modding and trying out different pickups. I bought the TB-4 because I really wanted to own a "real" Seymour Duncan to see what all the fuss is about. In general, I think the obsession over premium pickups is a bit "overwound" (see what I did there?). At the end of the day, you're talking about a magnet coil with a bunch of wire wrapped around it. There are a million variables including the composition of the guitar, amplifier, and electronics that go into the resulting tone, and whether or not you happen to like that.

All that being said, I have no complaint with the TB-4, it's a very nice pickup! It has pretty high output (16.4k), which translates to a robust low end and well-defined highs. One unique thing about the SH-4/TB-4, however, is that many players prefer it with 250k tone pots (as opposed to 500k), which are warmer than those used with most humbuckers. Without these, the high-end can be a bit piercing. In a "Fat Strat" with a bridge humbucker and 250k pots, the TB-4 sounds terrific. The other reviewers who described it as "smooth" were dead-on. The magnet is an Alnico V, which can be bright and punchy, but I think the degree of winding just thickens up the tone all over the spectrum.

I'm not sure I would necessarily recommend the SH-4/TB-4 in a Les Paul style guitar, given the other options. Also, there are a lot of cheaper options out there from companies such as GuitarFetish and Tonerider that do an excellent job. But if the premium price isn't too prohibitive, you won't regret purchasing a Duncan - they're extremely well-made, reliable, and sound great.

I bought this transducer/EQ for a Takamine F-389 12 string acoustic I was rebuilding. For the price, it's a good unit, although extremely sensitive and thus a bit noisy. Built-in tuner seems accurate, and the 5 band EQ (actually 4 band: bass, mid 1, mid 2, treble and presence boost/cut) is useful, albeit noisy in the treble and presence. The under-saddle transducer is rubber-clad, and a bit wider than the saddle slot, requiring widening the slot and replacing the saddle with a wider one. Also, the transducer is thicker than most, requiring the slot to be routed about 1/16" deeper to accommodate the transducer.
Templates were not provided, but I was able to find ideal locations for the EQ unit and the battery/output jack box by placing each along the edge of the guitar and marking the locations. I then put strips of white vinyl tape on those locations, carefully peeled the foam gaskets from the EQ and battery box, and used them as templates, tracing the interiors. Thirty minutes with a Dremel, and the fit was perfect for each.
I was able to reduce some of the noise by using an electrical shrink sleeve on the wire from the transducer to the jack that plugs into the underside of the EQ.
I was a bit dismayed that the transducer was still active after turning power off on the EQ unit! This necessitates removing the battery when not using the EQ.
Overall, I'm giving the unit four stars for what it is for the money. For a more expensive guitar and professional applications I would certainly recommend investing in a far better transducer/preamp/EQ. But for inexpensive instruments, amateur uses and occasional gigging, this is a very inexpensive, usable item.
Summary: Good Acoustic Guitar Transducer/EQ For The Price

I've used these pins on a lot of guitars, and I always hear a huge improvement over plastic. Bone pins will add a bit more nuance than these do, but 200% of the money for a 5% tone difference just isn't worth it at times.

These pins are size 1.3T, which means they have a .203" diameter (or a hair more) just under the skirt of the pin, with a 3 degree taper. It seems that MOST modern guitars have 3 degree pins, although there are a few exceptions. It's pretty easy to see the difference between a 3 and 5 degree pin though, so if you're unsure there's a difference they are probably the same.

These pins may be very slightly tight in some guitars - or in some specific holes - and in that scenario I'd recommend using some 320-600 grit paper to sand each pin until it fits barely snug in the hole you're fitting it to. You do NOT want the pin to be tight when the skirt of the pin touches the wood of the bridge, or the head of the pin sticking up over the bridge. When this happens, it is possible for the bridge to split between the pins if the humidity raises very much; not to mention it can also make the pins very difficult to remove in general. When properly fit, the pins will fall to the bottom of the hole and may be just a little "sticky" at the bottom when you push down on it. If you have to push really hard and the pin doesn't go all the way to the bottom, it is not fit properly.

Because these pins are all injection molded and therefore very consistent in size, I like to use them as a guide for reaming out inconsistently cut bridge pin holes. On some guitars I've put these in, one of two will fit nicely at the bottom but all the rest will stick up somewhat. When this happens I like to use the Grizzly 3 degree bridge pin reamer (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00012YFS0/ref=ppx_od_dt_b_asin_title_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) to very slowly (1-2 revolutions at a time) enlarge the holes until all the pins fit the same. This reamer only has one flute, so it makes it much more difficult to take out too much material and permanently screw up your bridge.

I've frequently used these pins in a lot of Alvarez and Takamine (Japan) guitars. In the first photo I have these pins installed in an Alvarez ABT610E Baritone guitar, and although the taper was fine, I did have to greatly enlarge the slots going through the low B and E pins before the strings would fit. Nonetheless, it was a great tone improvement that I immediately noticed. Same thing goes for the vintage Takamine F365S in my second photo, although I had to ream those pins quite a bit due to the varying depth of the holes.

Thanks for coming to my TED talk - I hope this helps everyone better understand bridge pin fitment.
Summary: Great tone-improving choice for most 1.3T guitars!

One of the better value-priced stands out there. The pros include excellent height adjustability (particularly good standing height), sturdy and steady metal music rest with good width and deep bottom lip, and the ability to adjust the base from narrow to very wide. Cons include the plastic parts at key points. No problem so far, but reports of failures aren't comforting.

As comparisons to Manhasset's stands are frequent, and because I also chose between the On-Stage and Manhasset myself, let me offer this: Manhasset makes excellent stands. They are made to take daily use and survive in tough environments (like schools) for decades. You can buy parts for them and repair them. On the other hand, I find they can slip in height relatively easily and you have to crank the tray tension to keep the tray from sagging if you are using books and not light sheet music. There's a reason they sell shaft locks and tray locks for these things. The fixed-base models are steady. I do not like their folding models. Finally, you will pay more for the Manhasset, 2x more, on average. The On-Stage is equivalently well-made, save for the plastic parts. A little care goes a long way.

Recommended for home use and light portability. Fine for heavy use and abuse if you can deal with repairing it yourself.

I actually did find a way to hang it upside-down with just the mic stand, but that caused the mic pole to be in front of the Halo, instead of behind. I asked Aston about this and they were very nice and said it should work. It did work about 90%, but found that method caused the tiniest bit of metal reflection sounds, even with scarves wrapped around the pole. The next solution was to buy a completely new mic stand that I had seen on Youtube that successfully hung the Halo—the Ultimate Support MC-125. Except that is $199! Anyway, I found a much cheaper $14 solution (since I already have a mic stand and boom arm), and my recordings sound perfect. If you already have your mic stand and a boom arm, you just need a mini boom arm or something like the On-Stage Posi-Lock Mini boom arm and attach that to your current boom arm. Mine holds the weight no problem, is easy to loosen and tighten, and is very secure. Remember, you need a boom arm first on your mic stand, and then attach a mini boom arm to that boom arm so it can hang down.

Text: Alright. Yes it is a cheap bass so you expect some downside. The bass itself is built like a tank. I bought a Sunburst P from Donner direct as they were out here on Amazon. I will give Donner credit. They do ship fast. Strings were DOA. Had so many high frets they put the string height at upright bass distance (3.20) and the relief was at .026. Supposed to be 0.22 or a bit less. I did a lengthy fret leverling, recrown and polish. Then a lengthy setup to set the relief correctly. Bring the string height down to perfect and the intonation was a mile and a quarter off. All of the saddles on this bass are now almost all the way forward which means someone didn't measure when they put the bridge on. I wanted to change the pickups but the Donner P-Bass pickups are not standard size. They are quite a bit bigger. I have three sets of new P-Bass pickups here and they were all to small to fit in this bass. Luckily the bass sounds good enough. There is no modding that on this bass which is a shame. The bridge is an odd mount also so you will not be putting a new bridge oin this either unless you completely re-drill. The nut was set in to high. I had to take that off as well and take a 32nd off the bottome to get it playable there. Finish is beautiful but if you are buying this as a beginner OR you have no tech skills this may not be the bass you want. I know what I'm doing and it took me hours to make this play like a bass should. Also something to keep in mind. This has a big wide neck with large spaced frets. The nut is 1 5/8ths and ends up at 3 3/4 at the top so this is NOT for a kid. This neck is a handful and that is also a shame because I probably will not actually play this bass very much because of it. It is just too uncomfortable. Maybe you'll get a better one. Maybe worse. Best of luck with that!
Summary: A LOT OF ISSUES WITH THIS BASS!

Text:
This microphone cable offers everything you could expect from professional-level equipment, but with a price tag similar to consumer-grade models.

The cable is great to handle, with a durable rubber jacket that's very flexible and readily lays flat on the floor, unlike the comparatively stiff PVC plastic jackets found on cheap stuff. This is a cable that will happily go wherever your crew and performers want, instead of trying to retain its previous shape and twisting/curling back up on its own.

The cable's metal XLR connectors are of very high quality, with gold-plated contacts and good soldering onto the 23-gauge wires. The connectors fit smoothly and precisely, and rubber gaskets at critical points offer a decent level of moisture/rain resistance. I like that this cable's male XLR features a full closed-shell design, which provides superior ingress protection compared to cheaper connectors that have an open cutout at the locking tab.

In use, the cable performs as expected, with excellent signal quality and strong EMF noise rejection provided by the star quad wiring design. The cable I received does not link pin 1 (signal ground) with the XLR shell (frame ground), which is my preferred configuration for avoiding ground loops.

Overall, I'm very impressed with the quality, performance, and construction of this mic cable. It's a professional-grade product in every respect. Highly recommended.
Summary: Professional quality at an affordable price

Text:
Great little keyboard, but with full-sized keys.

I have two other controller keyboards. Both M-Audio, one is 49 keys, one is 61 keys. They're good, but this is great. Actually also might make one a better keyboard player, by forcing you to concentrate on just two octaves, rather than noodling around the length of a longer keyboard. With just two octaves, you can "see" patterns and chords easier. Though you can go up and down to full 88 keys with buttons. But two octaves at once is a good teaching exercise.

And since it's smaller, it leaves room for a cat on my keyboard stand. And there's pretty much always a cat there now. (Stand is a board on a towel on a keyboard stand).

PROS:
--Solid build. Keys are good. Pads have an amazing feel.
--Can control your DAW - almost makes a soft synth into a hardware synth.
--You can sit across the room and play it, without being a slave to sitting at a computer. Once auto-mapped, you can change pre-set patches on a softsynth. And on some, you can control some of the parameters. Plus, play keys and drum pads. (M-audio is the other keyboard that can do that, but not nearly as easily and elegantly as this one does.)
--Easy to map your DAW (download software from manufacturer's site after registering)
--Pretty lights that change color on the pad when you play them! Looks trippy in the dark.

CONS:
--Keys are kinda stiff. Some people might hate it. Probably not good if you have hand pain issues. On the other hand, playing it may actually strengthen your hands.
--Keys are physically kinda loud when you press them. Make a dull thud sound.

EDIT AFTER 2 WEEKS OF PLAYING IT A LOT: The keyboard dull thud got much less after a little while. And I think the keys are still stiff, but my hands actually got stronger playing it (!), so it's not an issue now. I dig the feel.

Someone else here said it takes two buttons to remotely change synth patches but that's not true on Cubase. Just takes one at a time, going up or down the list in your DAW from this keyboard.

All in all I'm very happy with it. It's a heck of a lot of controller for 100 bucks.
Summary: Love it! Love it! Love it!

4 Months Later (December 2021): If you look at my "Initial Thoughts" below, you'll see that I wasn't particularly impressed with the pedal or the default sounds. The default sounds and IR presets aren't anything special, but there is a huge collection of free and paid IR emulations you can download from (Celestion, JBL, and other sources). I've spent, probably, 2-3 hours messing with programming this thing and I love it. I don't do many 5-star reviews, but in time I can imagine not being able to resist giving it that last star :-). Honestly, companies like Zoom, Line6, and, especially, TC Helicon provide awful software for their emulation pedals and cost as much as 10x this unit.

The distortion options are nothing special, but I'm not a big fan of distorted guitar anyway. With the speaker and amp IR loaded, I have created 3 terrific default sounds and I can quickly dial in other sounds for temporary use.

Initial Thoughts (September 2021): A friend bought one of these from the actual manufacturer direct from China a few weeks earlier and really liked it. He isn't particularly discriminating as far as tone and performance is concerned, but for $50 I thought I'd try it for my Jamkazam sessions, instead of mic'ing my amplifier. The default tones are pretty lame and the volume settings are just silly, the direct output (no effects) is 12-20dB quieter than the 3 default settings volume. The software, CubeSuite, isn't bad for basic operation and settings but you'll quickly find that the installed amps and IR models are pretty lame.

Figuring out how to use the CubeSuite software for downloaded IR models pretty much requires foreign language skills that I don't have. I did find a couple of YouTube demos that had links that gave me a couple of half-decent model sets, so I know it works. Don't expect this pedal to be competitive with the Zoom, TC Helicon, Roland, etc high end pedals because it isn't. It is a really nice device for travel (decent headphone output) and it isn't terrible as an effects pedal. Most of the clean sounds are pretty decent, but the distortion FX are super-cheezy.
Summary: Pretty good for $50, but with some programming and IR download work it can be terrific

Text:
I bought both from GC to compare. Truth is i like the cosmetics of the traditional fenders (I own a "real" 64 deluxe reverb and 65 vibrochamp and 61 blonde bassman) and I franky do not like the black on black of the 50XL. But sound is more important. I bought the 40 and found the bottom end a little anemic so I also ordered the 50 and would only keep the "winner". I have no interest in anything beyond the simple, yet amazing sound of a fender blackface so I only used the "blackface" voicing of channel 1. Additionally I have a very nice pedal board and was not interested in any of the on board effects. So I won't comment on either of those.

In testing the 40 and 50, along with my fender blues junior and my original deluxe reverb... I measured decibel output at 10 feet and also monitored the overall output bandwidth to see how they each performed across various frequencies - with my primary interest in their bottom end. The 40 put out 102db at 10ft, the blues junior and the 50 put out 103db. but oh boy it was immediately apparent how flabby the bottom end was in the 40. Funny thing is I even swapped out the stock speaker with a very nice Weber speaker and it didn't help the bottom end much at all. The 50's bottom end (considering its a $200 amp) was reasonably tight, held up well and even a little deeper than my blues junior (though the blues junior sounds superior overall). I probably don't need to say my deluxe reverb took them all to school, but considering it's current value is almost 10x the Champion 50, it's not a fair comparison.

Aesthetics aside I immediately returned the 40. From a sound perspective the extra $30 in price is a no brainer. I could do a small gig with the 50, i wouldn't even try with the 40.

The 50 is a decent sounding amp - remember I'm only interested in the traditional blackface sound - and I wouldn't hesitate to take it to a small gig.
Summary: Compared the Champion 40 to the Champion 50

It's hard to review the Clarke original tin whistle because frankly, it is what it is, a piece of folk music history preserved more or less in its original form from 1843. It's deserving of appreciation but not everyone will find it pleasant to play.

The antique design has several pros and cons. It delivers the rough, airy sound that the tin whistle is stereotypically known for and is sometimes lost in more modern and professional quality instruments. Whether you want or like this old fashioned sound is subjective. Unlike other cheap whistles, Clarke whistles are hand finished so the quality control tends to be better than brands like Generation.

The simple folded tin and wood block design also makes it difficult for beginners because it requires a lot of air. It's quieter than most whistles which may be a good thing depending on your living situation but its a poor choice for playing in a noisy atmosphere.

Ultimately I think every whistler should own a Clarke original at some point to have an appreciation for where the instrument came from, in its modern metal form anyway, and how the low priced instrument became a part of British folk music tradition. As a beginner's learning tool however, the Clarke Sweetone is much easier to play, sounds nicer and is cheaper.

Text:
I also have a Boss Katana MKII Artist and also bought its CA-FC foot controller. I mention this because it includes a button that let’s you toggle between patch selection or effects selection. This is hugely useful. In contrast, this Positive Grid footswitch, which so far otherwise works wonderfully, requires you to select its mode of operation from the pulldown menu on whatever digital device you’re also required to stream everything through. So this would be an inconvenience if you were miking up this amp at a gig, something worth considering since the tones on the Spark 40 amp are the best modeled tones ever heard at an amp in this price range, and it’s loud enough for you to use as your own stage monitor.
Then again, it was likely never the designers’ intent to use the amp this way; it is foremost a home practice and recording amp at which it succeeds spectacularly. That said, while the amp itself can be used without attaching it to a smart device, the footswitch cannot; there must always be a smart device connecting the two through Bluetooth. While this is technically an inconvenience, it is again likely exactly what the designers intended, as you can also not do deep editing, nor the smart backing tracks, nor any of the other powerful things the amp is capable of, unless its hooked up to its app on a smart device.
So I am docking the footswitch one star because of the opportunities missed in not addressing these possibilities when designing it. But it does work great, and since my practicing and recording in my basement likely makes me their target audience, the product succeeds very well at this mission.

Text:
With any decent high-gain tube amp or analog preamp, and this pickup in a TELE, you can NAIL the tone of Jimmy's classic rock riffs. I tested this with "Whole Lotta Love" "Communication Breakdown," "Heartbreaker" and "Moby Dick." This is also perfect for Jimmy's solo on Stairway where its bite and razor edged clarity leave most humbuckers in the dust.

When combined with a balanced neck pup, this gives a better-than-vintage chickin' pickin tone. It’s just as clear but LOUDER so it can push your preamp into lovely square-wave woolliness.

Although it has a bit more output than vintage pups, it does not get muddy even with ridiculous gain and distortion. Of course part of that mojo comes from the 10-degree angle and position of the Tele bridge set-up, but THIS PICKUP does all the heavy lifting.

The rail configuration does not exert too much magnetic drag, especially near the bridge, so these do not affect intonation even when adjusted very near the strings. These are sensitive to height adjustments, but not in a bad way. Close or near they sound good, just different. You'll need to set those adjustments with a clean tone to hear the subtle differences.

For the rock tones, I've found it's better to bring the bass-side down a 16th" or so and let the 100-watt plexi and four-12" cab reproduce the low end. For smaller combo amps and cleaner sounds, you can get away with raising the low side a bit and using the tone knobs on your amp for balls. Through a twin with volume above “3” it gets all the Joe Barden / Danny Gatton bite without the boutique penury. As Danny would say, “It barks like a show-dog!”

For purposes of comparison, I have six Teles: One vintage stock circa 1964, an American standard Fender with their V3 Noiseless pups and four other custom Teles. One of those has Kinman Hot tele pups, another has this barking beauty. (The other two have humbuckers so I don’t count those here)

The only other pickups I know of that make less noise are the Zexcoils, and at the time I bought mine they did not yet make Tele pups. These are only slightly more noisy, equivalent to any good humbucker. If you are recording with a DAW, then the Zexcoils are definitely worth checking out. With digital amp farms and processing, you can tweak any tone you want. But for REAL LOUD TUBE AMPS in a live setting, the tiny amount of extra noise is inaudible and you will drool for the power and tone of this dual blade baddass. If you’re doing any Zep covers live, you should really check these pups out!

Although this is a versatile pickup, it is not for everyone. Some prefer the old-school look of individual pole pieces. Some believe in magic mojo of vintage designs. Of course, SOME people believe in astrology and voodoo too.

The only way to hear for yourself is to A-B a stock Tele against another Tele with this pup with the same licks through the same amp with the same settings in the same room. Do that, then decide to keep it or not. Remember, both DiMarzio and Seymour Duncan have liberal return policies that guarantee your satisfaction.

As for myself... I'm keeping mine and building another Tele with another one of these snarlin' nasty bastards. Makes hairs on your arms and neck stand at attention.
Summary: NAILS those classic Zeppelin riff tones!

My prior experience with synthesizers was largely with software synths, including VST's on desktop and the wealth of great (affordable) synth apps on iOS devices. Coming from a software background can actually lead to some disappointment when you start to look at hardware (particularly analog hardware) and realize just how expensive it can be to get even basic features like complex polyphony, choice of waveforms, and sequencing in hardware form. Fortunately, Volca Keys and the Volca series as a whole are absolute freaks of nature, offering far more quality and functionality than a $160 plastic box arguably ever should! While this is more of a "4.5 star" review and I slightly prefer the Volca Bass (for reasons discussed below), I'm going with a 5-star rating anyway based on sheer "value" offered in this insanely portable little package.

FEATURES - The Volca Keys has a few distinguishing features that, at first glance, would seem to give an upper hand versus the other Korg Volcas. First, the Keys offers 3-note polyphony (or maybe "paraphony", some have argued), which on a very basic level means the ability to play 3 separate notes at the same time. For people new to synthesizers, the expectation is probably that a synth operates similar to a grand piano - mash down any many keys as you want, and each of those notes will play individually. But with synthesizers - and especially affordable ANALOG synthesizers - true polyphony is actually somewhat rare. If you're looking for a "first synth" or "only synth", I've heard a lot of people argue that the Volca Keys is the way to go, since it will allow you to do chords, leads, and bass all to some degree.

Another unique feature of the Keys is that it actually has a 27-key touch keyboard laid out like a traditional piano spanning just over 2 octaves. (By contrast, the Volca Bass and Korg's earlier Monotron/Monotribe products had variations of a straight-line ribbon keyboard). I'd be lying if I said the keyboard is easy to play with adult-sized hands, but the buttons respond well and for sketching and on-the-go functionality, it's certainly preferable to have this versus a straight sound module with no keys at all.

You can play the notes live like a keyboard, or record one-bar sequences through a variety of live inputs. (If I am not mistaken, the Keys does not have a programmable step sequencer as does the Volca Bass or something like a TB-303). While I'm still learning the ins and outs of the Keys, I believe that default live recording setting quantizes inputs to the nearest 1/16th note, or you can turn on "FLUX" and record non-quantized patterns that basically record your exact inputs. You can save up to 8 different sequences in memory banks linked to keys 1-8, and change these on the fly.

I said that recordings were limited to 16 steps or 1 bar, and that is technically true. However, you can "game" the system a bit by using the 1/1, 1/2, and 1/4 tempo adjustments, which cut the TEMPO and effectively allow you to record 2- or 4-bar passages. Actually, the Keys is the best of the Volcas at this functionality, as the other units are more strictly limited to 1-bar loops, unless you get creative with the tempo settings.

The pitch range of the keys is controlled by the Octave knob, which has settings for 32', 16', 8', 4', 2', 1'. It's an impressive range of sounds, and while the device is called "keys", you can absolutely get bass as well as lead sounds from the device. There are settings for the VCO (which, in most cases, is set only to a sawtooth wave), a voltage-controlled low-pass filter, and an LFO that allow for pitch and/or filter oscillation. Finally, Korg threw in a delay with time and feedback controls. While the quality of the delay is just so-so (it sounds more like a decaying analog delay than a crisp digital, to my ears), Korg's implementation is excellent, as always. By pressing FUNC + Key 13, you can correspond the delay tempo to the overall BPM tempo of the device. The "TIME" knob then shifts between 1/4 note, 1/8 note, etc. delay patterns. This is particularly useful if you are doing sequencing or chaining the Volca Keys to other Volcas using a 3.5mm cable and the "SYNC IN/OUT" jacks. For those unfamiliar, the Sync feature is a primitive but effective timing system that synchronizes BPM between Korg devices by sending out a brief electric pulse. So it's possible to have multiple Volcas chained together, all playing at the same tempo, and with delay on the Volca Keys synchronized to BPM (and all devices powered by battery). Really an amazing feat for entry-level equipment.

SOUND QUALITY - I think that the entire Volca line sounds incredibly good, even factoring in that the only audio output is a stereo headphone 3.5mm jack, and that the device is tiny and battery powered. It's worth noting that there is a little bit of background "hiss", moreso on the Keys and Sample than the Volca Bass, in my experience. It's only really noticeable when you turn up the volume and use a set of headphones, and it hardly ruined the experience for me.

The Volca Keys, at first glance, seems to have worlds more tonal flexibility than the Volca Bass, though that's a bit deceptive, as I discuss in the comparison section below. The 3-note polyphony is absolutely capable of producing rich, analog chords. However, if you happen to bump a fourth note (as is easy to do on the mini-keyboard), it will kill all of the notes and re-trigger, which sounds artificial. This was probably my #1 disappointment in using the Keys, but again, at this price point, ANY degree of analog polyphony is pretty amazing, and many sub-$1,000 devices have very limited polyphony. It's also worth pointing out that the all of the Volca devices remain in tune amazing well, which is not true of many analog synths (some of the cheaper ones are absolute horror stories in this department).

The UNISON mode is monophonic, and stacks the three sawtooth oscillators on top of each other for a thicker sound. You can use the DETUNE knob to make slight (or less slight) variations in pitch between the oscillators, which makes your bass and lead sounds even fatter sounding. OCTAVE setting uses two sawtooth waves at one pitch and the third at a pitch higher. FIFTH setting does the same except the higher note is a fifth instead of an octave higher. The two ring modulation settings incorporate a square wave and a have a unique sound, though probably more niche in their usefulness. Overall, everything sounds great. Raw analog sawtooth sounds can be a bit harsh, though you can tame this with the VCF cutoff or add external effects.

MIDI FUNCTIONALITY - If I'm being honest, I probably didn't "need" a Keys in addition to the Bass, but wanted one primarily so I could play 3-note chords with an external keyboard. Unfortunately, the MIDI functionality is limited in several ways. First, I do not believe it is velocity-sensitive (correct me if I'm wrong in Comments). Second, it accepts only 5-pin DIN traditional MIDI cables. While this was the standard for many years and especially in the 80's and 90's, virtually all cheap and compact MIDI controllers nowadays transmit MIDI data by USB. So many of the popular MIDI keyboards that people already use with Ableton or iPad apps simply won't work with a Volca Keys. I recommend the CME Xkey 37 or discontinued Alesis Q25/Q49 as some relatively affordable 5-pin MIDI keyboards that are smaller than the size of an office desk. I have the Xkey 37, and it's MUCH easier to play accurate 3-note chords with a keyboard versus the mini keys.

VOLCA KEYS VS. VOLCA BASS - When I researched which Volca(s) I wanted to buy, I saw a lot of debate on Keys vs. Bass, and it was about as evenly split as internet debates can be. The best way I can describe it is that the Keys is a more "optimistic" device, whereas the Bass is better at is specific stated task. If you know that your primary goal is to use your Volca for single note bass grooves or lead tones, get the Bass. There are apps sold for $10 to $20 on iPad and iPhone that offer true polyphony and far more variety of sounds than the Volca Keys offers, so you could use that as your lead synth. The Bass also has more traditional step sequencing in the tradition of the 303, and you can trick it into doing cool unison and faux polyphony sounds by setting the 3 oscillators to different pitch settings. But, as I said before, if your goal is to play as many different styles on a single device, the Keys has wider ambitions, and will at least allow you to input basic chords. However, you may need an external keyboard plugged into the Keys to truly take advantage of its POLY setting.

CONCLUSION - The Volca Keys is simultaneously the most amazing and the most frustrating of the Volca series. It's absolutely ridiculous that a battery powered device the size of a VHS tape can sound this good, be analog, and offer this range of features. At the same time, it can be maddening trying to input notes on the mini-keyboard and killing your chords by bumping a 4th note accidentally. You may inevitably choose to own more than one Volca, and if you do, the Keys is a great addition to the lineup. If you can only afford one, however, I hope my comments on the Bass and Keys are helpful in picking the right one for you. Enjoy!
Summary: Amazing (though limited) polyphony from a versatile analog mini-synth

What i like and what i don't like:

What i have to compare this to are two other holders i had.

One was the one i had in high school in the 60s and used to play a few Dylan songs, when i was first learning, i just went to a music store and bought "a harmonica holder," there weren't a lot of different choices, or any different choices, and all i wanted was one that looked like what Dylan and others had because i thought that's what harp holders look like. The one i got looked just like that and i didn't give it any thought. I put it on with the harp in it, and started learning some songs. The holder itself was never an issue, learning progressed easily, and i just got out of doing it because my life got turned upside down and i was moving around and unstable, and then a year and a half later, i left home on my own for Haight Ashbury and was traveling very light.

The second harp holder i had, i got 15 years ago, i wanted to play harp with guitar again so i got a holder, i don't remember where, online? or at a store? don't remember but it was much bigger than the one i used to have in high school that looked like what Dylan used. It was black and it had a wide round neck and it wouldn't stay in place, it was really awkward, it didn't stay tight, it made harp playing more than hard, it wasn't worth it. Just stick with guitar.

I didn't try anymore until last year, i had never learned blues harp ever, or second position, and i wanted to learn that so i got harps and took you tube lessons. And i also wanted to play some Dylan songs, Neil Young, Arlo Guthrie, so, i got this Stageline holder on Amazon.

i looked at all the holders on Amazon, there were so many different ones. I was looking for one just like the one i had as a teenager because it always worked fine and was easy to use, and it was the kind Dylan and others used, but nothing like that was on Amazon, or other online stores. Either they were kind of elaborately bent and shaped, with various adjustable things, some with only a wing nut on one side, some with no wing nuts, instead having round screw turners.

i wanted one like i used to have, and i found this one. This one looks pretty much like the one i used to have back when companies were making functional inexpensive simple 10 hole harp holders. The main difference of this one is that it's wide for larger harps to fit. (Do people actually play 24 hole harps with holders?) on Amazon, it was really hard to find one that was just designed for a 10 hole harmonica, and one or more of them were TOO narrow, so that you couldn't move the harp around very far if you wanted. i don't know why no one makes the kind that the best well known 10 hole players always used. i guess there's no market for that?

What i like about the Stageline:

wing nuts on both sides
wing nuts tighten easily, easy to grab both at the same time and turn.
easy and pretty fast to get harp in and out of clip
harp is stable in the clip, it's held sturdily

what i don't like about it includes:

it's too big and loose fitting
It can move to different positions on the neck, where i don't want it
related to its size, the harp is not in the right angle and proximity to my mouth.
the harp is too far away from my mouth, even though i can get my mouth to it,
when i get there, i can't get good traction and have a hard time controlling sound,
i have a hard time on some holes getting enough volume, getting too much air
because i'm too far from the harp. on most holes i can't bend very well because
not able to get a good snug correctly angled position, while moving around to different
notes/chords.
Or, to minimize these problems, i have to place the harp and tighten the holder too close
to my mouth so that i have to turn my head to the side to sing, or awkwardly up or down,
or sing into where the harp is, and sometimes make harp sound unintentionally.
Even when i do that, the angle isn't right for bends on certain notes in certain keys.
None of this happened with my original holder that i got in the 60s, which was the size
and shape of the ones performers were using then.

The main problem for me with this harp holder is that it's too big which makes it
loose fitting and less than stable, which is a tolerable problem BUT
also related to too big is that i can't get the harp in a good position related to my mouth.
That's a deal breaker, if there were other alternatives.

I went on eBay and looked for vintage holders. I found one that looked like what i had in the 60s
but when it arrived, i could not get it to hold the harp securely, harp slipped out the front if i put it on the shelf
of the clip, with the back against the up-bent part on the back edge of the shelf, the same way
i place it with this Stageline holder which is stable and secure, one of the best things about it for me.

i couldn't figure out how to get the old vintage eBay one to hold onto the harp, had to give up.
So, that's when i got a second Stageline, i am a home player, not a performer, i am having fun learning, so i
wanted one for my main room where i hang out and one in the bedroom (i keep guitars in both
places, ready to do things on impulse and inspiration).

So, bottom line, i got the first one, it had pros and cons, very frustrating to not be able to find the
kind of holder that used to be the only kind and were widely used and no one complained about them,
so, despite the frustrations of the inability to position the Stageline holder right to get the most playability out of
the harp, i got a second one of these, given the positive things i experienced with the first one.

As my technique improves, i get more frustrated with the harp holder getting in the way. I just bought
another vintage one on eBay last night, 10 hole side, "normal" looking, not all the fancy stuff so many
of the ones on Amazon have. Meanwhile, today i was messing with the other one i previously got on eBay and i put the harp in the clip in a way that seemed precarious and unsupported, but it held and i had
the greatest time playing, wow, what a difference. I hope the "new" vintage one will be the same.

If you’re just looking for reverb, this pedal has a pretty good spring reverb sound. The other settings are rather. . .unique, with some being really quite good, and others that I could do without. Someone had a lot of fun creating the DSP effects for this pedal, with many of the settings sounding like two pedals in series (e.g. a tremolo+reverb, or a flanger + reverb, or delay + reverb, etc.) or two pedals with parallel mixing (e.g. mixing a vibrato with clean, then adding reverb). It’s almost like you have presets of various series and parallel two-pedal combinations, in which the 2nd pedal is always a reverb. But not in all cases. Sometimes the effect is only applied to the reverb portion of the signal, or only to the non-reverb portion.

So, just a few up front thoughts, then you can read about each setting in depth. First, if you already have a huge pedal board with all the varieties pedals, you can already get these sounds. But, if you want these sounds in a single pedal, then this is a pretty neat package. What you lose is being able to insert other pedals in between these effects (notably distortions). I’d say this pedal is more suited to clean playing than overdriven or distorted inputs. It’s also stupidly big (imho). I opened it up, and only ½ the space inside is being used. This could have easily fit in a 1590B enclosure, and saved some space on the pedal board (see pic). Instead, it’s in a huge 1590BB. The only reason I can think why they did this is to print the control knob functions on the pedal. But, I’d rather have the more compact size. Also, the selection switch on mine is installed at a tilted angle. See the side profile pics to see what I mean. So, maybe lacking a bit in quality control.

This is a DSP pedal, and it consumes 62.7 mA. None of the effects have any gain to speak of, everything is at about unity. Since it’s DSP, the designer can change the function of the knobs depending on the setting, and they certainly make use of this, a bit too much. For example, the mix control knob changes between settings. Sometimes it’s the far right knob, sometimes it’s the middle knob, and sometimes it’s the left knob. This is a bit annoying, and it should have just been kept constant across all settings.

Aesthetically, you can judge for yourself. There is no fancy boutique style artwork, but none of that affects the sound anyway. It comes with 4 little grippy feet, but no velcro.

Here is a detailed description of each effect:

Long Reverb: I would call this “delayed reverb” if I was naming it. The reverb doesn’t kick in until after about a 200ms delay (see oscilloscope pic). You cannot adjust this delay time, it’s fixed at 200ms. I can’t hear any effect of the tone controls on this setting. They must be very subtle, and only programmed to effect the wet signal, which would indeed be hard to hear. The delayed wet signal seems to be compressed as well, with a rather slow attack. Minimum decay time is about 200ms, Max decay time is 1500ms.

Spring Reverb: This is exactly as you’d expect, a standard reverb setting. Min decay is about 300ms, Max decay time is about 1500ms. The tone controls are a bit more noticeable on this setting, but still super mild.

Phase Vibrato Verb: This adds vibrato only to the reverb signal. There are two mix controls. You can mix the reverb with the dry, and you can mix more or less vibrato with the reverb. The width control is pretty subtle, and doesn’t sound like it does very much. There is always quite a bit of vibrato in the reverb signal, even with the vibrato mix knob at minimum. It’s not a subtle effect. It adds a lot of de-tune into the reverb.

Tremolo Reverb: This is just a standard tremolo, with a sinusoidal envelope (see oscilloscope pic). The speed range is from 2.5Hz (400ms) to 10 Hz (100ms). The mix control lets you adjust the depth of the tremolo from 0 to 100%, and the reverb mix lets you mix in reverb from none (pure clean tremolo) to full reverb mix (about 600ms of reverb).

Flanger Reverb: This can be just a pure flanger (with reverb mix at zero, it applies the flanger signal only). The depth control allows you to “mix” in any amount of flanger, from zero to full. The flanger rate goes from about 0.6Hz to about 6 Hz. The Reverb mix control lets you add some reverb to the flanged signal, but to about 300ms decay time.

Vibrato Reverb: This one is interesting because it applies vibrato to the reverb signal, then mixes it back with the dry. Under normal circumstances, when you mix vibrato+dry you get a phasor. Well, this is mixing reverby-vibrato with dry, so it sounds reverby-phasor-ish. It’s a unique, kind of fun sound. You can get crazy space warbler sounds on this setting, or some nice slow subtle phasor with reverb.

Pitch Reverb: This is basically a chorus, in which you have lots of control over the pitch of the 2nd voice. With the pitch knob at 12 o’clock, the 2nd voice is exactly the same as the dry signal, and you hear no effect. But if you move it clockwise, you start mixing in higher pitch 2nd voice, and counterclockwise mixes in lower pitch 2nd voice. The range is pretty wide, several semitones, and you can really get some deeply detuned sounds. The “pitch mix” knob doesn’t do anything from what I can tell. It definitely does NOT control the mix of the 2nd voice. I can’t hear it doing anything, or see it doing anything on the oscilloscope. The reverb mix knob just lets you mix in some reverb, as if the reverb is the 2nd pedal after the chorus.

Octave Echo: This setting has a fixed delay of about 50ms, and the echo pitch is set by the pitch knob. The other knobs don’t do anything, and you can’t mix any reverb into this setting. This is your standard “octave up” or “octave down” sound, but you can smoothly vary the pitch between the two extremes, with the 12 o’clock setting being zero pitch change. It’s basically like the Pitch Reverb setting, without the reverb. Plus, the fixed 50ms delay.

Of all these settings, I find the ones with fixed delays to be a little bit annoying, especially since you can never change the delay time on any of them. But the Spring Reverb, Tremelo Reverb, Flanger Reverb, Vibrato Reverb (i.e. Phasor), and Pitch Reverb (i.e. Chorus) sound the best. In particular, this can create a beautiful deep chorus sound, and is a fairly good basic tremolo too. So, even if you don’t use any of the other interesting effects, you get 3 good pedals in one (spring reverb, chorus, tremolo). Plus there are all the other effects, most of which sound pretty good, if you dial them in right.
I’m only going to knock off one star, because my selector switch is at a goofy angle, and because the box is just way bigger than it needs to be. Pedalboard real estate is precious! But, for the wide variety of other effects, it gets to keep the other 4 stars.

Final Rating: 4 stars. This is a pretty cool combo pedal that creates some great sounds, but it's just a bit too big, with a crooked selector switch, which lost it a star. But it's a great value for the price.
Summary: Very interesting pedal, with a lot of cool sound combinations

This is the one! After using the 1202 (rotary channel knobs, 4 stereo channels) and then changing to the 1204 (channel sliders, but only 2 stereo channels), I am really liking the 1222. It has the sliders, 4 stereo channels, AND 2 sliders controlling monitor and effects send right down with the rest of them where they should be, not some hidden knob hard to get to on the fly, AND a slider for the 2-track return too! FINALLY I can balance all my inputs on the mixer and not fuss with volumes/gains on the computer/phone/cd player I'm sending from. All the channels are in a vertical row, much easier to keep track of the inputs as opposed to the stacked channels on the 1202. This does not have a PFL button BUT I think the separate level setting yellow LEDs up by the gain knobs are better for my mobile DJ use...maybe not as accurate as using PFL on the main meter but they are a constant visual aide to keep the input gain levels hot but not too hot. You simply keep them dialed to where the input occasionally flashes them. I would prefer the main XLR outs to be on the back like they are on the 1204 and I might miss the Solo buttons that the 1204 has too but I'll swap mixers if a gig needs that. All in all the 1222 has a great mix of features. I like the onboard graphic equalizer with feedback detect, stereo expand feature, and a great FX section. Good job Behringer!

My most important criterion in any instrument is its overall playability. In my hands, at least, this bass feels great. The setup was flawless right out of the box, the intonation is true all the way up the neck, the action is low. The neck itself is narrow across the fret board, which lends itself well to bass chords and complex voicings. Once again, the big surprise here is how well-suited this bass is to jazz. Text:
Wow! This is the kind of neck you'd find on a 2k+ guitar, but first I gotta say, I'm a little annoyed by other reviews that knock a star off because the nut needs to be replaced. That's Fender. That's the way all their necks are, except the higher end American models, & they should all be replaced to get most out of your guitar. They're not the only company that's like this, but it is annoying. If you can't craft a nut or aren't willing to pay for someone else to do it, don't buy this neck.

Now to the neck. Wow again! The craftsmanship is so fine it shocked me. The Mexico plant has become something special over the last decade, they're not just building great guitars, but great guitar craftspeople. Some people think the neck building process is done by machine, but that's not the case entirely; only about 3/4 is machine lathed, but the most important part, the form & finish work, is still done by hand, & by some highly skilled craftspeople. The roasting process appears flawlessly executed, & isn't overly dried, & the satin finish on the back of the neck is fast! The slab of wood is so loaded w/maple figuring that the fingerboard looks holographic, & the fret work is flawless, I mean not a single issue, not a burr even. I find myself starring endlessly starring into the figured fretboard, & I rarely look at the fretboard, even when soloing. It's just that beautiful. I probably just got lucky w/the figuring, but they've have chosen some really beautiful maple for this neck. I bought mine directly from Fender, so I can keep all my Fender gear in one place on their site, but I'm so impressed that I wanted to leave a review, & encourage anyone that might be thinking of upgrading. Just do it, you'll be so happy you did. -Cheers
Summary: This is the kind of neck you find on a 2k guitar

Switching channels seemed to help but then again, 5 minutes later a split second drop out wasn't that big of a deal until I finally replaced this digital system with an analog UHF system also from Amazon. Sounds better with lower latency and zero interference from my WiFi. Digital systems add A to D conversion time, latency that is almost undetectable but analog ends up being instant transfer with zero latency where digital isn't. Go figure. I wanted to give this pedal a try because of the fantastic price. Plus, I could use a drive pedal for quick use when I practice. And I wondered if it really was Klon-like. I played the pedal using a BC Rich Mockingbird through the pedal alone into a Hughes and Ketner TubeMeister amp head pumped into a Carvin sealed cabinet.

First, for the pros. Construction is solid. It can function as a drive or a clean boost. It has two voices, one with a more aggressive overdrive than the other. Being small, it would be a space saver on a pedalboard.

Now for the cons. The pedal is a bit too honky for me. It’s not a bad sound. It’s just not quite the smooth sound I like in a drive. I own a couple dozen excellent drive pedals. They all make playing the guitar a little easier. This pedal did not. I actually had to put a little more effort into getting a smooth sound out of my guitar. And compared to those pedals, this one sounds thin. Finally, there is a high pitch oscillation sound that became slightly audible as the guitar sound fades. It was barely perceptible, but I could not ignore it. I would never record with this pedal although it’s likely fine for everything else. Finally, sound like a Klon? I don’t own a Klon. That 6 months worth of groceries. But I own 6 other Klon-like pedals, clones. This pedal sounds like none of them.

It would be even better if that battery could be charged via USB.  Alas to be a truly portable independent unit you're stuck using regular or rechargeable AA batteries.  I get about two hours out of a full charge, which although is about what I expected, it isn't stellar.  I use it for recording the comm system in the cockpit so on a long cross-country I'll need to rig it up to an external battery pack.  Not the end of the world but battery life is definitely the glaring issue with what is otherwise an absolutely stellar little portable recorder.  I did a fairly extensive review on my YouTube channel "Unexploded Minds" you can check out for the gory details.  The recorder itself is fantastic and the mic preamps are very very good for the price.  I'm super pleased with the flexibility this portable recorder offers.  The shortcut buttons are very well thought out and the user interface is easy to navigate.  Except for the battery issue, I truly love this little recorder.
Summary: Great little portable recorder but begs to be rechargeable

I was looking for a cheap way to get some drums miced up in a hurry for this Saturday's St. Patrick's Day parade. I took a chance on this kit, even though I have never purchased anything that says "Pyle" on the label. Upon receiving this kit, my first surprise was the quality of the case, and then upon opening, I was surpised to find that these were the EXACT same microphones as the ones I borrowed once from a friend to do some recordings, but branded differently. He paid about 350-400 for his kit (still cheap by today's standards).

I pulled out 1 overhead condensor and the kick-drum mic and mounted them, fired up the PA and had our drummer play a bit and was shocked at the clarity of the overhead mic! We could probably get away with just using this one microphone to mic the entire kit, or two overheads; they pick up everything very clearly. I turned up the volume on the kick-drum mic and was even more surprised to hear the thump of a much more expensive mic coming out of this seemingly too-small mic. Now, I have a wonderful drum mix coming from only 2 microphones and my mixer has more channels free than I would have expected. For fun, I added one of the tom/snare mics and they sounded equally clear.

After purchasing this, I can tell you that there is absolutely NO way I would purchase one of the "high-end" drum-mic kits. If you are looking for a solution for recording or live sound, this is it. I promise you will LOVE the sound and you will be ecstatic about the price you paid to get that sound.

I own the Pioneer Toraiz SP-16 sampler, and though this bag isn't exactly designed for it, it will definitely do the trick for my light transport, storage and protection needs, as I just couldn't justify spending almost 3X as much for the officially branded product.

There's not a lot of slop, but as this case wasn't designed for the SP-16, there is a bit of space around the unit - (you could tuck the power adapter on one side) the foam insert helps.

The zippers are good sized, and look like they should hold up to regular use. The outside of the case is semi-rigid ballistic nylon, so I wouldn't describe this as a "hard case" per se, yet it will provide a reasonable amount of protection.

For me, this is a decent product, but I docked it a star because:
There is only one foam insert included, and that's a free (unattached) piece - the interior of the bag itself is not padded. There also aren't any rubber feet or cushioning on the back edge of the bag, should you choose to stand it up vertically. Finally, the two handles are independent - there's no velcro closure or snaps to join them together once the bag is closed. Like I said though, for the price, this bag will meet my needs. :)

This is a little expensive and totally a one-trick-pony, but it does exactly what it claims and it does it really well. I swear I can feel it stretching my strings and after my first use with a string change right before a gig, everything was stretched great and held in tune.

Honestly, I’d pass on this for the average player if you are changing strings less than twice a month. But if you’re tinkering often, have multiple guitars you’re stringing constantly, it is definitely worth saving a tiny bit of time and finger pain from hand stretching.

That's not to brag but to illustrate my experience with AMPS. Everything you can imagine. This AMP ranks up there with the best of them. I'm surprised as I've hated (with a passion) every DSP solid state amp I've ever played. This hybrid is incredible. The effects are excellent. The built in compression is amazing and the amp works excellent for recording. It has many onboard effects but I have racks and pedals that outdo those, so I don't use them for recording.

It's not a band amp unless you're an acoustic band or your drummer has electronic drums. It's 15 Watts, but it's loud... it's just not quite loud enough to get those cleans over the drums, though you might be fine for overdrive -- depending on the venue and situation.

It's not going to emulate certain amps like a VOX very well, but it does excellent with a Fender Black face (excluding the tube reverb). It does a Bassman ok, but doesn't quite capture that chime and nuisances tone of the original '59 Bassman. Doesn't cost $11,000 dollars other. It does a Marshall pretty well. Marshall's based on '59 Bassman without the delicate touch, so there's no wonder. The acoustic gives a very clean sound and makes that clean sound more full, yet doesn't sound like a filter. 0, 6, 7, 9 and 12 are amazing voices. You can bypass that and use it without effects or voicing and it sounds a lot like the original Super Champ.

I also have a 2x12 Vintage 30 box I connect it to for even more of a wonderful fully dynamic and full rich sound. When I'm just playing around the house or need a quick recording and don't wanna have to dial in sounds with my Vox AC30 or Fender Deluxe Reverb then this my amp of choice. It is miles ahead of a Fender Blues Deluxe.

Yes, this is indeed the best amp you will find for the price and the most versatile amp I've played outside of a $2000 mesa boogie.

Buy it. In fact, buy two. This is a future classic.
Summary: I have more AMPS than most people have TV's.

Way back in the day, a mic pre-amp (often tube for harmonics), compressor, de-esser, and parametric equalizer would have be be bought separately. This Helicon unit replaces all of that and does it with much less fuss - the controls on the pedal are optimized and combine multiple dials into one and tailor the pedal for vocals. All of these functions with the addition of a noise gate are included in the racks I mentioned at the beginning of the review. Each one of these racks has upwards of a dozen dials, 10 or more switches, and dozens of blinking lights on it. It takes a very long time to fuss with the controls on the racks to get it right - and the levels are prone to overloading all the units in the chain - without actually clipping levels. Furthermore, after fiddling with all the controls to get it right for one song, often they need to be adjusted again for another song. In addition, towards the end of the chain of one of these vocal channel strips, I would place an exciter (Aphex or BBE). The Helicon replaces all of that, including the exciter, but not including the noise gate.

It's hard to believe it does this with 3 lights, one switch and two dials. But somehow the folks at TC have managed to do it. There's a lot of research that went into this and using it saves me hours and fiddling with dials in between songs, trying to optimize levels.

Now what's bad about it? There is no way to insert or pull the signal out of it mid-chain. The racks would allow me to record just the pre-amp without all the other parts - and I can also do the same just after the de-esser, compressor, or pre-eq. When recording, I often like to record the signal completely dry and then process it post production. But also be able to hear myself through all the effects with the addition of some delay and reverb for my monitor mix. There is no way to pull the signal out pre-effects here. The pre on the TC is quite good and I would have liked the option to pull out a pre-amp only signal to record dry. However, the processed signal is quite good, so I might just record it as-is. The mini-USB plug for updating firmware is quite old and showing it's age as we are now in the world of USB-C and even the micro-USB is slowly disappearing. Most people will not have a mini-USB cable handy, but thankfully, updating firmware is not a frequent thing.

When I first found the rack-mount channel strips, it answered a lot of the mystery of how to get studio quality effects for vocals. I started back in the day of cassette 4-tracks, and these effects used to cost upwards of a thousand dollars for a handful of separate units in addition to the 4-track. The rack channel strips consolidated all these effects into boxes that were around $300-500. This TC box crams all that into a box that is usually around $100, even though at the time I'm writing this review, it's about $140 on Amazon. This box takes care of the mic-pre, de-esser, compression (usually opto), and parametric eq portion of the vocal chain. However, additional effects needed are delay, reverb, and a noise-gate. Some TC boxes have all of these in one, some of these have just the delay + reverb, and there are also TC boxes for just delay or just reverb. An exciter at the end of the chain is no longer needed, somehow the adaptive eq and compression takes care of that and makes the vocals shine and stand out in the mix. The difference is very apparent when listening through headphones.

However, this will not make your voice better than it is, it will not make you sound like Rod Stewart, Joe Cocker, or Justin Timberlake. It will make you sound like a better, cleaner, version of you. It will not help you sing in tune, although there is a TC box for that. The compression will help control the dynamic range - softer sounds become louder and insane louder sounds will be tamed. The dynamics are still there, just not as extreme. Often for live performance, a sound man will be fiddling with the volume slider as well as eq - and this minimizes the need for that.

The effect is more apparent in higher fidelity equipment. A clean full range chain with some good monitoring headphones, and its very apparent what it's doing. Listening through a bluetooth speaker that was $30 at a big box store, it's not so apparent.

If you understand that the pros use a quality mic pre, compressor, de-esser, and eq at the beginning of their vocal recording chain and what these things do, then you understand what this device is. If you know what a vocal channel strip is and understand what all those dials and lights do and why it's put in the chain of most recorded vocals, you will understand what this does. If you have tried to mess with one of these channel strips and have been frustrated at getting the levels right, even though nothing is clipping and have been frustrated at having to adjust in-between songs, then this will be a miracle box. It's amazing how they stuck all those dozens of dials, lights, and buttons into 3 dials and three lights and threw in the circuitry that auto adjusts to the incoming signal. Just realize you are giving up the flexibility of inserting anything between the parts of the chain or pull out a signal from the middle of the chain.

However, you still need the talent and ability to use it.

I own quite a lot of TC boxes. I have a vocal rack unit, reverb+delay box, and also the pitch correct box. I don't always use those boxes, but this vocal T1 is always at the front. I also have an audio interface by TC and will leave a review for that shortly. It doesn't disappoint and as long as someone knows what it is, it does what is supposed to, fantastically.

For singing: This unit --> another TC Helicon effects unit with Delay, Reverb, and Noise Gate
For speech for video work: This unit --> another TC Helicon effects unit with only Noise Gate
For remote video conferencing --> This unit --> even another TC Helicon unit with Delay (to sync up with video speech) --> Digitech unit with noise gate.
Summary: Replaces Vocal Channel Strip costing hundreds and does it better. FOR VOCALS only.
