Bought this to replace the original white pickguard on a Mexico made strat. Like I have heard before, the hole for the humbucker is cut in the wrong place. The hole is back towards the bridge about 1/4" farther than the factory pickguard. I have heard other reviewers complain about this and the seller tell them they are wrong, that this pickguard is for newer American and Mexican strats. They are both right, sort of. I also bought a white pickguard for my American strat, and it is cut the same way. The back edge of the hole for the humbucker on my Mexican strat was routed straight, and with the pickguard loaded, it dropped right in the Mexican strat. My American strat originally came with a single coil in the bridge position, but the body is routed for a humbucker. The back edge on the American strat was not routed straight, and was a little curved. This would not be a problem for a Fender HSS pickguard, because the hole for the humbucker is cut about 1/4" farther forward than the IKN pickguard. For my American strat, I have to tilt the humbucker back at an angle to get it to drop in the guitar body. Once it clears it is fine, and does not hit the body under the pickguard.
I have uploaded 2 photos to show what I mean by the pickguard not being cut properly. The first one shows the red IKN on top of the original Fender pickguard. Everything lines up perfectly, except for the humbucker hole. The photo shows about 1/4" of white at the back edge of the hole, The 2nd photo shows the original white Fender pickguard on top of the IKN guard. All the holes line up perfectly, except for the humbucker hole. The 1/4" of red shows the hole is too far back towards the bridge.
This pickguard looks really great, and except for the humbucker hole, is drilled and cut perfectly. I had not problems installing this pickguard in my 2009 Mexican strat. My American strat was a different story.
If you have a newer Mexican of American made strat, this should work. If your model says Vintage, this will not work unless you want to re-route your body cavity. Beautiful pickguard at a great price. I also like the assortment of colors. You can even get this in pink pearloid.
Summary: Not cut correctly, but still works....

I am using it with my BC Rich Mockingbird as well as my Epiphone Dot 335 into my Crate solid state amp (can't remember the model number), so keep that in mind, but the rest of this review is opinion only. Most of the settings I dialed in on the VINTAGE setting were too dramatic to be usable--I have to crank the TONE knob to keep it from sounding muddy. I prefer the MODERN vibe sound to the VINTAGE one... it has some nice phaser-style sounds and more subtle tones. Crank the SPEED and DEPTH knobs to get a pretty cool seasick John Scofield-style tone in this setting.

I like that DigiTech combined the TONE and DRIVE knobs because it keeps the layout nice and clean, but I can't get into using the sound produced by the DRIVE knob, especially in the VINTAGE setting. Inclusion of the MIX knob is genius for this pedal, and almost bumps this review up to 4 stars. VENTURA VIBE has an added feature in which you can hold the footswitch, and the LED light will turn green as the SPEED ramps up to max speed. This is supposed to emulate, presumably, the speed of a rotating Leslie speaker cone being manipulated. It's a great idea for this pedal, but poorly executed. It speeds up way faster than I want it to; I would prefer to be able to control the rate of acceleration somehow.

The secret weapon of this pedal is the ROTARY setting, which I find to be highly usable and very convincing. It can give a cool Zombies "Odessey And Oracle" era vibe or give your guitar a neat liquidy kind of sound on a clean tone, especially if combined w/ a tremolo pedal. I haven't tried it on a keyboard yet but definitely have that on my list of things to do. Also haven't used it in a live setting so I can't comment on that.

Text: great product

For a budget pair of studio monitor headphones, these are exceptional. The soundstage is close to neutral and there is zero line noise. I can hear every detail as I record and edit the audio for my videos. They even look good! Haha.

As I've said in the past, I'm no audiophile. I've just got regular ears that enjoy music....So here's a review from a regular eared person.

I have another set of over-ear monitors (ATH-M40X) that are double the price. I've had them since 2015 and they're still going strong. Honestly after five years of using those and a week of using these...There isn't that big of a difference! Strange as it sounds, these are very close in audio quality. I'd say the M40X is a bit more neutral, but these are not far off.

Pros
1. Neutral - not a huge amount of added bass, treble, mids, highs, lows, whatever. Almost FLAT. Highs are a bit more pronounced than with the M40X, but that could also be because these carry 50mm drivers as opposed to the 40mm drivers on the M40X.
2. 50mm drivers - huge, clean sound. Nothing was muddy at any volume.
3. Comfort - lightweight and very well padded. They fit my giant head without causing pressure, even after several hours of use at a time.
4. Connections - 3.5mm OR 6.35mm connections.
5. Cable - this twisted cable. It's SHORT, too, so no extra cable dangling on the floor or bundled up on the desk. Perfect for small studio spaces where everything is right at hand.

Predominantly, I will be using these in recording and editing voices for my videos. For that scenario, these are fantastic. Lots of detail. MOANO just does a great job with budget studio equipment.

I've also used these to listen to some music - ran them through my usual series of headphone testing songs. Everything sounded fantastic. I connected these to my phone with Hi-Fi DAC, to my laptop with Hi-Fi DAC, to my Hi-Res MP3 player/DAC, and to my home stereo system. The sound remains just about the same no matter how I'm connected or what I'm connected to. The LG V60 is powerful enough to run these! Seriously, nothing sounded off or weird. All genre of music sounded exactly the way the artists intended.

These studio monitors are really an exceptional buy. My only complaint is that the cups don't rotate like on the M40X. Not that big of a deal, though. I really like these.

I finally gave the UCA202 a try and was blown away at how easy-to-use and low-latency it is! I use my Apple devices as little portable recording studios - nothing professional, just looping, sketching, and small compositions for fun. I'm a guitar player, so I have an Apogee JAM interface for instrument cable, and it works great. But the UCA202 expands those possibilities even further. It allow me to capture pretty much any line level or headphone output audio signal into the iPad using AudioBus.

My experience with Behringer products and guitars has been, well, mixed. They're very affordable and decently built, but I've had a few other products that either sounded poor or were a nightmare to set up on PC. The UCA202 couldn't have been easier. I was able capture a great guitar signal using a Vox Amplug headphone amp (plugs directly into the guitar) and an inexpensive 3.5mm to RCA cable. This is fed into the UCA202 input, which leads to the Camera Connection Kit (basically a USB jack add-on for iDevices), and directly into my iPad or iPhone. Sounds complicated, but it's actually a very simply hookup, and requires no plug-in power source!

Even better, I was stunned to find that the there was very little latency with the guitar playing and monitoring using headphones plugged into the iPhone! Despite the fact that UCA202 has to convert the raw audio signal into digital and then send it into the iDevice, it did so very efficiently and with no extraneous noise. You could similarly capture full size amplifiers with a line level output, MP3 players, or synthesizers/drum machines. Behringer has very useful $30 tool here that makes capturing raw audio very easy, and further turns my mobile device into a portable studio. Highly recommended!
Summary: Great as iPad/iPhone interface using Camera Connection Kit!

Look, MIDI keyboards are controllers. They do not make sound on their own. You should never expect them to. Portability in this keyboard is a GREAT feature, you want it to be easy to handle and work with both in one spot and when used on, say, a tour, you know? Portability makes great sense whether this makes sound on its own or not. Quit buying stuff before you do enough research to know whether the $400 you're about to spend is going to actually do the thing you are wanting to spend money to do in the first place.

What this is, is a fully class-compliant (that is, universally functional) MIDI controller keyboard that also includes faders, knobs, drum pads (with multiple banks for up to 64 sounds quickly accessible), and transport controls so you can control your DAW software from the keyboard to an extent. It also has a great onboard arpeggiator.

You use this to control things that can receive MIDI, like synths, or plugins inside your computer. If you have none of that, then this is just going to be a pointless piano-looking thing with all kinds of stuff all over it. It isn't like a Casio keyboard with on-board sounds that it can play, it's just a really nice controller. Of course it has a software bundle that includes some things that WILL make sounds for you, when you hook it up your computer, but if you're looking at a ~$400 keyboard controller surely you have preferred sound software already or at least an idea how you'll use it.

I have tried a number of these in the $250-$400 price range and I am fully convinced this is the best one. Shout out to Novation for second place with the highly affordable Launchkey 49 Mk3, but it does not have aftertouch on the keybed and of course you get what you pay for when it comes to fit and finish to an extent - Novation Launchkey Mk3 keys are not nearly as nice as the Akai MPK249 keys, and it's not close Akai is way out ahead there. Still, I really liked that one (got the 37-key version to use along with my Akai MPK249 in fact) so if you're trying to spend around half as much and don't care if it has keybed aftertouch, maybe look into it.

But if you want to get the best, most mature, functional & proven unit in the price range, you can't go wrong with the Akai MPK249. I feel it is the standard-setter at this time, giving you what you should expect for the price in a modern controller, with no disappointments.
Summary: Some bad reviews seem to be ignorant of what a MIDI keyboard does. This is a great one!

I was pleasantly surprised to unbox this beast. I expected it to be made of plastic and it's not. It's very solid metal construction, and consequently a bit heavier than expected. Finding a road case for this is difficult but not impossible. There are oversized cases on Amazon at <$150 at this writing.

I bought this unit so I could record band performances on the road without having to be distracted by a PC. I've tried that and wound up with wounded (damaged) PCs, or failed recordings. This unit can't do 96x24bit, which would be nice for the intended use. Since it's made of metal, it's heavier for the road than I would like. That, and the fact that modern version of this unit no longer support MIDI or include a DVD for burning rounds out the list of my complaints. Otherwise, if you're familiar with multi-track workflow, don't require user interface bling, this unit is a fantastic value. You can always export tracks into a DAW if you want or need to. But you don't need to take a PC on the road or on-stage to capture your performances on 8 tracks, and you can come up with mixes the same night in a hotel room, or whatever your situation may be.

Tascam's DP-008 EX (and related models DP-006, DP-03SD and so on) uses software that follows the same workflow (although project files are not interchangeable!). If you're familiar with using these beasts, this unit will seem familiar. I have both.

It's pretty good. It is not without its issues. Here go the pros and cons.

Pros:

If you have an archtop guitar, this works well. Most other models require a round sound hole. Archtops have F-holes. This one doesn't go in any hole.

It works, as long as you keep it full, and it's easy to tell when it needs more water.

Cons:

It needs very frequent refilling. Like every few days--more than once a week in my apartment during winter. Not a problem if you only have one guitar. I have four, in separate cases. At any given time I'm only really playing one of them regularly, and it is a bit of a chore to drag all the other cases out and open them up just to refill.

It has these little clear plastic-looking beads inside. They are made of some sort of chemical. They become gooey when soaked. They apparently are required in order to regulate the rate at which water evaporates through the blue cloth lining of the humidifier. The product comes with a label saying the state of California finds these things to be known to cause cancer. I don't like that. At all.

The clip that holds this thing in your case is pretty neat, it loops over the lip of your case and it is magnetic. There is a metal bar in the lining of the humidifier, so it sticks to the clip. But if your guitar case seals shut in a way that precludes the clip looping over the edge, then you'll have to use the adhesive option. There is a metal plate with a peel-off sticky side which you attach in the case. But adhesive tape on a furry lining isn't 100% solid. I have had this adhesive fail twice, resulting in a humidifier rolling around in the case, making contact with the guitar. Mine didn't leak, but potentially it could and that would be disaster.
Summary: Not perfect but the best I've found

I'm not a professional drummer, or even a very good amateur one. But I do have an engineering background, and this set is designed well. Could it be better? Absolutely! But for the price, I doubt it. When I see all the complaints about assembly and weakness, I noticed while I was putting it together that you have to be careful to adjust things properly to get good performance. Don't just tighten things down in any old order, or make them so tight they break! Treat each clamp on the frame like a drum-head, and tighten things in sequence, a little at a time. The kit will work a lot better (and stand up to hard hits) that way.

The instructions for assembly are OK - they could be more detailed. Someone that has never assembled a drum set before would probably have a bit of a hard time, and someone that is not familiar with midi and electronic drums will be doing a little head-scratching. I notice that the instruction to attach the cymbals to their mounts was left out completely, which is a little awkward, because they have an extra component or two that need to be put in place - they are not quite as simple as the drum pads. You might view Tommy Igoe's "Getting Started DRUMS" to help you out - it's about setting up an acoustic kit, but a lot of the same principles apply. By the way, Tommy Igoe's DVDs are fantastic!

It sounds great. Period. When you listen through headphones connected directly to the DM10 module, it's perfect. When you hook the module output to a stereo or a mixer, you have to be careful not to turn up the output too much, or you get muddy sound. I thought my stereo speakers were bad when I first hooked it up to my stereo, but it turns out the output signal was over-driving it. When I turned down the output from the module, it sounded great on my stereo too!

I bought the kit primarily to play along with Rock Band. It works directly with a Mad Katz MIDI interface, and I only had to change one of the cymbal MIDI output settings on the module to make it play nice with RB3. There was no noticeable audio lag. It can get a bit confusing, though - be sure to understand that you can program a MIDI signal output from the module that is NOT the same as the sound the module supplies to headphones or its audio outputs. In other words, the module is extremely flexible. So I might want my tom to sound like a cowbell in my headphones, and I can program it to send a bass drum MIDI signal to the MIDI output jack at the same time.

I bought Amazon's inexpensive Coda DH-208 kick pedal to go with the kit. The pedal works perfectly with the Alesis kick pad.

Yes, the pads are not nearly as quiet as mesh pads. Especially the kick pad. But with the door closed on the room where I play, nobody really complains in the rest of the house. It's quiet enough to be family-friendly, and if you want to do so, you can always add mesh pads for less than $100.

In short, I am extremely pleased with this purchase.

I've played a couple dozen or more tin whistles over the years, of many different varieties. This Clarke style, which is a metal tube with a seam along the back, which tapers slightly (the end near the mouthpiece is slightly larger), is one that I don't particularly prefer, but it's certainly common. I would tend to recommend the cylindrical, seamless, Walton's style over this tapered style... but, to each their own.

For the beginner, this is a nice set, with a decent book of instructions and tunes to play, a storage back and a cleaning brush.

The tone is very nice, with a breathy quality that lessens the harshness the higher register can give on these whistles. It's not a pure tone, and that's a good thing.

I've played through both registers one note at a time against a tuner, and also played tunes and stopped at certain notes to check the tuning, and I can say that it is irregular at best. When played solo, you probably won't notice a thing. Playing along with other instruments, though, and the intonation issues jump out at you. Usually the notes are sharp, with a couple of exceptions (low F#, for instance), and in the lower register adjusting your breath intensity can correct this, but in the upper register you're kind of stuck with it. I'm over analyzing this a little, because the beginner isn't going to care much about any of that.

I can also mention that you could buy a dozen of the same penny whistle and notice slight variations in both tone and pitch... although there is deep science behind the shape of the tube, and the positioning and size of the finger holes, there is some natural variation from instrument to instrument, which is actually kind of fun.

4.25 stars, with a slight ratings ding due to tuning and my less-preferred whistle style (tapered/seamed). Worth picking up. If you're not a beginning, spend half the $ and get the whistle by itself.

Text:
...and takes away some of the mystery about making music.

As the result of years of saying something like "I sure like the way a banjo sounds and sure wish I could play one..." whenever we would hear some evocative bluegrass or American roots music, my daughter surprised me with a banjo last year.

And when I went for my very first lesson --after a lifetime without instruction in practical music or music theory of any kind-- the first thing my teacher did was grab my banjo and place it tune.

For the stringed instrument novice, tuning your string instrument is, of course, a fundamental step in everything that follows. On a 5-string banjo (an instrument notorious for not wanting to ever stay in tune), this begins with tuning the "D" fourth string, either by ear or to a piano. If you have neither of the ear, the piano or the experience for this, then an electronic tuner is a must-have item.

Clip this to the top center of your peghead, pick a string, and you'll get an intuitive visual display of where you are actually tuned (both via an index line that shows you how far above or below the desired note you are, and an text readout of the note you have played).

When taking on a new musical instrument, there's plenty to occupy your hands, eyes, ears and brain. Free some of that up with this easy to use tuner. Easy to operate, it is also easy to read even in direct sunlight, or --thanks to its backlight-- dim rooms.
Summary: Must have for the musical novice; it just works...

These are the Elixirs to get-- the PolyWeb ones.

I normally play flatwound strings for their superior sound and feel, but recently bought a Carvin guitar that doesn't have ideal hardware for my favorite flatwounds to work well. After finally getting the guitar I'd shelled-out almost 2k and waited 12 weeks for, I was disappointed by the sound of the instrument when unplugged, clean, distorted, etc. -- Nothing seemed to make it sound like it was worth the money I had just spent.

I was about ready to send it back to Carvin (as they'll let you try it for a period and send it back for a full refund if not satisfied) but I had a deep suspicion that the instrument would sound fantastic if I found the right strings, and since that instrument came equipped with Elixir nanoweb strings and I was completely unhappy with their brittle sound and harsh feel, I did some research and pondered my options.

Though initially dead-set against Elixirs from my introduction to them, I checked out their website and found that Elixir made this polyweb variety and it was supposed to be a bit smoother and less brittle sounding (a bit closer to what I prefer in a guitar string set). I decided to try them and the improvement in sound and playability was dramatic. Much less of that irritating string squeak, no more jangly brittle-sounding open strings, fewer harsh overtones; much more balanced and musical overall.

These still sound like roundwound strings, but they sound like *good* roundwound strings with pleasant, consonant overtones and a great balance in quality between the sound of fretted and open notes.

Sound? Clean, they sound great-- bright enough for most who need crystalline treble, but easily tamable just by rolling back the guitar's tone pot a bit. Overdriven and distorted, again, they sound like top-quality roundwound strings with a pleasant 'burn' or 'grind' of the notes in most chords during that crucial initial decay after the strings have been struck. For distorted single note work they have a pleasant ability to sing without as much of the 'garbage' (as I often think of it) during that decay immediately following the string snapping past the edge of the pick, which is likely due to their (seemingly) more balanced harmonic content.

Personally, I would like them to feel a bit smoother, sound less bright, but I am a huge proponent of flatwound strings and as such my tastes are likely different than most. For me, these are a good compromise when owning an instrument that cannot accommodate my preferred type of string.

Magnetic output? Loads of it. They're steel strings through and through-- just coated in a super-thin layer of tough stuff.

Hold their pitch? Yes. Even with repeated 'dumps' of the whammy bar to complete slack all the way to major third pull-ups. No problem with holding pitch at all.

The coating? Yes, it's there for a reason and it does its job well.

These are the longest-lived steel strings out there not just in terms of tone but also the feel of them. They feel the same; your fingers glide along them the same even months from when you first installed them. That kind of consistency if nearly impossible with non coated strings in my opinion since the crud and oxides build up on the surface of the uncoated nickel and steel ones even if you don't play often. String cleaners *never* completely restore the original sound or feel to those strings-- the polyweb coating solves this issue for certain.

I have noticed in the region most often struck by the pick during strumming that the coating on some of the larger strings has become fuzzy-- as if compromised-- but there has been no noticeable change in sound or trueness-to-pitch so I'm inclined to think it's just a cosmetic issue and nothing to discourage me from continuing to play the set until something breaks.
Summary: Much much better than Elixir NanoWeb-- these are the ones to buy

Text:
This is a straight up metal headphone practice amp. Tested with my EVH Stripe Series.

There is no clean mode, only chug.

Seems to be based (aesthetically at least) on a Mesa Boogie dual Rectifier amp.

With the gain all the way down, it sounds weird and uncomfortable with itself: not crunchy, not clean, kinda stuttery and broken sounding. Slowly rolling up the gain causes a sudden and awesome rush of distortion and a noticeable volume hike, with the gain just saturating more and more from there.

Rolling back your guitar volume knob cleans things up slightly but only barely, from high gain down to medium high gain.

The tone control takes you from “slightly muffled” to “piercingly bright”.

The FX switch adds in a fixed amount of delay / verb, which is nice for soloing.

The Aux input works well for connecting an external media player and jamming along. I tested with an iPhone and a Lightning to 3.5mm adapter, worked great.

But this is a one-trick pony. If you play different styles, or even just want to mellow out and play Clean once in a while, this isn’t the model for you. If you just want to plug in and rip, you’ll love it.

Build quality is nice, fits fine in a Strat style body (see pic) and won’t have issues plugging into pretty much anything else (might be harder to see?).

Overall audio / sound quality has a noticeably high noise floor from all the gain. Fine for practice and messing around but you likely won’t want to record with it.

For me, it’s a little too limiting due to the complete focus on a single high gain tone that can’t be tamed from the guitar volume.

So 4 stars because there’s no versatility here at all.

Text: I learned to hold my guitar by crossing my right leg over the left.  The guitar would be well supported and in the correct position, but after a while (plus an older body), this position becomes cramped.  With my legs uncrossed, my guitar would be too low and would feel like it would slide off my lap.  I also would slouch to reach the lower positioned neck; bad posture plus not a good position for more advanced fingering.  I've experimented with lower chairs, elevating my right foot on something, neck/shoulder strap, various pillows.  I saw a guitar support for the first time recently, did some research and decided to try a guitar cushion (rather than a suction cup support).  I'm still experimenting with positioning the cushion for the best positioning of my guitar and so far it's been comfortable to use and the guitar is stable on the cushion.  I use it on my right thigh curving around to between my legs, sometimes resting on the seat between my legs.  I'll probably have to adjust the position for different chair heights and, no, I never wear skirts, so between the legs is not a problem.  One star off for being something I'll have to carry around with my guitar, but it comes with a bag I can clip to the case.
Summary: Such a simple yet effective solution.

Update: I was about to return my Gator case, sadly because except for size it was exactly what I wanted. I thought maybe I could crush the foam at each end of the case enough to make it fit my guitar. Put the guitar in the case to see how much to squish and the guitar fell right into place. What happened? I put the headstock in first this time. The foam is hollowed out more at that end near the the bottom of the case (at least I think that's what's going on). If I put the bottom neck strap pin in first, in the space hollowed out for it, the headstock does not fit at the other end. Needs another inch or so before it will go in. If I put the headstock end in first, everything lines up better and I have a VERY snug fit. So I'm increasing my stars from 2 to 5 (I'm reviewing the case, NOT the packaging). No longer returning, happy again. Gator also responded to my comment, very important to see that they care. So, your mileage may vary, but this case works for me.

Original review:

Description says it holds a guitar up to 39.5" long, with body length up to 19". My guitar is that size (I measured before buying). Body length dimension is about 1/2" too short and overall length is an inch too short. My guitar doesn't fit even though it matches the the size listed. Guitar is a Schecter Omen 6 extreme. Very disappointed the description is so misleading (or they can't control their sizes, or someone decided to cut costs). Now I need to go through the hassle of returning it and picking out a different case. One reason I chose this case was because dimensions were given in the description. I won't trust Gator again (same dimensions are listed on other sites, so it's not an Amazon fault).

Case seemed to be made well and was just what I wanted: lightweight and sturdy with some storage space inside for pedals, tuner, slides, picks, recorder, etc., and a pocket outside for music books and note sheets. Looks great also. If you have a smaller guitar this might be a perfect choice.

Packaging was bad. It was shipped in a very large box and the tape was not holding the flaps shut by the time it arrived. Case could have easily fallen out of box and it was so loose that case was scuffed up from rubbing against the cardboard box. Why they bothered to put a single piece of crumpled paper in the box I'll never know; maybe there was more that fell out.
Summary: Very nice but not the size listed in the description (but size is deceptive)

I installed this into my Yamaha DGX-650B, and it snapped into place with barely any trouble. The frame is sturdy, and the design matches the strong and tight fitting piano stand. There were notches where it slips into the frame, and two holes on each side. I was able to unpack and install it in about 10 minutes. You would never have known it wasn't included with the piano already.

The peddles also are set into a sliding screw-hole that allows them to be adjusted up or down depending on the height of the floor beneath the piano stand. This is useful if you're placing the piano in a room with a thick carpet, or a flat floor.

The springs are most definitely strong and they have a consistently firm resistance throughout their range of motion. Firmly in place, they actually seem to add support to the overall design of the stand itself.

The price may seem steep for what amounts to 3 pedals that you barely even notice, but if you're hoping to make your Yamaha piano even more realistic and match the function of a real one, this is a fantastic addition to an already wonderful instrument.

The first, as has been mentioned, is the odor. It's not that it is terrible, it just isn't plesant and it is very strong. I would highly recommend using it outside if possible. Mostly because it is hard to breath when using it indoors. The odor doesn't linger though so if you must use it inside a particulate filiter may help.

The second is it didn't get my cymbals as nice looking as I expected it to. It definitely made them better but nothing like new. Again, they are much cleaner than before but because they are still not new looking I actually think I'd have been better off leaving them.

The third, and part of the reason it may be better to just leave them, is it started to remove the printing on the cymbals. It didn't completely remove the printing but it made it very light. Another cleaning with this stuff and it would likely be gone.

I'd say this stuff would be more useful in a couple of situations. First is if you used it occasionally on new cymbals to keep them looking new. Mine were older and quite dingy and stained. As I said they did get brighter but no where near new. If you used it on newer cymbals every so often it would likely keep them looking like new. The second thing is that you would have to be willing to lose any lettering printed on the cymbals. I know some people have no issue at all with this as most cymbals are stamped anyway. The Dispatch Master can produce some lovely effects and it's totally intuitive to use, but to my ear it's not quite as good as it could be.

The good stuff: The pedal is painless to use. Adjust one or two knobs and get back to playing. A brilliant "feature" is that the Despatch Master will not self-oscillate. This is the tendency of delay pedals to pile on infinite layers of repeats until excruciatingly loud (and utterly non-musical) noise is produced. This is a real flaw in pedals like the Belle Epoch and Carbon Copy, and can get you thrown out of your apartment if you're not careful.

The Dispatch Master's reverb is very nice. You don't get a dozen different types and all sorts of adjustible parameters, so hats off to EQD for making such great choices!

There are things that could be better. To my ear, the Dispatch Master makes things just a little tinny or pingy. It's not huge, but it reminded me of my Boss DD-2, the original digital delay pedal. When I compared to the DD-2, the Dispatch Master was even a little brighter. With single coil pickups, I thought it was a little harsh, but it might be perfect with a guitar that's dark sounding.

The other thing is the lack of adjustable modulation (pitch). I have a bunch of delays, and after reverb, the two things that make a delay sound really huge are modulation and stereo. I agree that on a simple pedal, stereo would add cost and not be taken advantage of by many players. But the ability to add a small amount of modulation would be fantastic. Not the awful "seasick" thing that just sounds out of tune, but a little pitch warble. Even a fairly inexpensive delay like the Carbon Copy has this feature.

Of course all the above is just my opinon and as you can see from the other reviews, people love this pedal. EQD seems like a really cool company, too.
Summary: What it does, it does well

One of the frustrations that I've felt--and that I've heard other guitarists express--about some of the other headstock tuners on the market is that they are a challenge to adjust so that you can actually see them.  That's not a problem with the Planet Waves tuner, which the user can swivel around and back and forth with ease.  It's also easy to turn on and off, which, again, is not necessarily the case with some of the smaller competing tuners.  But what some of those other tuners have is that they are small; this one's pretty big for a headstock tuner, and the vibrant color of the case means that there's no disguising it on your guitar.  Because of the size and depending on how you guitar case is designed, you might not be able to keep it attached when the guitar's in the case.  Tuning can be pretty accurate with this tuner; however, as is the case with all of the tuners out there that do not show you exactly how many cents sharp or flat you are, it is not as precise as the box tuners from companies such as Korg.  Overall, a perfectly usable, reasonably accurate tuner, with a few quibbles.

That said, setting it with the volume all the way up, and the drive all the way down, and roll off a bit of the tone knob to 11:00, and using the switch on LF - into the front end of my Mesa Boogie Roadster on Ch3/Modern = pure GOLD. That's the sound I've been looking for out of this amp!

So far I've only used it on a few of my amps, and, so far, I've not found it to be unusable or even as a one-trick pony. I'm impressed, and that says a lot for someone who just a few years ago, hated the idea of putting anything between his guitar and his amp...if the amp couldn't do it 'naturally' when it comes to dirty tone...then it's the wrong amp...I still think that way, but a good pedal up front can add a nice twist...and goose that front end a bit where shifting channels might not be what the Dr. ordered...

I am not a guitar person so I have no idea if this is a great unit or not, but I can give some insights. For one, it definitely feels well made and sturdy. If someone had me name a price, I would say this was worth at least $200. As far as sound goes, we had some issues with a high action as some noted. It was hard for my wife to play, probably because she is a newbie but it was very harsh compared to her mother's guitar that she originally used. I watched some youtube videos on how to lower the action by sanding the saddle. I used a marker to note each side of the saddle and preceded to sand it down a few fractions of an inch and installed extra light string. That made it much easier or my wife to play. I think we got it a bit too low because I noticed some buzzing on certain chords, so we loosened the truss rod (to create a more upward bow) and those noises have since disappeared. There is still some buzzing coming from what I think is the string pins but I am going to do the right thing and take it to it professional. Regardless, I learned a lot and hopefully it will come in handy some day.

What a terrible choice Alesis made in this regard.

Also of note: The music stand is flimsy, and there are no holders for the microphone or headphones.

The stool and piano stand are of good quality, however, and there's a decent number of sound varieties one can use. I tend to stick with the standard organ sound or one of the synth strings.

There are a number of features for play-along demos or recording what you've done. The other aspect everyone should note is that the keys are weighted but slim. Oddly, the weighted keys are supposed to mimic a real piano, but what real piano has smaller keys? In other words, if you want to get more of a piano experience, this might not cut it. It's probably best for not just beginners but for young beginners who may struggle with reaching keys to make chords. So, I'd recommend this for children who want to learn piano on a sturdy little electric piano with which they can use headphones and not disturb the whole house.

The workmanship on this instrument is very good. I could find no finishing flaws or assembly mistakes. The frets are clean, the nut is cut properly, and everything looks very good.

The one issue, which does not effect appearance or playability, is the fact that, when properly adjusted, there is a 10 mm gap from the P 90 pole screws to the strings. This is at least 7 mm too much space. The dogear P 90 cannot be adjusted for height, so I will have to shim up this pickup in order to get some real volume out of this guitar. The neck angle is pretty severe, which means the bridge [ which needed to be moved rearward ] is set pretty high, and so there is simply too much space between the pickup and the strings for any kind of volume.

Aside from that, I found no other real issues with the guitar. It is a very attractive guitar, and has a small block under the bridge area to lessen the feedback that hollow body guitars are prone to have. So It's still a good bargain.

Text:
I am a solo musician playing folky guitar and vocal music at live gigs. I needed a PA kit that would be convenient to transport, carry, set up and take down. I also needed it to be capable of handling small to medium sized venues. The STAGEPAS was just the ticket. It is an awesome package and worth every penny of the price I paid.

Everything you need to set up the system is included, i.e., speaker and power cables. Of course, you will need to provide your own mic and instrument cables. I bought speaker stands and was glad I did, as well as the Yamaha accessory that lets you mount the mixer on a mic stand. The accessory is very handy, because it means you don't have to depend on a table being available, so it makes you totally self-dependent.

As far as the sound, I could not fault it. If you are a solo (or duo) act, the mixer has everything you need. Good equalization on each channel, great reverb, feedback control, and iPhone/iPod support for music or backing playback. The speakers sound terrific, both for my guitar and voice, as well as for fill-in recorded music between sets, which sounded like a professional DJ setup! There is a separate monitor output, both left and right (use left only for mono).

I really cannot fault this system, and have no hesitation giving it five stars. Just one caveat: if you have more than a duo, or need to play to a bigger-than-medium venue, get the 600i, not the 400i.

I absolutely love this system, and highly recommend it for a live solo or duo acoustic act playing to small-to-medium venues.
Summary: Perfect system for solo or duo acoustic musical acts

Text:
I've now owned this pedal for about 2 weeks, but I've messed around with it significantly in that time period, with a couple different amps and several guitars. I bought it sort of on a whim to try and beef up my guitar tones in the studio for a new record we're cutting right now, but as soon as this pedal hit my board, it was there to stay. The Big Muff is the only real "fuzz" pedal I've owned (I mostly prefer tube screamer/OD type tone), although I did use a ProCo Dirty Rat for a while, with disappointing results. The DR was supposed to be a fuzzy, creamy, sustain-y version of the RAT, but it's lack of versatility sort of turned me off to the fuzzy type of distortion until I found the Big Muff, which has all that in spades. Now, I'm a convert. So here's what I've found in terms of Pros and Cons.

Pros:
1. The thing I like most about the Big Muff is the massive, massive bottom end. It can make one guitar sound like 3 (which is likely why it was such a favorite of Corgan's). Strat, tele, and assorted HB pickups all sound great, although my favorite so far is my Tele with a Duncan Designed Jazz HB in the neck. Holy cow. Huge, creamy sustain for days with power chords and screaming notes for weeks with lead runs. Basically, like others have said, listen to Siamese Dream and, well, there you have it.

2. Tone Versatility is amazing with this pedal. Low, growling mayhem, mid-saturated cream or buzzing scooped scream, you can do it all. Anyone who claims otherwise hasn't spent enough time playing with settings not only on the pedal itself, but on the amp and the guitar. All these have to work together to get the wide range of tone available from the big muff. The guitar volume knob is your best friend and can really tame this beast when you need to get a little more note separation with a big low roar still present. My favorite setting is the tone knob at about 1:30- leads cut through but power chords still have a bludgeoning low end.

3. Volume. I love volume. I hate when a pedal sounds good but just can't jump much above unity with the amp, but like the tone knob, the volume knob is versatile in the sense that it can really boost above the amp level. It helps that this pedal is pretty unique sounding, but when you hit that switch, the audience knows the Big Muff just kicked in. It's just huge in every way.

4. Electroharmonix is a cool company. I mean, even aside from the fact that they've been around for forever, and that Hendrix, Gilmore, Mascis, Corgan, Mark Arm, etc. played through the Muff, they're an American company and they make their products here(except for that whole move to Russia for a bit in the 80's...). I also like that the EHX East River Drive (an 808 clone released last Fall) put just in front of the Muff adds a whole new dimension of tone. Try it- it's crazy for lead work and it really smooths out the rough edges of the Muff on long bends and such.

5. Price. For 80 bucks, this is a heck of a lot of pedal.

Cons:
1. It's huge. Now, personally, I kind of like that it's so big because, BIG Muff. But it does take up a lot of real estate on the pedal board, and for some people that could be an issue.
2. 1/8 inch Power Jack. This is kind of annoying, since most pedals use the Boss-style 9v power supply. The 1/8" jack adapter is available for the Visual Sound One Spot, which I use, so it's not really a huge deal for me, but be aware that you're going to have to get an adapter (5 bucks or so) or use batteries, which I hate doing.

And that's about it, really. I think if you're into massive tone and you like the feeling of joining a tradition of musicians who have sculpted their sound around this really versatile pedal, the Big Muff is for you.

I bought the Tascam DP-004 to record the room when my band plays live. I didn't think that was asking a whole lot. I quickly learned how crabby this unit it. First, I use it with an AC adapter, and I noticed if you unplug the unit while it's recording it loses the entire recording! Hours of audio are gone in a snap. I learned my lesson. Now after each recording I carefully press the stop button and power the unit off. That was only the beginning of my troubles.

Next I popped the SD card out and put it in my computer, but noticed the card showed like it was empty. Turns out Tascam stores all audio in a proprietary format, and to get it onto your computer you have to export the track as a WAV file. The export process takes about as long to do as the recording is long, so a 2 hour recording takes about 2 hours to export. Extracting is a long, tedious, one-at-a-time process. It would be much easier if my computer could have direct access to all audio. As inconvenient as it was, it was just something else I had to get used to for this recorder to work for me.

Because exporting was slow, I had some shows recorded that I hadn't gotten around to exporting yet. I plugged it in and began that process. When I came back a couple hours later to see if it was done I noticed the Tascam was off, which was odd. I live alone in my apartment with no pets, so I know it hadn't been touched. When I turned it back on I got "MOUNT ERROR: 0c Please PWR OFF". WHAT?!!! No matter what I did I could not get the error message to go away. If I pop the SD card into my computer, it told me the card was unreadable. Apparently, while exporting a track as a WAV file the unit crashed and wrecked ALL of the data on the SD card. Unbelievable! A Google search quickly concluded I was not alone, and the only thing that could be done was format the SD card, which erases everything.

Ugh!!! This thing is more trouble than it's worth. Do NOT buy this product!

UPDATE:
I've since bought a XOOM digital recorder and have been much happier. You can configure the format you want to record (WAV, MP3, etc.), which is immediately accessible with no dumping! And the audio quality is FAR superior. The sound is clear, full, and in stereo. The Tascam sounds muddy in comparison. Glad I upgrade and GOOD RIDDANCE!
Summary: Crashes and Loses Data. XOOM is better.

I have to start by saying I was skeptical of this pedal, but I'm helping a buddy start his rig and this hit the right price point.

The first impression I had of it was the packaging.
1) the pedal is heavier than most mini-enclosure size pedals, and it stands up much more stable than other ones.
2) It's packed very well
3) They included a patch cable and pre-cut velcro for the pedal. So with that my interest got started.

Upon plugging in, I quickly bonded with the chorus options, these do a really good job at getting very usable tones. You may need to crank the mix knob to get the sweet spot.
I also really like the trem options, they each had different voices and I could get a couple of cool tones from each. The rate knob has a lot of range and can get really fast and slow
The flange and phase sound like classic pedals, I don't personally use those effects much, so I quickly skipped over them.
The LoFi mode is nuts, it's going to take some time to get used to it.

A few notes/concerns.
1) This pedal was picking up noise from another pedal I had on a simple daisy chain, powered on its own it was dead quiet. So isolated power is probably the right move, which may be an issue for starter pedalboards. If you're looking for a good power solution, Sonicake has a really affordable one.
2) The LED knobs will not be as abuse resistant as metal ones, so be nice to it
3) I couldn't really find a use for the tap tempo, it's a good feature but since it doesn't do sub-divisions I had a hard time getting the trem to the right rhythm

So, all in all, I would say this is a great pedal for the right people. If you're after an affordable place to start on modulation effects, a bedroom player, or need an effect with a very small spot available on your board, this is a great pedal. If you're a boutique or vintage aficionado, you may not like this and should be looking at the products made for your market.
Summary: Great option for starter boards and small rigs

Minor detail for me because I'm always building something anyway and I have the tools. But if you aren't handy and without the right tools, this may be an issue for you. I can see this mount being used for smaller drums and maybe they should offer a 2nd bracket that would accommodate larger drums and/or wider bolt patterns.

I bought this after I totally ignored it after multiple visits at my local guitar store. However, I tripped over a few reviews on Amazon, which led to several other online reviews and further research, and, I now own this awesome amp. Note: I'm not a solid-state fan, but, the video/reviews/promos on U-tube really got me excited. The THR10 is packed with features. And, said features are packed with technology. Yahmaha thought of nearly every practical/portable thing a home guitar player would want with little sacrifice to tone (in a small package). I'm shocked/amazed..... at the tone, warmth and response this amp has to all peripherals (including your mp3 device, which this unit could sell alone for this use - it sounds remarkable). Anyway, as for the guitar amp, the sound is if you were playing live, but, as if the live sound were a mastered recording. ...Kind of strange to get your head around that concept, but think about it.. All the controls on this amp react diferently to your pick attack/guitar pick-ups and the model of amp you select on THR10. So, my advise is to test this amp VERY, VERY extensively, and you will gain an appreciation for the technology which went into it. Each model breaks up differently, and you can set your bass/mid/treble accordingly to get your tone perfect. Not too muddy, or crisp - just right. Every model is outstanding. Based on my research and thougts here are the models: there is a Fender DRev., VOX AC 30, Marshall JTM 45, Marshall JCM 800, and MESA Dual Rec. Note: they are not called this on the amp, but I surmise this is what they modeled, and they did it so well.. There are quality effects here too: Flanger, Phase, Chorus, Delay, Reverb (Spring and Hall); tap tempo. Oh, you get software too to further modify your favorite tones in 5 presets. I could write on for SEVERAL more paragraphs on how great this amp is. It's loud for it's intended use (playing at home); I get terrific tone at non-ear shattering volume! You will too. All I can say is go to you tube and see the vid done by Soren Anderson (there are a few other terrific vids on this thing). This is a must have, and certainly will scare the crap out most amp makers. PS - anyone giving this a bad review didn't try numerous gain/master/guitar volume/master volume configurations on each model (inluding pick-up differences). I play a strat on the clean channel (high gain/high master) and a PRS on the 5 other models (dual humbuckers). You'll get the most out of this amp by having a guitar with a humbucker and two single coils, or a two separate guitars, one with humbuckers, and one with single coils. Oh, it glows like it has tubes, looks cool, and has terrific software. BUY with confidence - and, play more guitar. If I'm Yamaha, I'm looking to expand on this.

**UPDATE**
- I'm still really loving this little amplifier - I'm not over it, like many of us get with a new piece of gear, or pedal. My wife is a bit happier that she can now watch her shows while I run off to play my guitar. Note: I have found if you put this amp on top of another amp with an open back cab in a corner - you'll get some nice warm reasonance and added tone. I cannot wait for the future of this technology. If you have reasonable expections, this amp will blow your mind - just be sure to test it out VERY thoroughly. Each of the modeled amps have very unique sonic properties; so, you don't have to turn the gain, or EQ all the way up to achieve great tone. I would love a full size version! Ok, a few other notes: usable volume really begins at 12'O clock. You can make the speakers pop if you turn the master/volume/gain all the way up on the high gain models (you don't need to turn the knobs all the way up to get great Marshall-like tone). Oh, you actually get feed-back on the high gain channels if you get close to the amp with your guitar - COOL! I imagine there will be a loyal army of THR10 followers. PS - this thing is a crazy-good phone/mp3-player amp too!

**SECOND UPDATE** - yep, still loving this thing. Love the Marshall-like tones on "Brit-High" setting. Just dial the Master and Gain to about 1 O'clock setting your mids and add some verb/delay. Oh, my! Very nice. Oh, and if you crank it up a bit, and play a while, your ears will ring too. Loud for what it is! Again, you really have to test this guy out to appreciate it. Soaked ‘em good in the tub, squishing them a bunch to force as much air out and to let as much water in as possible. After wringing them out by hand I let them sit in the sun for a couple hours, turning them every once in awhile since the sun was at a pretty low angle. Should have done it at high noon but that thing called a job gets in the way sometimes. Once I lost direct sunlight I took them in and used the hair dryer on them (Note: don’t get a too hot nozzle too close) for a few minutes until they felt fairly dry to the touch. Then I placed them on a bath towel and let them sit overnight. Next morning there was a tiny bit of moisture feel where they had been touching the towel so I stuck them back outside to air out in the sun for a few hours.

Voila! So they may not be perfect, geometric formations they appear to be “full size,” fairly uniform and good to go. Akin it's golf counterpart, the AKG 271MkII is the Big Bertha driver of headphones, more forgiving in its reproduction of a much wider spectrum of recordings (player capabilities), more tolerant with lesser quality recordings (drives) in terms of quality and genre. Like all AKGs, it features patented Varimotion speakers that provides realistic sound with a wide frequency response. Comfortable as the headset is self-adjusting to fit most.

These closed-back headphone have great sound isolation and its auto-cut off is a useful recording feature....preventing sound bleeds during recording or if used in close proximity where privacy is required. Comes with two screw on stereo adaptor jacks - gold-cladded (1/8" & 1/4"), two sets of donuts (one velvet, the other leatherette) and two sets of headphone connectors - one 5m coiled, the other 3m cable which is attached to/detachable from the left earpiece of the headphone - connectors/port are robust. This allows for a cable upgrade/ replaceable to survive more rugged long term studio use.

**UPDATE**: Having used this sparingly in the past year for the clavinova, it had not had the chance to burn in. The past 3 months however, my nephew borrowed it and presumeably he must have left it running for hours, it came back, sat back in the drawer till I took it out last week for a relisten. AND... I was simply amazed at what I heard - I have a dramatically different pair of headphones. Without comparing to my higher end cans, I can say this could become my default listening pair. At the unboxing, the K271MKII was dull and unremarkable, I had instantly regretted my purchase. However, the headphones have really "opened up", I can literally hear the 3D soundstage, layer and different instruments that I couldn't before coming together beautifully. The bass resonance unlike the K702 is beautiful, natural and has depth. I had originally been a little disappointed though it served the purpose of a closed pair but NOW, I'd be listening to it a whole lot more. Sounds brilliant with most repertoire: classical (be it orchestral, ensemble, chorale to opera), Buble, Black Eyed Peas, Hromek's Celtic Guitar, Sting, Amici. Quite the all rounder close behind Sennheiser HD598 if not at par already. RECOMMEND FOR THE PRICE. STEEPLY DISCOUNTED. ONE DOESN'T NEED TO CHASE THE LATEST MODEL, THESE SUPERCEDED ONES ARE A REAL DEAL.

Sound performance ... still trails the K702 but still a great pair of hps - losing out a little in the spatial soundstage and sound separation category. But has fuller thumping bass unamped. It delivers for some...good design & utility. Some have said it's really AKG's legendary 240s in closed form. And some have mentioned preferring the semi openness of the 240s. Where one requires a closed back set, this is it. Or if you listen to a lot of legacy or other recordings of lesser or varied quality and want an all rounder pair from AKG without paying much more on headphone amps, DACs or the like.

First look, great AKG packaging from the outside. The item itself is lighter than expected but that just means it's more comfortable to wear. Touch, look and feel ... well I bought these hps steeply discounted, so can't really complain... ... the (attempt at a)"3D" logo & L/R marker buttons have an aberrated iffy look (fr an angle) which has an overall cheapening visual effect and the edge of the leatherette headband feels just a tad rigid and sharp to the touch unlike the softness of leather. I have no doubt however that this is based on AKG specification and endorsed, I might add. The dbl wire-frames allow the hps to be hung-up. A great quality look overall if you don't look too hard.

Put it this way, AKG clearly decided chinese manufacturing has come to its own, or decided for the volume churn making the chinese line accesible to the masses at half to a third the cost of its austrian counterparts... I believe that with a co like AKG everything is made to specification - on purpose. hm. If AKG edicted, I believe the made in china lines can also be made to look, feel and sound the same as its made in austria family members. Remember... it's all about perception and marketing. There are those who buy the brand there are those who buy the utility - and a lot of us in between. This provides a choice across the market spectrum.

This is accessible utility riding on a reputable "snob" tag. Perhaps that is also why the MKII studio lines are made in china whilst manufacturing of the higher end lines "K700"s (where more perceived uberness is required) are retained in Austria and built to that set of spec. All up a great pair for the studio at amazon special prices. Just wished AKG would do something about the logo/badges which could have a better finish.

Personal headphone ranking: 1) AKG K702; 2) Sennheisser HD598; 3) AKG K271MKII
Summary: Good on a wider spectrum of recording quality & genres than K702 - richer bass unamped - amazing after burn-in!

Text:
Had to bring in a smaller bass amp for my bedroom, and switch out from my Ampeg BA112 (50 watt version), so
I compared them even though this is kind of like comparing apples and oranges, but it was there, so what the hey.
I was actually looking around for a smaller cab 1x12 to replace the larger BA112, but there is no such thing The orange, and Kustom
are a bit smaller than the BA112, but not enough. This is due to a bass amp (more than guitar amp) needing a larger cab for lower frequency resonance created by the speaker, so in most cases, you have to match the speaker size with the cab: Small Speaker=Small Cab,
Large Speaker=large Cab.
The Rumble 15 (I also have a Rumble 100, 1x15 Combo) sounds much better than I had anticipated, considering my other two bass amps are a 1x12, and a 1x15. The BA112 is much louder, and can handle the E without breakup which the 15 cannot. With this one exception aside, the 15 has excellent sound (at about half the volume), and you will have to adjust from the larger amps by turning up the guitar, and amp volume more
than you are used to.
For the price, and small footprint, this is a great choice for the bedroom (apartment, Etc.) where room, and volume is limited.
For those that (unrealistically) expect a big sound out of this 8 inch speaker amp; GET REAL!

As the reviews herein have indicated, there is a wide variety of uses for studio monitor like the M-Audio BX5. With the proper cables, you can hook up everything from an iPad, to a home computer, to a musical instrument or stereo. I will preface this review by saying that I am no "audiophile". I have a basic understanding of speaker and musical equipment, but my primary goal here was to find a small speaker that I could use to monitor guitar playing through either a preamp pedal or iPad modeling software.

With those goals in mind, I was pleasantly surprised how good the BX5 sounded. The goal of any "studio monitor" is to convey as much of the true sound of the source material as possible without coloring the tone with additional equalization. There are some monitors in a comparable price range like the Rokkit 5 and options from Mackie and JBL - I have not tried those out. But the BX5 performs we well or better than I hoped.

For guitar playing, I use it in close proximity on a desktop. I found that it had a surprising amount of low end punch for a 5" woofer, given that my Fender tube amp has a speaker twice the size! The bass is tight and articulate, which is what you want. Again, if your goal is just to drown out the sound with additional base, go get a pair of Beats headphones or hook up a dozen subwoofers to it. That wasn't really my goal. But all that aside, having enough low end was important to me, and the BX5 delivers. Using modeling of "Fender" and "Vox" type amplifiers, it also handled the high end "chime" well without sounding "tinny".

I should note that I got an XLR (microphone) cable that converts to TRS on the other side. I had heard/read that this was the best way to get a guitar signal into the thing, though there are likely adapters and other cables you could use to accomplish the same thing. There are both XLR and TRS inputs on the back. The monitor is powered, so there's a power cable, as well. There is a volume knob, but no independent bass/treble adjustment, as on other monitors. So if you want that, look elsewhere, but if the monitor is actually relaying most of source tone, you shouldn't be using it anyway. Really enjoying my BX5 so far, wish I had the budget/space for a 2nd one!

For the record, my tuner is the first pedal in the chain, and right after this is an overdrive.

One of the reasons why I opted for this over some EQ pedals that are finer grained when it comes to frequency bands is I wanted simplicity. This one is divided up into bands that are well matched to a guitar and does not get into the bands that are not as useful,such as in the sub 100Hz or 8K and above. For me personally, less sliders means less complication. Here are the bands this pedal does cover and why they are important:
100Hz Punch and lower mid warmth
250Hz Sweet spot for mid range
630Hz Body and tone
1.6KHz Edge and bite
4KHz Clarity

There is potential, though, for over or under EQing since the plus or minus 18dB is a bit too wide. A range of +/-12dB would have been more appropriate in my opinion because too much or little offset from zero can quickly ruin EQ and that extra 6dB in both directions is too easy to add or subtract. An example is maxing out to +18dB in the 100Hz range will be too boomy, whereas too far in the opposite direction can sound thin and cold.

This pedal requires a power supply since there is no battery compartment. It only draws 8 mA so just about any regulated 9V DC with a 2mm negative center jack will work. It's totally compatible with a [[ASIN:B000RNB720 Truetone 1 Spot Combo Pack]].

A final note: this is well made and very compact. It takes up little space on a pedal board, and the true bypass claim is absolutely valid.
Summary: Effective, uncomplicated and works well; does not take batteries and needs a power supply

It's really hard to go wrong with any of the Wampler overdrive/distortion pedals - I own a Pinnacle and Black '65, but there are literally a dozen in the Wampler catalog I'm sure I would enjoy. But the Euphoria might end up being the one I use the most. It's incredibly smooth, surprisingly versatile, works well stacked or by itself, and sounds great placed in front of a clean amp, or driving one that's already breaking up.

Let's get a couple items related to the pedal's description out of the way. The "Euphoria" is the new name for what was originally the Wampler "Ecstacy" (I believe there was a minor quarrel with Bogner over naming rights, since Bogner has a well-known amp called "Ecstacy"). But I believe the design and sound are virtually identical. The Euphoria (in "Smooth" mode) is promoted as a "D" (Dumble)-style pedal. Let's be real - I have never played a Dumble Overdrive Special, and neither have virtually anyone who will read this - they are custom-built amplifiers and are sold for absurd amounts of money. But I had an "idea in my head" of what a Dumble tone and gain structure should sound like and, for what it's worth, the Euphoria met that expectation as soon as I tried it out.

A "Tubescreamer" tone is a good reference point for starting to describe how the Euphoria sounds, though there is actually quite a bit of difference between the two. Like the Tubescreamer, the Euphoria has a smooth, sustaining high end that operates in the low to moderate gain range. Unlike the Tubescreamer, the Euphoria offers quite a bit of low end, which can be dialed in or out quite dramatically with a dedicated "BASS" knob. The other reviewers were correct when they recommended to try the bass knob at around 9:00 to 12:00 first. In front of a clean amp, the Euphoria can stay relatively clean while taking over the EQ structure of the amp to give it "Dumble" aesthetics, and still maintain or boost the volume quite a bit. Turn up the gain in "Smooth" mode and you get a loose, tube-like response that can handle everything from rock power chords to bluesy solos.

I bought the Euphoria primarily for the "Smooth" setting, but it's pretty impressive how varied the tone becomes simply by flicking the mod switch to one of the two other modes. Wampler describes the "Open" (middle) position as the least overdriven and offering the most volume boost. The bottom switch position ("Crunch") is the most gainy, and sounds more like a traditional overdrive or distortion pedal. The three modes are not footswitchable, and I prefer the "Smooth" setting as the Euphoria's signature sound, but it's pretty cool that you bring this one pedal to a performance and have three fairly distinct sounds in one box.

One of the great ironies of Wampler pedals is that they are $200 boutique pedals made with the needs of professional musicians in mind, yet the powerful EQ controls and low-end response of their dirt pedals really pairs well with smaller, less expensive combo amplifiers. Many overdrive pedals are great provided that you play them through a cabinet loaded with 12" speakers and at a "cranked" volume level. The Euphoria (and all Wamplers, really) seems to have been designed to perform at low and high volume levels, alike. As for the "D-Style" tone, I tried a Mooer Rumble Drive and the Euphoria just blows it out of the water. Even if you don't care about "Dumble" tone, the Euphoria is an excellent alternative to the sea of Tubescreamer clones, offering something unique, powerful, and flexible.
Summary: Dumble-style "smooth" overdrive, and so much more

The Vandoren V-12 reed seems to have been a response to the needs of plays several decades ago who turned to brands such as Olivieri and Morre.  As a professional clarinetist who has played a variety of mouthpieces and reeds over the years, it has always been my experience that these thick-blank reeds work best on mouthpieces with a long facing, and usually a mouthpiece with at least a medium tip opening.  The Vandoren V-12 reeds might not possess the mystique of the Morre (which were always difficult to obtain, but they are closer to the classic thick-blank style of the past than the Vandoren traditional cut reeds.  Generally, I have found that the V-12 reeds are more consistent than Vandoren's traditional cut reeds.  If you are a Vandoren user and never tried the V-12 reeds, just be aware that you may need to try a different strength than what you are used to.  It has been my experience that the V-12 cut is more flexible at the tip, so (contrary to what conventional wisdom might suggest) sometimes people use a 1/2 strength higher with the V-12. TL;DR: What a great little amp this is.

This is actually my second Blackstar. I bought my first-generation HT-5 almost ten years ago, when Blackstar was basically still a startup company. Blackstar owes its early success in large part to the HT-5. It is one of the greatest low-wattage amplifiers of the last 20 years, a real classic.

I'd known about the Fly 3 for awhile. But my HT-5 already gives me a good, Marshall-like sound. Did I need another Blackstar? Not really. The HT-5 has a tube preamp, too, while the Fly 3 is all solid state, so I didn't think the Fly 3 would be as warm and full sounding as the HT-5, anyway.

But the thing is, I get a little tired of hauling out the full rig and setting it up when I want to play--even if it only takes a few minutes. Sometimes I just want to plug in and let 'er rip. I was starting to get an itch for an amp that could give me that spur-of-the-moment option. And that's when the Fly 3 started to make sense.

Normally I like a lot of gain in my sound. Lately, though, I've been playing a lot of Jimi Hendrix songs, especially from his first two albums, before he started playing Marshall Plexis. So I'm steadily moving toward lower gain, JTM-style Marshall sounds. That's what this amp seemed to offer, based on the demos I saw.

The one demo on YouTube that really impressed me was by an amazingly talented guitarist from the UK named Dave Simpson. While he had a few reservations, he really liked the Fly 3, and his demo was wide-ranging and well-played. More than any other, it was his demo that convinced me the Fly 3 would be a smart purchase.

And his demo really nailed it. As I was hoping, the Fly 3 gives me that pre-1968 Hendrixian tone really well, no matter how the gain is set. It's even changed my playing to some degree. For the first time, I'm not afraid to play at lower gain, and even with cleans. With the gain set at around 9 o'clock, I get a nice crunchy sound at the bridge position, and a nice signature Strat sound at the neck position. On the Fly 3, I'm having great fun playing songs I'd previously never attempted, like '51st Anniversary,' 'Remember,' and 'Can You See Me?'

Since I already have an earlier Blackstar amp, I'll note here about their proprietary ISF control and how it's voiced on the Fly 3. On the HT-5, the left half of the dial is meant to give us a kind of Mesa-like (US-style) sound, and the right half is kind of a Marshall-like (UK-style) sound. On the Fly 3, it's a bit different--the ISF acts more like a presence control, brighter before noon and darker after noon. My impression is it's more about tone than voicing. The size of the speaker and the amp's wattage may also play into this. It's not a drawback, necessarily, just a note that the ISF does not have the same effect on both amps.

On a moderate setting, the Fly 3's delay acts kind of like a reverb, adding dimension to the sound. I set delay on the Fly 3 with level at about noon and timing at about 9 o'clock. That gives me a nice thickening effect without slapping back. A slapback effect can also be dialed in as desired. I think the delay timing maxes out around 600 ms, which is reasonable. It's not an especially powerful delay, but it's very usable.

So far, I have tried the headphone input but not the auxiliary input. The headphone input sounds quite good.

To its credit, Blackstar decided to include the first set of 6 AA batteries with the amp, which keeps all new Fly 3 owners (like me) happy right as we crack open the box. That little detail cannot be overemphasized.

I can also attest that the Fly 3 makes a great bench test amplifier--I recently swapped out a humbucker in one of my Strats, and I grabbed the Fly 3 and plugged in the guitar to verify that the new pickup was working properly. Not having to set up a power cord with the amp makes that little task much easier.

I think Blackstar has another classic in the Fly 3, right alongside the great HT-5. This is a great little amp for a very affordable price. Just imagine if every beginning guitarist had an amp like this for starters.
Summary: It's a great little amp I didn't know I needed

Text:
I built a set of PA speakers utilizing a Celestion 15" driver and a Pyle PDS182 compression driver. When I purchased the Pyle compression drivers I did so mostly based on price and the specs. Even at the time I had the thought in the back of my mind that the Pyle's may be cost effective but that their performance may not be great.

After building the boxes, installing the drivers, building a crossover, and firing them up it was immediately apparent that I needed to install some Lpads as the compression drivers were much more efficient than the woofers and therefore over powered them. Once those were installed I fired up the speakers and started giving them a workout. Everything was going pretty well and I was very surprised at the nice sound the Pyle's had at both moderate and very elevated levels. I was very pleased. Then all of the sudden I got a weird sound out of one of the speakers, a pop, and then one of the Pyle's was dead. It seems the Behringer EP2500 was just too much for it.

Once that happened I decided I would experiment with a little more expensive compression driver to see if there was some better sound quality to be had by spending a few more dollars. I searched around a bit and decided to order one of these drivers and do an A/B comparison between the $18 Pyle that was still working and this $50 Selenium driver.

The results were a little surprising to me. The fact is, this driver definitely sounds better than the Pyle. But, not by very much. This driver is what a would call a little smoother or a little less harsh. Volume is pretty similar and the response also seems to be pretty similar. Where the Pyle has just a slight bit of harshness at the top (only when comparing the two, when not side by side the Pyle is perfectly acceptable) this driver is smoother. It is a nicer sounding driver overall. Again though, very slightly. For less than one driver you can have two Pyle's that sound about 95% as good.

For someone looking for some very good budget compression drivers I wouldn't hesitate to go with the Pyle's. The Selenium D220Ti gets the nod based one two things though. First, one Pyle did fail. The coil burned out from too much power. I think for the most part the power rating of the Pyle is overly optimistic. Not too big of an issue if you keep the power levels at sane amounts. Also the drivers very high efficiency don't really require lots of power to get them to very high SPL levels. I'm willing to bet that the Selenium is much more accurately rated in the power handling department. Second is that with the Selenium if you do over power one and burn out the coil a replacement diaphragm is available and costs less than the PDS182. In addition to those two things the Selenium does sound better, however slight.

Instead of dropping a star or two by comparing this driver to the PDS182 I give it 5 stars based on its very good performance, decent price, nice sound, and available replacement diaphragm. If your looking for the best bang for the buck the PDS182 is worth a look. If your looking for a little nicer driver with very nice sound this is a good choice.

In terms of just tuning your instrument, guitars (especially classical guitars with un-adjustable scale lengths and nylon strings) are idiosyncratic and every guitar, every time you pick it up, every piece you play, requires an idiosyncratic tuning. The ear just works better, in my opinion, than a tuner. That said, they are useful for setting intonation (checking the 12th fret harmonic vs. the 12th fret fretted note). But I don't have shop tools so I digress :)

I ended up returning this and just using my ear. I'm happy and my guitar sounds fine. I can see how it might be useful in a concert situation though.

I did boatloads of research on this signal processing unit (UberPedal) before buying. I watched lots of videos, read the user questions, watched the company vids and subscribed to TC Helicon's YouTube channel.

I finally got one of these today and wow, it's the best money I've spent on gear in a while.

My peculiar situation is that I am hard-of-hearing, so my right ear is better than my left but overall I struggled to hear my guitar and the vocals I'd sing with it. This made me play a lot louder just to hear something. I missed nuance. I have a hearing aid (I should have two, but one is broken) and I had to put it in my GOOD ear just to hear myself...which meant I was panned right. Terrible audio situation.

You can see where I am going with this. Because the TC Helicon has a headphone jack and decent volume, I could HEAR MYSELF PLAYING (and singing) with incredible nuance I never really heard before, and with my hearing aid properly in my bad ear for more balance. Then, I used my good quality Beyer-Dynamic closed headphones to monitor everything...guitar and vocals together. It's not just that I am hearing the dulcet sounds of the fantastic vocal reverbs and other FX along with my guitar in its fully BodyRez glory, but I can hear more. So, if you're hard of hearing, this is already a value just to be able to use headphones with an acoustic-electric guitar. If you need more volume, just do what I did and get a quality headphone amp and route a mini-jack from the Play Acoustic to the 1/4" in.

For the unit itself, this thing is just packed with features. The looper is fantastic, and as a beatboxer this will come in handy just to set up beats for myself to play with or to loop guitar parts when I want to pick out some solos. The BodyRez feature makes my $99 Jameson guitar (from Amazon, by the way) sound incredible...warm, rich, acoustic—yet amplified. Instead of throwing money at a guitar well beyond my skill level, the BodyRez really just gives me options that really appeal to me and my hard-of-hearing self, filling all the right gaps. It can make your inexpensive learner sound like a $3000 Martin. Heresy? Perhaps...but it makes me happy.

The subtle blend of auto-tune is nice for vocals, and being able to add a chorus is fantastic. I've also discovered that you can monitor the Play Acoustic even if it's plugged into an amplifier. If you want to get that full volume but allow others to hear it at a reasonable level, then the Play Acoustic serves this function too. For anyone, this is a benefit. For the hard-of-hearing, it's pure magic.

For me, this thing isn't just an inspiration to my playing, but a way to actually HEAR what I am doing without funneling everything through a $139 hearing aid that isn't necessarily made for audio of this type, and simply doesn't give me the volume I want or need. My playing got softer, more nuanced, my vocals got instantly better (because I could hear what I was singing)....just incredible. I can even play during later hours because my playing can be softer and more nuanced and I have all the volume I need in headphones.

5 big fat juicy stars!
Summary: Must-have for acoustic performers AND a boon for the hard-of-hearing!
