I have owned several "budget" guitars and don't fool yourself - this is a budget guitar.

Compared to the Fender Stratocaster Squire or the Epiphone Les Paul Special 2; the Epiphone LP-100 severely outshines both in construction, tone, and overall quality. I wish I had known about this model before starting my guitar journey with a Fender Squire Strat Pack - which is absolute garbage even with a proper setup. What I thought would be a step up from that pile was an Epiphone LP Special 2; while it isn't the worst choice it wasn't a good one. That guitar was a plank of wood and the tone reflected that. Stear clear of those models. They will end up in a closet gathering dust. They both suck to play and I really do mean that.

The LP-100 on other hand is VERY impressive for the price and would be a good starter guitar for anyone interested in learning how to play. Looks wise, it begs to be taken off the wall and played. The iconic sunburst finish really shines, doesn't look cheap at all, and can take a ding or two without showing. The sound is great, the humbuckers really sing, and the volume/tone knobs are responsive. String changing is a breeze and adjusting the action is also very simple given the tail piece and bridge are easily accessible. You can get a wide variety of rich tones out of this when coupled with a decent amp - I used a Fender Mustang 2 and not some silly mini speaker. In fact, if you are buying this for a gift or as first guitar for yourself do get a Fender Mustang 2 at around $100 on here. One of the biggest blocks for learning can be things not sounding right, Part of the equation to having a successful start with playing guitar is a combination of good equipment at the start. My recomended setup for those I give lessons to:

-Epiphone LP-100
-Fender Mustang 2 amp (the bigger the better, don't buy some mini cheapo POS)
-6ft Fender L-shaped cable for this particular guitar
-Dunlop Gator Grip picks ,58mm thickness or one of the variety packs
-Dunlop String conditioner - helps your strings last and helps condition the fretboard.
-Fretfast - helps slick up the strings and back of the neck.
-Ernie Ball slinky strings
-Chromatic Tuner (or if you have a smartphone there is an app called G-Strings and you will save a boatload of money)
-Floor or wall stand, brand makes zero difference until you're playing on some $1K+ Gibson.

With that equipment you get the feel and sound you want from your equipment to keep you moving along.

I have some "better" guitars in my collection such as a Fender Telecaster and an Epiphone Sheraton 2 but I keep coming back to this LP-100. I like the way it feels, the tone, the presence that it has overall. My only complaint with this guitar is the stock tuners/tuning pegs. It doesn't hold D or C tunings for as long as I would like but that is minor when considering the overall quality of this great guitar. If you buy this stellar Les Paul and keep it around, plan on upgrading the tuners to Grover tuners for around $20-$30 and an hour of your time.

To conclude my ranty review; you cannot go wrong with an Epiphone Les Paul 100. If you're a beginner, you will love it. If you're more experienced, it will be a nice addition to your collection and put some variety in your sonic arsenal.

Do not buy a Squire or a First Act, start off right or you are wasting your money. The LP-100 is hands down the BEST budget guitar I have played. New or used, it is worth the money if you are serious about learning.

First off, I wound up with this guitar because Amazon sent the wrong one! I had ordered the Ayv Emerald Green Les Paul knock-off (which costs about $60 less than the PRS knock-off). My initial reaction was to be ticked off that they screwed up the order. But then I got a close look at the PRS copy and the rest, as they say, is history.

What an amazingly unbelievable price point for a guitar of this quality. Mine arrived in rather flimsy packaging, but was not scratched or dented in any way. Setup was minimal. The fretboard was dry as a bone, so I took off the strings, oiled up and cleaned the frets, and lowered the bridge very slightly. I also added a set of .10 D'addario (or however you spell it) strings.

I had planned to just carry it to gigs in an old gig bag I had lying around here, but the thing is so nice I dropped another $100 on a nice, hardshell Gator case. I used it this past weekend at two festival shows and man, it sounds as good as it looks! I was able to get a nice clean sound for rhythm and a smooth, gritty sound for leads. The pickups are hot, but not overly-so. The sound is fat and warm and there is virtually no microphonic nonsense coming from them.

The inlay work and finish is VERY good, again for this price point. I've had several Epi Paul and PRS copies over the years -- been playing professionally since 1971 or so -- and none of them were nicer than this, though a couple were probably "as nice," which they should be since they cost me three times what the Iyv costs. The headstock and all the joint points are excellent. And on my unit, at least, the finish is flawless.

On the downside, the tuning pegs seem maybe just a little bit wimpy. I may wind up swapping out for some Grovers at some point. Also, they've spray painted flat black inside the F-holes and the interior part of the guitar doesn't seem to have received much sanding and/or finishing. But since I can't see through wood, this doesn't bother me much.

As some others have noted, this is NOT going to be as luxe as a "real" PRS, but man, for $250 or so, it is unbelievably close! In fact, I like it so much, I went ahead and re-ordered the Emerald Green Les Paul, which is what I wanted in the first place. I figure with the PRS and the Tele I already own, this will give me a wide pallet of tones from which to choose.

There are many great pickup options for acoustic guitars these days. My absolute favorite pickup, all things considered is the K&K soundboard line of pickups. No battery, no ugly and superfluous controls added to the guitar, just pure perfect sound. However, the quality of sound produced by the K&K is highly dependent on the installation. Since my hands are way too large to enter the soundhole and accurately place the pickups, I have to rely on someone else to do it. One installer did a great job but said never again. A second installer (2nd guitar) did not spend the necessary time to properly locate the pickups so the sound is not as great as it could be. So...

Lately I have gone the soundhole route. I own the M1 LR Baggs soundhole pu, and it is great. I like that it is designed (strap jack feature) to connect to the amp cable through the strap button at the rear of the guitar. But, it is a bit pricey ($130+) and is rather bulky. Sounds good though.

This time around I decided to try the Fishman Neo-D and I am about to order another one. It sounds amazing. I have tried it direct to the mixer, to the mixer through a DI box (UltraSound DI+), and direct to a guitar amp. Either way it sounds great. What is amazing is that it retains the character of the guitar, not just picking up the strings. I know, that is impossible right? I tested it using headphones thus blocking out the natural sound of the guitar, and I could hear the nuances of the guitar acoustics.

It is well made, I appreciate the cork pads on the clamp surfaces. My only gripe, and I knew this going in, the cable extends outside the soundhole and down the front. I route around and past my strap to kind of get it out of the way, but I prefer the LR Baggs M1 method (strapjack). Also, and maybe it is just the guitar I am using, the pickup is a bit narrow for the soundhole, I had to position it at the very top of the soundhole.

Regardless of the incredible price ($40), this is an excellent pickup and I plan to order a second for another guitar.

PS: After writing this I forgot to mention that I purchased the single coil version. I have not experienced hum and it is perfectly quiet,
Summary: Great Sound. Easy to Install. Incredible Price! A Guitar Pickup Trifecta!

Definitely good for the beginner. The Fender Play card (subscription, really) sits nicely in the range of offerings that are available today. At the high end there are in-person, one-on-one lessons. VERY expensive! Next, there are offerings like Artist Works, which provides a substantial community as well as personalized feedback from very prominent musicians/teachers. But it's also expensive! At the low end you have self-teaching through music books. At the bottom are a number of free offerings, though you can supplement with books, too. Fender Play sits nicely in the middle. The expense is very modest and is affordable for most. The quality of instruction is high. The range of styles, however, isn't very broad, being more pop and rock oriented. Techniques apply to all kinds of music, but practice in different genres matters a lot, too. If you are interested in styles other than pop and rock, then Fender Play may not be the best choice for you, though if you are a *total* beginner, it is worthwhile for basic techniques.

So, if you are looking for a leg up for decent instruction at a good price, for a good duration of time, then a Fender Play subscription might be just the thing for you. Take a look!

To be fair, with my rating, as above, I'm venting my frustrations, here, with the totally inadequate manual that comes with this device. This unit may be really great, but I can't tell, because of the almost indecipherable manual. That manual has 152 pages and, in its great verbosity, it explains, very poorly, how to operate this unit.  Yeah, this thing can do just about everything except cook you a gourmet meal, I guess, BUT, you need to slog through pages and pages of material to even begin to approach a rudimentary grasp of its mind-boggling features.  Going through the menus are incredibly tough and not exactly intuitive.  Some are counter-intuitive:  One button does one thing in one mode and something totally unrelated in another mode.  The manual just confuses you by slapping everything together. The "support" from the manufacturer is that in name only.  Going to their website you will find there basically is no support, save the horrible manual that you can download.  Have you ever been to Jamaica and tried to figure out what the locals are saying, right to your face, in Patois? Frustrating as hell.  You can make out many of the words but, to save your life, you cannot grasp the meaning of what's being said to you.  That is what the manual is like, in many cases.  There is hope, though.  Go to the main user group sites out there. They will help you, greatly.  Do go to them before you start tearing your hair out in frustration.  (I had the links in my original review, but Amazon pulled them.  Nice.) It is very telling that support groups exist for this line of recording devices.  What comes through in most postings is that scores of folks cannot use the manual to figure out much about the unit.  Once I have a good understanding of how to use this unit, I'll update, here. UPDATE: 5/10/12:  OK, I added another star.  While the manual is terrible, I am now figuring things out for myself and I'm starting to like this unit, more.  Expect another update once I teach myself how to use the multitrack features. UPDATE: 8/16/12:  I have now given this unit 5 stars.  I am using it in multitrack mode to make excellent quality demos.  It does the job in very fine fashion.  It is worth repeating that the manual is very frustrating to use. After having it for a few months, though, you will learn, on your own, as I have, how to navigate the menus, and that will greatly increase your enjoyment of this unit.

This does just what it's supposed to do:  get the subwoofer off the ground so it doesn't couple to the floor, creating boomy noise and generating standing waves.  Removing these problems is important to get the most out of your sub, and improves the 'Spousal Acceptance Factor' of the sub, too.  Spikes help, but not enough. It's not 'pretty' -- a velour-covered one can be had for $10 more -- but seems well-made.  As others will probably point out, it's just a piece of wood, covered in carpet, on foam blocks.  You could probably make it for half that price -- except that it includes foam 'pyramids' on the bottom to prevent generating its *own* set of standing waves; this foam isn't easily found in an upholstery shop.  It just about perfectly fits my SVS SB12-NSD, which is about 14.5" on a side, looks like it was made for it.  It should fit a 1-12" guitar amp nicely, too.  Auralex makes a larger version called the GRAMMA for amp use on stages and recording; if your sub is really big (15" or 18"), you might consider that instead.  But for your typical compact Velodyne, Polk, Hsu, SVS, or Klipsch woofer, this is the ticket!

I see at least one reviewer complained that the protective foam (or whatever it is) doesn't completely cover the entire underside of the tool. Funny thing when looking for a Harmon mute, this one popped up. The idea of of full sound with out disturbing anyone along with a little reverb was an interesting concept. I ordered it and it came super fast. Directions are ok but not very specific in regard to little things like which cable to use or securing the strap. The end that attaches to the mute has a screw on connector. Don't use the 3 lead cord. That's for external stereo output from the amp unit which is about the size of a small walkman. Be sure to connect the headphones and input pickup before playing. Don't plug in your phones or the pickup cable or it will pop loudly. Like the guitar amp you forgot to turn down. So how's it sound? Very nice, clean but the reverb is a bit weird. It starts out with a cycle that gets louder and louder as though there is a mic feedback loop but when you begin to play it seems to be okay. Weird circuitry in this thing. It's a very good mute even with out the power on and using the mute part only. The supplied earbuds sound ok but I wanted to try the Klipsh earbuds and my Bose QC 15 phones. Both sounded very nice. Yamaha does not make junk in my opinion. I wouldn't necessarily record with this unit but it is intended for practice/rehearsing anyway. It sounds great in any volume or key played on the horn. When I hit those high note klinkers, nobody is around to complain. I highly recommend it. Great tool.

A word about back pressure. Really, there isn't much more than what you find with a regular soft, or Harmon mute. It didn't bother me and I you'll find the same results. I like it. It is a quality piece of equipment. Not sure of the output impedance but this opens up all kinds of possibilities for effects with a good sampler at home. No doubt players have tried this. If not, they should. Good product for sure. You can have no reservations about getting one. You're probably a better player than me but I'm playing for fun anyway.

Add: I've had this for a while now and can say for sure that the back pressure is not an issue for me. It could be for some but not enough to worry about. Text: Here is a mini-review of my recent purchase: Blue EnCORE 200 vs. 20 year old EV PL20 which I have been using in all my recordings up to now. I love the PL20 because it is a passive dynamic with a very smooth proximity effect, that means it is very forgiving in positioning. It is also a classic broadcast desk mic that has a very pleasing response and a bit of high midrange boost. It is great for vox as well as instruments. However there is a detectable graininess which turns into outright distortion at a certain resonating frequency which sounds like the area where the boost occurs. This is not the so-called 'baby rattle' syndrome since there is no rattle when shaken. Now, to compare my new Blue EnCORE 200 - First this is the phantom powered version of their dynamic mic, and can be had at about 1/3 the cost of a new EV PL20. Phantom power is no problem for me, my cheap Focusrite 2i2 has it, as do most all interfaces and preamps. I bought this mic on the strength of it's reviews and it does not disappoint. It lacks the smooth proximity effect of the EV's (as expected) so I will have to be more careful with positioning in the 'sweet spot'. It seems to have a much flatter response, the graph even shows a low midrange dip. Very slight graininess around 5KHz to my ear, rapidly turns to distortion when overloading the preamp - proximity effect again. Overall seems like a great mic...Time will tell.

I was hesitant to purchase this, as I really like the display of the previous models. At first it seems like it might be less accurate. It has less granularity in the display for example. However, it does seem to respond noticeably faster. It appears to be a bit more sensitive and better at tuning bass notes. And it may in fact be more precise, though it takes learning how to work with the display.

On earlier Snarks, the display has individual tiny gradients for each cent of pitch above or below the note. And they seemed pretty dead on, especially if you tune from the harmonic at the middle of the string. But I also found that the note would occasionally stall briefly causing me to over-tune. (Though once you get used to it, it is easily avoided.)

Anyway, on this unit, I am not sure what each bar represents, but it is very sensitive. If the string is not quite perfect, the "On pitch" bar will be lit up, but so will one next to it. Then a slight turn of the tuning peg will bring it right on. Then only the "On pitch" bar will be lit (unless you turn too far). And the result sounds really right. I think I'll be putting one of these on most instruments from now on.

I threw together a quick demo of some raw tracks played through the Arena2000
I wasn't trying to duplicate any original sound, I just pick some of the presets I found while roaming all the presets. I used the Arena 2000 as the USB interface. I sent the raw recorded tracks to the Arena from the DAW, and then recorded the output back through USB. My DAW skills aren't great but I also didn't do any more signal processing to or from the Arena 2000

All of the presets show some features - but it would take tens of thousands preset patces and a whole lot of time to do all the combinations.

I see numerous reviewers listen to a couple of presets, then start tweaking them to their own taste. I think that's a good way to go. You'd need a decoder ring to figure out what the creater of each preset was trying to do, but tweaking them yourself you're more likely to put the patches to your own sound. Really, try as many of the built in presets. They really explore the power of the arena2000. They are great examples. You'll get the real value when you create your own for your own sound.

The original patches are stored in ROM if you want to reset to factory defaults in the future.

One thing for sure is you'll want to go through the patches and normalize the levels. Some are screaming loud while other too quiet. It's not a lot of work to do this, but just do the ones you like.

50 slots is massive for an ir loader. Plenty of room to expand. 23.2 MS per slot gives you all time and resolution you'll ever need to reproduce the essential sound of a cabinet. This is not going to be enough for room reflections, but you can add reverb to simulate rooms and halls. When you are playing live, you'll want the essential cabinet IR and be glad you can control room/hall reverb response separately.

I would like a longer looper and one that lets you do multi layers.

The drum rhythms are handy for practice and the aux in can accept any mp3 or phone apps

The PC software works great for me on Windows 10. On both the iPhone and PC the response from the Arena 2000 is instant. Arranging the order of the pedals is just drag and drop on the PC. The App, plus the foot pedals on the Arena will get you through all the settings without having to drop to the floor.

I haven't got into the MIDI yet. I haven't found a published MIDI map, but there is a table in the Arena where you can view the CC's. Furthermore, I can use a really cheap low power PC with a DAW to control MIDI as the Arena 2000 saves the PC from having to do Audio DSP loads. Donner makes the PC or iPhone load negligible.

Value of the Arena 2000 is high. You'll save a lot of time trying to collect and build a pedal board to do what the Arena can do, and sound as good as the Arena. Additionally, just fit in a small, lightweight bag to carry around. The Arena does take 9v from a pedal board power just fine.

Text:
My expectations for the DC-20 were pretty low, given its price point but…

This is a great little mic for anyone on a budget.

Excellent build quality, metal construction with some heft to it. The only detail that betrays that this is an affordable mic is the slightly crinkled decal that looks a bit naff.

It’s a “large-diaphragm” mic but the capsule is only 16mm.. by most definitions it’s too small for an LDC but also too large for an SDC. Donner isn’t the only company using 16mm capsules in their “LDC” mics, and as long as it sounds good I don’t really care.

There are no switches for low-cut or pad, but at this price point, I wouldn’t expect any. My interface has those anyway. Speaking of interfaces, you need 48V phantom power for this mic to work.

Accessories are cheap but.. you’re getting a LOT for $50.. there’s a plastic shock mount that, whilst not the most effective, securely holds the mic. Theres also a hard mount if you prefer. There’s a metal pop filter / screen that has plain round perforations (not angled as found on more expensive screens), which again isn’t super effective but works “okay”. The XLR cable is cheap looking and feeling but does the job well.

The only accessory that I don’t like is the tripod, which is very small, doesn’t really work with the shock mount when a cable is plugged in, and seems designed for a completely different product.

Tested using an Audient iD44 audio interface into an M1 Mac mini running Logic.

Vocals -
Suitability for voice is VERY dependent upon the individual’s voice (low / deep or high / thin sounding) but I feel the DC-20 works pretty well with mine (not particularly deep, not particularly high).

For spoken word, it picks up my voice very clearly and the top end - surprisingly - lacks the harshness I almost expect from cheap condenser mics. As always, using a condenser in an untreated room can result in poor recordings since it’ll capture any reflections.

At this point, I want to mention the AT2020, a VERY popular “affordable” condenser that is almost universally recommended as a first condenser mic for beginners but (to me) has a pretty brittle top end and not great self noise (hiss). I’d always recommend the Neat Worker Bee II (MUCH lower self noise, smoother top end) and honestly.. I think the Donner DC-20 would be a better choice for many people also at half the price!

Acoustic Guitar -
My acoustic is a lawsuit era Takamine. A little bit dark sounding but the relatively bright DC-20 handles it really well. Normally / ideally I’d use 2 mics and blend them in the DAW but the DC-20 captured a usable recording on its own.

Electric Guitar -
Didn’t close mic but placed it about 1.5ft away from the cab (greenback). Also had an SM57 right up on it. Blending the 2 mics in the DAW resulted in a very good recreation of what I was hearing in the room.

Overall.. a very decent sounding mic for under $100. A GREAT sounding mic for the current asking price of $50.

So for value.. this thing is insanely good. Happy to have it in my mic locker, if only for use with my acoustic that it happens to pair excellently with.

Text: These are expensive cables and take forever to get to you. Why did I give it 5 starts? Well, when you buy them you know the price and if you didn't notice the 3-5 week shipping notation it is right in your face when you place the order. That is what happened to me and I cancelled my first order trying to find a good cable at a similar price with 2 day Prime shipping. No luck so I placed the order again and just waited. I gave it 5 stars because it is a very good speaker cable to connect your amp head to a cabinet or two. WARNING- do not use a guitar cable as a speaker cable! They are designed for two separate animals. The center conductor of a shielded guitar cable is a very small gauge and will give way too much resistance. Friends in other rock bands have told me they burned out expensive amp heads by using a guitar cable as a speaker cable. I did not want to chance burning our my new bass head so the $11 for just the right cable (nice short footer) was worth the wait. You would be surprised at the number of musicians using instrument cables for speakers "hey I just use a guitar cord". These cables are heavy 14 gauge, a guitar cord is probably 22 or maybe even lighter with a shield that is useless for speakers. Even if you don't burn out the amp, you are drastically cutting your signal, hence sound.
Summary: Don't use a guitar cord in place of a speaker cable. These speaker cables are the real deal.

Great cable. I have dozens of guitar cables and have used hundreds or thousands as a studio and live sound tech, from the likes of Mogami, Monster, ProCo, Canare, Fender, Radio Shack, Monoprice, etc etc etc...

My criteria for an instrument cable is that it should:

- Lay flat when uncoiled, to avoid tangles and snags, and;
- Coil and uncoil easily, and;
- Not exhibit any handling noise from being moved, rotated, wiggled, etc, and;
- Have connectors that snap in and out of jacks solidly, easily, and securely, WITHOUT deforming the jacks (looking at you, Monster), and;
- Have good strain-relief, and be difficult to bend at a sharp angle.

Every cable is eventually going to get wrecked, on the road or in the studio. Chairs, racks, or flight-cases, are going to get rolled over it, it's going to get snagged, stepped on, yanked, jerked, bent, crumpled, tangled... you just can't be a piece of cable around musicians and roadies without getting abused. I mean, maybe in a home studio, or a pure church-audio setting or something, but not in my world.

So the fact that this cable has a lifetime warranty is great. But realistically, what matters more to me is how much life I can get out of it, and whether it's going to fail or cause problems at a gig or a studio session. This is a great deal on great cable. I have a bunch of them so far, and plan to gradually phase all the other brands as they fail. Kirlin just seems to hit the price/performance knee exactly right.

Right off the bat, I'm not a audio professional, so I can't technically tell you why this mic is great. But for my uses, it is absolutely FANTASTIC! I got this to replace my AT2020 because I learned that Dynamic mics are better for picking up vocals only in front of the mic itself, and that's exactly what this does. I use this for streaming, gaming, and generally talking to friends on discord, and it's extremely nice not needing to use any software processing to isolate my voice and get a clean sound. The reason why I didn't put the price as a con is because it's much easier (and possibly cheaper) than treating my room with sound dampening foam and such. It really does a great job at isolating my voice, and running through the Focusrite, my gain can be high with almost no static from the gain being near max. This is where the cloudlifter will come in. From my understanding, it's recommended that your interface be capable of outputting ~75dB to power this mic, however the cloudlifter can boost your interface by ~25dB without introducing static. Basically the cloudlifter lets you phantom power your dynamic mic (dynamic mics don't directly take phantom power). Since you will probably need a cloudlifter, you'll also need another xlr cable because.

Aside from likely needing a cloudlifter, there's not really anything negative I could come up with. It does exactly what it's supposed to do with great quality. If you're eyeing this, you probably already know that they used the SM7B to record Michael Jackson's Thriller back in the day, so it rightfully has Legendary status. If you're new into higher quality audio, I recommend the Focusrite Scarlett Solo which is right around $100. I wouldn't recommend going less than that because you start risking less clean audio. It's also a must to get a cloudlifter so you're not maxing out your gain. The volume and quality will be much better.

All in all, this was a solid purchase. Audio is very subjective, so definitely listen to some sound tests on YouTube before you make your decision. While this mic is perfect for my needs, it might not be for yours. When investing in equipment like this, generally, the price reflects the quality, and you need multiple components to get it working properly. These are all things to consider before making a purchase. If you're looking for a really good Dynamic mic, you can't go wrong with this.

I am a huge fan of Zoom products generally. I've owned two of their studio multitrack units, four of their field recorders, and various mic capsules they make for the H6. This mic was a huge disappointment. I can only assume they were trying to cash in on the podcasting fad and new work-from-home trend due to the pandemic.

This mic has a tremendous amount of handling noise, yet it's actually not very sensitive. You have to get your face right up in the mic-- almost touching it-- to get a decent sound (even with moderate gain). Once you get the sound level up high-enough, it's still a rather dark tone and not very flattering for voices (unless you're going for that middle-aged male, smoky, smooth jazz DJ vocal tone).

There are only two things I can say positive about the mic: It's cheap, and it doesn't require phantom power. But still, you'd be better off getting a Shure SM57 if you must have a dynamic mic (about the same cost, but twice as good). If you can swing the phantom power, upgrade to an Audio-Technica AT2035 (yes, twice as expensive, but ten-times better than this Zoom).

As an aside, let me mention that the Zoom U-22 USB interface is excellent, whatever mic you choose. Just get a different mic than this one.

Looked over a lot of reviews before picking this one to review. The hollowed out ones lacked the musical quality that I appreciate. Then too have been a didgeridoo player for decades and nothing beats a musical instrument crafted from a good hardwood.

LingTing's Wind Whisperer has an awesomely solid base, attractive wood, excellent bridge, and was tuned on arrival. Came in an attractive box, a case, and lots of goodies inside. The tines are in perfect harmony, clear, and well defined while playing. Nice, soothing tones. Can feel the music through my hands even.

Now when I play I found myself rocking the kalimba up and down. Seems natural for me, as you may seen in my unrehearsed 1 minute video. The camera's microphone did not pick up as clearly from what I heard when I play, so you might need to turn the volume up some.

While having an engraved letter of the notes could be a plus, I can see why there are none. Those engravings take away the rich tones of the tines to some degree. And I would not use a sticker, as that could dampen the nuances of the notes being played in their own harmonic orchestra. So, the only thing that I could see doing is to put the stickers on the tine brace. That would be the only place where the soothing siren's songs would not be affected by unnatural enhancements.

The chain adds a different effect. Unsure if this could be heard as well when being recorded, but playing it is a far more enjoyable experience. I did try the piezo pick-up, and placed it underneath the bridge. Unsure if I needed a phantom powered device before connecting the PC's USB port, but the results were not good. As such, I asked the instrument for its forgiveness as I removed the pick-up.

If this is your first Kalimba, then by all means buy it. The hardwood plank will give YOU far more enjoyment than a hollowed out one. I chose C tones as my singing bowls, didgeridoo, and other instruments are in C which is the closest to Earth's harmonic resonance. However, the B has a even more mellowly rich deep tone that sounds so pleasing.

As for the cons. hmm. The edges are a tad sharp, but that does not bother me in the least as I have large hands. Wished was a way to have this LingTing's Siren to sing outwardly more, but that may be due to the instrument or thumb powers. And lastly the piezo pick-up was not very good. For the price I would only of expected the kalimba and maybe a case.

If there were motifs engraved into the wood, like a dragon, faerie, or something along the mystical side it could be more aesthetically pleasing. And am trying to find a way to openly display this on a wall or angled on a shelf. The musical instrument is a beauty to behold, and should be shared and revered. The wood & texture is beautiful.

The extras was some rubber thumb covers to help pluck the tines, I suppose. I never used them. There are stickers, and a small piezo pick-up with 1/4 inch jack, a tassel, and a chain. You get a soft case with a zipper, and a burlap carrying bag if you choose. All in a presentable box ready for gift wrapping.
Another chain of stainless steel might provide a better effect, although I am fine without it. The tassel I put on almost immediately.

Highly recommended, even if you cannot play music, Merely attempting might send you into a blissful nap state.

Like the previous user said try other options. I have the Shure SM58 along with this usb adapter. It's not bad for a first usb adapter made by Shure. However, I do not recommend this product except if you extensively work on your laptop. It's heavy and the four controls can be messed up easily. The X2u has a latch that secures the XLR connection pretty well. On the negative side, I would seriously recommend using duck tape for both the four controls and the base of the X2u. If you don't the Mic Gain control (like the other controls) will be either too high for recording or too low since three of the controls are not secured when one holds this heavy adapter. Tape up the controls when you get the standard settings for good wave file recordings without the hiss.
The base of the X2u seems to loose connection too often with the cable, thus ruining recordings. This adapter sound quality is just not that clear. The Mic Monitor function is excellent feature but if you get this, "use electrical tape or even duck tape" for the background hissing noise and ideal control settings. A XLR cable adapter to a quality external sound device may be your best option for both laptops and desktops.

Shure has been making excellent products for a long time but this product is not what I expected it to be in terms of quality.
Summary: Just not that good of product for a Professional XLR Microphones

Since specific equipment can make a difference in a person's playing, there's often a "Holy Grail" quest to find the optimum. Years ago people just used the old metal band/2 screw ligatures but some had teachers who suggested others, and then the Internet happened and anyone with the curiosity could go to sites like Sax on the Web and read all sorts of suggestions. Some players had these old Harrison ligatures that held the reed in a different, sensible manner.

How different mouthpieces, reeds, ligatures and instruments work depends partially on the physical makeup of the individual player and greatly on what effect that player wants to achieve. But basically the reed needs to be held on the mouthpiece securely enough that it doesn't move while being played. Then there is the issue of holding the reed in a manner that does not impede its vibration. That's where these 4-point systems can be valuable. That's how this H ligature is designed - it holds the reed at 4 points instead of with a band like the old standard lig or the newer fabric or leather Rovner ligatures. I tried those Rovners for quite some time until I determined that they muffled the reed.

I happen to like this re-creation of the old Harrison ligature that is now hard to find. I use the vintage, larger mouthpieces with my current favorite being an old Buescher - kinda fat and used these days by folks who play the old, first half 20th century instruments for which that standard issue mouthpiece was designed. If you have the slimmer, more modern "jazz" mouthpiece, this is likely to be too large. That you should ascertain before ordering.

To me the gold plating is of no consequence although there are those who think something like that makes a difference. I admit that I like the ligature to match the color of the metal of my instrument; that's the only relevance to me of the gold. Or silver.

To a large extent you just have to borrow or buy these things and try them. I'd say this is not too terribly expensive for what you're getting.

My favorite "bundled" rods of this type are Pro Mark's Hot Rods. I like the feel and natural sound of the wood dowels. However they wear out prematurely, even with applying duct tape around the shoulder for added durability. It gets expensive replacing them. Next I tried Remo's Blastics.
Not bad for plastic rods but a little short for my taste. Finally I settled on Vater's wood handle Whip. Their longer rods are a plus for me. Adjusting rings are beefier than the "O rings" Remo uses. The Vaters outlast the others in general. However, the rods have an annoying tendency to all work loose in a bundle from the metal collar of the handle. Vater's binding process is not sufficient to keep the entire bundle from separating from the handle. In the past I believe it took awhile for this to occur. Then I started to preemptively glue the base of the rods to the metal collar. Now it seems the rods work loose much more quickly. Gluing sometimes keeps the rods from popping out en masse but not
always. To be fair, I use the Vater Whip for home practice to keep volume down. I do play them fairly hard, but still, they should not be coming apart while still new. That's the only reason I took off a star. If you're playing with only light to moderate force, you probably won't have this issue. Other than that, the Vater Whip is still my first overall choice. Now I simply glue when new and strengthen overall with duct tape.
**Update: Borrowing from my practice of duct taping the wooden dowel Pro Mark Hot Rods to minimize wear around the shoulder of the rod, I did the same with the V. Whips. I eventually wound up taping from the bottom of the bristles up to about an inch or two from the tips. However doing so made the whips heavier. I was ok with that but curiously noticed that in short order, the whips developed a bending of the duct tape in the middle. Attempting to straighten proved futile as the whips quickly became bent again. It then occurred to me that it might be the weight of the tape with the repetitive downward and forward force from playing that was causing or at least contributing to the poly bristles coming out of the handle individually or en masse. So I tried a new pair of V. Whips, still preemptively gluing the bristles at the wood base, experimenting with the adjustment bands, but NOT applying any duct tape. Voila! After a month of my usual hard playing, the bristles have all remained intact. It would appear the weight of the duct tape may have been the significant factor in the bristles coming out of the wood handles. Time will tell.
Summary: My favorite "bundled" rods of this type are Pro Mark's Hot ...

I'm a bit of a later adopter of the Arturia BeatStep, but I put a lot of thought into which of the affordable pad/knob MIDI controllers I thought would work best for me, and the BeatStep was the clear favorite. To seal the deal, Amazon randomly put it on sale for quite a bit less than the usual asking price of around $100 U.S. At that price (or even at the usual street price), it feels like a very nice device for the money.

PROS - The build quality of the BeatStep is impressive. The overall unit has a weight and toughness to it that you just don't find in products in this price range. I've owned comparable MIDI controllers from Akai and Korg, and while they function just fine, the lightweight plastic feel of them just doesn't feel like as nice of a product as what you get from Arturia. The additional heft from the metal backing probably help stabilize the pads during finger drumming, too.

The original BeatStep is a MIDI controller and (very basic) sequencer that doesn't necessarily excel at any one task, but is capable of more than you might expect. I thought the connectivity options were amazing - USB MIDI and 5-pin DIN MIDI out, plus CV Sync in a $100 controller!? It's pretty amazing that you could hook this single device up to a desktop DAW, iPad, or hardware synth and have all sorts of options for controlling notes and sequencing. A lot of older hardware gear only uses 5-pin DIN, so that's a major advantage to have that connectivity right off the bat. A lot of popular affordable gear from Korg, Teenage Engineering, etc. uses CV to sync between units, also. I haven't tried it with all my gear yet, but I've seen enough online to suggest it should work, and you can adjust the voltage and other parameters though a very robust online editor.

I primarily bought the BeatStep to use as a MIDI controller, and it's probably best suited for that purpose. Plug this thing into an iPad sampler, and it's like have the control surface of an MPC with a powerful software sampler behind it. With 16 rotary knobs to adjust CC parameters, plus 16 more pads (and a single large knob usually mapped to volume, but it can be reassigned), there's a lot of flexibility here. I actually thought the pads needed to be more sensitive, but again, that can be adjusted by the software.

In sequencer mode, the BeatStep is very easy to use and interesting as a creative tool. The pads light up in this mode to visually display progress through the sequence. You can change the step time to stretch single bar patterns into multiple bars, or morph slow progressions into frantic note runs. You also have the ability to play the sequence backwards or at random. You adjust the note on each step by turning the 16 corresponding knobs (which are notched for feel), kind of like an old-school step sequencer. It's not a terribly deep or one-size-fits-all solution for writing music, but it's still well-implemented and a lot of fun to work with the sequencer in this way.

CONS - Overall, I'm happy with the BeatStep, but there are some limitations you need to know about. The sequencer is basically monophonic, so you cannot really use the BeatStep to sequence proper drum beats. There's also no velocity control in the sequencer, unlike in controller mode where the pads are velocity-sensitive. As I've hinted at already, there are sequencer apps on the iPad costing a fraction of this already affordable device that are infinitely more powerful.

Arturia has addressed some of the other complaints, such as the CC knobs not working fast enough to be used for filter sweeps, etc. As a controller, the default setting for the pads are chromatic notes. You can change this to a number of different scales, which is neat. But there isn't a convenient way to switch octaves like you would on a keyboard with octave up/down buttons. I believe you can hold "shift" and turn the big knob to transpose a number of steps, and this feature was expanded in a later firmware update. But I can't imagine that would be a practical way to reach the "D" note in the octave above after you just played a "B" note in the lower octave on the pads.

Finally, the BeatStep has no visual display, and in my experience with some of the other budget equipment I've used, this becomes a limiting factor pretty quickly. For example, how do you use the BeatStep to sequence other gear via MIDI or CV if you have no visual readout of the BPM setting? Or, if you want to transpose a sequence by 5 semitones, how can you tell how far you've turned the knob without a display? I think the original BeatStep had the bones of a much more powerful controller and sequencer, but Arturia left out just a few important things that could have taken it to another level. This appears to be part of the lesson that led to the BeatStep Pro, although that's a notably more expensive device at about $250 U.S.

CONCLUSION - Despite everything it's missing, I really like what the BeatStep offers as a controller, and think I might enjoy some of the sequencing features as well. Considering I got it for not much more than the price of a Korg NanoKontrol2, there's really a lot to like here. Also, the software editor is one of the more straightforward experiences I've had with a piece of hardware, and that's a big help. The BeatStep doesn't do everything, but I've found that what it does do is handled efficiently and reliably in an attractive package.

UPDATE (09/26/16): It's been a frustration of mine that the pads on the BeatStep are a bit stiff and really require a firm touch to register. I'm not talking about "touch velocity" - they definitely sense velocity, but it seems like you should be able to configure it so that even very light touches register as hits, and I haven't really figured that out yet. Considered downgrading to 4 stars, but I'm not doing that yet because there's a lot of other good things about this controller, and I suspect it might be user error or my own inexperience with pads talking. But I am considering a used Korg nanoKontrol (the 2006 model) or another option.
Summary: Solidly built MIDI Controler with 16 knobs, 16 pads, and some bonus sequencing capabilities

Note that this is not intended for road use, and there is no front or rear cover.

Roland, in its TASCAM line, produces broadcast-quality (maybe low-end studio quality) audio recorders. I've used a couple of DR-40s for this purpose for several years, and loved them. (I also own a DR-44WL, which I'm not as happy with, but it also does the job.)

The R-07 audio recorder seems to derive features from the high-end line, in an everyday consumer package. The microphones are fixed-placement, but do the job of capturing high-quality audio. If you're used to one of the TASCAM recorders, the interface on the R-07 will be very familiar. The concept of pressing RECORD twice (first for standby and leveling, then again to start the virtual transport) is second nature to me, but I had a learning curve. It will certainly trip up someone who thinks they're already recording.

I can also picture some confusion for people new to the interface when they've recorded more than one track, then look for their first track. Time spent with the manual will be rewarding.

Like all of Roland's devices, this recorder includes a small, but serviceable, playback speaker. It's good for checking whether you got a track or not (see "standby" above), and you won't want to use it to play back a music track to a roomful of listeners—but that's okay.

I can picture carrying this in my pocket for spontaneous capture. It's not nearly as heavy or bulky as a DR-40 (which actually is only large by comparison with this unit), and I can picture the two AA-size batteries running down more quickly than the three on the DR-40. But it's easy to take out of a pocket and startup. Just remember to push that RECORD button twice!

Using a camera with a huge piece of glass and a big sensor is a huge advantage, especially once you find a good way to mount the camera on either a tilt/pan tripod or a nice handheld rig.

Given how ungainly DSLRs are to keep steady when handholding, the bulk of the DR-60D will only exacerbate things when attached to the bottom of the camera. As others have suggested, mounting it above or to the side is much easier to deal with.

I use a semi-cheap steady-cam rig and the extra weight of this and the microphones affect the ability to use this at all. Until I can come up with a better steady-cam rig, I may have to make a microphone hat and attach the DR-60D to my belt! :D

One thing I love about the recorder is the ability to use XLR microphones. Before, all I could ever use were cheap unbalanced mikes and the extra sound quality really shows.

The safety track feature is fantastic and will save my butt, I'm sure.

The recorder is very easy to use. Buttons are placed intelligently and the display lets me see what's happening easily. The configuration menus are easy to understand too.

The battery compartment is a bit flimsy, but has held up ok. Changing the SD card and batteries are both fast and easy to do.

One thing I've wanted for a long time is a portable digital recorder for going to concerts where taping is allowed. The DR-60D will work perfectly for that. I can mount a couple of XLR mikes on either side of the recorder and use either a monopod or small tripod so I don't annoy my neighbors.

I was very happy to find this recorder and I plan on making it a tool I use regularly.
Summary: Great way to improve audio quality when recording video with a DLSR.

Since my review is less than 5 stars, I'll start off with my only complaint (but...there is a Happy Ending).

The Bridge pickup in this Fleor "Zebra" Humbucker set was miswired ! I should note that before separating the Red/White "tap" wires, the pickup did measure about 15k as advertised, but...I separated the Red/White "tap" wires so I could measure the Inductance and DC Resistance for each coil. The Black/White coil was "open" (same for the Red/Green coil). Based on many sources and reviews, Fleor Humbuckers follow the Duncan wiring scheme and color codes. So, the Black/White wires should go to one coil, and the Red/Green wires to the other coil. The Duncan wiring matched the neck pickup, and, another set of Fleor Humbuckers I purchased, so I am sure the Bridge pickup was miswired.

I was considering returning the set, but my curiousity (and impatience) got the best of me ! I carefully disassembled the pickup, and was able to swap the wires from the individual coils to the correct wires on the cable. I wasn't 100% sure about the phase of the individual coil wires (Start/Finish windings), but I guess I got lucky, because after reassembling the pickup and installing the set in the guitar, they sounded great and there were no "out of phase" problems !!!

Hopefully this situation is not very common. I'm glad I was able to fix the issue, and I would purchase the same pickups again due to the excellent sound quality and relatively low cost.

I bought a handful of these to see if they can help keep some of my heavier guitar straps secured. I tried 7 guitars and it only provides a modicum of usefulness on my acoustic. The problems using them are as follows:
1) Will not work with leather straps, or straps with leather ends, due to tolerance between strap and guitar and button head.
2) Hole designed for easy on/off installation is too small for almost all of my guitars. Had to remove the buttons and put it between the strap and head and screw it back on... pointless.
3) When I do finally manage to get the part on my Danelectro that has smaller plastic buttons, it comes off after a few minutes because it doesn't "lock" in, it relies on friction.. also pointless.
4) The piece is made of two thin pieces of plastic which come apart when attempting to install. Again this is due to the tolerance, but also the weakness of design holding the pieces together.
5) One broke when trying to install on another guitar, because of its brittle plastic material make-up.

After dicking around with these for a couple of hours, I finally decided it was less trouble to remove the buttons and use a few appropriate sized zinc washers and rubber donut gaskets. Cost about .15c each. Just screw the button with strap and the washers back on and done.

Chalk this one up to a clever idea poorly executed by Jim Dunlop. DO NOT BUY!!

-Glenn

I have been playing a Vox Mini-Super Beatle for a couple of years now and I liked it a lot but I have been wanting to check out the Tweedy since it came out. One of the things I was curious about was comparing the Nu-Tube preamp to the 12AX7 preamp. I can get some pretty cool sounds out of the Vox but it only has one channel and you have to do a bit of fiddling around to go from clean to drive. I also like the tremolo on the Vox but not the Reverb. I just wish it had more reverb than it does. The Tweedy has two channels that are foot switchable and it comes with the foot switch. The channels are adjustable independently and have some cool features. The gain and volume are what you expect but they also have voice and tone knobs. The tone knobs go from a low boost or high cut counterclockwise to a high boost or no cut clockwise. Very much like tone knobs on my Epiphone Les Paul. So no bass mid and treble but a sweeping tone adjustment that works and is easy to use. The voice controls how clean or dirty it sounds. All the way counter clockwise is clean and the more clockwise you go the grittier it gets. I match the volume of each channel and then play around with switching to the second channel for choruses. I don’t have any pedals yet so I’m just playing around. The Tweedy is just easier to play around with because of the second channel. I am considering running the Vox in the effects loop to play with it’s tremolo. Overall I am really happy with it and I think I will pick up the Jackman as well.
3/13/2023 Update: I put the Vox in the effects loop and it worked but added mud that I didn’t like. That is the last time I have used it. I have been playing through the Tweedy since the day I got it. I might sell the Vox if I had another extension cabinet. I also put a WGS ET10 speaker in the Vox cabinet and I like it a lot too. It didn’t change the tone much but it comes in a lot clearer at low volume and I live in an apartment so I don’t play too loud.
Summary: Loads of fun for a low price!

I’m a professional musician, conductor, and teacher of 40+ years. But I’m a wind player with only presentable bass skills and no chorded string skills. I’ve tried to learn guitar for 50 years but always give up due tiny fingers and hands. Enter the 4-string strummed instruments. Much better success.

I bought the Rogue bari some years back to learn chord shapes in “Chicago tuning” which happens to work for tenor banjo to rhythm off beats. It worked for that purpose but mostly stayed unplayed as my “for fun” choice. The poorer quality of the money saver just made it hard to play. I know better - I keep making the same mistake. I’m glad I chose to step up to the Kala.

Enter this KA-B; the difference is just staggering. It’s easy to play and most importantly it’s fun to play. The tone and projection are super nice and perfect for parlor playing.

The build quality is great. It’s a ply body but you’d not know it from the finish. I can’t speak to tone, this is the highest model Uke I’ve played. I suspect solid top and sides is better but that price is $100s more. The stock strings are clear and bright. The factory set-up is great! Action is near perfect, intonation is spot on. I truly like the closed tuners which hold the strings pretty well as stretchy strings go.

I appreciate that they shipped it with string tension off but if you’re new, tuning it up will make you nervous. It’s not supposed to ship tuned - that’ll damage the neck.

What it’s really good for: it’s a small four nylon string guitar. The tuning is identical to the four small strings on any guitar. It’s great for parlor playing and songwriting. Fits small hands and short fingers beautifully. It’s ideal for learning the chord shapes that also apply to tenor/plectrum Chicago tuned banjo and to tenor guitar. It’s quiet enough to be a good hotel practice instrument but loud enough for parlor playing.

What it’s not: it’s not the smaller ukuleles and is tuned differently and isn’t reentrant tuning you expect from ukulele. The same chord shapes work though, they just produce a different chord. Ie: C on the soprano/concert is G on the bari. It’s likely not ideal as “beginner ukulele” since it differs in tone/timbre as well as fingering. Reentrant tuning is part of what makes a ukulele and the baritone is linear - sound is very different.

I’ve immediately ordered the KA-TK-T tenor to cover that “ukulele sound” adding to my very old Harmony soprano banjolele. I may get a KA concert in the future.

It is just so pleasant to play it’s going to stay out on a stand for random pick up. Kala did an awesome job here.

Hint: I IV V covers a ton of tunes. That’d be G C and D in G major. Three easy chords and you’re playing lots of songs. If you’re playing alone in parlor play, the key doesn’t matter - the chord progression is all that maters.

To start with; if your concept of making music is to sit down on the couch and tap pads, changing sounds and making short patterns to chain together; this is the device for you. If instead you also enjoy playing a regular midi keyboard, you can work with this device too; although you start to loose portability in that way, and start to add cables and a midi keyboard to the setup.

This is more of a portable travel "idea maker" device. You drop beats on it, maybe a few synth patterns and then move to the next. There is no concept of track here; there are "parts". Each pad is a part, and you can assign a different sound to it. When you tap the pad, the sound play at C3 I believe. You can make variations in various ways: you can use the touchpad, to move up and down a scale you set in the preferences, you can use the keyboard mode, which transform the 16 pads in a sequence of notes (using the same scale you set in preferences; each row is an octave, so can't use the upper row for black keys). or you plug a midi keyboard in.

Each part can be either a synth part, a sample or a rhythm part, like drums, percussion or what else; you have no limitations, except that some samples or instruments takes more than one "voice", and the device support 24 voices max at the same time. But there is a gotcha: when you use effects, this steal a voice, so while you think you can play 24 concurrent notes, that may not be true if you use effects on each of the parts.

The variety of sounds is OK; the main problem is that you can't add sounds, synth engines, samples or anything else. Everything is set in stone, so you may want to hear the sounds included in the ROM of the device, to get an idea if this is what you want. There is a variant of this device that is called "sampler"; which allow you to use your own samples; but you cannot add more synth presets, so the sampler is more for musicians that need a sampler box, more than a synth.

You don't have songs per se, you make a pattern, which is 4 bars at most. This is huge as limitation, considering that you can only slow down tempo to get more notes, but the notes are quantized by default, so you have very little room for anything that is not the canonical 4 step beat. You can work around this limitation by chaining different patterns, and make longer patterns, but there is no way to make a song per se. You can chain pattern A to B, but if you want to add pattern C, you have to chain it to pattern B, and so on. If you have 10 patterns, each of them has to chain to the next, and this means to chain each one singularly. I hope you won't change your mind later, because then you have to change the assignment for the chained patters!
This kill productivity, unless you always worked with patterns in such way; I use a DAW most of the time so for me, this is quite the mood killer, when putting together a fully fledged song. Not sure why they didn't put a chain sequence mode, where you put patterns in a chain and save it as song; but sadly Korg is well known for abandoning early the development of the software for their devices, so unless you can get the firmware unlocked and deciphered, the last update you get is from 2016

Synth sounds are OK; you get the basic sound shapes, plus mix of different types of shapes with effects and such; there are some digital instruments too like brass and piano, but nothing to write home about. As synth, this device is not worth much to be honest. The sound can be changed a bit, but all you get is pitch variation and a wave morph dial. The rest of the work has to be done on filters, which are pretty nice with 3 different categories of filters, then you have envelopes and effects; which can give you some good results, at the cost of voice stealing though, since some if not most of the effects, take voices.
In short, if you get this for its synth capabilities, you are better off getting a minilogue XD to be honest. this is not what this device was made for.

Of course this does not mean that you can't make great music, but you have to be creative, and work around the limitations of the device. Portability is great, and with 6 AA batteries and a pair of headphones you are good to go. The SD card slot allow you to save and load patterns, but not sounds. The sampler model can load samples from the SD card. The USB port allow you to connect your electribe to the computer, to use it as midi device if you like. You can get 16 channels output and play each part separately from the device, via midi, but keep in mind that USB does not transmit audio, so you still need to connect the stereo L R cables to your computer to grab the audio signal.

If that's your thing, then this device is a great alternative to more expensive and less portable grooveboxes (the Roland for example is a much better device but it cost also much more than this); but if you want to use this connected to the computer as module, for its sounds, then you can get probably much better modules with much better sounds on other products. This device is mainly for the person on the go that makes very specific type of music.

Text:
EDITED Feb 2015 - revised to positive review because (read below):

I originally gave this a 2 star review because a corner bit on the plastic cover that wraps around the rails broke when i was going to install it, so I never installed it at that time. I still contend, that the plastic bits should be sturdier so as not to break when I accidentally bump pickup into pick guard while installing (it was a solid 'bump', but not anything I would have expected to break a pickup cover!). That was the substance of my original review - 2 stars, based on having never installed it.

I have since managed to super-glue the plastic bit back on and installed it in the neck position of a homebrew (ie: built from near-scratch by me) guitar. I must say, I am just ridiculously incredibly happy with how this sounds. It is AMAZING - better than any factory pickup I've played in any guitar ever. This is my new favorite budget pickup (by a mile), and I'd have to spend a whole ton more to get one I think I'd like better. I would describe the sounds (in the neck position anyway, haven't tried it anywhere else) with adjectives like thick, rich, sultry, hot, smoky, boozy, sexy, steamy, sweaty, bold, and from there I would just keep going until this wasn't a family friendly review. Playing it through my Vox stomp-lab into a vaguely decent stereo system with the volume set at medium-loud and gain/drive on the stomp-lab at about 2 or 3 on a 10 scale, the experience is just screaming hot sexy goodness. It's also incredibly responsive for a ceramic magnet pickup too - I can instantly access sounds from almost totally clean to in-your-face-right-now just by going easy (or hard) on my pick attack. Usually that kind of awesome stuff only happens on lower output Alnico based pickups, and ceramics tend to be 'one sound, all the time'.

Anyway, it would get 5 stars from me now, but i still ding it 1 star for the broke plastic bit.

Oh, one other thing to note (that I don't consider a negative at all), is that they say these are like 5kohm resistance. My volt/ohm meter says it's more like 10 or 11. kohm's is a lousy method of evaulating pickups, and these sound pure awesome, so why would you care? I don't know, but if you do, these are hotter than 5kohm by a lot.

Enjoy.
Summary: Sounds AWESOME, but be careful when installing, plastic bits are flimsy and easy to break.

This is a quick release capo by Kyser which you'll see on many, many professional's fretted instruments. They really are the industry standard with a great price. There are definitely other styles of capos and some of them definitely work better, opinions vary. But as far as ease of use, this is the one, and this being a banjo capo, it works well.

The trouble with capos, as briefly I can explain, is they make the instrument sharp. And I'm afraid, again opinions vary, that the tighter the capo clamps, the sharper the strings go. Kysers clamp VERY hard, likely in order to ensure that the strings never 'fret out" or make a ticky noise. And they never do with a Kyser. But out of all my capos, and I've tried most everything, they do make the strings go the most sharp.

Now, the simplest solution to that is to put the capo on and then tune the guitar, and if you're lucky enough to have a tech to do this for you, be thou blessed, you will be precisely in tune and your singer and keyboard player will never complain. Also, in solo performance, what the heck if you go a little sharp, you're the one singing, just sing a little higher. And when you are recording, you'll have time to tune with the capo on. The thing that gets some people about quick release capos is that they are designed to be changed from fret to fret easily, so folks want to do that because it's so easy, and then you get with your band and they call you you out for being out of tune. So it can kind of negate the purpose of the "quick change". Also note that generally, the flatter your frets, the less the sharpness. But to me, a little sharpness can sound even worse than a lot when playing with a band that is exactly in tune. Just something to know if you are new to using capos.

This is a banjo capo, and I've found the sharpness there, but not nearly as bad as a guitar with my particular banjo. Banjos can be a bit persnickety with tuning anyway, and the solid, tight clamp will actually help. So get this. Everybody needs a Kyser in their capo collection. If you don't like it, you didn't pay much for it. Oh and singers, if you've never experimented with capo changes, you're gonna love this.
Summary: Kyser is the industry standard today.

These mics are ok for the beginner home studio if you are just looking to get your drumming ideas recorded. They are also fine for recording practices with your band. They are also fine if you are going to use them for mic-ing your drums live at shows and putting them into the mix a little, as I used the kick drum mic from this 4 pack placed into the kick drum and would send it to our PA to beef up the kick during live performances. Just keep in mind these mics require xlr plugs. So if your mixer does not have xlr jacks, these mics will be useless to you. That being said, I would not try to record a demo or an album with these mics. The highs fall off very fast on these mics after about 10khz. This leaves you with a very dull and unlively recorded drum sound. These make terrible overhead mics for drums. They will sound decent if you use each mic as a close mic to only one drum, however you will still need to use some better condenser mics for overheads to brighten up your highs (cymbals) and liven up your sound. Generally I find these mics to be very dull (even with equalization), flat, cold, sterile, and unlively sounding. They are not bad sounding or awful, they just arent going to give you the warmth or liveliness you are looking for when recording drums for professional recordings. I think you could get a better recorded sound with two decent large diaphragm condenser mics (like two AT-2020 ($90 each, or two MXL990 $70 each) used as overheads and a cheap dynamic or condenser mic shoved in the kick drum. Those three mics would produce a better sound than these four mics for not much more money. Of course you would also need stands too though. So though this is the cheapest way to get your drums recorded, I think spending a little more on two decent overheads with stands is a better choice with better results and will get you farther down the road in your recording endeavors.

The Good:
Cheap, I paid 149 for my 4 pack and that includes four mics and three sets of mounting clips. They are a cheap way to be able to record your whole drum kit. They have excellent noise rejection and do not pick up background noise much at all. They are easy to use and set up. They are also smooth sounding and never get shrill, and do not distort easy. They also feel very solid and durable. Ive had mine for years with no issue.
The Bad:
They are extremely flat sounding. They are also dull sounding due to the highs cutting off at 10khz. Not very lively sounding when used for recording. They are ok for recording things in the low to mid range like toms and kick drum, but are too dull for a good snare sound and suck for the recording of cymbals. You will still need a decent set of overhead mics if you want to get a decent recorded drum sound.
Summary:
These mics are good for using to mic your drums for live applications. They resist high sound levels, distortion, and dont feed back easily. They are well made. They are also ok for a practice studio or rehearsals.
These mics are not good for recording anything that you would want to put out in public such as a demo or album. You will need better mics for that. You get what you pay for, and your not paying much here for four mics with mounting hardware.
Summary: The cheapest way to get your drums mic-ed, but not great by themselves for recording.

I was shopping for a set of speakers for a computer I have in my university office. The speakers that were currently there were OK Logitech (apx. $50) computer speakers. They were alright for what they were but as I move more music applications to that computer (it essentially is becoming a mini-DAW), I knew I needed much better speakers if I was going to seriously use it for music creation purposes. First, I looked on Amazon with a search for something like "small bookshelf speakers". I found a number of highly rated speakers that I had never heard of before. Looking through the reviews of those speakers it became clear to me that most of the reviewers had no idea about what they were referencing when they made "professional sounding" remarks about things like "body", "boom". "treble response", "bass response", "roominess", etc. Oddly, in one of the listings, the little Amazon "you may like this insert" was the PreSonus Eris 3.5 speakers. After looking at many of the Chinese no-name speakers in the $75 - $100 price range, finally, a name that I knew and respected. As an musician, engineer and producer, I have had used many PreSonus products, and the main DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) is a PreSonus Product (Studio One Pro 5). When I saw the price of $99, I immediately looked for reviews from professional music sources that I trusted. As one would suspect, given the brand name "PreSonus", the reviews were more than spectacular for a small speaker with a 3.5" woofer and a 1" dome tweeter. Nobody would expect such a speaker to have tremendous bass response, but looking at some of the representative frequency response curved obtained from "real" spectral analyzer equipment and decent microphone capsules, it was amazing to me how flat the bass response was down to 80Hz. While that may not sound impressive, the KRK V6 monitors in my studio are only as flat down to about 60HZ! That, I did find amazing. Also, in the upper end, the frequency response of the Eris 3.5s was remarkable, considering their price. I guess that inclusion of the same 1" dome tweeter that PreSonus uses in some of its larger "real-size" studio monitors may account for that. At any rate, after seeing all of the glowing reviews from sources I trust, I decided to buy a pair. Well, they arrived today and I wasted no time setting them up on a "work computer" in my studio that was similar to the one in my office. After playing a number of tracks through them (some of my own productions included) I was amazed at just how good the little speakers sounded. For the hell of it, I also ran them with an old 10" Mackie subwoofer I had sitting around. After acoustically balancing the setup for it odd position in my studio, when I heard the overall response I immediately concluded that I could definitely mix using them. They were that good. Text:
First thing I notice when I take this ukulele out of the box is that it has a nice smooth organic body shape. The body looks like smooth plastic. It does not have a woven look like I expect from carbon fiber. Some other ukulele brands are made out of woven carbon fiber (like Klos and Blackbird). This one looks like it is mostly plastic with maybe a small fraction of loose non-woven carbon fibers mixed in to the plastic. The ukulele feels and sounds more like plastic than carbon fiber.

Second thing I notice is that the ukulele is very heavy. My kitchen scale says the weight is about 1 pound 12 ounces, which is very heavy for a concert-scale ukulele. Other concert-scale ukuleles that I own are 1 pound even and 1 pound 2 ounces. This one is 75% heavier. That extra weight makes the ukulele harder to handle, especially if you like playing up and down the fretboard.

On the plus side, this ukulele does appear to be sturdily built so it should survive most bumps and bruises. It should also be more resistant to heat and humidity than a typical wooden ukulele. The metal frets should be more durable than the plastic frets that some budget-priced plastic ukuleles. Plastic frets can wear out in a couple of years of just normal use.

On the minus side, the sound quality is at best mediocre. The product photos say the ukulele has "carbon" strings, which I assume means fluorocarbon, which will generally give an ukulele a bright lively sound. However, the product description says the strings are really nylon, not "carbon". To my fingers, the strings feel thicker and softer than fluorocarbon strings, which could contribute to the less lively sound and feel. I played and re-tuned the ukulele every day for a week and the tuning still felt unstable. Most new ukuleles will settle down for me in 2-3 days, but this one still sounds muddy after a full week.

In summary, Amazon sells many different plastic ukuleles. This one is more expensive and better looking than most others, but sound quality is mediocre at best. Considering these flaws, I think the $150 list price for this ukulele is high for what you get. I wish they put more effort into improving the sound quality. Most of the time, a lighter weight ukulele body gives the ukulele a more lively and vibrant sound quality.
Summary: nice looking ukulele, probably durable, but heavy and sound quality is not great

What's not to love? Right out of the box observations; The case is a heavy duty coated metal possibly anodized aluminum or a powder coated stainless. The manufacturer states, "Material: Aluminum alloy with stoving vanish (sic)" Definitely not plastic EXCEPT for the chintzy battery compartment cover. The potentiometers are first rate; they are made of a non ferrous metal with just the right amount of stiffness when you turn them. The frequency HI - LOW toggle switch is the best quality; you can just feel and hear the quality when flipping it up and down. And, the toggle switch is protected, surrounded by 3 burly soldiers named Gain, Tone and Level. Just like the OCD, of which this pedal supposedly is a clone and has been sufficiently tested and compared and 'proven' by others. Some very expensive pedal manufacturers leave that skinny little toggler right next to the KICK SWITCH!! In fact, I almost bought the hot tubes nano.

The bypass switch has just the right feel, as well. So the knobs themselves are plastic but I took one off to see how they are put together. There is a metal set screw into a threaded metal insert that is embedded in the knob.

The performance is an overdrive with a capital OVER. The manufacturer states, "It is intermediate between distortion and overdrive.." For my taste, I run the Gain at less than 9:00, the Level just under 10:00, and the Tone between 1:00 and 3:00 when I play my Les Paul. I haven't tried this box with my Telecaster yet. Plenty of gain for any shredders I predict.

This is not the first Chinese pedal I have bought (I will leave the moralistic guilts to others as well), but it is by far the best made, even better that some USA made boxes. That is, if the Joyo Ultimate Drive endures. Only time will tell on that. In the event of any failure I will do a follow up. But so far I would say for 30 bucks this is the bargain of the year.

[[VIDEOID:ae0b1e9370f98f0a233a94c700ab03c7]] Yamaha is a great company that offers very judicious clean sound. I suppose it’s a Japanese aesthetic. In this video I am presenting the piano with the sound coming out of the piano itself as well as out of a Bose speaker connected to my logic pro Bösendorfer patch. As a physical instrument, this piano plays like a real piano and the response of the piano is very much like a real piano in terms of dynamics and wait realism. When you hit the bottom the entire keyboard rumbles. This is how it should be and this is not how it happens when you play piano patches on midi through this same keyboard. I just wish it had a control on ambience and reverb because it feels a bit dry. So I plugged it into my logic program and use Bösendorfer piano patch that by default comes with a bit of reverb and ambience. This is what you’re hearing. When you plug this piano into a MIDI situation, and try to hit the low and rumble the whole keyboard it will not happen. That is why I use a combination of the sounds. In a recording session you could just out from the keyboard and adjust for reverb & ambience. You have to like and prefer the clean sound of the Yamaha piano as opposed to the Steinway or other pianos to enjoy this instrument as an instrument in itself. The piano does not offer sounds that come incidentally with a piano such as the noise from pressing pedal or the noise from dampening the strings or the noise from the keys, which you might find on other midi patches.

EDIT UPDATE: need to revise my negative stance on the reverb quality of this instrument. Like any instrument, the effects happen at different intensities based on volume output. Put the piano at about 70% volume, which is where I think it behaves correctly. You will get the sufficient reverb expected from a piano. Make it softer, and like anything else it will give you less effect. I love this instrument. I absolutely love it.

Note for Stereo Out:
