I've been playing ukulele for several years and own some ukuleles that cost more than $1000 each. This Lankro ukulele is a mixed bag. 10 years ago, I would say that an ukulele of this quality was a great value for the $65 price (I got the soprano size). In the last couple of years, however, quality control of these made-in-China ukuleles has improved a lot. My review here is a comparison of the Lankro ukulele to other ukuleles that Amazon sells for less than $100.

Overall specs:
- The ukulele comes with a lightly padded gig bag that has one sling strap and one small pocket. The accessories are basic quality; only the tuner looks really useful to me.
- Scale length is 13.5 inches and total length is 21 inches; both are typical of soprano ukuleles.
- Ukulele is relatively lightweight (15 ounces) making it easy to play without a strap.
- A strap button is pre-installed at the bottom of the ukulele. Strangely, the included strap is a cheap clip-on style that does not fit on the strap button. If you want to use a strap, I would buy a guitar or mandolin style strap that attaches to the strap button on one and and ties around the headstock on the other end.
- The ukulele uses a string-through bridge. This style of bridge is becoming more popular on ukuleles and is also used on some guitars. Don't believe the review that complains that the bridge is defective. Changing strings on this type of bridge is not difficult. There are plenty of tutorials on YouTube.

Plusses compared to other ukuleles in this price range:
- The installed strings appear to be lightweight nylon, rather than the white Aquila strings that most name-brand beginner-level ukuleles use. I actually think the nylon strings are easier for beginners to play and they produce a pleasing sound. If you want to switch them for Aquila, read my previous paragraph about string-through bridges.
- Intonation (the strings play the correct notes at different frets up the fretboard) sound good.
- Gloss finish is attractive (to me anyway).
- Solid mahogany soundboard does sound more vibrant and multi-dimensional than the plywood soundboards that you usually find in this price range.
- Tuning pegs work smoothly.

Minuses compared to other ukuleles in this price range:
- Some people will say the classical guitar style headstock is attractive, but the wood is thicker and heavier than standard ukulele headstocks. The ukulele feels top-heavy and out-of-balance when I play it.
- The ukulele has fret markers installed on the front of the fretboard, but not on the side of the neck. Most ukuleles, even in this price range, have fret markers on the side as well as the front. Side fret markers are especially important for beginners so you can see what frets you are playing without having to look at the front of the instrument.
- The fret ends are sharp and need to be filed down. If you buy an ukulele from a real music store, the store will take care of this, but Amazon does not. This job is not hard to do yourself if you are careful.
- String action (height of the strings above the fretboard) is 1.2mm at the first fret and 2.5mm at the 12th fret. 1.2mm at the first fret is very high and makes the instrument hard to play, especially for beginners. Fixing this is difficult without expertise and expensive tools. If your instrument has this problem, I recommend returning it or taking to a good ukulele or guitar store who can fix it for you (for a fee).
- The neck is 35mm wide at the nut with a rounded C-shape. A lot of cheaper imported ukuleles use this shape neck, but I prefer necks that are wider (37 or 38mm wide) and flatter shaped like you see on most American brands as well as many better quality import brands.

Conclusion:
I would have given this ukulele 5 stars for value if it had inlayed side fret markers and the string action was set up better and the fret ends were filed smooth and the neck was wider. The main body of the ukulele is attractive and appears to be well made from good materials. The company just needs to spend more time on the finishing touches since fixing these issues are difficult for customers, especially beginners. Amazon sells lots of other brands of ukuleles and many of them are doing much better on these details.
Summary: needs a setup, no side fret markers, narrow neck width

I want to make clear that this review is of the Mackie Mix5, which is the smallest and most affordable of the Mix series (the review page is combined between the Mix5, Mix8, and Mix12FX, but the latter two have some additional bells and whistles that the Mix5 does not have). So if you are like me and have a very elementary knowledge of mixers, hopefully this review of this excellent budget mixer will be of some help!

I had two primary reasons for seeking out an affordable mixer. First, I am a guitar player and effects pedal enthusiast, and there are a series of preamp pedals (Tech21 SansAmp/Tri-AC/Character; Joyo Sound series) that are designed to go directly to a mixer and played through studio monitors or a PA. I have a single M-Audio BX5 studio monitor but had the realization: "Wait, how would I even hook up a second one?" Second, I have an assortment of iOS music apps, ranging from virtual synthesizers, to drum machines, to guitar modelers, and needed a better way to play those apps through the same studio monitor(s). To a lesser degree, I also was interested in the XLR hookup to use with dynamic or condenser microphones (but with some limitations on the Mix5, which I will discuss).

The Mix5 is solidly constructed. It has a mostly metal casing, and is more compact than some of the similarly-priced alternatives from Harbinger and Behringer. The Mix5 ships with an 18V power supply unit, though as many people have noted, there is no On/Off power switch. This is an annoyance, but the unit is so compact, that I suspect many people will only bring it out when they want to use it anyway.

The dashboard is fairly straightforward and free from clutter. They promote the mixer has having 5 channels, though 2/3 and 4/5 are stereo inputs, so it is arguably more like 3 channels. Channel 1 accepts either an XLR mic input or an instrument cable (guitar, etc.). There is also a bass/treble EQ control, which is nice for an entry-level mixer. One thing I noticed about using the guitar through the mixer was that there was considerably more volume available as compared to running the preamp pedals directly into the speaker. Of course, the mixer is also a necessity for adding a second speaker and then having a L/R channel setup. The connections can be balanced or unbalanced - in my case, I believe I have a cable that goes from TS (instrument cable) to XLR (plugs into the monitor). If you want a mixer with XLR outputs, consider the Yamaha MG06, which I nearly bought, but which costs over twice as much. Guitar sounded great running through the Mix5, and you can of course throw reverb pedals and other effects in the signal chain before the mixer. I was also pleasantly surprised how good the guitar sounded simply monitoring with headphones - this was something I could not do with that setup before I had a mixer.

The RCA (red/white) in/out connection is quite useful for mixing in different types of audio sources. 3.5mm-to-RCA cables are very inexpensive, and allow you to hook up MP3 players and other audio sources like the aforementioned iPad instruments. The overall sound levels are displayed colorfully by the green/yellow/red display and to help prevent "clipping" of the audio signal.

The drawbacks of this device have been noted in other reviews, and they notable criticisms, but also part of the give-and-take of buying an entry-level device. In addition to no main on/off switch, there is no on/off switch for phantom power. Also, phantom power offered is around 15V, instead of the 48V needed to use many condenser microphones. The Mix5 also does not have any on-board effects, such as offered by the Behringer and Yamaha models for a little more money. Finally, please note that this is a mixer, NOT a recording "interface" with USB output to a computer. If you are looking for a USB interface, I considered the Behringer Q502USB, but decided that I did not need an interface for my PC.

The Mackie Mix5 is very basic, but seems to suit my limited needs perfectly. It retails at $50, so I consider it a great "first mixer", and I would always have the option to upgrade to something with more features, if needed.
Summary: Quality entry-level mixer for combining and balancing audio sources

Who IS this guy, and why does he care about the M350?

I've been a semi-professional live musician for many years, mostly low-key, "house of worship" stuff, but there was also a time when I actually toured the US and Canada as a rhythm guitar player with a contemporary Christian music group. I've never fussed much with big banks of guitar or vocal effects, because the kind of music I do generally doesn't require them. However, in more recent years, I find myself doing a bit more live PA work, both for myself and for other musicians/singers, so my interest in these accessories has increased. What I started looking for in particular was a very simple, rackmount effects processor that would just allow me to do a bit more by way of "warming up" live vocals, e.g., reverb, delay and compression.

Studio vs. Stage

With the explosion of digital recording and "post-production" processing of every kind of media imaginable, something of a split has occurred in the huge variety of audio signal processors available in the market, e.g., between platforms designed for highly controlled, computerized studio and "post-production" work, and platforms designed for "real time" stage and live performance. The TC Electronics M350 can be used in either setting, but its rackmount format and system of external knobs and buttons for control of all its functions is really ideal for "dinosaurs" like me, who don't want to have to haul a laptop computer around just to add a reverb and effects loop to a few channels on their mixer in a live setting. This review is written for all you live stage techs and analog dinosaurs out there who are looking for the same thing, and don't want to negotiate an animated replica of a control panel on a computer screen, or a baffling array of "soft-keys" and LCD/plasma menus whenever you want to change effects or kick the gain up a notch. I'm here to tell ya, the TC Electronic M350 fits that bill.

What the heck does "dual engine" mean?

The M350 is a true "dual engine" device. That means it has two distinct signal processors combined in one unit. One of these processors is dedicated to "effects" and the other one is dedicated to "reverb." That also means that when the M350 is hooked up to the right kind of mixer (e.g., one that has at least two separate "aux" inputs/sends available to dedicate to "efx"), the amount of "effects" and "reverb" you're applying to any particular sound source can be separately controlled at the mixer. The nature, sound and character of the signal processing itself still has to be selected and controlled from the face of the M350. For those of you that don't have such a mixer, or only one aux send available for "efx," you can still access both "engines" in the M350 by setting it up in serial or parallel mode, running both effects through a single aux send/return, and controlling the balance between, and amount of signal processing by each of the individual "engines" from the face of the M350.

The effects "engine"

On the effects side, the M350 provides a total of 15 distinct effects, with potential applications to both instruments and vocals, including several unique delays, chorus, phaser, flange, compression and de-essing. Each of these individual effects can be modified to suit individual tastes, assigned a number between 1 and 99, saved in the M350's memory as a user preset, and then later recalled on demand. Don't be intimidated by all the jargon, however. This thing couldn't be any easier to use. Getting any one effect up and running is as simple as turning the selector knob to the effect you want to hear, and putting the adjustment knobs at 12 o'clock. At this setting, you'll hear the "default" effect, or what the factory guys consider a basic example of the effect you selected. You can then use the adjustment knobs to tinker with this sound if you wish, or if you think the "default" sound is fine, just leave it alone and enjoy. The functions of the adjustment knobs automatically vary, depending on the effect you've selected. There's even a "tap" button on the face of the M350 that allows you to synchronize the timing of your chosen delay with your "real time" playback. Nice touch.

The only problem I noted with the multiple effects provided with the M350 is the fact that you can't combine any of them. You may select and use only one effect at a time. That's not surprising for an "entry level" effects processor like the M350, but it's kind of sad, since many of these are effects you might like to combine, like continuous compression and de-essing on a vocal track/channel, or continuous delay and chorus on a keyboard or guitar. In this particular configuration, however, the only way to combine effects in "real time" is to have multiple M350's in your effects loop. I took off one rating "star" for this limitation, but I admit it could just fall into the "you get what you pay for" category, and not necessarily be a legitimate basis for complaint.

The reverb engine.

The "reverb" side of the M350 operates in the same way as the "effects" side, but the reverbs are really what this gizmo is all about ... a total of 15 "canned" reverb formats, easy to select, use and modify. Check out the detail of the M350's faceplate on the TC Electronic website, if you'd like to see the manufacturer's descriptions of its individual reverb or effects settings. I've tried most of the "default" reverbs through a typical PA/mixer set up, and I thought they were great ... quiet, clean and polished. If you're like me, and just want the ability to quickly and simply put a touch of quiet, quality reverb into any channel on your mixer, you WILL be happy with this product.

The M350 and MIDI

While you can only access one distinct effect or reverb at a time in either of the two processing engines found on the M350, the device is MIDI-compatible, and can receive/send signal in either digital or analog format, so I assume that anyone who wants to incorporate the M350 into some kind of computerized sequencing system can alternate effects and settings in a single playback through a series of MIDI commands, with the same limitation, however. MIDI may allow you to jump from effect to effect, or from reverb to reverb in a single playback track, but you'll still only get one effect/reverb at a time out of the M350. Using MIDI to control a device like the M350 is far too complex a subject to talk about in any detail here ... it's just good to know you can do it if that's your thing.

The bottom line.

The M350 lists at $249, but most of the major music retailers I looked at offer it at $200, which I consider a decent value. If that's a bit rich for your blood, you can probably find a used one for a little less on E-bay, and most of those will be indistinguishable from a new unit, as there really isn't much that can be damaged or fail on a unit that's been properly used in a typical rackmount application. The M350 is solidly constructed, lightweight, provides an effects loop that's silent as a grave, easy to use, looks really cool in your rack, and its connection options, effects and reverbs are all great. Most amateur/casual users will never need much more than what this thing has to offer, and even pros will find it useful for limited applications ... like monitor feeds for those insecure prima donnas who just can't seem to drag themselves on stage without a little "post-EQ" delay and reverb added to their voice ...

For me, this gizmo fit the bill in every respect, and if your goals/needs are similar to mine, I think you'll be satisfied with the M350 too.

When I started looking at the Korg Volca series, the original plan was to own one or both of the Bass and Keys, and then pick a rhythm machine between the (newer) Volca Sample and Volca Beats. So much for that plan - I ended up with all four, and possibly even 5 after the Volca FM becomes more readily available. But the Volca Beats - despite its broad popularity - was the one I had the most questions about and ended up buying last. The verdict? The Volca Beats is an impressive little analog/hybrid drum machine with powerful sounds, but also some notable limitations even beyond some of the functionality constraints common to the whole series.

PROS - Much of what I like about the Volca Beats applies to the other devices in the Volca line. This is a truly analog musical instrument that is 100% portable, powered off 6 AA batteries for about 10 hours (or an AC adapter sold separately). The housing, while largely plastic, is extremely well-executed, and the device feels like a quality product, even relative to the $160 street price. The ribbon keyboard, while a bit clunky for the pitch-based instruments, actually responds quite well for live tapping and programming rhythm patterns. There is even 5-pin DIN MIDI input (though no real velocity control that I am aware of) for hooking up a separate keyboard, pads, or a sequencer - impressive at this price point.

The ribbon keyboard has 16 buttons, but actually only 10 sounds. Six of those (Kick, Snare, Lo Tom, Hi Tom, CL Hat, and OP Hat) are truly analog, and can be easily tweaked with a series of corresponding knobs on the dash. The remaining 4 sounds (Clap, Claves, Agogo, Crash) are basically PCM samples, and you can't do much with them other than adjust their playback speed. I wasn't impressed by the PCM sounds, but only use those instruments pretty sparingly anyway.

The kick drum and toms sound amazing, and the pitch and decay control allow you to vary things quite a bit. Going off of ear, I estimate that you get perhaps an octave-and-a-half of pitch range (around 18 semitones, maybe) in each of the toms. I hear more "808" than "909" similarity in these sounds, but it has a nice character of its own. In reading other reviews, I suspect that a lot of people might end up with the Volca Beats as a "first drum machine", and that's great. But it also leads to some confusion about what "analog" sounds are and what style of music the Beats is best suited for. The Beats certainly has a electronic or "synthesis" approach to drums - if you are buying it expecting it to sound like a "rock drummer in a box", you're likely to be disappointed. More on the snare drum in the "CONS" section below...

Wrapping up the positives of this device, I thought the audio quality and output level through the headphone jack was fully acceptable. While I would need to experiment with recording some more to determine if it's truly "line level" output, it certainly can power a quality pair of headphones through the 3.5mm jack, and while there may be some faint hissing or extraneous noise in the background, it's totally acceptable and impressive how good it is at this price. As with the other Volcas, several of analog instrument parameters can be "recorded" or "automated" during play back. So, for example, you could have a Tom that changes pitch from steps 1 to 16, or a hat that changes decay length throughout the pattern. Unfortunately, I don't believe you can automate "part volume" to do volume swells with particular instruments, though you can use that knob to set levels for the different instruments, kind of like a primitive mixer.

CONS - While my review of the build quality and sound quality of the Volca Beats is largely positive, there are two main issues that stick out as significant problems with the Volca Beats, enough to lower this review to a 4-star rating. First, as has been noted in great detail by many others, the snare drum is an abject disaster. It seems far-fetched to me that a reputable company like Korg would actually release a finished product with an accidental production error (such as completely omitting a part from the circuitry), but when you hear the snare drum, you wonder if that might be the case. I don't mean to imply that the snare is completely unusable - with the snappy and decay knobs set around 12:00, you get a short, percussive snare sound that is passable, albeit very limited in scope and a bit weak in output. Turn up the decay knob and it becomes a horror show mess of static and noise. Again, I'm not a expert at drum machines or drum synthesis, but I've heard synthesized snares in many other drum programs, and it can be done much better than this. It's an unfortunate oversight because the kick drum and toms are actually surprisingly good.

Second, the Beats is just a bit too limited in functionality to be a fully practical songwriting tool. The programming is largely married to 4/4 time and 16 steps, though you can trick it to 3/4 time by using active step and trimming the loop down to 12 steps. You can only save 8 drum patterns on the device, and there is no song mode. So, while you can absolutely record off the device and manually switch between intro, verse, chorus, and fill patterns that you create, it isn't the most practical workflow you could imagine. Especially given the fact that you can buy a fully functional drum app for $5 to $20 on iPad/iPhone with far greater synthesis and sampling capabilities plus a detailed sequencer with song mode, and record it with the 3.5mm cable or an audio interface.

There are some other omissions, as well. There is no "ACCENT" feature, which was a key feature on the 808 and other popular drum machines. The tweakable parameters will always affect playback, so if you switch from Pattern 1 to Pattern 2, I believe that Pattern 2 will just start playing using whatever knob settings you had inputted for Pattern 1.

VOLCA BEATS VS. VOLCA SAMPLE - As I mentioned in the intro, I actually bought the Volca Sample first, and I think if I had to own one or the other, I would stick with the Sample. While the Sample is criticized for memory limitations and being "only" able to store around 100 instruments, that's still about 90 more than you have on the Volca Beats. Also, the Sample has neat functionality with pitched samples, so you could do some basslines and melodies, in addition to rhythm parts. Still, I ended up purchasing the Beats anyway, because there is something very fun and straightforward about a dedicated drum machine that allows you to fine elements of drum synthesis in a very portable enclosure. The Sample offers a more diverse experience and is arguably the more "useful" of the two, but the Beats remains a very enjoyable drum machine with a character of its own.
Summary: Deep, powerful analog/PCM drum machines with a few forehead-slapping limitations

I don't think I can say enough good things about the Samson SP01 Shockmount. Long story short I was trying to get a podcast going from scratch about three months ago. I did some research and discovered that a shockmount is necessary to keep any noise from anything securing the mic from being picked up by the mic while recording. A shockmount is an absolute must, especially when looking at using a tabletop mic stand where the table will also be used as a work surface.

The build quality is fantastic. I just recently purchased my THIRD shockmount for an additional mic to be used on the podcast.

What I've grown to appreciate so much is that it seems to fit just about any condenser microphone I can get my hands on. If you are considering buying this for your own condenser mic, make absolutely sure that your mic has threads on the bottom to be screwed into some type of stand or shockmount. Nearly all do, but some companies like Blue (Snowball, snowflake, etc.) are designed not to be used in conjunction with shock mounts. I have used the MXL 007.USB with this shockmount as well as the AT2020 USB and XLR version. The MXL fit like a glove, perfect. The AT2020, once threaded in, seemed just a bit loose, so I added a couple foam bumpers around the base to act as a washer. It made a tight fit and further insulated it from any sound interference from any movement.

In short, I haven't found a better shockmount for condenser mics. The attachment screws onto any desktop tripod and traditional mic stand. Fantastic. Buy two of these!! :) Thanks Samson, now just make better mics!

The sounds are all pretty dang good, I wanted to see what it sounded like without being colored by my amp so I just plugged right into the headphone port and into my audio interface and it really sounds much better than I expected at this price. The battery seems to do pretty good, I haven't ran it dead, but I would think you could get somewhere from 4-6 hours out of it based on my experience so far. It also includes a nice little travel case that you can throw in your guitar bag/case and not worry about the device getting damaged.

Overall if you are looking for a multi effect unit or headphone amp this is my #1 pick especially considering the price. Of course there are products out there that do everything this does but much better, but they also cost 10x more. For the money I haven't used anything that comes close to the Mooer Prime P1

Text:
Wanted to make an audio upgrade from standard gaming headset to a legit headphone now that I'm PC gaming full time. I had the SteelSeries Arctis Pro, and don't get me wrong, that headset is excellent. You can't do better for console in my experience. But compared to audiophile style headphones, there's a significant jump.

With these audiophile style headphones comes other expenses, like the required headphone amp and 3.5mm to RCA cable. Let me save you the trouble of testing things yourself. 250 ohms needs extra power that your standard audio interface simply cannot provide. Know this ahead of time and buy an amp. I went with the Schiit Magni and it does a good enough job. I run these headphones at about 70% volume through the headphone amp and that's more than enough.

Anyway, with the proper setup, these headphones are a major W. Super comfortable, look good, and great audio quality for a really reasonable price. Under $200 is super cheap in the audiophile headphone space. Can't beat the price and the sound quality. Consider the other expenses that go along and are required for a more realistic overall cost. Likely $300ish. In my limited testing and experience, these headphones have definitely given me enhanced and upgraded audio quality without question while gaming. Highly recommend.
Summary: W upgrade from typical gaming headsets

Some sound best with 80/20s. I still have an all Koa Martin guitar that is *so* bright that it sounds best with the normally tone-killing Elixir Polywebs. Got a guitar-banjo? Try silk-and-steel or silk-and-phosphor. Trust me. I've been through my John Pearse phase. Pyramids? Yep. Tried 'em. I really liked LaBellas. The problem was that back when I was using them, they would tarnish in the packaging. I don't know if that's still the case.

Anyway, the bottom line is that D'Addario phosphor bronze are my go to string. They set the baseline for every guitar I've ever owned. (Note: That's baseline. In some cases, I've decided something else sounded better.) For many guitars, including my J-45, there's nothing I've found that I've liked better.

Also worth noting: The string that sounds best depends not only on the particular guitar, but also on the type of pick one uses, the type of music one plays, and the way one approaches the instrument. The string that's best for bluegrass with a hard attack may not be what's best for delicate finger style.

Bottom line: Don't follow leaders. Watch the parkin' meters. Experiment. But, D'Addario PBs are a great place to start.
Summary: There is NO perfect guitar string.

I've been playing over 30 years and got one of these for my 7-year-old because he wants to play guitar like daddy does. For $100 it's an OK starter guitar for a kid (and I guess really short people who can't play a regular Fender), but not something I'd recommend to anyone else. And my kid thinks it looks cool, so he'll be more likely to stick with it.

Even though it has a laminated body, the headstock and unfinished neck are decent wood. The frets are crowned OK but have some sharp ends to them, and I feel silly investing the cash to have them fixed. It's light and easy to handle. The hardware isn't bad, with a stable bridge (good idea not to put a floating trem in this), 5-way blade switch, solid jack and strap anchors, and smooth knobs. The pickups are not top notch but work well enough (a decent replacement set would cost more than the whole guitar does, so I'm not complaining). It has a nice red paint job.

On the down side, besides some sharp fret ends, it required a few truss rod and bridge adjustments to bring the action close to where it should be. The fretboard uses cheap rosewood and in one spot has some extra glue showing around a fret. The nut on the one I got is sunk lower on the treble side than on the bass side, so the low E string is farther from the fretboard than the other strings. It has one small pit in the red finish. It has no paperwork or owner's manual. The tuners are kind of choppy. And the body/neck flexes so if you put too much pressure on it the whole thing will go out of tune.

It comes strung with Fender 9's, which combined with the short scale makes the strings loose and easy to press down, so it's good for a kid just starting out. I actually enjoy messing around with it because the pickups have a punkish scratchy sound. But as soon as he gets bigger we'll ditch this for something better.
Summary: OK starter guitar for a kid

Pros: If you don’t want to pay for a proper hard case this is a good option. I would say it’s better than some similar cases. The case looks good, and looks like it will last a while. No padding besides a little on the lid. It will not hold the body neck cap securely, which means that the horn can bump against the key posts. Otherwise my horn was secure. The mouthpiece and neck compartments are divided by a poorly attached divider. It may not fall out altogether, but the top inch of mine was not attached at all. The metal strap hardware may or may not break. It’s thick enough, but obviously cast, so it could break depending on the casting quality and metal - IDK. Backpack straps are not removable. The front has places for two small pockets, but only one is functional.

This worked for selling a horn on a budget. Ok for the price. IMO these “hard” styrofoam cases aren’t strong enough for permanent use. It may last for several years, but they’re basically disposable. They provide limited protection. Much better than a gig bag, but considerably worse than a proper wood case.

A few good things. The battery compartment on the receiver is just large enough to accept rechargeable batteries - a big plus. The transmitter accepts both XLR and TRS inputs - big plus.

The carrying case and wall wart are bummers. The case is twice the size it needs to be to fit the transmitter and receiver alone. i don't need that bulk so the case won't be used. And alas - a wall wart. An IEC power cable is so much easier to use, find replacements and so on. I have several 1/2 rack devices that use them. I know it adds a few dollars but i would gladly pay for it for a more reliable setup. I won't deduct any points because of the case or the wall wart but they could have done much better here.

So after a 3 hour rehearsal.
- The noise: When the band is playing at medium to full level the noise is masked, but at low band volumes I notice it. Not as in "I'm intentionally listening for the noise", but rather even when I'm not trying to "listen for the noise" it can be loud enough for it to catch my attention. I'm not a snob, but I can tell if a drummer is using wood or nylon tipped sticks when playing their high hat. I'm not trying to be a snob, but it's just a fact i notice this kind of stuff, so yeah I will be more more sensitive to noise than others. That's not good or bad, it's just the way it is :) So it may not bother you one bit, and thats great! But if you are sensitive to this kind of stuff, I'm letting you know...
- The signal: The transmitter was sitting on a table no more than 5 feet from me. Several times it crackled but only a very brief moment. One time it had a real hissy fit :) and crackled and spit at me for 3-4 seconds. Next rehearsal I'll set it up on the other side of the room and see how it goes.

For me it's "good enough" to buy at this price point but it's not a screaming deal. Thats a 3 star in my book.

Text:
I bought this looper a few months ago and wanted time to familiarize myself with it prior to writing a review. If you decide to buy one, please take the time to read through the comprehensive owner's manual that comes with it before you attempt to use it. It will reduce your frustration level that has been experienced by some individuals who may have posted earlier reviews without reading the instructions. After reading the manual, I was able to produce my first loops within minutes. As my ability to use the device has increased, I am now able to produce loops containing several instrument parts. The unit itself is well-constructed and having multiple foot switches that operate it is preferable to some of the smaller units that have only one or two switches. The switches do make an audible "click" when you press them, but if you're using the machine in a live performance where the music is loud, no one will hear it. However, if you wish to play some soft acoustic guitar loops (or using any other instrument, for that matter), someone in the audience that is nearby could hear the click as you change the loops up or down. That slight clicking noise does not detract from the fact that this is a well-built unit that enables me to capture song ideas if one suddenly pops into my head one evening. Another slightly negative observation is that the tap tempo button is not as accurate as if the device possessed the ability to have a tempo set by dialing in a tempo or using a tempo button. In addition, the included rhythm patterns are minimal and primitive. They enable you to keep time but that's it. Those shortcomings are the main reason I took off one star in this review.

I've developed my own method to record a song idea. I calculate the number of measures for the verses, for the chorus (if different from the verses, and for any other parts of the song. Then I tap in the tempo and record the number of measures for each part. Then I begin recording each instrument that I'll need in each part of the song. It sounds easy, but you have to be precise in the number of measures you'll need and stopping the loop at the correct ending point. Otherwise, your loop will stop prematurely or go on too long. It takes some trial-and-error but persevere and you'll get the hang of it.

I haven't plugged the unit into my desktop to utilize the included software. Once all the loops on the device are filled, I'll then get a mini SD card and eventually fill that up. At some time, I'll need to work with the included software. I have a DigiTech RP 500 foot pedal and I haven't yet encountered any problem using the software that came with that product, but the two software packages might not even closely resemble each other, so take this last comment of mine with a grain of salt.

All in all, it's a fairly easy device to learn to operate. It has the shortcomings that I've noted before, but its ease of use and the multiple foot switches trump the design omissions. My friends that have listened to the loops I've created have commented on how life-like the recording sounds. It will also make you a better performer, as you'll hear every mistake you make when attempting to create a loop. In summary, I'm happy that I bought it.

Addendum (September 10, 2014): I finally got around to plugging in the DigiTech to my PC. I use a Windows-based computer, so my PC automatically downloaded the software to run the unit. Once that happened, a main screen pops up on your monitor and after a few moments, you can open the internal memory of the looper and see the location of your loops. From there, you can rename them or copy and paste them to another open spot in the device or you can copy them to your PC, so the process is fairly easy.

A couple of caveats, however. When you copy a loop, you'll only hear the music you recorded. If you use the built-in "drum machine" you will not hear that on the copy, although the rhythm pattern you choose will still be heard in the original loop in the internal memory. Also, although you have the ability to alter the tempo of the rhythm you originally chose when you open the software, don't do it. It will alter the rhythm in the original loop, but that doesn't alter the tempo of the accompanying music you originally recorded. As an example, I noted that a verse of a song I had recorded had a rhythm tempo of 105 but the chorus was a little faster, at about 105.6. So, thinking I was smart, I altered the tempo of the chorus to 105 while I had the DigiTech hooked up to my PC. That did change the tempo in the verse, but my music was recorded a little slower. As a result, the verse is just a little off-tempo. That's one experiment I won't repeat.

I haven't attempted to download other music from an outside source into the device nor have I utilized a memory card yet. When that happens, I'll amend this review again.
Summary: Easy looping capabilities; a few drawbacks, however

The vender, Adorama Camera, did a great job sending this guitar to me in a timely fashion. This review is about the Ibanez GRGM21MJB MiKro short scale guitar - NOT the vendor!

OK, it only costs around $150 bucks, and even with the issues listed below, for $150 it is a decent value (i.e. 3/5 for an INEXPENSIVE guitar). If you are buying this for a beginner, then I suggest you have the following done before giving it to them: Replace strings (use regulars), adjust neck truss rod, adjust bridge height and (very important!) the string intonation. Optional: replace neck nut to increase string sustain.

PICKUPS are pretty good, although the fabric wrap merely hinted at providing any protect to those teeny tiny 44AWG pickup wires: improved by removing wrap and sealing with liquid electrical tape. The pickups are mounted using only 2 screws - so they are wobbly: fixed by 3D printing a new 3-piece pick guard with 1 (top) + 2 (bottom) holes and a 1-to-2 hole 4-40 screw adapters (see pic). NECK is decent, but the fret ends are very rough: fixed by smoothing them down using a mildly abrasive rotary tool end. NECK NUT sucks, it is some kind of vibration dampening plastic! Fix: Replaced with a TUSQ blank - sounds a LOT better now. INTONATION: except for the low E string I was able to adjust the bridge saddles for correct intonation, while not perfect, the low E is close enough to work with. ELECTRONICS: decent pots and switch, I did add an EMG After-Burner (had to route out a pocket for the 9V battery and PCB/SW circuit). PAINT: Really cheap, really really cheap and easily chipped or scratched. TUNERS: Not the worst, but could use an upgrade as they have a lot of play in them. WEIRDNESS: When I took the neck off the body there was a 0.5" x 1" piece of sandpaper wedged between the neck and the body: huh? Anyway, NOW it is a 4/5 inexpensive guitar that now plays and sounds really nice!
Summary: Decent, inexpensive, short scale guitar, but needs some upgrades.

I've used a variety of MIDI controllers over the years and wanted something that I could drag around or let the kids borrow and not worry about too much.

The Samson 49-Key controller has an extensive set of knobs and sliders which are all programmable using your favorite DAW or soft instrument on PC, Mac or iOS device.

The keyboard action is decent, but not up to the build quality of a higher grade instrument which is perfectly fine given its price point. It's possible to do hammond-style glisses and the keys feel solid and not like they're going to tear off.

The sliders all work fine, but one is a little stiff feeling but has slightly improved with use. The knobs all work well, but feel a bit flimsy. Be sure to choose a case that will protect them when traveling.

The pitch wheel is the most annoying control so far. It works fine, but makes a scraping sound when you use it and it just screams "CHEAP!!!".

I like the inclusion of Komplete Elements. Komplete is a great collection of soft instruments and the Elements version has many of the synths you'd want to produce most sounds you're likely to use while starting out.

If you're looking for a decent quality keyboard with a collection of good soft instruments and don't want to spend a fortune, this unit does the job pretty well.
Summary: A good controller and set of soft instruments for people starting out.

Text:
I've been playing 12-string guitars for over 50 years, and I've never had a capo that I really liked . . . until now. The problem for traditional12-string capos is the difference in diameter between the two strings in each of the lower pairs. Especially the lowest two pairs. When the capo tension is correct for the low E of the lowest pair, the higher E of that pair is not adequately depressed, and produces a sickening dead "plunk." You can increase the downward pressure on the capo and hope that it will fully depress the thinner E string, but then the excess pressure will sharpen the thicker string. pulling it out of tune.

The G7th capo solves the problem by being compensated. That is, there are notches in the rubber pad that allow adjacent strings of different diameters to be adequately depressed at the same capo pressure. (It's such an obvious idea, why didn't anyone think of it before?)

Furthermore, the guitar does not require retuning when the capo is repositioned on a different fret (a common problem with uncompensated capos).

Bottom line: my 12-string has never sounded better . . . and my wife doesn't shudder when I bring out my capo!

As a multi-instrumentalist songwriter, I find myself switching back and forth between instruments a lot as I record, making small changes in how the different parts fit together. I had a 2x2 interface that I used for a long time, but it really cramped my workflow, since I had to unplug/plug/set levels every time I wanted to change. So, I went in search of a better way.

At first I looked at upgrading my 2x2 to a 6x4 or 8x6 interface. But I couldn't find anything I liked. Most of the step-up interfaces still only had 2-4 preamps, and the TRS inputs on the backs often lacked a way to set gain, making them nearly useless for recording stereo trs instruments direct. Also, many of the cheaper interfaces don't have a second headphone jack, which is handy when you're recording your bandmates. The interfaces i did find that were large enough and fully featured enough to cover all my needs were way out of my price range. Bummer.

Then I discovered this gem. The soundcraft notepad 8fx. What a brilliant little piece of hardware. It has a 2x2 interface built into it - but instead of statically routing the two preamps to the computer, it comes with a control program that allows you to route any of the first six inputs on the board to USB. This means I can leave all my instruments plugged into the board and leveled properly, then just use the soundcraft panel in my computer to flip between inputs, without touching a single cable or dial. It's the perfect solution to my problems. To top it off, the aux jack doubles as a second stereo headphone jack, so I can run two pairs of headphones when I'm recording my buddies, without the hassle of using a splitter.

Since we're talking about recording, let me just say that the preamps in this thing are excellent. It will easily compete with any 2x2 interface in this price range. They remind me a lot of the way focusrite preamps sound, but without as much sibilance, which I think is actually an improvement. Fun fact, one of the founders of focusrite later went on to found soundcraft. So perhaps the similar sound is no accident.

The electronics in this board are dead quiet, beginning to end, and the converters work well. Overall, the sounds I get out of it are clean and clear, both from the USB, and from the analog outputs. I use the main outs to drive my studio monitors, and since I do all my work in the same room (home studio) I love that I can source my headphones mix from the aux bus - because it means I can have different mixes for the monitors and the phones so the mics don't cause feedback when I decide to bring up the mains to listen to the mix on my monitors.

A couple things you should know about this board if you're looking at it - the aux bus sends are pre-fader, which is exactly what you want if (like me) you're using the aux as a mix bus for your headphones or other monitor system, but since the aux bus doubles as the FX bus, when you're using it for FX you have to be mindful of the fact that your FX do not scale up and down with the main level on the channel.

The other thing you should know is that you need to install the soundcraft control panel to switch the usb to inputs other than main L/R sends. I saw a review of someone complaining that they couldn't change their input and it didn't sound like they installed the software to be able to do so. The different inputs do not show up as separate sound interfaces in your computer, because this is not a true 8x2, it's a 2x2 that can select between four input configurations. You must install the software to make the selection.

The only cons I can think of are that I kind of wish it had a power button and indicator LED, but I'm not going to ding it a star for something that petty. I use a power strip in my studio to turn it on with all my other equipment anyways, so do I really need a power button? No, not really.

Also, it bears being mentioned that, even though I bought this as a portable recording and livestreaming interface, it also makes a great little mixer for small gigs or test purposes. I've found myself digging it out to try out speakers and other audio equipment when I didn't want to drag out my regular, full-featured mixer.

All in all, I'd say soundcraft knocked it out of the park on this one, and the price puts it right in line with other recording interfaces. If you're in the market for a 2x2, consider one of these instead. Not only do you get great sounding preamps, you get a device that can accomplish more and perhaps even improve your workflow.
Summary: Notepad 8fx - a step above the 2x2 Audio Interface

Text:

Cable is very nice coax - very flexible yet solid construction. Cable cutter works very well for a cheap cutter - cable was cut clean with no stray wires from the shield to short out signal.

I especially like the inclusion of both straight and angled plugs - very handy. Including the cutter and screwdriver in the kit makes it self contained - giving you everything you need to make a bunch of cables.

The only negative I could find for the whole system is the screwdriver - the blade is too thin for the slots in the set screws, and it can slip when one is trying to tighten down on the cable. If one is not very careful, one could stab oneself easily. Be sure you have the plugs braced in such a way that the cable is held tight and that your hand (or other body parts or items which could be scratched) is out of the way. You do need to torque the set screws pretty hard, and slipping could be dangerous. It is also not good for the heads of the screws to have an undersized screwdriver - could mess up the heads. If you have a good set of hollow ground screwdrivers, I would advise using one from that set which fits better. I would deduct half a star for that - if you are careful, which you should be with your hands and gear anyway, it is not a serous problem.

Other than that, I love this kit and look forward to making more cables, and buying supplies to keep going after the kit runs out. Good job D'Addario!

Text:
Wanted to give this bag 3-1/2 stars really. It's an OK bag and good value for the price (compared to other bags). It has lots of pockets and is a snug fit for a standard dreadnought-size acoustic. It's a roomy fit for the 000 size (Yamaha FSX) acoustic-electric I have in it at the moment. . . . but the padding does not protect 100% of the guitar. And isn't that the one job that this bag has?

The bag consists of an outer ballistic nylon shell and an inner thin polyester lining with a layer of foam padding sandwiched between them. It is this foam layer that does not make it all the way to the edges and is not stitched in place so it can move around internally. With a guitar zipped up inside you can feel that the padding sort of covers 90% of the guitar but you can clearly feel the edges of the guitar (unpadded) through the bag where the top and back meet the sides and all around the edges of the headstock. These are exactly where you're most likely to bang the case into a wall and where the guitar is most vulnerable . . hence my 3 star review.

That might be a quality control issue. Your bag might have sufficient foam to reach edges and protect the guitar better. But mine does not.
Summary: Ok budget bag but let down by spotty padding.

I purchased these to compare to my normal brushes (Regal Tip Ed Thigpen model). The all metal construction of these brushes makes them very different from the Ed Thigpen brushes, but the sizes (length, diameter and brush fanout) are very close.

These are a bit too heavy for gigs that call for a lot of brushwork. I play a lot of assisted living facility gigs that only last an hour, but are 100% brushwork. These would quickly grow tiresome because of the weight even on those short gigs. However, if you are only occasionally using brushes these are not bad.

The wire gauge is decent for most styles - not too thin, and the brushes stay put. What I mean by that is I usually play with my left brush fully fanned out and my right one with the fan a little tighter so I can get a nice legato sound with my left hand and a more staccato sound on the right hand pattern. My Ed Thigpen brushes hold those settings, but many other brands and models do not. These do.

I play with brushes more than sticks, so I am probably not going to purchase more of these, but that is based on personal preference and playing style. If you need a decent pair of brushes for occasional work these are better than some of the name brand ones out there (in my opinion, of course.)
Summary: Surprising quality; on the heavy side

Don't believe me? Listen for yourself. Look up "LIVE: Everything Klon Centaur (History, Circuit and Shootouts)" by JHS Pedals on YouTube. Begin at 48:34 - they A/B against a real Klon, even switching back and forth during a song and there's literally ZERO discontinuity.

Now in bypass mode, the Klon is buffered and this is true bypass, but you can always bring your own buffer.

Aesthetically the Pegasus is totally different than the Klon. But I think it looks nice as its own thing. It's smaller than a Klon which is a good for my pedal board. Another distinction is that the control knobs are a little different - not better or worse. Instead of, left to right, Gain, Treble, Output, as on the Klon, here you get, from left to right, Tone (Treble), Gain, Vol. (Output) - so the first two knobs are swapped. No big deal!

Finally, this guy comes with a removable battery adapter. I do like knowing that I can use a battery if want, and, heck, with the adapter I can probably use it on most pedals that require the same voltage and current. I might prefer having a dedicated compartment for the battery, but, honestly this is fine and probably easier. DEFINITELY easier than unscrewing the bottom of a pedal. Those are the worst!

This pedal rocks, and I definitely recommend it if you are smart and/or do not have unlimited money. It sounds exactly the same as the original, 100%.
Summary: Sonically identical to the Klon Centaur

Text:
This set of stainless steel parts is an upgrade for an Original Floyd Rose 1984 model that I bought earlier this year.

I shouldn't even have to be writing this, but the sad fact is that I needed to buy aftermarket parts because of a quality control issue with my Floyd Rose. Some of the string lock screws were stripped at the factory, and it's apparent that the threads of some of the saddles were stripped, as well.

I could make a warranty claim here--and I probably should, because the workmanship is unacceptable.

Even so, I went searching for parts that might help salvage the purchase. After looking at a few pricey options which made me hesitate, I found this full set of stainless steel parts at a really good price.

I bought this set for two reasons, mainly--I wanted to upgrade the (reputedly) fragile factory string blocks; and I wanted to replace the stripped set of string lock screws, hoping the stainless steel threads would be strong enough to hold in the saddles.

I didn't really need stainless steel screws for the nut clamps, but they're nice to have. The original intonation screws for the saddles were just fine, too, but again, these are nice to have. And I didn't need the fine tuning screws, partly because Floyd Rose made it impossible for me to remove the factory brass screws, and truth be told, I prefer those anyway.

I'm very impressed at the quality of this set. Everything is an exact fit--the nut screws, the intonation screws, all went in smoothly, perfectly threaded. The string lock screws fit nicely into the string blocks, and I was able to confirm that at least two of the saddles had threads stripped at the factory, judging by how roughly they turned.

Kaish has another winner with me. This set is excellent and a great value. They make good parts at attractive prices, and they haven't let me down yet. I will gladly continue buying guitar parts from them.
Summary: Floyd Rose let me down--this set is better than factory

Text:
The Volca Sample is the 4th addition to the Volca lineup (I own the Volca Bass also), and arguably offers the most versatility. In fact, I was looking for a fairly straightforward beatbox, and struggled between this and the analog drum sounds of the Volca Beats. Ultimately, I felt like the Beats had a few weaknesses (snare not very popular; limited arsenal of sounds) and that I could cover most of the Beats' sounds plus a whole lot more with the Volca Sample.

That being said, I think this is a 5-star product...provided that you educate yourself in advance of what it does and doesn't do. It's an extremely small plastic box that runs on 6 AA batteries and features no slot for external media (USB, SD card, etc.). I don't know how you reasonably look at those specs and expect this to be a $150 mini-MPC. But if that were your expectation, yes, you'd be a little disappointed.

The Volca Sample is special from the other Volca machines in just how flexible it can be towards a variety of needs. You could load it up with acoustic or drum machine samples and have up 10 instruments loaded with 8-instrument/note polyphony. You could load up a series of tuned notes and generate a walking bass line using either motion sequencing/automation, or by setting the same sample to different pitches. Pitch control is handled very well on the Volca Sample, in my opinion. You can change pitch with a numerical up/down value, or by semitones (2 octaves down all the way to two octaves up). This is done by the speed knob, and while lower pitched notes are basically the same sample played back more slowly, you can edit sample length, decay, and other features to balance things out. In fact, the 4x4 matrix with mini knobs in the gray section are 16 step programmable sampling parameters for you to adjust. Not only can these be adjusted for each sample, but you can live record automation or program the changes to occur at different steps. Is it a professional caliber sampler? No. Is it accessible to all levels of users and deceptively powerful for a battery powered, affordable device? Absolutely.

SAMPLE EDITING & iOS INTEGRATION - Some of the biggest complaints about the Sample are that the device was marketed as requiring an iOS device to change and edit samples. However, I view that as one of the device's selling points, and an excellent 3rd-party app from the Caustic developer quickly emerged to allow even more power over sample creation and uploading (I believe this is also available for Android and PC). iOS integration is a strength of the Sample, in my opinion, because there is such an insane wealth of affordable music content in the iOS app store. The Caustic Volca Editor easily links up with an app called AudioShare to import samples stored on your device, or imported from a cloud service like DropBox. Aside from uploading obvious samples (like .wav files of 808/909 sounds available all over the web), you can create your own without leaving your iPhone or iPad and store them in AudioShare. For example, I recorded a simple C2 note in a great app called iFretless Bass, sent it to the Caustic Volca Editor via AudioShare, and had a pitch tuned electric bass sound available on my Sample, and the whole process took maybe a couple of minutes.

Some tips/caveats: Some people have complained about the 4MB storage limit on the Volca, which is admittedly quite small. The best way to deal with this is to use the Caustic or AudioPocket editor and identify some of the longer factory samples (1 second or longer) and target those to be replaced. There are 100 sample slots for storage, but whatever you upload needs to be in place of something else, so you can free up more storage that way. Generally speaking, the Volca Sample is better suited for "one-hit" brief samples like a drum, brass hit, or clap. Sampling can also involve longer clips like 5-second guitar riffs, but the Volca Sample really isn't suited to handle that.

The fact that patterns are limited to 16-step single bars is another oft-cited problem with the entire Volca series, but there are workarounds. You can set different patterns and chain them with Song mode, or trigger them with the ribbon keys. Part of the fun of the entire Volca series, however, is taking a very brief and straightforward musical idea and then mutating with filter sweeps, modulation, and effects. The Sample excels at that, and the sound quality is great (through headphones or monitors though, just skip the built-in mini speaker). I like the "Analogue Isolator", which is basically an fancied-up name for a 2-band EQ, but which allows for some additional tone shaping and automation possibilities.

MIDI ISSUES - Unfortunately, the Sample isn't controlled via MIDI the way you might expect it to be. My understanding is that the 10 different samples respond to different MIDI Channels (1-10), as opposed being triggered by separate pads/keys on a single MIDI channel. That's a bit of bummer, but less than the other Volcas, since Live Play actually responds quite well with the touch keys (and quantizes to nearest 16th note), and you'll spend most of your time programming grooves with the step sequencer anyway. It does not respond to velocity control, though you can set the "Level" for each sample.

One final note - I think some of the negativity for the Volca Sample comes from the fact that what it offers isn't as "rare" as the Keys, Bass, and Beats. There are desktop and even mobile sampling apps that do much of what the Volca Sample does, and perhaps even more cheaply. In that sense, it isn't the same "freak of nature" that my little Volca Bass is, belting out warm, analog tones from an inexpensive, battery-powered box. But that doesn't make the usefulness of the Sample any less impressive - this little box really can do a ton. While the other Volca devices surprise you with quality of their sounds, the possibilities with the Sample are limited by only your imagination and willingness to experiment.

UPDATE (06/28/2016): Just a quick update on my review to attach a picture showing how much of a giant nerd I am, as well as the versatility of the Sample. I created a micro-sized table showing all the instruments uploaded to the device, as well as a table showing how many semitones away different notes are (since I am pretty bad at music theory). All of my pitched samples are tuned to a "C" note, so it becomes pretty easy to generate basslines and simple melodies using these charts for quick reference. The Sample allows you to load the same sample in multiple instruments slots, and since you have 8-note polyphony, you could program chords or even set up a custom keyboard where each note is within the scale/mode of your song. Text:
A year ago, I wrote a lengthy comparison of the [[ASIN:B000FPQFKO Edirol R-09 WAVE/MP3 Recorder, Black]] and the [[ASIN:B000VIGQCW Zoom H4 Handy Recorder + 2GB Accessory Kit]] (pre-accessory kit). I wanted a high quality, easy to use recorder, so even though the H4 had all of the features of the Edirol and sold for considerably less, I kept the Edirol because it was so much easier to use.

Zoom has responded with the H2, a scaled down version of the H4 with all of the features of the R-09 and all of the controls right where you need them. The H2 even has additional features over the R-09, but they don't get in the way. For example, there's a choice of a 90 degree recording pattern, a 120 degree recording pattern, and even a surround sound option. Samsontech has some nice video demonstrations on its website.

One big complaint I've had with the Edirol is the cost of its add-on stand. Unlike the Edirol, the H2 comes with a simple stand. In addition, the H2 has a threaded hole so that it can be mounted on a standard digital camera tripod! On a separate note, it's much easier to replace batteries with the H2 than the Edirol.

Recently, I got together with friends and recorded the same live acoustic music on both the Edirol R-09 and the Zoom H2. I used Adobe Audition only to normalize both tracks (that is, equalize their loudness). The first time we played them back, I thought I detected a VERY slight preference for the Edirol, with the overall opinion of the group split between the two units. The second time we played them back, my preference was for the H2, with overall opinion continuing to be split. We all agreed that the differences were so small as to be negligible if there were any at all. The sound files can be found at [...] for those who'd like to hear for themselves. We were sitting in a circle with the recorders located next to each other on a mantle above and outside the group.

I do prefer the Edirol's control buttons to the H2's membrane and I'm not about to sell the Edirol, perhaps because I am more familiar with the Edirol and don't want to give it up just yet. Also, the Edirol R-09 is the darling of the moment. However, if I owned neither, I couldn't justify the huge bump in price of the Edirol over the H2 and would opt for the H2. When I went to a music party last weekend and knew I'd need only one recorder, I grabbed the H2.
Summary: As good as the Edirol R-09 for about half the price!

This problem is unique to this synth, it doesn't happen with any other analog synth I've ever used, and I've used quite enough synths, including modular setups with CV to MIDI modules. The only way to avoid this problem in the "Boog" is to disable "legato", but then you can't have this behavior when you actually need it (by extending the previous note so that it overlaps with the beginning of the next note). Despite this very annoying problem, I'm still giving it 5 stars, because the value for the money is off the charts, you get truly proper, high quality voltage controlled oscillators and ladder filter.
Summary: Best bang for buck ever in analog synthesizers.

Text:
This mixer is meant to be a stereo mixer giving you two channels, LEFT and RIGHT.
If you use this mixer's AUX output you can have three independent channels to record with. If you use "half" of the inserts on channels 1+2 you may get a total of five independent outputs. This is pushing the limits of the mixer to the max.

If you want to record more than one stereo track or two tracks using channels panned LEFT and RIGHT, you will need a special audio card or interface that will allow you to do so. Usually if you want to record an entire band live and separate the tracks for mixing/mixdown you will need a special audio card to allow for more than one stereo input. Most times they are 8-16 channels, and also function as a soundcard.

If you want to multi-track record more than two channels using THIS mixer, you will need to install the Cubase software (included) or something similar like Cakewalk Producer, etc.

To record:
Read all manuals for equipment and software.
Set up a recording project in your software.
Arm the first two tracks or arm one stereo track.
If you use two tracks, you will need to set one track to record the MAIN LEFT and one track to record the MAIN RIGHT outputs. You could have a vocal mic panned to the LEFT and a guitar channel panned to the RIGHT, thus giving you two independent mono tracks at once.
Record the first stereo track. (or two mono tracks)
To overdub and add other parts to your recording, UNARM the tracks you just recorded and ARM a new separate track to record.
When you record the next track, you should hear the the tracks you recorded previously and add to them on a separate track, isolating them.
Keep recording tracks until you are finished with your project. You should expect to get maybe 20 tracks (or more) depending on your computer's specs and the limitation of the software.
Adjust all the levels to your liking adding FX and EQ and export your mix to a Stereo WAV file or MP3.

Here is a typical home studio routine:
Program a drum machine. Hook it up to your mixer. Record the first stereo track drums only.
Hook up a bass guitar and record the bass part on a separate track while listening to the previously recorded drum track. Do this for your guitar, keyboard, vocals, harmony vocals, lead solo, etc., tracks until finished.
You "build" the song or project one part at a time until finished.
Mix it down to stereo audio file.

Text:
I hate guitar products like these, slides and finger picks and such, that are critical to one's style, technique and sound. You really need to try before buying and really you need to try a dozen or two. But it's one of those things that the best you'll get is an in-depth Amazon review so here's my take:

PRELIMINARIES
This is a heavy brass slide so the first thing you will want to know is, if you don't refit your guitar with a super-high nut (or what is known as a "nut adapter"), this slide will bottom out on your frets and be unusable, worse than glass and steel. Even with the nut refit you'll still need to start using a heavier gauge string set: 13 - 56 at the lightest with 15 - 64 probably better still, especially with drop tunings and especially with the nut adapter (which is still not as high as a custom nut or a conventional lap steel or dobro nut). This goes for both acoustic and electric and really goes for any usable slide because slides must be heavy and dense for good tone.

Then you must be mindful of the added stress heavier strings (and higher tunings) will have on the soundboard and bridge (acoustic) and neck (acoustic and electric). For that reason I go mostly with open drop tunings or, if I up-tune, I don't go higher than Open G and then I must be mindful not to leave anything higher than Open D or Standard E tuned high for very long. To do open tunings right you'll need to purchase a Dobro-style capo since a conventional capo will no longer work because of the greater nut height; if you don't have the correct open strings your harmonic and stylistic opportunities are diminished greatly for all slide styles.

THE SLIDE
The best thing about this slide is that it includes the adapters for different size fingers which means yes, you can now experiment with placing the slide on different fingers instead of "whichever finger it fits." Plus brass is soft and can be easily re-polished if it gets some dings. Steel and glass cannot be re-polished easily.

The "reversible" feature is of less benefit than I had hoped. I find that reversing it with just one hand is difficult and if I need to reverse the slide quickly (most often the case), the only way to be sure I make the transition in time is to use my other hand to spin it around. Better than having to pull the slide off but not quite as smooth a transition as what I was hoping for.

So it still has advantages: it is heavy and dense, it can be reversed instead of removing it, it has the size adapters, and perhaps equally important, your finger doesn't sweat; the open design has adequate ventilation so you won't be feeling sweat and condensation like you will with closed designs.

Overall this has been my favorite slide for a few years but until I refit my nut and started using heavy strings, it sat in a drawer languishing for many years prior.
Summary: Very good, very heavy slide, reversible function is merely good

First ... let me say I'm a total beginner. I purchased this for my used Yamaha FG JR1, small 3/4 guitar. As expected, due to its small size, its sound seemed small as well. So I decided to invest in a few upgrades. First I put on a high end set of Elixir strings and added bone bridge pins which, real or imagined, seemed a bit better with more sustain. The B & E strings didn't seem to ring out nicely as they should ... or could.

Since I have no intention of buying another guitar, I contacted GraphTech for the proper TUSQ part numbers for my JR1. They replied quickly and I ordered as recommended. Then I replaced both the nut and saddle with TUSQ.

The nut suggested fit almost perfect with only a very small adjustment. The saddle required a bit more work. It was very slightly too thick and too long. I made those adjustments first. Next came the height adjustment. Hand sanding off 1/16 inch would take forever so I marked carefully and used a belt sander to knock of the bulk of the material. When I got close I hand sanded the final amount. Plus I had to lower it a very small amount. Yes, the fitting of the saddle was a rather tedious. You need to go about it patiently.

The end result was satisfying. The little Yamaha now plays probably as good as it ever can. The small strings seem brighter and cleaner sounding. For such a small body guitar I think it now puts out a nice, big sound. Plenty satisfying for my at home learning. Yes, the change was fairly small but occurred where I wanted it to.

This inexpensive mod was worth the time and effort. It was the first time I ever changed a nut or saddle and it wasn't that hard. Watch a couple videos. Take your time. You can do it too. If you get even a 10 or 15% improvement in tone it will be worth it. Especially if you have a low end guitar like me.

(Don't cheap out on strings either. Get the best ones for your guitar and playing needs. Added up, your cheapie or high end instrument will surely sound a wee bit better)
Summary: Nice Upgrade to a Cheapie Guitar

I used this to create a shockmount for my Zoom H2N which I used for many years for audio books, trainings, etc.

The trick for mounting an H2N in this is you just need to go to the hardware store and pick up some rubber and metal fender washers and a good 1/4" screw that fits. After that, you can easily mount the H2n, windscreen and even a USB cable or so to it. The benefit?

Well, it's pretty substantial as long as you do it correctly (ie, nothing is touching the mic that is directly coupled to the stand).

The benefit is that if you accidentally hit your stand or if something is vibrating the desk or stand, that it won't translate into your audio nearly as much as if it were directly mounted to the stand or whatever.

To best demonstrate the difference, once you have it setup. Put the mic in the mount and then tap the stand with your fingers. If the mic is suspended correctly, you'll hear the sound probably, but then make one change. Take a pen or something that's solid and connect the mic to the stand. You don't even have to make a "great" connection between the two. Then, simply tap the stand the same way again. You'll notice in the recording that the tapping is SIGNIFICANTLY louder in the one without the mount whereas the tapping with the mount might very well be impossible to hear at normal volumes.

This will prevent jarring sounds in your audio and is most useful in "live" or "near live" recordings where you're not going to be able to go back and correct mistakes or whatever.

If nothing else, it looks cool, so if you're looking for that - well, here ya go :)

There aren't really any problems with it, so 5 stars!
Summary: VERY good for isolating a mic (used for an H2n)

Text: Great

This is an excellent set of headphones for the current $69 price tag. The sound quality is nice across the board and could be even better with some minor tweaks. It is a big set of headphones but still quite comfortable to wear.

►► SOUND QUALITY ◄◄

The sound quality is pretty flat and natural across the spectrum, which is a good thing. The bass is accurate and the mid-range and high-end are both clearer than a lot of headphones that I have tested out. My only complaint here is that the mids and highs appear a bit off in the distance due to the amount of space that is between the speakers and your ears due to the over-sized earpads.

While listening to songs I know very well I'd listen then press the headphones a bit closer to my ears and the sound difference was quite substantial. Instruments like acoustic guitars and xylophones that seemed a bit muted and not quite lifelike through these headphones immediately came to life with the speakers just a bit closer to my ears.

►► BUILD QUALITY & FEATURES ◄◄

This is the first set of headphones I have had in this price-range that had removable cables and I really appreciate that feature as when things go bad in headphones it is usually in a cable that has been abused in some way. The ability to easily swap a new cable in should keep these working a nice long time. The headphones come with two cables, a long straight cable and a long coiled cable. They lock into the headphones and stay there securely. There is also an adapter included to use the headphones with the larger 1/4" jack.

There is a lot of metal in the build but the headphones do not feel overly heavy. They fold up nicely and fit into the included carrying case for storage.

►► COMFORT ◄◄

The earpads are soft and comfortable and I had no issues with them during extended listening from a comfort standpoint. The headband is well padded as well making these feel great when you're wearing them.

►► CONCLUSION ◄◄

This is truly a nice set of headphones that sound good and are comfortable to wear for long sessions of audio or video editing. I wish there was an easy way to remove just a touch of the padding as, for me, the sound quality definitely improved moving the speakers a touch closer to my ears.
