SUMMARY
Nice tuners, and a reasonable price. If they fit your guitar, I think you'll like them. Same locking mechanism as most locking tuners, with a thumbscrew on the back. I like the auto-trim feature a lot. When you tune the guitar, it just cuts those strings right off. Nice. Seem to have a nice snug feel and a decent tuning ratio. Not a good choice to replace modern Fender/Schallers because they don't cover the alignment pin holes. Fits well in 25/64" peg holes. (You can measure with drill bits if you aren't sure what your headstock has.) I wish they made these with a housing that would cover the alignment holes of most other tuners (Fender 2 pin and Sperzel 1 pin look like they would leave holes these can't cover.)

PROs
- Reasonable price for locking tuners
- Nice fit/feel
- Very secure once installed (properly)
- Black everywhere (unlike sperzel's black lockers which have a silver center peg.)
- Fits in 25/64" hole, typical of many guitars.
- They appear to be available in multiple finishes. I bought black.
- Small silver "dot" on center peg aids visibility/string insertion in darker environments. (like a club)

CONs
- Will not cover the 2 alignment pin holes on Stratocasters/Telecasters that use modern fender/schaller tuners. (as shown in photos on product page)
- Center peg is flat black, while the tuner handles and back casing are more of a shiny black.
- Washers and nuts seem thin/flimsy. I was concerned the nuts might strip really easily, but they went on ok using a socket.
- You will probably need to drill the holes for the alignment screws.

DETAILS, INSTALLATION HELP, OBSERVATIONS

I bought these to put on a Fender Custom Telecaster FMT HH that had black tuners, and they worked out great.
I was really annoyed that the tuners on that guitar had the 2 alignment pins about 1 pin width closer to the center peg than a normal fender/schaller tuner. But because of that, these Planet waves tuners were able to just cover the two holes. I wouldn't buy these for an American for Mexican strat or tele because as shown in the photos - they do not cover the alignment pin holes -- so they leave an unprofessional looking installation. But for this particular guitar, they worked great.

I really like the auto-trim feature. The locking knob could be slightly larger in diameter as it is the same as the tuner housing so is slightly harder to grip than it would be if it were a little bit larger, but it works ok. I prefer the shape of a fender/schaller tuning knob, so I may try taking the tuning knobs off the old tuners and putting on these, but I'm not sure if that will work or not.

Overall, these have a nice feel to them when installed. The basic mechanism is the same as any locking tuner, and they have a little silver pin on the center shaft that helps to show you where the string hole is. (Nice because with the black tuners, in a low light environment like a bar or club, when you have a broken string, the black is hard to see, but that little silver button/dot helps a lot. The nuts and washers on the front seem a little cheapish/flimsy, but they worked ok. These fit without issue in the 25/64" tuner holes in my head stock, no modification there. Before you drill, install all 6 tuners into the headstock holes, tighten them snug but not so firm that you can't rotate them with a little resistance. Then put a ruler across the back, align all 6 so they are straight, slightly tighten the nuts until you have them all aligned perfectly. Now drill the alignment screw holes using a 1/16" or smaller drill bit. Be careful to drill no deeper than the length of the screw. If in doubt, drill slightly less deep.I used the tiniest drill bit I have (1/16") to drill pilot holes for the anti-rotation screws...worked well. You can mark the drill bit with a black marker for the depth by holding it up to the screw to determine how deep it should go into the hole. Then drill slowly to get just the right depth for the screw. (Drill with the tuners in place.)

UPDATE 7/24/15 - I've had these installed for 6 months or more now on one of my guitars. I think they are really great. In fact I have upgraded my star rating from 4 to 5 stars after using these for a while. I've also expanded my own exposure to a variety of other locking tuners from Grover, Schaller and Fender and I have to say these would be my favorites if only the center post finishes matched the rest of the tuner, and if the mounting could conceal the holes of other original tuners better. Functionally, I love these. Cosmetically, they leave minor issues for me. I see they are now offered in some other finishes like Gold, Chrome and that's good except they all have the same black center post? I'm not crazy about that. I also see both 3x3 and 6 inline offerings which is good. Would love to see them offer additional button options like keystone shaped, grover kidney bean shaped, etc. Another clever option would be to offer some thin mounting adapter plates that would allow the tuner to cover the mounting holes of other popular tuners like the Fender/Schaller tuners. Planet Waves team - feel free to take those ideas and grow your tuner business! I would have put them on 5 more guitars by now if they hadn't lacked the ability to give a clean looking installation.
Summary: Nice tuners, good value, perfect fit for my specific application

I perform live as a soloist/1manBand... I play 2 guitars, keys, tracks on an Ipod so I have a lot of stuff to hook up. I was into the idea of snake cables to it all and made my last one with the little brass connections that are solder less. Those are ok, but the connection does go bad and you have to keep trimming the cable back to make the new connection. I still found that I had to plug into all of the pedals and wore those connectors out. I also run all in stereo for a great sound from processors and this time I used small xlr type cable that shares the ground and has 2 inside signal cables for interconnection. The Planet Waves does have 8 cables, each with a ground/shield and 2 signal wires, set up for XLR or stereo...this totals 24 of the 25 available in the D connector end.
This time I took the pedal board that has my track volume, guitar effects, vocal harmonizer and keyboard sustain and attached the open wire end of this Planet Waves system to that end. I glued the D connector to the end of the broad where it will meet the cable with two D connectors. This comes in two lengths 5 and 10 feet I believe. Then the other end where my rack is has another D connector tie wrapped and the open wire end has 1/4 inch and xlr connectors I soldered custom as I did for the pedal board end. I simply set every thing down, open my rack cases where the 5 foot cable stays connected and plug it into the pedal board. I ran a separate extension cable that is hardwired in the rack and goes down to the pedal board where I plug in a male ac cord that supplies power to the 2 ac adapters. You want to keep AC running separate to the signals or else you can get hum..but I did tape the run down to the pedal board next to the planet waves cord and it seems that the shielding they use does its job as I did not get any AC hum induced.
Now the big advantage besides a heap of time saved unwrapping and wrapping connectors, cables etc. is that these plugs are plugged in once at the pedal board and all of the connections are saved the wear of constantly being plugged in and unplugged... and the Planet waves D connectors have a much longer life of this type of wear...and when they go bad..I have 2 spare lines in the Planet Waves cable unused...or I just replace the one cable.
I play on the beach a lot and have constant salt mist and often get rained on to boot... I expect this is a durable and fast set up solution especially if you are using it around a studio or dry/clean environment.
I am glad that Planet Waves has this system...did not find anything else like it and did not want to try to solder a D connector without a big expensive machine to help... The connectors are very reasonably priced for any experimentation.. If you wire them the same you can have a 2nd back up rack that everything plugs into for different volume gigs or just if a rack goes down. I plan to buy another D with bare ends and a double D and do just that with my old rack.
I most always find Amazon has the best price and is hassle free when it comes to returning stuff. PayPal and EBay on the other hand, if you have a problem...well contact is like sending a Carrier Pigeon to the Moon.
Summary: Great system for fast connection and customizing your gear.

Text:
I purchased the Zoom G1Xon Guitar Effects Pedal without the expression pedal (one less moving part to possibly fail or break) and I'm thoroughly impressed. I've used everything from classic 1970's pedals to studio-grade rack-mount gear. This little pedal is a amazing value and packs an unreal amount of features and effects into such a small and inexpensive package.

Consider for a moment that the effects contained in this pedal are better than anything Buddy Holly, Elvis, or The Beatles had access to for any of their studio albums-- at any price. Then consider that you can not only have all this for about half a Benjamin, but in something about the size of a sandwich. The only thing you gotta remember is that this thing is very densely packed, and it's all digital.

Let's start first with the digital aspect. Digital is good because digital is efficient. You can pack a lot more effects into a digital patch-based pedal like this than you could if any of the effects were analog. The downside is that some of the effects will sound a little sterile or cold (namely the distortions). But for most uses, that's not going to be a problem. Even if you were to forget the overdrive and distortion options of this pedal, it's worth the price alone for all the delays, reverbs, and modulation effects. They sound excellent.

Then let's talk about the user interface (the UI). It's fine, but you're going to need to take some time to get used to it. Don't get frustrated and give up. When I was a kid, Boss pedals were all the rage. One pedal per effect, and they were expensive. The nice thing though was that you could just start twisting knobs and dialing-in the sound you wanted. With this combination effects pedal, you're going to have to get used to bouncing in an out of countless menus. It's a bit tedious, but you'll get into a groove where you know how to get around soon enough. Given the compact size and the price, it's worth the trade off. My suggestion would be-- once you go through all the effort to create a pedal combo you like-- save it for later reference. Many of the presets are over the top and when you get a half dozen sounds you like, that's going to be plenty for practicing and jamming.

The last thing I want to talk about is the rhythm patterns. I actually wish there were just a few more drum sounds to better distinguish the styles of music, but the number of styles is still very impressive. Even if you forgot about all the effects and distortions, this pedal would STILL be worth it's value for the fact that it's a tuner and for about a third of the cost of any drum machine, you get 66 practice patterns that cover nearly any style of music, and you can adjust the tempo (BPM) to your liking. This not only makes practicing fun, but less boring. The patterns they use here are NOT a metronome, but rather decent quality drum sounds. It's just great for practicing and jamming on a lunch break or after school/work.

Buy this pedal. It's about the best value I've seen in a multi-effects pedal in 25 years.
Summary: An Unreal Value, But You Gotta Learn the UI

I did not buy this through Amazon but rather at a center for guitars, but only because I wanted to play it first. You see, I bought an Epiphone DR-100 through Amazon several weeks ago. I liked it. I began learning to play, looking at justinguitar.com and freeandeasyguitar.com, sites I have no affiliation with, but I find them full of useful information. So, as I was playing and learning more about guitars, I looked at reviews of other guitars. I began thinking about which guitar I would buy if I should continue playing and outgrow my cheap guitar.

I bought the Epiphone thinking that I wanted to make a minimal investment in case I opted not to play. I now think if should have spent the extra $100 for this one. Why?

First, this is an amazing guitar for the money. It is extremely popular and almost universally praised. I have found reviews in four separate places that had tons of praise for this instrument. There was the rare poor review but I guess that will happen. So, one reason it's worth it to get this guitar over a cheap one is because you can resell it easily and probably for not a lot less than what you paid for it. Even among guitarists who are experienced and have other guitars, this model is still popular. If I was to try to sell the Epiphone, I bet I wouldn't get $50 for it.

Another reason is that this guitar sounds beautiful. It is rich and full. The tone is balanced and has sparkle, especially compared to the cheaper guitars I have heard. My son has a cheap Fender model and the Yamaha beats that one, too. It's not even close or debatable in my opinion. Those aren't really bad guitars. They just aren't as good as this one. It also feels ever to play, to me. I feel like I can fret chords better and that the strings buzz less. So, the action (the distance between the strings and frets) is better, or at least just about right.

Additionally, I would tell a beginner to get a decent guitar instead of cheap one. Why fight the guitar while you're trying to learn? And, if you really like your guitar like I like mine, you will want to play more and more often! I enjoy picking it up. The neck feels better. The resonance is amazing. I feel a sense of delight and pleasure when I handle this guitar (that sounded dirtier than I meant it to). This instrument is well made and designed. The tuners hold tune and are sensitive enough to make fine adjustments. The finish (I bought the Sandburst finished model) is beautiful. The frets are not sharp and I don't see any flaws in the binding or other areas of construction.

One small drawback is that the guitar only has one button for a strap, on the bottom of the guitar, so you will need something to attach the strap to the other point. I found a thing called Planet Waves Acoustic Guitar Quick Release System here on Amazon that I bought. It is used to attach to the headstock behind the nut without marring the finish of the guitar. This way you don't have to drill a hole in the body of the guitar and risk altering its tone. I haven't used it yet but it had a lot of good reviews.

I think this is a no-brainer for beginners. Get this guitar. If you have to save up for it, do it. Or buy one used. It is one of the most popular guitar models for good reason. If you have any questions, please ask and I will try to answer them. I love this guitar!
Summary: My second first guitar. I love it!

Text:
I have always wanted to play violin, and a few weeks ago I decided what the heck, I'm going to just get one. I did some research on Amazon and came across this set; the negative reviews made me question if I should buy it or not, but the amount of positive reviews helped me decide to just go ahead and get it.

When the violin first came, the strings were all set and everything, but (as expected) it was not in tune. I tried to tune it and I had some trouble. I've tuned a guitar before, so it's not like I was completely clueless- the problem was that I never used an instrument with a bridge before, so I knocked it over when tightening the strings. I wasn't 100% comfortable setting the bridge back up because everything feels so fragile and I didn't want to break anything. I took it to school (I'm a teacher) and had someone in the music department help me. If this is your first experience with tuning a stringed instrument, especially one with a bridge, I would highly suggest taking this to a music store or to someone who can help you. Tuning it after that initial setup isn't so hard; I purchased an awesome tuner to help me. I would HIGHLY recommend this tuner to anyone: [[ASIN:B004XNK7AI Snark SN-5 Tuner for Guitar, Bass and Violin]]. It's easy to use and really helpful!!

Next, I tried to assemble the shoulder rest. Lo and behold, I found that it did not fit...it must not have been made for a 4/4 full size violin because it wouldn't even reach across the bottom. Since the order was fulfilled by Amazon, I contacted them to see if they could replace the part. Amazon customer service is amazing and they said I could either return the whole set for a new one, or they would credit me for part of the cost of the violin so I could buy a new shoulder rest that did fit. I did not want to send the whole set back after the bridge/tuning business, so I had them credit me and I bought the [[ASIN:B002QJVTNA Everest EZ Series Shoulder Rest for 4/4 Violin]]. It fits perfectly, is affordable, and I can tell it's more comfortable than the one that came with the violin would have been.

After that, I took out the bow and began to work on that. I am not thrilled with the bow; when comparing all of the hairs on the bow, some of them were (and still are) more loose than others. However, when you buy a violin set for 60-70 dollars, you can't expect something mind-blowing and amazing. I used the rosin (you have to start it with some sandpaper or something) to get the bow ready to go. I actually ended up buying some better rosin because the stuff that came with the violin set seemed really cheap; after doing some research, I went with [[ASIN:B000BNG668 Pirastro Goldflex Rosin For Violin - Viola - Cello]]. I'm sure the cheap stuff is good enough to get by, but I wanted something of just a bit higher quality.

The violin set does come with an extra set of strings and an extra bridge; I like having those extra pieces as backups just in case. As for the quality of the strings, I've seen from other reviews that the strings really make a difference in the sound the violin makes; maybe in the future, I'll get some nicer strings, but for now the ones that came in the set work fine. I have friends that play the violin and I know the one I bought off Amazon doesn't sound half as nice (and it never will), but this Mendini set is such a great starter. It's affordable and sounds pretty good, which is all I need since I'm just teaching myself in my free time.

One last thing- I live in the middle of nowhere and do not have access to lessons (and the school I teach at doesn't even have orchestra- band only, so sad), so the book I've been using is [[ASIN:0634038176 Essential Elements 2000 for Strings Plus DVD: Violin Book 1]]. It's easy to use and comes with a DVD (which I didn't find too helpful) and a CD so you can play along with the tracks (which IS very helpful). I have also been using various YouTube videos for technique, like the bow hold, because those aren't covered as well in that book/on the DVD.

I am very pleased with this violin and I would highly recommend it- especially if you're an adult looking for something affordable to putz with!

Text:
When I'm playing at home, I play with a Peavey Vypyr amp. Those amps have terrible tuners. Never seems to pick up the correct note on my guitar. This tuner is much better. Easy configuration, you can set it for guitar or chomatic or flat steps down, etc. The interface is super easy to read. I personally like the style where it looks like the LEDs are spinning right/left for sharp/flat, but they have the standard off from center tuning that most tuners use. All in all, this is a great tuner pedal, and I'm very happy with it. It does what it does very well.

The thing I really like about this tuner is that there is an output and a bypass. Output gets cut when the pedal is active. If you are playing live, this is the one you will want to use. Bypass never gets cut. It's great for at home or if you are tuning somebody else to your instrument. But there's another awesome use for it; you can use it as a splitter and run your signal through 2 amps. This is fantastic for recording. Setting one amp up for the low end and another amp up for the high end and then mixing them together in the studio software makes for a very full sounding recording. If you want to run the same effects, put the tuner last, if you want to run different effects, put the tuner first.
Summary: Double duty pedal, tuner and a splitter

The clip is also much larger than the image would let you believe; however, the base is curved to allow your music to easily lay on top.

Some comments have indicated that when plugging the AC adapter into the base apparently did not disconnect the batteries as expected. The unit I purchased does disconnect the batteries upon insertion of the power cord into the clip. To confirm this on your unit: (1) DISCONNECT the AC adapter from the wall and from the light, (2) load batteries into the clip, and turn on the light, finally (3) with the AC adapter STILL DISCONNECTED from the wall outlet, plug the cable into the base. The light should go out. If it doesn't, your unit is not isolating the batteries from the AC adapter, and may present a fire hazard if the batteries are installed when the AC adapter is plugged in.

I've used the previous incarnation of this capo, and I thought I'd give it another shot.

Basically, there are the clamp action capos, which sometimes put too much pressure on the strings/frets and can cause premature fretware (an example is the Keyser Quick Change) and may also sharp the strings but are really handy and are operable with one hand; and there are the capos you put on with two hands and turn a dial to get the proper amount of pressure (such as the famous Shubb and Planet Waves own), harder to use, won't clamp onto the headstock for easy access when not in use, but won't damage anything or cause premature fretware or sharp your strings.

Generally, I stick with the latter, the Shubb and the Planet Waves capo of this type.

This capo tries to combine the best of both worlds. It can be clamped to the headstock for easy access and generally only requires one hand once you have the pressure dialed-in correctly.

The bad news is that, even using light-gauge strings, this capo, like its predecessor, just does not put enough pressure on the strings, even cranked all the way. The strings buzz because of this when they're open.

So, great idea, but I guess I will have to stick with the Shubb, the Shubb-like Planet Waves, and the like.
Summary: Not enough pressure for the first fret

The sanding block worked great. I levelled the frets of 2 guitars with one set of sandpaper, and still have the second set to do my other 2.

You won't get away with going cheap on the file, but if you only need to do a handful of your own guitars, this sandpaper/block is sufficient. And you don't need to spend $100+ on a Stew Mac file, the Fret Guru is proper, for ~$50.
And the metal fretboard protectors don't work, either, because when they're on, the file doesn't go close enough to the fret to file it. You gotta use like blue painter tape to protect the wood. I got a set of 120yds each of 1/4", 1/2" & 3/4" on Amazon pretty cheap that worked perfectly. It's enough to do 100+ guitars.
So the only thing useful in this package is the sanding block. It's still worth what I paid, but if you can buy just the block+sandpaper, do it. Don't bother with this file or the metal "protectors".
And I don't know why people need to further polish the frets with even finer grip paper or those Baroque sticks, my frets are as smooth as they need to be after this sander and the filing.

This is a great pedal, and although it is digital, it is more comparable to analog delay, as the delays are gritty, and tend to get the highs rolled off at the repeats, especially at long delays. The delays won't overpower your original sound, so you can have more delay volume without getting that washy digital delay sound, Tap tempo is a bonus. Tape simulation (basically a detune w/ lfo) works very well. Built like a tank, just like all the other Wampler pedals.

Shade control can be used to make the delay more predominant as it is a treble boost, but the delays are very noisy when the shade knob is turned up past, particularly at longer delay sounds. It adds a constant hiss under your guitar sound. This knob adds highs to the delay, so it makes sense that it would add noise, but it is really unusable at anything over 12:00 for medium delays, and must be turned down for long delays I actually prefer it all the way down, because I like a dark delay. But the point is, even though you can get a nice, gritty delay with good highs in it, you will end up with an underlying hiss under your guitar sound. So if you are looking for a crisp delay, look elsewhere, but if you want a thick, dark gritty delay, this is the one for you.
Summary: Good, gritty delay that doesn't get in the way, but can be noisy.

This is the 3rd humidifier that I've bought. It's very safe to use in any acoustic guitar and it's easy to see when it needs more water. This is the ONLY humidifier that I will trust in the guitars that I build.

UPDATE:
it's January 2, 2018. The humidity is extremely low. Even in my workshop, which has 2 large evaporative humidifiers, to keep the humidity at a constant 45-50%, is a struggle this year. It's dipped below 40% at times, which puts all of the guitars in my shop, many worth 10s of thousands of dollars, in peril. I'm getting ready to order 5 more Oasis humidifiers, to put into the soundholes of 5 new builds in various stages of completion. I still consider the Oasis to be the best humidifier on the market.

I urge you to keep a good hygrometer in your case. Anything above 55% can dismantle your precious guitars as easily as too low of a humidity. Whether you live with high, low, or fluctuating humidities, it's best to create a microclimate for your acoustic guitar. The best method is to store it in its case, with a good hygrometer (caliber IV for cigars is excellent), so you can respond to humidity extremes quickly. You should be aiming for 45-55%. Long periods below 45% or above 55%, are dangerous. Use the Oasis, unless you see humidity that exceeds 55%. Use a couple packs of dessicant if you see high humidity.

For those of you who leave your guitars out of the case, you must control the humidity in your chosen guitar storage area. You need to humidify, dehumidify, or use a combination. Remember, 45-55%, is the max range.

The rubber in the Oasis will disintegrate if it becomes totally dried out; it will also harden over time, when you fill it with hard water. Use distilled water to prolong the life of the crystals and rubber membrane. I have a weekly alarm on my phone to remind me to refill the Oasis humidifiers. If the membrane hardens or is allowed to dry out, you'll see water drops form on the seam. You should always check for this and if you see it, discard the humidifier.
Summary: I'm a Luthier and this is my recommendation

Text:
Having a nice selection of overdrive pedals has been interesting as each has their sound and nuances. This pedal does not come with foam on the back pre-glued. That right there is a huge plus for me.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a box with four optional feet of silicone to press onto the back recessed areas in the four corners. there is a 9 volt adapter for a battery, and there is a pretty decent instruction paper with this if this is your first overdrive pedal.

CONTROLS
The knobs on this are pretty easy to control. They are easy to see on an area with subdued light being that they are white against the black background. The switch between normal and special has to be used up close as it is not easy to quickly access in the middle of a performance. It is somewhat recessed.

BYPASS?
This seems to be a true bypass as advertised.

PERFORMANCE
This pedal is a decent overdrive. It has a bit of messiness to it, but not so much that it is muddy. It has some really fun effects and I like to be able to mess with the different tuning knobs. It really helps me get some interesting effects as compared to some pedals with minimal knobs and tuning.

SIZE
This is a full sized pedal not a mini pedal just in case you did not notice that and are new to pedals.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a great pedal if you need to have a pedal for your board, or just a single and are on a budget. Performance is decent and the adjustments are more numerous than other pedals I have used. I am THRILLED that this does not come with foam glued on the back so I can put my own velcro strip on the back for my board.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is solid. I am really happy that this does not come with foam on the back so we can customize it as we see fit. The performance is decent and I am happy with it.
Summary: Decent Overdrive Pedal For A Budget

Text:
This is my first time trying a “Lerodite” pedal. However.. in the photos, it says Mosky on the pedal so.. it’s a Mosky brand / rebrand. I’ve got a few Mosky pedals and mostly love them.

Not much in the box.. no instructions or explanations about the various modes.

But Gain and Level need no introduction, so the only mystery is the D/M switch.

The D mode seems cleaner, louder, maybe less compressed.

The M mode seems slightly dirtier, more compressed and quieter.

What the modes have in common is VERY subtle gain changes until you get to around 3 o’clock and then the dirt piles on exponentially.

Might be a dodgy circuit.. could be a weird pot taper. But it means you have to crank the Gain all the way to hear this pedal sing.

When going all out, the pedal has a slightly retro / fuzz vibe that is, to me, really fun.

There’s no Tone knob, so whatever brightness you put into the pedal, you mostly get back out. Might benefit from pairing with a cheap EQ pedal.

With humbuckers, it’s pretty easy to dial in classic rock riff tone.

With Single Coils, you can dial back the gain and get some very sweet low gain, edge of distortion tones. Roll back your volume for
More subtle changes.

Overall, it’s a very basic, cheap pedal that seems kinda flawed but it’s worth spending some time with it to unlock some genuinely fun tones. Kinda reminds me of the EX Chickenhead distortion that similarly has a “freak out” zone towards the end of the Gain taper that goes nuts but sounds cool.

For $30.. I think it’s a 4 star pedal.
Summary: Cheap and cheerful low gain (mostly) pedal

This little pedal is taking stepping up to fill the overdrive slot on my gigging pedalboard. And it does a respectable job.
Is it exactly like any other overdrive pedal? No, it's its own thing. But it is very much like my tube screamer and does all the jobs I've asked it to.

The switch on the pedal is a quality switch, there's no switching noise on the pedal I ordered. The knobs are small, obviously, but they offer plenty of range. On my rig, I set it this pedal to one sound and leave it, so the small knobs aren't an issue. I have a second distortion for a second sound, so I never have to reach down to twist knobs. These things are small, so why not have more than one distortion/overdrive?

Like any gain pedal, it will amplify noise in your signal chain, but it doesn't seem to add much noise of its own.

I'm really enjoying building a new, tiny pedalboard, and the Green Mile overdrive is earning its place in my signal chain.

I hope this review helps you!

Got this unit with some reserve....I had an M-audio Fast Track, and I was not sure why the Alesis was so affordable and with 2 IN for the instruments or mic.

The quality of the case is very low; cheap plastic for the case and the knobs, same for the switches and mic connectors; the only metal parts are the 3.5 inch jack where you plug your guitars or your external equipment, and the headphone OUT

The unit itself looks cheap, but what it matters is what it does; and this pup does it right.

I've hooked it to my Mac pro via USB, and as soon as i plugged it, Snow leopard recognized it; I just had to switch my audio settings to redirect the audio in, audio out and system sounds to the io2 and everything is set up.

I am happy to hear no noise even if the volume is cranked up, while wearing headphones; this means that either the circuit board is well done, or the unit is well shielded from external interference (the fasttrack would give a disturbing hiss now and then; that would disappear if i would change position to the unit of few inches)

The mic in works great; plugged in a mic and it works just fine; setting the knobs is a cakewalk since they are pretty precise and does not make any noise while twisting them (again, means that the people that put this together did a good job shielding the unit; we will see how good is shielded from dust, since that is one of the main causes of noise while twisting the knobs)

the Line in/Guitar in works also great; plugged in my guitar and increased the gain and the sound was really good; tried it with garageband and guitar rig 4 and the latency was under 10ms; versus 18ms with the FastTrack; the Phantom +48v is also useful if you just plug the guitar without amplifier; in this way you can use a sound modeling software like guitar rig and play nice effects directly into your computer, saving the hassle to bring in interference and other noise that would come from the amplifier or pedal.

The recording was also awesome; you can tell that the quality is high when you listen at something recorded with the io2, using Bose headphones or a good audio equipment; the quality was same if not better of a 196kbps MP3, even at high volume and using software equalizer.

The chance to use 2 IN at the same time (2 guitars, guitar and mic, mic and line in and so on) opens up a lot of possibilities; tried with mic and guitar and it works fine; giving you control on each separate channel (the +48v gain works globally on both IN ) with separate knobs for the gain and 2 extra knobs to control the mix between the wet and dry sound (so you can listen the sound of the instrument before being processed by the computer, and after)and to control the main level.

In the end i give this unit a 5 star, since even if is cheaply made; feels pretty solid when you actually use it; and cost much less than any other comparable external usb unit for mac.
Summary: perfect for mac, affordable and reliable

I've been working on a personal music electronics project for months. It requires a non-latching (doesn't toggle between "on" and "off" positions with each click), momentary (only goes "on" [that's a "normally open/off" switch] or "off" [that's a "normally closed/on" switch] when you push the pedal) footswitch. I have now looked at and/or actually tested/used three different brands of such footswitches: Philmore 30-17090; Hosa FSC-502 and Boss FS-5U. All the makers have different versions of the same switch ... if you know you need a "momentary" switch, then you have to find out if the type you need is "normally open/off" or "normally closed/on." As explained below, the Boss switch eliminates that problem.

The Philmore switch is the cheapest pre-fab switch I could find "out there," and comes with a basic 1/4 inch cable pre-installed. It "works," but it's like a noisy little tin can, and the guts of it are just too crude to really work effectively/consistently with any modern digital music devices. I couldn't get it to work properly/consistently with my project ... this switch is really designed for analog control of lights, ham radio mic/audio, etc.

The Hosa switch is "OK," also comes with a pre-installed cable, and SHOULD work, but it's basically a glorified version of the Philmore device, designed/made a little better for use with digital music devices ... that is, the internal circuitry is better designed for that function.

Then there's the Boss switch, which doesn't come with a pre-installed cable ... you'll have to provide your own. I've already been using two of these switches for years, as a controller for an Alesis SR-16 drum machine. One switch for "on/off," the second for switching between "A" and "B" patterns. They've worked so great for that purpose, I NEVER had a switch-related problem until one of them finally became so worn/glitchy that I had to replace it. That took about 10 years of regular (more than weekly) use.

Inside and out, Boss is the best such device out there. The case is thick, solid aluminum with a hard rubber base, and is basically bombproof. It has modular grooves on the right and left sides that allow you to lock multiple units side-by-side, and create a "bank" of as many separate switches as you want/need. The pedal is firm and the switch action is QUIET. The design that transfers the heavier action of the pedal to the more fragile/delicate internal circuit-board push-button is the best I've seen, and the internal circuitry is specifically designed to properly interface with the highly sensitive circuitry of digital music equipment.

Unlike the other two, the Boss pedal can also function as EITHER a "normally on/closed" OR "normally off/open" switch, by use of a toggle switch mounted next to the 1/4 inch input jack. This switch is simply labeled "polarity," but what it actually does is change the way the switch operates ... from "normally off/open" to "normally on/closed," and back again, so you know this one switch can easily be made to work with either type of input ... no experimenting with different model numbers.

In sum, if you know you need a "momentary" footswitch, spend the extra money and buy the Boss. It's the best-designed, most durable and most reliable option out there for the price, and it will save you a lot of headaches in the long run.
Summary: Inside and out, best passive momentary switch out there for the price.

I have been doing music for years. Recording is not something new to me, and at this point I am looking for something that is going to make recording easier, not harder. I thought that the Focusrite Solo was going to do that for me, but I was apparently sadly mistaken.

From the minute that I got this device, it has been nothing but a headache. From the installation process, registration before it could even be used, and the lengthy process of installing everything needed, I already had a headache. But whatever, the device was plugged in and turned on. Plugged in the mic and headphones, and everything is sounding good. Then, as soon as I hit the record button, all hell breaks loose.

The audio that is supplied through the box is distorted, electrical, and overall completely unusable even for the most basic home recordings or living room sessions. The direct-monitoring makes it seem like there are no issues with the sound, as everything directly monitored is perfectly crisp and clean. However, that doesn't mean much of anything when you can't record anything at all, and the device you were relying on to work simply does not.

A friend and I sat down and attempted to figure out what was causing this issue, thinking it may have been the software rather than the hardware. However, using a different software gives the same results. We read online that toying with the settings will oftentimes resolve this issue, but every time we attempted to reset something like the buffer rate or sample size, the computer either completely crashed, or the device immediately reset itself, because apparently it doesn't matter what the user selects, the device will still automatically reset itself.

After messing with it for the better part of an hour, we weren't able to figure anything out and decided to reach out to Focusrite Customer Service. This turned out to be a bigger joke than the product. Looking through their FAQ was useless (and considering how may comments report this issue, that alone is an absolute absurdity, Focusrite KNOWS this problem exists, it would be impossible not to with how many negative reviews state an issue exactly like this), and required me to write into the company. Yes, you'll have to email Focusrite and hope that your matter is important enough for them to get back to you in some kind of timely manner. And I'll tell you a secret, they won't get back to you in a timely manner.

Overall, you really need to pass on this. Unless you are willing and prepared to go through the headache of trying to screw with your settings for hours, search online forums for several days, and then have to wait for God only knows how long for Focusrite to get back to you, and even returning the unit to try a different one, I cannot in good conscience recommend this item to any musician. Our money is valuable, and should be put towards things that will actually do what they're supposed to do, and work how they're supposed to work, or at very least be a little more user friendly when things don't work.

Focusrite Customer Support, I hope you are paying attention because you have an absolutely LIVID customer.

The Ernie Ball MVP is a great volume pedal. I am used to a Morley Little Alligator volume pedal, which is optical, not controlled by a volume pot. There are advantages and disadvantages to both. For instance, the string that controls the volume pot on the MVP will eventually fray and need to be replaced. Likewise, the pot itself may go bad over time – hopefully not during a live show!

The optical is certainly more reliable, but I’ve noticed that the sweep on the Morley is not as smooth as the sweep on the MVP. There are advantages and disadvantages to this as well. For instance, the Morley is great for cello-like single note attacks. The MVP is far better (IMHO) for ambient swells. I use ambient swells in the church setting where I play, almost like giving the keyboard player a break when he/she is covering more piano parts and we need the added pads.

The MVP, like the Morley, has a minimum knob which allows you to set a lower volume in the toe up position. Personally, I have never used this feature as I prefer to do swells from no volume to full volume. That being said, I can see where this feature would be very helpful before OR after your drives. Before the drives you could use it to adjust gain/distortion levels – after the drives you could use it as an overall volume boost. The MVP also has the added feature of a decibel boost knob. This is great, especially in conjunction with the minimum knob, or by itself if you need the added gain. Personally, I don’t use this feature as well but I can still see the added benefit.

What is also nice about this pedal is the fact that it is buffered/powered (9v). So, if you use the tuner out (as I do) you don’t lose high end frequencies. In other words, it doesn’t suck your tone.

All in all, this is a great volume pedal and I have it secure on my pedal board. I won’t say that I’m not apprehensive about the string eventually fraying and breaking, because I am. However, it is especially smooth and works most excellently for ambient volume swells. Definite five stars from me!

Text:
There is a much-respected set of headphones made by Audio-Technica called the M-50 (the current model is the ATH-M50X)

It is a recording industry standard and, when someone says they are considering buying an overpriced pair of Beats headphones, the most common response from anyone knowledgeable is - don't waste your money - just get a pair of (Audio-Technica) M50's, they're a better headphone for way less money.

By their name and how they LOOK very much like Audio-Technica M50-s, and how they say "pro" in the name, these Rockville "Pro M50's" appear to be specifically trying to get people to buy it based on the Audio-Technica M50 legacy. Rockville is not Audio Technica, of course.

There ISN'T actually anything automatically bad about cloning a classic. I can't count the number of GOOD clones of the Neumann u87 microphone out there. I've got a Chinesse sE electronics se4400 that was very obviously made to go up against the much respected AKG 414 and it is excellent at half the price - cloning in and of itself is NOT bad.

However if their specific appeal is cloning the AT M50, I would want to see the specs, charts, perhaps some references to reviews putting them head to head. Maybe a link back to a page on the Rockville website with info about Rockville M50' vs Audio-Technica M50's. Without this information I think it is kind of unfair selling them like this, simply hoping to catch the unaware?

Searching for 10 minutes online, I can't find any reviews on any of the gear-oriented forums or websites of the Rockville - AT M50's are sold as pro audio monitor headphones. Rockville "Pro-M50's" appear to be available at Walmart. IF their plan was to make an affordable clone, where are the reviews they should be soliciting? From Harmony-Central to Gearzlutz to Sound on Sound to Head-Fi, there is dead silence regarding these headphones.

To sum up, if you want some M50's GET some real Audio-Technica M50's. If $50 is your price range, do your research, see what is best for your purposes in that price range. IF these are an honest attempt to clone the performance and quality of the M50, then it is a shame there is no information out there about them.

I went to the rockville audio website and there was no frequency response chart for this model headphone. Their website has a number of products under Pro Audio that have the appearance of classic pro audio gear - for instance, they have some studio monitors that look similar to KRK Rokit studio monitors. If Rockwell is trying to sell affordable quality audio to the masses, and there is certainly a niche/need for that, I hope they get their products out there for review to trusted reviewers.

First of all, these are NOT isolated. The adjustable outputs aren’t isolated, either. However, I bought two of these, knowing that they aren’t isolated, in advance. I also bought them, anticipating having to replace them, if I did have any problems. I have a LOT of pedals. Some vintage, some new, and everything in between. I’ve had no noise issues or any other problems. (Please note that some pedals (mostly vintage ones) have a positive ground, which won’t with this power supply. (If using it with negative ground pedals, as well.) You’ll have to either power those pedals separately, or get a TRUE isolated supply.)  The power adapter can provide 2 amperes (2,000 ma) of current, which is more than most of these less-expensive supplies can deliver. Keep in mind, that this is the total current that the supply can deliver. Each ‘port’ can supply 300ma, with one adjustable port supplying 500ma. However, this is the rating of individual ports. You can’t add up all of the ports and expect that much current. Adding them up might make some people believe that it can supply 2,600ma of current. It will only deliver what the power adapter will provide. (2,000ma) This isn’t a problem, or a criticism of it. It just something that you should understand, if you’re planning on using tons of pedals. It’s unlikely that you’ll use that much, anyway. Most pedals don’t use more than 25ma. (You should check your pedal’s specifications, though. Some CAN draw a lot of current.)  Personally, I think that this supply works great. It’s quiet and powers all of my pedals. Depending on YOUR setup, you MAY have problems with it. Some people do, most people don’t. Luckily, you can return it, if you do. I’m an EE, by profession. I have opened the unit and it appears to be well made. Is it as good as a OneSpot supply? Of course not, but it’s also not $179.00  I would definitely recommend trying it. Out of all of the ‘inexpensive’ power supplies, this one had the best reviews, which is why I chose it. I’m glad that I did. I saved a bunch of money and I’m very happy with it. If anything changes, I’ll update my review.  Rock on!
Summary: Not isolated, but I haven’t had any problems.

Text:
Nobody had done it and I wanted to know, so I compared this Hotone with the Morley mini-wah/volume and the new mini-Crybaby after buying all three.

First, the good stuff about the Soul Press: it's nice and small. It does volume and wah. You can adjust the volume sweep. It's solidly made of good metal.

But I didn't keep it, for one main reason: the wah sound is like a harsh Crybaby with way too much distortion added. Which is fine for Jimi-style leads, but a lot of the time I just want that old wacka-wacka Shaft thing on clean rhythm parts, and this can't do that as cleanly as it should. No matter what volume or gain level you hit this thing with, it cracks up the signal and adds that squonky Crybaby midrange harshness that, while helping an already-distorted lead cut through the mix, is not at all what I want added to my clean tone, and clean wah is vital on many tunes. So I guess this Hotone is less Hot One and more Ho Tone.

That said, if all you need wah for is lead, then this might be just what you want, as it sure does leave plenty of room on your pedalboard. However, it was a bit small for my size 11 shoe, which overlapped it considerably and ended up hitting the pedal next to it, which is never good. It's also got the adapter jack on the side, a big minus for me. If you're trying to conserve pedalboard real estate, which this was clearly designed to do, put the plug on top, kids. I just don't get why some firms don't understand that. Don't you guys play? Or do you all have mega-PedalTrains with space for 27 pedals?

The Soul Press is also a decent volume pedal, though I'd guess the pot will go within a year or two if you're on it a lot. I still prefer the Morley-style light-pots that never wear out. You must also be careful not to turn off the wah or volume by accident when using the Soul Press, as it happens pretty easily. Not great when you're gigging and perhaps a little wild and out of control.

One real negative is that you can't switch wah to volume or vice-versa by foot; you need to bend down and switch them by hand on the side. Being able to go from wah to vol via the footswitch is a key thing that both Morley and Hotone neglect, and that's truly unfortunate for those of us who'd like that feature. Having it be optional via a side switch would be perfection. Hello, engineers working for one or both of these firms...

So, if you have small feet (or lots of room around the pedal on your board), only want a raw, wailing wah sound, and need a tiny pedal that does both volume and wah, this is not a bad choice. It can also function as an expression pedal when hooked up to a device that uses one, but I don't use one of those, so I can't say how well it does that, sorry.

By the way, as far as true bypass goes, the Morley is the most transparent of the three when not on. That matters a lot to me as I put the wah at the start of the chain and I don't really want much of a buffer there, despite what some folks say about a buffer up front. Vintage wahs are infamous for making noise due to that, and none of these does, so that's a plus.

The mini-Crybaby sounds the best of the three, but not by much, and is wah-only. Pretty much the same size though, so if you only need a tiny wah, I'd go for the Dunlop over the other two.

But I ended up keeping my mini-wah/volume from Morley instead, as its wah is easily adjustable from clean to fuzzy (though it has a tone some like and some don't), its pot won't wear out, and you can change the volume and wah tones to your preference by moving the led lights inside. You do have to use a button to change from volume to wah, but that also means you won't switch them by accident while wailing away. It also fits my foot better. Plus, surprisingly, it's twenty bucks cheaper. And it's made in the USA, a rare thing for any low-priced pedal these days. This Hotone is made in China, and my Chinese pedals always seem to crap out within a year or two...caveat emptor.

All told, while neither is perfect, I much prefer the Morley mini-wah/volume, but the Soul Press is still a good and versatile pedal at a fair price.

Still, I'll take Made In USA and cheaper any day, as those two things rarely go together these days.
Summary: A comparison of this Soul Press, the Morley mini-wah/volume, and the mini-Crybaby

I picked up the Onstage GS7361 at my local music shop for $50, and it's a keeper.

1) Build quality: there’s a bunch of bad reviews here, so I was leery. However, the machining on my stand is perfect – screws holes are where they’re supposed to be, everything fits just fine, and the end product is sturdy, stable, and level. Either Onstage had production problems that have been fixed, or the bad reviews are from people who can’t assemble something from scanty instructions. It’s fine for home use, but nowhere near as sturdy as pro gear would be. I don’t gig, but if I did, I’d look at more expensive stuff, like the Hercules.

2) Assembly instructions: scanty, but adequate. Anyone with an IQ higher than the 2019 occupant of the Oval Office will do just fine. Make sure the two base pieces have the foam padding facing up and to the inside, and the upright pieces have the padding facing forward and to the inside.

3) Storage: I need compact storage for two acoustic guitars, and it’s perfect (see photo). Because the two bottom-rack dividers are removable, you have four configuration options. I removed the right-hand divider for the two acoustics in the picture.

4) Don’t even THINK about using this for two acoustics and an electric – there just isn’t enough room (see photo). You will bang your guitars against each other, every single time you move one in or out. Don’t do it! It's just plain wrong of them to advertise this as safe storage for acoustic/electric/acoustic.

5) One acoustic & two electrics – it’ll work, but be careful.

6) Three electrics – ditto.

7) The actual storage space, on the inside of the frame, is 13.25 inches. Subtract from that the width of either or both of the removable base dividers. The outside width of the stand is 15.5 inches, and it’s 21.5 inches deep.

8) I rated it 4 stars for two reasons: First, the foam padding on the side pieces and the uprights is thin, and doesn’t feel like it’ll stay glued down for very long. I may add a layer of foam tape, just for the extra padding. Second, it's flat-out false advertising to state that you can safely store two acoustics and an electric.

I’m happy to recommend this for most any home/studio guitar storage EXCEPT acoustic/electric/acoustic.
Summary: Excellent for home use.  Build quality:  Just fine.  Space for guitars:  use wisely!

YES, it's another chinese knockoff SM-57... NO, I didn't want to like it... YES, I bought it "just to see..." And YES now I want 2-3 more of them !!!

I don't have a real SM-57 to compare with, but I have 2 x (real) SM-58's, 2 x Sennheiser e825s, and a few cheap-o-depot mics for down-n-dirty applications. IMO, the GLS ES-57 goes toe-to-toe with ANY mic I ever heard in the $100-$150 range - and blows them all away in terms of value.

Granted, I'm just a hobbyist musician goofing around with at-home recording. I really don't "know" what I'm talking about. All I can tell you is what I HEAR. I've used this mic (with a generic windscreen) on female vocals, to mic a guitar amp, to mic a cajon, and as a single overhead mic for an entire drum kit. Everything coming thru this mic sounds wonderful right off the bat. Thru my MG10XU mixer and Turbosound iP2000 speaker, this mic is crystal clear with excellent transient response - and IMO, tracks from this mic seem to be especially responsive in post-production.

Maybe it's not as durable as a real 57 (I dropped my GLS 57-clone from atop a mic stand and it didn't miss a beat.) Maybe it doesn't handle higher SPL's as well as a real 57 (I haven't tried it on a kick drum yet.) And at the end of the day, it IS a chinese knock-off of (one of) the most iconic microphones in history. But it's also $36 vs $99.

So if you're new to microphones in general, and looking for some quick solid advice, here it is: Buy a real SM-57 or SM-58 for good karma (seriously) then grab 3 of these little gems. You'll be all-in for under $250 with a set of 4 excellent mics that cover 90% of the musical applications you'll likely encounter for years to come.

If you can only afford or need one mic right now, buy this GLS 57 clone and don't look back.

It really is that good.

JM2C :-)

Text: Exactly what we needed to rest the guitar on.  Fits great, and I would recommend it.

There is a lot more to this controller than meets the eye. You get 32 mini keys but they are really nice to play. In fact, the aftertouch is easily the best I've ever used on any keyboard of any size. I love playing this keyboard. It doesn't have any sliders, pads or knobs you can assign to softsynths, so it's possibly more suited to using with desktop hardware synths. I use mine with a Waldorf Rocket and it has basically turned it into a mini workstation.

The device itself has real heft to it and feels very well made. Because it's designed as a box, you can stand it up on it's front to plug in cables. It surprised me how cool it was to do, very handy. It's got lots and lots of connection options and you can sync the arpeggiator and sequencer to several different sources (USB, MIDI, Clock).

You get 8 sequences. Each can be up to 64 steps and each step can have up to 8 notes played. But that's not all. Via the MIDI Control Center software you can create, edit and store all the sequences you like. Then, through a simple drag and drop interface, you can copy new saved sequences into the KeyStep's memory, even while it is playing. It allows you virtually unlimited sequences, even when playing live on stage (if you are brave enough). Patterns can also be transposed, which is also very handy.

There is also an arpeggiator with 8 preset patterns. You can latch the arp and use aftertouch to get some variation into proceedings. It is very usable. The Arp and Sequencer can be set to a different MIDI channel to the keyboard, so you can control two instruments at once.

It's not all fabulous, though, The pitch bend touchstrip isn't nearly as good as a proper wheel, although the mod strip works OK. You can't change presets from the controller, either, which seems like a massive oversight that will limit its appeal. But if you can live with these problems and the mini keys, I think this is a really, really good controller and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

1. Brutally overpriced for what it actually is imo. The dilemma is that there are so few (if any) quality contact mics like this available. About the only other options are cheapo knock-off versions so whatcha gonna do?

2. Yes... everyone is right about that stupid, thin, fragile wire. At this price point you'd think they could splurge and make the cable a mm or two thicker. You feel like you have to handle this thing like it's a basket of raw eggs balanced on a stack of fine china. I try to take good care of everything but with this I worry if, for even a few seconds, it's left alone on the stage floor where it might get stepped or tripped on and not survive it. It's not like it will be cheap to replace. Time will tell how it holds up but, at this point, I feel slightly ripped off seeing that it appears to have been constructed solely for a musician working all alone in a private home studio and not built for the real world stage and gig work. Cable is longer than I need it to be. Giving the buyer a couple-three options in this regard would have been thoughtful.

In the end this is a very useful mic with a nice clean sound and a smooth-ish frequency response that is easy to work with. Where you position it in the first place will greatly affect the sound. Find the spot you like and eq gently from there.

Very glad I didn't end up going with some sort of clip on or stand held mic for our violin. This is so much easier to deal with in a (non-studio controlled) live stage situation. If a contact mic is what you're after then I think you'll be happy with this one... if you can put the price tag in the rear view mirror AND then vow to take extra good care of it. You'd think they might supply a decent storage/travel bag at this price. At least one of ours came with a tiny bag but Id never want to coil a cable that tight... especially a super thin one like this thing has. I ended up buying a pair of Shure Beta 52A bags off eBay and they seem to do the trick.. a tad larger than they really need to be but the mics stay safe.

Note: didn't get ours on Amazon so I'm not a "verified purchaser." Bought from those guys who follow up on your purchases and send you free candy along with your item:)

Text:
For inexpensive DMX lights, these things are packaged very nice. They come in nice white boxes rather than generic brown cardboard shipping containers. The support e-mail address is clearly listed on the packaging.

There is a nice English manual included. It has COLOR in its diagrams, and is a fold-out thick paper manual, and not some crappy black and white photocopy looking manual light most of the low end lights I have. The grammar is even good. It came folded over and in a cardboard envelope - fancy.

The manual explains all the built in functions you can do from the back menu, but is missing the DMX settings. I found those in a photo posted to another review of these lights.

The lights have the standard MENU/UP/DOWN/ENTER buttons, and the expected modes -- set a color, set a color fade pattern, set a jumping color pattern, set a strobe effect, and sound modes. You can also manually set any color and brightness by setting the R, G, and B levels. Just like all the other lights I have.

Where they shine is their warranty. They claim "lifetime guarantee".

I did not believe it, so I wrote the e-mail to see if they even answered. A day or so later, I got a response. They claim to stand behind their lights. This, alone, makes me want to choose AOELLIT for cheap DMX lights since they can "replace, refund or repair it free of charge" if there is an issue.

Nice.

The build quality isn't bad at all -- certainly better than some real cheap lights I buy in bulk from eBay. The power cable is permanent, which is what you get at the price point usually.

The remote looks identical to ones I have gotten with U'King and other brands.

No issues. If one dies, I'll update this review with how they handle the warranty.
Summary: Well packaged. Non-removable power cable. GREAT warranty. Fast response from company.

These are a far cry from the same straps of yesterday.

The nylon strap material is cheap feeling and just flimsy. These are not particularly comfortable straps. I mainly use these on my instruments while recording at my desk in a seated position, to prevent accidental drops. I would not trust these on stage for any type of dynamic performances. Not to mention a guitar of any substance will cause this strap to dig into your shoulder. You don't need that.

If you're sitting on a chair, In a coffee house, and just need some drop protection - they are ok, and cheap. Anything more, and this strap will be a huge disappointment.

The leather ends are really cheap cuts of scrap, too. They used to be so substantial, you would have a hard time getting them onto your strap button when they were new.
They are much easier to put on your strap buttons now, because the leather is so thin and cheap. The opening will stretch quickly on these cheapos, so you may need strap locks of some sort. Consider that and add the extra cost to your investment. Also keep in mind that using this on a nitro finish or even lighter color finish guitars is probably not advisable as I would imagine the cheap leather will allow the dye to rub off over time. No one needs that, little surprise.

Anyway, for what I use them for, when they were on sale for six bucks, that's a reasonable deal. Otherwise, especially if you are a beginner, do not assume, cheap is good, because you are just starting out. It's not, and will only dampen your enjoyment of playing. Get something better, and be happy.
Summary: Don't make'em like they used to

This is not my first Wampler pedal. I have an Ecstasy and a Paisley OD, and both are top notch pedals. This one is no different. I purchased it to take the place of my Blues Pearl Perplexed, which is another "Marshall in a Box" type of pedal that is also loosely based on the Marshall Guv'nor. That pedal has not been produced in 10 years, and has a big footprint.

I was able to get a near exact tone with the Pinnacle by manipulating the tone and contour. Being that the Perplexed has a bass, mid and treble control, it goes to show just how versatile the Contour control really is.

But the pedal can do SO much more. While I prefer the warm mids of the Vintage mode, the Modern mode will give you a brighter edge suitable for 80's thrash metal through modern rock. There is a ton of gain on tap, even without the boost, and plenty of volume to kick the front end of an amp.

But I ended exchanging the pedal for the Deluxe model. The main reason is that with the gain at anywhere above 12:00, kicking in the boost does add hiss (expected for this much gain). So I wanted to be able to control it with the pedal to kick it off (and the noise) during quiet parts of our songs. Also, it is just so much more handy having the boost on a footswitch for lead boosts. Not only does it give you a slight kick in volume, but it gives you that stacked OD pedals "butter" lead sound with infinite sustain. Having the boost on the pedal allows me to just use this one pedal on by board for rhythm and lead OD sounds, where before, I'd use a second "tube screamer" type pedal afterward to boost mids and volume for leads.

Overall, you can't go wrong with this pedal, but if you do want the versatility of having a dynamic OD for rhythm, plus a super compressed OD for leads, think about the Deluxe model.
Summary: Great pedal, but consider the Deluxe version.

All of the karaoke devices I’ve been seeing online are basically a glorified speaker and a microphone or two. As a musician, I see this as just a tiny, sub-par p.a. system. What’s the point? Obviously, for folks that don’t have a p.a. system, one of these little contraptions might work just fine.

When I saw this system, though, I started to get excited… with the key feature being a BUILT-IN tablet that connects to wifi and Bluetooth and can download karaoke apps. It also has TWO wireless microphones and a bunch of options on one panel of the speaker…

As this is listed at a much higher price than other karaoke systems I’ve been seeing, I immediately thought: high quality, lots of features, this is a no brainer!

I am afraid that I have to report that the system does NOT deliver. The “tablet” is the worst tablet I’ve worked with since the first cheapo one I got in the early days of tablets, and even a little worse than that. The touchscreen is barely responsive, especially if what you want to press is near the edge of the screen. The processor is extremely weak, so there is a significant delay when doing just about ANYthing on the screen… and it’s already at max capacity: I tried to download two different karaoke apps from the prominently-displayed Play Store (I’ve never seen that “Pending” message for so long!), and immediately started getting those “you are running out of memory” messages. The tablet is just… not good. And when you fold it closed, there’s no “click” and no safety piece that slides over any part of it to hold it in place, so it wobbles when you move the unit.

The unit comes with a large leather strap that’s fine if you want to carry it on your shoulder, but there should be some kind of a small handle to move it from place to place or readjust it.

The wireless mics ‘find’ the unit without a problem. For us there was a steady undercurrent of static, though, whenever you’re making any sound into the mic, which you may not notice, and isn’t really that big a deal for the purposes of karaoke, but still… this is a pricy unit!

The eq (Bass and Treble) knobs are almost entirely useless; they barely adjust the sound. I ended up with the bass almost all the way down and the treble almost all the way up to get a reasonable sound on the mics.

If you want to mess around with vocal effects for the mics, you have to go into the ‘karaoke magic’ menus on the dreaded tablet. There are some fun options… the overly auto-tuned sound of the ‘electronic’ setting, the modulator that makes you sound like The Chipmunks, the spacy reverb that makes you sound like you’re in a cathedral, and a few others. They’re so-so, and frankly should be better for the price. You also get some more nuanced eq effects for the music, which work reasonably well if the system is functional enough to let you slide them up and down...

Ultimately, we’ve given up on using the tablet for the lyric scroll, or for the source of the music. We’re using a phone connected via Bluetooth that’s dialed into the free karaoke section at YT, but of course this means staring at a small screen in front of your face, making it harder to get your superstar on.

When the power got low on the unit in the middle of a song, it gave us a ‘power low’ warning, and then shut itself off a mere seconds later. How about a little more warning, eh? You can get maybe 2 hours of heavy use out of it on one internal battery charge. It will also work plugged into a wall outlet.

There are several other features, and other ways to get music to play in this thing (USB ports, an SD card, HDMI, aux cable) and other ways to enhance the output… you can wire up stereo speakers to it to make it louder... you can hook up a wired microphone, apparently, using an 1/8” plug (not a ¼” or xlr)… you can plug headphones in…

There is a supposedly a feature where you can pipe some music in through a USB port and it can cut down the volume of the vocal so you can turn the song in to an ad hoc karaoke song.

But most of the features are kind of irrelevant when the main feature of this unit, the permanently-attached rotatable large-screen tablet, doesn’t work very well and is immensely frustrating.
The speaker itself is nice and loud, considering its small size.

But any of the positives here unfortunately are outweighed by the negatives. I would recommend giving this unit a pass.
Summary: A big disappointment and definitely not worth the price

The Yeticaster kit is a complete microphone package for voiceover, podcasting, recording-nearly every desktop audio function-that includes the Yeti USB microphone, the Blue Compass boom arm and the Radius III shock mount. Assembly is quick and intuitive and, when you plug the lengthy USB cable into your computer, the OS will load the appropriate driver and you’re ready to go. This is certainly one of the easiest ways I have found to get started in audio.

There’s nothing cheap about this all-in-one kit. Working your way from the bottom up, the Compass boom arm is a sturdy stand, designed to carry the weight of the Yeti microphone at full extension. A heavy clamp attaches the base to your desk and when the arm is set into that base, it enables the microphone to be moved 360°. The articulating arm is composed of two sections for a total length of about 32 inches. Though it will bend in different directions, you’ll discover that the proper orientation has the Blue logo right side up. Tightening the arm in the opposite direction won’t hold your settings. The tubular metal segments are joined with plastic clamps and I’m a little concerned about the longevity of these clamps as I had to screw them together pretty firmly to set the arms, but time will tell.

The isolation mount for the microphone suspends the mic using elastic cord woven around the metal ring. With the entire rig attached to my desk on which I’m working while I use the microphone, the Radius III seems to do a pretty good job of isolating the mic from picking up any of the desk – generated noises. It’s a sturdy design that appears to offer a long life, unlike some of the rubber band designs I’ve seen for other microphones.

Topping all this off is the well-known Yeti microphone. Reviewers have voiced their opinions of this mic for years and many, many users love it and some hate it. I find that the sound quality of the capsule is very good for my uses, which include video production and voiceover, computer dictation and podcasting. I do have more expensive shotgun microphones and they may produce a marginally better signal, but when a good clean, strong audio stream can be tweaked in software if necessary, the Yeti more than serves its purpose. One of the features of the microphone that beginning users may not see the benefit of is the variety of audio patterns that can be set for a single microphone. Turning a selector switch on the back of the microphone allows the Yeti to set the pattern to cardioid for a single user, stereo for a wider soundstage and even bidirectional for placing the microphone between two people in an interview situation. Being able to select various patterns for various situations also allows you to selectively reject other sounds in the area, something that the Yeti does quite well.

The Yeticaster kit is a great value for new and experienced audio users. The USB connection is simple and direct and in enables you to use the audio software installed on your computer. Blue also makes a similar microphone with XLR connections that would perform all the same functions but require an audio interface before connecting to the computer.

When it comes to guitar, I am all into learning different ways of approaching playing. I am not opposed to exploring new methods. I got this to hopefully learn something new. What I got was a chart I don't understand.

HOW THIS COMES
This literally comes as just a heavily laminated sheet.

HOW TO USE THIS
I could tell you to go all over the internet and find out how to use this. That is about the only way you will learn anything about this sheet. It comes with no instructions or information at all about how to use it.

WHAT YOU CAN EXPECT
This sheet is only for those who already know this method of guitar chords for CAGED approach. I am sure if you know the method, you are probably thinking to yourself " Well, DUH, of course"

I on the other hand want to let people know that you will not be getting anything of value with this if you do not already know what the CAGED approach to guitar chords is. So make sure you learn it before you get it, or have something set up before you get it to help you learn.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I am sure this is valuable to those who are already into the CAGED approach to guitar playing. I got this hoping to learn from it, but I guess until I learn the method, this will just be a laminated piece of paper with chords on it.

It is SO weird having to charge your capo, and seeing it light up. So weird!

But this new product from "Jowoom" has solved a typical problem acoustic guitarists have: the clip on tuner and the capo both protruding off the headstock. With this capo/tuner, you have only one attachment, and, mind you, one that looks great. Although: the company name in large letters going across your fretboard is NOT COOL.

I like the concept: one row of lights along the top that you can view while USING the capo, and a separate row of lights on the side that you can use to tune with while the capo is not in use, clipped to the headstock.

In the near-dark of a stage setting, the in-use capo lights aren't too useful, and the not-in-use lights (which actually have the note name printed in front of each light) are too hard to see for someone with less-than-perfect vision. But in normal lighting, these aren't really issues.

The way you tune relates to one dot being blue for flat, green for in tune, red for sharp, with blinking speed indicating how far sharp or flat you are. It's a little hypersensitive, and takes a little getting used to. But it seems accurate enough.

The instructions suggest using this for (steel string) acoustic guitar or ukulele.

Let's also remember that tuning while the capo is on can be a little hazardous... always tune without it first.

So far, no operational issues at all, with the on-off slider and mini-usb port working fine, and so on. The unit claims to have an auto-power off so if you forget to turn it off you won't drain the battery all the way (which is supposed to be good for 7 hours on a full charge). The surface is slick and wipes off easily, and the capo locks into its own little protected carrying case.

Plus, this thing is currently listed at $23, which is a solid price, barely more than a typical Kyser capo alone. Ditch the corporate logo and smooth out the blue-green-red blinking arrangement and this is a no-brainer, every-guitarist-should-have-one situation. 4.5 stars!

Time was when a "looper" was three things: Expensive, complex and more than a bit of a hassle. Donner's Looper Effects Pedal undoes all three, and, using other Donner gear, goes even further.

First off I love the simplicity of this unit. It is not my only looper -- I have several, including some fairly pricey ones -- but they do stuff beyond mere looping. Cool stuff, maybe, but for just traditional looping they are complex and a bit fussy.

The Donner Looper is none of this. Its one-button design assures that. But for all that its a tough little unit and sounds great doing just what a looper is basically designed to do. -To allow you and me to play this, then play that, laying dub over dub, building up a layered, complex, musical performance all on our onesy.

To make a pedal this simple Donner's engineers had to first understand how we guitarists use 'em, and this Donner's engineers obviously did. The pedal is a winner. Sound-wise, yes. Use-wise yesser. And solid as a proverbial brick. This I like!

Okay, but I took mine a step further (hee hee!) using another Donner delight -- a some of their excellent DWS-3 wireless guitar units. This not only simplifies set up -- no wires beyond the DC in! -- but it allows my layered loops to go to places other than my guitar amp if I so choose. This by setting the "in" ("amp") unit to the guitar's channel and the "out" ("Guitar" marked) unit to the wireless channel I use on my sound reinforcement system. (See the attached pic!)

I'm only starting to see this units possibilities. With a looper timing is everything, and if one does complex things this takes some practice. But the one-button system is a super plus here.

Okay, enough said. Now back to the music making.

Fun? Yeah. Recommended? Oh, yeah! Doubly so.

Thanks Donner for providing me with this unit for review. I love it!
