Text:
This box gives you essentially 3 classic tones at the crank of a knob. It's perfect for working, gigging musicians who need simple analog modulation while still preserving your core tone's warmth and integrity.

Tone #1 (dial kept very low) is a classic 70s flange. Not the heavy-resonating EVH stuff. Not the Tom Morello stuff. I'm talking about the pleasant, subtle analog flange from old Rush and Heart albums.

Tone #2 (dial between 9 and 1 o'clock) is a juicy 80s chorus effect. When it's clean, it gives you that Police vibe. When it's dirty, it gives you a nice full distorted sound without getting too cheesey. The best "just enough" chorus tone on the market IMHO.

Tone #3 (dial kept very high) is the classic leslie effect. Nobody uses this tone too often, but this box gets you there. If your band plays "Black Hole Sun," you've got it. Yes, I know it's a stereo leslie on the album, but what exactly do you expect?

All three tones are so darn pleasant, warm, and otherwise *PERFECT* that it's kind of hard to believe. You can find fancier chorus pedals that will take you a long time to dial in all the parameters just so. Any chorus pedal will give you these three tones, but how many of them can give you these tones with just one knob and a price so low? Dunlop really had their heads screwed on straight when they designed this one. Five stars.

The only downside: I have a tube-buffered effects loop, and this box hums like crazy when it's in the loop. Keep it in front of the amp.

Text:
In an A/B comparison using my hand in front of my mouth while saying “P”, “B”, and blowing air—this filter WORKS!
As far as inhibiting air flow and softening the plosives, this screen works. No question about it. The problem that I have with it and the reason it still sits unused in my mic locker is because it’s bulky and “rebellious”. LOL!
You can adjust the angle of the filter in 3 ways; however, I had some issues. First, the clamp is a pentagon shape. This might work fine for mounting to a round mic stand like a floor stand, but this becomes fiddly when you’re mounting to a square tube. I have the Rode PSA-1 boom arm which is made of square tube. Also, typical of boom arms, each section of it is a set of 2 parallel tubes. The Shure bracket is bulky and doesn’t fit nicely on this sort of thing so I had to monkey with it more than I think should be necessary. Secondly, the flexible neck that holds the screen to the bracket has a mind of its own. I’d bend it in a U shape to position the screen and it would contort out to its own angle and put the screen where I didn’t want it. We had words over it, but in the end, the flexible neck turned out to be not so flexible with my demands. I ended up trying 4 different locations for the bracket in order to try to get the screen to sit where I wanted it. Each time, the “flexible” neck gave me fits and we never got along. At first, I was about to turn into a movie diva and scream, “I can’t work like this! I’ll be in my trailer!” Then I remembered I don’t have a trailer. So instead I had to put this pop filter in a long time out in the mic locker. I doubt I’ll try to work with this filter again. I’ll probably end up trying to find another voice actor to give it to—maybe a competitor who’s trying to audition for roles I want. LOL! I mean, Shure, the actual screen section of this kit works very well for its intended job, but the mounting and support system for it leaves some things to be desired.
Summary: Filter works. That mounting system, tho!

I concur with the other 5 star reviews. I used the DR-07 to record our band practicing. The first time I used it in MP3 mode with the auto limiter engaged and got "pumping" from the limiter. The second time I used it I decided to go for the .WAV mode for better quality and disabled the limiter and had the band do a "level check" (driven by drum loudness) where I set the input manually. This proved to be MUCH better as the sound was slightly better and more importantly, there was no pumping due to using the limiter. One other thing you should know is that if you just keep recording song after song without hitting the stop button, instead of having invididual files for each song (ready to load into iTunes), you end up with one large audio file. If you record in MP3 format you need a computer application (I use SoundTrack Pro on the Mac) to chop up the file on your computer as the DR-07 provides no way to chop up a big MP3 file into individual songs. HOWEVER, if you record one big file in .WAV format, the DR-07 DOES provide the onboard tools to chop up the big .WAV file into indvidual songs right on the DR-07 without using a computer. Then when you plug into your computer all the songs are ready to load into iTunes (where you can then name them, convert to MP3, and discard the big .WAV files).

The quality of the built in Mics is surprisingly good. The sensitivity is amazing. We had a train go by while our band was practicing and you can not only hear the train with all the bass rumbling/shaking, the sound of the train moved from left to right in headphones as it went by the house. Amazing pickup. Amazing frequency response too as bass notes sound great on playback.

The controls are foolproof. To start recording you hit the record button once (flashing red light) to "arm" for recording. While the red light is flashing the input meters are active so you can do level checks prior to recording. To actually start recording you hit the Record button a second time (solid red light).

I also use the line in on the DR-07 (cable out of my Behringer mixer) to record song ideas playing my guitar thru my Pod X3 and using the Digitech Vocalist 4 for vocals. Once I adjust the input level of the DR-07 line in signal, I get really clear recordings playing thru the mixer into the DR-07. You can also have headphones plugged in (to the DR-07) to monitor what you are recording from either the line in or built in Mics. I have the headphones coming out of the mixer and just use the visual level indicator on the DR-07, but you could monitor directly out of the DR-07 if you so choose.

I just replaced the 2G SD card with a 8G SD card and for all practical purposes I now have more than enough memory to record my band playing in .WAV format. The MP3 quality recordings are pretty but the .WAV recordings are better (obviously). Also, I like being able to chop up the recorded audio file into individual songs when I get home using just the DR-07.

And to top it off, you can use this thing as a plain old MP3 player if you want.

Only gripe is that I had to buy the AC adapter seperately from Guitar Center.

All in all...an amazing piece of technology at a great price point.
Summary: Incredible Value, Ease of Use, and Sound Quality

6-month update: My impression of these speakers has only improved. I have used them very heavily for over 6 months now and they have not let me down. They are extremely accurate, yet very comfortable to listen to for long periods. I have done dozens of critical mixes on them and they translate perfectly. I would very happily buy these monitors again, and likely will.

Original review: Wow. These things are so great I almost can't believe it. I have worked in professional audio and video production for over 20 years and I have owned a lot of very high quality audio gear. I needed to set up a new small video editing suite and needed a pair of accurate near field monitors with the ability to reproduce deep bass. I had heard good things about these monitors, so I figured I would give them a try. For the price, I couldn't go wrong. I AM SO HAPPY I DID!

These monitors sound like much more expensive monitors. I had a pair of JBL LSR-28Ps that I loved and these have a very similar sound. They have a deep but tight low end, mild mids, and accurate but pleasing highs. Like the JBLs they are very pleasing to listen to for long periods of time, but are accurate enough to do critical mixing on.

The only slight (and I mean very slight) negative to consider with these speakers is that they are ported and if your speaker placement isn't ideal they can sound a bit tubby. Because of my room layout, when I first set them up they were a bit higher than they should have been and the ports were right at ear level (about 40 inches away from my ears). Using my speaker pads to aim them down a bit and moving them a bit further back completely fixes this. The dip switches allowed me to get the speakers sounding flat in my room very quickly and easily (they print the instructions on the back of the speaker for easy setup).

Even if you have the budget for more expensive monitors, unless you know exactly what you want,I highly recommend these speakers. I promise you won't be disappointed.

I bought this so I could record my guitar at home. I'm running a tube amp into a load box, the line out from the load box into a modeler with cabinet IR modeling, then the XLR out from the modeler into my recording interface.

The connection from the load box into the modeler was causing a bunch of hum which made it impossible to record clean tones because the clean tone wouldn't mask the hum.

I decided to give this box a try. It arrived today and I spent a while messing with it. Here are the results.

Pros:

It eliminates about 60% to 70% of the hum. Enough to be able to record clean guitar tones without the hum being audible in the mix, although the very faint hum does need to be gated out during passages in the song where the guitar isn't playing. It's fine for a casual home recording but I'd find a different method for a professional recording. I'd either use the modeler 100% for amp and cab modeling instead of just as a cab modeler, or I'd use my regular amp into an actual guitar cabinet and mic it old school.

Cons:

It causes a dramatic drop in the volume level. I have to wonder if the drop in volume level is making it seem like the hum is being removed but it only seems that way because the overall volume level of everything, including the hum, is being attenuated by this box. I think that's partly the case but not entirely because I compensated for the volume drop by increasing the output gain from the modeler to the interface, and the input gain on the interface to bring the level back to where it was without the box being in the signal chain and the hum got slightly louder but wasn't as loud as when the box isn't there. That's why I'm saying it gets rid of maybe 60% to 70% of the hum.

Overall, it gets rid of most of the hum but at the cost of lowering the volume level. You can compensate for it though by adjusting your gain settings in the rest of the signal chain.
Summary: Eliminates hum, but at a cost.

I came close to giving this a 5 star review all the way. However, as some have mentioned it does require a little bit of set-up to make it a superb value. I have been a luthier for a long time so what I consider minor adjustments others might consider a major undertaking. If you can do a little bit of work for yourself, don't hesitate to jump in. Here's what I discovered on the one shipped to me.
First negative: the string height at the nut was terrible. The plastic nut, though was quite hard (not sure what it is) and once filed and shaped works fine. Secondly, there were a few high frets which had to be dressed, crowned and polished. Third the intonation was only fair. It took me maybe an hour or two to correct these items. Finally: as you would expect at this price point , the hardware is usable, but not great. The tuners should probably be the first upgrade and the saddles might be the second.
Now, on to the good. The neck feels very good and has roughly the same dimensions of an American Fender neck. The fretwork on the 12" radius neck was pretty good overall (other than the already mentioned high frets) , fret ends were dressed nicely and the action was able to be adjusted to a very low string height. It is actually a lot of fun to play. Next: the finish looks really good (especially from a foot or two away). What looks like tiger striped maple is most likely "photo-flame." There is however, real wood underneath (maybe poplar, but can't say for sure) and it resonates nicely. This guitar is incredibly lightweight and comfortable to play. Third: the pickups are better than I expected at this price point (still, a bit microphonic). I bought this with the idea of making it a project, but I've decided to leave it as is for a while. Truthfully, I'm having too much fun playing it.
Again, if you can do the work yourself, go for it. I think you'll be happy. If you have to pay someone to do the work just use the money you would pay to buy a little better instrument (although, you'll be hard pressed to find a better looking guitar at anywhere near this price point!).

I bought 4 and a cross bar to use with an old speaker stand to provide some lighting for DJ gig. I bought 4 more of "another brand" to add to the other stand for band applications. The "others" are 36 x 1 watt PAR's which are clearly lacking in matching the color intensity, brightness and projection of these even though there are twice as many LED's. I am getting 4 more the replace the 36 x 1 fixtures which I will use to up-light the drum kit in close proximity.

For my small bar band applications, they look and work great. I have them mounted to the cross bars and ready to plug into the power strips I have attached to the stands so they are up and running in literally seconds. I have them set on the slowest transition mode where they fade in/out by color and combination thereof. In fact, they set up so fast and easy in my configuration, I even bring a set to most practices!

All in all - a great product if: You manage your expectations: These will not light up a 50' stage from 30' in the air. You pre-rig them for easy, fast set up and transport and store them safely.

Everyone has their own theories on what gauge/composition of string they want to use, so I won't go into why I prefer light top - heavy bottom, or why I prefer round wound nickel, I'll just review D'Addario strings as a whole.

- Which string is which within a pack is denoted by colored wrapping at the bridge end of the string. The color coding of the strings is really nice for quickly determining which string is which gauge, especially if you are trying to replace a string quickly during a performance. It isn't exactly tricky without the color code, but I like it. I know lots of players who HATE the color coding because depending on the instrument, you can see it after they are installed. Personally, I think it's subtle at best, and you'd really have to be looking for it, but on a lot of fixed bridge instruments, the colors are visible.

- The strings come in a plastic bag to reduce exposure to air, something along the lines of a sealed opaque sandwich bag. I have no clue how "fresh" the little baggy is keeping my strings, but I do know that I've had packs of these strings rattling around in gig bags for a pretty long time and they have never come out of the package tarnished.

-The big reason I buy D'Addarios is they don't seem to break as often as other string manufacturers. It's most noticeable on my bass, where D'Addarios never break, but Ernie Balls and others occasionally do. If you have issues with strings breaking you might want to give D'Addarios a try.

- I don't notice a tone difference between these and much more expensive strings like Elixers. I know people who claim to, so you'll have to see for yourself. I think they sound great.
Summary: These are what I use and recommend.

I put my 88-key Yamaha P-120 keyboard on this thing, and it's solid. It doesn't sway or anything while I'm playing. After a few minutes I forgot that I was even testing out the stand and just had fun playing. That's a good stand right there.

I took off a star because I agree with other reviewers in that there needs to be some kind of instructions for initial installation. Maybe even something simple on the outside of the box. It's not really complicated, but it's not immediately intuitive, either. When the stand arrives folded up, you have to remove the two center knobs completely and then reattach them in a different place. Once you got that, it's a piece of cake. Also note that the vertical adjustment has notch holes for the screws to go into. I didn't realize this at first and put a couple of circular dents in the posts (although I don't think this compromises stability). I think it would make more sense to use pins instead of screws with knobs.

The other reason I took off a star was because one of the screw knobs was kinked during manufacturing. The screw was at an angle compared to the plastic knob, but it was still fixed in place. This didn't affect the performance of the stand, but it was just a little annoying. Also, the brackets didn't quite fit all the way on the posts, so I kind of had to work them on there. I think over time with repeated fastening of the screws, the brackets will bend into shape. Despite these two setbacks, the stand still works great.

But hey, it's a great stand at a great price. Very solid. I wanted the Z-stand so my knees wouldn't get knocked with an X-stand, and it works great for that. Also, this stand goes as low as 24", which is great if you're not a very tall person and accustomed to the height of a real piano with a piano bench.

UPDATE: There are assembly instructions! But you have to download them from the website, and they're not included in the box (why not?). Go to [www] [dot] [onstagestands] [dot] [com] and then click on Support > Replacement Parts. Then type in the model number "KS7350", then click on the product link, and it will show all of the replacement parts available for this product. Scroll up a little and click on the "Documents" tab. There you will find a spec sheet and official assembly instructions (note that it's in MS Word doc format). I'm going to post a screen snapshot in the customer images.

ANOTHER UPDATE: I contacted On Stage Stands to request a replacement knob, and they happily did so. Great customer service.

It is difficult to rate something poorly when it is clearly not pretending to be something it is not. But you do get what you pay for, and in this case, you get exactly what you should expect, if not just a little bit more for a $40 mic stand. I am rating this as a mic stand between $20 - $50 price range. I've owned them all.

This mic stand is extremely stable using regular SM57 and SM58 style microphones. Under a load with the Audio Technica AT4050 condensor mic AND an isolation shield with metal mesh and foam (approximately 2 lbs.) can prove to be a little precarious, but this can be remedied by zip tying a 2 - 5 lb hand weight or divers weight to the end of the boom arm in order to counter the weight. As it stands, I mainly use this stand for Shure SM57 and SM58 style microphones and it has performed very well. I love the feet on this stand. The width of the feet placement is adjustable as well, so you do not have to use the pictured configuration if that doesn't suit you.

If you are on the fence because of the extra $10 - $20 difference, do yourself a favor and get this mic stand over "a mic stand that will do the job". It is worth the difference in price, and its stability is key. As someone who has spent the first 5 years of my musical existence fumbling with garbage mics and stands, I know what counts in these guys and this stand will deliver, ESPECIALLY if you have only owned inexpensive mic stands.
Summary: Probably the best in class for a $20 - $50 mic stand.

The is a very nice and versatile overdrive. With a clean amp, it provides a nice a very smooth overdriven tone. Not harsh at all. Very amp-like compared to some other OD's i've tried, including the TS9. For overdriving a clean amp, this is the best OD i've tried.

It also works well boosting and tightening a distorted tube amp into heavier territory, which is my main application for ODs. The low freq knob is especially useful here allowing you to EQ for just the right amount of tightness. For boosting already distorted tones, each OD has its own response that different players prefer and this one is up there for me, but i think i prefer the Delta Labs Tube driver for boosting. Still, gain at 0, level at 8-10, eq to taste, this will get you chugging nicely. It seems compress things a bit more than i'd like - but some folks would prefer the compression, and i may be able to dial that out. i haven't tried it at rehearsal yet to be sure if it will permanently replace my Delta Labs, but it's in the running. Still, I'd pick this up again over a TS-9 for sure. Plus it's well built and looks good on my board. Try this before you spend $250 on a hand painted boutique. Very versatile and sounds great

Text:
I have some to regard Puresound as a manufacturer of well designed and made snare wires. In the past eight years of using them on many of my snare drums (which during this period has numbered in excess of sixty), every set has consistently been free of flaws and defects.

Regarding the number of strands - many drummers insist on more instead of less strands and balk at 16. In truth, more wires in many cases are not necessarily better, and in a few cases are actually detrimental. I have found that most modern snare drums have relatively shallow and wide snare beds. 20-, 24- or more snare wire configurations tend to be less responsive. That seems to defy logic, but I have discovered through trial and error that my snare response and note articulation seems to improve with less snares. And I have found 16-wire sets to be the best general purpose configuration. Also, I get less sympathetic snare buzz from 16-strand wires than I do from 20+ wire sets.

On snare drums that have narrow and/or deeper beds (many vintage snare drums) I typically use [[ASIN:B004DGI41O PureSound Concert Series Snare Wire, 12 Strand, 14 Inch]], but that is a special case and I am mentioning it because if you are considering snares for a vintage drum or one with narrower beds, you may want to consider that model.

I've been playing guitar for about 8 years now and my 9 year old daughter has been playing for almost 4, so I have a little bit of a grasp of entry level guitars and what's worked for me and her as she's grown into standard guitars. First glance, it looks outstanding. The sculpted "arch top" and comfort bevel on the back are usually features in higher end guitar models. The clean bright chrome hardware against the glossy black is eyecatching. The white trimmed edge also sets this apart from traditional entry level slab monocolor guitars. The setup is a traditional les paul tunomatic bridge and tailpiece in a dual humbucker setup, with controls as volume/volume/color and a 3 way pickup toggle. Its a bolt on neck with a thinner profile that makes it easier for younger or smaller hand players to play comfortably. My big old hands did fine with the neck and the guitar is extremely playable and comfortable.

My daughter loved the black as well, which surprised me since she's also in love with her Atomic Pink metallic flake electric. Her first question to me was... Can I play it? Then.. Is it for me? She went on to lay out her plans to do add metallic pink skulls or hello kitty to it -- Which, would look pretty cool for a 9 yr old rockstar... After a strumming through run of a few Taylor Swift and Christine Perri songs she pretty much just took the guitar up to her room and I will have to go get it back later - hoping that it isn't already 9yr old girl customized.

What I liked about it for the sub $300 price point:
* Solid look and doesn't scream entry level
* passive 150 pickups are sensitive to play style and bright, with fairly little noise.
* aggressive cutaway makes the 24th fret usable.
* jumbo frets are comfortable and easy for beginners
* neck profile also good for younger or small hand players
* back profile or "waist cut" makes it a comfortable guitar to sit and play

Cons:

* Never been a fan of the ESP model number inlay in the middle of the fretboard. This guitar doesn't scream entry until you look at the huge EC-100AC across the fretboard. Should we inlay the barcode and price sticker as well?
* Under $300 this guitar is still at the high end of entry. The tuning machines are solid in maintaining tune play to play, but it would have been nice to see some locking machines and strap locks.
* Looking at the ESP line, if spending this much for this style I'd be tempted at looking at the higher end set-neck EC-256 with the transparent stained maple tops.
Summary: Great features, solid sound.  Excellent top level entry guitar

Text:
By definition, medium is an in between size. But when it comes to guitar strings, most of the range goes from extra light to medium. On that scale, these strings would be above a literal medium. For me, the guitar is not an everyday instrument. I don't typically spend five hours a day with one, and sometimes go weeks without picking one up. But I do have periods where I will spend many hours a day playing and don't want something that will kill me.

Medium in the guitar string sense of the word is too much for me. Light and custom light are easier to play, but can make a higher end Martin guitar sound like one closer to the bottom of the line. For me, these light-medium are exactly where I want my strings to be.

If you like Martin's medium, find them a bit much at times, but find that you give up too much when you play much lighter ones, you may find that these are a great choice. I don't feel I am missing anything compared to the Medium. If I had two identical guitars with new strings of each type, I would probably find differences in a side by side comparison. But without that, I don't think I'd notice the difference with normal listening. With the lighter varieties, that would be far from true.

If Martin extra light and light were the skim milk and 1% milk of strings, these light-medium would be the 2% that came along for people who wanted something lighter but still came close to the whole milk taste.
Summary: A great choice for Martin strings

Text:
TL;dr - This boom arm is solid quality at a reasonable price. I recommend it.

I bought a much cheaper arm (which I have also reviewed) that cost a whopping $12.50 shipped to my door. At less than what I've spent buying a movie ticket, that thing was killer. A real space saver and the flexibility of having a boom arm when it comes to positioning a mic compared to a stand was really handy. To be honest, if I wanted to get real picky there were some obvious points where "value" had been the priority over "quality", but for the small stuff I do, it fit a minimum budget at did everything I needed it to do.

Fast forward several months and I get this arm as a gift. I'd been eyeing it as a "nice to have", but hadn't bought it as my other one was still footing the bill just fine, so this came as a pleasant surprise! I get it home, unbox the thing, and immediately I can see that aesthetics were more important for this arm than the old one, and the quality of the hardware is indeed improved. A few of the things, obvious to less obvious, that stand out are of course the internal springs, which are firm and silent, the C-clamp is more robust, the threads on the mic-mount are better cut and no need for an adapter, and there's a small plastic "bushing" where the arm connects to the clamp, instead of the metal-on-metal fit of the other one. Overall, this arm was 4x the cost of the first arm (yet still under half the cost of the Rode PS1A or Blue Compass, and still being able to be used on lighter mics), but the quality of the finish reflects the cost boost. Definitely a niche product, but given the de facto standard that pedalboards have become, it's one that electronic musicians (and I include my electric violins in this) have come to depend upon.

But read on.

The solution most have arrived at, and I must say not a solution that pleases me, is a potpourri of stompboxes instead of a VST-driven solution with a rack mount computer. Nor is it a wireless solution, though one must see that coming eventually, because for this application, wired is the safest solution.

Not by design or preference, I do have a similar collection, along with rack effects that must be routed to/from the pedalboard. But one size does definitely not fit all of them.

The alternative is just too unwieldy, unless you can keep the box count down below 5. The alternative is a hassle for setup and take-down, and likely to stress connectors and cable alike.

There may be compatibility issues: e.g, the solution for Eventide involves a different connector type and routing to their rack mount PSU. Adding to this worry is that the product description doesn't say in advance what you'll be getting. Plug size and polarity sometimes matter, even though most stompboxes use the same setup.

If your rig is relatively static, I'd opt for soldered, old school connections because reliability is just too critical.
But for in-studio testing and reconfiguring, this might be a net plus over alternative methods that involve purchasing individual parts in this kit.

You should estimate what you'll need; the cable lengths overall may be adequate, but the plug count might not.

Echoing other reviewers, I know this is easy stuff once mastered, but do we really have to search for a blog post, review of YouTube clip to figure out if we're doing it right?

And then there are still devices that don't comply with the stompbox format, and you've got to wire signal *and power* to these as well. Some of these devices are important -- EV pedals, or signal processors that are made bigger. For example, I have used this pedal arrangement to manage MIDI triggers, volume and effects, and it clearly is outside the stompbox footprint: https://www.amazon.com/Roland-FC-300-Controller-Extended-Warranty/dp/B018V8HXBG.

Meanwhile, I'm waiting for a single connector back to a rack-mounted computer where the sounds are all VST's. After all,this is 2018, not 1975, when the stompbox design was catching fire. I regularly review acts coming to our local theater,and I'm amazed at how many guitarists and fiddle players pull off the pedalboard puzzle without a hitch. Often not everything fits in the pedalboard anyway.

And what are you doing again with your power cable routing? You really wouldn't depend only on batteries, would you?
Summary: Play music not Cable Croquet. Know your requirements: e.g., ideal in-studio reconfiguring

Enough that you can(with some work) run it through the arm and still have a good 2.5 feet left. Any more though and you'll need an extension. All in all everything is well built and sturdy.

Audio quality is everything I would ever need. I've recently been using it to chat with my brother when playing online games and he commented that it sounded great. Text:
These are very, very nice for the price. The condensers get a very nice quiet noise floor and capture the tone of my cymbals very well. I play a bit darker-sounding cymbal set than most and I like to get a bit more upper-mid range in the condensers. These have the warmth to capture that. Actually the two condensers and the kick mic are a pretty adequate rig.

The kick mic is not a Beta 52. Don't let your imagination go crazy. With inside the drum micing it particularly shines - middle of the drum aimed at the beater impact point. Give a steep parametric boost around 8k and keep the rest flat for a nice tap and punch. There is plenty of body and low end. You may want to roll some of that off for certain types of music. It does particularly well outside the resonant head without a hole. It is very "present" in even a crowded mix because the low frequency boost is a wide spectrum. Be careful to EQ out some space for the bass guitar or you will have a VERY muddy mix with this mic. Like I said...it isn't a Beta 52. There is no "set it and forget it" here. With some care this is a useful mic and an improvement over using a vocal mic (or SM57).

The mounts aren't my favorite as they take considerable space above the drum. Some setups would be more forgiving with this but space is tight on my recording rig. They do, however allow the placement that I like to use with a boom stand -1" above the rim aimed at the impact point. The tone is fine. Tune your drums and you will get nice sounds out of these...comparable to the Shure PGs or most decent dynamic vocal mics. I still prefer the SM57 on the snare. It's a bit hotter and at the same gain captures more of the instrument.

I'm really cheap in this wonderful age of budget music gear. I don't have a lot of expendable $ for microphones. Do you? If you do, check out the set with 3 SM57s and a Beta 52 and add two SM81s or get all fancy with a pair of AKG 414s. You will get in that setup for $600-$2000. Your four-piece kit will be in heaven and you can spend less time EQ-ing your mics and more time driving your 911 Turbo. Otherwise, pick this set up, check out some YouTube vids on mic placement and using a parametric EQ and start saving up for your 911 Turbo.
Summary: Way too much analysis for a $150 set of drum mics? They are fine...

Tuning Your Instrument
Many individuals have their own tuning method. We recommend standard guitar or bass tuning to A-440, using a tuning fork, electronic tuner or pitch pipe. The following chart shows standard tuning. The 1st string is the smallest diameter. Tune the two outside strings first, then tune towards the center. This equalizes the pressure on the bridge and allows rapid tuning.

Action Adjustment
Action is the distance that a string must be depressed before it meets the fret. Action measurements are taken in 64th’s of an inch, and are calculated from the top of the 12th fret to the underside of the string. GBME sets the action on all instruments at the factory for optimum playability. On occasion, lower than standard settings are desired by the player. This can be achieved by adjusting the bridge studs (See Tune-o-matic Bridge). Lower than standard action can often result in “buzz” or “rattle.” This is caused by the string vibrating against the fret. Buzz or rattle caused by lower than standard action is not considered a defect of the instrument.

For action at the first fret, all instruments are set at the same height. Treble strings are cut to 1/64" and the action progresses up to 2/64" on the bass
strings. Be sure that the truss rod is properly adjusted before setting action.

Truss Rod Adjustment
All guitar necks are subject to great stress as a result of string tension, humidity or changes in climate. Occasionally the neck may need adjustment. The truss rod is adjustable at the headstock on electric models and through the soundhole of acoustic models, using an allen wrench or an adjustment wrench.
NOTE: This adjustment should be performed periodically and only by qualified repair personnel. Over-adjustment can result in damage to the instrument and will not be covered under warranty. Intonation and Saddle Adjustment for a Tune-o-matic Bridge

The Tune-o-matic bridge comes to you pre-adjusted, but several adjustment options are available:
1. String Height or Action* The height of the bridge can be adjusted by turning the two slot-head screws on either side of the Tune-o-matic bridge;
clockwise to lower, counter-clockwise to raise.
2. Adjusting The Intonation* Intonation adjustment is usually only necessary when different gauge strings are used (it can also be affected by the angle of a tremolo unit). The saddle positions are adjusted by the individual slot-head screws located on the front of the bridge, sliding the saddles forward or backward.
To check the intonation: Use an electronic tuner and tune the guitar to a standard pitch. Play the harmonic at the 12th fret, and compare it to the fretted note at the 12th fret. These notes should read the same on the tuner. If the 12th fret harmonic pitch is lower than the fretted note, slide the saddle back (toward the tailpiece). If the 12th fret harmonic pitch is higher than the fretted note slide the saddle forward (toward the neck).
* Adjusting the intonation and string height will affect the playability of your guitar. If you are unsure of any of the above operations please take your guitar to an experienced guitar technician

Text:
Because I find myself traveling a lot, I began to realize the need for a portable keyboard to help in my music arranging and composing. I've used QWERTY piano patches before...but nothing beats the actual feel of piano keys. Several options came to mind, but I settled for this M-Audio Keystation Mini 32. And I have been happily using this unit on plane flights, long distance train rides, and some other spontaneous places where music ideas just hit me suddenly.

First off, the Dimensions:
It is (16 & 1/3in. X 2/3in. X 4in.) and was able to fit comfortably it in my computer back (which typically packed my laptop, my ipad, and a book. I was able to even pack in my flute, as well.

Durability:
At first I was afraid of this breaking due to it's plastic build...but it was actually very durable and solid. It sustained being packed in a tightly packed backpack as well as some accidental "rugged" situations (such as my backpack falling). All the functions are still operational and it still has a pristine look.

Features:
Well, first off, this is a plug-n-play keyboard that can work and interact with most DAWs, Music Notation programs, and midi/sampling programs. It features an editable interface (personally I haven't needed to use this feature, yet, so I can't comment) as well as typical octave up/down buttons. It also has a sustain button to mimic a pedal. And of course there is a volume control that interacts with your preferred DAW. Keep in mind that this is not a self-contained unit, but a midi controller. So you need to plug this into a midi-utilizing software. It is powered through the USB when plugged into the computer.

Response:
It has a fast response...no delays when playing it.

How does it feel?:
Honestly, for its purpose, it feels great. The keys are smaller and definitely light (understandably so), but they do have a good rebound. I would not make this my primary keyboard for performance (though I would gladly add it as an auxiliary unit to my main), but as an on-the-go musical/compositional tool it is wonderful.

All in all, I am very satisfied with my care. This fulfilled my needs for a portable notation/input keyboard. I even find myself using this over my main rig at home if I just need to do some small and quick inputs. It's just that easy ^_^

I don't work for Oscar Schmidt and I don't get paid by them. I own five Oscar Schmidt instruments (all from Amazon) and would never hesitate to buy another. In their price range they offer remarkable value. Obviously, these are mass-produced instruments and not hand-crafted masterpieces. Yet I see some very unfair comments in these reviews. When dealing with mass-produced instruments bought sight unseen from an internet dealer you can expect to hear bad reports once in a while. You will get poor reports from inexperienced players who expected more than they should have, and from experienced players who compare them to much more expensive instruments. Here's what my experience tells me to expect from Oscar Schmidt:

Top quality laminated woods. Not hand-selected solid tone woods, but really nice laminates that work well, lay well, and sound good. If you see 'solid wood' advertised at this price point you can expect garbage. Great quality solid wood is expensive! I've seen 'solid wood' ukuleles at this price made out of old packing crates, but they are solid wood.

Good fit and finish. No cracked or open seams or misaligned joints. A neck might bow or warp but this is usually due to how they are handled after they leave the factory. The manufacturer can't control that. That's what return policies are all about. It's a risk we take buying online.

You may find a tight or rattling tuner. I really wish Oscar Schmidt (Washburn) would use better tuners and increase the price a couple of dollars. It would avoid a lot of disappointments. That's my strongest criticism of the products.

All instruments need to be set up. That's the process of making small adjustments to get it playing its best. Getting rid of little buzzes and rattles, getting the strings just right, and so on. That doesn't get done at a factory, it gets done at a music store. But if you buy online you have to do it yourself or take it to a music store and pay extra. That's how it works for any brand at any price. It's normal and expected.

One of the most common complaints is that the ukulele won't stay in tune. Ukuleles use nylon strings. They need to stretch out for a few days. There's nothing wrong, it's supposed to be like that. Don't be upset, just keep tuning and playing and everything will be fine. Another complaint is that the strings are 'bad'. The Oscar Schmidt ukuleles use Aquila strings, one of the most famous brands. But instruments can sit around a long time before the sell. The strings may be old by the time you buy your instrument. Old strings need to be replaced, even if they haven't been played. Again, nothing to be upset over. You will replace the strings lots of times over the years.

Look, if you want a well made ukulele for not much money that is better than 99% of the junk out there selling for more, don't hesitate to buy an Oscar Schmidt. You'll get a good product and if there's really a problem it will be dealt with. They are a 100 year old company with a top reputation, not a fly-by-night brand that won't be there tomorrow.

Text:
The good first: these brushes have a heavier and thicker staccato sound than wire bristle brushes. That makes them perfect for Afro-Cuban and Brazilian music. As a substitute for wire brushes they work poorly because legato sweeps are not very distinct. As an additional tool, though they will add to your sound palette.

What I do not like is the fact that they are 'throw out' style retractable brushes. You push the bristles into the handle to retract them and a throw motion will extend them. That in itself is clever, but if you use different fan outs for each hand this brush is a distraction. For example, I typically will keep the fan of my right brush tighter so I get a more staccato sound, while fully fanning out on the left one for a legato quarter note sweep. That is awkward to do with these the way they are designed.

Physically these have a relatively thick handle at .579 inches, but it's light and the added thickness does lend itself to Afro-Cuban and Brazilian playing. The overall length is 13.75 inches, of which 5.25 inches are bristles. The balance is very nice. I have heard of handles cracking, but I have never experienced that. As far as construction these brushes appear to be well made and should last a long time of used properly (i.e., as brushes and not played like sticks.)
Summary: Adds to your sound palette, but has some issues

Purchasing professional instruments for children is a ludicrous proposition.

That is where this product comes in. For my oldest son we purchased an intermediate Trombone. He did not appreciate and has treated it poorly. Now I am left with angry feelings everytime I see it. We purchased it used from a local music shop that rents to students. They gave us a payment plan but charged us nearly full price for it, something we didn't realize at the time.

My wife and I decided after this that we would pay less for a first instrument, and if they liked it and stuck with it, then later purchase an intermediate when they would appreciate it and know better how to care for it.

After that experience we started looking online for instruments. I was very nervous at first as there are so many ways this can go wrong. However, it didnt exactly go right buying locally. For my next child we bought a flute off of Amazon for a very low price. It has worked pretty well, but had some problems. We probably paid too little for it. That said she has played for three years on it and it continues to work well.

This trumpet was purchased for my 2nd son and I am very happy with it. Having played trumpet myself I am quite satisfied with its quality. The valves have excellent movement and it makes good sound. I prefer my Selmer student model to this one but they are quite similar and you cannot purchase the same Selmer that I had 20 years ago, they are now made in China like this one. Seating of the valves is a little tricky in the Hutchen but once seated they are good. A key has stuck on a couple of occasions, but with some oil this is not a problem.

The case was very nice and sturdy and provides ample protection with some storage for accessories. I would and have highly recommended this trumpet for a first trumpet to any who would listen. I definitely recommend buying online for the first instrument. The local rental shops take advantage of students and their parents. Online can be the same, but at least the total bill is less.

If the student sticks with it they will be able to make an informed decision later when it is time to buy an intermediate instrument.

-- Update 3/2013 --

It has been almost a year now and the trumpet is working beautifully. My son's teacher has gone out of her way to comment on multiple occasions about the quality of the sound from this horn. My son was a little dissapointed at first, he wanted a black one(come on who paints horns black), but as he has used it and learned about it he has completely changed his mind and is quite proud to have it.

-- Oct 2013

My son manged to do some pretty substantial damage to the bell on this horn, it is still functional, but not nearly as pretty. Best part was I didn't have to kill him for destroying a $600 horn. Should he decided to continue, which I do not expect, I am sure that he would treat his second horn with much greater care.

My youngest son will enter Jr High next year and start learning and instrument. I have asked him which one he wants to play and it looks like I will be buying another trumpet. I have no hesitation in saying it will be another LJ Hutchen Trumpet.

Text:
The Microphone:

I was actually surprised by the sound of this mic.. At this price point I figured it would be like most of the low cost USB mics., cheap and cheap sounding. When I connected it to my mixing board, I was surprised at the quality of the sound. This is an XLR condenser mic and requires 48v phantom power. If you don't have an interface that provides that, this is not for you. If you do and are on a budget, This might do the trick for you.

The mic. is decently constructed. It has a little weight to it. Not heavy like a professional studio mic., but, not light, all plastic, either. The outer shell is some sort of metal. There are little to no specs provided on the mic itself. You cannot see the diaphragm, so I can't tell what size it might be. I can say that in testing, it sounds good enough for the average podcast or YouTube content creation on a budget. The clarity is good and the cardioid pattern is consistent. I tested both through headphones and monitor speakers and it sounded nice. I wouldn't put it on a par with several much more expensive mics that I have, but, I think it is good enough that if I needed to mic an additional person, it could hold its own and not be noticeably worse in general conversation. It will remain in my home studio arsenal.

The Rest of the Kit:

It comes with a boom arm, shock mount, XLR Cable, foam windscreen, pop filter on an articulating arm and the requisite adapter for attaching the mic to the boom arm.

Boom Arm -- Light weight and cheaply made. Definitely not professional grade. The base does mount solidly to the desk/table/counter and has a hook on it that could hold a coiled cord or set of headphones. The arm itself articulates well and stay in place where ever you set it with the mic on it. The part that inserts into the base is adequate but much less solid than many I have tried/used. It will likely be relegated to a back corner of a closet here. I'm not ready to toss it out, but, I have a couple on standby that are much better.

Shock Mount -- The shock mount is advertised to be of metal construction. That is NOT true. It is constructed of plastic. It seems reasonably solid and is easy to work with. It does not seem to provide as much isolation from bumps of the arm as it should. It is however, better than a rigid mount which transmits the smallest taps on the desk.

XLR Cable -- The cable works fine. It is cheaply made and it shows in the fit and finish. Not something I would buy, but, for a throw-in, I'll keep it in my cable bag.

Foam Windscreen and Pop Filter -- The foam windscreen is typical and works fine. The pop filter is on an articulating arm with a metal clamp. It stays positioned well whenever put in place. It is a fabric screen and seems to work fine for handling plosives.

Conclusions:

I think it is not a bad kit at the price point. The mic itself is very usable and will stay in my cache of equipment. The boom arm is disappointing. It is functional and does what it was designed to do, but, the construction quality is not good. The shock mount is also functional and can serve the purpose for which it was intended. It is not as advertised. The cable is, as with everything in this kit, functional. Not a high quality cable, but, it does work fine. Finally, the windscreen and pop filter are of good quality and function as intended.
Summary: OK XLR condenser mic kit for the money

This was an impulse buy on Amazon Warehouse (AW) on a bitterly cold night in early February, an evening when I had had a few too many glasses of wine. I was vaguely aware of the Korg Volca series, in that I had seen a few negative or neutral comments about them on various music forums, but I hadn't listened to any audio demos or watched any YouTube demonstration videos. Honestly, these tiny boxes had never appealed, as I like my synths with keys or something I can put in a rack and MIDI up to my rig. So when this popped up on AW in a "Used-Acceptable condition for what seemed to be nearly 50% off the retail price, I thought, well, if I don't like it, I can sell it on for a profit.

I'm glad I did. I love this little box, and it looked absolutely brand new in the box when it arrived. Go figure. I like it more than my Pro-1 monosynth -- I think the Volca Bass sounds better than most of my keyboards, with the exception of my Korg Radias. I mean to say, the Volca Bass is fat sounding, and oh!!! it has that distorted squeal that is very similar to a Roland TB-303 (or the Behringer clone). The filter resonance (peak knob) on this wee thing self-oscillates, so if you're looking to do a bit of Daft Punk or Chemical Brothers-style late 90s and early 00s techno work, this little guy can do it, and do it very nicely.

Let's get the cons out of the way:

The speaker is rubbish. I get why Korg put it there, but the speaker doesn't have the range to actually hear what all the glorious goodness this synth can make. Tip: Use headphones if you're going portable with this. Otherwise, hook it up to your mixer / monitoring system / amp.

The MIDI implementation is good, but you can't modulate the filter via MIDI. What???!!! Why not, Korg? What are you thinking? Sigh... So, you must use the Volca Bass's filter knob in real-time. Also, no MIDI out, but it is possible to modify the unit so that it can do MIDI out, so at least there's that option for the hardcore modders.

Pattern storage is limited to 8 memory slots. You will use those up quickly, and then you'll have to decide on which patterns to get rid of for later sessions. Also, there is no pattern chaining, so you must manually change patterns in real time, and you will need to do that in perfect sync as there is also no "wait to change pattern" functionality. If you're sequencing a pattern, know that the filter knob adjustments do not get recorded. The octave knob's movements will be recorded, however. On the other hand, it is possible to create 24 patterns when in individual three-osc mode, and with a bit of clever muting, you can probably do quite a bit with that.

The smaller, clear knobs ... it's sometimes difficult to see what their positions are. Also, when I reach for the tempo or the EG attack knobs at the top center/left of the unit, I often accidentally brush the big filter knob.

No noise oscillator... that's a shame. But not a deal breaker...

So them's me cons. On the the pros:

Three very stable analog VCOs (digitally tuned for stability, but these bad boys are definitely analog oscillators), any of which can be a Saw or Square wave. You have the options of three independent VCOs, two stacked together, or all three stacked together. There is also a tuning knob for each VCO, so you're able to create a very thick and fat super saw sound. Note range can be adjusted per voice but only if you are sequencing a pattern. Otherwise, all three VCOs will change depending on where the octave knob is set.

The playing surface (ribbon?) is really responsive to touch and it's fun to play and slide around on it, but it is important to note that the playing surface is not velocity sensitive. The Volca Bass responds to velocity when connected to MIDI controller, though. Keep that in mind if you want to get the most you can out of this tiny box of joy. It took me a few minutes to work out what the deal was with the black and gold "keys." Tip: The gold keys are the black keys on a keyboard. The rest are the white keys. The lowest note on the surface is an "A". Maybe an "E" would have been better, which is the lowest note on a bass guitar, but from keyboard perspective I suppose it makes sense (an 88-key keyboard's first note is an A.)

The filter on this insanely good. I read somewhere that it's based on a Korg 700s filter. I dunno if it is or not. And I don't care. I really like a lot.

The envelope seems limited, but it actually has two modes and it is perfectly serviceable. One mode with no sustain segment, just an attack and delay, which is superb for punchy bass tones, and the second mode is with a sustain feature, which is great for more synthy sounds and self-oscillating the filter rez. These modes are switched by holding down the function button and pressing the number 11 key marked Sustain.

Pattern sequencing is quick, if not a bit imprecise when doing it in real time. There is some sort of quantization going on, which can be distressing if your timing is off. I much prefer to sequence a pattern in Step Rec mode. Speaking of modes, the Active Step mode is useful and fun.

At the moment, I tend to use a Beat Step Pro to sequence more complex patterns. Other times, I will set up a zone on my workstation to play the Volca Bass via MIDI in real time. I'll even swipe at the playing surface from time to time when playing other synths. You'll definitely want to put some effects in the signal chain, such as pedals or some other multi-fx unit, as the dry sound may be a bit in your face. But even dry, it can sit in a mix at low volumes.

All in all, I'm really impressed by the sound of the Volca Bass. I had no idea that I was missing this in my life, and I'm glad I bought it. I'm now considering selling my Pro-1, as I have had that turned off since the beginning of February when the Volca arrived and I don't need two monosynths which cover the same sonic terrority.

For its size, it's a little powerhouse in a tiny, tiny box. Could the UI (knobs), memory storage and MIDI implementation be improved? Sure, those could be better, but if you can snag one of these for $100 or less, it's definitely worth it.
Summary: The Little Bass Synth I Didn't Know I Needed

My favorite guitar pick has been the Dunlop Big Stubby 2.0mm, but that might change. Just bought some 477P505 and 477P508 Dunlop Primetones and the 477P505 Primetones picks are simply a joy to use.

The contoured body provides a secure grip and its 5mm width demands that grip be loose. Loose is good for fast; loose is good for accurate; loose is good for deliberate. If any of those describe your style or aspirations, this pick will help.

The beveled edge allows the guitarist to glide onto the strings, transfer some energy, and glide off like a thief in the night. The results are two-fold: the guitar strings issue their notes with a soft attack and your pick hand is guiltily carrying the strings' silverware (shame shame!).

If you're not used to picks thicker than 2-3mm, it can feel like gripping a piece of hard candy. If you're used to dragging more than a few microns of pick over the strings to transfer energy, the tactile difference can feel odd (I probably drag 0.75mm's worth of Dunlop Big Stubby or Fender Hard over my strings like a dog dragging its heinie on a shag carpet). The payoff, though, is brighter tones and a little boost in tremolo picking speed (and a loss of a gross dog analogy). Definitely not needed and some people prefer the sound of thinner picks, but what a great pick!

Also tried the 477P508, but that thing was hyooj.

Slight update:

Most of my experiences with this pick were with an unplugged Epi Les Paul 100. Plugged into a Vox 'Metal' amPlug headphone amp, two other features lept out regarding harmonics:

1. Tremolo picking with the bridge pickup is very bright and sometimes squeaky unless the tone is rolled back slightly on the guitar or amp.
2. Pinch harmonics of a Pantera/Lamb of God nature are a breeze.

Nother update - Due to the soft attack of the strings, I mistakenly said they added warmth to the strings. That was stupidity on my part. The attack is soft, not warm, and the overall experience is an increase in brightness. On naturally bright strings such as Dunlop Heavier Core strings, the softness of the attack offsets the increase in brightness, so as not to cause an avalanche of white noise. On naturally warm strings such as SIT Power Wounds, the overall boost in brightness keeps the warmth of the strings from blending with the warmth of a mahogany-bodied guitar in muddy ways.
Summary: Feels like a Jolly Rancher and sounds even sweeter!

I love Tascam gear, and have used it for nearly 30 years. I was excited to try out this interface and see what it could do. Unfortunately, I was disappointed.

While the construction and mechanical function of the device itself were good, the actual function with the computer left much to be desired. Also, the complete lack of a manual with the one I got made it very difficult understand the functions. (Sorry, but with a device this expensive and which includes 2 CDs of software, how hard would it be to include a full manual on the install CD?)

There was a very small quick start guide included, which basically just named the various switches, inputs, and outputs, and gave extremely sparse directions about using the software mixer screen. I was forced into trial and error to see if I could get a serious recording in anything remotely resembling a multi-track mode. I could not. I could record and layer multiple tracks (I was using Audacity, didn't want to install Cubase), but I could not get playback from the previous tracks while I also had live input. Now this could have been my computer or Audacity, as it is an older Win XP machine, but it played back multiple tracks without problem.

There was nothing in the mini-quickstart guide to address this, or even hint where one should look, other than going to Tascam's web site. I'm sorry, but that is just not good enough with a device this expensive. There should be a complete manual, at least in pdf, included with the product. If I am going to use this to do serious recording, the last thing I want to do is waste huge amounts of time digging information out of a website, or worse, from "user community" threads in some blog.

Which brings me to another minor complaint - no Linux drivers included. I use mostly Linux, with only one Windows machine for software which I can't get on Linux. I wanted to try the software under Wine on Linux but was under time constraints.

Then there are the generic problems with software interfaces replacing hardware. With a hardware mixer, I can access as many controls as my fingers can handle (3 or 4 on some mixers) at the same time. Computerized mixers can only do 1 thing at a time, and one must be constantly moving the cursor from one thing to another to access controls. The controls on this interface were very fussy, and you have to position the cursor just exactly on a very small portion of a button to get it to react. I found it very tedious, and again, no actual instructions were included to help with that process. With a touch screen, it might be easier, but then why not just use buttons on a real mixer in that case? (Yeah, I know, touch screens are COOL.)

Also, software based functions are always limited by your computer and OS, and that means everyone can have a different experience - consistency is much harder to maintain.

I am old school, and find hardware mixers far more responsive and useful. I know that lots of people are all excited about having software versions of hardware in their computers, and saving space, etc., etc. I value function over fashion, however, and that is what I have always liked about Tascam gear: it was supremely functional. This software falls far short of what I expect from Tascam, and the lack of a manual for the interface is inexcusable.

Good mixers, especially for multi-track recording, can be complex and difficult to learn. The layers of signal interconnection can be hard to understand at first, and takes some time to get comfortable with. Old Tascam manuals actually used to have a certain amount of instruction in multi-track recording, which was helpful to aspiring recording artists. Not so here.

I had really hoped to give this 3 or 4 stars, but sadly, it only rates a 2 (2.5 if I could) for me. Come on, Tascam, you can do better than this.

Text:
If I had access to inexpensive pedals like this in the 80's, musical history might be different, at least my personal music history, lol.

I was building my first pedal board in 20 years, as I had been using multi-effect boards from Boss (Me-80), an old A.R.T. multi-ffects, as well as the presets on my Fender Mustang III and Marshal Code amps. I had tried a handful of el-cheapo pedals from Don*** and Cal*** and was sorely disappointed.

I had a Strymon Blue Sky and EH Canyon and Proco Rat to start with, and this was the 4th piece of the puzzle.

The Proco Rat is a vintage one I got from my late father in laws estate, but it was too harsh to my ears...it seemed brittle, angry and unpleasant, and frankly, unusable. I had never stacked pedals before, but on a whim, I put this right after another inexpensive purchase I made at the same time, a Joyo JF-10 compressor then into the Rat.

Holy schnikes...I was about to dump the Rat on the market, but pairing this pedal with it gave it new life. I can go from dirty to the umpteenth level to just a slight breakup for some searing blues work. That's cool, but how does it stand alone? Well...

I turned off the Rat, and just played with the Orange Burst, and and fell in love with it. Dropping the gain all the way down and using it for just a signal booster for lead sections is effortless and just what I needed. Cranking the gain to 70% or so gives me close to what I had with my old Tubescreamer 808 in the mid-80's. I remember saving every penny I earned for 2 months at my part time job to buy my first pedal, the ill-fate TS that took a header off the stage and busted. The tones I was wringing out of this were just what I hoped for. She's a beaut.

It would be a bargain at double the price for me. Were it stolen/lost/damaged, I'd buy another without thinking about it. I'm thinking about going on a Joyo pedal buying binge, actually. When I kick the bucket in 20 years or so, my poor wife is going to discover boxes stuffed with pedals like this. I hope like hell they don't end up in a yard sale, but if they do, well, they served me handsomely.

I own a Decibelics Golden Horse. It is an EXACT copy of a Klon. Germanium transistors and all the weird capacitors and the like. It sounds exactly the same-check YouTube. The Mosky Golden Horse is the next best thing period. All of these other pedals priced over $100 don’t use germanium transistors either. They all claim to go “beyond” a Klon. Horsepucky! If you play rock/metal you will never hear the difference. If you play blues jazz or clean stuff, you will notice it a little. However, for $30, it’s a no brainer. Every guitar player should own one. I use my Decibelics for my classic rock band, and my Mosky for my 80’s rock band when I need a little more gain in some solos. The fact that this one is slightly harsher than the real thing, makes it great for 80’s rock. Only slightly harsher. In other words, you wouldn’t be able to tell unless they are side by side. (The real Klon and the Mosky). Ya, it really is THAT good. There’s a YouTube video with the Decibelics and the Mosky, and a bunch of overpriced ones that don’t sound as good. Check it out. You’ll by one of these. Don’t expect it to be versatile. It only does one thing, but it does it great.

Text:
I bought this to interface between my Winfield Typhoon tube amp (5w) and my Focusrite 18i20, hoping to remove the need for my isobox. I had Winnie build a dummy load for the Thru output, so I didn't upset the amp. I powered the unit with phantom power from the interface, and ran into REAPER (Win7).

I fully appreciate that there's zero ambience with a direct box, but even bearing that in mind the sound was completely lifeless. Yes, I tried adding room sounds, too, but the source sound was just pretty awful. Naturally, A/Bing the Redbox with the signal coming from the isobox made the poor quality even more glaring, so I spent a few days without the isobox at all, so I could be as subjective as possible with the Redbox. Still wasn't impressed. The amp sounds really nice with a 12" speaker, and this box just makes the amp sound like some cheap transistor thing :-(

The Vintage / Modern switch had zero impact on the sound and the Tight / Loose switch did nothing either. There was a *very* slight bass hump on the Large setting on the Large / Small switch. I set the amp for a very slight breakup; volume and tone were at midway.

After this disappointment I thought I'd try a VST, and bought Waves GTR Solo. I found that there was no discernible difference between going through the amp and Redbox and going straight into the front of the interface, so I returned the Redbox. Those $99 are better in my pocket.

Sorry to skew the average for this unit, as others seem to have had much better results, but it really didn't cut the mustard for me and therefore I feel this is valid.

I was shopping for a capo that had enhanced rubber buffering at the string contact edge so that the thin strings would be pressed to the frets as much as the thick strings are. But that is not the case here, it's just another standard capo and the thin strings will mute or buzz unless you crank it down hard right on top of the fret, which is not good for your frets or neck wood. When I started guitar, I found the Dunlop Big Stubby pick to be very comfortable, but upon recently coming back to guitar, I found it to make too much of a racket against the strings, so I switched to a far less comfortable though also far less noisy Fender celluloid pick. I have recently been looking for a pick that is both comfortable and not noisy, and after testing a couple variety packs I have found this Tortex Flow to meet most of my requirements. I really like the Tortex material because it is a matte, chalky feeling material, which is both very comfortable to hold and also provides some grip to make it harder to slip out of your fingers (though not too much grip that you can't move your fingers around at all, which is almost the case with Dunlop's Max Grip picks). (Note: When I opened the package, I did find that they came in a thin layer of powdery, white dust, and from many of the pictures, even the ones on Amazon, this seems like this may be the case for many in new packages - while it is mildly annoying to have to clean them, the dust brushes off easily and then the feel like normal Tortex). As far as shape, I have found pointier picks tend to be more accurate, and despite this Flow pick having a wider point than something like the Jazz III XL or TIII, I have found that these picks are at least, if not even a bit more, accurate than those picks. The regular-sized Jazz III's are likely a bit more accurate than any of these larger picks, but that is slightly negated by the fact that sometimes it feels like my fingers, slightly on the larger side, are sometimes getting in the way, and also the larger picks are much better for strumming. Also, while I found the TIII picks tended to be a bit less comfortable than the Jazz III XL shape, the wider shoulders of the Flow pick make the Flow design more comfortable to hold than the Jazz III XL shape. I also experimented with a pack of Ultex Flow picks in different sizes, and I found I tend to prefer the Tortex material. The thicker Ultex (2mm+) is definitely not appealing, since similar to the Big Stubby picks they make a racket against the strings. I have found this to be the case with other thicker Ultex picks, as well. The thinner ones are better, but the Tortex is much more comfortable to hold. I have heard mentioned that the Ultex Flow picks have a sharper point than the Tortex Flow picks, and that this causes the Tortex ones to not perform as well as the Ultex ones. While I have found the Ultex ones to indeed be a bit sharper, I have not found this makes a difference when I am picking. There are two different Flow pick sizes, a normal-sized Flow pick and a "jumbo" which is slightly wider, and the Tortex ones seem to be the normal-sized picks, as you can see in the second to fourth pictures attached. The second one shows the Tortex Flow pick on a jumbo Ultex Flow pick, and you can see the Ultex peaking out from behind, while in the third and fourth pictures you see the Tortex on top of the regular-sized Ultex and the Ultex on top of the Tortex, and you can see that the one underneath is completely covered up. The only pick I prefer more than the Tortex Flow pick is the Hetfield Black Fang pick, which I like the shape of the most especially with the pointed tip and I also like the feel of, which feels like a cross between the regular Ultex and Tortex, since the colored Ultex of the Black Fang pick makes it seem more matte and grippy than regular Ultex. There could also be some subconscious elements seeing as how the Black Fang pick also just has a really cool design and I am a fan of Metallica. However, the Black Fang pick costs $1+ a pick, while this Tortex Flow pick costs less than $0.50 a pick, and it is nearly as good as the Black Fang. Also, I have found my preferred pick thicknesses are between 1mm-1.5mm, so the 1.14mm Tortex Flow picks fall about in the middle of this range, and they are my favorite color, purple. :) Overall, if you want a good all-around pick that works for both strumming and high accuracy, and feels comfortable without making a lot of extraneous noise against the strings when used, this pick is both excellent and priced well. I highly recommend trying out this Tortex Flow pick!

Note that the other pictures are: 1) A number of my favorite picks for comparison, 2-4) as described above, 5) a Tortex Jazz III XL on top of the Tortex Flow, 6) a Tortex Jazz III on top of the Tortex Flow, 7-8) a Tortex Flow on top of a Black Fang and vice versa, 9) a Tortex Flow on top of a TIII.

When I started guitar, I would use Dunlop's Big Stubby pick since it was the most comfortable pick I used. However, I recently started playing again after a few years' break, and I found the Big Stubby pick to make an unacceptable level of clacking against the strings when I played. I switched to a Fender celluloid pick, which made much less noise against the string, and used that for a bit but found it is one of the most uncomfortable picks to use, especially when going from the Big Stubby. I therefore sought a pick that was both comfortable and wouldn't make us much of a racket against the strings, so I picked up two Dunlop variety packs from my local Guitar Center, one of them being the artist variety pack which included this Hetfield Black Fang pick. I recently saw Metallica on their most recent tour, so I was particularly interested in trying the Kirk Hammett and the James Hetfield picks. When testing picks from the non-artist variety pack, I found I tend to prefer picks in the range of 1-1.5.mm with sharp tips. The Jazz III's I found to be very accurate, which I liked, but they were also rather small for my fingers and sometimes it felt like my fingers interfered too much and it was also difficult to strum with. I thought I might like the Kirk Hammett or the John Petrucci picks upon first opening the artist variety pack, but I found the Kirk Hammett pick to not be much different than a regular Jazz III, and the John Petrucci Jazz III was more comfortable to hold being a bit bigger, but it made almost as much racket against the strings as the Big Stubby pick (I have also recently purchased a variety pack of the Ultex Flow picks, and I have found that thicker Ultex, about 2mm+, tends to make much more noisy against the strings than thinner Ultex). I wasn't expecting to like the Hetfield pick, but it turned out that this Black Fang pick was my favorite in the artist series. Not factoring in the price ($1+, versus $0.50 or less for many other picks), this pick is my favorite. The sharp tip makes it feel more accurate, about the same accurateness as the Jazz III XL or the Tortex TIII, but the colored Ultex material used for this pick is very comfortable to hold and it is just slightly narrower than the TIII, which further makes it a more comfortable shape to hold. Since getting this pick, I took a second look at the Ultex Sharp, and I found their shapes are nearly identical, the Ultex Sharp being even closer to the Black Fang in shape than the  TIII is. However, for some reason I don't like the Ultex Sharp as much as the Black Fang. The Black Fang feels a bit more grippy, more like the Tortex material (which I tend to prefer over Ultex due to Tortex's increased grippiness and I like the chalky, matte feel of Tortex). I'm not sure why the Black Fang feels so much nicer than the Ultex Sharp - I think either the colored Ultex has slightly different properties, or it is possible that it is subconscious. The Ultex Sharp is an unappealing, sickly yellow color, so it is possible just the look of the Ultex Sharp makes me dislike it subconsciously, while the Black Fang not only feels nice to hold but also looks awesome. Whatever it is, I tend to prefer the pointier Tortex picks over the Ultex Sharp, but I like the Hetfield Black Fang better than any of the Tortex picks. It is a bit pricier than other picks, though, so I will likely use the Tortex picks more and save the pricier Black Fangs for when I feel like treating myself, since the Tortex picks aren't too much worse than the Black Fangs. The Tortex picks I like the best are all 1.14mm in thickness, and the shapes I like most are the Flow, followed closely by the Jazz III XL, followed closely by the TIII. If you need high accuracy and don't care about strumming and/or comfort (or perhaps your fingers are smaller and a smaller pick feels more comfortable to you), then the regular-sized Jazz IIIs are probably the best, but I find them too small. If comfort is most important to you and string noise doesn't bother you, I recommend the Big Stubbys, and if price matters then I recommend one of the Tortex picks I mentioned above. However, if price is no concern, these are the best all around (and coolest looking!) picks you will find! Rock on!
Summary: Though a bit on the pricey side, this is the best all-around pick there is!

The AKG K 240 Studio headphones are awesome! Straight forward review. No technical talk for those that understand great specs do not always mean great headphones. These do have great specs, by the way.

I have a pair of older 240s that are 600 ohms. These are essentially the same except they are 55 ohms. So, it takes less power to drive them. What that means is that if you use a low output device (phone, computer, etc.) you will get more volume. The volume is considerably louder than the older 240s and most studio reference headphones. However, they are not nearly as loud as headphones designed specifically for portable devices. All that said, they sound great with my Galaxy S4 and Galaxy Tab Pro. You do not need a separate headphone amp. Normal people do not use headphone amps. I dont; know why everyone always talks about them. No amp needed. If you are using these with mixing board or plunging them into an old-fashioned stereo, you certainly do not need an amp. they are loud. With a portable device they are louder than most people would need. but again, not as loud as something designed for a portable device.

As far as sound, these are some of the best sounding headphones I have tried. The sound is flat - like it should be. All sounds, highs, mids, and lows, come through crystal clear. Unless you want to spend several hundreds of dollars more, I really haven;'t heard anything even close to the 240s. Cranked up, they handle loud volume without distorting.

As far a comfort, these are the single most comfortable headphones ever made. Period! They are circumaural, which means they fit completely around your ear. They completely go around your ear (at least my ear) without any on-ear pressure. They are light weight and the adjustable band literally makes them weightless. Within a few minutes you will forget they are on. I watched a movie on my computer and had these on for about 2 1/2 hours. There was no strain or pressure anywhere. My ears and the top of my head didn't feel anything.

The 240s also have a detachable replaceable cord. this is abig plus as cords are the things which seem to go bad before anything else.

I realize sound preferences and fit are completely subjective. For me they are the best phones I have ever owned. For sound and comfort the AKG 240 Studio headphones are as good a it gets.
Summary: One of the best headphones out there!
