If this is going to be your first strat... Expect to spend some time and maybe money to get it set up right....
First of all, strats tend to have fret buzz or a sort of wobble on the G string specially because of the single coil magnetic pull...
It is expensive compared to a netter instrument in my opinion like a Gibson . But if your heart is set on a Strat , I would consider some things ... The naole necks are suposse to make the tone brighter and snappier with loads of sustain... I, personally would have bought a rosewood fretboard... It sounds warmer and more natural... They use some heavy coating on the maple necks , making it a little harder to pkay and to add your own vibrato... Kinda like trying to slide on a basketball court.... The material just makes it harder to slide.... So another reason to chose rosewood over maple...
Finally, single coils... Mmmmm not for me... I hnderstand they cut through the mix better and they have a very distinctive twang.... But the hiss and hum they create plus rhe low output doesn't make them ideal.... The bridge pickups are extrmely bright... Almost unuseable for me... I basically only use the neck and neck and middle pickup combination... But it will definitelly expand your tone range...
Personally, now months agter buying my first american standard.... I can say that I will buy another one... I will get a rosewood neck strat and it will be Made In Mexico! Seriously, they say how superiror the us made ones are... They are not... They do have better electronics but if you switch the pickups to some fat 50's or some setmour duncans... There is no way in hell anybody can tell the difference between a us made or a MIM model.... Except they are almost a third of the price...
Overall I was a little dissapointed with the performance of my strat... Have to be adjusting it constantly, have to compromise between fret buzz and high string action... The si gle coild hum is just too annoying.., and finally, yes... Nothing is quite like a strat.... I bought an amazing Gibson Les Paul that is superior in everyway to my strat... But funny enough I've come to appreciate the strat now even more than before I had the Gibson.... I find myself reaching for it more than before... It's starting to grow on me.... But only after many mods, setups and finding the right strings for it.
Summary: I was forst dissapointed, now I can't be without it... But...

As far as portable recording devices go, this should be awarded 4 stars...but as far as recording devices in general, it's more of a 3.

TASCAM is big into the all-in-one recording devices, which in my opinion, are a dying breed due to the ease of recording on laptops these days. If you have the option, I would actually spring for an interface for an iMac and use garageband over any all-in-one devices.

The best thing about this device is the portability. It's about the size of a VHS and can be battery operated (although the batteries don't last very long). I would actually get an adapter, which isn't included, because it can be annoying if the batteries die while you're recording.

You can do pretty much anything you want on this recorder - cut/paste, master, loop, etc. It also supplies phantom power for mics that use it. The one big problem I have with it, and all TASCAM recorders for that matter, is that there is a lot of feedback while you are recording. It doesn't come out on the mastered track, but it can get very annoying while you are trying to record anything.

***Pros :)
-Portability - size of VHS tape
-Full functionality of the larger 24 track all-in-one studios
-Able to produce a pretty decent, mastered product

***Cons :(
-Digital portastudio is much more cumbersome to use when compared to inexpensive computer software
-Feedback while recording is annoying
Summary: Love the portability, but still has feedback while recording like other TASCAM portastudios

Text:
Sound: excellent rich sound. Very clear "ringing" low notes, and very pleasant high pitch notes which do not have distortion. I can produce all the notes very clearly. The range is beyond one octave. I am an amateur in music, but I can easily figure out and produce standard do re mi fa sol la to do, plus 3 very high pitched notes on top of that. The thing that is a useful feature on the ocarina is that because of the design and large holes, you can easily produce the sharp and flat notes by covering half of the hole, similar to how it can be done on the piano with the black keys. Additionally, this Ocarina design has umvery useful small holes next to two big holes, one in each side of the Ocarina. You can cover them to get sharps or flats. Basically there are no issues with the sound this Ocarina makes. It is pretty excellent.

Design: No visible flaws with the design. All holes easy to cover firmly. The holes are positioned in a way that is comfortable for the fingers.
The outside appearance, color, finish, are just exceptionally impressive. People I showed this "Forest Whisper" ocarina to thought it was made from some kind of dark Cherry or Mahogany wood. The appearance is pretty much indistinguishable. At least it is the case with my individual Ocarina.

Extra: the Ocarina came with a nice pouch. I personally don't intend to travel with the ocarina but it should be in some kind of soft bag, or preferably a box of you take it somewhere. For me this bag is very useful because it I intend to put it away for extended period of time I wouldn't want dust settling on it, or some scratches appearing on the outside.
Another accessory that I found only two weeks later is a nice necklace string to attach to the ocarina. It's nice to see that it wasn't just a string. It has nice greenish beads on it.
Only small issue is that it wasn't attached and it might be tricky to attach it the right away so the tin nylon cords don't self untie and cause the instrument to fall.

Small Issue: there is one minor problem I found with the instrument coating which is that when you put a mouth to it you can smell the paint or laquer that it is covered it. I think it is just the paint. It does not smell too strong, nor does it really bother me, but it is noticeable and I guess some people may not like it. The coating/paint doesn't "bleed" or smear. The instrument has been baked and dried thoroughly. It's hits the smell.
I would subtract half the star from the five stars but since it is not an option I'd rather leave it at five stars.

[[VIDEOID:e94a6c6e20d001cee7401f06bf18cad0]] Today, I am reviewing the RockJam 20 watt electric guitar amplifier. My first impressions of it were that it is rather small for an amp of its wattage, I have several other amps of smaller wattages that are bigger in size. However, a smaller size does not make an amp good or bad and as such there are pros and cons that come with it being a smaller size.

The aesthetics of the amp are pretty nice, the carrying handle is unique, being a strap that fits onto the buttons on each side of the amp. The grille is metal, a feature I often don't see on cheap amps. The power cord is removable, which is another feature not commonly seen on these practice amps. At the top of the amp, there are five knobs. One for gain, one for volume, and a 3 knob eq. There's also the power switch, headphone jack, and input jack, as well as a boost switch which engages distortion.

Now as for the quality of the sound, it's not bad. It sounds better than my two Squier SP-10 amps I have, and is kind of on par with my peavey backstage in terms of clarity. The three level eq is very useful in finding the right level of bass or treble depending on how I need my guitars to sound. One thing this amp does that I have not seen in other amps is that the gain knob also affects the clean channel. Most of the time gain knobs have no effect on an undisturbed sound, but this gain knob increases the volume of the clean channel, too, which is neat. The headphone jack does pretty much what a headphone jack is supposed to do, and I've had no issues with it.

Overall, I'd recommend this amp, if you're looking for something to play around with, I'm not sure how well it would do on stage with other instruments, but it does a great job of being a practice amp.
Summary: Decent practice amp that has a few neat features.

Text:
Overall:
Good value and a great tool to learn songs. There's a lot in this little box for the money. I use this as a learning tool to learn songs for 2 cover bands I'm in. I don't plan to use the record feature, however, I think you could record your own backing track and jam on top of it.

Bottom line: I don't know how I could play in cover bands without something like this.

Quirks:
Tascam provides high value products where you get a lot for the money but they come with their quirks. I've had the unit freeze up on me twice now. You can't turn it off and back on, you have to unplug the power supply (if it's being used) and take out the batteries and put them back in.

Deficiencies:
Deficiencies include a tiny screen that's hard to read. You have to be on top of it and at just the right angle to see it well. And some of the data on it is 'small'. They could have made the unit bigger in my opinion.

I wasn't able to take this out of the box and start using it right away. I had to read the manual. It wasn't 100% intuitive.

If I change the key of a song to learn it in a different key then move on another song the key change carries forward to the new song, which I don't think should be the default.

I needed to use the Fine Tune feature of the key change to sync to a song and I swear the 'Fine' doesn't work. I couldn't get synced up. I need to read that manual again; there might be something about that feature I'm missing.

When you set a Loop, to learn a tough passage or something, and while looping you hit stop, when you restart it takes you to the top of the loop. I'd rather it continue from where I stopped. I need to read the manual to see if it's configurable.

I use it with battery power because I don't like the extra cord in the way. It chews through batteries pretty good for a unit without any moving parts, like a CD player has.

This is minor, but when you're in storage mode to download or upload songs from it, then unplug the USB cable the unit turns off. Most of the time I intend to keep using the unit after connecting it to my PC. Just have to power it on again.
Summary: Great idea, good value, works pretty well, but has some quirks and deficiencies

Text:
Small powered speakers don't typically get scratched and scraped when in use up on a tripod, the battle scars occur mostly during transport and storage. I have four QSC K10's. The 2nd pair via a special promotion came with free K-Totes and still look new 5 years later. The first pair, although very well cared for were starting to show a bit of wear, so I recently bought a pair of the less expensive Gator bags to protect them. Here's my direct side-by-side comparison:

Pro's: Sized correctly, gets the job done, and are less expensive than the very nice QSC bags

Con's: Not as well padded or as softly lined as the QSC. Lacks the top access flap of the QSC that allows you to grab the top handle of the speaker (a feature I rarely use with the QSC bags, but others might miss it more than myself) The zippers are a bit heavier duty on the QSC, but the ones on the Gator's seem to be adequate.

Both bags feature sturdy carrying straps which are more-or-less identical. The exterior pocket is the same size on either bag, big enough to store the power cable but not much more (grrr). Double the size would be far better as then you could also store a 50' audio cable. The QSC has a longer Velcro strip on the pocket flap.

Verdict: The Gator bag is perfectly adequate, but the QSC K-Tote is a bit better all around. If you are carrying $150 Harbingers (yuck) and want to keep them looking nice than the Gator makes more sense. If your speakers cost $600+ each and are frequently transported, then you might want to pay for the extra margin of protection that the QSC bags provide. I decided to keep this pair of the Gators, certainly good enough, no specific concerns.

I love cheap guitars, so long as they have a good sound and decent hardware that allows proper adjustment, This model qualifies!
It came from the box in nearly perfect adjustment, even though it suffered rough handling in transit. The selector switch was snapped off. It still worked, but needed replacement to work properly. Amazon treated me right on that repair. (good on ya Amazon!)

Once the guitar was restrung with good strings and minor intonation tweaks, it sounds GREAT! These are cheap pickups, oversized-humbuckers... but they are humbucking so noise is not an issue as it always is with single coils.

Throughout the decades, I've noticed that cheap pickups tend to sound better... by which I mean, they have more high end and a higher resonant frequency. I suppose that's because manufacturers use less wire to wind the pups, and that reduces the power, but raises the resonant frequency. The nice thing is, these are not really weak pups. They have enough OOmph to push the front end of several amps I tried them with... Marshall, Hughes & Ketner, Peavey, and two Fender combo amps.

The neck is made from nice rift-sawn maple, which is nearly as good as quarter-sawn. I've noticed most of the Indonesian guitars (like this one) are generally better than the Chinese imports, and good neck wood is one of their best features. I've seen far worse wood selection in necks made by Warmoth that cost more than this whole guitar! I like the "vintage" yellow finish on the neck.

The body is not too heavy considering that, like most Fender style guitars, it is just a slab of lumber. Still, whatever CNC machine they use for these makes accurate routs. The neck pocket and control routs are clean and precise. Everything fits. Nothing rattles.

The bridge is simple; one of fender's best designs. It adjusts easily and stays put.

The pickguard is rather thick, which many consider a sign of quality. I look for accurate clean edges with neat evenly-cut chamfers. This is easily as good as every aftermarket pickguard I've seen.

Since we had to repair the switch anyway, i took a look inside while it was on the bench. The pots are small and probably not the best quality. While they are new, that is no problem, but I can foresee a time when they may need replaced. While the pickguard was off, I also noticed the quality of wood in the body was VERY nice, especially for a guitar in this range. I might just sand off the black paint to see what's underneath!

All-in-all, this is a great bargain! After I play it enough to break it in, I'll level and dress the frets. It already plays pretty nice: low action, very little fret-buzz. Once it "settles in" to it's new environment, I bet I can tweak it to play as well as any expensive guitar short of a custom made job. I might get back with photos after some modifications and more playing time with this thing. In the meantime, every one of these Indonesian Squires I've seen has been far batter than Squires of the past. Highly recommended for budget minded guitarists or those wanting a cheap guitar to modify.

The Tortex Jazz III's are my favorite because they are pretty grippy due to their matte, chalky surface, but not overly grippy and it is still relatively easy to move your fingers around. These Max Grip picks are true to their name, in that once you take one of these picks it is, for all intents and purposes, impossible to slide your fingers around on it. I haven't played much with these when I have been sweaty, so it might become a little easier to slide your fingers around if your hands are sweaty (I will update this review if I ever have the chance to test this out), but these Max Grip picks are the grippiest picks I have tested. I tend to prefer either the new Flow pick shape or the Jazz III XL shape, so I wish these Max Grip picks came in a shape I preferred, but if you are looking for a pick that won't let your fingers slide around at all, I highly recommend this pick, in either the Jazz III shape if you need a lot of accuracy or the regular pick shape if you want more comfort. These Max Grip picks really do attach themselves to your fingers well.

This is a sturdy product that has the features I need to offer a premium lighting option for my live shows. My only caveat is a "fit" vs. "function" consideration. Read on.

My setup relies on MIDI as I'm an electric violinist who uses a sequencer (Cakewalk Sonar) along with software for video orchestration (Resolume). I normally would not offer lighting with my shows, but it's a definite plus for a dance gig, or for a alternative venue (e.g., a fundraiser which features a full band in a larger room, but with DarkViolin in an adjoining space).

The lighting standard uses the DMX protocol, as other have mentioned. That is clearly the industry standard, but it's not the one in my laptop + outboard MIDI gear's sweet spot. To fully exploit DMX, which the GB 400 supports in and out, I would use a VST such as the DMXIS Show Buddy, which would give Sonar away to send "scene" changes over DMX but using MIDI note commands.

I have multiple MIDI floor control units such as the [[ASIN:B000QGDZUK Roland FC-300]] which would allow for live lighting updates - e.g., an improvised tempo or volume change.

The sturdiness is appreciated. Seriously. But the weight of the unit and its bulk make it somewhat more difficult to carry, even though it is roughly the size of a small guitar amp or the mass of the [[ASIN:B000ECX6FA Roland KC-150 4-Ch Mixing Keyboard Amplifier]]. If I were to bring this along on a regular gig, I wouldn't be a happy camper.

That said, I doubt if there are better alternatives out there. Like those folks who manufacture 150 LB speaker cabs, it suggests Marq is somewhat unconcerned that real people have to deal with gravity and bulk when adding lighting to a portable gig. Bad intonation is one result of a tired violinist fatigued by gadget transport.

See photo for a height comparison if you have clearance issues. The shipping dimensions apply to you if the as-shipped box is your transport method.

Misc gig note: Keep in mind the power consumption added by this unit.

The Marc FAQ for this product is readable and indispensable.

Upshot: This device will be used at a wedding party shortly and will add the sort of visual sparkle that nothing else in my gadget arsensal could.
Summary: Sparkle that Every Lumens-Starved Electric Violinist Should Crave

I've been using a Scarlett Solo but lately I've been using two mic's to record acoustic guitar (the Solo only has one XLR input), so the 2i4 was a perfect upgrade. Installation was pretty easy - for PC you have to download some drivers and then I just went into "manage audio devices" in Windows and set the Focusrite USB as the the default device for playback and recording. Of course you'll also need to select it as the ASIO driver for your DAW, amp sim, etc. I bumped up the buffer size to 256 and everything seems to work perfectly now (I was getting some crackling in the audio at the smaller buffer size that it defaults to, but even with the larger buffer size there's no noticeable latency).

It's working great for me as far as recording. You've got two inputs which can each accept either a microphone XLR cable or a 1/4" instrument cable. There's 48 volt power for condenser mic's. On the back you've got MIDI in and out for a keyboard. Of course there's the USB plug on the back for connecting to your computer, along with two sets of phono cable outputs and one set of 1/4" outputs, all for connecting to your stereo gear or studio monitors.

Using my condenser mic's, I really like the preamps in these Scarlett units - they're very natural sounding and I feel that I get an accurate recorded representation of what I'm hearing in the room when I'm playing acoustic guitar. Of course running an electric guitar or bass through it and into my PC amp sim works just fine as well.

Overall I'm very happy with the unit and it looks great sitting on my desk as well.
Summary: Great for the small home studio

First I am not a professional sound guy, this is not a professional review. I am a hobbyist, and am using this as part of a setup to stream video gameplay to the Internet on twitch.tv/scottjohnsonvope.

Coming from a somewhat comparable mixer in size and features, the Behringer 1204FX Xenyx Premium http://amzn.to/1Ux29jo, I like this mixer better. The pots on this are solid, there is no noise when turning the gain knobs, the same cannot be said of the Behringer. The built in USB is so much better than the UCA200 dongle. The sound in general is cleaner and very pleased with the switch.

The manual is very thin, and contains several languages, resulting in perhaps 3 pages of english, with only descriptions of the knobs and sliders. Know explanation of other features. For instance I have no idea what the USB ADC/DAC is capable of in bit rate and frequency.

We had an issue where we were sending sound into the mixer, through the USB and back into the mixer, causing confusion controlling the volume. I couldn't believe that this was what was happening because there was no echo/delay in the final output which included both the pre USB and post USB audio signals. Ultimately, though that was the issue and we resolved it. Not a problem of the mixer, my mistake, but amazed that the USB input had so little latency on it that it wasn't even noticeable. This was not the case with the UCA200, which would lag unbearably during recording until it was minutes behind.

My one beef with this, and thus the 4 stars, also stems from the USB. There is no way to control output volume to the USB. Also I had hoped that there would be support for independent channels over the USB, not just the Stereo mix. There is only a pot to control the USB volume coming back into the mixer, and no way to assign it to a slider or even route the stereo signal to the slider.

Perhaps I am missing it but I have checked several times, there does not appear to be a stereo send for the monitor send or the fx send, though both seem to have a stereo return. Had there been I potentially could have routed the USB output through that and back in, where there is a slider. Although that still would have failed, as there is not Mute/Solo for the USB return.

A further oddity, difference from the 1204, is that the gain on channels 3/4 5/6 does not control the 1/4" inputs. The only stereo in that has a gain control is 7/8, which does not have an XLR in. The gain on 1 and 2, mono inputs, does control the line as well as the XLR input.

The individual dials for FX and MON are nice, but a positive on/off switch and led would be welcome as a positive on/off. Switching between inputs while testing by turning dials up and down is not nearly as useful. That said, without stereo output of the MON channels, they are of little use.

We are using a Monoprice Lollipop mic, http://amzn.to/1XtqINo, and the sound is great.

There is a charge indicator if you remember to watch, but it's probably a good idea to use up the rest of the power during practice. This fretboard oil was easy to apply and made the fretboard, on my IYV IP-350, look great. If you buy a guitar that was made in a country with high humidity and live in an area of low humidity, oiling the fretboard is a must. IYV Guitars are made in Vietnam, and I live in Northern Nevada, which is a much drier
climate. The 6554 Dunlop Fretboard Oil worked nicely to remedy that dry fretboard.

Since I had already installed new strings, I used a cotton swab to apply the oil beneath the strings and between the frets. I dabbed the cotton swab on the top of the Dunlop 6554 dispenser and rubbed it on the fretboard, bending and lifting my strings to get beneath and around them. I've watched many videos on guitar care and maintenance; it's important to not over-oil your fretboard. Be sure to apply a light coat and buff it off, after letting it set for a bit. I applied a light coat to half of my fretboard then went back and buffed it with a clean, micro-fiber cloth before applying it to the other half. After I completely oiling and buffing, I used a paper towel under the strings to absorb any oils I may have gotten on the strings. I then applied Dunlp 65 string conditioner, retuned and was good to go!
Summary: Made my fret board look much better

I’ve been looking for a reverb pedal to complete my pedal board and the MIMIDI surprised me with its design and sound.

WHAT YOU GET

Mini reverb pedal (~3 ½” x 1 ½” x 1 ¼”) with instruction manual and optional hook/loop tape for pedal board attachment. It is important to note that this pedal requires an outside power source (not included) to be used … its minimal design does not allow it to accommodate a battery compartment.

HOW IT PERFORMS

Honestly, I was looking at more expensive full-size reverb pedals but thought I’d give this little pedal a shot. The technology is available now to cram a lot of options into miniature versions of the “standard” pedal without losing a thing. The MIMIDI reverb pedal (named “Ocean Verb”) provided a surprising array of reverb options, all while being housed in a tough little stompbox. The aqua colored pedal offers a palette of sound options to tweak so you can find that “sweet spot”. The three main options are spring, room and shimmer (controlled by a metal selector switch knob). To fine tune, there are two small dials for mix and tone. The large central dial controls the decay of the effect and the standard metal on off footswitch is at the bottom (with an LED on/off indicator). I like that there is a chrome bar located just below the decay knob that protects the controls at the top from being stepped-on when turning the pedal on and off. It is evident that a lot of thought was put into the presentation of the pedal’s construction. The bottom of the pedal is covered with a rubber pad, but you can peel off the rubber pad and use the hook/loop tape if desired (which is what I did).

While this pedal can be used as an effect for multiple instruments, I use it for guitar. This digital reverb pedal has a bright overall tone that “behaves” differently, depending on the tools I’m using (single-coil Fender or humbucker Gibson). Of the three main options, I find the room and spring reverb being more practical for my style of play, but like playing around with the shimmer. This little power block is absolutely perfect for my needs. When I'm performing, the area around the base of my mic stand and my foot pedals does not need to be cluttered up with an extension cord, power adapter, and power cables. In addition, the AC power on many stages is very unreliable, causing noise in the pedal chain. I also do some "busking" shows outdoors with a battery-powered amp, with no power at all available for the pedals. This unobtrusive, professional-looking battery pack is a great solution for all that.

It's tiny and lightweight, so it slips right into my gig gear bag. It charges easily with a standard USB-C cable, with a red "charging" indicator LED and a green LED to let you know when it's topped off. There is a rocker-style on/off switch and blue LEDs over each output to indicate that it's getting power. It even comes with seven really nice 14-inch power cables.

I have used it for one performance so far, running a robust guitar pre-amp for nearly three hours. I'm not equipped to critically measure the battery capacity of the battery, but after the gig it took less than half an hour to recharge the power block. This suggests to me that the 10,000 mAh claim is no exaggeration. Theoretically then, I could run seven pedals in my pedal board for 11 hours on this - that will never happen!

Bottom line, I love this little power block, and it will live in my gig gear bag for a very long time.

When I first got this little controller I was pretty happy with it. The build quality felt professional and solid, the design was nice, and I figured it'd obviously play well with my various Arturia VSTs in the Reaper DAW. The keys seems nice and full with a nice amount of give and weight.

As I got around to installing things and trying to get it to work ... the picture got a little iffier. While the keyboard is basically plug n play, getting the knobs properly assigned is a bigger headache than it needs to be. You have to (or at least it first appears you have to) assign the sensitivities of the knobs through an Arturia software app that is just annoying to use all around. Once you get past that, it's still very fiddly getting knobs properly assigned with the kind of response correlation you expect, even on Arturia's own apps.

While this was disappointing, you can actually bypass the Arturia app I later realized, and in most cases I could at least manage the basic assignments I wanted with a little bit of elbow grease. But then other little things started bugging me. The USB connector is incredibly flimsy and it's easy for the cord to wobble around or even pop out. It's also positioned in a way that is very inconvenient relative to my tabletop/desktop set-up. The pad buttons feel sluggish and unresponsive, but in fairness I don't use pad buttons much, so I'm not sure if that's unique to the product or just symptomatic of why I've never gravitated towards using those kinds of buttons in the first place.

Even with all of this, I still felt that overall I had a reasonably decent if somewhat fiddly controller that looked and felt good on the whole. Then one -- maybe two -- of the keys started acting weird. They just will flake out and not trigger the note being pressed periodically, maybe once in every 8 or 9 presses. This only seemed to affect 1 or 2 specific keys.

That was kind of the final straw, given that I spent $100+ on the thing. In the time since my purchase, I've read that Arturia keys have a bit of a reputation for being ... not-stellar. They look good and make a good first impression, but I'm not sure the build quality under the hood is really there.

I write this review maybe 2 years after purchase? Something like that. I don't use MIDI controllers a lot so I've managed with it for this long, but I'm now shopping for a replacement and figured I'd leave my experience with this one. I've heard some of the Korg's are pretty good so I'll probably try one of theirs.

I have been playing through the Electro-Harmonix Metal Muff distortion pedal for about 5 years now. When I was in the market for a pedal I took my main guitar (a Carvin 7-string with active pickups) to the shop and tried hooking up several different distortion pedals to the same store amp. I compared the Metal Muff to the [[ASIN:B0002CZVA0 Boss MT-2 Metal Zone Pedal]] and the [[ASIN:B0002E3M0E DigiTech XMM Metal Master-Distortion Guitar Pedal]]. I found the Boss Metal Zone to be lacking in tonal range. It was good for high-treble shredding but not so good for midrangey riffing like Black Sabbath and Led Zeppelin. The biggest problem with the Digitech Metal Master was the lack of a true bypass - it colored the clean sound of the guitar even when the pedal was switched off. The Metal Muff was just right with a true bypass and an extremly wide range of tonal control.

For years I have used the Metal Muff for jamming and recording and for the occasional live performance. Once when I played at a church the sound guy didn't want me to play through my amp, so I plugged my guitar through the Metal Muff directly into the PA. The Metal Muff performed admirably.

This guitar pedal is a tonal beast! A small turn of a knob makes a big change in sound. The nice thing is that there are so many sweet spots that if you lose one you are bound to find another. You will have no trouble cutting through the mix with this pedal. If you need an extra little bit of treble (or a lot of extra treble) to cut through a guitar solo, there is a seperate treble boost swtich with its own control. You probably won't need it very often. Hard rock, Black Sabbath grooves, Metallica riffs, Steve Vai shred, Black Label Society, Korn, grunge, punk, death metal, black metal, industrial noise. In the world of heavy guitar playing there is not much you cannot do with this riff and lead monster. If you keep the gain fairly low and turn the midrange up there is an excellent clarity of notes when playing chords. If you have a decent amp you can play this pedal on top of the amp's distortion channel and still get a fairly clear sound, but you don't really need to. It works much better when the amp is on the clean channel or with a slight overdrive.

This pedal sounds excellent with active pickups, humbuckers, and single-coil pickups. However if you use active pickups like me you may want to invest is a noise supressor pedal.

What can't this pedal do? I really can't recommend it for blues and AC/DC style hard rock. An overdrive pedal is better than a metal distortion pedal for playing those styles.
Summary: Best distortion pedal I have ever used.

So if you are looking for your “typical” style guitar digital delay pedal, this may not be what you are looking for. However, if you like “experimenting” with different delay effects, need the ability to dial that effect in and save it, and have a basic 80 looper to boot, then this pedal is right up your alley!
Nicely designed, built well! You will need a typical 9v 300ma power supply (neg center) as most delay pedals require. No battery operation. This is a true stereo in/out device for your keyboards, etc...
You have seven (slots) or memory banks to save a created patch, with the last (seven) being the looper.
You have your standard style delays of course, but as you get further in to it, you have some very unique, different
functions available to you. Along the top, you have 3 controls for mix, speed and feedback control, then below those are two “tweak” knobs that make things even more interesting. The tweak knobs control different functions based on the patch you are in. I would download the instructions, as things can get a bit complicated without them.
I have not had this long, and only been able to play and test it out for a few days, but the amount of delays and “special effects” you can get from this pedal is impressive. Sounds great, bypass is clean, input/output volumes for your looper, and fade out functions as well. A great “unusual” delay that is a bargain at this price, and if you like to “experiment” for that sound, this pedal should take up residence on your pedal board!
Summary: Not Your “Typical” Delay Pedal & That’s Good!

I have had 3 of these. Yes, 3. I bought the JS-8 and really loved it. But being a guitar enthusiast more than a really good player, I change a lot:) So I sold the Js-8 to a friend while I concentrated on a tube amp setup. Then, about a year later, I desired the JS-10 and purchased one. I liked it but again went with a newer tube amp model and eventually sold the JS-10.

That was over 1 year ago. After much playing, working with pedals and setups, testing the Fractal FX-series and the Kemper head (both about 2 grand), I finally decided that what provides my real need, playing style, and life, is the JS-10. Here's why...

I love 4x12 cabinet sounds, tube heads, delay/phaser/chorus pedals, and I have used a Rockcrusher attenuator so I can dime out the amp volume without losing any tone. But I do not play in a band. I play only at home and 99% with no one ever hearing or seeing me. I don't need the big stuff. But I like the sound of the big stuff. So, I simply use the JS-10 with speakers attached, along with internal speakers and BOOM - the sound is awesome. The range is more in line with house speakers so the sound is more all/everywhere. It is near - not exactly - but nearly what the amp setup is.

The JS-10 has so many features that I like that the Amp setup do not have - like an auxiliary input, song looping, tuner, headphone jack, and so many effects that can be tweaked galore.

Also, for my taste, I can just sit and play by dialing in the presets available.

I am now selling all of my other gear. The JS-10 is my go to from here on out.

I also completely wash each harmonica every 3 weeks in very warm water. (you can do that with these harps
because they do not have wooden combs that swell up and crack.) I then shake out the excess water and
blow on each hole for 30 seconds or so, to be sure all the water is out of the reeds. Dry overnight and play
the next day. I'm not what you would call a hard rocking blower, so I don't tend to put too much stress on my
reeds. Even though I play at least once every day. I must say the Bluesmaster has the sweetest sound, ease of playing and bending, plus a clean design that
doesn't put stress on my lips or tongue and never have a bad taste. I highly recommend these to beginners.
Take good care of these little beauties and they won't let you down. My thanks to Suzuki for making such a fine
instrument. I'm trying to think of another key to buy like maybe an A flat. I'm not bothering with anything lower than

Text:
If you're looking for a portable stand on par with the standard non-portable variety in terms of stability and durability, this is one you should strongly consider. Unlike other portable stands of this sort, it's music holder divides into two pieces, which makes for a much less awkward carrying bag. It is decidedly the best portable stand I've owned over several decades now. Price-wise it's more expensive than the typical portable stand, but that's because it is designed to be on par with non-portable stands, plus it has the nifty music holder that breaks down to a smaller footprint.

The is the second one of these I've purchased, and is a heavier version since its music holder does not have holes cut into it to reduce its weight. Albeit a little bit heaver than its counterpart, that also makes it a tad sturdier. As already noted, the music holder divides into two pieces, which connect together using a clever pair of thumb screws that can only be loosened/tightened, not removed. The telescoping mounting post uses metal screw downs that have a large plastic knob for tightening. The screw fits into a (replaceable) nut slotted into a hard rubber friction fitting. Should for some reason you turn the screw all the way out (or your kid does), and should the nut gets lost or you damage it by cross threading when putting it back in, it's just a standard hex nut available from any hardware store. I particularly like that the tray can accommodate a fake book that might collapse a flimsier stand. The legs when fully spread provide a heavy duty base that is as stable as a conventional non-portable stand.

I find it almost as quick to set up as the flimsier portable stands, the only real difference being the need to put the two halves of the music holder together. If it's of interest, the stand also has the typical spring ties downs for use in windy conditions. It can also be laid out flat for use as a sturdy platform, something a percussionist might want to know.

It comes with a good sized bag, one much less bulky than for similar stands that don't have the divided music holder, but with room for additional items, in my case my stand light and a trumpet mute.

Text:
This is a useful product if you need a stand pretty much anywhere (and who honestly doesn't?). The holding clasp is quite wide, so it is suitable for both strat-style and classical guitars with a two inch nut. The clasp rotates, so it can be clamped to a drafting table or other slanted surface and still function well. The clasp also folds flat, making it even more portable. Also, the clamp in back opens to just over an inch and a half (5 cm) so it should accommodate nearly every shelf or desk to make a portable stand.

The stand must at a height where the bottom of the guitar rests on the floor, so be aware of that - the front neck clasp is a full three inches wide, which seems a little strange, honestly. If the bottom of the guitar does not touch the floor, the neck could slip through this clasp, and it will at the very least nudge your tuners (one on a stratocaster style, two on a dual tuner headstock) enough to knock them out a little. If you have this low enough so the guitar body rests on the floor, no worries!

So it's good at what it is, if a little pricey. For a super useful and portable guitar accessory, check out the [[ASIN:B005Q9Z5XW Ravel SSRAVELDESK Desktop Music Stand]], and its relatively low price... still, since this portable guitar stand is something you shouldn't have to buy more than once, it is ultimately worth it.

Years ago I first spotted the MS-2 in a store window on 48th St and thought it was a promo item - the sort of thing manufacturers give out to retailers to catch peoples' eyes. The irony of a pint-sized version of the iconic Marshall stack was hysterical - and this was years before today's 3 and 4ft mini-stacks that, for some reason, I don't find quite as amusing.

The MS-2 was considerably cheaper back when I got mine (it's stamped 'Made in Korea' which I doubt is still the case), and that's my main problem: relative bang for the buck.

Considering not just Marshall's other practice models but the sheer range of amps in the 1-15 watt space, buyers should really ask themselves what they want such a small amp for.

I will say the little guy has been a favorite conversation item, but a useful piece of playing or recording equipment? Not really.

The plastic box is so light that you'll have to steady it when you're plugged in. As someone else mentioned, I noticed problems keeping battery power constant and would recommend a 9V DC adaptor to squeeze what little power there is out of it. The clean tone for such a small speaker is not bad, but like ships, that's not what Marshalls are made for (IMO). Unfortunately, the distorted tone is, well, just not very realistic.

And yeah, I did try close-miking the MS-2 once to see if I could get that Physical Graffiti crunch on tape. What I got was interesting in its own right but wouldn't fool anyone. (Maybe if I triple-tracked it...)

The 1 watt ouput would have a hard time being heard over some acoustic instruments so if you're at all interested in playing with others, you'll need more juice.

If you're an electronics experimenter, the MS-2 is useful to have on your bench for low-volt audio output. I took the back off once and the board and construction are actually quite clean. I'll bet it's a great candidate for circuit benders and hardware hacks and somewhere there must be a site dedicated to outrageous mods.

I don't mean the knock the MS-2 too hard for being what it is - a 1 watt wonder. At half the price it's going for it would make a great stocking stuffer and a fun gift.

But if you're really interested in a decent-sounding small amp for practicing or recording and you're already considering spending $40, I'd strongly suggest you explore what's available for another 20 or 30, including a classic Pignose that can sound terrific close-miked if that's your thing. Decide whether you'd rather play a 5-10 watt amp cranked or a 15-20 watt amp clean; either way there's plenty to choose from.
Summary: Bonsai Marshall / Not A Lot of Price Value

By way of brief background, I got my 935s after testing them extensively against many Shures (including 58s and Beta 58As), as well as the awesome Sennheiser 835, which I'd been using for years, and I've been really happy with the 935s. The only reason I even thought to try the 945 was that I read some reviews saying that it was as good as the 935 if not a little better and, most saliently, that it was even less susceptible to feedback. I'm disappointed to say that my experience with respect to feedback has been the opposite. I've studied the diagrams of the polar patterns and the optimal monitor placement, and this thing seems to feed back all over the place. I perform in some venues where I can't control the precise placement of monitors, and in that kind of environment, I suspect this mic would be a disaster. Even just testing it in my living room using my Fishman Loudbox Artist as a monitor, I'm getting feedback from almost every angle, including the angles that are supposed to be outside the polar pattern. In an ideal controlled environment, the sound is a cut above the 935, and I'd love to see a way to make it work. In the real world, I think I'll probably just stick with the 935s, which I also love, and remember that the 945 and I will always have Paris.

I’ve got a few other compressors: Bogner Harlow v2 (single knob compressor with the boost), an EQD The Warden (studio level optical comp tweakability in a pedal), and a Pigtone Compressor (Dyna Comp clone I think).

The Coolmusic Comp Pro sits in a unique spot, costing far less than the boutique compressors but having more controls than the cheap compressor pedals out there.

Build quality is solid, despite the quirky design. The large footswitch LED is great and the mini LED dots inside the knobs are a nice touch. Pots turn smoothly. Solid all round. Mine came without any rubber feet or rubber plating on the base, which. Is great because I use Velcro and have a clean area to attach to.

The Level is an overall output control, so if the comp is squashing your signal down and you lose some level, you can compensate here.

Sustain, as the name implies, holds onto your note and can be subtle or, at extreme settings, impart a ringing character into your tone. At that point, you’re using it as an effect, not as a utility pedal. The sustain function is playing with the gain to extend your notes and the cost of that is an increased noise floor at any setting past noon on the dial. Pretty normal behavior, even for more costly pedals.

The Tone knob can be use to soften the hiss caused by the Sustain or just to shape your tone warmer or brighter as you see fit.

And the Attack knob determines how quickly the compression engages as you strike the notes. Fully clockwise, there’s really no effect and everything feels “open”. But the further counter-clockwise you set it, the Attack will cause a near-instantaneous clamping down on your dynamics, which evens out your notes.

So for clean playing where maybe your picking isn’t as even as it could be (hitting some notes harder, some softer) you can hear the overall level even out and it sounds “better”.

You need to spend some time with any compressor to find the sweet spot between losing your dynamics entirely and hearing a benefit from it. With this pedal, I found a happy medium pretty quickly and enjoyed noodling around with the pedal engaged.

And that’s my truest metric of how much I like a pedal: do I lose myself just playing and does the pedal inspire me in some way.

For the Coolmusic Comp Pro, the answer is a resounding yes; I spent a long time playing cleaner and in a style I wouldn’t normally because the pedal made that possible. Really cool!

Really enjoy playing with this pedal and at this price it’s well worthy of 5 stars.

WHO IT'S FOR: DSLR/Mirrorless video shooters who want to take their microphone OFF CAMERA (it can be mounted to the camera, but I can only think of a few small instances where you'd want to do that) and most importantly WANT A SAFETY TRACK.

SAFETY TRACK: Unless you need all 4 channels, the dual mode safety track is a life saver. Note that if you turn the volume up too loud in the monitoring headphones that the unit will shut down if you peak out the audio to protect the monitors ears. So, if you think peaking is at ALL a concern, keep the volume on the headphones down (not at level 10!). As for the feature, all it does is record a quieter version at the same time so that if you get mic distortion, you have a version of the same audio that has less or no distortion at all. For most cases, -6dB would be plenty of safety for just people talking. This really helped as I had this issue on my zoom recorder a few times and without using autogain (which introduced a LOT of hiss and weird ups and downs in the audio), it would ruin a take. Great for one-man crews and even those with inexperienced audio engineers. If you're interviewing people that are out of town or perhaps doing you a favor, you can't afford to lose an audio take over distorted audio so - this is a CHEAP solution.

Pre-amps: Very quiet, on high gain with near maximum knob-controlled gain, it's still nearly silent with only a hint of hiss which is pretty darn good for the amount of gain we're talking about. The only way to get much quieter is to use a hotter signal mic. Speaking of mics, I've used this with two RODE mics: the VMP and the Lavalier. Both need high gain because they are not terribly hot signals even with the +20dB setting. I'd imagine a NTG-3 or something wouldn't need high gain. Both of these mics produce VERY, VERY clean and clear signal with no hiss with the right settings however. I am not an audiophile but the audio from this recorder does sound cleaner and less colored vs my zoom h2n.

Size: Good size, smaller than a DSLR, slightly bigger than a mirrorless NEX camera. I'd like to find a carrying bag or case to give to a boom op, but for a one-man crew, it easily attaches to a light stand or something to connect to a stand-mounted mic. Weighs essentially nothing, yet has pretty much all the controls on the front - which is awesome because I don't like digging through menus (where was that setting again?) when I'm in a rush as I usually am with video. You can also mount something like a NEX 6 on top of this and put a shotgun mic on the shoe if you want. It's a little weird to hold, but I think I might use this setup a little bit when I don't have the luxury of a boom op or a good lapel mic. Interested to try a similar setup with a wireless lapel receiver.

Build-Quality: honestly, I don't know why other reviewers call it plasticy and flimsey. It is plastic, but it seems very sturdy to me. Maybe not good enough to throw off a stage, but easily going to survive a camera bag or whatever.

CONS: I do NOT like that it actually shuts off when the output to the headphones gets too loud. Yes, I appreciate it saving my hearing, but there's a better way than just turning off. I have not found official documentation on this issue, but I don't think it's a problem with my unit per se. I haven't tested since I updated the firmware. However, be aware that it CAN turn off if the levels peak really badly (usually when you change gain drastically) and you have the headphones set very high. I only experienced this problem with the headphones at like 9 or 10. I had no issues at lower volumes no matter how hard I tried to trip this protection. That said, test yours and become aware of this limitation before you head out to record something really important.

Biggest Surprise: I REALLY like that I can set the file name to a custom value. That's really helpful for me as I can sorta sync it close to what's on my cameras so it's a little easier to manage to audio+video tracks. Granted, it's not perfect, but it sure does beat random numbering and the ability to name it something that will remind me of WHO or WHAT I recorded, is GRRRREATTT!

AC ADAPTER: Tascam sells an ac adapter for this, but it's $20. Don't bother, it's an expensive cell phone charger and that's it. If you have a USB phone charger that you can plug a MINI USB cable (not the more common these days micro usb) into then you've got an AC adapter for this thing already. Actually, I use a 20ft long usb cable I bought on amazon with a wall wart for a smartphone. The tascam one is rated at 1.5amps but I believe it only needs 0.5amps (output listed on almost all chargers). You can use a usb adapter with MORE amps than necessary, just make sure you have enough (0.5amps=500mA fyi). A nice feature here is that when plugged into the AC adapter, if you remove the adapter it will seamlessly switch to battery power. So you have kind of a "fail over" battery backup. Not sure if that'll ever save my butt, but it's nice to know I can add additional levels of safety on those critical shoots.

Final Verdict: I still use Zoom recorders for cheap "wireless" lav mics and for more portable ways to mic something like a PA system when I don't have an aux cable. However, this has replaced the zooms for my primary recorder.
Summary: Dual track mode is worth it! (see note about AC adapter too)

I got this guitar as a "beater," or something I didn't care if I knocked around, that I could work with and enjoy and take to the camp, or plug in and play through the amp. I was hoping it would feel OK and sound OK, but my hopes were not high.

Maybe that's why I think this thing is darn near perfect. The sound is terrific. It has good tone, solid resonance and sounds great unplugged. Plugged in, it's so-so, but that's to be expected.

The feel, fit and finish are also terrific. Cheap guitars often have strings that are too far from the frets, or that hang on the higher frets. This one feels about right. The strings press down into the frets perfectly and it feels good in my hands, so much so that it has become my favorite guitar to pick up and fiddle on.

It comes with only one strap button and I wish it had another. I am a little scared to try to install one near the head of the guitar on the back of the neck connection point for fear of damaging this thing. That would break my heart. After owning it, I'd certainly be willing to pay more than this for another should that be necessary. It's worth double its cost (and I am cheap, so it could be worth triple its cost).

Pros
Great sound and capable of strong volume
Good fit and feel
Medium-thin body makes it easy to hold and play
Has a plug for amplified play
Holds its tuning well
INCREDIBLE value

Cons
Amplified play is a little so-so (most in this style are)
One strap button, not two. I hate tying string around the headstock.
Summary: Better than a "beater" guitar. Way better than an $80 guitar.

Text:
This is the perfect tool for small crew field recording needs and/or DSLR film work.

Let's say I need to record a piano, a singer, and a cello in one live take.

Vocal mic, straight into DR 60. Cello mic, straight into Dr 60. Stereo mic pair, running into a dual input preamp, sent out by a simple 1/8 stereo plug, into the 1/8 stereo input of the DR 60. and BAM, 4 channels, no syncing in post.

Then, run 1/8 stereo cable from the DR 60 into your DSLR, while you are filming said instrumentalists, and BAM, music video with no syncing in post!

Ok, so in terms of the actual performance of this unit. My biggest fear was the pre amp signal to noise ratio. I desperately did not want to have any hiss to contend with. The DR 40, when used with external shotgun mics, added an unacceptable level of hiss. So, since the DR 60 is a Tascam unit, I was concerened, But after buying it and testing it, I can assure you that the level of background hiss is as low as the ART dual pre, and almost as good as the Riggy Assist. In other words, the signal to noise issue with the DR 60, is not really an issue.

It sounds great. The Pre amps have really been upgraded and you can hear the difference.

The buttons and MILLIONS of features make this thing a complete joy to use. I am in love. It is also, tiny tiny. Like a little child's toy. Almost silly looking tiny.

It does have a plastic feel to it...like, "do not drop me" feel. So, don't drop it.

I am so happy I bought this thing.

btw, my background is, professional sound recording engineer/mixer/producer/music teacher/videographer, etc. also, professional cheapskate. so i like things that don't cost a billion dollars.
It took a sec for me to rig this the way I needed to use it, but this is actually a great little attachment, especially for the price.

Having upgraded from a Scarlett Solo I was fairly pleased with the setup here, in terms of size it's a bit bigger in every dimension but looks nearly the same. I personally never used the ProTools that you see included with the Scarlett products, so if you have no intentions of the same then this should do you fine. I found that it was detected perfectly on my MacBook for Garageband and Windows for testing in Audacity.

I use this for mostly instrumental inputs for guitars, which is why I wanted the two separate 1/4 inputs unlike my solo and the ability to change gain for either input is a huge benefit.

In terms of input sound, compared to my Moanocaster AU-AM100 and Scarlett Solo, I didn't notice a sound difference in a hiss test or after a sound recording (1/4 or XLR).

I did test the XLR inputs and phantom power with a few microphones and found no issues with the microphone picking up and adjusting the gain for clipping. On this particular unit, the knobs don't glow like other solo alternatives, but instead, you have two separate LEDs for CLIP and SIG which is where you'll make most of your adjustments.

Overall, if you need something basic as an alternative to the more expensive unit this is based on then I can recommend this for those looking for instrumental recording and/or streaming setups on a budget.
Summary: Good basic alternative to the Scarlett you may be used to

Text:
Overall this case is an awesome value.

With that being said, the Cons:
Assembly wasn't a cake walk, but it wasn't exactly difficult either. There are a few fit issues where enough wiggle room in the design could POTENTIALLY be an issue for some folks. However, with a little ingenuity and patients, it comes together rather nicely.
This case isn't going to survive a full-on World Tour. Based on the material thickness and joint attachments, I would imagine a fall from a moving vehicle would break it into pieces. So... if you are looking for a military grade crate for your gear, you will need to spend a lot more money.
The top (mixing board) compartment is a bit limited on size. Read the description and know the size of your board. I have the larger model of Yamaha rack mount mixer which is just a couple of rack spaces too large to fit. My smaller Peavey fits with room to spare.

The Pros:
The case wasn't a nightmare to put together. The instructions were fairly easy to follow. I would recommend a 2nd set of hand (I had my kid help me hold corners and the such) and a cordless drill. I was completely assemble the rack and load my gear into it in an hour (in no hurry).
Once assembled with gear installed the rack is pretty solid.
The front and back panels simply pop in and out with a fairly snug fit. The lid secures with a tight latch. Its is very easy to access all the gear quickly.

Bottom Line:
I use this rack to hold a small mixer, power conditioner, effects process, and a couple of EQs. I could EASILY fit a lot more gear into the bottom. My band uses powered speakers, so there isn't anything very heavy mounted in the rack.

Not a good experience with this. First off, this was going in a Yamaha Transacoustic, which has it's own built-in reverb & chorus. Much as I like those, I also wanted to have different reverbs & other effects at my disposal from the Tonewood. But it was very difficult to find a good place for the Tonewood's x-brace inside the guitar, since the Yamaha has an actuator inside that the x-brace's powerful magnet keeps being strongly drawn to. (On a normal acoustic you wouldn't have a huge piece of metal inside, so it wouldn't be a problem.)

Sonically, I was very disappointed in the Tonewood's effects. I got used to the naturalness of the Transacoustic's reverb; it's so organic that it becomes a *part of your sound & style* as you play, not a separate-sounding, sorta-delayed gimmicky effect like the Tonewood. The sound of the strings being picked or strummed was significantly louder than the effects, which swirled around inside the guitar body seconds after notes were played, like they're trapped in there. Trying to adjust the gain is useless; most of the effects cause squealing feedback at anything approaching a higher level, and I had to keep my pickup volume really low to avoid that. I didn't like any of the effects, despite adjusting the parameters considerably. Overdrive & auto-wah are unusable jokes; the delay doesn't have enough parameters to make it anything like a normal pedal delay, etc. I'd seen Youtube videos of the Tonewood sounding fairly decent in the hands of certain people with certain guitars, but they were often plugged in to an amp. It sure sounded like an artificial-sounding toy on my unamplified guitar. I'd seen the bad reviews prior to buying it, but I conveniently overlooked them because it's so unique & I *wanted* it to be great. It isn't.

My experience with the company wasn't good either. I bought directly from Tonewood to save some money with their coupon code, and ended up regretting it. They charged $5 for initial shipping - I was ok with that - but after I returned it, when the total amount of my purchase price was finally refunded (a week after they got it back, which had me concerned), they took out $10 total for shipping. So they not only didn't refund the original shipping, they charged me an extra $5 for no reason, with no explanation. Not only that, I had to pay $14 to return it! So they make a big deal about the 60-day money-back guarantee, BUT, they grill you hard about why you're returning it, and make it very difficult to find out exactly how to get an RMA on their site, and double your unrefundable shipping charge while making you pay for return shipping! I ended up paying $25 out of pocket just to try the thing for 1 day. Rip-off!

So if you're gonna buy it, buy it from Amazon so that you don't have to deal with Tonewood's costly, slow returns. Even better, don't waste your money and save the inevitable hassle. It sounds like a cheap toy, eats batteries like Rosie O'Donnell at a buffet, and is way overpriced. If you want natural-sounding reverb & chorus without an amp, get a Transacoustic; they did it right.
Summary: Don't waste your time or money

Text:
I've long been a glass slide player but I've been experimenting with tone recently and decided to see how I felt about metal slides after avoiding them for decades. These were a nice surprise - particularly the smallest length. I have large hands but can wear the smallest slide on my middle, ring, or small finger and play comfortably (I use all three depending on the texture of the music).

These aren't the chrome, shiny cheap metal slides we used to get in music stores. They're more of a brushed steel, almost pewter, finish that's fine ground enough to feel smooth, with just a touch of friction resistance, against the strings both horizontally and during any inadvertent vertical movement. I've played unbuffed "frosted" glass slides and don't necessarily mind some extraneous noise, but these steel slides are relatively quiet.

No need to sand or file the inside ridges, they're smooth and comfortable. And they're heavy - not as heavy as my large brass Dunlop, but comparable in weight and finish to my medium brass slide. Bottom Line: Happy with the purchase, an unexpected great deal.
Summary: Better than expected weight, feel, and fit

I've been playing 5-strings since the 60's and was looking at buying a new neck for my old frailing/clawhammer banjo. Necks are not cheap, so I thought I would give this Jameson a try to see whether the neck, pot or tailpiece are capable of upgrading my old banjo.

OK. So salvaging parts is not why most people buy this thing, so let's talk about the banjo as it stands. First of all, it sounds like an inexpensive banjo. I lay the blame for that primarily on the head. It's inferior to most good/great Remo heads and should be something to consider for upgrade as soon as possible. The headstock tuners are also something that I would consider replacing as soon as practicable. They don't hold position very well, allowing the banjo to cycle out of tune rather quickly. The 5th string tuner works very well and is geared, which is a real plus.

The neck was not parallel to the body of the banjo. This can be easily remedied by removing the small wood screw inside the pot, adjusting neck angle and redrilling the pilot hole for the screw. And, I'd use a larger American-made wood screw. The Chinese screw is brittle and likely to break, resulting in more problems.

The tailpiece is nice as well as the coordinator rod (which I wouldn't have expected at this price point). The tension hoop is a little flimsy. But, overall, I was favorably impressed with the amount of work and hardware that went into a 5-string for less than $200.

I'm certain this banjo can be made to play, but it will take some effort to get it there. As to the neck itself, there was quite a bit of fret sprout and 4 or 5 frets sat too high, requiring a fret job. All in all, the banjo doesn't meet my needs and I see quite a bit of frustration ahead for beginning banjo enthusiasts. There are a number of very good reviews of this product on Amazon, so I might have received one of the few bad ones. But, it was defective enough to return and work on purchasing parts for my upgrade.
Summary: Not the best bulb on the Christmas tree.

Obviously, you don't want your connector to determine your pedal order, as sound is the determining factor in all things pertaining to music. Way too much is being made of assembling these cables. They do not need to be stripped with a micrometer or even thought about. Cut the cable to length, clean and straight. Squeeze it round if you wish, but the connector barrel will do this for you. Shove the cable securely into the connector, bend it, put the cap on, next. stripping the sleeve on these could result in a much less secure and durable connection and NOT stripping them does not result in a short. I check cables with an inexpensive voltmeter for continuity and short, an old habit that has proven unnecessary with this product. I use them on a synthesizer rig full of effects pedals and have purchased longer lengths of the almost impossible to find 4mm cable from China. This system drastically reduces weight when compared to soldered Switchcraft and .255 or larger cable. Is this Mogami or Monster? I can't answer that because the resistance isn't published, but for short runs on stomp boxes or in rack effects and even on 10' for keyboards these are excellent for what they do - reduce clutter and weight. I used to have a forest of 1/4 straight jacks on top of my mixer. Switchcraft and other heavy right angle connectors, even the molded plastic ones, all fought for space. The footprint of these connectors is perfect. however if they were to offer these connectors for heavier cable I'd be all over them.
Another question was about whether these can be had for less, or as cable or connectors alone. Yes. BUT - by the time you add shipping to $1.87 each for the connectors you're right next door to this package with 10' of cable. And you get wait a couple of weeks.
Last thing - if anyone knows somewhere besides China or George l's $2.40 per foot!) for 4mm OD shielded cable, post a reply.

When you look at the Fender and Squire P-bass's you will see how low profile the input jack is. On the top is one of the nuts to hold it in place, but on the backside there is supposed to be an adjuster nut (identical to the one on top) that locks the jack fully to the pickguard so it cannot slide back and forth. This is the same thing for p-bass's that do not use pickguards, but are directly set in the drilled out hole on the top of the body.

Why does this matter? The nuts that are used for the pots and jacks are specialty. You can't just go to a home center and expect to find these. You have to get them through a place like Stewart MacDonald's, or another luthiery company.

It is unfortunate that the manufacturer of this jack failed to considered how this are typically mounted and it is mandatory that having the adjustment nut is vital for these to be held in place. Also note that these are SAE not metric so when ordering that extra nut you need to choose that.

Sure I "could" have just used a mess of flat washers, but that is NOT acceptable. If I buy something I do need it to be a direct drop in place item. That's how this is marketed.

Again this is NOT a complete drop in unit. You will have to have that adjustment for basses that use top mounted jack placement.
Summary: Does NOT come with secondary adjustment nut (needed for Fender/Squire P bass pickguards)

This was a great purchase for a wireless guitar setup. Only $40 w/ free prime shipping??? Oh yeah!!!

They arrived quickly, in perfect condition and were super easy to setup and use. I took them out, plugged them into a USB brick using the included Y charge cable, and let them charge for several hours. Unplugged them, slid on the power switches, tapped the pairing buttons, and viola - instant wireless guitar signal with zero latency and zero signal noise. (Transmitter = black / Receiver = silver)

First time charged and powered on, I jammed for a couple of hours with no issues whatsoever. In fact I've charged them only once more since then, and that was because I left the transmitter switched on one day and it ran the battery down. I figure they're good for around 3-4 hours total playtime per charge.

Since these are for my portable guitar rig (for traveling, jamming alone, etc. and not for on stage performance) the signal range, number of channels, and stuff like that was of no concern to me. The sole purpose of this rig for me is eliminating the need for a bulky 1/4" cable between my guitar and multi-fx unit. Mission accomplished !!! (see my review photo attached, and check out my YT channel - JM2C - for the entire portable rig)

Touring pros would never consider something like this, and for good reason. But for bedroom playing, jamming with friends, and band practice, these are an amazing value. I would even say they are "good enough" for live performance in many situations. But at that point, why not drop another $15 on the Getaria 5.8ghz setup for more range, more channels, and more piece-of-mind?

Highly recommended for a simple, cheap, functional wireless guitar setup.
Summary: Perfect for my portable guitar rig: simple, affordable, easy setup, zero latency, no noise

Has many features for a rather low price, but it is hard to know how to use all the features because the documentation is lacking.

The manual does not describe how to use all the mixer buttons, sends & returns; (seems like they assume you have been a sound engineer for a long time, or won't use all the features).

Behringer has not yet published the USB version of the Schematic drawing, but does have the non-USB version (nearly identical) on their website, to show how everything is internally connected with a simplified drawing. [Google search 1204FX_P0554_V3_YY.pdf ]

This mixer is also close to the Mackie Mixer, which explained some of the similar functions very well in their manual at: [Google 1202VLZ3_OM.pdf, or download at Mackie web site]

The effects are nice (they are programmable, I use weaker settings than the defaults for reverb & Chorus).

The main attraction for me of this mixer was the built in compressors, (one of my singers doesn't consistently move away from the mic for loud passages). However, the compressor sound wasn't pleasing when turned up very high. (So I ended up getting the FMR Audio RNC 1773 "REALLY NICE COMPRESSOR", which cost as much as the mixer). If you don't need all 4 mic inputs, you can patch the channels to run several Behringer compressors serially at low settings, which does sound nicer).

The Pre-amplifiers worked well with my sensitive Condenser mics (w/ 48V phantom), but my dynamic mic needed more gain and didn't sound as good (pre-amps seem to have more noise at maximum settings). So I use an external standalone pre-amp for mics needing more gain.

Some of the sliders/fadders and buttons have wiggle in them, but work well enough.

Since this has just one headphone output, I also got (and am happy with) the low cost Behringer HA400 Microamp 4 Channel Stereo Headphone Amp, with individual volume controls for each singer/musician.

All-in-all, you get a lot for the money. Similar units are made by Yamaha (also good value), and Mackie (sturdier but more expensive).
Summary: Schematics drawings helped (found here, not included in manual)

This cross platform audio interface is easy to set up and has all the basic features for a desktop home studio. Connectors on the front can connect 1/4 inputs (such as from a guitar) and XLR inputs (for a microphone). There is a jack and level control for headphones, and a direct monitoring switch. Outputs on the back are 1/4 inch, and the audio device is connected to the computer via USB-C. The included cable is USB-C to USB-A, with a USB-C adapter. The phantom power switch for powered microphones is located on the back as well. The case is made of metal with a matte red finish.

The built-in mic preamps are decent enough - noise free. Sound quality is a bit subjective, but to me it sounds fine - well within the bounds of price. It is a plug and play device that should work with most modern audio and music production software across different computer platforms. I tried it out with several tools on my Mac and it worked with them all. It is powered via USB, and draws enough power that it should be plugged directly into the computer, not through a USB hub. My only minor criticism is that I wish the monitoring LED’s were a bit larger - as it is, they are adequate. Overall, this interface works well as a budget option for a small home studio.

This guitar headphone amp with "effects" is not bad, but has several issues that keep it from being great.

It looks good. The fit and finish are nice. It is pretty much all plastic except for the jack, but that does keep the weight down. Having dropped it several times during testing, it seems to hold up well. It comes well packaged and includes a USB micro charging cord (no brick), a set of mediocre ear buds, a 1/8" trs to 1/4" trs cable and a soft velour type bag. It came with NO written instructions. Luckily the operation is pretty intuitive and straight forward.

While charging, there is a red light lit near the battery symbol on the top face of the unit. Once charged, the light goes out.

I tested this on 3 guitars and a bass. Two were acoustic, one with a passive pickup and one with an active pickup. The electric is a semi-hollow body with passive humbucker pickups. The bass is a P/J with active pickups. It worked similarly on all the instruments although the active pickups were definitely louder. I first tested using the provided ear buds, then a set of over the ears (decent not studio) headphones, then the direct out cable into a mixer and powered speakers. The unit performed similarly with all outputs tested. This unit does add noise to the signal which is not surprising since it is a mini preamp of sorts. How much noise is dependent on the settings used. It does have a volume slider, but, the output is so low that you pretty much have to leave it fully up to use it. The slider does work.

The "Clean" setting is relatively quiet and does render a good clean tone. Depending on what level you set the guitar knobs at, there is a bit of distortion when played hard. It can be eliminated by cutting back on the volume on the input. This is the case with all the "effects" presets. The clean setting is very usable.

The "Chorus" setting is horrible. It's very noisy (at least 3 times noisier than the other settings). The effect is not very present. There is more hiss and noise than chorus. Essentially unusable in my opinion and I am not holding this to a high standard. This is a headphone amp for quietly practicing. I would not be attempting to use the effects for anything else. The chorus setting is a bust.

The "Flanger" setting works and is not too noisy. It is however, very low output and seems to be more delay than flanger. There is a noticeable latency with this effect. It is however, a pleasing tone. Just not what most would consider a classic flanger. The flanger setting is very usable.

The "Metal" setting works well. Since it is a high gain distortion effect, the noise is not a factor. It was amusing to hear heavy distortion coming out of my acoustic guitars and even the semi-hollow body, but it definitely delivers a metal sound. The metal setting is very usable and probably the one with the highest output volume.

The "Wah" setting is actually a good effect. The rate of "wah" is preset and cannot be adjusted, but it is a pretty clean sound and sounded particularly interesting on the bass. There is a fair amount of noise with this effect. You can hear the whooshing of the effect when you are not playing. But, when you are playing it is not a bad effect at all. The wah setting is absolutely usable and probably one of the best effects on the unit so far as execution. It's a shame there is no way to adjust the tempo of the effect.

It has a Bluetooth input function as well. It allows the playing of music from a Bluetooth source like your phone or tablet while also playing along. This was easy to connect. Just go to your Bluetooth settings on your phone or tablet and look for "B6" and connect. The volume of the Bluetooth is controlled by the source (phone/tablet). The volume slider on the unit controls the volume of the instrument.

The bottom line is this; it works. It is not perfect. I have another similar unit of another brand (different effects) that works similarly for much more money. For the intended purpose of being able to listen to your guitar without plugging in to an amp, it does the job. The volume levels are all over the place from effect to effect and there is a good bit of noise generated by the unit. It works better with the over the ear headphones than the provided earbuds. Plugging it into my mixer and running it through powered speakers allows for a lot more volume adjustment but kind of defeats the purpose. The Bluetooth integration is simple and works. At the current price of $36.99, I can recommend it if you are in the market for this type of product.
