I've tried this as both my primary amp and personal monitor as a keyboardist in 3 different bands - a class hard rock band, an 80's cover band and a blues band. In all 3, power is short of what I really need. This unit failed as an effective monitor in the rock band and I was forced to return to using my 180 watt Roland KC-550 amp. In the other bands, when cranked it can usually keep up. Now, if the rest of the band was also using L1's, the sound of the whole band would have likely been much improved. The sound quality is truly lovely. But of course, the L1 and its more expensive cousins are practically prohibitively expensive for most musicians!

This being said, if you're playing in a full band in any of these genres, you're likely going to need the L1S or L2 to truly be satisfied, most especially if you play along with an electric guitarist. In my experience, electric guitarists are "bothered" by any sound other than their own happening in the same frequency range and will naturally want to turn themselves up even louder to compensate. You will not be able to compete or even stand toe to toe with a guitar amp with the L1 (except at wide angles), so inter-muscian discipline will be required to achieve proper balance. Good luck with that!

Bass response on the L1 compact is only down to 65Hz as well, insufficient for playing sub bass lines on the keys.

Power considerations aside, the rave reviews for sound quality are well deserved. The L1 is a 'mini line array' whose internal speakers are angled at offsets to provide a wide sound field. Sound is crystal clear, certainly far better at close range than any traditional amp I've heard.
Summary: Just short of the power I need.

When I first received these I realized they were made differently from similar humidity packs by Boveda but thought nothing of it and started them with my acoustic guitars. Several weeks later and I realize that they don’t seem to working, so I place on of them in a ziplock bag with a hygrometer. Several days later and the humidity in the bag hasn’t changed. The reading on the hygrometer was 26% RH.

It dawned on me that these humidity packs were bone dry and instead of maintaining the humidity of my guitars they were only sucking the humidity out of them! I removed all the packs and placed them in a large ziplock bag with a bowl of water and placed it in a warm place for a few days until the humidity packs were charged. They are now working but I had to hydrate them all myself.

Be careful with these because if they are not properly hydrated when you receive them they will draw moisture from your guitar even if your guitar is already too dry. To test them just place them in a ziplock bag with a hygrometer and the humidity in the bag should slowly increase to 49% RH give or take a few percent.

[[VIDEOID:mo19FD5VGUKGKGS]]The Blue Nessie is a joy to use, despite my very limited knowledge of audio recording. Compared to my PC's built-in webcam mic it's night and day. But what surprised me the most was how it smooth the recording was even in a room with screaming kids. It instinctively focused on the sounds in close proximity of the mic while filtering out background noise, breathing, or desk vibrations. I compared it to the audio from my [[ASIN:B003QKBVYK Zoom ZH1 Handy Portable Digital Recorder]] (see video) and while they both added fullness to my voice the Zoom's auto-gain sometimes went too hot and it picked up all of the background sounds (which may be useful if you're recording the background).

The design is also very attractive however despite all the chrome and metallic finish it is mostly plastic other than the weighted base. I don't see any problems with this since all the plastic is very strong and well made and it probably keeps the weight and price down, but it's worth mentioning. I have a couple of friends with the [[ASIN:B002VA464S Blue Microphones Yeti USB Microphone - Silver Edition]], and while it seems more versatile with it's multiple pick-up patterns, for single person recording I would choose the Nessie every time for it's drop dead simple capability to create clean audio. The mute button is touch sensitive and not a physical button, which is nice so that it won't pick up a click sound when you press/depress it. The headphone monitoring works well, but I found the output volume knob required a little bit more force than I would've liked, but since I don't adjust it during recording it doesn't cause any problems.

PROS:
+ Shock mount built-in
+ Pop filter built-in
+ 3 Modes Voice, Music, and Raw.
+ Pleasant LED ring indicates on (solid) and mute (flashing) modes

CONS:
- No recording software included or recommended for novices.
- Headphone volume requires two hands (one to anchor the mic) to operate.
Summary: The simplest most adaptive mic, even if it's not the most versatile.

This violin--to be honest is very cheap. Not just in cost but in quality.

BUT overall, not too horrible. Especially if you don't have an option on renting one, or if you don't mind buying one to have.

It isn't perfect, but there are some decent qualities about it. I'm very persnickety about instruments, my woodwind instruments cost well into and beyond thousands of dollars range, even my beginning ones.

This little guy, for what I want it for--learning the basics (fingering, bowing, proper care) is PERFECT for anyone.

Here are my notes about this violin:
1. The appearance of the violin is alright. It isn't anything special. In fact, it looks as if paper has been placed over the wood frame, and painted to look like it has groves, or actual wood designs.
2. The bow is acceptable, it works well enough for a beginner (young and old). It takes some effort getting the strands to be tight enough. I had to do a lot of pushing in and turning of the screw to get it to do its job. Once I had that settled and had enough rosin on it, it looked pretty great! And it even helped to produce a decent sound.
3. The tuning pegs are just awful! BUT how to prevent slipping:
-Remove pegs (untwist them, get the wire off.
-once the pegs are removed, rub them over the rosin. Make sure the cover the part of the peg that sticks into the violin with rosin. You will want the pegs to look white, or at least dusted white.
-Once pegs are covered with rosin, re-insert pegs/restring violin. PUSH THE PEGS IN ALMOST AS FAR AS THEY WILL GO!
**The rosin prevents slipping. The pegs are not in all the way to begin with, but with out the rosin, they will not stay pushed in.

After that is done, carefully tune the violin. YOUR VIOLIN WILL NOT STAY IN TUNE WITH NEW STRINGS! You will need to tune each string sharp, about a whole note sharp. With all strings (violin, guitar...) the tuning will slip for a while because those strings are not use to being 'pulled' and they will slip on their own.

Tune it sharp, let it sit. Retune it sharp, and let it sit again. Do this often the first day. This will help your violin stay in tune while you attempt to play it. the strings need to be stretched enough so they will not slip and become flat.

Most high quality stringed instruments don't need to be fussed with so much, but since this is not high quality, you will need to be patient and work with it longer before you can start.

Now, here are my final suggestions:

Do not buy this violin if you are serious about learning. Pay more money for one.

Do buy this if you 1. Can't rent one (no option to) and 2. If you have a beginner who is a little rough on things. If they like it, have them use this until they get a little less violent, or have them use it at school. Kids destroy their instruments at school, I can't tell you how many instruments I repair while working. You can buy a nicer one, but only allow them to play it at home, during lessons, and for 'chair challenges' at school. It will keep the nicer one safe, while allowing them to still learn how to play.

In the end, if you really don't like it, re-sell it or return it, or hang it up on your wall as decoration. They look awesome as a decoration.

This is not a marvelous instrument, but it is exceptable if you or a child want to get an understanding or feel for the instrument before spending more money. This instrument will do the job, but it isn't perfect. Make sure to take care of the pegs first, or you will hate this instrument!
Summary: Review done by a music teacher

The posts were a direct fit into the original bushings mounted in the guitar, and I was able to check the fit of the bridge on the original mounting holes confirmed that it was a good fit. After confirming this, I used the original mounting pins, a claw hammer, block of wood, and thick piece of leather to gently remove the original bushings. There was a bit of trepidation doing this, due to the risk of damaging the finish, and concern if the new bushings would drop into the old holes correctly. The old bushings popped out with no issues, and after some debate, I just pressed the new fittings into place with the hammer and the piece of leather covering the bushing to prevent dings or marring.

For the money, (A real 'Gibson' Tune-o-matic bridge will run you about $150.) you can't beat it. Perhaps the finish isn't perfect mirror quality, but for a players guitar it's perfect.

The mic customization settings are absolutely great. You've got a built in noise gate, full EQ band (for the full size version), compressor, and de-esser all ready for your tweaking. If you've never used a mixer before, the physical sliders are such a convenient way to quickly adjust your audio levels. The full size version's sliders are motorized, so whenever you mute or adjust levels in the software, they actually move to the desired position and back. It might not have any practical function, but it's nifty little addition.

I could go on and on about this thing. It has to be the best all in one audio device out there for the price. If you are interested, or do get one and need help setting it up, I recommend watching Harris Heller's (alpha gaming) setup tutorial on YouTube. When I heard about this device, I was intrigued by the fact that Korg is no stranger to me, so I assumed this device would be easy to pick, but it was not the case, Not sure if it is just me, but any attempt to get any decent sound out of this device, failed miserably. I can get great space sounds and noises; which would be perfect for a moody soundtrack probably; or for some sound effects in a videogame, but beside that, nothing much.

The touch strip is uncomfortable; I am used to real keys, and even if they are made of rubber, like some cheap hardware, they are fine, but those keys are nice but the keybed is too small, making quite hard for me to even use it.

On top of that, controls didn't make what I was expecting they would; changing parameters was erratic, and the output sound was mostly unusable for the applications I had in mind (electro-pop, techno and electro-rock).

In the end it is not a bad device; probably it is more aimed at experts with synths; which I am not. I can easily make patches on the Monologue, while I can't get the Volca Keys to do what I want.
If you can, give it a try first and see if its inner workings make sense, and if the sound is what you are looking for.

Text:
I purchased this for quick desktop recordings because setting up my Mackie 10 channel mixer takes a bit of time. I wanted something that sounds good but that I could just leave on my desktop for quick use. Also, I wanted it to be compact and have decent sound.

I did some test recordings with an acoustic guitar, an electric guitar and a condenser microphone. The sound is very clear and solid. The noise is pretty much nonexistent. The recording levels are great, with plenty of power. My system is Win 10 and I use Cakewalk as my DAW.

This unit is clearly built to be small, light and simple. I don't know how durable it will be but I don't think it's built for that. The layout is pretty logical for the small footprint. I normally like the mic, line and instrument jacks to be on the front but there is no room for that on this little box. Not a big deal.

My favorite feature is that they put a recording mix knob on it. Many other audio interfaces don't include this and it is SO handy to record with. If you don't know what that is, here's an example: When you're recording a track the mix knob lets you choose how much of your currently recording vocal or guitar, etc. you hear in the headphones vs how much of the previously recorded track. This makes it super easy to quickly record a track without fussing with your DAW settings.

One downside is that most of the power is up at the end of the input knob range. It works fine to dial it in just before clipping but you do need to tweak it a bit toward the top of the range.

Another slight downside is that the headphone amp isn't that powerful so you need to keep the volume pretty high.

All in all, this little audio interface does exactly what it says. Great sound in a compact package. Easy to set up and get started. Perfect for a small home studio!
Summary: Perfect for a Small Desktop Application!

Text: It is 30' but effective length is about 10-15'. If you are getting 15' out of 30' cable that means 15' is just sitting their sucking life from your tone. Do yourself a favour and A/B Bullet 30' cable with 10-15' regular good quality cable - eg. Planet Waves. You WILL hear the difference. Bullet would be OK if your amp was bright and you wanted to kill some highs but it is also HEAVY and producer made (IMHO) design mistake by not adding about 4' of straight segment of cable on both ends. That would have allowed the coiled part to just lay on the floor. Instead the whole thing dangle between and and guitar - all 1.6 pounds putting constant stress on input jack. If you go to floor pedal then that is one thing - no stress on input to pedal and on guitar end you can use slightly longer straight segment on right-angle end to plug into guitar and have less of the coiled part dangling in the air. I admit it is cool looking cable but not very well designed or useful if your instrument is not very bright.
Summary: Cool but: heavy, sucks tone and puts strain on jacks

Text:
This is a wonderful device.

Real simple, you plug your player into the 3.5mm female plug in the voicelive. Choose what type of harmony you want and the Voicelive does the rest of the work. There are many types of harmonies to choose from.

There is also vocal effects, some are really neat, but highly impractical.

The Microphone onput is XLR, you can use a regular microphone or one that needs phantom power. To use phantom power, you need to change a setting in the setup menu.

This device is limited in the way that it can be used. I will work well if you are a "one man show" and only ise backing trax like me, but it would be extremely difficult to use as a rack mounted device with live music and band, and it would be difficult to use in a recording setting.

This is how I use mine:

I have music coming from the computer via 3.5mm going to the input.
I have my microphone plugged into the XLR jack.
On the Voicelive, I have the 3.5mm headset jack going to my Bose Sound Dock 3.5mm in jack.
There is a microphone volume setting on the side of the Vocallive Play.
I control the volume of the music with the computer's volume buttons
I control the total mix volume with the volume buttons on the Bose.

Thing I wish were better:
I would really like the Voclive to run on batteries. I have a mixer (with phantom power) that runs on 2, 9 volt batteries and the Bose runs on batteries too. That way I would not need to look for an outlet.

I sing at churches and special church events, the ability not to need a extension cord is wonderful, especially when singing outside for Christmas, Easter, funerals and weddings.

Not having a battery extremely limits where I can use this device.

Good:
The Vocalive Play is extremely fun to practice with. It is a piece of equipment I wish I had purchased earlier.
Summary: This is a wonderful device. Real simple

Text:
I've been using a Seymour Duncan SA-6 Active Mag Mic run through a Fishman Loud Box Mini, to amplify my SeaGull S-6 for the past 5+ years. The sound quality was A+ great, I just didn't like having so many items attached to my guitar. When I found the K&K Pure Mini system on Amazon, I read review after review about how simple and amazing the K&K was (no batteries to change, nothing attached to the sound hole, amazing natural guitar sound & NO need for a $110-$200 K&K Pre Amp... All this for $110! Was I excited !Must Buy!!!

The instructions say to use super glue gel to attach the three dime sized mics to the underside of your bridge to achieve the best sound. No problem, since after reading ALL the very positive reviews on the K&K pickup system, there is NO way this is going back to Amazon!

Installation took about 45 minutes. It wasn't easy, but I did manage to get the mics glued into the proper location. Now...The moment of truth...
I plugged my 1/4' cable into my Loudbox Mini, turned on my amp and strummed some chords..... I wasn't liking what I was hearing at all. It was much too boomy and muddy sounding compared to the Seymour Duncan SA-6 I've been using for years. Feedback was also present, even at low volume levels! I tried adjusting the gain, volume, eq levels, chorus & reverb for about 15 minutes and nothing I did really helped. That's when I realized that I just made a $110.00 mistake...Damn!

Buyer Be Ware! DON"T glue in the mics until you're sure you like what you hear. Tape them in place. It may not sound as good as glued in mics, but it should give you a good enough idea of the sound.

It says "Free Returns" Yea right...try removing super glued mics off your guitar...not!
I could have spent another 1-2 hundred more dollars and tried using a K&K pre-amp to see if that "might" give me the sound I'm looking for??? Nope! Time to cut my losses right here!
I cut the wires leading to the 3 K&K mics & re-installed my Seymour Duncan back on my guitar, along with the battery...etc.

For me...Sound trumps convenience every time when it come to guitars!

I'm not sure when these strap locks first hit the market, but the great Ritchie Blackmore is the first I know of to sink a set of Dunlop strap locks into the body of his guitars. It's something I discovered while constructing a strat like Blackmore's to play in a Deep Purple tribute band. The guitar feels much more "snug" as a result... and it is.

These strap locks place the weight of the guitar firmly inside the body. You don't have the leverage created by a half-inch peg sticking out, which puts a lot of stress on the screw. Text:
I played trombone in high school and wanted to pick it back up as a hobby. Marching, Jazz, Pep, and Concert. I just needed a starter trombone for some scales and simple songs so I could evaluate whether I should invest in a full instrument again. This is perfect for that, and I think it's actually great for anyone who wants to learn trombone at home - not just kids! I'm not sure I ever really need the brass anymore, until I want to get a trigger trombone again - and even then, a competitor makes a trigger version of the pBone!

Pros:

It's a real trombone. So many people try to talk down the pBone as though it's a toy, but this is a true plastic trombone. It sets up and handles almost identical to a real trombone. A professional could play this just like a regular brass trombone. Someone who goes to rough gigs, like ska bands, may want to consider a pBone so they don't have to lug brass around.

Full-featured. Has everything from a real mouthpiece port if you want to use brass mouthpieces, to a spit valve, to a slide lock. The only feature this trombone is missing is that the point between the bell and slide if friction-fit, which I'll cover below. But for the most part, again, this is a real trombone.

Lightweight. I wish I could go back in time and give one of these to myself when I was marching. It's so light and easy to handle, it's great.

Attractive colors. I got the purple one, and it's a gorgeous deep color. It's high-quality plastic.

Great sound. Sure a brass trombone will "ring" better than plastic, but unless you're playing Beethoven in a quiet concert hall, you probably won't notice. For practicing or playing in a small club, this trombone will suit anyone. The sound is absolutely fine for tuning and improving form.

Damage resistant. I know it sounds silly to say that plastic resists damage better than brass, but consider what happens if you ever do really whack the slide so it starts to stick or becomes unusable. With brass, you could be in a situation where you need to go into a repair shop and pay a specialist to gently heat and bend the metal into shape. That could be expensive, or even require new brass at great expense. With the pBone, either the plastic will bounce, or if it cracks and you buy another one. Buying a new pBone is likely still cheaper than repairing a trombone. Heck - buy two! You could go through quite a few pBones before adding up to the price of one brass trombone.

Cons:

Small hands warning. The major downside is that the major joint between the slide and the bell is friction-fit. This means you're using your thumb around the bell's cross bar to hold the instrument together. This is the natural position used to hold a trombone, but anyone with especially small hands or a weak thumb could have trouble holding the two together. If you have trouble wrapping your thumb around the cross member when holding a trombone, you'll need to consider some other way to help reinforce this joint. They really should fix this and just make a tab to fix the bell at a specific angle. I'd rather have the trombone fixed at 90 degrees, than have to baby it. I'm sure you could use something simple like a rubber band to assist a small child if their hands are truly too small for the hold. You could easily glue this joint permanently if you intend to keep the trombone on a stand anyway, although you'll lose the ability to store it in a gig bag.

Out of the box the pBone slide really is scratchy and a bit slow. This is fine for anyone new to the instrument, as it's quite tricky to maintain a brass slide for a newcomer anyway. I'd say the slide feels no worse than my first trombone did before I learned to maintain the slide. The manufacturer says the slide will wear in with just spit and time. I'll probably add a dab of cream to assist the process, but for practicing scales and simple songs this is perfectly fine as-is.

Neutral:

The slide has a lock and a pinky lug so during play you should wrap your little finger around the lug to hold the slide in place. I'm used to the older style where the slide's first cross bar is higher so you held the cross bar with your little finger. Adjusting to the lug is weird but I'll learn.

Overall:

I love my pBone so much I don't really need a brass trombone anymore. The pBone is plenty for practice, basement jams, and even gigs. The only reason you'd ever need to upgrade is if you need special features (trigger), or if you play concert halls. Parents of children who may someday compete in concert should still consider the pBone. Not only is it better for learning (lighter, inexpensive if you change instruments) but a child should be more comfortable playing without worry that they'll damage an expensive instrument.

I held down the fog control and completely and totally fogged out my garage to the point that I could barely see the red light on the remote feet from my face in one cycle burst of 8-10 seconds!!! MUCH more volume and thickness than my old 400 watt machines!

I left the unit in the garage floor for a few days and when I went to use it on Halloween, I was surprised to see just how much fluid had leaked from the front. I was careful to lift the unit as straight up as possible, but when I did, twice as much fluid poured out of the bottom of the unit. It stopped leaking, but literally dumped 1/4 of the tank on the floor!!!! And yes, it stained the concrete. I moved the unit to the front yard and placed a length of drainage pipe in front of the output to spread the fog through a grave yard scene. It worked extremely well. I used an American DJ remote set for long bursts quickly. The unit ran smoothly and put out a ton of fog for about 5 hours, and only used half of the remaining fluid in the tank. I did notice a little bit of fluid leakage out the back of the machine during it's run time.

So, for an outside unit, or maybe hidden for an effect, this unit fogged great and the price was great. However, this is one of the few cheaper units that have a mounting bracket for a lighting rig, which is what I really bought it for. There is NO POSSIBLE WAY I could hang this unit from a DJ lighting rig! There would be a puddle in no time, and possible damage to other equipment. I guess I'll try and fill the unit half way and see if it still leaks, if not, it could possibly be mounted. If not, it gets saved for Halloween only, and that is a shame!!!

Text:
How much do you expect to get for $30? I think that this is a pretty decent stand for the price.

The collars that join the telescoping sections are made out of plastic but have a metal nut embedded in each of them for greater strength. Still I would be cautious to avoid over tightening, especially while in storage. Each collar is equipped with a cotter pin on a cable tether - nice.

The stand has 3 telescoping sections: 1 1/8 diameter, 1" diameter, 7/8" (Good to know if you plan to use and "O" clamp on the shaft. )

The crossbar has a square cross section. The 8 mounting points might be a bit of an exaggeration as each is only 4 1/2 " apart. This may make it impractical to use every mounting point unless you have very narrow fixtures.
UNLESS
You can alternate the mounting bolts to have every other one up or down, and mount half of your fixtures above the cross bar. You also have a 9th mounting bolt in the center top.

Stability:
At maximum spread, the legs form an equilateral triangle 3 feet (or 36") on each side. The crossbar is just under 40" wide. If you stay within the 50lb weight limit, you should be fine. Motorized lights would be best kept as centered as possible. I doubt that fixtures with moving mirrors (Derby etc...), would cause a stability problem. Spider lights would also probably be OK as they do not throw a lot of mass from side to side - UNLESS you have a spinning head type Spider light. (I would not recommend mounting a heavy moving head light on the crossbar - let's face it, if you are going to spend that much on a fixture, why not get a sturdier stand?) The more mass you are swinging around, the more likely that you are to set up a resonance and tip the stand. This would be especially true in a rhythmic, sound active mode.

End caps:
Each of the three legs is capped with a cheap plastic cap. Two of mine fell off in shipment, or while unpacking. While not a big deal you should plan on gluing them in place, or replacing them with something better. Scratching your, or someone else's floor would not be good.

Summary - Excellent, inexpensive stand for PAR Cans, fixed lights, and minimally motorized lights (moving mirror types). You might get away with mounting a single moving head light, low down on the center shaft, close to the legs.

Text: Great Strap

The Line 6 HX Stomp ("HXS") is my entry to high-end guitar modeling, and after a few weeks of use, it has prove to be an excellent product. I will try to go over some of the major features, as well as the key pros and cons, while trying to avoid making this review excessively long. But I want to go into some detail, since the HXS is an extremely deep and versatile unit that can be as complex or straightforward as you want to make it.

OVERVIEW:
The HXS basically the entire Helix modeling software shrunk down to the size of a dual-footswitch effects pedal (like a Strymon, or two BOSS pedals side-by-side). Debuting a street price of $599.99, this represented the most affordable entry point for a high-end modeler at the time of release, though the Headrush Gigboard is arguably a comparable product announced only four days earlier! Modelers like the Helix and Helix LT had typically costed $1,000 to $1,500 in price, and were significantly larger in size. Since my primary interest was in gaining access to the Helix amp models in an affordable, portable package, the HXS was of immediate interest to me.

HARDWARE:
The HXS is a sturdy unit that uses a clever combination of three touch-capacitive footswitches, a relatively small LED screen, and just a few more buttons and encoder knobs to access all of its features. The enclosure is painted in a glossy black sparkle finish, which is a fingerprint magnet, but I actually like quite a bit. There are stereo inputs on the top of the unit, balanced/unbalanced stereo outputs, the jack for the 9V, 3.0A proprietary power block (included), and a USB "printer" cable port. On the left side are a headphone output and in/out DIN MIDI ports for external control of the unit. Finally, the right side has jacks for a stereo FX loop, though this can be reconfigured to work as an "AUX IN" jack for playing along to external gear.

Overall, I find the unit to be very well-built. Footswitch longevity has been a concern on past Line 6 units (like the M5), but these "soft press" switches are different and feel built to last. Some of the encoders have a little bit of wobble to them, but should hold up with care. I would definitely work out some type of case to protect the unit - I am using an Apache 2800 hardshell camera case with foam cutouts for the HXS and power adapter.

AMP & CABINET MODELS:
In Helix, Line 6 uses what is called "component-level" modeling to create virtual models of real-life amplifiers by taking them apart and capturing what each physical component of the amp is doing. In theory, this means that you get the same control knob and switches available on the real-life amp, and they should behave in almost the same way. I found the HXS amp models to be largely excellent, though I strongly recommend setting up your own presets from scratch, as this will accommodate your tastes and the power amp, mixer, or headphone output particular to your setup.

The Helix library of amps is already dozens large with great guitar and bass options, and you can visit the Line 6 website for details on that ever-expanding list. While primitive modelers were favored by high-gain players, I tend to prefer the classics - sparkly Fender cleans, chimey Vox tones, and the bluesy crunch of vintage Marshalls. All are well represented here, and the "Placater" model of a Friedman BE100 is an immediate standout for driven rock tones.

Since the HXS functions either as a multi-FX unit (into a guitar amp's front end) or a direct box (into either a mixer, a flat-EQ power amp, or monitored by headphones), it includes endless cabinet simulation options to handle the "direct" option. The HXS has an IR loader that accepts third-party impulse responses in the proper format. However, I've been favoring the built-in cabinet simulations recently, as these give you more flexibility with microphone selection and placement.

An important tip about both cabs and IR's is warranted here. Guitar amps have a much narrower frequency range than a full-range studio monitor, with most guitar frequencies falling between 100Hz and 6400Hz (or, arguably, an even narrower range). But the Helix is capable of putting out a full frequency range, which means that some of the sounds will be either "boomy" (low end) or "fizzy" (high end) unless you apply low and high cuts on the cabinet or IR to match that range. Experiment with different settings and see if that cures any unpleasantness with your setup.

EFFECTS:
In addition to having great amp and cabinet models, the HX Stomp offers a full suite of effects options, ranging from overdrive/distortion to delay, modulation, reverb, compression, EQ, and even some off-the-wall options like pitch shifters and synth/note generators. There is also a noise gate built into the input slot of the effects chain, so you do not need to add a separate noise gate block.

I won't even try to go through the merits of the various effects, as there are dozens. But I think there are two key takeaways regarding the Helix effects. First, they are crafted with the same "component-level" approach as the amp models, so they really are meant to interface, behave, and interact with other gear in the way the real-life versions do. One of the reasons I wanted the HX Stomp was that I had been obsessed with guitar pedals and acquired way too many of them. I have found the models on the Stomp to be good enough that I was happy to sell over half of my pedal collection. Not only do I not feel like I am "missing out" by using the Helix version of these effects, but I truthfully have far more options having added the depth of the Helix library. There are effects in Helix that are either so niche I would never buy a dedicated pedal for them, or would cost in excess of $200, each, if I did.

Second, even if the HX Stomp effects are not always 100% as good as the source material, they still benefit from being assembled together in a cohesive ecosystem that allows you to do things that are expensive and complicated to do with a traditional pedalboard. The most obvious of these is powering all of these effects - you don't need to worry about dealing with different voltages and power supplies, as everything is done through the Stomp. But there is also effects switching and chaining - this can be done conveniently through presets and snapshots that change not just the on/off status of the effect, but individual effect parameters. Time synchronization is also a major advantage of a multi-FX approach. I can run two parallel delays or simply time-sync everything to a specific BPM setting using the tap tempo footswitch. After some initial time to learn how everything goes together, I think you'll find that advantages of this type of setup greatly outweigh the feeling of missing out on a few specific sounds from your pedals.

Of course, it doesn't have to be either/or. You can run pedals into the front of the HXS, or set up an effects loop that you move around to anywhere in the signal chain you want.

DRAWBACKS:
Having largely gushed about the HX Stomp, I should point out at least a few items that might be of concern for some users, and some software items that may benefit from additional tweaking to the (still-new) firmware for the HXS. The number one complaint, by far, about the HX Stomp, is that you are only limited to 6 blocks. This is due both the layout of the HXS, as well as its limits in processing power compared to its larger brothers. To be fair, I would basically never use 6 effect pedals at one time in anything I am doing. But if you running direct or otherwise using the amp and cab simulations, you have to account for 1 or 2 of those blocks occupied for that, plus reverb, compression, EQ, and other effects that you might want to use on virtually every patch. I don't find the 6 blocks to inhibit much of what I do, but if you are hoping to use a stereo setup, then you can run out of options fairly quickly.

The one other caveat that I would point out regarding HX Stomp and Helix and general is that it is NOT a plug-and-play solution for anything. You need to have a specific setups for headphone, running into an amp, running into a PA, etc., or the results can be pretty bad. I'm sure that the default presets sounded great with the gear of whoever created them, but I found them to be largely unusable, as modeling presets generally are. You need to start from scratch with your patches, don't afraid to experiment, and then avoid the "paralysis of choice" that comes from obsessive tweaking and the feeling that you can always make things "just a little better". I found that running the amp models (without cab simulation) into a power amp was pretty quick to get good results, but there was a huge learning curve for setting up direct guitar sounds due to the sheer number of variables (cabinet/IR type, mic placement, hi/low cuts, volume/gain settings). The good news is that if there is some way you want your tone to be shaped, there is almost certain to be way to do it with all of the amp, effects, and output options offered by HXS.

Many people have complained that the stomp only has three footswitches, and it is actually only TWO if you leave the third one as a tuner/tap tempo. I thought this would be a major annoyance for me, but it really hasn't been. Snapshots give you massive flexibility to change several effects at once, so you can think of it as having three "presets within a preset". And footswitches can be assigned to bypass multiple effects at once, so maybe your "lead" switch turns on a boost, activates a compressor, and adds some delay, all with one press. You can also expand to two additional (momentary) footswitches, two expression pedals, or one of each, if desired.

I should also note that there have been anecdotal reports of freezing, volume drop, and (very rarely) hardware/software failure on message boards I have been active in discussing this product. Many of these complaints may have already been troubleshooted as of the release of the v2.71 firmware. Others appear to be extremely anecdotal, and as a policy, I try to base my reviews only on the positive and negative experiences I have had with the device on a firsthand basis. My HX Stomp, thus far, seems to be well-built and has performed without incident thus far. I would amend my review in the future if that ever changed, of course.

SUMMARY:
At a street price of $599.99, the HX Stomp opens up the world of component-level amp and effects modeling to a whole new subset of guitar enthusiasts. While it is still one of the more expensive single items of guitar gear I have ever purchased, it arguably replaces and improves upon thousands of dollars of gear that I previously owned or would need to purchase in order to be able to do what I can now do from the convenience of a single, compact box. You are not required to like every amp and effect offered by the HXS - I certainly do not. But only a few weeks in, I've quickly identified some go-to amps and effect chains that are as good as anything I had created with analog hardware in the past. The amps are amazingly touch-sensitive and varied in what they offer. And the convenience of being able to plug a guitar, bass, or keyboard into a single box that serves as my iOS recording interface, amp/cabinet sim, and multi-FX platform is truly amazing.

UPDATE (02/21/19) - Glad to see my (absurdly lengthy) review was helpful! As I have had more time to use and learn the HX Stomp, my appreciation for it has continued to grow. It has effectively replaced all of the other ways I used to play guitar. I sold my largest amp, sold dozens of pedals, and with just my HX Stomp plugged into either headphones (Beyerdynamic DT880) or a FRFR speaker (Alto TS312), it seems like I have infinite tonal possibilities. The Yamaha/Line 6 development team and surrounding Facebook/online community is also incredibly helpful, knowledgeable and fun. I had zero affinity for Line 6 products prior to this purchase, and openly despised the brand because of some of their budget modeling products in the early 2000's (Spider amps, red POD, etc.). The acquisition by Yamaha and continued development of Helix has truly made Line 6 into a top-flight brand for component level modeling. The HX Stomp makes my playing more rewarding, and the only problem now is finding more time to play!

UPDATE (10/17/22): It's been over 3 years and a global pandemic since my last update, but the HX Stomp remains the focal point of everything I do with guitar, and I have no interest in "replacing" it. Line 6 has continued to support all Helix devices, and several of the updates since 3.0 have added significant features. I find that York Audio IR's greatly improved my experiences with the amp models, and I am STILL learning tricks and workarounds to improve the overall quality of tones. But my patch-building is pretty straightforward and I've found that it does play well with pedals if you set it to auto-impedance and keep your compression block after the amp block (like a rack effect). No, it didn't "end" all other gear purchases, but it significantly reduced them, and also just gave me much better success with whatever sounds I was going for.
Summary: Lowering the bar for entry on affordability and portability for high-end, component-level modeling

Text:
I have always used Korg products- tuners and metronomes and swear by them.
I have had an ancient Korg Chromatic Tuner (see photos) that I've had through my time at my music conservatory and well beyond. This dinosaur of a tuner has been banged, dropped, scratched, scraped and STILL works perfectly.

However, this updated Korg Tuner has brought me out of the Mesozoic era of tuners and into the 21st century. At more than half the size (weight, thickness, etc), it is far more portable. The addition of the metronome is fantastic and I love that I can subdivide the beat into triplets, 8ths, 16ths, 32nds, etc for those tricky rhythmic patterns. The tap button feature really works when I'm listening to a recording and there are no tempo markings on my music, I just tap the red button to the beat of the music and it tells me how fast they're playing.

The other fantastic feature of this is that you can use it as a recording device. I've always used self- record practice as a way of self-evaluation for tone, rhythm, intonation, musicality, etc. as it's difficult to do that objectively when behind the instrument. The volume playback is not very loud at all but there is an input (I haven't tried to put an external mic on it to see if that would improve the recording). There is also a headphone jack.

I purchased the additional attachment cord that can attach to your instrument (in my case my bass bridge) which has helped me tune more quickly and efficiently especially in a large rehearsal room where everyone is playing and you can't really hear your own instrument clearly.
Summary: Best Korg Tuner/Metronome/ Recorder - 3 Practice Tools in One!

Text:
I bought the 100W version rather than the 40W version as a home practice amp, as the 40W has garnered less than stellar ratings for sound quality.

First, the good...the control set up and LCD screen work very well and intuitively. There was really no learning curve, and it allows you to control many aspects of the modeling. It has many amp models built in, probably over a dozen, plus dozens of pedal emulations. It has 150 built in presets that are pretty self explanatory, including a set of basic presets for each amp model emulation. Bluetooth and wifi both worked very well, and the unit updated without a hitch. I thought the app was intuitive and easy, and has even more presets to download. Backing tracks played effortlessly through the unit. There were at first a number of poor reviews based on connectivity problems, but it seems fender has resolved them through firmware upgrades.

As to the bad, the sound quality is adequate, not great, which is disappointing given the 12" celestion speaker. The sound is muffled at lower volumes but better when volume is about halfway up, which is quite loud. I found I could help the tone at low volumes by turning the volume halfway up and reducing the guitar volume to a very minimal setting. Some of the amp emulations (like the 57 Champ) sound like an emulation of the speaker embedded in bulletproof glass in the subway. I have several of the tube amplifiers which this unit emulates, and the tube amps sound livelier, no question.

IMHO, there are too many presets...I think it would be better if Fender was more discriminating about the presets out of the box. The amp invites fiddling around with it, so if you don't want to do that, you should buy a traditional amp.

Overall, I will probably keep it. The functionality and wireless capability provide a lot of usefulness. I also considered the Boss Katana 50, which garners better reviews for sound quality, but it is not bluetooth or app enabled, and lacks the LCD screen.

Update: I replaced the speaker with an eminence Swamp Thang. Changed the amp entirely. Sounds great now.
Summary: great functionality but sound quality could be better

Text: Once you try flatwounds you will never want to go back to roundwounds.  They feel SO good under your fingers and you get rid of finger squeak.  I use them on ALL my guitars, electric or acoustic.  They give any acoustic guitar a bit warmer sound than bronze roundwounds which are almost the universal acoustic guitar standard.  I like the flatwound sound better and the feeling under your fingers is incomparable.  Add some Finger-ease spray lubricant and your fingers glide effortlessly over the strings with absolutely no finger squeak.  All the Chromes gauges are great, I personally use 11's on my electric guitars and 12's on my acoustics.  I may use other brands (LOVE Thomastic-Infeld) but I will simply never again play roundwound strings.  Flatwounds do cost more but you get much longer string life because your finger oils and other gunk does not get into the windings to degrade the strings the way it eill with roundwounds.  Even coated strings wear out sooner than flatwounds and you get the nasty shreds of coating as it begins to peel off with use.  As I said in the headline, dat's dat.  Never will I use roundwound strings again.  Flatwounds just rule and are addictive both in feeling and sound.
Summary: Once you go flat, dat's dat

I've tried a few of these momentary pedals, including Boss FS-5U (switchable), Hosa FSC-502 (normally open/off) and Roland DP-2 (normally closed/on). The Boss is the best, but it's also the most expensive, and doesn't come with a built-in cable. This pedal is designed a little differently than the Boss pedal, but it shares a feature with the Boss pedal that the Hosa and Roland pedals don't: an external switch that allows you to go from "normally open/off" mode to "normally closed/on," so this single pedal will work with pretty much any piece of equipment/feature that requires a momentary pedal. It's quiet; the construction is very heavy duty ... steel bottom and top, with thick rubber non-skid material on both; it comes with a built-in cable, all at about half the cost of the Boss pedal. At this price, nothing else I've tried even comes close. Very pleased.

[After reading a few older reviews, I came across one that explained the remarkable cost difference between this pedal and the Boss FS-5U ... the "guts" of this switch are FAR more rudimentary and prone to glitch/failure than the Boss design (M-Audio switch is activated by two bare internal wires being pushed into contact when you press the pedal). The Boss switch relies on a more sophisticated mini-button momentary switch mounted on an internal circuit board, so I still favor the Boss switch in terms of quality/reliability, but this one DID consistently work for my application, right out of the box. Buyers should also note that the manufacturer seems to have responded to older complaints about the rubber pads coming off/loose by changing to pads with little spikes on their bottoms that stick through corresponding holes in the metal case, to hold the pads more permanently/securely in place. So, still a great value, as long as you're aware of its limitations/potential shortcomings, and the more rudimentary design works for your application. My five star rating still stands.]
Summary: Best I've seen/tried for the price.

Just so you know where I am coming from, I replaced a cheapo, $13 Neweer microphone boom with this one. I have been wanting a Rode PS1 (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B001D7UYBO), or a Blue Compass (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B078MLBGRM) microphone boom but they were priced a little more than I wanted to spend. I figured they were all about the same, so I bought the cheapo Neweer (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00DFUEZZI), which turned out to be much like all the others I had ever used. They did their jobs fine.

Then recently I saw this one for $60 that looked a lot like the Rode but was half the price, so I bought it and MAN am I glad I did. I didn't really know just how lightweight and crappy the Neweer was until I unboxed this one. You can see the difference in size in the picture I included with this review. The Neweer is much smaller and the extra range that this Innogear has is so nice. I also like the fact that the springs are internal and somehow sound dampened when they move so it doesn't make that "sproing kriiiing" sound that the cheaper one makes when you move it. This one moves silently.

It is a bit stiffer than the Neweer, but I like that; though I presume I could adjust it with a phillips screwdriver if I wanted... Checking: Nope, the stiffness isn't really adjustable, so that may be an issue for some people, but I quite like it.

The one thing that I would ding it for is that the table clamp base is made of plastic instead of cast metal like the Neweer is. So far it seems sturdy enough and isn't worth a whole star so I'm leaving the review at five stars, but if they were to make it with a steel or cast aluminum base with a nylon insert to make pivoting smooth, then I'd be a little happier.

Overall it's a superb microphone boom arm and you definitely cannot complain for the price. I haven't directly compared it to the Rode PSA1 or Blue Compass, because I haven't gotten my hands on either of those, but I can't imagine a better boom arm than this one, especially after having used the Neweer and other cheapies in the same class, for years.
Summary: This is an AWESOME mic boom arm.

I was on the fence about whether to choose this unit or the comparable Boss TU-3 unit. They're both the same price, and both get good reviews. I finally decided to go with this unit because it's a newer design and offered both conventional and "strobe" style tuning. The latter appealed to me because I have been using a Peterson Strobo-Clip tuner for some years, and really like the strobe tuning method. I decided I wanted a stomp-box tuner so that I could mute the sound and do quick tune-ups more conveniently than the clip-on tuner permits.

I play electric bass. I found that the conventional tuning mode on this Polytune 3 pedal was just fine for my needs, and I have not yet even tried the strobe version. It also revealed that I need to touch up the intonation on my jazz bass -- playing various notes up and down the fretboard showed some deviation from the correct tuning. All the more reason not to need the micro-precise tuning of the "strobe" style display.

When I say "conventional" tuning display, I mean a display that shows a needle that is positioned to the left of center if the tuning is flat, or to the riht of center if the tuning is sharp, and dead center when the tuning is correct. Some tuners have arrowheads on either side of center that light up when you are not quite at the correct tune. With this unit, the needle itself changes color, displaying as red when the note is sharp or flat, and green when it is correct. It is very quick to go through the four strings of my bass and tweak it for the needle to be green.

This is a chromatic tuner, meaning it listens for the incoming note and displays what it thinks the note is. That works fine for me. It is only necessary to know that the standard 4-string bass tuning is E A D G. There are handheld (not stompbox) tuners, like the Boss TU-12, that have fixed presets for tuning a guitar or bass, but that is not generally available on a stompbox.

The Polytune 3 has a "soft" pushbutton that puts it in and out of tuning mode. By "soft" I mean that there is no mechanical ka-chunk as the sawtich is operated. When the unit is tuning, the output is muted. When tuning is finished (by pressing the switch a second time), the output is connected again.

There are three modes available, which are selected by internal DIP switches. The first mode provides "true bypass" switching when the tuner is turned on and off, which means that when it is not tuning, there is a direct connection from the input jack to the output jack. The second mode provides "buffered bypass," which means that the incoming signal passes through a "buffer" amplifier when not tuning. (This can be advantageous in a number of situation, especially if long cables are being used.) In both of these first two modes, the tuning display lights up only when the tuner is active and the output is muted. In other words, you can immediately tell whether you are muted or not by looking to see whteher the tuning display is lit up. The third mode is also buffered, but the tuning display remains active all the time. Thus, in theory, you can watch your tuning as you play. I have only used this unit in the second mode (buffered bypass, display on only when tuning) because that best suits my needs.

There are many features which I may never use. For example, while the factory setting is A=440 Hz, it is possible to adjust this reference. Also, the unit is advertised as allowing the user to play all the notes on the instrument at once, whereupon it claims to be able to sort out which of the notes are off. I don't see any particular benefit to this for the bass, and I have read that users do not believe the tuning accuracy is quite as good in this "polyphonic" mode. Frankly, it doesn't take very long to tune 4 strings individually, and that's what I do. Since my bass keeps tune pretty well, it only requires minor tweaking to deal with room temperature change, etc. This takes no more than a minute at most.

All in all, I'm very happy with my choice of the Polytune 3. It's very easy to use, has quite a readable display, and makes keeping in tune during a show very simple. I suspect the competitive units out there (like the Boss TU-3 or the Korg Pitchblack) are also fine, which may make the choice more difficult in this category. All I can say is that I think people would be happy with this well-made unit, so hopefully that will help with the decision.

This is a phenomenal kit that makes the awesomeness of custom made pedal cables accessible to anyone.

The is a reason why custom made cables are preferred for a pedal board. Depending on your pedals and layout the perfect amount of cable between pedals and the orientation of the jack is rarely the same. this kit gives you the flexibility to achieve that perfect layout without having to go to all the work of buying the cable and jacks and then stripping and soldering the connections. It additionally gives you all the tools you need to get the project complete including the wire cutter and screwdriver needed.

Some thoughts on the kit itself.
* Wire cutter. Worked surprisingly well. Built like a cigar clipper the cut that I get out of it was a LOT cleaner than the one I got from using my wire snips, something I totally did not expect. Awesome.
* Screwdriver. The weakest part of the kit as it is pretty cheap and a bit undersized for the screw heads. No biggie as I have a ton of screwdrivers around the house and another fit perfectly.
* Cable. On par with other cables I've gotten in the Planet Waves line.
* Jacks. Very solid and obviously all L-shaped.
* Adjustable. After putting together my first cable realized I had the orientation of the jacks misaligned. Loosen the screw rotate and retighten and everything was ready to go.
Durability. Well a pedal board isn't generally something that is torn down after every gig but the should last as long as you aren't constantly pulling on the cable.

Other thoughts: I hope that Planet Waves releases some straight jacks as some of my pedals would be better off with those over L-shaped jacks.

Summary:
I can't recommend this kit enough if you are interested in looking at an easy way to clean up you board with custom cables.
Summary: Better than pre-made pedal board cables.

Text:
I’ve always been fascinated with phono cartridges and I really enjoy trying out different ones in different tonearms, etc. Lately, I’ve been doing this a fair amount. Like many audio geeks “of a certain age”, I had a number of old phono cartridges stuffed in drawers, awaiting new styli to bring them back to life. These included a vintage Shure M44 series, an M91ED, a Stanton 681EEE, a couple of old Grados and more. Fact is, they all have their certain “charms”, strengths and weaknesses. The sound they deliver depends a great deal on which stylus is installed in them, as anyone who has ever played with cartridge/stylus combinations knows only too well.

After messing around with all of these 40-60 year old designs for a while, I thought it would be fun to try a truly modern cartridge, but I didn’t want to spend very much doing it. The Audio Technica AT VM95 series seemed like a great choice. They are quite affordable and are extremely easy to upgrade with a better stylus from Audio Technica. The choices go all the way from a simple conical stylus, through two different ellipticals (one bonded and one “nude”), a “Microlinear” and a “Shibata”. There’s even a 78rpm stylus available! The basic elliptical AT VM95E is priced at right about what I was willing to spend on this experiment.

I’ve only had it for a day, at this point, so I don’t know if it will sound noticeably different after it’s “broken in”. Many reviews I’ve read say that it will, some say not. I’ll just have to experience this for myself, if it happens. So, my review is based on a brand new cartridge and stylus, for what it’s worth.

The cartridge is currently installed in a 1980 vintage Technics SL-Q3 turntable where it tracks quite well at 2.0 grams. It’s on the lower side of medium compliance and that tonearm is of medium mass so it’s a good match. I’m pretty impressed with the tracking ability of it, considering it is a bonded elliptical, not “nude” and not a more advanced stylus profile. Yes, I’ve heard a couple of small instances of sibilance at the inner diameters but nothing serious, believe me. In fact, so far, most of the time, it seems to track very well, even near the label. Inner groove distortion (IGD) has always bothered me and I’m quite sensitive to it. (In fact, when I got my first CD player, way back in 1983, I just LOVED the fact that there was NONE of it!) I presume, this would be even better with the nude elliptical and even better yet with the Microlinear or Shibata styli. And, again, this may improve as the stylus breaks in.

So, how does the AT VM95E sound? Very, very good, especially for the price. (I paid $49) The first quality that was immediately obvious is how dynamic it is. Some reviews have called it “punchy”. The dynamics of the music are there in spades. Drums and percussion have plenty of bite and impact. Instrumental solos and vocals leap out and grab you. I like that a lot. My old Shure M-44 with Jico N55E stylus sounds great but it doesn’t come anywhere near what this thing does in that regard. The Stanton 681EEE with Pfanstiehl stylus is more dynamic than the Shure but, at least right now, I think the AT VM95E is even more so.

Separation is good, not fantastic. It’s certainly adequate and a good sense of space is maintained. It’s about on par with the Shures but is definitely bested by the Stanton. That thing has a very wide sound stage, indeed. It’s rated at 35db separation at 1Khz, compared to 20db on the Audio Technica. That’s a lot and it’s audible but not really a big issue for me. There are times, depending on how a record is mixed that a little less separation can actually be a good thing. It can keep the music a little more “glued together”.

The AT VM95E is slightly on the bright side, at least in my setup. This varies with the capacitance that the cartridge is looking into so it will sound different with different turntable/preamp setups. It’s not a glaring, unpleasant kind of brightness. It’s well controlled and gives the music a bit more presence and bite, without an ugly edge. It will be interesting to hear if this changes as the stylus suspension breaks in. The top end has been described by others as a bit “soft”. I don’t think so. It seems right about where it should be, to my ears. If you like a lot of “sparkle”, this cartridge may sound “soft” to you. The midrange is very nice, giving the cartridge a slightly forward but still full (or “warm”, if you prefer) sound. The low end may not be as prominent as some other cartridges (My M44 is definitely fuller down there but sometimes is a bit too much, actually) The bass is very tight and well controlled on the AT VM95E. I would rather have a little less bass, overall, but have it tight and under control.

Overall, this cartridge gives a very musical and, one could say, “exciting” presentation while still keeping things under control. I never had an old AT 95E, but some reviews have said that the AT VM95E is more “refined” and “polite”. If true, I’d say that’s a really good thing because, to my ears, this cartridge is as bright and forward as I think any phono cartridge should ever be. Any more and it would just be too much and would start to get irritating. I think Audio Technica has really gotten it just right with the AT VM 95E, and, I presume that would hold pretty much true for the other styli (not “styluses”, as I see all the time in other reviews!) that are available as upgrades. I actually plan to buy the Microlinear stylus for the cartridge at some point. Many reviews have said that the two sweet spots in the AT VM 95 range are the bonded elliptical and the Microlinear styli, in terms of “bang for the buck”.

That about sums it up for me after 1 day with the Audio Technica AT VM95E. I think this cartridge is an excellent value. A lot of “bang for the buck”. At $49, I don’t think you’ll find anything that will sound as good in a new phono cartridge. And the upgrade path is so easy. You don’t even have to change the tracking force when you change the stylus! I think you’d have to pay well over $100 for anything that sounds as good or better. If you don’t have a lot to spend on a cartridge right now, this is the one to look at, in my opinion!

Text:
I like a good cable! These cables do not crackle when moved about, they are, however, fairly stiff.

An inspection of one of the 1/4” TR plugs (see pics) shows decent holding technique. Not sure what the blue compound it at the end of the cable case, but it does a good job so securing the wires which is important as loose wires lead to failed connections over time. The end’s I looked at also had heat shrink tubing to help insulate the tip solder joint from shorting to the plug’s housing, cool.

There are 2 inner signal wires instead of one. This is normal for balanced cables like microphone cables, but in this case it is used as a redundant single path. I’ve had mixed results with cables like this as some will actually crackle when moved. Happily, neither of the cables I tested had this problem and were dead silent - as they should be.

The gold plating is a nice visual touch, but only time will tell if it was properly applied…

I played these cables using a Fender Twin Reverb amplifier and used a couple Ibanez guitars. Everything sounded fine.

Measurements indicated a low capacitance (1nF) and decent DC resistance (~1ohm round trip) which puts the cutoff reference so high up as to NEVER be a problem in the audio range.

Good cables, albeit a bit stiff (4/5 stars), but defiantly worth the cost. Would be excellent as patch cables in a studio environment, too.

I've started playing guitar after several years of not playing at all and decided I needed to get some finger picks. This looked like a reasonable package and so I ordered it. The comments on this package and a bunch of others focused on how the picks didn't fit, they were too small but I got them anyway.
The picks are great, very colorful and like everyone said, they were too small. The thumb pick worked ok, but the rest were too small to fit on my fingers. I tried adjusting one of them, and it broke, so I did a bit more research.
I found a comment that said the picks needed to be molded to your fingers and gave some advice about putting them in hot water. I did that and I guess I took some out too soon and left others in too long. The end result was that some of them became totally flat rather than round. I had left them in the water too long or it was too hot, or both.
The ones I took out at the right time were able to mold to my fingers well, but it took some effort to get it right. Now I have some picks that are too big (see the picture) and some that are still too small, and a few of the "Goldilocks" picks are Just Right.
So, the picks are good quality; however, there is a total lack of instructions. Some simple and accurate instructions would elminate a lot of negative reviews. And, it's not enough to just say "put them in hot water". It is much more hepful to say heat the water to 180 degrees (or whatever is right) and then put them in, one at a time for 3 minutes (or whatever is right). Then take the pick out and mold it to your finger. Repeat for the rest of your fingers and then put them in cold water for another 4 minutes so they set properly. Otherwise, we are all in the dark and will end up with no useful finger picks.
Summary: Good set of picks, but definitely needs instructions on how to size them for your fingers

Looking at the pictures online, I was expecting something a little beefier so I was surprised when I opened the box and saw these; they are small and lightweight. These are ON-the-ear headphones, not OVER-the-ear like I was expecting. Honestly, I can't think of a good reason to make ON-the-ear headphones other than they are likely cheaper to produce. On-the-ear doesn't do as well at isolating sound as over-the-ear headphones do. They are also less comfortable when using them for hours on end. At least these are nicely padded (ear-cups and head band) and don't squeeze TOO tight (unlike the Monster Diesel headphones that I used to use a while back). At first I thought, "Hey, maybe I can use these smaller ear-cups to my advantage and let my kids use these in the car (or whatever)," but a quick test revealed that the head band is too long, even on the smallest setting, for someone with ears that would fit INSIDE the cup. I had to wind up putting a stuffed animal on my 2-year-old's head in order to keep them from falling down to her jaw. Although she didn't seem to mind too much, it wasn't the ideal use for these cans like I had hoped. -1 star for being on-the-ear instead of over-the-ear.

I thought the sound was perfectly decent, at least in the quiet room that I was testing these in. There was plenty of low-end without being excessively boomy. The highs were clear without being too bright.

I appreciate that the adapter that makes these compatible with both 1/8" and 1/4" phono jacks actually screws on to the end of the plug (see picture). It isn't necessary, but a nice feature that just makes the experience nicer if you are using the larger size.

The fact that these swivel around as much as they do makes for convenient storage. The headphones also come with a little bag to store them (and the adapter, as needed) in.

All in all, a decent set of headphones, although at this price point, I would have expected the superior over-the-ear design.

That eats up all five slots before you get to an amp or cabinet emulation, or a distortion box (which I rarely use.) The expression pedal also uses up a slot if you engage it.

The delays, reverbs and modulations are not quite Helix/Pod Go quality but they sound good and the interface is way less complex and I got up and running on it in about 10 minutes. Not to mention its about 1/4 the price of the Pod Go. Plus this pedal is tiny and fits in the pouch of my guitar case and will run on 4 AA batteries.

Text: Let's cover the basics of what this is: Is this as good as a $1800 Fender American Telecaster? No. Is it a good copy of a Telecaster for $120.00 (the price on Amazon when I bought one)? Yes. Is it as good as a $450.00 Fender Player Telecaster made in Mexico? For practical purposes, almost and close enough to be just as playable. Is it as good as a $230.00 made in China or Indonesia Squire by Fender Telecaster? Pretty much yes. It's a very nice looking Telecaster copy with good enclosed smooth tuners, a decent maple neck, good frets, a great looking glossy wood finish and nice looking chrome. The switch and pots seem OK, long term use will tell. Pickups for sure have to be ceramic but are in the ballpark for Telecaster sound. Fit and finish of parts to body acceptable. Not too heavy. The paulownia wood looks very nice and for a guitar like this wood snobbery is sort of silly. Plays great. Bottom line is: you play music not wires, pickups and knobs. For a very budget priced guitar it's impressive. Of course almost any guitar needs some action adjustment out of the box to suit each player's ideas. But if you're on a tight budget this is definitely worth a try.

Text:
I love this device and I want to give it 5 stars, but there are some issues that you should know about before purchasing.

The keys feel a bit like toy keyboard keys. I don't mean smaller versions of standard keyboard keys - I mean it really does feel toylike. However, after using the keyboard I fell in love with the low travel and the pressure response actually works very well. But you MUST expect a "toylike" key feel when you first get it.

This keyboard has no control for velocity curve at the hardware level. If you use FL Studio that's fine, just set it there. But if you use an application like Reaper which has no global velocity curve, you're stuck with keys that sound a bit quiet unless you press them harder than you probably want to.

The firmware is easy to update and the keyboard has performed reliably once I addressed an issue --- if you find the keyboard to disconnect or seem like it crashes, it is most likely it's not getting enough USB power. This is a known issue with devices powered by USB, so if that happens just connect it to a powered HUB. I mention it though because I have two computers - one of which is a laptop - where there wasn't enough USB to power both my Focusrite Scarlett Solo AND the keyboard.

The pads feel amazing. They are incredibly responsive. The ribbon controllers feel good. The knobs feel good.
You also get some free software at the Focusrite website, which is nice.

All in all it's an excellent product, but the lack of velocity adjustment is unfortunate because it's a little unpleasant in software that doesn't have a global velocity setting.

PS. It lights up in glorious dancing rainbow colors after a few minutes of inactivity. It looks cool, but if you find it distracting you can turn it off. It's called "Vegas mode" and you can find out how online.

Text:
I had been looking for an amp for home practice and for live playing. Ultimately, my search was narrowed down to this Spider and a Fender Mustang. After reading many Amazon reviews, I ultimately chose the Spider over the Fender because (i) I read that the Fender amps gave off a hissing noise, particularly with the clean channels, and (ii) the Spider had better rock/metal tones, which is one genre I play, among others. Regarding the sound, it is unbelievable! And, to be quite honest, I've only been using the presets! The cleans are ultra clear, and the rock tones are amazing. And, this thing is LOUD. In conducting some internet research, having a mega-watted amp is not necessary and is, in fact, not recommended. I discovered that the reason for this is because the "sweet spot" for the volume is going to be when the amp is about three-quarters of the way up. In home practice, unless you aren't married and live in the boonies, you won't get there. With live play, this could hold it's own and in the sweet spot. As another reviewer mentioned, if you need something louder because you're in a larger venue, the amp will be mic'd anyway.

One note...Line 6 does somewhat force you to purchase one of the pedals because you need the pedal to update the amp. I purchased the [[ASIN:B002GYWBKU Line 6 FBV Express MkII 4-button Foot Controller]], and I'm very happy with it. I like the larger foot pedal switches on this 4-pedal switch, rather than the small buttons on the model up from that (a 6 button pedal board).

Finally, I chose this Spider IV over the Spider IV 120 amp version, in part, because this Spider has a larger speaker (a 12") and the other Spider IV 120 watt model has two 10" speakers. I feel that the larger speaker provides better lower tones.

The reason I bought this camera specifically is because of it's XLR inputs. I've used condenser mics with great success, and also fed audio from digital and analog mixers. Sounds great. But some of the VIDEO aspects of this camera are seriously lacking.
Ironically for a camcorder that is from a company named Zoom, the zoom function itself is pretty weak. It has 5 fixed positions, closeup to wide angle. It is suited for music performances where you want a camera close to the performers. Further than 15' away and it will look like you're miles away, even at most zoomed in perspective.
But the biggest bummer is the HDMI output. It's broken after only 4 months and probably less than 10 times using the HDMI output. I was careful to provide strain relief so there was no pressure on the port.
I'd recommend a better camera that allows for fully adjustable zoom function, capable of much further zooming, with a mic in jack and at minimum an HDMI mini output jack, NOT THE MICRO. A mini HDMI looks just like the full size HDMI type A jack that we see in home theatre equipment. I use the Canon HF R800, and I'm impress so far. And to add the capability of high quality audio: Saramonic SR-PAX2. Camera mounts to the top of it, tripod to the bottom. 9v battery power provides an LCD screen to monitor levels, and for 48v phantom power for 2 condenser mics, and a couple different ways to get signal into it. 3.5mm output for a TRS cable from the SR-PAX2 to the camera's mic input. Sounds great. Only downside is it's 9v will need to be monitored, and you'll chew up batteries regularly. Worth it for the sound it provides.
Bottom Line: if you aren't using the zoom Q8 for HDMI output, and you are ok with having the camera's view limited to within 15 feet, and 1080 max resolution, it's great for it's ability to capture great audio and a decent image. If you're using it for HDMI output, I can't recommend it.
