Text:
Drumeo Pat Petrillo P4 Practice Pad vs Offworld Percussion Invader V3 Red

I own both of these pads and love them both. I do not favor one over the other; each has small advantages and disadvantages. In order to help those buying new, I thought I’d share some of my findings about each of these excellent pads and post them on the reviews for each item.

Sound: Your favorite video channel has many sound videos for each of these pads, so you can listen there with headphones and judge for yourself. I do notice that, a couple reviews for the Petrillo P4 pad state that the distinction between the red and black pads is not enough; I disagree, although the distinction on videos seems not as noticeable as in real life. I think all four pads on the Petrillo P4 pad are distinct, and I could tell with my eyes closed. Note: when I place the P4 on my snare stand, and the bottom is open as opposed to resting on a table, the distinction is ever greater. The Offworld V3 pad has a solid single sound, but oddly enough, I can hit the 2” nameplate Offworld badge on mine that has the branding and that has a distinct pop of its own. So, it can make two sounds. I have a friend that cut a piece of laminate, like you’d find on a countertop (aka Formica) and stuck it on half his Offworld pad and that gives it a very sharp and distinct sound, if that’s what you’re shooting for. The variety of sound on the Petrillo P4, though, is a plus for that model if variety is your goal or you typically play on a drum kit. I enjoy the variety and hand movement while practicing more than I thought I would; it adds to the sometimes mundane task of practice. I wondered if the middle pads, in particular, on the Petrillo P4 would be too small to hit consistently, or if I would miss and hit the edges, but this has not been an issue.

Rim: The Petrillo P4 has no rim, the Offworld V3 has a full-sized rim. This alone makes the Offworld perhaps the better choice for marching drummers, and for players who do plenty of rimming, such as jazzy shuffle players. The Offworld rim seems to take a licking and not get dented; it’s some sort of hard plastic that truly seems solid.

Weight: Honesty, to the feel, they weigh about the same. The Offworld is a touch heavier, but not enough to make one choose the Petrillo P4 over it for carrying. The Offworld can be carried short distances by it’s rim, though, like from room to room, which might be helpful in a crowded band room setting. The Petrillo P4 might better fit in a carrying case than the Offworld.

Quietness: hands down, the Petrillo P4 has the quietest pad on the gray middle zone. I can play it on my apartment balcony in the summer without the neighbors calling the cops. The larger blue pad on the Petrillo is a touch quieter than the Offworld, the black middle pad is about the same volume as the entire Offworld surface, and the red top level of the Drumeo Petrillo P4 is sharper but again about as loud as the Offworld surface.

Cost: the two pads are roughly the same cost, in the sixty dollar range as of early 2018. Note: currently, the Petrillo P4 pad is free if one signs up for a year pre-paid membership to Drumeo, so that is something to consider if video lessons are your goal. It’s on their website (and may change at any time; what I mention is applicable at the time of this review).

Construction: I feel this is a tie. Note that they are both robust and look to stand up to the test of time (I will update if they do not). An Amazon comment from Drumeo on one of these reviews states that the P4 Petrillo model is made in New Jersey; I do not know where the Offword model is manufactured. The P4 ships in a cellophane shrink wrap, the Offworld in a plastic clear bag. Neither feels loose, slippery, sketchy, or cheap. They both feel robust and like you bought something that will last. The hardwood of the Petrillo pad can be seen on the black painted sides, and I like that even the risers for the tiers are stacked hardwood; they are not some cheap foamy riser. The Offworld shows no hardwood, just the hard matte plastic rim and the surfaces top and bottom. There are a couple reviews of each pad stating some glue runs or paint flaws, but mine at least, for both were completely flawless. Neither has even a hint of “homemade” character to them. Solid.

Pad material: I included photos so you can see the surfaces after a few days of use, uncleaned. The Petrillo P4 shows stick marks, especially the black pad, but these clean off with Windex. The surfaces show no overall signs of wear or degradation, although they are generally (even the blue area) softer than the Offword surface. Time will tell if they slowly wear in striking locations, but that is the trade-off for a generally quieter, less strident-sounding pad. The Offworld pad has some sort of proprietary material that is stiff and strong, feels like it will not wear, but certainly catches anything in the air on its sticky surface. The company says to use Armour All car cleaner on the surface, and I have done this with great success. That said, it only takes a day of use for things floating through the air to catch on the surface (dust, hair, anything). If you’re a neat-nick that is bothered by that, the less sticky Petrillo might be better for you unless you plan to Armour All your Offworld every couple of days. Storing it in a bag might help, but I don’t do that. As to rebound, I find them both to be pretty authentic to my snare. The Offworld surface and the main Blue Petrillo P4 surface are pretty much indistinguishable for rebound; the other P4 pads vary on rebound (with the quietest gray level being the least rebound). I like the rebound character of both pads, but rebound is a personal thing and this may be the most difficult for me to help you with in a written review.

Bottom: The original Ludwig (older) P4 Petrillo pad had a threaded cymbal stand mount on it; the current (newer) Drumeo version sold here does not. The bottom is a black, medium weight closed cell foam that works well to keep the pad in place on a flat surface. That said, I would not drum on the bottom foam as it looks not to be robust enough for long-term sticking. The Offworld pad also has no cymbal stand threads, and has the same sticky material on the entire bottom as it does on the top striking surface. So, the bottom can be used as a practice pad, and one without a rim if one does not want rim interference as they play (for instance on a high table). The downside is that the bottom, like the top, will pick up everything that you set this on (food crumbs, lint, dust, etc.).

Size: The exact measurements you can read on the listings for each pad, but this is key: the Petrillo P4 pad fits inside the playing surface of the Offworld pad (see photo). There is about 1/8” all around the P4 pad (i.e. showing surface of the Offworld pad) when placed like this. In essence, though, one can think of the playing surfaces as roughly the same (P4 ever so slightly smaller), and the thick plastic rim is what adds to the overall diameter of the Offworld pad. Playing on either pad is not a problem…I never feel as though one is too small or too large compared to the other. Some might say I want the rim and don’t mind a bigger overall profile, others might say if it’s only the rim adding the size, I’d rather have more portability. They both work well, but I just wanted to give a size comparison. I must mention that the Petrillo P4 placed inside (atop) the Offworld does not allow rimshots, the Offworld rim is too low. Note that the top tier of the P4 is slightly higher than the overall surface of the Offworld, but it’s not an issue when playing (and is an advantage for simulating the movement around a drum kit). I will say that the rim of the Offworld does get in the way when I’m playing on a high surface, like sitting on my barstools and playing on the bar; the solution is to either flip it over and use the bottom (which mades it 1.0” higher, though, the thickness of the upturned rim) or to place it on a lower surface or snare stand. Otherwise, I have to sort of reach over the rim to play, if that makes sense…where a rimless pad like Petrillo P4 does not have a rim to contend with. That said, rimshots are fun, so it’s a trade-off.

Summary: I can try to answer any questions you have in the comments and hope this review helped you decide between these two premium and popular practice pads. Overall, I truly love both pads and feel glad to have paid a premium compared to the many thirty and forty dollar pads available. I use both regularly and enjoy them. I love the variety of the Drumeo Petrillo P4 pad (Pat Petrillo shows how to make best use of the tiers with even something as simple as paradiddles on this YT videos; check them out), and the rimshots and marching band similarity of the Offworld. You can’t go wrong with either pad. Thanks. Wayne :-))
Summary: Drumeo Petrillo P4 practice pad versus Offworld Invader V3 practice pad: Comparison

I really love this amp modeler, but there is a very steep learning curve, and the instructions are, not necessarily horrible, but are woefully incomplete. You’re basically on your own figuring out how this works, because the manual is missing most of the relevant information. The instructions do talk about a few things, like how to use the looper and the tuner, but don’t list any of the FX or presets.

My box showed up a little damaged, but the unit was packed well enough that it didn't sustain any damage. It comes with a reconfigurable plug for US, European, and a few other style outlets, as well as a USB-C cable for PC connectivity (that isn't supported yet, more on that later).

This is first, and foremost, an amp modeler more than it is a multi-effects processor, because amp modeling is where this unit really, really, REALLY shines. It’s a little light on the multi-effects, but there are plenty enough FX models to let you get by, and still get most of the sounds you’re going to want. I have several other multi-effects units from other manufacturers (Line 6, Zoom, DigiTech, Mooer, etc.), and they generally have more “effects” than the Arena2000, but not as many amp and cab models.

Like with any amp+cab modeler, I didn’t want my own amp or cab to color the sound for this review, so I used a pair of high-end Sennheiser head phones. You can certainly plug it into your own amp, but then you get the modeled amp+cab being played through your actual amp+cab. Because of this, you can turn off the amp and cab models independently, as you please. The sounds this thing can create are truly quite astonishing, and the amp and cab models just sound fabulous. 80 amps and 50 cabs. Quite the range of combinations! I tested everything with a Carvin DC127 superstrat. Of course, I haven’t played through all 80 of these “real” amps for comparison, I only know if the model sounds good or not, but they all do. At some point you just have to trust that they modeled it right.

Here are a few things you need to know!

Every little light on the display is also a touch sensitive button. They don’t click or anything, they are just touch sensitive (like a touch screen. . . but the actual screen is NOT a touch screen). This is how you select, activate, and change effects settings. They each cycle through different functions, not just on off. For example, if you tap FXA once, it opens the settings, if you tap it again, it toggles it on/off. You have to double tap a lot. It’s the touch-light buttons that took me a while to figure out. This isn’t mentioned anywhere except that the A in “Arena” is a touch sensitive button, which got me thinking. I just kept turning the knobs not knowing why nothing is happening.

This is not well suited to live performance. The foot switches basically select between the adjacent 3 presets, and bank up and bank down if you hit two in unison (the manual does cover this). However, there is a goofy scheme of pressing the left foot switch to go into a “control mode” for that preset, then pressing one of the other foot switches to alters one of the assigned FX in the signal chain, then you have to exit the “control mode”. The whole process is just kind of clunky. You’re better off not using it for live gigs. Or making sure all your presets are right next to each other so you can bank up and down easily to get to them.

Perhaps most importantly, the manual does NOT have a list of the available effects, amps, cabs, presets, or anything else. The only way to discover what these are is to literally scroll through the menu and look at them all. Does this have a phasor? I don’t know, the manual doesn’t say anything. I guess I’ll poke around in the device until I find one or not. This is a huge waste of time when you want to just look up an effect or preset in the manual. Let’s say you want to look over the presets to see which ones have Marshal cabs. . . .nope! You have to poke around every preset in the device and look at what cab it has. What a pain.

While it’s way too much work for me to try to list all of those here, I will give you a high level overview, which hopefully helps.

It has 8 pre-defined effects, and two user-selectable effects, for a total signal chain of 10 effects.
The predefined effects are:

Compressor, 10 types (incl. Dyna Comp).
Drive, 20 types (incl. Klon, Rat, OCD, Big Muff Pi, Zen).
Amp, 80 types – all the famous ones, and then some.
Cab, 50 types – all the famous ones, and then some.
EQ, 5 types (3 band to 10 band, and custom defined)
Noise Gate, 3 types.
Delay, 10 types (incl. reverse, stereo, pingpong, etc.)
Reverb, 10 types (all the standards, plus some odd ones like “Distortion Reverb”)

Each of these predefined effects has several types to choose from, but not an overwhelming number. But each of them is very good. However, there are 80 amps, and 50 cabs. Because that’s what this thing really is, and amp+cab modeler. One thing that drives me crazy about all these tube amp models is that they all model the noise too! Why? So, then you have to also model a noise gate in front of everything. This unit is no exception here.

The two user-defined effects are called FXA and FXB, and you can select from about 20 and 18 effects, respectively, within each one. Some of the effects are the same for FXA and FXB, but some are unique to one slot or the other. For example, FXA has 4 types of wah, but FXB doesn’t have any. FXA has two choruses, FXB has those, plus a stereo chorus. It’s kind of strange, and I can’t understand the reasoning here. Why not let any slot be anything, like Zoom does on all their units? There must be some processor limitation or something, I don’t know.

Here are the available types of effects for FXA and/or/maybe/also FXB:

Wah, 4 types (only on FXA).
Gate, just one on FXA.
Boost, 2 types.
Chorus (2 or 3 types).
Filter, just 1.
Flanger, 2 types.
Vibrato, just 1.
Phasor, 2 types.
Tremelo, 2 types.
Ring Mod, 1 type.
Both FXA and FXB have 1 each “LoFi” “auto swell” and “step phase”.
Only FXA has 1 each, “pitch shift” and “Octave”.

So, there are not a huge number of user-selected effects, but still plenty enough. The effects that are here also sound amazingly good. I was very surprised at the sound quality, actually, it’s really, really good. Sounds just as good as my Line6, and honestly, better than some of my actual pedals.

But, there are definitely some limitations in your ability to control the effects order. For example, you can’t have a vibrato feed a wah, which drives a fuzz, then add a chorus or phasor afterwards. This is because FXA MUST be the wah, then you can use FXB to be either the vibrato in front of the wah, or the chorus or phasor after the fuzz, but not both. We’re only talking about 4 effects in the chain here , but you just can’t. We’d need an FXA -->FXB -->Drive -->FXC, and there isn’t a 3rd FXC slot. You also can’t select FXA or FXB to be one of the other pre-defined effects, like a drive, or delay, etc. So, you can’t feed one drive into another drive. . . like an OCD into a Rat. . . it just won’t let you do that, because it has exactly 1 drive slot. Similarly, you can’t have two delays bounce the sound all over the place, because it has exactly 1 delay slot. More versatile multi-effects units have no problem with this.

Ultimately, these limitations are not a huge deal, but just be aware. I still don’t have any problem getting awesome sounds from this, even with these limitations. I do wish I had a few more flanger options, for example. You DO have the power to put ANY effects ANYWHERE in the signal chain, so that’s nice. I mean, you could even do weird things like put the cab first; if you wanted to, it will let you.

There is also a 60 sec looper and a Drum Machine with 40 drum styles, and adjustable tempo and volume on all of them. And they all sound pretty good. Way more fun than a metronome (which I can’t actually fine anywhere on the device, although it’s listed in the app). I actually like these drum styles on the Arena2000 better than the drum machines on any of my other multi-effects units. The Looper is nice too, since it uses more than one foot switch to record, dub, play, stop, delete, etc. There is on-screen description of the controls, and it’s fairly intuitive, and similar to most other looper controls.

A cool trick is that the expression pedal has two modes called “on” and “off”, but really should just be called mode 1 and 2. You can assign different functions to each mode. For example, it can be a volume pedal, then just toe-down to switch modes, and it can be a wah pedal. Toe-down to switch modes back to the volume pedal when you like. You can also plug in ANOTHER external pedal, if you like, for a 3rd control. It’s also got most of the standard XLR/balanced, MIDI, aux input, and USB-C for connection to a computer. Actually, many multi-effects units don’t have an Aux input these days, so kudos for Donner for keeping it (because I actually use this from time to time).

Last, but not least, you can add your own Impulse Responses (IR), though the manual doesn’t tell you how. I presume you can do this through their software, which I haven’t downloaded yet. Why haven’t I downloaded it yet? Well, the software has not actually been posted on their website yet. Under the “Arena2000” download section, there is currently nothing. I contacted tech support, and they said they’d “email me the software” (but haven’t yet, after several days, besides I expect it would be too big for email, so they must have meant email me a link, but I still haven’t received anything). I also asked tech support to email me a list of all the effects, cabs, presets, and other info that should be in the instruction manual but isn’t, and they said they’d “try” to see if there is any other documentation they can email me. If/when they do, I’ll update this review. Hopefully using the PC software is easier to figure out, though, honestly, I’m not sure I’ll ever really do this. I’m perfectly happy with selecting from the 50 cabs already included.

The manual also points you toward a QR code to download the Arena2000 app for your phone (using Bluetooth connectivity). The app is actually in the app store, so you don’t have to side-load it. It’s actually legit! Once you download it, you have to figure it out yourself, but it’s actually more intuitive than the on-unit controls. After opening the app, click the Bluetooth icon to connect. With the app, it’s way easier to select presets and effects from the on-screen touch menus, and move the effects orders around by just dragging them where you want them (see screenshots). On the app, each effect has an on/off button, which I find less intuitive than just tapping the effect to turn it on or off, but it works.

However, the app doesn’t let you do everything you want to, so you still need to use the on-unit controls for the looper, volume, drum machine, and (obviously) the expression pedal. Other than the expression pedal, these should all work from the app. The app even lets you control the midi interface. . but not the master volume? By master volume, I mean the actual volume knobs for line out, XLR, and headphones (not the modeled volume of the amps and effects. . . those do work from the app). The app also has a few dead functions. Like the metronome. You can set a tempo for a metronome on the app, but it doesn’t actually control anything. Doesn’t turn on a metronome, doesn’t affect the tempo of the drum machine.

Everything is labeled v1.0.0, so I’m sure there will be some updates to fix some of the jankyness of the app, the on-board controls, eventually get the PC software rolled out, and hopefully later units ship with better instructions. I’m going to give them a LOT of leeway here, since this is v1.0.0, and I did not dock any stars for this, even though it’s frustrating. Because this thing really does just sound awesome enough to justify a full 5 star rating. I struggled with giving it 4 or 5 starts, but it’s all I’ve been playing through for the past week, and I just love it.

Final Rating: 5 stars, for pure awesome audio quality and first-class amp modeling. I’ll forgive Donner for their absurdly poor instruction manual, janky app, and non-existent PC software, because this thing is just so good (once you figure it out). And, I'm going to ASSUME the jankyness will be fixed soon with some updates.
Summary: Just AWESOME – Sonically just flawless, but lacks some FX versatility, and v1.0 has some bugs still

If you want a quick review of this pedal (the Behringer TM300) let's just say it might work for you but be prepared to send it back.

I'm trying to sell a keyboard amplifier combo that has 65 W, with a 15 inch speaker and a horn tweeter (it's a Peavey KB-100). You can use it for keyboards, bass guitar, and vocals without changing anything about it. But because it's a solid-state amplifier from around 1990 it doesn't sound good with electric guitars. So I looked for a cheap pedal that would make the amplifier really howl.

This Behringer pedal, like most Behringer pedals, is a clone of a more expensive pedal. I believe it's a copy of a Sans Amp GT-2, which costs typically close to $200. For around $25 it seems something that I should look into. It "changes" your amp into a Fender, Marshall, or Mesa Boogie. Since to get one of those amps would cost you probably over $1000, the $25 seemed reasonable.

The controls on the Behringer pedal let you choose between the three makes of amplifier I mentioned above, and there is a mic position switch, and three varieties of drive. As well as this there's a volume control, bass and treble knobs, and a drive (distortion) knob, so you can dial in the exact sounds you like. I saw a YouTube demo of this pedal, and was very impressed.

When I received this pedal I tried it out and the first thing I noticed was an intrusive hiss. There are several solutions to this, but I was worried that the prospective purchaser would find the hiss annoying, and of course I had no idea which instrument they wanted to use it with. So in the end I wrapped it up and UPS came with a label to send it back to Amazon for a full refund.

I'd like to address some concerns that I see about Behringer pedals. The main criticism is that it costs too little "and it can't be any good." The electronics of today is different from those of yesterday. When you don't have any development costs to design circuits, and you already have market research from companies like Boss, pedals can be cheap.

But the big cost saving in reproducing a pedal is modern assembly methods, particularly Surface Mount Technology (SMT). Because you don't need human hands to assemble circuits, components can be very small. Circuits are put together by machine from spools of components at the rate of tens of thousands parts an hour and automatically tested.

Another issue with Behringer pedals is that "They're plastic, so they'll break." There is a video on YouTube of a guy trying to destroy his pedal by kicking it across the room, throwing it what looks like a metal statue, and standing with both legs on the pedal. It still works. Think about the remote control for your TV - you sit on it, then push it down into the couch, and your dog decides it is a new dog toy. But usually when it fails, it's not the case but the internal parts. I don't see anyone advocating metal cases.

I was impressed by the thickness of the plastic of the pedal I had. I would use it to throw at the head of some dirty thief who stole my irreplaceable Squier Affinity Strat, and with the metal baseplate I'd use the pedal to hammer in nails. If you give it the slightest amount of respect it will last. If you're intent on apeing that bats*** guitarist and jump on it, remember he probably has a whole boxfull of pedals and a roadie to swap them.

The only complain that affected me was installing the battery. Behringer uses this method in most of their stomp boxes, and it's not obvious how to do it. Where the pedal pivots on the case there are black lugs on either side. Use a ballpoint pen tip to push these in, one at a time, and when each one is completely pushed in you should use your third hand to push the foot switch cover up and away.

Inside you can see the battery compartment with the connector for the nine-volt battery. Place the battery (that you supplied) into the compartment, connect it, and you're all set. This sounds worse than it actually is (especially if you have a third hand), but my advice is to get the Behringer power adapter. With the adapter you have the space in the pedal for the battery to hold whatever you want, and no indication that you have a secret compartment. Do you get my drift . . . drift . . . drift?

I'm feeling a little guilty about returning this pedal - not because it was faulty (it was) but given a little more time and no prospective buyer to impress I might have been able to deal with the hiss. The amp I'm keeping is a solid-state Fender Princeton 65 (watts), and most people's verdict on this is that it's LOUD. I try to keep the volume down on it and also on my guitar. That means that the signal is not very loud, and so any extra noise from a pedal is noticeable.

So, had I not been pressed for time, I should have experimented with volume levels, particularly with my guitar. Any pedal that hisses or hums is going to sound worse with a low signal. Another fix would have been a noise gate. That's a pedal that waits for a strong signal before it lets it on to your amp. Between songs your amp is silent, but when you play, a hiss or hum will sound from anything before the noise gate. Usually the guitar signal is so strong that it will drown out this extra noise.

So this hasn't put me off Behringer pedals, and YouTube demos of the TM300 show it performs pretty well. If you're concerned about getting a clone, almost every company has produced a pedal based on the circuit of Ibanez's Tube Screamer under their own name. If you know exactly which make of amp you want to emulate you could use one of a range of Joyo pedals (JF-13 through 16) which reproduces the sound of one of the amps here (Fender, Marshall, Mesa Boogie, and on Joyo alone, Vox). These have only one company's sound but a greater range of controls, are made of metal (for what that's worth) and cost in the low end of the $30 range. Each of them has YouTube demos.

But I guess I was spoiled by getting the $50ish [[ASIN:B00IOSJ68C Zoom G1oN Guitar Floor Multi-Effects Pedal]], which has far more effects, many different amp sounds, and is completely silent. I think we'll see a Behringer competitor to the Zoom before too long, and I welcome the competition.

Text:
2nd purchase of a Grote Telecaster. For the money, they are really good playing guitars. No, its not a Fender MIM Telecaster or USA Tele but the guitar plays great and sounds great for its price. Guitars have come a long way in past 2-3 decades. Knowing how to fix/repair/setup guitars helps tremendously with these guitars. I'll explain

Pro's:
Neck is nice satin C shape - Very comfortable playing guitar
Good sounding pickups - No hum/overtones
Nut height cut well - Approx 1/64 - 1 1/2/64 across all six strings

Cons:
Fret ends a little sharp

Frets are not polished/smoothe - When bending strings, Noticeable grinding/scratching sound across neck - Guitar is playable but could benefit from level/crown/polish

Tuners are pretty decent for price - With tightening nut on top of peghead during string change and phillips head, Tuners are pretty good.

Neck pocket was a little shallow from factory causing high action with saddles lowered as possible. Created/fitted shim in bottom of neck pocket to adjust angle and plays much better.

Overall:

Keep in mind this guitar is 109. Its expected that the guitar should be playable out of the box. However if your familiar with setting up guitars and tweaking them to your preference. This, just like any guitar can benefit from the following:

Crown/Level/Polish frets
Possible neck shim to adjust angle
3M Scotchbrite pad (Purchased from Dollar Tree) to smooth back of neck even more to play fast/smoothe
Tighten hardware
Lube on stringtree/nut/saddles
Set pickup height

Overall, Very happy with guitar and definitely would purchase another Grote soon
Summary: Great guitar for the money - Could benefit from setup

Text:
For 12 bucks, what I paid here in July 2015, this is a great deal. It's now 14, still a fine price. Anything under 16 or so I'd say is very good value on this cable. It's very well made, doesn't add any noise or lose any signal---often a concern above 10 or so feet---and can be easily opened at the jacks to fix if it goes out, as most do after a while.

But, good news, I've used one of these in rehearsal for over 100 hours and have had zero issues with it. It tangles up a bit, but so do most cables, and if you straighten them every hour or two, and leave them straight on the floor when not playing, they stay pretty flat. That is the sole issue I could find with this cable, but it does somehow manage to get all coily pretty easily, even while you stand in one place (how DOES that happen?), so if that drives you nuts, this might not be your best call. Most vitally, this cord sounds completely transparent, as good as any of my Monster or other cables that cost two to three times as much per foot.

I got the black and white one, very nice low-key color. Be careful of the "royal blue" ones though, as they are half blue and half red and turn out to be purple-looking, not blue. Just a note to those wanting blue, not purple.

I'll probably grab another one or two of these for future use, as I've rarely seen a cable this good for this cheap, and when the 10 foot is only a buck or two less, and the 20 adds no noise, why not get the long one. Seeing as you "lose" a few feet of any cable at the guitar and pedalboard, those extra ten feet can come in handy when you need to get to the rehearsal room fridge for another cold one.
Summary: Very good value at less than 65 cents a foot, totally transparent signal

Martin M600 strings came standard on my Martin ukulele. I like the loud bright clear sound and bought a new set when the originals wore out. These are thinner and lighter and easier on my fingers than the thick nylon Aquila strings that are standard on many mid-priced ukuleles. I think the Martin fluorocarbon strings give me more detail and just as much volume as the Aquilas. The Martin strings also break-in faster. In less than a week, I only have to tune them once a day (compared to 3 weeks to break in Aquilas). Martins are also cheaper than Aquilas ($5 for the Martins when I bought them). You should be able to find Martin strings for inexpensive prices at most music stores as well.

Fluorocarbon strings are all the rage for ukuleles right now and Martin strings are a cheap and easy way to try out fluorocarbons. Other brands of fluorocarbons are somewhat more expensive as well as more difficult to buy, but the sound difference between Martins and the others is much more subtle than the difference between Martin and Aquila.

The Martin M600 strings are for soprano and concert ukuleles only. Tenor ukulele owners should buy Martin M620 strings instead. [[ASIN:B000ZNKELC Martin M620 Ukulele Strings Fluorocarbon, Tenor]]
Summary: very good fluorocarbon ukulele strings for a great price

Text:
Folks, we need to clear the air on these types of microphones. These can be described as 'condenser' microphones, but a better, more technical term for them would be 'electret' microphones. They work a bit differently than the usual condenser microphone that requires 48 volt phantom power. The electret microphones only require 2-5 volts of DC current in order to function correctly. Without this current, they will sound very weak and thin.

Most sound card microphone ports provide enough power through a process called PIP, 'Power In Plug' that sends a voltage through the 3.5mm microphone in-jack on most computers. This gives additional voltage to the electrolyte coating on on one of the diaphragms in the microphone. Many desktops have USB ports that do have a 5 volt power provided, although plenty of laptops do have USB ports with lower or no voltage to them. USB unpowered ubs may have some problems providing enough power to get a good sound from these types of microphones.

Larger, more expensive condenser microphones do require the 48 volt phantom power, as they do not have any electrolyte coating on the diaphragms. The electret microphones can give a very good reproduction of sound if they have a decent electrolyte coating, which is magnetic. However, if the coating is very thin, or of low quality, then it will not be as effective. In any event, the magnetic coating will weaken over time, and the mic will eventually not work very well, although this might be many, many years. There is some controversy whether 48 volt power is too 'hot' for the electret types of microphones, but experience seems to indicate that it works OK with them.

Just be aware of these things when considering the electret type of condenser microphone.
Summary: A different type of condenser microphone.

I had several drum machines, but never kept one to actually use it. The worst one was the best "looking" one from the fancy French company Arturia. Unless you want to create the worst of the 70s sound on purpose, steer clear of that lovely looking stuff.

I've had one of those little Korgs, and a few others, and they all sound canned.

The Beat Buddy is fun, and sounds amazing in comparison any others I've played with or heard.

Someone else reviewing it mentioned all it does is playback .wav files. That's a very unthorough way to look at this device. If you slow or speed up a .wav file, it doesn't take long for it to sound "wrong," because you either lose top or bottom end quickly, and all the character can go away. That doesn't happen here; any speed sounds full, dynamic, loud and correct.

This device does not just play files. It allows you to play them at whatever speed you want, with a super intuitive KNOB to turn. It adds FILLS, seamlessly and reliably. There's a tiny screen but it doesn't ask you to navigate ridiculously-hard-to-manage menus. And they're not trying to upsell anything more than any other company. To "accuse" them of not giving you the "best" beats before even listening to the AWESOME beats they give you? C'mon.

This is a great drum machine, which requires nothing other than power. You do not have to plug a guitar into it; it is not a guitar pedal. Any beat can go any BPM, and volume is KNOB-controlled on the fly as is BPM. If you're a performer thinking of using this for a show, buy it. You'll love it!

I'm a semi-professional musician - which means I play regularly and I get paid to do it, but I don't do it for a living. I bought a pair of these to try out as a possible solution for some wireless in ear monitors at 2 gigs this weekend.
I charged both units, and paired and tested them with my guitar rig at home, and they seemed to work fine. I also set up my board and connected them to the aux out to make sure I could use them as a transmitter from our mixer board with the receiver plugged into a Behringer P2 IEM without any issue. That worked too. All in, this makes it about a 120.00 personal wireless monitor setup, so that's pretty cool.
However, during both of my tests, this was the only wireless device running. When I'm playing live, there are at least 4 other wireless systems running.
All gigs consist of 45 minute sets with 15 minute breaks. I turned off both the transmitter and receiver during these break times.
In both cases, the battery on both the transmitter and receiver lasted the whole show.
Also, in both of these cases, I'm within 5-15 feet of the transmitter with the receiver attached to the Behringer P2 on my belt behind my back. However, at gig1, the transmitter is behind me, at gig2 the transmitter is in front of me.
Gig #1 was 3 hours, in a suburban bar. For the most part, they worked. I noticed a few dropouts that seemed to start happening later in the gig. They were very brief.
Gig #2 was 4 hours, in an urban bar. Here's where I noticed a lot of dropouts, and they seemed to get worse as the night went on. It's worth noting that at this location, one of my other older 600MHz systems picks up a lot of interference, but that interference goes away when I turn on the transmitter, and that system doesn't drop out. It's possible that my own body was in the way.
Overall, I'd have been thrilled with this system 10-15 years ago. Compared to the XVive, these fall far short. The build quality is clearly lower than the Xvive, and I absolutely wouldn't trust these for playing a show simply based on that. The XVive swivel feels sturdier, and stays where you put it. That means, if you bend it into a U shape, that's how it stays. These simply flop around. Also the XVive people even put padding on the unit where it will impact your guitar to prevent any damage. These have none of that. Combine that with the dropouts, and it's a deal killer.
I'd say, if you're practicing in your house and you want a cheap solution to get rid of the cord that your roomba keeps sucking up, buy these. If you're gigging, look elsewhere - possibly XVive or Boss.

*edit*
I have now used these with that behringer p2 as a wireless monitor for at least 5 shows varying between 2 and 4 hours. The dropouts are manageable, but consistant. I am still willing to deal with them since the cost is so low and I'm the only one listening.
Summary: Wouldn't recommend for "stage" use, unless you're prepared for the drawbacks.

Text: These strings are essentially a coated version of the EJ16 light phosphor bronze strings I've been playing since I first picked up acoustic guitar 14 years ago.  I remember when I first started playing I thought that the similarly-coated Elixir strings were the bee's knees, but after playing for a while began to prefer the tone of the less expensive D'Addario strings as they seemed to break in quicker and not retain that twangy sound as long as the Elixirs.  The coating on these strings is not as slick as on Elixir strings, but it's noticeably there in comparison with the standard D'Addarios.  If you're interested in these strings, I think you need to ask yourself why you prefer coated strings--do you want them to last longer? Do you want them to be easier on your fingers and make less string noise when playing?  Or, do you just prefer the tone to other strings?  After playing for quite a while, I've come to feel that guitar strings are meant to have a limited life--sure, you don't want your strings to be dead in just a few hours of playing, but by their very nature, they're going to wear out even if they're coated--for about half the price you can get two sets of regular strings and easily more than twice the life in terms of good tone, though you will have to change them (which you should probably learn how to get good and quick at anyway).  Avoiding string noise is a reasonable goal, though these are a far cry from flatwounds in that department, and if you're worried about how hard playing is on your fingers, you probably should just keep playing and learn that it only takes a few days of heavy playing to build up some very useful calluses--it's part of playing the instrument!  What I'm saying, ultimately, is that, though the strings sound fine and very similar to the EJ16s, the price isn't justified by the qualities of the string coating.  If you're looking for $11 strings whose tone quality more accurately justifies the price increase, check out UK brand Newtone strings.  Otherwise, the standard D'Addarios remain my choice for value strings.

I use the Zoom U-24 as part of a portable recording rig with a small laptop (and sometimes a small tablet) and AT2022 stereo microphone, and its compact form factor and ultralight weight make it ideal for that application. I was considering purchasing the U-24, and when I saw it listed for half of the regular price, I snapped it up. Having used it for a few hours over several location recording sessions, I would recommend the Zoom U-24, even at full price, if compact size and lightweight are paramount considerations. If you can work with larger, heavier interfaces, there are many similar offerings in the same price range that are heavier duty, perhaps more durable, have more spacious control/connector layout and are worth considering as alternatives. The Zoom U-24 mic preamps sound excellent, with low noise, clean signal, and have adequate gain. The various input and output options are very useful, as are the dedicated preamp, monitor and headphone volume control knobs. I have used the U-24 with Cubase (on a W10 laptop) and Cubasis (on an Android 8 inch tablet), with excellent results.

The multiple options for powering this interface come in handy, especially the ability to use rechargeable standard AA batteries when I have the U-24 connected to a tablet, via a OTG USB connection. A pair of fully charged low self-discharge AAs lasted me 3 hours with no issues. Best to have backup fully charged AAs and to change them before you run out of power unexpectedly, like mid-take! Fortunately, battery swaps are fast and easy on this interface. In the alternative, you can easily power the U-24 by a portable power bank, a 5V micro USB cell phone charger cable or directly by the USB buss power supplied through the same USB cable (included in the box with the U-24) that connects it to your PC.

I have been very pleasantly surprised by the low recording latency I have been able to comfortably achieve while using the U-24 with my not-very-high-performance devices. The hardware and parts seem well made--albeit mostly of light plastic, especially given how light this unit is. It lacks the solid professional feeling of, for example, my Steinberg interface, which is made of steel, and is bulkier and much heavier. The U-24's plastic construction makes it seem a little less durable, so I recommend getting a good protective case for it. Amazon sells small, light, hard pistol cases with foam inserts that are perfectly sized for the U-24, and offer excellent protection at very low cost. For the U-24, I prefer to use a larger 2-pistol case that also has room for my stereo microphone and other accessories. For this use, inside the pistol case, I keep the U-24 further protected in a neoprene tablet sleeve case that perfectly fits it. Here is that sleeve --https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00RK1HZB4/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o02_s01?ie=UTF8&th=1

That neoprene case alone would probably adequately protect the U-24 in many situations.

For best audio recording results, I strongly recommend installing and using the Zoom manufacturer-supplied U-24 USB driver software, and making sure you understand and correctly use the buffer and other DAW and PC settings that affect CPU performance and DAW latency. I never use "direct monitoring," so cannot comment on that feature of the U-24. Instead, I monitor the playback through my DAW while tracking overdubs. The low latency of the U-24 is perfect for my DAW monitoring approach, and it works in true stereo.

I have not compared the U-24 to pricier competitors, like the newer Audient. I might be worth looking at those before you buy. But for a grab and go compact recording kit, the U-24 is ideal at its current price.
Summary: "Handy" describes it. Very lightweight, portable, great sound, nice features

There is both good and bad with this wireless set.

The Good:

It comes in a very nice case along with the charging cable and a couple of lanyards.

When turned on they match up in a matter of seconds and are ready to go.

The controls are easy to see and use.

On the front there is a button to set the channel. There are 4 channels available so you can try to avoid interference with other units or equipment operating on the same frequency. There is also a battery life indicator. I did not do a battery life test. The manufacturer claims 6-9 hours of useable battery life and 3-4 hours to fully charge.

On the left side are the Off/On switches which just slide to the desired position

On the side opposite the Off/On are the charge ports (USB C). The charging cable is provided and has two leads so that you can charge both at the same time.

On the transmitter there is a volume up button on the Off/On switch side, and a volume down on the charging port side. This is a nice addition, especially if you are using this on more than one instrument and don't necessary want to change the settings on your amplifier when swapping out instruments. There is not a large range to increase the volume, but there is some. You can turn it all the way down to silence.

The jack swivels up to 270*. This is very nice depending on the type of instrument you are using it on. If your jack is front facing you can swivel the head out of the way. If you have a Fender Strat it will also fit in the angled front jack. This makes it very versatile for use with many different instruments.

During use, I did not experience any drop out or interference. It maintained connection well.

The Bad:

It is inconsistent in its output volume depending on the instrument/pickups being used.

I tried it with two acoustics, one with passive pickup and one with active pickup and it worked well in both cases. There was some volume drop with all the instruments tested vs cord or another wireless set I have, but it was not bad in the case of those two guitars. I was surprised that the output was very similar between the active pickup and the passive.

When I used it with my Semi-hollow body (335 clone) with passive humbuckers, there was a very marked loss of output volume. The sound was also a bit muffled. Increasing the volume on the TX to its max helped a little, but overall, the sound was unsatisfactory. I swapped out this wireless for another that I have (Brian Fay) with the exact same settings on the guitar and amp and there was about a 50% increase in volume and everything brightened up the way that guitar usually sounds. I don't know why there seems to be an issue with this particular instrument, but there is. Your experience may be different depending on your instrument.

I also tested it with a bass guitar with active pickups and it performed very much like it did with the acoustics. Some volume drop, but overall tone and usability was acceptable.

The build quality on this set is ok, but I expected a little better at this price point. Most of the assembly is made of plastic. This makes it very light, but gives it a cheap feel. The Off/On switch is plastic as well. It makes me wonder about the longevity of everything. The switch seems to be a weak point and would be my bet for the first thing to fail. The swivel for the jack does seem very solid and moves smoothly. It stays where you put it (not floppy).

My conclusions:

On 3 out of 4 instruments I tested this with, I got acceptable results. Is is as good as a cable? No. Is it worth the tradeoff to be untethered? Probably. I have tried out other cheaper units that were basically unusable. This is not the case with this product. At $130 I expected more, but the results are, in 75% of the instruments I tested it gave usable results. My suggestion is, if you get it, put it through its paces with your equipment during the return period. That way you can return it if it doesn't work for your particular setup.

In a careful comparison, the Boss had a cleaner and slightly more clear sound, which is not really an overdrive, but more of a distortion, but a clear distortion, if that makes any sense. I've tried various ways to humidify my acoustic guitar over the years. Until I bought this unit, they were all either a nuisance, a mess, ineffective, or all of the above. The Humitar is so simple, I wonder why it took so long to come to the market. It fits very easily between the strings of the guitar, and when the guitar case is closed, the Humitar remains in place--no sliding around. The sponge is made of foam with cells so fine I cannot see them. I know it's foam by the way it absorbs water and the way it feels. Perhaps because of this micro-size cellular structure, the foam doesn't drip, holds a lot of water, and doesn't dry out too quickly. Using distilled water is recommended to prevent minerals or whatever from accumulating on the foam with repeated use. No problem. A gallon jug costs less than a dollar at Walmart and will last for years. Just pour a small amount of water into a dish and put the sponge in the water. After the initial soaking, future soakings are fast and easy. Gently squeeze enough of the water out to prevent dripping, and you're good for at least a week even in very dry conditions. The sponge gets hard when it is dry, so you can easily check on it; however, I prefer to put it in water once a week, to avoid exposing the guitar to dry conditions. So the sponge is always soft and moist. This ridiculously simple device works great. It's well designed, well made, and looks like it will last indefinitely. I recommend it enthusiastically to everyone.

The problem with all of these tuners is this. A simple program and mic on your phone will be able to accurately convert the frequency to a digital format that can be read for accuracy. i.e. you can download a tuner software on your iPhone and tune your guitar.

But - that's just not easy for me - and many others. I want something right there on my guitar that I can use.

I have looked for super high end, high quality tuners but have not found one. I wanted one with extreme accuracy that is made of high quality materials - that will last a very long time.

Here's the problem. Every one of these guitar tuners (similar to this one) believes they are competing with the iPhone software that's free. So they make these things and CHEAP AS POSSIBLE! yes - low quality plastics and parts. They try to hit the 10 dollar mark.

If you look around, you will see ones that come with capos. (really?! how much money did they actually spend making that tuner if they are including a 5 dollar capo for 10 dollars total?!)

That said. you will see these cheap plastic tuners for around 10-30 dollars. I have bought and returned the ones above 10 bucks for various reasons (reason 1) they could not tune the guitar. hitting a D string seemed impossible - which meant their components were junk - thus they are making bank by putting super low quality parts inside. Reason 2) the plastic buttons were so cheap that you could not turn it on. yes, I bought a 25 dollar "best of the best" recommended tuner and it struggled to tune the d string A AND I could not turn it on as those super cheap plastic buttons were just broken on arrival - complete garbage. there are other reasons - just assume all cheaply made - poor quality components).

After buying the - "best", I went and looked at this brand. keep in mind that I bought a few of the best of the best (as I wanted a tuner on my guitar that I could access at any time). they all had crazy problems with quality. yet - I bought a few of these at completely different times and all worked. that's amazing as zero of the expensive ones worked.

For around 10 bucks, you can't get better.

Memo to these tuner makers (yes - I am an engineer). you are not competing with that software app on the phone. Guys like me would pay to get a super high end quality tuner with super high end parts to have off the end of my high end Martin guitars. I have no desire to use the software on my iPhone. yes - I have a great ear but in concert - its super hard to hear and that thing at the end of my guitar had better be amazing. for now I am ok with 10 dollar cheap tuners (and this brand has proven to be the best that I have found) but I plan to either make my own with great parts or find a maker willing to make something high end.

in any case - get this one if you are looking for a solid tuner. they are very nice and cannot be beat for the price.

I have now used this snake on a few jobs, and have dropped my rating down to 2 stars. This is a very unreliable snake, it's got gremlins! During the first show I used it on, I had a channel go out in the middle of the show. Suddenly my wireless mic stopped working. So I moved it to another channel. The third time I had a channel go out during the show, and again, when I got it home, I could not make it fail. These were all different channels, and all different cables, different instruments/mics, and so on.

At this point, I am calling this snake COMPLETELY UNRELIABLE. Obviously I cannot have channels randomly going out on me in the middle of shows! So, I will be moving this thing to the low-end, backstock piles of random stuff. it will not be going to any more jobs as a primary choice.

**The following was the ORIGINAL review I had posted**
This review is written on first impressions.... I have an event coming up in 2 weeks, so I will edit the review after that if needed.

One of the big questions I had on this thing was "What material is the cable sheath made of?" I could not find any information on this at all, suggesting it is probably vinyl or PVC, rather than a quality rubber. Rubber stands up to heavier abuse, more extreme weather for outdoor use, and is generally more flexible and durable over time. But I also did not have the budget to buy a Rapco, so I figured I would give it a try. Upon receiving the unit, I found the sheath to be relatively rubber-like, but not quite all the way there, so who knows, it could be durable, or not... Don't know yet. My gig in 2 weeks is outdoors, it's going to get sun and heat so we'll see how it holds up.

Overall so far, the unit appears to be fairly well built. The stage box is solid, substantial steel with a nice big grip handle on the top, and wall-mount keyholes on the back. There is a woven strain relief on the box side, AND a metal wire pulling sock on the loose end. both the box and the cable end come with protective fabric bags to keep dust and minor surface abrasions out. The shipping crate is double-layered cardboard so it's heavy and thick for good protection, however it's cardboard so it won't last you very long if you intend to use it for any length of storage or transportation.

The cables are broken into 3 groups of 8, with red, yellow, and blue groupings. They are clearly labeled and there is a small space on the box side that you can write small labels on if you wanted to note something. in-line XLR connectors appear to be decent quality with good strain relief on each one.

I was a bit disappointed to note a couple issues:

First, the strain relief on the box side was woven so tight that it cut into the sheath and there is a permanent groove or nick in the sheath.

Second, the unit is packed so tightly into the shipping box that the cable is almost permanently kinked. Note the photo of the snake here on Amazon, see how tightly the cable is bent under the box as it standing up leaning back on the spool of cable? It's almost permanently stuck like that right out of the box. Not sure how I feel about that in long-term use and frequent transportation. I have some concern about stressing the conductors if I tried to bend it back out straight.

Third, the loose end comes with a thin fabric bag to protect the connectors, but it does not connect to the pulling sock, so it leaves a lot of room for some snagging or damage to the individual cables if you pull it from the pulling sock.

So far it looks like the snake will work for our needs, but I have a mild concern over the durability of the cable sheath. Time will tell, eh?

The Boss VE-2 is just right for my needs (Professional solo singer-guitarist). You can switch the foot pedal to "momentary" which is a must for me because I often use it to punctuate a short phrase here and there. The foot pedal action is smooth and quiet, much better than those clunky stop box metal switches. I like that the unit only has one pedal because I can't look down every time I step on it and if there is more than one foot switch , it is easy to step on the wrong one.

The pedal does not offer multiple harmonies like some others. You chose only one harmony voice, like a 3rd up, 5th up, or octave up (and the same for below). This does not bother me because I think it seems fakey when a solo singer tries to sound like the Eagles or a Gospel choir. I usually just leave it on a 3rd above and put the harmony volume a bit lower than my natural voice. That gives some nice variety to my sound without hitting my listeners over the head with it.

The unit tracks very well and the harmonies sound natural. I have owned and used 3 different brands of harmonizers, and all in all the Boss VE-2 is the best one for my needs simple needs as a solo guitarist-singer.

A tip for first users for a unit like this... If you strum all of your songs you will not have a tracking problem. But if you are finger picking and it seems like the unit is late in finding the right notes, it is because it needs to hear more notes from your guitar in order to make the right choice of harmony notes. To cure this, develop the ability to strum your chord on beat one and then finger pick until the next chord change. That also gives a nice full guitar sound and variety to just repating the same pattern over and over.

The Sampson C01U is the direct-connect USB version of the of their same mic that uses a standard XLR cable connection to a mixer, etc. It allows you to connect the mic to a PC with no other hardware needed. You can use it with a free audio editor such as Audacity or a commercial product such as Adobe Audition. [I did use the software that came with it, so I have no comment on it.]

There are no volume controls on the mic, it is all set via your software system. There are pros and cons to this. On the con side, it is not as easy to make small adjustments to the volume. On the pro side, once the mic is set up to your needs, it stays that way.

I have been using a Blue Yeti mic and tested this mic in exactly the same conditions, literally one after the other. To my somewhat practiced ear, using headphones, the sound of my voice was nearly identical. There have been some reports of people not able to get a decent level out of this mic, but it seems a lot has to do with finding the place in the Control Panel where the level can be adjusted. This was my experience.

Both mics are USB, the Yeti has volume controls, changeable mic patterns and a headphone output.

I would check prices and decide if the features of the Yeti are needed by you. In either case, you will get the same audio results for voice work, etc.
Summary: Good sounding mic, but volume must be adjusted via software.

Text:
I've tried several types of finger picks on my classical guitar and these are the best I've tried. They aren't ideal but they have some good qualities, namely...
-they make a nice, bright sound.
-the tip length is easy to modify (I like mine farely short and they clip easily with fingernail clippers and sand with fine sandpaper).
-they stay put pretty well while I am playing. That is essential when playing in church!
-they work equally well on my thumb. Much more suitable than standard thumb picks.
-they are comfortable enough and don't cause any fatigue or notable pain.
-they are the closest I've tried to feeling like natural fingernails. They are very thin and flexible.
-the price isn't too bad for 12 picks (large size).
-so far they have been durable. I haven't broken one yet.

There are also a couple negatives in my opinion, which are...
-you do need to have farely long fingernails to use these. Not as long as the picks, of course, but long enough to hold them in place under your fingernails.
-they are a little tedious to put on. I usually put um on before I get up to play in public because it takes me a couple minutes to get them on just right.

So, bottom line is, until I find something better these are my best option. If the negatives aren't a problem for you then I recommend trying these.

There are many mini synths that comes and go and for this I must admit, Roland has done a fantastic job with the JD-xi Groovesynth.

I was very hesitant to buy this since I see so many people complain about the lack of creation and producing.
What I soon discovered after watching only 3 videos is that most only cover "quick" pattern making and not the entire structure of a complete song.

Building a complete song is extremely easy. You simply chain patterns together by saving the parameters of each pattern first, then simply copy the pattern.
Another things that is overlooked is how you can "tap" full chords or phrases using the pattern tracks.

Another important feature is many say it only has 4 tracks. That is true until you discover how to "add" a fifth track. If you take the time to discover how to use this Groovesynth (which is very easy to learn), you will soon discover the hidden secrets. The "shift" key has many hidden options.

You can also set up a permanent "template" in the system settings to allow quick song creation where you do not have to set up each pattern over and over. Create a blank pattern using the system functions like "tempo, measures, recording time, click" and other options. Then start to create your pattern. Once you have one created, simply copy and "save" to a new location. Once you have 4 or 5 patterns created, simply "chain them" together.

Another issue many have stated is the lack of sounds? Yes there are not to many until you unlock the creation tools to make the sounds and save them in empty banks. you can also download sound sets from Roland's Axial site.

The large "dial knob" is a bit on the stiff side when selecting your desired selections like vocoder, brass, bass, seq etc. Also when you are using the vocoder and have a live mix and decide to change the big knob to another selection, you will hear the "click" when you turn it thru your speakers.

When you use the vocoder it will also "cut" off track 2 in place of the vocoder. There is a workaround for this. Record your patter first with the "vocoder" parameter fucntion turned "off". once you record your track, enable this setting and when you switch the big knob to another selection like "synth" it will allow you to use the vocoder and track without losing the second track.

The vocoder on the Rolannd JD-xi is 100% better than the Korg Microkorg, Novation MiniNova, Roland FA and Juno DS.

The reason it is better is because of how you can change and access the parameters like effects, depth, tuning on an instant without having to go into settings. The vocoder processing chip is in my opinion more advanced.

If you need more bass or lift on the outputs signals you can change this in the system. You can also assign individual effect for each track and save them. You can turn effects on and off in real time as well.

When you first unbox the Roland JD-xi you will think (wow what a toy), then you plug it in and start to play around with it and think (wow, what a toy).

Until you learn the basic layout and template if the JD-xi you will feel that way. After about 2 hours or so you will say (WOW - this thing really kicks butt)!

Another issue many have complained from reading forums, threads, blogs & videos is the sounds feel "cheap" or don't sound professional like the FANTOM, FA series. That is true because this is not in any way related to those workstations. This is a Groovesynth. Another issue is the "final mix" when ouput to a DAW or digital recorder again the sounds lack the feel of a mastered production.

The workaround for this is simply "add the final effects" once you complete an entire song.

If you take a bit of time to learn the "hidden" feaures and understand how the "shift" key utilizes more functions than most will tell you, you will soon find that this little Groovesynth is the bomb.

I have a couple of grooveboxes like the Roland MC 101 and the Akia Force. I love them both but they take time to learn and have more tools to use to create your songs which can overwhelm you. If you want "SIMPLE", the the Roland JD-xi Groovesynth is for you!

With roughly 64 banks in each category you have plenty of storage space to create patterns and songs. So far I have 22 complete songs saved. You can also "offload" your song data if you lack space or memory to a PC via USB or midi.

To get around the"mini" keys I have a Roland Juno DS that I use as a main controller and the parameters form the JD-xi simply work flawlessly including, Record functions like "start, stop, Rec, Pause, Tap, Erase. Track" etc.

Roland did a very good job on how this works with other modern Roland series controllers or workstations.

I give this 5 stars and 100% production fun!

PROS:
Easy to learn layout
Powerful pattern and step sequencer
Chain patterns
Fantastic effects
Excellent vocoder (compared to Juno DS, FA)
Full integration with 3rd party DAWS like REAPER, MIXCRAFT 8,9 and Audacity.
Works with Zoom R16 & 24 for saving files
Sound engine of the JUNO series and D20

CONS:
The rubber buttons feel a bit cheap
Hard to read lettering on the dashboard
Tweak knobs feel a bit cheap (compared to FA, Juno, Yamaha)
Big dial knob is hard to turn

I am very happy to have purchased the Roland JD-xi, It is not a toy by any means and I have already updated the entire sound library. This review is from what I have learned, discovered and took the time to go "in depth" on the dashboard of the Roland JD-xi.

It is truly worth the price compared to others competitors as a minisynth. The Roland JD-xi has so many features to take advantage of.

In conclusion, you do not even need a DAW, PC or software to create complete songs as this is a stand alone Music creation Groovesynth.
Summary: Better than Expected for a mini GrooveSynth. It's powerful! (in depth review)

While taking a guitar theory lesson, the professor mentioned that he'd been using these strap locks for over twenty years and they were not only super cheap but easy to use and had never failed him. I wasn't even aware of their existence, being familiar only with the more elaborate strap lock systems that require you to install them on your guitar and so on.

I bought a couple and started using them on my guitars and I couldn't be happier. Maybe if you're one of those acrobatic guitar players that like to make the instrument spin around like a rotor this would fall short of your expectations, but for most purposes it seems to work like a charm. I've tried it with a Strat, a Tele, a thin Epiphone SG and a much heavier Les Paul, and it works great with all of them.

Non-professional - as well as non-rich - guitar players know the horrible feeling of having your strap come loose (or even break) while you're in the middle of jamming or performing and, when the guitar is on the heavier side, this often runs the risk of having it fall to the floor or smash into something or someone before you can react. Well, this greatly reduces the chances of that ever happening. You can't beat a deal like that for a couple of bucks.

Text:
[[VIDEOID:70a7651aeadbc44d3991645082ac1cf6]] I recently acquired two new pedals, a Diezel Herbert and an Alexander Jubilee Overdrive, and I especially liked the Diezel Herbert. However, it did not have a headphone jack for silent practicing. I have a Valeton Rushead Max headphone amp which helped a bit when listening through headphones but still wasn’t great, so I tried out a Boss Pocket GT, a Fender Mustang Micro, and this LEKATO headphone amp.

I was very intrigued by this LEKATO headphone amp since it had a separate section for cab sims. I had been thinking about getting a cab sim pedal for the Diezel Herbert, but cab sim pedals seem quite bulky and require a second power supply. For adding a headphone jack to the Diezel Herbert pedal, I found it sounded the best through headphones when I used this headphone amp with the preamp section turned off and only the fourth stock cab sim, a VHT Deliverance cab, turned on. It sounded very similar to playing the Diezel Herbert through my Code 50, however the Fender Mustang Micro sounded pretty close but looser and less defined. With the Fender Mustang Micro, I also enjoyed a lot of the preamp settings and found the Uber amp model on the Mustang Micro sounded pretty similar to the Diezel Herbert pedal, while this LEKATO headphone amp’s preamp models sounded terrible to me. So I decided to keep the Mustang Micro since I can see frequently using it just by itself for silent practice, and sometimes plugging it into my pedals and still having a pretty good tone. The Mustang Micro’s design is also more compact than this with similar build qualities.

Overall, if you are looking for a headphone amp you can use by itself and sometimes plug into your pedals, I would recommend the Mustang Micro even though it is one of the pricier headphone amps at around $100 used or on sale. If you are looking for a headphone amp solely to use to plug into pedals, I would recommend this one since it is less than $50 and makes pedals sound very good through headphones with the option to just have a cab sim on. Supposedly you can even record with this like the Mustang Micro, which I haven’t tried with either, and with the LEKATO apparently you can even upload your own IRs. So especially if you have some cab sims you know you like, you can get this and essentially use it as a cheap, super portable, rechargeable cab sim pedal. So I would essentially recommend this in place of a cab sim pedal or as a headphone jack for pedals, but not as a standalone headphone amp. I do really like the cab sim idea, and hope to see Fender, Vox, and other headphone amp makers add separate sections for cab sims on their headphone amps and include the ability to upload third party IRs. Lastly, I have added some comparison pictures, lists of the preamp models and cab sim models, and a video showcasing the 10 preamp model sounds (I used the stock VHT Deliverance cab sim for all clips, as well as my Epiphone Les Paul Traditional Pro on the neck pickup, and I played through a Vanzom ClimberZ portable speaker).
Summary: Neat idea with cab sims included, but preamp tones sound terrible

If the hole in the headstock is larger than the post, wrap masking tape around the post so that they all are centered in the holes - critical.
Tighten the locking knobs to protect the threads - critical
Insert all 6 tuners and press a piece of straight wood (1/4" thick) up against the bodies of all six at the same time.
At this point, all six tuners are centered and snug (from tape) and in perfect alignment (from the wood).
Hold the wood against all tuners tightly!
Using a hard rubber mallet, tap each tuner. This makes indents where you need to drill.
Use a small punch, awl, or nail, and gently mark the center of the indents - this keeps the drill bit from wandering/walking.
Using a 3/32" bit to drill 1/8"-deep holes.
The indexing pins are .092", and 3/32" is .094 - these will be very snug.
Now you should be able to press these all in nice and tight.
Summary: How to install these great tuners

The Korg Pitchblack is probably, along with the BOSS TU-2/TU-3, considered one of the industry standards for compact pedal bypass tuners for use with guitar and bass. Both the TU-2 and Pitchblack are excellent, and I don't really have an opinion yet as to which is better. However, there are some strengths of the Korg Pitchblack that may lead you to prefer it over other tuners. The primary draw here is the bright light-up display with wide color bars. The tuner displays the note you are closest to, and the colors guide you to the perfect pitch, marked by the green light in the middle (almost like an airplane landing guide). But not only do the lights indicate tone by turning on and off, they actually dim and transition into one another as you go across those semi-tones. You could argue, therefore, that the visual guide is giving you a lot more precision than you would get from a simple on/off light. The tuner works quickly and reliably.

The build quality is outstanding, and it's true bypass. When you step on the pedal, the tuner is on and the guitar signal is off. The switch is also of the "soft button" variety, similar to what you find on some Vox pedals and many boutiques. It has a nice feel to it, though it could be easier to bump if it's in a high traffic area.

This is a great tuner at a reasonable price. It really comes down to user preference, but I've heard many guitarists prefer this one because of its high accuracy and visibility.
Summary: It's an industry standard for a reason!

My Wife bought this instrument for me for a holiday gift, but I wanted to check it out before it gets wrapped.. just in case of damage. I am glad that I did. I also know how to setup and do maintenance on both electronic and acoustic instruments.

The good things about this instrument:
This instrument sounds really good, as it seems to be structurally sound. I do not see any cracks in the body or missing glue around the neck joint.
The strings are nice wrapped around to tuning pags.
The open faced tuners and gears seem to be of a higher quality than others that I have seen.

The bad things about this instrument:
The bridge saddle is WAY too high. I have no issues in regards to setting up a bridge saddle, but I expected Yamaha to be a "bit more" on the quality control side of things and at least have the saddle to a more "normal" height.
The fretboard and body of this instrument was "very" dry. I used some Music Nomad f-one oil on the fretboard and some of the body as it needed it "badly".
The thing that was VERY surprising to me, is there were run-offs / rough spots in the back and sides of the instrument. For a more inexpensive instrument from a no-name company.. I could see that. .but for the price and the Yamaha name.. again.. VERY SURPRISING. I'm also having some issues in regards to getting a partial from Amazon for some reason, but I have amplified that further up the chain on the Amazon side.

Other things to think about:
I was able to tune this to a standard guitar tuning, that is very possible.
The neck is "wide" just like a classical guitar. A lot of people think this is a hybrid instrument of an acoustic guitar and a baritone ukulele. It's really a cross between an Classical Guitar and a baritone ukulele.

Conclusion:
I am sure that I will have a really awesome time opening this on Christmas day and setting up the saddle on the bridge. And I can probably buff out the rough spots in the finish.. but buying this really changed my mind in regards to Yamaha quality control.
UPDATE: I was able to take off a lot of material from the saddle, and lowered the strings, so the playability is better, but I still am a bit suprised in regards to the rough spots in the finish. The instrument should be priced in the $50.00 USD mark. Other than that, it does make a nice portable instrument in regards to classical guitar or baritone ukulele. - Tom

I play in an 80's band and I use this on "And We Danced (Hooters)". The original Melodica he used was the Hohner Piano 36 which is long discontinued and considered by many one of the best ever. I have one (and love it) so was able to compare the Performer 37 to the Piano 36.

The Piano 36 is quite mellow while the Performer is brighter, a little thinner sounding, and slightly louder. The Piano 36 keys don't need to be pressed down far to get sound (they don't go down very far actually) while the Performer 37 keys have about twice as much travel and need to be pressed down a little further to get sound. The Piano 36 keys are a tiny bit wider but not really noticeable while playing. Weight-wise, the Piano 36 is a little heavier and feels very solid (it should, there's more metal than plastic in it) while the Performer case is all plastic, thus lighter. Despite what some negative reviews have said, my Performer 37 came very much in tune, better than my Piano 36 and as good as my (very expensive) Polverini professional Accordion. Another plus for the Performer 37 is that it doesn't need as much air pressure as the Piano 36 to produce good volume.

I purchased this to use live while leaving the Piano 36 at home out of fear of theft or breakage. I can't replace my Piano 36 easily while the Performer 37 is easy to find and VERY cheap to purchase. I'm glad I got it as it sounds great, easy to play, easy to replace (if needed) and comes with a decent gig bag.

I have uploaded a pic of the Performer 37 next to the Piano 36 and an old Hohner student model for comparison.
Summary: Great Melodica at a great price.
