Text: Great cables atva great price.

I really like these fixtures. They're long, and narrow, so that makes them ideal for up / down lighting, mainly because they take up less room across the floor. They're less likely to be accidentally kicked, or tripped over by patrons when used on the flower as up plighting.

I like that the power connectors are set one at each end of the fixture. Makes for more sensible daisy chaining. My only gripe there, is the power output connector is an IEC type. This means you have to go get an IEC male-IEC female cable if you want to daisy chain the fixtures.

These are very bright, but the beam is constrained to about 40 degrees.

These fixtures do an amazing job of back lighting a stand / table scrim.

One thing that makes these fixtures great for washing a wall, or scrim is the fact the red / green / blue LEDs are arranged in a dithered pattern, which helps eliminate the possibility of unwanted shadowing that happens with fixtures that have the LED colours lined up in rows. On the flip side, these fixtures are not really intended to be viewed directly by the audience, so DMXed dancing light patterns are not really feasible. They're great for very nicely washed walls / scrims.

There are other similar fixtures that do have the LED colours lined up in neat rows for those looking to have direct viewable lighting for visual effect with DMX.

Speaking of DMX, these do have DMX in / out, so you can program excellent colour changes, and other cool effects. Oh, I lied about there only being one gripe. There is another. The DMX in / out ports are right next to each other. Would've been nice had they been placed one at each end, the way the power connectors were arranged, but no big deal, really.

The power cords that come with these are very thick, and heavy duty. They should hold up for frequent away missions, ect. However, you will need to spend some time training the factory curls out of these cords so you can neatly coil them for stowage, and lay them out flat for use.

The fixtures are fairly easy to operate, and come with an IR remote. I kind of wish the remotes had directly addressable colour buttons, not just RGB dimming buttons. It seems the numbered buttons are for accessing the various programs. To get to a given colour, you must cycle through the colours with the mode button. However, if your controlling with a DMX board, then you should have not bother at all, other than designing your show.

I do like that on the simple side, you can set these fixtures up as master / slave configurations. Great if you don't have a DMX board. Just use the remote, or control panel to change all fixtures at once. Pretty cool.

The LEDs are HUGE! They're 10mm LEDs. This makes them powerfully bright, and do a nice job of washing, with less shadowing.
Summary: A GREAT WASH LIGHT FOR UP / DOWN LIGHTING OF WALLS, SCRIMS.

I have a grand piano at home, but this Casio is used without resentment when my playing is disruptive to others, or when traveling. Just to be very clear, I am only interested in using this as a piano. I'm not interested in all the computer functions, and other sophisticated electronics that this keyboard has.

I had three major criteria: lightweight, good keyboard action, and good sound. It has all. In fact, sound, with decent headphones, is wonderful. Actually, is pretty close to my grand piano. I do sometimes use the metronome function and also adjust the tension adjustment for the keys to suit my preference, which almost matches my grand piano.

This review will show my purchases is not verified through Amazon. I bought it last winter from our local Guitar Center, on sale for $100 less than offered here. I suggest you shop around, as many vendors on Amazon do not offer the best prices. (however, the price on Amazon is a fair price. I just happened to get 20% off because it was on sale.). Also, I got extended warranty contract, so that the occasional warranty issues others complain about should not be an issue. Fortunately, after five months, so far everything is working perfectly.

Also, I bought a sustain pedal from Amazon, because the one that comes with it is not satisfactory. The music stand that attaches to it is good, and I bought a piano light from Amazon---rechargeable battery, for approximally $20, that is also excellent. I had a piano bench and Yamaha keyboard stand from a prior purchase. Otherwise, for home use, it would have been nice to have the hard stand contained in the bundle, or perhaps purchased separately. Also also have a generic keyboard bag, which I recommend for travel. Mine is quite large, so it accommodates a bunch of music music and everything needed for set up.

Over the years, I have tried many different keyboards and owned five. Also, I tried out several keyboards just before purchasing this one. If I were doing gigs, I may have gotten the Casio Privia 360, for ease of quick adjustments. But for my use, I could not jestify more than double the price I paid. Anyway, I know its subjective but along with the mentioned improvements I have to say this cartridge does indeed deliver in the sound department, it sounds clearer and more defined than my old 95E, and I always loved that cartridge so I wasnt keen to swap it out for some years, but after reading reviews and seeing the engineering changes in both sound and ease of mounting curiosity got the better of me and im glad it did it sounds great -- (Orto-who-?) I play every single day. I've played almost every single day the last 28 years. I mostly finger pick because it is more versatile than flat picking. My finger nails take a beating to the point where they grow out thin and grow out jagged on my strum hand. I bought these on a whim in hopes to grow my nails out and I have been very happy with them. I had to shape up the tip a little bit with a dremel to mimic my finger shape. I also had to change how I plucked/stroked the strings, but it was very minimal and I adapted quickly. The sound is obviously louder than natural nails. The response isn't as good as playing with natural nails, but if you need to give your cuticles a break and or are in fear or ripping a nail from the bed down, these are a good option to use to help grow them back out in a healthy way without resorting to gels or other nail conditioners. It does hurt a little pushing against the top of your nail bed on your cuticle, but if you take a few minutes to re-shape it, it'll feel like nothing is there at all. I have normal man hands, a large fits me perfectly. I have no doubt I will end up buying more of these because Ill lose them. Wish they were a little cheaper though, but still worth it.
Summary: I bought these on a whim in hopes to grow my nails out and I have been very happy with them

The shape and thickness of this pick also enables me to play upstrokes with the pick, getting a good tone, without causing the pick to slip on my thumb. The tone of this pick is clearer and brighter than my old, thick thumbpicks, but the tone is not thin; it just has a clear, well-balanced tone. I have only used this pick a few days, but I think with practice I will learn to hold it between my thumb and index finger like a flat pick when I choose to do so -- not often, but occasionally useful. The stiffness of the medium pick is just right -- not too flexy and not too stiff. I can pick and strum with this pick like never before.

Fred Kelley also offers a "speed" thumbpick. It also fits my thumb well and feels good when I use it, but the tone is brighter because the part of the pick that contacts the string is narrow. I prefer the "more normal" tone I get with this "slick" pick. However, the "speed" pick has also received good reviews. I suggest you try both picks; you may prefer one, or you may want to have both for times when you want the different tones they produce.

[[VIDEOID:a3083c6bf29395bb5f32f86feb90d8ec]] I decided to take a chance on the $169 dollar 7v kit since the $500 dollar jem would have to be upgraded with all new hardware and wiring anyway and man I am pleasantly surprised.
I only really wanted to use the body and neck but after I put it all together I don't want to put it down, I can't stop playing it!!
So I ordered a second to upgrade with all top quality components to see if I myself can build a guitar to rival the $1500 guitar.
I've put 4 days of work in and I've got a guitar that rivals my old S Series that I paid $800 for, It actually feels and plays better than my old JS100.
The body needed sanding.
The neck was only 1/8 turn of the truss off, not bad.
The frets were filed good enough, they need finishing off and tapered, ends smoothed.
The neck pocket fit perfect.
The trick is to take your time, get blueprints and measure and testfit everything 3 or 4 times before bolt/screwing it together.
The pots are audio taper, I didn't expect vintage for $169 anyway.
The pickups sound good enough with an effects box.
I've already ordered FLEOR alnico 5 humbuckers with the second kit. I would be nice if this kit had the option for better pickups at extra cost.
It all depends on how well you put this together.
Measuring the scale length to bolt on the neck is most important.
I've got mine so close to perfect that only the high E had to move closer to intonate using Slinky 9's.
I'll update with a video of the 5 different kits with stock pickup sounds when I get a chance.

Edit: I've now built 5 Leo Jayms kits, the 7v is the best for the money and easiest to assemble.
The (TC Kit) Telecaster is a close second.
I'd advise to not buy the 335, or Strat kits unless you are very experienced in building guitars.
I had Multiple problems with Quality control on both the 335 and Strat kits.
The ST kit (Strat):
The ST kit neck holes were drilled too large and off center,( they need to check the jig at the factory or the empoyees drilling the holes need closer supervision or training) the screws stripped the wood upon hand pressure with a screwdriver. To fix this I'm going to install inserts(adding to the cost)
The Strat copy neck had no relief with the Truss rod all the ways loosened.( to fix this I'll have to file the frets and install a neck shim adding to cost and time)
I won't buy another ST even for a cheaper price. The problem is just a lack of pride in worksmanship and a lazy or nonexistant QC.
That being said you may luck out if you do buy one. The one I was sent was bad.
The 335 kit:
The 335 had binding glue all over it.
The 335 is Pita to wire up and assemble through the resonator hole.
The (wood) block in the body of the 335 looks and feels like pressed cardboard and is so soft you can pierce it with a screwdriver with minimal effort.
My honest opinion is the 335 is nothing but a barely playable wall hanger which seems to have QC problems as well. The same lack of pride in worksmanship and lack of QC shone through on this one.

The TC kit(Telecaster)
Seems to be better QC than the two mentioned above.
I'll update after I get it playable.
I'd guess the 7v and TC kits are better crews at the factory or a different factory altogether. The quality is so vastly different it seems as if the 7v and TC are made in better quality controlled and more skilled factories.

I got this delivered October 20,2017. today is 3/22/2018. out of the box, the finish was nice and uniform. Looking inside the sound hole, you could see everything such as braces and all had been put together professionally, no rough or jagged edges, no extra glue squeezed out from under braces, this guitar was very well built. The tuners are "ok" as some are tighter than others, the strings provided were not that bad, not my preference, but very serviceable. I play every single day  and have played for over 20 years, and they lasted me a very long time. As with any guitar, I took the time to adjust the neck, the saddle and checked for proper intonation. The nut and saddle are made from plastic, which you should expect on an "entry" level guitar for under $100.  The bridge pins are also cheap plastic. Like i said, for an "entry" level guitar, it has more advantages than not. Since I have had this guitar, I knew I would replace the plastic parts with quality pieces if it stood up to my use. This guitar has done that and very well I must say. I busk alot, but never in weather that would do harm to the guitar and the Jasmine S35 has hung in there like a champ. By saving so much money and it being worth it in my opinion, I have replaced the plastic nut saddle and bridge pins with Brass pins and Bone saddle and nut that was purchased from kmise-us, and their products are a wonderful addition to this guitar. Immediately after doing so, I have noticed the tone of this guitar soften and warm up considerably. The guitar was already great for what it was but now with better quality components, it is just getting better and better. I personally use Ernie Ball Regular Slinky .42-.10 gauge strings and I think I might go a little bit thicker but that is a maybe. With replacing the plastic parts, this guitar has elevated itself considerably. For those of you buying this to learn or as a gift to a beginner, do not hesitate, this is a wonderful guitar to learn on, however as I said i have been playing for over 20 years. If you take the time to have it set up out of the box you will enjoy this beast way more than if you leave it alone. By saving money on this guitar. it is easy for me to justify spending extra to get better parts. The plastic nut that was on it was being cut by the tuning of the strings and HAD to be replaced anyway, so if you are just starting out, keep that in mind. I plan on purchasing Grover tuners to replace the ones that are on there now, and again, the money saved by this guitar being priced where it is makes these purchases to me to be of no consequence. I have to repeat here, if you are a beginner or purchasing this for a beginner, please, have the action set up  before going too far with it as this will help learning and hand and finger strain. Out of the box, this guitar will provide you with the tool you need to learn and grow as a musician, but in my opinion, if you want to enhance the quality of this guitar, replace the plastic pieces with those of quality of your choosing.

This was for a pickguard cut out for a strat shaped bass. Two pickup cutouts, some tight radii around the neck and 6 holes for pots and switches. Then the holes were drilled for the pickguard screws –about 1/4” from the edges. It was a chore, but the cuts were clean and the material stayed intact.

I used the Dremel Rotary cutter at low speed and a coping saw blade when things were a straighter cut. If it’s your first time, try it on similar material or use a portion that isn’t on your finished line –for practice. Things can go terribly wrong when the dremel walks or chatters. This can be controlled with technique, but it requires practice. Also a drill bit can get a bit too aggressive on this material near the edge and cause breakout. Plastic bits or a glass spade bit are nice to have and cut without grabbing the material. A Unibit also works well.

There was no chipping of the top layer and the finished product looks as good as anything coming out of a guitar factory these days. Compared to a Sterling or Ibanez pickguard, it’s on par. I got tortoise and pearl green. Both are very typical of the popular instrument wrap on higher end drums or plastic pickguard material. This plastic doesn’t present like a cheap knockoff. Top layer is pretty thin, but it isn’t just a decal. It’s a plastic layer of durable material with depth and a pearl look to it. It was a GOOD BUY... ok, Good bye

Text:
Realistically, there is no best ukulele string for everyone. I love these strings on my laminate mid-range ukulele. The girlfriend thinks they are too harsh for her solid-acacia ukulele and she replaced her strings with flouro-carbons. If you read the ukulele nerd forums, you will see long discussions about ukulele strings and different people disagreeing about which strings are best even for the same brand and model of instrument. Bottom line is the best strings for you are a personal decision, based largely on what sound you like and what kind of music you play and what is your skill level. Strings are cheap enough and easy enough to install that, as soon as you develop a good enough ear to tell the difference, you may as well try a few on your ukulele and figure it out for yourself.

As with all ukulele strings, they do take a while to settle in. I had to tune them after every 15 minutes of playing for the first couple of days. Every 30 minutes for the next few days. Once an hour for the next week. After a month, I only have to tune them a couple of times a week (or when the room is much cooler or warmer).

Note that Aquila "New Nylgut" strings can come in either a brown package or a yellow package. Apparently, they are the same thing, but the brown ones are last year's version. There is a different darker brown package labeled Aquila "Super Nylgut" that is a slightly different formulation for a somewhat higher price. Most reviewers say the price difference is not worth it.
Summary: I like Aquila strings, but my girlfriend doesn't

I've been using this amp for about a month, typical loud house party type music.

At first I was a bit bummed since I chose this one based on a recommendation from a friend, but without much research. Then once I had it, I started seeing similar "4000W amps" advertised for not too much more $$ from other manufacturers and I started to wonder if I had overpaid for what I got. After some testing and more research into the other amps, it's clear that the advertising for the other amps is misleading, and I'm glad I picked this Crown amp as it's a solid amp and works exactly as advertised and expected. The other branded / higher power amps in this price range are advertising momentary-peak power, not RMS power, and they don't even seem to deliver what they're promising in terms of RMS -or- Peak power output.

To do diligence, I pulled out my oscilloscope and checked my Crown amp running into 8-ohm PA speakers with a loud rock mix, and found it's real-life power exceeded the advertised power this set-up. A pleasant surprise! I was seeing Vpeak > 70V, with Vrms ~42V, giving a measured peak output of over 600W/ch instantaneous, and 220W RMS power. This beats their advertised 215W RMS output power into an 8-ohm load by 5 watts without clipping. I haven't tested lower impedance speakers yet, but from what I've seen so far it looks like this amp is solid.

The amp sounds very clear, I haven't been able to notice any distortion or weirdness unless I overdrive it into clipping. It also has all the self-protection features I wanted included, which is important to me as a casual user. Sometimes I screw things up or connect things wrong, so having the amp protect itself is important to me! It's lightweight, loud enough for most any house party, and would cover an audience of 80-100 people with some decent PA speakers on stands in a rock-band or small club setting.

The only complaint I really have is that it needs a 1.4V input to drive it fully, whereas my iPod only puts out about 0.8V. This is more of an iPod output level issue than Crown problem, but it took me a few hours to figure out what was going on at first when I tried plugging my iPod directly into the Crown amp. It worked, but wouldn't really crank as loud as I expected it to and the green output-level LEDs were only about 1/2 way up at full volume. I figured out that to drive this amp from an iPod requires a mixer or pre-amp to get the iPod levels up to a true 1.4V "line level" output. This isn't really a bad thing as Crown correctly designed their equipment to accept a +4dBu signal, but a -10dBu/+4dBu input level switch would have been appreciated by people like me. The work-around I settled on is to just add a small $50 mixer to the loop. Run the iPod into a stereo channel, set the levels appropriately, and send the mixer outputs to the Crown amp. This works great, as the mixer will easily push it to clipping and the levels are matched. Another advantage with this approach is that you get parametric EQ on the mixer, and an easy way to adjust the volume.

My next amp will probably be a bit more powerful, as I'd like to be able to drive my PA speakers to 500W each, but this amp will absolutely be kept as a workhorse, and I'll probably put it into service powering a pair of 500W Subwoofers in bridge mode. I think it's perfect for that task as it will output 1000W into 4-ohms without trouble.

Short version: buy it if you need an amp in this power class. It takes the abuse, and puts out like they say it will. 5-star rating from me. Great for running subs or mains.
Summary: Good amp, power is true to advertised specs

I have had this Roland Mobile Cube for several years now and have been pleased with its performance.  I use it for my solo gigs as an acoustic guitar player and singer. The reverb and guitar modeling are impressive with a classic Roland sound that I feel is really good if not excellent in most cases.  Two channels are on the amp with 1/4" inputs; one for vocal mics; one for guitar (an XLR mike cord will need an adaptor).  To protect and transport the unit I store it using an old leather purse my wife gave me that actually fits perfectly, although Roland does sell a case separately if you wanted to buy one.  My only other reco is to buy the power adaptor with cord---and a separate 25 foot or so extension cord to give you added flexibility when setting up---and saving money on battery costs.  I would buy this amp again if I had to-----and I also value its concise footprint where set-up space is limited.
Summary: Very nice reliable and nice sounding Roland amp for smaller venues

It’s incredibly durable, has a fantastic build quality/design, and it captures audio incredibly well for an interface in this price range, but on the other hand Mackie has really gone downhill with customer service and support.

Prior to this I was using a Presonus AudioBox, but the pre-amps are weak and it injected noise into my signal. The AudioBox was also $100, but the Blackjack is clearly superior in most respects. The only pros for the AudioBox is that it has MIDI in/out and the Blackjack does not, and also with the AudioBox I could plug it into any USB power source (such as a phone charger) and use it as a headphone amp but the Blackjack needs to be hooked up to a computer, though this won’t make a difference for most people because most will want it to be connected to a computer anyway.

I see some reviewers complaining about a hissing noise though I do not experience this at all. I can easily get a really strong and natural sounding signal. This box is definitely built like a tank! My AudioBox feels very cheap in comparison. I really like the tilted design with controls on the front and ins/outs on the back. This thing is simplicity in its finest!

The design/engineering is great, but it’s almost like their engineering team and software/support teams are all on completely different planets. If you do any research you will see that this device was plagued with driver issues which were completely ignored by Mackie for almost a year. It took two years before they were able to release a usable driver. I see a couple reviewers here trying to blame the driver issues on the customers, but it’s clear that the customers were not at fault, it’s just that many of these negative reviews were created when this device was having these issues. It’s quite easy to do a little searching and go back in time on the web to see how bad these problems were (they were bad).

I contacted Mackie about future driver support and they responded saying that they will only officially support up to Windows 7 or OS X 10.7. OS X 10.7 is Lion, which was released way back in 2011! Mackie even said in their email that they haven’t tested the device on newer operating systems. This is bogus because you can still find this interface in retail stores, if they’re going to keep selling it brand new via retail then they should at least support the OSs that people are currently using!

Luckily I’m running this with OS X which doesn’t usually require drivers for these sort of things (thanks to Core Audio) therefor I shouldn’t see a problem for at least awhile (working fine for me on Yosemite 10.10.5), but if you’re using Windows then be warned that Mackie simply doesn’t care about future driver support so if the aging drivers fail to work in the future then this thing is pretty much a brick, unless you want to use unsupported (and often very buggy and/or laggy) drivers.

The interface itself is an easy five stars. This thing is awesome for the price, but these type of products extend past hardware alone and because Mackie is so apathetic with their customer support and they continue to sell these brand new knowing they don’t support current OSs, I must remove a star out of principle, and I nearly removed two.

If you are using a Mac then this is a choice worth considering, drivers aren’t usually a problem, but if you are running Windows then beware! It may work now, but after an OS update you maybe SOL, I don’t think it’s worth the risk.

Text:
Don't get weird about my four stars instead of five. It's been out plenty long enough to pop a few bubbles. If this is the first model you buy in this series, you will surely give it five stars, however, if you had the SP404, or the SP202, SP303, or SP505, then you might notice a few eggs they broke to make this omelette, and I have had this since it came out, so none of this is a knee-jerk reaction.

Lets start with the superficial aspects: the faceplate is the same gorgeous metal layout as the standard SP404, but with the chrome toned-down to a darker shade, and the type contrast reduced as a result. The knobs are the same, if possibly a bit more snuggly nestled into the molded plastic around them (shut up!). Although I prefer real metal or hard plastic, nobody does that, and the pencil-twist action on these knobs is hard to deny.

More pros: The sample time is absolutely ridiculous with the max card. I honestly don't think it's possible to use 32 gigs on this thing, unless you are recording a whole concert onto each pad...literally. Save your 32gig card for your dad's camcorder, and just get a 16gig for this...no, REALLY! You won't run out, I promise! However, this is the key upgrade to this model. The other prime upgrade is effects section was rearranged and beefed up.

Lets take a second to talk about the effects. I am not going to ramble a laundry list to you, but those who got comfy with a certain workflow on the standard SP404 (which is still worth considering, if you get a great deal and need to save loot), those 404 users will need to redesign their workflow. The quick menu on the face is even shuffled, not just the long sub-menu. As usual in the SP line, the effects are sort of cheap around the edges, though notably less so than any model before it. you will find a handful of the effects very useful for your personal needs, and eventually ignore most of the others.

To discuss my effects I prefer, I have to explain a key function that has slowly been phased out of the SP series, which is the real-time action of the mark points and reverse controls. On the very first, the Sp-202, you could use the mark point control as a stutter, and the reverse as a turntable scratch, by pushing them repeatedly. However, in later versions, taking the reverse or mark point off, causes the sample to start over. So, they installed the DJ looper FX to compensate, and with a little practice (or a Kaoss pad on the output) it's easy to forget it's not a real reverse or stutter. That said, the stutter it does provide in the DJ FX is amazingly useful to create sounds never possible prior. As for the other effects, due to the submenu being a crazy long list with only a few useful tools, I started leaving it on the default of reverb a long time ago. The last thing you want at a gig is your face down close to the gear making you look novice, and the reverb is actually incredible anyway.

What I like about the reverb is the depth, whereby it can render drums into ambient sounds. The filter/drive function, the delay, and everything they moved from sub-menu to quick menu made me grumpy at first, but now I insist that these were killer choices, and I use all the face effects all the time live, even with a Kaoss pad beside it.

You may enjoy the sequencer, but I don't. I would rather just use resample and forgo any of their awkward wonky quantization (is there a secret "swing" function I never used?). I don't like to sequence in this button-trigger based way. The SP505 was clearly the superior sequencer of this line, and I think they drug it through the proceeding models just to beef up the stats on paper, but without the detailed screen of the 505, the Sp404sx sequencer is just laughable. However, it can be fun to just toy with a bit for some weird loops. I just could never make anything useful with the sequencer section, and this is the central sampler in my performance rig, with two Kaoss pads.

If you don't use the "resample" feature, then you might be new to the SP series, and not realize what this series really brought to the game to distinguish itself from other styles of sampler. Basically you can perform freely for a crazy amount of time, and have it all recorded on a new pad. In the case of the SP404sx, you can do this over and over and over and over, and hardly ever notice the sound quality drop EVER. This is a really big deal, coupled with this crazy array of effects. So, those effects that I never want to dig for onstage, I can easily dig for at home and resample into a permanent state.

All in all, the eggs broken to cook this up are nothing really, in the big picture. However, if you come across the older models at a great used price, and you think they are just inferior versions of this model, you are wrong. The change to the data card technology changed everything, every time, and each generation of data card, while seemingly less limited, promotes a different workflow, and different effect styles entirely. This is why Madlib/Doom/Dilla insisted that the Sp303 was superior for vinyl sampling, and it's resale value is stupid high as a result. Each SP box has cool tricks that can be done based solely on it's special limits. On the SP202 I used the real-time delay to make a RZA loop sound like an ever-varrying drum-n-bass beat, but on he SP404sx the delay pauses between each timing change, so I would have to resample several timings on several pads, taking much longer and possibly failing even after that time. So, if you have any earlier SP series samplers, I deplore you to NOT trade them in, but just save the extra money needed to keep them as you buy this or other models.

The sp404sx is a truly amazing box, which could wind up being the final generation of hardware in the SP line, but it very much caters to the experimentalist, who is willing to overlook things like no clock saying how many minutes into a sample you are, or no visual for cutting the start/stop point of a WAV. The way the samples are loaded from a computer to the card has never been faster or smoother, and really this makes up for almost all my gripes, considering how my KP3 and Koassilator pro pick up the slack. The compact design and darkened industrial face plate are very welcome design elements. Some people hate the glowing orb, but your pals will probably act impressed at first glance. Overall, this is one of the greatest samplers ever made, and every bit as unique as every other pervious model. You really can't get anything better for under $1,000, unless it's a controller/software bundle, and maybe not even then.
Summary: Another unique entry to the SP series, unlike any other sampler.

Text:
Got board within a year plucking a new Taylor elect/acoustic on this little pup. Thinking as I was going back to electric, I'd sell the Fish too. I assumed the input would be voiced for piezo pickups and the tweeter would be fizzy even when treble is rolled off. Basically not usable for an electric unless the tweeter was unhooked right?

Wrong. I plugged in a Les Paul style guitar and was amazed at the rich, full clean sound. The EQ was responsive and dialed in quickly to a warm tone where the treble/tweeter seemed transparent not brittle. The shocker is how well it takes to pedals. I first ran an analog delay which sounded sweet. Out came the Zen Drive which adds overdrive simulating tube breakup. This thing sounds great! I left the tweeter in and use in exclusively as my main amp. Treble is about 9:00, bass 12:00, mid 9:00 and it sounds neutral not crispy.

I am a solid-state amp hater by nature. They don't have tube sag or that damped feel. They produce uneven harmonics tube amps filter out. They can have brutal attack. This Fishman has changed my mind. I can get a full, warm, tube-like sound out of this thing and prefer the internal reverb to spring cans. At "living room levels" you can turn it up a bit and she fits in very nice for jams sessions. Got some odd looks from my "snob boutique" amp friends that spot it. Guess I'll have to pop the emblem off and glue on a Marshall logo. The haters are blown away when they hear this thing. I love the vintage look and size. Keeper!
Summary: Dare to plug in an Electric??

In response to another reviewer, which complained about the adjustment procedure (which takes only a few seconds). Am I alone or is it the "tune" of the guitar that is most important issue when changing capo position? When using a capo further up the neck, why would anyone assume that spring pressure is equal? I've used Both types for years and nothing comes close. Very little weight, small and simple, fits easily in your pocket and adjustable for all types of music, using just the right amount of pressure to where you capo. The more you use it the more automatic it becomes to adjust. It is never in the way, and does not ever become an obstruction when playing (like a roller capo). Then again, there are those that probably never even notice if the additional pressure of a spring type capo is pulling their strings out a bit (which if you aren't tone deaf you'll need to retune). Grant you, there are capos that claim to be more automatic in process, but at a cost of adding additional weight to your axe, thus changing your neck weight, which affects specific guitar tonality. I’ve been a casual guitar player for many years, using Boss and Behringer pedals, running them through a clean amp to get the sounds I want. With all of the electronic advancements for smartphones and tablets that provide an all-in-one experience, I find that I like using an actual foot pedal, choosing exactly what I want rather than relying on a myriad oftentimes inferior programs to do the work. I also like the ability to plug into something tangible that I can fine tune without using a magnifying glass on my smartphone or tablet.

I had never heard of GOKKO pedals before. They fall into the mid-price range of $30 to $100 and come with a variety of bells and whistles. I've never been a fan of amps with the distortion built in. I've always preferred a clean amp with the option to add in pedals. Generic distortion is fine when you’re just starting out, but over time, once you discover all of the remarkable sounds you can get out of a few select foot pedals, you’ll never go back. GOKKO’s SonicFire Distortion Guitar Effect Pedal provides the means to pull some crisp sounds from your speakers with the ability to fine tune level (volume), gain (distortion), and tone.

The results I got out of the amp where what I expected – clean, clear gain and sustain. There was no interference, no pops, static, or lost connections. With the metal casing and a heavy duty switch, it’s a solidly built foot petal that should last for years.

It comes with a 9 volt battery adapter that plugs into the DC-adapter plug. You will have to supply your own 9 volt battery or DC adapter cord.

Unfortunately, the pedal comes with no paperwork or explanation of any kind, so you have to have some idea of what you’re doing and what you want to accomplish. The GOKKO site doesn't offer too much in the way of helpful information either. Essentially, your guitar plugs in on the right, and the cord out to your amp is on the left. Set the level for the volume, the gain for your distortion, and the tone for clarity.

Overall 3 and ½ stars – average of 4.
Summary: A Good Mid-Range Pedal for Crisp Distortion

This is a good stand. It's sturdy and doesn't creak. It comes with everything you need to set up a mic, including a holder for the handheld types. I got a Yeti X just like every other streamer, and this stand has everything you need. The pop filter is big and works well enough. The clamp has foam on top, but not the bottom, so maybe stick some cardboard in there if you don't want to mess up the underside of your desk. The built-in headphone holder is nice, but can be awkward to use if the closed end of the clamp is facing you. It probably works better if you mount this thing near a corner so that the holder faces your side instead of facing away. This arm doesn't reduce vibrations, so a shock mount is still a good idea. My mic still picks up the pounding of my keyboard while on this arm. I wish that the joint connecting the two halves of the arm could swivel, but I suspect that would require a different (and significantly more expensive) design. There are cheaper solutions available, but they're not strong enough for this beast of a microphone. The gooseneck pop filter is awkward to get into place, but it's good once it's attached. Overall, I'm very happy with this product and would recommend it.

I’ve spent an hour noodling with this “Digital Mixer” (figuring out its features takes all of 5-10 min). For me it was an “upgrade” from my ICICLE XLR to USB encoder (and an analog Yamaha mixer). I bought the X3+ for two reasons:

1) direct to USB connectivity;
2) tone controls (technically I wanted a compressor but I figured the tone controls would give me a reasonable home office caliber approximation);
3) price.

It all works and it offers a feature set that lets the marketing folks at Creative check a bunch of “has feature x, yup” “has feature y, yup” checkboxes. But don’t be fooled. The A/D in this thing is COMPLETE GARBAGE. Mixing any inputs produces a low res, clumpy mess for about a half second until the firmware in this thing catches up. Later it will tend to fall back to clumpy garbage every few seconds as it becomes overwhelmed. Even when it’s “on song” the output has an obvious “flip phone” sort of vibe.

If you don’t need multi channel mixing just get a (Blu) ICICLE (5 stars but single purpose). The tone controls are “just ok” and the entire experience is soured by the garbage encoding. The sound clips and karaoke tuning crap are well... just crap. If you want similar mixing and such functionality drop the $500 it takes to get a device from Rode or it’s competition. I won’t be sending my X3+ back but I’m not the least bit impressed.

[[VIDEOID:56c16335fbb0b50993ed10f60b762bfd]] It's $100 more for the integration of a $10 LED matrix panel that doesn't even show up correctly on camera most of the time. But does it work? Yes.

The mic quality is definitely decent, equivalent to a good $60 mic, but toss on the Razer tax and its $80, then the RGB tax and its $180. The main problem is with the idea as a whole. Recording a person and a screen at the same time always bring difficulties, often with the screen being too bright and blending together or washing out the rest of the scene. Unless you dim everything down on the mic (with its poor customization, having to map each pixel one at a time), it'll become a glowing blob. I don't see why you would want to use this rather than an on-screen emote system with a much higher resolution and with no negative impacts on the rest of what's in-frame.

It does feel like a proper finished product, however. In many games, it'll have preset animations that it does at different stages. In Apex Legends, as an example, it'll pulse red as you're loading, and go through dozens of transitions/animations as you're running around, using your abilities, getting shot, shooting, etc.

The software was a pain to get working, but once I got it working, the twitch implementation worked essentially flawlessly. You can set custom emotes to chat messages, subs, follows, cheer, raids, etc, and they all work with almost no delay. But in the end, it's an expensive novelty. Razer is selling a $60 mic and a $10 LED matrix together for $180. I don't think it's worth it, but if you've got money to burn and want to play around with a new toy for streaming, it'll work.
Summary: It's not worth the money, but it works

I play guitar a lot, but I've only been playing a few years and I have limited exposure to strings. That said, I have a background in piano/keyboard and I've been playing music all my life. I've been through about a dozen different sets of strings on a few guitars I own. These run the gamut from inexpensive (Ernie Ball Earthwood) to standard (D'Addarios) to high end Elixirs and Cleartones. The Elixir Nanoweb is my second favorite I've used on both my Yamaha and Ovation A/E guitars with the Elixir Polyweb being my favorite thus far. Here's why:

The coating does affect string sound and I noticed it for the first session or two of playing. After that, what stood out to me was that the strings never lost their tone. For weeks. Ernie Ball Earthwoods sound great when installed, but after a week of playing, I can feel and hear them start to deaden out. The Elixirs take a hit on day one and two, but they don't wear down for weeks at a time. Months even. To me, by the time I am on my fifth session of playing (in one-to-two hour sessions), the Elixirs start to surpass the others and they continue to shine at that level for quite a long time. In fact, degradation of sound was so minuscule on my last set that I never heard it. I changed out the strings when I began to see visible marks at the fret and pick area (assuming where the coating was starting to chip/wear). The change did make them sound better... I could tell after I put the new ones on that the old ones were worn, but it was minor.

In short, you pay three times more for these strings, but you should get five times more life out of them. To me, choosing a $5-$6 set of strings instead is being penny wise and pound foolish.
Summary: The durability of these strings plus good sound makes them a smart buy

I have mixed feelings regarding this KLIQ UberTuner. They are below and I hope they are helpful to someone purchasing it.

PROS:
1. The tuner only picks up pitches when the device is clipped onto the head of the instrument. This is a neat feature because sometimes it is difficult to get an accurate reading from other brands because they are potentially picking up other sounds; other instruments trying to tune or background chatter.
2. It has a sturdy look and feel to it. It looks like a serious device and feels like one too.

CONS:
1. I am not a fan of the slide & snap piece to replace the battery. It tends to get stuck and there is not an easy grip on it so pull off; the device is small and that makes it difficult to get any leverage. It also is strong enough to stay on tightly, but because it is a chip of plastic you don't want to be too forceful that it might break. It's a pain to get on and off is what I am saying.
2. I cannot tell if this tuner is too sensitive in it's reading or inaccurate. I have another brand of tuner that is specifically designed for Ukulele's and it picks up the pitch to good accuracy. This tuner, on the other hand, gets very shaky on the reading that an instrument is under or over-tuned. It'll start to waver when you appear to have it in perfect tune (when the digital dial is right on the center)---it bouncing backwards or forwards.

OVERALL: I have tried this on a guitar and an ukulele and I appreciate that it has multiple settings so that you do not need many tuners, but I find that it's functionality and overall design are not great. It kinda has a crummy user interface in my opinion.
Summary: Maybe more features isn't always the greatest

This is a pretty great looper pedal, and it's definitely been fun to experiment with. Here are my key takeaways that you should know before purchasing:

- When it says 3 tracks or 3 loops, what it essentially means is 3 distinct songs. There's an aspect of multi-track recording (which I'll comment on in a second), but the switch lets you toggle between 3 of your separate recordings.
- Within each loop, however, you can record multiple layers one-at-a-time. What I did was use my keyboard to create a basic drum loop. Then, record a rhythm guitar track on top of that. Then while that is playing, I practice my lead guitar skills. (Spoiler, I need more practice)
- One you record one layer (like drums), and you start recording the next, you can delete that next layer. This allows you to record one layer at a time to get things right.
- It definitely is up to you to create good loops, and it takes some practice. It starts recording immediately when you hit the switch with your foot. It takes some coordination to record those 2 or 4 bars before hitting stop. It helps to put the drums down first as a quasi-click track.
- It stores the songs on internal memory. Even after turning off my power switch and unplugging it, it keeps the recordings.
- It has the good new standard layout: IN on the right. OUT on the left. Power along the top.
- Remember to place the looper all the way at the end of your pedal board

The only downside (and this is mentioned in other reviews as well) is that the LEVEL knob behaves a little weird. The LEVEL controls both the playback and the recording volume? It's hard to describe, but regardless, I found that playing my unrecorded lead guitar over the loops works fine.

I'm having a lot of fun with this, and I'm slowly getting better. I normally play guitar while sitting in a beanbag chair, but accurately clicking this pedal pretty much demands you stand up or sit in a chair so that you have good control over hitting the record button.

The controls take some getting used to. Double-click to stop. While stopped, hold down the foot switch to delete, etc. You'll want to keep the small manual next to you.

(One note: I don't really like it when pedal vendors create one page for multiple completely separate pedals. This review is ONLY for the looper. I have no idea what the other effects are).

Thanks for reading! I hope you found this review helpful!
Summary: Great budget looper pedal;  definitely takes some practice

Decent construction, and can not knock the price for the quality. Compare apples to apples, as a budget mic boom this fits the bill. If you have a lighter mic like the Blue Snowball or Yeti this will do the trick. The mounting bracket is separate from the arm in the box, just loosen the clamp screw attach to your mounting surface (I chose a glass topped desk) tighten, insert the arm and tighten the arm screw and your good to go. Assembly and attachment took all of five minutes. I tried on a couple different thicknesses of desk to check the stability of the mounting clamp and all seems fine. As a budget item this arm is fine, sure it won't stand up to the $1,000 super quiet broadcast arms... but then this things under $20. For someone doing a podcast or someone who wants to get that mic stand off their desk this is perfect.

I tried three different Microphones in the arm, and as expected it could not handle the weight of the larger mics. The Blue Snowball and the Blue Yeti work just fine. but the Blue Bluebird was too heavy with the shock mount cage and all. I am not one bit surprised by this, and as I said as a budget arm this does the job well. The only ding I would give the arm is that there is no way to easily tighten the part where the mic screws to the arm. There are quick release screws on the base and on the middle of the arm, so you can't completely tighten it down rock steady if you need to. This is a small issue for me, I would buy this again and I would recommend to anyone.

This adjustable keyboard stand is one of those things you need if you are in the habit of taking your keyboard on the road or only set it up occasionally.

Just make sure you get the longer ones on the bottom, and place the bars so they even out. (The holes in the crossbars are offset to match the legs.)

The hinge seems sturdy enough, and the locking mechanism is easy enough to operate. The real test is to see how it holds up over time and stands getting tossed around on road trips. This is good if you want something light; heavier/sturdier variations are available.

If you know audio or have been in the industry Mackie is a well respected name and rightfully so. This manufacturer is well known as their products speak for themselves. The Mackie condenser microphone is well built and offers crisp clean audio. With the built in controls you can adjust audio capture to suit your environment. Like many others, I have and absolutely love the JDS Atom headphone amp.

Except for the knob...
I don't mind the plastic build quality at all. What bothered me about the Atom's volume knob is the depth. It's very shallow and smooth, so it doesn't provide much "feedback" when turning it.

A quick search led me to these knobs. NaturaIly, ordered a set in blue, as it's the greatest color in the known universe. They're also available in other colors. As much as I love the blue, others have used the black version and it looks pretty slick on the Atom.

Changing out the knobs is easy; the stock Atom knob pulls off without a lot of force. The aluminum knob fits the Atom pot shaft perfectly and is held in place by a set screw secured to the flat portion of the Atom's pot shaft with the included allen wrench.

I love the feel of these knobs. They're knurled, but not sharp, so you get a good grip on them without shredding your fingers. The depth is perfect; more than the stock Atom knob, but not so much that it looks like you have a clown nose on the front of your amp (unless you get the red one...). It's also slightly smaller in diameter than the stock Atom knob, so more of the power led behind the knob is visible.

A worthy upgrade to the amazing Atom.

[[VIDEOID:17abe274782674bcb2032be3838a19b6]] This is a very cool audio console for the beginner or intermediate level podcaster OR someone who wants to do some basic voice over work. The "Pro" sound effect with everything adjusted to personal preferences using the included XLR mic sounds EXACTLY like making a recording from a sound booth. This would be an ideal setup for someone recording their voice while reading a script.

CONSOLE FEATURES:
For the price, it is definitely the most capable console I have used. There are a lot of options here that are not found on others in this price range, and a few that work substantially better. The ability to adjust LO, MID, and HI as well as the recording volume and microphone volume all at the same time is the main selling point for the console. You can't get anything else at this price that does ALL of that and has the extra features. This brings the CONSOLE up to intermediate level, for sure.

I had a lot of fun with the different voice pitches, too. The female voice can get glitchy, but if you adjust how you talk you can get a nice effect. If you speak too softly, the audio does sort of vanish, though. The other voice effects sounded fine, though. Robot voice....eh....more like B-Movie Monster. It's not bad, really, but should probably be labeled differently.

Some of the built in sound effects are great. Kids cheering, applause, booing, and the crow sounds are pretty useful. Would like to see a firmware update allow you to overwrite these with your own effects, though. That'd be pretty useful. Definitely more useful than only having only four programmable buttons.

Music Only, Side Chain, and Loop Back work as expected. No complaints! The De-Noise button, however, cuts words off very abruptly causing some distortion if you have a lot of short pauses and it will take practice to use. If you speak clearly and fluidly, this may not be an issue for you...I, however...pause often... Luckily, with the foam cover on it there isn't much background noise on the recordings anyway. I didn't use the De-Noise button, and I didn't have to do any cleanup in post.

The auto-tune works really well overall. I'm not much of a singer, but I imagine this could be useful for someone who wants to do a little bit of music work. There are definitely a plethora of outputs and in inputs to facilitate song production for someone just starting out.

My recording software picked the device right up. Output through USB-C to PC was flawless. I didn't have any issue crossfading through the sound effects or music (using my MP3 player). It just worked really well and is pretty intuitive. Big labeled buttons and wheels are a lot easier to understand than thirty tiny knobs like my first console.

MICROPHONE:
The included microphone is just okay. It's going to give you a voice-over sound, but it isn't anything special. I would absolutely advise investing in either a quality lapel mic or even a shotgun mic or two to pair with this. It has TWO microphone inputs so you can easily set this up for interviews during a podcast. I prefer the audio I get using a powered shotgun mic with built-in gain settings.

One thing I want to make note of here is that this does NOT supply enough power to run other XLR microphones through the console and included XLR to 3.5mm cable. I have not tried using this in conjunction with a phantom power supply, however....If you plan to, do so at your own risk! It does provide enough oomph to power basic shotgun mics, desktop microphones, and all other mics natively meant for or compatible with the 3.5mm jack.

CONCLUSION:
If you're just starting and want a solid audio experience that just works and doesn't have a huge learning curve...This thing is great. This is absolutely podcast making gold, even using the included beginner microphone. If you have a good 3.5mm mic, I can see this being a great upgrade to more inexpensive consoles. If you've got a nice console already, this isn't going to bring you much you don't already have. For me, this is a total upgrade. I'm still experimenting with different microphones, but the console itself is well worth it.

Text: I have had quite a few amps over the years and have heard so many people say these sound really, really good for the money. My Les Paul sounds darker than my Midtown and my strats also sound different from each other(one has Dimarzio Areas and the other vintage pickups).  The gain comes on pretty fast and it'll do 70's rock and roll all day and sounds really good.  The reverb is better than I expected and gets pretty lush if you turn it up.  When you turn it up the guitar gets very reactive and you can really have some fun.  It's pretty darn loud for a little amp.  It's also light weight and relatively small for a 12" speakered amp.  It does have an FX loop but I haven't tried it.  No standby switch which you would expect for something in this price range.  I'd say if you wan't a fun little practice amp with good tones for cheap this is it.  You definitely won't find anything better at this price.

24 pieces of 12in x 12in acoustic foams for under $100 is an inexpensive way to improve room acoustics. It removed all perceptible echos in my room. On some reviews...I've read a few people comment on reviewers trying to pop their bubble that this foams don't have any soundproofing abilities in them. So here are a few questions for you know-it-all people:

1. If the Auralex Studiofoam has a NOISE REDUCTION COEFFICIENT (NRC) rating of .80, meaning it absorbs about 80% upper-mid to high frequencies...does it mean that it does NOT reduce the sound transmission to other materials behind the foam?

2. Then you would argue that soundproofing is the art of isolating the sound from one room to the next or from the outside world. And sound absorption does not stop the transmission or movement of sound. I would counter argue: if parts of the sound have been absorbed by the foam then the transmitted sound have been reduced. Is it safe to say that a reduced sound is a quieter acoustic transfer?

3. If the foam can absorb some frequencies & reduces the amount of sound being transferred from the foam to whatever material behind it then isn't having some sound-absorbing abilities also the same as having some soundproofing abilities?

I am not an acoustician but a big part of sound is subjective dependent on how each individual perceives it. Yes, there are scientific ways to interpret sound but there is no concrete evidence if there is a standard way of how individual brains interpret perceived sound. So just because these people have read definition of things on the internet doesn't mean they have keener or more sensitive ears than everybody. If a reviewer says that he thinks his room got quieter after he installed these foams then that is his perception. Read reviews as you please, take it with a grain of salt and no need to pop other people's bubbles by commenting on their reviews that they're wrong.
Summary: Will reduce upper-mid to high frequency trasmission.

Text:
I actually have three of these - a red one, a blue one, and a black one. The black one is the one pictured here, with 'chromed' hardware and inserts for the legs which are included with it (unlike the blue and red models). The pickup on the black one is hotter than the ones on the other two.

I bought the red one first. I bought it to learn to play lap steel ten years ago (I played guitar for many years and was familiar with slide guitar already, but this is a different animal). Then I bought the blue one to keep tuned to a different key, and hot-rodded the red one with a Seymour Duncan pickup. Then I bought this black one with the legs. I also bought a Carvin 8-string along the way, so now I have 10 years of experience playing lap steel. Now on to the review -

You will find this model of lap steel marketed under different names - Rogue, Artisan, etc; they are all the same instrument. As I wrote above, the black one has a hotter pickup than the others, but the hardware is essentially the same on all three. The bridge and saddles are like those on a Telecaster, and the tuners are the type found on slotted-head classical guitars. They have a shorter scale (21", IIRC) than most professional lap steels, but that isn't too big of a deal.

For the price, this is definitely an adequate instrument to learn on - you can't expect professional quality for $100 or less, can you? Here are a few "cons": The input is in exactly the wrong place for a right-handed player; you need to use a cable with a right-angle plug so that the plug is not in your way when you play. The nut is made of wood (it appears to be rosewood), and breaks easily (it also can be replaced easily). The pickup is very noisy. The inserts and legs are made of the cheapest metal possible and must be handled with great care or they will break in very short order.

All in all, these are pretty cool for a guitarist (or anyone else) to fool around with and learn to play lap steel. There are many many youtube videos and a wealth of information online to get you going. Buy yourself a decent steel like a Lap Dawg and you're good to go.

- I dumped my Shure SM58 for Sennheiser e838/840 about 6 months ago, the reason was the e838 sounds clearer and has much higher output than the SM58. Have 4 e838s and have been looking to buy 2 more but can't since the e838/840 are now discontinued.
- Then I came across the C195. It was sold as a B-stock for $29, so I bought 2 figuring it was cheap enough to take a chance.
- I just did a comparison between the e838 and C195. Have them both connected to a Presonus Studiolive 16.0.2, set for the same gain & eq setting (which I usually use for the e838s during live events - I do live sound for events as a side job for fun). Obviously the C195 requires 48V, which is not a problem with the Studiolive.
- The C195 sounds much clearer, yet it also sounds fuller on the low frequency. It was much louder than the e838, so I had to bring its fader down, as well as decrease the low EQ by 1 notch.

Here's what I had on the Studiolive in order to get the same volume level and almost the same sound on both mics (you can refer to the Presonus Studiolive 16.0.2's console picture to get an idea):
- Sennheiser e838: fader at U, Mic/Line Gain at 2 o'clock (+3 notch from middle), Low Freq 155, Low Gain -4
- CAD C195: fader at U, Mic/Line Gain at 11 o'clock (-1 notch from middle), Low Freq 155, Low Gain -6
At the above settings, I still prefer the clear presence of the C195 over the e838 (and I have been happy with the e838 for over 6-month use & over 10 live events).
- Also important: the e838 gave more handling noise than the C195 (I rubbed my hand on them while holding). I could not really hear any handling noise from the C195. It seems CAD really knows how make quiet mic, as I also have an E100S Equitek which is also dead quiet.
I guess it's time to dump my e838s and upgrade to C195, even though the C195 is cheaper.
I have no connection nor being associated with CAD.
Summary: Better than Sennheiser e838/e840, and obviously much better than Shure SM58, if you can give it Phantom power

Pretty much Mackie’s answer to the Behringer Xenyx 1202FX mixer. They are extremely similar in function, channels, layout, etc., with only a few parameters like EQ frequencies being different, as well as being a bit larger.

One wonders if Behringer is OEM-ing these for Mackie, they are so alike.

Sound quality is good, fit and finish are good, except for a sharp edge on each side of the mixer, where the side pieces come up above the main board level. The Behringer version has a better fit and finish - no sharp edges. A small nitpick, but could be important to some.

The special effects (mostly reverb, with some chorus and flanging) are pretty much par for the course for a small mixer like this, and I assume they all use the same DSP chip for that. Not super studio high end effects, but usable for many tasks.

The connectors are all tight, the slider moves well and seems good quality, all the pots and controls seem to work well, and there is not a lot of noise. This is a very nice little mixer, and I think you would not go wrong if with it if you are in the market for this kind of mixer.

These small mixers won’t cut the mustard for your new hit release, but they are great for podcasts, small PA setups, and various other small mixing uses, even computer audio systems. I use a great many of these kind of mixers in my “day job,” and they are great.

Now that Mackie has thrown their hat in the ring in this small mixer market, those who are brand loyal can have a nice Mackie branded small mixer to do all those small to medium mixing tasks. I have had to access Mackie customer service directly once in the past due to a reseller’s intransigence, and the regional rep was instantly in touch and fixed the problem immediately without hesitation. That quality of customer service can be worth a lot.

A bit more expensive than a Behringer, but then there are a lot of people who feel that the Mackie brand name on an item is worth it. In any case, this is a nice little mixer, and I will not hesitate to put it to work on any number of audio projects.

Recommended. Definitely give this beastie a look.
Summary: Mackie's idea of a small mixer

Text:
I have put this style strap lock on nearly all my guitars (and I have a LOT of guitars). However, once you mount the other half on your favorite strap (or few straps) you have a bunch of "tops" left over.

So it is nice to be able to buy just the bottom button, save a few bucks, and not grow the collection of tops.

They should include the felt washers with these as they do with complete strap lock sets. After all, the felt washer goes with the button portion of the system. But you can buy those washers separately in 12 packs - enough for 6 sets of buttons.

These are reliable when properly installed and when used with a compatible top half. I've used these for more than a decade, including live gigging. I have them on at least 25 guitars and I've never had a failure.

Make sure you know how to install them. I hear some people talking about these failing but it's inevitably always improper installation or lack of maintenance in every case I've heard.

You don't use your old screws. You use the provided screws and you shim the old holes with wood shims and wood glue before screwing the new screws in, if the old screw holes are larger. This is what a pro luthier will do if you pay them to install the strap locks. You can use toothpicks or match sticks cut to size to do this, along with any wood glue. Not super glue or whatever basic glue you have sitting around - Wood glue such as titebond or elmers WOOD glue.

You also need to make the the top half that mounts to the strap is TIGHT. Use wrenches. TIGHT! It is not a bad idea to put thread locker on the threads of the nut so it can't come loose once tight. But regardless, you should periodically check the strap to be sure the nut is tight on the strap lock. You should also clean the button and the top half with Deoxit and then oil it with WD-40 or a light machine oil periodically - this is a metal to metal contact. It eventually starts wearing metal grindings if you don't lube it.

If you start trying to modify them, or you use them with cheap knockoff top halves...don't be surprised when your prized guitar takes a hit on the concrete. Do it right and protect your guitars. If aren't sure you can do it right - pay a luthier to install them properly including mounting the top half to your strap and installing the buttons on your guitar.
Summary: Great if you have several guitars with straplocks, but tend to use 1-2 straps for all of them.

What is interesting is that I normally just tear open the wrapper, decimate the box, take it out, plug it in and get to work, but not this time. This time for some unknown reason, I took the time to read the installation instructions. I downloaded software and driver updates and then proceeded to install the unit. I got the "unknown device".

Here is where I decided that Presonus is not my idea of a good product provider. I see a lot of discussion about this problem. So, it is obvious that Presonus is aware of the problem. Yet, there is no one available over the weekend to help customers through the issue. What if it is a procedure to follow or a file to download or even an issue that can be resolved via remote access? All of these would be fine. Then if there is no resolution the customer at least feels like Presonus cares about their customers enough to at least try. I am then not opposed to buying other Presonus product.

I am not unrealistic. I know, sometimes even expect, products to fail prematurely or even to not work at all. However, what i do not expect is the company leaving their niche customer community without help from 5:00 p.m. Friday to 9:00 a.m. Monday morning (Central Time). maybe this is not an issue to some, but this is far below the "fails to meet the standard" grade in customer service for me. Does Presonus realize that there are competitors, very strong competitors, in the market? Does Presonus realize that once a customer has paid for the Presonus product, the $50 or so difference in price between theirs and a competitor's more expensive offering is not so great a chasm anymore?

When I train sales professionals, I always tell them that mishaps and errors are almost inevitable. However, these are not what break business relationships. It is the lack or poor execution of a plan to address them. Presonus has made it into my "what would be your response as a customer, if... ?" lessons.

Purple has always been my favorite color and I have no plans to buy a purple guitar anytime soon, so I decided to add some purple to the cherry sunburst Epiphone Les Paul Traditional Pro that I purchased last fall. I saw that this Amazon page mentioned that the pickguard would only fit Gibsons, but I didn't see any other purple Les Paul pickguards and I figured these should still fit the arched-top Epiphone Les Pauls, which should be essentially identical to Gibsons, and that the page was likely just warning about the cheaper flat-top Epiphone Les Pauls. When I got it and put it on top of the original pickguard for my Les Paul, it seemed that it was essentially identical. However, when I took the old pickguard off and attached this one, I found the upper screw hole in the pickguard did not align well with the screw hole in the guitar. I'm not sure if this is because this is a cheap pickguard which wasn't cut 100% accurately or if it is because even the arched-top Epiphone Les Pauls are ever-so-slightly different than Gibson Les Pauls. Luckily, the cut-out for the neck pickup on the pickguard is very tight, and the pickguard seems to stay on the guitar well without the upper screw being in (this pickguard also came in a plastic bag, so I just put the old pickguard and the screw in there for now). It doesn't look great with just having a hole there and not a screw, but I don't currently perform with this Les Paul and, especially since the purple doesn't match perfectly with the cherry sunburst finish, if I ever did perform with it I would probably put the original white pickguard on. Other than how it looks with just an empty hole, I actually kind of like the idea of the neck pickup cut-out on the pickguard being tight enough to just hold the pickguard on and wish someone made a pickguard without any upper screw that worked like this, since I think just not having a screw hole there would be more visually appealing. Lastly, while my original Epiphone pickguard for my Les Paul doesn't seem super high quality, the quality of this pickguard does seem slightly lower than it, so I imagine if you are buying this for a Gibson Les Paul the drop in quality will be even greater. The main quality issues with this is that the plastic seems slightly thinner and cheaper than my original Epiphone Les Paul pickguard, and also there is some plastic fuzz on the front edge of the pickguard which I tried to take a good picture of, though had some trouble getting it clearly. Overall, this pickguard is only $7-8, so it is very inexpensive as far as pickguards go, and I don't think it is bad considering its price. I may eventually see if a luthier or someone with more technical experience than I have can cut it better and clean up the fuzz, but overall it seems nice for a cheap pickguard I can use on my Les Paul around the house. If you are playing live, you will likely want to either find a higher quality pickguard or take it somewhere to have it cleaned up so it looks nicer. And if you have an Epiphone Les Paul and are playing live, you will likely want to either get one that fits better or take this one somewhere to get someone to cut it so it fits better, especially since while the pickguard seems to stay on nicely even being more active around the house, I'm not sure if it would stay on well without the screw when performing live. So considering the cheap price, if you are thinking about getting one of these and like the color, I think you should go ahead and get it, just know you may not want to use this elsewhere except around the house and that if you have an Epiphone it may not fit exactly, even if you have an arched-top Epiphone Les Paul. I have attached before and after pictures of the guitar as well as close-ups of the plastic fuzz on the front edge of the pickguard.
Summary: Decent Les Paul Pickguard For the Price, Though May Not Fit Even the Arched Top Epiphone Les Pauls

Well built, professional grade multi-reverb pedal. 8 out of the 10 types are great. The other two are really good. The controls are wonderfully simple and intuitive. If you want, it has stereo ins and outs. The Long/Short switch gives two distinct characters to each reverb type. In some settings it can pull off a tasteful slapback echo. The clean output of this pedal is true bypass. There are two switches inside to control optional buffering of signal, and a wet-only setting for use in effects sends.

I tried all the reverb pedals I could find in the under $250 range, and this was the obvious winner. There are a few specialty units that have a truer spring reverb, but that's all they do. This pedal has room, hall, spring, plate, church, modulated, lo-fi, tile, ambient and gate.

On top of these ten reverb types (of which my personal favorites are room, plate, church and lo-fi, which is a garagey sort of retro-spring sound), this pedal GOES TO ELEVEN. The eleventh setting is the Tone Print setting, with which you may download settings created by veteran professional guitar and bass nerds and/or soundlabs. There is a setting called "Reverb" by a French sound gadget design firm that is a great spring reverb. Very smooth. They have roughly twenty Tone Prints available for this pedal right now, with more to be added. Many are specific to certain styles of music, but there are some nice general reverbs as well.
Summary: There isn't a reverb pedal this good in this price range.

Text:
The Donner XLR/USB Podcast Microphone, Vocal Dynamic PC Microphone for Recording, Live Streaming & Gaming, All Metal Cardioid Mic with Built-in Headphone Output, for iPhone & PS4/5, Black, UA-44:

Is both an XLR dynamic broadcast mic and a USB mic. Let’s get the obvious out of the way right away, it is what it looks like, it is an SM7b style microphone. Both in looks and in the frequency response curve. And to that ends it is an incredible version of an SM7b, without the presence boost and the low end roll off. You can, of corse achieve that in software or with a mixer or preamp. The frequency response curves are very similar with maybe less high end character. The curve of the UA-44 is overall a smoother curve but other wise very similar frequency response. In fact all the SM7b and SM7b style mic software presets I tried worked great and sounded very similar. Overall this is an outstanding version of that style of microphone and works and responds very similarly. As an XLR microphone this is an all around workhorse for everything from vocals and podcasts to guitar and bass as well as brass or anything else.

As a USB microphone here I was really blown away as well. I will admit I have not thought very highly of USB mics before now. Having been raised in production I’ve always had ways to plug a mic into a computer laying about. However this one seriously impressed me. The built in converter is fantastic and on a Mac is plug and play. It’s capable of 24 bit 96Khz audio recording and just works. It works with my MacBook Pro, the iPad Pro and an android phone no problem. It’s one USB C cable and it just works and sounds great. The mic takes post processing very well as do all the version of this style of mic.

The build quality and materials is fantastic. The mic has an all metal body and shock mount with a slip on foam windscreen. The mic has a good weight to it and mounts well to any standard stand or desk mounted boom arm. There is a little bit of self handling noise so a good isolated boom or stand would be best. Some desk vibrations may get transmitted to the mic if not well isolated. Over all off axis sound rejection is great. This mic sounds best when you are close up on it, like all of this style. Sound is on par wether using USB or XLR, of corse preamps and mixers can effect the sound much more than USB.

In conclusion this is a stunningly great mic at a crazy low price. The build and features are top notch and the sound is exactly as you expect it to be for this style mic. I could not be more satisfied and this mic will be getting allot of use. This is the 3rd interesting Donner product that has come across my radar, I hope I get an opportunity to try some of their other interesting offerings. They are a company to keep an eye on. They are quietly putting very capable, interesting and affordable gear. This one is very impressive to be sure. I highly recommend this to Audio professionals, musicians, voice over artists, podcasters, radio stations, streamers and anyone looking for an all around great SM7b style microphone. Well done Donner!
Summary: Sleeper hit of a microphone, truly awesome

Text: Yes, this is Jamie's take on a tube screamer, but it is not all that close to a tube screamer.  The tone knob is usable throughout its entire sweep.  Counterclockwise gets you closer to your dry tone; clockwise increases the mids/highs and cuts low end.  The pedal has 3 clipping options.  In the middle is no clip--just pure volume and power.  This is outstanding for using this pedal as a boost.  Combine that with the tone and gain, you have a super powerful overdrive/boost that can turn any of your existing gain pedals--or your amp--into a saturated, harmonic beast.  The other clipping options turn the plumes into an overdrive that's useful on its own.  I'm not a big tube screamer guy, but the plumes really does a lot.  Plus, it's $99 new.  That's insane in the world of boutique guitar pedals.  In closing, if you haven't been happy with the dirt pedals you have, get the plumes and breathe new life into your rig.
Summary: Don't call it a tube screamer!
