Text: Overall useless after 5 years of trying.

First, this is the only modeling amp I've ever tried that fulfills its promise of sounding like the amps it's supposed to be modeling. All the other solid state modeling amps sound awful. They take what ever is coming out of your guitar and add what they thing the amp "should" sound like. The result, a very generic, uninspiring tone regardless of what guitar you're using. An expensive guitar, a cheap guitar, it sounds pretty much the same and certainly not like a tube amp.

Along comes the Yamaha THR10C in 2013, one of three new Yamaha models designed for a more specific audience than their "original THR10" which is a more general purpose model. I don't play metal so I have no need for several of its "high-gain" settings. However, the THR10C emulates the sounds of the lower gain, boutique style amps. The guitar amps that it simulates are: the Fender DeLuxe, a Matchless DC 30(Sampson era), Fender Blues Jr., a Marshal Blues Breaker combo(Clapton from the "Beano" album), and finally a Dr. Z, Mini-Z. The biggest difference between the THR10C anything other companies have made is, this actually sounds and acts like the tube amps it's emulating. Yamaha's digital sound processing involves emulating the actual "components" of a vacuum tube amp like the way resistors, capacitors, potentiometers, vacuum tubes, etc. and how they interact to the way you play. This is the closest any company has come to capturing the sound of a tube amp via a solid state technology.

Runs off either a wall wart or eight batteries, the software that accompanies the THR10C is very good and give a few extra effects and the ability to fine tune the sound when connected to a computer. Because it's only about the size of a loaf of bread, it's portable but with a very big sound when placed on a desk in front of you via its two full range speakers. This is not an amp you would perform with but I've seen videos where you can use two mikes into a p.a. and get more than adequate sound for a larger room, lots of possibilities if you're creative.

I have tube amps similar to the ones the THR10C emulates but to get the nice, warm, over-driven tones, I need to really turn up the volume of my tube amps which can be a problem with my neighbors. I can get those same over-driven, sounds at a sane volume with the THR10C. Again with the same tonal characteristics as a tube amp, i.e touch sensitivity, harmonics, clean tones when the volume is rolled off, etc. You can connect an ipod and play along with music , backing tracks, and there's even a Yamaha free app for on itunes that allows you to edit music and play along at different speeds of minus the guitar track.

There are a ton of YouTube demonstration videos on this little amp and they're all quite informative but the bottom line is, the THR10C is everything it claims to be and nothing in its price range is even close, add in the various software that's included and this is an outstanding buy if you're just starting out or a seasoned professional, it won't disappoint!

It's 2:00 am, and I have to be at work in a few hours, but here I am, so happy with this device, that I'm sacrificing sleep and writing a review.

I'll spare you my background, but let's just say I'm slightly above beginner when it comes to music production, but I do own a few gadgets (mainly midi controllers/keyboards) and I'm very computer savvy. The main reason I wanted to buy this, was to connect my iPad to Ableton, and easily record music using all the amazing synths available on iOS. I ended up with a lot more functionality that I didn't even know I needed until I found out it was there.

At first, I had an issue with latency. I had connected all my keyboards, computer, and iPad to this device, installed iConfig (companion software) and was so lost I spent hours trying to understand how all the mapping worked, and why I wasn't getting sound out of my iPad, even though keystrokes seemed to trigger notes in synths. After messing with window's audio settings I found iConnectMidi in the recording devices and enabled a "listen to this device" check box. Eureka! I had sound coming from the iPad to the PC triggered by midi controllers, but the latency was quite unpleasant. I spent a lot of time researching and troubleshooting every part of this setup, (I didn't contact customer support because I do this stuff at late hours,) and after seeing that midi was actually getting through on time and without latency to the PC, and the iPad was sending midi to the PC on time as well, it was an audio pass through design flaw.

Well, I was wrong. As I finally decided to arm an audio track in Ableton and route audio to it through ASIO 4 ALL, and disable window's "listen to this device" check box, a big s*** eating grin took over my stupid face when I heard every single note I played having close to 0 latency coming from my keyboard connected to the iConnectMIDI4+, routed to the iPad triggering my synth, sending audio back to the iConnectMIDI4+, then to my PC, to Ableton, to my spearkers, to the air, to my eardrums, and to my sleep deprived and brutally abused brain.

My point is, this device is amazing. It got a golden award from the guys at Sonic Touch (a great youtube series.) If you're having issues, don't give up, contact customer support, or do some research, it works awesomely, and is kind of the only product of its kind.

Hope this helped you make your decision.
Summary: Incredible device, latency issuess are user error.

I'm going to be completely honest. I know nothing about guitar pedals and switch toppers. I'm a keyboardist, and I recently bought a Neo Ventilator II along with the additional foot switch pedal for use with organ sounds. I like to play barefoot when I'm at home. The switches on the Vent and its accessory foot switch are very stiff and not exactly pleasant to smack quickly with your hand or stomp on with your feet. So I started to look for a solution to this problem.

I assumed, incorrectly of course, that all guitar pedal switches were the same size. Well, evidently they are not. The Vent's switches are probably bigger than a typical effect pedal's toggle switch. I don't own any other pedals, so I have no idea. But I do know that the Flamma toppers didn't fit my Ventilator II. I bought these because I really liked the pretty colors and because they were made of metal. After unsuccessfully trying to put these on for longer than I'd like to admit, I gave up and tried to find out if anything at all would fit my Vent, but I don't have any calipers or measure the switch's diameter and I couldn't find any specs online either.

So after a bit of despair and head-scratching, I wondered how easily it would be to modify the Flamma toppers by carefully widening out the plastic connector inside the topper. And you know what? It was super easy to do that. I grabbed a cordless drill, a bit slightly larger than 3/8" and a vise and a microfiber cloth to protect the metal, and got creatively busy on these things. The plastic in the toppers is pretty thick and firm, so there's plenty of strength even after gently widening the diameter a wee bit. Did one as a test, the drill at its lowest force setting, and after a few quick and careful blasts with the drill, I was able to press the topper securely onto the Vent's switch. So I did the other four toppers, and as you can see in the pics, they fit great and look smashing!

So these didn't quite work out of the bag, but gosh, they're pretty. :)
Summary: I bought these for the pretty colors.

Text:
This is a very nice keyboard and a definite step up from the PSR line of Yamaha keyboards. The graded hammer action does give you a little more realistic keyboard feel over the Yamaha keyboards without it. The layout of the buttons is easy to use once you understand how it's laid out and the wheel to make choices is much nicer than mashing buttons over and over to cycle through settings. 76 keys is a nice compromise between 61 and 88 keys. All and all it's a nice stop up from the PSR line of keyboards. I recommend it over the PSR line if it's in your budget and don't mind the larger size and weight. It's almost a foot longer than the PSR and close to twice the weight. For the extra money you get a nicer key feel, a nicer display, better sounding speakers, the wheel for making menu choices, more features and an over all higher quality feel.

This is a great beginner level keyboard if you don't have the requirement for a full 88 keyboard with weighted keys. I think everybody who is serious about learning piano should start with weighted keys, but to get that you have to get in the $500 range of keyboards. (the P45 is the current least expensive keyboard in the Yamaha line up with weighted keys) but it's size/weight and cost doesn't make that practical for everyone.

The two things I'll mention is that it uses D-cell batteries which not a lot of devices use anymore and are more expensive compared to AA batteries. It's also important to note that this keyboard does NOT have a Aux line-in so you can't attach a phone/tablet/computer audio to this keyboard to hear through the keyboard speakers or headphones.For me this was a requirement so I had to return the keyboard. I took a star off for this since the less expensive Yamaha keyboards have a line-in so it feels missing on this model.
Summary: Great beginner keyboard or step up from entry level keyboards.

Surprise, its another positive review for the Korg Kaossilator. You can find this used for under US$100, and even at Amazon's price I would say this is worth it. Its a fairly simple design: you select the sound with the dial, then drag and tap your finger on the touch pad to create sounds. You can then record sequences and have them loop while you out another sound. Pretty simple, but there's just enough ways to tweak the over all sound that you'll have fun making simple songs in relatively little time. The device is also just about the perfect portable size; it fits in my back pocket. 4 batteries supplies plenty of juice and the thing sounds great with just headphones connected. The sound quality is beyond what you would get out of phone apps (i've tried a few on android, and I know there are more music creation apps on iOS) but if you want to make something that sounds good, this is actually a decent little unit.

I love this little thing. I am planning on recording loops into Garageband and maybe putting together simple songs that I can use as background music in howto videos. This is perfect for me because all these great 'techno' sounds come included, and there's tons of little tweaks with the Arp Gate as well as loop length and the scale settings to keep the sounds fresh.

Now on to the 'complaints':

The record button (used to set your loops) is on one side. It would have been nice to have dual record buttons in case you are right hand dominant. I find that I can get a good rhythm or sequence going with my right hand, then have to cross my hands awkwardly to record the pattern.

No sound expansion. There are tons of great synth sounds, but this may not be to everyone's tastes and you can't swap them out or add to the list.

no save feature: once you turn the unit off, you lose all your settings (arp setting, maybe you were using a particular sound but don't remember the number, etc.) You better write down your settings, otherwise you'll be hunting to get things "just right" the next time you turn it on.

I bought my unit used and the buttons seem to be a little stiff.

However, when you take into account that this unit is kind of a "sandbox" and not really a "work bench" music production unit, I can understand the shortcomings for getting a lot of fun out of this small package.

MOOER GWU4 appears to stand for "Guitar Wireless UHF 4-channel"

These are in the UHF 917-923.5 MHz bands and not overly crowded WiFi/Bluetooth 2.4Ghz bands.

UHF was for TV, but FCC opened some for use with wireless microphones when TV went digital.

Problems with the 2.4Ghz band is crowding by ever WiFi and Bluetooth device, additionally Microwave ovens can leak and cause 2.4Ghz interference. I know people who loose WiFi access when their microwave is running. This kind of interference will not happen with these MOOER GWU4.

Furthermore, the 917-923.5 MHz are lower in frequency than 2.4Ghz. The 917-923.5 MHz are lower, and thus why you see a little antenna sticking out of these. Lower frequencies have longer wavelengths and therefore use a longer antenna than WiFi. This offers some advantages, such as longer distances between the transmitter and receiver. It also allows some radio waves to travel around objects. This can mean less cut-outs when you move around on stage.

Additionally, I found these have been fully FCC tested and approved. The FCC confirms these work as advertised. There will not be any issues with FCC usage of MOOER GWU4 Wireless System.

With this particular pair, there are four channels available:
917.0 MHz
918.0 MHz
920.0 MHz
923.5 MHz

You select the channel on the transmitter and receiver by pushing the power button. They will light a different color LED for each channel. Be sure the transmitter and receiver have the same color LEDs and you'll hear the sound go through.

There is a limitation. You can only have 4 people on stage with these as you run out of channels. There is no automatic channel switching, so just be sure to cooperate with other players. I can only hope FCC opens more UHF frequency bands in the future.

Additionally, there is a handy feature where you can have a single transmitter that send to multiple amps if you buy additional receivers. Just make sure they're all the same color LED showing. For example, you might have two combo amps and want to transmit to both, buy another receiver, plug in receivers into both combos, and set the same channel. Very handy. Carry an extra combo and if the gig requires more volume you can be louder by sending to both. There's no hard limit on how many receivers you can use.

It can also transmit in parallel to your combo and the PA or recording console by adding a receiver on the console. This is a big opportunity to get radically clean recordings during live shows. I don't know of any other wireless guitar pair that can do this.

Here too – four people can send their selected transmitter frequency to a multiple of the receivers. No mass of guitar cables going every which way to connect multiple amps and consoles.

These do have digital processing with undetectable latency of less than 0.3ms. This digital processing cuts out any RF noise you would otherwise hear. Just a good clean signal, "No static at all".

Charging time is fast with a good charger. They include a dual head USB cable, which seems handy. To keep the batteries fresh, remember to charge them at least every 3 months if you put these away for a while. This will keep the batteries maintained for a long life.

Get another case to store these in, don't use the box. The antenna should be kept fairly straight, so it doesn't suffer from metal fatigue from being bent and crammed into a small box.

I can hardly believe MOOER can manufacture and sell GWU4 Wireless System at such an affordable price. Even if you have another brand wireless guitar pair, you owe it to yourself to also have a set of these if the need arises.
Summary: This is UHF and not the crowded 2.4Ghz WiFi/Bluetooth bands

Text: good item for guitarists

I originally purchased it with the intention of recording some high profiles lectures ill be attending so i wanted something that i could place in the room and control remotely if i couldn't get close enough to the presenter already. Battery life is lacking when you use the WiFi feature though so that is one drawback. At least they have a power adapter that you can use if you need prolonged periods of wireless usage.

Another usage i have with this device is the personal recording of our churches worship set on which i am apart of the worship team. We are a 500+ week service that typically pushes 95 db in the service. I started recording our sets so that i can listen to transitions from the first service and personally review if i could have done anything better and to overall review how we sounded. I used the device on the loud setting and used WIFI to adjust the gain from the stage (Sound guy was too busy and doesn't need another obligation) and the recording came out great. The lows/drums (our music has some deep parts) came out very good with no mud. I was impressed. I used the playback feature on my ride home from the first service to listen and review so i was ready for service 2 and 3. The sound quality was exceptional in my car speakers and i was able to get an accurate representation of the room and crowds reception.

Finally, i began using this device in my own individual practice. I use and electric metronome and a small amp (Fender Princeton Reverb) for my practicing. I found my practice time as far as quality and focus have gone through the roof since i began recording them. No more endless noodling for hours and not learning anything new. The recorder is setup about 3' away from the amp with its volume at 2 (Dead clean, no distortion). The guitar comes through clear with the metronome also in there so i can hear if i was drifting from tempo during my review time. Since i bought this device, practice times have gotten better as well as shorter since the efficiency this device brings to the workflow. I am able to be accountable to the time spent, the quality of the effort put forth, and then able to listen back during an off time (Usually my ride to work next day) and accurately gauge where i am in relation to my goals.

The other thing that suprised me was th roughness of the Pao Ferro fretboard. I double checked at a music store and Pao Ferro can be sanded as smooth as glass. Text:
So first off let me tell you that I have the older model with only 2 modes (fast and normal) for attack and release, so I can't speak for this exact version, though from what I understand the guts are the same. I do know that with upgraded tubes (I use an ElectroHarmonix) these compressors sound great! Punchy and warm with low noise and some nice functionality. The price, of course, is killer, but don't let that fool you- there IS a lot of gear out there that is cheap because it's no good, but the VLAII is a good value as well as being a good product.

The unit is well-built and the pots are smooth. Easily accessible on/off switch on the front is nice and the backlit meters are classy looking, I guess. If you do decide to switch out the tube, you can get at it pretty easily by taking out a few screws (ART tells you not to service it yourself, so choose your own adventure... but part of the fun of having a tube-driven comp is trying out different tube flavors.)

I use this in my vocal chain on every recording, set to just a DB or two of gain reduction- not really enough to slam the signal but enough to warm it up. I also love it on Snare drum with a bit more gain reduction and a fast attack. The snare gets fat and deep. Put a good preamp and EQ ahead of it and it's a tracking machine. I'm not sure I'd use it for outside-the-box mixing (it's not exactly a LA-2A) but for the front end it's fantastic, as far as I'm concerned. Finally, It's nice to be able to bypass the compressor as well just to A/B your signal with and without compression, and the metering is generally accurate (though, perhaps, a bit of overkill... why do we need THIS many meters?)

Cons: Too many meters (redundant, I know. Like the meters.) Also, while the analog meters look cool, my needle eventually got stuck since the plastic cards in the windows buckled with the heat of the lights and now I have to give the unit a little knock to loosen them. So I guess in this case the redundant digital metering comes in handy. Also, make sure you have rack room since this takes up two rack spaces- it's a beast. Finally, you'll have to deal with every snooty engineer you know giving you "that" look (you know, they same one they give your MIM Telecaster or your C1000 condenser mics but you know what? You saved enough money to buy another 3 MIM telecasters and your snare sounds warm as a mother's hug. Who cares what it costs if it sounds good?

Overall the VLAII is a solid, cost-effective tube compressor that is right at home in any studio that cares more about performance that looks.

DESCRIPTION: This is a ceramic guitar slide with an unglazed interior that absorbs some moisture from your finger. I was looking for a large slide, so I reviewed the Extra Large size.
APPEARANCE: This is a very attractive slide, with the graphics from Dunlop’s Rev. Willy guitar strings package stenciled on the slide under a clear, possibly salt glaze. I like the strings, and I like the look of this slide, although I mainly bought it for the sound.
SOUND: The sound was very mellow. Compared with my steel slides and tone bars, there was a treble cut-off — good if your sound is too wiry or edgy, but bad if you are seeking that high shivering sound. For example, on my Fender American Tele, the slide tamed the high end of the bridge pickup, but made it sound more like the mellow fingerboard lipstick pickup.
SIZE: Unlike most of Jim Dunlop’s products, the packaging of Billy Gibbons Mo-Jo slide does not give any dimensions. That may be because the hand-formed tube is not completely round. My inside diameter varied between 21-23 mm (0.83-0.9 inches). That’s not much, but it was enough to make the slide stick uncomfortably on my finger. Oddly, the inside diameter of one end was slightly different from the other end, so if I turned the slide around, it fit better.
The outer diameter of mine was 30-31 mm. The length was 70 mm or 2.75 inches, although there was some very slight variation. So, if the size is critical, be aware that the dimensions you read may not exactly match the hand-formed slide you receive.
RECOMMENDATION: Unfortunately, I was looking for clarity on the high strings, and the sound didn’t give me what I wanted, which was somewhere between glass and brass. If you focus your music on the lower strings, you may like the sound better. But remember that sizes vary on this hand-formed product.
I hope this review was helpful to you.

For testing this Kimafun I used Cad E-300 and a B2 condenser microphone, both are 48v phantom and an Art Digital Preamp System in our studio. The Cad uses two 8.4 volt lithium internal batteries and I made sure they were charged. The Kimafun gave me cutouts at every setting I could try. I then set up the B2 condenser microphone and it did not cutout, but neither mics gave a strong clean signal as using a cable and I tested them back and forth for 2 hours. Background noise on the B2 was considerably less using a cable. There was no background noise using the Cad on a cable. Trying other channels did not make a difference in sound quality.

Overall the cable rules. Using the cable both mics sound best with plenty of headroom using the Art Digital mic pre with all different settings.

The distance using the Kimafun was all good without any dropouts ever and I tested at about 70 feet not using the antennas. The exterior design seems very strong and solid whereas it wouldn't break easily.
The XLR connectors on the Kimafun are all good. In the manual, it says that the actual sound quality effects vary with different brands and models of condenser microphones. So there we have it and in my case it’s true on the Cad. I didn't have any dynamic mics handy to test and they may be a better choice to use with this wireless device.

This is a useless product. A pair ships with each set of Puresound snare wires, and the best thing you can do is throw them away and use a quality cord like Ludwig's orange cord or [[ASIN:B003V8BE6M Pearl SNC40/6 Snare Cord, 6 pack]], both of which work well.

If you can get by with flat ribbon (preferred if you are installing on a modern snare drum that does not demand the use of cord), then I recommend grosgrain ribbon. In most cases the simple (and inexpensive) replacement of the plastic snare wire straps with grosgrain ribbon will result in an immediately noticeable improvement in snare response.

Most plastic snare straps are 3/8" wide, but I typically buy 5/8" wide grosgrain ribbon because it perfectly fits almost every modern snare drum throwoff and butt. The thinner, 3/8" ribbon can cock when threading it through the strainer and butt clamps, skewing your wires. You can purchase this item, in a variety of colors, from Walmart and any fabric store

If you absolutely must use cord, do a search for "How to Properly Thread Snare Cord", which should lead you to an illustrated page of instructions at Snare Drum Addict. Just avoid the Puresound blue cord at all costs!

I love space and liked a lot of the space straps so I decided to buy a second $8 space strap from Kasstino to use as a backup strap (I was considering using the space strap instead of this one as my Les Paul strap, but this one matched better and was higher quality). The Kasstino strap had ends that seemed weaker and lower quality even compared to these ends, and the printing was much less clear. Considering they were both the same $8, the lowest price for a strap on Amazon, this one has much more bang for your buck since it is higher quality than other cheap Amazon straps. If you are looking for a cheap strap that looks amazing, then I highly recommend this strap!

I also like the interesting Chinese fire-bird on the strap. I looked up the "rosefinch" on Google and didn't find any Chinese bird called the "rosefinch", but the other name listed, "Vermilion bird", yielded results. If you think the bird on this strap looks like a phoenix, as I did upon first seeing it, this is because, interestingly enough, even though the Vermilion bird is a bird associated with Chinese constellations, it is also often confused, due to its similar appearance, with another bird in Chinese mythology: the Fenghuang which, for superficial similarities, is known as the "Chinese phoenix"! If you want to know more about the interesting mythology behind this very cool strap, I highly recommend Googling “Vermilion bird” and reading about it! (I found Wikipedia particularly helpful.)

I have attached picture comparisons between this strap and the Kasstino strap of both the image on the strap and the ends of the strap, as well as a picture of the strap with my Les Paul. Note that even though not pictured, this guitar strap also comes with a string for acoustic guitars.

First, if you are practicing dynamics, this is an excellent tool. Of course it's designed to develop a sense of time, but it produces a beat in the 60 dB range at one meter. For a drummer this is somewhere in the P to PP range, so if you combine time keeping exercises with dynamics, this is an invaluable tool that I suspect most drummers will overlook because it's based on a design that is literally hundreds of years old. Trust me, this is effective. Moreover, since it is not incredibly loud it reinforces listening skills. I used this for a solid week in my practice room before writing this review and can make the claim that if you are a trained drummer this metronome has the potential to improve your dynamics, listening and time.

A nice thing is this is not as delicate as the old style metronomes upon which the design is based. It's not a toy and does need to be treated with care, but I owned a much older instrument that was temperamental and did not like being moved or handled much. This one is more robust.

Bottom line: if you are uncertain if this will be loud enough, download a copy of [[ASIN:B0054KJND6 Decibel-O-Meter Free]] and measure your own instrument's sound pressure level at one meter and determine if this metronome will be loud enough. For some instruments it may not be, but for many like an acoustic piano, guitar, etc. it will be. For folks like me this works for certain exercises like those I mentioned and it is a lot more pleasant than some of the electronic metronomes I have tried.
Summary: Solid instrument that can help with not only time, but dynamics and listening skills

These work fine for the most part. They do tend to become loose and you get intermittent connections after a while. They also fit loose in some gear. Pretty much fit loose in all Shure microphones. Always the female end is the problem.

If they fit snugly enough in your gear, and if you don't plug/unplug them often, and they have no strain upon them they work well.

The problem is always the female end. From the face of the female connector to the widened base is usually 13 mm for those with a solid metal base. Many XLR's use a plastic or rubber ring at the base and the widened metal will be between 13-13.5 mm with the o-ring taking up the difference like in say Neutrik or Amphenol connectors. Those in these cables are 13.8 mm to the widened metal base, and the soft rubber o-ring after a short time fails to take up enough slack. The connector becomes intermittent at that point.

If you connect and mostly leave them alone like in use with an amp in domestic use, not a big problem. At the end of a microphone where you make and break many connections and there is stress on the connector from movement. It will only be a short time until they no longer maintain a good tight connection. Really a shame. If they'd tighten the dimensions on this you'd have great cables at a great price.
Summary: Good for awhile for stationary use

Text:
Reading the reviews from others, I expected to have issues with general quality, assembly, and stability. Nevertheless, the next best stands would cost about twice, so I decided to give it a shot.
As reported by others, the bag containing the screws/nuts and an Allen wrench was torn, but all parts were included. This was at best a minor nuisance. To my pleasant surprise, the instructions were decent and printed on glossy paper, so the company must have responded to the reviews posted here. I was able to assemble the stand within 5 minutes. It needed a bit of twisting for the last screw to fit, but this was also expected for such a stand (think of cheap BBQ or similar...).
There are some rough spots/irregularities in the paint in a few areas - probably particles that got stuck to the metal before the paint was applied. Nothing dramatic, and nothing that bothers me - it's not an exhibition stand. The most important part, the foam padding, is pretty thick and no metal is exposed in any areas that could get into contact with a git. So, one doesn't have to worry scratching the neck or body of a git (but see below).
Once fully assembled, it becomes pretty stable, and the weight of the guitars adds to stability. As already mentioned by others, 7 hollowbodies or acoustics will not fit, but it holds 7 solid body or semihollow guitars (one probably has to be careful with stiff trem handles). Here the greatest disadvantage: one has to be careful not to bump gits into one another. It also requires a bit of adjustment to get the angle right so that the git properly sits on both bottom bars. The git might otherwise tilt over into neighboring gits. I suppose that this issue would be valid for any stand of this type? For this reason, I wouldn't use these stands in a live situation.
In conclusion, the stand is well worth the money, but do not expect anything of great workmanship or ingenious design.

This is not a high-end Ukulele for the most scrutinizing aficiando who would think nothing about spending a 'grand' on a Martin, etc., but this ukulele is an overly-fantastic deal on what most people want a ukulele for. Pleasant strumming, camping & fireside get-togethers, beach, serenading, whatever.

Pure & Simple Enjoyment:
I also own a Luna Pineapple Tattoo Soprano (my first good one after making the mistake of buying a cheap-o.) The intonation, care and craftsmanship that goes into these ukuleles are by talented luthiers that take pride in producing a very musical and playable ukulele that stays in tune (once you stretch the strings to a stable state) and plays remarkably well in all registers/positions on the neck without any annoying dissonance. I was amazed at the difference between playing a "beginner Ukulele" and a well-made quality one. The cheap ones do not inspire you to play, sound horribly out of tune all over the neck, and hard to tune and slip out of tune even after the usually semi-tightening the tuning key screws on the reverse so they will hold the peg a little tighter. (Don't over-tighten these machine head screws, they need to be firm to hold but not "hard" to turn. This is common and should be 'checked' with every new ukulele.) Is the intonation absolutely perfect, no, but it is so slightly off on just one or two strings all the way up at the octave that only experienced ears could distinguish it, and face it, EVERYBODY loves a ukulele sing-a-long and really cares less about any virtuoso technique at the beach, right? :-)

The electronics actually blew me away!
I was expecting a cheap POS as an 'added frill' but the small built-in preamp and pickup system works more than remarkably well to be included in a ukulele of this caliber and price. The BASS & TREBLE sliders have a good range, but I have found that if I adjust them sparingly (Bass at 3/4 and Treble at 1/2) and then use the amplifier or PA system's EQ I can dial in great warm tones as well as a lively jingle-jangly strum!

The electronic pickup control is mounted on the top side for easy access & adjustments of Bass, Treble and a Volume slider making it easy to boost a little solo or adjust on the fly.

The pickup system has the output jack mounted on the bottom, a standard 1/4" guitar cable jack that inserts smoothly with no 'hard click', and again it is remarkably loud. I was playing quite loud right in front of my amp and it never even hinted as to wanting to go into feedback or squealing. I even held it up right in front of the amp's speaker front and it was quiet, actually silent with no added hiss or hum.

Since it IS mounted on a ukulele, the pickup control is of a compact design, but large enough for stubby fingers to easily adjust. What I thought was kind of cool (jury is still out) was the fact that it used two each CR-2032 watch batteries, about the size of a quarter. (3 volts) One thing to note is that when my ukulele arrived the batteries were dead, but I had two CR-2025 batteries, a small bit thinner but worked well nonetheless. The batteries are easily accessible from the top of the EQ/Volume Control Unit for a quick change, but remember it takes two batteries. I found a deal on Amazon for 5 packs of 5 each (25 total) for less than $5 w/free shipping.

Unplugged, the tone of this ukulele is warm but lively. A surprisingly full range of frequencies and harmonics and well as great projection (loud) is produced by using real mahogany wood and careful attention to installing the frets.

The fret edges appear to be filed for a smooth feel to the edge of the neck while playing. There are absolutely no buzzing frets/strings/notes, and when you play simple chords, normal fingering by most novices and intermediate players will have little problem making the chord ring out in tune with little pressure. (a common problem with cheap ukuleles that sound 'off' even when in tune.) Play it normally with medium dynamics while in good tune and you won't believe how well it plays and sounds compared to costly ukuleles (without any expensive extra appointments i.e. - fancy inlays, gold plating, special rare or exotic woods, etc.) This ukulele can hold it's own in any situation.

Likewise the great warm & lively tone and play-ability comes through when using the built-in electronic pickup. I am completely impressed.

The neck is made of mahogany and the fingerboard is made of rosewood. It also looks as though the bridge is made of rosewood, too. Very nice design and finish on the bridge/tailpiece.

Tattoo design is very attractive. Not gaudy or overly done. I highly recommend that you go onto YouTube and search for Luna demo videos. There are a few out there, but the ones by Luna are the best. Also go to the Luna website for much more fun and informative stuff.

I also own a soprano pineapple Luna, my first good one, no electronic pickups but was blown away by the great tone, fairly loud, very warm but balanced highs and lows. This is not one of those cheap obnoxious tinny-sounding $30 toys.

It comes with a gig bag, but this as well as my pineapple both deserve a good, sturdy wooden hardshell case, and so they reside inside a protected latching case that doesn't look like a cheap violin hard foam high school-type case. (yuk.) A fairly good one will cost from 40 to 50 bucks and are available from Amazon.

If you don't need to play up high on the neck, and also if you don't need to play through an amplifier, you can purchase a Luna ukulele without these features in a standard 'guitar-type' body form without the "cutaway", and even try out a smaller soprano-size ukulele (like my pineapple - highly recommended) Sure love my soprano, but the slightly large Concert size ukulele will probably be my favorite and the smaller soprano will become my camping ukulele! The prices are a good chunk lower than the larger ukuleles or ones with electronic pickups, and the soprano-size may even work well for smaller fingers. My 'stubbies' can play a soprano just fine once you get the 'hang of it' but I do like the extra width of the Concert size.

The shark-fin 'mother of pearl' fret marker inlays is a nice touch as well as an attractive appointment.

I was so impressed with the Luna soprano that again for the money, it was a no-brainer buying another Luna ukulele having complete confidence is getting a most excellent ukulele for the money with great intonation and they even put the best quality strings on them straight from the factory - Aquila brand strings.

I have played guitar & drums, keys and sing professionally for over 27 years and use tons of high-end pro gear, Gibson guitars, Fender tube amps, recording equip, and play full-time. My advice: Unless you are a Berkelee/Juliard virtuoso graduate with a butt-load of money...this is a wonderful playing instrument and probably the best sounding & playing deal out there. If it were stolen I would definitely get another one RIGHT AWAY.

I can't tell you the fun it is to learn obscure, quirky, funny, and general great sing-a-longs and every time I play my ukulele (pronounced "ooh-koo-lay-lay") just alone in my room, I escape all the crappy realities of life...if but for a little while and it always leaves me in a calm & content happier mood.

Once you learn three or four basic simple chords, go online and search for ukulele "stuff" on YouTube. There are just tons of videos online to show the beginner easy to play-right away songs, up close, slowly, and you can always pause and rewind.

Newbies give yourself a couple weeks and you will be off and running.
My secret: Learn easy songs you can play right away. Easy standards, corny as some of them may be, they are fun, attainable, and will put you on the right track to getting better faster by playing songs right away!

WARNING: If you buy a cheap $50 ukulele, you will NOT be inspired to really go on to get over the first small beginner's hump (memorizing two & three finger chords) and your playing will sound like 'poo-poo' even if you are a virtuoso on a crappy ukulele. A cheap-o ukulele is a very painful thing to hear and play. Kids seem to learn to play quite well very fast!

Good luck, and once again...it is really easy to pick up once you spend a week or two training the muscle memory in your fingers. 30 minutes a day for two weeks and you are there...trust me!

For newbies who already are familiar with a little bit a guitar and chords...you can pick this up in no-time at all! Chicks dig it, guys dig it when chicks play it, and I am sure ukulele music has the same effect of all genders and sexual orientation! (maybe more!) lol.

Best wishes - The Luna ukuleles are a pleasure to play and one of the most important simple joys that I look forward to in my jaded and sordid life!

Hope this helps!

I now have 4 of these lights washing a karaoke stage. You CAN configure these in a master/slave setup without a DMX controller...though there is nothing in the manual to either tell you it can be done, or how to do it. Here is how I got it to work:

1. Set the DMX address on the Master and Slave lights to D001 and daisy chain your DMX cables to link them. Be sure to press "Enter" on each unit so that they remember the address. Leave the Slave units displaying the D001 DMX address and do not set a light mode.

2. On the Master unit, select any light mode and this should now be replicated across your Slave units. Your Master now controls all of the functions of the Slave units. Just be sure that you save the light mode so that it returns to the same mode when you power off/on.

3. Do not use the remote controller in Master/Slave mode as it will give you confusing results. My advice would be to "set and forget" these lights using the buttons on the back and store the remote until such time that you wish to use each light as standalone.

Have fun!
Summary: Budget wash light that you can configure as master/slave

Text:
I'm a retiree looking for a decent digital piano / keyboard to self learn piano.

Firstly, this is a musical instrument, not a toy. It's made for someone who wants to own a quality instrument that will be enjoyed and appreciated for years to come.

The digital piano has a high quality keyboard. Not as stiff and difficult to play than a similar Yamaha, more like on the light side of a piano feel. It feels and plays like a very good quality piano with a light touch, well tuned.

The main piano sound is a sampled Kawai grand piano. If you were blindfolded you wouldn't say it plays and sounds exactly like a grand piano, but its as close as you are going to get in a digital piano. It sounds good, and the more your ear gets used to it, the more it just grooves with you.

I've owned Kawai many years ago. That instrument was outstanding and this is no different. The build quality is maybe a tad below what I owned thirty years ago (that instrument cost me $2,000) however the technology far supersedes it.

The speakers are just loud enough. I plugged in my high fidelity open back headphones to see if I would get a much better sonic experience, and low and behold, not much improvement over the speakers. That's a testament to how well the speakers deliver crisp, defined sound on this model.

The main piano sound is great. It doesn't sound like some old creaky grand piano sitting on some dusty stage, it sounds like a brand new Kawai grand. And that's good enough for me. All the other sounds are great, however I'm just going to stick with the one sound thank you very much!

I was learning from a book yesterday and I played for one hour and hardly noticed the piano. It doesn't get in the way of what you are doing at all. That's the sign of a great instrument.

Who is this instrument intended for? I would say beginners who want to spend a little more and get a quality instrument. Also, intermediate players who just want a great instrument. Heck, even pro's could use this instrument, no problem. it's really that good.

I wouldn't say it's super light to lug around. I plan to keep it in once place.

I haven't tried the midi yet, or some of the other features. This is a fairly feature packed piano.

So, well done Kawai. Not surprising, since they pretty much focus in on real and digital pianos, they know what they are doing, and they are not producing something for a couple hundred dollars less to sell someone a piece of junk, but rather an quality instrument that will be appreciated for years to come.
Summary: Instrument that will be appreciated for years to come

Text:
Meinl overs these shakers in three "volume" levels (red, black, and silver cases) designated soft, medium, and loud. I have all three.

This silver model has very sharp-edged pellets inside, and with two shaker tubes makes a lot of noise. I am confident it would cut through well in a live playing situation. I have found that it tends to be a bit much in more "unplugged" settings, where the shaker is meant to be more subtle.

The red "soft" version feels like it has sand or something really gentle inside. It has a more diffuse sound that sets a more indistinct beat.

The medium model is somewhere in between.

All three Meinl shakers take a bit of practice to develop a clean sound. Unlike the egg-type shakers, the amount of area that the internal pellets can cover in the two tubes is much larger, and therefore one's hand movements have to be more intentional and controlled to keep all the pellets marching in step and creating a consistent and clean sound. It's not a problem once the issue is recognized.

In a more intimate setting, especially if a microphone is being used, these Meinl shakers may be too much, and an egg shaker may work better. I have all at my disposal, and it's nice to have the choice. Overall, if I had to pick only one of the Meinl units, I would probably pick the medium one (black). But I would also have an egg shaker with me just in case.
Summary: Loud One is Really Loud, Soft One is Really Soft

I so wanted this thing to be everything claimed. I'm not sure what the 5-star reviewers are thinking. The harmonizing is OK (tracking is so-so), the whammy feature, especially going up is really cool for doing Tom Morello stuff, the detuning is a nice liquid sounding effect. The problem with this pedal is that it is unacceptably NOISY! There is a constant hiss coming from this thing, even when the pedal is turned off - which means no true-bypass. On strictly clean sounds, the hiss is barely noticeable, but if you apply any gain at all, the hiss is horrible. When I take this pedal out of the mix, my amp is dead-silent on clean settings and almost silent on high-gain settings. Put this back in the middle (with no other pedals), and hiss-city. The instructions say that "on rare occasions, interference from OTHER sources may cause noise" and to get rid of this, you unplug from the input, wait a minute and then plug back in. Nope - didn't work. I would never use this live or in recording - the noise is absolutely ridiculous. And I was using a 9-volt battery, not a power supply. I have no explanation other than this is a piece of crap. It does some cool things, but there is absolutely no excuse for this much noise. Too bad - I was really excited to get this at such a low price; now I know why the price is so low.

I do not recommend this pedal.

P.S. I could live with the hiss if it only happened while using the effect - but to have the constant noise when not engaged was a deal-breaker.
Summary: Noisy even when not using the effect = NO true bypass.

I bought this and a Line6 HX Stomp at the same time to compare and figure out which one would work best for me. The short answer? I returned the HX Stomp and kept the Ampero. But was that the right choice? Maybe. Read on!

What the HX Stomp does better than Ampero:

- HX Stomp is built like a tank and feels stage ready. Ampero does not feel like it would stand up to regular onstage use.
- HX Stomp online community is much bigger, it is easier to find quality presets.
- I was able to find sounds on the HX Stomp that I liked quicker than I was on the Ampero
- The desktop application for the HX Stomp is better
- HX can do stereo input if that is something you're into
- Both units and use third party impulse responses to simulate cabinets, but the HX Stomp software seems better for managing this.

What Ampero does better than HX Stomp

- An extra footswitch (there are 4 instead of 3) really is helpful
- Controls on the panel are more intuitive
- Ampero has XLR and 1/4" outputs. Note that the Stomp has 1/4" outputs that can use balanced OR unbalanced cables - on the Ampero you need XLR if you want a balanced out.
- Has a built-in expression pedal, but I wish it didn't. The pedal is so tiny that it is hard to use. You can plug an external expression pedal into both units
- Hardware switch for input type (electric/acoustic/line). HX Stomp can adjust the input type but this is buried in a menu and a bit of a pain to get to.
- Ampero has a drum machine and looper built into it. These are features that to me, signify that Ampero has a different use case - it is geared more towards the bedroom guitarists rather than someone using this as an onstage effects processor/amp simulator. I wasn't interested in these features but I have played around with them and they can be fun.
- You can send two outputs from the Ampero that have different signals. One great use of this is onstage if you plan to have your guitar signal straight into the PA but still want an amp onstage that is not mic'd, you can send a signal that has effects, amp and cabinet simulation to the PA, and send a second signal with just effects and amp to your onstage amplifier (assuming it has a transparent tone). The other excellent use case is that if you use the Ampero as an audio interface for recording, you can send a wet signal and a dry signal at the same time, and record both tracks together. Then, if later you're unhappy with your guitar tone, you can re-amp the dry signal, either through an amp simulator or through an actual guitar amp/mic.
- The Ampero is almost half the price of the HX Stomp.

Using the desktop application to set up and adjust your Ampero is crucial. Also, make sure you update the firmware as soon as you get it, as there are bugs that affect the looper and other things.
Summary: It does a lot of things... just not all of them well. But it might be perfect for you

The only issue is I didn't want to drop the $150 on a Wazazone or spend $50 on a used Metal Zone and then modify it. I needed a decent option. Are there better metal pedals out there? Of course! If you want to drop $200 on a Wampler Dracarys, $150 on a WazaZone, or $200 on a REVV G3, more power to you. Let's also not forget that ultimately, real 12AX7 preamp tubes running hot in a metal amp sound better than any pedal, but for one song that has to be recorded, I'm happy with my little Joyo.

After seeing John Batiste on Colbert's show, I knew I wanted to try a melodica. The first one I had was Hohner's 37 key one with a colorful tropical design on the body and a matching case. This--the black and white colors of a small piano--is exactly the same musically as that one, which was about 3 times the cost. It is so much fun--with a sound a bit like a harmonica and a bit like a saxophone. So easy to play--just learn to read single notes from "F" below "middle C" to "F" three octaves higher. It's just like that part of the piano keyboard--all the same notes, it even looks the same though the keys are a little narrower.

This melodica sounds as good as my Hohner. I tested all 37 keys and everyone was in tune. (It is so lightweight that I would always get the 37 key instrument rather than the 32 keys unless it's for a child who has no musical knowledge.

Although it also comes in pink or blue, after carrying around my very colorful Hohner for over a year, I found the "piano style" in black with a matching black bag (very sturdy) to be tasteful, unobtrusive and very nice. You want to dry it after you're done playing each time. Just take off the mouthpiece or tube, turn it so the opening is face down and shake it gently onto a cloth. You should see some saliva come out--important to do that to keep it clean and relatively dry.

It comes with two hoses and two mouthpieces. You can do it either way--hold it to your mouth with the mouthpiece like a clarinet or put it flat on a table or your lap and blow through the plastic tube (I sprayed mine black--with two, you can afford to experiment.) That's all that's involved in playing this genuine instrument--blowing into it and hitting the piano keys. It looks like a piano, but plays like a woodwind in the sense that you don't use a reed, but reeds are built in below each key. Each one has phosphor bronze reed and copper base. Although its inexpensive and the body is resin, it is very well made.

There are short "feet" on the bottom so that it doesn't like flat on the table. The sound comes from the top, with air released from a hole above each key. You can read any music for it--three octaves from F to F, or you can think it has middle C and two full octaves above it, plus four whole notes below it and above the highest. The sound projects so well--nice volume--but musically, you can't really control the dynamics. You need your breath to produce the sound especially on the upper and lower notes; it's not possible to modulate the volume much.

The melodica has a hand strap in the back, but no shoulder strap. The carrying case has an adjustable carrying strap. The whole thing is so small and so lightweight--about 1 1/2 feet long. You change keys while blowing but the note sustains--it's not choppy.

This is so easy, so fun. If someone doesn't see what you're playing, they'll think it's a lot more difficult instrument. It's very easy to play with others, too. This is a great instrument for children to learn on, too.

I've been playing ukulele for a few years and own a few other ukuleles. This is the cheapest one that I own; some of the others cost many hundreds of dollars. While this ukulele obviously sounds and feels like an entry-level instrument, it is a real musical instrument and I am surprised by how much performance you can buy for $30 these days. Just a couple of years, I bought my nephew a $70 Kala for Christmas and this $30 Caramel is just as good or better.

The Caramel ukulele weighs just under 1 pound, which is easy to hold and play without using the strap. It uses lightweight clear fluorocarbon strings which are not real loud, but they are easy to strum (easier than the white Aquila strings that most cheaper ukuleles use). The ukulele is surprisingly responsive and resonant; better than the $70 Kala. The headstock is extra thick to accommodate the guitar style tuning pegs, but it doesn't feel out of balance when I'm playing. The tuning pegs all operate very smoothly.

The fretboard is nicely finished with no sharp fret ends. There are fret markers on both the front and the side at frets 5, 7, 10, 12, and 15. This is an improvement over most ukuleles in this price range that do not have side fret markers. When you are playing the ukulele, the side fret markers are much easier to see than the markers on the front.

Intonation is great up the fretboard, meaning that the ukulele plays the correct notes all over the fretboard, which isn't always the case for cheaper ukuleles.

String action is OK, but not great. The string height is about 1mm at the 1st fret and 3mm at the 12th fret. That is playable, but if you buy a ukulele from a good store instead of by mail order, the store can lower the string height to make the ukulele easier for a beginner to play.

The width of the neck is 36mm at the nut, which is 1mm wider than our Kala. String spacing is also 1mm wider than the Kala. A wider neck and wider string spacing gives you more room for to hold complex chords with your fingers. Most imported ukuleles (like Kala, etc) are 35mm wide at the nut while many US-made ukuleles are 37 or 38mm at the nut, so this one is a comfortable medium. People with bigger fingers will almost always prefer a wider nut width.

You get a few useful accessories included with the $30 price. The gig bag is better quality than you usually find in this price range with backpack straps and some padding to protect your instrument as you carry it to class or to jam with friends. If you play regularly, you should plan on changing your strings at least every 6 months, so the extra set of strings is nice to have. I'm not a fan of straps or picks, but since they are included for free, you are welcome to experiment with them.

All in all, I have to say this is the best-sounding and easiest to play $30 ukulele that I have tried. While the sound quality is less rich than a $130 ukulele, it does compete well with $70 ukuleles. Overall build quality is better than I expected for $30. This isn't a great ukulele, but it is a tremendous value for $30.
Summary: much better than I was expecting for $30

I’m a keyboard player and usually use a 3 ring binder with paper sheet music. I have avoided using plastic sheet protectors in the past because of the extra weight when playing out. I do appreciate them if I’m playing outdoors and expect wind. On the plus side, the Sier Fins plastic sheet music holders weigh a bit less because of the unique mounting design, compared to the familiar double-sided plastic sheet protectors.
Well, I do like spiral-bound music books, they lay flat at 180 degrees and they can also be opened to 360 degrees to display a single page. The drawback with spiral bound binders is that for practice and jamming sessions the different music sheets cannot be delineated with section dividers like a 3-hole binder. Section dividers really help save time when searching for a tune that was added to the middle of the book. This can be solved using removable adhesive-backed tabs on the edges of the plastic sheets. I plan to try these removable tabs very soon.
As a default, I usually print my documents on both sides of the page. Bear in mind. that this binder has only 30 pages, of which 60 sides are available. Therefore you can use 60 one-sided music sheets or 30 double-sided sheets (the back of the plastic sheets are quite transparent, but may reflect a little light using 30 double-sided printed music sheets)
I tried putting together a portfolio of the music for my next jam session in the Sier fins folder recently. I didn’t have enough time or all the music sheets downloaded and tried to estimate where and how many plastic sheets to reserve space for the unfinished sheets that weren’t downloaded yet. So, the takeaway to this scenario was, you must have all the music in hand to effectively use this unique music binder.
Summary: This binder might be a useful addition to your portfolios

Construction of the unit is solid - the knobs and sliders all feel smooth with enough resistance that I'm not worried about accidentally bumping the table and knocking them out of whack. The phantom power lets me use a really nice supercardioid mic into the XLR port, and the app is okay. I'm not really much of a fan of apps - this one, like almost all the others I've used is a little clunky. There's no real visual indicator that something succeeds for example - so when you assign a sound to a button, there's not a great way to be sure that everything went to the right place without mashing the button live. That's fine if you're setting everything up ahead of time but if you want to do anything on the fly it's not the best.

I've got it installed as an audio device on my Windows machine, and it works flawlessly. There is a little bit of a delay between video and audio, but that's a processing issue and it's unavoidable. If you're using something like OBS then you can actually inject a frame delay to sync the two up.

I do wish I had more inputs, and I'm always looking for other ways to bring in guests but this is a really solid, well thought out device. Five stars from me.

The banjo tuner was slower getting the tuning information displayed. Since the ordinary NS and this banjo tuner use the same head, I reason that the bracket is not receiving/passing the vibrations as strongly as the same device on the headstock. Note that the two tuners on the head always agreed on the tuning. The banjo tuner was often different, sometimes showing showing a different key. (Dunno why?) The Snark S-1 was the fastest to show the tuning and with the bigger and color display was by far quicker and easiest to read.

In summary it is kind of cool, being designed for a banjo. I will keep it on my banjo and maybe I will grow to love it. Until then I will be using the Snark S-1 (aka Son of Snark) on the head of the banjo, for it's easy to read face, as my primary tuner. The NS tuner on the head is still an excellent tuner. I bought this keyboard to teach my 10 year old grandson piano.  Amazon tends to mix reviews for different models so be sure you are reading one for the right product. The CTK 2550 is a very similar product but with one big difference: It is not "touch sensitive" so you cannot vary the volume (velocity) of the sound by key press pressure. The CTK 3500 I purchased IS touch sensitive so you can vary the volume by the amount of pressure on the keyboard, similar to a real piano. Although the keys are not weighted, touch sensitivity will make it easier for a student to eventually transition to a real piano. I was surprised that at this price, it even has a level 1 MIDI jack (USB A-B type) so you can use it with MIDI software on a PC. I have Cakewalk MIDI sequencing software installed on my PC that I use for my other keyboards,  but have not yet tried the MIDI function for this keyboard,  but nice to know its there for future use. Although my grandson will mainly be using the piano tone for his lessons, I did try out a few of the other features and tones and is what you would expect for this price, and adds a little fun. For the price, it is a great keyboard to learn on. It also has a decent collection of  built-in songs that you can use for lessons and the display even shows fingering to use for those songs, which is very important to learn correctly in the beginning.  Notes are also displayed on a staff in real time as the songs play. The package deal comes with headphones and a keyboard stand. I would also recommend purchasing a piano bench/stool and a sustain pedal to complete the package (be sure the sustain pedal is compatible with Casio keyboards or at least has a 'polarity' changeable switch if not specified for Casio). I would highly recommend this for anyone wanting to learn piano,  or instructing beginning piano lessons.
Summary: Great beginners keyboard; Great price for the included features.

Seeing this Podcast Equipment Bundle advertised, I made me curious to explore it and potentially serve as the catalyst for future podcasting. While that ‘podcasting career’ hasn’t materialized just yet, I like the possibilities of this product.

This bundle is a tremendous get for anyone who is into podcasting and live streaming. The key piece of the bundle is the mixer, which features buttons assigned sound effects which can enhance the show or stream. It is lightweight, battery powered, and can connect to smartphone, tablet, and laptop. On this mixer, there are knobs and sliders controlling volume, treble + bass levels, and mic effects. As far as inputs, there is no shortage, including one for a 48v mic – not included. What is included is a respectable condenser mic with stand, which uses a 6.5mm XLR cable. Also, how about a set of headphones, monitor earbuds, and a couple of additional cords fo various inputs, found on the back of the mixer? This is, indeed, a complete package.

So, with all those components, how easy is this product to use? Well, as with everything, reading the instructions is key. There is a manual covering multiple usage scenarios, though as an amateur, I still had to think how to make this product work optimally for me. Ultimately, it was including this device as an input into one of my DAWs (Digital audio workstations) on my MacBook Pro (Logic Pro X). I assure you, if tinkering is not your thing, you can still have success with this product – it provides ample opportunities. I have played quite a few different pedals over the years: at first a Ludwig speed king, then a DW 7000 double pedal. After a 10 year break of not having drums I got back into it with a cheap Ludwig chain driven pedal, then a Tama Iron Cobra powerglide double pedal with single chains, and even tried a strap drive Pearl pedal. These pdp 502 pedals are every bit as good as the best of these pedals, and they had me grinning ear to ear the first time I played them. About as fast as a speed king and nearly as robust and as powerful as the DW pedals. I can't say how long they will hold up so far but after a few gigs and some heavy playing sessions no loosening of anything and they appear they will last a long time. I do not understand the complaining of people getting hit in the shins though.. are they playing incorrectly? And those that say these are slow are wrong, they may not be as fast and easy as an axis pedal but are equally as fast as anything DW makes (I've tried a 9000 on a kit at a local store). Perhaps some of these reviews are on the lesser pdp 402 pedals?

Anyways, one annoying thing about the 502 pedal is the tab on the left post on the left pedal gets in the way of a regular 3 leg hi hat stand. After the return period I cut it off easily with a hack saw so I could better position the hi hat pedal. It almost cut too easily, like the post is made of aluminum or some lighter weight alloy. I ended up getting a swivel type 3 leg hi hat stand later anyways which I'd recommend for even better placement. The spring tensioning screws on the 502 are made of plastic, but have not been a problem. Also, there are no felts on the beaters and the grey side seems almost as hard as the black one. If you want a warmer thud sound I find I can get this by putting a pair of my infant's socks over the beaters haha. The beaters are also very lightweight, more so than the dw ones I've had. I think this could contribute a lot to why these pedals feel quick to me. I love the look and feel of the footboards, just enough traction but can still slide your foot around enough for other types of playing. And they just look cool too. They have been good for heel down playing, heel up, heel/toe, you name it and right out of the box too I never felt like I had to adjust anything unlike my Tama pedals. I find the sharp logos from the DW and Tama pedals annoying because they catch your shoes or socks. I am convinced these pedals are the best value out there and Amazon had the best price at less than $120, arrived in like 2 days too with standard shipping! They are made in Taiwan and come in a cardboard box without a case. If you are careful when transporting them though and don't throw a bunch of heavy hardware on them you should be fine.

Update: Have played many 3 hour outdoor mall gigs with these and an underpowered PA system so I really had to lay into these pedals to project enough sound. Plus weekly band practices, almost daily solo practice, and no issues whatsoever over the last year. Every once in a while I put some bike chain lube on the chains and a little phil wood bearing grease on the springs and they are still silent and smooth. There is a slight bit of side to side play in the pedals from getting more worn in, but not a big deal and I would trust taking these on the road.
Summary: Great pedals, don't think I'll ever need to upgrade

Text: I’m purely a music hobbiest, and have recently tried a couple of other plug-in guitar headphone amps.  Plug-in guitar headphone amps are a great concept, but the others I’ve tried, while they also sound great, the fact that you can’t really control the settings during play (because the controls are out of reach, down at your guitar jack) really hinders maxing out the benefits.  The NUX has what turns out to be a very good cell-phone app that overcomes this problem, letting you adjust through your phone or tablet that you can set in easy reach.  The only complaint is the instruction manual does a poor job of explaining how to do this, but if you go ahead and set up on your Android or Apple phone or tablet, it turns out the app is very intuitive, and works fine (the manual simply does a poor job of explaining this).  But if you’ve just a bit of common sense, you’ll be fine and, if you’re like me will have a very positive experience with this.  I may try the Fender version too, which is about 50% more expensive, but I have to say NUX did a nice job with this, and it really lets you have a nice, easy way of getting a lot of great electric guitar sounds, very quick and easy, to simply let you enjoy your guitar through headphones.  NUX - Good job!
Summary: A great electric guitar headphone amp with effects and an intuitive cell-phone interface

I bought this to replace my Blue Snowball because I've reached that point where I require something that sounds a little bit more professional than what I was using. Before I begin my review, I'd like to mention that I use this with a Behringer 302USB Premium 5-Input Mixer with XENYX Preamp (copy and paste that into Amazon's search to find it). So my review is based on this thing being plugged into that thing.

Okay, my pros and cons.
Pros
1. My voice sounds great with this thing. Before I was using a Snowball and my podcast partner told me it sounded like I was in a "chamber". With this, my voice is strong and clear...and even a little bassy which is nice because I don't have a naturally bassy voice. I'm extremely satisfied with how well this thing makes me sound. It is WORLDS better than USB mics like the Blue Snowball. Worlds better.

2. It's heft, heavy, and feels well made. This might be the most expensive-feeling device I own. It's heavy but it in a good way. The materials feel high quality. This feels like a professional microphone.

3. It comes with a mic stand holder thing. Never say no to free stuff.

Cons
1. The only thing I can think of is that it doesn't come with its own cable. You'll need to buy an XLR cable on your own. It's not bad enough to deduct a star.

There are people who are comparing this to the Shure SM57 and other microphones. Here's the thing, I am an amateur. Before I owned this mic, I was using a Blue Snowball and before that, my laptop webcam mic. So I am not the authority. All I can tell you is that this thing sounds freaking amazing. My podcast co-host immediately noticed the difference and couldn't tell me enough of how much better I sounded and that's over a Skype call (we podcast using Skype). So if you're looking for a vocal/podcast mic, this is a great, cheap option. Are there better options? Sure, but not for this price. Not even close. Recommended wholeheartedly.

**Update 10-11-2015**
Just wanted to drop back in and say that this mic still works great. It's still my go-to mic for everything (podcast and YouTube videos) and still sounds as crisp and clean as the day I bought it. Unless there's another level that blows this one away (or unless I become rich), I'm sticking with this one. For how inexpensive it is, it really does work extremely well.

Yes, still plugged into the Xenxy302USB :)

*Update*

I have been using this thing for...9 years now?! Good lord.

I'm a fair bit more experienced than I was back then, but I wouldn't trade my Xenyx 302USB and my GLS ES 57 for anything. It's more than anyone would need for an amateur podcast or YouTube voiceover setup and you can get the whole thing (mic, cable, audio mixer) for less than the trendy USB mics.

I still consider this the best professional purchase I ever made, and I literally recorded a YouTube video voiceover with this thing 2 weeks ago.

I'm going to keep it until it breaks, and then probably buy another one. At this rate, the mic might live longer than me hahaha.
Summary: Great for voice overs and podcasts

Text:
Did that attenuate 90% of your noise? It did for me.

Unfortunately, it was also a huge performance drop for my PC, and there was still a hint of the old distortion. Obviously, not an ideal lasting solution, but if this works for you, then there's a great chance our noise problems have a cause in common.

I have a beefy self-built PC running a USB Scarlett 18i8, which outputs balanced TRS cables to an active Yamaha sub and HS80M monitors. Since the day I unboxed my monitors, they haven't been able to sit quietly, even with nothing happening. There was a constant whisper of a sound, which got worse the more the processing load increased. Move the mouse, buzzzzzzzz. Load a project or flatten something to audio, GRIIIIIIIIIND. Lots of spontaneous distortion on complex sounds and tracks, too.

A real nonstop kick in the beanbag, to have so much expensive audio gear make itself sound ugly. If you're here, I'm sure you know the feeling.

After years of trying and failing to build a tolerance to the noise, I stumbled on the "Power Saving" trick and finally was able to have an effect on the issue. From a technical standpoint, I still don't know what happens or why (something something ground loop...), but after verifying that particular symptom, it was suggested to try a hum box, so I scooped this one up and crossed my fingers.

Welp... it works. Simple as.

Passively patched in between my soundcard and my sub, this unit completely scrubbed my signal of all distortions and hum. I was worried about complications from the active sub being on a separate, unconditioned power circuit, but the stages after the eliminator did not reintroduce the noise at all.

I see a lot of reviews 1-starring this unit because their interference was caused by something else, so please try the "Power Saving" trick to see if there's a chance that you and I are experiencing the same flavor of problem; if we are, you can feel that much more confident taking a chance on this unit, or one like it.
Summary: Try this: put your PC into "Power Saving" mode

I purchased this TOM bridge to replace the stock TOM bridge on my Epiphone Les Paul Special II LTD (Player Pack model).

The stock Epiphone TOM bridge uses a retaining wire to hold down the string saddles, and after only 6 weeks of playing the wire loosened up a little and generated a lot of open string buzz due to both the now lose retaining wire and saddles that now bounced around.

The Metallor TOM bridge design eliminates the need of a saddle retaining wire, and once I installed it the bridge rattle and buzz went away.

The Metallor TOM bridge snugly fit onto the existing bridge posts, whereas the stock TOM bridge had a little more play on the posts.

Dunlop 927 Long Dawg Tone Bar
Tone bars are used play lap steel guitars, pedal steel guitars, Dobroes and Hawaiian style guitars with a high action, often tuned to an open chord. They are designed for use on a guitar that is held horizontally, on your lap, on a table, or at your waist with a strap.
To use a tone bar, hold it firmly and slide it up and down the strings while you pluck or pick the strings near the bridge with your other hand. With practice you can perform gliding glissando notes, notes between frets, slant chords with the tone bar at an angle, hammer-ons, and pull-offs.
I compared Dunlop RR1, SP2, Long Dawg, and Ernie Ball M bullet tone bars for this review. Test guitars included a 2021 Martin 00-15M acoustic with a custom bone nut and bridge, a 1970 Lotus F215 acoustic, and a 2011 Gretsch G5715 Electromatic Lap Steel guitar. All guitars were strung with Dunlop extra-light strings.
DESCRIPTION: The Dunlop 927 Long Dawg tone bar is a rounded tone bar with straight ends and an integrated grooved metal handle that will accommodate two or three fingers or can be held between finger and thumb. It weighs 5.6 oz, it is 0.75 inch wide and it is 3.1 in from end to end — the straight edges allow you to use the full length of the bar in contact with the strings.
Unlike similar looking Dunlop tone bars that are made of polished stainless steel, the Long Dawg is made of heavily chromed brass. The plating was incomplete on the corners which made them sharp to the fingers. There were a few pinpoint irregularities in the chrome finish on the handle that did not affect appearance, feel, use, or sound. Its price is slightly higher than other Dunlop tone bars. The package said made in China.
COMPARISON: This bar has a longer string contact area than the Dunlop SP2, the Dunlop RR1, or the Ernie Ball Medium. It is narrower than the EBM, the same width as the Dunlop SP2, and wider than the RR1. It weighs more than the Dunlop RR1, the same as the Dunlop SP2, and less than the Ernie Ball Medium.
SOUND: The midrange and low notes sound smooth and full of harmonics while the highs are clear and bright, but not quite as bright as with the polished stainless steel Dunlop tone bars.
HELPFUL HINT: This is my favorite tone bar so far. The midrange and low notes sound deep, dark, and smooth at the cost of a little less twang. I love the sound.

Text:
For the money, this is a great keyboard, aimed squarely at people who want to learn - adults or children - or those who knew a little bit and want to see if they can get their feet wet again without spending a bundle in the process.

As others have said, it does not come with a power adapter. So you know. It does run on batteries (six AA batteries), but it would be best to get a [[ASIN:B000WS1QC6 Power Adaptor]] as well for a few extra bucks.

What you get with this is a very lightweight keyboard (you can lift it comfortably with one arm) with 61 full size keys that are velocity sensitive (meaning louder as you hit them harder) and built in speakers. What makes it great for beginners is the suite of tutorial software built in. The keyboard will play and simple scalar sequence while displaying it on the LCD screen, then have the learner repeat it. These start very simple, but what makes them great is that there is a drum beat playing and a bass - so even though it's a simple scale, you hear it as musically 'valid'. This has always been a gripe of mine with academic musical pedagogy - the lack of musicality in favor of raw scales, or worse still, finger permutations that are decidedly unmusical. Those are ways to turn off a beginner indefinitely. So that this keyboard makes the exercises 'groove' is a terrific step in the right direction.

Now, to be sure, this is a beginner keyboard. I have both a [[ASIN:B0193QFPGK Yamaha YPG-235 76-Key Portable Piano]] as well as the great big [[ASIN:B003ZYELTY Kurzweil PC3K8 88 Note Performance Controller]]. This has 61 keys, the keys are not weighted (meaning they do not feel like acoustic piano keys) - it does not have multiple outputs (for connecting to an amp or recording console) and no dedicated MIDI. It also does not have a greatest piano sound. That all said, it doesn't have to have any of those things! It is a beginners keyboard, and is perfect for that purpose. The light weight and suite of learning software is great for kids or adult starters, and if you played piano in the past and want to try your hand at it again, this is a GREAT option. Hence the five stars.

Another neat feature is splitting the keyboard in half to create the same range of notes twice - like two two-octave keyboards next to each other. That's great for a teacher sitting next to a student, or even two people just having fun! Again, a very friendly feature, especially at this price point.

I would also recommend a [[ASIN:B00063678K M-Audio SP-2 | Universal Sustain Pedal]]. You'll want one as soon as you start to get serious. And face it - for a beginner the pedal always sounds better.

Excellent beginner keyboard!
Summary: Great for beginners and casual use!
