Text:
This will not be another, "good amp for the price" review. Early '60s Valco amps were good amps for the price. Now, try to buy one at a reasonable price. They are not good because they are older, they are good because they SOUND good and always did. Other than some US made boutique amps that employ point to point wiring and NOS tubes (which may or may not SOUND good), a tube amp is like a cheese pizza... the ingredients are readily available to any builder and in volume they are not expensive. It is how you put them together that make the difference. This amp was put together in a way that causes it to SOUND good. I have a Fender Princeton and a Vox AC15 (also 15 watt) and while this amps sounds different, to me it is in that league. By the way, this amp is smaller, weighs less, costs less and has an effects loop unlike those amps.

Fortunately there are a few fixable issues with it, otherwise 5 stars would not be enough. The reverb as noted by others is crap. Your options: 1. Don't use it... not everyone likes reverb. 2. Buy a MOD 8EB2C1B and replace it... requires some soldering skills. 3. Use a digital reverb pedal in the effects loop... and isn't it a nice feature that there is one.

If you go with option #2, I would put a high gain/ low noise 12AX7 tube in V2 position to regain some of the gain that is lost by using an 800 Ohm reverb in place of a 600 Ohm reverb and lower the noise of the reverb circuit. Other than that, I consider the stock Chinese tubes and Celestion 70/80 speaker to sound good. Given that I have lots of tubes and more than a few speakers that could not find a home in my other amps, I will probably do some swapping to see if I like something better, but you would not be making a mistake by keeping it stock.

OK, OK, It's a GOOD amp for the price! There I said it. So if you want an excellent tube amp for a low price, get it while you can. Full disclosure: I bought mine directly from Monoprice because they were having a 15% off deal at the time and it was delivered the next day. That said, many people will feel more secure buying through Amazon and I often find myself in that group as well.
Summary: What "Real Tube Tone" pedals promise... and yes, at about the same price.

I have been playing ukulele for a few years and I have seen worse instruments than this one. However, I cannot give them more than 1 star because the product description is full of lies. Not just mistakes, but outright false statements that are intended to deceive the customer.

One of the big features that buyers look for when purchasing any wooden stringed instrument is what kind of wood is it made from. The product description here says: "Quality mahogany" and "The solid mahogany body gives the ukulele a vivid and balanced tone." That would be great if it was true, but looking into the soundhole, I can see that the wood is plywood and not solid mahogany. Experienced musicians should know that a solid mahogany ukulele will not cost less than $100 (and usually not less than $200 either), but someone looking for a beginner instrument will easily get fooled by the false advertising.

Some other false statements: "Low action of 2.7mm at the 12th fret". Low action is great for beginners. The ukulele I received does not have low action. See the attached photos. According to my ruler, the string height is 3.2mm at the 12th fret and 1.2mm at the 1st fret; both numbers are high enough to make the instrument hard for a beginner to play.

"The nickel silver frets are properly seated and well finished. You have no need to worry about being scratched when playing the ukulele." The frets on the ukulele I received are not the worst I have ever seen, but the ends are still sharp enough to scratch me unless I file them down myself. I properly finished instrument would not have this problem.

"Vangoa soprano ukulele features 14.32 inch scale length". How can they make that claim? The scale length is easily measured as the normal 13.5 inches for a soprano ukulele. 14.32 inches would be an interesting design decision, but somewhere along the line, the manufacturing department did not get the memo.

"Easy to Learn: Modern C shape neck". A C-shaped neck is not easy to learn. Most people prefer a wider, flatter neck. The neck on this ukulele is only 34mm wide at the nut. A narrow neck is OK for children with thin fingers, but American adults usually prefer a 38mm neck, like many made-in-America ukuleles use. Also, the neck on this ukulele only has fret markers on the top of the fretboard, which you cannot see when you are playing. Beginners always prefer fret markers on the side of the neck, which most other brands have, even in this price range.

If this ukulele had a more honest product description, I might have given it 3 stars for build quality. As it stands, it only gets 1 star from me.
Summary: product description sounds great, but it is full of lies

First of all, I use this as more of a 6 band EQ using the lower and highest more for LP and HP filters. The middle four have the most dramatic effect on the tone. You can also use this as boost box, using the gain and volume sliders. The box is solid and fairly easy to manipulate on stage, but I tend to set and forget.

In reviewing other posts maybe these bullets may be helpful.

-If you turn your gain way up, you will have hiss. Period, this holds true for any effect box or amp that has a gain on it that I have been exposed to. Have a reason for upping your gain, if it is to add volume consider doing this on your guitar or amp.

-EQ is to ENHANCE your tone, not create it! A Strat cannot be made to sound like a Les Paul and vice versa. Your tone is made up of many, many variables. The resulting tone can be SHAPED or COLORED by adding or subtracting certain frequencies. That is the function of an EQ, nothing more. IT can range from dramatic to very subtle. Very small changes can have large effects. Small bumps in the higher range really enhance the harmonics I am able to produce.

-I tend to put the EQ in much later in my effect chain, but feel free to experiment.
Summary: If you know how to use EQ, this box is ROCK SOLID

Text:
It always bugged me that my Nord Stage 2 never sounded like the million bucks I knew it was capable of while coming through my studio monitors. Its pianos were good but not great, its organs which Nord is famous for lacked depth, and synths lacked the punch you need for modern composition.

I started upgrading the whole loop, picking places where I'd get the biggest bang for the buck first.

- Invested in a quality audio interface
- Got Mogami Gold TRS cables running to the speakers
- Power conditioner to eliminate background hum and improve speaker performance

All of these immensely helped the sound of the overall system, but nothing really helped the Nord Stage 2, so I went for the last piece of the line and replaced my existing 1/4"s, certainly not the cheapest cables on the market, with 2 of these Mogami Platinums.

To compare with my older cables, I started up a wide-range synth arp on the NS2 with sharp and padded elements so I could gauge the different aspects of the keyboard's voice. With the arp running, I swapped out the right channel cable with the new Mogami Platinum. As has always the case when upgrading to Mogamis, I immediately had to turn down the volume after plugging it in because the signal was so much stronger with the Mogami cable.

Instantly, I was stunned to "discover" the reverb that the NS2 was applying to its sound. Something that was barely audible with the previous cable was now clear and beautiful.

After further comparisons of left vs. right, I went ahead and swapped out the left audio channel as well for the full Mogami setup.

I equate the experience to someone reaching to your face and taking off a pair of dirty glasses you didn't even know you had on, revealing the world you thought you had been seeing clearly in new crystal clear 20/20 vision.

Indeed, it hurt forking over $320 for 2x20 feet of cable, but after hearing the difference I'd do it again in a heartbeat! Just like you'd never pair a cheap bow with an expensive cello, I've learned that you shouldn't be pairing cheap cables with expensive equipment. No doubt, I will be buying these cables by default for any future 1/4" cable necessities!
Summary: Lift the Fog Off Your Sound

Text:
I recently received an SD-1 for my birthday after having asked for one. It sounds good stock but in my particular setup it was a little too muffled, even with the tone knob turned all the way up (which seems to boost the upper mids moreso than the high end). However, there is an easy mod for the SD-1 in which you remove a capacitor (C6) to restore some of the high end that the pedal cuts out.

I opened up the pedal and was initially annoyed to find that Boss has moved to surface mount components for the SD-1. Now, there is absolutely nothing wrong, sound- or durability-wise, with surface mount components in a pedal, but it's *really* difficult to mod a pedal with surface mount components. By luck, however, C6 was positioned in a relatively easy to access location on the PCB, where I could grab it with some needlenose pliers and just snap it off.

It now sounds perfect to me--I love it. If stock or the C6 mod will work for you, I definitely recommend it. But if you're interested in any other mods it's probably best to find a used SD-1 from 2016 or earlier.

One upside to the surface mount components and new layout is that, as far as I can tell, it resolves a problem older SD-1's had in which it would sometimes inject noise into the bypassed signal.
Summary: Great, but difficult to mod now

3. It has a USB out to connect to your computer for editing and recording.
4. Factory tones are decent and can be changed on the fly to suit your
own needs.

Overall, this product is way ahead of anything in its price range and it SOUNDS GREAT. I totally recommend it to anyone of any style. I play an eclectic array of music, so the flexibility appeals to me. I am able to go from a JC-120 jazz sound to a Plexi. The stomp box modeling also are great. It would be nice if there was an effects loop, but you don't really need it with all the effects you can produce with this box alone.

Go buy one already... that's my advice :)

I was so thrilled with the Joyo American Sound that I ended up buying the British Sound roughly a week later. While the British Sound is a good deal overall, it just doesn't sound as good as the American Sound does (to me). This has nothing to do with how accurately it emulates a real Marshall amplifier (same thing with the American Sound), as opposed to how usable the sonic flexibility is when going straight into a (guitar) power amp. It's impossible to get a decent balance of bass/middle/treble frequency response, regardless of how clean or distorted the gain is set to. Along with that, there an unpleasant solid state-like harshness when the gain is set higher. While the American Sound isn't foolproof with how you can set it, there's a lot more usable sounds that are pleasing in a guitar amp way. Again, I have to stress that I'm using this pedal to be representative of a guitar amp's preamp, in its totality. If someone is just using this as an OD or distortion pedal, or if only using it as an emergency backup into the PA, it's probably potentially great for that.

Also, the British Sound seems to have the potential (depending on where the gain is set) to have a much higher noise floor than the American Sound, too.
Summary: Not as good as the American Sound

Text:
Compared to other highly rated headphones in the same price range (sub-$100), this is one of the best I've owned. At the lowered price since the release of the K240 Mk II the value is well worth it.

Note these 'phones are higher impedance (55ohms) than average, which provides several benefits you can find on Google. This means using these 'phones for mobile listening without proper supporting pre-amplification will not do them justice.

With a suitable support system (Dragonfly Red on a MBP, or direct through a hi-fi preamp) I found these 'phones to be much clearer and flatter in response than many others in the price range. They do well on everything from symphonic to folk to metal, on either CD or vinyl. These will not do booming bass so if you're a bass player, like Beats, or prefer pop/rock concerts you may not like this. These are great for studio mixes where bass and drums are tight and sharp and sounds well in the mix as opposed to over the rest of the band. It does similarly well with acoustic instruments where you can hear nuances on the string, and also with rock guitar where great grinding distortion tones come across with clarity.

Like its name, these phones are for you if you are like clear, controlled, balanced listening that you find in studio settings. If however you enjoy grooving out to different audio experiences I would look elsewhere.

Text:
SETUP
Simply attach the beater to the pedal and adjust to the desired height. has both felt side and plastic beater side.

PROS
1) I like the wide, slick footboard
2) The clamp adjustment is towards the outside so the footboard wouldn't hit it as some pedals I've seen
3) Easy adjustable throw angle to bring the beater back further for power
4) The pedal, when in position, actually seems to be closer to the head, than other pedals. Which means you don't have to raise the front of the drum up too high to ensure the angle of the beater is at a perfect vertical position.

CONS
1) It's noisy. Just operating without hitting the drum, you can hear the mechanisms as they move. Recording may be an issue
2) The beater is actually longer than other beaters, so you can't position the beater to hit dead center if you wanted to. It would rub against the head. That's when I realized that the beater was a bit longer than usual
3) The bottom of the pedal has the velcro hooks so if you set on carpet, it grabs it immediately. This is a problem because usually I'd lift my bass drum just enough to slide the pedal into the hoop. This one you can't. Once you set it down, that's it. You'd have to lift the drum higher than usual, attach to the hoop and THEN lower the drum. Problem is if you have your Toms and everything on top then you got that weight you need to lift. Thankfully, I have my rack Toms on independent stands. If you need to adjust the Bass drum position, it makes it difficult

OVERALL
Thus far in using it, with minor adjustments it feels good. It's just awkward with the pedal height being longer than normal, and the velcro on the bottom is not a good idea. It does come with spurs for carpet so that would keep it from sliding. Or maybe just the back end of the pedal should have the velcro, but not the whole pedal. It just made it awkward to place on the drum.
Summary: Some design issues, but decent pedal

My 8 year old daughter has a Yamaha GL1, but needed a bag/case to carry it to jam sessions/lessons. The instrument is 27.6" but this bag still works due to it's lack of rigid structure, and it echos her style and tastes perfectly!
I am impressed with the quality out of the box. This is a much nicer bag for this price than I expected. As another buyer commented, the bag is folded in a plastic bag when you receive it. There doesn't seem to be residual folds however after placing the Guitalele inside. The fabric itself is a nylon weave reminiscent of ripstop. The purple flower print is a rich plum purple, with white and magenta accents. The trim and stitching are black. It is smooth and won't pick/shred your clothes when the bag rubs against your back which is nice for a bag that will probably be carried slung over one shoulder or worn cross body. The side grab handle is nicely padded, however my daughter's instrument is very light (less than 2 lbs), so the padding almost seems superfluous. A nice touch would have been to pad the sling strap. The nylon tape of the strap will dig in a bit if the bag moves around at all. A strap pad is easy to obtain or make.
The interior is just as much a delight as the exterior. The fabric is a black fleece knit. The front pocket is lined, and just right for extra strings, pics and her snark tuner. It is too small for any of her music books however. The silver piping on the pocket is also a nice touch for the bag's aesthetic. The zippers aren't the highest quality, but the metal pulls, and nylon teeth are adequate in strength and scale for this application and price.
The padding feels more substantial than advertised, and will provide plenty of protection against the bumps and bruises transport could yield.
Overall we are thrilled with this bag, it's just what we needed to feel comfortable to take the Guitalele out of the house!

One year update:

This mic is outstanding, especially for the price. The trick to making it amazing is to look up the frequency response and set up an EQ that is opposite, to flatten the tonal balance.

Without EQ it has a significant boost around 9.4k and it can be very sibilant... But if you create EQ that inverts the tonal balance what you end up with is a neutral sound. Save the preset and use it again.

Then you can use a second EQ or a channel strip to flavor the flattened sound to your liking, but neutralizing it is key to having a good starting point.

The case & shock mount it comes with adds a lot of value. The rubber bands that suspend the mic wore out after some time, but they include replacements. I ended up using rubber bands and it's perfect again.

This is the perfect LDC mic for someone on a budget. Just use EQ to correct the tonal balance and it will sound like a high end mic.

The first thing to understand about a device like this is that it should last for a very long time. There's nothing in it that should just sputter out and stop working. Sure, you could ruin a pot, knob, dial, or jack, but barring one of those things happening, it shouldn't just stop working. It's a solid-state circuit board and it sits on a desk in a pretty beastly housing. At 25 months, mine died. I can count the times it has been moved around without taking off my shoes. It has been cared for well, never abused, and used in a non-smoking environment. Minus a star. At about 760 days of ownership, this little devil cost about $0.30 a day to own. By itself, that's not a terrible number, but given that I've got music equipment I've gigged with, hauled all over the place, and abused to no end that's been running for a decade or more, I'm pretty upset with it.

Native Instruments (who have aggressively bad customer service) offered to replace it with a refurbished product sometime in the next three to six weeks if I paid them $170. Sorry guys, that's an AWFUL deal. It also took seven business days of going back and forth with their technical support team, answering the same questions repeatedly, explaining that I had tried their ludicrous troubleshooting steps (they wanted me to try it on two Mac AND a Windows computer before ascertaining that it had a problem) to reach that laughably bad solution.

When I got it new, the direct monitoring (which is hardware level) didn't work. It still doesn't work, but I wasn't too fussed, and that represented well less than <1% of my need, so whatever. But, regardless of my needs, minus one star for a totally defunct hardware level feature right out of the box. Issue number two: the S/PDIF input never worked. I didn't even learn this until a full year after I'd bought it, but as far as I know it was also dead when I got it. Minus another star.

But how is it? Well, it's pretty good. The preamps are good enough for the price tag. It's clear, and you don't hear its internal electronics ever. The headphone jack on mine wasn't great, and I'd frequently hear a little noise when adjusting the volume, but that's not a huge deal. The drivers are solid, though Native Instruments' update system / software is some of the worst I have EVER used.

All in all, when it works, it's not bad. But, mine came with two DOA components, a headphone jack that crackled when adjusted, and it died in just over two years, costing me about $9 a month to own. I couldn't recommend it, and I wouldn't buy it again.

By way of a footnote, I also had a Native Instruments Maschine for a while, and I had hardware problems with it as well. Native Instruments does some great software work, and their hardware does feel wonderful when you're using it, but they just don't seem to have the kind of quality control you'd expect for the prices they charge.

I am in love with the Neck Humbuckers in my Gibson's. Unfortunately Gibson does not make a Strat Body guitar and I am a sucker for a black strat. So, I bought a Black Squire, these pickups and a new 24.75 neck.

Installation - Since the strat body was a single neck pickup heavy modification was required to the body of the guitar as I needed to route a swimming pool for the new neck humbucker as well as modify the neck joint for the shorter scale neck. I am happy to say that this loaded pickguard went in with ease and aside from soldering the output jack and the ground the install was super easy. Sure the screws needed a few new holes but the four corners lined up and I carefully pre-drilled whichever screws did not line up and you would never know the difference. (Besides, pick guards NEVER line up!)

Sound - For the low price that this product is, one must assume the sound is not going to be that of pickups that cost 10 times as much. That said, I was very surprised to hear the neck position! It's deep, bluesy, and full of tone! I have been comparing the guitar to one of my favorite gibson's that has stock pickups and these have more output. If you wanted to play some SRV "Mary had a little lamb" this is the combo. Now if you were to upgrade the pots and add some caps from AxeGrinders you are playing with some fire. Your tone is gonna make the neighbors either rip their clothes off and dance in the streets or call the cops on the delusional tones coming from your house.

Price - Why give a product like this less than 5 stars? Over expectation. Its cheap, buy it and experiment like I did. Put some work in. You will come back and buy another... like I did...

That's all this inexpensive foray into some custom guitar building is going to get from me today... I am off to go play my new toy!

[[VIDEOID:a8dacb2c6fb3facaa959f623294a8136]] This little amp does a decent job for quiet practice or jamming along with your music player. Kit includes a headphone splitter, an auxiliary 1/8" stereo cable, and a charge cord (no wall charger).
Charging is visually managed by LED indicators, showing the level. It charged quickly, and not having to swap out batteries is a bonus.
The guitar jack is fixed in position, unlike some that swivel. It worked well in multiple guitars, including a Stratocaster with the recessed/angled input jack.
To me, a good practice amp must have a clean tone above all else. Effects are cool, but when you need to listen critically clean is best. Unfortunately, this little amp distorts even at low volume levels.
The CHORUS and REVERB effect are not adjustable. Simply on/off. GAIN cranks up the distortion, which this amp excels at producing. TONE offered the least change in sound, taking out some of the higher frequency.
Is it the best headphone amp out there? No. But it has a fun metal sound and can be very useful for practice without breaking the bank. Or waking the neighbors.

In any recording process there are several components that come together to make a good recording. A good microphone is just one part of the whole setup, albeit a key item. As with any technical equipment, a great deal of experimentation is involved to test out the system. The mic, pop screen and extendable arm are well-manufactured and comfortable. The arm clamps to your desk and can swing into a wide range of positions to match whatever your desk setup is. When not in use I swing the arm up and behind my monitor so that it's completely out of the way and not intruding on any of my regular workspace.

The USB cord is generous at nearly 8 feet long, so you shouldn't have any trouble reaching your computer in most situations. The mic also comes with its own foam wind filter that fits over the end of the mic. You can use it in tandem with the included pop screen or either one by itself. You'll need to experiment with the sound quality to determine what kind of sound qualities you want. Generally you'll get slightly crisper sounds without the wind filter, but this can depend on your recording software and how you have your bass, midrange and treble set up. Experimentation is the key. The good thing is that all the hardware feels solid and it assembles easily and quickly without feeling cheap—quite astounding for such a reasonably priced system.

A major part of your recording is the software you use. On the Mac you have the included Garage Band at no additional cost. It's fairly intuitive and works directly from USB input or you can put it through a variety of signal processors from many different companies. Many people use a simple USB mic run directly into Garage Band and are very pleased with the results for podcasts, video voiceovers and Skype or other conferencing software. As your skills and knowledge increase you may want to buy other recording software and signal processors.

Overall, I would recommend this unit as an excellent starter system that could extend into semi-professional recording. For the price, it's an affordable means of testing the recording waters to see if it's something you want to do. Recommended.
Summary: Still experimenting but appears to be an excellent product

Text:
This moving head could be a great addition to any mobile DJ or party lighting setup. The unit offers two types of bright beam effects, best used with some fog or haze in the air.

Six RGBW LEDs and rotating lenses create a swirling/scanning light pattern, while a central laser produces a wide-spread field of green dots/beams. Both effects look good, but it’s worth noting that the RGBW is non-blended/non-mixed, and there’s no focus adjustment.

For those seeking a light show with minimal effort, the fixture offers sound-activated and fully-automatic operation. The preset modes incorporate a variety of color and movement, and they thankfully don’t rely too heavily on high-speed strobing (as many inexpensive moving lights do). A remote control is not provided, but multiple units can be linked using your own 3-pin XLR cables.

For advanced users, 15-channel DMX offers good control over the unit. The RGBW and laser are independently dimmed, but their strobe and rotation are shared. The fixture generally behaves well under DMX, except for small pan/tilt movements, which run at low speed regardless of anything commanded on the XY-speed channel.

The unit is decently built, with sturdy plastic panels over a metal chassis, and the cooling fans are quiet and unobtrusive. I was disappointed, however, that the RGBW lenses arrived very dirty, with a heavy layer of factory grime on both sides. They can be accessed for cleaning, with minimal disassembly, but extra care must be taken because the lenses are weak plastic and get scratched very easily. I ended up with swirls on my lenses after using a soft cotton cloth.

Overall, this little light is capable of making a big impact, but it’s unusually slow at completing small DMX movements, and the lenses should have been made of more durable material. Four stars.
Summary: Bright multi-beam/laser, but sluggish during small movements, and has fragile lenses

Text:
This isn't a particularly terrible drum kit but I still can't recommend it.

The best "feeling" part of this kit is the snare drum which uses a mesh drum top which more accurately imitates the feeling of playing a real drum kit. Unfortunately, this is the only drum to have the mesh build while the rest of the kit feels and works about as good as a rock band drum set.

I know its a beginners kit, but there are so many alternative kits on Amazon that are either slightly more expensive and much higher quality or slightly less expensive and still higher quality. Here's some of my biggest gripes:
- Only one mesh drum - The snare, the best feeling drum in the kit, doesn't even register hits if they're not decently strong and in the center of the drum. This is consistent with the rest of the kit where you really have to whack it to make any sound.
- Insensitive drum heads with little sound variation - Usually you'll get a wide range of sounds and volumes when you tap a drum vs whack it, but this kit doesn't have much variation outside of volume. It also seems to completely miss the ~25% lightest hits. You'll also have noticeably different sounds if you hit a cymbal that was just hit, but on this kit, it will just loop the same sound over and over instead of blending it.
- Poor pedals and hi-hat - Basically every decent drum kit has an actual pad that the bass pedal hits, but this one does not, nor does it have good sensitivity or range of volumes. The hi-hat, when ever you change the pedal, immediately stops the previous sound and plays an opening or closing sound with no blending whatsoever.
- Low quality parts - The headphones work decently for how cheap they are but are still uncomfortable and unadjustable, and seem to exist only to increase the overall price. The main control unit also feels like its made from the cheapest plastic available and doesn't seem sturdy at all.

Despite all of these complaints, it still might work well enough for you. Its definitely not "quiet" as you have to hit the drums pretty hard to get them to reliably register, but in a basement it'll be fine. But still, there are alternatives here on Amazon that at least appear to be much better than this kit (with alternatives as much as $100 cheaper with all mesh drum heads). This kit would make much more sense with a third of its price chopped off.
Summary: Theres much better for the money

Text:
GraphTech TUSQ is unlike any other nut material out there. It is a high-pressure laminate material that is easy to work with when using the proper tools. What is so amazing is that the material is actually "tuned" for resonance, acting very much like a tonewood. If you were to drop the nut (or any part made from TUSQ or Nubone material) onto a hard surface, it actually rings a note like tonewood does when you tap hammer it. Yes, its a musically sonic material! This allows string vibration to transfer tone to your neck in a way no other nut material can. It truly makes your instrument that much more resonant, and as a bonus, the "XL" means it's impregnated with PTFE (Teflon) so it's slippery. Even when cut improperly, string winding don't usually get caught in the string slots due to the PTFE. I HIGHLY recommend getting any nut professionally installed as it will need to be shaped, seated and cut properly. YOU DO NOT JUST BUY A NUT AND SLAP IT IN... IT MUST BE FIT TO YOUR INSTRUMENT!

Hope this helps,

I was skeptical at first when I saw a nut, saddle, and bridge pin set made of genuine bone for such a cheap price but since I didn’t really like anything else I was seeing, I took a gamble. After inspection under a light, I was pleasantly surprised to discover these are, in fact, bone. I could see the natural “grain” and inconsistencies that bone has and they also have that unmistakable clinky sound when you shake them in your hand. They’re also pretty high quality too. They seem like they’re machined very well. Nothing about them looked or felt cheap to my eye. The pieces sanded down well to fit my Alvarez.

But you don’t buy this set and upgrade your guitar for it’s looks. You buy it for the sound difference and let me tell you, other than buying lighter or heavier gauge strings, there isn’t a cheaper way to improve the overall tone of your guitar than to upgrade to bone. This set madr my guitar sound brighter, a little louder, and has much better resonation. I can even feel the increased vibration of the guitar against my body as I play. You don’t realize how much a plastic nut, saddle, and bridge pins can muddy up the sound until you switch to bone.

The craftsmanship on the abalone inlays on the bridge pins are just okay. I’ve seen better but you really can’t tell unless you’re really inspecting them closely and for the price, you can’t expect a set of Waverly quality pins. From afar they look fine.

One thing I wish Blisstime would offer is an unbleached set with a black dots on the pins. I was trying to find white pins with a black dot, as I like that traditional look, but that proved to be harder to find than I thought so I settled for these. And the stark white is okay but I’d prefer that natural off-white look of unbleached bone.

All in all it’s a great purchase. Expect to sand everything at least a little bit to custom fit your guitar

Text:
Mini Looper pedal that can handle 9 loops, with a built-in Tuner.

The loops are recorded at 48KHz 24-bit quality, which is indistinguishable from the source. Since there’s no detune / octave effects here, there’s no need for oversampling / higher frequency rates.

The loops can be accessed with the little Left and Right arrow buttons.

Pressing those buttons together enters Tuner mode, which silences any output - nice!

Tuner is super basic but does everything you need. Shows the current pitch and little dot LEDs indicate if you’re sharp or flat.

Overdubs are easy to do / undo, no limit on those (other than you can only undo 1 overdub; undoing an undo brings the overdub back again).

The LED indicator (circle of LEDs around the main screen) for where you’re at in the loop is VERY useful.

Overall, it seems really well thought out.

Value wise, it is 2 pedals in a mini pedal format, saving space and cost. No complaints there.

Can be used at the front of your board to create a riff and dial in your tone, or at the end of the board to capture a riff to jam along to. Most people can benefit from a little looper.

5 stars because it does everything I expect a single switch looper to do (plus a little more).
Summary: Simple to use Looper AND Tuner

To all guitarists, or anyone using a signal processing app----JUST BUY ONE AND BE DONE WITH IT!

I'm using iOS Amplitube as my mobile "ideas at the speed of thought" device. I think that's a quote from director Robert Rodriguez by the way, but the point is this app is my go-to studio for recording, playing, and working out ideas as they come for songs on my guitar. Of course, it's not a replacement for a professional studio, but I'm continually amazed at what it can do. It's one of the VERY FEW apps I have any real use for.

That said, the interface is critical between instrument and device. This first iRig interface was (is) pretty noisy. The same for the AmpKit by Peavey. This product, though not 100% perfect, is nonetheless a 100% improvement over the first generation interfaces. In my opinon, this is not just a novelty item, and can be used for true productivity.

The product description says it all. It is an all encompassing interface for instruments, both 1/4" and XLR input, as well as MIDI in. It also offers phantom power to condenser mics, and the interface is connected to the iOS device by the 13 pin connector, and/or the new lighting connector. But, it also has the ability for standard USB connection to a Mac computer.

All cabling for your iOS device connectivity is supplied minus your instrument/mic cable. From get go you can plug in your guitar, synth, or mic and start playing a minute or two after opening the box. I've used the iRig Pro for Amplitube, and Garage Band, using guitars, mics, and a portable, cheap toy like MIDI capable keyboard. All have been not only usable, but much more EXPANDABLE because I can now make fairly decent demo tracks with fairly professional results in more ways than one.

Beforehand, I've had to use a Focusrite Scarlett, iOS USB camera kit, and powered USB port just to get something quiet enough to record to iPad. I'll still use this setup, but the iRig Pro makes it to where all I need now is just one interface! I can throw this in a guitar case, go to wherever, not have to worry about powering one device or another, and I can get some REAL work done pretty much wherever I'm at, and have fun doing what I love to do----make music!

I don't like the price of the iRig Pro, but I'll admit to being a cheapskate. But the quality of the VERY LOW noise level is worth the price alone, and is the primary reason I can get those more than doable audio recording tracks. This device is truly a must have piece of gear if you're going to expand your mobile recording, and even live sound capabilities.

I feel more than comfortable using Amplitube and other apps for iPad during live gigs, providing the gig is not much more than a large coffee house, or campus setting at the extreme side of size. However, there is room to say that size may not matter with the right setup----no pun intended! But, I believe the iRig Pro has made this a real possibility for the ingenious performer that can, and will make that happen regardless of venue.

Look, I'm just another guitar player looking for something to add to my creativity and ease of use without paying out the nose for a setup I can't afford without having to sell a kidney. The iRig Pro provides a real usable device for that, and is a product worth the price tag.

I first tried an alto reeds on my modest but reliable EM Winston soprano sax years ago and liked the way they covered the mouthpiece opening and felt more substantial on the lip - especially once they’re broken in, soften up and shred a bit at the corners. With more material to work with they just hold their own longer.

Most importantly, alto reeds give my horn a slightly heftier and consistent tone than the 3 ½ Rico soprano reeds I’ve used.
I tweak them a bit both for comfort and appearance. You have to loosen the clamps more than you may be used to, but there’s still plenty of thread left for a secure fit. The alto reeds extend about 3/8” towards the back than soprano reeds. That length doesn’t interfere with playing hands but for appearance I use a thin blade hobby saw to cut about half of it off, roughly matching the soprano length – an X-Acto knife or equivalent sharp blade will also do the trick.

Where I prefer the X-Acto or a razor blade is to slice the small slivers of reed that extend just beyond the corners of the mouthpiece opening. I hold the mouthpiece in one hand and lightly glide the blade along the edge – two or three strokes at most are all you need for a solid-fitting reed.

The ten-pack D’Addario Reserved reeds are consistently clean and unchipped at the thin end and have similar coloration and consistency at the thicker base end. The plastic sliding holders have a slightly different holding mechanism than Ricos must that appears more like an attempt to head off a look and feel challenge than anything functional.

If you play soprano and have never tried alto reeds I’d recommend giving them a try. Sometimes it’s good to shake up your mechanics a bit; it can force your technique into new areas that in turn can lead to new musical results, which is ultimately what’s it’s all about.
Summary: A Little Work Makes a Better Fit for Sopranos

One of my guitars is a Fender 2007 Standard (MIM) Strat. I've always liked how that guitar felt, but not how it sounded. The stock pickups were kind of bland, and did not have the signature bite and punch that a good Strat should have. I knew eventually I would swap them out for a brighter, more dynamic set.

For years I wanted the much-hyped Fender Custom Shop '69s, due to the legend that those were essentially the same pickups used by Jimi Hendrix.

At first I was gassing for a Fender Classic Player 60s Strat, which had those pickups as standard equipment. Later on, I thought about getting a set to replace the pickups in my MIM Strat. But I hedged at the price--CS 69s were typically not discounted by much, if at all.

It wasn't until earlier this year that I discovered Pure Vintage '65s, after hearing a guitarist on YouTube nailing an early Hendrix tone with those pickups. With that in mind, I went to the Fender website and matched up the specs of the Custom Shop '69s with the Pure Vintage '65s. I was surprised to find that both pickups were almost identically spec'd, and the Pure Vintage '65s were at least $50 less expensive.

From that point, I was sold on the '65s. It was like I forgot all about how I lusted after the Custom Shop '69s. I bought a set of Pure Vintage '65s and couldn't wait to put together a new pickguard and wiring harness for the MIM Strat.

Note the following about these pickups as shipped:
(1) This is a 'pure vintage' set of pickups, so there's no reverse-wound middle pickup for controlling noise in positions 2 and 4;
(2) Fender does not indicate the output of the pickups, so you're on our own if you want to test your own set;
(3) Fender does not advise us on which positions to mount each pickup--that's up to us to figure out as well.

There was no way I was going to drop these pickups in without knowing which one should go where. That's why I have a multimeter. So I tested my set at 6.29k, 6.25k, and 6.07k. (Of course, not all pickups are exactly the same, so YMMV.) I wanted the highest output pickup--the 6.29--in the bridge, and the next highest--the 6.25--in the neck, since those are the positions I play in most often.

Also note here that prior to wiring the pickups for mounting, I completely lined the pickup routs and the underside of the new pickguard with copper tape--this creates a mini Faraday cage for controlling hum from the single coil pickups. Doing so was a revelation, as the finished guitar is extremely noise-free. I highly recommend this to anyone who owns a Strat.

With the pickups wired in and the installation completed, the Pure Vintage '65 pickups are a huge improvement over the stock pickups, as expected. They have much better dynamic range and clarity, although I would not say they are 'punchier.' These are vintage, warm-sounding pickups. They handle distortion much better than I expected, as well. Using a dirt pedal, I was able to get an early Van Halen tone out of the bridge, which was downright shocking. You can go from glassy, delicate cleans to an old-school rock roar. I currently like using them with moderate gain at the amp, and then I can dial back to clean tones with the guitar's volume knob. These pickups make lots of tone choices possible.

The only thing lacking in this set is the reverse-wound middle, so the 2 and 4 positions do not combine with the middle to make the output noise-free. You simply do not buy these pickups if you want a reverse-wound middle. (A correction to the earlier version: the 2 and 4 positions do have the distinctive Strat 'quack' sounds.)

All in all, I'm glad I waited and found out about Pure Vintage '65s. I don't miss the more hyped Custom Shop '69s at all. These are very versatile, sweet sounding pickups. It's made my MIM Strat an entirely different animal.

TLDR: If you don’t know much about microphones, I’d recommend a Shure SM 58 instead of this, in the price range - sounds richer. If you know a bit and are looking for a cheap condenser… this one is overhyped, for whatever reason, perhaps because it’s so ubiquitous, but it works for me on spoken word by taming sibilance during recording, yet requires some heavy but easy processing (compression/eq) to get the recorded signal sounding great.

The sound is flat and boring… I know, those aren’t technical terms. It feels like there are ‘pieces’ missing in the signal. I used it to mic an amp first and it sounded like a cheap mic sounds, in some regards. Almost transistor radio-ish. Lack of clarity, no character… I thought it was my amp.

For acoustic, haven’t tried it. Vocals, same, I’m not a singer. Spoken word is what I’m using it for - it’s dark (but not bass-y) and flat and has a slight upper mid boost and sounds overall hollow… HOWEVER… it lacks in the sibilant range, which is perfect for me as I’m ssssssibilant. That’s the big plus for me. But it’s also a lack of clarity in the upper range… but it doesn’t pick up much background noise… and by the time I EQ it and add compression, the recorded signal sounds ballsy with no harsh sibilance. The raw recorded signal however…. meh.

All in all, this may not be the condenser you’re looking for, maybe MXL has something comparable in the price range, but if a dynamic will suit you, I’d go with SM 57 or 58. If you have sibilance issues and can process the sound on your own (rather than turning in an untreated recording) this might be for you. I can recommend it as a low budget condenser for that very specific voice-over purpose. Probably if you heard my finished voice-over/rant, you’d be impressed with the sound… or it may be a bit compressed/terrestrial radio guy sounding.

Also, it’s always tough to judge by youtube vids, some add ‘a bit’ of EQ and/or compression, some don’t say, and who knows what mixer or preamp they’re using even if the sound is untreated. I’ve heard this mic sound better on vids than in real life.

Text:
Best all-around harmonica for any reasonable money? I did a ridiculous amount of research on this before I bought. I looked at Lee Oskar Harmonicas, at the Suzuki, and other brands. Some guy named Ian Chadwick, for example, provides extensive coverage of his own experience with an amazing spectrum of brands and models within those [http://www.ianchadwick.com/essays/harmonicas.htm] which is worth checking out, as of course are the reviews you'll find here on Amazon. And yes, within Hohner there are other options besides the Special 20, the most notable perhaps being the Hohner Blues Harp. The difference between the Special 20 and the Blues Harp is mainly--so the story goes--in the comb, the part your mouth actually rests on and glides over. The Blues Harp is wood, the Special 20 plastic. Despite what you first might think, lots of players go for the plastic because it doesn't swell and warp with the large volume of--let's face it--spit that gets driven through a harp. I grew up playing cross-harp along with one of my best high school buddies as he strummed his guitar, and it's fun. Do check out the basic mapping from the key of the song to the so-called "2nd position" (aka cross-harp) key. For the likely songs you encounter in popular music, blues, etc, they seem to be as follows:
KEY OF SONG / HARP KEY
E / A
F / B-flat
G / C
A / D
B / E
C / F
D / G
This set gives you keys C, G, A, D, & E. There seems to be a consensus that if you buy F and B-flat you're pretty much set, though the Special 20 comes in 14 keys, maybe in case you want to play Mozart. These are so much better than the cheap Hohners I grew up playing, real musical instruments that produce sound effortlessly, bend notes with considerable expressiveness, and work very well on both the blow and the draw--if those are the right terms. I remember my cheap set being a trial for note-production on the draw notes. These are made in Germany, as printed on the harmonicas, and as stated on the Hohner website. Don't panic, the case of course is made in China, and that sticker is the first thing you see, of standard Case Logic type quality, but very nicely fitted for the harps plus space for a couple more, which in due course, for me, will be that F and that B-flat. Btw I also checked the price all over the 'verse (as they call it on Firefly), and every place has the same price, so you can just stop looking and get it here. Great way to enjoy playing music. I own a pretty complete set of tools for that job--nice Yamaha stage piano, Gibson Les Paul electric, Martin dreadnought acoustic, and recently a cool Yamaha electronic drum kit, which is the bee's knees, let me tell you. But this is the ultimate portable, entry-level musical instrument, very unpretentious, and honestly you can sound pretty passable on them soon enough that you won't toss them aside with a snarl of frustration. Also a great gift. But folks, don't play like Bob Dylan. I just bought the mono recordings box set of his first eight albums, and the guy, genius though he is, sounds like he's signaling ships at sea when he blasts that harp. I'm not the only one who seems to think his headache-inducing harmonica work renders many tracks unlistenable. Bobbie, think of the neighbors! I mean, am I missing something or is Mr. Robert Zimmerman truly bad at playing the harmonica? OK, you're a bard, but stick to the lute, will you?
Summary: My research indicates this is the best all-around set. Very sweet-sounding.

I've been using these stands for 25 years and they are hands down the best available. What makes them so good? The guitar hangs from the claw and the body rests against the tripod. On stage they are very easy to navigate, and when going on break between sets you can just set your guitar on the claw and you're done. One issue I have run into over the years is the knobs with threaded shafts used to tighten the vertical arm and the tripod which, under heavy use eventually strips. No matter how careful one is, the threads eventually begin to wear to the point of stripping. If you are not a gigging musician this is not an issue, however with repeated use they will wear out. In the past I have emailed Hamilton customer service and they have been very good about sending replacements knobs. They have even acknowledged the thread problem, but that is there catch comes in. They no longer respond to any attempts at contact. And they know the threads are a problem. So now I have half a dozen stands that are no longer useful. And that's a big problem.

Again, if you are a casual user and set up your stand at home these are great. If you're a gigging musician, try to be as careful as possible. If it weren't for the bolt problem these would be 10 stars.

I am a guitar tech and I found this installation to be difficult and time consuming. I had to pull the parts back off several times to get a proper fit. If you are not used to modifying small parts and familiar with setting intonation, you should probably have a professional do the installation. Once installed it is a very nice looking bridge and works good. My ears could not detect any modification to the sound of the bass or its sustain. Before I bought this unit I read all of the reviews and most were favorable. I own the Line 6 Pod and initially thought this was sort of a Pod ripoff. But I have tried other units that were more expensive that did not yield the results I was looking for. Something told me to give this a try so I took the $110 dollar gamble. I am so glad I did!

This unit features guitar amplifier and cabinet simulation. I wanted something that I could go directly into the PC or mixing console with, that would sound good without having to mic a cabinet. I had tried other units that just didn't yield quality results. This one did, even though it was much cheaper. When I first plugged it in, it gave a fancy light show and I thought, "Wow, that looks pretty cool, I just hope it sounds as good as the light show looked." It did.

I ordered it off of Amazon and had it the very next day. I got it just minutes before I left my house for practice with my bass player. So I brought it with me. I had my cheap beat-around electric guitar with me at the time. I plugged it directly into my Peavey powered mixer and it sounded pretty good. I was immediately impressed, as was my bass player. When I got home, I plugged my Les Paul into it and it was even better! I went through some of the presets and found one close to the sound I was looking for. Then I tweaked it a bit, with headphones on, and it was amazingly close to what I had in mind. Then I plugged it into my PC through my Line 6 UX2. It sounded excellent.

One thing I noticed, though, is that it really does sound very much like a guitar amplifier with a miked speaker cabinet. There is a volume for the patch and a main volume. When your patch volume is too high, it is very much like a miked cabinet with the volume set too high, which would detract from clarity. So I lowered the patch volume and raised the main volume and the clarity improved greatly. It is important to remember that you really have to play around with it to find the sound you are looking for.

At the time of this writing, I haven't really tried the USB adapter that was provided with it. So I can't really speak to the latency issues some have complained about regarding that. But I can speak to the fact that it sounds great when run directly into a mixing console for live applications, thereby making it unnecessary to drag a small guitar amp around to mic for gigs. That's a big plus for me. Really quick setup time. You gotta love that!

It comes with many effects and they are decent quality but I was disappointed by the fact that it didn't include a pitch shifter that would allow for a dropped tuning or for harmony leads. However, I have a zoom pedal I can use for that. I can go out from that into this unit. Of course, It'll probably throw off the sound a bit and may require some more tweaking to set it straight again, but, oh well, nothing in life is easy.

The paperwork you get with it isn't really the greatest. You can download a PDF manual for it off of the Behringer website that is much better. Do that before you try to figure out how to use it and end up getting aggravated by not being able to figure it on your own.

So, to sum it up, I'd have to say it is well worth the money regardless as to whether or not the USB interface is good or not. The unit itself is great.

I really like this Kalimba. feel like the people who gave it a bad review just didn't take the time to tune it properly. You really can't expect a mail order instrument to arrive in perfectly tuned, playable condition; that's just crazy!

You need to loosen the screws until you can push the keys around somewhat easily. Don't be affraid to tune the pitch up fairly high. mine sounds a bit better at higher pitches.

push each key back until you get it into a register where it doesn't sound "tubby" if you pluck the key lightly. then get it into a scale that sounds nice to you. you can use a tuner or download a tuner app for your phone or you can just tune it by ear or to a piano.

Also, you want to make sure that none of the keys are touching each other, because this will detract from the tone.

After you get it tuned, tighten the screws just tight enough that you can pluck the keys pretty hard without them rattling. it's really worth it to spend 20 or 30 minutes to get your instrument tuned well. Mine sounds really nice now... just don't expect it to sound great out of the box.

Pros:
Lightweight and very portable
runs on AC or AA batteries,
61 keys is just enough for scales (covers double octave contrary in any key),
plug and play midi,
velocity sensitive,
full size keys.

Cons:
#1) NO PRESETS (OR REGISTRATIONS) AT ALL. Only a few settings (tuning, lcd contrast, and auto-poweroff) are saved when you power off. Everything else, you have to tap the function key up to 19 times depending on which setting you want to change--with NO WAY OF SAVING ANY OF IT!.
#2) The music rack is almost useless. Unless you have a lightweight booklet, anything else will just slide off. I have a couple music books ~150 pages and they will not stay on while playing. The book has to sit inside a slot is just not wide enough. Also, that slot is not long enough to accommodate a 3-ring binder, even a little 1/2 inch with a few pages, the slot is not long enough for the open binder to rest in. Plan on taking a music stand with you as well.

As for the 400 sounds, yeah that sounds a bit impressive, but they are a bit "cheap" sounding even through good headphones (which are way better than the built in speakers). The "dance" accompaniment is kinda cheap sounding as well--just nothing to write home about there.

As a practice keyboard (not your main practice keyboard) I think is it's only redeeming quality. For piano students, it is better than not practicing at all when you're on the go--good for scales and sight-reading exercises.. The "piano feel" is not there and getting the proper expression will not match a real piano, but that's expected in non-weighted keys. I would not suggest it as the only practice keyboard for piano.

Overall:
- For taking to parties (I'm assuming by the "Dance Music" feataure) I would suggest spending a little more and finding one that has presets so you don't have to stop and mess with the function key all the time and has better sampled sounds.
- For a piano students looking for a primary practice keyboard--get one with weighted keys.
- For a lightweight, portable practice keyboard or for just entering MIDI, it should do okay.
Summary: Missing important features, okay for practice

Text: This M-Gear SP-2 sustain pedal has a feel of being well-built, sturdy, and stays put on a smooth floor.  This is the second I've bought, this one for the purpose of engaging the push-to-talk (PTT) function on a ham radio, and it works fine for that.  It takes about 8 pounds of weight to fully depress which is a bit heavy, but not too bad.  It functions bascially as a momentary electrical on/off switch, and there is an switch on the bottom to change whether it opens or closes the circuit when depressed.  The resistance I measured for the closed position was between 1-10 ohms, but it was not continuous over the range of pedal motion, it just varied randomly across those values after depressing the pedal about 75% down.  So this is not a variable or 1/2 sustain pedal.  It's either on or off.  This is different from the first SP-2 pedal I bought 10 years ago, which I still use today on my Triton Extreme.  On that SP-2 the resistance varies continuously from 175 ohms 75% depressed to 80 ohms 100% depressed.  So it can be considered a variable or 1/2 sustain pedal.  A global setting on the Triton Extreme allows calibration for half damper which works for this older pedal, but not for the new one.  Only a few of more advanced sound patches make use of this feature.  I deduct 1 star for the change in design and function over the years for the same product model number, but otherwise a fine product (so far, but not so sure after reading some of the recent reports of the newer ones failing within a year).
Summary: Works fine, sturdy, no half damper pedal function

This is a great sounding, full featured little amp. It's only about the size of a loaf of bread. But it's well made, with a metal chassis. The effects and the presets are nice, and the built in tuner is a nice bonus.

But here's where this little amp really shines:
1) it has built in bluetooth so you can pair your phone or tablet and play it through the amp. Individual volume controls mix your guitar and input.
2) it's battery powered
3) it's compatible with the Line6 Relay G10T wireless guitar transmitter (not included) that charges through the input jack.

Here's what's not so great:
1) the volume. Keep in mind that this is designed as a practice amp and only has a pair of 3" speakers. They sound good, but they're not going to blow you away.
2) the price. I think it's a little overpriced. Not that it's not worth it. I don't regret spending the money. I just think it should be a little cheaper.

Bottom line: I don't think you'd regret buying this as long as you realize it's a practice amp, and nothing more.
Summary: Great for what it is designed for.

[[VIDEOID:ce2986e6766bfc8e1594babffb82c10f]] These are nice pins and worked well on my "stratacoustic" acoustic electric guitar. The string pin holes in my guitar were apparently rather small and, at first, I thought that the pins would not fit. They were too large. However, I used a sharp knife and a 180 grit sanding block, to gently and evenly scrape each pin. I was able to shave down to the size needed while maintaining the round shape of the pin. The end result is that each pin to fits beautifully. Like players, each guitar is unique. Tthese may fit perfectly or may need a small adjustment to fit your baby. I suspect that these are the standard size and will fit the vast majority of guitars and the my classic budget Fender Stratacoustic has smaller than standard pin holes.

In closing, these are nice pins that will look and sound great on any guitar. I'm glad that I bought them.

Text:
It is so hard to find heavy rated strings. I love the extra mass and resulting tension of heavy strings...makes for a much better attack and tone. For finger playing, the tighter tension really brings out the attach and punch, particularly when playing at the bridge pickup. This also tends to avoid a lot of fret "clicking" common with looser strings that flap all around with harder plucking. One can attack the strings pretty hard and they stay under control. I also found the heavy strings hold their tuning much better than lighter strings, as well as have much more consistent sustain. Light strings quickly lose volume when left ringing... These strings maintain volume for several seconds after the initial attack. For a long time I used DR heavy strings, but these are significantly cheaper and sound very consistent to DR strings.

Pros:
1. Super clean, refined tone,
2. Brighter attack that cuts through the mix,
3. More consistent volume, and maintains volume during sustain. If you don't use a compressor to regulate your volume, these strings help quite a bit,
4. Just a better, deeper, punchier, more consistent tone when compared to light gauge strings.

Cons:
1. If you're are used to light gauge strings, you will have to get used to these. These higher tension strings require a harder stroke. You may experience some fatigue when first trying these, but the tonal advantages are well worth the effort of getting your fingers in better shape.
Summary: Strings have great punch and attack.

Text: This tube preamp is amazing. What really makes it shine is the option to send as much or as little input audio through the tube. I got this to replace its smaller sibling, the UR22 (which is also terrific). I needed more inputs and preamps, and trust the quality and performance of Steinberg products.This did not disappoint me. I am using the UR44 with Cubase. There is almost nothing I don't like with this interface. Easy to use, works really well with Cubase, spectacular preamps for its class, superior hardware quality. Jacks, pots, switches, case--everything about this oozes solidity and quality. It inspires confidence in its reliability. I especially like the ability to have phantom power on for two inputs and off for the others, because I often mix types of microphones. The recordings I get with the UR44 are very smooth-sounding and clean, really professional results.

The only cons with this unit don't diminish my high esteem for it one bit. These involve the included guitar amp effects that can be used as either hardware based (in the UR44 itself) or as plugins. The included amp models take a bit of fiddling to get a natural, pleasing sound, and I do not like them nearly as much as the ones that are included in Cubase. I usually use third party guitar amp plug ins (I love Bias Amp Desktop), if I go that route. For serious recording, for me, nothing beats a mic on a speaker cabinet, driven by a cranked non-master volume tube amp. Also, the included algorithmic reverbs are adequate to get lower latency monitoring, but I prefer convolution reverbs for printing in final mixes. Finally, the mixer interface within Cubase to handle the UR44 routing and settings is a bit clunky at first, but easy once you get the hang of it.
Summary: Great sounding preamps,superior hardware and build, professional sounding recordings

Text: This is not the same thing as a surge suppressor. Don't be fooled by ill informed store associates into thinking a surge suppressor will protect your equipment from fluctuations in power. Most are too small to trigger a surge suppressor. Power conditioners are like water filters, they filter out all the oddities and small fluctuations in power that slowly destroy electronics. In my opinion a power conditioner is one of the *BEST* investments you can make in prolonging the life of sensitive equipment. I took a chance after moving and my equipment was without a conditioner for a short while, but have used this non stop since ordering in August of 2011 with no issues. I immediately noticed a huge difference when I started using it. My monitors immediately stopped 'humming' when no audio was playing and I stopped hearing faint static that had developed when adjusting the volume on one of my mixers. If, like me, you don't have a whole house power conditioner, this is a small and affordable unit that should save several headaches in early equipment failures down the road. I use mine for studio and computer equipment, but it will also work just as well for a home entertainment center and HDTV's.

So much has been written about these that I will not bother. I will only add my voice to the chorus: these are stupendous and amazing cans that are still *entirely* relevant and ferociously competitive in mid-2020. It's entirely evident these were designed for professional mixing/mastering environments. Many other reviews cover the how and why. I'll just say they are just spectacular. The detail, stage and imaging are perfection for my ears at this price (and I received mine from a used Amazon Warehouse Deal to boot).

A couple notes that I've not seen mentioned elsewhere:
First, I do not find them as inefficient as many have claimed; they are absolutely power hungry and their 62ohm potential can only be realized while amp'd, but running these from a DAC-dongle or portable is entirely adequate. I've also listened to them directly fed by an LG G8 phone's quad-dac and there's little to really complain about. A bit anemic perhaps, but not unlistenable. I've been running them off an old C&C BK itny portable amp and it's been outstanding.
Second, just a cosmetic note: the actual orange color of these is nowhere near as bright & loud as it appears in literally every photo or video of them I saw before seeing them in person. The color is actual a much more subdued sort of "burnt orange", significantly darker than it appears on-screen. I didn't think I'd care for the orange, but in person I actually really quite like it.

That's all I have to add. These are going nowhere and will be my default go-to for mastering sessions as well as critical listening of just about anything. They truly shine with classical and jazz but they are pleasant and revealing with anything I've thrown at them. I prefer my Fidelio X2HR for more casual, dynamic, fun listening (very different sound signature in every way), but the K712Pros are nowhere near as "clinical" as I feared they might be, remaining engaging, unified and remarkably natural across the entire frequency spectrum. After less than a week, filled with hours and hour of listening, I'm in love with these cans.

I've been considering getting a separate compressor for my bass rig for a while, and I have to admit I found the idea of an AmazonBasics box sort of humorous as I ordered it. When it got here, it was actually better than I expected. This is a small box with an all-metal chassis, and it has full bypass via a metal stomp button. It has soft, almost spongy rubber feet to keep it from slipping.

It has three controls - SUSTAIN, LEVEL and ATTACK. Level pretty much is the volume control, which is surprisingly handy even if you just need to add some volume and presence. It did a good job of that for my passive basses with little to no noise. SUSTAIN doesn't add sustain, but you probably guessed that if you've used a compressor. It's more the compression sensitivity, and it works fine. And attack - you can use this to dial in more compression, but it also adds noise. If you have a decent noise gate, you probably won't notice; if you don't, you'll definitely hear it. With SUSTAIN and ATTACK up, you get plenty of compression and it also evens out those peaks.

There are some things to be aware of. First, this doesn't come with an adapter and it doesn't work with batteries, but if you have a pedalboard, you've probably already got power for it, and if you own other effects boxes, there's a decent chance you can use one of their adapters. If you're new to pedals, be aware you'll need an adapter. They're not expensive. Next, the rubber feet are soft, and I'd guess they'll wear out before other rubber feet would, but for now they're fine. And while not an issue, if you play with a label-centric band, they may lift their eyebrows at the small, subtle amazonbasics logo with its familiar smile under the stomp button.

If you need a small compressor with a few basic controls, this one is worth considering - heck, if you just need boost for your volume/presence, it's worth considering by using only the level knob. It's solid and sturdy and gets the job done. I wish the attack control added less noise, but that's not unusual with this sort of pedal. Overall I quite like it.
Summary: AmazonBasics makes effect pedals - who knew?

GraphTech TUSQ is unlike any other nut material out there. It is a high-pressure laminate material that is easy to work with when using the proper tools. What is so amazing is that the material is actually "tuned" for resonance, acting very much like a tonewood. If you were to drop the nut (or any part made from TUSQ or Nubone material) onto a hard surface, it actually rings a note like tonewood does when you tap hammer it. Yes, its a musically sonic material! This allows string vibration to transfer tone to your neck in a way no other nut material can. It truly makes your instrument that much more resonant, and as a bonus, the "XL" means it's impregnated with PTFE (Teflon) so it's slippery. Even when cut improperly, string winding don't usually get caught in the string slots due to the PTFE. I HIGHLY recommend getting any nut professionally installed as it will need to be shaped, seated and cut properly. YOU DO NOT JUST BUY A NUT AND SLAP IT IN... IT MUST BE FIT TO YOUR INSTRUMENT!

To test I installed one pad and left the original pad on the other side of my 440's. The 840 pad has a larger surface area (see my pics with the old pad on the left in all shots) so I guess that spreads out the pressure over a larger area. But it's really minimal and I did not notice a huge difference pressure wise. The material is nicer/softer than the original so that is a plus. Every so often I would flip the headphones around to see if I could tell anything. The larger pad does cover more of the ear- almost surrounds it. But seriously, if you had me blindfolded I wouldn't bet my life that I always knew which side were which. But in general the large pad and softer material seems to be a better set up. I can't imagine any set of cans actually feeling truly comfortable to wear for an extended period of time.

Sound difference? Yes, one side in my test sounded better I felt... until I switched them around! Just like eyes your two ears are not 100% equal and over time they lose their edge but not at equal rates. I think those who make any kind of big deal out of any significant improvement or degradation in sound might be imagining it. I would have to see some measureable proof to believe that whatever millimeters' worth of difference in how the drivers may sit in relationship to your eardrums affects how the sound waves actually strike them. Wishful thinking or all inside their heads maybe? Notice the contradictory reviews- more bassy, less bassy etc??? It becomes highly subjective and I wouldn't buy or not buy these pads based upon those claims. If you need replacements this is no brainer as a cheap way to keep your expensive headphones alive. If you need more comfort then these may do the trick for you but I'm glad I didn't pay any more for them than I did from Amazon. That's my 2 cents.

This is just behind the Harley Benton and not by much. Fit and finish A+++. Frets on mine were perfect. The neck a bit more of a handful that the Harley Benton but still comfortable. Electronics are good but you will want to replace the tuners which are not near as good as the ones on the Harley Benton. I bought these strictly to use in music production with Ableton Live.

These are precision cans. The do NOT have a huge soundstage, meaning there is not a lot of separation between left and right channels.

They are as a close as to a flat response as you can get with these drivers, HOWEVER!!! This is what you want when you are trying to clean up the muddiness in your mix. Trust me on this, they do a fabulous job!

I immediately went back into one of my old mixes using my new DT 770 PROs (250 ohm) and in a matter of minutes I had used a para EQ and was able to clean up a mix that I had thought I had finished from before and it sounded beyond pristine.

The best way to describe the 250 ohm cans is they are studio scalpels -- they DO give you a lot more definition in the high-end area (meaning they are bright and trebley) but if you are using these to mix with, you really want this kind of detail.

A lot of people complain, "Where's the heckin bass?!?!" and it's suppressed slightly with the 250 ohm model enough so that if you have a bit of overdriven lower frequencies, you can immediately tell because it's sooo easy to discover where the boominess is coming from and you can go cut that right out because the bass is not overdriven compared to the other frequencies.

NOTE: ****If you want cans that have big stereo separation and deep bass response, get something else****

Also, there are a lot of dummies on YT that have no idea what they are talking about and a lot of them tend to parrot each other. Don't get these if you are wanting to listen to music as a casual listener, you will not like the flat response in the 250 ohm model.

Don't complain about how these closed-ear cans are tight on your head -- they are built this way to help cancel out ambient noise, so you can mix better and pick up on details without having to crank the volume.

Also, I would highly recommend using an audio interface to "drive" these headphones. I use a Steinberg UR22 to run these. If you don't know the difference between 32, 80 and 250 ohms, look it up online.

I love these cans for mixing! If you found this review helpful, let others know!

Great little cable - the audio feed from my television runs too hot and is not adjustable within its settings, so I ran the feed through this little guy to my stereo system. Because of this setup, after my initial adjustment I haven't touched it and have left it alone behind the television.

I'm an audiophile - I'm all about collecting vinyl albums and preserving CDs in lossless codecs. So far as I can tell (and I have a keen ear) this cable tuned down the signal with a very minimal loss of quality. I didn't require a major change in signal strength, only enough to bring the signal to normal levels again to prevent speaker pop. The first quarter spin or so didn't so much change the volume as it did clean up the signal to a usable level. After you reach a certain point it will decrease the volume quite a bit for a very small fraction of a turn.

Now - If you plan to use this cable with your iPhone or iPod, I would skip it 100%. Although it carries the brand name SHURE on the packaging, this is definitely a "made in china" product repackaged. It has what appears to be gold tipped connections, however the cable seems fragile, and under stress of pocketing and constant re-adjusting I am confident it would be broken in a matter of weeks. I don't appreciate the way it was packaged - the male end was attached to the female connector - putting extreme stress on the cable's weak points.

If you plan to use it like I did - i.e. a primary adjustment for a simple entertainment center setup and no more - I'd go for it. It does the job very well.
