I've heard a lot of people sing praises of the Xotic pedals (particularly the "triolgy" of the EP Booster, SL Drive, and SP Compressor), but this is my first experience with the brand. Part of the reason for holding off was that I was skeptical of a micro pedal priced over $100. Another reason was that I simply didn't appreciate what the EP Booster did, or how it differed from other (more affordable) boost pedals. The use of this pedal is so simple and straightforward, it makes it challenging to review. But I am confident that this an excellent product at a fair price, and will probably quickly become my favorite booster.

BUILD QUALITY - I've written probably dozens of these reviews (ranging from $20 Chinese pedals to $200 boutiques), and in virtually any pedal I bothered to own, I probably made some reference to "sturdy build quality". Well, the Xotic's housing takes sturdy to a whole new level. I was stunned how hefty and bulletproof this thing felt in my hand when I removed it from the box. The single gain knob as has a solid firmness as you turn it, and the I/O jacks and switch are also top-notch for their kind. Opening up the back, I discovered that part of the extra weight might have been the fact that this thing actually can run on a 9V battery! This is an extreme rarity for pedals in this "micro" form factor - virtually all of the "Mooer-style" enclosures can only be run on an external power supply. The EP Booster can also do this (up to 18V, I believe), but the battery option is a great added feature, especially given the low power consumption. All in all, this thing is solid and built to last.

SOUND & ORIGINS - The "EP" refers to "Echoplex", which was a (large) vintage delay unit with the added benefit that a lot of guitarists decided they loved the sound of the effect's preamp engaged irrespective of the delay. Xotic has figured out how to take just that preamp and turn it into a booster in a micro pedal, which is awesome. But, for all intents and purposes, the EP Booster is a clean boost pedal. Boosters are relatively simple circuits, and while they can color your sound in a variety of ways, their value is more in their interplay with your amp versus the sound coming from the pedal itself. That being said, the EP booster has a subtle, warm character to it that rounds out harsh treble frequencies and adds a hint of saturation and dynamic content to your tone, even on lower gain settings. Of course, as you turn the EP Booster up further, you get up to 20dB of additional gain, which will be louder, more complex, or gainier - depending on the amp and other effects that come after it.

INTERNAL SWITCHES & FLEXIBILITY - My understanding is that Xotic released a new version of the EP Booster (around 2011?), and that this current version has two internal DIP switches. The one on the left sets the starting position of the gain at +3dB, even when the knob is all the way down (default position). If you flick this switch down, however, it sets the starting point to true "unity gain". I use the latter setting because I'm more interested in the coloration of tone the EP Booster provides, and want to achieve this at bedroom/basement volumes. The second (right) DIP switch is a "bright" setting. The default position is with this "engaged", though this is actually the "flatter" of the two EQ settings. If you turn the bright switch off, the tone become darker, which was a characteristic of the original vintage Echoplex circuit. These two options provide some hidden flexibility to an otherwise very simple, one-knob design.

CONCLUSION...DIFFERENT THAN OTHER BOOSTERS? - The key question about the Xotic EP Booster, to me, is not whether this is a quality, well-made product...it absolutely is. The question is whether this is a booster you need, and whether it does anything truly different than other boost effects, most of which are probably cheaper. I currently own an EHX LPB-1, a clone of a ZVex Super Hard-On, and a number of clones of transparent overdrives (Klon, Timmy, Sweet Honey, etc.) that function largely as clean boosts. Of those, probably all of them are brighter than the EP Booster, except maybe the LPB-1. The EP Booster works best as an always-on tone enhancer or as a clean volume boost after other gain pedals. Paired with a good tube amp, I think the EP Booster was the best of the bunch, and with the unity gain feature, I'm starting to wonder why I'd turn it off.
Summary: Well-made adaptation of a vintage Echoplex preamp...morphed into a compact boost pedal

I bought this On Stage stand and another stand of similar style (ChromaCast CC-MSTAND Folding Music Stand with Carry Bag).  I was going to buy two ChromaCast stands because they were only six dollars and some cents apiece.  However, the seller or amazon (I don't know which) limited me to buying one ChromaCast for that price.  Since I wanted two stands, I went ahead and also got the slightly more expensive On Stage stand.  The On Stage stand comes pre-assembled.  All you have to do to use it is pull it up to height, fold out the music holder part and tighten a few turn knobs.  The On Stage case is a nice heavy canvas-like material with a Velcro closure.  The ChromaCast case is a thin nylon case with a zipper, and the case seems of lesser quality than the On Stage case.  The ChromaCast stand came in four pieces, so it took a little bit of assembly, which wasn't hard.  Once the ChromaCast stand is assembled, all the pieces can stay together and the stand simply collapses down when you loosen all the turn knobs; then it fits nicely into the included nylon case.  Whether one stand is better than the other remains to be seen---I won't know until I use them both. Neither stand appears to be a heavy duty stand for using with big books, but instead both stands seem to be just right for taking along to music events and for holding sheet music. Both stands, once folded down and put into their cases, are about 18 x 3.5 inches.  Neither takes up very much space and would easily fit into a carry bag or a suitcase.  Both stands, in their cases, seem to weigh about the same.  My initial impression is that the On Stage stand might be the one I end up liking better.  However, given that we intend to use these for music meets about 10-12 times a year, I suspect both will work just fine.

I had purchased a really inexpensive Chinese pre-loaded S-S-H pickguard for a Strat project I was working on. I had only paid $35 for the project guitar, so I wasn't going to drop big money into it. The cheap pickguard arrived, and it looked great, but I was really let down by the pickups that came in it. (what was I expecting for $30?) The humbucker wasn't a big issue, because I already had a replacement for it, but the single coils just sounded so thin and cheap. They had to go. At first I was looking on eBay for old Strat pickups, but you never know what you're going to get.

I decided to gamble on these based largely on other Amazon reviews. They come from China, so expect a few weeks for them to arrive. There were no instructions included at all, but I figured it out. (I taped up the already coiled red and green wires, ran the white to the 5-way and the black to ground) I'm not doing any coil tapping or anything fancy - just straight up replacement of the single coils. I did have some issues with fit. Nothing requiring a Dremel or file, but I had to use a bit of force to make them fit through the holes while getting the screw holes alligned.

It isn't a single coil sound, and I knew that going in, but they are very quiet and to my ear sound very good. I think the biggest difference is the fullness of the sound; more musical. They respond well to pick attack. If you lower the neck pickup down pretty good you can get an almost Hendrix-y sound out of them.

What can I say? They turned a $35 pawn shop purchase into my new favorite guitar.

There are already other videos showing how it sounds so I won't reinvent the wheel here, but let me cast my vote towards this being a really classy electric piano. Synthetic pianos have gotten incredibly good these days, and this is definitely a good example. Granted, touching the keys is immediately obvious that they are plastic on particle board, but no one should be expecting ivory at this price. The pedals do what you expect, the headphones are a nice touch, the keys are semi-weighted so they actually respond playing harder versus lighter, really it's everything I wanted in a budget piano for my kids to practice on. It is so much nicer and classier than our midi keyboard on a stand that was here before, and even adds some elegance to the room while we are at it!
There is a USB port on the back to use as a midi interface as well, however I did not experiment with that. This is, in my opinion, meant to be more like a piano than a midi interface. It's also too heavy to easily move into my office to plug into my computer! But if you want to do some music production on a laptop or something plugged into the midi port, it's nice that you have that option too. It even comes with a bench! Really a beautiful product, I'm very happy with it!
Summary: So much nicer than a keyboard!

Overdrive channel is surprising good for power chords and rhythm but as often the case with these low end built in distortion kinda fizzles out on screaming lead playing. Love the spring reverb. Interesting reviews. I was highly concerned by reading the reviews that this little unit wasn't going to meet my expectations and almost didn't purchase. But after having it and using it on a day to day basis I have come to quite a different conclusion. I believe many people do not understand the use model for this little gem.

The unit is capable of bringing in 10 mp3 tracks. You can play the mp3 while wearing headphones and while you sing you can hear your voice through the mic along with the mp3 along with chromatic pitch feedback at the same time. I have had no complaint about the volume at all. Without headphones it is almost audible, but if for some reason I wanted the mp3 to play through a speaker, I would use the headphone jack to output through another device or just play the mp3 on a different device all together. With headphones I can clearly hear both the mp3 (controlled by volume) and my singing input (controlled by distance to the mic and volume of your voice).

I do wish on playback (and even recording) that I could independently control the mp3 and recording of my voice volume. But overall I have greatly enjoyed being able to sing to the mp3 and hear the mix through the heaphones. Without headphones you get a lot of bleed over and it would impact what you hear.

So for this workflow model I think it works extremely well. There are some what I would call "downsides". The first is the cost. It is a fairly expensive unit. Part of the thinking I think was to package the trainer with a training program. I can't attest to that portion of the program although I took a little time to preview, the book in my opinion was fairly basic but some of the exercises seemed a bit more advanced. I would have greatly preferred the option to buy the unit without the training pamphlet and loaded exercises but the value of having a chromatic tuner that I could import mp3's to sing along too made up for it.

Also the user portion to load mp3's is limited to 10. I would have greatly preferred not pre-loading and giving me the option to use the space.
The unit is lightweight which is nice but has a tremendous plastic feel to it. It does not give comfort holding it in the palm of your hand, you feel like you are holding thin plastic. Also the ability to govern the volume of the recording AND playback would be a needed addition.

So far though the chromatic tuner has greatly aided my singing practice. I am glad I bought it and would recommend to anyone wanting to sing to an mp3 and check pitch at the same time.

Decided to put together a minimalist guitar rig so I could play while traveling. This led me to discover the Session Cake interface. The SC-01 is a great device and love the fact you can easily tweak the mix right from the device. You could use the Session Cake as a standalone headphone amp but it lacks any effects (like reverb) which would make playing much more enjoyable. The big discovery was that I could use an interface like Session Cake to run apps like Jamup or Bias FX on my iPhone, iPad or computer to open up a whole world of amp and effects simulation - and these apps sound really amazing with tons of options for tweaking your tone. The Session Cake unfortunately (like many of these older interfaces) work via analog 3.5mm (headphone jack) connection - this results in lots of hiss underneath the signal. Luckily the apps include a noisegate to partially filter out the hiss but it's still there - you can still use it & enjoy - but it really bugged me.
To solve the noice issue and give more options, competitors like iRig and others have come up with new superior digital interfaces. No noise! There is really no reason to own an analog device anymore. Just buy and iRig or other digital interface. While I thing the Yamaha Session Cake is a great device and well implemented, it has been overtaken by superior digital technology. Now only if Yamaha would make a smaller, portable DIGITAL interface.
My rig includes the super small and light Traveller guitar and a digital interface and iPhone - I can get tones that meet or exceed my vintage tube amp rigs all in a super small package. Makes me want to travel more.

[[VIDEOID:4abc378f6df071c10822a59cc9a70dcf]] I have the Coolmusic compressor which I like, so I was glad to try this new pedal.  There was a previous "Reverberry" (model A-RE01) with 9 reverb types, but this new Reverberry is actually a Multi-effects pedal and not just reverb.  The extra modulation options like Delay, Echo, Chorus, Flanger, Tremolo, etc. do NOT include reverb but are straight effects.  In fact, only half of the effects here are Reverb at all.

I tested the pedal using a Fender Stratocaster through a Fender Champion 20 amp.

What Is Good About This Pedal?

1. The Coolmusic pedal form factor is awesome - the slim metal body, the top-mounted power jack, and the green LED lights. They just look....cool :)

2. The pedal does seem to be true-bypass and I did not notice any volume changes when the switch was on or off.

3. The Reverbs themselves are mostly usable, some are pretty good. Some have more depth than others - the "Metal" in particular sounds very cavernous. I'm not sure what "Sur-1" and "Sur-2" are, but they sound like a digital attempt at a slapback effect.

4. The Delays are usable. There are 2 digital delays, a tape echo, and something called "Mod Tone" which sounds like a Reverse delay, although not a great one. The Mod Tone sounded much better when I dialed in some reverb from my amp.

What Is Not So Good About This Pedal?

1. The Chorus, Wah, Flanger, and Tremolo are not good at all and are basically useless. It would have been better for the company to include other reverb types instead like Spring or Shimmer.

2. There is some noise going on when the pedal is engaged. The noise is minor unless you turn your amp up past bedroom levels. At lower volumes it is not that noticeable.

3. There is some tone suck going on when the pedal is engaged. The pedal sucks some of the bass and midrange out, so to compensate you need to fiddle with the tone control on the Reverberry as well as the tone controls on your amp. That might not be too practical in a live situation, but for bedroom playing, it's fine.

4. The Reverbs are useful but they are not deep or as malleable as on a more expensive pedal. This pedal would not be the best choice for creating lush, ambient soundscapes, but in combination with another pedal or amp effects, you could pull something together that would be quite decent

SUMMARY: At this price point, it is hard to find a comparable reverb pedal which has decent Reverbs and also some very usable Delay features. You can find other multi-reverb pedals by Donner, Joyo, Caline, Flamma, iSet, Behringer, Sonicake, etc. but they will not have other options beyond Reverbs. So at this price, the Reverberry is like a very budget version of an EHX Canyon - not as good or as versatile, but very worthwhile if you are on a budget and just want to play around, experiment, and get your feet wet in the Reverb pedal space.

If you are looking for something more high-end and better for ambient or shoegaze, I'd say save your money and look into any of the following (all are combo Reverb/Delays under $200): Earthquaker Devices Dispatch Master V3, Boss RV-6, EHX Canyon, Keeley Caverns V2, Matthews Effects Cosmonaut V2 Void Delay/Reverb Pedal, Wampler Ethereal, and the NUX Atlantic pedal.

If you can go over $200 the following are some top choices: Source Audio Collider, AmpliTude X-Space, Line 6 DL4 Mk2, Earthquaker Devices Avalanche Run V2, and Strymon BlueSky.

I purchased this to upgrade from my previous audio interface, the Behringer UF0202. That device worked quite well for this purpose as well but lacked two things: a volume knob, and balanced in/outs. The volume knob thing I could work around, but my current monitors seem susceptible to ground loops (even with a ground lift plug), so I needed to go with balanced cables. I'm glad I did. The balanced cables completely eliminated my noise problems. This was a good purchase. However, I would say to anyone who doesn't need balanced cables and is on a budget that they should consider the Behringer. It's a tiny fraction of the price and it works pretty well. I have some good things to say about the Focusrite Scarlett 2i2 (all about the hardware) and some bad things (all about the software). I've tried using the driver version 2.1, which came with the disk, and the udpated 2.2, which I downloaded from Focusrite's website.

To let you know what I need in an interface:

1. Balanced stereo in/out
2. High quality headphone amp
3. Volume knobs for headphone amp and for the main line
4. Good digital-to-analog conversion
5. Low output latency (input latency not important to me)

I don't use the Mic preamps, which is one of the big selling points of this device.

================ The Good ====================

This box is simple and well-designed. It does what you want, has very convenient controls, and has high build quality. I'm pleased with the digital-to-analog conversion. It has a great big volume knob and another for the headphone amp. It has switches so each input can be a line-in or microphone pre-amp. It has a switch for zero-latency monitoring (of whatever is coming in).

* The headphone amp was of particular concern for me. I use headphones a lot and a poor headphone amp can be quite a problem. The Behringer headphone amp was only ok. Specifically, it has an output impedance of 50 ohms. The rule of thumb for good headphone/amp matching is that the output impedance should be 1/8 the impedance of the headphones--my hd 595's have 50 ohms of impedance. Breaking this rule you get distortions of the frequency response. In my case mostly this meant attenuation of the bass. Most manufacturers don't list their output impedance, possibly because they are embarrassed. Anyway, Focusrite does, which is one reason I trust them a little more. The output impedance is less than 10 ohms--respectable but not amazing. Still not as low as I would need in principle but I can notice an improvement in the bass response in my headphones. There's plenty of extra voltage here too, so I could drive higher impedance cans if necessary. Anyway, good headphone amp. Check.

* Balanced ins and outs work very well, The ins accommodates a 1/4 TRS style in and XLR. The light around them shows when something's actually coming in and shines red when it's in danger of clipping. There's lots of gain available. I have them turned all the way down almost. The outs are TRS style (balanced or unbalanced) and are located on the back.

* I like the look of the box, with a red metal case, and the front and back are sturdy and attractive as well.

* The USB cable is just a type B port. This means you can replace it if it gets damaged or whatever. The Behringer, for example, was hard-wired to its cable...king of annoying.

* It's bus-powered. I actually would have been fine with a wall-wart, but this is even more simple.

I really have no complaints whatsoever about the hardware.

===================== The Bad =========================

The driver for this thing is horrible under Windows XP. I have a clean installation with nothing installed except my DAW software, acrobat reader, and this driver. I mean, my computer is really stripped down. Performance using the Behringer was good. The latency (time between playing a note and hearing it out the speakers) was 8 ms using the Behringer, which isn't really perceptible.

Unfortunately the focusrite driver, though it's technically ASIO apparently, doesn't have anything like an acceptable latency. The lowest latency I could set it at and get sound out instead of crackles and pops was 23 ms. At that level the instrument begins to sound very sluggish and laggy. It's very difficult, at least for me, to work with a large latency like that.

I was ready to return this device when I decided as a last ditch effort to install ASIO4ALL. That's sort of an ASIO driver to use if you absolutely cannot make the manufacturer's driver perform at a decent level. I installed it and it worked. The output latency was a tiny 4.3 ms (only .3 of which are actually output latency, so this is REALLY impressive). I conclude that the hardware is very, very good in this machine, but the software is horrible.

Unfortunately, you can't actually uninstall the focusrite driver because otherwise windows doesn't recognize the device and it never even turns on--it's not class compliant, unlike the Behringer. So now I have two drivers for it installed, only one of which I use.

The bad news is that this configuration is very buggy. In general when I just turn the computer on and try and play my VST instrument, all I get is crackles and pops until I open the ASIO configuration panel and increase the buffer. The funny thing is that it doesn't matter where the buffer starts out, I always have to increase it before I get any good sounds out. I can start it out with a huge buffer--lots of latency--and it will crackle until I open it and increase the buffer yet more. I have to do this every time I turn on the computer. Also, sometimes if I leave it on for a while and come back, it will be crackly again until I increase it yet another step. We are talking about major bugs here.

I decided to try ditching ASIO4ALL and trying to make the focusrite drivers work again--maybe there was a setting I was missing. As I was trying to set the buffer size, I heard the sound of an explosion and then my computer rebooted. When it came back I couldn't get good sounds out, even when I turned the buffer way up. Tried rebooting a few more times, still didn't work. So I uninstalled and re-installed the focusrite software. At first it didn't work. I had to install ASIO4ALL as well, and now I can sort of get sounds out of it, half the time.

I hope you are getting the idea. These drivers are terrible. Awful. A monkey could have written a better driver. I would give it 1 star if it wasn't for the fact that the device works very, very well when all the stars align and the driver recognizes the drive and allows it to play. I guess I'm willing to sacrifice convenience and stability for nice hardware when it works. I would never use this in a live situation or when time is critical.

The good thing about drivers is that they can update and fix them. I'm hoping for that. They have already revised the driver once, which is amazing because even the 2.2 driver is seriously an abomination, just like the 2.1.

================ Closing Thoughts =======================

Unfortunately, there really isn't a USB interface that has a good driver. The Behringer driver always worked, but if you moved the interface from one USB port to the other, it was no longer recognized and you had to reinstall the driver. However, you didn't have to use the Behringer driver and ASIO4ALL would give you 11 ms and perform without any complications. That's about as trouble free as I've seen in this type of device.

If you read about the Presonus Audiobox USB and the M-Audio Fast Track Pro (probably the two closest competitors to this focusrite), what you get is a bunch of comments just like this one...horrible, horrible drivers that never get fixed. Actually Mackie makes a competitor as well, the Onyx Blackjack--but the reviews of that show that the driver is possibly even worse than this one. Unfortunately none of the pro music manufacturers cares about their drivers, so we have to live with unstable systems that only work half the time. Maybe it's better under mac. I don't know.

Interestingly, this is really the only USB 2.0 device in this range. That's quite shocking considering how long the USB 2.0 standard has been around. The only real implication of this is that the USB 1.1 devices like the M-Audio and Presonus can only do two channel 24/96 audio in OR out, not both at the same time. There's not enough throughput in USB 1.1.

So in light of the competition, the Focusrite looks kind of ok. Unfortunately all audio interface manufacturers--at least in this range of device--think there's no need for good hardware and (especially) good software. At least the hardware in this one is up to spec. We can cross our fingers for improved drivers in the future.

Bottom line: this is a fantastic, 5-star device...if you can make the software work consistently.

If you are on a tight budget or don't care about balanced in/out, I'd recommend you go with the Behringer UCA202 or UFO2020. They are tons cheaper, class complaint, and have better drivers. If you use a high impedance headphone with it, even the headphone amp is pretty good on that one.

================ Update May 2012 ==============

A new version of the driver, 2.3, came out since the writing of the above. The new driver actually works. I have stopped using ASIO4ALL and I get decent latency. Once in a while--not too often--it will inexplicably require me to edit the settings and increase the buffer, and some percentage of the time when I do that it will reboot my computer. If I don't change anything, most of the time, it works ok. I would never use this in a mission-critical setting (i.e., gigging or pro work), but for my home use, it's good enough now. If you have issues with the driver, definitely update.

I traded a Frontman 212R for this because the 212R was too large and heavy, and too loud at even 3. Where that amp excelled, though, is a key strength of this one: very clean with a decent amount of headroom. I realize that headroom is more of a tube amp characteristic, but this one stays clean no matter how loud I crank it.

Since others have discussed the FUSE engine and most of the other features I am not going to cover those. I did play around with FUSE and despite my technical background (I am a retired IT consultant) it was not the most straightforward modeling environment I have run across. I'll probably use the presets, and thus far the 59 Bassman model is my favorite for jazz.

For some styles of music the fact that this amp is difficult to distort is a detriment, but for jazz and other styles it's a plus. If you are looking for an amp that distorts this is probably not going to make you happy. Despite the 40 Watts this is plenty loud. If you play lighter music or jazz this is easily sufficient for a 100-150 patron venue. If you are playing heavy rock or metal, again, this is probably not your best bet. It also makes for a great practice amp. I tested it with an electric-acoustic guitar and a key board, but honestly it was not optimum for either. Don't get me wrong, it was adequate, but honestly my Fender Rumble 100 bass amp was better for those two instruments.

Another thing I love is the weight. At 24 pounds I can carry it with one hand. In fact I can carry both this and the bass amp I mentioned in a single trip - one in each hand. That is a convenience for me since I am getting a little on the old side and my 66 year old body ain't what it use to be.

Bottom line: if you want a practice amp that will double as a performance one in smaller venues (or for lighter music) this may be all the amp you need. The tone is incredible for a solid state amp, and if you like tinkering the FUSE engine will provide you with endless hours of both frustration and fun. As for the straight across trade for the 212R I traded for this, I feel as though I got the best part of the bargain, although the person to whom I traded feels the same. This amp does everything I want at half the weight and size. Plus it has features like the USB connection and FUSE engine that were not dreamed of at Fender when the 212R was designed.
Summary: Impressive cleans and a lot of versatility

Text:
Pros:
* Works with all USB compliant devices without drivers and includes the proper adapter for iOS devices.
* XLR output
* Headphone monitor (3.5mm)
* One tap muting (USB mode only)
* Works with PS4/PS5 consoles
* Includes XLR cable
* Easy to drive (XLR mode does not require much gain - 35db gain gives me about over 1.5ft distance to center of microphone for audio pickup)
* Price/value for target user (amateur podcasting, gaming)
* Solid metal construction microphone all around

Cons:
* Does not seem to have any dampener built internally or externally. Picks up all sorts of audio when touched/moved around
* Needs a pop filter - wind filter is fine but would recommend a pop filter
* Picks up all noises around and afar. You need to use this microphone in a quiet room. Keyboard typing, etc, you’re gonna record it thru this microphone
* Very sensitive microphone for an XLR dynamic microphone (not a deal breaker, just be aware how sensitive it is)

First off don’t let the cons break your decision. It’s there because well it is what it is. One particular thing to note is that I am driving this microphone both in USB and XLR (not at the same time) - in USB the microphone is very nice and works with M1 iPads/iPhones (with a powered hub) and even with my PS5 console it works great. There is absolutely nothing wrong with performance and in fact it’s definitely better than the built in controller mic on the ps5 dual sense and better than any webcam microphone/headset hands down. It is very sensitive and it will pick up on all audio directly in front and even to the side of the microphone.

I am driving this in XLR mode with a Motu Ultralite MK5. The gain for this mic is around 35dB and I can be about nearly 2 ft away and it will pick up my voice clearly. It will also pick up ambient noise from about 25 feet away with the door open from another space in the home as well! It’s really sensitive for a dynamic microphone but the sound is actually great without much help (from typical compression). I really like the sound of the microphone and it is more than adequate for any podcast session. Just that it’s very sensitive it will pick up alot of ambient noises around your microphone. You definitely do not need any fethead or cloud lifter to drive this microphone.

I did get some strange reverb that I cannot seem to turn off. It is not presently active from my Motu but for some reason when recording the audio I can hear the reverb - it’s not karaoke type reverb but subtle. I don’t know if this microphone is doing this but it does not show up in USB mode (at least I cannot detect it). In XLR from my Motu I can definitely hear it via the headphone monitor on the Motu. Perhaps this is just a setting I enabled I will have to further investigate and update this review when I find out.

It is a value microphone that will not break your bank/wallet. Sure you can get an expensive SM7B but you’re gonna need all the other hardware to drive that microphone and if you really need that caliber of a mic you’d never even look at this one. But I will say I am not an audio engineer nor a professional recording artist so I use microphones mainly for documentary video creation and some gaming. The build quality and cables that are included justify the price. Easy to mount on a boom mic or a simple microphone stand and if you aren’t going to be moving the microphone around alot you don’t have to worry about the lack of vibration dampening feature it’s missing. One more note about the noise floor of this microphone - if you crank the gain on your XLR input from your dac the noise is highly perceptible vs another mid-range/high end microphone I have on hand. This isn't a problem just get closer to the microphone or turn down the gain. But this microphone is indeed very sensitive to pick up audio but the audio picked up is very clear, however.

A nice solid microphone that will work and last a long time. Solid 4-star microphone for it’s price point.
Summary: A good but highly sensitive microphone for all general purpose use

I wish I could report that this guy solved all of my ails with 60 cycle AC hum, but unfortunately it does, and it does not.

When engaged, it definitely kills the hum, but there are still a few transients that get past what it gates out. It turns loud AC hum into a light sparkle, for lack of a better way to put it.

That I could deal with, but what I can live with is the fact that it is NOT transparent in the signal chain. There's a definite loss of boost when engaged, and on top of that (and the most unfortunate) is when the gate closes there is a very harsh, electrical sound as the pedal engages. To describe it better - if you're playing something using a high gain amplifier, and you have a rhythm section that has a stop in it (where the guitar volume is still up, but you mute the strings) there's a definite sound as the pedal plays catch-up between the ("good") noise generated by the guitar preamp and the pedal trying to lop off the "bad" noise. As another reviewer said, it definitely sounds similar to a cheap reverb.

If you're just jamming with friends and want to kill the AC noise when you're not playing, this will do the job. But unfortunately, anything you record using one of these inline is going to take a lot of editing to get it's noise out of the track - you're better off just filtering the AC hum instead.

When the jamstik came out I was so excited the world finally had a compact midi guitar that, supposedly, worked wonders for the expert and the beginner player. I went to the apple store and planned on purchasing it but, before I did, I read the reviews. The reviews were underwelming and the word 'lag' was everywhere. I decided to wait for the next iteration of this potentially amazing instrument. I waited and waited, then, the Jamistik+ came out.
Granted: I am a guitar noobie; I know how to play chords and strumming patterns but I play mostly acoustic and cannot play solos on electric guitars. That being said: this guitar is not for me, but let's start from the pros.

Positive aspects
The latency in this iteration is negligible. I experienced lag but only when I was using bluetooth headset. With wired headphones there was no lag at all. The strings feel like a real guitar. The action is manageable for beginners but you will be sore after a few hours of playing and, of course, since there are real guitar strings you wll have to develope calluses. The fact that you can sound like a piano by playing a guitar is pretty sweet. I was afraid it wouldn't work picking the strings with my fingertips rather than a guitar pick, since I read it in a previous review, but I had no problems once I set the sensitivity to minimum (highest sensitivity). The instrument does not feel like a toy. It is heavy enough to feel sturdy and the battery lasts forever. Easy to pair. Fits in any bag. Light when compared to a normal guitar.

Now for the negative aspects.
I play with my acoustic resting on my leg, the Jamstik+ is too small for that. The Jamstik+ has only 5 functional frets and I relized it was gonna be a problem playing this guitar when I started doing bar chords. The stick it is too short and light to quickly switch to bar chords and back to nornal chords. Also, chords don't sound like chords, they sound like individually played strings but at the same time. On a real guitar the sound from all the strings in a chord blends togheter to form a beautiful, full sound, this felt artificial...well it is artificial.

That being said I feel that, If I was playing solos witha distorted electric guitar sound, this Jamstik+ would suit my needs. Also, if I would have played with the included strap, standing like you play most electric guitars, I would probably have had a different experience. But I don't play that way, This stick, as many small keyboards, only has a small range. I undertand that rage is sacrificed for portability and I would have overlooked that if the chords played sounded like chords. But they didn't. Also, there aren't many apps that allow you to use this stick as a midi input but, I haven't tried to look for them that hard so don't uote me on that.

Overall, I have returned the Jamstik+ and purchased a portable guitar from another manufacturer that I will not mention because I deem it desrespectful to Zivix. Zivix is pioneering this sector and I think they are doing an amazing job at it. This time their product did not suit my needs but I will definitely try their next version of this item. I believe in their products and company.
Summary: Did not suit my needs but read on and see if suits yours

Text:
0) If you want to learn Ableton Live, the more power to you!
1) I'm using the Launchpad MK1 with Ableton Live 8 lite, very similar to this latest model. Even Novation admits this.
2) Useless without Ableton, unless you're an experienced MIDI programmer.
3) Ableton is very difficult to learn, even the simplest application of the Launchpad to trigger a MIDI clip. You basically have to learn Ableton thoroughly before even applying Launchpad to do ANYTHING!
4) YouTube videos and Ableton books are too advanced or do a bad job for the beginner. Using the Ableton Reference Manual is like using a dictionary to learn how to speak English. No grammar or syntax, just definitions. What is needed is a short, step-by-step example book that is very detailed, and shows a few simple examples from start to finish.
If you do the Tutorials that are available in Ableton Help in the Ableton program, they are still lacking detail and step-by-step instructions for a few simple cases.
5) My recommendation for the musician is to use GarageBand or the SynthStation app on an iPod, and hook it up to the Akai SynthStation. You can buy a cable that goes from female 30 pin to Lightening, and it is thousands of times easier than trying to learn Ableton! More fun too, and you spend your time creating rather than trying to figure out Ableton Live.
Summary: Too complex with a steep learning curve, use GarageBand for your iPad or iPod!

Text:
For my job, I suddenly found myself in LOTS of Zoom meetings. At first, I used the camera and microphone that are built into my computer. However, I'm really interested in getting the best possible sound and image, so I slowly upgraded -- first using a gaming headset for a better mic, then adding my mirrorless camera for a better image. Finally, I upgraded to a better mic, in this case a Sennheiser e835 mic that I already had. (The mic plugs into the camera, which feeds the computer via a USB capture dongle. That way, the sound and image are synchronized.)

I needed something convenient to hold the mic, something that wouldn't be in the way, yet would hold the mic in the right position. I decided on this ZealSound Microphone Stand, hoping that it would be sturdy enough to hold the fairly heavy Sennheiser mic. It definitely is sturdy enough -- in fact, it's a little stiff, but not so stiff that the stand is impractical. And it holds the Sennheiser mic with no droop or sagging. The stand clamps to my table firmly and I have plenty of room under it for my mouse hand.

I make a lot of videos and do some voiceover work, so I also use the ZealSound Microphone Stand for that. Of course, I need a quiet, acoustically dead space for voiceovers, so I move the Zeal stand into my big closet where all the hanging clothes completely dampen the sound. I use the same Sennheiser mic plugged into a Tascam recorder, and it is great for voiceover work. The ZealSound stand is easy to move and set up for this, which is a little bonus that I did not expect.

I definitely like the ZealSound Microphone Stand and recommend it.
Summary: Handy mic support for vlogs and Zoom meetings

Text:
I purchased the S49 MK2 specifically because of its supposed great DAW integration and of course support for NI Komplete instruments. I currently own the NI Maschine MK2 controller along with the full Komplete Kontrol suite upgrade. Thus, I am fairly invested in NI plugins and software. My DAW of choice is Logic Pro X, so all opinions are with this setup.

First as a controller with the NI Complete suite of sounds, it is definitely a 5 star. I'm not sure how they could integrate this midi controller any better with their software. Also, its ability to control Maschine is a nice benefit, if you own Maschine (which does NOT come with Komplete unfortunately).

Next, in terms of being a general midi controller with Logic Pro X, I give this a 4 star. Transport controls work, along with ability to navigate tracks and rudimentary mixer controls, all good. However, there is no pre-mapping of Logic's "Smart Controls" which are predefined midi controller parameters for each instrument. I know this is possible because I tried out a Nektar LX49+, which did automatically map Logics smart controls to its fader and rotary knobs, very nice. Komplete Kontrol MK2, does NOT do this, leaving you to have to try to assign each instrument, which can cause conflicts and problems.

Finally, hardware. I give it 4 stars again. Solid and good, but not great. I also have an Akai MPK249, which hardware wise is definitely better, the key action is nicer, etc. However, the Akai's software integration was almost non existent, which is why I got the NI KK S49 MK2. So, DAW integration is good, not great, NI Komplete integration is great, hardware is good.
Summary: Solid hardware, great integration with NI software, OK DAW integration

[[VIDEOID:e944f84eebdd7fc95cbc91fdd1f60b03]] I love this tuner pedal, it’s just wonderful! It’s very small. . . my cables take up more space than this thing. The entire display IS the foot switch, but the display portion is recessed a few millimeters from the surrounding edge, so when you stomp on it, your shoe does not actually touch the display, just the surrounding ring. I love how they optimized space this way, it’s a neat idea for the display to be the foot switch. It’s very bright, and easy to read in a dark environment. You stomp once to go into tuning mode, which is silent, and it does not pass the signal any farther. Stomp again to go back into bypass mode. There is absolutely zero electrical switch pop noise. It is super simple and intuitive to use.

Both the packaging and the unit itself are super sturdy. The build quality and physical feel is excellent. It came with a grippy back already installed. The grippy back is like a square border around the pedal. It also came with 2 sizes of Velcro. One size fits inside the grippy border, and the other size fits the entire back of the pedal (you have to remove the grippy border first, according to the instructions). No power supply is included, but it takes standard-for-pedals 9V negative-center power. I might as well mention the instructions make a few odd statements like “please use the attached charging cable” when it doesn’t come with a power cable, and isn’t battery powered. There are several weird little mistakes like this in the instructions, but nothing that keeps you from figuring out how the pedal works.

In bypass mode, there is a little white “dash” icon, indicating signal pass through. In tuning mode, if there is zero input signal, you see two green lights with NO note letter. As soon as there is a signal, the note letter appears, and you get very intuitive red or green LEDs indicating sharp, flat, or in-tune. The manual states that it’s accurate to +/- 0.5 cents, but the product page says +/-1 cent. Either one is good. I have no way to verify this, so I’ll take their word for it. My phone tuner apps (which don’t even agree with each other) don’t agree with it, but I don’t expect the phone to be accurate. I’ll trust this pedal as my “absolute truth” now.

One nice thing is that it recognizes octaves and harmonics. It clearly recognizes harmonics at the12th and 24th frets, which most of the cell phone apps won’t do. The recognition is quite fast too, almost immediate. It’s easy to play up and down the entire fingerboard quickly to check intonation at any fret.

You can also deviate from the standard A=440Hz reference standard if you want (e.g. A = 439Hz, or whatever), though I never do this, nor do I know anyone who does. But the instructions explain how.

A few things this does NOT do that I wish it did: It does not distinguish the octaves from each other. You can accurately tune an E2, or an E3, or an E4, but it just calls them all E, E, and E. This isn’t a big deal, but it would have been nice to indicate the octave. Also, the instructions never tell you how many cents each red LED bar is. I know the accuracy is supposedly +/- 0.5 cents, but the red bars MUST be courser than that. The coarseness of the LED indicator is not stated anywhere. Without knowing that, it’s hard to really “utilize” the +/- 0.5 cents accuracy if, say the LED bars only change every 2 or 3 cents (or more). A little explanation would be nice here, but the instructions are silent on this. I would guess (just a wild guess, mind you) that the +/-0.5 cent accuracy is only for when the green “in-tune” LEDs light up.

It’s also a bit expensive; it’s definitely at the higher price range for tuner pedals. I assume most of this cost went into the build quality, which is truly superb. Hopefully, presumably, some cost also went into superior electronics as well, to deliver on the promised accuracy. I almost subtracted a star for the higher cost, but in this case, I really do think you’re buying “better” with this one.

Overall, 5 stars. There are a few extra features I wish it had, and it's kind of expensive, but it’s really a superb tuner overall.

After several off and on months of looking at trumpets, it became clear that to get a good trumpet, you had to spend over $500, or end up with something inferior. That was the thinking until I spotted this trumpet on Amazon. The thing that particularly stood out about this trumpet was the very high number positive (5 star) reviews. It frankly was hard to find much wrong with the trumpet based on the reviews, and if there was the odd problem reported, most people who had the problems indicated that things were quickly corrected by the seller.

Well, after long consideration ( and what felt like a gamble), I ordered this trumpet. Besides, I felt that if I was duped, then $220 was not a horrible hit, and this was much easier to swallow than a $500 or more trumpet - especially if you are not sure your kid is going to stick with it. One good thing though being an occasional trumpet player myself, it would get used either way.

So the order went out in mid February, and the trumpet was received very quickly. That was the start of being impressed. We opened the case, took out the trumpet, and noted an instrument that is better looking than the pictures show. Exceptional finish, and all valves and tuning slides were smooth as silk to operate. Long story short: My son and I have been playing together as he learns, and it's been great. It's now June, and we've had zero problems. It is the same as when we received it. Valves still smooth. This audio interface is simply one of the best you can find out there. There are many things about it that are advantageous for recording that I find delightful. Essentially, in my mind, I think of it as its own CPU, running plug-ins and NOT taxing your computer's CPU. Here are a few things about the Apollo that make it great:

Design:
I used many different interfaces over the years, and this is by far the most simple and elegant in appearance. The front of the Apollo seems as if to give a nod to the older days of NASA when the name "Apollo" was a household word.

The rear panel of the Apollo has the basics. Two Mic/line inputs, Monitor L/R, Two Line Out, Optical in, Headphone port on the front, and a Thunderbolt port. The minimal approach allows for a compact design, but can also limit usage.

Connectivity:
First off, let me say that I love the usage of a Thunderbolt port for an audio interface. Not many company's have done this, and it allows for some of the fastest data transfer possible. The only negative sides is that they don't supply a cable. For an interface at this price point, they should.

Audio Quality:
In the end, this is what matters the most. With either a mic plugged in or a line level instrument everything sounds warmer, clearer, and bigger than any other interface that I've used. Between the clarity and warmth of the pre-amps combined with all of the "vintage" plug-ins puts this interface at the forefront of the comparable brands on the market. This is, where the Apollo Twin is a winner!

2nd Update: I’ve since swapped the bridge to something sturdier, tuning machines (to locking ones), knobs (to witch hats), and pickups (to Seymour Duncan Seth Lovers). Still plays like a dream.

Update: I cleaned and treated my fretboard and I changed my strings. It plays even better now. Instantly improved.

Overall, great bang for your buck. Great for entry level. Great for seasoned vets that want to make a project out if it. Definitely buy one when they’re back in stock.

But, I got it wet yesterday and it was in the guitar all night and today. The sponge was a little drier, I noticed.

The hard plastic ring, according to the manufacturer's instructions, is made of a plastic that won't react with the guitar's finish. So, I left it on. Basically, get the sponge wet and then squeeze out all excess water. Use a towel and thoroughly dry the exterior of the humidifier. I remove the hard plastic ring for that. It's easy because the rest of the humidifier is a soft plastic material. So, once dry, put the humidifier over the sound hole, under the strings. Slip the "wings" under the sound hole. The hard plastic ring is between the body of the guitar and the humidifier.

This is a great instrument for a beginner to intermediate player. I play clarinet myself, and although I prefer wooden instruments, there's no way I would entrust a 5th grader with an $1800-$3000 clarinet. However, I also don't want to give her one of those $100 ultra-cheap clarinet-shaped-objects to learn on. This Yamaha, which I purchased from a local music store, is the happy medium.

While $600-$650 might seem a bit much to spend on an instrument for a beginner, especially considering that you may want to replace it with something better once they become more advanced, don't forget that once they reach high school and start marching band, they'll need a decent plastic clarinet anyway. My oldest daughter started with her Buffett plastic clarinet in 4th-5th grade, and continued to use that instrument for marching band throughout high school even after receiving a wood clarinet, and it also has served as a backup for when her main clarinet had to go in for the occasional repair. So, with that in mind, I consider it a worthwhile investment to buy something that will hold up throughout the years.

That said, I've played on this Yamaha a bit, and it sounds and feels great. Plays well across all registers, and the included mouthpiece is decent as well. So, while an advancing clarinetist might want something better later on, I do also believe that this instrument would be just fine through high school. Text:
This little box is incredible. Sound quality is great for a mini, much better than the minuscule size. It’s by far a class above other mini/micro amps I have owned (haven’t tried the Boss Katana Mini) and also above the 10W & 15W corded practice amps I’ve owned. It’s not going to be loud enough for busking (unless you’re in a preternaturally quite place) or even coffee houses but for practicing and just enjoying yourself, it’s great. The headphone jack passes a great signal, much better than the actual headphone amps I have which are admittedly much smaller and more convenient but cost 2/3 as much. And the auxiliary input is great, crystal clear and, since it’s volume is controlled by the signal device rather than by the FLY3, easy to control to your preferred level.

There are a couple negatives, neither of which affect me. The power adapter is not included, is unique (which I appreciate - otherwise the noise reduction circuitry has to be baked into the amp) and from what I understand can be noisy. I use it wirelessly and so far I’m twelve hours into my first set of batteries with no signs of fading, so I don’t plan to buy the adapter. (Note to Blackstar: Inflating adapter pricing lowers quantity which increases cost and lowers profit. A cheaper adapter would sell more copies (just in case) and might lead to higher profit in the long run.) The other negative is the controllability. I’m not impressed with the range of tones available, and one of the knobs seems totally useless. Again, this isn’t a negative for me as I use it clean only and I don’t expect a full range of Blackstar’s vaunted effects reproduced in a sixty dollar product with a 3” speaker. But if you intend to use distortion, try it first, especially against its Vox, Orange and Laney competitors. I don’t think you’ll find better distortion and effects in this size and price range, but preferences vary, and if these are important then you might be happier with the Katana Mini (which costs 2/3 more.) Same with busking; I don’t think you’ll find better volume in its class, but you might be happier spending more. Otherwise, this is clearly the best value in its class. Blackstar hit a home run with this one. I did a ton of research before choosing this mini amp and I am completely satisfied.
Summary: Excellent product for practicing, jamming and just having fun

Text:
The Zoom G5 is a solidly built, well engineered amp simulator multi-effects pedalboard. I've owned a few competitors in the past and I feel that the amp and effects models on this unit are pretty spot-on replicating a multitude of amps and effects. I played out with it for the first time on 1/12/13 and got several comments on how realistic the amp and effects models were in comparison with my POD Xt, M-Audio Blackbox and real solid state and tube amps mic'd up.

I have only consulted the manual a couple of times as the multiple LCD screens are easy to navigate and everything is organized very intuitively. Imagine a big pedal board that you can arrange in any order, with your signal chain going in either direction and you'll get the picture. Amp simulators with their associated cabinet models are mixed in as part of the overall chain. It is so easy to add, remove or rearrange effects/amps in this unit! The addition of the Z-Pedal is icing on the cake. The tube booster really warms the signal up and can be used for that purpose (leaving it on all the time) or as a boosts to make your solos cut through with a subtle db bump.

The unit also has a built-in tuner, basic drum machine and looper. It makes for an awesome practice tool or live performance device. I have not yet explored the Edit & Share software, but I will most likely download that soon and play around with it as well.

I would have given this device 5 stars, but the only thing holding it back is the way you switch back and forth from the patch view and the individual stomp box/amp view along with the looper and drum machine. When you are in patch view you have to hold down the 4th button to switch to "home view" to view the individual amps/effects. It's not that big of a deal, but tweaking an indivudal setting requires shifting through a menu. Also, to engage and stop the looper you must hold down the 2nd button to switch into "looper" mode. You can then switch back to patch or "home view," but then you can't turn the looper on and off without holding the 2nd button down to switch back to the looper to turn it off. A small quibble, but with some more creative engineering that could have been avoided. Again, that's the only thing holding this back from my 5 star review.

If it broke, would I buy it again? The answer is yes! I strongly considered the Boss GT-100 instead of this, but could not justify the extra expense ($500-$549 at current prices). Plus, I think this box's tones are as good if not better than the Boss unit. I have a music room in my basement full of amps and effects and I think this one will get a lot of use. Keeping stage volume at a minimum was why I looked at this as an alternative to a mic'd amp and it really fills the bill nicely.

I also picked up the Gator Cases Micro Keyboard Bag (GK-2110). It's not a perfect fit, but it leaves room for cables, straps, adapter which is a nice plus. Samson doesn't make a case specifically for this yet, so the Gator may be your best bet for toting this thing around.

This is an excellent product that I can't wait for updates to the patches and software to make it even better.
Summary: Zoom G5 really rocks like an amp with a huge pedal board attached!

I used this on every new guitar I buy and you can audibly tell the difference. The difference after ToneRite is different for each guitar. I most recently bought a Cervantes Crossover I. It was on the ToneRite for about 12 hours and I played it again and it had more sustain, the sound was more full, and the notes sounded more complex (more blooming). Contrast that with my Taylor 512ce 12-fret where after the ToneRite there wasn't much difference.

I've used it on a Breedlove Master Class Northwest Classic. The effects on this guitar was quite dramatic. I've used it with success on a Martin Dreadnought Jr (a difference), Gibson Keb Mo (a little difference), Bedell Angelic Bellisima (a difference), '10 Taylor 412ce Spring Ltd (walnut back and sides) (big difference).

People say this is snake oil, but some of them have never even used it. For those who used it and didn't like it, the ToneRite likely just didn't work with the one guitar they owned. I own several guitars and while it doesn't have a huge effect on all of my guitars, it works on most guitars and to me it is worth it. There are also different frequencies of the vibration and that may have something to do with success and failure of the ToneRite to affect change on different guitars. I think the claims of a guitar sounding "vintage" doesn't even make sense though.

Over the years my hands and fingers have succumbed to a variety of nerve and arthritis, which has diminished my ability to practice and play classical guitar. So finding something that is easier on my hands is a big deal for me. I had a standard cordoba c5 for that 4 years, which when I could play I enjoyed a lot. So I figured that hopefully a smaller scale finger board would work. Much to my delight the small decrease in nut size (52mm to 50mm) and scale length (650mm to 630mm) works well for my hands. I had tried 48mm crossover guitars before, but the string spacing never felt correct. 50mm at the nut with a thin Cordoba neck works well. I can play for about and hour without great difficulty or pain.

Now the guitar itself is a marvel, it's well finished and well balanced to play as most Cordoba's are. The sound is very good for a small guitar. The sound across all string is very even which is nice, and it has a warm sound with the Saverz strings. For comparison the C5 is a bit more 'Bassey' with clear trebles (When payed with normal tension strings). The Dolce by comparison has the same tone and good sustain for this level of guitar. The Dolce is basically 5mm smaller in all body measurements, and it does feel smaller.... but in a good way.

I expect the sound to changes a bit when I switch to lower tension strings, I normally play low tension basses and normal tension trebles (something like Augustine Blacks) .

This is a nice surprise in a small package.
Summary: Basically a smaller C5, that is a good thing

I actually wanted a midi controller at first so that's why I went with this. Although they will tell you this is not a control surface, they're lying. Every single knob sends CC, and every time you move the switch you get four different controls, so technically this has a total of 24 knobs you can assign to 24 different controls in your DAW. Not a fan of the small keys but they're not that bad, just not ideal for piano, strings and other instruments you don't only play single keys with. The only issue is that the slots for the buttons on the guitar were a little small for my instrument. I had to increase the length of the slit.

Instructions to increase the length of the slit.
1. Tools: sharp knife and cutting board. I used a kitchen knife.
2. Place the end of the strap flat on the cutting board.
3. Position the point of the knife approx 1/4 inch past the end of the slit. NOT THE HOLE.
4. Push down firmly on the knife until it cuts through the two sides of leather.
5. Test fit the strap on your guitar. If it fits wipe off the cutting board and knife and put them back where they belong. If it doesn't fit, repeat the above, increasing the slit by about a 1/4 inch each time.

Text:
Hello,

I'm a songwriter/composer under performance rights organization BMI, Inc as well as a writer/publisher under the mechanical licensing collective (The MLC). I write and record commercially licensed music as well as for retail sale. Here is what you need to know about this Tascam DR-05X recorder.

The good:
The recorder has a small profile to it. Highest quality files it can make is .mp3 files @ 320k bps and also 24bit 96k Hz .wav files.

The unit that I have there is not hardly and "floor noise" and the microphone pickup audio well.
I have no issues transfer files to my computer from the micro SD card as well as using this as a computer usb microphone for direct recording on my computer.

The bad:
The reason for my 4 stars not 5 stars is the company could "at least" include a small micro SD card. Yes, you need to buy one separately, there is a lot of them to choose from on Amazon. Also, I did not get any "micro" USB cable in regards to my unit for transferring files and for direct computer recording.. There is nothing stated in the product description in regards that the cable is "not" included. I reached out to Tascam in regards to asking about the missing cable, no email back after almost a week now from their support... so I find they lack customer facing after the sale.

Other things you need to know:
There are some posts in here on Amazon and I also found some on YouTube and other social media platforms that this recorder picks up a lot of electronic magnetic interference (EMI). Honestly, mine does not and I have way more computers and other electronic devices around me than most people. It is possible that either there was a "bad batch" that was released with out the proper internal "shielding" and maybe that was corrected? Any mass produced product, your going to find bad apples out of the bunch no matter how great your QA/QC is. If this recorder was say stolen, I would take a chance again and buy it again.. it's that good. Also another possibility, is people may have bought a fake reproduction of the unit.

Conclusion:
I'm using this to record acoustic nylon stringed instruments such as ukulele, guitarlele and classical/folk guitars mainly for commercially licensed music. And so far, for a portable recording solution, it's been great. - Tom
Summary: Really great recorder, what you need to know.

Text:
These speakers are loud and clear, no mistaking it. Battery life is good and they're light. We use them every week. We've used Bose in niche settings for over a decade.
Now for the caution:
If you intend on sending music tracks via Bluetooth to perform with, don't The on-board Bluetooth for the S1 is 3-4 generations old and creates at least a 1/2 second delay most times. Impossible to play with. Granted, it appears that their intent isn't for this use, but all the documentation on their Bluetooth specs are conspicuously absent and it's impossible to know this in advance before purchase because the details are omitted in the specs. It's VERY old Bluetooth. Not low latency, not aptX or aptXHD. So planning on streaming Bluetooth to it for live play? Don't bother.

Solution: We got around this Bose S1 deficiency by using 4.2gHz transmitters and receivers. This allows us to send our entire mix wireless to mains and monitors.
You can get around the low mid-range feedback chronic Bose issue also by pre-eq'ing the output to notch eq the known feedback issues with these speakers. This will save your pickeup'd acoustics and not have audience leaving. Then, enjoy like we are.
Summary: We use 4 Bose S1's. Good sound, poor Bluetooth - be aware.

Text:
Most of our studio is wired with Mogami snakes and Neutrik or Switchcraft connectors. Which is awesome. Those are professional brands, with scrupulous engineering and quality. Mogami snakes are unlike any other: supple, soft, dense, lay flat, easy to strip and splice, with spectacular shielding. You just have to hold it, and you can immediately tell the difference in build-quality versus something from Hosa or the like. It doesn't crackle when you move it, nor die if someone rolls an amp over it, nor twist itself into knots.

Same with Neutrik and Switchcraft connectors. They fit tightly but smoothly, they are well-made, the strain-relief works, they last through thousands of pluggings and unpluggings without fault or failure, it's just a professional-grade tool, for people who need their equipment to work day in and day out. Moreover, they are SERVICEABLE, easily and quickly. There is generally nothing wrong with a Neutrik connector, that I can't fix in under a minute with a soldering iron. That's not true of even some very expensive (Monster) brands.

So, ideally, I would recommend anyone in pro audio use Mogami cable and Neutrik or switchcraft connectors for everything. It will work great. But it also costs a fortune, if you want to rig out an entire live setup or pro studio.

I have bought several pieces by seismic over the past few years, and while their quality is definitely not in the same tier as Mogami/Neutrik, they get most of the important things right, for a fraction of the cost.

The connectors are pretty good. Not as good as switchcraft/neutrik, but they are sturdy and serviceable, and strain-relief is decent. The snake and cable are similar. Not awesome, but pretty good. If nobody's going to be rolling an Ampeg SVT or a big lighting rig over it, I think it would probably last indefinitely.

I bought this to use with an Epiphone Les Paul, an almost 10 pound, solid body guitar. Ten pounds doesn't sound heavy until you're carrying it on your shoulder for an hour. I considered a cheaper, non-leather strap but decided that comfort was critical factor. Let's face it, if you're in pain, you're not going to want to play.

Here are my initial thoughts after a week of use (~8 hours):

-COMFORT-
I'm glad I chose a leather strap over a nylon strap. Even though I can feel the substantial weight of the guitar, the strap does not dig into my shoulder. The 2.5 inch width makes a difference as well since the weight is distributed over a broader area.

-LOOKS-
This strap makes you look like a serious player. If you're spending a few hundred dollars or more on a decent guitar, why cheapen the overall look by not having a nice looking strap? Nylon straps look like they belong on a plastic Guitar Hero guitar. There other straps that are more "designer" but this has a subtle professional look to it and doesn't take the attention away from the guitar.

-FIT-
Although this is adjustable, I found it comfortable on the shortest setting since I wear my guitar high (I'm 5'8). Part of it is because I'm not a guitar pro so I still need to look at the frets from time to time. Also, I was able to put this through the guitar buttons with no problem.

-DURABILITY-
This feels like a thick, sturdy leather belt. I've only used this for a week but it seems like it would last a generation.

-RECOMMENDATION-
If you're using acoustic or other light instrument, you can get away with non-leather strap; it won't look as good but functionally you'll be fine. If you want to look like a pro, have a sturdy strap literally do some heavy lifting for you, and have a $20 budget, buy this!

I will attempt to find a better instrument and will gladly pay more money. BTW, it's okay to slam a product, but remember, through Amazon, returns are both possible and easy. Make sure you do it within the 30-day window.

I compare 3 guitars in this video.
The first is an Ovation Applause with old electric guitar strings (my beach jam guitar). It sounds tinny and buzzy, but it allows me to play along to songs as if I was playing my electric. The G-string is plain, not wound so I can bend it.
The second guitar is the carbon fibre Donner. It sounds richer and bigger and is very easy to play after I adjusted the action and took one shim out from under the saddle. Unfortunately, it's too small for my adult sausage fingers. Decent bass response as well..
The third guitar is the all carbon fibre Enya with on board effects and a pickup. The effects 'magically' come out of the guitar (after charging it via USB) without the need for any amp or external speaker. It's very cool. Much richer tone and much easier to play than the Donner due to the adult scale length and string spacing. I did have to adjust the action to my taste by lifting the neck about a millimeter. To do this I loosened the allen bolts inside the guitar (a real tight squeeze for my large hands) and gently wiggled the neck up to where I wanted it to sit. I used an electronic caliper to measure the string height at the 12th fret and adjusted to taste.. Then I simply squeezed my hand into the soundhole again and fumbled with the allen key again and tightened the neck down. Other than that, it was great.
The Applause cost me $25 at a Pawnshop, the Donner was $299 (special price for the yellow body) and the Enya was $599.
Each are great in their own way and if I had to choose only one, the Enya wins hands down.
The Enya is a pro quality instrument that gives Rainsong, Emerald and a few others cause for concern. It comes with a very classy (think symphony cello) gloss black hard shell case.
Oh, and the onboard effects are a hoot. Playing David Gilmour style acoustic stuff with delay, chorus or reverb (2 of 3 at once) kept me busy for hours. Not sure how effective (pun intended) they'd be in a live setting, but sitting on the couch or jamming around a bonfire is a blast.

I am a somewhat old school musician in that I still have lots of hardware based synthesizers, mixers and such. At first I just had a couple rack mountable synths that I just stacked on each other on a desk. However as time went on I found other toys to buy and that stack started to get in the way and started to get all cluttered. I needed a rack mount system. The common systems for musicians tend to come in sturdy cases for touring and such. However since I am only using my gear in a home studio the added expense made getting one prohibitive. Then OnStage came along with this baby, and now I am worry free.

This rack stand is simple, sturdy, versatile and very affordable. I have three rack synths, mic preamp, multi-channel mizer and a rack power strip to mount up. This stand fits it all with room to spare. There are mount sections for 11 single unit rack mountable pieces of gear (or six 2U and a single 1U or three 3U and one 2U... well you can do the math). The stand comes with easy to tighten mount screws and can be placed anywhere the space allows it. The stand is NOT adjustable, but that only serves to keep everything nice and stable.

If I need to make any patch changes on the back I simply grab on end and rotate it around. Simple. The only gripe I can have (and it's a tiny, tiny one) is the protective end caps tend to pop off every time I move the thing. They are easy to put on, so I suppose that makes then easy to come off too. Like I said no big thing, and it's about the only negative I have to say on this rack stand.

OnStage is known for making affordable equipment, and this time they hit the nail on the head with the perfect blend of form, function and value. You get a good deal of quality from this little rack.

Without getting into a zealot like opinion review, I'll just say these strings have been my favorite classical guitar strings for a of years.

Nothing technical to bring up. Nylon trebles and wound bass strings - seems like every manufacturer has the same basic design. But the D'Addarios tell my ears these sound the best for my playing. I've tried so many different brands over the years - cheap to ridiculously expensive.

For the sound and price these hard tension strings are hard to beat. Some elitist may say otherwise, but I say don't listen to anyone including me. Discover for yourself what sounds best for you. These may not do it.

But, they're a great place to start!

In a pinch, can I use another? Sure, if I'm at a show and mine is lost or whatever...

But lets be real, these things last forever, and you only really buy a new one when the old one gets lost or broken (or stolen!). I've bought 5+ cakes of this stuff over the past 20 years and some of those were $20+ at local luthier shops! Even when it was expensive, it was worth it. I thought I could skimp and use other similar looking stuff, but there's a difference I tell ya!

I tell all my students to get exactly this brand, and the Light is easier to play imo than the dark for most cellists (most of my students, in the styles that I teach, at least!). I'm not sure how it feels to violinists compared to other rosins, but I describe this as "soft and forgiving" that there's a lack of bite, but in a good way. I can add bite with my arm, but if it's built into the icky sticky rosin, then it's almost impossible to take it out and play really smooth/warm notes.

I play with Larsen soloist A/D strings, and Spirocore Tungsten G/C strings. I've also used this rosin with Jargar and Jargar Superior A/D, Obligato G/C, Eudoxa/Chorda gut strings (it was a little too light for that) and played on my students' instruments with Kaplan and other brands of strings, and it feels great on all of them.

The "tone" of a guitar is said to be "in the fingers" but on a cello, the left hand gives intonation and vibrato, not tone. The tone comes from the right hand, or more specifically, the bow. The rosin is one of the most critical parts of the whole equation of tone, and Hill Light Rosin (from england) is exactly what fits the bill.

These days I'm playing all carbon fiber. I have a CodaBow Classic (~15y old) and a Luis&Clark carbon cello. I also have a couple of wood instruments in the house, as well as an electric cello. Other than being allergic to pine, I have no reason to ever stop using this rosin. I could write a whole book on how much I love it! Actually recently tried Magic Rosin (synthetic) to avoid breathing problems from my allergic asthma, but it was just not the same. I'd rather sacrifice some breathing so that my cello can breathe better!

I've tried the more professional looking bricks, but they aren't really any better, and I had one short out and fry a pedal. The One Spot seems like just an adapter, but it's industrial strength.

For those giving this a low rating because it buzzes more than running batteries, learn a thing or two about electronics (and don't say things like "I'm a professional"). The ground is key. Try plugging the One Spot and your amp into the same circuit. Problem solved. Never had any issues with buzz from these (several bandmates have 'em too), and after 6 years of playing out with my one and only One Spot regularly, there's no sign of degradation in the cable (Boss and Ibanez power supplies I had would need to be wiggled after a few months). I must say, it's the best pedal power supply I've ever used.

I'm a home musician and my stage days are gone, so I don't need 20 plus foot cables anymore. For most practicing or bedroom musicians, a 6 foot cord is plenty long enough. Plus there's less resistance, which means a cleaner signal. I needed a right angle plug because I first plug into a Morley wah pedal with the plugs on the side. With the limited space in my setup, a regular straight plug stuck out too much and got in the way.

This is a good 20 gauge cable with a nice thick rubber jacket and sealed rubber plugs covering gold plated 1/4" connectors. If I were gigging it would still come in handy for backstage use or something. It's too short for anything else, but that's what makes it great for for practicing and such. For my use it's the perfect length, not too short but not so long it gets tangled up and stuff. I don't run around the room, so it's just right for playing the guitar by the desk. Unlike a few other budget range cords I have with sealed plugs, the molding on these plugs aren't any bigger than a regular metal sleeve plug is. This can be issue if the guitar has a recessed output plug and it's too big to fit, or you have to jam it in there. The 1/4" connections make solid connections on both ends and it works like it's supposed to, with no static, humming or any other noise. Just a clean guitar signal from the guitar to the pedal. I received this cable at a discount in exchange for my honest review and I happily recommend it.

The design of this unit fits my needs perfectly for use in improving short wave radio listening through headphones.

Short wave audio is typically endowed with a lot of artifacts at different frequencies that blot out the part that we need to hear which is most typically voice between 500 and 5000 cps.
