Needed a set up that could be used by pretty much anyone without me worrying (or really caring) too much about what happens to it. It also needed to be highly portable, unobtrusive and able to handle a mic, guitar and music playback all by itself. This bag was the obvious choice for the speaker, hopefully reducing wear and tear on the box itself as it's tossed into car trunks, hauled between buildings in the rain and used by young and old alike. It will see action ranging from church campouts to reinforcing a teacher in classroom with older folks to just sitting in a corner playing music via Bluetooth during youth group and maybe for outdoor summer events where we don't want to bring out the big guns.

So I think this speaker and bag combo will be just the ticket for our new little multi-purpose "pa system."

The bag itself fits this model speaker with a bit of room to spare; there is space in the main compartment (especially on top) for us to, at the very least, bring along the power cord, a mic cable, a 58 in pouch, an instrument cable and a (as back-up )aux cable. The bag looks fantastic and well made. I didn't really see any other options to choose from out there so sort of went with this by default. I don't think On-stage makes a speaker bag in this size. Something to actually compare this too (more options) would be nice.

While it is a very nice bag I only went four stars for a couple reasons.
1) The pouch on the side (I can only speak to the 8" speaker bag) is pretty small and not of much use to me. Even the power cable doesn't fit in there too cleanly. It might be a good place to stow an aux cable, spare guitar strings and winder or things like that- but not much else. They really should have made the pocket larger and perhaps even put a second one on the other side. It would have been an extremely simple way for Gator to make this a much more desirable product.
2) The other issue I have with the bag is the lack of stiffness/thickness/padding/protection on the bottom; the place your dentable speaker grill (the one part of it people always see) is resting all the time. I personally would like to see the speaker's face better protected since it's taking the weight and takes is subjected to the bumps and bangs every time the bag is set it down.

If this was an expensive speaker that I actually needed to take good care or I might have some reservations about using this style bag/cover.. For good speakers I prefer slip cover covers and hence keeping the speakers stored upright. But for the new mighty Harbinger and it's "Grab-n-Go PA in a bag" purposes I think the Gator 8" Speaker Tote Bag is definitely a winner. It's all still new so really hoping that as the bag show signs of age and use/abuse the speaker will remain fairly presentable... assuming it still works. of course! Will update this if the bag blows up or turns to dust or something prematurely.
Summary: Like It but could be improved

WOW, I'm surprised this is not a more popular amp. I see a lot about the combo version of this amp, which has a 10" speaker and leaves a good amount to desire. I've seen a 12" cabinet option which im sure sounds much better than the 10" combo option.

I'm using this amp on a 2x12" closed back cabinet with 2 12" Celestion Vintage 30's, and it sounds AMAZING.

I am also very surprised that a lot of people do not experiment with the Fuse software for this amp. It makes a HUGE difference and gives you the ability to change a wide variety of the effects and voicing sounds. First thing i did was go into the Fuse software and roll down the Mid Range EQ to about 4-5, as everyone knows that Fender Amps tend to be a bit much on the mid range scoop area. That alone makes a big bump in sound quality.

I have not gigged with this set up, but im sure it would be plenty loud enough for a smaller group and in a smaller area. I usually only play with a few other guitarists at a smaller bar, not full volume or with a loud drummer or anything. So a very good and powerful 15 watts, i have yet to feel like i needed "more power or volume".

I see folks being turned off by this being a hybrid style amp, but in my opinion you get a decent tube sound out of this and the Voice Modeling is very handy and gives you a wide variety of classic fender amp tones. A great amp for recording or goofing off at home. I have a 50 watt Tube Bugera Infinium T50 Amp, and this sounds every bit as good and loud and warm and true Tube sound. This Fender Amp actually gives me more of a broader EQ range and the effects and voicing sound good. I feel like i have more of a bottom end with this Fender than i do with my larger and all tube Bugera T50.

You can't just switch between voicing and expect each one to blow you away, you need to set the Gain and EQ appropriate to the Voicing that you are using. Once i stopped switching back and forth, and spent a few minutes on each Voice, they sounded better and more useful. Its nice being able to dial into a vintage sound, then switch over to an entirely different genre and tone, on the same amp!

The effects stock right off the amp are decent, but editing them on the Fuse software makes all the difference. Being able to modify the presets and tweak each of the voice settings really allows you to dial in a plethora of good tones. Stacking effects and changing their order is very nice feature as well. (with Fuse)

Only thing i can complain about is there is no Effects Loop on the amp. Which depending on your choice of effects, its not the end of the world.

I have not changed the Tubes, i think they sound decent and "fender" enough as it is. I would totally buy it again.

Is this meant for studio recording? No.
Is it meant for putting in your gear bag for a weekend trip and you might want to break out the keyboard and jam some tunes out? YES!
If you're looking for a cheap MIDI engine as a traveling keyboardist, this is prefect for you. Now you can break out the midi engine and lay down some notes right next to the guitarist and plug right into the amp, instead of lugging out the ol' MBP laptop and starting up the MIDI software, and telling the band to hang on while you've got an OS update, or software update to run "real quick." Then troubleshooting why OsX can't see the midi device routing...

The sounds are fine, there are some programs that have some noise but if you're playing on the go, you probably won't notice them. So don't expect studio quality.

It has USB host and MIDI interfaces, so you can plug in old style MIDI barrel plugs, or USB keyboards. Which is great removing a USB host device from the travel bag. My current set up has a USB Host box, a MIDIPlus S-Engine box, going to the mixer and out to headphones. This replaces all three of those devices! I won't replace my current set up with it, but it's great for powering up the keyboard and getting some notes tested and written down.

It's got a great selection of programs, some odd ones (like gunshot...), but most are pretty good.
No, again, it's not studio quality to record from... but for this price you better not be looking for studio quality. It's great to jam out from, and test some tracks without the hassle of breaking out the laptop, and starting up your midi set.

Mini amps really aren't a "new" trend - there have been micro-sized amps from Pignose, Marshall, Fender, etc. on the market for several decades. The part that is new is that some of these mini amps (yes, even the Fly 3 with its 3" speaker) actually put out quality tone to the point where you would actually want to practice with them. By contrast, the similarly priced Fender Mini-Twin has become an attractive desk ornament. But the Fly3 is absolutely no toy...

FEATURES - As mentioned above, you are getting 3 watts of solid state power through a single 3" speaker. The controls are very basic, but surprisingly versatile. The clean channel will range from completely clean to slightly crunchy, and the OD channel morphs the tone into a much thicker, gainier overdrive. Blackstar did not include a reverb because reverb circuitry is very power-hungry, but instead offer a simulated "tape delay" which can be adjusted for delay level and repeat time. This is actually a terrific feature because the delay can be set to simulate almost a "room-like" ambient reverb effect. Or, it could be used as a more traditional quarter or eighth note delay for soloing. It doesn't have the features of a dedicated delay pedal, but as an add-on to a $60 amp, it's pretty outstanding.

The Fly 3 also has a jack that doubles as a line out (with cabinet emulation!) and headphone output. The Fly 3 really sounds excellent with headphones - plenty of fullness and power. So, if the small speaker is a concern for you, keep in mind that the Fly 3 doubles as a pretty great little headphone amp. There is also an MP3/Aux input for playing music with a 3.5mm cable, or jamming along with your favorite sounds. (Note: the volume and other controls only affect the guitar input - MP3 volume controlled externally).

The amp does not come with a power adapter, and it is 6.5V, so you can't use a standard "Boss" 9V power supply. However, they sell an expansion kit for around $30, I believe, that has both the adapter and an add-on speaker cabinet to plug into the back, which doubles the output. One advantage for the Fly3 over the ID:Core10 is that it is truly battery operated (6 "AA" batteries). Blackstar claims that battery life can vary dramatically (4 to 40 hours!) based on volume of play. But if it ends up being somewhere in the middle, I think that is acceptable.

TONES - The "ISF" control is offered in place of a tone control, and I've actually been critical of it on other Blackstar amps. I previously owned the ID:Core 10, which is basically this amp in 2x3" configuration, and with some additional effects and amp models - but felt that the ISF on that amp was a weak link, and missed a traditional tone control. Currently, I have a Blackstar HT-1MC ("Metal") small tube amp, and the ISF control on there also leaves a bit to be desired. But for whatever reason, I find the ISF to be much more effective on the Fly 3. On the "0" side of things, it is supposedly doing an "American" sound, but to me it actually sounds brighter and more open. The "10" side of the control they claim is "British voiced", though I swear it actually sounds more bass heavy and scooped. I'm never quite clear on what the US/UK "tones" are supposed to be, anyway, but the good news is that ISF actually offers a good variety of tones here, especially noticeable through headphones.

I'd be lying if I tried to convince you that a 3" speaker in a plastic housing is going to have anywhere close to the fullness and complexity of full-sized guitar combo. But at the talk-over volumes this amp is designed to operate with, it's perfectly satisfying. And the overdriven tones coupled with an ambient delay that can be set to very subtle levels make this amp sound larger and better than it really has any right to.

There are some great mini amps now available on the market, but I consider the Fly3 to be a class of its own, given the $60 price point, and EXTREME portability. This is an amp that could literally go anywhere, and is good enough and versatile enough that you'll actually want to play it. It's really worth a look from any level of guitar player.

UPDATE (02/04/2016) - Still enjoying my FLY3, and have been impressed how long the batteries last with it. The fact that I can just throw some Eneloop rechargeables in there and pull it out of a cabinet without any plugs needed has made this my preferred "okay, I have 5 minutes to jam" amp. I also appreciate that it has the AUX IN jack - it's fun to plug iPhone apps, a Vox Amplug, a multi-FX unit, or pretty much anything with a headphone/line out into the FLY3 and use it as a low volume cabinet. It's borderline criminal that people are still paying $35 to $50 for the desktop ornaments Fender and Marshall call micro amps, when they could be playing the FLY3 instead for slightly more money. This is absolutely a serious piece of musical equipment - not a toy.
Summary: The new killer battery-powered micro amp

Text:
On the plus side, it looks pretty. The device is a small, single, round speaker that connects with your cell phone via an app.

Now, the negatives. There is no way to connect it directly to your computer to extract files, and with large, audio files, uploads can quickly eat up your monthly data plan. Not to mention, uploads move at glacial speeds, draining your cell phone battery in the process. I learned (after a day and a half of trial and error) that you need to turn off the device before uploading the files. This isn't documented anywhere. Once uploaded, your computer doesn't recognize the file type so all uploads need to be sent up as tracks (wav files) rather than as project files (proprietary software). Again - not documented. There are very few You Tube instructional videos, and the company website doesn't offer much help. The chat support tool only works for product purchases - not tech support.
I used the device to record a live-gig with my string quartet, and I'm sorry that I did. The device had difficulties capturing the sound accurately. There was a great deal of distortion, rendering the recordings useless. To be fair, they seem to be targeting the non-classical music world with their device, so perhaps that explains the terrible sound quality results that I received.

If you are a serious musician, you may want to consider something that renders a better quality result, and one that is compatible with your laptop/desktop computer.
Summary: Hard to use, poor documentation, hard-to-get tech support -- distorted sound

It has, over a dozen-plus sessions, almost elminated my back tweaks, and my neck muscles are also more relaxed after playing for extended periods. This pad slides easily over the strap, too easily in fact; one negative for me with the pad is it slides up and down the strap too easily and makes my guitar much more slippy in my hands than without the pad. So I put two-sided duct tape on both sides of my strap across the whole area where I put this pad, then wrapped the pad around it with its velcro. presto, problem solved, and now the ax sits perfectly, better than without the pad, as the pad keeps it stable on my shoulder. I tried one side only at first and the tape came loose fast, so two sides all the way across the strap is the way to go.

The other minor quibble is that the somewhat rough sewn edge of the pad digs into my neck, so I spent a few minutes a few times folding it back hard against itself. After a while it started staying bent, and now it doesn't rub on my neck.

Aside from those two things, both fixable, I love this pad. It's a bit heavy but that's a very fair tradeoff for the serious softness and support it gives, and how it stabilizes the guitar once I taped the pad to the strap. Moving the guitar while taped like that is no big deal, I think, and I don't really do a lot of those Joe Rockstar headstock-to-the-sky moves anyhow. The weight distribution is the real bonus here, and my heavy instrument seems half its weight now.

Which goes to show how vital a wide strap is. A good thick leather strap is wonderful, but it's cumbersome and costs five to ten times what a simple nylon strap plus this pad cost. And I find this combo just as good and even better in some ways to the SRV-style thick leather straps I've used. The gel keeps my shoulder cooler and breathes better than leather as well. Plus it doesn't seem to hold the smell of sweat like leather can, a real plus for those of us who aren't Lemmy.

For twelve bucks, this is a true bargain. It could end up saving you thousands in doctor bills over time---back problems are no joke, ask anyone with one---and it also mkaes playing long gigs or practices much more pleasant. I rarely even think about the weight of one of my heaviest guitars any more. It's easy to take off one strap and put on another, and fits in most any gig bag's front pocket.

I never would have thought of this gel concept, but I really have benefitted from it, so thanks to whomever came up with this better mousetrap!

Text:
Expectations are key to how this piano should be rated.

I've played with various pianos at Guitar Center for over a year just for fun while shopping for guitar equipment and realized that all onboard speakers on digital pianos are rather terrible. This made me think that even the cheapest pianos, if properly processed and amplified, should technically sound good, just like any other electric instruments out there. Of course, it will lack the "authenticity" that some people are adamant about but there are always small annoyances found in any improperly maintained instrument.

What's included?
The Allegro is currently on sale for $200 at guitar center. The body is sturdy and not cheap-looking at all. It has a metronome and the ability to record (but haven't tried this feature). The sustain pedal included looks and feels plastic-y so i bought an m-line sustain for around $40 which has a grippier surface to minimize movement.

How does it play?
I've only played Grand Piano 1 (i think) so this review is only regarding that setting. The action on the keys are surprisingly firm out of the box. The speaker doesn't have a very good bass so the low notes will not sound well. However, I noticed that after playing for a bit, the lower keys loosen up somewhat and become more sensitive so I don't have to punch the keys to get a sound. Also regarding the action, overall it is not very consistent and hard to gauge the stroke(?) to volume output, but i'm ok with it, and i'm hoping that it'll eventually loosen enough to be more sensitive (like the lower keys).

Final thoughts
I'm pretty new to digital pianos and didn't know what was involved in creating the right sound. But, after some research, i've realized that an external monitor is rather necessary to get the sounds that the digital piano CAN make. I haven't purchased the studio monitors yet but have tested the piano with my Logitech Z-5500 to see what kind of sounds the piano can make and it blew my mind regarding its untapped potentials. The onboard speakers sounds too muddy when used with the sustain and each individual notes can't be heard when you're speeding things up (like the 3rd movement of the Moonlight Sonata). With a proper speaker system which also can handle the bass, I think it's definitely worth buying a combination of a cheaper piano with a nice studio monitor, if you're on a budget. With the money i didn't spend, I opted for the 2-year warranty for $40 which covers any damage, even accidental, which is nice if you plan on travelling with it.

Finally, I would've given this 5-stars but I knocked a star for selling the music stand separately. $20 for a piece of bent metal.

If you ask people who know about guitars: "What's the one relatively inexpensive change I can make to my guitar that will improve tuning stability (and possibly tone)?", upgrading the nut is a common answer. Inexpensive guitars, such as my Squier Bullet, often use an inexpensive plastic nut, which tends to catch the string and result in that "plinking" sound as the string catches and lets go. Even more than the tuners, the friction points of a guitar are usually responsible for tuning issues. People talk about the type of wood, tremolo blocks, etc., but "nut to bridge saddle" really is the point A to point B where your string is played, and any problems with those contact points is a BIG problem for the guitar.

The TUSQ nut is pre-slotted and made a little large so that you sand it down to size. You can install it yourself without being a professional luthier, but I chickened out and turned mine over to a Guitar Center tech ($30 or less) because I wanted it done right.

Very happy with the result - my guitar has excellent sustain, though I can't say for certain if it's "better" than with the plastic nut. The bigger difference, however, is that the string travels easily through the nut without catching, and the guitar stays in tune. You're starting to see these standard on some newer guitars, and I hope that manufacturers take note of that and install teflon or synthetic ivory on new guitars!
Summary: Teflon/Synthetic Ivory really should be the standard on all new guitars!

I finally managed to solve the problem of getting a really durable flight case for my prized vintage Conn New Wonder II ("Chu") tenor with this Gator Deluxe ABS case which to my surprise accommodates the opposing bell keys. That's always the big question with these shaped cases. In fact there is a bit of extra room lengthwise so that I think I will add a piece of material to the top of the end plug to make things nice and stable. The case closes without any hint of it being too small and when I shake the case, I can't detect any movement of the instrument inside. That's what you want so that in case of major impact, the instrument is not damaged by the inertia of movement inside its case.

In fact, it's a good idea anytime you take an instrument outside the house and especially when transporting in a vehicle or if shipping it, to pack it judiciously with some extra foam or fabric. Not too much and not too little. If you use a cotton scarf or towel, that will also be useful to dry moisture that escapes from inside when playing and the like.

With this Gator case I like the ABS shell rather than fabric, the metal clip closures rather than zipper and the shoulder strap with its well-designed clips which puts the handle in just the right spot for me to be able to guide the case if necessary. This is not totally lightweight but considerably lighter and more maneuverable than my Gard case which I like but is a tank. I also like that this case is designed with little feet to sit on a flat surface although its body is curved. It will even stand upright on feet, which from experience I know is a good feature at a space-challenged situation. (Note I would stand it upright only when the instrument is not in it, say at a rehearsal, due to the inherent instability of that position. Or I might stand it in upright position if it could be securely wedged or roped to prevent a tumble.)

Text:
So I'm not suggesting there aren't better products out there, just that this is the nicest chorus I've ever played in my 15 years of practicing, touring, gigging, rehearsing, and recording. Again; the keyword here is USABLE. This is a beautiful sounding AND looking pedal - it's super classy with its chrome knurled knobs, bright blue LED, and custom sparkle teal color.

It's hard to find an unusable tone in this thing except at the most extremes of settings - the tones are even useful for crunch and distortion/OD and are especially if you're running a dual amp (stereo) setup. The stock presets are nice with great usable throws of the knobs; nothing that will blow your speakers if you turn one knob too far. You could find a great setting and just leave it on all the time (I like CHO2 with SPEED and DEPTH around 12 o'clock and FX LEVEL dimed) for clean and distortion/OD alike.

Then there's the TonePrint feature. This is the cat's pajamas, SERIOUSLY. Not only can you download TONS of tones from famous artists and beam them directly to the pedal via your iPhone into the guitar's pickup, you can download TC E's TonePrint Editor, which allows you to alter the tones and create your own with loads of tweak-able parameters. As for anyone who complains there isn't enough control over this pedal, they obviously haven't messed with the TonePrint Editor. It's staggering what you can do, if you ever get bored of all the endorser's tones.

There are lots of good demos on YouTube. I just posted a 32 minute video demo/review of this pedal over there - just search for "zakhansonfan dreamscape" and mine's the first video that pops up. I go through almost EVERY possible tone with both clean and distorted guitar.

Cons:
-I probably would have preferred the inclusion of a phaser instead of the vibrato feature, but I almost never use phaser anyway, so it's not a big deal (though maybe I would if it sounded as nice as this pedal does).
-The toneprint was a little finicky to get set up because at first my firmware needed to be updated. Once I settled down and followed instructions, that only took a minute of two, so no biggie.
-The included USB cable is WAY to short; unless you want to disconnect the pedal from your system and move it closer to the computer, you can't really get at it using the TonePrint editor. This is a minor gripe, but given that if you want to make tweaks, it helps to be able to hear how your changes are affecting your overall sound. This can be fixed with USB extension cable (or just a longer USB cable).
-If you want a different preset, you must actually bend down and turn the knob, which wouldn't be a problem except...
-Knob positions are global, and not all "neutral" setting are "neutral" for all settings. So if you like your settings in CHO2 and you turn the knob to FLA1, you're gonna have to adjust the speed, depth, and level, otherwise it will sound bad too extreme.
-It does have some extreme settings, which are pointless and novel; but it only takes a second or two to reign the sound back into a usable range.
-What this pedal can do is far greater than advertised, so a lot you're gonna have to figure out by trial and error - for instance, I suspect using the TonePrint editor, I can go in and make the 12 o'clock settings for all the presets useful, so that when I change from preferred settings in CHO1 to FLA2, the current knob positions are still useful - maybe needing only some MINOR tweaking.

I know it sounds like I have a LOT of complaints. But in reality, I had to scrape the bottom of the barrel for these and they're very minor. You're gonna LOVE this pedal. I know it's one of my few (along with a tuner, Bad Horsie 2 wah, Ibanez TS808, and Deluxe Memory Man analog delay) that are now officially a part of "MY" sound. Watch my video and try one out yourself - you'll love it.
Summary: The only USABLE chorus pedal out there.

I really hope that the THR10 is doing good sales for Yamaha because, in my opinion, they might have just made the perfect home/portable practice amp. I would further say that it is the ideal "beginner's amp", too, except that at $300 for the THR10, it's just a bit high for (most) brand new players starting out. But it is worth every penny of that cost.

Let's get some misconceptions out of the way first. This is not a tube amp. When you turn it on, it glows orange, but this is a stylistic effect (and one I rather like). Also, this is not a preamp, even though it kind of resembles an Orange Micro Terror or Vox Lil' Night Train. The THR10 is an all-in-one-stop combo amplifier (some refer to this style as a "lunchbox" amplifier). It is a solid state amp, but also a modeling amp. It also does not have a "line out" of any kind, though there are apparently online discussions about how to add one. The amp is intended to be plug-in-and-play, though you can use it as a USB recording interface (a lightweight version of Cubase is included), and you could (probably) go to a small speaker using the headphone jack.

BUILD QUALITY - Top notch. The facings and front grate are metal, and the sides are plastic. It has enough weight to sit on a table and not be bothered by the instrument cable, but is lightweight enough to be extremely portable. Actually, the metal handle is a terrific idea because otherwise you would have no good way to carry it without disrupting the knobs. The main power switch is a metal toggle, and seems built to last. The knobs have enough resistance to them that you won't accidentally change settings. In other words, this thing is not a toy. Most importantly, although I haven't really "cranked" it yet, this amp seems more resistant to annoying rattling and metal noises when you hit a lower note. Mini amps are notorious for this, and even my two other apps (a 20+ lb Fender Super Champ X2 and a solid state Vox Pathfinder 15) do this to an extent when pushed. That just speaks of precise design and manufacturing.

(Note: there is apparently an issue with electrical noise on some units that is VERY easily corrected - it literally requires a bundle of wires to be zip-tied away from some other wires. I haven't had this issue yet, but I am not concerned)

SOUND & TONAL FLEXIBILITY (THR10 Model) - Note that this is a review of the THR10, not the THR10C (boutique) or THR10X (high gain), though I did demo both of those models and found them equally impressive! The THR10 has 5 basic models (plus 3 multipurpose ones). Yamaha reps have all but acknowledged that they model the following amps:

CLEAN (Fender Twin)
CRUNCH (Vox AC30)
LEAD (Marshall Plexi)
BRIT HI (Marshall JCM800)
MODERN (Mesa/Boogie)

What the THR10 does that is (allegedly) different than other modelling amps is to basically re-create the actual circuitry of those amps with the modelling technology. The significance of this is that, in particular, the AC30 and Plexi models will reflect the full range of gain for those amps. (A Yamaha rep even joked that the THR's tone controls on the Marshall amps "don't really do anything", since they don't do much on real Marshalls either!). Therefore, despite having only 5 amp models, I find plenty of usable clean tones between the CLEAN, CRUNCH, and LEAD settings, and they all have their own character. The BRIT HI model has a good deal of output, and can run from classic rock to some metal. And the MODERN sounds downright mean, and insanely "large" for an amp that is, well, so small! Remember, this is two 3" speakers for a total of 10 watts, yet it probably as much or more volume (and better quality) than many 8" speaker combo amps.

People tend to neglect the other three settings, but they also intriguing. The BASS setting is probably intended for plugging a bass guitar for practice (haven't tried), but it completely functional as a bassy sounding guitar amp (Fender Bassman, anyone?). The ACO is the acoustic setting, which would allow you to plug an acoustic/electric in and take advantage of the excellent reverbs on board. FLAT sounds boring, but is extremely useful - this would be the setting you would us to plug an external device (synthesizer) or perhaps a preamp pedal like a Tech21 to use the THR10 more or less like a PA or power amp.

What really makes the THR10 great is that they thought of so much of what the home guitar player would want in a single package without just throwing a mess of everything at the user and making it a nightmare to navigate. It has a built-in tuner, separate effects knobs with Delay/Reverb and Chorus/Flanger/Phaser/Tremolo, tap delay for tempo setting, and a handful of simple amp models that are high quality and extremely versatile. This one was and is an instant classic.
Summary: Instant classic; almost a "must-have" for home/low-volume practicing

Self-lubricating is how all guitar string retention points should be made coming out of every factory! Outside of having a good initial setup, having self lubricating type parts just make sense for every guitar thats being made or has been made. String breakage is easily one of the most common problems and can be effectively minimized with a few low cost upgrades. And in tuning stability these along with a properly cut quality nut will make a night and day difference on your tone, sustain and tuning stability. Collectively they all add up and matter equally.
Having a 3k guitar does you absolutely nothing if you're constantly breaking strings or having tuning issues. 99% of the time that can be relegated to your nut, NOT your tuners. I can't say these will make all the difference in the world to you or your sound but they surely don't hurt and it's an extremely low cost upgrade that you can do yourself. Anything I can do to relieve string pinch tension without sacrificing tuning, tone or sustain is to me worth the price of a lunch.

As you'd expect from a small amp, they are limited in how much air they can move and can only produce so much volume of the deep bass sounds a 76 keyboard can produce without rumbling. These are a great economical choice for room treatment for audio recording. The sellers would probably cut out a lot of bad reviews if they changed their description to not say, "soundproofing." That's not what these are designed for and it seems a lot of people are confused about that in their reviews here. These are designed for fixing problem spots in a room where you're doing audio recording- they help to cut down bad reverberations and reflections of sounds that cause issues in your recorded sound.

I got the 12 pack of the 'mushroom' panel type to help treat some corners in my home studio that I hadn't addressed yet. These did the trick and were cheap.

You absolutely need to use the method described of soaking these in water and then drying in your dryer on medium. In my case they needed more time than the 20 suggested minutes- it was more like an hour in total. That method absolutely did the trick though and they puffed back up to their normal size perfectly. I had tried jsut leaving them out on the floor to puff up on their own as I've done with other acoustic tiles- and that approach just does not work with these.

Great and inexpensive tiles and I highly reccomend these to anyone doing audio recording at home!

Makes tremolo sounds without noise for $25. Good bargain pedal, doubtful about the durability and a few minor nits noted below.
I bought it to use on 1 song. Should work for that purpose.

PROS
- Cheap price
- Good sounds and range of sounds
- Form factor (size/shape) is good - doesn't hog the board, but not so small you step on adjacent pedals stomping it.
- "standard" 9V center positive power supply jack.(same as a boss pedal)

CONS
- Plastic case
- power supply jack on right side can interfere with positioning input patch cord in certain positions.
- pots (controls) feel cheap
- not sure the waveform knob is really required. A better choice might have been just an output level jack although I don't notice it raising or lowering the volume.

DETAILS
Rate, speed, and waveform adjustment knobs allow for a variety of tremolo sounds. Price is great at $25, case is plastic and that's a concern for durability. Behringer puts the power supply on the right side, and I don't like that because it can be in the way of right angle patch cord plugs. The overall form factor (size and shape) is good, the power supply is standard (9v, Center positive), and it makes the sounds it should and doesn't seem noisy. I can't complain at $25 but I'd rather see them move the power to the back vertical surface and put this in a metal case. The pots feel kind of cheap to me too. Its not an effect I expect to use a lot, just a few songs. If I fall in love with tremolo and decide I need a more durable unit, I'll buy a more expensive one from someone else. But for the occasional user, this seems like it can work. I basically like it because its cheap, it works, it doesn't require any weird power supply plugs or different voltages, it has a standard form factor and it sounds decent.

My downgrade of 1 star is based on my perceived quality and durability of the product. I rather expect that I'm going to step on it one day and its going to crush under my foot or the switch inside will be cheap and not last very long. Time will tell. I've recently purchased 3 behringer pedals for effects I don't use a lot but wanted to use a little. We'll see how they last.

UPDATE: I've had this about a year and a half, although have not used it consistently during that time. It still works, never had any issues when I was using it weekly. The one problem that emerged on this , and both of the other 2 Behringer pedals I bought around the same time is that the back label came off when I pulled these off my pedal board. i.e. the velcro is a lot stronger than the glue bonding the label to the pedal. Find a better glue fellas! Overall I think this is worth it's relatively low price but probably would buy a better one if this was an effect I wanted to use a lot.
Summary: Great price, does what it is supposed to.

Went through two of these before giving up. The first one I sent back because of an extremely noisy (static) output jack (the one on the preamp to the endpin jack). Contacted Brandon with Kempa and sent a video demonstrating the issue. He said this was not common for that pickup so I sent it back to Amazon for replacement. Unfortunately, the replacement also had exactly the same issue. I believe all/most of them have this issue, but once the pickup is installed and wiring secured you may not even notice it, but it should not do this!  The other reasons I returned this second pickup is that 1) It sounded too magnetic/metallic, as many soundhole mag pups do, especially the further up the neck you play. I knew this before buying but was sure I could dial out most of the nasty tones between onboard controls and a good EQ but, unfortunately, I could not....not through my acoustic amps or PAs at 2 separate open stage events. And yes, I blended plenty of mic signal in as well, but this didn't help much and makes it more prone to feedback. Reason 2) The internally mounted transducer, which is what turns your guitar into a speaker, had very low output making it barely audible while playing, even after adjusting the transducer output pot to 100%. I placed it where recommended, on the back - across from bass side of the bridge. Maybe it had low output because of the Jumbo size body (Taylor 815-C)? I don't know. For comparison, I played a couple different Yamaha Transacoustic models (parlor & OM? size) that have Yamaha's own similar version of this setup. No magnetic pup... I believe they're using a UST. Nothing is obstructing the sound hole, unlike the Kepma. I noticed the transducer (speaker) in the body is huge compared to the Kepma's. The sound (even out of a relatively crappy Yamaha) was much more pleasing to the ear and much louder. I really wanted this Kepma to work out, primarily as a pup system for gigging and open stages. The internal transducer effect was secondary. I was disappointed with both features. YMMV, depending on the guitar and your sound preference. Obviously, many people have and love this system, but it's not for me. Thankfully, Amazon/Kepma gave me a full refund. I ended up installing the K&K Sound Ultra-Pure Mini Guitar Pickup/Preamp and couldn't be happier.
Summary: Preamp jack issues. Mag/metallic sounding. Low output from transducer

I bought this speaker as a portable music and karaoke solution. I've been use to carrying around the Bose F1 812 and F1 sub everywhere. Even to small get togethers. The small get togethers are what prompted me to purchase the S1 Pro.

The good:
Ultra portable sound solution. The sound quality exceptional. The built in EQ and reverb worked well enough for karaoke. The battery lasted 5 hours at a very high volume. I was expecting less even though Bose advertised up to 11 hours. The fast charging is great, but you can't use fast charge while the system is on. Did I mention its portable?

The bad:
The mids and high ends were perfect. The low end lacked a lot. This is probably done for as much sound clarity as possible. But I really felt the low end was really lacking. I have a Harmon Kardon portable speaker that delivered deeper base than the S1 Pro. I wish the bluetooth and 3.5mm aux channel had some sort of EQ solution as well. It may have helped balanced some of the missing low end. When a song with a lot of base plays at a higher volume, there woofer flutters and sounds extremely bad.

If you're looking an extremely portable sound system for karaoke or some live acoustics, this is the perfect balance. If you need something that can deliver base, I don't recommend this speaker at all. I may pair this with a B1 sub for a more rounded sound.

I used my PC for recording and playing back music I created. I had a ridiculous amount of USB/electrical noise coming through my audio system to and from my PC audio and my Behringer XENYX-1204USB mixer. That was making any attempt to produce a solid recording impossible. I decided to start isolating and replacing gear.

QUICK AND DIRTY RESULT = I NO LONGER USE USB AUDIO OF ANY KIND. I now limit how many USB items I use with my main editing PC. I will be buying a stand alone digital recorder with XLR and Line inputs. I will only use my PC for Post Audio file editing and software music creation.

I have found that USB 3.0 and 2.0 are angry at each other so be wary of using both, use either or. I think that the power requirements of USB 3.0 make the system more susceptible to noise and interference with USB 2.0 wireless devices.

BELOW IS WHAT I WENT THROUGH TO MAKE MY FINAL DECISION ABOUT DISCONTINUING USE OF USB AND/OR ON-BOARD AUDIO RECORDING.

PROBLEM: I had huge, ugly, noise coming through my mixer from my PC in the form of system/USB noise and general scittery power noise related to my PC (unrelated to buffering, ASIO, midi, or audio hiss).

1) I bought a highly rated PC power supply (SeaSonic 650 GOLD plus) - That made things much more visible (worse).

2) I bought a Monster Power PRO 3500 power conditioner from guitar center - that did not help with PC audio noise at all, but did help with some buzzing of new JBL monitors.(My guitar amp is bad and-needs to be replaced.)

3) I bought a PYLE PDC22 lift BOX and ran my PC analog audio card out through the PYLE PDC22 to my mixer. That worked well, but not 100%. I still had migrant, but low level bursts, of electronic chatter. Thank you for a good effort PYLE.

4) I isolated every power cord and audio cord from each other and from my PC. I kept my PYLE box isolated - even from its own audio cables. That killed a great deal of my audio-through issues pertaining to PC system noise.

UPDATE: I found HUGE pieces of the USB and audio electronic noise puzzle.

5) I replaced my standard magnetic hard drive with a Kingston v300 240 GB SSD drive. POOF, Noticeably less USB scrittle. It turned out that the reading and writing was causing noise in the whole system as well.

6) Through trial and error, I found that the USB connection of the Behringer XENYX 1204USB is just plain crap. No matter which computer I plugged it into (three different laptops and my main PC), HUGE USB noise was generated. Once the USB was disconnected and the drivers removed, the audible noise was noticeably reduced.

*Tertiary Note: I found, through trial and error, that the Monster Power supply "broadcasts" a huge amount of interference which wreaks havoc on my gear if placed anywhere near the supply. Now I keep anything related to power generation, away from all of my gear by a meter or so, and all of my audio cables separated as well as I can.
PLEASE SEE MY DECISION ABOUT USB AUDIO AT TOP OF THIS POST.
Thank you so much for reading this. I hope it helps would be private musicians.

The Golden Gate F-3303 is intended for extending the nut on resonator guitars that are ordinarily set up for fretting.  In other words, this is a device that allows the player of a round neck resonator to set up the instrument for square neck-style lap playing.  With this extension nut, the player can change back and forth from having the instrument set up for fretting (or a combination of fretting and slide playing) or alternately for steel bar playing.  The buyer needs to realize that although the extender simply fits non-obtrusively over the top of the guitar's regular nut, you must slacken the strings in order to make the switch.  In other words, it's not something that you're going to be able to do in between songs at a gig.  However, the Golden Gate is very sturdy, seems to fit a wide variety of string gauges, and changes the guitar's intonation set up very little.  Do note, though, that because changing the angle of the strings from bridge to nut also changes the length of the scale ever so slightly, tuning the open strings perfectly in tune means that the frets will not mark 100% precisely where the touched notes need to be played.  Since so much of slide playing relies on the ear and not on precise visual placement of the bar directly over the frets, it is not a problem.  This device is ideal for the players who plan to do, say, some Delta blues with a combination of fretting and use of an over-the-finger slide (normal, short nut setup), and then maybe work on Bluegrass lap-style resonator playing in the future.  It's not for someone who is going to change set up hour by hour or day by day.  The only way you could probably do that would be to own two instruments.  If you don't need to make quick, frequent setup changes and don't want to own two resonator guitars, the Golden Gate F-3303 does the trick! At less than $10 compared with the price of a second resonator guitar, it's a no brainer.

Text:
I have been playing guitar for a lot of years, and have also worked extensively as a professional studio engineer and live sound technician. I have never met an acoustic guitar pickup that sounds right, but sometimes they are just infinitely more practical than trying to mic the guitar.

There are basically two "flavors" of acoustic guitar pickup:

- Magnetic pickups (such as Dean Markley) are the same technology as you find in an electric guitar. They can actually sound pretty decent for fingerpicking, but they sound and respond more like an electric guitar than an acoustic, which is especially problematic on fast strummy stuff.

- Piezo pickups are the more common built-in type. They do actually sound kind of like an acoustic guitar, but like a terrible one. They have a plasticky, brittle, thumpy, obnoxious sound that is perfect for ruining the dinner experience in a casual-dining restaurant, while strumming and singing EZ guitar versions of 90s rock songs. There are some things you can do with eq, compression, and reverb to try and de-awfulize the sound of piezo pickups, but nothing will restore the rich, woody resonance that a real acoustic guitar has.

The purpose of this pedal is to help with that "piezo" sound. It does. It doesn't "cure" the piezo-ness, but it makes a noticeable improvement if you dial it in. The "blend" control is really helpful in balancing the compression/saturation effect of the "level" control.

It won't make your acoustic guitar sound like a properly-miked acoustic sound, and I still think a magnetic pickup (or just an electric guitar) is probably better-sounding for most players, but if you must play with piezo acoustic pickups, this box will help tame some of the obnoxious brittleness.
Summary: Not a cure-all, but good for what it is.

I play jazz and have been playing drums since 1964, so I keep my top hi-hat loose. This allows me to fan it, as well as get that sloshy sound when I ride it (and for you rock drummers, keeping the top hat loose was how Ringo, Mitch Mitchell and a number of others coaxed a great sound from their hi-hats too.)

The problem I was having is when I would loosen my top hat in just about any other clutch, eventually the bottom retaining nut would come loose and drop into the cup of the bottom hat. On some clutches this would happen on every set, which meant messing around with the bottom nut often. I was introduced this well-designed clutch when I purchased a [[ASIN:B0002F4ZSQ Drum Workshop CP6500 6000 Series Hi-Hat Stand-Flush Base]], which comes equipped with it. Immediately I noticed the small set screw in the bottom nut, which was tightened with a drum key (see the stock photo at the top of this page.) It allowed me to loosen the bottom nut as much as I wanted (or the top, locking pair - same affect and same problems with conventional clutches.)

Since using this clutch I have never had a bottom not drop and I do not have to give my equipment a second thought while playing, which is the way it should be. I was so taken that I ordered these clutches as replacements on my other hi-hats (mainly Pearl and Tama) and even carry a spare in my stick bag for jams. If you are old school and experience the same frustrations I described, this is the cure.
Summary: Perfect for jazz and old school drummers

The whole trick to using a looper - especially live - is getting the start and end points perfectly in time, and it is no easy feat (feet?) if the start/stop switches /buttons aren't exactly as they should be. The stomp switches on this unit are certainly rugged and will takes thousands of stomps, but there's enough resistance in the downspring that unless you're wearing steel sole shoes, there's going to be enough 'give' in the sole of your shoe (or flesh of your bare foot - if you're that classless enough to go on stage that way) to cause a delay in the actual start of the loop. That cuts off the very front edge of the note or chord you begin your loop with. I don't know a good solution other than a more sensitive switch that would probably fail sooner. I purchased this kit locally after going through the frustration of buying 2 Alesis kits online untested. Initially, I bought the Alesis DM6 ($329) as a starter kit and a component of my mid-life crisis figuring for a few hundred bucks the risk was minimal. Ultimately the quality and performance was minimal. Then I saw the Alesis DM10X ($1,050) and, boy howdy, it shore was purty. Unfortunately, once I turned it on I realized Alesis was at least consistent in their level of quality. I even went so far as to have it evaluated by a long time electronic drum player, who suggested at best with a lot of tweaking it might be functional. I packed it up and sent it back to Amazon (who is very good about returns by the way.)
So... I go to the music stores and badger the drum guys for feedback and recommendations. Pretty consistently vague at best about Alesis. Roland and Yamaha seem to be the conventional choice while Alesis promises big and falls short in reality. I have written reviews on both kits if you want to hear more of my whining or perhaps my specific complaints.
The TD11K does everything it promises. It is responsive and functions precisely as you would want or expect it to with a decent variety of kits and voices to satisfy in all likelihood any level of drummer. Simply put, when you hit a pad it makes a noise which sounds like a drum... If you don't hit a pad it doesn't make a noise.
The TD11K is user friendly and easy to navigate and tailor voices and kits to your preferences. The USB thumb drive allows you to load loops as well as full MP3 tracks which you can play along with.
Don't be mislead by physical appearances. The TD11K looks very similar to the Alesis DM6 which both look like a toy next to the Alesis DM10X but neither of the latter are worth taking out of the box in my opinion. Read some blogs, there are people that are very happy with Alesis products. I was not and have reviewed all 3 kits in an effort to same some of you the trouble I encountered.
Now... If you can afford the Roland TD11KV (with mesh heads, about $1600) I would heartily recommend that upgrade or you can do like I did and upgrade with mesh pads purchased separately. The TD11K comes with PD-8A pads which are rubber and single zone pads for the toms, and a PDX-8 (8" dual zone mesh pad.) for the snare. I have upgraded to a PDX-100 (10" mesh head dual zone) for a snare and PD-85 (8" mesh head dual zone) for the toms. The feel and response is worlds apart.
I like the TD11K I anticipate using and enjoying it for years to come. If someone hands me $4,500 I would confidently throw it at a TD30K-V pro even though it would be wasted on a poser like me.
Read the blogs... Do a search for Roland Vs Alesis vs Yamaha... Do the research before you invest... Better yet, go to Guitar City or Sam Ash or any local retailer that carries electronic kits and TRY THEM OUT. Amazon is always competitive in pricing with reputable sellers.

Installed this into an Epiphone Les Paul Standard Plus. Originally replaced the pickups with uncovered Seymour Duncan SH-1's, though the guitar can with covered pickups.

Liked it for a while (5 years, to be exact), but, having bought a 2012 Gibson LP Standard Plus, and it having burstbucker pro's, I figured I'd show the Epi a bit of love and swap to some covered pickups, and, why not Gibson 57 Cl/Cl+?

Yes, I know, I could have just bought some covers, soldered them on, and potted them myself, but, that's a PITA I didn't want to deal with. These are already potted.

Removed the SH1's, installed these, and there's a difference - these are a bit 'hotter'. Granted, that could be pickup-string distance differences, but, overall, I still think it was an improvement. No matter, asthetically the Epi looks better, though tonally it can't touch the Gibson.

Text:
All bone with abalone pins of this type are the same. They're all made in China and sold under various brand names. There are things you need to do to fit the pins to your acoustic guitar, regardless of brand. I see some questionable advise in the reviews. So I thought I'd give you a luthier's perspective.

Will they improve the sound? Yes, if you're changing from plastic, you'll notice better note separation, clarity, and longer sustain. It's even better to change your plastic saddle to bone. I use exclusively bone or buffalo horn pins, saddles, and nuts when I build a guitar.

Sizing: there are a few different pin sizes. Depending on the age and brand of your guitar, there are 2 angles and a couple of sizes. These pins can be used in the majority of modern guitars. Here's how you adapt them:

Pins should fit nicely, so that they don't fall out when the guitar is unstrung, but not so tight that their difficult to remove. Wood is a barometer; it swells with high humidity and shrinks in low. If the pins are tight and the wood swells, you'll crack your bridge, something you definitely want to avoid.

When you put the pins in, if they don't go all the way in, you MUST ream the hole. A plumber pipe reamer, which usually is ~ 6° will work, even though it's not exactly the 5° of the pins. Ream a very little at a time, until they sit in the hole without falling out. DO NOT FORCE THEM OR HAMMER!

If the pins are a tiny bit loose, string the guitar to see if they'll secure your strings. If so. You're okay. If they're ridiculously loose, don't use them. For these guitars, you need special larger pins, offered at luthiery sites. If they're just a little loose, you can spread ca glue (super glue) around their shanks. After it dries, use 220g sandpaper and sand them until they fit nicely in your holes.

Ramping may be necessary for proper fit. Ramping involves filing the bridge pin holes, straight down through the top, to make room for the strings. I have special tools for this, but in a pinch, you can use a micro file. Take your time and file a "trench" so your string will fit within the pin groove.

BTW, even well-fit pins will be difficult to remove when you change your strings. Here's how to remove your strings:

Push the string into the hole. It'll release your bridge pins! You should never have the need for a tool. If you consistently need a bridge pin removal tool, even after pushing the string in, then you should enlarge the pin hole, just a smidgen with a reamer. Remember, you want your pins just tight enough that they don't fall out (without strings).

I hope this information is helpful. The photos show me reaming, then ramping, the holes on a Martin bridge that was raising. I had to remove to reglue it.
Summary: I'm a Luthier. This is the right way to fit the pins

OK... lots of things to say about this pickup. Bottom line: If you are looking for a cheap solution to plug an acoustic into pre-existing gear without buying additional parts, you MAY be really REALLY disappointed.

Pros:
- Sound is actually pretty good
- Install is easy
- Fits in the soundhole of a Big Baby Taylor
- Comes with extra rubber feet

Cons:
- If you don't have a preamp look elsewhere
- If you have to buy a preamp, this is NOT an inexpensive solution
- Volume (as in, there isn't any)
- You'll end up turning your amp up so loud that if you get feedback (and you will), God help you
- It picks up the cable moving against the guitar body
- The rubber pads that hold it in are kind of wonky... definitely prefer screws

So now for the full deal... This pickup is the only thing I have ever seen that is more passive than my ex-girlfriend. If you don't have a preamp to amplify the input signal (either external or built into the amp) you might as well forget about it. To give you an example, I have a 300 watt 1x15 combo that has a high-gain input for passive electronics. This works OK (just OK) and I can get reasonable volume out of this pickup if I crank the amp WAY up. BUT, with the amp that high, if there is feedback or interference, you better be ready to hit the kill switch. That said, the pickup actually sounds beautiful in my BBT. Nice FAT low-end and really clear highs (which I would expect running through a bass amp of course, even though I have the lows cut on the EQ). Overall with a little EQ I was able to balance the sound, and it was incredibly clear and pleasing. The volume seemed uniform across the strings. Nice job.

I also have a Boss 100 watt Katana MKII head running through an 8ohm Carvin 4x12 cab. The head has a single, low-gain input (no preamp), and in order to even hear the speakers over the actual acoustic using the amp's acoustic patch I had to run it at a full 100 watts at a volume around 7 (of 10). In comparison, my LP at these settings would be ear-splitting, terrifyingly loud (like, you-better-be-wearing-hearing-protection loud). Again, feedback at these volumes could actually be damaging to equipment and biologicals.

All said, I just think this kind of misses the mark. The point (at least for me) of an inexpensive soundhole pickup is so I can amp an acoustic with minimal cost and hassle. I didn't want the expense or trouble of installing an onboard preamp or purchasing an external one. Now, with a passive pickup I didn't expect miracles in the volume department, but it is honestly kind of unusable. Having to "turn it up to 11" to hear it just isn't tenable. I don't tend to return stuff and had already tossed the box when I minimally verified it was working, and I am sorry I did. If I have to go buy additional stuff, I might as well have taken my guitar back to the luthier and had them install an active system.

The other thing I noticed (maybe common with this type of setup) is that MAN does this pick up any movement of the cable against the body. Any time I moved I could hear sliding and tapping in the mix.

I guess this would be useful to throw in a gig bag as a backup for an existing rig if you have access to a preamp, but for a guy like me that just wants to hear himself play at home without throwing a ton of cash at it, meh. Two stars for the fact that, if you do get enough volume, it sounds really nice, but considering it is a partial solution, two stars is all it gets.

The quality of sound on this interface is great - you simply can't beat it for the price. I've come to expect that from Behringer. I would have given it 5 stars if not for 2 issues.

2. The Windows drivers really limit the device if you're using a lower-end recording software. The Windows drivers don't see the interface as 1 device with 4 inputs (which is what one would expect). It sees it as 2 separate devices each with 2 inputs. So if you plan on using this with something like Audacity, which is limited to recording from 1 device at time, then you don't get the ability to record all 4 tracks at once - at best, you get two. Even if you're using a higher quality DAW that can take inputs from multiple devices simultaneously, this opens up the door for potential time/sync issues.
Summary: Good Unit but Windows Users Beware

The VOX seemed like the best bet, so I shelled out $240 at Best Buy. Needless to say I'm not happy about seeing the amp now selling for $80 less than that. MY biggest problem with this amp is the noise. It's virtually unuseable in a recording situation...and it seems to be something that the VOX people are passing off as "normal". The only remedy for the noise is to turn down the "power" control on the back of the amp. But that severely limits the volume you can play at. Changing the top control settings ("gain" and "volume", and "master") do nothing to change the noise. So, it's either the tube or some cheap IC's (Integrated Circuits) that are at fault. I would sooner suspect the solid state components than the 12AX7 tube as this particular noise does not sound like the typical noise associated with bad12AX7 tubes. I would like to make a point here concerning the proliferation of "tube" equipment that currently is flooding the market and appealing to those old-schoolers and tube lovers. This is not a "pure" tube amplifier, but one which simply inserts a vacuum tube in a circuit containing mostly solid-state components. The 12AX7 tube was designed as a two stage hi-gain preamp tube used in audio amplifiers to bring guitar and microphone levels from microvolts up to millivolts and consequentially drive the output stage of a common tube amplifier. For the 12AX7 to operate properly, it requires 150 volts DC. And therein lies the biggest cost factor in designing a tube amp; the power supply, which must take 120 volts AC from the wall and convert it to 150 DC. This requires bulky transformers, capacitors, and diodes. The manufacturers found that a 12AX7 would run on as little as 50 volts DC but would not provide any real gain. So they make up the gain with transistors which run on very low voltages requiring minimal power supplies. This is how amp companies can now claim "it's a tube amp" without it really being one, just so long as there is ONE tube in there. There are many fine amplifiers that use this design. I've used one for 33 years and love it. As long as the quality of the solid state components used is up to par, there should not be a problem. Even one 12AX7 will add a certain harmonic distortion and warmth so coveted by all guitar players. But noisy components on either side of the tube are going to be heard at the output.

What I do like about this amp is its power. It's damn near loud enough to use on a small gig. And the reverb is one of the nicest I've heard in any amp. I'm not much for 'modeling' but there's a huge pallette of tone available. I generally stick to the "super 4X10" and "AC30" amp selections because I'm old school and play pretty clean. There's a bunch of effects available also. A footswitch (around $64) is available that will allow you to switch from a bunch of presets.

Overall, for the money, a pretty good amp. Just wish it was quieter.
Summary: Noisy...and not really a TUBE amp

I own one, I like it and will keep it, but there are things you should know. It may not be a noise gate, but it behaves like one. When you stop playing, it can be heard quickly adapting to the changing signal. It does not entirely remove all hums and buzzes, but it does get rid of 99 percent of them. And what is there is much, much quieter. Also, the power supply (included) is recommended as the only way to power it (using as it does less than 9v), so no 1 spots will do. This last is a hassle, but worth it. I play strats and teles, and it works like a charm with them, but it doesn't render them utterly silent. (I've encountered humbuckers that were noisy as heck, and this would doubtless help them too.) Also, the high setting on the Debugger can create some slight, metallic delay pedal-like sounds, but they are very subtle and not to be feared. The normal setting will likely be your choice, as it is mine. Just remember that it's basically a 'smart processor' that is reacting on the fly to your signal, and the tiny flaws in performance will not bother you. Note: put it first in your signal chain! - Sound quality: I really like this mic. It just has a balanced tone and fairly low noise. Compared to my Rode NT1a, it doesn't go as deep in the bass range or as high in the treble. Still its tone is balance and extended enough to cover an acoustic guitar and most people's vocal with a fair degree of accuracy. Its cardioid pattern is not as tight as my PR20, but has enough rejection for studio use. See the Recording Hacks website for its on axis graph with the focus button on and off. The Focus just seems to reduce the low end which can help reduce rumble. Notice it also is a low noise mic, though it doesn't seem to be as low as the NT1a. It's still very useful and sensitive enough for quiet instruments.

- Reliability / Durability: Very well made mic. It's heavy and solid with a decent shock mount and a beautiful wooden case. Seems to be a league ahead of the NT1a in this regard.

- Would you buy this again if it were stolen?: I would. In fact I have 2 just in case something happens to one in a clutch and so I can do some stereo recordings. I got them for $159 on sale. That seems to be what they are commonly available for at the time of this review.

- Features that stand out: The best part about this mic is that it seems ideal for the one person and his/her guitar. The response, sensitivity, and low noise make that its ideal use.

- What I don't Like: The pop filter looks nice, but isn't particularly useful. It certainly doesn't muffle the sound though. If you get the older version, the shock mount was poorly built. They sent me a new replacement and it is fine, but still not as nice as some spider mount style ones. I can't say it's given me any problems though.

I suppose for the price you shouldn't expect a fine furniture product. The bench looks good and is sturdy, which is what really matters. The bench comes securely packed in in a flat pack with the legs inside the bench top.  A pack of screws is stapled to the inside surface of the top, which has a nice cloth liner. The assembly uses metal brackets designed to pull the legs securely into each corner when you tighten the supplied nuts to pre-installed mounting screws on each leg. My only real complaint is that the legs do not fit snugly enough to close the small gaps where the legs fit to the frame, which immediately identifies the bench as less than fine furniture. A throw-away wrench is supplied to allow you to firmly attach each leg using a washer, lock-washer, and nut. The directions supplied are superfluous since the assembly is obvious. Some have complained their bench does not sit flat on the floor, but I think that's the fault of the installer. You first put the legs on without fully tightening the nuts, then sit it flat on the floor while you tighten the nuts down. There is enough play in the fittings so that as long as your floor is perfectly flat your bench will stay perfectly flat while you tighten the nuts. My 4-star rating is a 4.5 stars with a deduction for the fit not being as tight as it could have been.
Summary: Good piano bench but not fine furniture

However, the OD312 is initially quite impressive. "Initially" is all I have so far because it was just delivered a couple hours or so ago. The first thing I noticed was that it is a beautiful guitar. The second was that the neck is straight. Third, action was pretty good right out of the box; in fact, lower than my newly beloved Yamaha FS730S when I got it new last week, or so. And the 730 is an awesome instrument which I subsequently set up with very good action. But as they arrived, the Schmidt had the better action. I noticed other reviewers mentioning good action as new, and frankly doubted it. But seeing is believing. Those unwilling to either set up their guitar or pay someone else to do so might just get lucky with this guitar (though there is yet room for improvement). All the woods look very nice, gloss finish well done. The guitar is fairly big, with a resonant spruce top.

Its sound is a bit light on bottom, but its jangly, bright tone is alluring and very pleasant. I began playing guitar using a 12-string from the sixties. My fingers met the 312's fretboard with the same feel I had back then, meaning the neck and string spacing all felt natural and very familiar, as the guitar became a time machine, for me, transporting me back to younger years. Fun, Fun, Fun.

Chances are, the bass end will improve with age, is my guess. The best solid spruce tops aren't available down here in the budget end of the product pool, obviously, which likely makes a significant contribution to the guitar's tonal characteristics. Very similar to that old Ventura I played decades ago and for twenty years. It got away from me, but I intend to be a better caretaker for my current small stable of instruments, hoping to pass them along to others who will play and hear them in their prime years after I am gone. That Ventura improved with age.

[Edit - Rest assured that this instrument is not anemic in the lower registers; I perhaps gave that impression. The sound is full range, with a very satisfying presentation. Also, further playing time has enhanced my already-good opinion of this guitar. Really good action makes it a joy to play, while its tonal characteristics are great, with that big 12-string sound ringing in the night while a million-dollar sonic presentation has banished all those fleeting feelings of buyer remorse, even though the price dropped twenty bucks a few days after my purchase - now is the time to order.]

I will add to this review over the coming days with more observation and play-time, but as it stands, so far so good. I am impressed with the Oscar Schmidt OD312-12 String at this point, and feel good about the purchase.

[EDIT: Okay, now that I've played it for a few hours over a couple days or so... The bottom end is better than I initially thought. Action, from the box, is so good that I have not done any set-up - nor will I. Very unusual, even for guitars at twice the price and more. It is something I'm fairly picky about, and I take it as routine that set-up is required when I make a guitar purchase. I don't even think of it as criticism for a guitar to need adjustment to my preferences. So I shouldn't think of it as a plus when it is not needed, but can't help finding this impressive nonetheless, especially for an instrument this affordable.

The guitar's tone is alluring, pleasant and as balanced as any 12-string I've played. It sounds great! Furthermore, I find it a joy to play. Its appearance also is excellent for the money - I like the binding around the fret-board. One of the rather small tuning keys (G-string) on mine is a bit stiff, but livable - as my only nit to pick, a minor one. I am amazed by my Oscar Schmidt, and the brand has risen in esteem for me due to this guitar. If you've ever wanted a 12-string, but thought a decent model too expensive to take the plunge then this is the one to purchase. Amazon has dropped the price for the Christmas season another twenty-something bucks - just a couple days after I received mine but I like it so much that I'm not disappointed.]
Summary: Action Good, Sounds Good On a Jingle-Jangle Morning;  Outstanding Value

Text:
I saw the new "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" debut this week and his band leader, Jon Batiste plays one (check Youtube for clips of him playing a melodica). As soon as I saw it, I had to have one. It just looked so fun and online info made it sound easy and so versatile--a little like a saxophone, a little bit like an accordion--and a lot like a giant harmonica (that is much easier to play). I've read these sometimes play a little sharp (but still fine), so I was actually surprised to test this inexpensive 32B melodia with my tuner and find that every key was pitch perfect (what variations there were weren't enough to register as a sharp or flat). Really surprised! It sounds great.

Despite having a keyboard, the melodica doesn't sound at all like a piano because when you blow into the mouthpiece and press down a key, your breath crosses a reed that vibrates under that key. It's a woodwind that's "free-reed"--you just blow into it--and the sound is produced like a harmonica which is also considered a free-reed instrument (and, of course, has historically been Hohner's specialty. Hohner also were the ones who developed the melodica, back in the 1950s. Because they have the trademark, the other companies making them--Yamaha, Suzuki, Hammond, etc.--have to call their melodicas something different--a pianica or melodeon, or "MYlodica", etc. But they're all the same idea as this, with slightly different designs, and different tones, build quality, action and performance, sometimes--but not always--related to price.) If you like the feeling of hitting piano keys, this is much easier to play than either a harmonica or an accordion. As Lauren Bacall said in the movie "To Have and Have Not" (in a different context, but it works), "You just put your lips together and blow."

The melodica's simplicity is probably why there are no directions with this, nothing at all, except a sturdy padded case with a carrying strap (about 18" long case) and inside the black mouthpiece (which I greatly prefer) and the white tubing that you can use if you are carrying it, or more commonly, if you put it on the table to play flat while you blow through the tube. That's an easy way to practice, but it looks a little strange. Because there aren't any instructions, I've included the few things that I do know about playing this below.

You can regulate the sound (which can be pretty loud--and I like that because beginning an instrument its often difficult to get decent volume). Blowing gently makes it softer which seems obvious, and harder of course makes it louder--and you can vary the dynamics in between more than I expected. Experiment with your breath control to see. It is a nice single note instrument that can solo or accompany others (guitarists can keep the guitar in their lap and switch back and forth pretty easily).

Yes, you can make chords, but personally, I like the single note (or paired notes) sound better for this. JMO. You don't always tongue each note like, for example, with a clarinet, because you'll usually tie a whole phrase together with one breath. But you should try the attack at the beginning of each breath, by seeing whether saying "two" or "do" or "who" gives a better sound for that phrase. Someone said that if you can get a growling breath coming from low in your throat it sounds a bit like a saxophone but I have not been able to do anything like that. Still trying.

For sheet music, just find songs that you like where the low note doesn't go below "F". I've found that "C" fake books work well--play the melody/lead, adding partial chords here and there as needed.. Simplified classical music works too, if it has a strong melody line.

After about 30 minutes, the melodica will have accumulated some saliva so depress the "spit valve" at the bottom end, remove the mouthpiece, shake the body gently, and then blow gently while holding the spit valve. I've actually found most moisture is in the mouthpiece so have something handy to shake that into as well . Surprisingly, people who've taken these apart after much use find them very clean inside--nothing like dirt or mold, etc. like you might expect. Maybe whatever residue remains evaporates quickly.

Unlike some other melodicas (like Yamaha), Hohner has a hand strap for your left hand. This is very nice to keep it steady. You can also lay it flat on a table or in the case, and use the tube.

I also like the Hohner "Airboard" (basically the same instrument sound-wise, but very colorful and a little more expensive.)[[ASIN:B00I0YOEC8 Hohner AIRBOARD32 32-Key Airboard with Bag]] All in all, to me, whether you choose the 32B or the similar airboard or a different style altogether, if you like the sound of harmonica and want to get that sound in a very easy and fun way, the melodica is a great choice.
