The BOSS VE-8 Acoustic Singer may be look like somewhat of a niche product, but it’s actually a successful marriage between 2 separate, capable units: a vocal processor/harmonizer and an acoustic preamp/multi-FX. Well, maybe 2.5 units, if you consider the basic looper that ties everything together. While not a perfect unit by any means, I think the VE-8 is very good at every it does, and screams “BOSS” quality and durability throughout.

ACOUSTIC GUITAR SIDE:
The left third of the controls and the confusingly-named “CHORUS” footswitch all apply to the acoustic guitar input. The VE-8 supplies everything you need to plug in your acoustic-electric and then from the unit directly to a PA speaker (or to a mixing board). There are controls the change both the “shape” (essentially, EQ) and the Acoustic Resonance of your guitar. It’s possible to use these just by playing around and not fully understanding what the different settings mean in the manual. My acoustic-electric is the budget-friendly, but generally solid Yamaha FGX800C. With the VE-8, I could change from a variety of deep to bright tones. There are notch and phase settings to help dial out unwanted string noise. And there’s a selection of ambient, room, and hall reverbs that aren’t dramatic, but get the job done for acoustic.

The only thing missing from the VE-8 that I wish it had was one of BOSS’ compressors. The guitar sounds out of the unit are great anyway, but I might experiment with a compressor in front of the VE-8 to see if the additional control over sustain, attack, and volume limiting is helpful. Oh, and there are a handful of effects included in the VE-8, not just “Chorus”. However, the octave is +1/-1, not -1/-2 like the OC-2/3/5, which I had hoped for looping. Nice addition of the Slow Gear here, which is a violin-like, swelling effect from the 80’s that BOSS never remade.

VOCAL EFFECTS SIDE:
I was originally looking for a dedicated vocal effects processor, but the acoustic portion of the VE-8 was also very useful to me. However, the VE-8’s vocal processing, connectivity, and harmonizing features look to compare quite well to TC Helicon, Zoom, and other offerings. I use a Shure SM48 (again, very affordable), but the VE-8 can handle a wide variety of microphones and offers phantom power, if needed. The “ENHANCE” knob seems to both compress and brighten your vocal as you turn it up, so it stand out better in the mix. The vocal reverbs are very nice, and far superior to the dry sound of plugging directly into a PA.

The harmony feature was the “fun” element of the VE-8 that really got me interested in the device, and it has not disappointed. You can set it to a specific key, or it can “follow” chords on the guitar input, or a hybrid combination of both. It takes some practice, and it will reveal flaws in your vocal technique, but it is super-satisfying once you figure it out. There are a variety of vocal options for different harmony ranges, vocal doubling, and a few effects. These can be saved to a few dozen presets so you can switch between songs.

The pitch correction feature also deserves a mention here – I really like it. It’s definitely not a robotic AutoTune effect, but is meant to be much more subtle. You can turn it off, or choose between soft and hard pitch correction. In addition to cleaning up inaccurate notes live, it helps the accuracy of the harmonizer by holding the reference note steady.

LOOPER/OUTPUT SECTION:
In most of the negative reviews you’ll come across for the VE-8, they’ll point out that the unit’s looper is “only” good for 80 seconds, and is missing some of the key features that other dedicate looper pedals have, like an “undo” option for overdubs. I’m not here to say that this is the best looper I’ve ever used, but: (a) it’s great that it was included at all; and (b) the implementation between guitar and vocal tracks is excellent. The problem I’ve always come across when using pedal loopers is that it is very easy to slam them with too much signal, and then you run into digital clipping, or degrading audio quality as you overdub. The VE-8’s integrated looper did not exhibit any of those problems, and I found it very easy to use. You also have dedicated level controls for the guitar and vocal tracks. I believe you can also add an external footswitch to stop loops immediately (and clear them quietly), which is useful.

SUMMARY:
The VE-8 is built like a tank, and really feels like a unit that you can use and abuse for many years. I appreciate that most of the critical controls are mapped to knobs and buttons, rather than having to menu-dive on stage or during a jam like you are using an iPad on the floor, or something. This unit succeeds in providing a ton of features, but is also quite simple to set up and use. It can even run for about 4-5 hours on 6 AA batteries, which will be of interest to buskers. I’m happy enough to be pretty average guitar player and an even more “average” singer. But the VE-8 gets the best out of me and – best of all – makes me want to play music instead of endless messing with gear.
Summary: Everything you need to plug in, play, and sing in a solid gold box

My dissatisfactions are so few and so so minor, I'm still willing to give this recorder full marks.

On the technical side, recording is "limited" to 96kHz / 24 bit, as opposed to true high def 192kHz / 32 bit recording. The audio difference is so minor, most people will not miss it, especially since recordings are typically mixed down to 48kHz. The cover for the SD card slot may be difficult to pry open. That's about it. Like I said, real minor points.

I returned the DR-05 to get this and I do not regret the difference in price at all. The mics are more sensitive than the DR-05 and the dual positions they offer is a great plus. I am still getting acquainted with my DR-40, so I've not used all the features, but it is already going a long way to filling the promise of being a serious field recorder capable of near studio recordings.

It will drain your batteries fast, but the DR-40 will even supply phantom power to condenser mics. Alternate power can be supplied through a USB connection to a computer, AC adapter or an external high capacity battery pack is available. With the built-in mics, the sound is clean without the brittleness usually associated with this type of mic. I can appreciate the difference in the two recording modes available, close and wide-field stereo, and can see application for both modes. The tripod socket on the bottom is a nice touch.

Yes, the case is plastic, but it does not feel cheap or flimsy in your hand. The contours make the DR-40 easy to hold, but I would use hand held recording only if I have no other choice as you will pickup handling noise. The combination line inputs are a real plus: you have both XLR and ¼ inch TRS inputs on the same unit. The headphone jack is still a mini jack, but I can live with that. The built-in speaker is good only for determining if you are actually getting any input. The fidelity is worthless, but I always check recordings through headphones anyway, so this is a non-issue for me. Oh yes, the output is automatically turned off when you record, eliminating an annoying source of feedback.

I have yet to evaluate some of the high end functions that are integral to the design: 4 track recording using both the built-in mics and two external mics, over dub, dual recordings at two different input levels at the same time and some studio effects, like reverb,are all tricks the DR-40 can deliver. You can also use the DR-40 with a digital SLR for some real high end audio to go with the video digital cameras are capable of. And yes, there are still more features to explore!

If you need something more sophisticated than memo recorder and still want to keep you outlay reasonable, look at the Tascam DR-40. It will fill a wide variety of niches for you, whatever your recording needs are.

Text: Works great

It's cleanly printed in a nice, large size with bright colors, which makes it easy to read (you don't have to get up super close to see what's what), but it's not so large that it takes over the wall. The canvas, wood, and string all feel like they'll last. A good reference to have on hand (on wall?), if you've got music with more unusual chords, or you're songwriting and looking for something that might spice things up a bit.

But, there are two flaws—as another reviewer noted, the color-matching is off for F & E, between the chord charts and the fretboard illustration. The other issue (for me) is a matter of sharps and flats. The fretboard lists every in-between note as a sharp/flat (#/♭), which does not match the product images, where only sharps are listed. Sharps are my preference, since I am not a jazz musician, and the split makes it harder to read/reference quickly. But the chord charts are all in flats (♭). So for example, we have chord charts for G♭m and D♭m, which the musician will have to mentally translate into F#m and C#m for most music. It's kind of an annoying problem (unless you're trying to be a jazz guitarist, I guess) for an otherwise very nice-looking and useful wall hanging.

I think for $15, knowing what you're going to get, this certainly isn't a bad buy—and it looks pretty good in my music room (the little rainbow guitar shapes at the bottom give it an aimed-at-teenagers vibe, but they're small enough for me—a 30-year-old adult—to ignore). Great choice for beginners, as long as they don't mind looking at the fretboard illustration to translate the flats to sharps depending on the music genre.

Text:
Obviously, this is a copy of the Mooer Echolizer which I have not tested but have seen tested by others. Buying the Donner will save you 53 clams. How is that possible? Both are Chinese companies. These mini sized pedals are the coolest looking / hottest selling effects these days, and Mooer is the "trendy" brand to buy. Oh, and Mooer now paints white lines on their little bitty micro knobs.

But for my money, this Donner pedal is tops. I tested it next to my Biyang Time Machine which is what I call a normal sized modern pedal, and it costs a little more. Both pedals have the same 3 delay controls but are called by different names. In fact, the Yellow Fall has labeled them just like the Mooer: Echo; Time; and F Back. This mini pedal won't take a battery; there is no room for one. The Biyang doesn't run on a battery for very long any how. A power supply is a must- have in both units.

The Biyang also has a selector switch for max 600 ms time intervals in one position, and 1000ms in the other position. The Donner will give you about 680 ms time which is the same as the Mooer again!

Important info: The Donner product manual that came in the box says this: "DC 9V regulated AC adapter (Positive Tip)". So any way I didn't notice that at first, and I plugged it right into my T Rex Fuel Tank Power Supply which is definitely Negative tip all the way and it works fine I guess.

I like both pedals equally even though this Donner has a nicer finish than the Biyang. I think the Biyang is less rugged also, because of that dinky toggle switch. And as far as the Analog / Digital thing goes, I will leave that to others. My take is; this one is digital (like the Mooer) but I really don't care one way or the other. Both of my delays that I tested side by side are great pedals for the money. But the Donner Yellow Fall is cooler by far.
Summary: My coolest pedal is this greenish yellow thing.

Text:
I bought one of these a couple of years ago. I used it to connect my Behringer BCR2000 (in MIDI mode, naturally!) to my computer for mixing duties in REAPER. It worked with no issues and I had zero complaints.

A few weeks ago it stopped working (I had bent the USB connector and so I thought that was the culprit) so I bought another.

The replacement arrived and installed with no issues, but I'm still having trouble getting it to send MIDI data into the computer. MIDI out of the computer to the Behringer is fine. I'm not sure if this is due to the adapter or some funky Windows update that's happened lately, but it's certainly not ideal! :(

In my haste, having seen it install OK but without trying to actually use it, I discarded the packaging. Unfortunately the replacement is displaying the same symptoms as the first unit, so now it looks like I'm stuck with two possibly-broken USB / MIDI interfaces. I have reinstalled Windows, tried both with another computer, uninstalled and reinstalled the drivers, all kinds of good stuff and I still can't get either of them to send MIDI data into the computer. I was v-e-r-y close to throwing my Behringer unit away as I thought it was broken too!

Thankfully I tried an old Yamaha interface and it is OK. This means I just need to get and buy some MIDI cables and I'll be back in business.

So, I'd say buy one of these, and make sure it works before you throw your packaging away! When they work they're absolutely great and they're SO cheap! If you receive a lemon, return it and order another. It's worth it if you're not in a hurry. If you *are* in a hurry then order a few of them, or just get something else.

I'd also like to advise people that reports of MIDI latency with these devices is quite probably a misnomer. I strongly suspect that the speed of transferring MIDI data into your computer through this device is much faster than you think, and the actual latency you're experiencing is that of converting your MIDI data into audio. This happens inside your computer and has **nothing** to do with this device's performance; it's purely down to your hardware and software configurations. All this talk of ASIO is only really going to help you on the audio side of things. If you're using this device to record MIDI data then you should have no issues at all... as long as you get one that works! :-)

Cheers.
Summary: cheap 'n' cheerful... ish... and watch your "latency"

This is a good quality inexpensive microphone for its price. The stand and pop filters and sock are a good bargain. The stand is good overall, and it stays put easily. The shock mount holds the mic with out slipping and the handling noise it pretty minimal. Its a good overall mic, its not too bright, and seems to be clean when you power it. The Included XLR to Headphone jack cable is no good, not that it doesn't work, but you'll want a phantom power XLR jack for this. You can do this by either by supplying 48v phantom power with an inline phantom power adapter, or by using a  USB interface which supplies it like in my case with the UM2. In my testing I found that it was just too quiet with say a USB sound card that supplied it with just 5 volts, it improved it but it didn't get anywhere near the UM2's clean input with a true phantom power supply. For me the UM2  is really clean and quiet with this and complements it nicely. The build quality is good, the condenser capsule housing the condenser is plastic, but the condenser itself is larger than you little cheep mic and it preforms pretty well. The metal body is solid and its not to heavy, its in the middle weight wise. The finish is good though, and the grill is pretty sturdy but I'd say it wouldn't be drop proof like some of the expensive ones. It would generally hold up very well though. Inside the PCB is good overall with a little hand soldering to the wire connectors they are wire to pad, so not though hole, and there is little flux and residue with clean component placement. Inside the grill there is some padding for it as well. Combined with the sock or the pop filter it seems to do a good job. Overall the build quality is excellent for the price, and it sounds nice. The price alone is good with out the Mic, I figured if I didn't like it I could upgrade it. Its done well for me with just some quick voice over work and for conferencing and gaming. Its not in Sure or AKG territory, but for the price you can't go wrong.
Summary: great price point for a good performance does need external power.

Text:
Things I like: Small size, classic tones, affordable, same ugly green color as the original.
what I don't like: cheap parts -- it uses a PCB-mounted potentiometer for the gain control.

Last night I plugged it up, and turned the gain knob to find it was acting like an on/off switch - full gain to completely clean with nothing in between. I pulled the pedal apart and put my Fluke meter on it to find the potentiometer had failed and contact cleaner didn't help. It's a mini PCB mount component. A plastic housing clipped together with tension pins. I've included photos of the delicate part under magnification. That's a 6mm shaft. It's approximately the size of a pencil eraser.

I ended up clipping the leads off the pot and cramming a 100k mini-size potentiometer wrapped in heatshrink in there just to get it back up and running. This one will go in the trash bin eventually.

It's a real shame. The originals are still out there after 30 years of use rattling around in gym bags or the trunks of cars, with paint chipped, dents in the chassis, knobs broken off, etc. but still working great. This one has lived a sheltered life, spending only a few hours of use on a carpeted floor.... and it fails.
Summary: not durable. Sounds great, while it lasts.

I've installed this tailpiece on three fiddles now, and I like it. It's plastic, so it's very light weight. The four fine tuners are great -- they are integral to the tailpiece so they don't add to its overall length, and the design makes it basically impossible to tighten a fine tuner so much that it touches and scratches the top of the instrument (like the old style metal add-on fine tuners can do.) They are also designed to accept ball-end strings more easily than the old style.

Installation is easy if one is comfortable taking apart one's instrument. Use the previous tailpiece to help set the length of the little tail (it has adjustment screws on both ends), and be careful not to bump the instrument when the strings and bridge are off, as it might knock over the sound post. That usually requires a trip to the violin repair shop.
Summary: Works well, great fine tuner design

Text:
My high rating is not for the quality, but for the VALUE of these inexpensive guitars. With few notable exceptions, (i. e. hand made custom guitars) absolutely ALL new guitars require set up. Any reputable dealer should do some set-up before selling a guitar. Although when you buy a guitar via mail, you're unlikely to receive that service.

But even with a cursory set up, each guitar will change over time. Wood moves. It will expand and contract. Frets bulge from the neck. Someone will need to do those adjustments and minor repairs. Would YOU risk working on a fine instrument without the best tools and plenty of experience?

My reasoning is, EVERY kid who wants to play guitar also wants to modify it. I've been teaching for over 40 years. In all that time, almost every youngster or teenager puts stickers on his-her guitars, draws on them, tattoos them, refinishes or carves them! You wouldn't want them to do that to a fancy expensive instrument.

Also, every guitarist must eventually learn how to work on his guitar: restringing at a minimum, but adjusting action, making small electronic repairs or upgrades. Bolt-neck imported guitars like these (or Squire) are wonderful platforms for learning that craft without fretting about destroying a fine instrument. (Fretting... ha!)

If your young guitar enthusiast wants to learn re-fretting, that's much easier to do on a bolt on neck with no binding like this. Want to hear the difference between pro-pickups and these inexpensive imports? Swapping pickups is an inexpensive upgrade. Even less expensive is trying different capacitors or potentiometers. Your fledgling guitarists may become a computer whiz kid in the future. Some electronic knowledge and basic soldering skills will give him a "leg-up."

The fact is, a good guitar technician can make one of these cheap guitars play almost as well as an expensive one. You won't have the bragging rights, but you will have a useable guitar that sounds good and inspires practice.

With just a few inexpensive tools, any kid can learn to level and dress frets. During that learning process, he will make mistakes, but those are also inexpensive to repair and provide a crucial learning lesson: NO ONE gets it perfect the first time. Only consistent daily effort brings improvement. What parent wouldn't want their kids to experience that crucial life lesson?

It is no longer speculation, but a well known fact that music lessons improve other scholastic scores because only daily practice improves any new skill. It doesn’t matter if that skill is playing rock and roll, or practicing math. Do it every day, and you WILL improve. Learning music helps inculcate that great life lesson. Learning to fix and personalize your own guitar makes that lesson deeply engrained yet FUN!

NO, as-is, this is NOT a great guitar, but it is plenty good enough for beginners to learn with. With a few tweaks here and there, these can be made to play as easily as pro-guitars so they don't hurt young fingers. And if you consider all the other factors in a child's development, these may be a better choice than funding an expensive guitar.

Over the decades, I've repaired, adjusted and modified hundreds of student guitars and taught hundreds more how to do their own guitar work. That is one advantage electric guitars like these have over other instruments. You would not want a kid to mess around with a grand piano or a fine violin or classical guitar.

Further, the young student can express his individuality, learn to be self reliant, and learn the great lessons of relentless steady effort. Some may think sports provide some of those life lessons too, but with guitar, you don't risk critical injury or regular public humiliation. What could be better for your kids?

These and the Squire brand guitars are a great positive “gateway” instrument that brings life-long appreciation for music and craftsmanship. They can be a springboard toward learning electronics, circuit design and even some computing basics.

If you are clever and know an experienced guitarist / teacher, you or your kids can learn about economics, how businesses make compromises at different price points, and what is REALLY valuable in instruments. You might just learn what is valuable in life too.

THAT is why I love cheap guitars like these, and this particular model is one of the best for all those noble goals.
Summary: Great VALUE for decent quality, plus many other benefits to these cheap guitars!

This product does power the microphone but it does not do what it also needs to do, which is amplify the signal so it is useful for connection to a computer. However, the recordings have little static and the switch that changes the type of microphone to alternate between microphone capsules for directional and non-directional recording does seem to work as promised. This device produces a recording volume level that is FAR LESS than the built in microphone on a PC or from a regular plug-in computer microphone costing $5 or less, even when the computer settings for recording volume are set to a maximum. You would have to be recording a VERY high volume sound source for this microphone to be truly suitable, and any normal level sound is recorded at a very low level even with the recoding level on the computer turned to a maximum. Recording volume levels using this device are almost identical to the recording volume of a Shure SM57 quality microphone that is USB powered but not amplified, which is to say totally inadequate and probably indicative of using common existing types microphone capsules in the Blue Microphone that are designed to other types of electronics, without adding the pre-amp needed for them to produce enough recording volume for use with a computer.
Measurements of recording volume of this microphone using the highly respected recording program Audacity indicate that the recording level of normal speech close to the microphone using this device would need to have output power amplified about 50 times (resulting in sound amplitude amplified roughly 7 times - these two values are precisely related by mathematics that I have not done but can roughly estimate from graphical results obtained using Audacity) in order to equal the recording volume of a built-in computer microphone or cheap $5 plug-in computer microphone. As a result of the very low recording volume using this device, even at maximum recording volume, this microphone is therefore almost useless for recording anything at normal volume on a computer without quite large post-recoding amplification using a program such as Audacity. Recording quality will thereby suffer due to the large post-recording amplification that is required. The need for post-recoding amplification of something the volume of normal speech is considerably greater for the non-directional microphone capsule (15 db up very close for normal speech ) than for the cardiod capsule (6db up very close for normal speech), with both capsules requiring about 20 db amplification at about 10 ft recording distance. These values are quite a lot since 10 db means 10-fold too little power and 3 fold too little amplitude, and 20 db means 100-fold too little power and 10-fold too little amplitude.
Devices made to use standard recording microphones have built in amplification as well as power and have no problem with low recording volume, so it is clear the Blue microphone simply lacks proper matching of output power levels to a computer due to lack of an internal pre-amp. Similarly, devices such as the $90 Behringer MIC800 Microphone Modeling Preamp provide both power and amplification and allow the Shure SM57 to record very nicely when hooked up to a computer, although sadly the Behringer does not allow USB connection and therefore will not allow both speakers or headsets) and external microphone to be hooked up simultaneously to my "modern" single 3.5mm jack computer that uses the single jack for both speakers and external microphones, and the Behringer also cannot use the USB connection of the Blue microphone. So far, I have found no good microphone that attaches to USB port or way to adapt a good microphone to a USB port. Therefore, things like overdubbing a sound track using Audacity are difficult or impossible using my current computer that needs a competent USB microphone when external wired speakers or headphones are simultaneously connected with a microphone..
Summary: Maximum Recording Volume Much Too Low

Well FDUCE just blew up the market with a clear sounding, well built, affordable XLR/USB mic. This thing is sturdy! The default USB output is pretty hot (which I like) compared to the XLR output, but sonically they both sound clear, present, and well, great. Also bonus, but I use an old Windows 7 computer, and the USB portion had no problem recognizing the mic. The MV7 is only compatible with Win 10. The only USB/XLR mic that competes in this price range is the Miktek Mio which is small condenser style and can be frequently found for $80 and under. But I’ve had several Mio’s and they all emit a small high pitched hum in USB mode. The FDUCE emits no hums or whines and is super quiet both in USB and XLR mode. If you’re looking for the MV7 style and don’t need bells and whistles software, this is your mic.

Let me preface this by saying that I have been playing for nearly fifty years, and always do my own guitar set-up and maintenance (which is necessary even on high-dollar guitars). This guitar is solidly made, and is certainly playable. It lacks any kind of cosmetic amenities, is made of mostly colored mystery plywood with painted stripes where the bindings would be on more typical guitars. It looks cheap but then again - it is cheap! Plywood does make it more sturdy, but it does have somewhat of a negative effect on the tone. If you want a guitar that will hang together while your kid is learning, this is it. If your child shows any interest at all, it would be wise to upgrade to a better guitar after a few months to a year. Many reviewers say the guitar does not stay in tune. Welcome to the world of nylon strings! I have to re-tune my $1000.00 classical every time I play it also. No guitar will stay in perfect tune indefinitely. Watch the pros at a concert - they will either re-tune their guitar after a few songs or pass it to an off-stage tech who will hand them another perfectly tuned guitar. Nylon strings stretch and are affected by temperature, humidity, etc. They will get better in time, but then when you change the strings it all starts over again. This is true of ALL guitars, no matter the cost or the type of strings it has. Part of learning to play the guitar MUST include learning to tune it!!! There, I'm off my soap box now...

All in all, for what it is, it is a sturdy, no-frills, beginners guitar that simply does what it is supposed to do and does it well.

Text: Just what I wanted and expected

I bought this cartridge to replace my previous daily driver, a Goldring 1042. Now, even though the 1042 retails for over three times as much as the VM95ML, the AT easily outperforms the Goldring.

To test the cartridge I put it through a number of objective and subjective tests. I tested the frequency response curve of the cartridge using a CBS STR100 test LP frequency sweep track. Result: response is very close to flat out 20khz, with very little unnatural peaking or early high frequency roll-off. This is with a 100pf/47k load at the phono preamp (a Graham Slee Reflex M) and another 100pf or so in tonearm cabling. Translation: this is a very neutral cartridge going by my measurements, not something to be used to compensate for "bright" or "dark" or "warm" sounding downstream components.

I also tested stereo separation and tracking ability using the Ortofon Test LP. Result: I was able to achieve 27dB of separation which is better than factory spec, and the only tracking test it could not pass was the 100um band. Note that very few cartridges will be able to track that 100um band - it will send most carts flying to the deadwax.

For my subjective testing, I grabbed all my difficult to track records with narrow inner grooves and hot cuts out of my 1300+ LP collection. Result: there was nothing the cartridge couldn't track extremely well, even records where the more expensive 1042 faltered at the inner grooves. I listen to a wide variety of music and my daily drive cartridge needs to perform well on everything, which the VM95ML does.

Note: I have seen a lot of people ask whether they should buy the VM95ML or the VM540ML for their turntable. The answer: it depends on your tonearm mass. The 540ML is ideally matched to a lighter tonearm, e.g. 10g or less in effective mass including the headshell. The VM95ML is ideally matched to medium-mass or medium-heavy tonearms ranging from around 15-20g in effective mass. If you have a tonearm that is say, 12g effective mass you are on the borderline and will have to make a judgement call. Once you set up your cartridge, I always recommend measuring the actual tonearm resonance using a test record rather than using a calculator, especially where Japanese style compliance numbers are given, as they are useless for such calculators and cannot be accurately converted in all cases.

[[VIDEOID:e49e6a25474a231669218759e404049a]] My use is less conventional than most: I'm using it to store/transport 3 C+ Stands. How well does it work for that? pretty nicely.

C stands are used in Film & video, they're heavy clunky suckers which are unfortunately the bread and butter of a lot of video work. I'm not a Grip/Gaffer, so i only have a few to haul and wanted a neat case to do so as well as for storage. That very question popped up on the G&E group and that got me to dig into find something. And here's my thoughts on this finding:

-Price point is great
-Material feels sufficiently thick
-Inner rubberized coating is great, feels like it can take a beating
-Sticking looks pretty nice
-Strapping doesn't go all the way around but weight test feels good.
-I made a few modifications....

Modifications:
C stands with turtle bases and extension arms/heads/knuckles/etc... are not a neat package, there's stuff sticking out all over. I opted for the double compartment bag because i wanted some separation, and planned on having to slice some of the inner separator out to make room for the bases. Slicing with a sharp knife and scissors was easy, and the material doesn't feel prone to ripping. With a large hole cut near the bottom for the turtle bases, and a smaller hole near the top for the bits and pieces to float around works rather nicely.

I also folding up some cardboard and foam to make a bottom brace, which ensures all the poles are confined to that area which i then put a thick bit of foam behind. I did this to keep things neat, as well as protect against all that weight when this bag is stood up on end.

Lastly, i tied some paracord between the two zippers, so they open together.

In it i'm storing a standard matthews stand, and two larger heavier impact brand stands. You might even be able to fit 4 regular stands in it, but the weight might become impractical. You could also store extra/other types of stands in there, regular light stands you could fit at least 4 of some of the 10' ones.

All in all i'm plenty happy with how it turned out. I makes for neat storage and an easy package to haul into the car for a gig.

UPDATE:
I reduced it to the two larger stands, it's a much more reasonable weight to manage

Text: The main reason I selected this stand was that it is very portable.  It stows nicely in the outer pouch of a violin case.  It fits the viola equally well.

Just got this unit itn. It sounds great, and as I play mostly classical, and light jazz funk works on theremin with recorded accompaniment, it seems to do the job nicely.

I like the way each channel has it's own effects volume, so the whole board is not limited to one level. My theremin needs jast a tad more reverb than the accompaniment, so that's huge. The red LED effects display is easy for me to read, and the selector knob is also easy to work. Just twist to select, and push to engage the selected effect.

The cables are long enough to work with on a porch sized stage, and all appear to be heavy duty. You should not have any problems with these even under heavy use. The mic connectors on the mic cable are metal. That's a big plus in my book.

I like the hidden mic stand holes in the speakers. No extra gear to attach there. Just slip the speakers right on to the stand, focus to the room, and you're on to the next setup steps. Pretty easy.

I like the metal grille over the cones.

For a large living room, or a small venue like intimate coffee shops, and restaurants, where talking levels in the venue are not too bad, it should do well. Pubs, and bars, well that might be a different story, but then they usually have their own house system. Should do well outside on a porch if you're not competing with too much other noise.

Set up went fairly easily. I had no problems figuring out what went where.

I wish there were a few more ports, but you can get round that easily by packing along a mini mixer, and running it's audio to the cd/aux inpurts, and there you go. :) However, for my solo gigs, this has everything I need.

I love the zippered bag in the unit for stowing all the associated cables. Even enough spare room for the mp3 player. :)

I do wish it had it's own legs, but then you can always use a handy projector table, or cart.

Would be even better if the lid were removable to make it look less bulky on stage, but once you've got your volumes set, you can just close the lid, and away you go. :)

I think if I do gigs where the room is much larger than 30 feet, or so, I'll likely have to upgrade to a 300 watt system, or more.

Most of my gigs don't require that amount of power just yet.

I still need a subwoofer for louder audiences though.

I do wish the unit had ports for monitors, and subs, but then we'd be looking at twice the cost. Might be possible to run the lines to a sub, and then on to the speakers if one can find a sub that sends the highs and mids on to the mains.

All in all, it's not a bad little portable sound system for small venues. I think it'll work even better than my Ion sound system which was only a third the power of this 150 watt system. so, I'll use the Ion for home / studio rehearsals. :)

Text:
This is a fantastic value for a tube amp. I've had this amp for a little less than a year now as of 12/18.

It has some pretty awesome features.

Let's start with how it looks. The highly polished chrome, and see through design is a bit of a wow factor, and gets noticed, though it may not be to everyone's liking, still I think it speaks well of the amp, and has the appearance of a much more expensive amp. It still has a bit of an old school vibe to it though, and not just flash or heavy metal. This head is heavy, all in all I believe it weighs in about 35-40lbs.

The INFINIUM tube life multiplier, which allows your tubes to last much longer, Bugera says 10x longer, but I don't know if it's true or not....time will tell.

This technology also allows you to use mismatched tubes,no more biasing needed!!!!!...no more buying matched pairs of EL34s, which is what it came stock with, but you can use any EL34s you have. But WAIT! ....you can use one EL434 and one 6L6..or one 6L6 and one 5881 at the same time!!!!!! Or two 6L6's etc... any combination of the three different types, so you have lots of choices, and no worrying if only one tube goes out. I believe this is also true of the 4 preamp 12AX7 tubes, A, B C, it doesn't matter, but I'm not 100% sure about them you'd have to ask Bugera to be sure.

The sound: It really seems pretty versatile, does nice cleans though may not be as chimey like a fender amp, but I'm using it with a Ibanez hollowbody with humbuckers and not a single coil strat at the moment. I'm working on getting my strat back together, I'll update when I do.

The first channel is called clean and has a gain, treble, mid and bass knob. The second channel is called lead and has gain, treble, mid and bass, but also has a volume knob. Also has a reverb, tone cut, and master volume, which allows for a lot of flexibility.

This amp does nice clean to pretty heavy distortion tones. I play more on the clean side, and don't use the amp for high gain tones that much, but I've read some reviews that call it more of a fuzz tone, but IDK for sure.

It has a switch on the back that allows the amp to run in A class or A/B class modes.

Also has stereo speaker jacks with a 4,8 or16 ohm slide switch so you can run just about any speaker configuration with this amp!!!

Includes a emulated DI input, with a 1x12 or 4x12 cabinet emulation for direct recording.

Also has an effects loop

A footswitch jack that works with the included footswitch, which toggles the channels, and reverb.

All in all, I say this is a fantastic bargain for the price, and you should get it before the price goes up by a few hundred. I also think Bugera has been trying much harder to fix issues with reliability, and has taken to heart some of the past issues to make better products overall.
As always mediabridge has always done solid products. Very happy no hum or noise
Summary: As always solid product at a great price

I purchased this "safety riser" directly from the manufacturer's website, because I didn't know whether Amazon was selling it on their website. Anyway, the price was the same. I researched various turntable safety risers including some selling on eBay that were much cheaper than this one. The reason I decided on the Audio-Technica was the quality-looks, the specs and the manufacturers reputation.

I wasn't about to take a chance on a cheaper item with a $1100 turntable and $285 cartridge. The more expensive safety risers looked good, but were well beyond my budget. It took me about 1.5 hours to get this thing to work due to the way my turntable is built, with the arm lift extending way past the base.

On their website Audio- Technica stated that I needed about 14mm to make this work and sure enough, that's about all the room I had to work with !

What I needed to do was to set the right height for the riser so it did not interfere with the normal functioning of the turntable and also set the right angle on the trigger of the safety-riser so that when the tone arm hit it, it would lift the tone arm off the record.

The only way to do this was by trial and error. I set the safety-riser's height(after it is triggered) to the same exact height of the tone-arm lift on the turntable when it's in the 'UP' position. I then turned the safety-lifter slightly until the trigger was activated when the tone-arm and cartridge reached about the middle of the trailer on the record(he smooth side with no grooves) about half way between the last groove and the record label. ** The tone arm has to be free wheeling for a while to have enough force to activate the trigger. Otherwise, if you set the tone-arm to lift when it reaches the last groove of the record, the trigger won't activate and the tone arm will just skip in place over and over again, without ever being lifted.

The stickers to stick the safety riser to the TT were a joke. I went through the whole set of 4 while performing my adjustments. Instead, I used some double sided masking tape and cut to size. This worked much better than the stickers.

The AT safety riser is very quiet and classy. Due to the hydraulics, there is no jerky motion like with other safety-risers. The tone arm lifts slowly and accurately, but at the same time very quickly ? It matches perfectly with my black turntable with polished steel buttons and switches. It blends in so well, that it looks like if it's part of the turntable itself !

The riser comes with 2 extra (polished steel) spacers to lift the safety-riser even higher if your turntables needs it, but lucky for me I didn't need to use them. Good thing, because this would have complicated things even further. The AT safety-riser also comes with a 7 language manual and 1 year warranty.

I bought this for use with my Roland TD30-KV drum kit, allowing me to use the 8 semi-separate outputs to send off to the PA system. Actually, I plug this into a 8-channel isolation transformer (By ART), which then feeds off to the PA System, to eliminate hum/noise, and, to turn the unbalanced outputs into balanced XLR to go to the mixer.

Anyhow, for this purpose, this works perfectly.

I had original thought to put this as a 4-star product...but found a fix that helped to to shine enough to get to a 5-star (I'll detail that at the end). But first the good stuff...

I'm not a huge fan of extreme and heavy distortions as a whole (I have my exceptions of course). For me, the ideal guitar sound lies closer to the Arena Rock styles (Survivor, Styx, etc.). Thus, I really wanted a pedal that would pull those sounds off with both punch and tonal clarity. I chose this one because I heard that it does precisely that...and with simplicity to boot.

I run this pedal after my OD and before my Delay and it fits perfectly in the front of my Mustang IV (1.10) or Stageworks PMA-9. I play on an Oscar Schmidt OE20G. And it sounds beautiful.

THE BUILD
This is a very small pedal but quite sturdy. Completely metal casing and surprisingly heavy. The knobs are plastic, but feel quite durable and are smooth, but snug to the turn. The switches are definitely tight, too. It also has a light to let you know when it's on. Because of the size, this does not feature battery power...you'll need a DC9V (a "One Spot" daisy chain what I currently use since I don't use too many pedals).

TRUE BYPASS
It really does feature real "true bypass". Whenever I switch this off, my original signal is not impeded, manipulated, or distorted (heh) in anyway.

THE TONE
As mentioned before, what I really love about this distortion is how it can carry a strong distortion, yet keep distinct tones and notes (not just rumbles and grumbles). Some may not like it because it's not a heavy distortion...but it fits my sound. It features a gain knob, level (aka volume), and tone knobs which allow for surprising versatility. I've pulled off some strong power distortions (a la "Survivor") and even some very creamy lead guitar sounds when coupled with my delay pedal. It also features a 3-way toggle switch to help augment the tones a little more...though in most cases, I admittedly don't hear the difference between the 3 (but then again, I don't often max the gain on this unit, so maybe that's why).

THE 4-STAR/5-STAR DILEMMA
So, the original reason I was about to give this 4-stars was because, though it had an amazing sound...it also had a fairly audible hiss when I stopped playing if I had set the gain past 12 o'clock. However, when I realized there was a built in amp noise gate (not one of the digital pedal effects), it really cut it down and had it playing the way it was meant to play...which is why I brought it back to 5. In a live setting, the hiss isn't so bad (unless you mic up) and is easily lost amongst the rest of the band, but it certainly was annoying when practicing on my own. It is important to note though, that this hiss only happened when run into the FX Loop. When running it into the front of the amp (my preference for a distortion), no problem whatsoever.
Summary: From Creamy Ambient Leads to Driving Rock With a Hint of Class.

Text:
I've been playing guitar for about 40 years and wanted to see if I liked playing the mandolin. Years ago a friend had a similar itch, bought a really nice Gibson, played it once and it now sits in his closet. That was an expensive itch. I figured I'd try something budget-friendly and upgrade if I liked playing mandolin. I bought the Rogue in black.

My Rogue arrived yesterday. First pleasant surprise was how well it was packed. Large shipping box opened up to butcher block paper wrapped around a smaller box. Opened the smaller box to find a "blanket" of puffy plastic wrapped around the mando and secured by rubber band. Opened that and the mando was encased in thin, clear plastic. The installed strings were covered by a piece of brown paper taped over them for protection. The pick guard has a sticky cover over it to prevent scratching (you remove it). The mandolin was in perfect shape, no shipping damage.

The finish is gorgeous. There are two spots near the F holes with very minor marks which I think will buff and wax out. Nothing near the issues I have seen on several $400 guitars I have bought. This is going to polish up nicely. The Rogue label on the headstock is beautiful. I did a lot of research and lubricated the tuners and the nut before tightening the strings. The tuners are better/more accurate than on my $300 Martin ukulele, and it came up to tune nicely. The binding is well-done, the frets look good. In fact, the whole mandolin looks really good.

I let it sit overnight. Today it's still pretty much in tune, strings need to settle (this is true with any stringed instrument I've ever owned). Intonation is a hair off - I didn't notice it by ear, but I used my electronic tuner to see that it is a shade sharp at the twelfth fret. With a floating bridge it's an easy adjustment that every mandolin requires. Height at the nut and bridge are a tad high, but even the one-page setup guide that comes with it advises you to lower the bridge and then raise it until you find the "right" height. I'm going to adjust the nut myself.

The bridge sits nicely on the soundboard, though I'm going to fit mine so it is perfect. The fretboard looks a bit dry, so I'll treat it with some fret lube. If I played it as-is I'm sure I'd be happy (thrilled) with the purchase, considering the price. I'll post again after I complete a thorough setup. I have a feeling, based on what I've seen so far, that I'll consider this the best bargain instrument I have ever bought. I haven't tested it yet, but my initial playing indicates that the frets are fine (this is the one area I would not want to try to correct). Everything else is adjustable if you know what you're doing.

Every other experienced buyer review said to replace the strings, so even though these don't sound as bad as I expected I am going to remove them all, clean and wax the mandolin, make the desired adjustments, put on D'Addario strings (purchased from Musicians Friend) and see how she sounds. As I said, I will make a follow-up post, but I think it will be positive.

One word about Musicians Friend. *After* I made the purchase I found another Internet provider with the same mandolin on special with books and gig bag included. I called Musicians Friend, they found the website and matched the deal. Incredibly friendly easy-going customer service. For an under-$50 mandolin. They own me from now on. : )

In summary, I am amazed at the quality for the price. Stunned. I can't wait for my visiting relatives to leave so I can spend some quality time with my new Rogue mandolin!
*** And, a couple of days later... I have lowered the action even a little more, the frets are still fine, no buzzing. I putzed around playing a few chords after work tonight, the volume projection is outstanding, and I like the tone. It's woody, not thin. I still can't get over the value of this mandolin. Buy it now!

Text:
Here in the early golden age of on-line shopping, musicians have it made. Especially if you're in a smaller town, you used to go to your local music store, and whatever they had, THOSE were your options. Now, on Amazon alone, you type in "10 foot guitar cable" and you immediately have access to dozens and dozens of brands and styles, ranging from $7 to $20, almost all with 4 and 5 star reviews. It's insane. [we won't talk about Mogami!]

Which is why I have to give only 3 stars for this cable. Not because of its quality, but because it is listing for over $31. Let's let d'Adderio tell you about the technology they use in this cable: "...cables feature a coaxial oxygen-free copper conductor with two layers of impenetrable noise-rejecting shielding formulated for low capacitance. The lower cable capacitance allows your instrument’s brilliance, presence and character...." you get the idea. Cable transmits sound from your instrument to an amp or p.a., and this is a fancy way of saying that this cable also does that.

Make no mistake: in my first couple of weeks of using this cable, I've been impressed by the suppleness of the nylon wrap, it hasn't gotten tangled... and I really like the permanent little cable tie loop. As most musicians know, the only way to really judge a cable's quality is over extended use, because they ALL work.... until they don't.

As a reviewer of free products, it's easy to forget to pay attention to the price. If this item was priced similarly to the majority of the other cables for sale at Amazon, my rating would go up. 4 stars for $18-$22 (like Pig Hog, Rig Ninja), 5 stars for anything under that.
Summary: Overpriced but well-made cable with built-in cable-tie

A friend of mine raved about one of these, so I had to try it out. I was concerned that it was a midi instrument so the Tonal range would be limited. I do have to say that it was a great deal of fun to play with it. I think the strum bar is a terrific idea. The melody option is great for keyboard players as it comes within included template that lays over the buttons. It will be immediately recognizable to a keyboard player.
I could see plugging this into a synthesizer or a mixing board to create all kinds of interesting background sounds, especially with techno music or anything with the ethereal sounds. But as a primary instrument, I found the midi voices fairly limited. If you remember the video games back in the 70s and 80s, then you will recognize a midi sound. A lot of improvement has been made for midi to the point that some devices can nearly emulate the real thing. But on the Qchord, No matter what I did, I could not get away from that video game type of tone. I tried all of the “voices“ for guitars and they just really didn’t sound like any kind of guitar I’ve ever heard. Keyboard instruments were better, especially the organ options, but in no way did it sound like a “ Grand piano.” The best sounding voices to me were the horn instruments and the various “effects” sounds.
If you’ve had any kind of musical training, especially keyboard, you will figure this out in about an hour. But I would say even a beginner could make a lot of fun sounds and even create some music with the various accompaniment options in a very short amount of time.
But I just couldn’t see myself using this as The primary instrument for Playing the type of music I like. Ithink that’s what it boils down to. I sent it back because I just couldn’t see it helping me out with Rock, blues or metal. If you watch the YouTube videos, that will give you a really good idea of the type of music that this device works well with.

By the way, I bought mine in March 2021 and it did NOT come with an AC adapter. It did come with 8 C batteries. I tested a couple of them before I sent it back and even after about four hours of messing with it, The battery voltage was nearly as good as a brand new battery.

In summary, I wish my friend would’ve pointed me to YouTube to search for “Suzuki Q chord.” That is my advice because you will get a good idea of what the instrument sounds like and how it can be used with the right kind of music. If Suzuki could add sampled voices, like you find in Apples “garage band“ app, then I think you would really have something That would appeal to a broader base of musicians. If I selected “distorted guitar” and it sounded like one, I would’ve definitely kept it.
I’ll finish up by saying that it’s a well-designed and well thought out instrument; there is even a video of David Bowie using the Q chord, which is pretty high praise. There are other use cases such as people with special needs or disabilities will find this a godsend compared to a typical instrument. Go listen to it on YouTube and decide for yourself if you could use it as a primary instrument or something for accompaniment.
Summary: Better as an accompaniment tool Rather than a primary instrument; at least for me.

For me, the best mat material is cork all the way around, but they're just too dang thick for that table. Every mat has this problem on this particular table, not to mention newer records as well, so it's really more an issue of outdated build standards. The MD-2 Mega Distortion was not released by BOSS until September 2001. By that time, the grunge, detuned, and seven-string culture BOSS was trying to cater to was already starting to die out, and experienced players had well-set impression of what a BOSS distortion sounded like - largely from the venerable, yet flawed DS-1 Distortion.

But a funny thing happened when I plugged in the MD-2 Mega Distortion: it actually kinda rocks! While the tone of this pedal probably isn't a complete reinvention of the DS-1, the "bottom" control gives it considerably more bass. In fact, this might be the only BOSS distortion pedal that gives you the low end control of a MT-2 Metal Zone without getting stuck into the niche tone of a "metal" pedal. While pedals like the MI Audio Crunch Box, Marshall Guv'nor, and others are referred to as "Marshall-in-a-box" pedals, the MD-2 actually does a brilliant job on smaller combo amps of simulating the "whomp" of a large cabinet pushing air with bass notes.

Also, there's a very cool interplay going on between the "Distortion" knob and the "Gain Boost" knob. Turning up only the Gain Boost actually creates a more vintage/overdriven sound. It's punchy, but not super saturated. The Distortion knob seems to dial in the more saturated heavy gain settings targeting nu metal and other modern players. But neither of those options sound "metal" - this is a rock pedal through and through.

It may look like a DS-1, but the MD-2 really is its own beast, and I like it. Some people may prefer the more fashionable ST-2 Power Stack, but I think the MD-2 is underappreciated, especially for bedroom/casual players who want some thickness to their tone.
Summary: An underappreciated modern upgrade to the DS-1

[[VIDEOID:885c6b38945b8541712576b0826b5b63]] These reeds don't work properly due to many flaws in design and craftsmanship.

The tips of these reeds were almost all torn and clamped (blunt cutter). The measurements were generally off. The vamp had jagged edges and was not smooth (as it should be). The slope of the vamp was uneven with pits and tears.

The underside of the reed was pitted and had cross-cut damage. It would not lie flat against the mouthpiece.

These reeds were packaged with a silica desiccant pack. I suspect the reason they include desiccants is because the reeds were not properly cured, drained and dried prior to manufacture, and that's likely why these reeds are so damaged... Wet reeds do not lend themselves well to cutting and shaping.

I've recorded a playing test (to be added), playing all 10 of these in comparison to one of my 6 month old Vandoren reeds. All of the Cecilio reeds were terrible. A few wouldn't play outright, with some I had to contort my ambouchure... Eventually, I was able to get them all to make noise, but not much better. I've been playing professionally most of my adult life. Teaching for 20 years as well. These reeds make playing clarinet well impossible.
--
All reeds are made of cane, known as Arundo Donax. It's not wood or bamboo... It grows around river banks and lakes and it absorbs the water for growth and nutrients. If not properly collected and dried, whatever was in the water may still be in the final product. Properly sourced cane is extremely important.

Nice Interface!

I had previously given this product fewer stars due to some driver interactions with webex software on windows that caused audio glitching.

I'm happy to report that Working with Motu's US based support was a great experience, within a week they were able to replicate the issue and about a day after that they had a beta driver that resolved the issue for me on my system.

With that out of the way, I see no reason this wouldn't be a 5 star product at it's price point.

Here are some Good points about the M4:
* Assembled in USA
* USA based support team that works for Motu (not outsourced) is great.
* Construction quality is great.
* Screen is great
* Knobs are great
* Connectors are great
* Powerswitch is great

If you do any kind of recording, the VERY granular meters on the screen in the front are SUPER important - recording a microphone or instrument too loud will distort the audio - this is true of all interfaces at all price points! - having visual feedback right on the device is EXTREMELY helpful and puts this in a different class from ALL the other interfaces in it's price range.

Sound Quality:

The M4 sounds 'fine' to me - I don't have 'golden ears' and after switching back and forth between this and a focusrite scarlet 4i4, nothing immediately jumps out as drastically different.

Also, I don't do recording, so I have no comments on the mic preamps.

Overall the Motu M4 is a great product - but it's in a weird spot. Knowing what I know now, I think the M2 model (the one with 2 inputs and 2 outputs) is an easy recommendation. The M2 is easily "best in class" on all counts I can think of. The M2 is a MUCH better choice than any of the 2 input 2 output competition I've looked at. Quite frankly the M2 is a steal.

The M4 adds two more inputs and outputs and this is where the M4 starts to fall down vs the competition. Adding those extra inputs and outputs adds the need for a driver that supports more than just basic routing. It adds the need for the driver to be able to control the gain of the different inputs and route audio (so you can hear inputs 3/4 on monitors connected to 1/2, etc) Right now the M4's competition is better at this, but I think it's something Motu can catch up to with software over time (this was written 11/2019)

So the bottom line is, if you need an audio device with just 2 inputs and outputs get the M2, it's HANDS DOWN the best in that class and offers more than ANY of the competition - honestly they will probably sell TONS of the M2's and It wouldn't surprise me if they run out of stock, it's that much of a value leader.

The M4 has that same potential - the hardware is great, I hope we'll see driver updates that bring it feature parity with other 4 input/output devices.

I bought a Cordoba C5CE years ago, loved it. Sadly, I sold it for some reason.

So after looking, i found this popular Yamaha. I've always respected Yamaha musical instruments...I grew up playing the PSR 280 keyboard and it's lasted for 20 years.

I wanted something great but I didn't wanna spend a lot of money. This seemed to fit the bill.

So i got it in the mail, and yes, the hype is real. The thing is built cleanly and with precision for this price point. I consider $140 to be ridiculously cheap when I'm buying any instrument other than a Eukelele. So, for this much money, I'd normally expect complete garbage. But what we have hear, I think, is an example of excellent consolidation and streamlining. This guitar has no features meaning: no special top of the line woods, no electronics, no fancy graphics or inlays etc. They put all effort in making a rock solid, decent sounding instrument.

Now, compared to my old Cordoba, it does not have that "wow" factor in terms of tone. But it does have the "goodness this thing is well balance and very playing" factor, couple with the "I only spend $140, this is insane" factor.

So, if you are needing a nylon string to keep around for various projects, gigs, and occasional professional needs, and you are on a budget, get this.

Like wise, if you are wanting something that just grab and play for fun at the office or in the living room, get this.

I'm a professional player, so let me tell you knew guys: a nylon string is a fantastic instrument for a beginner to get started on because it's easy to play, like an electric, and the neck is fat, so it'll help you learn to splay your fingers properly.

Likewise, for a pro or seasoned musician, this guitar is perfect to keep around because it's light weight, easy to play, satisfying to noodle around on, and just feels and sounds great.

As a keys player, i don't play steal string as much as I could, so my fingers aren't always 100% callused up. So this nylon is great to noodle around on, write with, keep handy. But, I also know it usable for recording purposes and live playing purposes when the needs arise for such an instrument.

This is a great pad for $15. Compare to StewMac's guitar workpad at $47 to 57!! Or Fender's at $56. This is a better mat than either of those, although those both have a plastic neck cradle. You will want to make or purchase a neck support to properly work on your guitars with this mat. You want the headstock elevated, especially if it is a headstock that angles back (like a les paul, etc.) so you don't crack the headstock or neck.

This is thick enough and durable enough that unless you are really careless, it should last a long time. Like any rubber mat - don't solder over it, or you'll get metal splatters and flux splatters that will then scratch your guitars if you don't remove them (which is hard).

Has been safe on all my guitar finishes, and I have a lot of different guitars...(about 30). I've had one for about a year.

Those saying it's too thin, too cheap, not good quality...are just wrong. This is the best mat I've found, and I've tried a bunch of them. And it's cheap. If it's too thin...buy two, they are inexpensive. But it's really not too thin. It's fine.

The length is also fine if you are using a neck support, as you should be. In fact, it is longer than the Stewmac and Fender mats.

There's really nothing to dislike about this mat, except it currently can't ship into California, which might be because they can't demonstrate their supply chain does not use slave labor...not sure. Must be some regulatory issue...

It's more than a stretch to call this a "heavy duty" xlr cable like they do in the title description (truth in advertising has never been Amazon's strong point) but for the price I obviously wasn't expecting a Road Hog equivalent. The cable is not overly flimsy and overall it's pretty much what you get from many other bargain cables. Grabbed this to have in the bag as back-up just in case I need to make a long-ish run and don't have anything else available. Not something I usually need to do but as any sound person can tell you unanticipated situations somehow always seem to pop up... and there is no such thing as it happening at a convenient time.

It isn't really worth it to me right now to me drop big money on an expensive 50' cable; especially since there's a good chance it will rarely, if ever, see much action. So from that standpoint this is bargain. If it fails after a gig or two then not so much. But only time will tell.

For primary, workhorse xlr cables I don't really like to use anything that isn't a proven name; Rapco, Live Wire and Hosa I've had good experiences with. But you get what you can afford and I've lived (and occasionally died) with many a cheap cable in my time. If/when they fail I don't act like I'm surprised. When they work no one but you knows the difference!

I like that the ends are serviceable, though honestly if a connector has issues I'll probably just replace it with a Neutrik end and call it good. I'll have to take their word for it that it is 24ga pure copper.. but yeah, as long as it works correctly it's worth having as a back-up, imo. Beats tying up $45+ on "good" cable that I will rarely, if ever, need. So recommended taking into account all of the above.

Text:
I wanted something to take with me while traveling in my motorhome that I would not worry about and that would allow me to continue to play while on the road. So, when this became available, I ordered it. Here is what I found:

1. This is very compact and fairly light weight. When extended, it is fairly solid and works well with a foldable piano stand. The cover, while light weight, does the job and keeps it clean. The cover should be treated with care so that it will last.

2. The power cord is less than stellar as it is about 3 feet in length. The charger is not impressive either, but they do work. The fact that this unit takes a standard C connector makes it easy to get a longer cord and a better charger. Maybe the concept was that since there is a onboard battery, you would only be charging up the battery with the cord so it could be so short.

3. Speaking of battery, that is a very nice option since it allows me to play outside at a campground without worrying about a power cord.

4. Supporting Blue Tooth is nice for headphones. Keeps the campground quiet while allowing you to play outdoors. You can also use speakers if you are playing for the neighbors.

5. No one will ever mistake the sounds from this piano for even a low end Yamaha. The reproduction just is not that good. It is good enough and it works, but it is a sub $300 instrument after all.

6. Speaking of sound, you can choose various voice effects by pressing that button and then using a rotating dial. That works, but it is awkward and takes time to get what you want. It quickly times out so that rotating the button just changes volume level, its default setting. Note that you cannot keep a specific setting when you power off and on the unit. It will revert to its default settings.

7. The manual is ok, but not very clear. For instance, they do not specifically tell you that the only way to get to the various options is to use a two step process. One, press the button for what you want to change and 2, then use the rotating knob to select what you want in the very small view window. Another example is NOTHING is said about there being an onboard battery or that when it is fully charged the light will change from red to green on the back of the unit.

8. The keys are NOT great. They work, but they are not consistent in what they deliver and where they deliver it at. It is close, but still has several misses along the way. The keyboard is responsive in its own way to volume based on impact level with key, but not consistently.

All in all, this is a good piano for someone who does not know if they want to learn piano or not. It is an inexpensive investment that lets kids and adults explore and decide if this is something they want to pursue. It is also good for a inexpensive traveling device that will let you practice and enjoy playing as long as you do not try to hold it to high standards. Think of it as the old piano that was left in the rental unit and all will be good.
Summary: Good for a motorhome or travel trailer

These switches are REALLY flexible (normal 5 way's are NOT). I used this to wire up a guitar where the whole system runs on a single switch, with no other controls. It's a pair of humbuckers, and runs like this:

Position 1: Bridge pickup direct to output jack (super-hot output, great for solo's or otherwise cutting through a mix)
Position 2: Bridge pickup with a 100kohm resistor between hot and ground (like turning the volume and tone knobs from 10 to 8.5 or 9-ish)
Position 3: Bridge + Neck w/ 100kohm resistor same as position 2.
Position 4: Neck pickup with 100kohm resistor same as position 2.
Position 5: off - short's hot to ground, turns it off like turning volume to 0.

That's just what I did for an example. There is really no limit to what you could do one of these, your imagination (and ability to think through a circuit design) is your only real limitation for what you can do. Phase switching, parallel vs serial, etc, all of it can be done with one of these. Standard 5 way's are extremely limiting, and will make your head hurt trying to figure out any cool custom circuits. This thing is a piece of cake (I didn't even use one of the 4 switched poles for my setup).

Text:
These things are tiny, almost invisible, especially in black (what I bought - there is also silver). Used in on bass: a vintage Gibson EB0 - very deep sounding bass - and it was indistinguishable from a 15' cable (we A/B'd it with both speakers and headphones). We were using a TC Electronic BH500 head and BC410 and BC212 cabs, and for headphones, a Behringer P16 system driven by a Behringer X18R with AKG 240S headphones. There was another wireless system in the room, a Line 6 Relay G10 - no interference. The batteries lasted through a three hour rehearsal.

I don't know yet about real world stage range, but in the area of the rehearsal, there was lots of WiFi and cell phone activity.

Additional information: I can no longer completely recommend these systems:

The first one I got (black) works perfectly; the second one (silver) had a touchy power switch on the transmitter - it would drop in and out. xVive will refund, though still not sure about the shipping charge for the unit back to them (that should be free for a defective product in the first day).

The replacement I bought (black) has a charging issue: the red LED blinks simply red (usually means "not charging") after glowing red for only a few minutes. I have no idea if it's really charging or not, but clearly something is wrong.

So, that's 2 out of 3 with a problem. Until their quality control improves, I cannot recommend this unit.

*** another negative: I found that when I used the xVive U2 to plug into the guitar input of my TC G-System, it experience all manner of drop outs. Apparently, if it's near digital effect equipment (and the G-System has a pretty heft extruded aluminum housing!), it interferes with the A/D in the xVive.

*** yet another one: it is possible to overdrive the xVive U2 with a powerful, though passive, signal. I sometimes us an original 1965 Gibson EB0 bass, and if I dime everything on the bass, the unit will "crackle" loudly if I play hard: sounds like digital distortion. With a 24 bit A/D converter, that should not be a problem, and isn't with my Line 6 G10 (or G30 or G50), it appears unique to the xVive.
Summary: Great, well priced wireless guitar and bass system. New Information: not recommended for now.

Text:
My Review for my Whirlwind IMP 2 is a bit different from any other review I have done as you see I purchased this DI, 17 years ago!
Yes, 17 years ago and still working great. I purchased a few DI's along with a bunch of Whirlwind cables and a Whirlwind snake to put my band on the road in my younger day. Most of these Whirlwind products survived 4 years of full time rock band road work in the most demanding environments imaginable.

After those hard touring years the DI then survived everything form full time club house PA ( 6 nights a week) to a Church environment in its later life and all I can say is Whirlwind stuff for me has a 99% still working score after almost 20 years. Thats amazing!

17 years and I only lost one DI (has a slight hum, never tried to fix it) and one cable got squished in the trailer door but still works! I do not think you can kill a Whirlwind!
With that in mind I do highly recommend this DI for solid longevity.

However, when I was a house Sound tech using this DI on a bass guitar... like I had done for years, I had a touring band plug-in a much more expensive brand tube DI and I was amazed at the difference. Was if the bass had an extra octave of low end or as if I had added a few 18" subs! I could not believe what I was hearing as the walls in the club were shaking more than normal with the kind of low end you feel; the Whirlwind did not do that.

I realized then this DI was missing something. Kinda made me sad as I thought about all the years I could have had so much more low end had I only upgraded my DI box as I had a killer PA rig. But keep in mind I am talking a big expensive PA system in a big room, not your normal club rig.

Later in my carrier I also had an artist drop over for a live show and use her much more expensive passive DI (6x the price of this IMP2) that featured Jantzen transformers with her Martin Acoustic guitar. I was blown away with what I experienced as the sound was so lifelike...Overtones to die for as those kinda sounds get lost with the IMP2 ,IMO.

With that in mind I find the Whirlwind to be as solid as a tank however if you are using a high end PA system or critical recording in my opinion you are only as good as your weak link and have better sounding options but at 6x to 20x ( or more) the price!

I am a full time sound tech and an audiophile nut so I hear the differences of upgraded DI boxes , tubes, cables and such but if you play high end Guitars and tone and sound is everything to you don't skip on your DI and cables.

However, with the low price and reliability of this IMP2 makes this the DI to buy when looking at budget DI boxes. if you are on a tight budget and a road dog working rock band living in you van this Whirlwind DI may be the one to buy as it will outlast just about anything you own but keep in mind when you get famous and get that record deal remember to upgrade your DI ( as tone is EVERYTHING IMO) but always keep this Imp2 DI in your gig bag as you will be assured to always have a DI that will work no matter what you do to the thing!

Text:
People love to shell out big bucks on mythical "bumblebee" caps as used in the 50s. Why? therein is the myth. Do desktop of laptop computers use tubes or transistors? Cell phones? No, that is old technology. Imagine if you had tubes in your desk tower, laptop or cell phone to do the same thing transistors do.
If you measured the value of one of those old 50s caps you will find them out of tolerance as they have degraded over 60 years. These orange drops are state of the art and do what a capacitor is supposed to and they will last 100+ years. You will be dead and your guitar will probably be in a trash heap before these caps go bad. Don't fall for the bumblebee nonsense as they have no magical ualities. Tone starts in your fingertips.
Sure, they don't say "Sprague" on them but they are orange drops.
Summary: These caps are the real deal for your guitar.

I have been trying out various gauges of strings for the last year or so, and I decided that 9.5s are my favorite with 9s as a close second. I was reading about different string materials for electric guitars (nickel-plated steel, stainless steel, and pure nickel), so this summer, I decided to try out some string sets with different wound string material. I tried this set of stainless steel strings from around the end of May to the beginning of July 2020. The first thing I noticed was that the strings did feel slightly rougher than normal strings, which I wasn't a fan of. The other main difference I noticed between these and the nickel-plated strings I had been previously using was that these had a considerably more "metallic" tone than the nickel-plated strings. I have an acoustic guitar simulator on my Marshall Code 50 amp, and I think if you wanted to get closer to a steel-string acoustic sound through it, stainless steel strings would be the way to go. I mostly play hard rock songs, and I did not like the "metallic" tone of these strings for that genre. I don't play funk or pop music or listen to it much, but based off what I know of those genres, I think the "metallic" tone of stainless steel strings would fit very well with those genres. Overall, given the type of music I play, I do not think stainless steel strings are worth using, especially since I do not like their rougher feeling for my fretting hand. Depending on the type of music you play, though, you may want these strings for their "metallic" tone, and their tonal qualities may override the rougher feel of the strings for you (or maybe you even like rougher-feeling strings). I definitely think these strings have their place in music, but they are not for me at my current stage in my musical journey.
Summary: These might be good strings depending on the type of music you play
