I attempted to do a quick repair to finish a jam session, but this thing is now rendered a single pedal instead of a double pedal, and I expect the other pedal will be following this one to the grave soon. Do not buy this.

Well, Ill start off with the good:

-Hardware is sturdy feeling, very solid, heavy, so far feels built like a tank.
-Has double chains, decent springs, 4 sided beaters (1 round felt, 1 flat felt, 1 round plastic, 1 flat plastic)
-Nice small toe stop that helps with using slide or heel-toe techniques

Now on to why I could unfortunately give this only 3 stars...

It's really almost a shame to see something so solid and beefy like this so sloppily assembled. I get it, you get what you pay for, but its SO close to being an absolutely insane deal, but considering the assembly flaws, it's back to "what you'd expect for the price."

The box for the product itself was totally crushed. This was not a shipping issue, the outer box was undamaged, but the inner box had holes in it and was smashed pretty badly. As far as I can tell, the only casualty from this damage was the instruction sheet, which was punctured and torn, but I've assembled similar products so I personally didn't need it.

Next, the first thing I noticed upon examining the unit was the angle of the right pedal. The pin that attaches the pedal to the heel portion of the base was machined in at a very visible angle, causing the pedal to be also visibly angled off to the left at the toe. Action seems okay at the moment, but this angle is definitely going to cause some premature wear under repeated use. Next, the chain itself on the right pedal was pulled off to the left because of the previously mentioned angle. The screw that attaches the chain to the cam via a small plate can be loosened to straighten this out, but only partially, since the main cause is the angled pin near the heel. The plate at the end of the chain was also attached at a steep angle, so I had to loosen that to straighten it, which very slightly improved the angle of the chain, but because the hole where the pin that attaches the pedal to the baseplate was simply machined improperly, this cannot fully be fixed.

The next problem... cross threaded set screws. The worst one, by far, was the set screw on the memory lock for the left beater rod. The angle this was screwed in was very steep and very visible. When I unscrewed it, it was covered with metal shavings. It screwed back in okay for now, but I suspect that after repeated use (which likely wont happen, I wont be repositioning the memory locks any time soon) that the threading will simply be stripped out and I will have to drill it out and re-tap it.

This brings me to another problem, which was more of an odd design choice rather than an assembly/manufacturing defect... the set screws themselves. The kit comes with a nice, heavy duty drum key, which is great, but the set screws have this weird flare on them, which is likely a cosmetic choice, but it prevents the drum key from fully seating, and over time these are probably going to get rounded off because of that. The large drum key also is a tight fit when trying to tighten down the beaters to the cam, so I tossed it in my parts bin and i'm using a smaller drum key. Still doesnt fit over the flared set screws properly, but it doesnt rub up against the adjacent set screw on the beater rod attachment point.

Carpet pins. They're too short. If you have berber or other thin, tightly woven carpet, these will probably be okay, but I have somewhat plush carpet, and they don't come out anywhere near long enough to dig into the carpet, and so they very quickly slide around. For me, this is only a problem on the left pedal. I'm using an roland v-drum kit, and the kick trigger has nice big spikes that do the job so the right pedal stays in place. This makes the left pedal totally unusable for me at the moment, within just a few doubles the pedal has slid so far forward I cant properly reach it. Beyond that, the carpet pins themselves (at least on the left side) were cross threaded very badly and it was extremely difficult to get them to turn. I wrapped some rubber around them to prevent damage and used a wrench to get them through, but they're less than 1cm when fully extended. The ray of sunshine in this issue is that the baseplate on these pedals has some predrilled holes that I can use to mount this to a board, but until I can fabricate that or figure out some other solution, I simply cant use the left pedal.

Tension spring adjustment- For my liking, these were a bit loose, but not bad, right out of the box. Unfortunately, I cannot seem to get much of any adjustment range out of these. After backing off the lock, the adjustment knob itself is very difficult to turn. It feels like its probably also cross threaded, but if I strip that out, it will render the pedal pretty much useless, so I'm not messing with it anymore. Both tension spring adjustments feel like this. It's also possible that there is just no more adjustment range on them, either way it's not exactly ideal, but as I said, it came fairly close to being dialed in to my liking right out of the box, I just wish I could get a bit more tension.

On the other hand, this may purely be a QC issue, and if you roll the dice and get one that is properly assembled, it might be awesome, but considering how obviously visible the defect is on this pedal that took me all of 2 full seconds to notice, I wouldn't bet on it personally. I won't bother returning it as Amazon is cracking down on the number of returns, and if my number of returns is limited, I'll wait until it's a bigger purchase, but I also won't be risking any more purchases from Griffin. I'll fabricate a mounting board and use this as an emergency backup pedal until the chain breaks, then I'll scavenge parts from the left pedal and turn it into a single kick, until that breaks, then it's going in the trash. So close, Griffin, if these things were assembled cleanly I'd be singing your praises everywhere, but it was just too sloppily built and kind of a sad waste of heavy duty materials.

Build quality is up to CoolMusic’s usual standard. I’ve tried a few of their pedals now and build quality has never been a concern. The footswitch, as on most / all their pedals has an LED ring around it to indicate if the pedal is on, to flash as the loop cycles, change color depending on if there’s a recording etc.

Another issue I encountered (only once so far) was the DSP getting confused and emitting a loop of feedback continuously until the pedal was power cycled (physically unplugged). Couldn’t recreate the issue but thought it should be mentioned.

So overall it’s a mixed bag.

Text:
These are advertised as "hand made." And they sure are. As in poor quality control, poor consistency, poor construction, poor sound. They have all the benefits of a product made by some teenager in his basement.

Quality control is poor. One of four shredded upon installation before even coming up to tune. And, yes, I followed the "manufacturer's" instructions to the letter (use pliers to make a sharp 90 degree bend, then cut). 25% waste is not acceptable.

The sound is poor. These have a tinny sound inconsistent with quality bass strings. Alas, this is not consistent from string to string, most noticeable on the third string, but also evident on the second. Not the rich tone of a true round wound, nor the thump of a flat. As stated, the consistency is poor. It would almost be better if all four strings had the same tone, because then we could just say they were poorly designed. These are poorly manufactured ("hand made").

The feel is poor. I disagree with those who say these need lubrication to handle slides properly. These feel like mushy round wound strings, although sliding is no problem. Still, it's hard to get the left hand feel necessary for decent playing. Basically, they're cheap round wounds dipped in paint. I haven't played them long enough to see whether the paint stays on or not. Other reviewers suggest it just chips off after a few days.

These strings only have two things going for them. First, they are billed as lasting upwards of double the life of an uncoated string. Maybe so, but given how nasty they feel and sound, that's hardly a benefit. Second, they look great, especially on my black JT Viola bass. Shame we have to listen to them as well. If you want cool looking strings you can hang on the wall, you'll love these. If you want acceptable sounding bass strings, these are not the way to go. So let's just look at them and not play them.
Summary: If you look at it, it's a barn.  If you smell it, it's a stable.

I wanted to find a device that let me record easily when at a gig, or just in my office. I did a LOT of research into devices that were USB only, even other ones that Focusrite sold. The main reason I picked this one was its versatility in being both iPad and USB compatible.

The complaints about the iPad connector cable are valid - it's too stiff and short. I feel like I might accidently break it off if I'm not too careful. Why it uses a proprietary connector on the back of the unit, I'll never know. To combat the included 30-pin cable I bought a [[ASIN:B008M12J9Y $10 3ft 30-pin extension cable]], which seems to do the job nicely. The GarageBand software on the iPad is simple enough to use, and while it can only record one of the 2 input channels at a time, that's fine for what I expected. To record from a live sound-board, I just use the XLR input, set the gain (with the awesome colored halo ring), and save the recording as a mono track.

Being small and solidly built, I've got no problem tossing this in the milk-crate with the rest of my cables and peddles.

In regards to how it records when plugging into a computer via USB (an iMac in this case), it's even better than I expected. The GarageBand software on the Mac does have the ability to record both input channels at the time time. The on-board monitor volume and headphone is fantastic. I thought it only would play back what was being input at that moment, but it does more than that. It's a real monitor (the GarageBand software recognizes it's the monitor output), and when you have a multi-track recording that you're working on, the software allows you to pass back other tracks from the computer while recording a new track.

For example, I recorded a track with just the guitar (track 1), I was using the 1/4" input channel, and laid down that track. Then I created a second guitar track and recorded a second guitar part (headphones plugged into iTrack Solo) and I was able to hear both the current track I was recording, and the first track. Lastly, I plugged in a mic into the first input, and created a 3rd vocal only track. When I was singing, I was able to hear both guitar parts with the headphones still plugged into the iTrack Solo as well as my vocals recording in real-time. I wasn't expecting this level of capability, and was very impressed by the lack of any noticeable latency in both the backing tracks and the vocals I was recording with all 3 going at the same time.

The last thing I want to mention is the XLR pre-amp. Focusrite has been making high-end professional recording equipment for a long time, and the thing they're most well-known for is the mic pre-amp. I have to say, it is spectacular. There is absolutely no noise (no hiss, or clicks) of any kind. The gain staging nobs with the color halos make it so easy to setup, it's almost too easy. The sound it captures is exactly what you expect, and you'll notice right away if you're using a low quality microphone. It definitely stands up to their reputation. Having 48v phantom power to use those top dollar condenser mics is also a really nice thing to have. The demos on their website show how simple it is to use. Once you start playing with it, you'll realize it is a really nice tool for a solo artist, or someone who wants high portability, but great sound quality.
Summary: Portable, durable, and GREAT mic pre-amp

Text:
I've purchased four GLS audio instrument cables. Two were 10' and the other two were 20'.

Pros: Low capacitance means highs are not lost in the cable. EXTREMELY flexible. Shrink wrapped ends. Look great.
Cons: Durability.

Of the four cables I bought, one became noise prone (lots of crackling when moving it) after relatively light use. That was disappointing. Maybe I just got a dud, but it makes me questions the durability of these cables.

That said, I have Mogami cables as well, and I find that these GLS audio cables are extremely close in their clarity and high-frequency retention to those more pricey Mogami cables. The Mogami cables do sound better to my ears, but only slightly (and "better" is subjective). GLS cables are SO MUCH more flexible than other cables because of the tweed jacket, which makes them so much better to play with if you move around a lot on stage. A tangled, twisted cable has got to be one of the most annoying parts about playing guitar.

Overall, if you're a bedroom guitarist, these are truly great cables. If you are a gigging musician who is going to abuse these cables, I would spend the money and buy something else. The tweed jackets on these cables do fray after a while and, after having one of the cables become prone to noise on me, I just wouldn't be able to trust them.

When you read all the raving reviews on these cables, remember that everyone wants to get something high quality for super cheap and people have to rationalize their purchases to feel good about them. All products have strengths and weaknesses. These are great cables, but, you usually get what you pay for. If these were the holy grail of cables you wouldn't be getting them at $1/ft
Summary: GREAT a for bedroom guitarist, but working musicians should spend more for something nicer.

Very impressed. Excellent strings. Now I understand the hype around this product. First of all, the strings are noticeably louder than other strings both playing through an amp or playing unplugged. That alone is worth their price.

I got the "hybrid" set, also called light/heavy. Meaning, the bottom 3 strings are light and the top three are from a heavy set. We guitar players have been experimenting with mixing string gauges from different sets for a long time. But this is way more convenient and cost effective. For those who have not tried hybrid string sets, please do yourself a favor and try it. It is absolutely the best of both worlds because you can have a more balanced string set for both string bending/soloing and chord playing. It is not too soft or too hard, just right in the middle. An even better benefit of this hybrid set is the ability to tune down without losing too much tension - which obviously is a problem with lighter string sets.

Note about hybrid sets: Depending on how your guitar nut is cut, you might have to modify it to receive the thicker bass strings. If the nut is cut for 10s, it will probably work just fine. Just make sure to use a lubricant for the strings to move freely thus reducing tuning issues. If it's cut specifically for for 9s you might really have to file the slots (most guitars are cut for 10s though). Not a difficult job, just need a bit of material removed. You do not want to go deep on the slots, just want to make them a bit wider. Really easy to do, can even use the new strings as "files" (like using a dental floss on the slots, just be gentle using light movements) if you do not have the right tools. But if you are insecure about it, better take the guitar to a luthier because if you remove too much nut material you can ruin your guitar's ability to be set up properly.

I got this unit for two purposes: Beach party, and for a unit to just sit on my desk at work to do music, scan through tracks do basic cue pointing etc.

It's nearly perfect for the money.

I also own the WeGO4, and overall, I find this unit better (and half the price).

What I like about this unit is that the platters feel good, and they feel right. They have the right shape, and work well and easily. The performance 'pads' are buttons not pads, but I actually rather like this for a more rugged setting like the beach where I'm more likely to fat finger things. I like that it has low, mid and hi EQs, which the WeGO4 doesn't. The tempo sliders are a good size, and have an okay feel, not as good as the DDJ1000 or DDJ800, the dead zone around the 0 mark isn't very easy to feel sometimes, and the zone where they slider doesn't produce adjustment is also kind of big relative to the whole slider.

What's not to like? Well - the headphone out is accomplished by splitting the stereo output of the computer; which means you're only getting mono out of the headphone jack, and so the overall signal power of the output is 1/2 which leaves the headphones particularly weak. And for me, the biggest missing is the load control on the unit. Every single other DJ unit has a load control, and I think if I could have put one more thing on the unit; it would be this. The performance pads can be switched to different modes from the laptop itself, which isn't awful; but my second wish would be a mode button for the performance pads. It's also missing any loop controls which is a bit of a bummer, but, it's a basic unit, so how much can I expect?!

This device also works REALLY well with the iPhone DJ app WeDJ (which works on the iPad also). Really really well. The iPad essentially functions as a Midi controller, and the buttons not present on the controller itself are present in the App, and it's very easy to use this way (maybe even better than with Rekordbox).

Did I mention it's very well priced?! if nothing else, this is a great backup controller that you can afford to just throw in a backpack and pull out in an emergency to get you through.

Would I recommend this unit: Absolutely, 100%. Buy it, it's fun!

I play an instrument on my church's Worship Team. Just recently we made the transition from printed song sheets to iPads, which is great. It's easier to swipe across the screen to turn pages than it is to actually turn paper pages, but it would still be nice to be able to go to the next or previous page hands-free. That's where this Starfavor Page Turner Foot Pedal comes in. It allows you to go forward and backward through the songs with a light touch of the illuminated left and right foot pedals. It's a SILENT touch too - no click whatsoever!

Some of the members use smaller Bluetooth pedals, but I prefer the Starfavor model for a number of reasons, not the least of which is that it stays put better than a smaller pedal instead of moving every time a page is turned. The illuminated arrows on the pedal are a great addition also as it makes the pedals easier to find under subdued lighting conditions. There are a number of different modes supported, including emulating the left and right mouse buttons. I'm sure that's useful in some applications, but for me I just need to turn pages.

It's not that the five mode buttons are useless, as different applications might use different modes to achieve the same result. For example, I first tried the pedal at home, just using the Books app to see if it would work. The leftmost mode button worked, but seemed counterintuitive since the left pedal advanced the page, while the right one sent you back one page. So I tried the SECOND mode button, and this one worked perfectly! Using the church's music sheet application, neither the first nor the second mode button worked at all. I was crushed, thinking that I wouldn't be able to use it for its intended purpose! But then I tried the THIRD mode and it worked perfectly!

I'm happy to report also that there was no lag between the pedal press and the page turn action on the screen. Only a very light touch of the foot is needed to trigger the page turn - there's no need to stomp on it, although the unit seems to be built tough, so I doubt that stomping would damage it. The case of the pedal is a strong plastic (ABS or like ABS), with rubber pads on the pedals, and a strong metal base. on the back is a recessed reset button, and on/off toggle switches for power, a "repeat" function (not sure what that is yet - need to look in the manual and experiment a bit), as well as a third switch to turn the lighting on the pedal on and off. Rounding out the rear-panel is a USB-C jack for charging the internal rechargeable battery. Included in the box is a fairly long USB-C to USB-A charging cable to plug into any USB power source, like your cell-phone's charger. A useful instruction booklet is included also.

I installed these pickups on an older Schecter Omen-6. The guitar is a second instrument that was gifted to me and the old pickups were mismatched and weren’t working properly (in fact, I ended up replacing the cable jack, the pots, the 3-way switch, and most of the internal wiring). This was my first time swapping out pickups, so it was a learning experience. Fortunately, despite the lack of clear instructions, I was able to do the swap pretty quickly and with little frustration.

To install the pickups you need to pay attention to the markings on the back of each pickup showing whether it’s for the bridge or the neck (they aren’t supposed to be interchangeable). The wiring for the neck pickup is longer than on the bridge as well. The red and white wires are pre-soldered together so leave them alone other than insulating the bare wire with some electrical tape. The black wires run to ground points on the tone pot(s) and the yellow wires run to the proper positions on the switch. You will probably want to search the web for a wiring diagram that matches your particular guitar. You’ll also need a good soldering iron, wire strippers, and the skill needed to solder the connections. Overall, it took me about 2 hours to install the pickups and all the other parts I was installing.

Now, the real question is how well they perform. Admittedly I am a novice guitar player, but I can compare these to sound on my new Schecter Omen Elite-6 that has no aftermarket parts (except strings). The Wilkinson pickups have comparable volume and using Super Slinky strings it seems to have a warmer tone than the factory pickups on the other guitar that has NYXL strings. Overall, I feel that for the average player, these pickups are an awesome value and worth trying on your guitar.

And round-wounds just didn't have that acoustic sound. There were quite a few choices for fretless strings, but I've always liked D'Addarios on my 6-string guitars. These flat-wounds were a perfect choice. They've got plenty of bottom, but the midrange is more pronounced than other strings. The bass sounds more like a 'real' bass. And the action is now so smooth. I can use a small vibrato when I like--no longer restricted to the wide Jaco-style.

There are all sorts of bassists who look for all different sorts of sounds. But there's something about a fretless that attracts a particular sort of player--the player who wants a bit of that upright bass sound. As soon as I put these on, I felt like I was home.

I have experienced the misfortune of thinking I needed new pickups only to find my innocent-looking cables were simply worn-out from the inside. The problem with cables is that the damage isn't always visible or even audible (your ears get accustomed to the "bad" tone/noise)... and they can be quite pricey to replace.

I found Planet Waves' AMERICAN STAGE CABLE to be a pleasant surprise by offering a higher quality cable at a respectable cost. Planet Waves is owned by D'Addario, a trusted company known for its guitar strings and guitar accessories. The AMERICAN STAGE CABLE represents the company's ongoing desire to serve musicians by providing innovative products that address common problems musicians face with their equipment:

- The Geotip design allows for a universal connection that accommodates the differences in jack design/quality. I immediately noticed this effect when the cable "snapped" into place exactly the same for all four of my guitars. The connection quality varies from guitar to guitar with my other cables.

- The noise reduction was immediately noticeable.

- I am hoping the "permanent bond" soldering process is true to its word as the connection between the wire and connector is generally the unseen culprit of cable problems. I like that Planet Waves is providing a cable that is designed to address this critical issue.

I am extremely satisfied with the quality of the AMERICAN STAGE CABLE and its performance. I am also appreciative that an American-made product of higher quality is so affordable.
Summary: A Fresh Approach to a Critical Element ...

Text:
I'll keep this short, since I'm a pedal fanatic but pretty new to loopers. I reviewed some of the different options, and the three main competitors in this price range are probably the TC Electronics Ditto Looper, the DigiTech JamMan Express XT, and the Boss RC-1 (and they were released in that order). The total loop time for those three is 5, 10, and 12 minutes, respectively. But realistically, it'll be pretty rare that I bother to loop an entire song, so even enough time to cover a cord progression of a few bars is probably sufficient.

The JamMan Express XT and the Boss RC-1 are functionally very similar, but I opted for the JamMan because I was able to find a used deal and save some money. The RC-1 has a visual loop indicator that this one does not have, so it's probably the "best" of the bunch now. But all of these function quite well, especially if you practice by yourself and just want a simple practicing aid.

The DigiTech has button that looks like an MXR, but is actually a soft press (which is becoming more and more prevalent). This is important to point out because one concern I initially had was that a click-press button would be too hard to activate repetitively on the fly. But that's not the case! The controls are quite simple - first press starts record, press again to end the loop. The loop will continue playing in "green" Play mode. You can play along with your guitar, or press the button again to engage "yellow" overdub mode. Double press the button to stop playback. Holding the button down for a few seconds in play mode removes the overdubs. Holding it for a few seconds while playback is stopped clears the loop. That's really about it. There's more challenge in the timing (and learning to play accurately) that there is in that actual operation of the device, which is fairly simple.

This is a basic-yet-simple looper that will suit the needs of most people that just want to experiment, practice, or do some songwriting & sketching. Effects pedals are tons of fun, but this pedal actually has the potential to encourage me to work on both my technical and creative guitar ability, which is long overdue.
Summary: A simple-reliable looper with the potential to redefine how you practice and create

Every set of headphones is different – each has a different personality and of course, a different sound. Perhaps that sounds crazy when speaking about an inanimate device, but as an avid user of a variety of headphones over the years, it’s true. The [[ASIN:B079CBHKZZ Mackie in-Ear Headphones and Monitors, Dual Driver (MP-220)]] is a model that has plenty to offer. The main attraction – the main thing piquing interest personally – was the ‘studio’ abilities of this model. Indeed, these aren’t unlike over-the-ear head models that are used for recording and mixing and such. What was surprising was the sound itself, packed into such a small but efficient model.

As Mackie advertises, the MP-220 checks off the boxes. The “lows” are low, and the mid(s) and high(s) are indeed “precise.” The headphone cable is made out of strong material, with excellent length. esthetically, not only do the headphones look awesome (in addition to the overall build), but the packaging is also an aesthetic triumph. Notably, inside the package, an included hard-shell case proves to be an excellent accessory, including extra buds and an audio adapter used in a number of ‘studio’ devices, including keyboards, mixers, and multitrack recorders. Summarizing, sound, accessories (case, extra buds, and adapter), and aesthetics (build, looks, package) serve as the pros.

The cons are few – mostly nitpicking. The biggest rub personally was ear comfort in extended periods of use. If you are sensitive to something being in your ear, after a while, the case will be no different with the MP-220 because of how it fits in your ear. Also, I found that there’s an adjustment to getting use to the project, particularly if you use on-ear phones more often or even a different set of buds for music listening (I used Powerbeats3 for everyday listening for example). To reiterate, it is nitpicking. All in all, Mackie in-Ear Headphones and Monitors, Dual Driver (MP-220) is an efficient and highly successful product through and through.
Summary: All in all, an efficient, highly successful set of in-ear headphones

Text: I play Bach and fingerstyle blues on a plugged-in Seagull Artist Studio, with a thumb pick, so what works for me may not work for you. But in the interest of being helpful, I'll point out that these are super jangly, buzzy strings. I think the aluminum might not be as stiff as the typical steel strings, because I'm getting a lot more fret buzz and finger noise than usual. The tone here is about as far away from phosphor bronze as you can get. At first I was willing to give them a couple of weeks, but they seemed to get shriller after a few hours' playing, so I had to chuck them, and go back to my (overpriced) Elixir Phosphor Bronze 12-52's. Some players may find them "bright," but I'm hearing way too much metal. On the other hand, they are very easy to bend, and so you can easily get those blues tones that lie somewhere between major and minor. Hey, I'm glad I tried them, but I won't be buying again.

Overall, for the money, this deal cannot be beat. Have been playing a long, long time, and I wish I had a guitar like this when I first started, would have been even more motivated! Anyhow, back to the guitar: The finish on my one (blue transparent burst) was very good overall, save for a 2 inch dark mark on the side of the neck by fret markers. Is not a deal breaker, but does not affect playability. Pickups are decent sounding, knobs turn fairly freely. My major problem is with the string buzz. I expected that it would probably need some sort of remedy to make it sound and play its best, and the nut is the culprit. It is cut too low on mine, particularly on the 6th, 3rd, and 2nd string. Causing tuning issues and lots of fret buzz, esp on the open strings. Ordering a new nut to replace the existing one, and hoping that will remedy problem. Other than that, it plays well, sounds good, and for the price, it is very hard to beat.
Summary: For The Price-Good, But May Need Work

This is a great gig bag for a classical guitar. Honestly, I was not prepared for it to be as good as it was for this price (currently around $32), so I would say this is an excellent value, and an easy 5 stars. Before I jump into the pros and cons, I just want to say none of the cons are big enough issues to knock off even 1/2 star. The pros far outweigh them.

Pros:

1) It’s padded pretty much everywhere, every surface, even the external pockets. The padding feels sufficiently thick to actually protect the guitar from minor bumps and jostles as you carry it to/from lessons or gigs (though for really gigging, you already know you need a hard shell case). For a kid just going to/from weekly lessons, this case would be an excellent choice.

2) I thought the “U shaped design” behind the head was just a gimmick, but it really is more comfortable to carry on your back. That “U shaped design” behind the neck really does keep your head from constantly bumping the case when you walk around in backpack mode.

3) It has 2 external pockets. The big one is the perfect size to comfortably fit music books, even fairly thick ones (see picture). And both sides of the big pocket are padded.

4) The rubber “shock absorber” pads on the bottom are kind of sharp, and made of hard plastic, but it’s nice that there are two of them, and it helps the case balance a bit better when leaned against a wall.

5) It feels very well built, the zippers are sewn in very securely, the case overall feels very strong, and it has an attractive design. I didn't test the waterproofing, but I think it should be fine for a quick run though the rain (say from the parking lot into a building).

Cons:

1) It ships all folded up in a small box. So, once you unfold it, it looks wrinkled (see pictures). I’m dismayed by this, but I understand that this saves cost. Still, even after the guitar is in it, it looks a bit frumpy and crinkled. It’s sad, because the design otherwise looks very nice.

2) The zipper only opens on one half of the case, so you have to slide the guitar in and out. The case doesn’t fold completely open, like a hard shell case. Not a big deal, but worth pointing out.

3) It had a pretty strong “chemical” odor when it arrived. After airing out a while, it’s not so bad, and I’m sure will eventually go away, but take note if you’re sensitive to strong odors.

4) The small pocket on the neck is really small. Too small to even fit a set of spare strings, and I can just barely fit a capo in there with some effort. It’s really only useful for some spare picks or something super small, and even then, the small size makes it difficult to get the picks back out again. Basically, an almost useless small pocket. But the awesome big pocket makes up for it.

Final Rating: 5 stars. For a gig bag in this price range, this is a super value. It’s well padded and pretty functional, and the cons are all super minor, maybe worth subtracting just ½ star overall, if even that. I just wish it looked more like the seller’s picture, and not so frumpy and wrinkled.
Summary: Great gig bag for a classical guitar – but looks a bit more frumpy than advertised

Text: If you live in a dry climate, it is important to provide humidity to the guitar. If you don't, you may experience some buzzing of the strings and bowing or indentation of the wood, which I was experiencing. This humidifier has to be re-watered about once a week, which isn't bad. As other viewers have stated, I also removed the hard ring insert which allows the humidifier to be more flexible so you can insert it. You can't really insert it like it is engineered. It is too hard to remove that way and you risk scratching the sound hole when you insert and remove it. So I just slip it under the strings and it is held it place by the pressure of the strings. It does still scratch the sound hole a little bit. So I'm very careful when inserting and removing it. I have noticed my string buzzing has disappeared. Don't expect major straightening of the wood on a damaged guitar, but it will improve the wood, no doubt. I do recommend it.

I decided to try some flat-wound strings on my Carvin bass, having liked the feel and sound of flatwounds that I have used on my other two, less expensive basses.  The Rotosound 77 Jazz Bass strings have the classic flat-wound feel; however, the bright ping in the sound suggests round-wound strings.  Right from the get-go these strings hold their tuning incredibly well and produce quite a lot of sustain.  It was a little annoyed by the metallic dust that came off the strings when I first took them out of the individual paper sleeves, but this might have been a result of the third-party Amazon retailer having had them in stock for some time.  Once I cleaned them off, though, I'm happy with the feel, sustain, and especially the intonation.  Unfortunately, I really was looking more for the sound of LaBella Deep Talkin' Bass flat-wound strings -- the Rotosounds decidedly are not deep and dark sounding. So, take the product description to heart: these are bright-sounding strings and probably are perfect for the player who wants the round-wound sound with the feel of flats.  Certainly, they seem less compromising than ground or semi-round strings.

I wanted a fully weighted midi controller that was affordable. I just received it and set it up. Will hopefully add more info later.

OVERVIEW
Affordable
88 weighted keys
Has a screen (small)
Putting together was easy.
Average speakers and sound.
Great price point for what you get

DETAILS
On sale with the "piano" look made it cheaper than buying just the keyboard and a separate stand. Took my daughter and I 15 minutes to assemble the pieces, maybe. Used my drill to mostly put it together and then a screwdriver to tighten enough but not too much.

Sounds on it are fine. Nothing great. But typical for such an instrument. I bought it for midi ultimately so it's built in sounds don't matter to me. But I am glad it has its own speakers and some decent sounds. It doesn't have a bunch of great assignable buttons or sliders for midi (I bought a
Korg nanoKONTROL2 MIDI Control). I'll be using a Mac and Mainstage.

The screen is small. So compared to other screens it's a weakness. But at this price point you can look at it and be thankful it has a screen. No scroll wheel for navigation is a negative.

The built in piano stand version comes with three footpedals which is nice, but I have yet to meet a piano player in the last decade that cares about two of those pedals.

Volume control is normal. Speakers are plenty loud for practice at home or group of 20 people singing with you. Sounds a bit better through a sound system and good speakers. Right now the sound comes thru its own speakers and the system speakers. Haven't researched yet, but there may be a setting to change it. I know my piano players will appreciate the built in speakers being in when plugged in.

Keys are nicely weighted - good enough for 90% or more of all piano players. They aren't fancy and don't feel as much like the real thing as some keyboards. Shouldn't bother most people.

It used to be that fully weighted midi controller keyboards didn't exist. So at this price point, I think it's a good deal.

Power chord isn't long.

Music stand is average.

Same height as the traditional piano it replaced.

The keys alone looked slightly longer than 88 piano keys - but close.

A piano student could use this for years and it would be more than adequate.

Even with the stand, it doesn't weigh much.

Why only 4 stars?
At its price point I could give it 5 stars. But too many little things could be better. I hope to review this in a few months.
Summary: Affordable, Playable, 88 Key Fully Weighted Piano

Pros:
———

This microphone includes BOTH usb and XLR capabilities. The price is great ($80) at time of review but what is amazing is the sound quality and versatility of this microphone. It includes a pop filter over the microphone which you can adjust to your liking.

In USB mode, the gain controls on the mic work in both PS4/PS5/MacOS. I’ve tested with all three and very little to low noise even with gain on max. Microphone is perfect for PS4/PS5 online gaming but it does pick up external noises pretty easily. Turning down the gain does help quite a bit but still picks up some minor noises (keyboard clacking, mouse button clicks, etc). The audio is natural and works good during gaming.

In USB mode under macOS Monterey, the microphone shows up as a fifine usb device. No drivers necessary just like for the ps4/ps5. You will have to turn up the gain, however, because the microphone needs to be amplified. I either need to be up about 1-2” at most to be able to decently get audio from the microphone otherwise I’d have to crank up my volume gain in my system. Obviously gets noisy if you crank all the gains up.

I am not a musician or a sound engineer but I do use microphones for podcasting and audio recording and this microphone is GREAT when paired with an interface. I chose UA Volt 2 interface and it sounds wonderful. I did not even need to use a cloud filter the gain on my volt is at about 2-3’oclock and it’s loud enough. I really think this mic shines in terms of being good at both USB and XLR connection. When connected via XLR, all the usb functions are disabled (obviously). No phantom power is needed and the mic has very low noise. Teams, Skype, FaceTime all work via the interface and connected to this microphone and it’s great quality!

You do not need to buy an SM7b just to do gaming/podcasts; microphones like this Fifine model are perfect and best of all you can use USB and if you want to step it up you can connect via XLR to an interface and the microphone really shines. For the price you pay and the quality build of this microphone, this is a really wonderful microphone. I have nothing but praises because it really surprised me; I expected some inferior quality at this price (because it’s dual interfaced) but the audio quality really surprised me. Yet you can also game with this microphone and use it for more professional audio recordings you get the best of both worlds. It gets expensive if you go with just an XLR dynamic microphone because you’d have to get all the other hardware but with microphone you have that option if you wanted to but at a later date.

Overall this is really worthy of a 5-star rating. I will recommend this for any gamer and or more serious into audio recording - just make sure you get an interface it will really bring out the quality of this microphone. But again it’s the choice you get with this microphone!

______________________________________________________________________________________________

I have had only a single problem with the product. The inputs randomly stop while recording / monitoring as if the driver simply stops working. This will happen within a few seconds or as long as 10 minutes. It will stop working no matter what I try to record with - Reaper, Sound Forge, Izotope RX4 and I have to restart the software in order to get it working again.

In Reaper luckily there is a fix. Go to Options - Preferences. In Preferences Go to Audio - Devices. There make sure that ASIO and Focusrite USB 2.0 Audio driver is selected AND check the box that says "Ignore ASIO reset messages (needed for some buggy drivers)."Without the Reaper fix I would have sent this thing back and given it 1 star. Luckily Reaper is my DAW of choice.

Otherwise it is a well built device with nice clean gain for microphones. Surprisingly it even works well with dynamic miscs that require a good amount of gain. I've used it with the Electro Voice RE20, RE320, and the Shure SM7b. Surprising because the 2i4 only has 55db of gain and ordinary you'd need a mic pre with 60 db of gain for the SM7b and Re20. There is barely enough for the Sm7b that requires the most gain - you'll have to crank it all the way up and still add some gain in your DAW. But absolutely no hissing - very clean.

Extremely low latency. I have the 2i4 running recording at 1 ms of latency. Barely noticeable when you monitor the recording live and processed. Of course you can always switch to zero latency monitoring unprocessed if you like.
Summary: Short life / never buying focusrite again

I’ve tried several different types of pick holders for guitar, music, mic stands, etc., and all have drawbacks of one type or another. Especially the more picky you are about them. Functionally it holds the smallest & largest thicknesses of picks I have, and they’re easy to get in and out. But what I like most with the Gator Frameworks holder is the addition of a slide holder. This alone is GREAT to have. Even the heaviest ‘beer bottle neck’ slide that I have rests perfectly on it. And being a plastic or silicone coated rod, it won’t ding up or scratch your slides.

Feels weird to leave a super detailed review of a ‘pick holder’ for a stand… probably is I admit…
but this worked MUCH better than I even imagined it might.

$6-7 bucks and you can’t really go wrong. If you need or just want a pick holder on your stand… this is the one you’ll want to get.

A few years ago, I heard an interview with Roger McGuinn, co-founder of The Byrds, on a podcast. During the segment, he mentioned using a Samson USB microphone for home recording and talked about how good it was. I looked it up and decided to give one a try and I have been a happy Samson C0-1U user ever since. I use it all the time for podcasts and radio ads/jingles.

When I got a chance to review this mini Samson product, I didn't expect it to be as good as the large size Samson (it isn't), but I thought it might offer similar quality on the go. Unfortunately, while it would be more than enough for podcasting (and certainly better than most built-in computer microphones), my attempts to use it to record two jingles tonight were not as good as I hoped. The tiny microphone seemed to pick up more background noise and was much more sensitive (I had to turn off my ceiling fan). That would be very good for recording multiple speakers around a laptop (and this seems to be the intended purpose). The audio quality was very clear and I expect to keep it with me for use on my laptop or old iPad (via Camera Connector Kit) to get decent recordings when I don't have my big Samson with me.

The packaging was awesome - very close to an Apple-style box. The small microphone came in a small zip up case, but the included USB cable had no where to fit so it will end up being tossed in a laptop bag. At least the zipper case protects the microphone.

One unique feature of the microphone is a switch to toggle between uni and omni directional recording. One side of the microphone has an LED that blinks between green and red (when overdriving), and there is a 1/8" headphone jack on it as well. This jack serves as an additional output so you could plug headphones directly in to it rather than the computer - a nice touch.

Trying to configure it with GarageBand was as easy as anything else, but I had not dealt with something that added an extra output and was a bit confused when I could not hear anything through my normal headphones (via laptop output). When I tried it on the Go Mic output, I was able to hear my GarageBand tracks, but still surprised when OS sounds came from my normal external speakers. A visit to the audio preferences cleared this right up as it showed the new ins and outs.

The mic is VERY sensitive and I had to crank the input level way down to get a non distorted recording. This is not an up close mic, really. But it is portable, has a nice manual, and a long USB cable (with a bolt and a clip - gotta go back through the manual to see what those are for). The microphone can clip to the side of a laptop screen (nice) and fold around in various directions - a very cool design.

Had this been out when I first started podcasting years ago, I probably would have opted for it for the price and convenience and been more than happy. I'm only slightly less impressed since I have a (seemingly) much nicer sounding big Samson microphone.

The Go Mic is a real nice thing for the size and I've never had a problem with my other Samson in all the years I have been using it.
Summary: Portable goodness, but won't be replacing my Samson C0-1U.

Excellent, durable, light-weight guitar that you can keep an arm's length away for easy access. So accessible, in fact, that I play it far more than my. 2 MIA Strats. I originally gave it 5 stars, but after owning it for a couple years, I do think it's overpriced relative to other guitars. Price notwithstanding, definitely 5 stars despite tuning stability issues.

Knowing what I do now, I'd probably be better off with the Hotrod version of the Traveler Speedster, as it has an onboard preamp. However, once again I think that particular guitar is priced very high. I purchased a new Steinberger Synapse for about the same price and while they have different purposes, the Steinberger is a true gig-worthy instrument.

Unplugged, the one-piece maple guitar has very little resonance and sounds very tinny - completely understandable from a guitar that weights around 3 pounds. When played aggressively whilst unplugged, it has poor acoustic tone relative to heavier guitars, but it can get surprisingly loud. One upside is that you can play it softly so as not to disturb those around you. When plugged in, everything changes, and it's no doubt an electric guitar with a hot, twangy humbucker. It's tone and power will surprise anyone who hears it, because it's a wolf in sheep's clothing.

The Good
* Decent rosewood fretboard, good medium frets, feels Fenderish. Action can get pretty low. Thin neck, radius seems pretty flat. Thin D shape.
* Durable, one piece design. Would have to try pretty hard to break this guitar.
* Versatile with string gauges. I think it came with .09s, but I switched to 12s to try to thicken up the resonance. Now I'm using 10s.
* Play it anywhere -- bedroom, bathroom, outside on trips, etc. Very lightweight and easy to tote around. I bring it with me anywhere I know I'll have to do some waiting.
* Headless design has advantages.
* Simplicity
* Removable lap rest
* Simple aesthetics. I like the fact that it almost doesn't look like a guitar. For that reason it doesn't look like a toy. Scaled down models of full sized guitars look funny to me. I wanted something very unassuming and simple. I get quite a few compliments and inquiries about the guitar.
* It's so portable that it makes a huge difference in my practice habits.
* This is a practice guitar not a pro performance guitar -- just an FYI.
* Sounds killer with my iPad and Line 6 Sonic Port, Line 6 Pocket Pod, and other portable modelers. Also direct through my Blues Junior amp. Not as good with Amplugs, because when you're limited to a single bridge pickup and have no reverb options, the tone is a bit too harsh and unforgiving for my ears. I own 3 Amplugs and discovered that the Amplug Twin is the best and most versatile match for this guitar because the chorus gives it more depth. I generally have to use a patch cable with it since the guitar output jack is against my body.
* Comes with a simple but handy loop strap at the head so you can just hang the guitar on a 3M plastic wall hook.
* Can easily rest it against a wall on a carpeted floor.
* Easy access to the truss rod.

Criticisms
* The stock tuners are not stable. I replaced mine with [[ASIN:B0007Y3XGW Grover 406C Rotomatic Mini 3 per Side Self Locking Machine Heads, Chrome]]. The Grovers were expensive. Moreover installation really requires that you drill a stabilizing screw. Not necessary but advised. On the thin wood blocks that mount the tuners, this can be tricky. As a result, my stabilizing screws bulge the woodblocks slightly.

* Changing strings can be a pain because the rollers on the butt of the guitar are floating -- so you need to make sure they are close together and centered before winding the tuning machines. No doubt that locking tuners make the chore a bit easier.

* I think the guitar is overpriced. Great little guitar, but you can buy a full-size decent electric for around the same price.

* Awkward jack position. Has to be there due to the design, but it makes playing with Vox amplugs challenging because they press against my body which in turn can change your dial settings and put stress on the prong. If in theory I were to do it all over again, I'd theoretically get the Speedster Hotrod instead (theoretically, because the price is prohibitive).

* The guitar is so light that slides and sliding double stops are more difficult; the entire guitar moves in the direction of the slide motion. Can't fault the manufacturer for this -- it's what you get with such a light instrument.

* To ensure light weight, etc., sacrifices are made: no tone knobs. I prefer on-board tone control.

* Gig bag is smaller than I'd like, and lacks dual straps for use as backpack. It has a single sling strap. I carry the guitar in my Steinberger gig bag. That way I don't have to remove the lap stand.

* I would prefer a tuning system that is like the Steinberger -- all tuning machines tucked away in the tail of the instrument.

* One very small ergonomic challenge is that the guitar can sort of roll up towards your head very slightly. This makes fretting the 6th string a bit of a burden on your wrist. If I'm lying down, I compensate for this roll by putting a small rolled up towel underneath (below the 6th string so that the guitar is more balanced and pivots flat. This is really hardly worth mentioning, but it's just the nature of having a super thin guitar.

Summary, it's a great guitar for what it is. You will find yourself reaching for it because it's just so accessible. As with all Traveler Guitars, my biggest issue is the price. If it was priced well I'd give it 5 stars.
Summary: Great practice guitar with some caveats

Text:
I’ve been leading worship with acoustic and electric guitars for a very long time and used a different, well-known brand two pedal option that worked for a long time. Then all of a sudden it quit out of the blue on a Saturday night, right before a big important Sunday service, too late to get another device. I use Planning Center’s app Music Stand for my music on an iPad. This device is great.

I ordered this a few days later after reading a lot of reviews and digging into other brands as well. This unit is expensive, and yes, a bit overpriced to my mind, but I love that it’s built out of a guitar pedal case, and runs on a 9v pedalboard power cord like any other pedal, or plugged in with a One Spot, or an internal 9v. It works great, had it set up and changing pages in under a minute, stays synced to my iPad even when one or both are turned off, connects quickly, and the switching is really quiet. I never had an issue with it being too loud during quiet parts of songs like some have said. I found it to be plenty quiet. No problems. If you need absolutely zero noise at all (like for studio work), get a cheaper plastic option from A*r T*rn. But I’m telling you, it’s plenty quiet. I was surprised to hear a few reviewers say it was loud. It’s actually very quiet. There’s no loud *click.*

The USB plug is very nice if you need to keep an iPad charged for multiple services or to charge your phone. I used this feature the very first Sunday. But please note, to charge a device with the USB port, it has to be plugged in and not just running on the internal 9v. Makes sense.

It needs a couple of tweaks to make it perfect IMHO. It needs the Bluetooth antennae to be inside the case, or more protected. I worry about the little nub getting stepped on accidentally. It’s a little odd to have a very rugged case but with the BT antenna exposed in a little rubber nub. Not a deal breaker though. And if it goes on your board with Velcro then it will likely never be an issue.

Second, it needs a little door for the 9v battery to be installed to make it easier. Not a huge deal since many guitar pedals require you to unscrew the back, but for $150 I’d expect that little tweak.

It would be perfect with these two small changes. But this is still the best one on the market if you need a rugged option like I do. These are a little nit picky, but I want to be clear: this pedal is fantastic and the best I’ve found. The cost is high, but I’m making the case that it’s worth the money.
*******************
PS - I have read that their customer service is great too, and that if needed, getting an extra BT wire for replacement is possible should it be needed.
Summary: Great alternative to plasticy options from other brands

Text:
I bought this product for only one reason: I have several amps that are not guitar amps, but stereo or PA-type, clean, high powered , two channels, that I want to use as guitar amps, either as the primary or backup. This tube modeler acts first as a pre-amp, and then adds gain, volume control, "crunch", whatever, to the non-guitar amps to make them sound like guitar amps. I don't really care what tube amps it models, or what mic placement, I just want the guitar amp sound and style. I also use it in front of a Behringer Ultra-G DI box, so that the DI box splits the signal coming from the TM300 and sends half to my non-guitar amps and guitar speakers on stage, and the other half to the house PA. I don't think that many people would do this.
The sound you get out of this box is affected by what amp, and kind of amp you are driving with it, and also what kind of speakers that amp is driving. The acoustics of the space you are playing in also affects the sound, but I've used this box with all of its settings driving PA amps, home stereo amps, bass amps, and guitar amps, all of which drove PA speakers, bass speakers and Eminence Commonwealth 12 guitar speakers, all in the same acoustic space. Each combination of amp and speaker with all settings on the box held constant, sound different: some more like guitar amps and speakers, some not. As I said, I don't really care about what tube amp is being modeled, only that I get an authentic guitar and speaker sound out of the box. It works for me.
I read reviews that say that this is a digital knockoff of the analog Sansamp GT2, and based on its performance so far, it has served as kind of like a cheap preview of what the Sansamp can do. I would consider getting the GT2 in the future, but for now this product is, for me, the poor man's tube amp.

Because it wasn't in the package, with the other things, and I can't find a way to make a direct report/complaint.

Too many small, 'convenient' devices include horribly over-thought interfaces: double/triple-function buttons, arbitrary and difficult-to-memorize sequences, cluttered displays, etc. I often feel like I'm negotiating some nuclear failsafe mechanism than getting quickly to what I want.

But fortunately someone at D'Addario felt the way I do when designing this tuner:

One button on/off, calibrate the 440 with up/down arrows- if I want to.

The display tells me clearly when diatonic pitches match. I'm not using this to micro-tune and I don't care if I'm twenty-seven cents off nor do I need to see a dynamic bar graph of out-of-tuneness.

The clamp is large enough to feel secure while grabbing and squeezing, and the padded clamp surfaces are large enough not to worry about the tuner popping off – especially nice for vintage instruments with delicate finishes.

A negative: the mount on the tuner unit swivels and tilts, but it doesn't 'scissor' and it’s not quite as flexible as a smaller Planet Waves tuner I use for mandolin and violin. The D'Addario display doesn't auto-adjust horizontally/vertically (not that I really expect it to) so the less-flexible mount means it takes some effort to find an optimal position.

Another negative is purely cosmetic and subjective: the hideous yellow color of the outer band. I'm sure it's easy to spot in dark spaces or inside a gear bag, but it gives the impression of a child’s toy and I don’t want to see it while I’m playing.

I’ll add my usual caveat when discussing tuners and fretted instruments:

Tuning open strings is a good starting point but may or may not get you ‘in tune’- and I don’t mean in the metaphoric Pete Townsend sense.

Variables such as nuts, bridges, neck relief, fret position, string gauge and degree of wear are all factors in intonation. Fretted instruments are compromises-by-design, each one is different, and the ultimate arbiter of ‘in-tuneness’ is the same for musicians today as it’s been for centuries: your ears.

I saw this same amp in what looks to be the same box...with different names by at least 3 different companies. I am perty sure they come out of some Chinese factory/city. Then, the company here in the USA that puts their label on it, also selects a Speaker..as we have speakers available here that are competitive and it helps cut down on the shipping. I chose the Rockville company that handles this as they stated they had the heaviest weight speaker installed of the other companies.
I bought two of these for a Bose like system on steroids..at 1/4 the cost. I bought 2 Galaxy 4 x 5" speakers for the line array style mid/high range as they cover up above what people can hear without a large fall in response up there. I also put a blocking network in them to block below 200 Hz from the Galaxys. So, I power them with a little one rack space amp of 200w per side...more than enough for my small to medium solo gigs, and am happy with the system I have put together.
The rockville subs cut start cutting off frequency at about 175 hz and sound somewhat mute for frequency above what they are designed...such as kick bass and low bass. There is a control that adjusts this frequency sweep...I have it set on the highest level. These have also a volume control and a Nutrix input and output that takes a Balanced input or 1/4" line.
I drive these full volume and they seem to take a large amount of low level signal to drive them. The box feels strong and they are a bit heavier than you expect...but that is good. The carpet cover appears of minimal thickness and quality from China, the corners have typical quality metal covers and the handles on each side are plastic and adequate. These also have pole holes ot the common size in the USA, I forget that dimension and if I remember...I am perty sure they are plastic and not metal...but could be wrong. All in all I like having been able to find a 10" little sub at this price to mate with my 10" 2 way Peaveys I some times use and also my new Galaxy 4 x 5" speakers that I also fly on top of these with poles. These subs are heavy enough to use a pole up to say 5' and put either of my mid/high sets of speakers on...as long as someone does not fall into them while intoxicated. The system has all the same perks of a Bose system that would range around 2 grand all for under 500. if you have a small amp in your rack to drive the mid/high speakers... I do it this way cause I play on the beach and like NOT to have amps or electronic that are exposed out in the high air to corrode from the Salt air... It also gives me flexibility to not use the subs in very quiet dinner settings. My friends have both over priced Bose and HK systems in the same design style of having no High end Horns that are harsh and cause feed back. I just dont like the sound of their little 2" multiple array speakers...so I went with the Galaxy with it's 5" array design and have a nice sounding system for cheap...I could have a quad surround sound system in each of the 4 corners of a performance room for the same price as the Bose system. Now I just have to have some custom bags made for the Galaxy mid/high speakers to keep them safe. If you want the maximum thump from 2 of these subs...place them side by side and make sure the phase shift switch...also on the back is set the same for each. That phase shift switch by the way compensates for the type of crossover on the top speakers. That top end crossover can make the top signal 90,180, or 360 degrees out of phase...as crossovers are named 1st order, 2nd order, 3 order and 4th order/360 degrees...the 360 is not so common but puts the tops completely out of phase with the bottom subs...so that is why subs have a phase switch and that is why your cords to them should be the same supplier or same polarity. You want the whole system pumping the same direction on hard hits of sound....and even small ones.
Summary: Great Value, Largest Speaker Weight...takes the place of the whimpy performance tower.

This is my first set of Fender Voodoo Child pure nickel strings. I usually use Ernie Ball Hybrids on my Strats (.009, .011, .016, .026, .036, .046), so this is a pretty significant change.

I keep one of my Strats tuned in Eb, and I consider that my 'Jimi guitar.' Recently I saw a video by Nashville-based guitarist R.J. Ronquillo as he tried a set of strings in the same gauges that Jimi Hendrix used (.010, .013, .015, .026, .032, .038). I liked how it sounded--notes on the low E string sounded tighter, and I liked how the G and B strings interacted, as well. It was definitely an intriguing prospect. It seemed to explain some of Jimi's chimey, midrangy tones.

I wanted to test drive the idea on the Jimi Strat, so I got a set of Fender Voodoo Child strings. That's not to say I had complaints about the Ernie Balls. I think the Hybrid Slinky set has been very good on that guitar. So as I put the Voodoo Child set on, I kept the string heights about the same as before (around 5/64). I immediately noted how slack the G string was, and how easy it was to bend notes. It was fun to play little runs on just the G string.

Still, the low E string felt . . . weird. It felt more like a traditional A string, and for a while I couldn't get over the irrational thought that the low E was lighter than the A string (it isn't--I double and triple checked!).

More discouraging was the fact that the low E was buzzing. While it felt good, the buzz was noticeable, especially unplugged. So like anyone else would, I tested out possible solutions. First, I raised the action on the low E to 7/64 and the A to 6/64. The low E still buzzed even at that height. After that, I adjusted intonation on all strings. I could feel a difference on the higher strings, but the low E still buzzed. Lastly, I checked the relief in the neck, and thankfully, the truss rod needed no adjustment (I would have had to take the neck off to adjust it, which I wasn't looking forward to doing).

In a bit of frustration, I lowered all the strings down to 4/64, and then dialed the intonation again. Now the strings feel very slinky, although the low E still buzzes when I play with a pick. I’m pretty well convinced that the low E string, at .038 and tuned in Eb, is too light for that position. So I'm afraid the Voodoo Child set will not last long on that guitar. It's kind of disappointing to have to admit defeat, even though I feel like I've done as much as I can to sort out the issue (short of raising the low E to 8/64, which is too high).

This experience makes me curious about how Hendrix set up his low E strings. Maybe he raised the string height, or maybe he played it more gently (I always thought Jimi had a heavy picking hand--I guess not). I will try to be patient and see a way through this issue, although at this point I hasten to say that this set is an acquired taste. I guess I'm no longer surprised that this set isn't more popular.

2020-01-30 update: Reluctantly I had to give up on these strings. I think for the right guitar they are an interesting set. The low E string was just too light for the guitar I put them on, and playing the low E required a much lighter touch than I'm comfortable with, even at 7/64. I have gone back to using a .046 for the low E.
Summary: Excellent, but not for all tastes

It never ceases to amaze me what a difference it makes upgrading the pots and switch in an import guitar can make.

MIM Fender Strats come with microscopically small 500k Ohm pots, which makes the pickups sound like ice picks. This kit comes with 250k Ohm pots, which is what usually matches low output single coil pickups the best.

The wiring diagram has you solder the bridge pickup to the middle tone control, which was another welcome upgrade to my 1990 MIM Strat.

Keep in mind if you're upgrading an import guitar, the pot shafts are bigger than stock, so you will have to use a reamer or a round file to enlarge the holes. A little slop is fine because you'll never see it under the knob. Just don't make the hole way too big. Otherwise buy a new pickguard. The stock screws for the old 5-way switch fit the new one just fine for me. Your old knobs and switch tip will also not fit here. Stewmac sells knobs that fit fine and course splined pots though.

I don't know if it's just different with 250k Ohm vs 500k Ohm, a different wiring scheme, or the new capacitor, but I don't notice the treble roll-off on the volume knob as much with this kit vs stock. It does come with a treble bleed mod but I didn't end up using it.
Summary: Massive upgrade to import Strats but will not fit old pickguard and knobs.

Text:
I'm new to ukulele, but not new to stringed instruments, so I know what to look for... I've had an itch to get a uke for a few months now, and like I do before any big purchase, I read A LOT of reviews and ukulele websites. Kala Makala kept coming up as pretty much the best under $100 uke that's still worth a dang. Well, all those reviews were not wrong! Yes, this Uke is made from Agathis, not paka or mahogony or other "tone" wood. Don't let that fool you, it still sounds great! Nice mellow tone, full projection, and a great sound overall. The action was set perfectly textbook (1mm at the first fret, 4mm at the 12th), and the black nylon strings that it came strung with seem pretty good. After the requisite string break-in period, it holds a tune quite well, and the tuners seem quite good. The finish was very nice, with no mars or blemishes, and the mahogany neck and rosewood fretboard are very nice looking, and feel good under the hand and fingers. The frets are all nice and even, and there is no fret buzz anywhere on the neck.

Yes, it's made in China. But the price is right, and the workmanship is good! It's not going to compete with a higher end Uke in terms of tonality, but it's got very respectable tone in its own right. If you are looking for low-cost, but still great sounding tenor uke, this is the one for you!

UPDATE: It's been several months now, and I'd just like to post a follow up to this initial review... I still LOVE this Uke, and after restringing with Aquila Nylgut strings (in the Kala brand package), this Uke sounds better than ever! Do yourself a favor and buy the Aquila strings at the same time as you buy this Uke. Keep the stock black strings on as you start to learn. They will help you toughen up your fingertips and build hand strength. Then, after you can make a bunch of chords, and you can finger pick a bit, put on the Aquila strings and be amazed! :) But the bottom line is that this was definitely a great purchase! I LOVE THIS THING! Absolutely zero buyer's remorse!

SECOND UPDATE (6/09/14): I still love Uke, and play it every day. With the Aquila Nylguts, it seems to magically stay in tune for weeks and weeks and has great resonant tone. Now that I'm "good" at playing the Uke, I can more fully understand what your $$ will get you on more expensive models (and I've played a few of those by now), but I honestly love this little kala Uke! I'm not planning on getting rid of it, and IMO, it really hits the perfect price/quality sweet spot for an instrument that you want to be able to keep and grow on. This was a great purchase.

I've only had this a few days, but I absolutely love it. This is what I think of this fine instrument.

The tone is a bit lighter or brighter than an equivalent clay or ceramic ocarina, which tend to have a mellower tone. If you are familiar with ocarinas, you know what I mean. This is not a bad thing, it's the nature of a lighter ocarina. It has a very nice tone, bright and loud. It is slightly louder than a comparable sized ocarina, but you can also play with less air without going out of tune. Cheaper ocarinas are notorious for not being well tuned to start with, and requiring a lot of air to sound good. This instrument can be played with less air and still sound good. The volume range is really good. The high notes are nicely in tune.

Mechanically, It feels good and is comfortable to play. The hole spacing fits my fingers perfectly. I have average sized hands, FWIW. It is light, being plastic, but it is solid, not at all flimsy feeling. It is very nicely finished, smooth and well constructed. The finish is not rubberized as some people say, it is not coated, but the plastic itself is textured with a satin like finish, rather than leaving it smooth and shiny. This, to me, makes it easier to grip and hold. It gets a well deserved five stars.

Update: After playing this for a few weeks, my initial impression is unchanged. It plays very well and is very well tuned. The high notes are easier to play than the Zelda style of Ocarina, though maybe not quite as easy as a high end clay ocarina. Still, the high notes sound good and are easy to play. Being plastic, it is lighter than an equivalent clay model, but still fits well and feels good in my hands. I would be interested in trying one of their larger models, I like this one so much.

Text: LOVE THIS PERFECT!

After DOD pedals were absorbed into the DigiTech brand name, I always felt like the HardWire pedal series was a direct response to the reputation of DOD pedals as cheap, unreliable effects for bedroom players. The HardWire pedals came with a very sturdy "BOSS-style" soft switch, and solid metal enclosure with a wide, low, and stable profile, and bells and whistles like Mod switches and metal knobs. In short, pedals like the Valve Distortion and Tube Overdrive were boutique-caliber pedals at BOSS prices, and you could argue that the RV-7 Stereo Reverb was one of the better pedals they ever made. As of early 2015, it still seems unclear if DigiTech has formally abandoned the HardWire line in favor of new products, but the RV-7 is a pedal that should stand the test of time.

There are a lot of quality reverb pedals nowadays that can cover a variety of reverb styles - including the Boss RV-5 and the TC Electronics Hall of Fame. Those are excellent pedals, too, but the RV-7 really does a nice job covering everything from vintage spring reverbs, to the subtlety of a room effect reverb, to the lush, deep effects of a hall reverb. And each of these settings actually seems to range from the very subtle to the over-the-top, which is where many reverb pedals fall short.

But what really sets the RV-7 apart in this price range is that the 7 reverb modes are supported by Lexicon algorithms. Lexicon may be unknown to many casual guitarists, but they are a legendary name in the development of digital reverb and effects. The rack-mounted equivalents of these effects cost thousands of dollars in the 80's, and even now are usually in a much larger form factor costing hundreds of dollars. This is true-to-life ambient sound effects in the size of a stompbox, and sold for $150 or less. Amazing. I don't know that this is the "best" spring reverb I've heard in a pedal (the Catalinbread Topanga deserves some mention), but it's a very good one in a pedal that does 6 other things. The Lexicon-supported Room and Hall settings are terrific, as is the Plate setting for a bright, 70's-like finish to your muted riffs. The Reverse, Gated, and Modulated settings along the top are a bit more niche, but all done extremely well. I truly believe this is the last Reverb pedal I will ever need, and that's not something a pedal addict can usually say with much confidence!

A few caveats to point out - the pedal has a hookup for a 9V battery, but it's basically decorative in a high-powered digital reverb pedal like this one. (By the way, if you were ever stumped how to access the battery compartment on a DigiTech pedal, as I stupidly was for awhile, the hinges on the footstomp portion double as release pins to kick off the cover - press inward with guitar plugs on both sides!) You will get zero battery life with the amount of power this demands, so you will want a good power adapter. The One Spot adapter puts out 1700mA, which is plenty of power, but some digital pedals run in parallel have issues with digital pedals. If this is an ongoing issue, an isolated power source like the one from Voodoo Labs should do the trick.

Whether or not these pedals are discontinued, they are still being stocked online and in many stores. I think it's an excellent pedal with hundreds of dollars of value compressed into a compact pedal, and at a reasonable price.
Summary: Unmatched versatility, backed by Lexicon, in a tank-like reverb pedal

Text:
Seagull guitars have intrigued me for years in photos and on their website, but there is no dealer anywhere near me, so I bought one sight-unseen from Amazon, based on the good reviews. I'm glad to say I can add my voice to the chorus of praise for this innovative design.

A traditionalist will need some time to become accustomed to the unusual appearance and construction. The narrow, reverse-taper headstock and wide fingerboard give this guitar a bottom-heavy look when viewed vertically. Back and sides are cherry with only a light stain, and the binding is dark. The top is natural cedar.

As dreadnoughts go, this one is very comfortable to play sitting down. It appears to be based on the Martin outline, but with a slightly rounder lower bout and a narrower upper bout. Weight is pleasantly light, and the semi-gloss finish is comfortable to the touch. Players with broad fingers will appreciate the wide fingerboard, but those with small hands should consider the ""Slim" version, with a neck 0.08" narrower at the nut.

Sound is what really counts, however, and this Canadian dreadnought has nothing to be ashamed of there. The maker has the good sense to ship the instrument with high-quality, fresh strings, allowing the new owner to appreciate the notable bass and clear midrange as soon as it is tuned up. Overall, it falls within the classic dreadnought tone category, with good volume.

Buying a guitar online saves money but leaves setup to the buyer. Both the nut and saddle on my guitar needed lowering, and the truss rod required adjustment (a long-reach hex wrench is included). If you are not experienced in these tasks, a local luthier should do it for no more than $30 or so.

Based on sound, playability once adjusted, and construction quality, this guitar should definitely be included when comparing instruments in this price range. It is a real standout in value.

Update 8 DEC 2012: The more I play this guitar, the more I love it. It delivers balanced sound with good dreadnought "snap", and once the action was dialed in, the broad fingerboard relieves finger crowding I didn't fully realize hindered my playing. I am considerng replacing my Takamine mini-jumbo with a Seagull equivalent.
