I've been using the MAONO XLR mic for the past week for various purposes including work (virtual meetings and documentation), gaming with Xbox live on Windows, and recording audiobook excerpts for librivox. In all applications this condenser mic exceeded my expectations.

The build quality is good-great. The base of the mic stand is metal and the mic itself feels well built. There were no factory defects or blemishes on the mic or the accessories. The pop filter is metal as well and slots into the mount.

As for the recorded sound quality I can't complain at all really.

I routinely create documentation videos of processes and workflows for our IT Dept staff. This mic picks up my voice clearly when recording and though I don't have the deepest voice this accentuates some of the bass which makes for a warmer sound signature. I could easily see this mic working for ASMR whispering videos with a better pop filter.

As for sibilance in some of the recordings, I didn't really notice my "s" sounds sounding harsh with just the default accessories (slotted in metal pop filter). The mic doesn't pick up on much of the white noise in my home office either (I have a fan and air purifier running while recording) so that was also a plus.

For connecting and powering this mic I used an all in one USB audio interface featuring 48v phantom power.

Overall based on the mic's performance in meetings and the quality of the completed recordings I would definitely recommend this mic, especially if you're looking at budget friendly xlr condenser mics.
Summary: Excellent mic for podcasting, documentation recording, gaming, or virtual meetings, needs 48v

What I like most about this product is that it really works to restore string tone. It lubricates as well, but my problem was keeping my guitar strings from going dead and that's what I was concerned with.

I tried other string cleaners, but without much success. But this one really works. It also seems to keep the fingerboard very clean. I never get any buildup of junk on my fingerboard anymore.

Here is an idea on how to use the product:

I remove the pad on the top of the bottle. There is a valve underneath the pad. This valve apparently opens when you press down on the pad, like when you are cleaning the strings. But I don't use the pad.

What I do is to put a piece of terrycloth over my fingertip and then press that against the valve on the top of the bottle while holding the bottle upside down. That makes a wet spot on the terrycloth where my finger is. Then I put my fingertip between the strings and run it up and down the fingerboard. This gets both the tops and sides of the strings. I also run the cloth up and down the fingerboard on the outside of the high and low E strings. That gets the sides of those strings too.

I've gotten amazing results this way. I've had strings go from dead (where the guitar sounded crappy) to brilliant like the strings were when you first installed them and stretched them.

Anyway, this stuff works very well for me and I'm going to stock up on it. It's reasonably priced (especially for how good it is) and a bottle seems to last a long time too. I strongly suggest using this before and after each of your guitar playing sessions.

These things are OLD. That must be why they aren't too expensive. Foam degrades over time because of the components in the air we breathe (Ozone, an unstable molecule, normally bonds with foam, oxidizing and destroying it and freeing the 03 to be 02). These things have clearly been sitting for a while, because they have that characteristic "crunchy" feel when you squeeze foam and it's turning into dust.

They went up without a hitch and look good, but the thinness of the product precludes any real noise prevention. The only thing these do is break up reflected audio so you don't hear room-reverb or an echo.

Would I recommend them to a friend? If I were mad at them I would. Otherwise only the most inexperienced would appreciate them. My recording studio and musician friends would likely say "No way, they're too thin and they're crunchy too!"

I'll put up with that. For now.

I picked up this pedal used along with DS-1 Keeley modded distortion pedal not entirely knowing what to think. Long story short, the mod DS-1 is getting returned and I'm keeping my Fulltone OCD.

First, a word about the negative reviews...it tells you something when a small handfull of people completely trash something, but the 13 other reviews (as of Sept. 2012) were all 5-star reviews. It tells me that the people who ripped on the tone of the pedal didn't know what the pedal was before they tried it. And anyone complaining about the price - this is a hand-crafted pedal that is extremely well constructed (the inside circuitry is pristine) and built to last for decades. I think the ratings should reflect quality first and foremost.

Now, let's talk about how the pedal sounds! It's marketed as an overdrive/distortion. I had a lot of people try to steer me away from it because I indicated I was looking for a distortion pedal, but I was actually quite surprised at how much gain and sustain the pedal has. It is much more an "overdrive" in the sense that it keeps the tonal characteristics of your guitar and amp, but boosts the level in gain in a very full, rich sound. The sound has a lot of "bass" to it, but unlike a Tubescreamer (TS-9), it's definitely not "muddy". In fact, if you're tired distortion pedals sounding tinny and weak on a combo act, this might be exactly what you need.

The battery is accessible behind 4 hand screws and moderately involved to get to, but an AC adapter is really the way to go. It's a standard plug like you find on BOSS and Ibanez pedals, but you can use a 9V or 18V. I've read some reviewers say that 18V gives you more headroom, while some actually prefer the 9V sound. Honestly, I tried both and didn't discern any difference - it probably only matters at very loud volumes with cabinets.

Finally, there is an LP/HP switch, and it's really a matter of preference and setup how you use it. I've been mostly using the LP setting, which has plenty of output but avoids the shrill highs that I hate. But in a live setting (or to use it as a boost for soloing), the HP setting could be quite useful, as it is designed the emphasize the mids and highs to "cut through" the other instruments on stage.

If I had to summarize this pedal, I would describe it as a Tubescreamer you can rock with. Which is not to say that it's "better" than the Tubescreamer, necessarily, but it definitely has a larger range of gain and tone. Put this on your pedalboard and you may find yourself using it as your go-to for rhythm/chord sections, soloing, or both.
Summary: Like a Tubescreamer you can rock with!

When I first tried this pedal, I wasn't that crazy about it. I have some other high quality Klon type pedals (including the 2nd gen "authentic" Klon KTR, a soul food, and a RYRA Klon Clone and a couple others I tried and sold off. (The RYRA is the best but the guy who makes them didn't impress me much when I dealt with him.) I was mostly playing it at lower volumes at home. And it was ok but I didn't think it was anything special.

Fast forward to the first time I took it on stage and played it in a band mix. I was soloing and needed a little more sumthin' to cut through the mix, which was kinda noisy and muddy anyway. Stepped on the Tumnus and ladies and gentleman...the guitarist is here. It was just the right eq, added drive fatness and boost level. I thought "I can't believe I was about to sell that."

I have used some really high quality KLON clones at quite a few gigs prior to that so I shouldn't have been surprised. I guess my point here is that if you are not liking it at home, low volumes, or while playing alone, try it in a band mix, at stage volume. It's good!

My only criticism really is that like most pedal manufacturers, Wampler must design his graphics on a computer at blown up size on a computer screen. Guys.. Puhleeeeeeeze...Make the knob label text LARGER and put it in colors that STAND OUT. I know these pedals are small but there is room for your giant pedal name text and artsy graphic of a mythical character - sacrfice THAT to functionality and make the knob labels readable please.

On the plus side, they use knobs that have a white line (THANK YOU) so you can see how they are set, and they don't use the super micro knobs. It would be nice if the pots were spaced a little further apart (maybe vertically instead of in a triangle) but pretty good. They also put the power jack on the rear vertical surface where it belongs (THANK YOU) and doesn't interfere with the input/output cables. (TC Electronics and MXR take note!!! it goes on the back!!!)
Summary: Solid Klon tones in a tiny package

Text:
After a 36 year run of of playing guitar, performing on the road, and being in more bands than I can count, I developed a condition in my right (picking) hand called Complex Regional Pain Syndrome accompanied significant nerve damage. The disorder is extremely painful and severely affects my wrist, pinky, ring and middle fingers. Surprisingly, I still have about 80% use of my thumb and 20% of my index finger. Holding a pick is useless because I cannot navigate the distance between the strings on a guitar. All of the skills I have learned over the years are still perfectly located in my brain, however, I am unable to make my fingers respond accordingly. For a musician like me, the only thing I can compare it to is losing my ability to speak. After seeing several specialists, I was told that my condition was permanent and there was little they could do. I tried for nearly 18 months to prove them wrong and finally had to face the fact I may never play or perform live again. NOTE, I hadn't given up yet and this story has an optimistic ending!

One evening, my wife was watching a Doobie Brothers concert on PBS. I was simply passing through the room when I looked up at the TV at just the right time. Patrick Simmons wearing some sort of pick holding apparatus on his his thumb and strumming his orange Stratocaster rather aggressively while not using his fingers at all. Needless to say, I became very intrigued. Then he did the unthinkable. He ripped into an entire solo using only his thumb. The next morning I desperatety tried to find out what Patrick was using, but soon realized that no one seemed to know what it was. Upon further investigation, I ran across the Shark Tooth Strum-N-Comfort Crossover pick. It's design gave me an idea and I immediately grabbed a bass that I only used for recording purposes. I then found a heavy thumb pick and strapped on with duct tape.

Well, it worked okay on the down stroke but failed miserably when trying to pick in an upward motion. Simply put, it kept slipping or falling off completely. It didn't matter that my experiment failed. I knew if I could find something that would stay in place, I was 100% sure that I a second shot at playing and performing again. I immediately called Greg Atkin at Strum-N-Comfort and we talked at length about my injury, my idea regarding exclusively using my thumb (for bass as a starter), and if Crossover pick would stay in place while doing so. Greg assured me that the his pick would work and built me two prototypes; one for bass and one for guitar. The price was astoundingly low and I received them in the mail in under a week. I then found myself procrastinating and afraid to try one out in fear of failure. This was it. If the Crossover didn't work I was out of options. It took a couple of days but I grabbed my bass, cranked up the tunes, and gave it a shot. I started with some light up and down strokes and it worked perfectly. About two hours later I was playing 8th notes with speed, precision, and delight!

Even though I'm not ready to tackle playing guitar just yet, I have no doubt that finger pickers of all styles will love the Crossover. AS FOR THE BASS, you can play practically any style you want without worry of the pick falling off. I have no doubt that THE BASS method I am working on will get me back in action. As well, I will be adapting a "thumb only" technique for guitar very soon! Even if you don't have major problems like I do, the Strum-N-Comfort Sharktooth pick is an awesome device that every guitarist or bassist should try out. One thing I should mention is that these also work wonderfully if you use both your thumb and index finger. (No more dropping picks ever)! Order today and you won't regret it. I will be posting some pictures and possibly a video very soon. DISCLAIMER: I am not associated with Strum-N-Comfort in any way.
Summary: PLEASE READ!  INJURED HAND?  DIFFICULY IN HOLDING A PICK?  THE STRUM-N-COMFORT IS ESSENTIAL FOR GUITAR AND BASS!

It's not exact in that the Rocket has the Top recessed and these Top/Bottoms are on top within that groove (stated in a way not to be technical, rather descriptive). Actually, it plays easier, out of the box, all Reeds.

All need a little play in, but this played will out of the box. The "Tone" is subjective and similar (this is my only B-key), so challenging to compare. I compared it to the Low-C and Low-D and this is NOT a Low Octave Harp, just a "B-Key" harp. So, actually, to be fare :) maybe did not play "better", however as well. (The Low-C is low and needs a more gentle Draw, and all the rest. Different Keys have different length and thickness/tunes reeds.

So, since purchase during our Global Quarantine, Mar 2020 period, - it looked good, clean and not played, but is not "Sealed"; none are really (some have been in the past some brand, but not these).
- So, I did wipe it down as I unboxed it; don't want to suck cleaner regardless of what the bottle may say :) So a gentle wipe. I know there is some kind of sterilizer machine? probably UV-C light... However, me, I gengly unscrewed the Top/Bottom and in a fine Sprayer, misted it with 91% - 99% denatured alcohol and gently dabbed it dry; then left it for a time.

So I can say, that, -- these ARE hand tuned, - the individual reeds may show that (take a little off and etc.), However all looked and played perfectly "aligned" no bindng, stuffness on Blow/Draw.

So, I am happy with it. I'd like one in Low-B, but don't see any. And I don't pay Electric Guitar Level Prices for these since not a "harmonica player" so to speak. To many instruments to use as well :)

I use this controller for several years in my home studio. It still works perfectly.

I've seen people using the APC40 with software like Bitwig and Resolume. So it's not tied to Ableton.

This device encountered a massive price drop as Ableton released Push and Push 2. If you are on a budget and want a controller, which can handle abuse instead of having the latest features, look for a used APC40.

I tested this pedal with 2 set-ups: 1) CLEAN (single-coil Stratocaster & Peavey Bandit 112 amp), and 2) DISTORTED (single-coil Stratocaster & Marshall Valvestate 8240 Stereo Chorus amp). Results:

1. CLEAN: The pedal is light and very small, but has a solid build and can be powered by a DC power adapter, a power bank, or a 9v battery if you have battery clip converter (see picture). Still have not found a setting that I'm 100% happy with, but was able to get some interesting sounds from the clean set-up. The delay has a good range, 50ms - 1,000ms, which is a wide range for a cheaper delay pedal. I did not notice any degradation in sound with it on or off, but there was a slight tonal change when the delay is switched on. The notes I played got a little brighter - nothing major, but noticeable.

In addition to the delay controls, there are 3 modes available to experiment with - Echo, Mod, and Normal. Echo is more subtle while the other two seem to have more of a pronounced effect. Normal seems to have the best slap-back echo while Mod is better for more way-out effects and sound modulation. A 3-way toggle switch places you in Echo, Mod or Normal modes.

2) DISTORTED: Here is where I noticed more tonal variations, not in a good way. First, with the pedal off, my distorted tone through the Marshall was not 100% true bypass. There was a very slight dampening of the sound of my chords with the pedal switched off. I tested it a few times and it was subtle but there. For a live setting it would not be a deal-breaker amount, but for recording it might be a situation that causes some concern.

Second, there was a noticeable (but again, slight) increase in noise with the pedal turned on. Again, I tested it a few times. And there was also a bit of a treble boost with the pedal turned on that I did not like. I was looking for a more cascading kind of echo and instead I got a little bit more of a harsh, biting high end. This was more noticeable on the Echo and Mod modes, whereas with the Normal mode, I actually got a darker sound with the repeats (counter-intuitive, I know).

I used to own a Roland Boss rack-mounted digital delay, and that had a smoother sound than this. Of course it was also 4X the price, but while I do not expect perfection I had trouble getting a useable sound with this pedal with distortion, beyond a slap-back delay that actually sounded pretty good.

When I switched on the chorus on the Marshall amp, the sound was better and fuller. Maybe that is the key when using this pedal through distortion, also having a chorus or other effect combined with it.

Another observation is that the "Level" and "Regen" knobs are very tiny and the indicator strip is not very visible so it is very hard to know where they are set. I don't have big hands but even for me, these knobs are too small and unreadable.

SUMMARY: Overall, I liked the pedal more with the Clean set-up and will continue to experiment with that. With the Distortion set-up, I did not care for the delay sounds enough to want to play with the pedal again unless I had a specific sound that I was aiming for. While I appreciate the wide range of delay available - as well as the 3 modes - I have not found much that is useable yet for just everyday playing. My Blackstar Fly 3 practice amp has an analog-style delay and I just like that better because it is more subtle, sounds less harsh on the high end, and adds some nice color for everyday playing. (Maybe I would prefer a straight analog pedal?) In any case, I will play with this delay pedal more but as of now I consider it more of a curious thing to play with rather than an essential part of the sound that I am looking to to build. Even if I were doing shoegaze or ambient music, I would probably want to try a different pedal for a little more money.
Summary: Wide Range Of Delay But Has Some Tonal Effects That Are Not Always Welcome

IF YOU ARE NEW TO STRINGED INSTRUMENTS, DO NOT ADJUST THE TRUSS ROD YOURSELF. Please ignore the poorly translated instructions in the item description. Truss rods are not really meant to adjust the height / "action" on the strings. A truss rod adjustment straightens or bows the instrument neck, and even experienced players only let professional repair folk handle such repairs.

Now that that's out of the way, here's some review info from a guitarist:

I was really excited to find a beginner banjo for review on Amazon Vine. When this Vangoa came in the mail, it did not have the floating bridge adjusted, and the tailpiece got a little bent out of shape during shipping.

It is best to take this instrument to your local guitar & banjo luthier or repair person to get it "set up" and ready to play. You will not regret it. The banjo came to me with a few obvious issues that a luthier can take care of: intonation issues, floating bridge installation, high action at the 12 fret (for my fretting hand), etc. The written instructions with the banjo do not help you do any of these things, and its translated pretty poorly, in spite of hinting at great ideas and support for new banjo enthusiasts.

Things I like:

- For beginner stringed instruments, I have two requirements: 1) it stays in tune while playing (doesn't aggressively detune), and 2) it plays fairly easily, meaning you're not dealing with any issues in the construction that would fatigue your hands quickly or otherwise make it hard to play the banjo for more than a few minutes. This Vangoa passed the test on both counts!

- Decent price for a mahogany banjo with a resonator back.
- flimsy gig bag, but excellent support around the top of the neck with a foam block and velcro
- You get a really nice little pack of strings, picks, tuners, and other instrument knick knacs.
- Really, really fun to play. I bought a capo and just started figuring out Gillian Welch and Sufjan Stevens songs on it.
- Nice mahogany, note forward tone (instead of overtone-forward) that's pretty simple to play

Stuff that could be worked on:

- Translating the manual to English. Need a good translator! Vangoa actually has a lot of useful information in the manual, but it's hard to understand the poorly constructed sentences

- Brand new users are encouraged to figure out how to put on their floating bridges--if you can, get someone experienced with stringed instruments to help

- The first string buzzes when fretted quite a bit. I haven't taken my banjo to a luthier yet. I'm thinking that I need to adjust the tailpiece and make sure the floating bridge is in the right place.

- action is high at the 12th fret, not the worst thing for most people, but my hands don't really like it

Overall my assessment is that the craftspeople who designed and built this Vangoa know what they're doing when it comes to building instruments--even if the construction materials are not the greatest, or the translated instructions are poor. The instrument speaks for itself, and it's a pretty good performing one.

If you play guitar, or know someone who does, the Zoom G1Xon is absolutely one of the best gift purchases you can make. There are many reviews covering technical specs and user operation, so no need to repeat any of that here. I'm only going to hit the highlights with this short review.

The unit is small, lightweight, surprisingly functional, and it sounds terrific with electric guitars AND acoustic-electric guitars. Basically you get a pre-programmed (and fully programmable) digital multi-effects processor, with an expression pedal, a built-in rhythm section, an AUX input (to connect any mp3 music source), and a 30-second looper with overdubbing - all for $69.95, w/ free Prime 2-day shipping. Come on now, that's a pretty good deal IF it works and sounds good... and it does!

Watch my quick-start video here: [...]

The G1Xon units currently shipping have 100 pre-programmed effects patches (10 banks of 10 patches each, up from 70 patches in the previous model) ranging from clean jazz, to Jimi / Stevie / Eddie, to borderline synthesized sounds thanks to full collection of digital stomp boxes (delay, fuzz, distortion, chorus, reverb, phaser, octave multiplexer, wah, amp modeling, and the list goes on) all of which produce amazingly good sound quality. Best of all, you can chain together up to 5 effects, in any sequence you like, for amazing tonal variety - and save your custom patches for future use.

The rhythm section / drum machine also sounds surprisingly good for what it is. (I've heard better, and I've heard much worse; this one is on the better end of the scale.) As for the looper, it can be a little tricky to get the exact pedal-push timing down for creating loops, but the looper itself is quite transparent and the playback level (volume) can be adjusted on-the-fly; as you can also do with the drum machine.

Is the G1Xon "stage worthy"? For sound quality: Yes. For durability: Probably. For usability in a live setting: Possibly. But the unit is clearly designed and built for playing, practicing, and recording in a home environment.

As for playing through the unit, most people will use headphones or plug into an amplifier. However, you do not need an amplifier - and it may even sound better if you don't use an amplifier! Here's why...

If you have (or purchase) a mini-stereo cable and 1/4" headphone adapter, you can plug this unit into any audio device with a mini-stereo AUX input. That means you can jam-out with hundreds of pedal combinations, a large variety of drum sequences, an overdubbing looper, and even songs or backing tracks on your mp3 player, using just about any blue-tooth speaker, table-top audio player, home stereo / theater system, or car radio as your amplifier / speaker. As long as it has a mini-stereo AUX input, you can play through it, and I've listed all the parts you will need at the end of this review. Other guitar mutli-effect units also have a headphone output (most individual pedals do not) but this unit is so small you can basically take it with you to plug-n-play just about anywhere you go.

(Personally, I have an older Samsung all-in-one home theater unit, with 5.1 surround. In default surround mode, this pedal sounds pretty amazing. Apparently, certain effect patches are picked up and rendered differently by the audio decoder, which delivers a surround-sound effect with different sounds coming from different speakers. I doubt this was intentional design by Zoom, and I can't say the results would be the same with other home theater systems, but through my home system this thing totally rocks.)

So if your in the gift-giving mode, here are a few "extras" for your gift-bag...

$7 Headphone adapter: http://amzn.com/B00XAVOW00 (this is a 3 pack for a great price)
$23 Headphones: http://amzn.com/B003LPTAYI (affordable Senheiser headphones)

This is a great seriously cheap pickup.  The only con is that the diameter is too large to mount on the bridge plate of an average flat top guitar.  If you're set on mounting the transducers on the bridge plate you need to go with a smaller diameter.  That means either spending actual money on a name brand pickup or rolling your own--buy the transducers, wire them in parallel, and solder them to a jack.  I was in an I don't care situation and mounted one transducer in the center of the bridge plate and the other two on the sound board.  For that guitar it was a reasonable solution.  If you're putting a pickup in a guitar you really care about you should think about a name brand model.  It'll cost you roughly 10 times as much but it will be better.  Diminishing returns applies always.  The name brand will be easier to tame and mount.  Remember too that you will need a preamp if you want a relatively true sounding solution.  That's true of any piezo setup.
Summary: Can't beat it for the money.

Pro DX8 has great potential, but its valuable smartphone app only sporadically connected with my BLU Studio Energy II android smartphone. Because this BLU also operated marginally with a few other audio-video-GPS smartphone hardware accessories, I suspect the fault lies more with my BLU than Pro DX8. Will later test with an Apple iPad II.

Pro DX8’s essential mixer features, such as volume, four effects, and channel selection, can be activated via its front panel, without using a smartphone. I tested-compared using a 4-channel-input, covered-with-dials, no-effects-features Soundcraft Notepad 124 mixer, high-end live speakers, medium-quality electric guitar, and high-end dynamic mic. DX8 can sound superior to the No-Effects Notepad 124 because DX8 has numerous mediocre effects. And DX8 is easier to set up and operate than the Notepad.

DX8’s smartphone app, MixerConnect, is DX8’s true value! MixerConnect enables a layman to easily become a soundman assistant because it is easier to learn than the numerous puzzling dials of a traditional mixer, and because such soundman assistant can operate up to 30 feet away from the mixer.

For example, after the band sets up and starts playing at a bar’s patio, they usually do not hear what the audience is hearing. A bartender notices the bass is loud and guitar is faint. So, he uses his smartphone’s MixerConnect app to balance mixer's sound output. Likewise, if a karaoke singer’s voice is weak, waitress ups MixerConnect’s mic volume and adds a “hall reverb” effect.

Between band sets, bartender uses DX8 to activate his remote microphone, announce a drink special, and turn on recorded music. If a TV sports game starts, restaurant staff mutes music and use TV’s own remote devices, turn on the TV with possible audio line feed into DX8. DX8 is easy to use, improves sound for the band and bar, and saves money for the bar. And there are countless applications where an occasional assistant soundman can be very useful. And, of course, a band member on stage can also adjust stage monitors and main speakers via his smartphone.

Problem is, the MixerConnect app sporadically connected my BLU Android. I’ve tried reinstalling the app, resetting DX8, rebooting BLU, complete reinstalls—results are sporadic. As mentioned above, I currently fault this problem moreso with BLU than with Mackie. I’ll see later what happens using an iPad instead.

Mackie’s tech support is outstanding. I reached them sometimes in as fast as 1 minute and no longer than 7 minutes. And they’re knowledgeable and friendly.

I've seen so many outdoor and some indoor performances where the band can sound far better by using an occasional soundman assistant. Currently a 4 star, and may become a 5 star.
Summary: Great potential and tech support, smartphone problems, opportunity for assistant soundman

After some brief research, the Furman M-8DX seemed to be the best balance of quality and performance for the price and seems to be the industry standard in line conditioning and surge protection. It is lightweight, yet seems solid in its construction. Voltmeter is dead-on accurate. My outlet read 118v using a Fluke power meter and the Furman.

It works well and does what it's supposed to do which is protect your equipment, but I can't give it a perfect score because...
1) The "Christmas light" bulbs are difficult to remove if they ever need to be changed and the manual does not specify how. Furman should have used LED lighting instead.
2) The 6-foot power cord it comes with is too short. No matter how close an outlet is to my DJ setup, I still have to use an extension cord. I think it should be at least 10-12 feet.

Despite these minor deficiencies, I still recommend this product.

It is so hard to get an honest review of any mike that isn't a Shure SM58. This is considered the gold standard by which all others are measured. Of course at least part of this reputation is deserved, but perhaps more for the durability of the SM58 than its sound. I have a couple of SM58s and a couple of PG58s. I was considering the SM48, but the PG58 has slightly better specs, and almost identical price.

The first thing I noticed out of the box was that the PG58 is slightly bigger and slightly heavier. It also has a different switch than the SM58. The metal screens protecting them aren't interchangeable. I then plugged in one microphone cable so the settings would be identical. I tried both mikes, one after the other, first with speaking and then with singing and playing guitar, and then I changed the settings, or more specifically, the effects and the EQ on the PA. I repeated the experiment, speaking and then singing while changing between mikes.

Here's what I noticed: The SM58 is slightly flatter in the mid range. The PG58 is slightly brighter and has a touch more presence. They are about equal on volume. The slight differences in tone can be easily manipulated with an EQ or just ordinary tone controls. Neither was susceptible to much feedback or vocal pop.

I haven't tried out this side by side comparison in a live situation or even in practice, as it's too time consuming and interferes with playing. It's difficulty to judge in those situations too, or at least awkward, but I have used a combination of the two in practice and no one seems to be able to tell the difference, except one person actually expressed a preference for the PG58, but that could be just the settings.

I looked at the specs for the two mikes side by side. The SM58 is a little flatter in response, especially at the high end, over 10K Hz, and it picks up a few dB before the PG 58, somewhere between 50 and 60 Hz. However, since the human vocal range is generally between around 300 and 3000 Hz, neither of these seems likely to have much effect, although the SM58 might be a tad more responsive for a bass singer.

I also tried out two different Behringer mikes and a Radio Shack mike. The Behringer 8500 was totally outclassed by both of the Shures, sounding tinny and thin and with little presence or volume. I tried out a Behringer 2000XM and was impressed by the similarity. These mikes sound almost identical (The B 2000 and the Shure SM). The Behringer 2000XM seems to have been discontinued, though, and replaced with the 1800XM, an inferior mike offered in bundles of three for under $50.

I then plugged in a Radio Shack mike that was a spare backup, not even taken out for practice. The model number is 33-3001, probably also discontinued. This was an excellent sounding mike, with good volume, presence and tone.

I didn't have any other mikes to test in this side by side experiment, but I did reach some conclusions:
There is quite a bit of snobbery in choosing microphones, with the Shure SM58 held up as some unreachable standard. They ARE sturdy, and they are good mikes and the price is not unreasonable, at around $100. However, there are other microphones which sound nearly identical and are also sturdy and reliable, at lower prices, including the Shure PG58, and most likely the SM48, though I didn't have any of those to test.

I wish more people would give unbiased reviews based on actual performance instead of condescension toward those who are either on a budget or looking for alternatives to the standard bearer. I'm giving this 4 stars only because I haven't had enough time to give an evaluation of how this holds up in comparison to the SM58.

This is identical to the [[ASIN:B000AORV3U Cannon UP638 Bass Drum Anchor]], which sells for nearly twice the price of this one. I own both models.

If you own a vintage bass drum with disappearing spurs, then this anchor will save you a lot of frustration. If you are not familiar with the term disappearing spurs, ut refers to the older (or cheaper on modern bass drums) spurs that are at a fixed angle and either fold or are pushed inside the bass drum when not in use. The [[ASIN:B0002F6WCS Gibraltar SC-BS2 Lt Wt Bass Drum Spurs With Bracket]] is an example of a modern model and are patterned after vintage spurs.

Some modern, less expensive bass drums like the older Tama Stagestar also require this anchor because they use modern disappearing spurs such as the Gibraltar SC-BS2. If you are an extremely heavy player and your bass drum does not stay put this will help anchor it.

This anchor works as intended, although even this anchor may not be enough for heavy players on vintage bass drums. In that case, do like we did back in the day and augment this with cord running from one side of your bass drum, around the back or your throne, to the other side of your bass drum (attach it to the T-Rod or tension rod between the claw and lug). In most cases you need not get this extreme, and at any rate you will still need the anchor to keep the bass drum from moving laterally.

I've uploaded some customer-supplied images at the top of this page that show close-ups of this anchor with detailed views of the wingnuts and how the bracket attaches to your bass drum hoop. If your bass drum creeps, you need this anchor!
Summary: Prevents bass drum creep and is required on vintage bass drums

Text:
How does a violin create tear-jerking high notes that vibrato and can actually increase in volume? Answer--the violin bow continues to supply energy. However, guitar strings, once struck, diminish in volume, and if used with pedals, the revised sound is usually a jump-into-effect-sound.

Ernie Ball Expression Overdrive (aka Expression) solves above problem. This variable-foot-control pedal adds crescendo and diminuendo to overdrive and boost. To explain, suppose one strikes a single string; then, its tone volume gradually decreases. Step on a standard overdrive stompbox's button, and tone suddenly adds (jumps into) distortion and boost. Press Expression, and the tone can smoothly crescendo upwards, adding distortion and boost, like how a violin bow can add more volume when playing those tear-jerking higher notes. More expressive—hence, appropriately named Ernie Ball Expression Series.

When playing chords, these crescendos and diminuendos can be played to sound like fluttering, also called interweave or layered effects. Expression on my Fender GDec30 modelling amp creates all kinds of new sounds... spacey, airey sounds, chimes, crunch, etc. Expression with my PA sounded mediocre.

Additionally, with Expression, there is no need to bend over to change gain. Shift from clean rhythm to robust lead rapidly. Fade in from low to high distortion. Go from clean rhythm to subdued distorted rhythm quickly. If coupled with its sister product Ernie Ball Ambient Delay, these two pedals produce remarkable sound effects. Add a variable wah pedal….you’d be a Variable Pedal God! :)

Looks durable, a smaller pedal than my wah pedals. When I'm pedaling Expression on carpet, a static noise creeps in. When pedaling on an effects board, no static noise. Still researching this static noise issue.

What’s strange is Expression doesn’t perform as a distortion pedal. Seems this should be its intended purpose—to foot control from clean to overdrive to distortion. But, I think this is intended as a new type of pedal sound.

A 5 star for an innovative product that creates crescendos and diminuendos in modern guitarist’s arsenal.

Updated October 18, 2022: When I first tried this pedal with a Fender Squire, I was getting almost no noticeable gain or dirt even with the drive knob turned all the way up.   However last week I was using it with an Epiphone Les Paul and it performed much better.

The positives:

1.  This is a fairly transparent overdrive and there is not much coloration to your original tone aside from a mids bump.  

2.  The pedal is touch sensitive and that is not easy to find in an overdrive or distortion pedal.  

3.  The pedal does not take up much space on your board and the power supply cable fits into the top.

4.  The pedal does seem to be true-bypass, as far as I could tell so far.

5.  Even with the tone control all the way up, this pedal never gets shrill or thin sounding.

6. With a humbucker guitar it delivers a nice low-to-mid-gain with some good harmonic overtones. Definitely a much more pleasant overdrive and a less nasal or abrasive tone than with most low-to-mid priced gain pedals.

The negatives:

1.  The pedal did not mesh well with either of my compressor pedals (the new Caline Python and my Coolmusic compressor) when the compressor was patched into the Overdrive.  The sound got squashed and there was barely any dirt at that point.  I had to shut the compressor off when using the overdrive.  Only bad thing about that was that the overdrive pedal did not really add much sustain to the signal.

2.  The footswitch on my overdrive pedal seems a bit flimsy and did not always engage when I clicked it.  

3.  As previously mentioned, there is not much gain / dirt coming from this pedal when using a single-coil guitar, even with the drive / gain knob all the way up.  It is like your foot is on the gas and not much is coming out. It performs much better though with a humbucker guitar.

Summary:   I bumped the rating from 3 to 3.5, rounded up to 4. Will continue to play with this pedal with my Epiphone Les Paul, but will use another pedal with the Squire Strat.  I like the transparent nature of the signal and the slight bump in the mids. The gain and the sustain come up a bit short compared to my T-Rex Diva Drive, which is roughly the same price. But I have a feeling that this Caline Overdrive was meant to be a more transparent, low gain pedal like the various pedals out there that try to capture the sound of the Klon Centaur.  Anyway, I am enjoying this pedal with a humbucker guitar, as it has some harmonic richness that other similar pedals lack.
Summary: Fairly Transparent; Works Better With Humbuckers Than With Single Coils

I've never played ukulele, but I have guitar experience, so I figured I'd get a tenor size with what little knowledge I have of them and research I've done. It weighs less than nothing, switching from this to my dreadnought makes me feel like I'm picking up some unwieldy monstrosity. It has good projection and sustain, and a warm, mellow sound, almost like what guitarists chase lol. But it's not your super happy ukulele sound, while still being very much a ukulele sound. You can tune tenors two different ways, which create in essence two different instruments. This comes tuned to standard ukulele gCEA. It has a curved back, which some low end ukuleles do not have.

And look at that wood! Black walnut? Much much nicer than I expected. The iridescence is top notch, makes you want to walk back and forth just to see the stripes change color lol. But is it solid, or veneer like the headstock? Can't seem to find a definitive answer to that. See my (blurry) pic of the inside; it sure looks like the side is at least solid wood, since the grain follows the strong outside pattern. The back, too. It would be weird that only the top isn't solid (the soundhole doesn't look like soundholes on solid top acoustic guitars). But solid wood doesn't really matter at this price point, and laminate means I won't have to baby it.

The sealed tuners are a bit wobbly but hold tune well enough; it would be the one upgrade I'd make. The accessories are great: padded gig bag, chord sheet, cleaning cloth, excellent nylon strap, excellent headstock tuner (better than some other headstock tuners I've tried; it actually matches up nicely to my onboard fishman tuners), 2 picks that may or may not be ukulele picks and remind me very much of my .88 tortexes, an extra set of quality strings.

Some fret ends are a little sharp, but you won't have to worry about that if you're just doing chords. There aren't any dead spots, I did have a little bit of buzzing at first, but that's gone away as the strings have settled in. I like the bottom loading bridge; that will make string changes much easier. I did notice some spacing, less than a mm, not sure if it's akin to the dreaded bridge lifting some acoustic guitars suffer. I'll update if that turns into a problem.

But overall, very beautiful, portable, playable. I'm glad I took a chance.
Summary: Beautiful iridescent (solid?) wood, curved back, warm and mellow sound.

There are a lot of cheap EQ pedals on the market, and most of them work just fine. But I opted for this Caline model because: (a) I have other Caline pedals and appreciate their value and build quality; (b) I wanted one with a master volume/gain control; (c) I wanted one affordable enough that I didn't have to feel sick about breaking if I used it improperly.

I got the CP-24 primarily to use with my guitar amp - it's excellent in the effects loop, where you can most purely impact EQ frequencies without then feeding those into a preamp, which itself has its own tone stack. You can also use it as a volume attenuator - set up your amp for the tone you want at any volume, and then roll back the gain using this EQ pedal in the FX loop. Works great for home/apartment practicing!

Guitar frequencies are more narrowly focused than this, and most frequencies below the 100Hz level are below what the guitar actually puts out. So you don't "need" a 10 band EQ, per se, but having one gives you more precise control. For example: maybe you want to boost mids, but really want to boost LOWER-mids, as opposed to a Tubesceamer-like effect. The CP-24 allows you to do that. I also want it because I could see using it with bass, synths, and other gear that much work more in a full range of frequencies.

The pedal itself is built very well, though I wouldn't put a lot of stress on the 11 slider knobs, which are plastic and could break off if rest or drop other things on top of it. The CP-24 is a great affordable option if you want a 10-band EQ and can't afford something like the MXR version.
Summary: Affordable, effective 10-Band EQ with universal gain/volume control

For those that don't know what this is, GraphTech has perfected a "man-made ivory" material that is basically made out of Teflon and is supposedly 500 times slipperier than graphite. Since most tuning instability comes from friction at the nut (even more so than bad tuners), people who know guitars will tell you that replacing the nut is an easy fix that might solve a lot of problems with the guitar.

I've used several of the GraphTech products now, including their nuts, string trees, and bridge saddles. All of them have been spectacular. I had one professionally installed on an older guitar I cared about, but recently got this Black TUSQ model to try installing by myself on a "project guitar". Before installing the GraphTech nut, the guitar was prone to going out of tune, and the original plastic bridge was angled or cut improperly, which was muting some of the higher strings.

Installation of the new GraphTech nut literally took all of 15 minutes. I did sand down the width a bit, but it was so close to the existing height I made no changes to bottom or slots. Secured it with some Elmer's glue, and now the guitar sounds much better tonally and, amazingly, stays much better in tune. It's made such a big difference, I'm thinking about what other cheap guitars I have now or might have in the future, that would benefit from this simple, inexpensive part.

I've been using Shubb capos for 30 years. I still have my original that I used on a daily basis for 15 years. I have three regular Shubb's, a Drop-D, and a partial 3-string is ingenious because let's say you have your guitar in standard tuning, and place the capo over the second fret on the D , G, and B strings-- you've got an A major chord. (Even if you strum the low E, that's the 5th of the A major chord. The slash chord is written like this A/E) So basically by using that capo you're playing an A major chord, but the GREAT thing is, because you DIDN'T change the tuning of the guitar, you can play around with adding all different upper register intervals and poly chords on top of the A chord, and then use regular barre chords, because you haven't changed the tuning, like you would in Open C or Open G tuning, etc.!

That's the brilliance of the partial capos!

🎼‼➡️ And try a full capo on the ENTIRE third fret, and then a 3 - string partial on the D - G - and B strings on the 5th fret and you've got yourself a C MAJOR chord! (MUTE THE LOW G STRING, OR AGAIN, LET IT RING OUT-- ITS THE 5TH INTERNAL OF THE C CHORD... WRITTEN C/G) There's your simulated Open C tuning... but it's NOT open C because you didn't change the tuning, you just added the capos, so you can STILL play barre chords or partial barres! You can strum the C chord, add a 9th (D- 10th fret on the high e string) and then play a partial Dm7 barre chord, to a G7 barre, back to the C chord that's capo'd, but add a 6th (A- 10th fret on the B string). You've got some basic 2 - 5 - 1 jazz going there.

Just use your imagination.

THIS IS WHY IT PAYS TO KNOW EVERY NOTE ON THE FRETBOARD! YOU CAN THINK OF THINGS LIKE THIS!

Text:
Anyone who knows even a little about acoustic guitars will NEVER confuse this guitar for a Martin or Taylor. Granted those guitars are priced in the thousands and this is $150. But this thing is really not even worth $150. The fact that this guitar comes with some decent beginner extras is the best thing about it.

If you're game to upgrade a few parts and do a little basic detail work you could make this guitar a little bit (but not much) better in terms of playability and performance. But I wouldn't recommend putting too much extra time or money into it because the neck and body just aren't of a quality to make it worth it. You'd be better off just buying a better guitar from the start. Construction feels super light and materials don't feel sturdy overall. It has the feel and sound of a guitar somewhere between a beginner instrument and a toy.

Sadly, some strings also fret out at the upper frets. That's a sign of uneven fret height and poor quality control. That relegates this guitar to a strummer at best. Tuners are not great but can be made better with some tightening of screws and hex nuts. Even with that though, it does not hold tune well.

To summarize, this is really not even a beginner level instrument. The sound and feel are bad enough to make playing generally unpleasant and would likely ward off many beginners from sticking with it. The beginners who do somehow stick with it will outgrow this guitar within a few months if not weeks. Spend a bit more than $150 and get a proper instrument that's higher quality. It will be worth it in the long run.

Text: I tried this pedal out, and there's only one reason for taking a star off.  On mine, the foot switch doesn't always register a change.  It's just a bad switch, and it can be replaced, which is a learning opportunity for me.  I actually do not need to turn it off most of the time, and to the extent that I don't need it, I have that much more impetus to get that effects loop selection pedal and leave this delay on in the appropriate chain.  The sound is fine.  I wasn't expecting any sort of Strymon spaced-out analog emulation awesomeness.  Delay pedals truly are BASIC these days.  I just needed a slapback, and this does that job fine.  Now, for someone like me, what really matters is how a few of these are going to sound in a row; budget multi-tap delay, anyone?  THAT is where this pedal is going to shine.  If you need a no-frills MTD setup, get a few of these and tweak away.  Get smart, and make your own reverb!  I only got one, but I'll spring for others.  As for the fact that Nux makes these for Amazon, I already expressed my sentiment in the title of this review.  I am not a believer in any sort of esoteric gear purity.  If you get the sound you want, who cares where the gear comes from?!  Again, analog delay pedals are a basic circuit nowadays, and if you don't want to build your own, then the less you have to pay, the better, ESPECIALLY if you are getting a sound that you can use or by which you can be inspired.  Anyway, enough preaching--this pedal is good enough for basic short-time delay needs and won't ask for a thousand hours of your time just to find a few sounds you MIGHT keep using for a few years at best.  So get one, and if you're too cool to be seen with it on your pedal board at the gig, it'll work fine in your studio rig or even as an inevitable hand-me-down (or Christmas gift!) for that younger relative that wishes they were you but doesn't have your chops and knowledge just yet.

I had the Peterson clip on for several years and recently dropped it, shattering the LCD. I really liked the accuracy of that tuner, but did not want to spend another $70. I did want something a little nicer than a Snark though, so I gave this one a shot.

It is built relatively well. Same quality plastic build as the Peterson. It is highly adjustable as far as position, and quite small. I can clip it to the bottom of the headstock near the nut on my Strat and position it behind the headstock, so it is invisible to the crowd on stage. I don't have a problem reading the tuner under lights. The display is thin and wide, but small overall. Not a huge border, so there is still a lot of screen real estate, and the layout of the display is clean and easy to read. It is straight forward to calibrate or compensate for lowered turnings, and the settings are saved after powering off. Bass and guitar settings are saved separately.

It is more sensitive to tuning than the $10 tuners I've tried like the Fender and Snark. It tunes up quite fast. I know some reviewers said otherwise, but maybe it's a matter of positioning? I'm not a fuzz guy. In 50 years of playing, I've owned one fuzz that I really liked, a first generation silver box Fulltone SoulDrive. I sold it when people were paying too much for them and I've regretted it since. Hated the others I tried, including a newer SoulDrive. I admit I haven't tried a lot of fuzz pedals over the years, but for the price I tried this one. I don't know what this circuit copies, but whatever it is I like it.

It's a mini sized pedal built in a metal pedal housing. There is rubber on the bottom and Sonicake includes a piece of velcro cut perfectly to fit on the bottom for pedalboard mounting. There's a business card with instructions for the pedal, but it's pretty intuitive. Regular 9v center negative center. You can't fit a battery inside, but you can buy very short 9v to the right size plug here on Amazon.

Now for the sound. Know how some fuzzes just get spitty? This one doesn't. It's creamy, as the name implies. That's the kind of fuzz I like. The fuzz knob is useful all along its path. The level control goes from zero to just a bit of gain above unity. Most of the volume change is in the first 50% of travel. The tone control seems to affect the high end and it has a pretty wide sweep. I like it at noon, so plenty of room to change the tone. The pots turn very smoothly and there's a nice bit of resistance which should keep them in place.

The footswitch is metal and feels substantial under the foot. Of note is that hitting the footswitch will light the pedal without any cables plugged in.

In conclusion, if you're looking for a small, well-built creamy fuzz, give this one a shot. And with free returns there's no risk. Glad I took that risk.
Summary: I'm not a fuzz guy, but I love this fuzz!

Interestingly, this lack of sensitivity is not mitigated by moving the tuner to other locations on the head stock. Also, although some clip-on tuners more readily pick up the twelfth fret harmonics, this unit doesn't seem to respond in that way. The tuner seems accurate enough, it simply lacks sensitivity making initial tuning and fine adjustments a challenge. Consequently, I can't see it being of much use in a performance environment.

Secondly, the metronome feature is absolutely useless. I've yet to figure out how this mode would benefit anyone. Overall, it's not a rip-off for the price; one can tune a guitar with it. But tuning with a standard guitar tuner or many of the other available clip-ons is an easier and quicker proposition. This unit will probably find a home on my travel guitar while my primary instruments will get continue to rely on larger and more useful units.

UPDATE:
After using this tuner on three different acoustic guitars and one electric in a variety of locations, I have to conclude it's essentially useless. The sensitivity issues noted above continue but I've also found this tuner consistently produces false readings compared with my Snark, Korg, and Intellitouch tuners. I changed the battery hoping this might be the root problem to no avail. Ultimately, any one of the free smart phone apps will serve you better than this tuner.

Text:
Had it for 8 months now. It comes with a urea saddle & nut, which are okay but I think for this price they both should've been bone. I had it tricked up: Colosi bone bridge pins; bone saddle; and a Zero Glide nut which I had custom made for this guitar for a drop-in fit, as well as a stainless steel zero fret. But truthfully, I wouldn't say any of that improved the sound or intonation to any major degree. But there is more sustain for sure, and the Zero Glide certainly changes the tone of open strings since they're now going over a fret at the nut. That helped greatly with the thin, pingy sound I was getting on the high E&B with certain string sets; that's no longer a problem. But overall, I'll say this to any future buyers: you don't need to do all the customizing I did, which cost me around $200 total. Play it just like it is and you'll be happy (unless you're extremely picky & precise about tone & tuning like I am.)

This guitar is above average, in fact unique due to the onboard effects, but I'm not thrilled with it completely by any means. It tunes rather poorly. The intonation is still off even after the new nut & saddle. The action has to be set fairly high to avoid buzz. It doesn't have very good projection; I use Newtone & TI Plectrum extra-heavy gauge strings and play with my thumb & fingers, rather aggressively sometimes, and it's sure not very loud unplugged - but not so soft that it's a problem. Using a pick to strum almost doubles the volume, but makes the tone too trebly for my taste. I like a more warm, woody sound like Kevin Eubanks gets, and can only get close to that sound with my thumb & fingers.

I play it every day, sometimes with reverb and sometimes not. I seldom use the chorus which does sound authentic but just isn't up my alley style-wise. The LL-TA sounds good enough that I'm motivated to go pick it up when the impulse hits. I just wish it tuned better and didn't have buzz & other noise problems unless the action is pretty darn high. It doesn't play very well higher up on the neck. The intonation goes off a little and certain strings get those buzzy sounds when picked hard. I keep raising the action via the truss rod to help with that, and it does help, but high action sucks for jazzy playing. A really precise setup by a true pro might help with these problems to some extent. It could be that the frets are slightly uneven straight from the factory, I'm not sure, but something is just not quite right, despite the Zero Glide making the strings even all the way down the neck and the saddle being sanded down to the appropriate height as far as I can tell. All of that should've helped with intonation & action, but it did not.

I used this on a 5string bass. I liked how this helps me slide around the fretboard easier. My friend tried it on her acoustic guitar and hated it.

Her reason for her opinion is simple. This stuff puts out a LOT more oil (or whatever it is) than you would think. This has the unintended consequence of the oil making your hard-earned callouses soft...which when playing guitar can lead to bleeding fingers pretty fast (and did for my friend).

To apply this you simply hold the handle and press down while running it along each string, one string at a time. I highly suggest you only use one slide down each string. At first it may not look like anything is getting on your strings, but give it a few minutes and you will start to see the excess oil appear and start pooling under the strings on your fretboard. That's ok. You will need to wipe away the excess, and I'm telling you, if you accidentally get too much, that excess oil may not come off easily (didn't for me at least). Mine left little pools of oil between the frets, and I only used one swipe and thought I had just a little on there. Naturally, this product also makes your fingers very oily feeling. My friend hated that part too, and I agree with her. Soft callouses = no callouses. This is a good product idea, and I like it in theory, and with my thick bass strings I didn't have the severe problem w soft fingertips that she did. Just be aware of the possibility of that being a problem for you.

It does what it says, but you may not like what else it does or how it feels on your fingers.
Summary: Good product idea, could causes problems for some people.

Text:
I'm not a keyboard player but always wanted to learn. Of course the first thing you need to do in order to play from sheet music is to memorize which lines/spaces on the staff correspond to which key. Well, I never wanted to learn THAT bad. This has the keys light up, which makes all the difference. I just hooked up my Nexus 7 tablet to it (it even comes with a USB cable that actually had the correct connector), downloaded the app from the Google Play store, and in a couple of minutes I was playing.

The sheet music comes up on your tablet or other device, and you can either play by yourself, at your own speed, just pressing the keys as they light up, or you can push "play" and it will play the song and you play along with it. You can change the tempo of the song (full tempo, 80%, 60% or 40% of full tempo), so keeping up isn't a problem. Of course the regular treble and bass clefs come up on the tablet, so you can get a feel for where the keys on the keyboard that correspond to the notes on the staff are located.

The amount of music available on the app seems fairly robust; they have categories for classical, traditional, jazz, pop, film score, as well as exercises. Some categories, like classical, exercises, and pop seem to have a good deal of music, while others like traditional, jazz and film score have less. For a beginner like me though, there's more than enough to keep me busy for a year or more.

I like the minimalist design - my last keyboard was covered in a plethora of sliders, buttons and switches, most of which I had absolutely no use for. This just has four controls: volume, sustain, tone (it has 20 built in sounds), and on/off. Sound quality from the speakers is okay, it's not going to fool anyone into thinking they're listening to a real piano, but for the money it creates a reasonable facsimile.

Overall I'm very happy with this unit and look forward to actually learning to play some music with it. And of course, hearing yourself playing something musical is the best inspiration there is as far as getting the beginner to practice more.

The jam feature seems gimmicky though I haven't played with it much. Overall, the presets, quality of effects etc are pretty good.

As a bluetooth speaker it's okay. The sound is reasonably balanced though it lacks true fidelity e.g. good sound stage, crisp clean high etc. I suspect part of the reason is a cheap SBC bluetooth audio codec. Codecs can make a huge difference. The should have at least used Apt-X which would produce better sound.

Overall, it's a piece of quality gear for those who want a solid practice amp in a tiny go anywhere form factor. As a bluetooth speaker it does fine but don't expect high fidelity.

These are advertised as "hand made." And they sure are. As in poor quality control, poor consistency, poor construction, poor sound. They have all the benefits of a product made by some teenager in his basement.

Quality control is poor. One of four shredded upon installation before even coming up to tune. And, yes, I followed the "manufacturer's" instructions to the letter (use pliers to make a sharp 90 degree bend, then cut). 25% waste is not acceptable.

The sound is poor. These have a tinny sound inconsistent with quality bass strings. Alas, this is not consistent from string to string, most noticeable on the third string, but also evident on the second. Not the rich tone of a true round wound, nor the thump of a flat. As stated, the consistency is poor. It would almost be better if all four strings had the same tone, because then we could just say they were poorly designed. These are poorly manufactured ("hand made").

The feel is poor. I disagree with those who say these need lubrication to handle slides properly. These feel like mushy round wound strings, although sliding is no problem. Still, it's hard to get the left hand feel necessary for decent playing. Basically, they're cheap round wounds dipped in paint. I haven't played them long enough to see whether the paint stays on or not. Other reviewers suggest it just chips off after a few days.

These strings only have two things going for them. First, they are billed as lasting upwards of double the life of an uncoated string. Maybe so, but given how nasty they feel and sound, that's hardly a benefit. Second, they look great, especially on my black JT Viola bass. Shame we have to listen to them as well. If you want cool looking strings you can hang on the wall, you'll love these. If you want acceptable sounding bass strings, these are not the way to go. So let's just look at them and not play them.

I "grew up" in the 1960's with a Fender Super Reverb, and used a Twin Reverb in the 1980's-2000's. The Twin was lost in Hurricane Katrina (all I have left is the beefy cast metal Fender nameplate). I went amp-less for several years, then bought a gadget called FootNote that combines a pedal board with a practice amp. That worked "OK" at best---too large for a pedal board, too quiet for an amp. So I treated myself to a Fender Champion 40 and am very, very pleased with the quality and sound (and light weight!). It's clearly not a military-grade device, but then neither am I. This amp will likely outlast me, and that's plenty good enough.

The amp has excellent tone on the clean side, similar to a Twin etc. The dirty side has some nice adjustments (as heard in the demo videos). It's plenty loud enough for practice and small venues, and will mic just as well as any other amp for larger venues. The reverb and effects are very good, with less "digital" sound than I am used to with simulated effects. Still, I prefer my separate Boss pedals that have a lot more control for the delay and chorus. But the Champion effects are plenty good enough for practice without hauling out my pedalboard.

BTW, the amp works fine with a two button footswitch P/N 0071359000 (which isn't clear in the online info or brief instruction manual). The footswitch controls the clean-dirty selection as well as effect off-on. The switch seems very well made and came with the required 1/4" cord.

So if you are a purist and like hauling 50-70 pound amps then get yourself a real Deluxe or Twin with nice hot tubes. But if you want a low price amp with very good sound and simple features this is a hard deal to beat.
Summary: Very good sound and quality in a lightweight amp

Text: I wanted an 88-key non-weighted keyboard that was light enough to take on the road to gigs, and that leveraged my existing Yamaha DGX keyboard knowledge.  This YPG-535 is all of that.  I found one used on e-bay for $300 with cosmetic damage (a few gouges in the top rear center--easily filled & painted, and a broken speaker grill on the right--easily bent back into place and barely noticeable now).  It was well packaged and arrived almost a week earlier than expected.  Beyond the cosmetic damage I noted, it works perfectly and fills the needs.  It adds many additional instruments and rhythms and songs to my existing DGX-220, and is the perfect "big brother" to that 76-key DGX-220.  I'm very happy with it.  They organ-style, non-weighted keys are very easy on the fingers and knuckles when running a hard glissando down the keyboard during some exciting rock song.  I'd been using my Yamaha DGX-660 on the road and discovered its weighted keys--although VERY nice for concert performances--aren't appropriate for rock/country dance gig performances.  A night of glissandos on it and one's knuckles would be scuffed--perhaps even bloody.  Not so with the YPG-535.  I recommend the 535 for home or road/gig use for its flexibility, full scale keyboard, and portability.  Do not expect weighted keys like in an analog or real piano--this has unweighted "organ touch" keys.  I grew up learning on a real spinet piano and loved its weighted keys, and I suspect weighted keys are probably best for beginners and folks taking piano lessons.  They provide the feedback and necessary resistance to teach a learner how to perform trills and repetitive rapid single notes better than an organ-style unweighted keyboard.  Buy one of these if you know how to play already, if you need portability and want a full 88-key digital grand piano with many different piano styles and sounds to choose from (along with full drum kits, orchestral instrumentation, and full-featured performance synthesizer sounds).  This one ranks a 9.5 out of 10 for me, leaving a tiny bit of room for some future feature of which I've not yet discovered.  Mine came with a wooden stand, music rest, power cable, and sustain pedal.  In retrospect I wouldn't opt for the wooden stand since I already have a Hercules X-stand for my DGX-220, and I simply bought a second tier stand to carry both pianos on one stand.  The wooden stand remains wrapped and unopened--perhaps I'll sell it to someone who wants one for their 88-key piano.
Summary: 88-keys, organ touch (not weighted keys), full-featured, light weight

This is a nice cover for the Evolve 50 base unit. It allows you to easily transport the speaker to/from your gigs, and also makes it easy to load the speaker in and out of vehicles. If you have an Evolve 50, I would say this is a must have.

This cover is very well designed. It has two well made zippers which you use to open a "flap", and you then slide the speaker base unit inside the case. Close up the zippers, and you are ready to move. There are handles on the top, sides, and even one on the bottom which makes it very easy to load the speaker. There are loop straps on the top which you can use to secure the top column array case that you got with your Evolve 50 onto this case for transport.

I do wish there were pockets for cables. It would be nice to throw the cables for the speaker into the case with the speaker, rather than having them go into a generic cable box. That would make setup even quicker.

This case has a telescoping "luggage style" pull handle, which makes it quite easy to move the speaker around. The instructions warn however not to tilt the case on two wheels and pull it. You should always roll the case on all 4 wheels - it is not made to hold the weight on only 2 wheels.

The padding inside is very well made. There are corner pieces that are made to hug the contours of the speaker (angled front grill). All of the padding is velcro'd in, so if you need to take it out to clean or replace it, you can easily do so.

Unfortunately, due to the design, this case does not fold flat at all, mostly because of the telescoping handle and also the protective foam. This makes it almost impossible to hide the case away under a table during a gig. I have to bring them back to my vehicle and store them there during the gig, then go back and get them. I would say this is the biggest negative of this cover.

If you need sound absorbing panels that will help decrease echos and appearance is important but not critical, these are highly recommended. They look pretty good but ATS also sells ones with a higher end looking fabric and tighter edges for just a bit more that are better if looks are very important to you.

To be clear: What these do is to absorb sound so it doesn't deflect around a room causing echos. Sound absorbing is NOT going to stop sound from passing through a wall. We have a 30x21 foot modern room with 22' ceilings that's all hard surfaces and glass. 6 of these on the second level reduced RT60 times from 5+ seconds of echo down to 3 seconds. When a car drives by the echo made it sound worse than it is and so while these don't stop the noise from coming in, they make it seem less impactful. We couldn't have 2 conversations at the same time in that room and now it's possible. Still far from where we want to be but we know we need approximately 315 square feet to get to our goal and at 48 ft2 our panels made a bigger difference than expected.

Other sound deadening tips: ATS also sells acoustic insulation. Use it to fill behind canvas art and wherever else you can. Also use memory foam carpet padding under any rugs, it is the singular most effective (and cheapest!) acoustic treatment we have found.
Summary: Excellent Accoustic Treatment, finish just OK

However, once I got the right drill and bit, it was cake and if I had it from the start, it would have been a flawless installation.

The good: This is an awesome pickup. I tested it running through a marshall halfstack, which as you know is not an acoustic friendly amp, and it still sounded like a woody, acoustic guitar. I have since then gigged and running it through PAs sounds killer. Switching to this, the audience is captivated when I play because it sounds the way it sounds acoustically. I actually prefer it plugged in now. Adjusting each string is easy as cake.

The downside: Not much really. I notice that I hear more string noise when I slide up or down the neck while playing, but it really isn't bad at all.

Recommendation: Get it. For the money, it is awesome. The tone is perfect, so if you have a cheap guitar, it will make it sound expensive. I would install this on a cheap or expensive guitar.

Full disclosure:  I am not a professional clarinet player but this Euro Cut Légère reed had good reviews here and also was recommended to me by several people.  My personal experience is that, ironic as it sounds, it needs a little breaking in and so does the player, to get used to it.  It vibrates pretty easily in low register  but I am struggling with it in the high register.  I do not struggle with cane reeds (Gonzalez being my favorite cane reeds).  The Légère lacks warmth...very noticeable.  It plays louder and sharper which for me translates to “cold.”  I will keep this reed and continue to work with it.  I bought a ligature recommended to me for this reed, a BG Flex, but not sure it allows enough vibration...had better luck with the old standard Rico everyone has.  I have purchased two more ligatures and will try them both with this reed.  I may also purchase a Légère Signature Classic to see if I like it better than the Euro Cut.  I don’t know one clarinet player who has not gone through multiple reeds, mouthpieces, and ligatures before settling on a set-up they find consistently reliable  for their music.  I am no exception to that!  UPDATE!  I bought and am using a Bambu ligature with a metal plate...it works fantastic with this reed.  Every note is sounding a lot better now and it’s easy to play altissimo with the new ligature (Bambu Nova). THIRD UPDATE:  I now love the Légère Reed EuroCut.  I needed to get used to it.  Furthermore, I am using the BG Flex ligature and find it is an excellent set up and works well in all registers.  I still maintain that the synthetic reeds lack the warmth of cane reeds but it’s a welcome tradeoff, considering how reliable and easy these reeds are to play.  I still use a cane reed at beginning of my practice to make myself work but then I switch to Légère to play music so I can focus on the music and not as much on working out my air support!

For a Made in China product, this initially felt good to the touch, but not sure if it is built for true professional use (despite the "PRO" in its nomenclature; because it is not built tough with professional-grade, heavy-duty materials. Too much plastic on this superlight device to withstand the wear-and-tear and everyday use/abuse under normal studio use. Although, the velocity keys are taut like a high-quality synth, they are not as sensitive (used with FL Studio 11). The sliders' friction is just right. And, the rubbery-feel of the knobs and pads seem to be made for heavy use. I might add that the pads are velocity-driven but not as sensitive, either. You'd have to make that extra effort to slap your fingers on the tiny rubber pads, to make your drum sounds go boom. Otherwise, you'd miss your timing mark because there is a fraction-of-a-second delay (which you can audibly discern) from the time you hit the pads to the moment you hear the sound on the monitor speakers. Still, compared with comparable keyboard controllers, this appears to be a better unit, for the price. Would I recommend this product? Yes, but only if you really need this many keys on a midi controller; the smaller Roland versions would probably suffice, with matching good price; I personally prefer Roland over the other brands for its consistent, relatively high quality across the many studio-grade instruments it offers over the years.

This is a simple humidifier for guitars with a round sound hole. It would not work for an f-hole archtop or other types of instruments such as mandolin or ukulele. Inside the sturdy plastic case is what appears to be an ordinary kitchen sponge. If you use distilled water (as recommended) it should last quite a while. The top comes off with a gentle press on the sides. The dry sponge can be a little difficult to remove with fingers but tweezers or needle nose pliers work perfectly. Don't push it all the way in after moistening and you won't have a problem. I drip a little distilled water on the sponge, squeeze out any excess, and the assembled case pops in easily between the D and G strings, suspended in the middle of the sound hole. They can't be seen in the photo but there are small ridges on each side that hold the top in place against the strings. I've never had one of these move from where I left it.

If the sponge isn't dripping wet you should never have a problem with drops of water in the guitar or case. When the humidity is very low (30% or less) the sponge dries out in 2 to 3 days even if the case isn't opened. As with most humidifiers of this type you will have to check every few days.

If you have ever had a crack appear in the top of favorite guitar (or don't want to see one) use a guitar humidifier! Especially during the winter - heating a house tends to drop the indoor humidity below safe levels (between 45% and 60% is ideal for most guitars). Air conditioning can do the same. For especially valuable guitars it would be worth buying a hygrometer to keep in the case but for most guitars having one in the room where you keep you guitar(s) is okay. For many reasons it's always best to keep your guitar in a case or gig bag when not in use. A humidifier is inexpensive extra precaution at those times of year when temperature or humidity changes quickly.
Summary: A Good Basic Humidifier for Round Hole Acoustic Guitars

The display was bright and colorful - had absolutely no trouble seeing it in a brightly lit room.

I didn't try any of the other modes because I only have a guitar, but this thing can also help tune a bass guitar and even a violin.

Bigger kids will need to have full-size keys in order to learn how to actually play and have proper spacing for their fingers.

My kids hop right on and like to play the pre-recorded songs, and also enjoy cycling through the sounds. I'd much rather have them beating this thing up than messing with my "real" keyboard, and I feel the same about this in classroom use for little kids. I don't think I'd like to see kids destroying keyboards that I spent a few hundred bucks on per unit.
