The sound quality of this wireless mic kit is phenominal...crystal clear, wide frequency response. The mic head has a built-in windsock that all but eliminated breath-pops. I found the mic to be not very sensitive and quite directional...best to keep it within 6" and pointed at you. At one point I had a pack of barking dogs around me and my wife said she couldn't hear them through the amp at all(she was inside, I was outside). With the receiver indoors on the second floor of the house I went outside to test the range of the mic/receiver. I generally found that I could get about 125' before the signal would begin to cut out, presumably will be further if the receiver is outside too. Since this is digital there is no static, only muted silence when the signal drops. Throughout testing we found that there was never any pops, clicks, static or other unwanted noises passed through to the amp. The mic switch has three positions - off, mute and on. I found that the mic and receiver were able to pair up and start working instantaneously when switched on from the off position, again with no unwanted sounds. The receiver has connections for both balanced mic and line-out outputs as well as a gain control. Both outputs are 1/4" phone plug, if you want to connect it to other types of inputs you'll have to provide your own cables/connectors/adapters. It also has LED's to show the RF link as well as received modulation...simple and helpful. There is an LED on the mic, but so far I haven't figured out yet what it's supposed to show, it only flashed for a moment when you first turn it on...maybe it will flash for low battery? If not then it seems kind of useless...oh well. Both the receiver and the mic have a nice solid build quality and feel to them, without being unnecessarily heavy or dense. The receiver runs on 12-15V DC, so it won't be difficult to rig it for non-AC operation...from a car or portable battery...but you'll have to provide that yourself, the kit only comes with a 15V AC adapter. The kit also comes with a VERY nice internally padded hard carrying case to keep all of the kit items safe and together. I put together my own kit of audio cables, connectors and adapters, and was able to store them in an open pocket in the carrying case. At this point I should be able to just grab the case and be able to connect to almost any type of audio input. Overall I am very pleased with this system.
Summary: Fantastic Sounding Mic! Solid build, good range...

I received my "updated" Enya U concert ukulele on January 14th, 2023 and I am primarily a fingerpicker. I've been eyeing the travel uke for a while. When it arrived, I instantly feel in love with the slim bodied stylish look and feel. I thought to myself, this is perfection. I played it daily having a great journey while bonding with my new uke companion. Fast forward 1 week to January 21st, 2023 and the honeymoon is over. The G string started to fray and to my surprise the A string decided too as well. A quick email to Enya and by the response from Emma at Enya it became apparent "strings for life" was a discontinued promotion. I've never seen stock strings disintegrate within a week. Emma at Enya offered a $10 refund to purchase a new set of strings which I declined. I decided to try a set of Martin M600 strings and as I was about to swap the strings out I discovered fret wear under the A string and G string. Another email to Enya with pictures and this is the response I received from Megan at Enya, "Please don't worry about ukulele fret wear, it is normal that there is no noise during your use." I'm sorry but I have never experienced fret wear on an instrument that you can see and feel with the first week of playing. I have had a Flea from Magic Fluke for at least a decade with a plastic fretboard and it only shows minimal fret wear. How can this be acceptable in a musical instrument? It is an absolute shame that this ukulele cannot stand up to regular use.

I cannot recommend this ukulele and I am disappointed by Enya customer service. There is no value in disposable instruments.

That said, I've played other Enya ukes and overall I am impressed by the brand but not this particular ukulele.

The Grover GP1103 Perfect Guitar Nut is a zinc casting that fits on top of your existing guitar nut to elevate the strings about 3/8 inches. Once elevated, you will play your guitar with a slide or tone bar, but you will no longer be able to press the strings down on the frets.
I used the Grover Nut to convert my 1970 Lotus F215 acoustic to high action so I could play lap steel and Hawaiian style. After 50 years, the neck had warped slightly, but that problem is irrelevant with the nut modification.
Before installing, I used files to smooth any rough edges, then I covered the surfaces that would touch my guitar with blue tape so that they would not leave an impression or scar the guitar surface. Card stock would have worked as well.
To install, I loosened all the strings of my guitar, inserted the Grover Nut underneath, and slid the nut to the top of the neck. You may need to loosen your strings more to get the new nut over your old nut and to avoid scratching your fingerboard. I placed the strings loosely in the corresponding slots on the Grover Nut. Then I positioned the Grover Nut so that the flat side faced the bridge and was exactly in line with the forward surface of the old nut. I centered the Grover Nut on the fingerboard, tightened the strings and tuned them. Total time: less than 10 minutes. The cost is low and the sound is great.
I consider this a superior product to the angle iron type (such as Golden Gate Accordion Accessory F3303.
Note, The intonation on your guitar will remain perfect if the leading edge of the Grover Nut is in line with your original nut -- otherwise, the notes may not correspond perfectly to the underlying frets any more. Once elevated, the guitar won't be fretted, though, so intonation is kind of irrelevant.
Helpful Hints:
1. Frequently the Grover Nut will extend beyond the edges of your neck. This probably won't affect your playing, but you may find it inconvenient or you may not like the look. If you have any doubt, measure the width of your current nut and compare. The Grover Nut is about 1.88 inches in width.
2. In my experience, after installing the Grover Nut, it is not always necessary to change the height of the bridge in order to play with a tone bar like a lap steel guitar. However, if you have a moveable bridge (like a Telecaster) you may wish to raise it, or you can get or make a higher bone bridge for your acoustic guitar.

The main thing is that this is a wonderful guitar rest that really does help me achieve a much more comfortable ergonomic playing position. I’ve tried several positions that work, depending on where I want the guitar, but my favorite is at the top of the lower bout. I’m a stickler for positions that let me play with a minimum of strain, tension, pressure, or contortion. I want to caress the strings with my left hand fingers when I am playing chords, not clamp them. I play jazz chords up to the guitar body. My thumb supports the guitar neck. The neck does not rest in the V between my thumb and my index finger. Despite this, I didn’t realize how much of my energy was going to holding up the neck and keeping the body from slipping until I tried this gadget. Suddenly the neck was where I wanted it without my having to support it. My tension cut way back, and I was able to play with much more grace, ease, and speed. Also, the guitar’s weight seems cut in half. I now sit with my feet flat on the floor, legs spread, very comfortable, and the guitar isn’t sliding, and the back of the guitar is several inches away from my body for the best tone. If you play seated, do try this. It’s definitely worth the money.

Little effort was used by VOX's production engineers to produce the same level of audio output from each preset. (A group of 13 year olds could have done an equally effective job). Sure - each preset shows some of the ways the StompLab can be utilized, but it actually shows you best how to NOT set up your user presets so they are useful.

The manual throws the various settings you can use in your presets in the appendix. Not knowing much about all the various amps and cabs it attempts to emulate - I'm a little at a loss as a beginner, and simply did my best to find a combo that sounded good.

There is no where in the manual where it details each of the 100+ presets in StompLab. They don't seem to list them on their website either. It is possible in edit mode to go through each detent of the knob and discover each setting selected, and use the stomp buttons to view the actual knob settings stored, but that's a job VOX should have done for us.

What I did with it, and why I gave it 5 stars.
1 - set up a clean setting - simply my amp/cab combo - with gain and volume set to produce a clean tone => store in your first preset
2 - copy that and add a little reverb to my next preset
3 - copy that and add a little chorus for the third preset
4 - copy that and boost the gain and lower the volume to give a little edge (or switch my amp to overdrive set low gain)
5 - use the last one with a medium gain and a lower volume (to maintain same level of audio output)
6 - use the last settings to create high gain and enough volume to match the volume out

This allows me to gracefully switch from simple to gradually edgier sound with out having to bend over and tweak knobs.
I gave it 5 stars because in spite of it's poor [?] presets and a steep learning curve, for the price - I would have a hard time achieving this variety of sound with anything else.

=====

[update] After having used the Stomplab for a few months - usually by itself with good headphones and NOT the Peavy (used Rage 158) - I decided to do some amp shopping. You would do well to look at my other review for the VOX Pathfinder if you are needing a practice amp at home and love VOX's clean/warm tone. The Peavey had clean ... but it felt sterile. The VOX feels more like a good book in an easy chair by the fireplace.

I'm going to sound like a fanboy for VOX. I'm sorry. This Stomplab and the Pathfinder make for a very compact and extremely effective pair in my sound chain. What the Pathfinder can't do - the Stomplab does perfectly. For the size and price, it may be a long time before I need to upgrade anything - and if I do - it will probably be something with 40+ Watts and a 12 inch speaker for performance (VOX are you reading this? I want a solid state Pathfinder 40 with a 12 inch speaker, Bass/Mid/Treble, Vol/Gain, and aux in for practice and headphone/line-out - and let it compete with the Fender Champion at the $200-250 price-point).

I love this little pocket amp so much. Here's what you're actually getting:
- No batteries. This charges (and charges quickly) via USB-C. The battery life is pretty amazing, but I can't estimate how long it lasts. At least 4+ hours
- It lets you plug in headphones and combine 4 different amps+effects
- You can easily connect your phone to the device via bluetooth. This let's you play music while playing guitar into the same headphones. You can control the mix between guitar audio and bluetooth audio by pushing volume up/down on your phone.
- AMP: Let's you toggle between 6 different amp models, but realistically what you get are 2 different clean, 2 overdrive and 2 distortion sounds. There is a gain knob that let's you control how much overdrive or distortion. My favorite is "Pink", which is supposedly based on "ENGL Powerball II"
- MOD: This let's you add one effect, such as Chorus, Rotary, Tremolo, Vibrato, Flanger and Phaser.
- DLY: This let's you toggle between 6 different types of delay effects (which I honestly didn't notice too much of a difference)
- RVB: This let's you toggle between 6 different reverb, such as Studio, Room, Hall, Church, Plate, etc.
- The output is 1/8", not 1/4". So if you want to plug this into an amp, you'd need an adapter.

For MOD, DLY or RVB, what you do is push that button to switch into that mode. Then the FX wheel let's you adjust just that effect. So you can dial up reverb and delay, but add only a little flanger. Obviously you're only getting a single adjustment per effect, and it's mostly the strength and mix. Max for most of the MOD effects is just wildly crazy.

You can also just have no reverb, mod or delay effect at all.

The final wheel is TONE, and that let's you control the tone of your guitar. Honestly, I just left it at 10. Turning down tone leaves your guitar sounding a bit muddy.

It's a ton of tonal combinations. You can go from metal to rock to trippy space rock with way too much delay and reverb and phaser. While I also have an Amoon Pockrock (which has many of the same capabilities, including adding drum beats), I was never really happy with the quality of tone. Plus that takes batteries or you have to plug it in. This seemingly lasts forever and is rechargeable.

You're obviously not going to gig with this. When you switch effects (like Delay to Reverb), the signal will cut out briefly. And if you change the FX value, sometimes you get a weird wobbling as the signal processor is changing the settings. But once you're dialed, it's great.

Anyway, I love this thing. I can play and get a great tone in my headphones while playing along to music from my phone. It's nice having all of the adjustments basically on my guitar so I can play on the couch while reclining.

Thanks for reading! I hope you found this review helpful!
Summary: I love this portable USB-C chargeable headphone effects amp

The Mini and the Joyo were exceptionally close in sound, and the East River was a lttle less harsh and a touch warmer, but all 3 sounded like an 808.

People have said on the interwebs there's a noticeable difference between the Mini and the TS808, but to my ears the difference is about the same as what you'd get from two TS808's, as they all have the tiniest of variable differences. Fortunately, Amazon promptly replaced it, but I'm still a bit disappointed that something with such an obvious defect made it through Fishman's quality control.

Now that I've got that out of the away, let me say that this pedal is the ultimate for getting your piezo-equipped acoustic to sound as if it were mic'd instead. It's VERY solidly built, but the main feature here is the ability to store 16 presets chosen from the vast library of sound sets available online from Fishman. To appreciate that, you have to know how this pedal works, so here it is.

Fishman has built, and maintains and updates a library of specific guitar/mic combinations. So the idea is to visit the library online, find your guitar, and then choose a mic combination and then download and assign it to one of 16 user-selectable locations stored in the pedal (using the large rotary knob in the middle). So, for example, you can download the patch for - say - a Taylor 414ce with a Neumann U87 or Shure SM 57 (or several others), and assign it to one of the 16 locations. Then you plug in your Taylor, select the assigned location, and play. Instead of piezo quack, you get an excellent emulation of your guitar with the specified mic. The sounds are very authentic sounding, and are a huge improvement over the piezo sound.

This is just an awesome piece of gear for gigging acoustic players who don't want to deal with compromises involved in mic'ing an acoustic guitar (you've pretty much got to be seated, while refraining from moving your guitar away from the proper proximity to the mic). Well worth the price assuming you don't get a lemon like my first one.

These Grover harps are good quality but need to be cared for like any musical instrument.
*Dry them off when your done playing.
*Don't pluck too hard (Learn how to get the volume from your mouth and throat)

It turns out the menu button was defective on TWO of the units I received. The second was a replacement, hoping I had received a dud with the original tuner. Pressing the right arrow to navigate into a sub-selection would result in an up or down navigation instead.

After experimenting with different ways of using the button for such a basic function (navigate right) I figured the button itself was to blame. So I sent it back and the second one had the same issue.

I remember another reviewer mentioning the 'random menu generator'. A better description would be: menus from directions other than those you've chosen.

A better button mechanism or software fix could probably improve accuracy, but this tuner isn't really ready for guitar players yet. It needs a data wheel to scroll through menu choices faster than the slow click-click-click-click...select of the current setup. Of course I never got far, due to the issue I mentioned. But I did see a couple of reviewers describe how long it took to scroll through the tunings.

For the record: I received a refund for the first tuner and got the second one for free. Not exactly sure what happened there. But I sent the free one back too. It's unusable without the ability to navigate right.

Now I have a Peterson Stroboclip HD and a TC Electronics PolyTune Clip (Black). The PolyTune lets you strum, then displays which strings are out (and which direction to tune - it monitors in real-time until they're correct). It also has a chromatic tuner and a strobe tuner, like the Peterson Stroboclip HD. Both have 'sweetened tuning' settings and capo options and additional features. Combined, they cost the same as the sad, defective Roadie 3.

Note: The Polytune Clip is much cheaper on Sweetwater and they stopped making the Peterson, so you'll have to get that one while you can.

Boss has a free tuner app for Apple and Android. Reviewers says it works well with a phone's built in microphone, but better with an external mic.

Peterson has a Stroboclip app for $4.99. It has the same software as all of their tuners - even the desktop models.

My advice is: wait until they iron out the kinks in this new product. I might try again in the future because it seems interesting. But in the meantime, there are plenty of great tuners from established brands that both work, and satisfy the need for incredible tech guitar gadgets.

Good luck in your tuner hunt. I hope you found this information useful.

Text: Good value for the money

Recently installed a pristine Pickering XV-15/625e I bought years ago but never got around to using.  Put it in a Marantz 6300, installed it in the bedroom, and got some great new records.  At first I was a little disappointed with the sound.  It was a bit thin.  I thought that the Pickering might have aged out and perhaps the internals had dried up, hardened or softened just sitting in the case for all those years. Tried several receivers with good phono preamps but the results varied little.  Dug out some vintage external preamps but was still not delighted.  I finally got the Shure SFG-2 Tracking Force Gauge.  That was the missing link in my meticulous setup.  I've had some fine cartridges over the years, but few had the little brush attachment. Never felt the need for a brush.  I take good care of my records.  They are clean and static free.  But despite my best efforts, I quickly learned how notoriously inaccurate the calibration of even a good tonearm can be if you don't have a proper way to measure the tracking force.  Turned out the extra gram I thought I had added per the manufacturers spec to compensate for the brush was not even close.  So I used the guage, got a good reference for the stylus, added the extra gram, checked again and now I'm blasting Miles Davis Jack Johnson.  It's full, bright, has a nice throbbing bottom end.  No skips, no rumble.  A world of difference and I owe it all to getting the tracking dialed in with the help of this sweet little gauge.  Talk about money well spent!  Now I'll be setting up my Technics SL-1200 MK2 with a Stanton 681EEE downstairs in my studio.  I use that table more and I think it is pretty well balanced, but soon I will know for certain. Lesson learned.  You can't set up a good turntable without a good tracking gauge.  This is the best one I've ever used. Don't see any reason to spend big bucks on a digital gauge.  This is accurate and inexpensive and an essential tool for serious vinyl lovers.
Summary: Magnificent.  I was nearly a gram light!

Text: Some people have asked for the height of this stand.  Well, that depends on "how far apart" you adjust the feet.  You can adjust the spread of the feet from narrow to very wide.  But, "the narrower the spread, the less stable the stand" becomes.  I adjusted the feet so that there was a moderate spread.  I then adjusted the tilt so that there was no tilt at all.  For my situation, the bottom of my amp will be about 21 inches above the floor.  And of course, if I tilt the amp back, the front of the amp will be more than 21 inches above the floor.  The only way to move the entire amp up or down is to adjust the spread of the feet. You can easily make it so that your amp will be lower than 21 inches.  But if you try to raise the entire amp higher than 21 inches by moving the feet closer together, the stand will become unstable.  I'm going to say that the max height from the floor to the bottom of your amp is about 21 inches.  On my stand, the SPACE BETWEEN the upright posts is 12 and 1/4 inches.

I also soaked the picks in hot water (boiling), and slipped them on out of the water to stretch them to fit my fingers. I’ve done this with the more traditional plastic finger picks in the past. I wanted a compact stand I could rest my bass, guitar, or banjo on. I have a couple of stands with the yoke and one of them can handle any of my instruments; however, m when setup, it was always seeming to be in my way. I tried one of these A frame stands in the past, but I was not pleased with the instability of the instruments when they were resting on the stand. I have several Fender basses, a G&L guitar and Deering Sierra banjo. You will need to set the instrument and make sure it is stable because the back of the instrument will rest against the padding, but the neck may not appear to line up with the top of the frame of the stand. I think the secret with this type of stand is set the instrument, give it a little side to side shake to ensure it is stable.
I did not have a problem with the cable being plugged into the bass or guitar while it was on the stand. Will this work for every instrument shape? Probably not, but for the price, it is worth giving it a try.
I would probably not use this on a stage unless it was tucked in behind an amp or cab where someone is unlikely to knock into it. A more traditional stand would provide a little more security, in my humble opinion. Stages are tricky places with cables, instruments, and gear scattered about and people moving around.
Bottomline, yes I would recommend this stand. It folds to be quite compact and when setup, it's stable.

So after an hour of playing my shoulder would inevitably start aching and the strap would start digging into my shoulder. Then I'd have to stop playing. Major bummer.

I needed a strap that was not only wide, but also thick and cushioned. This strap fits the bill perfectly. I got the medium brown one. The materials and craftsmanship are easily handsome enough to be attached to a Les Paul. But the main thing is that it is not only wide, but also very thick and cushioned. It has plenty of length too so it is adjustable to nearly anyone's size and playing preference. I am now able to play for a longer time with far less pain and discomfort.

Straps are often an afterthought for many guitar players. A lot of times they are chosen based on cosmetics first. Don't get me wrong, I like a nice looking strap too. But the first consideration for any strap should be support and comfort. If you are comfortable and not in pain you will play better and you will play LONGER. Text: I love this little amp, it's just fantastic! I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this amp to anyone. I'm very very pleased.

[[VIDEOID:4e10ee8844898cab9835dac606f5bd29]] I had previously bought a Valeton Rushead Max headphone amp which I liked, but I was curious about the Vox AmPlugs since they are the most well-known headphone amps. I decided to give the AC30 version a try since the AC30 is probably Vox's most famous amp. I found the sound quality to be pretty good, though I typically play harder rock so I wasn't impressed with the low amount of gain available on this. The Valeton's two more distorted amp models are definitely far better for higher gain options. The Valeton also has more effects options, where I can mix a delay, reverb, and either flanger, chorus, or tremolo, and control how much of them I have via knobs on top. The AC30 AmPlug just has more tremolo I can add via a button on the side. For the clean tone, I find the Valeton's clean rather bland, while this Vox AmPlug's clean tone had just a slight bit of crunch to it which gave it more character. So if you are after solely a nice classic rock clean tone, I think this AC30 AmPlug would probably be better for you. Build-wise, I wasn't overly impressed with this AmPlug. The rotating hinge was a small benefit to make it a bit more portable, but it wasn't a huge improvement and the plastic this is built from seems much weaker than the plastic the Valeton is made out of. I had to make sure I gripped this Vox AmPlug right by the guitar plug when I pulled it out or else I worried I would risk breaking this, while the Valeton I feel pretty comfortable gripping anywhere to pull it out and it never feels like it is going to break. Also, while you can use rechargeable batteries in this AmPlug, the Valeton having an in-built rechargeable battery where you can just plug a micro USB cable into the device to charge it is much more convenient than having to change batteries.

So overall, the Valeton feels sturdier and has better distorted tones. The AC30 AmPlug does have a rotating plug which makes it slightly more compact, and the clean tone is much better on the AC30. I have gotten both a Marshall Code 50 and a Digitech RP255 multi-effects pedal in the last year or so, and I have played a number of different tube amps at local guitar stores including a Vox AC10 a few times. This AmPlug gets pretty close to the AC10's tone, though it sounds noticeably thinner though most of that probably has to do with playing it through headphones or a portable speaker instead of through a 1x10" guitar combo amp. The AC30 model on the RP255 pedal and the "Brit '50s" model on the Code 50 both sound very similar to this, so there doesn't seem to be anything particularly special about Vox's modeling of their AC30 amp. I ended up giving mine to a relative who plays acoustic guitar and is starting to look into getting into electrics, as well. I would recommend the Valeton Rushead Max to most people looking for a headphone amp with its better build quality, distorted tones, and extra versatility, but if you really love the AC30 tone and want a little headphone amp with a close approximation of it and a neat design, then this may be the way to go. Note that even though they are called "headphone" amps, you can plug an audio cable from this into a portable speaker with an AUX in and effectively have a mini amp (I use a Vanzom ClimberZ, which sounds particularly good for this usage). I would recommend using this sort of setup to beginners. Since most people generally have a portable speaker to listen to music, it costs the same (or less) to get a headphone amp than a small practice amp and it will sound the same (or better) to go this route. Plus, when you progress to more advanced amps, a cheap beginner combo amp you'll probably be looking at getting rid of (and likely for a loss), while a headphone amp you'll always want to have handy for travel or for quiet headphone practice.

Update September 26, 2021:
I recently purchased two new pedals, a Diezel Herbert and an Alexander Jubilee Overdrive, and was looking for a way to listen to them with headphones. So I decided to try out a Boss Pocket GT, a LEKATO Headphone Amp, and a Fender Mustang Micro. After trying these out, my new favorite headphone amp is a Fender Mustang Micro. It is pricey at around $100 used or on sale, but it sounded better and less fizzy than the Valeton Rushead Max, is more compact probably even than the Vox AC30 without being flimsy like the Vox one, and can even record which I haven't tried yet. The LEKATO was also interesting with a separate section for cab sims, and I would love to see Fender or Vox add cab sims into their headphone amps, but the preamps on the LEKATO were by far the worst and so I ended up keeping the Mustang Micro. If you can swing the extra cost, I would definitely recommend the Fender Mustang Micro.
Summary: Pretty good clean sound, but build quality is lacking

I recently bought a Blue 101i enCORE instrument microphone to amplify acoustic guitars. The only microphone I have to compare the Blue 101i microphone with is a Shure SM57 (which happens to be exactly what I should compare it to since their price-points are similar and they are both dynamic instrument microphones). Both microphones do a great job amplifying acoustic guitars, but I am giving the Blue 101i microphone the nod over the Shure SM57 microphone because of it's more consistent proximity effect. The Shure SM57 tends to create a deeper bass as I move the guitar closer to the microphone while playing (and it also gets a little "boomy" and muddy-sounding if placed close to the guitar's sound-hole), whereas the Blue 100i tends to be more consistent in it's bass and treble effects as I move my guitar while playing (which tends to be more true to my amplifier settings). The Blue 101i microphone will sound a little more "bassy" as I approach the guitar's  sound-hole, but not to the same degree as the Shure SM57 microphone does. This next statement is kind of hard to explain without you being able to listen to the microphones, but I'll give it a shot....the Blue 101i microphone allows the acoustic guitar to sound, well, more like an acoustic guitar; much more so than the SM57 microphone. Like I said, you'd have to hear the microphones in a side-by-side comparison to be able to tell the difference. Having said all of this, modern preamps, mixers and amplifiers, etc can tweak any sound-difference between similar microphones to a point where they sound nearly identical, but if you don't have that equipment, microphone choice is more crucial. Both microphones are excellent choices, but due to the proximity-effect, I feel that the Blue 101i is the better instrument microphone for use with an acoustic guitar, especially for live stage performances or studio recording, or when you're just sitting around your family room strumming some tunes.

Let me start by saying there are some good things about this pedal.
For one, the crybaby effect is pretty good.
The fact that you can change the order of the effects in the software is nice.
Some of the effects are cool.
The software is easy to figure out, and connecting to the unit is fast.
Switching patches has nearly no noticeable lag.

Then there are the things I really hated.

I hated the expression pedal.
There is no visual indication of the state of the expression pedal. Is it on? Is it off?

The expression pedal, on most patches by default, operates as both volume and expression. This means that if you want to use the expression pedal for something like the crybaby, your only option is full volume - because you first have to push the expression pedal all of the way down in order to activate the crybaby.
Certainly you can remove the volume pedal from the patches - but then you probably want an external volume pedal - which kind of defeats the purpose of a multi-effects unit in my humble opinion.

Also, it's way too easy to accidently turn the expression pedal on and off. If you're not very careful, every time you press it forward, it switches state.

I hated the user navigation.
I purchased the optional FS3X to use with this, and honestly it's kind of a joke. While it makes it slightly easier to use the looper, the FS3X operations are by-and-large redundant to what you can do with the existing buttons. Beyond using the extension for the looper operations, you can put it into "FS3X" mode - which basically just turns two of those switches into 'up' and 'down' buttons - which are accessible from the main unit regardless of which 'mode' you put that into.

Furthermore, when you put the FS3X into FS3X mode, with the current firmware - if you accidently activate the looper by pressing the looper switch JUST ONCE, it goes into record mode and will then start playing the loop - and depending on the mode the main unit is in - there's no way to stop it from looping.

There's no way to switch between the 3 modes without getting down onto the floor, and navigating through the menu by hand.

There are basically 3 modes this can do, arguably the most useful is 'stomp box' mode which allows you to turn 3 different effects on or off within the patch. You can leave the unit in 'stomp box' mode, then hit the 2 right pedals simultaneously to switch to "patch mode" - however it's design makes it quite difficult to do this, and it's difficult to not accidently activate the looper when doing this. When you're not in stompbox mode, there is no way to switch to stompbox mode using any combination of foot switches.

I hated the echo effects.
To my ear, the echo effects on this unit sounded fake, harsh, and distorted. I tried several of the 'stomp boxes' and settings, and just never could make it sound real enough for my tastes. This is completely subjective, of course. You may like them.
Summary: Not a replacement for a full size effects unit - even with the optional FS3X.

I buy TOO MANY effects, a common disease. Many, maybe most, wind up in this drawer I have. Not this one. I bought it to punch up the treble on my Supro Blues King 12, an amp which I love dirty (as in "Bluesy") but which I found lacking a little in the treble/presence department for the full range of clean sounds. The amp when clean was great for jazz, but too subdued high up for country, for example, or to make the most of a Strat's in-between  or bridge-only positions. This pedal solved that...completely. I leave it on pretty much all the time now: it's great at what it does. Understand, though, that although it does have a "Gain" pot, it is NOT an overdrive pedal unless by that you mean a pedal with enough gain (as in amplification) that it can drive your pre-amp or power tubes to interesting distraction  - THAT it will do, but it won't otherwise fuzz up your sound on its own. Even at max, there very little clipping to be heard. I call that a good thing. I use it for clean, and it's great for that. I usually have the Gain knob all the way down, then fiddle with the level knob. I suspect others will find that Gain knob just the thing, but we're all different, thankfully. The little toggle, by the way is VERY handy, gives you three entirely different ranges of effect. As I guess you can tell, I love this pedal. Use it in line with its make-up, and you'll love it too. My qualifications? I've been playing for 50 years. You decide whether that's good or bad!

Text: Good and well packaged

Well, kudos to a guitar manufacturer that actually wants to help people learn to play the guitar. For a very low one-time price, a person who wants to learn can skip the 25 dollar-per-half-hour in-person lesson cost and learn at their own pace when they want to and have the time.

Personally, I played guitar for a number years in my twenties, and I two years ago began playing again and practicing on my own. I've spent many hours binge watching my favorite old shows and movies while doing finger exercises, and I can do anything I've seen in any of the videos that are part of this plan. But still, I was fascinated by this approach to getting a beginner a "foot hold" through on line education.

This approach lets a student choose a "path" (a sequence of videos that builds toward a goal) or just randomly watch videos in a certain area, like theory, exercises, etc. There really is a wealth of knowledge for a beginning guitar student, and the videos are of a consistent professional quality.

So, even though I've mastered most everything I've seen after a number of hours watching these videos, I'm going to get through as many as I can before my six months are up. I'm sure I'll learn something somewhere.

Also, since I have not been up on pop music continually for the past 40 years, I'm discovering some modern pop music classics that I may never have known about any other way.

Finally, my only criticism is that there should be a video on pain management. Seriously. Getting started on guitar hurts. You have to build your callouses on your fingers. Without callouses, you bend a string, and the string goes nowhere but sinks into your finger tip and it hurts. I wish a video addressed this issue and told beginner up front that there is a "no pain, no gain" aspect of learning guitar.

But this is seriously a cost effective way to build a body of knowledge on-demand and to get a foothold in guitar playing.
Summary: Great guitar manufacturer teaches people how to play guitar!

All I need to do is add some warm/mild space echo to my amp's reverb. I don't need tap tempo, a looper, dotted 8th notes, etc. A cheaper delay might have been a acceptable choice for me, but this sounds so good that I don't mind the price. I had the MXR Carbon Copy and found it too subtle, and turning up the level just made my tone muddy. So as far as sound and versatility, I give this a 10.

Tap Tempo: People have a clear misconception about the "tap tempo" feature. I wouldn't call it a tap tempo at all. Rather, it's a way to adjust the delay time BEFORE you start playing a song w/o having to bend down to adjust the control. However, I prefer the more common design that allows you to change the tempo on the fly in mid-song. This isn't that.

There are much better loopers out there, but keep in mind that this pedal's forte is in its tonal versatility.

Battery life: if you think the battery life on this is bad, you need to understand that battery life is typically low for any time-based effect. You absolutely need a power supply for time-based effects pedals. Moreover, I wouldn't imaging that anyone using this delay pedal in a pedalboard would rely on batteries in the first place.

Overall, I'd say this: if you look up review ratings about the MXR Carbon Copy, it seems to get quite high marks. Though it's a great sounding pedal, I find the FlashBack Delay far better sounding and more versatile.

There are more features than I've reviewed here, such as internal switches. Look to other reviews for more info.

(3) Height and width can be independently adjusted. This is significant. With an X stand width decreases with height.
(4) Wide range of height and width adjustment.

You want to read the assembly instructions. They are not included in the box. Instead, go to the On Stage website and locate the product; as of this writing, you will find a Word document with very clear instructions. This stand is of an ingenious design and you have to understand how to set it up In particular:

(1) As in the box, the stand it broken down but screwed back together into a single, easy to carry unit. By unscrewing two of the knobs you end up with three pieces to proceed with the assembly. I found this aspect of the stand to be impressively clever.

(2) As mentioned in other reviews, the height adjustments, for strength, are performed by tightening a knob that inserts a pin into a hole of the upright for strength. While there are no markings, if a hole is lined up with the top of the vertical tube, the pin will go into the proper hole. This is very easy to do, just put the vertical in the tube, tighten it gently until you feel resistance on the vertical , they loosen it a bit, move the vertical, and tighten gently until you feel the pin in the hole, then tighten securely. Very easy to do.

(3) For the width adjustment, the knobs turn a screw that presses against a plate that in turn presses against the horizontal to prevent it from moving. This keeps the screw from marking the horizontal and also provides additional strength. But what this means is that the knob has to be tightened down more than you might think. Again, simple, just pull the horizontal out half way and then tighten the knob until the horizontal is secure and you cannot pull it out. Also, the maximum width is somewhat less than full extension, but once you know how much the knob has to be tightened, if you pull the horizontal out too far, you will know it, because the knob will take too many turns and will not secure the horizontal. Again, simple.

(4) The instructions mention that attaching the horizontal bars to the vertical might take two people, but that was not my experience; it was very easy to attach the horizontal bars to the vertical one side at a time.

Again, this is a fantastic stand and customer support is fantastic as well. I can't imagine why anyone would not love this stand, it is very strong, very stable, breaks down to a small size, adjusts to a wide range of heights and widths, and has a deep support rack. The stand also comes with four glue on neoprene pads to position on the rack to protect your equipment. In my case, I bought four magnetic soft rubber vise protectors so I could easily reposition them.

Great stand, great support, great price. Buy this stand.

Text:
I read the reviews and was skeptical about the positive remarks from a low-priced, Chinese Banjolele. Once I got it, it was as described and it lived up to the reviews. For $90, this little Banjolele is pretty well made, sounds great and has good playability. But, I do want to point out some things that you should know.

To get the best tone, you will need to replace the strings and take off the resonator panel. For $6, you can replace the stock strings with a nice set and it immediately and noticeable improves the tone. Also, the cool, tinny sound of a Banjo seems muted with the resonator panel on (I thought resonators were supposed to make Banjos louder. but this one mutes the sound). Once removed, you will hear a brighter, louder, crisper sound that you can control with some body placement. I was hoping to put spacers between the body hoop and the back panel to allow some sound to escape but the screws are tiny and the rim is made from cheap wood and has small stress fractures from the bending process, so you can't take off and put on the resonator over and over without risking stripping out the holes.

The action is a bit high but if you carefully sand down the bottom of the bridge, you can get it down to a more reasonable height. I took .5mm off of mine and it was worth it.

The head is rough and not made of great material. The roughness allows for a cool scratching sounds when using a scratching strumming technique where your fingers graze the head material. The tuners are a little loose but once quality strings break in, it is staying in tune fairly well, but not perfectly.

This is a great value at $90 and a great way to see if you like playing a Banjolele. If you do, and you do it a lot, you will feel better about dripping $400 next time.

Overall, four solid stars!

Text: This brush is non-metal and thus can be used to clean the long thin tubing of a trombone without fear of scratching the surfaces. If you are a trombone player, you really must clean your instrument periodically. There are several reports you can find on people suffering from upper-respiratory infections caused by a dirty trombone. The inside of the inner slide portion starting at the mouthpiece gets a shower of food bits, saliva, etc. as you play. Microorganisms can live inside this slide--it is warm and humid in this slide after you stop playing--and some of those could cause disease! This is a gentle and effective cleaner. The first time I cleaned my instrument, I found not too much in the larger bell or ascending side of the slide, but the descending portion below the receiver was FILTHY. There was a gray-slime that just coated this brush when it came out. I was nearly gagging thinking about every time I was doing those rapid slide motions that we do to make sure the lube is good realizing that the "exhale" backing up the mouthpiece was passing over this gunk and shooting into my face! Yuck. Buy one and use it well. I am not sure how durable this will be as it is new, so I'm holding back a star to "wait and see" so clearly "I like it" but I'm not sure that "I love it" yet.

I've always hated the garish, bright, overbearing sound of new strings. This was not a problem with strings in the past, and is less so a problem with 80/20 bronze, but it's a huge issue with strings today. Phosphor bronze strings are popular, rightly so, and sound great, but for me personally, I hate how they sound out of the box, and I hate waiting for them to break in. This problem is even more pronounced with coated strings. Martin's coated strings are the worst offenders, and the issue continues with Elixirs and pretty much every other coated strings.

For me, personally, I actually prefer the sound of dead strings to "new" strings. On crappy guitars, sure, it can be nice to hear the string instead of the guitar, but if you have a deep-sounding, solid-wood Martin, Guild or Gibson, that's unnecessary.

D'Addario has taken a nod from strings of the past, and like Martin's "Retro" series of strings (which I still find too garish until they break in, taking ages), John Pearse's Pure Nickel (which can be a little dead on some guitars), and a few others, these strings are meant to let you hear more of the nuance of the guitar and less of the string itself. They sound more broken-in, right out of the box, and when they hit the sweet spot (right away), they keep it longer.

I would rank these with Martin's "Retro" strings. Many people love them, but to me, they still sound too new, too bright and garish, and, again like the Retros, these actually seem to take LONGER to break in than PB, 80/20, or coated strings. Bummer.

For me, the only true nickels are the John Pearse Pure Nickels, but, again, these can sound a little dead on some guitars.

So, it's back to D'Addario's other varieties for me--PB, 80/20, Flattops. I find that for most guitars, the 80/20 are a nice blend of vintage sound, fast break-in, and not too garish--sadly, they do not last as long. These Nickel Bronze last forever, and once they break in, they do sound as advertised. I just hate that break-in period, and I thought that was part of the point, for them to sound broken-in right out of the box.
Summary: Still sound too new and bright and take FOREVER to break-in--similar to Martin Retros

Text: Recently, I became interested in using partial capos to simulate alternate guitar tunings, and I wanted a 4-string capo, but I couldn't find any guitar capos that only capoed four strings. I figured something like this may work well for my purposes, and I am pleased to say that it does work. For example, I have a song that I had played with the E and the A strings tuned down a whole step from standard tuning with a 6-string capo on the second fret, and with this, no alternate tuning is required. I simply play with the four higher strings capoed on the second fret and some minor changes to the fingerings that are very doable. I will say that the capo is just slightly long for this purpose, so it can be a little tricky to get into place without muting the A string, but it's doable with some practice. It works very well as a 5-string capo for simulating drop-D style tunings, as well, so definitely a good value even if it is not marketed towards guitar players as it saves you from buying a separate drop-D" capo. I've also experimented with using the capo on the lower four or five strings, and this could create some unusual tunings as well. If you use it in combo with a 6 string capo you can use it to get all sorts of combinations of drop and standard tuning. I do not currently own an ukulele, so I have no comments on its intended use, but I can't see how there would be any issues. Very useful product!
Summary: Great for creating alternate guitar tunings

If you are a Luthier or just like to do your own work on a guitar you need these. They aren't a critical tool for the casual user as most quality guitars should be set up properly and not need to be adjusted. If you plan to replace your saddle then you need to ensure the new saddle has the correct radius which is where these tools come into play. There is some disagreement over this but generally the radius of the saddle should match the radius of the 12th fret. Having said that I should point out that not all guitars have the same fret radius up and down the neck.
It is somewhat surprising how little difference there is from one radius to another but it is important its correct if you want the guitar to play well.

Those who are unhappy with this product either are using it for the wrong application or are not following the directions.

First, these are for brillant finish cymbals only. Think Zildjian A Customs - mirror finish cymbals. If you use this on Zildjian As or "traditional" finish cymbals, it will put a brilliant finish on it.

This stuff is nothing more than a swirl remover. It's a very fine liquid abrasive. If you've ever used Meguires Swirl-X you'll know what this is. It even smells like Swirl-X.

Use it only on brilliant finish cymbals and follow the directions and you'll get great results. Just know that you'll need to whipe down your cymbals will several clean cloths to get all the black off. Use old white T-shirts if you have them. You'll use a lot of cloth.

I have several acoustics, a 20yr old Takamine cedar top which has aged up, a brand new Ibanez acoustic artwood, and now this Yamaha. The way that wood ages does change the sound and it's hard to describe and not that easy to notice without an a and b comparison, but the first notes I played on the Yamaha, I was struck by how clear they rang out. The torrefaction aging they are doing to the wood isn't snake oil, and it has an easy to hear change on the tone.

The upper mid range of the guitar for instance is louder, and there seem to be more overtones. If you could imagine starting with a soft, wet wood, how it would tend to muffle the treble freqencies because it's not very stiff, and then imagine you somehow made that wood as stiff as carbon fiber, and then played it, how much brighter it would sound, it's something like that. The notes sound very clear, and project very well. It actually 'sounds good'. Like play an A chord and someone can tell it's an expensive guitar just from that. It just has that sound.

The electronics are also great. I wish it had a built in tuner like my Ibanez but the magic wizardry that is the built in chorus and reverb is pretty incredible. It takes 2 AA batteries from down by the TRS jack, and I haven't had to change them yet after about 20 hours of playing. The chorus especially gives you a 12string sound on a 6 string.

The plugged in sound is better than my Ibanez, but still sounds like a piezo. It's okay for using an amp but if you're recording guitar, you're still better off using a microphone pointed at the 12th fret.

Now the action......is great. It's the easiest acoustic action I've ever used. It's not as easy to play as an electric, but you won't struggle with it even if you don't play acoustic. It's nothing like my Takamine which is a finger destroyer. The neck also has that knurling down both sides to kind of protect your hand from fret sprouting and such so that even wrapping your thumb around the neck you have nothing grinding on your hand on either side moving up and down the neck. Very smooth, and a matt neck finish so it's not grabby.

The tuners are very fast, which is usually a sign of quality. It takes very little movement to tune up or down and once the strings stretch out, it stays in tune. It also does not affect tune very much if you're pulling on the neck or pushing on it which is a good sign. I did not have to adjust the action to get a buzz free experience. The action as a whole is a little higher than I'd like, but you won't get any string buzz with it set like that.

My fit and finish is flawless. No scuffs, dings, flaws, from the factory. The guitar uses thick top wood which is much thicker than my Ibanez or Takamine. The guitar also weighs more than my other 2 acoustics and it feels solid.

I expect this guitar to last a lifetime.
Summary: On first strum I immediately heard what torrefaction aging does to the wood and I liked it.

Text:
If you plan to use this pedal as a traditional volume pedal in a Guitar > Volume Pedal > Amp configuration (inserting effects pedals anywhere you like), this is a POORLY engineered pedal. It can't be "true bypass" as long as the signal travels through a potentiometer but they can use pots that are a virtual short when adjusted properly and with the pedal forward.

Anyway, the difference between plugging my guitar directly into the amp and placing this pedal in the chain between the amp is immediately noticeable. The tone becomes duller, the output drops. I would expect that from an Asian knock-off, not from an A-list gear maker. I might be over-stating Ernie Ball's reputation, though they make some fine guitars I gotta say, and I've used their strings for many years.

If you plan to use this EB-6180 pedal with digital effects you should be fine. This is because the digital device will take two measurements of pure resistance at either end of the rocker. The signal processing takes place in the unit, not the pedal. (Those units have their own tone problems but that's another review.)

It does occur to me that any pedal with a buffer (NOT "true bypass" in other words) may fix this problem, which is more than likely related to impedance, like a tuner pedal, between the guitar and the volume pedal. I will need to try that out, but it does not excuse Ernie Ball from their responsibility. Major FAIL on their part.

2 stars is generous because EB fails to honor the simple "first do no harm" principle. It harms your tone. How dumb is that? The pedal itself is very attractive, appears indestructible, though I have my doubts about their "string" mechanism over time. The rocker feels smooth and the weight gives the pedal stability on the floor.

I have no recommendations for a volume pedal. Because of the feel, and esthetics, I do plan to keep this for the digital device use, but wish it was able to do what it promises, and fails so miserably, to deliver.

I'm pretty much a know-nothing concerning this product, primarily a keyboard player who happens to own a nice Gibson and a nice Martin. My issue as an amateur is that because I know the intervals I can accompany almost any music in a fingerpicking style, which I hope will lead to a better grasp of chords, since I can accompany both melodically and in chordal blocks on the piano. So here I am stuck with fingerpicking, but a) doing so with the bare hands sounds kind of blunt, b) a regular wedge pick seriously limits facility in playing rapid sequences of individual notes, and c) my fingers hurt, as in ow--not just the fingertips, but the whole index finger, because I'm plucking the strings like some bozo. So I shelled out for these Fred Kelly picks (you get three), and also for the [Fred Kelly Picks D5TB-M-3 Delrin Bumblebee Teardrop Large Medium Guitar Pick], which I use on the thumb. With these Poly Freedoms on the other usable digits, play is both more clear and less difficult. And while the thumb pick is very good, these are a game-changer for me in terms of sound clarity and comfort. The fact is that we overuse the right-hand digits like mad in this modern world of ours, especially the index finger, so fingerpicking without tools like this is a shade idiotic. Much of this same review is reproduced in the Delrin Bumblebee review. I'd definitely give these Fred Kelly picks a try. They're clearly designed by a thoughtful guitar player, with fingerpicking in mind. Again, any real guitar player will recognize my lack of knowledge, but these picks give a sweet sound and feel like natural extensions of the digits, which is all I ask for.

Update: Btw if you want some pics of these picks, you can try fredkellypicks.com

Update #2: I just ordered a second set so I have them ready to hand in the two rooms where I have guitars on stands. These things are pretty great, and I'm already finding them to be indispensable. They're just terrific for both acoustic and electric play, though again readers should note that I have no idea what I'm doing on the guitar. People tell me that fingerpicking the way I do on a Gibson Les Paul is the work of the Devil and so on, but because my legion of screaming fan-girls adores me, what care I for such piffle? All I'm saying is that playing is vastly more comfortable, the picks feel like extensions of the digits, as they are no doubt supposed to feel, and that the sound is very clear and lucid, both with amplified and with acoustic strings. Nice.

I've been playing guitar for over 30 years both teaching & performing and never used a pedalboard. I used to carry the FX's in a briefcase and setup the ones I needed. I'm old school when it comes to these boxes... I run compression, wah, overdrive, super-overdrive, delay & reverb pretty much in that order. Sometime I use a phaser or a tremolo... I also have a few distortion pedals laying around as well but don't use them much. I currently have 8 pedals setup on this board. I have room for one maybe two more. The board itself is built like a tank and travels well. The bag that comes with it is road worthy for local gigs but I wouldn't take it on tour without a metal case. I did go ahead and Velcro down all the pedals that I always use leaving a little room for add ins. Be sure you want to Velcro down the FX chain because to get the best, most secure, it won't fall off the board when you pick it up off the floor...I found that I had to remove all the rubber feet from each pedal. The Velcro is very strong and may test the durability of some of your cheaper pedals. Use great care when removing them from the board as you can easily rip the backs off of some of them. Low end wah pedals and boxes made out of plastic be warned....Boss, MXR, Mod Tone and other high end, well made pedals work best once set on the board. You can run any number of power sources to it. There is plenty of room for all my needed connections...I leave the choice of that to you the reader.
At the end of the day it's easier for me to move my FX pedals around and setup on the gig is in minutes. Plus it looks much cleaner and gives me a little more room on tiny stages and less chance of tripping over a cable.. I'm very happy with this product and would replace it should anything happen to it.

The genuine article! Certified, authentic Fender replacement part. Nice. The caveat. Do you REALLY want to modify your Fender Stratocaster? That is the question you most want to ask yourself. Why? Well, the first thing I noticed upon examining the plastic bag the plate and 'SCREWS' came in was the LENGTH of the "SCREWS."

Pretty long I said to myself. I'll just go ahead and use the screws from the plate that was on there to screw this on. D'OH!!! Maybe you noticed on your Tele or Strat that the "LONG SCREWS" go THROUGH THE BODY then into the NECK of the guitar.

Really. I did not realize that before asking myself upon examining the task I was not sure whether I would undertake or not once the realization hit me that I'm actually removing a part that holds the neck of the guitar to the body. I do NOT know what I was thinking.

Later, since the idea of doing this or NOT was just there bouncing around between my ears not consciously thinking about it really. It was just there. So among that calm subconscious reflection I found myself loosening the strings almost completely so there was no tension on the neck whatsoever.

I put down some acoustic tiles on my designated 'work' bench and laid that baby face down; ensuring the 5 way pick-up switch was centered and between two of the tiles. You can probably use soft rags; however you choose to care for your guitar. Judging by the looks of some 60s era Strats for example, that get such high praise for tone, but the body wasn't shown much respect; they're always 9 times out of ten beat to I don't know what, again 'BUT' supposedly still worth thousands. Personally I wouldn't pay $50 bucks for one looking like that... anyway... careful there.

Take note of how there might be a slight separation between the neck and body after having so carefully removed those screws. I find it wise to remove the screws by hand with a screwdriver initially rather than using a drill with a Phillips head screw bit so that you can get a feel for the tension of the screw, or the amount of torque you want to apply when putting the screws back in.

I had to lift gently on the neck holding it by the headstock to ensure the screws individually at the top especially went STRAIGHT back into the holes from which they came. Long story short, the operation was a success. If you don't consider yourself a 'handy person' that usually doesn't get things right the first time, I don't recommend buying this to swap out for a generic looking one that came on your MIM Strat or Tele. I have a Tele made in Indonesia, but it is one solid piece of wood with no neck plate. I was going to practice on that one til I saw there was no neck plate.

So be advised in the event you think it would be cool to replace the existing generic, no-name or initial plate withan 'F' plate because you will actually be taking apart your guitar! Things that came to my mind (LATER) after having received the plate and "before" starting the job was: how would this affect the truss rod? Wow. I'll be removing the screws that hold the neck and body together.

You would be wise to ask yourself the same questions. Oh well, in the words of Mr. Floyd (perhaps???), but NOT to Mrs. Floyd whom years later he kept hanging up on in perhaps familiar to you a song, of Young Lust but just the same "Careful with that axe Eugene."
Summary: ".. a long distance call...he keeps hanging up.." Careful with that axe Eugene... Seriously.  Read on.

I use a mixer mainly for recording podcasts and occasionally for recording acoustic guitars and vocals. Previously to using the ZED-14 I was using an older Behringer XENYX mixer for a few years and I was pretty satisfied with for the price point it was in. Moving up to the ZED-14 was definitely and upgrade though, as the board is just overall quieter.

The ZED-14's preamps are excellent for an integrated solution and have a nice, quiet sound. My main microphone is a Heil PR40 and this board has no problem driving it. It will also drive my Shure SM7B which is known as a very hungry microphone. I've posted a quick audio sample on the major video site, just do a search for "ZED14 SM7B" and you'll find it.

I briefly tried out an Allen & Heath ZED60-10FX but was disappointed that unit didn't have individual inserts for each microphone channel. If you're not using inserts and want a smaller form-factor unit with the addition of some basic effects you can take a look at that unit.

The ZED-14 is a very versatile mixer as it gives you a multitude of options on how you want your signals routed. You have the final stereo mix, the pre-processed stereo mix, pre-processed aux channels and post-processed aux channels and any of these can be sent to USB for recording. It's a simple press of a button to change between these options and it's easy to understand just what is going on. The variety of routing options means you can let a singer have some reverb in her headphones when recording a vocal but you can still record her voice dry.

Overall, I am very impressed with the ZED-14. It's a big, heavy and well built mixer. The preamps are excellent and the board overall is very quiet. The first time I plugged it in I thought something was wrong until I spoke into the microphone as I didn't hear any hiss or electrical noise at all. If you're looking for a quality mixer that is versatile and easy to use I would highly recommend the ZED-14.

I bought two sets of these, for two different guitars. They work great, I'm 100% satisfied, and you don't need to spend more money. Yes, there are two straplocks in each package -- the product description doesn't make that clear at all. Two, as in one pair, as in one for each end of your strap.

Here's what you should know:

1) Fender's wood screws are smaller than my guitars' original screws, so Fender's screws don't lock down. The big original screws don't fit through the small hole in the new Fender button. Easy solution: put two pieces of toothpick in the screw hole on the guitar body, snip 'em off flush, and put a drop of good ol' wood glue on the screw threads. Works fine -- the new screws are locked down, and won't pull loose.

2) The round pull-pin head screws onto machine threads on the shaft, and can work itself loose. A couple reviewers here report that it came apart -- that would be a royal pain if the strap is attached to the guitar. Easy solution: unscrew the head, put one teensy drop of blue Loctite on the threads, screw the head back on, and let it set for twenty minutes. You're done.

Four stars, because it's a great product, but Fender could easily have avoided both these problems.
Summary: Works fine, here's how to make it perfect:

Text:
With all of the well-received efforts put into their Music Man guitar line and the popularity explosion in the boutique pedal market over the past several years, it's no surprise that Ernie Ball would jump on board and put their spin on an expanded effects line. I think most people who have heard of this "Expression" series were probably at least intrigued at the concept--a delay and reverb pedal where the repeat level/mix control is an expression pedal rather than a knob. In my usage of the pedal, I've found it to be solidly built with some thoughtful design, but a number of issues that will probably make its mileage vary with different users according to their needs.

Pros:
-It's beautiful - I think of the finish as copper rather than rose gold, which makes a little more sense to me. Of course, it's shiny and fingerprints and any scratches you might pick up will show up pretty well.
-The moderately bright built-in plate reverb sounds good. Contrary to some things I've read, I wouldn't say you can use it as a reverb-only effect by turning down the other effects, as the lowest delay setting still has one repeat. That said, the reverb meshes really well with the delay sounds and doesn't overpower even at high settings of all the parameters.
-For an expression pedal, it takes up a small amount of real estate, and having the jacks on the end of the pedal enhance its small footprint.
-Operation of the expression pedal and knobs is smooth but firm, which is pretty important for a pedal like this, for me at least, where you don't want your settings easily bumped by accident.
-The digital delay sounds are nice and full, pretty warm, and natural sounding.

Cons:
For my purposes, there are a number of issues with this pedal that prevent it from being especially usable as a studio tool, which is my primary need.
-Maximum settings are pretty tame on all fronts--if you need oscillation or cavernous reverb, you're not going to find them here--it's like the designers tried to determine the "most useful" range of settings and then limited the pedal to only those. If what you're looking for fits within that range, you will probably love this pedal (and 1 full second is a pretty solid delay time range however you cut it), but for me it introduces limitations that my music is often going to butt up against, particularly in terms of repeat feedback, for which I need to have an "endless" option available. Similarly, even with the toe all the way down, the volume of the repeats don't start at quite the same level as the original signal, which is another unfortunate limitation and one not shared by my numerous other delays (e.g., Seymour Duncan's Vapor Trail even allows for initial repeats louder than the original, for some reason).
-I like the idea of marrying parameters to an expression pedal, but having the only option be delay level is both limiting and a bit irritating at times. Most of the time, if you want to set and forget a delay level setting, it's probably going to be below full volume, and it's pretty tough to accurately nail the same setting every time with a foot control. The instructions, short though they are, indicate that there's a trim pot "on the underside of the pedal" to adjust the maximum mix setting (so you could, for example, make the "toe down" setting a lower volume). This could mitigate the difficulty of finding the sweet spot, but then you're also robbed of the ability to reach full volume without re-accessing the trim pot, which, from what I can tell, is only accessible by removing all 4 foot screws.
-If you adjust any of the parameter knobs while the pedal is actively delaying, the delay sound completely stops until more signal from your guitar passes through. This is a big bummer for me, as my studio work often involves tweaking parameters of reamped guitar parts on the fly, and this completely nullifies that ability.
-Not necessarily a con depending on your use of the pedal, but it's important to know that the delay circuit receives your guitar signal even when the heel is down, i.e., if you keep playing while your heel is down, your delay settings are still repeating and reverbing the signal and those remaining repeats will be heard as soon as you push your toe down, even if you've stopped playing (depending on the settings, of course).
-Needs a 9v power supply and doesn't come with one.
-No tap tempo included (though there is an input for one); I'm sure people who want to use this live will be especially irritated by this. Pretty tough to make tempo adjustments without that functionality, and for the price, people are going to wonder why a tap isn't included.

Overall, I think this pedal has a lot going for it and is a pretty good first attempt at an interesting concept, but there are a lot of design improvements I'd like to see before it would be really useful for me. In its current state, I think it would be most useful in a live setting, where the "preset" nature of the settings will probably fit in a lot of people's ideal range, and you can use the expression functionality to enhance a guitar solo, fingerpicking, or even vocals, totally on the fly and probably to great effect to enhance the drama and production values of a live performance in a way that a typical on/off delay can't quite do. I'm looking forward to continuing to experiment with what I can use it for in a live setting--pedals with increased functionality always get more useful with practice.

For the more mad scientist types (among whose number I count myself), one of the main improvements I'd like to see is the ability to change which parameter the expression pedal controls. The ability to alter delay time, feedback amount, and even reverb with the expression pedal would all be equally (or more) useful for what I'm trying to do and would add serious flexibility to the pedal and really make it something special that nobody else is doing. For examples of using an expression pedal with delay time, check out demos of the Boss DM-2W and you'll likely have your imagination piqued as to what would be possible if the expression settings of this pedal were expanded. In its current incarnation, I would recommend you get your hands/feet on one to demo and see if it's what you're looking for.
Summary: Probably best suited to a live setting

I had used a borrowed DR-05 a few years ago to assist in audio recording for a local TV commercial, as the pure WAV or high-bitrate MP3 options outmatch the camera's mic hookup, as on-camera audio is compressed terribly into the video file, and there isn't much left to play with in the editing side. The only problem was that we could ONLY record from the built-in speakers, or from the line-in jack, but not both, and there was no way to use the studio mics without a mic-amp in between.

So now I have this beast. Full 24-bit WAV capabilities, with two stereo recording streams, one from the Tascam's mics, and one for the two mic inputs on the bottom. Even better, the bottom jacks can handle amp-powered via a 1/4" pole jack, or condenser mics with the XLR plug (with phantom power, too)! You also have the ability to stick with one stereo mic set, and record on two volume intensities (so if one peaks you can fill in with the lower, for better quality), but I say if you record in 24-bit, drop the intensity until you won't peak, and then if you need to boost it when editing, 24-bit offers a HUGE range beyond the abilities of the human ear, and your audience won't be able to tell after the final output, which is usually down-sampled to 16-bit.

Camera mounting is easy using a hotshoe adapter, or you can easily add a stand or tripod and move the wire mess into a more manageable position.

Power is easy, with 3-AA cells doing the job. Using high mA-H NiMH batteries (I use Eneloop), you will see 8-10 hours on a single set, but for the paranoid, a wall USB adapter and the included cable will keep this running until the power company goes down (or you run out of SD card space).

The audio produced by this recorder, and in truth ALL TASCAM products, are clean, without the hiss that even the most high-quality laptop PCs have, so there is no clean-up before editing. And of course this offers an amplified line-out, that can be fed into the camera, or you can attach a good quality set of headphones and hear exactly what the machine is recording.

This is an audio studio for your pocket. Enjoy!
Summary: The big dog, for the big geek!

Text:
The Zoom R16 is great for home studio recording. I love the fact that you have 8 dedicated inputs for keyboards, mics, guitars and other gear. Though it only has one phantom power it does work well. I give this 5 starts for 2 reason only. The dedicated inputs are a MUST HAVE compared to the Zoom R8 which only has 2.

The second reason for the 5 star rating is that it has a dedicated USB host to PC, This is great for REAPER, ABLETON and STUDIO ONE.

The downside is simply this. It will not work with Audacity, Ardour, LMMS or FL. (latest driver release).

You have to download and install the Zoom driver for windows 10 even though it says it will install it automatically. This is NOT true if you have your firewall active on Windows 10.

The other issue is that the unit has not updated the firmware since 2018 and that is a huge issue when connecting to a dedicated DAW like a Roland Fantom or Motif.

I will still give this 5 stars for fact that Zoom has good products and they pack their multi-track recorders with features that others like Tascam simply do not offer.

The price is a bit high for an older unit however ask yourself a simple question? How many Multi-track recorders today offer more than 2 inputs for the price of the Zoom R16?

Lastly the R16 is a dedicated Audio interface for PC & Mac. It will run very well on software listed above however some older versions or "open source" software may not work or have issues.

Out of 9 DAWs (digital audio workstations) here is the ones I have found to be MOST reliable in the order I have listed.

1. - REAPER (5 stars)
2. - ABELTON (4 stars)
3. - STUDIO ONE 4 or 5 (5 stars)
4. - Steinberg Cubase (4 stars)
5. - Apple Logic Pro (3 stars)

Others not listed have not worked or connected properly to test. REAPER by far was the winner for conneciton, control, ease of use and mix down.

There are a lot of Fulltone OCD clones/variants available nowadays, but I was willing to pay a slight premium for the Mooer Hustle Drive because I felt it was the most faithful micro pedal clone of an OCD. If you're somehow unfamiliar with the OCD, it's a very amp-like overdrive pedal that does well in front of a completely clean amp and can range from spongey low-gain crunch to driven overdrive sounds. The LP/HP switch is kind of like a presence control for dialing into different types of amps. But I also found the Tone control to be useful in rolling off high ends to the degree necessary for your rig. The Hustle Drive has some similarities to a Tubescreamer in the way it pushes mids, but it has better low end response and does better in front of a fully clean amp.

There are a lot of pedals that cop the OCD circuit - I actaully own two of the other popular ones: the Joyo Ultimate Drive and EHX Glove OD. But both of those have a bit of their own character mixed in (gainier, darker), and I find the Hustle Drive to be the closest 1:1 clone of the OCD I previously owned, but flipped for other pedals. Doesn't hurt that it's about half the size and half the price, as well.
Summary: Well-built OCD clone with wide-ranging overdrive versatility

I like the form factor of this pedal. It's low profile and the lit up knobs make it super easy to see what state the pedal is in.
It has a lot of modes- the slap back echo, and the Mod Tone are notable. The Mod tone setting essentially doubles your signal, and you can transpose the pitch in increments- so it can be an octave up or an octave down, or a fifth, or a sevent. Cool feature.

The controls are a bit lacking for echo effects. It has Mix (how much processed signal is added to the original) Tone (tone) and Decay (how quickly the processed signal decays) but it does not have a feedback setting- so you are kind of stuck with a preset feedback.

The "chorus" and "flange" effects suffer from this lack of feedback adjustment, making them rather extreme with the pre-set.

There are no preset settings on this device- so that means when you switch from slapback echo to Mod, your mix and decay is dependent on where the knobs are set. You have to twiddle each knows every time you change settings for a different song.

This is a versatile pedal for exploring, and in that regard, it's good value. For gigging, I'd use it for one effect and not try to change it between songs- so for me, I'd keep this on the board to use as an octave divider, but nothing else.

It's not expensive and fun to play with.
