Text:
*Portability*
I wanted a very small lightweight yet versatile amp I could literally toss on the back of a motorcycle with my Kala Ubass & use at bluegrass jams and other small informal gatherings.

*Volume*
I bought this to use while playing in groups with mostly acoustic instruments. If your instrument must be amped to hear yourself (like the Ubass), when you pull out an amp the banjo & mandolin players are not going to be happy with you. At least with this tiny little thing its small enough that no one really raises any objections. Then, once they realize I am just using only enough volume to be heard & to blend in, everything is fine. If you need it, this amp does have surprisingly good volume - It's not going to blow the doors off the barn, but you should not expect it to. If you want big and loud, buy something else. I wanted something that sounded good while using fairly low volume yet loud enough to be heard when I wanted to turn it up, while also being physically small, lightweight & made for bass frequencies. In other words, this amp is perfect for my needs.

*Features*
Every feature on this amp works very well and it is a lot of fun to play around with all the different effects. When actually playing with other people I play flat (no effects) to get the most natural sounds from the Ubass. Occasionally I will put in a little something extra just bc I can, and to liven things up a bit ;) Overall tone sounds great no matter what settings you use.

*Summary*
This is also a great little practice amp. I needed a new practice amp anyway so this fits that spot too. I only wish it had a lineout, that would make it perfect for so many more uses. If it had a lineout I could use it onstage sometimes instead of lugging my main amp around. I knew it did not have a lineout when I bought it, so can't ding a star for that. But If I could wave a magic wand over it & change anything, that one thing would make this amp pure awesome, and it's already pretty great.

Overall I am very happy with this purchase. Hope this helps.

It isn't overly long, though, so if you have a giant desk, you may need something a bit longer. This doesn't stretch all the way across my desk, but it gets halfway there (to my face), so no complaints.
2. The clamp is strong enough to connect to my desk. It wiggles a little bit when I move the desk (I type really hard) but I don't feel like it's going to fall off or anything. The top of the clamp has a bit of foam/rubber so it doesn't mess up the top of the desk, which is appreciated.
3. The arm itself seems to be pretty solid. It goes where I put it and doesn't move or fall at all. I stays where I need it to stay. Of course, it's practically brand new out of the box so I'd be pretty angry if it didn't work perfectly at first. I'll update my review if things start going south but as long as it holds as well as it does now, I'm a happy camper.
4. It was inexpensive. I've seen boom arms go for double this price and some upwards to $100. I know those are probably freaking amazing but, frankly, if it holds the mic in place, why spend an extra $80?
5. Feels like it'll last a while as long as I take care of it. Of course, this applies to all things as all things will last a while if you take care of them, but this doesn't feel flimsy or fragile.
6. I finally have some freedom with my microphone. No more desk stands to use (they take up SO much desk space), no more mics in my face while i'm reading stuff. This also lets me put my mouth closer to the mic which lets me turn my levels down a bit while still maintaining the same voice volume, which then translates to less background noise (it doesn't get louder :) )

Cons
1. The piece that holds the microphone holder swivels which is great, but the piece that swivels is also connected directly which is great, but it's also directly connected to the microphone holder. So, while adjusting the mic, the holder may become unscrewed a bit which causes the mic to wave around a little bit. This isn't a big deal, but I wish there was a way to tighten the mic holder and then swivel it without the two motions interacting with one another. It's hard to explain, but screwing the mic holder in also turns the swivel while swiveling it the other way unscrews the mic holder. They're two separate pieces, but they interact which is weird
2. The mechanism that screws in the clamp is quite large and trying to place the arm near my computer tower has caused some issues. A more minimal clamp mechanism would've been appreciated.

Overall, for under $20, I definitely feel like I got my money's worth. I use this for podcasting and voice-over work on YouTube videos. My old desktop stand was always in my face, meaning I had to peer over the top of it just to see what was on my screen. This makes things far easier and it's much easier to organize and move things around. Plus, I get that kinda small sense of professionalism. I have a mic arm, that makes me cool...right? :P

If you're on a budget, I would recommend this, just be a little cautious of the potential design flaws (I say potential because the design isn't bad, it just interferes with how I personally do things). Otherwise, it's a nice little arm. I'll update my review if anything starts go wrong, but otherwise, assume I'm still happy with it.

4.5 out of 5 stars.

Ok, I probably didn't need to replace my tubes, but my Peavey Classic 30 is 6 years old, and until I got my Vox VT20+, I was playing it an average of 1-3hrs/day. I had a static problem that I thought was coming from the tubes, but which wasn't. A word to the wise: if you hear static, popping and crackling when you rub your hand against your guitar's pickguard, it's the pickguard, not the amp! All you have to do is rub a Bounce drier sheet on it periodically, and the static will go away. As for these tubes, I stuck them in, even though I had already solved the static/popping problem before they arrived. They sound just as good as the originals, which I stuck back into the box these came in, so now I have a backup set, should I blow-out one of the new tubes. I play on the overdrive channel mostly, with medium to heavy gain, and these tubes make my amp sound brand new. I can definitely tell that the gain sounds stronger with the new tubes, so instead of cranking it to 12, I only have to crank it to 11 (yes, my amp really does go straight past 10 and 11, to 12 :D ).

Update 02/09/2014: I haven't been playing the Peavey much (I have a Vox VT20+ that I'm having a LOT of fun with, and it's a heck of a lot easier to throw in the car to jam with friends, and plenty loud for its size). I went to play the Peavey for maybe the 5th time since installing the new tubes (wanted to jam some SRV), and my gain channel was totally dead. I checked the tubes, and sure enough, one of the 12AX7's had a white powder coating on the inside. It was toast. I popped back in one of my old tubes, and the amp worked just fine. I probably will just keep it the way it is. I doubt the seller will exchange it after this long, and I have 2 more spares if I need them. I'm not impressed with the quality, that's for sure. I doubt I had more than 20hrs on the new tubes, and I didn't even have the gain cranked-up that high (maybe 6) when it blew (and I ran the old tubes with the gain over 7, often over 9, almost constantly for 6 years w/o a failure). If I ever buy new tubes again, I'll be sure to beat on them good for a few months to make sure they don't fail.
Summary: They sound good in my Peavey Classic 30

I got this because of the reviews saying how loud it is. And it is louder than most metronomes. They have the speaker in a tube shaped chamber with a little slit at the bottom and that chamber resonates to make it louder - but it is very dependent on the acoustics of where you set it. If you set it in the wrong spot, it is really easy for reflections to cancel out and make it seem very quiet. It is the loudest (usually) if you lay it on its back on a flat surface like a table or desk. Sometimes you can set it on a solid back music stand and the reflections off the music stand help it get loud enough.

It has a 2-3 and 3-2 clave pattern and a rumba clave too. For me this was the reason I bought it (I already have other metronomes that I like - but they don't have clave) ... and the light that flashes on ONE is really helpful when working with a 2-3 clave.

People complain about it not shutting off automatically and running batteries down. Well here is a tip for you - get eneloop or other rechargeable batteries. I haven't had to buy new batteries in the past 15 years - just recharge them every few weeks. The new KDM-3 has auto shut off because of all these complaints. I'm perfectly happy with my KDM-2 and wish it were still available at the normal price.

Text:
This is a well-built, nicely designed USB microphone that requires nothing more than plugging it into a USB port.

The manual is out-of-date and speaks of downloaded from the Samson The website which is no longer available. Instead, the mic works with just about any contemporary program with sound recording capabilities. In my tests on a Windows 8.1 system, it worked out-of-the-box with the free open source Audacity audio program, Microsoft Movie Maker, Cyberlink PowerDirector, Skype, Google Hangouts and several other programs.

The unit appears designed to be used a handheld mic, but it comes with a sturdy little stand which I used exclusively. It also comes with a ten foot cable and a very basic cloth carrying sack.

There are two things you must remember when using this microphone, lest you become frustrated and disappointed.

First, the mic has a “Super Cardioid” pick-up pattern. For the non-expert (like me) cardioid means “a heart-shaped curve traced by a point on the circumference of a circle as it rolls around another identical circle”. In simpler terms, this is a pretty directional mic and if not pointed directly toward the source of the audio, you may not capture it. This also makes this microphone very effective when recording in rooms with high ambient noice as long as the noise source is not behind you.

Second, it is a dynamic microphone. The further the mic is from your audio source, the higher you need to set the gain. This can introduce noise into the recorded audio. Personally, it didn’t happen to me when the mic was about 18 inches from my mouth and I had the gain cranked up to 100% in Audacity.

My experiments with the Q1U were limited to recording my voice and the recording sure sounded like me. Since I never record live music of any kind, I have no idea of how it would function in such circumstances.

Overall, I think this an excellenjt microphone for vocal recording and think it a fine addition to my kit.
Summary: Excellent vocal recording performance at a very modest price

As is true for other Behringer pedals I have used the EQ700 is quiet, solid, basic and effective.

Some find fault with their plastic construction but for most purposes I do not. Motorcycle helmets and the like are made with modern plastics. These appear tough.

On the other hand the slider controls themselves are probably a bit delicate, and even if not broken by an errant foot their settings would be easily disturbed. There should be a cover that fits over the sliders.

But for all this the EQ700 is a useful tool, enabling shaping of the tone with a precision beyond that of an amps tone controls.

My own favorite uses is to 1) tighten the bass without thickening the overall bottom end. I do this by raising the 100 hz slider about 8db and at the same time decreasing the 200hz output just enough to compensate for the 100hz slider's influence on the the frequency centered above it. (The hz designations give the center point of the slider's action. Picture it as a hill of beans that grows wider at the base as it get taller) and 2) to add sparkle to the upper frequencies with the slider most effective for this depending on the guitar and its PUP type. This only requires a small (3db) increase and thus does not noticeably influence any frequency outside of the slider's own range.

I installed this bridge, the Golden Gate GB-3 5/8 height, on my banjo. My banjo is a Gold Tone OB 150 Masterclone. My banjo has no fretboard radius.This bridge is great on banjos like this. Radiused necks are kinda a new thing these days and I can't speak for a radiused fretboard banjo. Anyhow.my banjo is stock out of the box. What tone ring, rim and head is what came with from the factory along with the other parts of the banjo. I have the head tension set to 90 at each lug using the DRUM DIAL. This is a must have tool for proper banjo head setup. IF you are going for that bluegrass sound the usual head tension puts its tuning to G# That is normal for most banjos.I have the Tailpiece set closer to the head than the standard 1/4 inch gap. A lot of banjos are set up at the factory with the 1/4 inch setting. I tightened the tailpiece to about the thickness of a guitar pick. This is what some bluegrassers prefer for increased volume. It puts more pressure on the bridge.

Now enter the Golden Gate GB-3 Deluxe bridge. This is going to give you the crack in the notes and you will notice an increase in volume with this bridge. I use the stock gauger strings but may change to 10's over the 11's. Some reviews say they had issues with the string slots not fitting the strings. I did not experience this. You can use a set of welding tip cleaners to lightly dress the slot but be VERY careful IF you do. You really do not need to do that to this bridge. Try this bridge with an archtop banjo and it will get good and loud too. My banjo is a flathead. For a traditional bluegrass sound this is one bridge you may love. You probably will bot find your self doing some sanding to thin the bridge as some bluegrassers do to get volume. This bridge, with the setup on my banjo as I have it gives me plenty of volume and crack that i wanted in the notes. You will find a few sweet spots in the banjo that may not have been heard before.

IF you are an experienced bluegrasser and have been playing a while you may already know what this bridge can do. I wanted to get a bit of Dr. Ralph Stanley's tone mixed with the old sound of Earl Scruggs from the 1949, original recording of Foggy Mountain Breakdown.I think I have reached the desired tone I was looking for.on this banjo. I know I love this bridge.for what it does for my tone. I hope this gives you a guide for selecting a bridge for your tone that your ears like.
Summary: This bridge turned up some volume and it cuts through the way I like it.

I bought this talk box shortly after trying to make my own out of an old PC speaker I was no longer using, a Maxwell coffee container lid, a large sized oil funnel, duct tape, and a tube. Only spent about 20 bucks and spent a couple hours to make it, but when I went to use it the sound wasn't as good as all those video you see of people using talk boxes.

Specifically, the videos I've seen were people using this product. That's when I finally decided to spend the money on this bad boy.

Whenever I buy music products its always the demo videos I see online of people using the product that sucker me in. The same thing happened with this. I have no doubt this talk box can produce amazing sounds, but it honestly sounded the same as the one that I built myself.
That's when I finally realized that buying a talk box is not going to magically give you that polished robotic, ear tingly, beautiful sound that you hear other people making. Just like any other instrument, you have to learn how to `play' this thing.

Coming from a talk box newbie, you definitely are going to have to put the time and effort into making words intelligible and clear sounding.

The way a talk box works is by forcing the sound/air into your mouth and then you have to shape that sound as all that air exit's you mouth. That being said, I'm still new to the talk box world and I have to mention that it seems to knock the wind out of me in a way. Who knows though, maybe it's just because I have asthma.

The actual tube that you place in your mouth has some weight to it and can be annoying keeping in your mouth. I'd say you are better off strapping it to a microphone stand to hold it up to your mouth. Trust me, you will save yourself some neck ache's by doing this.

I'd say if you are capable of building you own talk box and want to save some money, then go for it. There are a few videos on you tube on how to do it. Its really not that hard.

But if you just want to save time and own a good, reliable and solid talk box then I'd recommend picking one of these up. In the end, it is definitely more pleasing to the eye compared to the talk box I made myself. Lol.

Text:
I am amazed at how innacurate the string action ruler that comes with this set is. I happened to have a similar one made by Baroque. I casually compared the blocks that you use to adjust string height with that run along the long edges of the ruler. I couldn't believe what I was seeing. All the blocks are off by about .025 to .030 on both edges! DO NOT use those blocks to adjust string height until you check them. If I had, for example, used the blocks to set my neck relief at .010", I would have actually set it to about .035" to .040"! I would have been off with string height too if I had used the blocks to check height. (By blocks, I'm referring to the black rectangles along the long edges on one side of the ruler that is used to measure string height by viewing them next to the strings.) Also, all scales on that side of the ruler (in other words, both edges that have blocks) that start on the long edges are off by the same amount. The scales on the short edges that also start on the short edges are accurate. The two scales on the opposite side that run along the long edge are also accurate but they base off the short edge. In other words, anything that bases off of the long edges is innacurate. The only way to fix this ruler would be to carefully file both long edges to make the "blocks" accurate thickness but that would take a long time and it's just not worth it. The whole purpose of this ruler is to provide accuracy and it failed terribly at that. Assuming they are all like the one I received, anyone who uses this ruler's "blocks" to check neck relief or string height without checking the accuracy of the ruler will have an incredibly bad setup - virtually unplayable. Everything will be off by .025" to .030" and that's HUGE. 200% + off! The whole purpose of this tool is precision. Think about this. If you use the blocks to set your neck relief to the pretty much standard .010", you're relief will actually be set to .035" to .040"! That's not even remotely close and you'll probably get bad fret buzz at the higher frets. If you then set your string heights with the blocks, they'll be so high that your guitar will be virtually unplayable.

There's absolutely no excuse for such terrible quality control.

When I saw how bad the ruler is, I decided to check the radius gauges that come with the set. They appear to be accurate but anyone who bought this set should them too before using them. I happen to have accurate radius gauges to compare with the ones in this set. The reason I bought this set is that I have un-notched (above the strings) radius gauges and also a set of Stewmac under-under-the-strings radius gauges. I wanted a set of notched radius gauges. Well, I got that but the ruler is dangerously innacurate. I'm going to throw it out so nobody ever uses it.

I hope the manufacturer happens to see this review so they can remedy the problem. If not, there'll be a lot of guitarist who mess up their setup terribly if they assume the ruler is accurate.

UPDATE: I first tried to contact the manufacturer using their contact form on their website. After filling out the form, it wouldn't send it. However, the site also listed an email address to contact them so I sent an email. The result? Nobody ever got back to me. I had even offered to send them close-up pictures of the ruler side-by-side with the one by Baroque. Those pictures showed the gross inaccuracy of the ruler. so much for customer service. Perhaps I just received a bad one but that would be a bad reflection of their quality control. After this experience, I won't be buying any products from this compay.
Summary: String action ruler is WAY off.  Don't use it until you check it.

If you examine the range of USB microphones for sale at Amazon, you will find lower end ones in the $25 range that are good for the times when you simply want to have a microphone and quality isn't much of an issue. Such microphones lack sensitivity and range, and give mediocre sound quality at best. This Samson microphone is not a high end microphone, but will give you good sound quality at a lower end price point. Its cardioid design has a heart shaped pickup pattern, meaning it works best with sounds coming from one side of it, and covering to a lesser extent those sounds coming from the surrounding area on the same side. So if you use it for vocals or with an instrument, it will be more sensitive to the side with the vocalist or the instrument, less sensitive to the audience side, but still pick up the band albeit at a much lower background level.

This mic is more sensitive than a typical cheap "rock band" grade mic, so it works best when you are about a foot away unless you use a screen (not included). It will pick up sounds from eight feet away, but they will sound like they are eight feet away. In other words, it works as a personal mic, and if you want something to record multiple people or instruments, you'd want one of these for each person or instrument.

If you are looking for something with a choice of patterns such as cardioid, stereo, bidirectional and omnidirectional, and want something potentially sensitive enough to pick up a sound clearly from 10 feet away as if it were at the microphone, you could expect to pay at least double for something like a [[ASIN:B008F4USMS Blue Microphones Yeti USB Microphone]]. If you want to pay less, there are a variety of options but don't expect the sound quality to be up to this one. If you are looking for a good mono recording mic, with a cardioid pattern (probably the best pattern for practical purposes) then you get a lot of quality for the price range.

For a home user who wants enough quality for something to sound good but who isn't ready to go all out and spend lots more money, this mic is a good choice. Likewise, if you need to buy several without breaking the bank, this will also fit the bill. It will work as a plug and play microphone with compatible systems, but you can download software from the manufacturer to get a lot more control over it.

Text:
Hmm....based on the glowing reviews I thought this cord would be an improvement over what I already had, but it's worse.  I've been using a cheap nylon-encased 10' cord, and apart from some crackling, the sound quality has been good.  Even with a cheap practice amp, I have been able to get a nice glassy tone out of my Squier Strat.

But as soon as I plugged this Jowkuny cord in, that glassy tone was gone.  I tried fiddling with the knobs on the amp and guitar but to no avail.  Comparing the sound through both cords, this Jowkuny appears to be doing the following:

1.  The sound output (loudness) of the signal is improved - (Good)

2.  The overall tones are getting muffled, with the treble coming out harsher and not as smooth as I am used to - (Bad)

3.  There is less headroom and the tones are distorting at lower volumes - (Bad)

This Jowkuny cord may be okay for people who play the high gain modern metal "chug" style, where some of the above subtleties are not going to be as important.  But for those of us who play a variety of music (or try to!) including blues, classic rock, and jazz, this Jowkuny cord is not cutting it.

The construction seems to be good quality overall and I like the seamless connections at the end, as well as the straight plug on both ends.   I am usually not a fan of PVC coverings because many plastic-covered cables contain lead.  But the inner specs on this cord sounded great on paper.   In terms of actual use however, anything that kills my glassy Strat tone is not something I want to use, so I will be searching for a better option.
Summary: Slightly Muffled Sound, More Distortion, and Harsher Treble Compared To My Other Cords

I was curious if these were the same as the Humidipaks D'Addario brought out 15 years ago - yep, apparently so, only apparently from the original manufacturer.

I bought Generation I Paks and used them until the recall. It took D'Addario 1.5 years to replace the Paks I sent in - and I heard from quite a few of stories of leaking Paks, and of D'Addario replacing higher end Taylors. When the Gen II Paks came out there was an issue with outgassing and (for some reason) the green velour interior padding (e.g. standard for Collings) of cases. The outgassing would discolor velour. I did not hear of any affect on the instruments in those cases.

I bought some Gen II Paks, but by then was fairly cautious about whatever I put in my cases, and set the Paks (in the original box) on a shelf in my closet. (I live in central Oklahoma, and am very fortunate in that the humidity range is usually between 35 and 55 RH -- I do have to watch it during the rainy or hot or extremely cold weeks.) A year or so later I opened the original box and found several of the Paks had leaked. I have pictures so don't accuse me of falsification.

My instruments are not professional classical $100k, but they are north of $3k up to $15k each. I will not ever have a potentially leaky product in my cases without some kind of protection --- and whatever protection ideas I've had would prevent the product from working.

I strongly suggest you monitor any Humidipaks or Boveda Paks for leakage. The original problems were in high humidity areas - deep south in humid months. Best for me is keeping my instruments cased, monitoring the ambient RH, and adding a (well wrung out) sponge in a tube or baggie and monitoring it frequently (how frequent depends on RH).

Oasis worked for me as well although I am cautious about placement in case of a tear or break in the fabric.

The tones were brighter all around and the sustain I could hold on my high E string was between 26-32 seconds steadily.

I know everyone has their favorite "go to" strings and I've tried some of those with "meh" results. These absolutely work so it's what I'm sticking with. I know they've gotten better since then but having flaking from the coating in my fingerboard and in my pickups is annoying and just something else that needs to be maintained for no real benefit and at an outrageous cost.

Text:
Many a guitar player looks for and can find something more than a novelty in a piece of gear. If you're really down the Rabbit Hole, you'll chase plenty of Mad Hatters for a good cup of tea. My purchase of the Orange PPC108 8" speaker cabinet was an exploration into some different ideas in sound coloration. I bought this little speaker for recording purposes.

Using a smaller speaker is a great approach to recording a huge guitar sound depending on microphone type and placement. Oh, right...we're in the new age where everything is digitally... Well you certainly don't need to be technically advanced to have fun with this little guy. It's your thing, do what you want to do.

I've been using my PPC108 in combination with a Bad Cat Cub III15R, a pretty slick amp with a lot of tonal variations to choose from. I was not so impressed with original "Voice of the World" speaker that was installed in said Orange (mine is Black) cabinet. To me, it sounded lacking in sensitivity. I also experimented in removing the the back cover to see if I could get a fuller response of the speaker. The outcome was only slightly better. For another $29 I switched out the Voice of the World speaker for a Celestion "Eight" 8" 15W 4 ohm model. This was a marked improvement over the original speaker loaded in this dinky cabinet. The guitar feedback I can get from the Celestion is much more musical than the VOTW speaker.

Regarding the PPC108 cabinet construction, these things must be slapped together rather quickly in the China factory. It was not so easy taking that back cover off. The glue for the tolex had not even dried when they put thing together. An area of toxel on the inner frame was stuck to the inside of the back cover. Otherwise, the construction of the cabinet is particle board. So if you are looking for a sound to the likeness of a small Fender Champ, there's no pinewood box here. Unfortunately, this little gem does not sound phenomenal, but it will get the job done. With the right speaker it will serve the purpose of a feedback loop and other guitar fun.
Summary: In Search of a Good Cup Of Tea

Great product from UAD. After 18 months, its still as good as the first day. When you think about buying UAD Apollo interfaces, you should consider a long term budget beyond this purchase price. Why? Because the plugins that really shine are sold separately. They may be expensive for some budgets, but the value is worthy. UAD plugins are amazing. You can demo them for 14 days, and the demos are renewed typically with new purchase/authorization of a plugin or UAD software update.

Pros:
- Solid build.
- Onboard UAD processing saves CPU and reduces increased latency. This is a major benefit, and you can add Satellite for more processing.
- Console software is versatile. I can route iTunes/System audio through the FX, and even send to DAW via virtual routing.

Cons:
- Front Hi-z input replaces rear input when plugged. So I can't use my guitar while having my keyboard plugged as stereo 1/4". To solve this I bought a Presonus Digimax D8, which allows me to send 8 audio inputs to the Apollo via ADAT. This has been my solution until my rack unit arrives this week.
- Not bus-powered. I know this is not possible because of onboard plugin processing. However, I wish there was a way to disable that internal card and just use as interface.
- Separate units for Windows/Mac. My Mac unit is currently not compatible with Windows. Recently, they released a USB3 version for Windows.

Overall, this is the best compact interface you can get if you have the budget to invest. I'm all about Thunderbolt, so this was a no-brainer for me.
Summary: Great minimal I/O solution with UAD processing.

Text:
Donner Bone Bridge Pins
Bridge pins are conical pegs that wedge into holes in your bridge to hold the ball end of your string in place. In addition to affecting your guitar’s appearance, bridge pins play an important part in transferring the sound of the string to the wood of the guitar, and many people believe that the type of pin affects the sound of the guitar. You must remove these pins every time you change strings — if one of your pins is damaged or missing, or if you just want to try a new pin, these are for you.
I compared Donner Bone pins with plastic pins, Martin Ebony and Martin Liquidmetal pins. Test guitars included 2021 Martin 00-15M and 1970 Lotus F215, with custom bone nuts and bone bridges, and Dunlop extra-light strings.
CONTENTS AND INSTALLATION: Donner Bone pins were delivered quickly. The package also contained a hefty pin wrench that will allow you to pry pins out of your guitars without damaging the bridge. I will continue to use this wrench for years and it may even be worth the cost of the pins.
The package contained sandpaper to shape the pins, but that was not necessary — the Donner bone pins fit easily into bridge holes of both guitars. After loosening a string, I just laid a slip of paper down to protect the bridge, inserted the wrench under the pin and popped it out. Then I inserted the new pin, pressed it into place and tightened up the string again. The Donner Bone pins were a breeze to install.
APPEARANCE: These pins are very attractive, with an off-white body and a small abalone dot. I like the appearance of these pins better than all others.
COMPARISON: Donner Bone pins sit lower in the holes than plastic pins, but higher than Martin Ebony or Martin Liquidmetal pins. They are more expensive than plastic pins but much cheaper than either type of Martin pins.
SOUND: Donner Bone pins have a slight, very high-pitched resonance when dropped or struck with metal bar. In the guitar, they produce brighter highs and more fundamentals, so that it is easier to hear individual strings in a chord compared with plastic pins or Martin Ebony pins. They are good for finger picking and solo guitar. Their sound is comparable to Martin Liquidmetal pins. Your guitar or ear may differ.
HELPFUL HINT: Some abalone dots will be lighter or more reflective than others. Take a look at them before you put them in and alternate light with dark, so you do not end up with a bridge that looks uneven.

All the Dunlop products are available individually and not everyone benefits from the package kits.  I use Dunlop 65 polish, the lemon oil, and the carnauba wax.  The others in this line really don't work for me.  To clean my fretboards I use 91% Isopropyl (rubbing) alcohol from the pharmacy.  Then I put on the lemon oil and really rub it in with a toothbrush.  Do NOT oil maple fretboards that have a finish on them.  The carnauba wax restores any scuffed or slightly scratched spots, like light pick marks.  However, if you have a satin finish be aware that too much wax will turn it into a gloss finish!  Then I clean and polish overall with... you guessed it... the cleaner and polisher.  For cleaning cloths I use old cotton T-shirts.  Ones that have been washed several times.  I have never needed any fancy chamois or micro-fiber gizmo.  A piece of Scotch Brite will polish the frets without hurting the wood.
Summary: Buy seperately to get the ones you really need

Since it seems the information surrounding this products is vague, I thought I would give a review with as much info as I can to help those who are thinking about buying, and or bought and have questions. I will also address some of the concerns I found in the reviews/questions areas.

First off, my opinion of this product. I am very happy with it, and it did what I needed it to do, which is replace the crappy wiring in my janky old Martin Les Paul copy with two humbuckers. This product is everything I hoped and expected it to be. I considered giving it four stars because it is a lower end harness, but ultimately I figured if peeps are buying and eight dollar harness, they ought to know they're not getting top of the line. Okay, onto the info:

#1 - Are the pots small? Answer: Yes. They are likely smaller than what you are replacing. They were smaller than what I was replacing, both in the body and in the threads. However, if you use a washer, and tighten everything properly, there should be no issues. My old knobs fit perfectly on these pots. No issues there. They're just smaller.

#2 - Is the switch huge? Answer: I didn't think that it was particularly huge. That said, it was slightly larger than my original switch, and I did stress a little that I was going to have to unsolder/resolder the switch, however, with a little finesse and uncharacteristic patience, I was able to work the switch through the cavity of my guitar and get it into place. One thing I didn't like about the switch was that the plastic knob dealie-bob does not appear to come off easily (it does not screw on). That didn't make it any harder to get through my guitar, but it did scrape a little on the way. Probably if I cared a little bit more, I would have covered it with masking tape. So, no biggie.

#3 - Is it wired incorrectly? Answer: No. I installed it as is (as pictured here on Amazon), and it worked like a charm. That is not to say that it is going to be wired exactly like the current set-up that you are replacing. If you google Les Paul wiring (like pretty much everyone who answers questions on this page suggests that you do), you will quickly see that there are MANY ways to wire this type of setup. MANY. I think a lot of the folks who are saying "it's wired incorrectly" are actually basing that on not being wired how their current setup is wired, or what they're familiar with. So this is one method of many to wire it, but a valid method. Look at the picture, if that is not what you want, then find a different harness or wire it yourself, or buy this one and rewire it. But, based on my experience, it is not wrong, just maybe different than what peeps are expecting. That is my experience only, though, so carefully look over the wiring to make sure it's all good.

#4 - Did it come broken? Answer: Okay maybe a little. Actually one of the ground solders had come apart during shipping. I can't speak to why or how this happened, but I think it might have to do with how it was packed/shipped, and not the product itself. In any case it was a quick fix, I soldered it while I was soldering the pickup wires to the pots. No biggie.

#5 - Where do you wire the pickups to? Answer: This is a question I had, and also one that is asked a bunch in the questions. It's also further compounded by the description saying that you hook the pickups up to the switch. You do not hook the pickups to the switch! The pickups get wired to the volume pots. The hot (insulated, usually white) wire goes to the post on the pot that also has a wire going to the tone pot. The ground (uninsulated) wire gets soldered to the back of the pot with the other grounds. Do this for each of the two pickups (depending on your application).

#6 - Where does that rando black wire that isn't attached to anything go? Answer: It's a ground wire that goes to the bridge. I already had a wire coming in from my bridge, so i just spliced them together.

#7 - Does it make your guitar sound bad? Answer: No. This is the best my guitar has ever sounded. Granted, I put new pickups in, but there is nothing bad that seems to come from the wires, eg. hissing, hums, buzzing, etc... I experience none of that.

I think that about covers it. I hope this is helpful to those who have questions and concerns about this product.

I've been hesitating to review this amp. A couple of years ago, I bought a Blackstar Fly 3, which I really like. I bought the Boss Katana Mini more recently, not to compare with the Blackstar, necessarily, but for something a bit different.

The Boss Katana Mini is billed as 7 watts, and I think much of that is in the 'brown' channel, which is noticeably louder than the other two channels, the clean channel and the crunch channel.

Bottom line, I really like the clean channel here, but I'm underwhelmed by the crunch and 'brown' channels, which sound ordinary to my ears. They sound flat, the bass is a bit dull, and the gain doesn't have much of an edge to it.

I like using the Katana Mini on the clean channel with the gain knob dimed. That's a really pleasing, well-rounded clean, leaning toward a very slight crunch.

The Katana Mini has a three-band EQ, which is nice, and it also has a pretty good delay section, which I set to a very slight slapback sound.

I'll be honest--I prefer the Blackstar Fly 3 over the Katana Mini. The clean sound of the two amps is about equal, and the Blackstar's crunch channel--although not spectacular--is better voiced than the Boss and more fun to play through.

The Katana Mini is, in my opinion, overpriced for what it delivers.

The nut and nut slot on mine are pretty bad, and the overall quality and build are very, very cheap, but it actually looks very nice sitting on the stand. It's got terrible "neck dive" because the wood in the body is very cheap and light, and the work inside the body is pretty awful. My pots were sitting crooked, and the knobs were rubbing the top of body, so the first thing I had to do was remove them and chisel some wood out from the inside so they'd sit straight.

Everything it came with (pots, pickups, etc) was pretty awful, and I didn't like the way it was wired (both tone pots effected both pickups), so naturally I've replaced EVERYTHING: strings, pots, caps, 1/4 jack, pickups, and the nut is next. Not only is the nut in severe need of filing b/c it's too high, and it binds the strings, but on the headstock side, the plastic near the strings is chipping away as I play it more. I also had to remove the nut to fix the nutslot.

This is actually a terrible bass guitar as it comes from the factory; it's just amazingly good for only $100, and for those of us that don't mind doing luthier or guitar tech stuff and chiseling, sanding, and soldering, it's a good value. However, given the amazingly bad build quality, and the non-existent post-sales support I've gotten, I just can't give this more than three stars. In retrospect, I wish I'd spent another $80 and upgraded to an Ibanez bass to get some kind of baseline build quality. Regardless, I had a ton of fun upgrading and learning guitar tech skills on this thing, and I absolutely love playing it now. I get why so many people have given it good reviews (it IS good for the money), but just know that it's probably going to need some work before it's properly playable or suitable for a beginner.

P.S. Sure would be great if the seller or manufacturer would just tell me which Graphtech nut to buy for a replacement. I'll measure it myself etc, but as bad as the nut is, they should have that info readily available on their FAQ's or something as the nut it comes with should be replaced, regardless.

First, as advertised, the Hydra is very sturdy and would be hard to tip over. However, there are problems. First, the Hydra is heavy. It ways about as much as, say, a jazz guitar in a hard shell case. I wouldn’t want to carry it around. If you have a roadie, fine. Second, the three head hangers are removable, sort of like a steering wheel, by unscrewing what is called a “D & A Cap”. However, I had a difficult time screwing it back on without it going at an angle and possibly stripping the threads. After close to ten attempts, I finally got it screwed on. Third, the height of the head hangers is adjustable with a “Tri Knob” that tightens a circular piece against the extendable neck. However, I’m the strong guy who gets called to unscrew jars, but I had to twist really hard to get this thing to hold the extendable neck in place. I was afraid I would break it. I thought I had it once, but it slipped and dropped my instruments a couple inches. (If it is all the way down, the instruments fit, but the bottom of my guitar bangs against the 3/4” space where the metal legs are covered by neither neoprene foam or the feet of the Hydra.) Fourth, maybe the foldout things that can rest against a guitars back are good for solid body electric guitars. I don’t find them necessary. It works better for my guitars body to rest against the neoprene on the legs. That’s more stable. If I were going to use these foldout things, I would cover them with more neoprene foam. I don’t like like the body of my expensive mandolin banging against a piece of plastic nearly as hard as a belt buckle. Fifth, I use little D’Addario tuners on all of my instruments. Often, they are positioned between the nut and the low E string tuning peg or its equivalent. After I hung my guitar on a neck hanger, I discovered that it was actually hanging by the tuner, which was about to be pulled off the instrument! Sixth, I discovered that my five string banjo was resting partly on the head but partly on two of the tuner knobs, which could damage them or make them turn, putting the instrument out of tune. I’ll have to think of a solution to that problem. The weight of a mandolin is not enough to close the collar around a neck hanger, but it closes it halfway. My square-neck Dobro does fit on a Hydra, with care, but my eight string square-necked resonator guitar does not. (Not a big surprise. I didn’t think it would.) I’ll use this and find a way to work around its problems, but it’s certainly a bit disappointing. For one instrument, I much prefer the Hercules stand that holds a guitar by its headstock. It’s easier to tip over, but less easy than most, and it’s much lighter though well built.

Great mic that is applicable in all the same situations as the old standby, the Shure SM57. I wouldn't say I like the i5 more than the 57, but I would say that it acts as a great compliment to it, especially when miking up an amp. Since I bought this mic (found mine in mint condition on CL for 40 bucks!!) I've not stopped using it in tandem with the 57 whenever I mic up an amp... the i5 is a bit richer and fuller in the mids than the 57, and if you use a stereo preamp you can blend the tones of the two to taste, almost using the i5 as a mid-boost to the standard 57 sound. As an example, this past week I recorded both blues-style lead guitar and pedal steel guitar using this combination. For the guitar (a Gretsch hollow body) I cranked the i5 for a sweet, thick mid tone, but for the steel I cranked the 57 for that glassy, country sound, letting the i5 lend a bit of body to the lower end, which steel recordings sometimes lack.

I've also used the i5 on snare, and found the tone to be a little more mid-heavy and "dense" than the 57. For live vocals, the i5 gets the job done well on a tenor voice especially, though for a lower male range like my own I prefer the Beta 57. One very nice perk of the i5 as a live vocal mice is that it has a much larger "target" than the 57 or Beta 57 and thus makes it a bit easier for a "passionate" vocalist to sing into.

So should you buy an i5? well, yes, obviously, but I think it really comes down to what you're trying to accomplish with the tone. The i5 is an excellent tool to have in your mic locker for certain applications, and it's affordable and incredibly solid, just like it's buddy the sm57.
Summary: Great Addition to the Mic Locker.

I make this review as a newer player who bought this pedal/modeler because it seemed like a great “do-it-all” pedal. I’ve used it on and off for a few months and overall I’m pretty unimpressed with it.

First, the positives. This pedal seems to be well-built and is pretty simple to learn. The amount of effects and the ability to tailor each effect is pretty impressive. That’s where the positives end for me.

Perhaps it’s because I’m still a novice player, but I found the M5 to cause a lot of noise in my signal chain when paired up with other pedals (powered by an MXR iso-brick power supply). The noise was so problematic that I thought my overdrive pedal was defective. When the overdrive was switched on, there was a lot of white noise. At other times, the overdrive would have very little output even when the M5 was switched off. Without the M5 in the chain, the overdrive works and sounds excellent. When I use the M5 as a stand-alone pedal, there is no noise. Pair it up with either of my overdrive pedals and there is a ton of noise.

Next problem is that the M5 only allows you to use one effect at a time. This is ok if you use it to supplement your other pedals (see problem above), but not great if you are wanting to use it as a replacement for a full pedalboard. At first I didn’t think that would be a big deal, but it’s a drag when you want to layer effects and don’t have the separate pedals you need.

Cables are somewhat thin; thinner than MonoPrice and CableMatters XLR cables. Very flexible though, which can be an advantage!

Doesn’t really give many specifics on the type of cable shielding. For example, CableMatters has multiple shields, insulates the individual wires within the cable, etc. Amazon just mentions an “inner copper spiral shielding”.

The connectors are solidly built, not exactly Neutriks but the locking mechanism feels solid on both and no issues plugging / unplugging. They’ve machined little grooves into the barrels that help with grip when unplugging, which is a nice detail.

The XLR barrels are a little shorter than on some other brands, which is actually very useful in tight spaces. The strain relief plastic is short and squishy, more so than on MonoPrice or CableMatters products. Not sure how effective it is but, again, it doesn’t get in the way and the overall shortness / flexibility can help. For example, the CableMatters XLR barrel rubs against my VIVO mic mount, putting a slight pressure on the SM7B connector. The MonoPrice XLR is even longer and I won’t even try it. The AmazonBasics fits just right!

Pins are brass, silver plated. Both MonoPrice and CableMatters use gold plated pins.

The shielding and pin plating being different or unknown / lesser quality might not be a big deal for 6ft and under. For longer cable lengths, go with a brand that has the best possible shielding to maintain signal integrity, especially when recording.

Testing with a Shure SM7B along with a Cathedral Pipes “Durham” mic booster, which needs +48V phantom power. Audio interface is an "old but gold" Focusrite LS56. Monitoring on Sennheiser HD280 Pros. Hopefully this lets me test every aspect of the cable accurately and fairly.

I used 2 channels on the same interface, one wired with a pretty expensive (and long) Monster XLR cable to a mic booster, then from the booster to mic with a short 3ft CableMatters XLR cable.
The 2nd channel was wired purely with the two AmazonBasics 6ft XLR cables, either side of the mic booster.

Noise floor was pretty indistinguishable between the two setups. Recorded audio quality was also close to the point of being unable to tell them apart.

For the short cable runs, whatever shielding Amazon is using is definitely up to par and I’ll likely permanently swap out the stiffer CableMatters XLR to reduce pressure on the SM7B’s XLR connector (the AmazonBasic’s shorter barrel really makes a difference here).

Text:
The Portastudio delivers clean audio mixing and recording with no discernible noise a portable package. Note that I describe this as a mixer-recorder: a few features prevent this from being the ultimate portable recording/mixing package.

Tascam offers two fundamentally different portable audio product lines: the DP-series Digital Portastudios, and the DR-series Digital Recorders. The two are actually deisgned for quite different purposes. The DP are for people who want to make high-quality audio recordings with a one-piece unit, without any mixing. They're great for gathering audio in the field, and have become very popular with filmmakers, music producers and news gatherers. You can plug in external mics, but the internal microphones are pretty darn good.

On the other hand, this DP unit is a digital multi-track mixing recorder, designed primarily for musicians and bands who want to mix and record tracks. Audio quality is excellent: I could not hear any noise through headphones. You can mix and pan tracks on board, and upload your tracks to a computer over an included USB cable. There are two onboard microphones for convenience: if you are mixing tracks, you are going to want to do so with better quality audio that you can only get from a microphone positioned immediately adjacent to the audio source. But the onboard microphone quality is remarkably good for casual recordings or music track composition.

There are two 1/4" jacks for plugging in analog mics-no USB input, which is understandable. But there are no XLR inputs either-1/4" jacks only. And this is the first flaw: Why omit XLR jacks on the DP mixer unit, given that the DR units have combined XLR-1/4" jacks? XLR is the connector standard for analog audio beyond guitars.

The mixer functions work well enough if you read the manual and practice using the keys and on-screen menus. It's not intuitive, but it's not difficult either. I'm not sure you can do much better in such a tiny physical package. We got a real kick recording four tracks, then panning them back and forth into a final mix we liked, all before uploading the tracks to the Mac. This unit would be great for a guitarist who wants to record herself, or a composer who wants to compare different arrangements.

Nice features include a solid feel to all the pots, red OL indicator LEDs when you have set the input level too high, and a jog wheel that works as expected in the menus and timeline.

Five stars for solid audio performance, minus one star for missing XLR jacks and having to push one too many buttons to record.
Summary: Solid audio performance, read for comparison with Tascam Portable Digital Recorders

I have to add my voice to the others praising this banjo. Of course, this is just a first impression. Things like instruments will either live up to the initial rush or not. This banjo arrived pretty much set up perfectly except for tuning, which I did not expect anyway. Out of the box it took about five minutes to tune (using a Snark, which I recommend) and since I am not a beginner (or a professional) I was able to pick out a tune almost immediately. All strings will take a while to settle in, and this is no exception. But after an initial "break in" period, it seems to hold tune well. Intonation up the neck is good as well. This has been a bane of my experience with inexpensive banjos. Glad to see it doesn't seem to be an issue here. I would recommend this banjo to anyone just starting out, or who wants to add a banjo "voice" to an existing repertoire without having to invest in a five hundred and up banjo. The geared fifth string works well and I am glad to have it, having dealt with friction tuners in the past. I'll be back to update this as I experience this instrument more. UPDATE: It's eight months or so later. I still like this banjo and I'm learning a lot. I'm also learning that better banjos ARE worth the money. I played a really pricey banjo (an ODE) and wow, is there ever a difference. So, this one is good to learn on, but if you have a chance to play a really good banjo, that may spoil ya. UPDATE: I still think this banjo is excellent, although I wouldn't put light gauge strings on it. I did put some LGS on it and it changed the tone completely. Light gauge also tended to buzz as well. I'll be going back to medium gauge, which is what I'm sure the banjo came with, they just felt more substantial. Of course LGS will be easier to "choke" and bend, but you'll pay in terms of tone and that buzzing. Anyway, the banjo is fine. But I'm getting the itch for a more upscale one already. UPDATE: As I expected I have outgrown this (I was guitar player for many years, finger-picking so the rolls came more easily it seems. I'm no prodigy by any means, but I've advanced to intermediate more quickly than some) and am buying a Huber Workhorse or equivalent soon. I will relegate this banjo to the "clawhammer" style that I'm going to tackle next. Oh, one thing. This banjo DOES NOT have a tone ring so it will NEVER sound as good as a banjo with one, unless you like a duller sound. (Some people do, for clawhammer and the like.) FURTHER UPDATE: Forget what I said about a duller sound for clawhammer. That was foolish. Get a decent banjo for both. I still stand by this as a good beginner banjo, but if you have a real love for the banjo you'll quickly outgrow it.
Summary: If you have a real love for banjo, you'll quickly outgrow this one

I must say I was looking forward to trying out my new Red Series Aquila strings for my tenor uke. I purchased both the four string set (AQ-88U) that came with the wound lower G string as well as the individual unwound lower G string (AQ-72U). I'm not exactly sure why they don't sell the unwound lower G red string in a set with the other three strings. The only thing I could find on the aquilacorde.com web site with regards to the Red Series string is the following statement, "*Warning: these sets are composed by plain RED SERIES® strings and wound strings. Unfortunately The set with all RED SERIES® strings is not acoustically balanced." This leads me to believe that the unwound lower G string is no intended to be used in conjunction with the C, E and A Red Series strings. Regardless, I installed the C,E and A strings long with the unwound lower G on my Kala tenor. I stretched it out carefully and installed the strings carefully as outlined in the official Aquila video. The lower G string constantly buzzed when playing. I couldn't figure out where the buzz was coming from. I checked the installation of the string, and it was just fine. Finally I got frustrated to the point that I removed the unwound lower G and installed the wound lower G. Being wound, it had a metallic sheath on the string which I didn't really want. I installed it carefully, but it snapped during the installation process. I wasn't happy about that. I installed my old Aquila Nylgut high G string back on the uke just so I could play it. I really did like the feel and the sound of the C, E, and A Red Series strings, but I wasn't happy that they had a non-matching, white regular Nylgut G string with them. A few days later I decided to put the unwound lower G Red Series string back on. During the installation process it broke too. I was being careful to ensure the string wasn't dragging through the nut while being tightened.

Regardless to say, I'm not very satisfied with the Red series. I've changed strings on ukes a number of times and never had them break like these. I was thinking everyone else who complained about breakage was just doing something wrong. I think the inherent nature of these strings is that they are much more susceptible to breakage. I don't give negative reviews unless I think they really deserve them. Here I think you can save yourself a few bucks. I have included a picture of the broken wound lower G string. The unwound lower G broken in nearly the same fashion.

Text: This nut is a bit taller than the stock Strat (MiM) nut. Because of this, the strings are raised higher than they should be on frets near the neck, making open chords cumbersome to play. This small discrepancy will throw your neck action out of whack, for me it required adjusting the bridge saddle, and readjusting string intonation. Apparently you can sand down the back of the nut to make it less tall. I tried that and ended up breaking it. You'd think a bone nut would be hardy, but I can tell you right now these things snap like a twig if you put too much pressure on it while shaping. Ended up having to buy another one. Maybe this is how its supposed to work with nuts. But it would be nice if just ONE of these "stratocaster nuts" were the actual size and shape they're supposed to be (like stock Fender nuts). I've purchased 3 so far and not one has been the appropriate shape or size. There are a lot of misleading descriptions for these products. A milometer discrepancy in width or height makes a huge difference. If you own a strat, be wary of which nut you purchase, as it can open a whole can of worms. Its not an easy installation like it should be.
Summary: Not the right size for Fender Strat, requires shaping and/or saddle adjustment

Text: I am not a fan of lugging around a hard-shell case, and as I get older, I'm doing everything I can to lighten my load when I rehearse and gig. There are plenty of places to attach items, like a Tick bag or other items like your earplug case, etc.  The pocket in front is extremely large, and I fit all kinds of items in it....iPad, page-turning pedal, strap, instrument cable, pens, tools, and a small voice recorder. - After lots and lots of reviews, I decided on this speaker to replace my Jet City stocker (a very nice Eminence 16 ohm). I had to swap because my Fender Super Champ amp is an 8 ohm head. For those who don't know you should always match impedance of speaker and amp. The speaker will sound a lot better as the push will match the pull (read-up on impedance if you need); and, if you use a lower impedance speaker than your amp's ohms you can destroy your amp, or catch stuff on fire.. Anyway, this speaker sounds very,very good out of the box, with good crisp response. According to Celestion, the H30 is a cross between a "Greenback" and a "Vintage 30". And, I was really torn between the Vin 30 and the Greenback, however, the H30 solves the debate. So, I went in between with this. I'm very pleased with the high gain it handles and it sounds amazing (cleans are also bright and full). Also, it handles pedals very well, and no rattle or buzzes. This speaker sounds broken in right out of the box, so I'm sure it will get even nicer. If you want Van Halen/AC/DC/The Who/and, high gain; blues, 70's/80's/90's metal-tone, look no further (this is so versatile). As for death metal, I just don't know about it. I think Vin 30 is a darker, slightly bassier speaker and might do better for it. The Vin 30's I've heard also sound terrific for all types of music.

**Update** - as I continue to break this speaker in... wow.. it really is opening up..meaner, nastier, growl-ier... Just plain incredible. And, part of your chase for tone (that is, if your a purist), ends here, with this very speaker. Try one in your cabinet - just match your impedance and your golden. They put Celestion high-end speakers in boutique amps for a reason - tone, baby. My H30 sounds terrific in a Jet City 1 x 12 cab (where I had to remove the stock 16 ohm-er due to mismatching head impedance). Oh my. I've played it for 6 or so hours,and it's really smoothened out. Don't even consider - buy, break-in, and love.

[[VIDEOID:421b26ee86677cb39277066f913459e8]] I was looking for an extremely portable amp that would be easy to carry in my backpack or luggage. I found the Vox amPlugs and thought those would be perfect since they are extremely small and I could plug them into any portable speaker I wanted, and even use my headphones for silent practice sessions at night. I had settled on getting the AC30 amPlug since it had some nice clean sounds and Vox's AC30 amp is a classic amp that many classic rock players use, but I primarily play harder rock and metal which use dirtier tones, so I was trying to decide which of Vox's dirtier amPlug models I wanted in addition to the AC30. However, I had this device, the Valeton Rushead Max, recommended to me, and after listening to a few videos and seeing a great Black Friday deal on it, I decided to go with this. I am very glad I did.

The Pros:
This is both very well built and extremely versatile. While I still don't have an AC30 amPlug (the clean sound on this is enough for me for now, though I will likely eventually get one and update this review when I do), I have read that they are somewhat flimsy. This pocket amp has no such issues and is very sturdily built. The sounds on this are also extremely versatile. Like most pocket amps and mini-amps, this has the basic volume, tone, and gain controls. However, the types of amps offered and the effects are where this pocket amp shines. Vox's amPlugs have only one amp per amPlug, but they give you three different channels (a green, orange, and red, and the sound gets increasingly dirtier the redder the color gets), but from what I have heard on YouTube, the channels on the amPlugs don't sound very different. On this Valeton pocket amp, they give you three different amps entirely. "CL" gives you a nice clean tone, "OD" gives you a hard rock-style overdrive, and "DIST" gives you heavy metal-style distortion, so you can switch between three of the most popular guitar styles all at, to quote AC/DC, a "Flick of the Switch". I mostly use the OD and DIST channels, and they both sound awesome. I also love being able to drastically switch sounds so easily, switching between the rock and metal tones I typically use all much quicker than dialing in the tones on my 20W Randall practice amp. Additionally, even mini-amps like the Nux or the Boss Katana only give you three similar options, so Valeton's pocket amp is on par with most mini-amps while being much smaller and letting you choose which speaker you want to use with it (when at home, I will typically grab the MOKCAO Power+, a speaker dock for the 2nd generation Echo Dots, which sounds surprisingly good for guitar and even rivals my larger 20W Randall practice amp, while on-the-go I will typically grab a little 808 NRG speaker, which doesn't sound as good but is significantly more portable). Lastly, this little device has a ton of available effects. Vox's amPlugs give you three different versions of Chorus, Delay, and Reverb, but you can only have one active at a time. Valeton's pocket amp lets you have Delay, Reverb, or Delay/Reverb active, and then you can add to that Chorus, Tremolo, or Flanger. It doesn't give you different versions, but you can change how each of them sound by adjusting a knob on the top of the device, ranging from not having any of the effect to having more of the effect.

The Cons (or Suggested Improvements):
While there aren't any major negatives about this device, I do have a few suggested improvements. The biggest is that I would add bluetooth. I know this device already has a ton of stuff packed into a small package, but bluetooth typically doesn't take up much space. Also, many speakers in today's world only use bluetooth, so adding bluetooth would make this pocket amp work with more speakers as well as eliminating messy cords. If possible, I would also make this pocket amp slightly smaller – when attached to the lower bout on my Les Paul, the top comes very close to contacting the ground when I have the Les Paul sitting on the floor, and I sometimes worry that the amp might get broken. Additionally, making it slightly smaller would increase portability. Lastly, I do somewhat agree with another reviewer on here who mentioned that it is a bit difficult to use for guitars where the input jack is on the lower bout, since you can't see the buttons. While I have mostly gotten used to controlling the knobs and buttons by feel, I think what would be nice is making the jack on the amp rotatable. Unlike on Vox's amPlugs, though, which rotate the jack side-to-side, I think it would make more sense to let it rotate front and back, that way those who have input jacks on the front of the guitar can leave it facing downward while those who have it on the side can have the jack on the amp rotated so it is pointing out of the main face of the pocket amp, making it easier to see.

Overall, the cons aren't hugely significant, and the pros make this one of the best pocket amps you can buy, especially if you are interested in versatility. If you know you want an excellent recreation of exactly one of Vox's amps, then one of the amPlugs might be better for you, but if you want something that will give you a plethora of different sounds on-the-go, then this is the pocket amp for you. The tones, particularly the overdrive and distortion tones, also sound excellent, so you are getting amazing tones (especially if you have a good speaker) in addition to superb versatility. I am blown away how Valeton, a company I never heard of until I found this device, managed to make a significantly better pocket amp than Vox, one of the world's leading manufacturers of guitar amps. The Rushead Max even lets you just charge the device by plugging a micro-USB phone cord into it, which is much more convenient than using batteries with Vox's amPlugs (even if you use rechargeable batteries, you still have to take them out and charge them, while the Rushead Max you can just plug in - it claims it only lasts 5 hours, but I think it lasts a bit more than that, since I have gone 2-4 days with hour-ish long practice sessions and I have only had it go down to 1/4 the battery dots left without charging). I still plan to eventually get Vox's AC30 amPlug, since the AC30 is such a classic amp, and when I do I will update this review to provide a more thorough comparison between the amPlug and this. Until I do, though, I think Valeton has put Vox to shame in the pocket amp department, and I highly and enthusiastically recommend the Valeton Rushead Max!

Updated March 14, 2020: As I said in the review, the little 808 speaker I was plugging this Valeton Rushead Max into sounded quite tinny while the MOKCAO Echo Dot base sounded really good. I was researching speakers the last few months to try to find if there was a smaller speaker than the MOKCAO that sounded significantly better than the 808 speaker, and I settled on getting the Vanzom Climber-Z speaker. It is about halfway between the 808 and the MOKCAO speaker in size, and it sounds much more like the MOKCAO speaker, possibly even sounding slightly better than the MOKCAO. Those are the only three speakers I have tried with this and out of those three I would recommend the Vanzom Climber-Z speaker - it is $60 new but there are frequently 20-25% off coupons on it, which brings the cost to less than $50 new. I did listen to a few speakers at Best Buy recently, and though I couldn't compare the sound directly since I couldn't bring the Vanzom speaker inside, I thought the Vanzom was clearly better than all of the UE speakers and all of the Sony speakers except for the XB41 (which was much more expensive and larger), and I thought the Charge 4 was only slightly bassier than the Vanzom (though also larger and more expensive) and the Bose Soundlink Revolve was only slightly clearer than the Vanzom (though also considerably more expensive). So, assuming that how music sounds through speakers is a good indication of how a speaker will work with this pocket amp, there are speakers that may sound better than the Vanzom, but for its size and price, I think the Vanzom is the best deal. I would definitely recommend the Vanzom Climber-Z if you want to play this through a portable speaker, or at least a speaker with 2 or more active drivers and 1 or more passive radiators should create a fuller sound which will make playing this through the speaker sound better.

Update January 1, 2021: A few months ago I finally got a Vox AC30 AmPlug, and I also replaced my main amp with a Marshall Code 50. First comparing the AC30 AmPlug to the Rushead Max, I found my previous thoughts based on YouTube videos to be pretty accurate. The Rushead Max in general sounds better, is more versatile, is more convenient with a rechargeable battery, and is sturdier. The two plusses I found to the AC30 AmPlug is that the foldable plug does make it slightly more portable when transporting it, and I prefer the slightly crunchy clean tones of the AC30 AmPlug versus the crystal clean, and to me almost bland, clean tone of the Rushead Max. After learning more about amp models, I would guess the Rushead Max's clean channel is based on a Fender amp, the overdrive channel on the Marshall JCM800, and the distortion channel on the Mesa/Boogie. Therefore, I did compare the Rushead Max's distortion channel to the JCM800 model on my Marshall Code 50, and I was surprised with how close it came. The Code 50 clearly had more details and intricacies in the JCM800 sound, but it also has a much larger computer and a 12" speaker. Considering how small the Rushead Max and Vanzom speaker are, the Rushead Max did a good job getting the general tone of the JCM800 down. Secondly, in addition to the new amps, I have more recently tried two smaller speakers with the Rushead Max, in an attempt to make it more portable. The first one I tried was a cheap, off-brand aux speaker, which is essentially just a very small speaker with a male aux jack attached, designed for use with phones to make them louder. It made the Rushead Max a bit heavy, but I found putting a rubber band around the amp/speaker connection and strapping it around a tone or volume knob kept it in place. It sounded better than I would have expected from such a small speaker, but it was still very tinny and muddy and had no bass. Also, playing the overdrive or distortion channel with high volume made it shake, and I'm sure the speaker could easily be broken if played on high volumes on the distortion channel for long periods of time. The second speaker I got even more recently was a JBL Clip 3. I found that the best way to make it portable is to hang the Clip 3 off of one of the top tuners and run a 3-4 foot audio cable from the Rushead Max to the Clip 3. The Clip 3 still lacked the bass of the Vanzom speaker, sounded a bit tinny, and did the weird buzzing thing, but it was a considerable improvement over the phone extension speaker. In comparison to that one, the Clip 3 was significantly clearer, does not shake at higher volumes on the distortion channel like it is going to fall apart, and also has a bit more bass to it. So while if you want the best sound with the Rushead Max I would still recommend a tabletop portable speaker, if you are looking for a super portable way to use the Rushead Max which would allow you to walk freely around the room, I would recommend the JBL Clip 3 hung over a top tuning peg. I did also try connecting an Aluratek Bluetooth 5.0 transmitter/receiver to the Rushead Max so it could wirelessly connect to my Vanzom speaker (which also uses Bluetooth 5.0), but I found the lag, while only being ~0.5 seconds, to be quite noticeable, so I would recommend a wired connection for this pocket amp. Lastly, I have attached a couple more pictures of the Valeton Rushead Max, this time comparing it to the Vox AC30 AmPlug, as well as a video comparing sound samples between the Rushead Max and AC30 AmPlug. The distortion tones were achieved on the Rushead Max by changing channels while the distortion tones were achieved on the AC30 AmPlug by increasing the gain.

Updated September 26, 2021:
I purchased a Diezel Herbert and an Alexander Jubilee Overdrive pedal a few months ago and was looking for an easy way to listen to them with headphones. Setting the Valeton to the clean mode and plugging into the output sort of worked but didn't sound the best, so I recently tried out a Boss Pocket GT, a Fender Mustang Micro, and a LEKATO Headphone Amp. The LEKATO was neat with cab sims and made the pedals sound the best when I only used a cab sim, but a clean setting on the Mustang Micro sounded pretty close just a little looser, and the amp models on the Fender were better even than the models on this Valeton headphone amp. I especially liked the Uber model on the Fender, which to my ears sounded fairly similar to the Diezel Herbert (my favorite of the two pedals). The Valeton sounds noticeably fizzier than the Mustang Micro, and the Mustang Micro is more compact and portable than the Valeton without being fragile like the Vox. The Mustang Micro also has more options. Though the Valeton does have a bit finer control over the options available, the knobs aren't super sensitive and after playing the Mustang Micro I realized the tone knob on the Valeton is slightly weird in that the volume decreases as you turn the tone down. Apparently one can also record with the Mustang Micro. I haven't tried it yet, but since this is the one I decided to keep out of the three new ones I tried, I definitely will try this at some point. Overall, I would recommend the Mustang Micro slightly more than the Valeton for its better tone, more compact size, and recording ability. However, the Mustang Micro is 3-4 times the price of the Valeton. I think it is worth it myself, but if you are on a budget and especially if you don't need to record, the Valeton is still the best headphone amp under $50 in my opinion. If you can find an extra $50 for a used Mustang Micro or a new one on sale, then I would recommend the Mustang Micro, though. I also added a couple more comparison pictures.
Summary: Excellent Pocket Amp and Better Than Vox!

MADE IN CHINA--three little words that mean low quality materials, cheap construction and the low price American consumers seem to be willing to accept for these Chinese made goods.

That said, this is a decent starter set. I bought it because I haven't had an electric guitar in some time and just wanted to see if I still remember what I used to know and if I still like playing without investing a lot of money. This package is fine for my purposes and, if I find I like playing again, will surely upgrade soon. No Made In China guitar is going to get five stars from me since only high end labels like Fender, Gibson, Ibanez and Paul Reed Smith deserve five stars in the category. The pros and cons are below:

Pros:
Guitar is reasonably well made--not high end just reasonably well put together.
Amplifier has a decent sound for a tiny amp.
Cable is long enough to play the guitar at a reasonable distance from the amp.
Strap is okay.

Cons:
The strings are real garbage. Your fingers will TURN BLACK after just a few minutes of playing. They're cheap and likely to break after a short period of time.
The fret wires are not rounded at the edges of the neck and you can cut your fingers and snag clothing on them.
The picks are cheap garbage.
The guitar body is very light weight--essentially meaning that the wood is not high quality.
The gig bag is cheap, thin canvas and smells like chemicals.
The amp has a very, very strong, unpleasant smell that goes away after about twelve hours.
The pitch pipe is useless--any pitch pipe for guitar tuning is useless and to tune any guitar correctly, you need an electronic tuner of some sort.
The amp overdrives easily and shreds sound even without turning on distortion mode.

You should DO THE FOLLOWING:
File down the ends of the fret wires so they're round and flush with the edges (sides) of the neck. Use a very fine, metal file and it won't take long.
Get some decent strings and replace the ones that ship with it as soon as possible. The guitar will sound better and your fingers won't turn black. AND who knows what the black stuff on your fingers is...
Get some decent picks of various thicknesses to replace the junk ones that ship with the package.
IF you can afford it, buy an electronic tuner to use AFTER replacing the strings with a higher quality set.

Conclusion:
This package is okay for a beginning player or someone who wants to get back into playing. The price is certainly reasonable and, even though you'll need to file the fret wires and replace the strings immediately it's an okay purchase.
Summary: Nothing Fancy-A Good Starter Package-Some Issues
